suitcase.example: Many seats carry reservation labels, while the luggage racks are festooned with backpacks and suitcases.
suitcase.exampleSense: A large (usually rectangular) piece of luggage used for carrying clothes, and sometimes suits, when travelling.

overturn.o: From Middle English overturnen, equivalent to over- + turn. Compare also Middle English overterven (“to overturn”), see terve.
overturn.example: We also found that the only emergency egress from the tram was by smashing the front or rear windscreens, and that emergency lighting had failed when the tram overturned.
overturn.exampleSense: To turn over, capsize or upset.

accelerating.o: present participle and gerund of accelerate. First attested in the 1520s. Either from Latin accelerātus, perfect passive participle of accelerō (“to accelerate, hasten”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), formed from ad + celerō (“to hasten”), which is from celer (“quick”) (see celerity), or back-formation from acceleration.

accelerate.o: First attested in the 1520s. Either from Latin accelerātus, perfect passive participle of accelerō (“to accelerate, hasten”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), formed from ad + celerō (“to hasten”), which is from celer (“quick”) (see celerity), or back-formation from acceleration.
accelerate.example: to accelerate the growth of a plant, the increase of wealth, etc.
accelerate.exampleSense: To quicken the natural or ordinary progression or process of.

p: suffix forming agent nouns from verbs, or forming adjectives with senses of being prone or tending to do the actions of verbs
accelerant.o: From accelerate + -ant (suffix forming agent nouns from verbs, or forming adjectives with senses of being prone or tending to do the actions of verbs).
accelerant.example: Hello Neighbor’s experience reflects the rise of video sites like YouTube as an accelerant for the video game business.
accelerant.exampleSense: Something that speeds up a process or the uptake of something else.

boss.o:
noun: Borrowed from Dutch baas, from Middle Dutch baes (“master of a household, friend”), from Old Dutch *baso (“uncle, kinsman”), from Proto-West Germanic *baswō, from Proto-Germanic *baswô (“uncle”), perhaps from Proto-Germanic *ba-, *bō- (“father, older male relative”), source also of the English terms babe, boy, bub, bully. Cognate with Middle Low German bās (“supervisor, foreman”), Old Frisian bas (“master”), hence Saterland Frisian Boas (“boss”), Old High German basa (“father's sister, cousin”), hence German Base (“aunt, cousin”). Originally a term of respect used to address an older relative. Later, in New Amsterdam, it began to mean a person in charge who is not a master. The video game sense is borrowed from Japanese ボス (bosu), borrowed from English boss.

noun: From Middle English bos, bose, boce, from Old French boce (“lump, bulge, protuberance, knot”), from Frankish *bottja, from Proto-Germanic *bautaną (“to hit, strike, beat”). Doublet of beat; see there for more.

noun: Apparently a corruption of bast.
boss.example: Chat turned to whisper when the boss entered the conference room.
boss.exampleSense: A person in charge of a business or company.

harm.o: From Middle English harm, herm, from Old English hearm, from Proto-West Germanic *harm, from Proto-Germanic *harmaz (“harm; shame; pain”). Cognate with Dutch harm (“harm”), German Harm (“harm”), Danish harme (“indignation, resentment”), Icelandic harmur (“sorrow, grief”), Swedish harm (“anger, indignation, harm”).
harm.example: Although not physically injured in the car accident, she received some psychological harm.

graceful.o: From Middle English graceful. By surface analysis, grace + -ful.
graceful.exampleSense: Having or showing grace in movement, shape, or proportion.

oracle bone script.o: Coined by American missionary Frank Herring Chalfant in 1906.

oracle.o: From Middle English oracle, from Old French oracle m, from Latin ōrāculum n.
oracle.example: The several oracles included in this haftarah presumably were uttered at different times to the people in exile, presenting diverse themes and using distinct styles.
oracle.exampleSense: A prophetic response, often enigmatic or allegorical, so given.

canning.o: present participle and gerund of can. From Middle English can, first and third person singular of connen, cunnen (“to be able, know how”), from Old English can(n), first and third person singular of cunnan (“to know how”), from Proto-West Germanic *kunnan, from Proto-Germanic *kunnaną, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵneh₃- (whence also know). Doublet of con. See also: canny, cunning.

yell at.example: The boy's father yelled at him for lying to him about cleaning up the mess.
yell at.exampleSense: To scold, to rebuke, often by yelling.

gloomily.example: [T]he sedate monk's hood lifted its head still higher and looked gloomily and wickedly down on it, while it nodded and kept time to the cuckoo's song, as if it were counting how many days it had to live.

innings.o: From the old verb inn (“to house corn”).
innings.example: Like father, like son. Sixty-eight. Not such a bad innings, really, when the old man was gone at fifty-three.

inning.o: Back-formation from innings, mistaken to be plural of the time period, not the entries of the batters/batsmen.
inning.example: It is a baseball tradition to sing "Take Me Out To the Ball Game" during the seventh inning stretch.
inning.exampleSense: A period of play in which members of a visiting baseball team attempt to hit a baseball pitched by the opposing home team until three players are called out, followed by a similar attempt by members of the home baseball team against the visiting team's pitching. There are nine or more innings in a regulation baseball game.

reinstatement.example: Many people are unhappy with the sacking of the chief constable and demand his immediate reinstatement.
reinstatement.exampleSense: The act of restoring something to its previous state.

reinstate.example: Of these nine days, six will be needed for jacking. The remainder of the time will be given over to removing and then reinstating track and overhead line, power and signalling equipment from a 200-metre stretch of the ECML above.
reinstate.exampleSense: To restore to a former position or rank.

hang on.example: Just hang on and keep going; this pain won't last forever.

narration.o: From Middle French narration, from Old French narracion, from Latin narrātiō. By surface analysis, Latin narr- + -ate + -ion.

haggard.o:
adj: From Middle French haggard, from Old French faulcon hagard (“wild falcon”) ( > French hagard (“dazed”)), from Middle High German hag (“coppice”) ( > archaic German Hag (“hedge, grove”)). Akin to Frankish *hagia ( > French haie (“hedge”))

noun: From Old Norse heygarðr (“hay-yard”).
haggard.example: A gradual descent into a haggard and feeble state.
haggard.exampleSense: Looking exhausted, worried, or poor in condition

quartermaster.o: From Middle English quartermayster, quartermaistre, equivalent to quarter + master. Perhaps reinforced by and merged with Dutch kwartiermeester, kwartier-meester. Compare German Quartiermeister, French quartier-maître.

segregationist.example: Her [Rosa Parks'] arrest launched a 381-day Montgomery bus boycott in which 40,000 Black people, mostly all working people, fought the segregationist bosses.
segregationist.exampleSense: A person who supports or believes in segregation.

segregated.o: simple past and past participle of segregate. From Latin sēgregātus, perfect passive participle of sēgregō (“to separate”), from sē- (“apart”) + gregō (“to flock or group”), from grex (“flock”). Compare gregarious, aggregate.

segregate.o: From Latin sēgregātus, perfect passive participle of sēgregō (“to separate”), from sē- (“apart”) + gregō (“to flock or group”), from grex (“flock”). Compare gregarious, aggregate.
segregate.example: One aim of the reorganisation on both routes is to segregate completely the operation of the District and Tilbury Lines between London and Upminster, removing physical connections between the two.
segregate.exampleSense: To separate, especially by social policies that directly or indirectly keep races or ethnic groups apart.

congregant.example: The wedding was at Timmyʼs fatherʼs church, and all the female congregants had cooked a meal fit to feed a king.

continuity.o: Borrowed from Middle French continuité, from Latin continuitas. By surface analysis, continu(e) + -ity.
continuity.example: Considerable continuity of attention is needed to read German philosophy.
continuity.exampleSense: Lack of interruption or disconnection; the quality of being continuous in space or time.

ablate.o: From Middle English ablat (“taken away”), from Latin ablātus, past participle of auferō (“to remove”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix). First attested in the 1500s, it became obsolete by the early 1600s. Returned into use as a back-formation from ablation.

levitate.o: First attested in 1673; borrowed from New Latin levitātus, perfect passive participle of levitō (“to levitate; to have one's motion directed upward, as opposed to the downward motion induced by gravity”) (first attested c. 1670), modeled on gravitō (“to gravitate”) (← Latin gravis (“heavy”)), from levis (“light”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).
levitate.exampleSense: To cause to rise in the air and float, as if in defiance of gravity.

multiplicative.o: From 6th-century Latin multiplicativus, from Classical Latin multiplicāre (“to multiply”).
multiplicative.example: Matrix determinants are multiplicative; if A and B are square matrices of the same size, then #92;mbox#123;det#125;(AB)#61;#92;mbox#123;det#125;(A)#92;,#92;mbox#123;det#125;(B).

payoff.o: Alternative form of pay-off. Deverbal from pay off.

ax.o: From Middle English axen, aksen, axien, from Old English ācsian and āxian, showing metathesis from āscian. Ax/aks was common in literary works until about 1600.
ax.example: Dolly: And if so be, why did you ax me to keep you company? Housekeeper wants me below to pick raisins.

self-important.example: The assistant manager was a self-important fellow who strutted about the office barking instructions.
self-important.exampleSense: Having, or behaving as if having, too high of an opinion of one's own importance.

cline.o:
noun: From Ancient Greek κλῑ́νω (klī́nō, “to lean, incline”). Introduced by English evolutionary biologist and eugenicist Julian Huxley in 1938 after British mycologist John Ramsbottom suggested the term.

noun: From c(ircle) + line; compare circline.
cline.example: Let C₁ and C₂ be two nonintersecting clines. Prove that there is a unique pair of points that are simultaneously symmetric to both C₁ and C₂.

removal.example: The board decided the removal of the branch manager was the best option after his misbehaviour.
removal.exampleSense: The dismissal of someone from office.

default.o: From Middle English defaut, defaute, from Old French defaute (“fault, defect, failure, culpability, lack”), ultimately from Latin de- (“away”) + fallo (“deceive, cheat, escape notice of”).
default.example: He failed to make payments on time, and he is now in default.
default.exampleSense: The condition of failing to meet an obligation.

slim.o: Borrowing from Low German or Dutch slim (“bad, sly, clever”), from Middle Dutch slim (“bad, crooked”), from Old Dutch *slimb, from Proto-West Germanic *slimb, from Proto-Germanic *slimbaz (“oblique, crooked”). The sense development would have been "slanting, cunning" (Dutch) > "insignificant, slight" and then "thin, graceful" in English, a shift that Liberman calls an "incredible amelioration" of word meaning. The pejorative sense found in Low German and Dutch is also found preserved in the archaic English noun slim (“worthless or lazy person”), also comparable to the South African use of the adjective as "crafty, sly." Compare Dutch slim (“smart, clever, crafty”), Middle High German slimp (“slanting, awry”), German schlimm (“bad”), West Frisian slim (“bad, dire”).
slim.example: Movie stars are usually slim, attractive, and young.
slim.exampleSense: Slender; thin. Slender in an attractive way.

faded.o: simple past and past participle of fade. From Middle English fade, vad, vade (“faded, pale, withered, weak”), from Middle Dutch vade (“weak, faint, limp”), from Old French fade (“weak, witless”), of obscure origin. Probably from Vulgar Latin *fatidus, from Latin fatuus (“insipid”).
faded.example: Some clients adjust their instructions as faded memories come into focus. Mr. Li recalled one prospective client who spent most of an hourlong phone call crying as she reminisced about her old home.
faded.exampleSense: That has lost some of its former strength or vigour.

caffeinated.o:
adj: From caffeine + -ated.

verb: From caffeinate + -ed.
caffeinated.example: For most of us, to be caffeinated to one degree or another has simply become baseline human consciousness.
caffeinated.exampleSense: Overly peppy or energetic; stimulated by caffeine.

decaffeinated.o:
adj: From de- + caffeine + -ated or de- + caffeinated.

verb: From decaffeinate + -ed.

caffeine.o: Borrowed from French caféine, from café (“coffee”), or German Caffein, Kaffein (cp. Coffein, Koffein), from Kaffee (“coffee”) (cp. Kaffe, Koffee, Koffe), or Italian caffè (“coffee”) + -ine.

bravo.o: Borrowed from Italian bravo. Doublet of brave.
bravo.example: Together they had bravoed the great tragedians, and together hopelessly worshipped the beautiful faces, enskied and sainted, of famous actresses.
bravo.exampleSense: To cheer or applaud, especially by saying bravo!

marguerite.o: From French marguerite. Doublet of Margaret (and various forms, q.v.), margarita, margarite, and Margherita, and related to margarine.

lay out.example: I laid him out on the sidewalk after he tried to grab me.
lay out.exampleSense: To render (someone) unconscious; to knock out; to cause to fall to the floor; to kill.

left over.o: simple past and past participle of leave. From Middle English leven, from Old English lǣfan (“to leave”), from Proto-West Germanic *laibijan, from Proto-Germanic *laibijaną (“to let stay, leave”), causative of *lībaną (“to stay, remain”), from Proto-Indo-European *leyp- (“to stick; fat”). Cognate with Old Frisian lēva (“to leave”), dialectal Dutch loven (“to have left over, save, keep”), Old Saxon lēvian, Old High German leiban (“to leave”), Old Norse leifa (“to leave over”) (whence Icelandic leifa (“to leave food uneaten”), Swedish leva (“to leave”)), lifna (“to be left”) (whence Danish levne). More at lave, belive. The noun is attested since the 19th century, with earliest references to billiards.
left over.example: I had some food left over after the party.
left over.exampleSense: simple past and past participle of leave over

bereaved.o: simple past and past participle of bereave. Inherited from Middle English bireven, from Old English berēafian (“to bereave, deprive of, take away, seize, rob, despoil”), from Proto-Germanic *biraubōną, and Old English berēofan (“to bereave, deprive, rob of”); both equivalent to be- + reave. Cognate with Dutch beroven (“to rob, deprive, bereave”), German berauben (“to deprive, rob, bereave”), Danish berøve (“to deprive of”), Norwegian berøve (“to deprive”), Swedish beröva (“to rob”), Gothic 𐌱𐌹𐍂𐌰𐌿𐌱𐍉𐌽 (biraubōn).
bereaved.example: Perversely, we love John Wick himself. That lethal, bereaved assassin is a good bad guy for our times, the natural extension of Tony Soprano, Walter White and all the other heroic antiheroes the culture has embraced.
bereaved.exampleSense: having suffered the death of a loved one

bereave.o: Inherited from Middle English bireven, from Old English berēafian (“to bereave, deprive of, take away, seize, rob, despoil”), from Proto-Germanic *biraubōną, and Old English berēofan (“to bereave, deprive, rob of”); both equivalent to be- + reave. Cognate with Dutch beroven (“to rob, deprive, bereave”), German berauben (“to deprive, rob, bereave”), Danish berøve (“to deprive of”), Norwegian berøve (“to deprive”), Swedish beröva (“to rob”), Gothic 𐌱𐌹𐍂𐌰𐌿𐌱𐍉𐌽 (biraubōn).
bereave.example: Death bereaved him of his wife.
bereave.exampleSense: To take away someone or something that is important or close; deprive.

equalize.example: No system of instruction will completely equalize natural powers.
equalize.exampleSense: To make equal; to cause to correspond in amount or degree.

completion.o: Borrowed from Latin completio(n), from complere (“to fill up, complete”). By surface analysis, complet(e) + -ion.

affecting.o: present participle and gerund of affect. From Middle English affecten, from Latin affectāre, from Latin affectus, the participle stem of Latin afficere (“to act upon, influence, affect, attack with disease”), from ad- + facere (“to make, do”). By surface analysis, af- + Latin -fect.
affecting.example: Within this sphere, then, the reader is allowed to follow Hull's growth both as an individual and as a poet. She moves from pieces that are affecting, though merely descriptive, to "conversations," and finally, to strong affirmations spoken in the first person.
affecting.exampleSense: Producing or causing strong feelings and emotions.

net-zero.example: Heath's home is defined as net-zero, which means it produces as much energy as it consumes throughout the year.
net-zero.exampleSense: Of a building or system, generating as much energy through solar, wind, and other renewable resources as it uses from the electricity network.

on top of.example: Living on top of one another in a refugee camp is stressful.
on top of.exampleSense: Very close to, in any orientation or in time.

limitation.o: Borrowed from Latin limitatio. Morphologically limit + -ation.
limitation.example: The lawyer obtained impunity by dragging his obviously guilty client's case beyond the ten-year limitation.
limitation.exampleSense: A time period after which some legal action may no longer be brought.

a priori.o: First attested in 1610. Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin ā priōrī (“involving reasoning from cause to effect; from first principles”, literally “from the former”).
a priori.example: In his opening argument, the student mentioned nothing beyond his a priori knowledge.
a priori.exampleSense: Based on hypothesis and theory rather than experiment or empirical evidence.

ephemera.o: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἐφήμερᾰ (ephḗmeră), neuter plural form of ἐφήμερος (ephḗmeros).
ephemera.example: Everything at the fair was considered “antiquarian books or ephemera”. Ephemera are things like maps, photos, posters, menus, autographs. A pair of shoes worn in Singin' in the Rain. Anything considered “historical evidence”.
ephemera.exampleSense: plural of ephemeron Manmade objects that are short-lived (under usual conditions), usually because their design intent is to be inexpensively made and thus affordably bought, a goal that often is an engineering trade-off versus durability. Especially, such ephemera that are collectibles, such as (originally) cheap publications (e.g., pamphlets, brochures), single-use packaging from packaged goods, and giveaway or throwaway trinkets.

ephemeral.o: From New Latin ephemerus, from Ancient Greek ἐφήμερος (ephḗmeros), the more common form of ἐφημέριος (ephēmérios, “of, for, or during the day, living or lasting but for a day, short-lived, temporary”), from ἐπί (epí, “on”) + ἡμέρα (hēméra, “day”).
ephemeral.example: The graben constitutes a depositional basin and a topographic low, underlain by Cretaceous shales, in which volcanic debris accumulated in ephemeral lakes and streams in Oligocene and early Miocene time.
ephemeral.exampleSense: Usually dry, but filling with water for brief periods during and after precipitation.

batch.o:
noun: From Middle English bach, bache, bahche, from Old English *bæċċ (“something baked”), of uncertain origin, but possibly from Proto-West Germanic *bakku, from Proto-Germanic *bakkuz (“baking, baked goods”), cognate with Middle High German becke (“something baked, pastry, baking, bakery”). Related also to Old English bacan (“to bake”), Old English ġebæc (“something baked”), Dutch gebak, German Gebäck, Dutch baksel.

noun: From Middle English bache, bæcche, from Old English bæċ, beċe (“brook, stream”). Doublet of beck. More at beach.

verb: Clipping of bachelor (“unmarried adult male”).
batch.example: The contractor batched the purchase orders for the entire month into one statement.
batch.exampleSense: To aggregate things together into a batch.

infant.o: Inherited from Middle English infaunt, borrowed from Latin īnfantem, accusative masculine singular of īnfāns, nominal use of the adjective meaning 'not able to speak', from īn- (“not”) + fāns, present participle of for (“to speak”). The verb is from Anglo-Norman enfanter, from the same Latin source. Doublet of infante.
infant.example: Thomas Humphrey Doleman died the 30th of August 1712, an infant, intestate and without issue; Lewis the next nephew died the 17th of April 1716, an infant about sixteen years old, having left his mother Mary Webb, ...

keep it up.example: Ever hear of Viagra? It's not my fault you can't keep it up anymore.

keep up.o: From Middle English kepen up (“to perpetuate, maintain, preserve”), equivalent to keep + up.
keep up.example: I always try to keep up with (or "keep up on") current affairs.
keep up.exampleSense: To ensure that one remains well-informed about something.

exhaustive.o: Borrowed from Medieval Latin exhaustīvus. By surface analysis, exhaust + -ive.
exhaustive.exampleSense: Including every possible element: fully comprehensive.

paddock.o:
noun: The noun is almost certainly a variant of dialectal British parrock (“enclosure; park; croft, small field, paddock”), from Middle English parrok, parrock (“enclosed pasture, paddock; coop; feeding stall; cabin, hut”) [and other forms], from Old English pearroc, pearruc (“fence used to enclose a space; area enclosed by such a fence, enclosure”), from Proto-West Germanic *parruk (“enclosure; pen for animals”), from Proto-Germanic *parrukaz (“fence; enclosure”); further etymology uncertain, perhaps related to Proto-Germanic *barō (“bar, beam; barrier”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *bʰerH- (“to pierce; to strike”). Equivalent to park + -ock. Doublet of park. The verb is derived from the noun. Cognates * Danish park (“pond”) * Dutch perk (“flowerbed; garden; pen”) * German Pferch (“sheepfold, sheep-pen”)

noun: From Middle English paddok, paddoke (“frog; toad”) [and other forms], from pad, pade (“frog; toad”) + -ok (diminutive suffix). Pad, pade is derived from Old English *pada, *padda, padde, from Proto-West Germanic *paddā, from Proto-Germanic *paddǭ (“toad”); further etymology uncertain, possibly ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰew- (“to swell”). The English word is analysable as pad (“(Britain, dialectal) frog; toad”) + -ock (suffix forming nouns, originally with diminutive senses). Sense 2 (“sledge”) is probably from the supposed resemblance of the object to a frog or toad.
paddock.example: You remind me of a two-year-old, Dinny—one of those whipcordy chestnuts that kick up their heels in the paddock, get left at the post, and come in first after all.
paddock.exampleSense: An enclosure next to a racecourse where horses are paraded and mounted before a race and unsaddled after a race.

prix fixe.o: Borrowed from French prix fixe, literally "fixed price".

rewind.example: I meant to pause the picture, but hit the rewind by mistake.
rewind.exampleSense: A button or other mechanism for rewinding.

anthem.o: From Middle English anteme, from Old English antefn, antefen and Old French antiene, anteine, anteivne, from Latin antiphōna, from Ancient Greek ἀντίφωνα (antíphōna), from ἀντί (antí, “over against”) + φωνή (phōnḗ, “voice, sound”). Doublet of antiphon.
anthem.example: The choir sang a selection of Christmas anthems at the service just before the big day.
anthem.exampleSense: A hymn of praise or loyalty.

run-down.example: Shepard: Give me a run-down of the damage.

telegraphic.example: It turned out to be no more than the weekly Reuter’s telegram sent as an ordinary letter from the nearest telegraphic office fifty miles away.
telegraphic.exampleSense: Of, or relating to the telegraph.

beneficence.o: From Middle English beneficence, from Latin beneficentia.
beneficence.example: Trump also promises to attack the sources abroad that he blames for the country’s malaise: economic interdependence, transnational criminals, traditional allies he sees as free riders on America’s long-running global beneficence.
beneficence.exampleSense: An act of philanthropy, a kind deed; an act which benefits someone else.

beneficiary.o: From Latin beneficiarius (“enjoying a favor, granted a privilege”) from beneficium (“benefit”), perhaps via or influenced by French bénéficiaire (“beneficiary”). Indirectly, by way of the etymology of the Latin word beneficium, the English word beneficiary ultimately has the same origin as the English word benefactor, its near antonym.
beneficiary.example: In a second step, the rights to the asset are divided between the trustee, who holds formal title, and the beneficiary, who receives the (future) economic interest.
beneficiary.exampleSense: One who benefits from the distribution, especially out of a trust or estate.

remit.o: From Middle English remitten, from Latin remittere (“to send, send back”). Compare Old French remettre, remetre, remitter.
remit.example: The Supreme Court today allowed major sponsors, including LG Electronics India (LGEI), to remit foreign exchange for the tournament.
remit.exampleSense: To transmit or send (e.g. money in payment); to supply.

combo.example: The jazz combo played nightly at the little restaurant.

tactile.o: Borrowed from Middle French tactile, from Latin tactilis (“that may be touched, tangible”), from tangere (“to touch”).
tactile.example: The delicacy of the tactile sense varies on different parts of the skin; it is greatest on the forehead, temples and back of the forearm.
tactile.exampleSense: Of or relating to the sense of touch.

displace.example: Freud considered shyness to be evidence of displaced narcissism.

stand out.example: Tourist guides often carry umbrellas so that they stand out in a crowd.
stand out.exampleSense: To be obvious or conspicuous, in contrast to the surroundings.

inattentive.example: He was inattentive in class and did not do well in his exams.
inattentive.exampleSense: Of or pertaining to a lack of attention; not paying attention; careless.

vegetarian.o: From vegetable + -arian; popularized following the foundation of the British Vegetarian Society in 1847.
vegetarian.example: Heh heh. You hit like a vegetarian!
vegetarian.exampleSense: A person who does not eat animal flesh, or, in some cases, use any animal products.

unacknowledged.example: [T]he use of both acknowledged and unacknowledged (silent) translations of non-English sources makes it difficult for users to determine if a certain term genuinely appeared in an English-language text.

foreknowledge.example: But two bottles would alarm and confuse him, would lead to a conversation, so I smashed it merrily into a skip, buzzed and lit with the comforting foreknowledge of the second one on its way.

knowledge.o: From Middle English knowleche, knaweleche, cnawlece (“knowledge”), from knowen (“to know, recognise”) + -leche. Related to Middle English knowlechen (“to find out, acknowledge”). For more on the Middle English suffix -leche, compare freelage. Compare also Old English cnāwelǣċ, cnāwelǣċing (“acknowledging, acknowledgement”).
knowledge.example: His library contained the accumulated knowledge of the Greeks and Romans.
knowledge.exampleSense: The total of what is known; all information and products of learning.

giantism.o: From giant + -ism, coined in the mid 17th century. In the medical or biological sense of gigantism from the 1880s.

shire.o: The noun is derived from Middle English schire (“region, shire, county”) [and other forms], from Old English sċīr (“administrative region under an alderman and sheriff, shire; district under a governor or official; status of an official, office”) [and other forms], from Proto-West Germanic *skīru (“district; status of an official, office”); further etymology uncertain, possibly related to Latin cūra (“care, concern; administration, charge, management; command, office”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kʷeys- (“to heed; to see”). The verb is derived from the noun.
shire.example: Yorkshire is the largest shire in England.
shire.exampleSense: An administrative area or district between about the 5th to the 11th century, subdivided into hundreds or wapentakes and jointly governed by an ealdorman and a sheriff; also, a present-day area corresponding to such a historical district; a county; especially (England), a county having a name ending in -shire.

enzyme.o: From German Enzym, coined 1878 by the German physiologist Wilhelm Kühne from Ancient Greek ἐν (en, “in”) + ζύμη (zúmē, “leaven”). By surface analysis, en- + zyme.

rubricate.o: From Latin rubricatus, past participle of rubricare (“to colour red”). See rubric.

rubric.o: From Middle English rubriche, rubrike, from Old French rubrique, from Latin rūbrīca (“red ochre”), the substance used to make red letters, from ruber (“red”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁rewdʰ-.
rubric.example: All the clergy in England solemnly pledge themselves to observe the rubrics.
rubric.exampleSense: The directions for a religious service, formerly printed in red letters.

refund.o: From Middle English refunden, refounden, from Old French refondre, refonder, refunder (“to restore; pay back”), from Latin refundere; prefix re- (“re-”) + fundere (“to pour”): compare French refondre, refonder. See fuse (“to melt”), and compare refound (“to cast again”), and refuse.
refund.example: If the camera is faulty, you can return it to the store where you bought it for a full refund.

construct.o: Borrowed from Latin cōnstrūctus, from cōnstruō (“to heap together”), from com- (“together”) + struō (“to heap up, pile”). Doublet of construe.
construct.example: A sentence may be constructed with a subject, verb and object.
construct.exampleSense: To build (a sentence, an argument, etc.) by arranging words or ideas.

bodybuilding.example: In my day, if you filled out your shirt, people assumed you played football or wrestled. The term bodybuilding had more to do with cars than lifting weights.
bodybuilding.exampleSense: Work done to construct or repair the body of an automobile.

keep fit.example: I keep fit by kickboxing every week.

outflow.o: From Middle English outflowen, from late Old English ūtflōwan (attested in the past tense as ūt flēow), equivalent to out- + flow. The noun is derived from the verb.
outflow.example: Borg’s home, which he built with his wife and two sons among tall conifers 33 years ago, overlooks the Nipigon River, an outflow from the lake of the same name.

baseline.example: A laser level generates a convenient baseline for interior work.
baseline.exampleSense: A line that is a base for measurement or for construction.

lobby.o:
noun: From Medieval Latin lobia, lobium, laubia (“a portico, covered way, gallery”), borrowed from Frankish *laubijā (“arbour, shelter”), related to Old English lēaf (“foliage”). More at leaf. Doublet of leaf, lodge, and loggia. Political sense derives from the entrance hall of legislatures, where people traditionally tried to influence legislators because it was the most convenient place to meet them.

noun: Shortened from lobscouse.
lobby.example: The influence of the tobacco lobby has decreased considerably in the US.
lobby.exampleSense: A class or group of interested people who try to influence public officials; collectively, lobbyists.

reframe.example: The woman in the shop was reframing a painting.

decorate.o:
verb: From Middle English decorat (“adorned”), from Latin decorātus, perfect passive participle of decorō (“to adorn, distinguish, honor”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from decus (“ornament, grace, dignity, honor”, decor- in compounds), akin to decor (“elegance, grace, beauty, ornament”), from decet (“adorn, befit”).

adj: From Middle English decorat (“decorated, adorned”), see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and Etymology 1 for more. Originally also used as the past participle of decorate; compare generate or communicate.
decorate.example: He was a decorated soldier who served in three wars.
decorate.exampleSense: To honor by providing a medal, ribbon, or other adornment.

lexicographical.example: More importantly, there is an untold multitude of Indian English terms that have never been given lexicographical treatment in any dictionary.

emancipation.o: 1630, from French émancipation, from Latin ēmancipātiō. In the US, with reference to anti-slavery, abolitionism, first used in 1785 by Charles Godfrey Leland. In Britain, with reference to easing of restrictions on Catholics, in 19th century.
emancipation.example: US President Abraham Lincoln was called the Great Emancipator after issuing the Emancipation Proclamation in 1863.
emancipation.exampleSense: The state of being thus set free; liberation (used, for example, of slaves from bondage, of a person from prejudices, of the mind from superstition, of a nation from tyranny or subjugation).

liberation.o: Borrowed from Middle French libération, and from Latin liberatio, liberationem (“a freeing”), from liberare past participle liberatus (“set free”); see liberate. Equivalent to liberate + -ion.
liberation.example: women's liberation... black liberation... gay liberation...
liberation.exampleSense: The achievement of equal rights and status, particularly as seen as freedom from historic and structural oppression.

emancipate.o: Learned borrowing from Latin ēmancipātus (“liberated, emancipated”) + English -ate (suffix forming verbs, and adjectives with the sense ‘characterized by the specified thing’). Ēmancipātus is the perfect passive participle of ēmancipō (“to declare (someone) free and independent of another’s power, emancipate; to give (something) from one’s authority or power into that of another, to alienate, transfer; to cause (oneself or someone) to become another’s slave; to make (someone) subservient”), from ē- (a variant of ex- (prefix meaning ‘away; out’)) + mancipō (“to sell; to transfer”) (from manceps (“owner, possessor; purchaser; etc.”) + -ō (suffix forming infinitives of first-conjugation verbs)). The verb emancipate has verb sense 1.1 (“to set free”) and verb sense 1.3 (“(obsolete) to place under one’s control”) which are contradictory. The Latin word ēmancipō had the same senses, and the Oxford English Dictionary notes that according to the Latin grammarian Paulus Festus (fl. 8th century) this is because both actions were effected by the legal process of mancipation.
emancipate.example: Emancipate yourselves from mental slavery, none but ourselves can free our minds.
emancipate.exampleSense: To free from any controlling influence, especially from anything which exerts undue or evil influence

liberate.o:
verb: Learned borrowing from Latin līberātus (“freed, liberated; absolved, acquitted; released”); see English -ate (suffix forming verbs, and used as the ending of participial adjectives and obsolete past participles from Latin). Līberātus is the perfect passive participle of līberō (“to free, liberate; to absolve, acquit; to release”), from līber (“free, unrestricted”), + -ō (suffix forming regular first-conjugation verbs); and līberō is ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁léwdʰeros (“free”), from *h₁lewdʰ- (“to grow; people”) + *-teros (contrastive or oppositional adjectival suffix) (*h₁léwdʰeros possibly originally meant ‘belonging to one’s own people’, excluding slaves who were captured from other groups of people, and thus later came to mean “free (not enslaved)”). Not related to deliberate.

noun: From Late Middle English liberate (“warrant for payment of an allowance, debt, pension, etc.; warrant for delivery of property from a sheriff’s custody”, noun), from Law French liberate, from Anglo-Norman liberate, and from their etymon Late Latin liberate (“name of such a writ”), a noun use of Latin līberāte (“deliver”) (commonly the first word of such writs), the second-person plural present active imperative of līberō (“to free, liberate; to absolve, acquit; to release”): see further at etymology
liberate.example: We didn't need IDs. We just liberated these beers from the back of the shop.
liberate.exampleSense: To acquire from another by theft or force: to steal, to rob.

write-up.example: The film had poor write-ups, but I ended up enjoying it anyway.
write-up.exampleSense: A review published in the print or online media for a film, book, etc.

write up.example: The supervisor wrote up the personnel report about him.

pathology.o: From French pathologie, from Ancient Greek πάθος (páthos, “disease”) and -λογία (-logía, “study of”). By surface analysis, path- + -ology or patho- + -logy.
pathology.example: Some sort of mental and social pathology seemed to sweep over the discourse later that autumn.
pathology.exampleSense: Pathosis: any deviation from a healthy or normal structure or function; abnormality; illness or malformation.

scenery.o: Earlier scenary, from scene + -ary, but now remodelled as scene + -ery.

peeper.example: So you go to see this peeper, this Marlowe. That was your mistake.

peep.o:
noun: From Middle English pepen. Compare Dutch piepen (“peep”), German Low German piepen (“to peep”), German piepen and pfeifen, all probably onomatopoeic.

verb: From Middle English pepen, variant of piken.

noun: Uncertain; perhaps variant of pip.

noun: Back-formation from peeps, a shortened form of people.

noun: Genericized trademark from the confection brand Peeps.
peep.example: When flowers first peeped, and trees did blossoms bear.
peep.exampleSense: To begin to appear; to look forth from concealment; to make the first appearance.

arrange.o: Inherited from Middle English arengen, arrangen (“to draw up a battle line”), borrowed from Old French arengier, arangier (“to put in a line, put in a row”), derived from reng, rang, ranc (“line, row, rank”), from Frankish *hring (“ring”), from Proto-Germanic *hringaz, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)krengʰ-, a form of Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to turn, bend”).
arrange.example: It had been arranged as part of the day's programme that Mr. Cooke was to drive those who wished to go over the Rise in his new brake.
arrange.exampleSense: To plan; to prepare in advance.

indifferent.o: From Old French indifferent, from Latin indifferens. By surface analysis, in- + different.
indifferent.example: Then she shrugged, the mildest, most indifferent gesture he had ever seen, and smiled.
indifferent.exampleSense: Indicating or reflecting a lack of concern or care.

plane.o:
adj: From Latin plānum (“flat surface”), a noun use of the neuter of plānus (“plain”). The word was introduced in the 17th century to distinguish the geometrical senses from the other senses of plain. Doublet of llano, piano, and plain.

noun: From Middle English plane, plaine, from Anglo-Norman plaine, from Late Latin plāna (“planing tool”).

noun: Clipping of aeroplane.

noun: From Middle English plane, borrowed from Old French plane, from Latin platanus, from Ancient Greek πλάτανος (plátanos), from πλατύς (platús, “wide, broad”).
plane.example: Mirrors in the compartments have been canted out of the vertical plane to reduce reflections to the passengers when seated.
plane.exampleSense: A flat surface extending infinitely in all directions (e.g. horizontal or vertical plane); a bounded portion thereof.

butler.o: From Middle English butler, butlere, boteler, botelere, from Old French buttiler, butiller, boteillier (“officer in charge of wine”), from Medieval Latin botellārius, equivalent to bottle + -er. Piecewise doublet of bottler.

subtraction.o: Borrowed from Late Latin subtractio, subtractionis. Can be decomposed to subtract + -ion.
subtraction.example: The teacher has set us ten subtractions to do by tomorrow.

aptitude.o: From Middle French aptitude, from Medieval Latin aptitudo, from Latin aptus (“apt, fit”). By surface analysis, apt + -itude. Doublet of attitude.

feudalist.example: Had I been born in a feudalist society, I would have attempted to batter myself into the nobility.
feudalist.exampleSense: Advocating or practising feudalism, or in which feudalism is practised.

feudalism.example: It was the beginning of a feudalism of the range, a barony rude enough, but a glorious one, albeit it began, like all feudalism, in large-handed theft and generous murdering.
feudalism.exampleSense: A social system based on personal ownership of resources and personal fealty between a suzerain (lord) and a vassal (subject). Defining characteristics are direct ownership of resources, personal loyalty, and a hierarchical social structure reinforced by religion.

folly.o:
noun: Inherited from Middle English folie, from Old French folie (“madness”), from the adjective fol (“mad, insane”).

noun: Uncertain. The most common theory is that term primarily denotes a clump of trees and relates to French feuille, feuillée and English foliage; it has also been suggested that it refers to some perceived connection or resemblance of the named place to an architectural folly, but many places so named have no architectural follies and cannot be named directly for them.
folly.example: The purchase of Alaska from Russia was termed Seward's folly.
folly.exampleSense: Thoughtless action resulting in tragic consequence.

regimen.o: From Middle English regimen, from Middle French regimen and its etymon, Latin regimen (“guidance, direction, government, rule”). Doublet of regime.
regimen.example: Pronouns may be nominatives, and of the direct or indirect regimen.

reliably.example: Genuine cowards follow the wicked and cannot reliably sustain any virtue.

relevancy.example: It is the malpractice of the courts to confine evidence and discussion to the bounds of apparent relevancy.
relevancy.exampleSense: The degree to which a thing is relevant; relevance, applicability.

recalibrate.example: Throughout the evening, Mr. Christie’s admonition about canned lines and rehearsed speeches hovered and seemed to recalibrate how the crowd — and television viewers — processed what Mr. Rubio said (and resaid, over and over).
recalibrate.exampleSense: To calibrate for a second or subsequent time.

recalibration.o: From re- + calibration. First attested in 1883.

celebration.o: From Old French celebration, from Latin celebratio. Equivalent to celebrate + -ion.
celebration.example: We will attend the Christmas celebration in church.
celebration.exampleSense: The formal performance of a solemn rite, such as Christian sacrament.

midnight.o: From Middle English midnight, from Old English midniht, from Proto-Germanic *midjanahts (“midnight”), equivalent to mid- + night. Cognate with Saterland Frisian Midnoacht (“midnight”), Old High German mittinaht (“midnight”), Danish midnat (“midnight”), Swedish midnatt (“midnight”), Icelandic miðnætti (“midnight”). Compare also Saterland Frisian Middernoacht (“midnight”), Dutch middernacht (“midnight”), German Mitternacht (“midnight”).
midnight.example: Thanks to its sonar, the narwhal can remain active even at midnight, unhindered by the darkness.
midnight.exampleSense: The middle of the night: the sixth temporal hour, equidistant between sunset and sunrise.

fickleness.o: From Middle English fikelnesse, equivalent to fickle + -ness.

fickle.o:
adj: From Middle English fikil, fikel, from Old English ficol (“fickle, cunning, tricky, deceitful”), equivalent to fike + -le. More at fike.

verb: From Middle English fikelen, from fikel (“fickle”); see above. Cognate with Low German fikkelen (“to deceive, flatter”), German ficklen, ficheln (“to deceive, flatter”).

unequivocally.example: They strove to make their product unequivocally the best in the industry.
unequivocally.exampleSense: In a way that leaves no doubt; in an unequivocal or unambiguous manner, unquestionably.

unequivocal.example: I want you to give me an unequivocal guarantee on that.
unequivocal.exampleSense: Unambiguous; without equivocation or ambiguity; singularly clear, unmistakable, or unquestionable

equivocation.o: c. 1380, from Middle English equivocacion, from Old French equivocation, from Medieval Latin aequivocātiō, from aequivocō, from Late Latin aequivocus (“ambiguous, equivocal”), from Latin aequus (“equal”) + vocō (“call”); a calque of Ancient Greek ὁμωνυμία (homōnumía).

equivocate.o: From Late Middle English equivocaten, from Medieval Latin aequivocātus, perfect passive participle of aequivocō (“to be called by the same name”), from Late Latin aequivocus (“ambiguous, equivocal”). Compare French équivoque.
equivocate.example: All that Garnet had to say for him was that he supposed he meant to equivocate.
equivocate.exampleSense: To speak using double meaning; to speak ambiguously, unclearly or doubtfully, with intent to deceive; to vacillate in one's answers, responding with equivoques.

equivoque.o: From Late Latin aequivocus (“ambiguous, equivocal”), from Latin aequus (“equal”) + vocō (“call”).
equivoque.example: [T]he black wisps of women bargaining behind those veils might turn out to be the ballet and coalesce in some dance gaily admitting their equivoque of concealing and proclaiming their sex.

equivocal.o: From Late Latin aequivocus + -al, from aequus + vocō. By surface analysis, equi- + vocal.
equivocal.example: For the beauties of Shakespeare are not of so dim or equivocal a nature as to be visible only to learned eyes.
equivocal.exampleSense: Having two or more equally applicable meanings; capable of double or multiple interpretation.

typo.o:
noun: Clipping of typographical error.

noun: Clipping of typographer.
typo.example: On the highest, rear seat was James Williams, of Cloverdale, Missouri, and his Bride.

disposition.o: From Middle English disposicioun, from Middle French disposition, from Latin dispositiōnem, accusative singular of dispositiō, from dispōnō. By surface analysis, dispose + -ition. Doublet of dispositio.
disposition.example: I have little disposition now to do as you say.
disposition.exampleSense: The way in which something or someone is disposed or disposed of (in any sense of those terms); thus: Tendency or inclination under given circumstances.

perturbation.o: Borrowed from Middle French perturbation, from Old French perturbacion, from Latin perturbatio.
perturbation.example: But her mind had never been in such perturbation; and it needed a very strong effort to appear attentive and cheerful till the usual hour of separating allowed her the relief of quiet reflection.
perturbation.exampleSense: Agitation; the state of being perturbed

seagull.o: From sea + gull. The second element is from a Brythonic language. Compare Welsh gwylan, Breton gouelan.
seagull.example: And while there are plenty of benches, there's little shelter from the wind (or predatory seagulls the size of dogs) out on the platforms.
seagull.exampleSense: Any of several white, often dark-backed birds of the family Laridae having long, pointed wings and short legs.

geology.o: From geo- + -logy, partly after Renaissance Latin geōlogia, from Ancient Greek γεω- (geō-, “earth”) + Latin -logia (“the study of”), from Ancient Greek -λογία (-logía).
geology.exampleSense: The geological structure of a region.

tutti.o: From Italian tutti, from Latin totus (“all”).
tutti.example: Even so, the orchestra endowed tuttis with a positively radiant glow.
tutti.exampleSense: A passage in which all members of an orchestra are playing

valve.o: From Middle English valve, from Latin valva (“double door, valve”). Doublet of valva.

unfamiliar.example: United were second-best for long periods as they struggled to adapt to an unfamiliar line-up and were ultimately fortunate to leave Merseyside with their unbeaten league run still intact.

neocolonialism.o: By surface analysis, neo + colonialism, or, by surface analysis, neocolonial + ism.

decolonization.example: But what does decolonisation have to do with place names? Place names are the meeting points of history and geography that shape part of our identities.
decolonization.exampleSense: The reverse of colonization, i.e. granting back autonomy to a group.

morph.o:
noun: Back-formation from morpheme, from Ancient Greek μορφή (morphḗ, “form, shape”). Compare German Morph, from Morphem. Attested since the 1940s.

noun: Back-formation from morphism. Attested since the 1950s. See also morphology.

verb: Clipping of metamorphose.

noun: Clipping of morphine.

noun: Clipping of morphodite.
morph.example: But what is this metasubstance that blinks at us from the apex of the morph, and that in Terminator 2 is hyperbolized in the quicksilver substratum of the T-1000?
morph.exampleSense: A computer-generated gradual change from one image to another.

unethical.example: He was sacked for unethical conduct.
unethical.exampleSense: Breaching the established standards of conduct or behavior within a particular organization or profession.

extrinsic.o: From French extrinsèque, from Latin extrinsecus (“from without, without, on the outside”), from *extrim, an assumed adverbial form of exter (“outer, outward”) + secus (“by, on the side”).

positiveness.example: Nobody knew anything about it although they all spoke with great positiveness and strategical knowledge.
positiveness.exampleSense: The quality of being positive; positivity.

energetic.o:
adj: From New Latin energeticus (16th c.), or its source, Ancient Greek ἐνεργητικός (energētikós), from ἐνεργέω (energéō, “to be active”), from ἐνεργός (energós, “active”). By surface analysis, energy + -etic.

noun: Possibly from a clipping of energetic materials.
energetic.example: Cosmic rays are energetic particles from outer space.

patriotically.example: The obsessive subject of our sterile confrontation between the two PCs ― the politically and the patriotically correct ― is clumsily labeled "multiculturalism".

relume.example: [H]e opened his eyes again; the spreading film retired, and love relumed them—he gave a look—it was never forgotten.
relume.exampleSense: To make clear or bright again.

resume.o:
verb: From Anglo-Norman resumer, Middle French resumer, from Latin resumere, from re- + sumere (“to take”).

noun: Borrowed from French résumé, past participle of résumer (“to summarize”), from Latin resūmere (“to take back”); compare resume.
resume.example: Ladies and gentlemen, please resume your seats.
resume.exampleSense: To take back possession of (something); to regain;

handover.example: The emergency regulations ordinance, created by British authorities to break up port strikes in 1922, had not been used for over half a century, and never since the handover of Hong Kong to Chinese rule in 1997.
handover.exampleSense: The transference of authority, control, power or knowledge from one agency to another, or from one state to another.

justified.o: simple past and past participle of justify. From Middle English justifien, from Old French justifier, from Late Latin justificare (“make just”), from Latin justus, iustus (“just”) + ficare (“make”), from facere, equivalent to just + -ify.

culprit.o: From Anglo-Norman cul. prit, contraction of culpable: prest (d'averrer nostre bille) 'guilty: ready (to prove our case)', words used by prosecutor in opening a trial, mistaken in English for an address to the defendant. See culpable. It may have been influenced by Latin culpa (“blame, fault”).
culprit.example: I have tightened the loose bolt that was the culprit; it should work now.
culprit.exampleSense: The person or thing at fault for a problem or crime.

double.o: PIE word *dwóh₁ From Middle English double, from Old French doble, double, from Latin duplus (“twofold”). Doublet of doppio and duple.
double.example: Saddam Hussein was rumored to have many doubles.
double.exampleSense: A person who resembles and stands in for another person, often for safety purposes

ultimately.example: Ultimately, he will have to make a decision before the end of the week.

noticeably.example: We all saw it: he paled noticeably.

academia.o: Borrowed from New Latin acadēmīa, from Ancient Greek Ἀκαδημία (Akadēmía), a grove of trees and gymnasium outside of Athens where Plato taught; from the name of the supposed former owner of that estate, the Attica hero Akademos. Doublet of academe, academy, and Akademeia. Modern sense of “the world of universities and scholarship” recorded from 1956.
academia.example: Academia continues to provide scientific education, despite attempts to turn it into a system of professional schooling.
academia.exampleSense: The scientific and cultural community engaged in higher education and research, taken as a whole.

conviviality.example: Keeping a relationship over social media just is not the same as experiencing in-person conviviality.

convivial.o: Borrowed from French convivial, from Latin convīvium (“a feast”), combined form of con- (“together”) + vīvō (“to live”).
convivial.example: I put the chief of police behind the bar, instructed him in his duties, and we four convivial spirits sprawled along the counter drinking ale and telling yarns till cockcrow.
convivial.exampleSense: Having elements of a feast or of entertainment, especially when it comes to eating and drinking, with accompanying festivity

conducive.o: From conduce + -ive, 1640s, from Latin condūcere, patterned after forms like conductive.
conducive.example: A small, dark kitchen is not conducive to elaborate cooking.
conducive.exampleSense: Tending to contribute to, encourage, or bring about some result.

transferable.example: To start a new career, you need transferable skills.

umbrella.o: Borrowed from Italian ombrella (“parasol, sunshade”), from Late Latin umbrella (influenced by umbra (“shadow, shade”)), from Latin umbella, from umbra + -la (diminutive suffix).
umbrella.example: The test facility was established under the umbrella of the company's quality program.
umbrella.exampleSense: Anything that provides similar overarching coverage of a range of concepts, purposes, groups, etc.

youth.o: From Middle English youthe, youghte, ȝouþe, from Old English ġeoguþ (“the state of being young; youth”), from Proto-West Germanic *juwunþa, from Proto-Germanic *jugunþō, *jugunþiz (“youth”), corresponding to young + -th (abstract nominal suffix). Cognate with Saterland Frisian Juugd, West Frisian jeugd, Dutch jeugd, German Low German Jöögd, German Jugend.
youth.example: I made many mistakes in my youth, but learned from them all.
youth.exampleSense: The part of life following childhood; the period of existence preceding maturity or age; the whole early part of life, from childhood, or, sometimes, from infancy, to adulthood.

choir.o: From Middle English quer, quere, from Old French quer, from Latin chorus, from Ancient Greek χορός (khorós, “company of dancers or singers”). Modern spelling influenced by chorus and French chœur. Doublet of quire, chorus, and hora.
choir.example: The church choir practices Thursday nights.
choir.exampleSense: A group of people who sing together; a company of people who are trained to sing together.

lustful.o: From Middle English lustful, from Old English lustfull (“desirous, wishful”); equivalent to lust + -ful. Cognate with Dutch lustvol (“lustful, lusty”), German lustvoll (“pleasurable”), Swedish lustfyllt (“pleasurable”), Swedish lustfyllda (“lustful”).
lustful.example: Many of the so-called rites of these secret societies were so patently ridiculous, that it is quite obvious that they were merely an excuse for men and women to indulge in sex-play and lustful gratification, frequently of an abnormal kind.
lustful.exampleSense: Full of lust; driven by lust.

nestle.o: From Middle English nestelen, nestlen, from Old English nistlan, nestlian, nistlian (“to make or build a nest”), from Proto-West Germanic *nistilōn (“to build or occupy a nest; nestle”), equivalent to nest + -le. Cognate with Middle Low German nëstelen (“to build a nest”), Dutch nestelen (“to nest, nestle”).
nestle.example: She made no answer, but her fingers nervously nestled the leaves of a book.
nestle.exampleSense: To move or place into a comfortable position

hitchhike.example: After much deliberation, he decided hitchhiking was his only way out of London.
hitchhike.exampleSense: To try to get a ride in a passing vehicle while standing at the side of a road, generally by either sticking out one's finger or thumb or holding a sign with one's stated destination.

chaperone.example: TfL has more than enough to be getting on with each day without having to chaperone TV crews.

sluice.o: From Middle English sluse, alteration of scluse, from Anglo-Norman escluse (“sluice, floodgate”), from Late Latin exclusa (“extrusion, gate”), from Latin exclūsus, form of exclūdō (“to shut out, to exclude”) (English exclude). Cognate to Dutch sluis.
sluice.example: Out of sight of the houses he took off his clothes and let the rain sluice down on his bare body.

spell out.example: He used Scrabble tiles to spell out “I LOVE YOU”.
spell out.exampleSense: To form (a word) from letters; say the letters in a word.

attendee.example: O'Reilly, the summit host, remembers a particularly insightful comment from Torvalds, a summit attendee.
attendee.exampleSense: A person who is in attendance or in the audience of an event.

state.o: From Middle English stat (as a noun); adopted c. 1200 from both Old French estat and Latin stātus (“manner of standing, attitude, position, carriage, manner, dress, apparel; and other senses”), from stāre (“to stand”). Doublet of estate and status. The sense of "polity" develops in the 14th century. Compare French être, Greek στέω (stéo), Italian stare, Portuguese estar, Romanian sta, and Spanish estar. The verb is first attested around the beginning of the 16th century. Related to English stand.
state.example: Never do anything against conscience even if the state demands it.
state.exampleSense: A polity or community. Any sovereign polity or community; the government of a country or city-state.

stated.o: simple past and past participle of state. From Middle English stat (as a noun); adopted c. 1200 from both Old French estat and Latin stātus (“manner of standing, attitude, position, carriage, manner, dress, apparel; and other senses”), from stāre (“to stand”). Doublet of estate and status. The sense of "polity" develops in the 14th century. Compare French être, Greek στέω (stéo), Italian stare, Portuguese estar, Romanian sta, and Spanish estar. The verb is first attested around the beginning of the 16th century. Related to English stand.
stated.example: Our stated policy of nonalignment has kept us out of any military alliance such as NATO and Warsaw Pact. However, in reality, we have had to concede ground to nations from which we import military hardware.
stated.exampleSense: Expressed in a statement; uttered or written.

troubleshooting.o: present participle and gerund of troubleshoot. Back-formation from troubleshooter; by surface analysis, trouble + shoot.
troubleshooting.example: When it comes to computer problems, his troubleshooting is first-rate.
troubleshooting.exampleSense: The identification and resolution of problems, especially problems of a technical nature.

out of hand.example: Clean things as you go so that the mess does not get out of hand.
out of hand.exampleSense: Barely under control; not under control.

magnification.example: His story included a magnification of the events.
magnification.exampleSense: The act of magnifying; enlargement; exaggeration.

legible.o: From Late Latin legibilis (“that can be read”), from Latin legō.
legible.example: Despite hardly having any energy to lift a pen, she left a legible note on the paper.
legible.exampleSense: Clear enough to be read; readable, particularly of handwriting.

sur-.o: From Middle English sur-, from Old French sur-, sour-, sor-, soure-, a syncopic form of the Latin super. Doublet of super-, over-, and hyper-.

expeditionary.example: [...] turned out in its best attire to receive the Brazilian expeditionaries and the group of soldiers representing the gallant U.S. 10th Mountain Division.
expeditionary.exampleSense: One who goes on expeditions, especially one who is a member of an expeditionary military force.

tubular.o: From Latin tubulus + -ar. By surface analysis, tubule + -ar. The sense meaning "cool" or "awesome" is believed to be a figurative extension originating in surfing lingo, from the way that an excellent wave encloses a surfer within tubular walls of water.
tubular.example: It was such a tubular party, Journal! But a few minutes later, I walked up to the Hermosa Beach Pier and left the girls with my things, thinking the totally bitchin' party would continue. But when I got back, they were all gone.

turbulent.o: From Middle English turbulent, from Middle French turbulent, from Latin turbulentus, from turba (“disorder, tumult, crowd”).
turbulent.example: The mid-19th century was a turbulent time in American history.
turbulent.exampleSense: being in, or causing, disturbance or unrest

turbulence.o: From Middle English turbulence (“turbidity, cloudiness”), from Late Latin turbulentia (“trouble, disquiet”). By surface analysis, turbulent + -ence.
turbulence.example: Turbulence was everywhere, within every blade of grass, every drop of dew on a leaf, every cloud in the sky, and every star beyond. The turbulence was purposeless, but in huge quantities of purposeless turbulence, purpose took shape.
turbulence.exampleSense: The state or fact of being turbulent or agitated; tempestuousness, disturbance.

turban.o: Borrowed from Middle French turbant, from Italian turbante, from Ottoman Turkish دلبند (tülbent), from Classical Persian دلبند (dulband), also the root of tulip.
turban.example: Towel hair wraps come in a mixture of materials, from microfibre to polyester, while satin and silk are the go-to materials for sleep turbans.
turban.exampleSense: A towel wrapped around long wet hair in a manner resembling a turban.

deficient.o: From Latin deficiens, present participle of deficere (“to lack, fail, be wanting”); see defect.
deficient.example: This was justified by the rationale that mental deficients, by definition, are not able to succeed in society.

stow.o:
noun: From Middle English stowe, from Old English stōw (“place, location”), from Proto-West Germanic *stōu, from Proto-Germanic *stōō (“a place, stowage”), from Proto-Indo-European *steh₂- (“to stand, place, put”). Cognate with Old Frisian stō (“place”), Icelandic stó (“fireplace”), Dutch stouw (“place”), German Stau (“congestion”). See also -stow.

verb: From Middle English stowen, stawen, stewen, from Old English stōwian (“to hold back, restrain”), from Proto-Germanic *stōōną, *stōjaną (“to stow, dam up”), from Proto-Indo-European *steh₂- (“to stand, place”). Cognate with Dutch stuwen, stouwen (“to stow”), Low German stauen (“to blin, halt, hinder”), German stauen (“to halt, hem in, stow, pack”).
stow.example: Yet everybody knows that a cargo properly stowed in a seaworthy craft reaches market in much the better condition than by rail, though perhaps it is some hours longer on the way.
stow.exampleSense: To store or pack something in a space-saving manner and over a long time.

osmanthus.o: From João de Loureiro's (1790) taxonomic name Osmanthus (“genus of flowering shrubs”), from Ancient Greek ὀσμή (osmḗ, “smell”) + ἄνθος (ánthos, “flower”), for the strong scent of the Osmanthus fragrans.
osmanthus.example: By 1969, the flower district had under cultivation over 13 hectares of rosebeds alone, 10,000 pots of osmanthus, 50,000 pots of magnolias, camellias and jasmine and several hundred thousand pots of chrysanthemums, as well as thousands of pine, pomegranate and iron trees.
osmanthus.exampleSense: Any of several widely distributed evergreen flowering plants, of the genus Osmanthus.

adept.o: Borrowed from French adepte, from Latin adeptus (“who has achieved”), the past participle of adipisci (“to attain”).
adept.example: Others, alas, had an instinct towards artificiality in their very blood, and became adepts in counterfeiting at the first glimpse of it.
adept.exampleSense: One fully skilled or well versed in anything; a proficient

mandate.o:
noun: First attested in 1521; borrowed from Latin mandātum (“a charge, order, command, commission, injunction”), substantivized from the neuter forms of mandātus, perfect passive participle of mandō (“to commit to one's charge, order, command, commission, literally to put into one's hands”) (see -ate (noun-forming suffix)), from manus (“hand”) + -dere (“to put”). Sense 3 in Canadian English is likely a semantic loan from French mandat.

verb: First attested in 1623; partly directly borrowed from Latin mandātus (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and Etymology 1 for more), partly from the above noun by metanalysis.

noun: From man + date.
mandate.example: Instead, May, more sheep than shepherd, has feebly allowed herself to be driven ever further towards an extreme, inflexible, take-it-or-leave-it stance for which she has neither mandate nor credible grounds.
mandate.exampleSense: An official or authoritative command; an order or injunction; a commission; a judicial precept; an authorization.

check up.example: The numbers she provided check up with my own data.
check up.exampleSense: To seem correct or plausible; to comport with known facts; to check out (with other facts).

maniacal.example: He suddenly exploded into about three seconds of maniacal laughter and stopped again.

maniac.o: From mania + -ac. Borrowed from French maniaque, from Late Latin maniacus, from Ancient Greek μανιακός (maniakós), adjectival form of μανία (manía, “madness”). Compare manic.
maniac.example: She was driving like a maniac.
maniac.exampleSense: An insane person, especially one who suffers from a mania.

mania.o: Borrowed from Latin mania, from Ancient Greek μανία (manía, “madness”).
mania.example: One of the manias of the present day, which especially excites my spleen, is the locomotive rage which seems to possess all ranks—that necessity of going out of town in the summer...
mania.exampleSense: Excessive or unreasonable desire; insane passion affecting one or many people; fanaticism.

persecution.o: Equivalent to persecute + -ion. From Middle English persecucioun, from Old French persecucion, from Ecclesiastical Latin persecūtio (“persecution; chase, pursuit”), from Latin persequor (“follow up, pursue”), from per- (“through”) + sequor (“follow”). Displaced native Old English ēhtnes.
persecution.example: Many apartheid perpetrators escaped prosecution for their persecution of black Africans and political dissidents.
persecution.exampleSense: The act of persecuting, especially a specific group of people; an instance of persecution.

persecutor.o: From Middle English persecutour, from Old French persecutor and Latin persecūtor. Displaced native Old English ēhtere.

persecute.o: Borrowed from Middle French persécuter, from Ecclesiastical Latin persecutor, from Latin persequor, persecutus (“follow up, pursue”), from per- (“through”) + sequor (“follow”) (English sequel). Compare prosecute. Cf. also pursue.
persecute.example: Humans have been persecuting wolves in this forest for centuries.
persecute.exampleSense: To kill many of one species of animal, with the intent of removing them from human habitats.

detoxify.o: Attested since 1905 (twelve years earlier than toxify), from de- + tox- + -ify. (Detoxicate is attested one year earlier, since 1904.)
detoxify.example: The severe disciplinary action taken by his daughter—who since taking over the FN in 2011 has led a drive to “detoxify” the party and move it away from the racist, jackbooted, antisemitic imagery of the past—was supposed to silence her father.
detoxify.exampleSense: To remove foreign and harmful substances from something.

easiness.example: Custome hath made it in him a propertie of easines.
easiness.exampleSense: The state or quality of being easy (in various senses). particularly: Lack of concern or care: carelessness, indolence.

upspring.o:
verb: From Middle English upspringen, from Old English uppspringan, ūpspringan, equivalent to up- + spring.

noun: From Middle English upspring, upspringe, from Old English upspring (“origin, birth, rising up, springing up”), equivalent to up- + spring. Cognate with Old Saxon upspring (“well; source; spring”), Middle Low German upspringen (“to spring up; grow”).
upspring.example: Might not its waters upspring in this new land, whose discovery was the great marvel of the age, and which men looked upon as the unknown east of Asia?
upspring.exampleSense: To spring up, rise up, originate, come into being.

upbringing.o: From Middle English upbringinge, equivalent to upbring + -ing.
upbringing.example: Through her upbringing, Mildred's father had carefully programmed her to expect very little from life.
upbringing.exampleSense: The raising or training of a child.

milepost.example: But beyond these cut-offs, to avoid the wholesale alteration of all mileposting and mileages—of bridges and culverts, for example—the original mileposts have remained unaltered.
milepost.exampleSense: A sign or post beside a railway marking the distance from the (actual or nominal) start of a line (usually the principal terminus or junction with a more major line).

milestone.o: From mile + stone. Compare Dutch mijlsteen (“milestone”), German Low German Mielensteen (“milestone”), German Meilenstein (“milestone”), Swedish milsten (“milestone”).
milestone.example: Death is another milestone on their way.
milestone.exampleSense: An important event in a person's life or career, in the history of a nation, in the life of some project, etc.

end point.o: Alternative form of endpoint. From end + point.

defraud.o: From Middle English defrauden, from Old French defrauder, from de- + frauder.
defraud.example: She is sinned against, because she is defrauded of her rights ^((i.e. sexual satisfaction)).

valuer.example: I'm a funny combination of loner and valuer of community.
valuer.exampleSense: A person who appreciates something and sets a value on it.

argumentation.o: Inherited from Middle English argumentacioun, from Anglo-Norman argumentacion, Middle French argumentation, or their etymon Latin argūmentātiō; by surface analysis, argument + -ation.
argumentation.example: His chain of argumentation is flawed.
argumentation.exampleSense: Inference based on reasoning from given propositions.

argumentative.o: From Late Middle English argumentatif (“syllogistic, sophistic”), from Old French argumentatif, argumentative (modern French argumentatif (“argumentative”)) and Medieval Latin, Late Latin argūmentātīvus, from Latin argūmentātor + -īvus (suffix forming adjectives).
argumentative.example: Your host was in his turn eloquent,—authoritative,—facetious,—argumentative,—precatory,—pathetic, above all, pertinacious.

actuator.example: The mind is the actuator of the body.

one-off.o: From one + off. Probably from foundry work, for which making reusable molds is expensive and expediency makes the rule for molds not to be used only once. A term long used by artists who are printmakers and sculptors to indicate a unique print or casting. If using traditional edition numbering, a one-off would be a "1/1", which is said, "one of one" meaning the first print in an edition of one.
one-off.example: I'll put together a quick one-off as a sample so we can taste the recipe.
one-off.exampleSense: Something that is done, created, etc. only once, and often quickly, simply, or improvisationally.

proclamation.o: From Middle English proclamacion, from Anglo-Norman and Old French proclamacion, from Late Latin proclāmātiō, from the verb Latin prōclāmō.
proclamation.example: The Tuesday meetings are only thirty minutes now. That proclamation was made in the previous meeting.
proclamation.exampleSense: A statement which is proclaimed; formal public announcement.

exclamation.o: Borrowed from Middle French exclamation, from Latin exclāmātiō, from exclāmō (“to cry out”) + -tiō.
exclamation.example: "And now, my dearest Lucy, collect yourself, for all depends upon our own resources." Such were the whispered exclamations with which Francesca cheered her trembling companion, whose courage was not heightened by the darkness and stillness around them as they proceeded on their hazardous enterprise.
exclamation.exampleSense: A loud calling or crying out, for example as in surprise, pain, grief, joy, anger, etc.

declamation.o: From French déclamation, from Latin dēclāmātiō, dēclāmātiōnem, from dēclāmō, dēclāmāre; see declaim.

acclamation.o: * First attested in 1541. * Borrowed from Latin acclāmātiō, acclāmātiōnis (“calling, exclamation, shout of approval”), from acclamo (“shout approval or disapproval of, shout out at”), from ad (“toward”) + clamo (“cry out”) * Compare French acclamation.
acclamation.example: Sometimes a member nominates a chairman and no vote is taken, the assembly signifying their approval by acclamation.
acclamation.exampleSense: A shout of approbation, favor, or assent; eager expression of approval; loud applause.

reclamation.o: Borrowed from Middle French réclamation, from Latin reclamatio. Equivalent to reclaim + -ation.
reclamation.example: From there, the material will be transported by rail to three sites across the country, to be used for land reclamation.
reclamation.exampleSense: The act of reclaiming or the state of being reclaimed.

precocious.o: From Latin praecox (“premature, precocious, ripe before time, early ripe”), from praecoquō (“to ripen beforehand, ripen fully, also boil beforehand”), from prae (“before”) + coquō (“to cook, boil, ripen”). Doublet of apricot.
precocious.example: The precocious plant was already blooming flowers by day 4.
precocious.exampleSense: Characterized by exceptionally early development or maturity.

strong.o: From Middle English strong, strang, from Old English strang (“strong”), from Proto-West Germanic *strang (“severe, strict, rigorous, strong”), from Proto-Germanic *strangaz (“tight, strict, straight, strong”), from Proto-Indo-European *strengʰ- (“taut, stiff, tight”). Cognate with Scots strang (“strong”), Saterland Frisian strang, West Frisian string (“austere, strict, harsh, severe, stern, stark, tough”), Dutch streng (“strict, severe, tight”), German streng (“strict, severe, austere”), Danish and Norwegian streng (“strong, hard”), Faroese and Icelandic strangur (“strict”), Norwegian strang (“strong, harsh, bitter”), Swedish sträng, strang (“severe, strict, harsh”), Latin stringō (“tighten”). Related to strict and string.
strong.example: A wise man is strong, yea a man of knowledge encreaseth strength.

solicitation.o: From Middle French sollicitation, from Latin sollicitātiō.
solicitation.example: "The instances you have quoted," replied the other, "are certainly very encouraging! Homer past a life in blindness and beggary; Columbus, in vain solicitation and feverish disappointment; and Luther's was spent in struggle, imprisonment, and danger...
solicitation.exampleSense: the action or instance of soliciting; petition; proposal

solicitous.o: From Latin sōlicitus, sollicitus (“thoroughly disturbed, anxious”), from sollus (“whole, entire”) + cieō (“move, disturb”). By surface analysis, solicit + -ous.
solicitous.example: The more solicitous of the two was Nurse Cramer, a shapely, pretty, sexless girl with a wholesome unattractive face.
solicitous.exampleSense: Showing care, concern, or attention, in any of several ways; thus: In a conscientious way, often with kindness.

soliciting.o: present participle and gerund of solicit. From Middle English soliciten, solliciten, from Old French soliciter, solliciter, borrowed from Latin sollicitō (“stir, disturb; look after”), from sollicitus (“agitated, anxious, punctilious”, literally “thoroughly moved”), from sollus (“whole, entire”) + perfect passive participle of cieō (“shake, excite, cite, to put in motion”).

funding.o: present participle and gerund of fund. PIE word *bʰudʰmḗn Borrowed from Latin fundus. Doublet of fond and fundus.
funding.example: The council is providing funding to the church to repair the roof.

break off.o: From Middle English breke of (“break off, terminate”), a dissimilated form of earlier Middle English ofbreken. By surface analysis, break + off.
break off.example: Both families want the lovers to break off any relationship they may have.

break.o:
verb: From Middle English breken, from Old English brecan (“to break”), from Proto-West Germanic *brekan, from Proto-Germanic *brekaną (“to break”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰreg- (“to break”). Doublet of bray. Cognates Cognates of Germanic origin include Scots brek (“to break”), West Frisian brekke (“to break”), Dutch breken (“to break”), Low German breken (“to break”), German brechen (“to break”), French broyer (“to crush, grind”), Gothic 𐌱𐍂𐌹𐌺𐌰𐌽 (brikan, “to break, destroy”), Norwegian brek (“desire, yearning”). Also cognate with Albanian brishtë (“fragile”), Latin frangō (“break, break up, shatter”, verb), whence English fracture and other terms – fragile, frail, fraction, and fragment. The modern pronunciation shows an irregular change of Early Modern English /ɛː/ to /eɪ/ in the standard language; contrast this with the development of other words such as speak and wreak.

noun: Clipping of breakdown (the percussion break of songs chosen by a DJ for use in hip-hop music) and see also breakdancing.
break.example: Crossing the break smoothly is one of the first lessons the young clarinettist needs to master.
break.exampleSense: The point in the musical scale at which a woodwind instrument is designed to overblow, that is, to move from its lower to its upper register.

interrupt.o: From Middle English interrupten, derived from Latin interruptus, past participle of interrumpere (“to break apart/off, interrupt”), from inter (“between”) + rumpere (“to break”).
interrupt.example: The interrupt caused the packet handler routine to run.
interrupt.exampleSense: An event that causes a computer or other device to temporarily cease what it was doing and attend to a condition.

park.o: From Middle English park, from Old French parc (“livestock pen”), from Medieval Latin parcus, parricus, from Frankish *parrik (“enclosure, pen, fence”). Cognate with Dutch perk (“enclosure; flowerbed”), Old High German pfarrih, pferrih (“enclosure, pen”), Old English pearroc (“enclosure”) (whence modern English paddock), Old Norse parrak, parak (“enclosure, pen; distress, anxiety”), Icelandic parraka (“to keep pent in under restraint and coercion”). More at parrock, paddock.
park.example: If the afternoon was fine they strolled together in the park, very slowly, and with pauses to draw breath wherever the ground sloped upward. The slightest effort made the patient cough.
park.exampleSense: An area of land set aside for environment preservation or recreation. A piece of ground in or near a city or town, enclosed and kept for ornament and recreation.

median.o: Borrowed from Middle French median, from Latin mediānus (“of or pertaining to the middle”, adjective), from medius (“middle”) (see medium), from Proto-Indo-European *médʰyos (“middle”). Doublet of mean and mizzen. Cognate with Old English midde, middel (“middle”). More at middle.
median.example: Why is not our jugular or throat-veine as much at our command as the mediane [translating mediane]?
median.exampleSense: A central vein or nerve, especially the median vein or median nerve running through the forearm and arm.
