adobe.o: From Spanish adobe, from Arabic اَلطُّوب (aṭ-ṭūb), from Sahidic Coptic ⲧⲱⲃⲉ (tōbe, “brick”), from Demotic Egyptian ⁠⁠ (tb, “brick”), from Egyptian Db-b-t:O39 (ḏbt, “brick, block, ingot”).
adobe.example: Many people in Texas and New Mexico live in adobe houses.
adobe.exampleSense: An unburnt brick dried in the sun.

outrageously.o: From Middle English outrageously, equivalent to outrageous + -ly.
outrageously.example: The hotel was wonderful, but the food was outrageously expensive.
outrageously.exampleSense: In an outrageous manner; to an outrageous degree.

outrageous.o: From Anglo-Norman outrageus, Middle French outrageus, from outrage; equivalent to outrage + -ous.
outrageous.example: The Irish-French rugby union whistler Alain Rolland was roundly condemned for his outrageous decision that lifting a player into the air then turning him over so he falls on his head or neck amounted to dangerous play.
outrageous.exampleSense: Violating morality or decency; provoking indignation or affront.

courageous.o: From Middle English corajous, from Old French corageus, from corage + -eus.

stop by.example: On our way back, we should stop by the grocery store.
stop by.exampleSense: To pay a visit briefly and informally.

reminiscence.o: From Late Latin reminīscentiae (“remembrances”), from Latin reminīscēns, present active participle of reminīscor (“remember”); see reminiscent.
reminiscence.example: Here was my chance. I took the old man aside, and two or three glasses of Old Crow launched him into reminiscence.
reminiscence.exampleSense: An act of remembering long-past experiences, especially positive or pleasant ones, often fondly.

reminiscent.o: From Latin reminīscēns, present participle of reminīscor (“remember”), from re- (“again”) + min-, base of me-min-isse (“to remember, think over”), akin to mens (“mind”); see mental, mind, etc.
reminiscent.example: That painting is very reminiscent of Picasso's later work.
reminiscent.exampleSense: Tending to bring some memory etc. to mind (followed by of)

reminisce.o: Back-formation from reminiscence, from Latin reminīscēns, present participle of reminīscor (“to remember”).
reminisce.example: I met up with Alastair McQueen [former Mirror colleague] and we had a reminisce.

earplug.example: In this same strain of mouse, earplugging from 17-22 days postpartum is effective in inducing susceptibility to audiogenic seizures...

plug-and-play.o: Alternative form of plug. From Dutch plug, from Middle Dutch plugge (“peg, plug”), from Old Dutch *pluggi, from Proto-West Germanic *plugi. Further origin unknown. Possibly from Proto-Germanic *plugjaz, but the word seems originally restricted to northern continental West Germanic. Perhaps ultimately from the same source as Dutch plag (“cut-out sod”), itself considered to be from a substrate. Compare German Low German Plüg, Norwegian plug (“peg, wedge”, probably borrowed from Middle Low German), German Pflock (“peg”, restricted to Central German and phonetically divergent). Possibly akin to Lithuanian plúkti (“to strike, hew”).

plug.o: From Dutch plug, from Middle Dutch plugge (“peg, plug”), from Old Dutch *pluggi, from Proto-West Germanic *plugi. Further origin unknown. Possibly from Proto-Germanic *plugjaz, but the word seems originally restricted to northern continental West Germanic. Perhaps ultimately from the same source as Dutch plag (“cut-out sod”), itself considered to be from a substrate. Compare German Low German Plüg, Norwegian plug (“peg, wedge”, probably borrowed from Middle Low German), German Pflock (“peg”, restricted to Central German and phonetically divergent). Possibly akin to Lithuanian plúkti (“to strike, hew”).
plug.example: He attempted to plug the leaks with some caulk.
plug.exampleSense: To stop with a plug; to make tight by stopping a hole.

revisionary.example: I conclude that there is good reason to suspect that adverbialist paraphrases are in fact conservative rather than revisionary.
revisionary.exampleSense: Having the character of a revision.

repercussion.o: From Middle French répercussion, from Latin repercussio (“rebounding; repercussion”), from repercutio (“cause to rebound, reflect, strike against”), from re- + percutio (“beat, strike”), from per- (“thoroughly”) + quatio (“shake”).
repercussion.example: You realize this little stunt of yours is going to have some pretty serious repercussions.
repercussion.exampleSense: A consequence or ensuing result of some action.

volatility.example: The recent volatility has come with the S&P 500 hovering just above bear market territory, or a 20 percent drop from its most recent high.
volatility.exampleSense: A quantification of the degree of uncertainty about the future price of a commodity, share, or other financial product.

aesthetics.example: At a glance, Thor Steinar resembles waspy American pseudo-collegiate brands like Abercrombie and Fitch, Hollister, and Aeropostale, while displaying a distinctly Nordic aesthetics.
aesthetics.exampleSense: The study or philosophy of beauty.

aesthete.o: From Ancient Greek αἰσθητής (aisthētḗs, “one who perceives”).
aesthete.example: Although Stanley was the political operator while Pick was the aesthete, it was Stanley who made the early running in Underground design.
aesthete.exampleSense: Someone who cultivates an unusually high sensitivity to beauty, as in art or nature, often in a manner perceived to prioritize beauty over other qualities such as virtue and utility.

sly.o: From Middle English sly, sley, sleigh, sleiȝ, from Old Norse slǿgr (“sly, cunning”, literally “capable of hitting or striking”), from Proto-Germanic *slōgiz (“lively, agile, cunning, sly, striking”), from Proto-Indo-European *slak- (“to hit, throw”). Cognate with Icelandic slægur (“crafty, sly”), Norwegian Nynorsk sløg (“sly”). Related to sleight, slay. In all likelihood, however, unrelated with Saterland Frisian slau (“sly, crafty”), Dutch sluw (“sly, cunning”), Low German slu (“sly, cunning”), German schlau (“clever, crafty”). Doublet of sleight and slöjd

toss.o: From Middle English tossen (“to buffet about, agitate, toss; to sift or winnow”), of uncertain origin. Perhaps from Old Norse (compare dialectal Norwegian tossa, dialectal Swedish tossa (“to strew, spread”)), or perhaps from an alteration of Middle English tosen (“to tease, pull apart, shred; to wound, injure”). Compare also Dutch tassen (“to pile or heap up, stack”). The Welsh tos (“a quick jerk”) and tosio (“to jerk, toss”) are probably borrowed from the English.
toss.example: "We are all in a toss, in our neighborhood," said Mistress Pottle.

unease.o:
noun: From Middle English unese, equivalent to un- + ease. Compare disease.

verb: From Middle English unesen, equivalent to un- + ease.

uneasy.o:
adj: From Middle English unesy, equivalent to un- + easy. Merged with Middle English unethe, uneathe (“difficult, not easy”). See uneath.

adj: From Middle English unesy, unaisie (“not comforting”), from un- + esy (“comfortable, at ease”). More at easy.
uneasy.example: I've been uneasy about your friend ever since I met him. Are you sure we can trust him?

start out.example: He started out writing for the school magazine, and now he's a TV talk show celebrity.

gentleman.o: From Middle English gentilman, morphologically gentle + man, partial calque of Old French gentilhome.
gentleman.example: Latrobe had extensive dealings with Jefferson, the most prominent gentleman-architect in the United States.
gentleman.exampleSense: An amateur or dabbler in any field, particularly those of independent means.

vilify.o: From Late Latin vīlificāre (“vilify”). Equivalent to vile + -ify. Compare vilipend.

breast-feed.o: Alternative spelling of breastfeed. From breast + feed.

breast.o: From Middle English brest, from Old English brēost, from Proto-West Germanic *breust, from Proto-Germanic *breustą, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰrews- (“to swell”). Compare West Frisian boarst, Danish bryst, Swedish bröst; cf. also Dutch borst, German Brust.
breast.example: Tanya’s breasts grew remarkably during pregnancy.
breast.exampleSense: Either of the two organs on the front of a female human's chest, which contain the mammary glands; also the analogous organs in males.

pregnancy.example: Viable non-malformed singleton pregnancies were selected for cerebellar measurements; transcerebellar diameter, (TCD), left and right cerebellar diameters (LCD, RCD).
pregnancy.exampleSense: The condition of being pregnant; an instance of this.

marital.o: Borrowed from Middle French marital, and its source, Latin marītālis, from marītus (“husband”).

subjectively.example: [Animals] are conscious; they are subjectively aware; they have interests; they can suffer. No characteristic other than sentience is required for personhood.

subjective.o: From Latin subiectīvus, equivalent to subject + -ive.
subjective.example: The general finite stem is the verbal stem which serves as the basis of inflection in the indicative present and past in the subjective conjugation and the objective conjugation with the singular and dual object.
subjective.exampleSense: Describing conjugation of a verb that indicates only the subject (agent), not indicating the object (patient) of the action. (In linguistic descriptions of Tundra Nenets, among others.)

unequal.o: From Middle English unequale, equivalent to un- + equal. Compare German unegal (“unlevel, uneven”).
unequal.example: Her manner to Francesca was very unequal. Sometimes it had all the frankness of their early intimacy; at other times it was forbidding, and even petulant.

consensual.example: He'd operated on an almost permanent adrenaline high, a byproduct of youth and proficiency, jacked into a custom cyberspace deck that projected his disembodied consciousness into the consensual hallucination that was the matrix.
consensual.exampleSense: With permission, with consensus, without coercion; allowed without objecting or resisting.

pee.o:
noun: The initial letter of piss. Compare eff.

noun: Spelling of the abbreviation p of pence.

noun: See peak.
pee.example: He was dying for a pee.

mangle.o:
verb: From Middle English mangelen, manglen, from Anglo-Norman mangler, mahangler, frequentative of either Old French mangonner (“to cut to pieces”) or mahaigner (“to mutilate”), of Germanic origin, for which see mayhem. Alternate etymology derives mangle from Middle English *mankelen, a frequentative form of manken (“to mutilate”), from Old English *mancian, bemancian (“to maim”). More at mank.

noun: Ca. 1700, from Dutch mangel, from Early Modern German Mangel (15th c.), enhanced form (by analogy with other tool names in -el) of Middle High German mange, from Medieval Latin manga, manganum, from Ancient Greek μάγγανον (mánganon). Doublet of mangonel.

noun: Borrowed from Spanish mangle, mangue, probably from an Arawak language (such as Taíno), or a Cariban language.
mangle.example: There was a bright-red plastic baby-bath, a car tyre, a rusty mangle, and something that looked like a primitive version of a washing machine.
mangle.exampleSense: The mangle attached to wringer washing machines, often called the wringer.

manga.o:
noun: Borrowed from Japanese 漫画(まんが) (manga), from Middle Chinese 漫 (MC manH, “free, unrestrained”) + 畫 (MC hweaH|hweak, “drawing”). Compare Mandarin 漫畫／漫画 (mànhuà), Korean 만화 (漫畵／漫畫, manhwa). After an 1814 book by Katsushika Hokusai. Doublet of manhua and manhwa.

noun: From Spanish manga (“sleeve”). Doublet of manche.

noun: Short for mangalitsa.
manga.example: Lately I've been reading a Brazilian manga.
manga.exampleSense: Any comic in such a style, regardless of the country of origin.

curled.o: simple past and past participle of curl. From metathesis of Middle English crulle (“curled, curly”), of uncertain origin but probably from an unrecorded Old English word or from Middle Dutch crul, crulle (“curl”), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *kruzlǭ (“bent or crooked object, curl”), connected to *krūsą (“curl”), of unknown origin. Cognate with Saterland Frisian Krulle (“curl, lock”), West Frisian krul (“curl”), Dutch krul (“curl”), German Low German Krull (“curl”), dialectal German Krolle (“curl”), Danish krølle (“curl”), Norwegian Bokmål krøll (“curl”). Related also to Saterland Frisian Kruus (“curl”), German kraus (“frizzy, crumpled, curly”), Danish krus (“curl”), Swedish krusa (“to crimp, curl”). Compare also Gothic 𐌺𐍂𐌹𐌿𐍃𐍄𐌰𐌽 (kriustan, “to grind, crush, gnash”).

curler.example: The captain sent a curler into the top corner of the net.
curler.exampleSense: A pass or a shot of the ball which swerves.

aero.o: Back-formation from aero- (prefix), from Ancient Greek ἀέρος (aéros).
aero.example: We've seen a lot of growth in the aero sector.

recess.o: The noun is borrowed from Latin recessus (“act of going back, departure, receding, retiring; (figuratively) retreat, withdrawal; (metonymically) distant, secluded, or secret spot, corner, nook, retreat; recessed part, indentation”) (also Late Latin recessus (“decree or resolution of the Diet of the Holy Roman Empire”)), from recēdō (“to go back, recede, retire, withdraw; to go away, depart; (by extension) to disappear, vanish; to separate; to stand back, be distant; to yield”) (from re- (prefix meaning ‘back, backwards’) + cēdō (“to go, move, proceed”)) + -tus (suffix forming action nouns from verbs); influenced by Middle French recès, French recès (“a break, pause; break between classes in school; school vacation; ebbing of tide; reduction”) (also Anglo-Norman recès and Old French recès (“hiding place; hollow”). Noun sense 5 (“decree or resolution of the diet of the Holy Roman Empire, etc.”) is possibly influenced by Italian recesso and refers to a decree or resolution made just before a meeting ends. The adjective and verb are derived from the noun. Cognates * Catalan recés * Italian recesso * Middle French recès (modern French recès) * Portuguese recesso * Spanish receso
recess.example: [T]he soldier looked to the oriel windows. The recesses within them were raised a step or two from the wall.
recess.exampleSense: A depressed, hollow, or indented space; also, a hole or opening. A small space created by building part of a wall further back from the rest; a niche.

haste.o: Blend of Middle English hasten (verb), (compare Dutch haasten, German hasten, Danish haste, Swedish hasta (“to hasten, rush”)) and Middle English hast (“haste”, noun), from Old French haste (whence French hâte), from Old Frankish *hai(f)st (“violence”), from Proto-Germanic *haifstiz (“struggle, conflict”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱeyp- (“to ridicule, mock, anger”). Akin to Old Frisian hāst, hāste (“haste”), Old English hǣst (“violence”), Old English hǣste (“violent, impetuous, vehement”, adjective), Old Norse heift /heipt (“feud”), Gothic 𐌷𐌰𐌹𐍆𐍃𐍄𐍃 (haifsts, “rivalry”). Cognate with German heftig (“vehement”) and Danish heftig (“vehement”).
haste.example: We were running late so we finished our meal in haste.

hasty.o: From Middle English hasty, of obscure origin. Likely a new formation in Middle English equivalent to haste + -y, found as in other Germanic languages (Old Frisian hâstich, Middle Dutch haestich (> Dutch haastig (“hasty”)), Middle Low German hastich (“hasty”), German hastig, Danish hastig, Swedish hastig (“hasty”)); otherwise possibly representing an assimilation to the foregoing of Middle English hastive, hastif (> English hastive), from Old French hastif (Modern French hâtif), from Frankish *haifst (“violence”), ultimately of the same Germanic origin.
hasty.example: Without much thinking about it they made a hasty decision to buy it.
hasty.exampleSense: Acting in haste; being too hurried or quick

cobbled.o: simple past and past participle of cobble. From Middle English cobill, kobill (used in various combinations with ston, stan (“stone”), note, nutt (“nut”), etc.), probably a diminutive of Middle English *cob, *cobb, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *kubb- (“lump; round object”). Equivalent to cob + -le.

stint.o:
verb: From Middle English stinten, from Old English styntan (“to make blunt”) and *stintan (attested in āstintan (“to make dull, stint, assuage”)), from Proto-West Germanic *stuntijan, from Proto-Germanic *stuntijaną and Proto-Germanic *stintaną (“to make short”), probably influenced in some senses by cognate Old Norse *stynta, stytta (“to make short, shorten”).

noun: Origin unknown.
stint.example: The majority of maiden mares will become stinted while at work.
stint.exampleSense: To impregnate successfully; to get with foal.

egoist.o: From French égoïste, from Latin ego + -iste. By surface analysis, ego + -ist.

egoism.o: From French égoïsme, from New Latin egoismus, from Latin ego. By surface analysis, ego + -ism.

cardio-.o: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek καρδία (kardía, “heart”).

cardio.example: I did some cardio today instead of lifting weights.
cardio.exampleSense: Exercise with the goal of raising the heart rate.

lollipop.o: By surface analysis, loll (“laze, hang loose”) + y + pop (“shot, try, burst, enter”); likely through lolly (“head, tongue”). Attested from 1784. Compare lollygag and lollypoop. An unlikely derivation is from Romani loli (“red”) + phabaj (“apple”); candy apples are often red and placed on a stick to keep the person's hands dry, similar to lollipops. However candy apples were not well-known until a century after the first known use of the word lollipop, and the original lollipop was likely a small item like modern penny candy.
lollipop.example: Mount Pleasant itself is a lollipop trail. Walking along the handle of the lollipop is a breeze—the perfect warm-up for the uphill climb at the beginning of the loop.
lollipop.exampleSense: Something having the shape of a lollipop: a linear stem connected to a round body.

newness.o: From Middle English newnesse, from Old English nīewnes (“newness, novelty”), equivalent to new + -ness.
newness.example: The newness of the car meant it still had that funny smell.
newness.exampleSense: The property of being new; novelty; recency.

nerveless.example: Little Sea and Desire, blessed, nerveless savages, were sound asleep.
nerveless.exampleSense: Devoid of nerves: calm, controlled, cool under pressure.

nakedness.o: From Middle English nakednesse, from Old English nacodnes (“nakedness”); equivalent to naked + -ness. Cognate with West Frisian neakenens (“nakedness”).

neatness.example: Both engines and carriages were maintained in admirable cleanliness, and a very high standard of neatness characterised the permanent way and lineside buildings.

nameless.o: From Middle English nameles, equivalent to name + -less. Cognate with Dutch naamloos (“nameless”), German namenlos (“nameless”), Danish navnløs (“nameless”), Swedish namnlös (“nameless”), Icelandic nafnlaus (“nameless, anonymous”).
nameless.example: The culprits shall remain nameless here, as some names have been changed to protect the guilty; just don't let it happen again.
nameless.exampleSense: Whose name is unknown; unidentified or obscured.

neediness.o: From Middle English nedynesse; equivalent to needy + -ness.
neediness.example: The kind of family neediness experienced by homemakers differed between classes.

needless to say.example: Having won the championship, he is, needless to say, a very happy man.

needlessly.example: He worried needlessly about his dog.

needless.o: From Middle English needlees, nedelees, nedeles, equivalent to need + -less.
needless.example: This new project of yours will only be a needless expense.

duo-.o: PIE word *dwóh₁ Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *dwóh₁ Proto-Italic *duō Latin duo English duo- From Latin duo (“two”).

congregate.o: The adjective is first attested in 1400–1450, in Middle English, the verb c. 1513; from Middle English congregat(e) (“(of people) banded together; (of liquids) accumulated; (of muscles) contracted; (of wounds) closed up”), borrowed from Latin congregātus, perfect passive participle of congregō (“to congregate”) (see -ate (etymology 1, 2 and 3), from con- (“with, together”) + gregō (“to collect into a flock”), from grex (“flock, herd”). See gregarious and egregious. Participial usage of the adjective up until Early Modern English.
congregate.example: Even there where merchants most do congregate.
congregate.exampleSense: To come together; to assemble; to meet.

vagrant.o:
noun: From Late Middle English vagraunt (“person without proper employment; person without a fixed abode, tramp, vagabond”) [and other forms], probably from Anglo-Norman vagarant, wakerant, waucrant (“vagrant”) [and other forms] and Old French walcrant, waucrant (“roaming, wandering”) [and other forms], perhaps influenced by Latin vagārī, the present active infinitive of vagor (“to ramble, stroll about; to roam, rove, wander”). Old French walcrant is the present participle of vagrer, wacrer, walcrer (“to wander, wander about as a vagabond”) [and other forms], from Frankish *walkrōn (“to wander about”), the frequentative form of *walkōn (“to walk; to wander; to stomp, trample; to full (make cloth denser and firmer by soaking, beating and pressing)”), from Proto-Germanic *walkōną (“to roll about, wallow; to full”), *walkaną (“to turn, wind; to toss; to roll, roll about; to wend; to walk; to wander; to trample; to full”), from Proto-Indo-European *walg-, *walk-, *welgʰ-, *welk-, *wolg- (“to turn, twist; to move”), ultimately from *welH- (“to turn; to wind”). The English word is cognate with Latin valgus (“bandy-legged, bow-legged”), Middle Dutch walken (“to knead; to full”), Old English wealcan (“to roll”), ġewealcan (“to go; to walk about”), Old High German walchan, walkan (“to move up and down; to press together; to full; to walk; to wander”), Old Norse valka (“to wander”). See further at walk.

adj: From Middle English vagraunt, vagaraunt (“having no proper employment; having a tendency to go astray or wander; wayward”), from Anglo-Norman vagarant, wakerant, waucrant (“vagrant”) and Old French walcrant, waucrant (“roaming, wandering”); see further at etymology
vagrant.example: Every morning before work, I see that poor vagrant around the neighbourhood begging for food.
vagrant.exampleSense: A person without settled employment or habitation who usually supports himself or herself by begging or some dishonest means; a tramp, a vagabond.

homeless.o: From Middle English *homles, *hamles, from Old English hāmlēas (“homeless”), equivalent to home + -less. Cognate with Dutch heemloos, Danish hjemløs (“homeless”), Swedish hemlös (“homeless”). Compare also German heimatlos (“homeless”), Icelandic heimilislaus (“homeless”), West Frisian dakleas (“homeless”, literally “having no roof, roofless”).
homeless.example: Whenever I pass the park, I see the homeless people sleeping on the benches.
homeless.exampleSense: Lacking a permanent place of residence.

congregation.o: From Middle English congregacioun, from Old French congregacion, from Latin congregātiō, itself from congregō (“to herd into a flock”). Adopted (1520s) by the English Bible translator William Tyndale, to render the Ancient Greek ἐκκλησία (ekklēsía, “those called together, (popular) meeting”) (hence Latin ecclēsia) in his New Testament, and preferred by 16th century Reformers instead of church. By surface analysis, congregate + -ion.
congregation.example: The critically low level of rainfall in the second half of 2020 – approaching 50% year on year for November – led the religious affairs directorate to instruct imams and their congregations to pray for rain last month.
congregation.exampleSense: A gathering of faithful in a temple, church, synagogue, mosque or other place of worship. It can also refer to the people who are present at a devotional service in the building, particularly in contrast to the pastor, minister, imam, rabbi etc. and/or choir, who may be seated apart from the general congregation or lead the service (notably in responsory form).

role.o: From French rôle, from Middle French rolle, from Old French role, from Medieval Latin rotulus. Doublet of roll and rotulus.
role.example: Local volunteers played an important role in cleaning the beach after the oil spill.
role.exampleSense: The function or position of something.

hint.o: From Middle English hinten, hynten, variant of henten (“to lay hold of, catch”), from Old English hentan (“to seize, grasp”), from Proto-West Germanic *hantijan, from Proto-Germanic *hantijaną. Doublet of hent. Related also to hunt.
hint.example: We shall not describe this tragical scene too fully; but we thought ourselves obliged, by that historic integrity which we profess, shortly to hint a matter which we would otherwise have been glad to have spared.
hint.exampleSense: To bring to mind by a slight mention or remote allusion; to suggest in an indirect manner.

sip.o: Inherited from Middle English sippen, of uncertain origin. Compare with Low German sippen (“to sip”). Possibly from a variant of Middle English suppen (“to drink, sip”) (see sup) or perhaps from Old English sipian, sypian (“to take in moisture, soak, macerate”), from Proto-Germanic *sipōną (“to drip, trickle”), from Proto-Indo-European *seyb- (“to pour out, trickle, leak out”). Compare also Old High German supfen (“to drink, sip”), from Proto-Germanic *sūpaną (“to sip, intake”).
sip.example: bright young things in jeans and T-shirts huddle around laptops, sipping lattes or munching on free food.
sip.exampleSense: To drink slowly, small mouthfuls at a time.

patrol.o:
noun: From French patrouille, from Old French patrouille, patouille (“a night-watch”, literally “a tramping about”), from patrouiller, patouiller, patoiller (“to paddle or pudder in water, dabble with the feet, begrime, besmear”), from patte, pate (“paw, foot of an animal”), from Vulgar Latin *patta (“paw, foot”), from Frankish *patta (“paw, sole of the foot”), from Proto-Germanic *paþjaną, *paþōną (“to walk, tread, go, step, pace”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *(s)pent-, *(s)pat- (“path; to walk”), a variant of Proto-Indo-European *pent-, *pat- (“path; to go”); see find. Cognate with Dutch pad, patte (“paw”), Low German pedden (“to step, tread”), German patschen (“to splash, smack, dabble, waddle”), German Patsche (“a swatter, beater, paw, puddle, mire”). Related to pad, path.

verb: From French patrouiller, from Old French patrouiller (“to paddle, paw about, patrol”), from patte (“a paw”).
patrol.example: Four members of the squadron were on patrol.
patrol.exampleSense: A going of the rounds along the chain of sentinels and between the posts, by a guard, usually consisting of three or four men, to insure greater security from attacks on the outposts.

stealth.o: From Middle English stelthe, from Old English stǣlþ, from Proto-Germanic *stēliþō, to Proto-Germanic *stelaną (“to steal, to sneak”) + *-iþō, equivalent to steal + -th (abstract nominal suffix). Compare Old English stalu (“theft, stealth”), Old High German stāla (“theft”), German Diebstahl (“theft”).
stealth.example: For example a sex worker complained about a client who 'stealthed' her by removing a condom and prosecuted him for rape. The court found him guilty (R v Campos).
stealth.exampleSense: To subject (someone) to stealthing (sexual intercourse without a condom through deception, for example removing the condom mid-act).

astral.o: From Late Latin astrālis, from Latin astrum (“star”), from Ancient Greek ἄστρον (ástron, “star”).
astral.example: Now both of you sit there and wait for any guides to come to you, any astrals or people from that life to make themselves known to you.
astral.exampleSense: A supernatural being from the astral plane.

tell off.example: The Recruit looked thoughtful and told off the days on his fingers.
tell off.exampleSense: To count (members of a sequence), to enumerate.

physiology.o: From French physiologie, from Latin physiologia, from Ancient Greek φυσιολογία (phusiología, “natural philosophy”), from φύσις (phúsis, “nature”) + λόγος (lógos, “word”). Equivalent to physio- + -logy.
physiology.example: So he clung to the sides of the vertical tunnel, le wormhole, employing the setules covering his legs, that is, millions of tiny spider-hairs with triangular tips, a wall-creeper physiology if you wish, a hang-upside-down-from-the-ceiling anatomical boon.
physiology.exampleSense: A branch of biology that deals with the functions and activities of life or of living matter (as organs, tissues, or cells) and of the physical and chemical phenomena involved.

exhilarate.o: From Latin exhilarō (“to delight, to gladden, to make merry”), from ex- (“out, away”) (from Proto-Indo-European *h₁eǵʰs (“out”)) + hilarō (“to cheer, to gladden”), from hilaris (“cheerful, light-hearted, lively”), from Ancient Greek ἱλαρός (hilarós, “cheerful, merry”), from ἵλαος (hílaos, “gracious, kind, propitious”), from Proto-Indo-European *selh₂- (“comfort, mercy”). By surface analysis, ex- + Latin hilar(ō) + -ate.
exhilarate.example: Good news exhilarates the mind; wine exhilarates the drinker.
exhilarate.exampleSense: To cheer, to cheer up, to gladden, to make happy.

provable.o: From Middle English provable, prevable, equivalent to prove + -able. Doublet of probable.

elevate.o:
verb: From Middle English elevaten (“to raise up, erect; to elate, inflate (e.g. with pride); (alchemy) to vaporize; (of a bone, excressence, blood vessel) to protrude”), from elevat(e) (“(in physical elevation, in rank, in altitude above the horizon) high”, also used as the past participle of elevaten) + -en (verb-forming suffix), further from Latin ēlevātus, the perfect passive participle of ēlevō (“to raise, lift up”), from ē- (“out”) + levō (“to make light, to lift”), from levis (“light”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix); see levity and lever.

adj: From Middle English elevat(e) (“(in physical elevation, in rank, in altitude above the horizon) high”, also used as the past participle of elevaten), see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and Etymology 1 for more. Cognate with French élevé.
elevate.example: The doctor told me elevating my legs would help reduce the swelling.
elevate.exampleSense: To raise (something) to a higher position.

forge.o:
noun: From Middle English forge, from Old French forge, early Old French faverge, from Latin fabrica (“workshop”), from faber (“workman in hard materials, smith”) (genitive fabri). Cognate with Franco-Provençal favèrge. Doublet of fabric and fabrica. Partially displaced English smithy. * Computing sense perhaps derived from the early SourceForge service, launched in 1999.

verb: From Middle English forgen, from Anglo-Norman forger and Old French forgier, from Latin fabrico (“to frame, construct, build”). Doublet of fabricate.

verb: Make way, move ahead, most likely an alteration of force, but perhaps from forge (n.), via notion of steady hammering at something. Originally nautical, in reference to vessels.
forge.example: Close to the hump-backed bridge on the lane leading into the Hambleden Valley is a mid-19th-century smithy, its inside walls hung with tools of the blacksmith's trade, though decorative wrought-ironwork is now the main product from its glowing forge.
forge.exampleSense: A furnace or hearth where metals are heated prior to hammering them into shape.

forage.o: From Middle English forage, from Old French fourage, forage, a derivative of fuerre (“fodder, straw”), from Frankish *fōdar (“fodder, sheath”), from Proto-Germanic *fōdrą (“fodder, feed, sheath”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂- (“to protect, to feed”). Cognate with Old High German fuotar (German Futter (“fodder, feed”)), Old English fōdor, fōþer (“food, fodder, covering, case, basket”), Dutch voeder (“forage, food, feed”), Danish foder (“fodder, feed”), Icelandic fóðr (“fodder, sheath”). More at fodder, food. Unrelated to modern French forage (“drilling”), whose first element is ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰerH- (“to pierce”).
forage.example: He [the lion] from forage will incline to play.
forage.exampleSense: An act or instance of foraging.

mediate.o: The adjective is first attested in the 1440s in Middle English, the verb in 1538; from Middle English mediat(e) (“intermediate; intercessory”), borrowed from Late Latin mediātus, perfect passive participle of mediō (“to divide in the middle; (in Medieval Latin) to be in the middle, be or become between, mediate”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from medius (“middle”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix).
mediate.example: Negotiators managed to mediate a ceasefire.
mediate.exampleSense: To resolve differences, or to bring about a settlement, between conflicting parties.

side-effect.o: Alternative form of side. From Middle English side, from Old English sīde (“side, flank”), from Proto-Germanic *sīdǭ (“side, flank, edge, shore”), derived from *sīdaz, probably from Proto-Indo-European *seh₁- (“long, lasting”). Cognate with Saterland Frisian Siede (“side”), West Frisian side (“side”), Dutch zijde, zij (“side”), German Low German Sied (“side”), German Seite (“side”), Danish, Norwegian Bokmål, and Norwegian Nynorsk side (“side”), Swedish sida (“side”). The LGBTQ slang sense was coined by sex therapist and author Joe Kort in 2010 and popularized in 2013. The sense was coined by analogy with top and bottom and based on the metaphor of a box which has a top, bottom, and sides.
side-effect.example: Hence, side-effecting the environment is equivalent to collaborating with an autonomous co-robot.
side-effect.exampleSense: To alter as a side effect.

neuter.o: Inherited from Middle English neutre, from Latin neuter, from ne (“not”) + uter (“either”), a semantic loan from Koine Greek οὐδέτερος (oudéteros); compare English either, English whether, and neither.
neuter.example: In The Cook and the Carpenter, Arnold used the device of a neuter pronoun "na," instead of assigning gender to the characters.
neuter.exampleSense: Having a form which is not masculine nor feminine; or having a form which is not of common gender.

mismatch.o:
verb: From mis- + match (verb sense).

noun: From mis- + match (noun sense).
mismatch.example: After all the trepidation born of Holland's toils home and away against these opponents in qualification for Euro 2012, and the pockmarked nature of the pitch, this was exposed as a mismatch from the opening exchanges.
mismatch.exampleSense: Something that does not match; something dissimilar, inappropriate or unsuitable.

infiltrator.example: Sometimes Israelis were attacked by Arab infiltrators, and hardly a month went by without a West Jerusalemite either being killed or wounded.
infiltrator.exampleSense: One who infiltrates an organization or territory; an undercover or covert agent.

infiltrate.o: From Middle English infiltrate (adjective), from Medieval Latin infiltrātus, from infiltrō.
infiltrate.example: One critical distinction to make is whether a focal corneal infiltrate is infected with bacteria or is a sterile immunologic response.
infiltrate.exampleSense: Any undesirable substance or group of cells that has made its way into part of the body.

filtrate.o:
noun: From the substantivation of New Latin filtrātus (“filtered”) past perfect participle of filtrō (“to filter”). Equivalent to filter (the verb) + -ate (noun-forming suffix).

verb: From New Latin filtrō (“to filter”) + -ate (verb-forming suffix).

lateral.o: Borrowed from Latin laterālis (“belonging to the side”), from latus (“the side or flank”) + -ālis (“-al”, adjectival suffix).
lateral.example: A fish senses changes in hydrodynamic pressure with its lateral line.
lateral.exampleSense: To the side; of or pertaining to the side. Situated on one side or other of the body or of an organ, especially in the region furthest from the median plane.

authorize.o: From Middle English auctorisen, from Old French auctorisier, from Medieval Latin auctōrizāre, from Latin auctor. See author about the orthography with ⟨h⟩. Doublet of octroy.
authorize.example: The General Assembly authorized the Council to take up the matter.
authorize.exampleSense: To grant (someone) the permission or power necessary to do (something); to permit; to sanction or consent to.

jointly.example: They jointly raised the child, even though they were no longer married.

behavioral.example: Becoming more aware of the progress that scientists have made on behavioral fronts can reduce the risk that other natural scientists will resort to mystical agential accounts when they exceed the limits of their own disciplinary training.

delegation.o: Borrowed from Latin dēlēgātiō, dēlēgātiōnis, from dēlēgō: compare French délégation.

ecological.example: Bats host many high-profile viruses that can infect humans, including severe acute respiratory syndrome and Ebola. A recent study explored the ecological variables that may contribute to bats’ propensity to harbor such zoonotic diseases by comparing them with another order of common reservoir hosts: rodents.
ecological.exampleSense: Relating to ecology, the interrelationships of organisms and their environment.

gateway.example: According to Mellody, love addiction is a gateway addiction leading to additional addictions: to sex, food, drugs, alcohol, and so on.
gateway.exampleSense: Any point that represents the beginning of a transition from one place or phase to another. Any thing or area of interest that tends to lead to deeper involvement.

shutter.example: Shutter the windows: there's a storm coming!

redraw.example: The treaty proposed to redraw the border lines between the nations.

audit.o: Borrowed from Latin audītus, from audiō (“to hear”). The sense of examine is because examinations were originally presented orally, and the examiner listened.
audit.example: Yet I can make my audit up.
audit.exampleSense: The result of such an examination, or an account as adjusted by auditors; final account.

declaration.o: From Middle English declaration, declaracion, declaracioun, from Old French declaration (French déclaration), from Latin dēclārātiōnem, accusative of Latin dēclārātiō.
declaration.example: I went to Miss Mills's, fraught with a declaration.

tailor-made.o: simple past and past participle of tailor-make. Back formation from tailor-made.
tailor-made.example: A breitschwantz stole edged with ermine is knotted over this black woollen tailor-made.
tailor-made.exampleSense: A piece of clothing made by a tailor; (specifically), a dress made by a tailor rather than by a dressmaker, and hence plainer in style.

standout.example: The band played well, but the acrobats gave the standout performance.

decisive.o: From Middle French décisif, equivalent to decide + -ive.
decisive.example: In truth, Tottenham never really looked like taking all three points and this defeat means they face a battle to reach the knockout stages -with their next home game against PAOK Salonika on 30 November likely to prove decisive.
decisive.exampleSense: Having the power or quality of deciding a question or controversy; putting an end to contest or controversy; final; conclusive.

in vain.example: This petition is the reverse side of the commandment against taking God's name in vain.
in vain.exampleSense: In a disrespectful manner, without honoring the proper meaning; insincerely or without proper respect.

imprisonment.o: From Anglo-Norman emprisonement, from Old French emprisonnement. See imprison + -ment.
imprisonment.example: Every confinement of the person is an imprisonment, whether it be in a common prison, or in a private house, or even by forcibly detaining one in the public streets.
imprisonment.exampleSense: A confinement in a place, especially a prison or a jail, especially as punishment for a crime.

imprisoned.o: simple past and past participle of imprison. Inherited from Middle English imprisonen, emprisounen, emprisonen, from Old French emprisonner. Equivalent to im- + prison.

imprison.o: Inherited from Middle English imprisonen, emprisounen, emprisonen, from Old French emprisonner. Equivalent to im- + prison.
imprison.example: [...] demand for the boots fell sharply after the Battle of Waterloo, and Brunel was imprisoned for debt in 1821.
imprison.exampleSense: To put in or as if in prison; confine somebody against their will.

criminality.o: From French criminalité, from Latin criminalitas, from Latin criminalis. By surface analysis, criminal + -ity.

criminalise.example: Thailand has dropped legislation to criminalise torture and disappearances after years of working on the bill, the United Nations human rights office said on Tuesday, leaving state employees unaccountable for serious crimes.
criminalise.exampleSense: Non-Oxford British English standard spelling of criminalize.

co-ordinate.o: Alternative spelling of coordinate. From Medieval Latin coōrdinātus, perfect passive participle of coōrdinō (“arrange together”), from co- + ōrdinō, equivalent to co- + ordinate. See -ate (adjective-forming suffix) for more. See also ordain and ordinate.
co-ordinate.example: To assist in this mind-bogglingly complex endeavour, Switzerland has developed sophisticated software tools that allow infrastructure managers (IMs), operators and local/national authorities to co-ordinate civil engineering projects with planned service enhancements, demand forecasts, pathing requirements, nationwide timetables, and asset utilisation up to 15 years ahead.

uncoordinated.example: Though occasionally a “flatliner” can be revived with a defib, it is most commonly used to change the uncoordinated contractions of the heart (fibrillation) into a normal sinus rhythm—that is, to defibrillate the heart.

capacitate.example: By this instruction we may be capacitated to observe those errors.
capacitate.exampleSense: To make capable of functioning in a given capacity.

helper.o: From Middle English helpere, from Old English *helpere, from Proto-West Germanic *helpārī (“helper”), equivalent to help + -er. Cognate with Saterland Frisian Hälper (“helper”), West Frisian helper (“helper”), Dutch helper (“helper”), German Low German Helper (“helper”), German Helfer (“helper”), Danish hjælper (“helper”), Swedish hjälpare (“helper”), Icelandic hjálpar (“helper”).
helper.example: And I routinely took more “helpers” when I woke up in order to maintain the fast pace and, more importantly, to study for my final exams.

adduction.o: Borrowed from Latin adductio, adductionis, from adducō (“to bring to oneself”), from ad + ducō (“to lead”). Compare French adduction. Equivalent to adduct + -ion or adduce + -tion. See adduce.

addiction.o: From addict + -ion; compare (Latin) addictio (“an adjudging, an award”).
addiction.example: Do your lethal addictions to self-prescriptions numb the ache of the darkest days?
addiction.exampleSense: A state that is characterized by compulsive drug use or compulsive engagement in rewarding behavior, despite negative consequences.

habit-forming.example: Many governments prohibit the advertising of habit-forming substances to minors.
habit-forming.exampleSense: Addictive; likely to cause dependence or recurrence of use.

addicted.o: simple past and past participle of addict. Borrowed from Latin addictus, past participle of addīcō (“deliver; devote; surrender”), from ad- (“to, towards, at”) + dīcō (“say; declare”)

addicting.example: similar in action to codeine salts but when compared with codeine on the basis of weight is more active, and more addicting.

commode.o: Borrowed from French commode (literally “convenient”). Doublet of comodo.

incommode.o:
verb: Learned borrowing from French incommoder (“to bother, disconcert, incommode”), from Latin incommodāre, the present active infinitive of incommodō (“to inconvenience”), from in- (prefix meaning ‘not’) + commodō (“to accommodate, adapt; to bestow, provide; to hire, lend”) (from com- (a variant of con- (prefix indicating completeness or intensification)) + modō (the ablative or singular of modus (“manner, method, way; bound, limit; measure”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *med- (“to measure”))). The English word is analysable as in- (prefix meaning ‘not’) + commode (“(archaic or obsolete) to provide (someone or something) with an appropriate, suitable, or necessary thing; to meet the requirements of (someone or something), suit; to repair (something)”).

adj: The adjective is a learned borrowing from French incommode (“causing discomfort; inconvenient; troublesome; undesirable, unwanted, unwelcome”), from Latin incommodus (“inconvenient; disagreeable, troublesome; unfit, unsuitable, unseasonable”), from in- (prefix meaning ‘not’) + commodus (“becoming, suitable; comfortable, commodious; convenient; useful; opportune, timely; friendly, pleasant”) (from com- (a variant of con-) + modus): see further at etymology
incommode.example: Information is all around us, now more than ever before in human history. You barely have to stir or incommode yourself to find things out.
incommode.exampleSense: To cause (someone or something) inconvenience; to hinder, to impede, to inconvenience, to obstruct.

livestream.example: In November, she expressed irritation with Sam, 29, in an awkward exchange on his livestream.

lifeline.example: Slowly I began to fill up some of the emptiness inside—writing had become my lifeline.
lifeline.exampleSense: A source of salvation in a crisis.

accrue.o: First attested in mid 15th century. From Middle English acrewen, borrowed from Old French acreüe, past participle of accreistre (“to increase”), from Latin accrēsco (“increase”), from ad (“in addition”) + crēscō (“to grow”). Compare accrete.
accrue.example: The monthly financial statements show all the actual but only some of the accrued expenses.
accrue.exampleSense: To be incurred as a result of the passage of time.

sassy.o: A modification of saucy, equivalent to sass + -y, originally used in American English. First attested in 1799, but in common usage only as of the mid-19th century.
sassy.example: Brought her down with a crack of the bull-dogs, jest as she was makin' off: she's the sassiest of the whole lot, as white wenches always be.
sassy.exampleSense: Bold and spirited, cheeky, impudent, saucy.

swear off.example: One of these days, he thinks he will swear off his nightly television regimen and get some exercise.
swear off.exampleSense: To quit or cease completely, or to promise to quit, as a bad habit.

swear in.example: The Chief Justice swore him in as President on Inauguration Day.
swear in.exampleSense: To administer an oath to, as an oath of office or of citizenship.

sabotage.example: The railway line had been sabotaged by enemy commandos.
sabotage.exampleSense: To deliberately destroy or damage something in order to prevent it from being successful.

landmine.o: Alternative spelling of land. From Middle English lond, land, from Old English land, from Proto-West Germanic *land, from Proto-Germanic *landą (“land”), from Proto-Indo-European *lendʰ- (“land, heath”). Cognates Cognate with Scots laund (“land”), Yola lhoan, lloan, loan, londe, lone (“land”), North Frisian loun, luin, lun, Lön, lönj, löön (“land”), Saterland Frisian Lound (“land”), West Frisian lân (“land”), Limburgish Land, landj, Laïnt (“land”), Dutch land (“land, country”), Luxembourgish and German Land (“land, country, state”), Vilamovian łaond (“land”), Danish, Elfdalian, Faroese, Icelandic, Norwegian Bokmål, Norwegian Nynorsk and Swedish land (“land, country, shore, territory”). Non-Germanic cognates include Old Irish lann (“heath”), Welsh llan (“enclosure”), Breton lann (“heath”), Old Church Slavonic лѧдо (lędo), from Proto-Slavic *lędo (“heath, wasteland”), French lande (“heath”) and Albanian lëndinë (“heath, grassland”).

nothing but.o: From Middle English nothyng but, from Old English nan þing butan
nothing but.example: Do you solemnly swear that you will tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth, so help you God?

steadfastly.o: Inherited from Middle English stedefastly, stedefastliche; equivalent to steadfast + -ly.
steadfastly.example: He steadfastly refuses to go out with her.
steadfastly.exampleSense: In a steadfast manner; firmly; with conviction

sovereignty.o: PIE word *upér From Late Middle English sovereynte, souvereynte [and other forms], from Anglo-Norman sovereyneté, soverentee, and Old French soveraineté, souveraineté (modern French souveraineté), from soverain + -té (suffix forming nouns, often denoting a property or quality). Soverain is derived from Vulgar Latin *superānus (“chief; sovereign”), from Latin super (“above; on top of”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *upér (“above, over”)) + -ānus (“suffix meaning ‘of or pertaining to’, usually denoting a relationship of origin, position, or possession”)). The English word is analysable as sovereign + -ty (suffix forming abstract nouns from adjectives).

flak.o: Borrowed from German FlaK, short for Fliegerabwehrkanone (“anti airplane cannon”).
flak.example: Alex McLeish, perhaps mindful of the flak he has been taking from sections of the Villa support for a perceived negative style of play, handed starts to wingers Charles N'Zogbia and Albrighton.

territorialize.example: The landscapes of group identity — the ethnoscapes — around the world are no longer familiar anthropological objects, insofar as groups are no longer tightly territorialized, spatially bounded, historically unselfconscious, or culturally homogeneous.
territorialize.exampleSense: To reduce to the condition of a territory.

territorial.o: Borrowed from Late Latin territorialis, from Latin territorium; equivalent to territory + -al.
territorial.example: Studies have narrowed the territorial focus to signage used in specific cities, townships, suburbs, precincts, etc.
territorial.exampleSense: Of or relating to geography or territory.

hegemon.o: From Ancient Greek ἡγεμών (hēgemṓn, “a leader, guide, commander, chief”), from ἡγέομαι (hēgéomai, “to lead”).

hegemony.o: From Ancient Greek ἡγεμονία (hēgemonía, “supremacy or leadership, chief command”), from ἡγεμών (hēgemṓn, “a leader, guide, commander, chief”), from ἡγέομαι (hēgéomai, “to lead”). Early 19th-century usage influenced by German Hegemonie.
hegemony.example: The two political parties battled viciously for hegemony.
hegemony.exampleSense: Dominance of one social group over another, such that the ruling group or hegemon acquires some degree of consent from the subordinate, as opposed to dominance purely by force.

defining.o: present participle and gerund of define. From Middle English definen, from Old French definer, variant of definir, from Latin dēfīniō (“limit, settle, define”), from dē + fīniō (“set a limit, bound, end”).
defining.example: The ability to reproduce is a defining characteristic of living organisms.

rebellion.o: From Middle English rebellioun, rebellion, from Old French rebellion, from Latin rebelliō. Equivalent for rebel + -ion.
rebellion.example: The army general led a successful rebellion and became president of the country.
rebellion.exampleSense: An organized, forceful subversion of the law of the land in an attempt to replace it with another form of government.

undercover.example: To oversimplify, if black males age 20 to 29 are undercovered by 50 percent, then the first stage sampling weights for black males age 20 to 29 are doubled to properly sum to known population totals.

obsessed.o: simple past and past participle of obsess. From Latin obsessus, perfect passive participle of obsideō (“sit on or in, remain, besiege”), from ob- (“before”) + sedeō (“to sit”); see sit, session, etc.; compare assess, possess.
obsessed.example: E. W. Sprague, 1915, Spirit Obsession Or a False Doctrine & A Menace to Modern Spiritualism, page 86, →ISBN.
obsessed.exampleSense: Influenced or controlled by evil spirits, but less than possessed in that the spirits do not actually reside in the victim.

plausibly.example: Plausibly, she said she'd been working at the time.
plausibly.exampleSense: Probably; not falsifiably, based on available facts and general knowledge.

hodgepodge.o: From Middle English hochepoche, a variation of hochepot, from Old French hochepot, from Middle Dutch hutspot (“beef or mutton cut into small pieces and mixed and boiled together in a pot”), from hotsen, hutsen (“to shake; jog; jolt”) + pot (“pot”), equivalent to hotch + pot. Compare German Low German Hüttspott (“hodgepodge”).
hodgepodge.example: His latest sculpture is a hodgepodge of kitchen clutter and scrap glued together.
hodgepodge.exampleSense: A collection containing a variety of miscellaneous things.

superimpose.example: He superimposed the company logo over the image.
superimpose.exampleSense: To place an object over another object, usually in such a way that both will be visible.

netizen.example: The netizen posted their question on the forum.
netizen.exampleSense: A member of the community of Internet users.

attendance.o: From Middle English attendance, from Old French atendance, from atendre (“to attend, listen”).
attendance.example: John's attendance for the conventions was not good.
attendance.exampleSense: The frequency with which one has been present for a regular activity or set of events.

nifty.o: From *nift + -y. First element is of unknown origin. Possibly theatrical slang, as a shortened, altered form of Magnificat. Alternatively, perhaps a special use of US regional niffed (“put off, peeved”).
nifty.example: The niftiest, snappiest slacks you ever saw!

clam.o:
noun: From Middle English clam (“pincers, vice, clamp”), from Old English clam (“bond, fetter, grip, grasp”), from Proto-West Germanic *klammjan (“press, squeeze together”). The sense “dollar” may allude to wampum. The sense "Scientologist" alludes to the Scientologist belief that human thetans (souls) previously inhabited clams.

adj: From Middle English clammen, clemen (“to smear, bedaub”), from Old English clǣman (“to smear, bedaub”). Cognate with German klamm (“clammy”). See also clammy (“damp, cold and sticky”) and clem (“to adhere, stick, plug (a hole)”).
clam.example: A whole Swarm of Wasps got into a Hony-pot, and there they Cloy'd and Clam'd themselves till there was no getting Out again.
clam.exampleSense: To clog, as with glutinous or viscous matter.

attacker.example: The targets suggest the attackers are sympathetic to the vast censorship apparatus known as the Great Firewall of China.

authorization.exampleSense: A document giving formal sanction, permission or warrant.

autonomously.example: Nonetheless, Mr. Musk has often described the technology as if it could fully drive cars or was on its way to operating autonomously.
autonomously.exampleSense: In an autonomous or self-governing manner.

punt.o:
noun: From Old English punt, from Latin pontō (“Gaulish flat-bottomed boat, pontoon”), from pons (“bridge”); readopted from Middle Low German punte (“ferry boat”) or Middle Dutch ponte (“ferry boat”) of the same origin.

verb: Possibly a dialectal variant of bunt. Rugby is the origin of the sports usage of the term.

noun: Borrowed from French pointe or Spanish punto (“point”). Doublet of point, pointe, ponto, puncto, punctum, and punto.

noun: Borrowed from Irish punt, from Middle English pund. Doublet of funt, pfund, pood, and pound.
punt.example: With five minutes remaining Hennessey was down well to block another Vukcevic shot, while Gunter was smartly in to punt away the dangerous loose ball.
punt.exampleSense: To dropkick; to kick something a considerable distance. To kick a bouncing ball far and high.

favorite.example: Has direct links to update good and bad lists, customized favorites with childsafe sites, easy installation from one CD.

engorgement.example: However, several enterographic findings are associated with increased disease activity, including wall thickening greater than 4 mm, intramural and mesenteric oedema, mucosal hyperaemia, wall enhancement (and enhancement pattern), transmural ulceration and fistula formation, vascular engorgement and inflammatory mesenteric lymph nodes (often with hyperenhancement).
engorgement.exampleSense: The process or the condition of becoming engorged, becoming over-filled with fluid.

disengagement.example: There was a quick flash, a disengagement, a feint, a lunge that was like a man's, and as her long left arm shot out like lightning, her foil bent nearly double.
disengagement.exampleSense: A circular movement of the blade that blocks an opponent's parry.

engagement.o: From French engagement. Equivalent to engage + -ment.
engagement.example: We are enjoying a long engagement, but haven't yet set a date.
engagement.exampleSense: The period of time when marriage is planned or promised.

handpick.example: Each year they handpick seven candidates for next year's committee.
handpick.exampleSense: To select carefully and with individual attention.

handwork.o: From Middle English hondwerk, from Old English handweorc (“work done by hand; handiwork”), from Proto-Germanic *handuwerką; equivalent to hand + work. Cognate with Dutch handwerk, German Handwerk, Swedish hantverk.

handbook.o: From Middle English handbok, from Old English handbōc (“handbook”), possibly reinforced as a calque of German Handbuch (“handbook”). By surface analysis, hand + book. Compare West Frisian hânboek (“handbook”), Dutch handboek (“handbook”), German Low German Handbook (“handbook”), Danish håndbog (“handbook”), Swedish handbok (“handbook”), Icelandic handbók (“handbook”).

deregulation.example: Some say the airline industry has been profitable since the government began deregulation of it.
deregulation.exampleSense: The process of removing constraints, especially government-imposed economic regulation.

legacy.o: From Middle English legacie, from Old French legacie and Medieval Latin lēgātia, from Latin lēgātum. The boardgame sense was coined by game designer Rob Daviau in 2011 with the game Risk Legacy.
legacy.example: John Muir left as his legacy an enduring spirit of respect for the environment.
legacy.exampleSense: Something inherited from a predecessor or the past.

evolutionary.example: The evolutionary history of marine mammals includes land-dwelling ancestors.
evolutionary.exampleSense: Of or relating to the biological theory of evolution.

evo.o:
noun: From evening.

noun: Clipping of evolution.

anatomist.example: A plant anatomist receiving such samples can remove pickled wood and bark for anatomical study, then dry the remaining portions for inclusion in a xylarium.
anatomist.exampleSense: One who studies, teaches, writes on, or does research on anatomy and anatomical structures.

anatomize.o: From Late Middle English anatomisen, anatomien, anatomen (“to dissect in order to investigate”) borrowed from Middle French anatomiser (modern French anatomiser), or from its etymon Medieval Latin anatomizō, from Latin anatomia (“anatomy”) + -izō. Anatomia is derived from ἀνατομή (anatomḗ, “act of cutting up, dissection”) + -ia (suffix forming feminine abstract nouns); ἀνατομή (anatomḗ) is from ἀνᾰτέμνω (anătémnō, “to cut open”) (from ᾰ̓νᾰ- (ănă-, “up”) + τέμνω (témnō, “to cut, hew; to butcher”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *temh₁- (“to cut”))) + -η (-ē, suffix forming action nouns). By surface analysis, anatomy + -ize (suffix forming (chiefly similative) verbs).
anatomize.example: He did not care the least about Fanny now: he wondered how he ever should have cared: and according to his custom made an autopsy of that dead passion, and anatomised his own defunct sensation for his poor little nurse.
anatomize.exampleSense: To inspect or investigate by dissection.

erasure.o: From Latin ērādō (“to erase”) + -tūra, equivalent to erase + -ure.
erasure.example: There were several erasures on the paper.
erasure.exampleSense: The place where something has been erased.

unforeseeable.example: Traincrew management has always been a bit of a black art, rather than a science. The present traincrew difficulties that beset the UK rail industry are neither new nor were they unforeseeable.
unforeseeable.exampleSense: Incapable of being foreseen or anticipated.

on site.example: The final paint touch-ups will be performed on site, after installation.
on site.exampleSense: At the site of a job, or at the location of the customer of a product or service, as opposed to at the vendor's factory or office.

incommodity.o: From Latin incommoditas. Compare French incommodité. See incommodious.

commodify.example: Our attention spans have been chopped up and commodified, sold off piecemeal to platforms and algorithms. We’re too busy, too lazy, too preoccupied to lose ourselves in books.
commodify.exampleSense: To make something into a commodity, sometimes at the expense of its intrinsic value.

cheerleading.example: Since its inception in the late 19th century, cheerleading has evolved from yelling encouragement on the sidelines to a competitive hybrid of gymnastics, dance and acrobatics.
cheerleading.exampleSense: A physical activity in which cheerleaders organize elements of dance, gymnastics, and tumbling for judgment or to cheer on a team.

cheerleader.example: Given these sentiments, it is unsurprising that ultranationalists have been the main cheerleaders of closer Russia-North Korea relations.
cheerleader.exampleSense: A person who rallies support for any cause.

incubation.o: From Latin incubātiō, from incubō (“to lie on”).
incubation.example: Incubation in the vicinity of burial places, cremation grounds, holy wells and sacred streams was common. The ancient Hebrews visited vaults or slept among tombs to get meaningful dreams.
incubation.exampleSense: Sleeping in a temple or other holy place in order to have oracular dreams or to receive healing.

centralise.example: The government decided to centralise the issuing of passports.
centralise.exampleSense: Non-Oxford British English standard spelling of centralize.

find out.example: He had been fiddling the books for years, but finally he was found out.
find out.exampleSense: To discover or expose (someone) as disobedient, dishonest, etc.

childcare.example: Today most childcare centres are woefully understaffed with poorly paid and underqualified personnel. Child care workers in both the USA and UK are in the lowest tenth of all wage earners.
childcare.exampleSense: The act, practice, or occupation of supervising and taking care of young children.

entrant.o: From French entrant, present participle of entrer.

cherry-pick.o: A metaphor, from the idea of picking through a bowl of cherries and seeking the best for oneself, or the idea of picking off the cherries for oneself from a cake or dessert.
cherry-pick.example: Screeners can help you cherry-pick a promising group of stocks that meet your exact specifications.
cherry-pick.exampleSense: To pick out the best or most desirable items from a list or group, especially to obtain some advantage or to present something in the best possible light.

borrow.o:
verb: From Middle English borwen, from Old English borgian (“to borrow, lend, pledge surety for”), from Proto-West Germanic *borgōn, from Proto-Germanic *burgōną (“to pledge, take care of”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰergʰ- (“to take care”). Cognate with Dutch borgen (“to borrow, trust”), German borgen (“to borrow, lend”), Danish borge (“to vouch”). Related to Old English beorgan (“to save, preserve”). More at bury.

noun: From Middle English borwe, borgh, from Old English borh, borg, from Proto-West Germanic *borgōn, from Proto-Germanic *burgōną (“to borrow, lend”) (related to Etymology 1, above).
borrow.example: I went out and borrowed him a night cap; put him my night shirt on, and wrapped him in a blanket.

hilarity.o: From Latin hilaritās (“cheerfulness”), from hilaris (“cheerful”), from Ancient Greek ἱλαρός (hilarós, “cheerful”). By surface analysis, Latin hilar(ō) + -i- + -ty.
hilarity.example: When the duck escaped into the birthday party, hilarity ensued.
hilarity.exampleSense: A great amount of amusement, usually accompanied by much laughter.

hilarious.o: Learned borrowing from Latin hilaris (“cheerful”) + -ious, from Ancient Greek ἱλαρός (hilarós, “cheerful, merry”).
hilarious.example: Cold Doctor Pell here refused a very considerable fee. He could on occasion behave handsomely; but I can't learn that blustering, hilarious Doctor Rogerson ever refused his.

headroom.example: The new bridge (6) gives headroom of 13ft at high tide, sufficient for present-day river traffic.
headroom.exampleSense: The vertical measurement, top to bottom, for example for clearance under a bridge.

vise.o: From Middle English vis, vys, vice (“screw”), from Anglo-Norman vyz, vice, from Old French vis (“screw”), from Latin vītis f (“vine”). Probably akin to English withe.
vise.example: Clamp this loop in a strong vise and twist the two ends evenly into one piece. As the twisting progresses, move the wire along so as to keep the grip of the vise close to the hands.
vise.exampleSense: An instrument consisting of two jaws, closing by a screw, lever, cam, or the like, for holding work, as in filing.

vice-.o: Derived from Latin vice (“in place of”), ablative form of vicis (“alternation, turn”). Compare viscount.

hark.o: From Middle English herken, herkien, from Old English *hercian, *heorcian, *hiercian, from Proto-West Germanic *hauʀikōn, *hauʀukōn, derived ultimately from Proto-Germanic *hauzijaną (“to hear”) + formative/intensive -k (see also the related hīeran, whence English hear). Equivalent to hear + -k. Cognate with Scots herk (“to hark”), North Frisian harke (“to hark”), West Frisian harkje (“to listen”), obsolete Dutch horken (“to hark, listen to”), Middle Low German horken (“to hark”), German horchen (“to hark, harken to”).
hark.example: But harke, I heare the footing of a man.

haik.example: Woollen hayks for garments are manufactured here of a curious texture, extremely light and fine, called El Haik Filelly.
haik.exampleSense: A covering for the head and body worn by Arabs.

forever.o: Univerbation of for ever, from Middle English for ever, for evere. By surface analysis, for + ever. First attested in the late 14c., and first attested in the late 17c. as one word. Noun first attested in 1858.
forever.example: Anything in the world of transport takes forever to do, and costs far too much.
forever.exampleSense: For a very long time, a seeming eternity.

restless.o: From Middle English restles, restelees, from Old English ræstlēas, equivalent to rest + -less.
restless.example: The night before his wedding was a restless one.

confetti.o: Borrowed (possibly via French) from Italian confetti (literally “confections”), used to describe sugar-coated almonds, and by extension things imitating them (like pellets of plaster), which were thrown in Italy during festivities like Carnival and weddings. (This practice is mentioned in English since at least the 1810s.) The French and the English adopted the practice of celebrating weddings and other festivities by throwing such candies, or (by the late 1800s) tiny pieces of colored paper symbolizing them, partially displacing their earlier practice of throwing rice.
confetti.example: … a pale and fair devotee of fashion who has left off eating confetti, and recovered her bloom.
confetti.exampleSense: Edible Italian sugar-coated almonds, especially those which are used as part of a traditional Italian wedding.

sidecar.example: Faux 19th-century bartenders in sleeve garters and baroque facial hair ply their trade in pre-Prohibition bars. Women wearing cloche hats order sidecars at speakeasies.
sidecar.exampleSense: A cocktail made with cognac (or brandy), triple sec liqueur, and lemon juice.

indignantly.example: When Samael saw that God had enlightened Adam, he yelled indignantly.

indignation.o: From Middle English indignacioun, borrowed from Old French indignation, from Latin indignātiō, from indignor (“to scorn, resent”), from indignus (“unworthy, not fitting”), from in- (“not”) + dignus (“worthy, appropriate”). Attested since ca. 1374. Doublet of indignatio.

indignant.o: Borrowed from Latin indignāns, present participle of indignor (“to consider as unworthy, be angry or displeased at”), from in- (“privative”) + dignor (“to deem worthy”), from dignus (“worthy”).

bureaucratize.o: From French bureaucratiser or bureaucrat, bureaucracy + -ize.

epee.o: Borrowed from French épée, from Latin spatha, from Ancient Greek σπάθη (spáthē). Doublet of spatha, spathe, and spade.

taint.o:
noun: From Middle French teint, from Old French teint (past participle of teindre (“to dye, to tinge”)), from Latin tinctum (past participle of tingere); compare tint.

noun: From Middle English taynt, aphetic form of attaynt, atteynt, from Old French atteinte (“a blow, stroke”). Compare with attaint.

noun: Reportedly from the phrase “'tain't your balls and 'tain't your ass”. Ascribed to E.E. Landy's Underground Dict. (1972) is the following explanation: ‘'taint their ass and 'taint their pussy.’

contraction: Contraction of it + ain't.
taint.example: Meat soon taints in warm weather.
taint.exampleSense: To be affected with incipient putrefaction.

dutiful.example: Ralph was a dutiful child, and took the trash out without being told.
dutiful.exampleSense: Accepting of one's legal or moral obligations and willing to do them well, and without complaint.

tangle.o:
verb: From Middle English tanglen, probably of North Germanic origin, compare Swedish taggla (“to disorder”), Old Norse þǫngull, þang (“tangle; seaweed”), see Etymology 2 below.

noun: Of North Germanic origin, such as Danish tang or Swedish tång, from Old Norse þongull, þang. See also Norwegian tongul, Faroese tongul, Icelandic þöngull.
tangle.example: I tried to sort through this tangle and got nowhere.
tangle.exampleSense: A complicated or confused state or condition.

piggyback.o: A corruption of pickaback, itself a corruption of pick-pack, like a pack.
piggyback.example: A Montreal-Toronto "Piggyback" freight of the Canadian Pacific.
piggyback.exampleSense: Pertaining to transportation of goods where one transportation unit is carried on the back of something else. For example, a truck on a train.

culpable.o: From Middle English culpable, from Old French culpable, from Latin culpābilis (“blameworthy”), from culpō (“to blame, condemn”), from culpa (“a fault, crime, mistake”). Compare also culprit.
culpable.example: I am culpable for stealing your money.
culpable.exampleSense: Meriting condemnation, censure or blame, especially as something wrong, harmful or injurious; blameworthy, guilty.

exculpation.o: Borrowed from Medieval Latin exculpātiō. By surface analysis, exculpate + -ion.

exculpate.o: From Medieval Latin exculpātus, perfect passive participle of exculpō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from ex- (“out, from”) + culpa (“fault; blame”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix).

nimble.o: With intrusive -b-, inherited from Middle English nymyl, nemel, nemyll, nymell (“agile, quick, ready, able, capable”), a merger of Old English nǣmel (“receptive, quick to grasp”) and Old English numol (“able to take, capable of holding”), both from niman (“to take”) + -el, -ol (associative suffix), corresponding to nim + -le. Compare German nehmen, Gothic 𐌽𐌹𐌼𐌰𐌽 (niman), Old Norse nema (“to take”). More at nim.
nimble.example: He was too nimble for the assailant and easily escaped his grasp.
nimble.exampleSense: Quick and light in movement or action.

apprise.o:
verb: PIE word *h₂éd Borrowed from French appris, apprise, the past participle form of apprendre (“to learn; to teach”), from Middle French apprendre, aprendre (“to learn”), from Old French aprendre, aprandre (“to learn; to educate, teach”), from Latin apprēndere, a variant of apprehendere, adprehendere, the present active infinitives of apprehendō, adprehendō (“to lay hold upon, grab, grasp, seize, take; to apprehend, arrest; to grasp with the mind, comprehend, understand; (Medieval Latin) to learn; to inform; to teach”), from ad- (prefix meaning ‘to; towards’) + prehendō (“to lay hold of, grab, grasp, seize, take; (figuratively, rare) of the mind: to apprehend, comprehend, grasp, seize”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʰed- (“to find; to hold; to seize, take”)). Doublet of apprehend.

verb: From Middle English aprisen, apprisen (“to determine or estimate the value of (something), to appraise, evaluate; to regard (something) as important, valuable, or worthy, to esteem, prize; to praise or worship (God)”), and then either: * from Old French apriser, aprisier (“to appraise, evaluate”), from à (“to”) + prisier, preisier (“to attribute a value to, to appraise, value”) (from Latin pretiāre, the present active infinitive of pretiō (“(Late Latin) to consider valuable, hold in high regard, to esteem, prize, value; (Medieval Latin) to estimate the worth of, appraise, assess, value”), from pretium + -ō (suffix forming regular first-conjugation verbs)); or * from Old French à pris (“to (put a) price (on)”) (pris (“price; esteem, (positive) reputation”) is derived from Latin pretium). Pretium (“cost, price; value, worth”) is ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *per- (“before, in front; first”). The English word is a doublet of appraise, appreciate, praise, price, and prize.
apprise.example: Thou apprisest the thief when an opportunity will occur.
apprise.exampleSense: To make (someone or oneself) aware of some information; to inform, to notify.

brunch.o: Blend of breakfast + lunch. Attested from 1895 in British English and from 1930 in the United States.
brunch.example: Feeling a bit peckish, Sandra made herself some brunch with the leftovers in her fridge.
brunch.exampleSense: A meal eaten later in the day than breakfast and earlier than lunch, and often consisting of typical foods from both of those meals.

blunder.o: Inherited from Middle English blundren, blondren (verb) and blunder, blonder (“disturbance, strife”), from the verb; partly from Middle English blondren, a frequentative form of Middle English blonden, blanden ("to mix; mix up"; corresponding to blend + -er); and partly from Middle English blundren, a frequentative form of Middle English blunden (“to stagger; stumble”), from Old Norse blunda (“to shut the eyes; doze”). Cognates include Norwegian blunda (“to shut the eyes; doze”), dialectal Swedish blundra (“to act blindly or rashly”), Danish blunde (“to blink”) or blunde (“to take a nap”), Icelandic blunda (“to nap; doze”). Related to English blind.
blunder.example: I was never distinguished for address, and have often even blundered in making my bow.

extenuate.o:
adj: From Middle English extenuat (“(medicine) made thin, emaciated”), from Latin extenuātus (“diminished, reduced, thinned”), perfect passive participle of extenuō (“to diminish, reduce, thin”) (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from ex- (“out-, thoroughly”) + tenuō (“to enfeeble, weaken, wear down; to lessen, reduce; to make thin”), from tenuis (“fine, slender, thin; feeble, weak”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *tenh₂- (“to extend, stretch; thin”)) + -ō (first conjugation-verb forming suffix). Compare attenuate.

verb: From Latin extenuātus (“diminished, reduced, thinned”) (more at etymology 1), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).
extenuate.example: [T]he Chinians can very cunningly beate and extenuate gold into plates and leaues.
extenuate.exampleSense: To beat or draw (a metal object, etc.) out so as to lessen the thickness.

extenuating.o: From Latin ex (“to delete, to cross out”) and tenuatus, past participle of tenuare (“to make thin”) + Middle English -ing. By surface analysis, ex- + tenuate + -ing.

wring.o:
verb: From Middle English wring, wringe, wringen, wryng, wrynge, wryngen, wryngyn, from Old English wringan (“to wring”), from Proto-Germanic *wringaną (“to squeeze, twist, wring”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *wrenǵʰ- (“to squeeze, wring”). Cognates Cognate with Scots wring (“to wring”), Saterland Frisian wringe (“to wring”), Dutch wringen (“to wring; to wrest; to writhe”), German ringen (“to wrestle; to struggle; to wring”), wringen (“to wring”), Luxembourgish réngen (“to grapple, wrestle”); also Ancient Greek ῥίμφα (rhímpha, “fast, nimbly, rapidly”), Lithuanian rangýti (“to roll up; to curl, twist, wave”).

noun: Partly: * from Middle English wring, wringe (“twisting or wringing (of the neck)”), from Middle English wringen, wryngen (verb); and * from the modern English verb. See further at etymology

noun: From Middle English wring, wringe, wrynge (“a press, especially for olives or wine”) [and other forms], from Old English wringe, from wringan (verb): see further at etymology
wring.example: I didn’t have a towel so I just wrung my hair dry.
wring.exampleSense: Often followed by out: to squeeze or twist (something moist) tightly so that liquid is forced out.

chide.o: From Middle English chiden (“to chide, rebuke, disapprove, criticize; complain, grumble, dispute; argue, debate, dispute, quarrel”), from Old English ċīdan (“to chide, reprove, rebuke; blame, contend, strive, quarrel, complain”). Cognate with German kiden (“to sound”); Old High German kīdal (“wedge”).
chide.example: Valentine: Well, you’ll still be too forward.
chide.exampleSense: To admonish in blame; to reproach angrily.

masculinize.exampleSense: To make masculine; to give typically male characteristics.

masculinity.o: From French masculinité, from Old French, equivalent to masculine + -ity. Earlier in same sense was masculineness.
masculinity.example: Over time, society's ideas of masculinity has greatly broadened.
masculinity.exampleSense: The degree or property of being masculine or manly; manliness.

masculinist.example: We live in a masculinist-oriented (as opposed to a feminist-oriented) society. That is, we live in a society which rewards masculine action, even if such action is taken by a woman.
masculinist.exampleSense: Relating to or in accordance with masculinism.

masculine.o: From Middle English masculyne, masculyn, from Old French masculin, from Latin masculīnus, diminutive of masculus (“male, manly”), itself a diminutive of mās (“male”). Displaced native Old English werlīċ (literally “manly”).
masculine.example: German uses the masculine form of the definite article, der, with Student.
masculine.exampleSense: Of, pertaining or belonging to the male grammatical gender, in languages that have gender distinctions. Being inflected in agreement with a masculine noun.

exacerbation.o: From Middle English exacerbacyoun, from Latin exacerbātiōnem, from exacerbāre (“to provoke, make harsh”). See exacerbate.

trampolining.o: present participle and gerund of trampoline. From Spanish trampolín and/or Italian trampolino; in English, a genericized trademark based on the Spanish word trademarked in 1936, but attested since 1798.

trample.o: From Middle English tramplen, trampelen (“to walk heavily”), equivalent to tramp + -le. Cognate with Saterland Frisian trampelje (“to trample”), Dutch trampelen (“to trample”), German Low German trampeln (“to trample”), German trampeln (“to trample”).

spurt.o:
verb: From earlier spirt, sprit (“to sprout”), from Middle English sprytten, from Old English spryttan, from Proto-West Germanic *spruttjan, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)per- (“to strew, sow, sprinkle”).

noun: Uncertain. May be derived from Etymology
spurt.example: I seem to remember talking wanderingly to myself during that last spurt.
spurt.exampleSense: A sudden brief burst of, or increase in, speed, effort, activity, emotion or development.

nostalgist.example: When I was a little girl, if they ever called me a backward child they must have meant a looking-backward child; for I grew up to claim the proud title of the world’s champion nostalgist.
nostalgist.exampleSense: A person who is prone to nostalgia.

nostalgic.example: But of course every well-brought-up person to-day knows that the Victorians were sentimentalists, nostalgics, escapists, self-deceivers.
nostalgic.exampleSense: A person who displays nostalgia for something.
