For the meaning development compare with Russian красть (krastʹ, “to steal”) and Russian кра́сться (krástʹsja, “to stalk, to prowl, to slink”). etymology notes Proposed etymologies beyond Germanic are numerous and include * Proto-Indo-European *ster-: compare Welsh herw (“theft, raid”), Ancient Greek στερέω (steréō, “to deprive of”) * Proto-Indo-European *stel(H)- (“to stretch”): compare Albanian pë/mbështjell (“to confuse, mess up, mix, wrap up”), Old Church Slavonic стєлѭ (steljǫ, “I spread out (bed, roof)”), Ancient Greek τηλία (tēlía, “playing table”) * Proto-Indo-European *tsel- (“to sneak”): compare Sanskrit त्सरति (tsárati, “creep, sneak up on”) and other forms under Pokorny 5. *sel- "schleichen, kriechen"
stealing.example: The politicaster is looking for small opportunities – for such pickings and stealings as a careless public may leave for those of his kind. The great politician is looking for great opportunities.
stealing.exampleSense: That which is stolen; stolen property.

lease.o:
noun: From Middle English *lesen, from Anglo-Norman *leser, Old French lesser, laisier (“to let, let go”), partly from Latin laxō (“to loose”) and partly from Old High German lāzan (“to let, let go, release”) (German lassen), cognate with Old English lǣtan (“to allow, let go, leave, rent”) whence let.

verb: From Middle English lesen, from Old English lesan (“to collect, pick, select, gather”), from Proto-West Germanic *lesan, from Proto-Germanic *lesaną (“to gather”).

verb: From Middle English lesen, from Old English lēasian (“to lie, tell lies”), from lēas (“falsehood, lying, untruth, mistake”).

noun: From Middle English lese, from Old English lǣs (“meadow”), from Proto-West Germanic *lāsu (“meadow”). See also leasow.

noun: From leash.
lease.example: I'm leasing a small apartment in Runcorn for a month while I'm there for work.
lease.exampleSense: To hold a lease as a tenant.

enforceable.example: President Biden is seriously considering legislative proposals that would dramatically alter the Supreme Court, including imposing term limits and an enforceable code of ethics on the justices, according to a person familiar with the ongoing discussions.

workaround.example: More significantly, rigid deference to [Justin] Bieber’s still-young core fan base keeps things resolutely PG, with any acknowledgement of sex either couched in vague “touch your body” workarounds or downgraded to desirous hand-holding and eye-gazing.
workaround.exampleSense: A means of overcoming some obstacle, especially an obstacle consisting of constraints, or laws or regulations.

unavoidable.o: From Middle English unavoidable, equivalent to un- + avoidable.

anomalous.o: From Late Latin anōmalos, from Ancient Greek ἀνώμᾰλος (anṓmălos).

corrupt.o: From Middle English corrupten, derived from Latin corruptus, past participle of corrumpō (“to destroy, ruin, injure, spoil, corrupt, bribe”), from com- (“together”) + rumpō (“to break in pieces”).
corrupt.example: Don't you dare corrupt my son with those disgusting pictures!
corrupt.exampleSense: To make corrupt; to change from good to bad; to draw away from the right path; to deprave; to pervert.

silently.example: There never was an English-language text, either in 1561 or 1859. Yule and Burnell have silently provided a translation.
silently.exampleSense: Of an edit or change to a text, without explicit acknowledgment.

architectural.example: Wheelchair users are restricted entry into many structures and public facilities by architectural barriers.

at gunpoint.example: At gunpoint I was told to hand over my money.
at gunpoint.exampleSense: Under coercion by someone with a firearm.

saturated.o: simple past and past participle of saturate. The adjective is first attested in the second part of the 15ᵗʰ century, in Middle English, the verb in 1538, the noun in 1921; inherited from Middle English saturat(e) (“satiated, satisfied”), borrowed from Latin saturātus, perfect passive participle of saturō (“to fill, satisfy, quench”) (see -ate (etymology 1, 2 and 3)), from satur (“full”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix).

computerized.o: simple past and past participle of computerize. From computer + -ize.

observational.example: The essential fact is simply that all the pictures which science now draws of nature, and which alone seem capable of according with observational fact, are mathematical pictures.
observational.exampleSense: Relating to observation, especially scientific observation.

observable.example: The strange new star was at the edge of the observable universe.

insurmountable.example: Getting everybody to agree proved to be an insurmountable difficulty.
insurmountable.exampleSense: Incapable of being passed over, surmounted, or overcome; insuperable

morphology.o: Borrowed from German Morphologie. By surface analysis, morpho- + -logy.

facade.o: Borrowed from French façade, from Italian facciata, a derivation of faccia (“front”), from Latin faciēs (“face”); compare face.
facade.example: Eight or so gunmen stood shoulder to shoulder in the gray-white trail before the barn, firing into the saloon's burning, bullet-pocked facade.
facade.exampleSense: The face of a building, especially the front view or elevation.

withhold.o: From Middle English withholden. Equivalent to with- + hold.
withhold.example: I’ll withhold from asking about it.

overdue.example: More join us at Colwall and at the lovely station at Great Malvern, although the place is in need of some TLC nowadays. The ornate canopy supports are overdue a repaint, and the closed cafe gives the place a forlorn air.
overdue.exampleSense: Late; especially, past a deadline or too late to fulfill a need.

unturned.example: [W]oman's loveliness had heretofore been an unturned page in the young man's life.

scraper.example: A scraper is a large scoop, mounted on pneumatic-tyre wheels, in which earth is collected by a steel cutting-blade at the front, and from which the earth is dumped wherever required. It is operated by the driver of the caterpillar tractor which hauls it.
scraper.exampleSense: An instrument with which anything is scraped. An instrument drawn by oxen, horses or a tractor, similar to a plow, that is used for scraping up earth in making or repairing roads, digging cellars, building canals, etc.

institute.o:
noun: From French institut, from Middle French, from Latin īnstitūtum.

verb: From Middle English, from Latin īnstitūtus, past participle of īnstituō (“to set up, place upon, purpose, begin, institute”), from in (“in, on”) + statuō (“set up, establish”).
institute.example: They have but few laws. For to a people so instruct and institute, very few to suffice.

dispatcher.example: The organization of Decline to Sign involved trained teams sent out to where 608/610 supporters were gathering signatures, alerted by dispatchers operating a hotline to which anyone could call in—from a mall, the ferry terminals, holiday events, etc. when signature gatherers were sighted.
dispatcher.exampleSense: In a transportation organization, a person who controls the movements of vehicles.

late.o: From Middle English late, lat, from Old English læt (“slow; slack, lax, negligent; late”), from Proto-West Germanic *lat, from Proto-Germanic *lataz (“slow, lazy”). By surface analysis, deverbal from let. Cognates Cognate with Yola laate (“late”), North Frisian leed, leet, lääs (“late”), Saterland Frisian leet (“late”), Dutch, German Low German laat (“late, tardy”), Danish lad (“languid, lazy, indolent”), Faroese, Icelandic latur (“lazy”), Norwegian Bokmål, Norwegian Nynorsk and Swedish lat (“lazy”), Gothic 𐌻𐌰𐍄𐍃 (lats, “lazy, slothful”).
late.example: The flowers were late in blooming because of the prolonged cold weather.
late.exampleSense: Not arriving or occurring until after an expected time.

rigidly.example: What could have been done by such a machine downhill can only be conjectured, for the maximum speed was restricted rigidly to 80 m.p.h.

inefficient.exampleSense: Not efficient; not producing the effect intended or desired; inefficacious

matricide.o: From French matricide, from Latin mātricīda (“person who kills his own mother”) and mātricīdium (“the murder of one's mother”). By surface analysis, matri- + -cide.
matricide.example: Nancy was a matricide; it happened four years ago.
matricide.exampleSense: A person who kills his or her mother.

patricide.o:
noun: Borrowed from Middle French patricide or Latin patricīdium. Equivalent to patri- + -cide.

noun: Borrowed from Middle French patricide or Latin patricīda. Equivalent to patri- + -cide.

decider.example: The Determination of his Majesty, who is the only proper decider of this Matter.
decider.exampleSense: A person, divinity, or authoritative text which decides.

cider.o: From Middle English sider, cidre, sidre, from Old French cisdre, sidre (“beverage made from fermented apples”), from Medieval Latin sīcera, from Ancient Greek σίκερα (síkera, “fermented liquor, strong drink”), from Hebrew שֵׁכָר (šēḵār, “liquor”). Doublet of cyser. Partially displaced earlier English apple wine.
cider.example: She liked an aged cider. He liked a harder cider.
cider.exampleSense: A non-alcoholic still beverage consisting of the juice of early-harvest apples, usually unfiltered and still containing pulp; apple cider; sweet cider (without pulp such a beverage is called apple juice).

genocide.o: From the stem of Ancient Greek γένος (génos, “race, kind”) (cognate with Latin gēns (“tribe, clan”), whence genus), corresponding to geno- + -cide (“killing”). Piecewise doublet of gendercide. Compare genticide. Coined by Polish Jewish lawyer Raphael Lemkin in 1943 or 1944 in reference to the Armenian Genocide (then known by other names; for more information, see Terminology of the Armenian genocide on Wikipedia), massacres of Assyrians (such as the Simele massacre and Seyfo) and the Jewish Holocaust.
genocide.example: Shaddam IV: I want fifty legion of Sardaukar on Arrakis at once!
genocide.exampleSense: The systematic and deliberate destruction of a group of people, typically by killing substantial numbers of them, on the basis of their ethnicity, religion, or nationality.

homicide.o: From Old French homicide, from Latin homicīda (“man-slayer”) and homicīdium (“manslaughter”).
homicide.example: Homicides in general and victorious warriors in particular are often obliged to perform a variety of ceremonies for the purpose of ridding them of the dangerous ghosts of their victims.

suicide.o: First attested in Thomas Browne's Religio Medici (1643) in noun sense 1, ostensibly from New Latin suīcīdium, from suī (genitive reflexive pronoun) + -cīdium (“act of killing or murder”), but often believed to have originated in English before entering Latin. Displaced native Middle English seolf-cwale from Old English selfcwalu (literally “self-slaughter”), after which suicide may have been modelled, or calqued (compare manuscript). Noun sense 3 is perhaps by analogy with words like homicide, patricide (see -cide), or, although unlikely, from Medieval Latin suīcīda; see the Etymology section at suīcīdium.
suicide.example: There had been half a dozen mysterious suicides which had been investigated by Scotland Yard.
suicide.exampleSense: A particular instance of a person intentionally killing oneself, or of multiple people doing so.

hierarchical.o:
adj: From hierarchy + -ical; compare French hiérarchique.

adj: From hierarch + -ical.
hierarchical.example: It has been said that only a hierarchical society with a leisure class at the top can produce works of art.
hierarchical.exampleSense: Classified or arranged according to various criteria into successive ranks or grades.

stateless.example: A stateless server treats each request independently.
stateless.exampleSense: Of a system or protocol, such that it does not keep a persistent state between transactions.

roll out.example: They rolled out the red carpet to welcome the visiting dignitaries.
roll out.exampleSense: Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see roll, out.

invocation.o: From Middle English invocacioun, from Old French invocacion, from Latin invocatio, invocationem. Equivalent to invoke + -ation.
invocation.example: As a matter of legal principle, the State should report whether all the necessary conditions for the invocation of the right of self-defense were existent.
invocation.exampleSense: An act of invoking or claiming a legal right.

armed.o:
adj: From arm (“to equip with a weapon”) + -ed.

adj: From arm (“the upper limb of the body”) + -ed.
armed.example: The naked eye then will immediately direct us, by means of the two stars just mentioned, towards the place where, in the finder, the armed eye will perceive the double star in question about ¾ degree from the 44th Lyncis.
armed.exampleSense: Furnished with something that serves to add strength, force, or efficiency.

attribution.o: From Middle French attribution, from Latin attributio.
attribution.example: The attribution of the quote is widely regarded as dubious.
attribution.exampleSense: An explicit or formal acknowledgment of ownership or authorship.

thrash.o: From Middle English thrasshen, thresche, threschen, threschyn, threshen, thresshen, tressyn, þreisshe, þresshe, (whence the modern English thresh), from Old English þerscan, þrexan, from Proto-Germanic *þreskaną (“to thresh; to tread”), from Proto-Indo-European *terh₁- (“to rub, turn; to drill, pierce”). Cognates Cognate with Dutch dorsen (“to thresh; to thrash”), German and Luxembourgish dreschen (“to thresh; to thrash”), Yiddish דרעשן (dreshn, “to thresh”), Danish tærske (“to thresh”), Faroese treskja (“to thresh”), Icelandic þreskja (“to thresh”), Norwegian Nynorsk treska, treske, treskja, treskje (“to thrash”), Swedish tröska (“to thresh”), Gothic 𐌸𐍂𐌹𐍃𐌺𐌰𐌽 (þriskan, “to thresh”), Finnish rehkiä (“to drudge; to toil”); also Welsh taradr (“auger, wimble; awl, borer; drill”), Latin terō (“to rub or triturate; to wear away or wear out, consume; to tread; to press with a mill; to pass, spend”), Greek τρίβω (trívo, “to grate; to rub”), Albanian tjerr (“to spin”), Belarusian це́рці (cjérci, “to rub; to polish; to pinch; to grind”), Bulgarian три́я (tríja, “to rub; to chafe; to grind”), Czech třít (“to rub; to spawn”), Polish tarć, treć, trzeć, trzyć (“to rub; to shred; to cut; to chafe; to crush; to spawn”), Russian тере́ть (terétʹ, “to rub; to polish; to grind”), Serbo-Croatian тр̏ти, tȑti (“to rub; to cause friction; to scour; to break, crush”), Slovak trieť (“to rub”), Slovene treti (“to crack open; to rub”), Ukrainian те́рти (térty, “to rub; to scrub”), Armenian թուր (tʻur, “sword”), Sogdian ܕܣܦܪܛܪ (dsprtr, “hand towel”), Hittite 𒋻𒌑𒍣 (tar-ú-zi, “to perform a round dance, to dance in twisting manner”), Tocharian A and Tocharian B tärk- (“to allow, let; to let go”), Sanskrit तर्कु (tarku, “spindle”).
thrash.example: But in the town it was well known, when they got home at night, their fat and psychopathic wives would thrash them within inches of their lives.

thrashing.o: present participle and gerund of thrash. From Middle English thrasshen, thresche, threschen, threschyn, threshen, thresshen, tressyn, þreisshe, þresshe, (whence the modern English thresh), from Old English þerscan, þrexan, from Proto-Germanic *þreskaną (“to thresh; to tread”), from Proto-Indo-European *terh₁- (“to rub, turn; to drill, pierce”). Cognates Cognate with Dutch dorsen (“to thresh; to thrash”), German and Luxembourgish dreschen (“to thresh; to thrash”), Yiddish דרעשן (dreshn, “to thresh”), Danish tærske (“to thresh”), Faroese treskja (“to thresh”), Icelandic þreskja (“to thresh”), Norwegian Nynorsk treska, treske, treskja, treskje (“to thrash”), Swedish tröska (“to thresh”), Gothic 𐌸𐍂𐌹𐍃𐌺𐌰𐌽 (þriskan, “to thresh”), Finnish rehkiä (“to drudge; to toil”); also Welsh taradr (“auger, wimble; awl, borer; drill”), Latin terō (“to rub or triturate; to wear away or wear out, consume; to tread; to press with a mill; to pass, spend”), Greek τρίβω (trívo, “to grate; to rub”), Albanian tjerr (“to spin”), Belarusian це́рці (cjérci, “to rub; to polish; to pinch; to grind”), Bulgarian три́я (tríja, “to rub; to chafe; to grind”), Czech třít (“to rub; to spawn”), Polish tarć, treć, trzeć, trzyć (“to rub; to shred; to cut; to chafe; to crush; to spawn”), Russian тере́ть (terétʹ, “to rub; to polish; to grind”), Serbo-Croatian тр̏ти, tȑti (“to rub; to cause friction; to scour; to break, crush”), Slovak trieť (“to rub”), Slovene treti (“to crack open; to rub”), Ukrainian те́рти (térty, “to rub; to scrub”), Armenian թուր (tʻur, “sword”), Sogdian ܕܣܦܪܛܪ (dsprtr, “hand towel”), Hittite 𒋻𒌑𒍣 (tar-ú-zi, “to perform a round dance, to dance in twisting manner”), Tocharian A and Tocharian B tärk- (“to allow, let; to let go”), Sanskrit तर्कु (tarku, “spindle”).
thrashing.example: Now Hodgson just has to work out a makeshift forward line against a Ukraine team who warmed up for Tuesday by doling out the obligatory thrashing to San Marino, knocking in four goals by half-time and another five in the second half.

aver.o:
verb: From Middle English averren, from Old French averer, from Early Medieval Latin advērō, a verb derived from Latin vērus (“true”). Compare Modern French avérer.

noun: From Middle English aver, avere (“workhorse; any beast of burden (?); things which are owned, possessions, property, wealth; state of being rich, wealth; ownership, possession”) [and other forms], and then either: * from Old French aver, aveir, avoir (“possession, property; (collectively) beasts of burden; domestic animals; cattle”) (modern French avoir (“asset, possession”)), from aveir, avoir (“to have”), from Latin habēre (“to have, hold; to have, own (possessions)”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰeh₁bʰ-, *ǵʰeh₁bʰ- (“to grab, take”); or * from Old English eafor (“workhorse; tenant’s obligation to transport goods”), further etymology uncertain.
aver.example: Horticulturalist Richard Lighty has a form [of Trillium grandiflorum] that he avers to open almost a cerise-red.
aver.exampleSense: To assert the truth of (something); to affirm (something) with confidence; to declare (something) in a positive manner.

confirm.o: From Middle English confirmen, confermen, from Old French confermer, from Latin cōnfirmāre (“to make firm, strengthen, establish”), from con- (“together”) + firmāre (“to make firm”), from firmus (“firm”).
confirm.example: Elizabeth, daughter of Henry VIII, was baptized and confirmed at the age of three days.
confirm.exampleSense: To administer the sacrament of confirmation on (someone).

particulate.o:
adj: From New Latin particulātus (“divided into small parts”) (also particulāta (“small parts”), from its neuter plural), from Classical Latin particula (“particle”), from pars (“part, piece”) + -cula (diminutive suffix), + -ātus (-ate). The verb is probably independently from the adjective rather than from Etymology 2.

verb: From Latin particulāt-, past participial stem (compare the verbal suffix -ate) of particulō (“to particularize”), from particula (“particle”) + -ō (verbal suffix).
particulate.example: Particulates in engine oil can abrade moving parts.
particulate.exampleSense: Any solid or liquid in a subdivided state, especially one that exhibits special characteristics which are negligible in the bulk material.

articulate.o: The adjective is first attested in 1531, the verb in 1551; borrowed from Latin articulātus (“distinct, articulated, jointed”), perfect passive participle of articulō, see -ate (etymology 1, 2 and 3). Regular participial usage of the adjective up until Early Modern English.
articulate.example: The lower jaw articulates with the skull at the temporomandibular joint.
articulate.exampleSense: to form a joint or connect by joints

articulated.o: simple past and past participle of articulate. The adjective is first attested in 1531, the verb in 1551; borrowed from Latin articulātus (“distinct, articulated, jointed”), perfect passive participle of articulō, see -ate (etymology 1, 2 and 3). Regular participial usage of the adjective up until Early Modern English.
articulated.example: The trains are a fixed formation of four articulated vehicles, and are fitted with large vestibules, wide aisles, open gangways and air-conditioning.
articulated.exampleSense: Of a vehicle, composed of component parts each with its own wheels and chassis, e.g. an articulated lorry, articulated bus, or certain kinds of streetcars and trains.

compatible.o: Inherited from Middle English compatible, fron Anglo-Norman compatible, from Medieval Latin compatibilis (“in compatibile beneficium, a benefice which could be held together with another one”), from Late Latin compator (“to suffer with”), from com- (“together”) + pati (“to suffer”); see passion.
compatible.example: This printer isn't compatible with my computer.

horrendous.o: Borrowed from Latin horrendus, future passive participle (gerundive) of horreō (“to dread”) + -ous.
horrendous.example: There was horrendous carnage at the scene of the plane crash.

dog eat dog.o: From dog + eat + dog. Derived from Latin canis caninam non est (“a dog does not eat the flesh of a dog”).
dog eat dog.example: As for the game I came on them, it was dog eat dog, anyway.
dog eat dog.exampleSense: Ruthlessly acquisitive or competitive. Describes a business or other set of circumstances where people try to succeed at the expense of other people.

veridical.o: From Latin veridicus (“truly said”), from verus (“true”) and dīcō (“to say”).
veridical.example: Few believe that all claimed religious experiences are veridical.
veridical.exampleSense: Pertaining to an experience, perception, or interpretation that accurately represents reality.

verisimilitude.o: From Middle French vérisimilitude, from Latin vērīsimilitūdō (“likeness to truth”), more correctly written separately as vērī similitūdō; from vērī, genitive singular of vērus (“true, real”), + similitūdō (“likeness, resemblance”).
verisimilitude.example: On July 12, Madame filed suit for divorce, naming one Jane McManus as his principal mistress. Other adulteries were noted in the interest of verisimilitude.
verisimilitude.exampleSense: Faithfulness to its own rules; internal cohesion.

verisimilar.o: From Latin vērisimilis, prop. vērī similis (“having the appearance of truth”), from vērī (genitive of vērus (“true”)) + similis (“like, similar”); see very and similar.
verisimilar.example: Joyce's objection was founded in [...] a reaction to the doggedly linear, heavily patterned artifice of the nineteenth-century novel, the verisimilar credentials of which existed – so, at any rate, the argument runs – in inverse proportion to the conventionality of its narrative style.
verisimilar.exampleSense: Appearing to be true or real; probable; likely.

warm up.example: I couldn't be bothered to cook another meal so I just warmed up yesterday's leftovers.

in favor of.example: He left school after just three years in favor of a professional sports career.

churn.o: Noun from Middle English chyrne, cherne, kyrne ( > Scots kirn), from Old English ċyrn, ċyrin, ċirin (“churn”), from Proto-Germanic *kirnijǭ (“churn”); verb from Middle English chyrnen from Old English ċernan, from Proto-Germanic *kirnijaną (“to churn, stir”), of unknown origin. Cognate with West Frisian tsjerne, Dutch karn, Walloon serene, German Karn, Kirne, Norwegian Bokmål kjerne, Danish kærne, Swedish kärna, Icelandic kirna.
churn.example: Now the cream is churned to make butter.
churn.exampleSense: To agitate rapidly and repetitively, or to stir with a rowing or rocking motion; generally applies to liquids, notably cream.

tear down.example: They're going to tear down the old shack when they redevelop the land.

homogeneous.o: From Medieval Latin homogeneus, from Ancient Greek ὁμογενής (homogenḗs, “of the same race, family or kind”), from ὁμός (homós, “same”) + γένος (génos, “kind”). Compare homo- (“same”) and -ous (adjectival suffix).
homogeneous.example: Their citizens were not of homogeneous origin, but were from all parts of Greece.
homogeneous.exampleSense: Having the same composition throughout; of uniform make-up.

hand-off.example: Vertex shaders are algorithms that transform the vertex information stored in the model before handoff to the rasterizer.
hand-off.exampleSense: The transfer of control to another subsystem.

warm-up.example: If you don't do your warm-ups properly you have a greater chance of injury.
warm-up.exampleSense: The act of exercising or stretching in preparation for strenuous activity

sun-drenched.o: Since the 1890s or earlier; figurative, conceiving sunlight as if it were a fluid that can drench (immerse) something.
sun-drenched.example: Sun-drenched beaches are vacation destinations for sunbathers no matter where the beaches are.
sun-drenched.exampleSense: Receiving lots of sunshine; bathed in sunlight; (of a place) frequently sunny.

drench.o:
noun: From Middle English drench, drenche (“beverage, drink; cup of drink, specifically a poisoned drink; medicinal potion, specifically an emetic (?)”) [and other forms], from Old English drenċ (“drink; draft, potion; dose (of medicine, poison, etc.)”), from Proto-West Germanic *dranki, from Proto-Germanic *drankiz (“drink; potion; dose”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *dʰrenǵ- (“to draw, pull; to gulp; to sip”). Doublet of drink (noun). Cognates * Gothic 𐌳𐍂𐌰𐌲𐌲𐌺 (draggk), 𐌳𐍂𐌰𐌲𐌺 (dragk, “beverage, drink”) * Old Dutch *dranc, (Middle Dutch dranc, modern Dutch drank (“beverage, drink”)) * Old High German tranc, tranch (Middle High German tranc, modern German Trank (“drink; potion”)) * Old Saxon dranc

verb: The verb is derived from Middle English drenchen, drench (“to drown; to flood, inundate; to consume (drink or food); to give (someone) a drink; to poison (someone) with a drink; to immerse, soak, drench; to descend, fall, sink; to penetrate, permeate; (figurative) to engulf, overwhelm”) [and other forms], from Old English drenċan (“to give (someone) a drink; to immerse, soak, drench”), from Proto-West Germanic *drankijan, from Proto-Germanic *drankijaną (“to cause (someone) to drink”), the causative of *drinkaną (“to drink”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *dʰrenǵ- (“to draw, pull; to gulp; to sip”). Doublet of drink (verb). The noun is derived from the verb (etymology 2, verb sense 1.2). Cognates * Old High German trenchen (modern German tränken (“to give a drink; to water”)) * Old Norse drekkja, drenkja (Swedish dränka) * Old Saxon dręnkian (Dutch drenke (“to get a drink”))
drench.example: But music alone, would not do—Some roast-beef was a necessary article, and some wine, to feed and drench the actors.
drench.exampleSense: To cause (someone) to drink; to provide (someone) with a drink.

genuinely.example: I thought they were joking at first, but it seemed they were genuinely interested in the talk about glaciers.
genuinely.exampleSense: In a genuine manner; truthfully, truly.

ground plan.o: Alternative form of groundplan. From ground + plan.
ground plan.example: In our ground plan, treatment follows management, care and assessment of the child.
ground plan.exampleSense: Alternative form of groundplan A framework or pattern.

as it is.example: As it is, Tokyo is relatively unaffected.
as it is.exampleSense: In the actual circumstances (and often contrary to expectations).

proceeding.example: The proceedings of the high commission.
proceeding.exampleSense: A measure or step taken in a course of business; a transaction.

overlay.o: From Middle English overleyen, from Old English oferleċġan, from Proto-West Germanic *obarlaggjan, from Proto-Germanic *uberlagjaną, equivalent to over- + lay. Cognate with Saterland Frisian uurläze, úurlääse, Dutch overleggen, German Low German overleggen, överleggen, German überlegen, Swedish överlägga, Norwegian overlegge. Compare overlie.
overlay.example: She will now overlay fruit on top of the crust.
overlay.exampleSense: To lay, spread, or apply (something) over or across (something else); to overspread.

deferral.o: From defer + -al, with ‘r’ doubled to clarify pronunciation.

oscillation.o: From French oscillation, from Latin oscillatio, from Latin oscillo. By surface analysis, oscillate + -ion.
oscillation.example: The trial running tests which were made with the vehicles showed that they ride very steadily laterally, with almost complete absence of oscillation at all speeds.
oscillation.exampleSense: the act of oscillating or the state of being oscillated

operational.example: Despite somewhat faded paintwork, 87017 Iron Duke is clearly very much operational, as confirmed here on September 4.

ill-suited.example: A considerable amount of beet comes from the Clonakilty and Courtmacsherry growing areas to Mallow and if the closure proposals mentioned are implemented this traffic will in future years be thrown on roads ill-suited to such heavy haulage.
ill-suited.exampleSense: unsuitable, unfit or inappropriate for some purpose

reassign.example: The offending employees were reassigned after the incident.

reclaim.o: From Middle English reclaymen, recleymen, reclamen, from Anglo-Norman reclamer (noun reclaim and Middle French reclamer (noun reclaim), from Latin reclāmō, reclāmāre. Equivalent to re- + claim.
reclaim.example: Once a term of homophobic abuse, the term “queer” has been reclaimed as a marker for some gay, lesbian, bisexual, transgender (GLBT), and other marginalized sexual identities.
reclaim.exampleSense: To bring back a term into acceptable usage, usually of a slur, and usually by the group that was once targeted by that slur.

enforced.o: simple past and past participle of enforce. From Middle English enforcen, from Old French enforcier, from Late Latin infortiāre, from in- + fortis (“strong”).

migrate.o: First attested in 1623; borrowed from Latin migrātus, perfect passive participle of migrō (“to migrate, change, transport”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).
migrate.example: To escape persecution, they migrated to a neutral country.
migrate.exampleSense: To change habitations across a border; to move from one country or political region to another.

elasticity.example: Her elasticity allowed her to recover quickly.

pronounced.o: simple past and past participle of pronounce. Recorded since c.1330 as Middle English pronouncen (“to utter, declare officially”), from Old French prononcier, from Latin prōnūntiō, itself from prō- (“forth, out, in public”) + nūntiō (“to announce”) from nūntius (“messenger”).

proportionate.o: Borrowed from Latin prōportiōnātus, see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and -ate (verb-forming suffix). By surface analysis, proportion + -ate.
proportionate.example: What is proportionate to his transgression.

bounded.o: simple past and past participle of bound. From Middle English bound, bund (preterite) and bounden, bunden, ibunden, ȝebunden (past participle), from Old English bund- and bunden, ġebunden respectively. See bind.
bounded.example: A compact set must be bounded.
bounded.exampleSense: That can be enclosed within a ball of finite radius.

existing.o: present participle and gerund of exist. From French exister, from Latin existō, exsistō (“I am, I exist, appear, arise”), from ex (“out”) + sistere (“to set, place”) (related to stare (“to stand, to be stood”)), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *stísteh₂ti, from the root *steh₂- (“stand”); see stand. Compare assist, consist, desist, insist, persist, resist. Cognate with Spanish existir, French exister, Italian esistere, German existieren.
existing.example: In his favour, Beeching declared that he supported carrying on with the existing modernisation projects, but that the rest of the business needed root and branch reform.
existing.exampleSense: That exists, or has existence, especially that exists now.

busty.example: I could see a busty blonde at the end of the boardwalk.

upfront.example: Appleby is an upfront homosexual, a devout Roman Catholic and a practitioner of the Black Arts.

adherent.o: From Middle English adherent, from Old French adherent, from Latin adhaerēns, present participle of adhaereō (“to stick to, cling”).
adherent.example: Half (49.9%) of patients were adherent to their regimens, 42.6% were underadherent, and 7.6% had medication oversupply.

adherence.o: From Middle French adhérence, from Latin adhærentia.

coupler.example: Another example of up-to-date practice is that all locomotives and rolling stock have automatic couplers.
coupler.exampleSense: Anything that serves to couple things together; but especially a device that couples railway carriages.

couple.o: From Middle English couple, from Old French couple, from Latin cōpula. Doublet of copula.
couple.example: A couple of police officers appeared at the door.
couple.exampleSense: Two of the same kind connected or considered together.

coupling.o: From Middle English couplynge; equivalent to couple + -ing.
coupling.example: It seems just as likely, though, that it simply never occurred to him to think about crime as something so tightly tied to place. Literary theorists and bridge engineers and police chiefs struggle with coupling.
coupling.exampleSense: A link between the performance of an action and the location where that action occurs or the method used to perform that action.

hijacking.example: The audacious hijacking in Paris of a van carrying the baggage of a Saudi prince to his private jet is obviously an embarrassment to the French capital, whose ultra-high-end boutiques have suffered a spate of heists in recent months.
hijacking.exampleSense: The instance of such an act; the seizure of a vehicle.

scatter.o: From Middle English scateren, skateren, also schateren, * probably a variant of shatter, which is imitative; * or from Old English *sceaterian, probably akin to a dialect of Old Norse, possibly ultimately related to Proto-Indo-European *skey- (“to cut, split, shatter”). Compare Middle Dutch scheteren (“to scatter”), Low German schateren, Dutch schateren (“to burst out laughing”); and is apparently remotely akin to Ancient Greek σκεδάννυμι (skedánnumi, “scatter, disperse”). and Tocharian B kät- (“to scatter, sow seeds”). Doublet of shatter.
scatter.example: Her ashes were scattered at the top of a waterfall.
scatter.exampleSense: To distribute loosely as by sprinkling.

panoramic.example: Scenic panoramics were not the best sellers. All commercial panoramic photographers specialized in pictures of large groups.

amortization.o: From Middle English amortisen (“to kill, alienate in mortmain”), from Anglo-Norman amorteser, alteration of Old French amortir, from Vulgar Latin *admortire (“to kill”), from Latin ad- and mors, mortem (“death”).

roundtrip.o: Alternative form of round. From Middle English round, rounde, from Old Northern French roünt, rund, Old French ront, runt, reont ( > French rond), from both Late Latin retundus and the original Latin rotundus. The noun developed partly from the adjective and partly from the corresponding French noun rond. Doublet of rotund.
roundtrip.example: Left with only her Sun-Times subscribers, she faced a 35-mile roundtrip to deliver to four of them.

ninja.o: Borrowed from Japanese 忍者 (ninja), of uncertain derivation but with an underlying sense of secret or hidden person. Popularized in Japanese by manga after World War II and in English by the 1980 novel The Ninja by Eric Van Lustbader and the 1981 movie Enter the Ninja Noun sense 3.1 (“Mongolian miner”) arose from the supposed resemblance of the bowls used to wash ore with mercury to the shells of the main characters from Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles. The Juggalo slang sense arose via influence from AAVE nigga.
ninja.example: Spies prowled Japan from the seventh century, but the secretive ninja left few written records.
ninja.exampleSense: A person trained in ninjutsu, especially (historical) one used for espionage, assassination, and other tasks requiring stealth during Japan's shogunate period.

trinity.o: From Middle English trinite, from Anglo-Norman trinite and Old French ternite (modern French trinité), from Latin trīnitās, from trīnī (“three each”), from trēs (“three”). By surface analysis, trine + -ity. Displaced native Old English þrines (literally “threeness”).

overuse.example: On a summer visit back to the farm here where I grew up, I think I figured out the central problem with modern industrial agriculture. It’s not just that it produces unhealthy food, mishandles waste and overuses antibiotics in ways that harm us all.
overuse.exampleSense: To use too much of (something); to use (it) too often.

correspondingly.example: He lived in a huge mansion, with a correspondingly large set of gates to keep out unwanted guests.

delicately.example: The gingerbread was delicately, if imprecisely, captured by the brushstrokes.

veil.o: From Middle English veil, veyl, from Anglo-Norman and Old Northern French veil (“sail, veil, shroud”) (Francien Old French voil, French voile), Latin vēlum (“cloth, covering”). Displaced Middle English scleire, scleyre, sleyre, slyre (“veil”) (compare German Schleier). Doublet of velum and voile.
veil.example: The forest fire was veiled by smoke, but I could hear it clearly.
veil.exampleSense: To conceal as with a veil.

fail.o:
verb: Inherited from Middle English failen, borrowed from Old French falir, from Vulgar Latin *fallire, alteration of Latin fallere (“to deceive, disappoint”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰāl- (“to lie, deceive”) or Proto-Indo-European *(s)gʷʰh₂el- (“to stumble”). Compare Alemannic German fääle (“to lack”), Cimbrian béelan, véelan (“to fail”), veln (“to be absent, missing”), Dutch falen, feilen (“to fail, miss”), German fallieren, fehlen (“to fail, miss, lack”), Danish fejle (“to fail, err”), Swedish fallera (“to fail, break, malfunction”), Spanish fallar (“to fail, miss”).

noun: Unknown. Compare Scottish Gaelic fàl (“hedge”), Scots faill (“turf”). Attested from the 16th century.
fail.example: There shall not fail thee a man on the throne.
fail.exampleSense: To be wanting to, to be insufficient for, to disappoint, to desert; to disappoint one's expectations.

fundamentally.example: What the science shows, he says, is that the brain of an addict is fundamentally different from that of a nonaddict.
fundamentally.exampleSense: In a fundamental or basic sense; reaching the very core of the matter.

cut down.example: They want to cut down several trees to make room for the parking lot.

threefold.o: From Middle English threfold, from Old English þrīfeald. Equivalent to three + -fold.
threefold.example: "We recognise that electrifying more of the railway is likely to be necessary to deliver decarbonisation," it stated.

hijack.o: Possibly from a blend of highway + jacker (“one who holds up”) (1915).
hijack.example: One lone "high-jack" held up 11 harvest hands in a freight car [...] last night, making a clean getaway with slightly over $180.

unveil.o: From Middle English *unveilen (suggested by past participle unveiled, vnueylyd (“unveiled”)). Equivalent to un- + veil. Ultimately from Latin velum (whence also English voile, English reveal, Russian вуа́ль (vuálʹ), Russian завуали́ровать (zavualírovatʹ) (compare typologically)). Also compare typologically uncloak, unmask, Russian разобла́чать (razobláčatʹ) (akin to облаче́ние (oblačénije)).
unveil.example: A sort of curtain, made of- mat, usually hung before them, which the natives were sometimes unwilling to remove ; and when they did consent to unveil them, they seemed to express themselves in a very mysterious manner.
unveil.exampleSense: To remove a veil from; to uncover; to reveal something hidden.

infeasible.o: From in- + feasible. Cognate to French infaisable.

remote.o: From Middle English remote, from Old French remot, masculine, remote, feminine, from Latin remotus, past participle of removere (“to remove”), from re- + movere (“to move”).
remote.example: A remote operator may control the vehicle with a wireless handset.

pigeonhole.o: The noun is derived from pigeon + hole. The verb is derived from the noun.
pigeonhole.example: Fred was tired of being pigeonholed as a computer geek.
pigeonhole.exampleSense: To place (someone or something) into a notional category or class, especially in a way which makes unjustified assumptions or which is restrictive; to categorize, to classify, to label.

honest.o: From Middle English honest, honeste (“honourable, appropriate, excellent”), from Old French honeste, from Latin honestus, from honor. For the verb, see Latin honestāre (“to clothe or adorn with honour”), and compare French honester. Displaced native Old English sōþfæst (literally “truth-firm”).
honest.example: We’re the most honest people you will ever come across.
honest.exampleSense: Scrupulous with regard to telling the truth; not given to swindling, lying, or fraud; upright.

bulletproof.example: We have to bulletproof this program before we let the users at it; check every input, catch every possible flaw...it must not fail in use.

absenteeism.example: Chronic absenteeism, for example, continues to be a problem despite some improvements.
absenteeism.exampleSense: The state of being absent, especially frequently or without good reason; the practice of an absentee.

ballooning.o: present participle and gerund of balloon. First use appears c. 1591, "a game played with a large, inflated leather ball" (possibly via Middle French ballon) from Italian pallone (“large ball”) from palla (“ball”), from Lombardic *palla. The Northern Italian form, balla (“ball-shaped bundle”), today a doublet, likely derived from Old French balle, from Frankish *balla (“ball”), and may have influenced the spelling of this word. Both Germanic words are from Proto-Germanic *ballô (“ball”), *balluz, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰoln- (“bubble”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰel- (“to blow, swell, inflate”). Akin to Old High German ballo, bal (“ball”), (German Ballen (“bale”); Ball "ball"). Doublet of ballon. More at ball.
ballooning.example: When he retired, he took up ballooning.
ballooning.exampleSense: The sport or hobby of flying in a hot-air balloon.

setup.example: Shapiro says KYW would keep two separate news staffs that would work together, similar to WBZ's setup.
setup.exampleSense: The fashion in which something is organized or arranged.

physical.o: Borrowed from Late Latin physicālis, from Latin physica (“study of nature”), from Ancient Greek φυσική (phusikḗ), feminine singular of φυσικός (phusikós, “natural; physical”), from φύσις (phúsis, “origin, birth; nature, quality; form, shape; type, kind”), from φῠ́ω (phŭ́ō, “grow”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰuH- (“to appear, become, rise up”).
physical.example: It's not so much a physical place as a state of mind.
physical.exampleSense: Of matter and nature. Pertaining to the world as understood through the senses rather than the mind; tangible, concrete; real. Having to do with the material world.

splash.o: Probably an alteration of plash (compare spatter, spill for the initial s-).
splash.example: There was a visible splash on his pants after he went to the bathroom.
splash.exampleSense: A mark or stain made from a small amount of liquid.

reversible.o: Probably from Middle French, equivalent to reverse + -ible.
reversible.example: [...] the Welwyn bottleneck will be relaid with high-speed turnouts and resignalled for reversible working.

suppression.example: In these circumstances the Communist guerrillas had survived Kuomintang suppression and in the autumn of 1931 they had launched a rising in the Huanglung Mountains of north Shensi.
suppression.exampleSense: The entirety of acts aimed at stopping or preventing the enemy to execute such unwanted activities like firing, regrouping, observation or others.

suppressed.o: simple past and past participle of suppress. From Latin suppressus, perfect passive participle of supprimō (“press down or under”), from sub (“under”) + premō (“press”).

aperture.o: From late Middle English, from Latin apertūra (“an opening”), from aperiō (“to uncover, make or lay bare”) + -tūra (“-ure”, action noun suffix). Doublet of overture and apertura.
aperture.example: The door was opened — ‘on the chain.’ The old lady peered at us through an aperture of about six inches.
aperture.exampleSense: A small or narrow opening, gap, slit, or hole.

block.o: From Middle English blok (“log, stump, solid piece”), from Old French bloc (“log, block”), from Middle Dutch blok (“treetrunk”), from Old Dutch *blok (“log”), from Proto-West Germanic *blokk, from Proto-Germanic *blukką (“beam, log”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰelǵ- (“thick plank, beam, pile, prop”). Cognate with Old Frisian blok, Old Saxon blok, Old High German bloh, bloc (“block”), Old English bolca (“gangway of a ship, plank”), Old Norse bǫlkr (“divider, partition”). More at balk. See also bloc, bulk.
block.example: After one disk is mapped, the next block starts at address 0 on the next disk.
block.exampleSense: A logical extent or region; a grouping or apportionment of like things treated together as a unit. A logical data storage unit containing one or more physical sectors.

waylay.o: From way + lay, likely a calque of Middle Dutch wegelagen (“besetting of ways, lying in wait with evil or hostile intent along public ways”). Compare Middle Low German wegelagen, German wegelagern (“to waylay; rob”).

on demand.example: Our new on-demand software delivery system is cutting edge.

endurance.o: First attested in the late 15th century. From Middle French endurance, from Old French endurance. Morphologically endure + -ance.
endurance.example: He has great endurance: he ran a marathon and then cycled home.
endurance.exampleSense: The measure of a person's stamina or persistence.

capitalize.o: From capital + -ize, the first element ultimately from Latin capitālis (“of the head”).
capitalize.example: In German, all nouns are capitalized.
capitalize.exampleSense: In writing or editing, to write (something: either an entire word or text, or just the initial letter(s) thereof) in capital letters, in upper case.

accelerator.o: * First attested in 1611. * (motor vehicle): First attested in 1900. * accelerate + -or
accelerator.example: As soon as you get onto the slipway, push the accelerator.
accelerator.exampleSense: A pedal causing the vehicle to accelerate when it is pressed.

propone.o: From Latin prōpōnō (“place before; offer, propose”), via Scots [Term?].

hob.o:
noun: Related to hub, but the ultimate origin of both words is obscure.

noun: From Middle English Hob (a diminutive of Robin, an Old French [Term?] diminutive of Robert), through its connection with Robin Goodfellow and (later) the devil. Compare hobgoblin; see robin.
hob.example: More fitter for the Country Hobs.
hob.exampleSense: A countryman; a rustic or yokel.

hub.o: From earlier hubbe, which has the same immediate origin as hob. Hub was originally a dialectal word; its ultimate origin is unknown. Compare German Hubbel (“bump on a surface”), from Proto-West Germanic *hubil (“bump, hill”) (which contains a diminutive suffix *-il); compare English hive, or perhaps ultimately from the same root as hip or hop.
hub.example: If you need to reload film, the cassette can be rewound slightly by turning the hub located on one end of its spool.
hub.exampleSense: The central part, usually cylindrical, of a wheel; the nave.

centric.o: From Ancient Greek κεντρικός (kentrikós), equivalent to centre + -ic.

recommended.o: simple past and past participle of recommend. From Middle English recommenden, from Old French recommender (compare French recommander), from Latin re- + commendāre (“to commend, commit; to recommend”), from con- + mandāre (“commit, intrust, enjoin”), from manus (“hand, handwriting, power”) + dare (“to give; to offer or render”). Compare typologically Bulgarian препоръчам (preporǎčam), Serbo-Croatian препоручити, Slovene priporočiti, Czech doporučit, Slovak odporučiť (the same meaning); Russian поручи́ться (poručítʹsja), пору́ка (porúka), поручи́тельство (poručítelʹstvo) (close meaning), all related to Proto-Slavic *rǫka (Bulgarian ръка (rǎka), Russian рука́ (ruká)).

artifact.o: Alteration of artefact, from Italian artefatto, from Latin arte (“by skill”) (ablative of ars (“art”)) + factum (“thing made”) (from facio (“to make, do”)).
artifact.example: Given increasing investment in an IT (information technology) artifact (i.e., online service website), it is becoming important to retain existing customers.
artifact.exampleSense: An object made or shaped by human hand or labor.

synergy.o: From Ancient Greek συνεργία (sunergía, “cooperation”), from σύν (sún, “with, together”) + ἔργον (érgon, “work”). By surface analysis, syn- + -ergy.
synergy.example: Others argued that the notion of a targeted war on a particular disease inevitably distracted from natural synergies with other areas of research.
synergy.exampleSense: Benefits resulting from combining different groups, people, objects or processes.

chokepoint.example: First, a hostile state could invade and occupy an oil producer or cut off a key chokepoint such as the Strait of Hormuz.
chokepoint.exampleSense: A point at which traffic or other movement can easily become blocked.

institutionally.example: Japanese retail stores have strove to, and have succeeded in, fulfilling these severe demands, and in doing so, have constantly had to innovate both technologically and institutionally in order to keep up with the competition.

institutional.example: Swindon's Model Lodging House was originally designed by Isambard Kingdom Brunel. The 1847-1849 recession led to delays and plan revisions, including smaller windows in the finished structure, resulting in a more 'institutional' appearance.
institutional.exampleSense: Of, pertaining to, characteristic of, or organized along the lines of an institution.

interdisciplinary.example: This journal is interdisciplinary: it has articles on everything from biology to electrical engineering.
interdisciplinary.exampleSense: Of or pertaining to multiple distinct academic disciplines or fields of study.

steadfast.o: From Middle English stedefast, from Old English stedefæst, from Proto-Germanic *stadifastuz, equivalent to stead (“place; spot; position”) + fast (“firm; fixed”). Cognate with Middle Dutch stedevast (“steadfast”), Icelandic staðfestur (“steadfast”), Danish stedfast (“firmly attached, secured”), Danish stadfæste (“to confirm; ratify”), Norwegian Nynorsk stadfesta (“confirm, ratify; establish”), Swedish stadfästa (“to confirm; establish”).

tailored.o: simple past and past participle of tailor. Inherited from Middle English taillour, from Anglo-Norman taillour, from Old French tailleor, from taillier, from Late Latin tāliō, from Latin tālea (“a cutting”). Doublet of tailleur. Compare typologically German Schneider (akin to English snithe); Macedonian кројач (krojač), Polish krawiec (akin to Proto-Slavic *krojiti).
tailored.example: His expensive tailored shirts didn't look that much better than off-the-rack, but they lasted much longer.

cockpit.o:
noun: Compound of cock (“rooster”) + pit.

noun: Either the same as above or from compound of cock (“boat”) + pit, where the first element is also found in cockboat and coxswain.
cockpit.example: India became the cockpit in which it was shown that trade was war carried on under another name.
cockpit.exampleSense: A site of conflict; a battlefield.

daisy chain.o: The noun is derived from daisy + chain. The verb is derived from the noun.
daisy chain.example: Like Brad Bird's playfully virtuosic Ghost Protocol, the high point of this franchise in more ways than one, Fallout creates an endless daisy chain of spectacle, so that one stunning display of acrobatic nerve is barely over before another begins.
daisy chain.exampleSense: A sequence of events where each one leads to the next.

hump.o: Probably borrowed from Dutch homp (“hump, lump”) or Middle Low German hump (“heap, hill, stump”), from Old Saxon *hump (“hill, heap, thick piece”), from Proto-Germanic *humpaz (“hip, height”), from Proto-Indo-European *kumb- (“curved”). Compare Proto-Germanic *huppōną (“to hop”), from Proto-Indo-European *kewb-, *ḱewb- (unnasalised root), and English hub (a softened variant without nasal?). Cognate with West Frisian hompe (“lump, chunk”), Icelandic huppur (“flank”), Welsh cwm (“a hollow”), Latin incumbō (“to lie down”), Albanian sumbull (“round button, bud”), Ancient Greek κύμβη (kúmbē, “bowl”), Avestan 𐬑𐬎𐬨𐬠𐬀 (xumba, “pot”), Sanskrit कुम्ब (kúmba, “thick end of bone”). Replaced, and perhaps influenced by, Old English crump (“crooked, bent”). More at cramp.
hump.example: Stop humping the table, you sicko.
hump.exampleSense: To rhythmically thrust the pelvis in a manner conducive to sexual intercourse. To dry-hump.

disambiguate.example: When necessary, the Greek spelling is disambiguated by an appended phonetic transcription.
disambiguate.exampleSense: To distinguish one word or lexical unit (from a different one which has a similar form).

indirection.example: In your case, I fear, confession is exploitation by indirection, profit-making by ruse, self-aggrandizement at the expense of God.
indirection.exampleSense: A lack of direction; deviousness or aimlessness.

up to speed.example: Is Mary up to speed on the situation in Kuala Lumpur?

farmland.example: Other common farmland butterflies to have suffered steep declines include the small tortoiseshell (64%), the wall brown (37%) and the large skipper (35%).
farmland.exampleSense: Land that is suitable for farming and agricultural production.

compulsory.o: Borrowed from Late Latin compulsorius, from Latin compulsus. Displaced native Old English ġenīedelīċ.

peachy.example: Although this is an apricot pie, it tastes peachy.

halfway.o: From Middle English halfwey, from Old English healfweġ (“half-way”), equivalent to half- + way. Compare partway. Cognate with Saterland Frisian hoolfwais (“halfway”), Dutch halfweg (“halfway”), German halbwegs (“halfway”), Danish halvvejs (“halfway”), Swedish halvvägs (“halfway”).
halfway.example: "He comes halfway and I come halfway," said Mr. Korson, 56.
halfway.exampleSense: Half of the way between two points; midway.

concentric.o: From Middle English concentrik, from Middle French concentrique, from Medieval Latin concentricus, from Latin con- (“with, together”) + centrum (“circle, center”). Equivalent to con- + -centric. By surface analysis, con- + centre + -ic.
concentric.example: Seven huge concentric semi-circular rings of stone surround the northern end, and quite rightly are Grade 2-listed by conservation body Historic England.

datum.o: Learned borrowing from Latin datum, a nominalization of datus, perfect passive participle of dō, from Proto-Italic *didō, from Proto-Indo-European *dédeh₃ti, reduplication of *deh₃-, or from *-ti. Doublet of die.
datum.example: A geodetic datum is sometimes also called a benchmark.
datum.exampleSense: A fixed reference point or set of reference points which precisely define a system of measurement or a coordinate system.

addressable.example: "Despite the prevailing external forces, we remain confident in our ability to profitably grow the business in our addressable markets," the company said.

unlimited.example: The Scottish Region is issuing a Day Rail-Rover Ticket, available at 12 hours' notice, permitting unlimited travel in an area bounded by Edinburgh, St. Andrews, Dundee, Perth, Comrie, Callander, Stirling and Falkirk for 25s. (children, 12s. 6d.). . . .

altogether.o: From Middle English altogeder, altogedere, equivalent to al- (“all”) + together. Cognate with Scots awthegither (“altogether”), Middle High German alzegater (“altogether”), Dutch altegaar. Compare also Old English ealġeador, eallġeador (“altogether”), West Frisian allegearre (“altogether”). More at together. The noun sense (nakedness): was popularized in George du Maurier's 1894 novel Trilby.

causality.o: From Latin as if *causalitas, from causalis (“causal”), from causa (“cause”). By surface analysis, causal + -ity = cause + -ality.
causality.example: But how do transformations like the evolution of language take place? A scientist looks for a cause inside time; a mystic knows that causality is essentially a process that is outside time-space.
causality.exampleSense: The relationship between something that happens or exists and the thing that causes it; the cause and consequence relationship.

abysm.o: From Middle English abime, from Old French abisme from Late Latin *abyssimus, a superlative of abyssus (“bottomless pit”), from Ancient Greek ἄβυσσος (ábussos). Cognate to French abîme. See also abyss.
abysm.example: Dr. Prunesquallor had circled around Steerpike with his head drawn back so that his cervical vertebrae rested against the near wall of his high collar, and a plumbless abysm yawned between his Adam’s apple and his pearl stud.
abysm.exampleSense: An abyss; a gulf, a chasm, a very deep hole.

stipend.o: The noun is derived from Late Middle English stipend, stipende (“salary, wage”) [and other forms], from Old French stipende, stipendie, from Latin stīpendium (“contribution; dues; impost, tax; tribute; military pay or stipend; military service”), from *stipipendium, *stippendium, from stips (“alms; contribution, donation, gift”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *steyp- (“erect; stiff”)) + pendere (the present active infinitive of pendō (“to cause to hang down or suspend; to weigh, weigh out; (hence) to pay”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)pend- (“to pull; to spin; to stretch”)) + -ium (suffix forming abstract nouns). The verb is derived from the noun. Cognates * Italian stipendio * Portuguese estipêndio * Spanish estipendio
stipend.example: My stipend for doing public service is barely enough to cover living expenses.
stipend.exampleSense: Some other form of fixed (and generally small) payment occurring at regular intervals, such as an allowance, a pension, or (obsolete) a tax.

gaslight.o:
noun: From gas (“flammable gaseous hydrocarbon or hydrocarbon mixture used as a fuel”) + light.

verb: From the 1938 stage play Gas Light by the English playwright and novelist Patrick Hamilton (1904–1962), and its 1940 and 1944 film adaptations, in which a husband attempts to convince his wife and others that she is insane by manipulating small elements of their environment. For more details, see also Gaslighting § Etymology on Wikipedia.
gaslight.example: Then as the darkness descended, they began to shine with the mellow radiance of gaslight.
gaslight.exampleSense: The light produced by the burning gas in such a lamp.

lint.o:
noun: From Middle English lynet, linet, from Old French linette (“grain of flax”), diminutive of lin (“flax”); or, from Medieval Latin linteum, from Latin līnum (“flax”).

verb: From the lint Unix utility, written in 1979, which analyses programs written in the C language, itself named after the undesirable bits of fiber and fluff found in sheep's wool (see etymology 1).
lint.example: Clean the lint out of the vacuum cleaner's filter.
lint.exampleSense: Clinging fuzzy fluff that clings to fabric or accumulates in one's pockets or navel etc.

linter.example: A linter checks your source code for syntax and style errors.
linter.exampleSense: A program or algorithm that performs linting.

factorial.example: This playing around with consecutive integers reminded one of the students of factorials, and he asked about products of integers, which I said could be expressed similarly as#92;prod#95;#123;k#61;1#125;ⁿk#61;1#92;cdot 2#92;cdot 3#92;cdotsn.But what does this equal?
factorial.exampleSense: The result of multiplying a given number of consecutive integers from 1 to the given number. In equations, it is symbolized by an exclamation mark (!). For example, 5! = 1 × 2 × 3 × 4 × 5 = 120.

palette.o: Borrowed from French palette. Doublet of pallet.
palette.example: The unified colour palette of reds, blues, and yellows used throughout the signage matches that of the institution’s logo and letterhead.
palette.exampleSense: The range of colors in a given work or item or body of work.

tab.o:
noun: First attested 1607, of uncertain origin.

noun: Apocopation (shortening) of (variously) tabulate, tabulator, or tabulation.

noun: Likely to have been formed by clipping the Geordie pronunciation of the word tobacco or alternatively from the brand name Ogden's Tabs.

noun: Clipping of tablature.

noun: Clipping of Cantab, from Cantabrigian, from Latin Cantabrigia (“Cambridge”).

noun: Clipping of tabloid.

noun: Clipping of tablet.
tab.example: We lifted the tabs on the cans and poured the brew carefully into glasses.
tab.exampleSense: A small flap or strip of material attached to or inserted into something, for holding, manipulation, identification, opening etc.

step out.example: They've been stepping out since he told her he was interested in a family.
step out.exampleSense: To date, to be in a romantic relationship.

step in.example: McCoist unexpectedly ushered back a defender of his own with Kirk Broadfoot taking over from Steven Whittaker. There was, of course, another change, Kyle Bartley stepping in at centre-half to replace suspended Dorin Goian.
step in.exampleSense: To act as a replacement or substitute.

stepover.example: Fernando Amorebieta seemed to have checked him, but a stepover created a fraction of room that became significant as the defender slipped, giving Falcao just enough space to curl a superb finish into the top corner.

side by side.o: Alternative spelling of side-by-side. From side + by + side.
side by side.example: The new houses were built side by side, facing the lake.
side by side.exampleSense: Beside or alongside one another; close to one another and abreast.

experiment.o: From Middle English experiment, from Old French esperiment (French expérience), from Latin experimentum (“experience, attempt, experiment”), from experior (“to experience, to attempt”), itself from ex + *perior, in turn from Proto-Indo-European *per-.
experiment.example: South Korean officials announced last month that an experiment to create artificial rain did not provide the desired results.
experiment.exampleSense: A test under controlled conditions made to either demonstrate a known truth, examine the validity of a hypothesis, or determine the efficacy or likelihood of something previously untried.

nanook.example: Let's build a nanook. A big one. Almost as big as a real one!

shard.o: From Middle English shard, scherd, scheard, schord, from Old English sċeard (“a broken piece; shard”), from Proto-West Germanic *skard, from Proto-Germanic *skardą (“notch; nick”), from *skardaz (“damaged; nicked; scarred”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to cut”). Akin to Scots schaird (“shard”), French écharde (“splinter”), Dutch schaarde (“tear; notch; fragment”), German Scharte (“notch”), Old Norse skarð (“notch, hack”) ( > Danish skår). The database sense is perhaps derived from the online gaming sense or from SHARD (System for Highly Available Replicated Data), name of a 1980s database product.
shard.example: You know there is something fascinating beyond that wall because someone's tried to stop you seeing over, and there are shards of glass embedded in the top.
shard.exampleSense: A piece of broken glass or pottery, especially one found in an archaeological dig.

dismount.o: From dis- + mount, probably a calque of Old French desmonter.
dismount.example: It was a stylish routine, let down by a sloppy dismount.
dismount.exampleSense: The part of a routine in which the gymnast detaches from an apparatus.

neuroanatomy.example: This flowchart suggested by the neuroanatomy corresponds fairly well with what psychologists see in the clinic and lab.
neuroanatomy.exampleSense: The anatomy of the nervous system.

krypton.o: From Ancient Greek κρυπτός (kruptós, “hidden”) + -on, used for all noble gases.

python.o: From Latin pȳthon, from Ancient Greek Πύθων (Púthōn), the name of the mythological enormous serpent at Delphi slain by Apollo, probably from Πυθώ (Puthṓ), older name of Delphi.

anaconda.o: From New Latin anacandaia (“python”), originally referring to a species of constrictor found in Sri Lanka, from Sinhalese හෙනකඳයා (henakaⁿdayā, “whip snake”), from හෙණ (heṇa, “lightning, thunderbolt”) + කඳ (kaⁿda, “stem, trunk, body”) or from Tamil ஆனைக்கொன்றான் (āṉaikkoṉṟāṉ, “having killed an elephant”), from ஆனை (āṉai, “elephant”) + கொன்றான் (koṉṟāṉ, “having killed”).
anaconda.example: I have chased after white women to find they only wanted to dance with my anaconda and weren't interested in me as a partner.

pickle.o:
noun: From Middle English pikel (“spicy sauce served with meat or fish”), borrowed from Middle Dutch, Middle Low German pekel (“brine”). Cognate with Scots pikkill (“salt liquor, brine”), Saterland Frisian Piekele (“pickle, brine”), Dutch pekel (“pickle, brine”), Low German pekel, peckel, pickel, bickel (“pickle, brine”), German Pökel (“pickle, brine”), Icelandic pækill (“brine”).

noun: Perhaps from Scottish pickle, apparently from pick + -le (diminutive suffix). Compare Scots pickil.
pickle.example: A pickle goes well with a hamburger.
pickle.exampleSense: A cucumber preserved in a solution, usually a brine or a vinegar syrup.

likeness.o: From Middle English liknesse, from Old English līcness, ġelīcnes (“the quality of being like or equal; likeness; image; copy; pattern; example; parable”), from Proto-West Germanic *galīkanassī (“likeness”), equivalent to like + -ness. Cognate with West Frisian likenis (“likeness”), Dutch gelijkenis (“similarity; likeness; parable”), German Low German Glieknis (“form; semblance; likeness; parable”), German Gleichnis (“form; semblance; image; likeness; parable; simile”). The verb is derived from the noun. Compare also Old Norse líkneskja (“figure, image, appearance, likeness”).
likeness.example: How he looked, the likenesses of him which still remain enable us to imagine.
likeness.exampleSense: That which closely resembles; a portrait.

purge.o: From Middle English purgen, from Old French purgier, from Latin pūrgō (“to make pure, to cleanse”), from pūrus (“clean, pure”) + agō (“to make, to do”).
purge.example: Stalin liked to ensure that his purges were not reversible.
purge.exampleSense: A forcible removal of people, for example, from political activity.

raptor.o:
noun: From Middle English raptour, from Latin raptor (“kidnapper, thief”).

noun: Popularized (and possibly coined) in 1990 by Michael Crichton in Jurassic Park; clipping of velociraptor, ultimately of the same etymology as above.

enclosed.o: simple past and past participle of enclose. From Middle English enclosen, inclosen, from Middle English enclos, from Old French enclose, feminine plural past participle of enclore, from Vulgar Latin *inclaudō, *inclaudere, from Latin inclūdō (doublet of include), from in- (“in”) + claudō (“to shut”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kleh₂u- (“key, hook, nail”). Equivalent to en- + close.
enclosed.example: The gas is completely enclosed within the bottle.

overdo.o: From Middle English overdon, from Old English oferdōn, equivalent to over- + do.
overdo.example: [...] it would be their shame for ever to be overdone in mischiefe, nor were they here exceeded.
overdo.exampleSense: To do more than (someone); to do (something) to a greater extent.

surrogate.o: From Latin surrogātus, perfect passive participle of surrogō (“ask”); a variant of subrogō, from sub (“under”) + rogō (“ask”).
surrogate.example: A mixture of horseradish and mustard often serves as a surrogate for wasabi.
surrogate.exampleSense: A substitute (usually of a person, position or role).

gaze.o: From Middle English gasen; akin to Swedish dialectal gasa and Gothic 𐌿𐍃𐌲𐌰𐌹𐍃𐌾𐌰𐌽 (usgaisjan, “to terrify”).
gaze.example: She counters the tendency to focus on critical strategies of resisting the male gaze, raising the issue of the female spectator.
gaze.exampleSense: In Lacanian psychoanalysis, the relationship of the subject with the desire to look and awareness that one can be viewed.

torso.o: From Italian torso, from Late Latin tursus, from Latin thyrsus, from Ancient Greek θύρσος (thúrsos, “Bacchic staff”). Doublet of thyrse, thyrsus, and torse.

athletic.o: Borrowed from Middle French athletique and Latin āthlēticus, from Ancient Greek ἀθλητικός (athlētikós, “relating to an athlete”), from ἀθλητής (athlētḗs, “athlete”): equivalent to athlete + -ic. For more, see athlete. The Super Mario sense is effectively a reborrowing of Japanese アスレチック (asurechikku, “obstacle course”), originally borrowed from English athletic; this sense was itself originally a clipping of the genericized wasei eigo trademark フィールドアスレチック (fīrudo asurechikku, “Field Athletic”).
athletic.example: You have such an athletic build—you must work out regularly.
athletic.exampleSense: Having a muscular, well developed body, being in shape.

slender.o: From Middle English slendre, sclendre, from Old French esclendre (“thin, slender”), from Middle Dutch slinder (“thin, lank”), from Proto-Germanic *slindraz (“sliding, slippery”), from Proto-Indo-European *sleydʰ- (“to slip”). Cognate with Bavarian Schlenderling (“that which dangles”), German schlendern (“to saunter, stroll”), Dutch slidderen, slinderen (“to wriggle, creep like a serpent”), Low German slindern (“to slide on ice”). More at slide, slither.
slender.example: Being a person of slender means, he was unable to afford any luxuries.

semaphore.o: The noun is borrowed from French sémaphore, from Ancient Greek σῆμα (sêma, “mark, sign, token”) + French -phore (from Ancient Greek -φόρος (-phóros, suffix indicating a bearer or carrier)). By surface analysis, sema- + -phore. The verb is derived from the noun.
semaphore.example: The arms of the semaphore at the settlement were, in fact, gesticulating with comical vehemence.
semaphore.exampleSense: Any equipment used for visual signalling by means of flags, lights, or mechanically moving arms, which are used to represent letters of the alphabet, or words.

dolphin.o:
noun: From Middle English delphyn, from Latin delphīnus, from Ancient Greek δελφίς (delphís), from δελφύς (delphús, “womb”); the modern form in -ol- is probably influenced by the pronunciation of Middle French dauphin. Compare Swedish delfin. Doublet of dauphin. Displaced native Old English mereswīn (literally “sea pig”), whence English mereswine.

noun: Ultimately from 3rd Duke of Alba (duc-d'Albe in French), who was the first to build this type of structure in the Spanish Netherlands in the 16th century. Possibly from Dutch dukdalf, or the plural dukdalven, through elision of the initial duk-.
dolphin.example: For a dolphin or buoy to be placed on the south point of Goat Island, in the harbor of Newport, one hundred and fifty dollars.
dolphin.exampleSense: A permanent fender designed to protect a heavy boat, bridge, or coastal structure from the impact of large floating objects such as ice, floating logs, or vessels.

leaflet.example: The new leaflets at the end of the branch were a lighter shade of green than the mature leaves.

penultimate.o:
adj: From Latin paenultimus (“penultimate”) + -ate (adjective-forming suffix), from paene (“almost”) + ultimus (“last”). Equivalent to pene- + ultimate. Compare French pénultième.

noun: From a substantivation of the above adjective. Equivalent to Latin paenultimus + -ate (noun-forming suffix).
penultimate.example: Antepenultimate is that before the Penultimate, or the last but two.
penultimate.exampleSense: A penult, a next to last The penultimate syllable of a word or metrical line.

desk.o: From Middle English deske, desque, from Medieval Latin desca, modified from Old Italian desco, from Latin discus. Doublet of dais, disc, discus, dish, disk, and diskos. See also German Tisch, "table".
desk.example: Each row of desked benches was stepped up a step from the other until the top row of desked benches seemed to hit its high ceiling.
desk.exampleSense: To equip with a desk or desks.

option.o: From French option, from Latin optiō (“choice; option; act of choosing”), from optō (“to choose, select”). Equivalent to opt + -ion.
option.example: There's a book out on us and there's gonna be a movie based on the book. ABC has bought the option for a movie to be made specially for T.V.
option.exampleSense: A contract giving the holder the right to buy or sell an asset at a set strike price; can apply to financial market transactions, or to ordinary transactions for tangible assets such as a residence or automobile.

mourn.o: From Middle English mornen, mournen, from Old English murnan, from Proto-Germanic *murnaną. Cognate with French morne (“gloomy”).
mourn.example: Abraham came to mourn for Sarah, and to weep for her.
mourn.exampleSense: To express sadness or sorrow for; to grieve over (especially a death).

commendable.o: From Middle English commendable, from Middle French commendable, from Latin commendabilis, from commendare (“to commend, intrust to”), from com- + mandare (“to commit, intrust, enjoin”), from manus (“hand”) + dare (“to put”).

lamentable.o: From Middle English lamentable, from Middle French lamentable, from Latin lāmentābilis (“full of sorrow, mournful; deplorable”), from lāmentor (“lament”), from lāmenta (“wailing, weeping”). By surface analysis, lament + -able.

skepticism.o: From New Latin scepticismus; equivalent to skeptic + -ism.

ticker.example: To my surprise, the ticker showed that the deal had already gone through.
ticker.exampleSense: A ticker tape, either the traditional paper kind or a scrolling message on a screen.

widen.exampleSense: To broaden or extend in scope or range.

replication.o: Inherited from Middle English replicacioun, replicacion, from Anglo-Norman replicacioun and Old French replicacion (“reply, answer”), from Latin replicātiō, replicātiōnem. By surface analysis, replicate + -(at)ion.
replication.example: That painting is an almost exact replication of a famous Rembrandt painting.

hyperreal.example: There's far more than just hot dogs to feast on too. The pizzas—gigantic, floppy, with a hyperreal waxy sheen—are mythic. They arrive exclusively in cheese, pepperoni, or supreme—the holy trinity—and will run you an eminently affordable $1.99 for a ridiculously huge wedge-shaped slice.

collocate.o: Borrowed from Latin collocatum, supine of collocō. Doublet of couch.
collocate.example: A list of collocations to accompany the SVL words providing their important lexico-grammatical associations could therefore be a useful supplementary resource. Thus, we took an extra step not present in previously developed academic wordlists and created lists of each word's discipline-specific collocates.
collocate.exampleSense: A component word of a collocation; a word that collocates with another.

percentile.o: Coined by Francis Galton in 1885, from percent + -ile.
percentile.example: She is highly intelligent—she has an IQ in the top percentile.
percentile.exampleSense: Any one of the hundred groups so divided.

bullshit.o: From bull + shit. Figurative use as a noun referring to useless or untrue information is attested from the 1910s.
bullshit.example: You’re bullshitting me. I called your office and you never even came in.
bullshit.exampleSense: To tell lies, exaggerate; to mislead; to deceive.

overclocking.o: present participle and gerund of overclock. From over- + clock.

adrenaline.o: From adrenal + -ine, coined by Japanese chemist Takamine Jōkichi in 1901.
adrenaline.example: Some people bungee jump to feel alive through the surge of adrenaline.

unaware.example: Luckily, she was unaware that I'd spent the last five years in prison.
unaware.exampleSense: Not aware or informed; lacking knowledge; unmindful.

entwine.example: And with the story of the booking office, we have a fortune deeply entwined with the stations encasing them.
entwine.exampleSense: To twist or twine around something (or one another).

come of age.example: Eager to find a better life, you joined the Alliance military when you came of age. You volunteered for an expedition to Akuze: a lush world on the outskirts of Alliance space that had suddenly dropped out of contact.
come of age.exampleSense: To mature, or become fully developed.

humanoid.o: From human (from Latin hūmānus m (“of or belonging to a man, human, humane”, adjective)) + -oid.
humanoid.example: That's how I came to be down there, Captain, pursuing the devil's own spawn, a thing I've chased across the universe. He's humanoid outside, but inside, he's a hideous, murdering monster. I'll get him, Captain. I swear it.
humanoid.exampleSense: Having the appearance or characteristics of a human; being anthropomorphic under some criteria (physical, mental, genetical, ethological, ethical etc.).

afford.o: From Middle English afforthen, aforthen, avorthien, from earlier iforthen, iforthien, ȝeforthien, from Old English forþian, ġeforþian (“to further, accomplish, afford”), from Proto-Germanic *furþōną, from Proto-Germanic *furþą (“forth, forward”), equivalent to a- + forth. Cognate with Old Norse forða (“to forward oneself, save oneself, escape danger”), Icelandic forða (“to save, rescue”).
afford.example: Ms Camisa and her husband have had to rejig their finances to afford tuition.
afford.exampleSense: To incur, stand, or bear without serious detriment, as an act which might under other circumstances be injurious; (usually after an expression of ability, as could, able, difficult) to be able or rich enough; to spare.

accordance.o: * (compliance): First attested around 1300. * (agreement): First attested in the early 14th century. * accord + -ance * From Middle English accordaunce, from Old French acordance (“agreeing, reconciliation, harmony”).
accordance.example: And what had been done that was not in strict accordance with the law of Parliament?

p: suffix forming abverbs from adjectives and nouns
relentlessly.o: From relentless + -ly (suffix forming abverbs from adjectives and nouns). Relentless is derived from relent (“(noun) act of relenting or giving way, yielding; (verb) to become less cruel or harsh; to become less intense”) + -less (suffix meaning ‘lacking, without’); and relent from Middle English relenten (“to melt; to soften; to dissolve in water; of weather: to be cool and moist”), from Anglo-Norman relenter, relentir (“to melt; to shrivel; to give up; to slacken”), and also influenced by Middle French ralenter, ralentir (“to abate; to slow down”) (modern French ralentir), from re- (prefix meaning ‘again’ having intensifying effect) + alenter, alentir (“to slow down”) (from Old French alentir, from a- (prefix denoting entering a state or progressing towards a goal) + lent (“slow”) (from Latin lentus (“slow, sluggish”), possibly ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *lentos (“pliant; soft; smooth”)) + -ir (suffix forming infinitives of verbs)).
relentlessly.example: The leadership team must believe in it and pursue it relentlessly, along with the leader herself.

engineered.o: simple past and past participle of engineer.
