The noun is derived from: * Middle English enginour (“one who designs, constructs, or operates military works for attack or defence, etc.; machine designer”) [and other forms], from Anglo-Norman enginour, engigneour [and other forms], and Middle French and Old French engigneor, engigneour, engignier (“one who designs, constructs, or operates military works for attack or defence; architect; carpenter; craftsman; designer; planner; one who deceives or schemes”) (modern French ingénieur), from engin (“contraption, device; machine; invention; creativity, ingenuity; intelligence; deception, ruse, trickery”) + -eor, -or (suffix forming agent nouns); engin is derived from Latin ingenium (“innate or natural quality, nature; intelligence, natural capacity; ability, skill, talent; (Medieval Latin) engine; machine”), from in- (prefix meaning ‘in, inside, within’) + gignere (the present active infinitive of gignō (“to bear, beget, give birth to; to cause, produce, yield”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ǵenh₁- (“to beget, give birth to; to produce”)) + -ium (suffix forming abstract nouns); and * from engine + -er (occupational suffix); and * from engine + -eer (suffix forming nouns denoting people associated with, concerned with, or engaged in specified activities), possibly modelled after Middle French ingénieur (a variant of Middle French, Old French engigneour; see above), and Italian ingegniere (“engineer”) (obsolete; modern Italian ingegnere). The verb is derived from the noun. Cognates * Medieval Latin, Late Latin ingeniārius (“engineer”) * Medieval Latin ingeniator (“one constructing or using an engine”) * Old Occitan engenhador, enginhador * Portuguese engenhador (obsolete), engenheiro (“engineer”) * Spanish engeñero (obsolete), ingeniero (“engineer”)

parenthesis.o: Learned borrowing from Late Latin parenthesis (“addition of a letter to a syllable in a word”), itself borrowed from Ancient Greek παρένθεσις (parénthesis, “insertion”). By surface analysis, par- + en- + thesis.
parenthesis.example: [T]he present research also made an effort to approach a greater accuracy in presenting the original sources of borrowed words. This was achieved by presenting etymons from Hindustani in the Devanagari script followed by a transliteration in the Roman alphabet in parentheses.
parenthesis.exampleSense: Either of a pair of brackets, especially (mainly US) round brackets, ( and ) (used to enclose parenthetical material in a text).

phony.o: Of unknown origin. Perhaps an alteration of fawny (“gilt brass ring used by swindlers”) (1781), from Irish fáinne (“ring”).
phony.example: He's such a phony, he doesn't believe half of what he says.
phony.exampleSense: A person who professes beliefs or opinions that they do not hold.

in turn.example: The boy was next in turn to sit on Santa's lap.
in turn.exampleSense: In due order; in proper sequence; in a determined or measured sequence, as a waiting line or queue.

triton.o:
noun: From trit- + -on. From tritium, from Ancient Greek τρίτος (trítos, “third”).

noun: From Triton, who blows such a seashell like a trumpet.

proceeds.example: They will donate net proceeds—whatever money is left after they pay their expenses—from the show to charity.

pseudo-.o: (but uncommon before Modern English), from Ancient Greek ψευδής (pseudḗs, “false, lying”).

monopolise.o: Alternative spelling of monopolize. From monopoly + -ize.
monopolise.example: Lord Norbourne wished to stay with the party till his nephew arrived, fully intending then to monopolise Lord Marchmont, and thus to leave Ethel to Courtenaye.

monopolize.example: Teachers try not to let any one student monopolize a class discussion.
monopolize.exampleSense: To dominate or to get total control of something by excluding everyone else.

responsiveness.example: Altogether, the present data show that the Toxoplasma-induced hypermigratory phenotype in a 3D matrix is consistent with integrin-independent amoeboid DC migration with maintained responsiveness to chemotactic and chemokinetic cues.
responsiveness.exampleSense: The quality or state of being responsive.

leaky.o: Likely a normalisation ( + -y) of earlier leak, leake, leke (“leaky”, adjective), from Middle English leke (“leaky”), from Old English hlec, *lec (“having cracks or rents; leaky”), from Proto-Germanic *lekaz (“leaking; leaky”). By surface analysis, leak + -y. Cognate with Scots lek, leck (“leaky”), Saterland Frisian läk (“leaky”), Dutch lek (“leaky”), German Low German leck (“leaky”), German leck (“leaky”), Swedish läck (“leaky”), Icelandic lekur (“leaky”).
leaky.example: The ceiling was so leaky that someone had to fix it.

microsecond.example: The data word processor 606 handles the in-flow and out-flow of byte-oriented input/output data and interleaved signals at a rate of, for example, 500 kilobytes per second. Instruction processing rates of four to eight per microsecond are required for such a data flow.
microsecond.exampleSense: An SI unit of time equal to 10⁻⁶ seconds. Symbol: μs It is commonly represented with symbol µs.

confines.example: It has not been used for many years, and although it was impracticable to photograph the engine in the small confines of the shed it was possible to obtain a picture of the plate which it still carries showing the former ownership.
confines.exampleSense: The borders or limits of an area.

functionality.example: Glu Mobile, who realigned its workforce towards centralized GaaS functions last year, announced earlier this month that it will shut down GameSpy Technology on May 31. The service provides multiplayer functionality for dozens of games on consoles, computers and mobile devices.
functionality.exampleSense: The ability to do a task, performance, or execution; a set of functions that something is able or equipped to perform.

escalation.example: Thousands of violent videos are still available on the internet, according to Alexander, who claims they lead to an escalation in offline tensions between rival gangs. "I believe some young people are losing their lives as result of this material on the internet," she said.
escalation.exampleSense: An increase or rise, especially to counteract a perceived discrepancy.

inspire.o: From Middle English inspiren, enspiren, from Old French inspirer, variant of espirer, from Latin īnspīrāre (“inspire”), itself a loan-translation of Biblical Ancient Greek πνέω (pnéō, “breathe”), from in + spīrō (“breathe”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)peys- (“to blow, breathe”). Displaced native Old English onbryrdan (literally “to prick in”).
inspire.example: He knew not his Maker, and him that inspired into him an active soul.
inspire.exampleSense: To infuse into the mind; to communicate to the spirit; to convey, as by a divine or supernatural influence; to disclose preternaturally; to produce in, as by inspiration.

allocate.o:
verb: From Latin allocātus, perfect passive participle of Latin allocō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from ad- (“to”) + locō. Doublet of allow. By surface analysis, al- + locate.

adj: From Middle English allocat(e) (“allocated”), originally used as the past participle of allocate, from Latin allocātus, see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and Etymology 1 for more.

noun: From Middle English allocate (the common first word of writs authorizing payment), from Medieval Latin allocātum, substantivized from the nominative neuter singular of allocātus, see -ate (noun-forming suffix) and Etymology 1 for more. Alternatively, from allocāte, the second-person plural imperative of allocō, compare English liberate (“a warrant for the payment of a pension, allowance, debt, etc.”).
allocate.example: The bulk of K–12 education funds are allocated to school districts that in turn pay for the cost of operating schools.
allocate.exampleSense: To distribute according to a plan, generally followed by the adposition to.

analogize.example: The teacher analogised swotting for an exam in terms of marathon training.

analogy.o: From Latin analogia, from Ancient Greek ἀναλογίᾱ (analogíā), from ἀνα- (ana-) + λόγος (lógos, “speech, reckoning”).
analogy.example: Is there any analogy, in certain constitutions, between keeping an umbrella up, and keeping the spirits up?
analogy.exampleSense: A relationship of resemblance or equivalence between two situations, people, or objects, especially when used as a basis for explanation or extrapolation.

analog.o: First attested in the early 19th century; from French analogue, from Ancient Greek ἀνάλογος (análogos, “proportionate”), from ἀνά (aná, “up to”) + λόγος (lógos, “ratio”). Equivalent to ana- (“functionally similar”) + -log.
analog.example: Not that I expect my children’s generation to be shocked by it all. Unlike my analog upbringing, they were born into a digital world.
analog.exampleSense: Not relating to, or pre-dating, digital technology such as computers and the Internet; relating to real life.

aforesaid.o: From Middle English aforesaid(e), aforeseid(e), past participle of aforesayen, aforeseyen, aforeseien, aforeseggen; formed with the prefix afore- and the several forms of seien (“to say”). Equivalent to afore- + said.
aforesaid.example: I soon took pity upon them and on myself, and rode off; but before I had crossed the aforesaid green glade, I heard their voices and laughter rising gaily as before. Very impertinent!
aforesaid.exampleSense: Previously stated; said or named before.

saguaro.o: From Mexican Spanish saguaro, from a Taracahitic Uto-Aztecan language, probably Yaqui, Mayo or Opata.
saguaro.example: The Pitella (pronounced Pitayo) and the Saguaro are the most prized.
saguaro.exampleSense: Carnegiea gigantea, a large cactus native to the Sonoran Desert and characterized by its "arms".

theft.o: From Middle English theft, thefte, þefte, þefþe, þiefþe, Old English þīefþ, from Proto-West Germanic *þiubiþu, from Proto-Germanic *þiubiþō, from *þeubaz (“thief”), equivalent to thief or thieve + -t (abstract nominal suffix). Cognate with Old Frisian thiuvethe, thiufthe (“theft”), dialectal Dutch diefte (“theft”), obsolete German Diebde (“theft”), Icelandic þýfð (“theft”).
theft.example: A suspect was arrested for the theft of a gold necklace.

alongside.exampleSense: Along the side; by the side; side by side; abreast.

terminate.o:
verb: From Middle English terminaten (“to bring to an end; to adjudicate; to end, stop; to border, confine, contain”) from terminat(e) (“bounded”, also used as the past participle of terminaten) + -en (verb-forming suffix), borrowed from Latin terminātus, perfect passive participle of terminō (“to set bounds to, bound, limit, end, close, terminate”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from terminus (“a bound, limit, end”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix); see term, terminus. Doublet of termine, cognate with French terminer.

adj: From Middle English terminat(e) (“bounded”, also used as the past participle of terminaten), see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and Etymology 1 for more.
terminate.example: One third is a recurring decimal, but one half is a terminate decimal.
terminate.exampleSense: Expressible in a finite number of terms; (of a decimal) not recurring or infinite.

hyphen.o: Learned borrowing from Late Latin hyphen, from Ancient Greek ῠ̔φέν (hŭphén, “in one, as a single word”), univerbation of ῠ̔φ’ ἕν (hŭph’ hén, “under one”), from ῠ̔πο- (hŭpo-, “under”) + ἕν (hén, “one”), neuter of εἷς (heîs, “one”).
hyphen.example: As the proud owner of my very own hyphen in a lovingly crafted surname, I have an especial soft spot for this most confusing of punctuation marks.
hyphen.exampleSense: The symbol "‐", typically used to join two or more words to form a compound term, or to indicate that a word has been split at the end of a line.

hymen.o: From Middle French hymen, from Late Latin hymēn, from Ancient Greek ὑμήν (humḗn, “skin; membrane”).

inheritor.o: From Middle English enheriter, enheritour. Displaced Old English ierfenuma. By surface analysis, inherit + -or.

registrar.o: From Medieval Latin registrārius, from registrum (“register”) + -ārius (“agent of use”). See more at register. By surface analysis, register /registry (“a record”) + -ar.

sandbox.example: Running a program in a sandbox can prevent it from doing any damage to the system.
sandbox.exampleSense: An isolated area where a program can be executed with a restricted portion of the resources available.

bar code.o: Alternative spelling of barcode. Compound of bar + code. First attested in 1963 for noun sense

bypass.o: From Middle English *bypassen, *bipassen (suggested by past participle by-past, bipast), equivalent to by- + pass.
bypass.example: Five of the 16 patients required simultaneous FF bypass and iliaco-femoral bypass; 2, required simultaneous FF bypass and iliac thrombo-endoarterectomy (Table II).
bypass.exampleSense: An alternative passage created to divert a bodily fluid around a damaged organ; the surgical procedure to construct such a bypass.

direction.o: From Middle English direccioun, from Old French direccion, from Latin dīrēctiō. Equivalent to direct + -ion.
direction.example: Keep going in the same direction.
direction.exampleSense: A theoretical line (physically or mentally) followed from a point of origin or towards a destination. May be relative (e.g. up, left, outbound, dorsal), geographical (e.g. north), rotational (e.g. clockwise), or with respect to an object or location (e.g. toward Boston).

front-end.o: Alternative form of front. From Middle English front, frunt, frount, from Old French front, frunt, from Latin frōns, frontem (“forehead”). Doublet of frons.

burnout.example: Ten years of this soul-sucking job would turn any ambitious young person into a burnout.
burnout.exampleSense: A person who has the experience of long-term exhaustion and diminished interest.

sociability.o: From Middle French sociabilité, from Latin sociābilis.
sociability.example: He was a true introvert, and his sociability lagged behind others of his age in the school.
sociability.exampleSense: The skill, tendency or property of being sociable or social, of interacting well with others.

depredate.o: Late Latin depraedari, depraedat-: Latin de- + praedari (“to plunder”).

degradation.example: There will be no poverty. All work will be done by living machines. Everybody will be free from worry and liberated from the degradation of labor. Everybody will live only to perfect himself.
degradation.exampleSense: The state of being reduced in rank, character, or reputation; baseness; moral, physical, or intellectual degeneracy; disgrace; abasement; debasement.

stiffy.example: Never leave home without a spare stiffy disc in your bag.
stiffy.exampleSense: A computer floppy disk of the kind supplied in a stiff plastic outer shell.

heterodox.o: From Ancient Greek ἑτερόδοξος (heteródoxos), from ἕτερος (héteros, “other, another, different”) + δόξα (dóxa, “opinion”).
heterodox.example: Most Christian denominations consider each other heterodox.
heterodox.exampleSense: Of or pertaining to creeds, beliefs, or teachings, especially religious ones, that are different from what a religion (or sect) believes to be orthodox, but (usually) not conflicting with that religion's established beliefs and therefore not heretical.

rephrase.example: Make sure to rephrase your thesis in your conclusion.
rephrase.exampleSense: To say or write something with different wording.

paranormal.o: From para- (“beyond”) + normal; compare supernatural. First use appears c. 1905.
paranormal.example: “We who study the paranormal always hope for strong readings with our equipment,” explains Nancy.
paranormal.exampleSense: That (ostensibly) cannot be explained by what scientists know; supernatural; especially of or pertaining to ghosts, spirits, and supposed abilities like telepathy.

guarantee.o: From Old French guarantie (perhaps via a later Spanish garante), from the verb guarantir (“to protect, assure, vouch for”), ultimately from Old Frankish *warjand, *warand (“a warrant”), or from guaranty. Doublet of guaranty and warranty.
guarantee.example: The cooker comes with a five-year guarantee.
guarantee.exampleSense: A written declaration that a certain product will be fit for a purpose and work correctly; a warranty.

not least.example: For a variety of reasons, not least because it is quite cheap.

securely.example: Check all personal items are securely stowed in the overhead lockers.
securely.exampleSense: In a secure manner; without fear or apprehension; without danger.

uncompromising.example: But Richmond, his grandfather's darling, after one thoughtful glance cast under his lashes at that uncompromising countenance appeared to lose himself in his own reflections.
uncompromising.exampleSense: Inflexible and unwilling to negotiate or make concessions.

compromising.o: present participle and gerund of compromise. From Middle French compromis, from Medieval Latin, Late Latin compromissum (“a compromise, originally a mutual promise to refer to arbitration”), prop. neuter of Latin compromissus, past participle of compromittere (“to make a mutual promise to abide by the decision of an arbiter”), from com- (“together”) + promittere (“to promise”); see promise.
compromising.example: A compromising photograph of the president was sold to the newspapers.
compromising.exampleSense: That compromises somebody or something; incriminating.

isolated.o: A rendering into English of French isolé.

non-negotiable.o: Alternative spelling of nonnegotiable. From non- + negotiable.

upside.example: The only upside of being over 35 is that you don't get raped as much.
upside.exampleSense: A favourable aspect of something that also has an unfavourable aspect.

variety.o: From Middle French varieté (“variety”) (modern French variété (“variety; genre, type”)) or directly from its etymon Latin varietās (“difference; diversity, variety”) + English -ty (suffix forming abstract nouns from adjectives); by surface analysis, various + -ety. Varietās is derived from varius (“different, diverse, various; variegated”) (possibly ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁weh₂- (“to abandon; to give out; to leave”)) + -tās (suffix forming feminine abstract nouns indicating a state of being). The English word displaced the native Old English mislīcnes. Sense 1.3.2 (“total number of distinct states of a system; logarithm to the base 2 of the total number of distinct states of a system”) was coined by the English psychiatrist William Ross Ashby (1903–1972) in his work An Introduction to Cybernetics (1956). Cognates * Galician variedade (“variety”) * Italian varietà (“difference; variety”) * Portuguese variedade (“variety”) * Spanish variedad (“breed; variety”)
variety.example: Capsicum annuum var. glabriusculum is a variety of Capsicum annuum commonly known as chiltepin or Indian pepper.
variety.exampleSense: A specific variation of something. An animal or plant (or a group of such animals or plants) with characteristics causing it to differ from other animals or plants of the same species; a strain or cultivar. A rank in a taxonomic classification below species and (if present) subspecies, and above form; hence, an organism of that rank.

para.o:
noun: Borrowed from Serbo-Croatian pàra /па̀ра, from Ottoman Turkish پاره (pare, para), from Persian پاره (pâre).

noun: Clipping of words such as primipara and multipara.

noun: Clippings.

adj: Clipping of paralytic.

noun: Borrowed from Urdu پاره (pāra), from Persian پاره (pâre).
para.example: She managed things with so much economy that she was enabled to save two paras every day, out of the piastre which he gave her.
para.exampleSense: A former subunit of currency in several countries in the Ottoman/Turkish and Yugoslav regions.

cornerstone.o: From Middle English corner ston; equivalent to corner + stone. The figurative sense is in part after Psalm 118:22, and is also quoted several times in the New Testament.
cornerstone.example: The cornerstone on the Flatiron Building is set on the Fifth Avenue facade.
cornerstone.exampleSense: Such a stone used ceremonially, often inscribed with the architect's and owner's names, dates and other details.

chancellery.o: From Middle English chancelrie, from Old French chancelerie (Modern French chancellerie), from Late Latin cancellaria. Doublet of chancery.

strikeout.example: We've had one strikeout after the other on the Jones account.
strikeout.exampleSense: An instance or the act of yielding nothing.

emeritus.o: The adjective is a learned borrowing from Latin ēmeritus (“(having been) earned, (having been) merited; (having been) served, having done one’s service”), the perfect passive participle of ēmereō (“to earn, merit; to gain by service; (military) to complete one’s obligation to serve, to serve out one’s time”), from ex- (prefix meaning ‘away; out’) + mereō (“to deserve, merit; to acquire, earn, get, obtain; to render service to; to serve”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)mer- (“to allot; to assign”)). The noun is derived from the adjective. The plural form emeriti is borrowed from Latin ēmeritī.
emeritus.example: Number and Description of Professorships. 1. An emeritus professorship of obstetrics.
emeritus.exampleSense: Retired, but retaining an honorific version of a previous title.

adjunct.o: From Latin adiunctus, perfect passive participle of adiungō (“join to”), from ad + iungō (“join”). Doublet of adjoint.
adjunct.example: When a female enters the profession, she is generally not referred to as doctor but as a lady doctor or woman doctor. The use of "feminizing" adjuncts designates a deviation from the norm, doctor, and does not carry the weight of the term unmodified.
adjunct.exampleSense: A phrase within a clause or sentence that is grammatically dispensable but not semantically so, modifying its meaning.

substitutable.example: Stevia is not substitutable for sugar in baking: the recipes won't work; they taste terrible.
substitutable.exampleSense: Capable of being used as a substitute; valid as a replacement or alternate item.

substantiation.o: From Latin substantiātiō. By surface analysis, substantiate + -ion.

unsubstantiated.o:
adj: From un- + substantiated.

verb: From unsubstantiate + -ed.
unsubstantiated.example: Such hedging is necessitated by the lack of in-depth knowledge of the contents, which also gives free rein to the scripting of unsubstantiated factoids concerning the book.

substantiate.o: From Medieval Latin substantiatus (“given substance”), from the verb substantiare, first used 1657.

plagiarize.o: From plagiary + -ize, ultimately from Latin plagiare (“to kidnap, to abduct”).

plagiary.o: From Latin plagiārius (“kidnapper, plagiarist”), from plagium (“kidnapping”), probably from plaga (“a net, snare, trap”).
plagiary.example: Without Invention a Painter is but a Copier, and a Poet but a Plagiary of others.

modelling.o: present participle and gerund of model. From Middle French modelle, from Old Italian modello, from Vulgar Latin *modellus, diminutive form of modulus (“measure, standard”), diminutive of modus (“measure”); see mode, and compare module, modulus, mould, mold.

peta-.o: Based on penta- (“five”) (from Ancient Greek πέντε (pénte)) with the middle letter removed, analogous to tera-.

giga-.o: From Ancient Greek γίγας (gígas, “giant”); cognate to giant.
giga-.example: Wow, I am giga-jealous right now.
giga-.exampleSense: Augmenting an adjective; intensely, extremely, or to an exceptionally high degree.

mega.o: From the prefix mega-, from Ancient Greek μέγας (mégas, “great, large, mighty”).
mega.example: We had a mega time until Peter fell in the fish pond and cut his leg.

coffin.o:
noun: From Middle English coffyn, from Old Northern French cofin (“sarcophagus", earlier "basket, coffer”), from Latin cophinus (“basket”), a loanword from Ancient Greek κόφινος (kóphinos, “a basket”). Doublet of coffer. Displaced native Old English þrūh.

noun: Borrowed from Cornish koghyn (“exploratory trench”), with spelling likely influenced by etymology
coffin.example: Indians do not hinder the progress of their dead by embalming or tight coffining.

spoof.o:
noun: Coined by the English comedian Arthur Roberts (1852–1933) in 1884 as the name of a card game involving deception and nonsense.

noun: Origin unknown; perhaps imitative of the spurting of a viscous liquid. Compare splooge, spoo (US slang), spooge, spaff.
spoof.example: However, MULTOPS assumes that packet rates between two hosts are proportional and the IP addresses are not spoofed.

spoofing.o: present participle and gerund of spoof. Coined by the English comedian Arthur Roberts (1852–1933) in 1884 as the name of a card game involving deception and nonsense.

musician.o: Inherited from Middle English musician, musicien, from Old French musicien (“musician”), equivalent to music + -ian.
musician.example: Jenny is a talented musician, playing the cello, saxophone, piano and guitar.
musician.exampleSense: A composer, conductor, or performer of music; specifically, a person who sings and/or plays a musical instrument as a hobby, occupation, or profession.

philosophise.o: Alternative spelling of philosophize. From philosophy + -ize.

misaligned.o: simple past and past participle of misalign. From mis- + align.

stocking stuffer.example: Gimbels is scintillating with last minute stocking stuffer ideas!
stocking stuffer.exampleSense: A small, relatively inexpensive Christmas present suitable for placing in a child's stocking, which was traditionally hung by a fireplace on Christmas Eve in anticipation that Santa Claus would fill it with gifts.

qualifier.example: But England's final qualifier, played out in the hostile surroundings of Podgorica City Stadium, turned on two incidents that will have cast a cloud over Capello's delight at reaching another major tournament.
qualifier.exampleSense: A preliminary stage of a competition.

nihility.o: From Renaissance Latin nihilitās, from Latin nihil (“nothing”).
nihility.example: Paeans and even poems have been written to the esoteric nature of the smallest building blocks of matter: how they manifest as everywhere and nowhere, seem to have come out of emptiness, and at the ultimate level seem to be distilled from pure nihility.
nihility.exampleSense: The state or fact of being nothing; nothingness, nullity; nonexistence.

nihilism.o: Probably borrowed from French nihilisme, German Nihilismus, or Late Latin nihilismus; the French, German, and Latin words are derived from Latin nihil (“indefinite nothing”), from nihilum (“nothing”), from ne- (prefix negating the principal meaning) + hīlum (“a trifle; not in the least”). The English word is cognate with Italian nichilismo, Spanish nihilismo, Russian нигили́зм (nigilízm), philosophical doctrine grounded on negation of one or more meaningful aspects of life; emptiness; lack of education and cultural refinement.
nihilism.example: The Government took up the word, and used nihilism to stigmatize all revolutionary, and ultra democratic and socialistic tendencies; and we have seen it play its part in the recent investigations into the attempted assassination of the Emperor.
nihilism.exampleSense: Alternative letter-case form of Nihilism (“a Russian movement of the 1860s that rejected all authority and promoted the use of violence for political change”)

retaliatory.example: The hostile forces were at an impasse; neither could attack with enough force and still defend against the retaliatory counterattack.
retaliatory.exampleSense: Relating to or part of a retaliation.

nuance.o: Borrowed from French nuance (“nuance, shade, hue”). Omitting several steps, from Latin nūbēs. Compare typologically Italian sfumatura (< Latin fūmus).
nuance.example: Understanding the basics is easy, but appreciating the nuances takes years.

repurpose.example: The town common was repurposed as a practice field.
repurpose.exampleSense: To reuse for a different purpose, on a long-term basis, with or without alteration.

consolidated.o: simple past and past participle of consolidate. Borrowed from Latin consolidātus, from the verb consolidō, from solidus (“solid”). By surface analysis, con- + solid + -ate.

ending.o:
noun: From Middle English endynge, endyng, endinge, from Old English endung, ġeendung (“ending”), equivalent to end + -ing. Cognate with Dutch ending (“ending”), German Endung (“ending”).

verb: From Middle English ending, endyng, endende, from Old English endiende, from Proto-Germanic *andijōndz, present participle of Proto-Germanic *andijōną (“to end”), equivalent to end + -ing.
ending.example: Spanish verb forms have different endings depending on the tense, mood and person.
ending.exampleSense: The last morpheme of a word, added to some base to make an inflected form (such as -s in "dogs").

insider.example: Heavy losses were sustained in Simms Petroleum, which took a greater toll from supposed "Wall Street insiders" than from the general public.
insider.exampleSense: A person who has special knowledge about the inner workings of a group, organization, or institution.

integer.o: Borrowed from Latin integer (“whole”), from Proto-Italic *n̥tagros (“untouched”). Doublet of entier and entire. Related to English tact, thack, and thwack.

miscellanea.o:
noun: Borrowed from Latin miscellānea, neuter plural of miscellāneus, from miscellus (“mixed”), from misceō (“to mix”).

noun: See the etymology of the corresponding lemma form.
miscellanea.example: Bright copper utensils, strings of onions, and gigantic sausages, wine-skins, chillies, and castanets hung with a miscellanea of all kinds from the roof and walls.
miscellanea.exampleSense: A miscellaneous collection of different things; a miscellany.

miscellaneous.o: Borrowed from Latin miscellāneus, from miscellus (“mixed”), from misceō (“mix”).
miscellaneous.example: A miscellaneous pile of clothing, buttons, tools and other junk.
miscellaneous.exampleSense: Consisting of a variety of ingredients or parts.

incremental.example: The replies to questions indicate that the technology provided noncontractually is generally more routine and incremental than that protected by contracts.
incremental.exampleSense: Occurring over a series of gradual increments, or small steps.

power.o: From Middle English power, poer, from Old French poeir, from Vulgar Latin potēre, from Latin posse, whence English potent. Compare French pouvoir. Displaced the native Old English anweald.
power.example: He's nominally president, but he does not have any real power.
power.exampleSense: The ability to coerce, influence, or control. The ability or authority to control, govern, command, coerce, etc., such as in a legal, political or business sphere.

trump.o:
noun: Possibly from French triomphe (“triumph”) or Old French triumphe. If so, it is a doublet of triumph and thriambus. Compare German Trumpf.

noun: From Middle English trumpe, trompe (“trumpet”), from Old French trompe (“horn, trump, trumpet”), from Frankish *trumpa (“trumpet”), from a common Germanic word of imitative origin. Doublet of tulumba and tromp. Akin to Old High German trumpa, trumba (“horn, trumpet”), Middle Dutch tromme (“drum”), Middle Low German trumme (“drum”). More at trumpet, drum.

noun: Ellipsis of Jew's-trump, which may be from French jeu-trompe (literally “toy trumpet”).
trump.example: He knew the hand was lost when his ace was trumped.
trump.exampleSense: To play on (a card of another suit) with a trump.

generalised.o: simple past and past participle of generalise. From general + -ise.

generalized.o: simple past and past participle of generalize. From general + -ize.
generalized.example: The generalized formula applies to all cases, the specialized one only works on simple problems.

diminished.o: simple past and past participle of diminish. Formed under the influence of both diminue (from Old French diminuer, from Latin dīminuo) and minish.
diminished.example: The diminished Roman Empire never recovered from the sack of Rome.

diminishing returns.example: He added, however, that the system operator is unlikely to use the cellphone alert often, lest Californians start to ignore it. The governor agreed that diminishing returns were a risk.
diminishing returns.exampleSense: A condition in which additional inputs into an organization, project or process produce progressively fewer or lower-quality additional outputs, and may, in extreme cases, cause the total quantity or quality of outputs to decrease.

diminishing.o: present participle and gerund of diminish. Formed under the influence of both diminue (from Old French diminuer, from Latin dīminuo) and minish.

estimation.o: From Middle English estimacioun, estimacion, from Old French estimacion, from Latin aestimatio. Morphologically estimate + -ion.
estimation.example: The publisher made an estimation on the potential value of the new novel.
estimation.exampleSense: The process of making an estimate.

count down.o: Alternative form of countdown. From count + down.
count down.example: The sound system counted down the seconds to meteor impact.
count down.exampleSense: To announce the passage of time to a precisely timed expected event.

authoritarianism.example: Instead of three co-equal branches acting as a check on each other, power has become increasingly concentrated over the years in the White House – a trend that is now being supercharged under Mr. Trump in ways that, to critics, raise the specter of authoritarianism.
authoritarianism.exampleSense: A form of government in which the governing body has absolute, or almost absolute, control. Typically this control is maintained by force, and little heed is paid to public opinion or the judicial system.

monocracy.example: A monocracy, as traditionalists called it, also seemed dangerous.

autocratic.example: Despite his lack of actual authority, his autocratic demeanour annoyed many of his colleagues.
autocratic.exampleSense: Of or pertaining to the manner of an autocrat.

autocrat.o: Borrowed from French autocrate, itself from Ancient Greek αὐτοκρατής (autokratḗs, “sovereign”), from αὐτο- (auto-, “self”) (combining form of αὐτός (autós)) + κράτος (krátos, “strength, power”) + -ης (-ēs). By surface analysis, auto- + -crat.
autocrat.example: Your salary is high; you are to have apartments in the house; and to be the autocrat of the library, where, I shrewdly suspect, your reign will be undisturbed.
autocrat.exampleSense: An absolute ruler with infinite power.

inverse.o: Recorded since 1440, from Latin inversus, the past participle of invertere (“to invert”), itself from in- (“against, in”) + vertere (“to turn”).
inverse.example: Cowgirl is the inverse of missionary.
inverse.exampleSense: An inverted state: a state in which something has been turned (properly) upside down or (loosely) inside out or backwards.

shamble.o: From Middle English schambyll, shamyll, schamel, from Old English sċeamol, scamol (“bench, stool”), from Proto-West Germanic *skamul, *skamil, from Proto-Germanic *skamulaz, *skamilaz, from Latin scamellum, a variant of scabellum (“footstool”). Cognate with West Frisian skammel (“shamble, trestle, stool", also (in the plural) "legs, especially when showing defects or deformities”), Dutch schemel (“footstool, bench”), German Schemel (“stool”), Danish skammel (“stool”). Icelandic skemill (“footstool”). The verb is probably derived from the adjective, itself from attributive use of the noun. Compare West Frisian skammelje (“to walk with a swaying gait, especially on deformed legs”).
shamble.example: I wasn't too impressed with the fellow, when he shambled in unenthusiastically and an hour late.
shamble.exampleSense: To walk while shuffling or dragging the feet.

rambler.example: I like being mother and wife. We've lived in a rambler in West Valley City, Utah for three years.

ramble.o: An altered form (with dissimilation of mm to mb) of dialectal rammle, from Middle English *ramlen, *ramelen, frequentative of Middle English ramen (“to roam, ramble”); compare Swedish ramla (“to stumble; fall; make a noise; rumble”), Danish ramle (“to stumble; collapse; thunder; boom”); equivalent to roam + -le. "mid-15 c., perhaps frequentative of 'romen' 'to walk, go' perhaps via 'romblen' (late 14 c.) 'to ramble.' The vowel change perhaps by influence of Middle Dutch 'rammelen,' a derivative of 'rammen' 'copulate,' 'used of the night wanderings of the amorous cat.' Meaning 'to talk or write incoherently' is from 1630s".
ramble.example: The river rambled through the mountains.
ramble.exampleSense: To follow a winding path or course.

amble.o: From Middle English amblen, from Old French ambler (“walk as a horse does”), from Old Occitan amblar, from Latin ambulō (“to walk”). Doublet of ambulate.

preamble.o: From Middle English preamble, from Old French preambule (French préambule), from Medieval Latin praeambulum, from praeambulō (“to walk before”).
preamble.example: The consultation preamble explains: "The planned timetable will be introduced in 2025 once we have completed the necessary steps required to ensure that we have enough resources to do so.
preamble.exampleSense: A short preliminary statement or remark, especially an explanatory introduction to a formal document or statute.

take over.example: If you will take over driving, I'd like to get some sleep.

architect.o: From Middle French architecte, from Latin architectus, from Ancient Greek ἀρχιτέκτων (arkhitéktōn, “master builder”), from ἀρχι- (arkhi-, “chief”) + τέκτων (téktōn, “builder”). By surface analysis, archi- + -tect.
architect.example: Plato made the causes of things to be matter, ideas, and an efficient architect.
architect.exampleSense: A professional who designs buildings or other structures, or who prepares plans and superintends construction.

entertainment.o: From Middle English entretenement (“support, maintenance”), from Old French entretenement; see entertain. Morphologically entertain + -ment.
entertainment.example: The delinquents are generally the adventurous type, who have little use for reading and other non-active entertainment.
entertainment.exampleSense: An activity designed to give pleasure, enjoyment, diversion, amusement, or relaxation to an audience, no matter whether the audience participates passively as in watching opera or a movie, or actively as in games.

crunch.o: From earlier craunch, cranch, of imitative origin.
crunch.example: The sound of our vessel crunching her way through the new ice is not easy to be described.
crunch.exampleSense: To grind or press with violence and noise.

tabulate.o:
verb: From Late Latin tabulātus (“having a floor; floored”), perfect passive participle of tabulō (“to fit with planks”), from tabula (“board, plank”), of uncertain origin, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *teh₂- (a variant of *steh₂- (“to stand”)) + *-dʰlom (a variant of *-trom (suffix forming nouns denoting tools or instruments)). Equivalent to table + -ate (verb-forming suffix).

noun: From Late Latin tabulāta (“thin board, plank, flooring”), or more likely a relatinized version of tablet through tabula.

adj: Back-formation from translingual Tabulata (“an extinct order of corals”) on the basis of -ate (adjective-forming suffix, corresponding to Latin -ātus (forming participles), itself seen in Tabulata), from Latin tabulāta, the nominative neuter plural of tabulātus (“floored”). See further at etymology

noun: From a substantivation of the former adjective through the associated taxon's name (Tabulata). Equivalent to tabula + -ate (forms nouns meaning "specimen of a corresponding taxon ending in -ata")
tabulate.example: The inevitable deduction from the figures tabulated must be that the material prosperity of the people as a whole is making good progress.
tabulate.exampleSense: To arrange in tabular form; to arrange into a table.

tribulation.o: From Middle English tribulation, from Old French tribulacion, from Late Latin trībulātiō (“distress, trouble, tribulation, affliction”), from Latin tribulāre (“to press, probably also thresh out grain”), from trībulum (“a sledge consisting of a wooden block studded with sharp pieces of flint or with iron teeth, used for threshing grain”), from terēre (“to rub”); see trite.
tribulation.example: Baltimore's tribulations were indeed sore; there was no peace for him day nor night.
tribulation.exampleSense: Any adversity; a trying period or event.

inhere.o: Borrowed from Latin inhaerēre (“stick in, stick to, inhere to”), from in (“in”) + haereō (“stick”); see hesitate. Compare adhere, cohere.
inhere.example: Sovereignty should inhere in the people and not the government, so governments forfeit sovereignty when they commit crimes against humanity.
inhere.exampleSense: To be inherent; to be an essential or intrinsic part of; to be fixed or permanently incorporated with something.

color.o: From Middle English colour, color, borrowed from Anglo-Norman colur, from Old French colour, color, from Latin color. Doublet of couleur. Largely displaced English blee, Middle English blee (“color”), from Old English blēo. Also partially replaced Old English hīew (“color”) and its descendants (English hue), which is less often used in this sense. The spelling color was popularized in modern American English by Noah Webster, to match the spelling of the word's Latin etymon, and make all American spellings of the derivatives consistent (colorimeter, coloration, colorize, colorless, etc).
color.example: There is a great deal of colour in his writing.
color.exampleSense: Richness of expression; detail or flavour that is likely to generate interest or enjoyment.

vowel.o: From Middle English vowel, from Old French vouel, a variant of voyeul (whence French voyelle), from Latin vōcālis (“voiced”), itself a semantic loan of Koine Greek φωνῆεν (phōnêen). Doublet of vocal and vocalis.
vowel.example: Facetiously is spelled with all six vowels in alphabetical order.
vowel.exampleSense: A letter representing the sound of a vowel; in English, the vowels are a, e, i, o, u, y.

along with.example: She fired all the journalists in the company, along with some of the administration workers.

shorten.o: From Middle English shortnen, schortenen, equivalent to short + -en (verbal suffix). In some senses, a continuation (in altered form) of Middle English schorten (“to make short, shorten”), from Old English sċortian (“to become short”), from Proto-Germanic *skurtōną (“to shorten”).
shorten.example: York came round to our heads and shortened the rein himself, one hole I think; every little makes a difference, be it for better or worse, and that day we had a steep hill to go up.

lengthen.example: You need to lengthen the story if you want to have it published.
lengthen.exampleSense: To make longer, to extend the length of.

succeeding.o: present participle and gerund of succeed. From Old French succeder, from Latin succedere (“to go under, go from under, come under, approach, follow, take the place of, receive by succession, prosper, be successful”). Partly displaced English speed, of which the original sense “to succeed” only survives in a few fossilized expressions such as Godspeed.
succeeding.example: At her invitation he outlined for her the succeeding chapters with terse military accuracy ; and what she liked best and best understood was avoidance of that false modesty which condescends, turning technicality into pabulum.

preceding.o: From Middle English precedyng, precedenge, present participle of Middle English preceden (“to precede”), equivalent to precede + -ing.
preceding.example: On the preceding Monday Shobana had gone on vacation.
preceding.exampleSense: Occurring before or in front of something else, in time, place, rank or sequence.

domestically.example: Athletic have been showing signs of fatigue domestically and they never quite seemed to reach the same pitch of intensity that had so unsettled Manchester United and Schalke 04 in earlier rounds.
domestically.exampleSense: at home, playing in one's home ground

domesticity.example: The Neolithic of 8000 to 6000 B.C. is in the sign of Cancer, a feminine sign associated with domesticity, retentiveness, and sentiment.

castoff.example: Found art is created when odd, disparate, unlikely, even long-abandoned castoffs are put together with other similarly unexpected remnants to create something new and, if all goes as planned, lovely.
castoff.exampleSense: Something that has been rejected or discarded; a reject.

cast off.example: However, with the dainty volume my quondam friend sprang into fame. At the same time he cast off the chrysalis of a commonplace existence.

discard.o: From dis- + card. Compare Spanish descartar.
discard.example: A man discards the follies of boyhood.

supposition.o: From Middle English supposicioun, from Anglo-Norman supposicion, from Latin suppositiō, suppositiōnem (“supposition”), from sub- (“under”) + positiō, positiōnem (“position; theme”), from positus (“position”), from the perfect passive participle of pōnō, pōnere (“put, place”).

intermission.o: Derived from Latin intermissiō, from intermittō (“interrupt, omit”) + -tiō.
intermission.example: We ordered some drinks for the intermission.
intermission.exampleSense: A break, especially between two performances or sessions, such as at a concert, play, seminar, or religious assembly.

tenured.o: simple past and past participle of tenure. From Middle English tenure, from Anglo-Norman, from Old French tenure, from Vulgar Latin *tenitura, from *tenitus, from Latin tentus (from teneō) + -ura.

gaming.o: present participle and gerund of game. From Middle English game, gamen, gammen, from Old English gamen (“sport, joy, mirth, pastime, game, amusement, pleasure”), from Proto-West Germanic *gaman, from Proto-Germanic *gamaną (“amusement, pleasure, game", literally "participation, communion, people together”), from *ga- (collective prefix) + *mann- (“man”); or alternatively from *ga- + a root from Proto-Indo-European *men- (“to think, have in mind”). Cognate with Yola gaame, gaaume, gaume (“game”), Old Frisian game, gome (“joy, amusement, entertainment”), Dutch gemelijk (“cantankerous, crabbed”), Middle High German gamen (“joy, amusement, fun, pleasure”), Danish gammen (“merriment”), Icelandic, Norwegian Nynorsk gaman (“joy, fun”), Swedish gamman (“mirth, rejoicing, merriment”). Related to gammon, gamble.

terminator.o: * Partly from post-classical Latin terminator (5th century), from Latin terminō; partly from terminate + -or. * (android that kills humans): After the 1984 film The Terminator.
terminator.example: Opposite of natural monsters there are technological monsters such as terminators, cyborgs, and robocops—all of which undermine dichotomies between the artificial and the organic, the prosthetic and the natural.
terminator.exampleSense: An intelligent android created to destroy humans.

destructive.o: From Middle English destructyve, from Middle French destructif, from Latin dēstrūctīvus, from past participle of dēstruere (“to tear down, destroy”) + -īvus.
destructive.example: The pastures are filled with gay political drop-outs, persons of reasonable intent who found the scene personally destructive.

rejection.o: From French réjection or directly from Latin reiectiōnem, accusative of Latin reiectiō. Displaced native Old English āworpennes (literally “thrown-out-ness”).

automatize.o: From French automatiser, from automate (“automaton”). Equivalent to automate + -ize.
automatize.example: Student responses are gradually automatized through repetition.

wiper.o:
noun: From wipe + -er.

noun: From white (bass) and striper.
wiper.example: Using her hands like windshield wipers, she tried to flick snow away from her mouth. When she clawed at her chest and neck, the crumbs maddeningly slid back onto her face. She grew claustrophobic.
wiper.exampleSense: Something, such as a windscreen wiper, that is designed for wiping.

power walking.o: present participle and gerund of power. From Middle English power, poer, from Old French poeir, from Vulgar Latin potēre, from Latin posse, whence English potent. Compare French pouvoir. Displaced the native Old English anweald.

solenoid.o: From French solénoïde, from Ancient Greek σωληνοειδής (sōlēnoeidḗs) (from σωλήν (sōlḗn, “channel, pipe”) + -ειδής (-eidḗs); see -oid).

slapdash.o: From slap + dash. First attested in the late 17th century, meaning "careless".
slapdash.example: They had seen Poland, and that was the sort of slovenly, slapdash place they were used to, but once across the German frontier they found everything—crops, roads, buildings—uncannily different.
slapdash.exampleSense: Produced or carried out hastily; haphazard; careless.

perfunctorily.example: Lim Cheng Po said an Anglican prayer or two, not too perfunctorily.
perfunctorily.exampleSense: In a perfunctory manner, without interest or concern for quality.

perfunctory.o: From Late Latin perfunctōrius (“careless, negligent”), from the past participial stem of perfungor, perfunct- (“perform, carry through”), from per- + fungor.
perfunctory.example: He then poured some wine for me to taste, and harassed me with perfunctory courtesies that had to be acknowledged.
perfunctory.exampleSense: Done only or merely to conform to a minimal standard or to fulfill a protocol or presumptive duty.

peaceful.o:
adj: From Middle English peesful, pesful, paisful, pesefull. By surface analysis, peace + -ful.

noun: Derived from the derogatory term religion of peace, which is used against Islam itself for its association with violent attacks by Islamic extremists, and alleged support and lack of condemnation against them by certain Muslim communities.
peaceful.example: Attractive cottages look out on a scene so peaceful that lapping wavelets, stirred by the breeze, are often the loudest sound to be heard.

quest.o:
noun: From Middle English quest, queste; partly from Anglo-Norman queste, Old French queste (“acquisition, search, hunt”), and partly from their source, Latin quaesta (“tribute, tax, inquiry, search”), noun use of quaesita, the feminine past participle of quaerō (“to ask, seek”).

noun: Blend of quiz + test, to avoid using the word test.
quest.example: Next day we quested in search of our caravan, and after some pains recovered it.
quest.exampleSense: To search for something; to seek.

populate.o: Borrowed from Medieval Latin populātus, past participle of populor (“populate”), from Latin populus (“people”).
populate.example: John clicked the Search button and waited for the list to populate.
populate.exampleSense: To fill initially empty items in a collection.

interpose.o: From Middle French interposer, influenced by poser (“to place, put”), from Latin interpōnō, from inter (“between”) + pōnō (“to place, put”).

factor.o: From Middle French facteur, from Latin factor (“a doer, maker, performer”), from factus (“done or made”), perfect passive participle of faciō (“do, make”).
factor.example: 3 is a factor of 12, as are 2, 4 and 6.
factor.exampleSense: Any of various objects multiplied together to form some whole.

disciplinary.o: From Medieval Latin disciplinarius, from Latin disciplina (“instruction, teaching, field of study, habit”).
disciplinary.example: We hope that psychologists will applaud good studies of scientific behavior and thought regardless of the disciplinary specialty of the author.
disciplinary.exampleSense: Of or relating to an academic field of study.

pedagogy.o: From Middle French pédagogie, from Ancient Greek παιδαγωγία (paidagōgía). By surface analysis, ped- (“child”) + -agogy.
pedagogy.example: A resource that profiles the important language of secondary disciplines by adapting the methods of EAP research could therefore be very useful for such pedagogy.
pedagogy.exampleSense: The strategies or methods of instruction; an educational philosophy.

pedagogic.o: First attested in 1781. From French pédagogique, from Latin paedagōgicus, pēdagōgicus, from Ancient Greek παιδαγωγικός (paidagōgikós), from παιδαγωγός (paidagōgós, “teacher, tutor”), from παῖς (paîs, “child”) + ἄγω (ágō, “to lead”).

pedagogical.example: The value of pedagogical material informed by objective methodological procedures developed in corpus linguistics is widely recognized.
pedagogical.exampleSense: Of, or relating to pedagogy; teaching.

bap.o:
noun: Originally Scottish English, of unknown origin.

intj: Onomatopoeic.

noun: Borrowed from Korean 밥 (bap).
bap.example: He lost the bap. ― He became angry.

abstract.o: From Middle English abstract, borrowed from Latin abstractus, perfect passive participle of abstrahō (“draw away”), formed from abs- (“away”) + trahō (“to pull, draw”). The verbal sense is first attested in 1542.
abstract.example: He abstracted out the square root function.
abstract.exampleSense: To separate; to disengage. To consider abstractly; to contemplate separately or by itself; to consider theoretically; to look at as a general quality. To produce an abstraction, usually by refactoring existing code. Generally used with "out".

pilot.o: From Middle French pilot, pillot, from Italian pilota, piloto, older also pedotta, pedot(t)o (the form in pil- is probably influenced by pileggiare (“to sail, navigate”)); ultimately from unattested Byzantine Greek *πηδώτης (*pēdṓtēs, “helmsman”), from Ancient Greek πηδόν (pēdón, “blade of an oar, oar”), hence also Ancient and Modern Greek πηδάλιον (pēdálion, “rudder”).
pilot.example: So we mounted our horses, and put out for that town, under the direction of two friendly Creeks we had taken for pilots.
pilot.exampleSense: A guide or escort through an unknown or dangerous area.

aligned.o: simple past and past participle of align. From Middle English alynen, alinen (“copulate”), from Middle French aligner, from Old French alignier, from a- + lignier, from Latin lineare (“make straight or perpendicular”), from the noun linea (“line”), from līneus (“flaxen; flaxen [thing]”), from līnum (“flax”), likely ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *līnom (compare linen).
aligned.example: AI research and development should be refocused on making today's powerful, state-of-the-art systems more accurate, safe, interpretable, transparent, robust, aligned, trustworthy, and loyal.
aligned.exampleSense: Allied or working together with a common goal.

parse.o: Possibly from Middle English pars (“parts, shares; parts of speech, grammar”), from Old French pars (plural of part (“part, portion, share”)), from Latin pars (“part, piece, share”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *per- (“to carry forth; to sell”).
parse.example: The parse will fail if the program contains an unrecognised keyword.
parse.exampleSense: An act of parsing; a parsing.

subsequently.example: It will be recollected that the ill-fated Halloway...distinctly stated the voice of the individual who had approached his post...to have been that of a female, and that the language in which they subsequently conversed was that of the Ottawa Indians.
subsequently.exampleSense: Following, afterwards in either time or place.

semantics.o: From French sémantique, displacing earlier semasiology. From Ancient Greek σημαντικός (sēmantikós). By surface analysis, semantic + -ics.
semantics.example: The semantics of a single preposition is a dissertation in itself.
semantics.exampleSense: The individual meanings of words, as opposed to the overall meaning of a passage.

specifically.example: Many laws are directed specifically at child abuse.
specifically.exampleSense: In a specific manner, applying to or naming a particular thing or things, expressly, explicitly.

aforethought.example: This act was not merely wrong; it was clearly done with malice aforethought.

aforetime.o: From Middle English a fore tyme, afore tyme, aforetyme, afortym, a-for-tyme, afortymez; equivalent to afore- + time.
aforetime.example: Prov. 8:23 מקַּדמי ארץ really means from all the aforetimes of the earth.

afore.o: From Middle English afore, aforn, from Old English onforan or ætforan; equivalent to a- + fore.
afore.example: A chap named Eleazir Kendrick and I had chummed in together the summer afore and built a fish-weir and shanty at Setuckit Point, down Orham way. For a spell we done pretty well.

aforementioned.example: It wasn't until later that we realized that the aforementioned caller and this taciturn man were the same person.

endangered.o: simple past and past participle of endanger. From en- + danger. Displaced native Old English frēcnian.

endanger.o: From en- + danger. Displaced native Old English frēcnian.
endanger.example: All the other difficulties of his reign only exercised without endangering him.
endanger.exampleSense: To put (someone or something) in danger; to risk causing harm to.

attach.o: From Middle English attachen, from Old French atachier, variant of estachier (“bind”), derived from estache (“stick”), from Frankish *stakkā, *stakō (“stick”), from Proto-Germanic *stakô (“pole, bar, stick, stake”). Doublet of attack. More at stake, stack. Displaced native Old English þīedan.
attach.example: The great interest which attaches to the mere knowledge of these facts cannot be doubted.

isolate.o: Back-formation from isolated, from French isolé, from Italian isolato, from Latin īnsulatus (whence also insulate), see -ate (etymology 1, 2 and 3).
isolate.example: To isolate the petroline the condensed oil is distilled again until fifty per cent. of oil has been obtained, and what is left in the still is petroline.
isolate.exampleSense: To separate a substance in pure form from a mixture.

by extension.example: He argued that the failure of a democratic government, by extension, meant the failure of the people.
by extension.exampleSense: Used to connect the internal logic of two statements.

preset.example: To save these settings as a preset, click the Add button in the lower-left corner of the dialog and give the preset a name.
preset.exampleSense: A setting that is set in advance.

primer.o:
noun: From Middle English primer, primere, from Medieval Latin primarius and primarium (“prayer book”) possibly via Anglo-Norman primer (“prayer book”), from prima (“prime the liturgical hour and office”) + -arius and -arium (suffix forming related objects). Its use for schoolbooks derived from the late medieval and early modern use of such prayer books to teach reading.

noun: From prime + -er.

adj: From Anglo-Norman primer (“first”), from Latin prīmārius (“first”).
primer.example: The percussion primer, known as the “ 110-grain percussion primer,” contains an igniting charge of 95 grains of black powder in addition to the essential elements of a percussion primer.
primer.exampleSense: Any substance or device, such as priming wire or blasting cap, used to ignite gunpowder or other explosive.

severely.example: After the first day they left her severely alone, their plea to their husbands, her uncompromising independence.

de facto.o: Unadapted borrowing from Latin dē factō (literally “according to fact”), from dē (“according to”) + ablative of factum (“fact, deed, act”).
de facto.example: Although the United States currently has no official language, it is largely monolingual with English being the de facto national language.
de facto.exampleSense: In actual use or existence, regardless of official or legal status.

region.o: From Middle English regioun, from Anglo-Norman regiun, from Latin regiō, from regō. Doublet of regio.
region.example: The average age of the club's members is in the region of 35.

aka.example: The Arkansas Legislature, aka the broligarchy, does not believe in the people’s right to the ballot process. This is as disappointing as is it unconstitutional, though the unconstitutionality isn’t stopping the bill’s sponsors.

quota.o: From Latin quota pars; see Latin quota.

enforce.o: From Middle English enforcen, from Old French enforcier, from Late Latin infortiāre, from in- + fortis (“strong”).
enforce.example: In a few minutes I was stealthily groping my way down my own staircase, with a box of matches in my hand, enforced by scientific curiosity, but none the less armed with a stick.
enforce.exampleSense: To compel, oblige (someone or something); to force.

unrealistic.example: How much of our thinking is based on unrealistic planted scripts of drama, romance and violence?

last but not least.o: Rhetoric: A possible/common pattern to arrange a speech or essay suggests putting your strongest and thus most important argument favoring your own opinion first and conclude with the weakest, thus least important argument.

squiggle.o: Probably a blend of squirm + wiggle.
squiggle.example: Even the cold ashes where a gipsy's fire had been sent little squiggles of fear down Laura's spine, for how could she know that they were not still lurking near with designs upon her own person?
squiggle.exampleSense: A short twisting or wiggling line or mark.

express.o:
adj: From French exprès, from Latin expressus, past participle of exprimere (see Etymology 2, below).

verb: From Old French espresser, expresser, from frequentative form of Latin exprimere.
express.example: This is also a TransPennine Express service which makes a mockery of the word 'express'.
express.exampleSense: A mode of transportation, often a train, that travels quickly or directly.

rift.o:
noun: From Middle English rift, of North Germanic origin; akin to Danish rift, Norwegian Bokmål rift (“breach”), Old Norse rífa (“to tear”). More at rive.

verb: From Old Norse rypta.
rift.example: The Grand Canyon is a rift in the Earth's surface, but is smaller than some of the undersea ones.

pierce.o:
verb: From Middle English perce, from conjugated forms of Old French percier such as (jeo) pierce (“I pierce”), probably from Vulgar Latin *pertūsiō, from Latin pertūsus, past participle of pertundō (“thrust or bore through”), from per- (“through”) + tundō (“beat, pound”). Displaced native Old English þȳrlian (literally “to hole”).

noun: Borrowed from Japanese ピアス (piasu, “pierced earring”), itself from English pierce.

self-awareness.o: From self- + awareness. Also equivalent to self-aware + -ness, though attested earlier.

significantly.example: The quality of life is significantly higher than it was twenty years ago.
significantly.exampleSense: In a significant manner or to a significant extent.

query.o: An anglicisation of quere, an obsolete variant form of Latin quaere, second-person singular present active imperative of quaerō (“seek, look for; ask”); perhaps suffixed with -y (“abstract noun”). Cognate with French quérir, Italian chiedere, Portuguese querer, Romanian cere, and Spanish querer. Compare question.
query.example: I refer you to your line above, where you use a query and a bang together.

abreact.o: Partial calque of German abreagieren, from ab (“away from, off, down from”) + reagieren (“to react”), equivalent to ab- + react.

secretarial.o: From a Latin-type formation *sēcrētāriālis, from Medieval Latin sēcrētārius + Latin -ālis. By surface analysis, secretary + -al.

drastic.o: From Ancient Greek δραστικός (drastikós, “active, efficient”), from δρᾶσις (drâsis, “strength, efficacy”), itself from δράω (dráō, “to do”).
drastic.example: If our third attempt fails, we may need drastic ideas.
drastic.exampleSense: Having a strong or far-reaching effect; extreme, severe.

multifold.example: There are many drug lords, each with his own corridor (think of it as a franchise of sorts) funneling narcotics into Texas. There are multifold methods of transport.

extermination.o: Borrowed from Middle French extermination, itself a learned borrowing from Ecclesiastical Latin exterminātiō.
extermination.example: Depending on the case, extermination of a group of people may constitute genocide or crime against humanity.
extermination.exampleSense: The act of exterminating; total destruction or eradication.

termination.o: Borrowed from Latin terminationem (accusative of terminatio).
termination.example: She speaks poniards, and every word stabs: if her breath were as terrible as her terminations, there were no living near her; she would infect to the north star.

verified.o: simple past and past participle of verify. From Old French verifier (French: vérifier), from Medieval Latin vērificāre (“make true”), from Latin vērus (“true”) + faciō (“do, make”); see -fy.
verified.example: Only verified cardholders are eligible for the discount.

defense.o:
noun: From Middle English defens, defense, from Old French defens, defense, from Late Latin dēfēnsa (“protection”). Displaced native Old English bewering. The verb is from the noun.

verb: From Middle English defencen, defensen, from Old French defenser or its etymon, Latin dēfēnsō.
defense.example: In fact, there is an increase in the effectiveness of the Five Cutter Offense when teams put pressure on, instead of sagging or switching in an attempt to defense the attack successfully.
defense.exampleSense: To employ defensive tactics (so as to block).

transversal.o: From Middle French transversal, from Medieval Latin trānsversālis, from Latin trānsversus.
transversal.example: Let l and m be two hyperparallel lines. All the transversals to l and m that form congruent corresponding angles with l and m lie in a pencil.
transversal.exampleSense: A line which traverses or intersects any system of other lines transversely. A line intersecting a pair of parallel lines.

antagonize.o: From Ancient Greek ἀνταγωνίζομαι (antagōnízomai), from ἀντι- (anti-) + ἀγωνίζομαι (agōnízomai). By surface analysis, ant- + agon + -ize.
antagonize.example: The other children constantly antagonized Joe to the point of tears.
antagonize.exampleSense: To work against; to oppose (especially to incite a reaction).

uppercase.example: In German, the ß character is called eszett. It’s used in “Straße,” the word for street, and in the expletive “Scheiße.” It’s often transliterated as “ss,” and strangely enough, it’s never had an official uppercase counterpart.

lowercase.o: From the noun phrase lower case, which itself consists of an adjective modifying a noun; when used as a noun adjunct then, to render its syntactical function clearer and simpler, it is written as a single word or with a hyphen as a sort of chunking.
lowercase.example: I never asked Rob e. Hanson why he lowercased his middle initial; I suppose he figured a man just shouldn’t accumulate too much capital.

separator.example: When applying polish, always use toe separators to keep toes apart.
separator.exampleSense: An object located between two or more things and hence separating them.

capitalization.example: I doubt if one of them was interested in any business the total capitalization of which exceeded a couple of hundred thousand dollars.
capitalization.exampleSense: US and Oxford British English standard spelling of capitalisation.

fallback.example: As a fallback, I suppose we can use typewriters if the word processing system fails.
fallback.exampleSense: A backup plan or contingency strategy; an alternative which can be used if something goes wrong with the main plan; a recourse.

fall back on.example: So I fell back on the simple methods of the plainsman and Indian and jogged along on their trail.
fall back on.exampleSense: To turn to as a substitute; to rely on as a backup.

latter.o: From Middle English latter, lattere, lattre, from Old English lætra, comparative form of læt (“late”). Equivalent to late + -er, thus a doublet of later; also, related to last, whose doublet is latest.
latter.example: On sale next to dried fish and chicken feet were rats and bats (the latter's wings in a pile like leather scraps, also for sale), plus cut-up pigs and monkeys, their faces intact.
latter.exampleSense: Relating to or being the second of two items.

multilingual.example: In reality, the multidimensionality of language contact in multilingual environments ensures no such neat compartmentalisation.
multilingual.exampleSense: Of, relating to, or involving multiple languages.

colon.o:
noun: From Latin cōlon (“a member of a verse of poem”), from Ancient Greek κῶλον (kôlon, “a member, limb, clause, part of a verse”).

noun: From Latin cŏlon (“large intestine”), from Ancient Greek κόλον (kólon, “the large intestine, also food, meat, fodder”).

noun: From French colon.
colon.example: A colon tells the reader that what follows is closely related to the preceding clause.

shade.o:
noun: Inherited from Middle English schade, from Old English sċeadu, from Proto-West Germanic *skadu, from Proto-Germanic *skaduz, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ḱh₃tús, from *(s)ḱeh₃-. Doublet of shadow. Cognate with Ancient Greek σκότος (skótos) (whence English scoto-) and σκιά (skiá) (whence English scia-, and uncertainly via σκίουρος (skíouros) English squirrel).

verb: Inherited from Middle English schaden, from schade + -en.
shade.example: The old oak tree shaded the lawn in the heat of the day.
shade.exampleSense: To shield (someone or something) from light.

causal.o: Borrowed from Late Latin causalis, from Latin causa (“cause”), equivalent to cause + -al, see cause.
causal.example: There is no causal relationship between eating carrots and seeing in the dark.
causal.exampleSense: of, relating to, or being a cause of something; causing

truncation.o: From Late Latin truncātiō, from Latin truncāre, past participle truncātus (“to cut off”). By surface analysis, truncate + -ion.

unsung.example: The backstage crew of the movie were the unsung heroes.
unsung.exampleSense: Which has not been lauded or appreciated.

arguably.example: In the early 1770s the bogey figure for opposition politicians was arguably not so much North in the Commons as Mansfield behind the curtain, the country's greatest lawyer (and another Caledonian to gratify the Scotophobes) keeping an irresolute Cabinet committed to waging war in America.
arguably.exampleSense: As can be supported or proven by sound logical deduction, evidence, and precedent, but without absolute certainty.

merry-go-round.example: Some of us are lucky enough to still have families that care. But more often than not, we find that we have lost contact with the outside world, which leaves us very vulnerable in the merry-go-round of the parole process.
merry-go-round.exampleSense: A meaningless cycle; a bustle of activity that gets nowhere

merry.o:
adj: From Middle English myrie, merie, mery, from Old English myrġe, myriġe (“pleasing, agreeable; pleasant, sweet, delightful; melodious”), from Proto-West Germanic *murgī (“short, slow, leisurely”), from Proto-Germanic *murguz (“short, slow”), from Proto-Indo-European *mréǵʰus (“short”). Cognate with Scots mery, mirry (“merry”), Middle Dutch mergelijc (“pleasant, agreeable, joyful”), Norwegian dialectal myrjel (“small object, figurine”), Latin brevis (“short, small, narrow, shallow”), Ancient Greek βραχύς (brakhús, “short”). Doublet of brief.

noun: From French merise.
merry.example: We had a very merry Christmas.
merry.exampleSense: Jolly and full of high spirits; happy.

downside.example: The downside of obtaining a higher rank is that far more work is expected.
downside.exampleSense: A disadvantageous aspect of something that is normally advantageous.

bard.o:
noun: (15th c.) from Scottish Gaelic bàrd, from Old Irish bard, from Proto-Celtic *bardos (“bard, poet”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʷerH- (“praise”), and reinforced by Latin bardus, borrowed from Celtic. Cognate with Latin grātus (“grateful, pleasant, delightful”), Sanskrit गृणाति (gṛṇāti, “calls, praises”), Old Church Slavonic жрьти (žrĭti, “to sacrifice”).

noun: From French barde. English since the late 15th century.
bard.example: A WEAPON, THE WARRIOR CARRIES. A SAW, THE IDIOT CARRIES. AN INSTRUMENT, THE BARD CARRIES.
bard.exampleSense: A professional poet and singer, like among the ancient Celts, whose occupation was to compose and sing verses in honor of the heroic achievements of princes and brave men.

playground.o: From play + ground. Compare Middle English playstede (“playground”) from Old English pleġstede.
playground.example: The kids have to go to the playground during recess, no matter the weather.
playground.exampleSense: A large open space for children to play in, usually having dedicated play equipment (such as swings and slides).

interface.example: The surface of a lake is a water-air interface.
interface.exampleSense: A thin layer or boundary between different substances or two phases of a single substance.

interfacing.o: present participle and gerund of interface. From inter- (“between”) + face (“shape, figure, form”).

thus far.example: Barry removed Pawlisch last July and the former board member has sought reinstatement to his seat, thus far without success.

thus.o: From Middle English thus, þus, from Old English þus (“thus, in this way, as follows, in this manner, to this extent”), from Proto-West Germanic *þus (“so, thus”), perhaps originally from a variant of the instrumental form of this, related to Old English þȳs (“by this, with this”), Old Saxon thius (“by this, with this”). Cognate with Scots thus (“thus”), North Frisian thus, Saterland Frisian dus, düs (“thus”), West Frisian dus (“thus”), Dutch dus (“thus, so”), Middle High German dus (“thus, as follows”). Compare also Dutch zus (“thus, hence”), Low German sus (“thus, hence”), Middle High German sus (“thus, hence”), a similar formation from the stem of Proto-West Germanic *swā (“so”).
thus.example: If you throw the ball thus, as I’m showing you, you’ll have better luck hitting the target.

regulation.example: Army regulations state a soldier AWOL over 30 days is a deserter.
regulation.exampleSense: A law or administrative rule, issued by an organization, used to guide or prescribe the conduct of members of that organization.

copyrighted.o: simple past and past participle of copyright. From copy + right.

misleading.example: The problem does not appear so hopeless when misleading metaphor is discarded.
misleading.exampleSense: Deceptive or tending to mislead or create a false impression, even if technically true.

necessarily.example: It is not necessarily true that children get their morals from their parents.

unintended.example: The most powerful and least divisive way to decrease abortion is to reduce unintended pregnancy.

accountability.example: The erosion of accountability doesn't seem to matter now, but it will matter when things start unraveling.
accountability.exampleSense: An acceptance of good faith of one's responsibility for something and of its consequences.

unclear.o: From Middle English unclere, equivalent to un- + clear. Compare Saterland Frisian uunkloor (“unclear”), West Frisian ûnklear (“inoperative, broken”), Dutch onklaar (“out of order, defective, broken”), German unklar (“unclear”), Danish uklar (“unclear”), Swedish oklar (“unclear”).
unclear.example: I'm still unclear about what she meant by that remark.
unclear.exampleSense: Not having a clear idea; uncertain.

seldom.o: From late Middle English seldom, alteration of earlier selden by analogy with adverbial datives such as whilom, from Old English seldan (“seldom”), from Proto-West Germanic *seldanā, from Proto-Germanic *seldanē. Cognate with Saterland Frisian säilden (“seldom”), West Frisian selden, komselden (“rare, seldom”), Dutch zelden, German selten, Danish sjælden, Norwegian Bokmål sjelden, Norwegian Nynorsk sjeldan, Swedish sällan, Faroese sjáldan, Icelandic sjaldan. More at seld and selly.

fairness.o: From Middle English fairness, fæȝernesse, from Old English fæġernes (“fairness; beauty; pleasantness”), equivalent to fair + -ness. Cognate with Old High German fagarnessi (“fairness”).
fairness.example: Some questioned the fairness of the new laws.
fairness.exampleSense: The property of being fair or equitable.

partially.example: In all 5 untreated coeliacs as well as the 3 partially treated coeliacs who were in relapse at the time of biopsy, villi were entirely absent.
partially.exampleSense: To a partial degree or extent, incompletely.

satisfying.example: As in much of biology, the most satisfying truths in ecology derive from manipulative experimentation. Tinker with nature and quantify how it responds.
satisfying.exampleSense: That satisfies, gratifies or pleases; that removes any feeling of lack.

inspector.o: Borrowed from Latin īnspector, from īnspiciō, equivalent to inspect + -or.
inspector.example: After that, with the help of the disk inspector, you can at any time compare the status of programs and system disk areas with the original one.
inspector.exampleSense: A software tool used to examine something.

either-or.example: Using existing housing better and building new homes are not either/ors but complementary. Doing both will mean a faster (and greener) solution.
either-or.exampleSense: A situation in which there is a choice between two different plans of action, but both together are not possible.

trillion.o: Borrowed from French trillion, from French tri- (“three”) + -illion, equivalent to tri- + -illion. The noun was coined by American basketball player Harvey Pollack, because of the way the numbers read across a basketball box score.
trillion.example: Javik: Stand in the ashes of a trillion dead souls and ask the ghosts if honor matters. Their silence is your answer.
trillion.exampleSense: A million (times a) million: 1 followed by twelve zeros, 10¹².

reach.o:
verb: From Middle English rechen, from Old English rǣċan (“to reach”), from Proto-West Germanic *raikijan, from Proto-Germanic *raikijaną, from the Proto-Indo-European *Hreyǵ- (“to bind, reach”). Cognate with Dutch reiken, German reichen.

noun: From Japanese 立直 (rīchi), from Chinese 立直 (lìzhí).
reach.example: the gulfe Iasius, and all the coast thereof is very full of creekes and reaches.
reach.exampleSense: A stretch of a watercourse which can be sailed in one reach (in the previous sense). An extended portion of water; a stretch; a straightish portion of a stream, river, or arm of the sea extending up into the land, as from one turn to another. By extension, the adjacent land.

sometimes.o: From Middle English sumtymes, somtymes, som tymes, equivalent to sometime + -s (adverbial suffix). Compare West Frisian somstiden (“sometimes”), Dutch somtijds, somwijlen (“sometimes”).
sometimes.example: Sometimes I sit and think, but mostly I just sit.
sometimes.exampleSense: On some occasions, over some periods, or in certain circumstances, but not always.

beyond.o: From Middle English biyonde, from Old English beġeondan, from be- + ġeond; related to yonder.
beyond.example: She had no reason for the conviction beyond the very inadequate one that she had seen him around London.

self-directed.example: I see a lot of self-directed anger on the part of the straight wives: What's wrong with me that I can't keep this man attracted to me? What's wrong with me in the first place for attracting a gay man?

directed.o: simple past and past participle of direct. Borrowed from Latin dīrēctus, perfect passive participle of dīrigō (“straighten, direct”), from dis- (“asunder, in pieces, apart, in two”) + regō (“make straight, rule”). Compare dress. Doublet of derecho. For the meaning development compare with Russian напра́вить (naprávitʹ, “to direct, to turn, to aim, to level, to point”), отпра́вить (otprávitʹ, “to send, to dispatch, to forward”) connected with пра́вить (právitʹ, “to govern, to rule, to drive, to steer”).

categorize.example: First, categorize incoming messages according to the needed actions.
categorize.exampleSense: To assign a category; to divide into classes.

categorization.example: It’s fair to say that Wikipedia has spent far more time considering the philosophical ramifications of categorization than Aristotle and Kant ever did.
categorization.exampleSense: The process of sorting or arranging things into categories or classes.
