constrained.o: simple past and past participle of constrain. From Middle English constreinen, from Old French constreindre, from Latin cōnstringō, from cōn- (“with, together”) + stringō (“to draw, bind or tie tight”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *streyg- (“to stroke, to shear, stiff”).
constrained.example: The epistle is opened and read—with a little wonder, most probably not a little vexation, at its constrained style.

primarily.example: Some Gold Cups are won primarily with class, others with stamina.
primarily.exampleSense: Of a primary or central nature, first and foremost

straight.o: From Middle English streight, streght, streiȝt, the past participle of strecchen (“to stretch”), from Old English streċċan (past participle ġestreaht, ġestreht), from Proto-West Germanic *strakkjan (“to stretch”). Cognate with Scots straicht (“straight”), Dutch gestrekt (“stretched”), German gestreckt (“stretched”), Danish strakt (“stretched”), Faroese and Norn strekti (“stretched”), Icelandic strekkti (“stretched”), Norwegian strekte (“stretched”), Swedish sträckte (“stretched”). Doublet of straught. Equivalent to stretch + -ed. In some senses, conflated with strait (“narrow, constricted”), which is from Latin strictus via Old French estreit.
straight.example: After four straight wins, Mudchester United are top of the league.
straight.exampleSense: In a row, in unbroken sequence; consecutive.

grit.o:
noun: With early modern vowel shortening, from Middle English grete, griet, from Old English grēot, from Proto-West Germanic *greut, from Proto-Germanic *greutą. Compare grist.

noun: From Middle English *gryt (“bran, chaff”), from Old English grytt, from Proto-West Germanic *gruti (“coarsely ground bits”), ablaut variant of Proto-Indo-European *gʰrewd-. See above. Doublet of goetta.
grit.example: We had no choice but to grit our teeth and get on with it.
grit.exampleSense: Apparently only in grit one's teeth: to clench, particularly in reaction to pain or anger.

domesticated.example: But I can take the calves and learn them to work and give milk, and learn them to become domesticated and useful.
domesticated.exampleSense: Selectively bred to live with or around humans. (of an animal or a plant, especially a pet)

instead of.o: From Middle English in stede of, in stude of (“instead of”, literally “in stead of, in place of”), equivalent to in + stead + of (cf. in one's stead). Cognate with Saterland Frisian insteede, ansteede (“instead of”), West Frisian ynstee (“instead of”), Dutch instede (“instead of”), German anstatt (von) (“instead of”), Danish i stedet (“instead of”).
instead of.example: He walked to school instead of taking the car.
instead of.exampleSense: In lieu of; in place of; rather than.

shine.o:
verb: From Middle English shinen, schinen (preterite schon, past participle schinen), from Old English sċīnan (“to shine, flash; be resplendent”; preterite sċān, past participle sċinen), from Proto-West Germanic *skīnan (“to shine”), from Proto-Germanic *skīnaną (“to shine”). Cognate with Dutch schijnen, German scheinen, Danish and Norwegian Bokmål skinne, Norwegian Nynorsk and Swedish skina, Faroese and Icelandic skína.

verb: From the noun shine, or perhaps continuing Middle English schinen in its causative uses, from Old English scīn (“brightness, shine”), and also Middle English schenen, from Old English scǣnan (“to render brilliant, make shine”), from Proto-Germanic *skainijaną, causative of *skīnaną (“to shine”).
shine.example: I shone my light into the darkness to see what was making the noise.
shine.exampleSense: To create light with (a flashlight, lamp, torch, or similar).

moreover.o: Inherited from Middle English moreover, moreovere, morover, mooreover, more-overe, mare over, equivalent to more + over.
moreover.example: For three years there had been pestilence, and in the last of the three a famine; moreover, there was imminence of war.
moreover.exampleSense: In addition to what has been said.

paraphrase.o: From Middle French paraphrase, from Latin paraphrasis, from Ancient Greek παράφρασις (paráphrasis). Doublet of paraphrasis.

revolve around.example: His life revolves around beer and bad jokes.
revolve around.exampleSense: To be essentially connected with; to concern.

revolute.o:
adj: Borrowed from Latin revolūtus, perfect passive participle of revolvō (“roll back”).

verb: Back-formation from revolution.
revolute.example: The Hawaiians have ‘revoluted’ and dethroned the fat squaw they have hitherto chosen to call a queen.
revolute.exampleSense: to participate in or incite a revolution or revolt

preclude.example: It has been raining for days, but that doesn’t preclude the skies clearing by this afternoon!
preclude.exampleSense: Remove the possibility of; rule out; prevent or exclude; to make impossible.

given.example: When evaluating this math problem, don't forget to read the givens.
given.exampleSense: A condition that is assumed to be true without further evaluation.

selective.example: The selective algorithm excludes the redundant classifiers to construct a streamlined ensemble learning.
selective.exampleSense: Of or relating to the process of selection.

selectively.example: Our prototype implements a basic pharming attack to selectively misresolve the client domain name requests.
selectively.exampleSense: In a selective manner, only affecting or applying to some selected cases.

llama.o:
noun: Borrowed from Spanish llama, from Quechua llama.

noun: Borrowed from Tibetan བླ་མ (bla ma).
llama.example: He was, as it were, a great Llama, shut up in a holy of holies, inscrutable, invisible, inexorable,—not to be seen by men's eyes or heard by their ears, hardly to be mentioned by ordinary men at such periods as these without an inward quaking.

decoupling.o: present participle and gerund of decouple. From Middle French découpler. By surface analysis, de- + couple.

vocalise.o:
verb: From vocal + -ise.

noun: Borrowed from French.

puppy.o: From earlier puppie (“a woman's pet dog”), of uncertain origin, but probably from Middle English *puppee, *poupee, from Old French poupée, popée (“a doll; puppet”). More at puppet. Mostly displaced native Middle English whelp (“puppy”), from Old English hwelp, whence Modern English whelp and whelpie.
puppy.example: I found my place taken by an ill-bred, awkward puppy with a money bag under each arm.
puppy.exampleSense: A conceited and impertinent person, especially a young man.

make sense.example: Maybe we should take a break. I mean, our relationship just isn't making much sense anymore.
make sense.exampleSense: Used to express interest or desire in something; to be pleasing or beneficial; to work, be operative, or be advantageous to.

identifiable.example: I don't know where he was from because he had no identifiable accent.
identifiable.exampleSense: Capable of being distinguished and named.

plural.o: From Middle English plurelle, from Old French plurel (“plural”), Borrowed from Latin plūrālis (“of or belonging to more than one, belonging to many”, adjective), from plūs, plūris (“more”) + -ālis.
plural.example: The plural of 'cat' is 'cats', but the plural of 'child' is 'children'.
plural.exampleSense: A word in the form in which it potentially refers to something other than one person or thing; and other than two things if the language has a dual form.

exactly.example: So you're saying that we have only three days left? — Yes, exactly!

consul.o: From Middle English consul, from Old English consul, from Latin cōnsul.

consular.o: From Middle English consular, from Latin cōnsulāris. By surface analysis, consul + -ar.
consular.example: If this is a consular ship, where is the ambassador?
consular.exampleSense: Of or pertaining to a consul, or the office thereof.

consulate.o: From Middle English consulat, consulate, from Latin consulātus, from consul + -ātus. In some senses, via French consulat. By surface analysis, consul + -ate (forms nouns denoting rank or office).

dithering.o: present participle and gerund of dither. Variant of didder, from Middle English dideren (“to tremble”). Compare Middle English bididren, bididdren (“to seduce, deceive”), from Old English bedidrian, bedyderian (“to deceive, trick”). Alternatively, perhaps with expressive voicing from *titeren, from Proto-Germanic *titrōną. If so, then a doublet of teeter and cognate with Old High German zittarōn (German zittern) and Old Norse titra (Faroese titra, Icelandic titra). Alternatively an unrelated reduplicative onomatopoeia.
dithering.example: Even though it became clear as early as 1766 that a separate policy for Quebec was required, eight long years of delays and ditherings lay between that recognition and actual legislation in the Quebec Act.
dithering.exampleSense: The act of one who dithers.

mingle.o: From earlier mingil, mengle, from Middle English menglen, equivalent to ming + -le. Cognate with Dutch mengelen (“to mingle, mix”), German mengen (“to mingle, mix”). More at ming.
mingle.example: Across the city yesterday, there was a feeling of bittersweet reunion as streams of humanity converged and mingled at dozens of memorial services.
mingle.exampleSense: To intermix; to combine or join, as an individual or part, with other parts, but commonly so as to be distinguishable in the product.

numerical.example: Harry Kane broke the deadlock from the spot eight minutes after half-time, the captain's superb pass releasing Jude Bellingham, who was fouled by Liam Scales, earning the defender a second yellow card and a dismissal.

tackling.o: present participle and gerund of tackle. From Middle English takel (“gear, apparatus”), from Middle Dutch or Middle Low German takel (“ship's rigging”), perhaps related to Middle Dutch taken (“to grasp, seize”). Akin to Danish takkel (“tackle”), Swedish tackel (“tackle”). More at take.

discipline.o: From Middle English [Term?], from Anglo-Norman, from Old French descipline, from Latin disciplina (“instruction”), from discipulus (“pupil”), influenced by disco (“to learn”), from Proto-Indo-European *dek- (“(cause to) accept”).
discipline.example: Economics is a messy discipline: too fluid to be a science, too rigorous to be an art.
discipline.exampleSense: A specific branch of knowledge, learning, or practice.

sign on.example: After 12:30 p.m., no new sign ons are permitted.

scaffolding.o:
noun: Inherited from Middle English scaffaldyng, skaffaldyng, equivalent to scaffold + -ing.

verb: See the etymology of the corresponding lemma form.
scaffolding.example: We refer to the process by which socialization agents support emotional activity within the child as emotional scaffolding.

close in.example: The police had not yet caught the thieves, but were closing in.
close in.exampleSense: To come or approach nearer to someone being pursued.

close.o:
verb: From Middle English closen (“to close, enclose”), partly continuing (in altered form) earlier Middle English clusen (“to close”) from Old English clȳsan (“to close, shut”); compare beclose, foreclose, etc.), and partly derived from Middle English clos (“close, shut up, confined, secret”, adjective), from Old French clos (“close, confined”, adjective), from Latin clausus (“shut up”, past participle), from claudō (“to bar, block, close, enclose, bring an end to, confine”), from Proto-Indo-European *kleh₂w- (“key, hook, nail”), related to Latin clāvis (“key, deadbolt, bar”), clāvus (“nail, peg”), claustrum (“bar, bolt, barrier”), claustra (“dam, wall, barricade, stronghold”). Cognate with Ancient Greek κλείω (kleíō), κλείς (kleís, “bar, bolt, key”), Russian заключи́ть (zaključítʹ) (via ключ (ključ)), German schließen (“to close, conclude, lock”), Dutch sluiten (“to close, conclude, lock”). Partially replaced Old English lūcan (“to close, lock, enclose”), (whence English lock). Doublet of clause.

adj: Borrowed from French clos, from Latin clausum, participle of claudō.
close.example: The runner in second place is closing the gap on the leader.
close.exampleSense: To remove or block an opening, gap or passage through. To move a thing, or part of a thing, nearer to another so that the gap or opening between the two is removed.

exaggerated.o: simple past and past participle of exaggerate. Borrowed from Latin exaggerātus, perfect passive participle of exaggerō (“to heap up, increase, enlarge, magnify, amplify, exaggerate”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from ex- (“out, up”) + aggerō, aggerāre (“to heap up”), from agger (“a pile, heap, mound, dike, mole, pier, etc.”), from aggerō, aggerere (“to bear, carry to (some place), bring together”), from ad- (“to, toward”) + gerō (“to carry”).
exaggerated.example: The Wycombe slowing begins at West Wycombe; to the High Wycombe curve itself most exaggerated respect was shown, with a minimum of 30 m.p.h.
exaggerated.exampleSense: That has been described as greater than it actually is; abnormally increased or enlarged.

exaggeration.example: They say he's a millionnaire, but that's a massive exaggeration.
exaggeration.exampleSense: The act of exaggerating; the act of doing or representing in an excessive manner; a going beyond the bounds of truth, reason, or justice; a hyperbolical representation; hyperbole; overstatement.

propertied.example: The Bolsheviks organized unity and class solidarity of the workers and peasants in the oppressed and oppressing nations to fight the propertied classes that exploited their labor.
propertied.exampleSense: Owning property, especially land or real estate that yields an income.

popularize.example: Saudi yoga trainer Dr. Nouf Marwaai has also been honored with one of India’s highest civilian awards, the Padma Shri, for popularizing yoga.

educator.o: From Latin ēducātor. By surface analysis, educate + -or.

monumental.o: Borrowed from Late Latin monumentālis, from Latin monumentum; equivalent to monument + -al.
monumental.example: Creating a complete map of the human connectome would therefore be a monumental milestone but not the end of the journey to understanding how our brains work.
monumental.exampleSense: Taking a great amount of time and effort to complete.

poised.o: simple past and past participle of poise. From Middle English poys, poyse, from Anglo-Norman pois, Middle French pois (“weight”) and Anglo-Norman poise, Middle French poise (“measure of weight”), from Latin pendere (“to weigh, ponder, think”). Doublet of peise.
poised.example: The Titanic stands on end, poised briefly for the plunge.

ponder.o: From Middle English ponderen, from Old French ponderer (“to weigh, balance, ponder”) from Latin ponderāre (“to weigh, ponder”), from pondus (“weight”), from pendere (“to weigh”); see pendent and pound.
ponder.example: I lit my pipe and had a ponder about it, but reached no definite conclusion.

discernment.o: From Middle French discernement, equivalent to discern + -ment.

discernible.o: From Middle French discernable; spelling changed from -a- to -i- in the 17th century to conform to Latin discernibilis. By surface analysis, discern + -ible.
discernible.example: There is a discernible performance difference between a Porsche and a Civic.
discernible.exampleSense: Possible to discern; detectable or derivable by use of the senses or the intellect.

indiscernible.example: The details of the room were indiscernible, lost in yellowish shadow.
indiscernible.exampleSense: Not capable of being discerned or perceived.

onwards.example: A Class 158 relegated from express duties turns up to transport me via the flower-bedecked Brighouse station to the trans-Pennine main line at Bradley Junction and onwards to Huddersfield.

laboratory.example: [Isaac Newton] was obsessed with alchemy. He spent hours copying alchemical recipes and trying to replicate them in his laboratory. He believed that the Bible contained numerological codes.
laboratory.exampleSense: A place where chemicals, drugs or microbes are prepared or manufactured.

equip.o: From French équiper (“to supply, fit out”), originally said of a ship, Old French esquiper (“to embark”); of Germanic origin, most probably from Old Norse skipa (“to man (a ship)”), from Proto-Germanic *skipōną (“to ship, sail, embark”). Compare with Middle High German schipfen, German schiffern, Icelandic skipa, Old English scipian. Doublet of ship.
equip.example: Take it down from a distance with a magic spell, or equip your sword and attack it at close range.
equip.exampleSense: To equip oneself with (an item); to bring (equipment) into active use.

acknowledgment.example: This is conveniently done by means of a written instrument, called a bill of exchange, which is, in fact, a transferable order by a creditor upon his debtor, and when accepted by the debtor, that is, authenticated by his signature, becomes an acknowledgment of debt.
acknowledgment.exampleSense: A recognition as genuine or valid; an avowing or admission in legal form.

precede.o: From Middle French précéder, from Latin praecēdō, from prae- + cēdō.
precede.example: It has been usual to precede hostilities by a public declaration communicated to the enemy.
precede.exampleSense: To cause to be preceded; to preface; to introduce.

broadly.example: [W]hen he caught sight of her running towards him like that, he smiled broadly.

drive.o: From Middle English driven, from Old English drīfan (“to drive, force, move”), from Proto-West Germanic *drīban, from Proto-Germanic *drībaną (“to drive”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰreybʰ- (“to drive, push”). Cognates Cognate with Scots drive (“to drive”), Yola dhreeve, dhrive, dreeve, drieve, drive (“to drive”), North Frisian driiv, driiw, driwe (“to drive”), West Frisian driuwe (“to drive; to float”), Alemannic German triibe (“to drive”), Dutch drijven (“to drive, push”), German treiben (“to drive, push, propel”), Low German drieven (“to drive, drift, push”), Luxembourgish dreiwen (“to drive, propel”), Yiddish טרײַבן (traybn, “to drive”), Danish, Norwegian Bokmål drive (“to drive, propel”), Icelandic drífa (“to drive”), Norwegian Nynorsk driva, drive (“to drive, move; to propel; to run”), Swedish driva (“to drive, compel; to drift; to run”), Gothic 𐌳𐍂𐌴𐌹𐌱𐌰𐌽 (dreiban, “to drive”).
drive.example: Some old model trains have clockwork drives.
drive.exampleSense: A mechanism used to power or give motion to a vehicle or other machine or machine part.

as such.example: This is a valuable artefact and should be treated as such.
as such.exampleSense: In the role or manner of the thing mentioned.

focus.o: Borrowed from Latin focus (“hearth, fireplace”); see there for more. Related to fuel. Kepler introduced the term into mathematics and the sciences in describing elliptical orbits of planets (quote from Nicholas Mee) : "One of the interesting properties of an ellipse is that if there were a light bulb at one focus, then all the light that it emits would reflect off the ellipse and converge at the other focus. This is why Kepler originally used the name focus for these points."
focus.example: I have to focus on my work.
focus.exampleSense: To concentrate one's attention on something; to have as one's central point of interest, concern, etc.

as.o:
adv: From Middle English as, als(a), alswa, from Old English eallswā (“just so; as”), thus representing a reduced form of also. Compare German Low German a(l)s, German als, Dutch als.

noun: Borrowed from Latin as. Doublet of ace.

noun: From a + -s.

adv: Shortening of as hell or as fuck or similar.
as.example: Under most circumstances, it will be possible to draw a distinction sufficiently clear as to allow an unambiguous allocation to one or other category.
as.exampleSense: In the (same) way or manner that; to the (same) degree that. Used to introduce a result: with the result that it is.

constipated.o: simple past and past participle of constipate. The adjective is first attested circa 1425, in Middle English, the verb in 1541; inherited from Middle English constipat(e) (“constipated”), borrowed Medieval Latin cōnstīpātus (“constipated”) (or through its Old French equivalent constipé), perfect passive participle of Medieval Latin cōnstīpō (“to cause constipation, to constipate”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from Classical Latin cōnstīpō (“to crowd or press tightly together”) (whence obsoleted sense 2 and 3), itself from con- + stīpō (“to press, cram”). Cognate with Middle English constipen (“to constipate”) and doublet of costive; related to stiff.
constipated.example: But there is no place for grand gestures but there's a basic contempt for women in this puny, constipated drama.
constipated.exampleSense: Failing to make a point or reach a conclusion; stifled.

constipate.o: The adjective is first attested circa 1425, in Middle English, the verb in 1541; inherited from Middle English constipat(e) (“constipated”), borrowed Medieval Latin cōnstīpātus (“constipated”) (or through its Old French equivalent constipé), perfect passive participle of Medieval Latin cōnstīpō (“to cause constipation, to constipate”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from Classical Latin cōnstīpō (“to crowd or press tightly together”) (whence obsoleted sense 2 and 3), itself from con- + stīpō (“to press, cram”). Cognate with Middle English constipen (“to constipate”) and doublet of costive; related to stiff.

constipation.o: First attested in the beginning of the 15ᵗʰ century, in Middle English; inherited from Middle English constipacioun, borrowed from Medieval Latin constīpātiō or its Old French equivalent, from cōnstīpō + -tiō. By surface analysis, constipate + -ion.
constipation.example: If you also knew how to combine foods—that is, what foods eaten together “set well,” you need never have indigestion, constipation or any of the headachy, stomachachy ills they lead to.
constipation.exampleSense: A state of the bowels in which the evacuations are infrequent and difficult, or the intestines become filled with hardened faeces.

canonize.o: From Late Middle English canonizen (“to declare as a saint; to appoint to an ecclesiastical office”), from Old French canonisier (modern French canoniser (“to canonize”)), or from its etymon Medieval Latin, Late Latin canōnizāre, the present active infinitive of Latin canōnizō (“to recognize as a saint, canonize; to declare as authoritative or official”), from Latin canōn (“measuring line; (figurative) precept, rule, canon; authorized catalogue”) + -izō (suffix forming verbs). The English word is analysable as canon (“general principle, rule; authoritative group of works; catalogue of saints canonized in the Roman Catholic Church”) + -ize.
canonize.exampleSense: To declare (a deceased person) as a saint, and enter them into the canon of saints.

quad.o: Shortened, via clipping or abbreviation, from various English terms. Ultimately related to Latin quattuor (“4”); compare quadri-, quadruple. The typography senses are from the abbreviation quad. for obsolete quadrat; the keyboard command comes from the verb sense.
quad.example: Other larger spaces – known as quads – were used to space out lines.
quad.exampleSense: Abbreviation of quadrat. A blank metal block used to fill short lines of type.

loosely.o: From Middle English lously; equivalent to loose + -ly.
loosely.example: It was an April Fool hoax, of course. 31200 had been rigged up with a single lightweight wooden [name] plate (loosely held on by Blu Tack).

indicative.o: From Middle French indicatif, from Late Latin indicātīvus. By surface analysis, indicate + -ive.
indicative.example: The fact that imperative forms were taken into English as indicatives suggests that the English speakers using the Hindustani verbs were most familiar (in some cases perhaps only familiar) with the imperative form.
indicative.exampleSense: A term in the indicative mood.

keep up with.example: Blake needed to run to keep up with the indignant Doctor.
keep up with.exampleSense: To manage to remain beside or just behind someone or something that is moving away from one.

illustrative.example: This latest incident is illustrative of his continued bad behavior.
illustrative.exampleSense: Demonstrative, exemplative, showing an example or demonstrating.

inner.o: From Middle English inner, ynner, ynnere, from Old English innera, comparative of inne (“within”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁en.
inner.example: As we age, the major arteries of our bodies frequently become thickened with plaque, a fatty material with an oatmeal-like consistency that builds up along the inner lining of blood vessels.
inner.exampleSense: Being or occurring (farther) inside, situated farther in, located (situated) or happening on the inside of something, situated within or farther within contained within something.

working.o:
noun: From Middle English werking, werkynge, warkynge, worchinge, from Old English wyrċing (“working”), verbal noun of wyrċan (“to work”), equivalent to work + -ing. Cognate with Scots wirking, warking, Dutch werking, German Wirkung.

verb: From Middle English workyng, wirkynge, worchinge, werchinge, workinde, wirkand, worchende, wurchende, from Old English wyrċende, from Proto-Germanic *wurkijandz, present participle of Proto-Germanic *wurkijaną (“to work”), equivalent to work + -ing. Compare Scots wirkand, werkand, warkand (“working”), Dutch werkend (“working, acting”), German wirkend (“acting, working”).
working.example: The working minimum focus distance is the distance from the closest focusable subject to the lens.

conceptual.o: Borrowed from Medieval Latin conceptuālis, from Latin conceptus, perfect passive participle of concipiō (“take hold of; conceive”); see concept and -al.
conceptual.example: The repeated exposure, over decades, to most taxa here treated has resulted in repeated modifications of both diagnoses and discussions, as initial ideas of the various taxa underwent—often repeated—conceptual modification.
conceptual.exampleSense: Of, or relating to concepts or mental conception.

humanlike.example: Crows are humanlike in their creativity and their ability to thrive in the ecosystems we shape, so their presence looks to some observers like an extension of human disruption.

far-off.example: Perhaps on some quiet night the tremor of far-off drums, sinking, swelling, a tremor vast, faint; a sound weird, appealing, suggestive, and wild - and perhaps with as respectable a meaning as the sound of bells in a Christian country.
far-off.exampleSense: Remote, either in time or space.

multivocal.o: From Late Latin multivocus (“expressed by many words”), from multi- + form of vocare (“to call”).

tailoring.o: present participle and gerund of tailor. Inherited from Middle English taillour, from Anglo-Norman taillour, from Old French tailleor, from taillier, from Late Latin tāliō, from Latin tālea (“a cutting”). Doublet of tailleur. Compare typologically German Schneider (akin to English snithe); Macedonian кројач (krojač), Polish krawiec (akin to Proto-Slavic *krojiti).
tailoring.example: A man got up in all the outward trappings of a gentleman: an extensive display of snowy linen, unimpeachable tailoring, ganté, botté, in perfection; nothing overdone.

leisured.example: The leisured class may produce great advances in the arts, or it may fritter away its time.
leisured.exampleSense: Having leisure time, especially as a result of not having to work for a living.

checkup.example: I took my car in for an annual checkup.

ineligible.example: Employees of the promoter are ineligible to enter the competition.
ineligible.exampleSense: Not eligible; forbidden to do something.

antigravity.o: Alternative spelling of anti-gravity. From anti- + gravity.

leftover.example: The entire wheel of cheese is a leftover from the party.
leftover.exampleSense: Remaining after a meal is complete or eaten for a later meal or snack.

outstanding.o: From outstand, equivalent to out- + standing or outstand + -ing.
outstanding.example: Charles S. Peirce, 1839 to 1914, was one of America's most outstanding intellects. Philosopher, mathematician, and scientist, he wrote profusely, the equivalent of almost 100,000 printed pages in all.
outstanding.exampleSense: Exceptionally good; distinguished from others by its superiority.

from time to time.example: On these red embers Hatteraick from time to time threw a handful of twigs.
from time to time.exampleSense: Occasionally; sometimes; once in a while.

ping.o: Partly onomatopoeic, and partly continuing Middle English pingen (“to push, shove, pierce, stab, prod, goad, urge, feel remorse, incite”), from Old English pyngan (“to prick”), in turn likely from pungere. Compare English pang.
ping.example: The microwave pinged. He forked the steak onto the plate and set the timer again.
ping.exampleSense: To make a high-pitched, short and somewhat sharp sound.

touch up.example: Use a small brush to touch up the paint anywhere it is uneven.
touch up.exampleSense: To make slight corrections or adjustments to; to fill in or perfect.

seasoned.o: simple past and past participle of season. From Middle English sesoun, seson (“time of the year”), from Old French seson, saison (“time of sowing, seeding”), from Latin satiō (“act of sowing, planting”) from satum, past participle of serō (“to sow, plant”) from Proto-Indo-European *seh₁- (“to sow, plant”). Akin to Old English sāwan (“to sow”), sǣd (“seed”). Doublet of saison. Displaced native Middle English sele (“season”) (from Old English sǣl (“season, time, occasion”)), Middle English tide (“season, time of year”) (from Old English tīd (“time, period, yeartide, season”)).
seasoned.example: Since these noodles are dried, they are often served with a side of seasoned stock.
seasoned.exampleSense: Of a food, often a liquid: containing seasonings

pivot.o: From Middle English pevet, *pivot, from Old French pivot (“hinge pin, pivot”) (12th c.), possibly from Latin pūgiō.
pivot.example: The weight of the body and the traction and braking forces are taken by the conventional dished bogie centre pivot with phosphor-bronze liner; this type of centre pivot facilitates passage over marshalling yard humps.
pivot.exampleSense: A thing on which something turns; specifically a metal pointed pin or short shaft in machinery, such as the end of an axle or spindle.

ocelot.o: From French ocelot, a word formed by Buffon from Classical Nahuatl ōcēlōtl (“jaguar”).

democratize.o: From French démocratiser, equivalent to democrat + -ize.

offering.o: From offer + -ing. Displaced native Old English hūsl.
offering.example: In recent seasons fetishwear has found its way onto the catwalk, with vinyl, PVC and lycra featuring among the most unlikely designer offerings.
offering.exampleSense: gerund of offer Something put forth, bid, proffered or tendered, such as for sale

lend.o:
verb: From earlier len (with excrescent -d, as in sound), from Middle English lenen, lænen, from Old English lǣnan (“to lend; give, grant, lease”), from Proto-West Germanic *laihnijan, from Proto-Germanic *laihnijaną (“to loan”), from Proto-Germanic *laihną (“loan”), from Proto-Indo-European *leykʷ- (“to leave, leave over”). Cognate with Scots len, lend (“to lend”), West Frisian liene (“to lend, borrow, loan”), Dutch lenen (“to lend, borrow, loan”), Danish låne (“to lend, loan”), Swedish låna (“to lend, loan”), Icelandic lána (“to lend, loan”), Icelandic léna (“to grant”), Latin linquō (“quit, leave, forlet”), Ancient Greek λείπω (leípō, “leave, release”). See also loan.

noun: From Middle English lende (usually in plural as lendes, leendes, lyndes), from Old English lendenu, lendino (“loins”), plural of Old English lenden (“loin”), from Proto-West Germanic *landī, from Proto-Germanic *landį̄ (“loin”), from Proto-Indo-European *lendʰ- (“loin, kidney”). Cognate with Scots lend, leynd (“the loins, flank, buttocks”), Dutch lendenen (“loins, reins”), German Lenden (“loins”), Swedish länder (“loins”), Danish lænd (“loin”), Icelandic lendar (“loins”), Latin lumbus (“loin”) (whence loin), Polish lędźwie (“loins”), Russian ля́двея (ljádveja, “thigh, haunch”).
lend.example: I will only lend you my car if you fill up the tank.
lend.exampleSense: To allow to be used by someone temporarily, on condition that it or its equivalent will be returned.

erroneous.o: From late Middle English erroneous, from Middle French erroneux, from Latin erroneus.
erroneous.example: His answer to the sum was erroneous.

redoubtable.o: The adjective is derived from Late Middle English redoutable (“worthy of honour, venerable; frightening, terrible”), borrowed from Anglo-Norman redoutable and Middle French redoutable, redoubtable, from Old French redotable (modern French redoutable), from redoter (“to fear”) (whence Middle French redoubter, redouter, French redouter) + -able (suffix meaning ‘deserving of, worthy of’). Redoter is derived from re- (intensifying prefix) + doter (“to doubt; to fear”) (from Latin dubitō (“to doubt, be uncertain, waver in opinion”), probably ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dwi- (“apart, asunder; two”) + *bʰuH- (“to appear; to be; to become; to grow”), in the sense of being in two minds). By surface analysis, redoubt (“to dread”) + -able. The noun is derived from the adjective.
redoubtable.example: The redoubtable New York Times has been called the "newspaper of record" of the United States.
redoubtable.exampleSense: Eliciting respect or fear; imposing; awe-inspiring.

transitive.o: From Latin trānsitīvus, from trānsitus, from trāns (“across”) + itus, from eō (“to go”).
transitive.example: Men have tried to turn "revolutionise" from a transitive to an intransitive verb.
transitive.exampleSense: Taking a direct object or objects.

cyclic.o: From French cyclique or its etymon Classical Latin cyclicus, from Ancient Greek κυκλικός (kuklikós). By surface analysis, cycle + -ic. Piecewise doublet of chakric.
cyclic.example: Benzene and cyclohexane are both cyclic compounds.
cyclic.exampleSense: Having chains of atoms arranged in a ring.

filiate.example: I shall, therefore, invite you to consider, as a suggestive analogy, the action which takes place when a bit of finely filiated platinum is introduced into a chamber containing oxygen and sulphur dioxide.
filiate.exampleSense: To establish filiation between (see "filiation" for the many senses).

foliate.o:
adj: Learned borrowing from Latin foliātus (“having leaves, leafy, leaved”) (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), a participial adjective derived from folium (“leaf; (Late Latin) leaf or sheet of paper”) + -ātus (participial adjective-forming suffix) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰleh₃- (“blossom, flower”) or *dʰelh₁- (“to be green”)).

noun: From a substantivation of the above adjective. Equivalent to folia + -ate (noun-forming suffix).

verb: From Latin folium (“leaf”) + -ate (verb-forming suffix) (more at etymology 1)

divisor.example: The positive divisors of 6 are 1, 2, 3 and 6.
divisor.exampleSense: An integer that divides another integer an integral number of times, the former being called a divisor of the latter.

high-level.example: It remains a key part of the busy Strathclyde railway system, with its high-level platforms served by trains to Lanarkshire, Ayrshire and England, and its low-level platforms a key artery at the heart of the busiest commuter network outside London.
high-level.exampleSense: Taking place or existing at a high level, altitude or elevation.

manifest.o: From Middle English manifest, manifeste, from Latin manifestus, manufestus (“palpable, manifest”), from Latin manus (“hand”) + an uncertain second element. Doublet of manifesto.
manifest.example: And usually this manifests as them trying to prove their parent's criticism's and belittlings wrong.
manifest.exampleSense: To show plainly; to make to appear distinctly, usually to the mind; to put beyond question or doubt; to display; to exhibit.

directly.example: I'm sick of asking you to fire him; I'll just do it directly.
directly.exampleSense: In a straightforward way; without anything intervening; not by secondary but by direct means.

dividend.o: From Middle French dividende, from Latin dīvidendum (“thing to be divided”), future passive participle of dīvidō (“to divide”), by surface analysis, divide + -end.
dividend.exampleSense: A number or expression that is to be divided by another.

point of view.o: Calque of French point de vue.
point of view.example: His point of view is that there is only one true religion.
point of view.exampleSense: An attitude, opinion, or set of beliefs.

electrical.example: For our final example let us finish the problem posed in the introduction to this chapter. The ideas and formulas needed will be familiar to electrical students, and would be handy for nonelectricals to know as well.

doghouse.example: "But, honey, whar yo' ole man gwine ter sleep?" "Dey's straw in de barn, en pine shatters in de doghouse!" she shouted, slamming the window.
doghouse.exampleSense: Any small house or structure or enclosure used to house a dog.

dither.o: Variant of didder, from Middle English dideren (“to tremble”). Compare Middle English bididren, bididdren (“to seduce, deceive”), from Old English bedidrian, bedyderian (“to deceive, trick”). Alternatively, perhaps with expressive voicing from *titeren, from Proto-Germanic *titrōną. If so, then a doublet of teeter and cognate with Old High German zittarōn (German zittern) and Old Norse titra (Faroese titra, Icelandic titra). Alternatively an unrelated reduplicative onomatopoeia.
dither.example: Everyone was in a dither; either in it or about to get in it or just climbing out of it. Naturally, the Madam was not in a dither. Dither was a foreign concept to her.

fundamentals.o: plural of fundamental. From Late Latin fundamentālis, from Latin fundamentum (“foundation”), from fundō (“to lay the foundation (of something), to found”), from fundus (“bottom”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰudʰmḗn.
fundamentals.example: While this stock has been trading at a low P/E multiple lately, I think its fundamentals are sound, and consider it a good buy for long-term investors.

testimony.o: PIE word *tréyes Inherited from Middle English testimonie, from Old French testimonie, from Latin testimōnium (“testimony”).
testimony.example: When ye depart thence, shake off the dust under your feet for a testimony against them.
testimony.exampleSense: Witness; evidence; proof of some fact.

successively.example: My last to you was of Oct. 8 by the Count de Moustier. Yours of July 18. Sep. 6. & Oct. 24. have been successively received, yesterday, the day before & three or four days before that.
successively.exampleSense: In a serial or successive manner; one following another.

realistically.example: The dream of a junkless, truly functional workspace is one fantasy you can realistically fulfill. It's downright exciting just to think about it!

oversimplify.example: But the report stresses that this comparison, based purely on the total transport performed, oversimplifies the picture. The kinds of work performed by rail and rail transport are not identical.
oversimplify.exampleSense: To explain or present something in a way that excludes important information for the sake of brevity, or of making the explanation or presentation easy to understand.

divergent.o: From Latin dis- (“apart”) + vergere (“to turn”) + the adjectival suffix -ent.
divergent.example: Four zebras stood despondent facing divergent directions like an old European film or a '90s band photo.

divergence.example: An angle is made by the divergence of straight lines.
divergence.exampleSense: The degree to which two or more things diverge.

one-shot.example: One-shot volunteering projects are also common, though possibly somewhat less so than hobbyist-like projects.

vocabulary.o: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin vocābulārium. Doublet of vocabularium.
vocabulary.example: The vocabulary of any language is influenced by contacts with other cultures.
vocabulary.exampleSense: The words of a language collectively; lexis.

recapitulate.o: From Late Latin recapitulātus, past participle of recapitulāre (“to go over the main points of a thing again”), from re- (“again”) + capitulum (“head, main part, chapter”), from caput (“head”) + -ulum (diminutive suffix); see capitulate. By surface analysis, re- + capitulate.
recapitulate.example: Similarly this concept of unity provided a powerful impetus for embryological studies and the idea that fetal development recapitulates the steps of phylogenetic development.
recapitulate.exampleSense: (biology, of an organism) To mirror or repeat in analogous form, especially in reference to an individual's development passing through stages corresponding to the species' stages of evolutionary development.

recapitulation.o: From Anglo-Norman recapitulaciun et al., Middle French recapitulacion et al., or their source, from Late Latin recapitulatio (“summing up, summary”), from the participle stem of recapitulare (“recapitulate”), from re- + capitulum (“chapter, section”), diminutive of caput (“head”).
recapitulation.example: one would expect God's final purpose to be expressed in his created world, since the doctrine of recapitulation showed that this is where his plans had worked out before.
recapitulation.exampleSense: The symmetry provided by Christ's life to the teachings of the Old Testament; the summation of human experience in Jesus Christ.

logic.o:
adj: From Middle English logike, from Old French and Latin logicus, from Ancient Greek λογῐκός (logĭkós). Displaced native Old English flitcræftlīċ.

noun: From Middle English logik, from Old French logike, from Latin logica, from Ancient Greek λογική (logikḗ, “logic”), from feminine of λογικός (logikós, “of or pertaining to speech or reason or reasoning, rational, reasonable”), from λόγος (lógos, “speech, reason”). Displaced native Old English flitcræft (literally “art of arguing”).
logic.example: Fred is designing the logic for the new controller.
logic.exampleSense: The part of a system (usually electronic) that performs the boolean logic operations, short for logic gates or logic circuit.

testimonial.o: From French testimonial, from Late Latin testimonialis (“of or pertaining to testimony”), from Latin testimonium (“testimony”). See testimony.

bubble gum.o: Alternative form of bubblegum. From bubble + gum.

move on.example: I think Shane is going to move on my ex tonight.
move on.exampleSense: To attempt a seduction, often in a way seen as disloyal or rude to another.

toy.o: Inherited from Middle English toye (“amorous play, piece of fun or entertainment”), probably from Middle Dutch toy, tuyg (“tools, apparatus, utensil, ornament”) as in Dutch speel-tuig (“plaything, toy”), from Old Dutch *tiug, from Proto-West Germanic *tiugī̆, *teug, from Proto-Germanic *teugą (“stuff, matter, device, gear, lever”, literally “that which is drawn or pulled”), from Proto-Germanic *teuhaną (“to lead, bring, pull”), from Proto-Indo-European *dewk- (“to pull, lead”). Cognate with Dutch tuig (“thing”), German Zeug (“stuff”), Danish tøj (“stuff”), Icelandic tygi, Norwegian tøy (“equipment, riggings, stuff”), Swedish tyg (“cloth, textile, fabric”). Related to tug, tow, taw, tew.
toy.example: A grown man like him does not play with a child’s toy.
toy.exampleSense: Something to play with, especially as intended for use by a child.

assumed.o: simple past and past participle of assume. From Latin assūmō (“accept, take”), from ad- (“to, towards, at”) + sūmō (“take up, assume”).

revisit.o: From Middle English revisite, from Middle French revisiter and Latin revīsitāre. By surface analysis, re- + visit.
revisit.example: On November 21 the restored Highland "Jones Goods" 4-6-0, No. 103, revisited its old haunts when it worked a Stephenson Locomotive Society special from Glasgow (Buchanan Street) to Blair Atholl and back; [...].

weightlifting.o:
noun: From weight + lifting.

verb: From weightlift + -ing.

weighting.o: present participle and gerund of weight. From Middle English weight, weiȝte, weght, wight, from Old English wiht, ġewiht (“weight”), from Proto-Germanic *wihtiz ("weight"; compare *weganą (“to move”)), from Proto-Indo-European *weǵʰ- (“to move; pull; draw; drive”). Equivalent to weigh + -t (abstract nominal suffix). Cognate with Scots wecht, weicht (“weight”), Saterland Frisian Wächte (“scale”), Gewicht (“weight”), West Frisian gewicht (“weight”), Dutch gewicht (“weight”), German Low German Wicht, Gewicht (“weight”), German Wucht (“massiveness, force”), Gewicht (“weight”).
weighting.example: Higher weightings were assigned to data from double-blind studies.
weighting.exampleSense: The weight or significance given to something, sometimes by means of a statistical multiplier.

weighted.o: simple past and past participle of weight. From Middle English weight, weiȝte, weght, wight, from Old English wiht, ġewiht (“weight”), from Proto-Germanic *wihtiz ("weight"; compare *weganą (“to move”)), from Proto-Indo-European *weǵʰ- (“to move; pull; draw; drive”). Equivalent to weigh + -t (abstract nominal suffix). Cognate with Scots wecht, weicht (“weight”), Saterland Frisian Wächte (“scale”), Gewicht (“weight”), West Frisian gewicht (“weight”), Dutch gewicht (“weight”), German Low German Wicht, Gewicht (“weight”), German Wucht (“massiveness, force”), Gewicht (“weight”).
weighted.example: Huntsman starts out with a vision of Theron that’s specific, unique, and weighted in character, but it trends throughout toward generic fantasy tropes and black-and-white morality, and climaxes in a thoroughly familiar face-off.

weighty.o: From Middle English weighti, weghti, wighti, equivalent to weight + -y. Cognate with Scots weichty, wechty, wichty, Saterland Frisian wichtich, West Frisian wichtich, Dutch wichtig, gewichtig, German wichtig, Danish vigtig, Swedish viktig. Compare typologically Russian ве́ский (véskij), весо́мый (vesómyj) (< вес (ves)). Also compare the same meaning development from cognate (by borrowing) Polish waga (< ... < Proto-Germanic *wēgō): ważny (whence Russian ва́жный (vážnyj)).
weighty.example: To fund the purchase, he had to sell a late Renoir, The Judgment of Paris, with its depiction of weighty ladies frolicking in a roseate garden.
weighty.exampleSense: Having a lot of weight; heavy.

pretty.o: From Middle English prety, preti, praty, prati, from Old English prættiġ (“tricky, crafty, sly, cunning, wily, astute”), from Proto-West Germanic *prattug, from Proto-Germanic *prattugaz (“boastful, sly, slick, deceitful, tricky, cunning”), corresponding to prat (“trick”) + -y. Doublet of pratty. Cognate with Dutch prettig (“nice, pleasant”), Low German prettig (“funny”), Icelandic prettugur (“deceitful, tricky”). For the semantic development, compare canny, clever, cute.
pretty.example: Some people are surprised, I believe, that that the eldest was not [named after his father], but Isabella would have him named Henry, which I thought very pretty of her.
pretty.exampleSense: Excellent, commendable, pleasing; fitting or proper (of actions, thoughts etc.).

addition.o: Sense of “what is added” dates from 14th century, from Middle English addicioun, addition, from Old French adition, from Latin additiōnem, accusative singular of additiō, from addō (“add, put”).
addition.example: The addition of five more items to the agenda will make the meeting unbearably long.

additional.o: Learned borrowing from Latin additionalis. By surface analysis, addition + -al.

separated.o: simple past and past participle of separate. From Middle English separaten (“to separate”), from separat (“separated”) + -en, from Latin sēparātus, perfect passive participle of sēparō (“to separate”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from sē- (“apart”) + parō (“prepare”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *per- (“produce, procure, bring forward, bring forth”). Displaced Middle English scheden, from Old English scēadan (whence English shed). Doublet of sever, also derived from the same Latin verb.

separate.o:
verb: From Middle English separaten (“to separate”), from separat (“separated”) + -en, from Latin sēparātus, perfect passive participle of sēparō (“to separate”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from sē- (“apart”) + parō (“prepare”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *per- (“produce, procure, bring forward, bring forth”). Displaced Middle English scheden, from Old English scēadan (whence English shed). Doublet of sever, also derived from the same Latin verb.

adj: From Middle English separat, see -ate (“adjective-forming suffix”) and Etymology 1 for more.

noun: From a substantivization of the above adjective, see -ate (“noun-forming suffix”) and Etymology 1 for more.
separate.example: The sauce will separate if you don't keep stirring.
separate.exampleSense: To divide itself into separate pieces or substances.

refined.o: simple past and past participle of refine. From re- + fine.
refined.example: Under current guidelines, refined sugar must be at least five times purer than its raw counterpart.
refined.exampleSense: Purified, reduced in or freed from impurities Highly-processed and pure.

packer.o: From Middle English pakker, pakkere, packare, equivalent to pack + -er.
packer.example: When his back problems kept him from lifting furniture, his skill as a packer kept him employed.
packer.exampleSense: A person whose business is to pack things; especially, one who packs food for preservation

packing.o: From Middle English pakkynge; equivalent to pack (“verb and noun senses”) + -ing.
packing.example: A kind of fine Norwegian hay, used as packing in the finnesko to keep the feet warm and to make the fur boot fit firmly.
packing.exampleSense: As a concrete noun. Material used to fill in the space around something, especially to make a piston etc. watertight or airtight.

along.o: From Middle English, from Old English andlang, from prefix and- + lang (“long”). Doublet of endlong.
along.example: Swiftly and silently he made his way along the track which ran through the meadows.
along.exampleSense: In a line with, with a progressive motion on; onward on; forward on.

irrelevant.example: Andy Kirby said that, on her second day in his class, Velvet declared algebra irrelevant to her life and strolled out the door. "Haven't seen her since," he said.

drown out.example: He uses the music to drown out other noises around him.
drown out.exampleSense: To cover, obscure, or overwhelm by being louder or more intense than.

normality.o: From normal + -ity, perhaps modelled on French normalité.
normality.example: Jessie was going to wear pants to school, but her brother persuaded her to wear shorts to preserve normality.
normality.exampleSense: The state of being normal or usual; normalcy.

three-dimensional.example: A good novel needs three-dimensional characters.

multidimensional.example: The Cosmic Woman is an integrated, multidimensional woman who has crossed both the Zodiacal and cosmic planes.
multidimensional.exampleSense: Crossing through or existing in multiple dimensions (spacial planes).

four-dimensional.example: We live in a four-dimensional universe.
four-dimensional.exampleSense: Relating to the four dimensions of space-time (three spatial dimensions with the addition of time as the fourth).

one-dimensional.exampleSense: Having length, but no width, height or depth.

unidimensional.example: Lives are not simple and homogenous or uni-dimensional.

interactive.example: The show includes computer interactives, animation, models and live parakeets (for an exercise in species identification).
interactive.exampleSense: A feature (as in a museum) that can be interacted with.

baker.o: Inherited from Middle English bakere, from Old English bæcere (“baker”), from Proto-Germanic *bakārijaz (“baker”), equivalent to bake + -er. Cognate with Dutch bakker (“baker”), German Bäcker (“baker”), Norwegian Bokmål baker (“baker”), Swedish bagare (“baker”), Icelandic bakari (“baker”).
baker.example: But through the oligopoly, charcoal fuel proliferated throughout London's trades and industries. By the 1200s, brewers and bakers, tilemakers, glassblowers, pottery producers, and a range of other craftsmen all became hour-to-hour consumers of charcoal.
baker.exampleSense: A person who bakes and sells bread, cakes and similar items.

used to.o:
adj: From used, past participle of use (“(archaic sense) to be in the habit of”) + to.

verb: From used, past of use (“(archaic sense) to be in the habit of”) + to (“infinitive marker”).
used to.example: I am used to cleaning up other people’s mess.  I became used to his ways.
used to.exampleSense: Accustomed to, tolerant or accepting of.

bake.o: From Middle English baken, from Old English bacan (“to bake”), from Proto-West Germanic *bakan, from Proto-Germanic *bakaną (“to bake”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeh₃g- (“to roast, bake”). Cognate with West Frisian bakke (“to bake”), Dutch bakken (“to bake”), Low German backen (“to bake”), German backen (“to bake”), Norwegian Bokmål bake (“to bake”), Danish bage (“to bake”), Norwegian Nynorsk and Swedish baka (“to bake”), Ancient Greek φώγω (phṓgō, “roast”, verb).
bake.example: She's been baking all day to prepare for the dinner.
bake.exampleSense: To cook (something) in an oven (for someone).

say.o:
verb: From Middle English saien, sain, san, secgan, segen, seien, sein, seiȝen, sugen, sægen, ziggen, from Old English seċġan, secgean, secggan, secggean, seggan, sæċġan (“to say, speak”), from Proto-West Germanic *saggjan, from Proto-Germanic *sagjaną (“to say”), from Proto-Indo-European *sokʷ-h₁-yé-, a suffixed o-grade form of *sekʷ- (“to say”). Cognates Cognate with North Frisian sai, seede, sii, sjide, sooi, säie (“to say”), West Frisian sizze (“to say”), Alemannic German ŝchége, ŝchegi, séege, säge, sägä (“to say”), Bavarian sogn, soon, sågn (“to say”), Dutch zeggen (“to say”), German sagen (“to say”), Low German seggen (“to say, tell”), Luxembourgish soen (“to say”), Vilamovian ziöen, zuön, zuø̄n (“to say”), Yiddish זאָגן (zogn, “to say”), Danish sige (“to say”), Elfdalian saja (“to say”), Faroese siga (“to say”), Icelandic segja (“to say”), Jamtish segi (“to say”), Norwegian Bokmål si (“to say”), Norwegian Nynorsk segja, seia, seie (“to say, tell”), Scanian siğa (“to say”), Swedish säga (“to say”); also Cornish hwedhel (“narrative, story, tale”), Irish scéal (“story, tale”), Manx skeeal (“story; news; narrative”), Scottish Gaelic sgeul (“story, tale; information, news”), Welsh chwedl (“story, tale”), hebu (“to say”), Latin inquam (“to say”), Ancient Greek ἐνέπω (enépō), ἐννέπω (ennépō, “tell or tell about; speak”), Latvian sacīt (“to say, tell”), Lithuanian sakyti (“to say, tell”), Bulgarian соча (soča, “to indicate; to point”), Czech sočit (“to blame, hate”), Old Polish soczyć (“to accuse, slander”), Russian сочи́ть (sočítʹ, “to emit (a liquid)”), Ukrainian сочи́ти (sočýty, “to emit (a liquid), exude, ooze; to drain, sap”). The adverb and interjection are from the verb.

noun: From Middle French saie, from Latin saga, plural of sagum (“military cloak”).

verb: Aphetic form of assay.
say.example: To this argument we shall soon have said; for what concerns it us to hear a husband divulge his household privacies?
say.exampleSense: To speak; to express an opinion; to make answer; to reply.

personally.o: From Middle English personally, personely, personallich, personaliche, equivalent to personal + -ly.
personally.example: 'There's a boy here who wants to speak to Miss Clara personally,' he announced.

common.o: From Middle English comun, from Anglo-Norman comun, from Old French comun (rare in the Gallo-Romance languages, but reinforced as a Carolingian calque of Proto-West Germanic *gamainī (“common”) in Old French), from Latin commūnis (“common, public, general”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱom-moy-ni-s (“held in common”), from Proto-Indo-European *mey- (“to exchange, change”). Displaced native Middle English imene, ȝemǣne (“common, general, universal”) (from Old English ġemǣne (“common, universal”)), Middle English mene, mǣne (“mean, common”) (also from Old English ġemǣne (“common, universal”)), Middle English samen, somen (“in common, together”) (from Old English samen (“together”)). Doublet of gmina and mean.
common.example: The two competitors have the common aim of winning the championship.
common.exampleSense: Mutual; shared by more than one.

exact.o: From Latin exāctus (the verb via Middle English exact), perfect passive participle of exigō (“demand, claim as due; measure by a standard, weigh, test”), from ex (“out”) + agō (“drive”).
exact.exampleSense: Precisely agreeing with a standard, a fact, or the truth; perfectly conforming; neither exceeding nor falling short in any respect.

goodness.o: From Middle English goodnesse, godnesse, from Old English gōdnes (“goodness; virtue; kindness”), from Proto-West Germanic *gōdnassī (“goodness”), equivalent to good + -ness. Cognate with Scots guidness (“goodness”), West Frisian goedens (“goodness”), Old High German guotnessī (“goodness”), Middle High German guotnisse (“goodness”), Russian годность (godnostʹ, “suitability, fitness”).
goodness.example: Rich, raisiny, smoky, coffee goodness: that is the flavor of urfa biber.
goodness.exampleSense: The state or characteristic of being good.

fast forward.example: Metallica have revealed that they plan to ‘fast-forward to the next chapter’ of working with Lady Gaga – sparking rumours of a collaborative album.

illustrated.o: simple past and past participle of illustrate. Back-formation from illustration.
illustrated.example: Siegfried Kracauer was to be a particularly vocal critic in the twenties of the shift in perception brought on by the illustrateds.

ineluctable.o: From Middle French inéluctable (whence in- + e- and -able), from Latin inēlūctābilis, from in- + ēlūctor (“struggle out”) + -bilis.
ineluctable.example: I throw this ended shadow from me, manshape ineluctable, call it back.
ineluctable.exampleSense: Impossible to avoid or escape; inescapable, irresistible.

hype.example: After all the hype for the diet plan, only the results ended up slim.
hype.exampleSense: Promotion or propaganda; especially exaggerated claims.

stuffing.example: The stuffing is made of synthetic goose down.
stuffing.exampleSense: The matter used to stuff hollow objects such as pillows and saddles.

succession.o: Inherited from Middle English [Term?], from Old French succession, from Latin successiō (noun).
succession.example: England gave away six penalties in the first 15 minutes and were lucky to still have 15 men on the pitch, but Kvirikashvili missed two very makeable penalties in quick succession as Georgia were unable to take advantage of significant territorial advantage.
succession.exampleSense: An act, process, or instance of succeeding: A sequence of things in order.

arbitration.o: From Middle English arbitracion, borrowed from Old French arbitration, from Latin arbitratio, from arbitrari (“to arbitrate, judge”); see arbitrate.

payload.o: From pay + load. From the early 20th century.
payload.example: 1990, Dave Mustaine, "Rust in Peace... Polaris", Megadeth, Rust in Peace.
payload.exampleSense: That part of a rocket, missile, propelled stinger, or torpedo that is not concerned with propulsion or guidance, such as a warhead or satellite.

preload.example: That nightclub is so expensive. Let's preload at your flat.
preload.exampleSense: To drink (cheaper) alcohol at home before going out socially.

recessive.o: From Latin recēdō + -ive, or directly from New Latin recessīvus.
recessive.example: The worker–client relationship is more recessive and has a more catalytic and enabling quality.
recessive.exampleSense: Not dominant; whose effect is masked by stronger effects.

scrutiny.o: From Middle English scrutiny, from Medieval Latin scrūtinium (“a search, an inquiry”), from Vulgar Latin scrūtor (“to search or examine thoroughly”), from Late Latin scrūta (“rubbish, broken trash”), from an extension of Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to cut”).
scrutiny.example: So much for the occupant of the britscha, who waits, as all the horses are out at a ball or a scrutiny.
scrutiny.exampleSense: Intense study of someone or something.

refundable.example: The entrance fee is refundable if you choose not to stay for more than half an hour.
refundable.exampleSense: Able to be refunded in case of customer dissatisfaction, loss, breakage etc.

dispatch.o: Borrowed from Spanish despachar and/or Italian dispacciare. Further etymology is uncertain. For first element des-, see dis-. Second element probably from either Vulgar Latin *pactāre (“to fasten"”), *pactiare or Latin -pedicāre (“to entrap, shackle”), from pedica, from pēs. Ultimately related to impeach through shared Latin root. The first known use in writing (in the past tense, spelled as dispached) is by Bishop Cuthbert Tunstall in 1517. This would be unusually early for a borrowing from a Romance language other than French, but Tunstall had studied in Italy and was Commissioner to Spain, so this word may have been borrowed through diplomatic circles. The alternative spelling despatch was introduced in Samuel Johnson's dictionary, probably by accident. Compare typologically deliver (for the meaning to bring or transport) (< Latin dē- + līberō).
dispatch.example: We must act with dispatch in this matter.
dispatch.exampleSense: The act of doing something quickly.

schedule.o: Inherited from Middle English cedule, from Middle French cedule (whence French cédule), from Old French cedule, from Late Latin schedula (“papyrus strip”), diminutive of Latin scheda, from Ancient Greek σχέδη (skhédē, “papyrus leaf”), from Proto-Hellenic *skʰíďďō, from Proto-Indo-European *skid-yé-ti, from *skeyd- (“to divide, split”). Doublet of cedula and cedule. This word was historically pronounced /ˈsɛdjuːl/, /ˈsɛdʒuːl/; the pronunciations with /ʃ/ and /sk/ are due to the spelling (the latter may have been reinforced by learned influence); compare schism.
schedule.example: To complete on time, we must follow the schedule.
schedule.exampleSense: A procedural plan, usually but not necessarily tabular in nature, indicating a sequence of operations and the planned times at which those operations are to occur.

certify.o: From Old French certefier (“confirm, assure, make certain”). Compare French certifier.
certify.example: These blankets have been certified as fireproof.
certify.exampleSense: To attest that a product, service, organization, or person has met an official standard.

certified.o: simple past and past participle of certify. From Old French certefier (“confirm, assure, make certain”). Compare French certifier.

accreditation.example: Remus Chen, head of Taiwan's Foreign Ministry's Department of European Affairs, told reporters that the new Lithuanian representative Paulius Lukauskas had arrived in Taipei earlier this month, and on Monday had formally applied for his accreditation.

conferee.example: A press conference was held at 1:30 with many representatives of the press from around the state eating lunch with the conferees.
conferee.exampleSense: A person who participates in a conference.

confer.o: From Early Modern English conferre, from Middle French conférer, from Old French conferer, from Latin cōnferō. Compare Dutch confereren, German konferieren, Danish konferere, Swedish konferera. Doublet of collate. See also infer, relate and refer, delate and defer, as well as prelate and prefer among others.
confer.example: They were in a huddle, conferring about something.
confer.exampleSense: To talk together, to consult, discuss; to deliberate.

despatch.o: Alternative form of dispatch. Borrowed from Spanish despachar and/or Italian dispacciare. Further etymology is uncertain. For first element des-, see dis-. Second element probably from either Vulgar Latin *pactāre (“to fasten"”), *pactiare or Latin -pedicāre (“to entrap, shackle”), from pedica, from pēs. Ultimately related to impeach through shared Latin root. The first known use in writing (in the past tense, spelled as dispached) is by Bishop Cuthbert Tunstall in 1517. This would be unusually early for a borrowing from a Romance language other than French, but Tunstall had studied in Italy and was Commissioner to Spain, so this word may have been borrowed through diplomatic circles. The alternative spelling despatch was introduced in Samuel Johnson's dictionary, probably by accident. Compare typologically deliver (for the meaning to bring or transport) (< Latin dē- + līberō).
despatch.example: Eldridge closed the despatch-case with a snap and, rising briskly, walked down the corridor to his solitary table in the dining-car.

immediate.o: From Old French immediat (French immédiat), borrowed from Late Latin immediātus (“without in-between, moderation”), from Latin in + mediātus, perfect passive participle of mediō (“to halve, to be in the middle”) (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from medius (“middle”). By surface analysis, im- + mediate.
immediate.example: Computer users these days expect immediate results when they click on a link.
immediate.exampleSense: Happening right away, instantly, with no delay.

ere.o:
adv: From Middle English er, from Old English ǣr (adverb, conjunction, and preposition), from Proto-West Germanic *airi, from Proto-Germanic *airiz, comparative of Proto-Germanic *airi (“early”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éyeri (“day, morning”) (compare Avestan 𐬀𐬫𐬀𐬭 (ayar, “day”), Gk. ἠέριος (ēérios, “at daybreak”), see also era, Albanian herët (“early in the morning, at daybreak”) ). The adverb erstwhile retains the Old English superlative ǣrest (“earliest”). Cognate with Saterland Frisian eer (“before”), Dutch eer (“before, sooner than”), German ehe (“before”).

contraction: Formed from is + there + a/an.
ere.example: The hill-tops rejoicing will ere long be at their ruddiest, and blush Good-night.

relieved.o: simple past and past participle of relieve. From Late Middle English releven, from Old French relever, specifically from the conjugated forms such as (jeo) relieve (“I lift up”), and its source, Latin relevo (“to lift up, lighten, relieve, alleviate”), combined form of re- (“back”) + levo (“to lift”). Doublet of relevate. Compare levant, levity, etc.
relieved.example: She was extremely relieved when the lesson finished.
relieved.exampleSense: Experiencing or exhibiting relief; freed from stress or discomfort.

sufferance.o: From Middle English sufferaunce, from Anglo-Norman suffraunce, from Late Latin sufferentia. By surface analysis, suffer + -ance.
sufferance.example: The sufferances which simply touch us in minde, doe much lesse afflict me, then most men [...].

particularise.example: To particularise the railway improvements required by the County of London Plan, 1943, a Committee under the Chairmanship of Professor Sir Charles Inglis was appointed in February, 1944, by the Minister of War Transport.
particularise.exampleSense: Non-Oxford British English spelling of particularize

misery.o: From Middle English miserie, from Old French miserie (modern: misère), from Latin miseria, from miser, equivalent to miser + -y. Doublet of misère and mizeria.
misery.example: Ever since his wife left him you can see the misery on his face.
misery.exampleSense: Great unhappiness; extreme pain of body or mind; wretchedness; distress; woe.

afflict.o: From Middle English afflicten (attested in past participle afflicte), from Latin afflīctō (“to damage, harass, torment”), from ad- + flīctus, past participle of afflīgō (“strike, beat”), from ad- + flīgō (“strike”) (whence af-).
afflict.example: [T]he wench was afflicted with religion and unapproachably austere.
afflict.exampleSense: To cause (someone) pain, suffering or distress.

leanness.o: From Middle English lenenesse, equivalent to lean + -ness.

humanly.o:
adv: From human (adjective) + -ly (adverbial suffix). Piecewise doublet of humanely (in Middle English as humanly, when human and humane had not yet become different words).

adj: From human (noun) + -ly (adjectival suffix). Used once in Middle English, as humaynly, modelled on Middle Dutch and meaning “characteristic of human nature”.
humanly.example: “Ouch!” exclaims Adam, expressing humanly emotion for the first time.
humanly.exampleSense: Of or pertaining to humans; human.

humanely.o: From Middle English humanly; equivalent to humane + -ly. Piecewise doublet of humanly.
humanely.example: The study was approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) of the University of Florida and the tortoise was humanely euthanized with an overdose of sodium pentobarbital performed by intracoelomatic injection [34 ].

superfluity.o: From superflu(ous) + -ity, Old French superfluite, from Medieval Latin superfluitas, from Latin superfluus.
superfluity.example: As they had almost all the conveniencies of life within themselves, they seldom visited towns or cities in search of superfluity.

surfeit.o: From Middle English surfeite, surfet, a borrowing from Anglo-Norman surfet, surfeit and Old French sorfet, sorfait, past participle of surfaire (“to augment, exaggerate, exceed”), from sur- (“over”) + faire (“to do”). The adjective is derived from the noun.
surfeit.example: Matter and argument have been supplied abundantly, and even to surfeit.

relieve.o: From Late Middle English releven, from Old French relever, specifically from the conjugated forms such as (jeo) relieve (“I lift up”), and its source, Latin relevo (“to lift up, lighten, relieve, alleviate”), combined form of re- (“back”) + levo (“to lift”). Doublet of relevate. Compare levant, levity, etc.
relieve.example: This shall not relieve either Party of any obligations.
relieve.exampleSense: To free (someone) from debt or legal obligations; to give legal relief to.

patrician.o: Borrowed from Middle French patricien, from Latin patricius, derived from patrēs cōnscrīptī (“Roman senators”). May also have been derived from Latin patricius + -ian
patrician.example: It will speed the shrivelling of the patrician “one nation” Tories, who tried to curb the extremes of Thatcherism and ended by providing its veils.
patrician.exampleSense: Politically active to help people in lower classes, especially in a patronizing or condescending way.

contexture.o: From Middle French contexture, from contexte + -ure after texture.
contexture.example: He was not of any delicate contexture; his limbs rather sturdy than dainty.
contexture.exampleSense: The structural character of a thing.

resolved.o: simple past and past participle of resolve. From Middle English resolven, from Old French resolver, a learned borrowing of Latin resolvō (“loosen, thaw, melt, resolve”), equivalent to re- + solve. Piecewise doublet of re-solve.

famish.o: From Middle English famisshe, from famen (“starve”), from Old French afamer, ultimately from Latin famēs (“hunger”). Compare affamish, famine. Cognate with Spanish hambre (“hunger”).
famish.example: The Lord will not suffer the soul of the righteous to famish.
famish.exampleSense: To suffer extremity from deprivation of anything essential or necessary.

conciseness.example: I shall endeavour to keep it with as much conciseness as possible.
conciseness.exampleSense: The property of being concise; succinctness.

plainly.o: From Middle English playnly, pleinly, pleyneliche, equivalent to plain + -ly.
plainly.example: She decorated the room plainly but neatly.
plainly.exampleSense: In a plain manner; simply; basically.

back end.example: The back end of the operation is kept out of sight of the customers.
back end.exampleSense: The rear, back, or unseen portion (of something).

anomaly.o: From Latin anomalia, from Ancient Greek ἀνωμαλία (anōmalía, “irregularity, anomaly”), from ἀνώμαλος (anṓmalos, “irregular, uneven”), negating the meaning of ὁμαλός (homalós, “even”), from ὁμός (homós, “same”).
anomaly.example: This ardent exploration, absorbing all his energy and interest, made him forget for the moment the mystery of his heritage and the anomaly that cut him off from all his fellows.
anomaly.exampleSense: A deviation from a rule or from what is regarded as normal; an outlier.

backbone.o: From Middle English bakbon, bakebon, bac-bon; equivalent to back + bone. Compare the semantically analogous English ridgebone.
backbone.example: He would make a good manager, if he had a little more backbone.

slapshot.o: Alternative spelling of slap. From Middle English slappen, of uncertain origin, possibly imitative. Compare Low German Slappe (“slap”), whence also German Schlappe (“defeat”). Compare also Italian sleppa (“slap”).

transcendental.o: The adjective is a learned borrowing from Medieval Latin transcendentālis + English -al (suffix meaning of or relating to forming adjectives; and forming nouns, especially of verbal action). Transcendentālis is derived from Latin trānscendentem + ‑ālis (suffix forming adjectives of relationship); and trānscendentem is the accusative singular form of trānscendēns (“exceeding, surpassing, transcending”), the present active participle of trānscendō (“to climb, cross, pass, or step over; to exceed, surpass, transcend”), from trāns- (prefix meaning ‘across; beyond; through’) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *terh₂- (“to cross over; to overcome; to pass through”)) + scandō (“to ascend, climb; etc.”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *skend- (“to ascend; to jump up”)). The noun is derived from the adjective.
transcendental.example: In deference to Christian usage we can say that the transcendentals constitute the Logos within which everything has its being and according to which everything is made.
transcendental.exampleSense: Any one of the three transcendental properties of being: truth, beauty or goodness, which respectively are the ideals of science, art and religion and the principal subjects of the study of logic, aesthetics and ethics.

salutation.o: From Middle English salutacioun, from Old French salutacion, from Latin salutatio (“a greeting, a wishing health to”), from saluto (“wish one’s health, greet”), from salus (“well-being”). Compare the Latin greeting salve (literally “be well”).

readiness.example: England had won just two of their previous six matches prior to facing Spain and manager Sarina Wiegman had been questioned about their readiness to defend their European title in Switzerland this summer.
readiness.exampleSense: The state or degree of being ready; preparedness.

bridge.o:
noun: From Middle English brigge, from Old English brycġ (“bridge”), from Proto-Germanic *brugjō, *brugjǭ (“bridge”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰerw-, *bʰrēw- (“wooden flooring, decking, bridge”). Cognates Cognate with Scots brig, brigg (“bridge”), Yola burge (“bridge”), North Frisian brag, Bröch (“bridge”), Saterland Frisian Brääch, Brääg (“bridge”), West Frisian brêge (“bridge”), Dutch brug (“bridge”), German Brücke (“bridge”), Limburgish brögk (“bridge”), Luxembourgish Bréck (“bridge”), Vilamovian bryk (“bridge”), Yiddish בריק (brik, “bridge”), Danish, Norwegian Bokmål brygge (“jetty, pier, wharf”), Faroese, Icelandic bryggja (“pier”), Norwegian Nynorsk brygge, bryggje (“jetty, pier, wharf”), Swedish brygga (“bridge; pier”). The verb is from Middle English briggen, from Old English brycġian (“to bridge, make a causeway, pave”), derived from the noun. Cognate with Dutch bruggen (“to bridge”), Middle Low German bruggen (“to bridge”), Old High German bruccōn (“to bridge”) (whence Modern German brücken). The sense of a part of a stringed instrument is a semantic loan from German Steg, from Old High German steg.

noun: From the earlier game biritch, probably from Russian бирю́ч (birjúč) or бири́ч (biríč); else from Turkish bir-üç (“one-three”).
bridge.example: Rugby players often break the bridge of their noses.
bridge.exampleSense: A construction or natural feature that spans a divide. The upper bony ridge of the human nose.

bridging.o: present participle and gerund of bridge. From Middle English brigge, from Old English brycġ (“bridge”), from Proto-Germanic *brugjō, *brugjǭ (“bridge”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰerw-, *bʰrēw- (“wooden flooring, decking, bridge”). Cognates Cognate with Scots brig, brigg (“bridge”), Yola burge (“bridge”), North Frisian brag, Bröch (“bridge”), Saterland Frisian Brääch, Brääg (“bridge”), West Frisian brêge (“bridge”), Dutch brug (“bridge”), German Brücke (“bridge”), Limburgish brögk (“bridge”), Luxembourgish Bréck (“bridge”), Vilamovian bryk (“bridge”), Yiddish בריק (brik, “bridge”), Danish, Norwegian Bokmål brygge (“jetty, pier, wharf”), Faroese, Icelandic bryggja (“pier”), Norwegian Nynorsk brygge, bryggje (“jetty, pier, wharf”), Swedish brygga (“bridge; pier”). The verb is from Middle English briggen, from Old English brycġian (“to bridge, make a causeway, pave”), derived from the noun. Cognate with Dutch bruggen (“to bridge”), Middle Low German bruggen (“to bridge”), Old High German bruccōn (“to bridge”) (whence Modern German brücken). The sense of a part of a stringed instrument is a semantic loan from German Steg, from Old High German steg.
bridging.example: All the joists and bridgings of the mezzanine floor to have stout double herringbone strutting not more than 6 feet apart.
bridging.exampleSense: The system of bracing used between floor or other timbers to distribute the weight.

groundwork.example: The discovery of the laws of electricity laid the groundwork for a century of innovation.
groundwork.exampleSense: The foundation; the basic or fundamental parts that support or allow for the rest.

governance.o: From Middle English governaunce, from Old French gouvernance, governance, equivalent to govern + -ance.
governance.example: But was it responsible governance to pass the Longitude Act without other efforts to protect British seamen? Or might it have been subterfuge—a disingenuous attempt to shift attention away from the realities of their life at sea.
governance.exampleSense: The process, or the power, of governing; government or administration.

authoring.o: present participle and gerund of author. From Middle English auctour, from Anglo-Norman autour, from Old French autor, from Latin auctor, from augeō (“to increase, originate”). The h, also found in Middle French autheur, is unetymological as there is no h in the original Latin spelling. The OED attributes the h to contamination by authentic. Doublet of auteur.

spearhead.o: From Middle English spere-hed; equivalent to spear + head.
spearhead.example: Spearheads of the NER bargain fares attack this year have been the introduction of weekend fares at a 7s 6d in the £ discount on ordinary rates between principal stations throughout the Region—[...].
spearhead.exampleSense: One who leads or initiates an activity (such as an attack or a campaign).

instability.o: From Middle French instabilité, from Latin instabilitas. Morphologically in- + stability.

decouple.o: From Middle French découpler. By surface analysis, de- + couple.
decouple.example: Decoupled tests would be nuclear explosions set off in massive underground caverns, a site that would greatly reduce the seismic waves caused by the explosion.
decouple.exampleSense: To muffle the seismic waves of (a nuclear explosion) by performing it underground.

silo.o: From Spanish silo, of unclear origin. See Spanish silo for more.
silo.example: Our networking is organized in silos, and employees lose time manually transferring data.
silo.exampleSense: A structure in the information system that is poorly networked with other structures, with data exchange hampered.

biology.o: Borrowed from New Latin biologia (1766), itself from Ancient Greek βίος (bíos, “bio-, life”) + -λογία (-logía, “-logy, branch of study, to speak”). By surface analysis, bio- + -logy. In English, first attested in the modern meaning in the work of English physician Thomas Beddoes in 1799.
