The term is also recorded in the sense of a biographical history in the work of Dudley Loftus in 1686, but this is considered by the Oxford English Dictionary to be an isolated use. The modern Greek βιολογία (viología) is borrowed from the English term and French biologie via international scientific vocabulary. Piecewise doublet of zoology.
biology.example: As in much of biology, the most satisfying truths in ecology derive from manipulative experimentation. Tinker with nature and quantify how it responds.
biology.exampleSense: The study of all life or living matter.

in reverse.example: The Satanic message can be unmasked by playing the song in reverse.
in reverse.exampleSense: Of a motion, sequence, etc.: backwards; reversed.

postsecondary.example: In its revised budget, the government has increased funding for postsecondary education.
postsecondary.exampleSense: Of or pertaining to education or educational institutions subsequent to secondary school or high school.

pursue.o: From Middle English pursuen, from Anglo-Norman pursure, poursuire etc., from Latin prōsequor (though influenced by persequor). Doublet of prosecute.
pursue.example: He now feared for his life, and believed US intelligence agents would pursue him.
pursue.exampleSense: To follow urgently, originally with intent to capture or harm; to chase.

unsupervised.example: Stop letting your children run around unsupervised!
unsupervised.exampleSense: Not supervised; not being constantly observed.

supervise.o: Borrowed from Medieval Latin supervisus, from supervidere, from Latin super + videre. Doublet of survey.
supervise.example: Without someone to supervise them, the group will lack direction.
supervise.exampleSense: To oversee or direct a task or organization.

pop-up.example: I came across this recipe when Helen Graham cooked it for Bracia and Friends, a pop-up whose USP is that chefs must cook a single dish.
pop-up.exampleSense: A business that opens for a brief temporary period only, such as a temporary restaurant.

quotient.o: Borrowed from Latin quotiēns, from quotiēs.
quotient.example: Dividing 12 by 4 yields a quotient of 3.
quotient.exampleSense: The number (either a fraction or an integer) resulting from the division of one number by another.

divided.o:
verb: See the etymology of the corresponding lemma form.

adj: From Middle English divided, devided, devidid, past participle of Middle English dividen (“to divide”), equivalent to divide + -ed.

amicably.o: From Middle English amcabily, equivalent to amicable + -ly. Piecewise doublet of amiably.
amicably.example: By 1849, they agreed amicably to disagree, and McCormick bought the Ogden and Jones half of the business for $65,000.

queue.o: From Middle English queue, quew, qwew, couwe, from Anglo-Norman queue, keu and Old French cöe, cue, coe (“tail”), from Vulgar Latin cōda, from Latin cauda. See also Middle French queu, cueue. Doublet of coda and cola.
queue.example: I was absent-minded at the moment and was last in the queue.
queue.exampleSense: A line of people, vehicles or other objects, usually one to be dealt with in sequence (i.e., the one at the front end is dealt with first, the one behind is dealt with next, and so on), and which newcomers join at the opposite end (the back).

enquire.o: From Old French enquerre, from en- + querre (“to search, to look for”), from Latin quaerere, of uncertain origin, but possibly from Proto-Italic *kʷaizeō, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷeh₂- (“to acquire”).
enquire.example: He enquired about the availability of rental bicycles in the town.

across.o: From Middle English acros, from early Middle English a-croiz, a-creoyz, from Anglo-Norman an (“in, on”) + croiz (“in the form of a cross”). More at cross. By surface analysis, a- + cross.
across.example: That store is across the street.
across.exampleSense: On the opposite side of (something that lies between two points of interest).

manipulator.example: The power lights blinked red and the amplifier failed, but not before Kassad had seen the tapering ovoid shapes, spotted with thrusters and cockpit blisters, each trailing a tangle of six jointless manipulator arms.
manipulator.exampleSense: A device which can be used to move, arrange or operate something.

kinesis.o: Borrowed from Ancient Greek κίνησις (kínēsis, “motion, movement”).

kinematics.o: French cinématique, from Ancient Greek κίνημα (kínēma, “motion”) + -ics.

atomy.o:
noun: A variant of atomi, the plural of atomus (“hypothetical particle posited as an ultimate and indivisible component of matter; mote of dust in a sunbeam”) treated as a singular form. Atomus is derived from Latin atomus, from Ancient Greek ἄτομος (átomos, “indivisible”, adjective), from ᾰ̓- (ă-, prefix forming terms having an opposite sense) + τομ- (tom-) (stem of τέμνω (témnō, “to cut”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *temh₁- (“to cut”)) + -ος (-os, suffix forming nouns of action or result). Doublet of atom.

adj: From atom + -y (suffix meaning ‘having the quality of’).

noun: Rebracketing of anatomy (“skeleton”) as an atomy; compare notomy.
atomy.example: Hostess Quickly. Ay, come, you starv’d bloodhound.

cranio-.o: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin crānium, borrowed from Ancient Greek κρᾱνῐ́ον (krānĭ́on), from *κρᾱν- (*krān-) + -ῐ́ον (-ĭ́on).

stereo.o: A shortened form of stereotype, stereoscope or stereophonic, all originally derived, via stereo-, from Ancient Greek στερεός (stereós, “solid”).
stereo.example: He liked to listen to classical music on his stereo.
stereo.exampleSense: Any object or device equipped with audio components that reproduces sound in stereo, such as a stereo console in the home.

tiling.o: present participle and gerund of tile. From Middle English tile, tyl, tigel, tiȝel, teȝele, from Old English tiġele, tieġle, tiġle (“tile, brick”), from Proto-West Germanic *tigulā (“tile, brick”), from Proto-Germanic *tigulǭ (“tile, brick”), from Latin tēgula, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)teg- (“to cover”). Doublet of tegula. Cognates Cognate with Saterland Frisian Tichel (“tile”), Dutch tichel (“brick”), tegel (“tile”), German Ziegel (“brick, roof tile”), Luxembourgish Zill (“brick, tile”), Danish tegl (“brick”), Faroese tigul (“tile”), Icelandic tigl (“brick, tile”), Norwegian Nynorsk tegl (“brick, roof tile”), Swedish tegel (“brick, tile”), Asturian teya (“tile”), Catalan teula (“tile”), French tuile (“tile”), Galician telha, tella (“roof tile”), Italian tegola (“roof tile”), Mirandese teilha (“roof tile”), Portuguese telha (“roof tile”), Spanish teja (“roof tile”), Belarusian цэ́гла (céhla, “brick”), Czech cihla (“brick”), Polish cegła (“brick”), Serbo-Croatian cígla (“brick”), Ukrainian це́гла (céhla, “brick”), Finnish tiili (“brick, tile”).
tiling.example: We spent all day doing the tiling in the bathroom.

timely.o: From Middle English timely, tymely, timliche, from Old English *tīmlīc (adjective) and tīmlīċe (“in good time; timely; soon”, adverb), equivalent to time + -ly. Cognate with Danish timelig, Swedish timlig, Icelandic tímalegur, tímanlegur.
timely.example: If the whistleblower submitted a timely response, pursuant to Step 9, the Claims Review Staff will consider the issues, along with any supporting documentation, and make its Proposed Final Determination.
timely.exampleSense: Done at the proper time or within the proper time limits; prompt.

amortise.o: Alternative form of amortize. From Middle English amortisen, from Old French amortir (via the stem amortiss-), from Vulgar Latin *admortīre, derived from Latin mortuus (“dead”).

amortize.o: From Middle English amortisen, from Old French amortir (via the stem amortiss-), from Vulgar Latin *admortīre, derived from Latin mortuus (“dead”).
amortize.example: extraordinary borrowing had been so extensive, Joly de Fleury reckoned, that even if it were amortized over the following decade, the state would still be running an annual deficit of over 50 million livres.
amortize.exampleSense: To wipe out (a debt, liability etc.) gradually or in installments.

back.o:
adj: From Middle English bak, from Old English bæc, from Proto-West Germanic *bak, from Proto-Germanic *baką, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeg- (“to bend”). The adverb represents an aphetic form of aback. Compare Middle Low German bak (“back”), from Old Saxon bak, and West Frisian bekling (“chair back”), Old High German bah, Swedish and Norwegian bak. Cognate with German Bache (“sow [adult female hog]”).

noun: Borrowed from French bac.
back.example: I still need to finish the back of your dress.
back.exampleSense: The rear of the body, especially the part between the neck and the end of the spine and opposite the chest and belly. The part of a piece of clothing which covers the back.

utilization.o: From French utilisation or from utilize + -ation.

abstraction.o: From Middle English abstraccyone; either from Middle French abstraction or from Medieval Latin abstrāctiō (“separation”), from Latin abstrahō (“draw away”). Equivalent to abstract + -ion.
abstraction.example: The cancelling of the debt would be no destruction of wealth, but a transfer of it: a wrongful abstraction of wealth from certain members of the community, for the profit of the government, or of the tax-payers.
abstraction.exampleSense: The act of abstracting, separating, withdrawing, or taking away; withdrawal; the state of being taken away.

order of magnitude.o: 18th century, in the sense "magnitude (brightness class) of a star", informed by the Greek τῶν μεγάλων τάξις (tôn megálōn táxis) (Ptolemy).

massively.example: Some of the most impressive applications of massively parallel computing have been in the context of wide-area distributed platforms.
massively.exampleSense: In a massive manner, in a way that appears large, heavy or imposing.

emerging market.o: Popularized by the International Finance Corporation, early 1980s.
emerging market.example: Government departments advised him to seek out new business in “emerging markets”, counsel he said was risible given the huge market on Britain’s doorstep.
emerging market.exampleSense: A relatively less-developed country or other trading region undergoing significant growth in production, consumption, or foreign investment.

over time.example: This graph shows the population of California over time.
over time.exampleSense: From a historic or evolutionary perspective.

spread.o:
verb: From Middle English spreden, from Old English sprǣdan (“to spread, expand”), from Proto-Germanic *spraidijaną (“to spread”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)per- (“to strew, sow, sprinkle”). Cognate with Saterland Frisian spreede (“to spread”), West Frisian spriede (“to spread”), North Frisian spriedjen (“to spread”), Dutch spreiden (“to spread”), Low German spreden (“to spread”), German spreiten (“to spread, spread out”), Danish sprede (“to spread”), Norwegian spre, spreie (“to spread, disseminate”), Swedish sprida (“to spread”), Latin spernō, spargō, Ancient Greek σπείρω (speírō), Persian سپردن (sepordan, “to deposit”), English spurn.

verb: Blend of speed + read.
spread.example: I dropped my glass; the water spread quickly over the tiled floor.
spread.exampleSense: To take up a larger area or space; to expand, be extended.

forgo.o: From Middle English forgon (“to go by, pass up”), from Old English forgān (“to go away, forgo”); equivalent to for- + go.
forgo.example: You might think that Americans buy roughly the same number of fitted sheets as flats. Or, considering the market for electric blankets, duvets, and other covers, that consumers buy even more bottom sheets, simply forgoing the tops.
forgo.exampleSense: To do without, to abandon, to renounce.

akin.o: From a corruption of of kin, from Middle English of kyn (“related, of kin”), equivalent to a- + kin (1550s). Compare Old English cyn, cynn (“akin, proper, suitable”, adj.).
akin.example: The faces changed, passing in rotation. Youthful faces, bearded faces, dark faces: faces serene, or faces moody, but all akin with the brotherhood of the sea.
akin.exampleSense: Of the same kin; related by blood.

pitfall.o: First recorded use in the 14th century from pit + fall in the sense of "pit trap, pit snare", from Old English fealle (“trap, snare”), from Proto-Germanic *fallą, *fallaz (“a fall, trap”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)pōl-. Cognate with German Falle (“trap, snare”).
pitfall.example: It's usually a simple task, but you should know the pitfalls before you attempt it yourself.
pitfall.exampleSense: A potential, unsuspected, hidden problem, hazard, or danger that is easily encountered but not immediately obvious.

traverse.o: From Middle English traversen, from Old French traverser, from Latin trans (“across”) + versus (“turned”), perfect passive participle of Latin vertere (“to turn”).
traverse.example: He will have to traverse the mountain to get to the other side.
traverse.exampleSense: To travel across, to go through, to pass through, particularly under difficult conditions.

locality.o: From French localité, from Late Latin localitas, equivalent to local + -ity.
locality.example: It is thought that the soul and angels are devoid of quantity and dimension, and that they have nothing to do with grosser locality.
locality.exampleSense: The fact or quality of having a position in space.

off the shelf.example: After the war, the invaluable experience gained with mass production of the TP engines saw Davey Paxman in a favourable position to supply such units almost "off the shelf", a facility found to be of great value by oil companies engaged in well-drilling; [...].

off-the-shelf.example: We can build a specialized part for you, but an off-the-shelf product will probably cost less.
off-the-shelf.exampleSense: As purchased or as commonly available, without modification or customization.

par.o:
noun: Abbreviations

prep: Borrowed from French par (“through, by”), from Latin per (“through”). Doublet of per.

noun: Borrowed from Latin pār (“equal”).

verb: Borrowed from Jamaican Creole, itself from partner.
par.example: He will need to par every hole in order to win this game.
par.exampleSense: To reach the hole in the allotted number of strokes.

cuddle.o: Origin uncertain, but probably from a frequentative form of Middle English *cudden, cuththen, keththen (“to embrace”), a variant of cuthen, kuthen, kithen (“to be familiar with, make known”), from Middle English cuth, couth (“known, familiar”), equivalent to couth + -le. Cognate with Middle Dutch kudden (“to come together, flock together”). More at couth.
cuddle.example: Give me a cuddle, Paul, it'll cheer you up.
cuddle.exampleSense: A snuggle; an affectionate embrace, often given to family members and close friends.

cuddly.exampleSense: Fond of or prone to cuddling.

spare no effort.example: This reflects credit not only on the railway staffs concerned but on the various signalling firms, which have spared no effort to carry out research work, and test and apply, when feasible, every new idea.
spare no effort.exampleSense: To do everything within one's powers to achieve something.

spare.o:
adj: From Middle English spare, spar, from Old English spær (“sparing, scant”), from Proto-Germanic *sparaz, from Proto-Indo-European *sph₁rós, from the root *speh₁-. Compare Dutch spaar(zaam), German spar(sam) and spär(lich), Swedish spar(sam), Icelandic sparr (“sparing”); also Latin (pro)sperus (“lucky”), Old Church Slavonic споръ (sporŭ, “plentiful”), Albanian shperr (“earn money”), Persian سپار (sepâr, “entrust; deposit”), Ancient Greek σπαρνός (sparnós, “rare”), Sanskrit स्फिर (sphirá, “thick”).

verb: From Middle English sparen, sparien, from Old English sparian (“to spare, show mercy to, refrain from injuring or destroying”), from Proto-Germanic *sparōną, *sparāną (“to save, keep, spare”), from Proto-Indo-European *sper- (“to be productive, earn”). Cognate with Scots spar, spare, spair (“to spare”), West Frisian sparje (“to save, spare”), Dutch sparen (“to save, spare”), German sparen (“to save, conserve, economise”), Swedish spara (“to save, save up”), Icelandic spara (“to save, conserve”).
spare.example: Kill me, if you please, or spare me.
spare.exampleSense: To show mercy, to have mercy on. To preserve (someone) from danger or punishment; to forbear to punish, injure, or harm (someone); to show mercy towards. To refrain from killing (someone) or having (someone) killed.

uninterrupted.example: Having departed Inverness on time, I take the advice of several guidebooks and sit in a right-hand-side seat, which should afford me uninterrupted views of the sea as the train winds its way north.

comparable.o: From Middle English comparable, from Middle French comparable, from Latin comparābilis. By surface analysis, compare + -able.
comparable.example: An elephant is comparable in size to a double-decker bus.

state-of-the-art.o: Alternative form of state. From Middle English stat (as a noun); adopted c. 1200 from both Old French estat and Latin stātus (“manner of standing, attitude, position, carriage, manner, dress, apparel; and other senses”), from stāre (“to stand”). Doublet of estate and status. The sense of "polity" develops in the 14th century. Compare French être, Greek στέω (stéo), Italian stare, Portuguese estar, Romanian sta, and Spanish estar. The verb is first attested around the beginning of the 16th century. Related to English stand.

state of the art.example: which is not only not advancing the state-of-the-art of management but also is believed to be regressing the state-of-the-art.
state of the art.exampleSense: The condition of scientific or technical knowledge, particularly the peak or highest level thereof, at a particular time.

penetrative.o: From Middle English penetratyve, penetratif, from Medieval Latin penetrativus, from (the participle stem of) Latin penetrāre (“to penetrate”).
penetrative.example: I've been in a relationship for nearly a year and we have an amazing sex life as is, but we've never managed penetrative sex.
penetrative.exampleSense: Pertaining to sexual activity involving penetration by the penis.

penetration.o: From Middle English penetracioun, from Old French penetracïon, and its source, Latin penetrātiō, from the participle stem of penetrō (“pierce”, verb). Morphologically penetrate + -ion.
penetration.example: Arsenal lacked urgency and penetration in a lazy, lacklustre opening half, sucked in by Forest's strategy of sitting back in blocks of defence waiting to hit them on the counter.
penetration.exampleSense: The act of progressing or moving forward through or into something.

futurist.example: ‘A passion for destruction is also a creative passion.’ This statement by the Russian revolutionary Mikhail Bakunin in 1842 could have been the rallying cry of the Italian Futurists around 1910.
futurist.exampleSense: An adherent to the principles of the artistic movement of futurism.

prescribed.o: simple past and past participle of prescribe. Borrowed from Latin praescrībere, from prae- (“before, in front”) and scrībere (“to write”).
prescribed.example: Short-term energy monitoring tuning follows a very prescribed procedure; building shell parameters are adjusted first, then HVAC efficiency.
prescribed.exampleSense: Of a procedure, specified to a great degree of detail; established as following a strict procedure or set of rules.

proscribe.o: From Middle English proscriben, from Latin prōscrībō (“to proclaim, forbid, banish”).
proscribe.example: Many Roman citizens were proscribed for taking part in rebellions.

anticipation.o: From Middle English anticipacioun, from Middle French anticipation and its etymon Latin anticipātiō, anticipātiōnem.
anticipation.example: Often the anticipation of a shot is worse than the pain of the stick.
anticipation.exampleSense: The act of anticipating, taking up, placing, or considering something beforehand, or before the proper time in natural order.

anticipant.o: From Latin anticipans, present participle of anticipo (“anticipate”).

return.o: From Middle English returnen, retornen, from Anglo-Norman returner, from Old French retourner, retorner, from Medieval Latin retornare (“to turn back”), from re- + tornare (“to turn”). By surface analysis, re- + turn. Compare beturn.
return.example: The boiler technician had to cut out the heating return to access the safety valve.
return.exampleSense: A return pipe, returning fluid to a boiler or other central plant (compare with flow pipe, which carries liquid away from a central plant).

reciprocation.example: ... the same pendulum alwayes maketh its reciprocations in equall times.
reciprocation.exampleSense: Alternate recurrence or action; as, the reciprocation of the sea in the flow and ebb of tides; oscillation.

payback.exampleSense: A benefit, reward, a form of recompense.

blog.o:
noun: Rebracketing of weblog, as if it means we blog. The Oxford English Dictionary says the shortened word was coined 23 May 1999 and references the "Jargon Watch" article in an issue of an online magazine which attributes the shortening to Peter Merholz. The form blog is now so much more common than weblog that some misspell the latter as webblog, as if from web + blog.

verb: (This etymology is missing or incomplete. Please add to it, or discuss it at the Etymology scriptorium. )
blog.example: Have you tried these, darling? They’re tempura zucchini flowers. Japanese-Italian fusion! My own invention. Shall I photograph it? We can put it on our blog.
blog.exampleSense: A website that allows users to reflect, share opinions, and discuss various topics in the form of an online journal, sometimes letting readers comment on their posts. Most blogs are written in a slightly informal tone (personal journals, news, businesses, etc.)

popcorn.o: Short for popped corn. By surface analysis, pop + corn.
popcorn.example: You've been cabling, twisting, popcorning and bobbling. See, we told you that they weren't so hard.

ruthless.o: From Middle English reuþeles; equivalent to ruth + -less.

unstoppable.example: However Russian Pavlyuchenko stunned his compatriots with an unstoppable 25-yard drive into the top corner.

upcoming.o:
adj: From up + coming.

noun: From upcome + -ing.
upcoming.example: The Federal budget lays out government spending for the upcoming budget year.
upcoming.exampleSense: Happening or appearing in the relatively near future.

last-minute.example: He's a last-minute replacement. After today, they'd have had to play with the original roster.
last-minute.exampleSense: Just before it is too late; in the nick of time.

per-.o:
prefix: Borrowed from Latin per and per-.

prefix: Borrowed from Old French per (modern French par).

per.o:
prep: From Latin per (“through, during”), from Proto-Indo-European *per. Doublet of par.

pron: Clipping of person, coined by American novelist and poet Marge Piercy in Woman on the Edge of Time (1979)
per.example: The medication is to be administered per os.
per.exampleSense: By the, by means of the, via the, through the.

systematic.o: Borrowed from Late Latin systēmaticus, from Koine Greek συστηματικός (sustēmatikós), from σύστημᾰ (sústēmă, “a composite; system”) + -ῐκός (-ĭkós, adjective suffix). Cognate with French systématique and Italian sistematico. By surface analysis, system + -atic.
systematic.example: And say, when them Gogs started out to put a thing through they did it systematic and thorough.

in on.example: We had to let him in on it after he overheard some of us talking.
in on.exampleSense: Part of or privy to; involved in (something private, especially a plan or plot).

inbox.example: The kids, my ex, my parents, the job, bills — my inbox is full.
inbox.exampleSense: The aggregate of items that demand one's attention or effort.

jargon.o: From Middle English jargoun, jargon, from Old French jargon, a variant of gargon, gargun (“chatter; talk; language”).
jargon.example: In fact all the competing theories have developed their own specialized jargons and have a tendency to be difficult to penetrate.
jargon.exampleSense: A language characteristic of a particular group.

serenity.o: From Middle English serenyte, from Old French serenité, from Latin serēnitās, equivalent to serene + -ity.
serenity.example: Forthwith a change came over the waters, and the serenity became less brilliant but more profound.
serenity.exampleSense: The state of being serene; calmness; peacefulness.

front.o: From Middle English front, frunt, frount, from Old French front, frunt, from Latin frōns, frontem (“forehead”). Doublet of frons.
front.example: Officially it's a dry-cleaning shop, but everyone knows it's a front for the mafia.
front.exampleSense: A person or institution acting as the public face of some other, covert group.

beamer.o:
noun: From beam (“balance beam”) + -er.

noun: From beam (“project, transmit”) + -er (agent noun suffix), or, for the ball, + -er (patient suffix).

noun: Clipping of BMW + -er.
beamer.example: For several days he went about his charge with disgust, trying everything he could to avoid the stench of rotting vegetation and of human feces, which was overpowering even as it all burned under the plasma from his beamer.
beamer.exampleSense: A device that projects or transmits matter, information, or energy.

multiply.o:
verb: From Old French multiplier, from Latin multiplicō, from multi (“many”) + plicō (“to fold”). The noun presumably derives from the verb.

adv: From multiple + -ly.

adj: multi- + ply
multiply.example: He had been multiplying, but it occurred to him he needed to resolve the exponents, first.

multiplier.example: The score multiplier increases each time you complete a level of the video game.
multiplier.exampleSense: A number by which another (the multiplicand) is to be multiplied.

proactively.example: [D]uring each lecture, an observation journal was kept to record what happened in the classroom, focusing on whether and when students enjoyed or proactively participated in classroom activities.
proactively.exampleSense: In a proactive manner; so as to look or plan ahead.

civil war.o: Calque of Latin bellum cīvīle, in English from 1651 in reference to the English Civil War, with possible early use in the 15th and 16th centuries as wer cyuile or ciuill warre. Displaced native Old English inġewinn.

civilian.o: From Middle English cyvylien, from Old French civilien. Equivalent to civil + -ian.
civilian.example: Three civilians were apprehended by the soldiers and taken away in a military vehicle.
civilian.exampleSense: A person following the pursuits of civil life, especially one who is not an active member of the armed forces.

civils.example: Our [ISO] 9000 (etc) accreditation extends, so far as I am aware, to cabling, ducting, poling and other civils activities.

civilization.o: Borrowed from French civilisation, equivalent to civilize + -ation or civil + -ization.
civilization.example: Modern civilization is a product of industrialization and globalization.
civilization.exampleSense: An organized culture encompassing many communities, often on the scale of a nation or a people; a stage or system of social, political, or technical development.

rejuvenation.example: Utnapishtim hears his wife's plea and tells Gilgamesh where he can find a miraculous plant of invigoration and rejuvenation.
rejuvenation.exampleSense: The process of rendering young again.

tortuous.o: From Middle English tortuous, tortuose, from Anglo-Norman and Old French tortuos, from Latin tortuōsus, from tortus (“a twisting, winding”).
tortuous.example: The badger made his dark and tortuous hole on the side of every hill where the copsewood grew thick.

market share.example: They continued to lose market share.
market share.exampleSense: The percentage of some market held by a company, country, (sub)sector or any other actor or aggregate.

euphoria.o: From New Latin euphoria, from Ancient Greek εὐφορίᾱ (euphoríā), from εὔφορος (eúphoros, “bearing well”), from εὐ- (eu-, “well”) + φέρω (phérō, “to bear”).
euphoria.example: The runner was in (a state of) absolute euphoria after winning his first marathon.
euphoria.exampleSense: An excited state of joy; a feeling of intense happiness.

poise.o:
noun: From Middle English poys, poyse, from Anglo-Norman pois, Middle French pois (“weight”) and Anglo-Norman poise, Middle French poise (“measure of weight”), from Latin pendere (“to weigh, ponder, think”). Doublet of peise.

noun: From French physicist and physiologist Jean Léonard Marie Poiseuille.
poise.example: The rock was poised precariously on the edge of the cliff.
poise.exampleSense: To keep (something) in equilibrium; to hold suspended or balanced.

barrel.o: From Middle English barel, from Anglo-Norman baril, Old French baril, bareil (“barrel”), of uncertain origin. An attempt to link baril to Old French barre (“bar, bolt”) (compare Medieval Latin barra (“bar, rod”)) via assumed Vulgar Latin *barrīculum meets the phonological requirement, but fails to connect the word semantically. The alternative connection to Frankish *baril, *beril or Gothic *𐌱𐌴𐍂𐌹𐌻𐍃 (*bērils, “container for transport”), from Proto-Germanic *barilaz, *bērilaz (“barrel, jug, container”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰer- (“to carry, transport”), is more plausible as it connects not only the form of the word but also the sense; equivalent to bear + -le. Compare also Old High German biril (“jug, large pot”), Luxembourgish Bärel, Bierel (“jug, pot”), Old Norse berill (“barrel for liquids”), Old English byrla (“barrel of a horse, trunk, body”). More at bear.
barrel.example: Barrels came in firkins, nine gallons; kilderkins, eighteen gallons; halves, twenty-seven gallons; barrels, thirty-six gallons and hogsheads, fifty-four.
barrel.exampleSense: A round (cylindrical) vessel, such as a cask, of greater length than breadth, and bulging in the middle, made of staves bound with hoops, and having flat ends (heads). The word is sometimes applied to a similar cylindrical container made of metal, usually called a drum. Such a cask of a certain size, holding one-eighth of what a tun holds. (See a diagram comparing cask sizes.)

line up.example: A number of famous actors and musicians have been lined up for the celebrations.
line up.exampleSense: To make arrangements for an event.

rounding.example: In the early Egyptian works, the relief was low, the surface flat, and but little if any attempt was made to show the roundings of the human figure, or to exhibit the inflexion of the human form.

subtrahend.o: 1670s, from Latin subtrahendus numerus (“number to be subtracted”), form of subtrahō (“to pull out from under, to subtract”) (English subtract). By surface analysis, subtract + -end (“patient (recipient) of action”).
subtrahend.example: In the subtraction 10 − 4, 4 is the subtrahend.
subtrahend.exampleSense: A number or quantity to be subtracted from another.

minted.o: simple past and past participle of mint. From Middle English mynt, münet (“money, coin”), from Old English mynet (“coin”), from late Proto-West Germanic *munit, from Latin monēta (“place for making coins, coined money”), from the temple of Juno Moneta (named for Monēta mother of the Muses), where coins were made. Doublet of money and manat. The verb is from the noun; Old English mynetian (“to mint”) is a parallel formation.

minuend.o: From Latin minuendus (“something to be diminished”), gerundive of minuō (“decrease, diminish”), by surface analysis, minus + -end.
minuend.example: In the subtraction 10 − 4, 10 is the minuend and 4 is the subtrahend.
minuend.exampleSense: A number or quantity from which another is to be subtracted.

turnstile.example: The fare was fixed at 2d., irrespective of distance, and was paid by passengers on passing through turnstiles at each station.
turnstile.exampleSense: A rotating mechanical device that controls and counts passage between public areas, especially one that only allows passage after a charge has been paid.

correctness.example: As a demonstration, we first establish the correctness of the Jacobian matrices for kinetic models of hydrogen, methane, ethylene, and isopentanol oxidation, then demonstrate the performance achievable on CPUs and GPUs using pyJac via matrix evaluation timing comparisons..

crosstalk.o: From cross- + talk. Usage in reference to the Chinese comedic performance is probably a loose calque from Chinese 相聲／相声 (xiàngsheng).
crosstalk.example: I couldn't hear the opening address because of all the crosstalk around me.
crosstalk.exampleSense: Conversation that is incidental to the topic under discussion.

quadrature.example: When the Moon is in quadrature, it appears in the sky as a half-moon.
quadrature.exampleSense: A situation in which the directions of two celestial bodies (or a celestial body and the Sun) form a right angle from the perspective of the observer.

quadrate.o:
adj: From Middle English quadrat, quadrate, from Latin quadrātus (“square”), past participle of quadrō (“to make four-cornered, square, put in order, intransitive be square”), from quadra (“a square”), later quadrus (“square”), from quattuor (“four”).

noun: From Middle English quadrat, quadrate, from Latin quadrātum. Doublet of quadrat; compare also quadrant (“square or quadrangle”).

verb: From Latin quadrātus, past participle of quadrō.
quadrate.example: Figures, some round, some triangle, some quadrate.
quadrate.exampleSense: Having four equal sides, the opposite sides parallel, and four right angles; square.

quadruple.o: From Middle English quadruple, from Latin quadruplus. Can be analyzed as quadri- + -ple.
quadruple.example: He's quite an athlete and can do quadruple jumps with ease.
quadruple.exampleSense: Being four times as long, as big or as many of something.

quadrilateral.o: Learned borrowing from New Latin quadrilaterus + -al.
quadrilateral.example: The Venetian quadrilateral comprised Mantua, Peschiera, Verona, and Legnano.
quadrilateral.exampleSense: An area defended by four fortresses supporting each other.

biquadrate.example: Two biquadrated is equal to sixteen.
biquadrate.exampleSense: To raise to the fourth power; to determine the result of multiplying by itself three times.

doctoral.o: From doctor + -al, probably modelled on Latin doctorālis.
doctoral.example: We have no need of doctorall consultations or collegian interpretations. Our senses tell us where it is and what it is.
doctoral.exampleSense: Pertaining to a medical doctor or physician.

acutely.example: I minored in physics at university, so am acutely aware of atomic structure.

therefore.o: From Middle English therfore, therfor, tharfore, thorfore; synchronically a univerbation of there (pronominal adverb) + for, literally “for that (reason)”. The spelling has been changed due to a reanalysis as there + fore (literally “forward from that; thence”). See also therefor, ultimately the same formation. Compare Saterland Frisian deerfoar, Dutch daarvoor, German dafür, Danish and Norwegian derfor, Swedish därför.
therefore.example: Traditional values will always have a place. Therefore, they will never lose relevance.
therefore.exampleSense: Consequently, by or in consequence of that or this cause; referring to something previously stated.

functional.example: A functional construction element generally must meet higher technical but lower aesthetical requirements.
functional.exampleSense: Only for functional purposes, notably in architecture.

unfolding.o: present participle and gerund of unfold. From Middle English unfolden, from Old English unfealdan (“to unfold”), equivalent to un- + fold.
unfolding.example: If I had the space, I'd cite dozens more examples of Gould's graceful unfoldings of various Beatle tunes.
unfolding.exampleSense: The process by which something unfolds or becomes revealed.

folding.example: Refrigerating the dough between rollings and foldings also makes the dough easy to handle and prevents the butter from becoming too soft.
folding.exampleSense: The action of folding; a fold.

innominate.o: From Latin innōminātus, from in- (“not”) + nōminātus (“named”).
innominate.example: Counsel for the Defence objected to the libel, on the grounds that the offence was innominate.
innominate.exampleSense: Having no name, nameless, unnamed; anonymous.

padding.o:
verb: See the etymology of the corresponding lemma form.

noun: From pad + -ing.
padding.example: That magazine is mostly advertisements; the rest is padding.
padding.exampleSense: Anything of little value used to fill up space.

donation.o: From Middle English donacion, donation, from Middle French donation, from Latin dōnātiō (“a present”), from dōnō (“to give”), from dōnum (“a gift”). Recorded in English since the 15th century. Equivalent to donate + -ion.
donation.example: They were collecting donations for the elderly at Christmas.
donation.exampleSense: A voluntary gift or contribution for a specific cause.

increasing.o:
adj: From increase + -ing (participial suffix).

noun: From Middle English encresing, equivalent to increase + -ing (gerund suffix).
increasing.example: Now begin the increasings for the chest by making 2 stitches in the fourth stitch; repeat this, increasing in every fourth row, but 1 stitch further each time, so as to form a slanting line, the same as a dress-pleat.

spacial.example: The spacial depths between the glittering threads of the web and the chef seemed abysmic and prodigious. He might have belonged to another realm.

connectivity.example: Since submitting our Strategic Outline Business Case to the DfT last summer, MPs, government ministers and even the new Prime Minister have started talking about our £2 billion proposals as the answer to poor rail connectivity between the East Midlands and the West Midlands.

certification.example: You do not possess the certifications required for this post.
certification.exampleSense: A professional qualification that certifies a person's ability.

pivotal.example: "Crucially, HS2 is already playing a pivotal role in helping Britain's post-pandemic economic recovery.
pivotal.exampleSense: Being of crucial importance; central, key.

dummy.o: From dumb + -y. Pacifier sense from dummy teat where dummy is in the sense of a nonfunctional replica.
dummy.example: To understand the effects of the accident, we dropped a dummy from the rooftop.
dummy.exampleSense: Something constructed with the size and form of a human, to be used in place of a person.

pendent.o: From Middle English pendaunt, Anglo-Norman pendaunt, pendant, respelled to reflect Latin pendēns, pendentis, present participle of pendere (“to hang, to be suspended”). Compare pendant, which retained the spelling.
pendent.example: Jandrell, Sa. three buckles, the tongues pendent ar. two and a one.
pendent.exampleSense: Hanging or pointed downward; (of a crescent) with its horns pointing downward.

transverse.o: Late Middle English, from Latin trānsversus (“turned across; going or lying across or crosswise”). Doublet of transversal.
transverse.example: Unlike the older trains, the new units have walk-through carriages and longitudinal rather than transverse seating.
transverse.exampleSense: Situated or lying across; side to side, relative to some defined "forward" direction; perpendicular or slanted relative to the "forward" direction; identified with movement across areas.

interleaving.o: present participle and gerund of interleave. From inter- + leave.

wavelet.o: From wave + -let; a calque of French ondelette, from onde (“wave”) + -ette (diminutive suffix).

congenial.example: What was it that made this notion of mimesis, in spite of its inherent difficulties that only the dialectical method enables him to avoid, seem so useful and congenial to Plato?

differential.o: Learned borrowing from Latin differentiālis. By surface analysis, different + -ial.
differential.example: [Caspar Schetz, Baron of Grobbendonck] was regularly in the pay of Sir Thomas Gresham, to whom he produced differential favours, and by whose government he was rewarded by gold chains and presents of hard cash, bestowed as secretly as the equivalent was conveyed adroitly.
differential.exampleSense: Of or pertaining to a difference.

instinctively.example: Fish instinctively know how to swim; most humans don't.
instinctively.exampleSense: Innately; by instinct; without being taught.

intransitive.example: This means that subcategorization properties do not allow us to distinguish between transitives and intransitives (both types of verbs are allowed, but not obliged, to take a direct object).

elementary.o: From Middle English elementare, from Latin elementārius (“elementary”), from elementum (“one of the four elements of antiquity; fundamentals”) + -ārius (adjective-forming suffix). Cognate with French élémentaire. By surface analysis, element + -ary.
elementary.example: At Lakeside Elementary I learned to appreciate the forest.

manipulation.o: From French manipulation, from Old French manipule, from Latin manipulus. Morphologically manipulate + -ion.
manipulation.example: The counselor was able to reach the disturbed teen through positive psychological manipulation.
manipulation.exampleSense: The usage of psychological influence over a person, event, or situation to gain a desired outcome.

ad hoc.o: Learned borrowing from New Latin ad hoc (“to this, for this”).
ad hoc.example: Contrary to the traditional condoning of ad hoc hypotheses, and in line with Popper's and Grünbaum's approaches, we see, once an ad hoc hypothesis is introduced we are unhappy about it and try to eliminate it.
ad hoc.exampleSense: Postulated solely to save a theory from being falsified, without making any new predictions.

excitation.o: From Middle English excitacion, excitacioun, from Old French excitation, from Latin excitātiō. Morphologically excite + -ation.
excitation.example: Generator excitation is obtained by a combination of the separately-excited and self-excited fields, and the output is controlled by a resistance in the separate field circuit adjusted by the load regulator under the control of the engine governor.
excitation.exampleSense: The act of exciting or putting in motion; the act of rousing up or awakening.

timing.o: present participle and gerund of time. From Middle English tyme, time, from Old English tīma (“time, period, space of time, season, lifetime, fixed time, favorable time, opportunity”), from Proto-West Germanic *tīmō, from Proto-Germanic *tīmô (“time”), from Proto-Indo-European *deh₂imō, from Proto-Indo-European *deh₂y- (“to divide”). Related to tide. Not related to Latin tempus. Cognates * Scots tym, tyme (“time”) * Alemannic German Zimen, Zīmmän (“time, time of the year, opportune time, opportunity”) * Danish time (“hour, lesson”) * Elfdalian taime (“hour”) * Faroese tími (“hour, lesson, time”) * Icelandic tími (“time, season”) * Norwegian time (“lesson, hour”) * Swedish timma, timme (“hour”).
timing.example: The officials used the latest technology to ensure timing down to the nearest millisecond.
timing.exampleSense: The regulation of the pace of e.g. an athletic race, the speed of an engine, the delivery of a joke, or the occurrence of a series of events.

govern.o: From Middle English governen, governe, from Anglo-Norman and Old French governer, guverner, from Latin gubernō, from Ancient Greek κυβερνάω (kubernáō, “to steer, drive, govern”). Displaced native Old English wealdan, whence modern dialectical English wald (“to govern”).
govern.example: Chance governs the outcome of many card games.
govern.exampleSense: To exercise a deciding or determining influence on.

prefer.o: From Middle English preferren, from Anglo-Norman preferer, from Latin praeferō. Displaced native Old English foresettan and foreberan. Doublet of prelate. See also infer, relate and refer, delate and defer, as well as collate and confer among others.
prefer.example: You don’t attack politicians because you prefer them; you attack them because you’re scared of them.
prefer.exampleSense: To be in the habit of choosing something rather than something else; to favor; to like better.

prototyping.o: present participle and gerund of prototype. From French prototype or Late Latin prototypon, from Ancient Greek πρωτότυπος (prōtótupos, “original; prototype”), from πρωτο- (prōto-, “first”) (from πρῶτος (prôtos, “first; earliest”)) + τῠ́πος (tŭ́pos, “blow, pressing; sort, type”) (from τύπτω (túptō, “to beat, strike”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)tewp- (“to push; to stick”)). The word is analysable as proto- + -type.
prototyping.example: ■ A Design and Build Contract for the design, software development, prototyping, factory testing, integration testing, installation, static and dynamic testing and commissioning of the TDS.
prototyping.exampleSense: The rapid creation of prototypes of a new product for demonstration and research purposes.

froth.o: From Middle English froth, frooth, froþ, likely a borrowing from Old Norse froða, from Proto-Germanic *fruþǭ; Old English āfrēoþan (“to foam, froth”) is from same Germanic root. Verb attested from late 14th century. Compare Swedish fradga.
froth.example: Froth or scum at the paper machine consists largely of clay, rosin, and starch.

frothy.example: For a frothy result, in a blender blend the hot chocolate in batches.
frothy.exampleSense: Foamy or churned to the point of becoming infused with bubbles.

postulate.o:
noun: Borrowed from Latin postulātum, a neuter nominalization of postulātus, perfect passive participle of postulō, possibly from poscō. See -ate (noun-forming suffix) for more. Cognate with French postulat.

verb: From Latin postulātus, perfect passive participle of postulō (“to request”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix) for more. Cognate with French postuler.

verb: From Latin postulātus, perfect passive participle of postulō (“to request”), see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) for more.

breakdown.example: After so much stress, he suffered a breakdown and simply gave up.
breakdown.exampleSense: (Sudden) worsening of physical health or (more commonly) mental stability, resulting in an inability to carry on normal activities; (countable) an instance of this.

portmanteau.o: From Middle French portemanteau (“coat stand”), from porte (“he carries”, third-person singular present indicative of porter (“to carry”)) + manteau (“coat”), literally “[that which] carries coat”. The lexical sense (sense 2) was first used figuratively by Lewis Carroll in Through the Looking-Glass (1871) to describe the words he coined in the poem “Jabberwocky”, based on the concept of two words packed together, similar to a portmanteau (sense 1). Sense 3 (“portmanteau film”) is derived from this.
portmanteau.example: Rodolphus therefore finding such an earnest Invitation, embrac'd it with thanks, and with his Servant and Portmanteau, went to Don Juan's; where they first found good Stabling for their Horses, and afterwards as good Provision for themselves.
portmanteau.exampleSense: A large travelling case usually made of leather, and opening into two equal sections.

hysteresis.o: Coined by Sir James Alfred Ewing from Ancient Greek ὑστέρησις (hustérēsis, “shortcoming”), from ὑστερέω (husteréō, “I am late, fall short”), from ὕστερος (hústeros, “later”). By surface analysis, hyster- (“higher, outer, latter, next”) + -esis.

curie.o: Borrowed from French curie. Named after French physicist Pierre Curie (1859–1906).

saturation.o: Borrowed from Late Latin saturatio, saturationem.
saturation.example: Modulation often requires that amplifiers operate below saturation.
saturation.exampleSense: The point at which the output of a linear device, such as a linear amplifier, deviates significantly from being a linear function of the input when the input signal is increased.

pine cone.o: Alternative form of pinecone. From pine + cone.

wrapper.o: From Middle English wrappere, equivalent to wrap + -er.
wrapper.example: Messy trains are horrible, but you can sort of understand passengers leaving their sandwich wrappers and paper cups if there is nowhere to dispose of them.
wrapper.exampleSense: Something that is wrapped around something else as a cover or protection: a wrapping.

investigator.o: Attested in the mid‐16th century; from Latin investigator, from investigare, equivalent to investigate + -or.
investigator.example: Over the past year, Hur was tasked with investigating classified documents found at Biden’s home and private office from his time as vice president. Hur was seen as a meticulous investigator during the probe, sources told CNN.

geometry.o: From Middle English gemetry, geometrie, from Old French geometrie (modern French géométrie), from Latin geōmetria, from Ancient Greek γεωμετρία (geōmetría, “geometry, land-survey”), from γεωμέτρης (geōmétrēs, “geometer, land measurer”), from γῆ (gê, “earth, land, country”) + -μετρία (-metría, “measurement”), from μέτρον (métron, “a measure”). By surface analysis, geometer + -y or geo- + -metry. Doublet of gematria.
geometry.example: ANY problem in geometry can easily be reduced to such terms that a knowledge of the lengths of certain straight lines is sufficient for its construction.
geometry.exampleSense: The branch of mathematics dealing with spatial relationships.

alteration.o: From Old French alteracion (French altération), from Medieval Latin alterātiō. Morphologically alter + -ation.
alteration.example: …and I saw by the alteration in your face that a train of thought had been started.
alteration.exampleSense: The state of being altered; a change made in the form or nature of a thing; a changed condition.

geometric.o: From Latin geōmetricus, from Ancient Greek γεωμετρικός (geōmetrikós), from γεωμέτρης (geōmétrēs). By surface analysis, geometer + -ic or geo- + -metric.
geometric.example: The architect used geometric techniques to design her home.

conjugate.o: The adjective (as “combined, united”) and noun are first attested in 1471, in Middle English, the verb in 1530; partly from Middle English conjugat(e) (“combined, united”), partly directly borrowed from New Latin coniugātus, the perfect passive participle of Latin coniugō (“to yoke together, combine; (New Latin) to conjugate, decline, inflect”) (see -ate (etymology 1, 2 and 3)), from con- (“with”) + iugō (“to join”). In Classical Latin, the word for conjugate (grammar) was dēclīnō, coniugō is a later back-formation from post-classical coniugātiō (“conjugation, declension”).
conjugate.example: The effects of hunger were often conjugated with epidemic disease.
conjugate.exampleSense: To join together, to unite; to juxtapose.

identification.example: The authorities asked for his identification.
identification.exampleSense: A document or documents serving as evidence of a person's identity.

filter.o: From Middle English filtre, from Medieval Latin filtrum (compare also Old French feutre (“felt; filter”)), from Frankish *filtir, from Proto-West Germanic *felt. See felt. Doublet of phin.
filter.example: The water filtered through the rock and soil.
filter.exampleSense: To pass through a filter or to act as though passing through a filter.

twiddle.o: Unknown. Perhaps a blend of twirl, twist, or twitch; fiddle.
twiddle.example: With a toot on the flute and a twiddle on the fiddle, O!

empty.o: From Middle English emty, amty, from Old English ǣmtiġ, ǣmettiġ (“vacant, empty, free, idle, unmarried”, literally “without must or obligation, leisurely”), from Proto-Germanic *uz- (“out”) + Proto-Germanic *mōtijô, *mōtô (“must, obligation, need”), *mōtiþô (“ability, accommodation”), from Proto-Indo-European *med- (“measure; to acquire, possess, be in command”). Related to Old English ġeǣmtigian (“to empty”), ǣmetta (“leisure”), mōtan (“can, to be allowed”). More at mote, meet. The interconsonantal excrescent p is a euphonic insertion dating from Middle English.
empty.example: The cinema emptied quickly after the end of the film.
empty.exampleSense: To make empty; to remove the contents of.

chile.o: From Spanish chile. A variant of chili, chilli; see that entry for more information.

capsaicin.o: Arbitrary alteration of earlier capsicine, capsicin (“material extracted from cayenne pepper”), presumably to prevent confusion, from German Capsicin, from New Latin capsicum + German -in. Name introduced by John Clough Thresh (1850–1932) in “Capsaicin, the Active Principle of Capsicum Fruits”.

capsicum.o: Borrowed from New Latin capsicum, from Ancient Greek καψικός (kapsikós, “like a box”), from Latin capsa (“box”).
capsicum.example: Celery is often combined with carrots and onions in gently fried aromatic base preparations for other dishes (French mirepoix, Italian soffritto, Spanish sofregit; in the Louisiana Cajun “trinity” of aromatics the carrots are replaced by green capsicums).
capsicum.exampleSense: The non-spicy fruit of the above plants, the bell pepper, contrasting with spicy varieties known as chilli.

projectile.o: From Medieval Latin prōiectilis (“projectile”), from Latin prōiectus, perfect passive participle of prōiciō (“throw forth; extend; expel”).

voltaic.o: From Volta + -ic. Named after Italian chemist and physicist Alessandro Volta.
voltaic.example: Around them, the air thrummed with the kind of voltaic wailing to power up the darkest night.
voltaic.exampleSense: reminiscent of the action of electricity: thrilling, shocking, dramatic.

perovskite.o: From Perovski + -ite. Named for Russian mineralogist L. A. Perovski (1792-1856) in 1839.

dwarf.o: From Middle English dwergh, dwerw, dwerf, from Old English dweorg, from Proto-West Germanic *dwerg, from Proto-Germanic *dwergaz. Cognate with Scots droich, dwerch (“dwarf, midget”); Old High German twerc (German, Luxembourgish Zwerg (“dwarf”)); Old Norse dvergr (Danish dværg (“dwarf, midget”), Faroese dvørgur (“dwarf”), Icelandic dvergur (“dwarf”), Norwegian Bokmål dverg (“dwarf”), Norwegian Nynorsk dverg, verg (“dwarf”), Swedish dvärg (“dwarf”)); Old Frisian dwirg (Saterland Frisian Dwärch (“dwarf”), West Frisian dwerch (“dwarf”)); Middle Low German dwerch, dwarch, twerg (German Low German Dwarg (“dwarf”)); Middle Dutch dwerch, dworch (Dutch dwerg (“dwarf”)). The Modern English noun has undergone complex phonetic changes. The form dwarf is the regular continuation of Old English dweorg, but the plural dweorgas would have given rise to dwarrows and the oblique stem dweorge- would have led to dwery. These forms are sometimes found as the nominative singular in Middle English texts and in English dialects. A parallel case is that of Old English burg giving burgh, borough, burrow, bury.
dwarf.example: It is possible to grow the plants as dwarf as one desires.

striate.o: From Latin striatum, past participle of strio (“to groove”).

receptive.o: From Late Middle English receptive, receptyue (“capable of receiving something; acting as a receptacle”), borrowed from Medieval Latin receptivus (“capable of receiving something”), from Latin receptus (“retaken, having been retaken; received, having been received”) + -īvus (suffix added to the perfect passive participial stems of verbs, forming a deverbal adjective meaning ‘doing; related to doing’). Receptus is the perfect passive participle of recipiō (“to regain possession, take back; to recapture; to receive; to accept, undertake”), from re- (prefix meaning ‘back, backwards; again’) + capiō (“to capture, catch, take; to take hold, take possession; to take on; to contain, hold; to occupy; to possess; to receive, take in; to comprehend, understand; to captivate, charm”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kap- (“to hold; to seize”)).

neo.example: This fabulous fannish cover illustrated the three stages of fandom: the neo, the trufan, and the BNF.

format.o: Via French format and German Format, from New Latin liber fōrmātus (“book fashioned”), from fōrmō (“to shape, fashion”).
format.example: I lost weeks of work when I inadvertently formatted my hard drive.
format.exampleSense: To prepare a mass storage medium for initial use, erasing any existing data in the process.

formal.o:
adj: From Middle English formel, borrowed from Old French formel, from Latin fōrmālis, from fōrma (“form”); equivalent to form + -al.

noun: See formo-.
formal.example: She spoke formal English, without any dialect.
formal.exampleSense: Being in accord with established forms.

foldable.example: This should speed up assembly, although many traditionally assembled foldables can be put together in 20 minutes or less; they can be knocked down faster.

conformable.example: In age well-balanced, in personal appearance fairly matched, and in domestic requirements conformable, in temper this couple differed, though even here they did not often clash, he being equable, if not lymphatic, and she decidedly nervous and sanguine.
conformable.exampleSense: Having the same shape or form; very similar.

deformable.o: From French déformable; equivalent to deform + -able.
deformable.example: The adaptive optical systems in modern astronomical telescopes compensate for atmospheric distortion by using deformable mirrors.

easel.o: Borrowed from Dutch ezel (“donkey; easel”), from Middle Dutch esel (“donkey”), from Proto-West Germanic *asil, from Latin asellus (“young ass or small donkey”), diminutive of asinus (“ass, donkey”), ultimately from an unknown source in Asia Minor. Essentially, the stand that a painting is placed on is being likened to a donkey carrying a burden; compare horse (“a frame with legs used to support something”), as in clotheshorse and sawhorse.
easel.example: It would also form part of a new carriage design, which had started out on Swindon drawing office easels two years earlier.
easel.exampleSense: An upright frame, typically on three legs, for displaying or supporting something, such as an artist's canvas.

essay.o:
noun: Since late 16th century, borrowed from Middle French essay, essai (“essay”), meaning coined by Montaigne at the same time, from the same words with the earlier meanings 'experiment; assay; attempt', from Old French essay, essai, assay, assai, from Latin exagium (“weight; weighing, testing on the balance”), from exigere + -ium.

verb: From Middle French essayer, essaier, from Old French essaiier, essayer, essaier, assaiier, assayer, assaier, from essay, essai, assay, assai (“attempt; assay; experiment”) as above.
essay.example: He retraced his steps to the front gate, which he essayed to open.

sodium.o: Coined by British chemist Humphry Davy in 1808, from soda + -ium.
sodium.example: From Keighley onwards we had obviously returned to civilisation, for the surrounding country was now studded with the sodium street lights of suburbia and a thickening industrial haze was blotting out the moon.

absent.o:
adj: From Middle English absent, from Middle French absent, from Old French ausent, and their source, Latin absens, present participle of absum (“to be away from”), from ab (“away”) + sum (“to be”).

verb: From Middle English absenten, from Old French absenter, from Late Latin absentāre (“keep away, be away”).
absent.example: When they were able to return to the clinic some months later, certain pieces of equipment were absent.
absent.exampleSense: Being away from a place; withdrawn from a place; existing but not present; (sometimes) missing.

assert.o: From Latin assertus, perfect passive participle of asserō (“declare someone free or a slave by laying hands upon him; hence free from, protect, defend; lay claim to, assert, declare”), from ad (“to”) + serō (“join, range in a row”).
assert.example: Since going to therapy, I've found it much easier to assert myself.
assert.exampleSense: To insist on the legitimacy of one's rights, opinion, etc; not to allow oneself to be dismissed; to ensure that one is taken into consideration; to make oneself respected; to be assertive. See assert oneself.

assent.o: From Middle English assent (noun) and assenten (verb), from Old French assent (noun) and assentir (verb), from Latin assentiō (whence as-).
assent.example: The princess assented to all that was suggested.

dielectric.o: From dia- (“through”) + electric. Learned 19th-century formation, coined by William Whewell (died 1866).

orbital.o: Borrowed from Medieval Latin orbitālis, from orbita (“a track or rut; a circuit, orbit”) + -ālis (“-al”, adjectival suffix), equivalent to orbit + -al. Doublet of orbitalis.
orbital.example: As with most power tools, orbitals can be divided into light and heavy-duty categories.

interpolation.o: From French interpolation, from Latin interpolatio. Morphologically interpolate + -ion.
interpolation.example: Today a widely established convention encloses all editorial interpolations in square brackets [like so] for clarity.
interpolation.exampleSense: That which is introduced or inserted; in contexts of content analysis of centuries-old texts, especially something foreign or spurious.

interposition.o: From Middle English interposicion, from Old French interposicion, from Latin interpositio.
interposition.example: As he spoke, he tried to catch the remnant of the paper, but was too late—Lady Anne's eye had been more accurate than to admit such an interposition;...
interposition.exampleSense: The act of interposing, or the state of being interposed; a being, placing, or coming between; mediation.

discontinuity.o: From Late Latin discontinuitās, from discontinuus, equivalent to dis- + continuity.
discontinuity.example: Shock waves are sudden discontinuities propagated in compressible media – usually air.
discontinuity.exampleSense: A lack of continuity, regularity or sequence; a break or gap.

magnetic.exampleSense: Having an extraordinary ability to attract: attractive, alluring, persuasive

civilised.o: simple past and past participle of civilise. From civil + -ise.

uncivilised.o: Alternative spelling of uncivilized. From un- + civilized.

civil service.example: He's got a steady job in the civil service.
civil service.exampleSense: The body of civilian employees of any level of government, not subject to political appointment and removal, normally hired and promoted largely on the basis of competitive examination.

civil servant.example: Policing the relationship between government and business in a free society is difficult. Businesspeople have every right to lobby governments, and civil servants to take jobs in the private sector.
civil servant.exampleSense: A person employed in the civil service; a government employee.

phonon.o:
noun: From phono- + -on. From Ancient Greek φωνή (phōnḗ, “sound”). Modelled after photon.

noun: From phono- + -on. From Ancient Greek φωνή (phōnḗ, “sound”).

relive.example: Replays in video games allow you to relive your greatest moments.
relive.exampleSense: To experience (something) again; to live over again.

heartfelt.example: She expressed her heartfelt sympathies at the death of his mother.
heartfelt.exampleSense: Believed or felt deeply and sincerely.

interpenetrate.example: [O]ur Religion is not yet a horrible restless Doubt, still less a far horribler composed Cant; but a great heaven-high Unquestionability, encompassing, interpenetrating the whole of Life.

translocation.example: There happen'd certain translocations at the deluge.
translocation.exampleSense: Removal of things from one place to another; displacement; substitution of one thing for another.

transposition.o: From Middle French transposition, from Medieval Latin transpositio.

cutlet.o: From French côtelette (recorded in English since 1706), from Middle French costelette (“little rib”), from coste + -elette, from Old French coste (“rib, side”), from Latin costa. Influenced by English cut, as if from cut + -let. Doublet of kotlet and kotleta.

interception.o: Borrowed from Latin interceptiō; compare French interception.

hence.o: A later Middle English spelling, retaining the voiceless -s, of hennes (henne + adverbial genitive ending -s), from Old English heonan (“away", "hence”), from a Proto-West Germanic *hin-, from Proto-Germanic *hiz, and Proto-Germanic *-anē. Cognate with Old Saxon hinan, Old High German hinnan (German hinnen), Dutch heen, Swedish hän. Related to Old English her (“here”).
hence.example: I'm going hence, because you have insulted me.
hence.exampleSense: From here, from this place, away.

spacer.example: "How do I know I can trust you?" asked BKR.
spacer.exampleSense: A person who works or lives in space.

written.example: Written language is a way of representing spoken language.
written.exampleSense: Of, relating, or characteristic of writing (i.e., of that which has been written).

blockage.example: There was a blockage in the sewer, so we called out the plumber.
blockage.exampleSense: The thing that is the cause of such a state, blocking a passage.

urinal.o:
noun: From Middle English urinal, urynal, orynal, from Old French urinal, orinal (“vessel for urination”), from Latin ūrīnālis (“urinary”). Use for plumbing fixtures attested from 1851.

adj: From Middle French urinal, from Late Latin ūrīnālis, equivalent to urine + -al.
urinal.example: This was the second time in the last few months that she was asked to install a urinal in a luxury residential project, and she said she knows many other designers and architects who have been specifying home urinals in their projects.
urinal.exampleSense: A device or fixture used for urination, particularly

waiver.o: From Anglo-Norman weyver, from waiver. Date: 1628. By surface analysis, waive + -er.
waiver.example: I had to sign a waiver when I went skydiving, agreeing not to sue even if something went wrong.
waiver.exampleSense: A legal document removing some requirement, such as waiving a right (giving it up) or a waiver of liability (agreeing to hold someone blameless).

waive.o:
verb: From Middle English weyven (“to avoid, renounce”), from Anglo-Norman weyver (“to abandon, allow to become a waif”), from Old French waif (“waif”), from gaiver (“to abandon”), ultimately of Scandinavian/North Germanic origin; see weyver.

verb: From Middle English weyven (“to wave, waver”), from Old Norse veifa (“to wave, swing”) (Norwegian veiva), from Proto-Germanic *waibijaną.

noun: From Anglo-Norman waive, probably as the past participle of weyver, as Etymology 1, above.
waive.example: but she might be waived, and held as abandoned.
waive.exampleSense: To abandon, give up (someone or something).

silly.o: From Middle English seely, sēlī, from Old English sǣliġ, ġesǣliġ (“lucky, fortunate”), from Proto-West Germanic *sālīg, from *sāli; equivalent to seel (“happiness, bliss”) + -y. Doublet of Seelie. The semantic evolution is “lucky” to “innocent” to “naive” to “foolish”. Compare the similar evolution of daft (originally meaning “accommodating”), and almost the reverse with nice (originally meaning “ignorant”).
silly.example: ... thrie Saturdayes befor Lambas and thrie efter called the six silie Saturdayes.

detachment.o: From French détachement. By surface analysis, detach + -ment.
detachment.example: Vietnamese sovereignty over the Paracels dated back at least to the early 19th century, when Emperor Gia-Long sent a detachment to Hoang Sa Island, it remained until the establishment of French protectorate over Annam, when France assumed responsibility for the islands.

detruncate.o: First attested in 1623; borrowed from Latin dētruncātus, perfect passive participle of dētruncō (“to cut off”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from dē- + truncō (“to maim, shorten, cut off”).

truncated.o: simple past and past participle of truncate. From Latin truncātus, perfect passive participle of truncō (“maim, reduce to a trunk”); see trunk as a verb.

truncate.o: From Latin truncātus, perfect passive participle of truncō (“maim, reduce to a trunk”); see trunk as a verb.
truncate.example: The script was truncated to leave time for commercials.
truncate.exampleSense: To shorten (something) by, or as if by, cutting part of it off.

optimum.o: From New Latin, neuter of Latin optimus (“best, very good”), from the root in ops (“work”) or omnis (“all”).

mortgage.o: From Middle English morgage and Middle French mortgage, from Anglo-Norman morgage, from Old French mort gage (“dead pledge”), after a translation of judicial Medieval Latin mortuum wadium, with wadium from Frankish *wadi (“wager, pledge”). Compare gage and also wage. So called because rents and profits from the land were owed to the lender for as long as the gage existed (comparable to interest on a loan today), as opposed to the living gage, in which rents and profits automatically reduced the debt (paying it off over time).
mortgage.example: We're renting a property in the city centre because we can't afford to get a mortgage yet.
mortgage.exampleSense: A special form of secured loan where the purpose of the loan must be specified to the lender, to purchase assets that must be fixed (not movable) property, such as a house or piece of farm land. The assets are registered as the legal property of the borrower but the lender can seize them and dispose of them if they are not satisfied with the manner in which the repayment of the loan is conducted by the borrower. Once the loan is fully repaid, the lender loses this right of seizure and the assets are then deemed to be unencumbered.

actuality.o: From actual + -ity. * (television): Influenced by French actualité.
actuality.example: This is a news report from the scene of the event. When a voicer and an actuality are combined into one complete story, it's known as a wrap.

dismal.o: From Middle English dismal, dismale, from Anglo-Norman dismal, from Old French (li) dis mals (“(the) bad days”), from Medieval Latin diēs malī (“bad days”).
dismal.example: Liverpool's efforts thereafter had an air of desperation as their dismal 2012 league form continued.

see.o:
verb: From Middle English seen, from Old English sēon (“to see, look, behold, perceive, observe, discern, understand, know”), from Proto-West Germanic *sehwan, from Proto-Germanic *sehwaną (“to see”), from Proto-Indo-European *sekʷ- (“to see, notice”). Etymology 1 sense 9 is a calque of Latin vidē (“see (thou)”, 2ⁿᵈ person singular imperative), which was also borrowed into academic English (see vide) as well as Portuguese. Cognates Cognate with Scots see, sei (“to see”), Yola sau, ze, zee, zey, zie (“to see”), North Frisian se, si, siin, siine, siinj, sä, säie (“to see”), Saterland Frisian sjo (“to see”), West Frisian sjen (“to see”), Bavarian segn (“to see”), Central Franconian sehn, senn (“to see”), Dutch zien (“to see”), Low German sehn (“to see; to look”), German sehen (“to see”), Limburgish séëne, zeen (“to see”), Luxembourgish gesinn (“to see”), Alemannic German gseh (“to see”), Mòcheno sechen (“to see”), Vilamovian zaon (“to see”), Yiddish זען (zen, “to see”), Danish, Norwegian Bokmål, and Swedish se (“to see”), Elfdalian sją̊ (“to see”), Faroese síggja (“to see”), Icelandic sjá (“to see”), Norwegian Nynorsk sjå (“to see”), sia (“to foretell”), Gothic 𐍃𐌰𐌹𐍈𐌰𐌽 (saiƕan, “to see”), and more distantly with Albanian shof, shoh (“to see”), Latin secūtus, sequūtus (“followed”), Ancient Greek ἕπομαι (hépomai, “to follow, obey”), Persian ا (a), از (az), ز (ze, “from, of”), Luwian 𒁕𒀀𒌋𒄿𒅖 (“eye”), Sanskrit सच् (sac, “to be associated with, familiar with, have to do with”).

noun: From Middle English se, see, from Old French sie (“seat, throne; town, capital; episcopal see”), from Latin sēdēs (“seat”), referring to the bishop's throne or chair (compare seat of power) in the cathedral; related to the Latin verb sedēre (“to sit”). Doublet of sedes.
see.example: I saw the latest Tarantino flick last week.
see.exampleSense: To perceive or detect someone or something with the eyes, or as if by sight. To watch (a movie) at a cinema, or a show on television etc.

seel.o:
adj: From Middle English sel, sele, from Old English *sǣle (“good, fortunate, happy”) (attested in Old English unsǣle (“evil, wicked”)), from Proto-Germanic *sēliz (“good, happy”), from Proto-Indo-European *sel-, *sēl- (“to calm, quiet, be favourable”). Cognate with Danish sæl (“blissful”), Dutch zalig (“blissful”), Gothic 𐍃𐌴𐌻𐍃 (sēls, “good, kind, useful”), Icelandic sæll (“blissful”), Latin sōlor (“to comfort, console”), Swedish säll (“blissful”).

noun: From Middle English sele, sel, from Old English sǣl (“time, occasion, a fit time, season, opportunity, the definite time at which an event should take place, time as in bad or good times, circumstances, condition, position, happiness, joy, good fortune, good time, prosperity”), from Proto-Germanic *sēliz (“luck, joy”), from Proto-Indo-European *sel-, *sēl- (“to calm, quiet, be favourable”). Cognate with Icelandic sæla (“bliss”), Dutch zalig (“blissful, blessed”). More at silly.

verb: From Middle English silen, from Old French siller, ciller (“to sew up the eyelids of, hoodwink, wink”), from cil (“eyelid”), from Latin cilium (“eyelid, eyelash”).

verb: Ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *sīgan (“to drop”). Compare Low German sielen (“to lead off water”), French siller (“to run ahead, to make headway”), and English sile (transitive verb).

reciprocate.o: From Latin recīprocātus, perfect passive participle of recīprocō (“to move back and forth”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from reciprocus (“back an forth, reciprocal, alternating”) + -ō (first conjugation verb-forming suffix), itself possibly from a phrase such as reque proque (“back and forth”), from re- (“back”), prō (“forwards”) and -que (“and”). See also reciprocal. Compare French réciproquer.
reciprocate.example: Nugget appreciates the generosity! Nugget will reciprocate with a Monstermon card!
reciprocate.exampleSense: To give something else in response (where the "thing" may also be abstract, a feeling or action) To make a reciprocal gift.

decimeter.o: Borrowed from French décimètre. Equivalent to deci- + meter.

normal.o: From Latin normālis (“made according to a carpenter's square; later: according to a rule”), from nōrma (“carpenter's square”), of uncertain origin; doublet of normale. The earliest meaning of the word in English was "perpendicular; forming a right angle" like something normālis (“made according to a carpenter's square”), but by Late Latin normālis had also come to mean "according to a rule", from which modern English senses of the word derive: in the 1800s, as people began to quantitatively study things like height, weight and blood pressure, the usual or most common values came to be called "normal", and by extension values regarded as healthy or desirable came to be called "normal" regardless of their usuality.
normal.example: A number that is normal for every base b ≥ 2 is said to be absolutely normal.
normal.exampleSense: According to norms or rules or to a regular pattern. Adhering to or being what is considered natural or regular in a particular field or context: In whose representation in a given base b ≥ 2, for every positive integer n, the bⁿ possible strings of n digits follow a uniform distribution.

buzzword.o: Coined in the 1970s in the United States, from buzz + word.
buzzword.example: Their salespeople know all the right buzzwords, but they can't really help you solve your problems.
buzzword.exampleSense: A word drawn from, or imitative of, technical jargon, used more to impress others than to convey meaning.

overpersuade.example: Opportunitie casting him into the company of foure French Gallants well attended [...]; over-perswaded him to goe with them into France, to the Dutchesse of Mercury, from whom they should not only have meanes, but also Letter of favour to her noble Duke [...].
overpersuade.exampleSense: To win someone over through persuasion; to convince (someone) to do something against their own judgement or wishes.

dissuade.o: From Middle French dissuader, from Latin dissuādeō (“to urge differently”, “to advise against”, “to dissuade”), from dis- (“away from”, “asunder”) + suādeō (“to recommend”, “to advise”, “to urge”).
dissuade.example: Jane dissuaded Martha from committing suicide.
dissuade.exampleSense: To convince not to try or do.

dissuasion.o: From Middle English dissuasioun, from Middle French dissuasion.

mower.o: From Middle English mowere, equivalent to mow + -er.

lawnmower.example: We replaced our old electric lawnmower with a new cordless one.
lawnmower.exampleSense: A device used for cutting grass to a chosen height, typically of landscaped lawns of residences or institutions.

pontificate.o:
noun: From Latin pontificatus, from pontifex (“high priest”), from pons (“bridge”) + facere (“make”).

verb: From the past participle stem of Medieval Latin pontificō, from Latin pontifex (“high priest”), from pons (“bridge”) + facere (“make”).

hallucinate.o: First attested in 1604; borrowed from Latin hallūcinātus, alternative form of alūcinātus, perfect active participle of alucinor (“to dream”); see -ate (verb-forming suffix).
hallucinate.example: In case you were wondering, the yahoo url above doesn’t actually exist, the model just hallucinated it.
hallucinate.exampleSense: To produce information that is not supported by the model's training data.

hallucination.o: Derives from the verb hallucinate, from Latin hallucinatus. Compare French hallucination. The first known usage in the English language is from Sir Thomas Browne.
hallucination.example: Hallucinations are always evidence of cerebral derangement and are common phenomena of insanity.
hallucination.exampleSense: A sensory perception of something that does not exist, often arising from disorder of the nervous system, as in delirium tremens.

omnivorous.example: The Beckettian progression appears occasionally: while Miss Counihan (static) is an omnivorous reader and Murphy (transitional) a strict non-reader, Cooper is an analphabete.
omnivorous.exampleSense: Having an interest in a variety of subjects.

neutrally.example: The terms of the contract were arbitrated neutrally by a third party.
neutrally.exampleSense: In a neutral manner; evenhandedly or fairly.

neutralize.o: From French neutraliser (first attested in 1642). By surface analysis, neutral + -ize.
neutralize.example: All the powers involved are committed not only to stay out of a given territory, but also to reenter it if any one of them violates the independence of the neutralized country.
neutralize.exampleSense: To make (a territory, etc.) politically neutral.

neutrality.o: From Middle French neutralité, from Medieval Latin neutralitas. Morphologically neutral + -ity.
neutrality.example: The official pretence of a scrupulous solicitude to maintain neutrality is flagrantly insincere.
neutrality.exampleSense: The state or quality of being neutral; the condition of being unengaged in contests between others; state of taking no part on either side.

neutralise.o: From French neutraliser (first attested in 1642). By surface analysis, neutral + -ise.
neutralise.example: It’s all based on immobilising your opponent, rather than punching or kicking them, which means you learn how to neutralise, for example, a stranger grabbing your wrist.
neutralise.exampleSense: Non-Oxford British English standard form of neutralize.

ritualism.example: A carousing zone is a place where the ritualism of generating antinomian excitement prevails and may even be institutionalized.
ritualism.exampleSense: The practice of engaging in rituals.

sluttish.o: From Middle English scluttish, slottesche, slottysch, sluttissche, sluttissh; equivalent to slut + -ish.

slutty.example: The makeup, high heels and short skirt made her look so slutty.
slutty.exampleSense: Of, resembling, or suitable for, a slut.

slut.o: From Middle English slutt, slutte, slute (“a dirty or slovenly person, usually a woman, scullery maid; messy animal to prepare as food; slush, mud”), probably from Old English *slȳte (“sleet”), from Proto-West Germanic *slautijā, from Proto-Germanic *slautijǭ (“sleet, hail”), related to Proto-West Germanic *slaut (“puddle, ditch”).
