Compare Dutch slodder and slet, dialectal Swedish slata (“idle woman”), Norwegian sludd (“sleet”), and the dialectal Norwegian slutr (“sleet, impure liquid”). Doublet of sleet.
slut.example: You could hire a slut for a few hours, if you're that desperate.
slut.exampleSense: A sexually promiscuous woman. A prostitute.

hack.o:
verb: From Middle English hacken, hakken, from Old English *haccian (“to hack”), from Proto-West Germanic *hakkōn, from Proto-Germanic *hakkōną (“to chop; hoe; hew”), from Proto-Indo-European *keg-, *keng- (“to be sharp; peg; hook; handle”). Cognate with Saterland Frisian häkje (“to hack”), West Frisian hakje (“to hack”), Dutch hakken (“to chop up; hack”), German hacken (“to chop; hack; hoe”), Danish hakke (“to chop”), Swedish hacka (“to hack; chop”), French hacher (“to chop”). Related to hatch. The computer senses date back to at least 1955 when it initially referred to creative problem solving. By 1963, the negative connotations of “black hat” or malicious hacking had become associated with telephone hacking (cf. phreaking).

noun: Variations of hatch, heck.

noun: Abbreviation of hackney (“an ordinary horse”), probably from place name Hackney.

verb: Unclear. Perhaps imitative; compare hock, hawk. Alternatively, perhaps from hack (“chop; do something difficult”) via the idea of doing something (like breathing) or with difficulty.

noun: From hackysack.
hack.example: Dason is nothing but a two-bit hack.

diligently.example: Instead, empty bags were folded diligently into the corners of underpacked suitcases, waiting to be jammed full with the familiar objects of home.
diligently.exampleSense: In a diligent manner, with appropriate effort, carefully.

reminder.example: He left a note as a reminder to get groceries.

strategy.o: Derived from Latin stratēgia, from Ancient Greek στρατηγία (stratēgía, “office of general, command, generalship”), from στρατηγός (stratēgós, “the leader or commander of an army, a general”), from στρατός (stratós, “army”) + ἄγω (ágō, “to lead, conduct”).
strategy.example: Oftentimes, the very simple strategies pay very great dividends.
strategy.exampleSense: A plan of action intended to accomplish a specific goal.

mitigation.o: From Middle French mitigation, from Latin mitigatio.
mitigation.example: Its [the gantry crane's] noise-mitigation characteristics even include a soft-landing feature to minimise the noise when containers are lowered.
mitigation.exampleSense: A reduction or decrease of something harmful or unpleasant.

deliverable.example: Due to inclement weather, we will be unable to provide our deliverables.
deliverable.exampleSense: The tangible end product; that which will be delivered.

scape.o:
noun: From Latin scāpus, from Doric Greek σκᾶπος (skâpos). Doublet of native English shaft.

verb: From Middle English scapen (whence also atscapen and ofscapen (“to escape”)), formed by aphesis from escapen, ascapen (“to escape”). Compare also Old French scapper, a variant of Old French eschaper, formed via similar process. Doublet of escape and scarper.

noun: Probably imitative.
scape.example: Not pardoning so much as the scapes of error and ignorance.
scape.exampleSense: A freak; a slip; a fault; an escapade.

satin.o: From French satin, which is derived from "Zaitun", the Arabic name for the Chinese city of Quanzhou, itself derived from Arabic زَيْتُون (zaytūn, “Zayton; olive”), from phono-semantic matching from Chinese 刺桐 (MC tshjeH duwng, “coral tree”) in 刺桐城 (MC tshjeH duwng dzyeng, “coral tree town”), an old name for Quanzhou.
satin.example: Ibn Batuta informs us that a rich silk texture made here was called Zaitûniya; and there can be little doubt that this is the real origin of our word Satin,—Zettani in mediæval Italian, Aceytuni in Spanish.
satin.exampleSense: A cloth woven from silk, nylon or polyester with a glossy surface and a dull back. (The same weaving technique applied to cotton produces cloth termed sateen).

prune.o:
noun: From Middle English prune, from Old French prune, from Vulgar Latin *prūna, feminine singular formed from the neutral plural of Latin prūnum, from Ancient Greek προῦνον (proûnon), variant of προῦμνον (proûmnon, “plum”), a loanword from a language of Asia Minor. Doublet of plum.

verb: From Middle English prunen, prounen, proinen, from Old French proignier (“to trim the feathers with the beak”), earlier prooignier. Likely influenced by Middle French rogner, Old French rooignier (“cut, trim”) (from Latin rotundo?), and possibly by Old French provainier (“provine”) (Latin propaginem? whence French provigner). The relation to the noun is thus unclear.
prune.example: I hardly left that spot in my pool that month even when my fingers pruned and chlorine dried out my skin.
prune.exampleSense: To become wrinkled like a dried plum, as the fingers and toes do when kept submerged in water.

tessellate.o: Learned borrowing from Latin tessellātus, from tessella, diminutive of tessera; from Ancient Greek τέσσαρες (téssares), from Proto-Indo-European *kʷetwóres.
tessellate.example: It is possible to tessellate the plane with equilateral triangles and regular hexagons.
tessellate.exampleSense: To completely fill (an area) when multiple copies of one or more two-dimensional shapes are placed edge to edge.

probability.o: From Middle French probabilité, from Latin probābilitās (“probability, credibility”), from probābilis (“probable, credible”).
probability.example: These waters wash from the rocks such glistering tinctures, that the ground in some places seemeth as guilded, that better iudgements then ours might haue been perswaded, they contained more then probabilities.
probability.exampleSense: An event that is likely to occur.

agglomeration.o: From Latin agglomerātiō. By surface analysis, agglomerate + -ion.

disprove.o: From Middle English disproven, dispreven, from Old French desprover, from des- + prover, equivalent to dis- + prove.

congestion.o: From late Middle English congestioun, from Old French [Term?], from Latin congestĭō (“heap, accumulation”), from congerō (“to bring together, accumulate, heap up”), formed by the root gerō (“to carry”) and the prefix con-.

digest.o:
verb: From Middle English digesten, from Latin dīgestus, past participle of dīgerō (“carry apart”), from dī- (for dis- (“apart”)) + gerō (“to carry”), influenced by Middle French digestion. Partly displaced native Old English meltan (intransitive) and mieltan (transitive), both “to melt, to digest,” whence Modern English melt.

noun: From Latin dīgesta, neuter plural of dīgestus, past participle of dīgerō (“separate”).
digest.example: Feelingly digest the words you speak in prayer.
digest.exampleSense: To think over and arrange methodically in the mind; to reduce to a plan or method; to receive in the mind and consider carefully; to get an understanding of; to comprehend.

overcrowd.example: The host of business travellers between Bishops Stortford and London would scarcely take kindly to devious routing via the Southbury line; on the other hand, it is not desirable that they should overcrowd the business trains to and from Cambridge.
overcrowd.exampleSense: To fill beyond reasonable limits, with people, animals, objects or information.

overcrowded.o:
verb: See the etymology of the corresponding lemma form.

adj: From over- + crowded.
overcrowded.example: I've spent hours on overcrowded trains, and time on ones which were almost empty, because the recovery [from COVID] has been uneven.
overcrowded.exampleSense: Containing too many occupants for an area of its size.

overcrowding.o: present participle and gerund of overcrowd. From over- + crowd.
overcrowding.example: Department for Transport statistics show that since 2010 overcrowding in the morning peak at 11 cities has risen by 48%, to reach 280,000 standing passengers daily.
overcrowding.exampleSense: The situation where a space holds more occupants than it can comfortably accommodate.

crowded.o: simple past and past participle of crowd. From Middle English crouden, from Old English crūdan, from Proto-West Germanic *krūdan, from Proto-Germanic *krūdaną, *kreudaną, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *grewt- (“to push; press”). Cognate with German Low German kroden (“to push, shove”), Dutch kruien (“to push, shove”). (group of people, mob): Compare typologically throng (<<~ Proto-Germanic *þrinhwaną); Czech dav (akin to Russian дави́ть (davítʹ), да́вка (dávka)); Polish ciżba, ścisk (<~ ciskać, akin to ти́скать (tískatʹ)); Polish tłok, Russian толчея́ (tolčejá) (akin to толка́ть (tolkátʹ)).
crowded.example: The train is usually crowded and half the township of Forres seems to turn out to watch it go off.
crowded.exampleSense: Containing a dense pack or mass of something; teeming.

inseparable.o: From Middle English, from Middle French inséparable, from Latin īnsēparābilis. Constructed as in- + separable.
inseparable.example: Jayanta does so in answering an opponent who declares that the very idea of a relation between two inseparables is self-contradictory. How can inseparability and relation be reconciled?
inseparable.exampleSense: Something that cannot be separated from something else.

separable.o: From Middle English separable, from Middle French separable and its etymon Latin sēparābilis.

superscript.o: From Middle French superscript, from Latin superscriptus (“written above”). By surface analysis, super- + script.
superscript.example: The ambient or unsaturated value of a variable is superscripted with a "*".

transpose.o:
verb: From Middle English transposen, from Old French transposer, from Latin trānspositus, perfect passive participle of trānspōnō (“to put across”), from trāns (“across”) + pōnō (“to put”).

noun: From the verb.
transpose.example: After e6, the opening transposed to a Sicilian.
transpose.exampleSense: To reach a position that may also be obtained from a different move order.

confident.o: From Middle French confident, from Latin confidens (“confident, i.e. self-confident, in a good or bad sense, bold, daring, audacious, impudent”), present participle of confidere (“to trust fully, confide”). See confide.
confident.example: I'm pretty confident that she's not lying, she's acting normally.

confidence.o: From Middle English confidence, from Latin cōnfīdentia (possibly via Old French confidence), from cōnfīdō (“believe, confide in”) from con- (“with”) + fīdō (“trust”). By surface analysis, confide + ence.
confidence.example: I tell you this in the strictest confidence.
confidence.exampleSense: A feeling of certainty; firm trust or belief; faith.

collate.o: From Latin collātus, perfect passive participle of conferō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix). Doublet of confer. See also infer, delate and defer (Etymology 2), relate and refer, as well as prelate and prefer among others. Not related to collateral.
collate.example: "Once collated, all files are sent to an external printing business with a turnaround time of about seven days, and then most of the distribution is done in-house.
collate.exampleSense: To assemble something in a logical sequence.

defaecate.o: Alternative spelling of defecate. Borrowed from Latin dēfaecātus, the perfect passive participle of dēfaecō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix). See also faeces; cognate with French déféquer.

urinate.o: Borrowed from Medieval Latin urinātus, perfect passive participle of urinō (“urinate”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), equivalent to urine + -ate. Compare French uriner.
urinate.example: Boys on their campsite should avoid urinating within 200 feet of the lake.
urinate.exampleSense: To pass urine from the body.

sarcasm.o: From Late Latin sarcasmus, from Ancient Greek σαρκασμός (sarkasmós, “a sneer”), from σαρκάζω (sarkázō, “to gnash the teeth (in anger)”, literally “to strip off the flesh”), from σάρξ (sárx, “flesh”).
sarcasm.example: Although the Celebrity was almost impervious to sarcasm, he was now beginning to exhibit visible signs of uneasiness, the consciousness dawning upon him that his eccentricity was not receiving the ovation it merited.
sarcasm.exampleSense: Use of acerbic language to mock or convey contempt, often using irony and (in speech) often marked by overemphasis and sneering.

iterate.o: The adjective is first attested in 1471, in Middle English, the verb in 1533, the noun in 1941; partly inherited from Middle English iterat(e) (adjective), partly borrowed from Latin iterātus, perfect passive participle of iterō (“to do something for a second time, repeat”) (see -ate (etymology 1, 2 and 3)) , from iterum (“again”) + -ō. Sporadical participial usage of the adjective up until Early Modern English.
iterate.example: The baptisme is good and may not be iterate and geuen agayne.

nerdy.example: I got a pair of nerdy glasses and clothes for Halloween.
nerdy.exampleSense: Of, pertaining to, in the style of, or appealing to nerds.

nerd.o: Unknown. Attested since 1951 as US student slang. * Perhaps an alteration of nerts (“nuts", "crazy”); see references below. * The word, capitalized, appeared in 1950 in Dr. Seuss’s If I Ran the Zoo as the name of an imaginary animal: *: And then, just to show them, I’ll sail to Katroo / And bring back an It-Kutch, a Preep and a Proo, / A Nerkle, a Nerd and a Seersucker too! * Possibly a rebracketing of inert as a nert, as in he's inert = he's a nerd, in reference to one's lack of competence or athletic ability. * Various unlikely folk etymologies and less likely backronymic speculations also exist.

machine gun.example: Whether modern, industrial man is less or more warlike than his hunter-gatherer ancestors is impossible to determine. The machine gun is so much more lethal than the bow and arrow that comparisons are meaningless.
machine gun.exampleSense: A type of fully automatic firearm that fires bullets in rapid succession by a single action of the trigger and is capable of sustained fire.

require.o: From Old French requerre (whence Modern French requérir), from Latin requīrō (“to require, seek, ask for”, literally “to seek back”), from re- (“back; again”) + quaerō (“to seek”, whence query).
require.example: I requyre the in the name of god, that thou torment me nott.
require.exampleSense: To ask (someone) for something; to request.

requirement.example: There was a requirement of the government on citizens for paying taxes.
requirement.exampleSense: A necessity or prerequisite; something required or obligatory. Its adpositions are generally of in relation to who or what has given it, on in relation to whom or what it is given to, and for in relation to what is required.

so long.o: Uncertain. Compare to Swedish hej så länge and Russian пока (poka). See Douglas Harper (2001–2026), “so long”, in Online Etymology Dictionary.

blank.o: From Middle English blank, blonc, blaunc, blaunche, from Anglo-Norman blonc, blaunc, blaunche, from Old French blanc, feminine blanche, from Frankish *blank (“gleaming, white, blinding”), from Proto-Germanic *blankaz (“white, bright, blinding”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰleyǵ- (“to shine”). Akin to Old High German blanch (“shining, bright, white”) (German blank), Old English blanc (“white, grey”), blanca (“white steed”), Spanish blanco. More at blink, blind, blanch. Doublet of blanc.
blank.example: It was an unloaded gun that fired only blanks.
blank.exampleSense: Short for blank cartridge. [since the 19th century].

divide.o: PIE word *dwóh₁ From Middle English dividen, from Latin dīvidere (“to divide”). Displaced native Old English tōdǣlan.
divide.example: Divide the living child in two.
divide.exampleSense: To split or separate (something) into two or more parts.

covariance.example: As we will see in Chapter 8, we see both covariance and contravariance throughout the Java Collections. They largely exist to ensure that the generics just “do the right thing” and behave in a manner that should not surprise the developer.
covariance.exampleSense: The conversion of data types from wider to narrower in certain situations.

identically.example: It was hard to tell the twins apart: they even spoke identically.

bibliography.o: From Ancient Greek βιβλιογραφία (bibliographía, “the act or habit of writing books”), from βιβλιογράφος (bibliográphos, “a writer of books”), from βιβλίον (biblíon, “small book”) + γράφω (gráphō, “I write”).
bibliography.example: The supplementary bibliography (in Vol. VI) attests to the comprehensiveness of the effort.
bibliography.exampleSense: A section of a written work containing citations, not quotations, to all the books referred to in the work.

prerequisite.example: A degree is a prerequisite for entry into this profession.
prerequisite.exampleSense: Something that is required as necessary or indispensable, or as a prior condition of something else.

acupuncture.o: Learned borrowing from New Latin acūpūnctūra, from Latin acus + pūnctūra. First attested in 1684. By surface analysis, acu- + puncture.
acupuncture.example: Chinese doctors at Chishan County Hospital in Shansi Province have used acupuncture on the scalp to cure a patient suffering from paralysis of the right limbs caused by inflammation of the brain’s blood vessels.
acupuncture.exampleSense: The insertion of needles into the (living) tissue of the body affecting the Qi or energy along energetic pathways of the body called meridians. This modality is traditionally used as a form of internal medical treating all disease and illnesses, in Western countries it is widely used for the purposes of pain relief.

pushback.o: From push + back, or push back.
pushback.example: Sweden, as well as the UK, recently announced pushbacks on green targets and budgets, while there are negative noises from Germany on building insulation costs.

flashback.example: As noted, that method provides limited support for multi-table flashbacks.
flashback.exampleSense: A query that operates against data from an earlier time, before it was changed.

opium.o: Borrowed from Latin opium and Ancient Greek ὄπιον (ópion), from ὀπός (opós, “juice of a plant”), from Proto-Indo-European *sokʷós (“juice, resin”).

outland.o:
adj: From Middle English outland, outlond, from Old English ūtland (“foreign land, land abroad”), from Proto-Germanic *ūtlandą (“outland”), equivalent to out- + land. Cognate to Dutch uitland, Afrikaans uitland, German Ausland, Danish udland. The use in the phrase "outland German" is influenced by (or is a calque of) the German cognate of the same meaning, Auslandsdeutsche (see Ausland). The use in the phrase "outland Chinese" is influenced by (or is a calque of) the Chinese term of the same meaning, 華僑 / 华侨 (huáqiáo).

verb: From out- + land.
outland.example: Whatever dependence the Pan-German chauvinist had placed on outland Germans proved to be a broken reed.
outland.exampleSense: Living abroad, living in a foreign land, expatriate.

theology.o: From Middle English theologie, from Middle French theologie, from Old French theologie, from Latin theologia, from Koine Greek θεολογία (theología), from θεολόγος (theológos, adjective), from θεός (theós) + λόγος (lógos). By surface analysis, theo- + -logy.
theology.example: In this context, one could conceivably hold onto the theology that baptism is essential for salvation.
theology.exampleSense: A particular belief within a religion.

annihilation.o: From Middle French annihilation, from Latin annihilātiō. By surface analysis, annihilate + -ion.

goblet.o: From Middle English goblet (= Middle Low German gobelet, kobelet (“goblet”)), from Old French gobellet, diminutive of gobel, from or related to the verb gober (“to ingest”).
goblet.example: At first Enkidu gags on the food, but then he grows to like the strong drink and takes seven goblets, until his face glows.
goblet.exampleSense: A drinking vessel with a foot and stem.

mathematical.o: From Middle English mathematicalle, mathematical, from Medieval Latin mathēmaticālis.
mathematical.example: The team has a mathematical chance of being promoted, but they need to win the next seven matches.

alignment.o: From French alignement, by surface analysis, align + -ment.
alignment.example: It turns out that there’s little overlap between the communities concerned primarily with such short-term risks and those who worry more about longer-term alignment risks.
alignment.exampleSense: The goals and values of an artificial intelligence, considered relative to human ethical standards.

with regard to.example: I am writing with regard to the advertisement that you placed in last week's Daily News.

selectivity.example: “We must stop conflating selectivity with excellence. We must stop correlating prestige with privilege,” he said.
selectivity.exampleSense: The quality of being selective, or extent to which something is selective.

swap.o:
verb: From Middle English swappen (“to swap”), originally meaning "to hurl" or "to strike", the word alludes to striking hands together when making an exchange; probably from Old English *swappian, a secondary form of Old English swāpan (“to swoop”). Cognate with German schwappen (“to slosh, slop”). Compare also Middle English swippen (“to strike, hit”), from Old English swipian (“to scourge, strike, beat, lash”), Old Norse svipa (“to swoop, flash, whip, look after, look around”). More at swipe.

noun: From the verb swap. First attested in 1620.

noun: From Middle English swap, swappe (“a blow, strike, lash from a whip”), from the verb (see Etymology 1 above).
swap.example: How much swap do you need?
swap.exampleSense: Space available in a swap file for use as auxiliary memory.

quasi.o: Learned borrowing from Latin quasi (“as if”).
quasi.example: The presiding officer of the assembly does not appoint a chairman of the quasi committee, but remains in the chair himself throughout its proceedings.
quasi.exampleSense: Resembling or having a likeness to something.

charge.o: From Middle English chargen, from Old French chargier, from Late Latin carricō (“to load”), from Latin carrus (“a car, wagon”); see car. Doublet of cargo.
charge.example: The child was a charge of the nanny.
charge.exampleSense: Someone or something entrusted to one's care, such as a child to a babysitter or a student to a teacher.

drop out.example: He [Bill Gates] dropped out of a better school than I dropped out of.
drop out.exampleSense: To leave (school, a race, etc.) prematurely and voluntarily.

anion.o: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ἀνιόν (anión, “(thing) going up”), neuter present participle of ἄνειμι (áneimi, “go up”), from ἀνά (aná, “up”) + εἶμι (eîmi, “go”). Coined by English polymath William Whewell in 1834 for Michael Faraday, who introduced it later that year. By surface analysis, an- (“up, away, forward”) + ion.

cation.o: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek κᾰτῐόν (kătĭón), neuter present participle of κᾰ́τειμῐ (kắteimĭ, “to go down, come down”), from κᾰτᾰ- (kătă-, “downwards, down, cata-”) + εἶμῐ (eîmĭ, “to go, come”). Coined by English polymath William Whewell in 1834 for Michael Faraday, who introduced it later that year. By surface analysis, cat(a)- + ion.

open circuit.example: Turning the switch to "off" makes it an open circuit.
open circuit.exampleSense: an incomplete electrical circuit through which no current can flow

steady.o: From Middle English stedy, studi, stidiȝ, perhaps continuing Old English stæþþiġ, ġestæþþiġ (“steadfast, stable, firm, staid”), equivalent to stead + -y; or calquing Middle Low German or Middle Dutch stēdig. Cognate with Saterland Frisian stoadig (“steady”), West Frisian stadich (“slow”), Danish stedig, stadig, steeg, Swedish stadig, Icelandic stöðugur, German stätig, stetig. Compare also Old English ġestedegian (“to bring to a standstill”) and Dutch steeds (“more and more”). Adjective sense 8 is a semantic loan from Singapore Hokkien 在 (chāi, “confident, skilled”, literally “steady”).
steady.example: Their feet steady, their hands diligent, their eyes watchful, and their hearts resolute.
steady.exampleSense: Firm in standing or position; not tottering or shaking; fixed; firm.

illuminated.o: simple past and past participle of illuminate. From Middle English illuminaten, borrowed from Latin illūminātus, perfect passive participle of illūminō (“lighten, light up, show off”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) for more), from in + lūminō (“light up”), from lūmen (“light”). Cognate with Old English lȳman (“to glow, shine”). More at leam.
illuminated.example: From this list are purposely omitted books printed upon vellum, Books of Hours of the Virgin Mary, and illuminated books; for these are rarities within reach of the wealthy only.

absorption.o: First attested in 1597. From Latin absorptiō (“a sucking in”), from absorbeō (“absorb”). Morphologically absorb + -tion.
absorption.example: the absorption of light, heat, electricity, etc.
absorption.exampleSense: The act or process of absorbing or of being absorbed as, the imbibing or reception by molecular or chemical action, of radiant energy; the process of being neutrons being absorbed by the nucleus; interception.

intertexture.example: At length, after walking a long way in the woods, we arrived at another thicket, through the intertexture of which was glimmering a pale rosy light.

kindly.o:
adj: From Middle English kyndely, kyndeliche, from Old English cyndelīċ (“natural, kindly”); equivalent to kind + -ly.

adv: From Middle English kyndely, kyndly, kyndeliche, from Old English ġecyndelīċe, equivalent to kind + -ly.
kindly.example: He kindly offered to take us to the station in his car.
kindly.exampleSense: In a kind manner, out of kindness.

noted.o: simple past and past participle of note. From Middle English note, from Old English not, nōt (“note, mark, sign”) and Old French note (“letter, note”), both from Latin nota (“mark, sign, remark, note”).
noted.example: In 1866 Colonel J. F. Meline noted that the rebozo had almost disappeared in Santa Fe and that hoop skirts, on sale in the stores, were being widely used.
noted.exampleSense: simple past and past participle of note

zenith.o: From Middle English cenyth, from Medieval Latin cenit, from Arabic سَمْت (samt, “direction, path”), from the fuller form سَمْت اَلرَّأْس (samt ar-raʔs, “direction of the head”). The -ni- for -m- is sometimes thought to be due to a misreading of the three strokes, which is plausible, though it could be a mere phonetic approximation.
zenith.example: In the east a pillar of cloud reared from horizon to zenith, with a kind of arm outstretched like a threatening colossus.
zenith.exampleSense: The point in the sky vertically above a given position or observer; the point in the celestial sphere opposite the nadir.

cutoff.example: If the treatment is approved, a script is written. If the script is approved, it goes into production. But this is usually a long and painful process. A cutoff can take place (and often does) at any step along the way.
cutoff.exampleSense: A cessation in a flow or activity.

irradiance.example: The geometry of the cone θ and the irradiance at the image of the carbon block were used to determine the absolute steradiancy of the energy in the cone θ as a radiometer calibration value.
irradiance.exampleSense: The radiant power received by unit area of surface.

assiduity.o: From Latin assiduitas, from Latin assiduus. Equivalent to assiduous + -ity.
assiduity.example: Disgusted with the insipid boastings of him who continued his unceasing assiduities to Miss Airey, without any advancement towards that issue doubtless anticipated by herself and friends—...

assiduous.o: A learned borrowing from Latin assiduus, from assidere (“to sit down to”), from ad- (“to”) + sedere (“to sit”). Compare sedulous. Cognate (via assidere) to assess.
assiduous.example: A good deal of assiduous attention had enabled Henry to win this place in her affections.
assiduous.exampleSense: Hard-working, diligent or regular (in attendance or work); industrious.

assiduously.example: They were all too assiduously engaged to talk to us as we passed.
assiduously.exampleSense: In an assiduous manner; diligently, industriously.

endeavor.o: The verb is from Middle English endeveren (“to make an effort”); the noun is from Middle English endevour, from the verb. Endeveren is from (putten) in dever (“(to put oneself) in duty”), from in + dever (“duty”), partially translating Middle French (se mettre) en devoir (de faire) (“(to make it) one's duty (to do), to endeavour (to do)”) (from Old French devoir, deveir (“duty”)).

house.o:
noun: From Middle English hous, hus, from Old English hūs (“dwelling, shelter, house”), from Proto-West Germanic *hūs, from Proto-Germanic *hūsą (“house”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kews-, from *(s)kewH- (“to cover, hide”). More at hose. Eclipsed non-native Middle English mees, meson, measoun (“house”), borrowed from Anglo-Norman mes, mies, meis, maisun (“house”). The uncommon plural form housen is from Middle English husen, housen. (The Old English nominative plural was simply hūs.) Cognates Cognate with Scots hoose, oos (“house”), Yola heouse, houze, howze (“house”), North Frisian hüs (“house”), Saterland Frisian Huus, Húus (“house”), West Frisian hûs (“house”), Alemannic German hous, hus, husch, hüs, hüüsch (“house”), Bavarian, Cimbrian, Mòcheno haus (“house”), Central Franconian Haus, Hous, Huus (“home”), Dutch huis (“house”), Dutch Low Saxon hoes, huus (“house”), German Haus, Hauß (“house”), German Low German Huus (“house”), Limburgish hoes, Huus (“house”), Luxembourgish Haus (“house”), Vilamovian haojs, haus, hoüz (“house”), Yiddish הויז (hoyz, “house”), Danish, Norwegian Bokmål, Norwegian Nynorsk, and Swedish hus (“house”), Elfdalian aus (“house”), Faroese and Icelandic hús (“house”), Crimean Gothic hus (“house”); also Cornish kudha (“to conceal, hide”), Welsh cuddio (“to hide”), Latin cutis (“human skin; hide, leather”), Ancient Greek κεύθω (keúthō, “to cover, hide”), Tocharian A kāc (“hide, skin”), Sanskrit स्कुनाति (skunāti, “to cover”).

verb: From Middle English housen, from Old English hūsian, from Proto-Germanic *hūsōną (“to house, live, dwell”), from the noun (see above). Compare Dutch huizen (“to live, dwell, reside”), German Low German husen (“to live, dwell, reside”), German hausen (“to live, dwell, reside”), Norwegian Nynorsk husa (“to house”), Faroese húsa (“to house”), Icelandic húsa (“to shelter, house”).

noun: Probably from The Warehouse, a nightclub in Chicago, Illinois, USA, where the music became popular around 1985.
house.example: The petition was so ridiculous that the house rejected it after minimal debate.
house.exampleSense: A building where a deliberative assembly meets; whence the assembly itself, particularly a component of a legislature.

allege.o:
verb: From Middle English aleggen, perhaps from Old French alleguer, or from Anglo-Norman aleger, the form perhaps from Old French esligier (“to acquit”), from Medieval Latin *exlītigāre (“to clear at law”), from Latin ex (“out”) + lītigō (“sue at law”), but the meaning from Old French alleguer, from Latin allēgāre (“send on a mission, depute; relate, mention, adduce”), from ad (“to”) + lēgō (“send”). See also al-.

verb: From Middle English alleggen, from Old French alegier, from Latin alleviāre (“lighten”), from ad + levis (“light”). Doublet of alleviate.
allege.example: The agency alleged that my credit history had problems.
allege.exampleSense: To make a claim as justification or proof; to make an assertion without proof.

lawmaker.o: From Middle English lawemaker, lawe maker, equivalent to law + maker.
lawmaker.example: “Many members are only now beginning to understand that,” one GOP lawmaker told CNN.
lawmaker.exampleSense: One who makes or enacts laws.

recycle.example: Recruits cannot fail this portion of their training and become a Marine. Anyone who fails may be “recycled” through training up to three more times to try again, but will be sent home if success in this program is not achieved.
recycle.exampleSense: To put (a person) through a course of training again.

overlap.o: From over- + lap. Cognate with Dutch overlap.
overlap.example: The mouse-mat overlapped the edge of the desk.
overlap.exampleSense: To extend over and partly cover something.

break down.o: Alternative form of breakdown. Deverbal from break down.
break down.example: She is back to work now, after she broke down the other day.
break down.exampleSense: To render or to become unstable due to stress, to collapse physically or mentally.

basically.example: They've added some fancy features, but it's basically still a crappy car.
basically.exampleSense: In a fundamental, essential or basic manner.

constrain.o: From Middle English constreinen, from Old French constreindre, from Latin cōnstringō, from cōn- (“with, together”) + stringō (“to draw, bind or tie tight”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *streyg- (“to stroke, to shear, stiff”).
constrain.example: But it's not just Castlefield Corridor capacity that constrains services. All the junctions on the lines feeding into the corridor are flat, so they create conflict points as trains pass.
constrain.exampleSense: To keep within close bounds; to confine.

extension.o: From Middle English extensioun, from Old French estension, from Latin extensiō, extensiōnem.
extension.example: Due to the unforeseen circumstances, you are allowed an extension of two weeks to complete the task.
extension.exampleSense: The act of extending; a stretching out; enlargement in length, breadth, or time; an increase.

come out.example: I came right out and told the boss what I thought of him.

utilize.o: From French utiliser, from Italian utilizzare, from utile (“useful”), from Latin ūtilis, from ūtī (“use”).

evict.o: From Middle English evicten, evycten, borrowed from Latin ēvictus, past participle of ēvincō (“to vanquish completely”). Doublet of evince.

walk through.example: On my first day at work, the secretary walked me through the process of using the photocopier.
walk through.exampleSense: To explain (something) to (someone), step by step.

recap.o:
verb: From re- + cap.

noun: Clipping of recapitulation.

noun: Clipping of recapitalization.

verb: From re- + cap (capacitor).
recap.example: He refused to buy recaps because he didn't trust them not to come apart on the highway.
recap.exampleSense: A tire that has had new tread glued on.

turn.o:
verb: From Middle English turnen, from Old English turnian, tyrnan (“to turn, rotate, revolve”), from Proto-West Germanic *turnēn (“to turn, lathe”) (also the source of German turnen and its derivatives) and Old French torner (“to turn”), both from Latin tornāre (“to round off, turn in a lathe”), from tornus (“lathe”), from Ancient Greek τόρνος (tórnos, “turning-lathe: a tool used for making circles”), from Proto-Indo-European *terh₁- (“to rub, rub by turning, turn, twist, bore”). Cognate with Old English þrāwan (“to turn, twist, wind”), whence English throw. Displaced native Middle English wenden from Old English wendan (see wend), and Middle English trenden from Old English trendan (see trend), among several other terms.

noun: Partly from Anglo-Norman *torn, from Latin tornus, from Ancient Greek τόρνος (tórnos), and partly an action noun from the verb turn.
turn.example: She turned the table legs with care and precision.
turn.exampleSense: To make a non-linear physical movement. To shape (something) symmetrically by rotating it against a stationary cutting tool, as on a lathe.

parallelism.o: From parallel + -ism and from Late Latin parallelismus.
parallelism.example: Plutarch (c. AD 46-120), in his Lives of the Noble Grecians and Romans, traced a parallelism between the most eminent men of the two countries.
parallelism.exampleSense: The state of being in agreement or similarity; resemblance, correspondence, analogy.

show up.example: Please come on time; don't just show up whenever you feel like it.
show up.exampleSense: To appear, arrive, or attend, especially suddenly or erratically.

bundle.o: From Middle English bundel, from Middle Dutch bondel or Old English byndele, byndelle (“a binding; tying; fastening with bands”); both from Proto-Germanic *bundil-, derivative of *bundą (“bundle”). Compare also bindle, Dutch bundel, German Bündel.
bundle.example: The fable of the rods, which, when united in a bundle, no strength could bend.
bundle.exampleSense: A group of objects held together by wrapping or tying.

contiguous.o: From Latin contiguus (“touching”) + -ous, from contingere (“to touch”); see contingent, contact, contagion.
contiguous.example: Supposing three such houses to be contiguous to a central one, each separated from the latter by a straight wall.

hoard.o:
noun: From Middle English hord, from Old English hord (“an accumulation of valuable objects cached for preservation or future use; treasure; hoard”), from Proto-West Germanic *hoʀd, from Proto-Germanic *huzdą (“treasure; hoard”), of unknown origin, but possibly derived from Proto-Indo-European *kewdʰ- (“to conceal, hide”), thus meaning “something hidden”. Cognate with German Hort (“hoard; refuge”), Icelandic hodd (“treasure”), Latin cū̆stōs (“guard; keeper”). For the meaning development, compare Russian сокро́вище (sokróvišče, “treasure”) related to Russian скрыва́ть (skryvátʹ, “to hide, to conceal”).

verb: From Middle English horden, from Old English hordian, from Proto-West Germanic *hoʀdōn.

noun: From Middle English hord, whorde, from Anglo-Norman hurde and Old French hourd, hourt (“barrier, palisade”), from Middle Dutch horde, from Old Dutch *hurd, from Proto-West Germanic *hurdi (“wickerwork, braiding of branches, hurdle, scaffolding, military company”).
hoard.example: Occasionally Scots and Irish coins are also found. The gold hoards consist entirely of crown gold unites, half unites and quarter unites from the reigns of James I and Charles I.

hoarding.o:
noun: From hoard (“structure”) + -ing.

noun: From hoard + -ing.

verb: See the etymology of the corresponding lemma form.
hoarding.example: The west side is one massive building site, although it's hard to appreciate what's going on behind all the hoardings.
hoarding.exampleSense: A temporary fence-like structure built around building work to add security and prevent accidents to the public.

sequentially.example: Then a dimensionwise heuristic and a vectorwise heuristic are applied sequentially.

sequent.o: 1550s; borrowed from Middle French sequent, from Old French sequent, itself borrowed from Latin sequentem, present participle of sequī (“to follow”).
sequent.example: The One is somewhat shadowy. It is sometimes called God, sometimes the Good; it transcends Being, which is the first sequent upon the One.
sequent.exampleSense: Something that follows in a given sequence.

utensil.o: From Middle English utensyl, from Old French utensile, from Latin ūtēnsilis (“useful, usable”).
utensil.example: We have convenient storage for all the kitchen utensils.
utensil.exampleSense: An instrument or device for domestic use, especially in the kitchen.

instantiation.o: A coinage of the twentieth century, from instantiate + -ion, itself coined in 1946 from instance + -ate. The latter, in the sense "a case, an example", from Middle English instance, from Medieval Latin īnstantia (“a being near, presence; also perseverance, earnestness, importunity, urgency”), from Latin īnstāns (“urgent”); see English instant.
instantiation.example: I can name numerous instantiations of this gift of luck at work in my hostʼs life.
instantiation.exampleSense: Something resulting from the act of instantiating; an instance.

immaterial.o: The adjective is derived from Late Middle English immaterial, inmateriall (“incorporeal; spiritual”), from Middle French immateriel (“not material”) (modern French immatériel), and from its etymon Medieval Latin immāteriālis (“not material”), from Latin im- (a variant of in- (prefix meaning ‘not’)) + māteriālis (“made of matter, material”) (from māteria (“matter, substance, material”) (from māter, from Proto-Indo-European *méh₂tēr, + ia) + -ālis (suffix forming adjectives of relationship)). The English word is analysable as im- + material. The noun is derived from the adjective.
immaterial.example: Objection, your Honour! The defendant’s criminal record is immaterial to this case.
immaterial.exampleSense: Especially of evidence; chiefly followed by to: not associated in any way that is important or useful to the context being discussed; irrelevant.

theorem.o: From Middle French théorème, from Late Latin theōrēma, from Ancient Greek θεώρημα (theṓrēma, “speculation, proposition to be proved”) (Euclid), from θεωρέω (theōréō, “to look at, view, consider, examine”), from θεωρός (theōrós, “spectator”), from θέα (théa, “a view”) + ὁράω (horáō, “to see, look”). See also theory, and theater.
theorem.example: Fermat's Last Theorem was known thus long before it was proved in the 1990s.
theorem.exampleSense: A mathematical statement that is expected to be true.

scoop.o: From Middle English scope, schoupe, a borrowing from Middle Dutch scoep, scuep, schope, schoepe (“bucket for bailing water”) and Middle Dutch schoppe, scoppe, schuppe ("a scoop, shovel"; > Modern Dutch schop (“spade”)), from Proto-Germanic *skuppǭ, *skuppijǭ, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kep- (“to cut, to scrape, to hack”). Cognate with Old Frisian skuppe (“shovel”), Middle Low German schōpe (“scoop, shovel”), German Low German Schüppe, Schüpp (“shovel”), German Schüppe, Schippe (“shovel, spade”). Related to English shovel, Japanese スコップ.
scoop.example: with a quick scoop, she fished the frog out of the pond.
scoop.exampleSense: The act of scooping, or taking with a scoop or ladle; a motion with a scoop, as in dipping or shovelling.

synchronization.example: The generator went off line when it lost synchronization with the power line.
synchronization.exampleSense: The state or property of being synchronized.

rupture.o: Borrowed from Middle French rupture, or its source, Latin ruptūra (“a breaking, rupture (of a limb or vein)”) and Medieval Latin ruptūra (“a road, a field, a form of feudal tenure, a tax, etc.”), from the participle stem of rumpere (“to break, burst”). Doublet of roture.
rupture.example: He knew that policy would disincline Napoleon from a rupture with his family.
rupture.exampleSense: A social breach or break, between individuals or groups.

mealy.o: From meal + -y. Cognate with German mehlig.
mealy.example: Below the hole the mice made in the woodwork was a pile of mealy sawdust.

prescribe.o: Borrowed from Latin praescrībere, from prae- (“before, in front”) and scrībere (“to write”).
prescribe.example: The property meets the criteria prescribed by the regulations.
prescribe.exampleSense: To specify by writing as a required procedure or ritual; to lay down authoritatively as a guide, direction, or rule of action.

ingratiate.o: First attested in 1622. From Italian ingraziare or Medieval Latin *ingratiatus, from Latin in grātiam (“for the favor of”).
ingratiate.example: He ingratiated himself with the Kurdish bloc when he stood up to aggressive Turkish rhetoric about the Kurdish border in May.
ingratiate.exampleSense: To bring oneself into favour with someone by flattering or trying to please them; to insinuate oneself; to worm one's way in.

directive.o: From Middle French directif. The noun senses are from French directive (feminine form of the adjective).
directive.example: A directive management style is stronger among owners with 'lifestyle' as a business objective than among those with business/economic objectives.
directive.exampleSense: That which directs; serving to direct, indicate, or guide.

poll.o:
noun: From Middle English pol, polle ("scalp, pate"), from or cognate with Middle Dutch pol, pōle, polle (“top, summit; head”), from Proto-West Germanic *poll, from Proto-Germanic *pullaz (“round object, head, top”), from Proto-Indo-European *bolno-, *bōwl- (“orb, round object, bubble”), from Proto-Indo-European *bew- (“to blow, swell”). Akin to Scots pow (“head, crown, scalp, skull”), Saterland Frisian pol (“round, full, brimming”, adjective), German Low German Polle, Poll (“round object, ball”), German Low German Poller (“head, tree-top, bulb”), Danish puld (“crown of a hat”), Swedish dialectal pull (“head”). Meaning "collection of votes" is first recorded 1625, from the notion of "counting heads".

noun: Perhaps a shortening of Polly, a common name for pet parrots.

noun: From Ancient Greek πολλοί (polloí, “the many, the masses”), as in hoi polloi.
poll.example: He polled a hundred votes more than his opponent.
poll.exampleSense: To register or deposit, as a vote; to elicit or call forth, as votes or voters.

assessable.o: From Middle English assessable, from Middle English assessen (“to assess”) + -able (“-able”). Equivalent to assess + -able.

underline.example: As to underbridges, the policy is to wait until the small underline bridges become due for renewal when they will be replaced by prestressed concrete structures.

statistics.o:
noun: From German Statistik, from New Latin statisticum (“of the state”) and Italian statista (“statesman, politician”), compare English statist. Statistik introduced by Gottfried Achenwall (1749), originally designated the analysis of data about the state.

noun: See the etymology of the corresponding lemma form.
statistics.example: Statistics is the only mathematical field required for many social sciences.
statistics.exampleSense: A discipline, principally within applied mathematics, concerned with the systematic study of the collection, presentation, analysis, and interpretation of data.

sophistication.o: From Middle English sophisticacion, sophisticacioun, sophisticacoun, from Old French sofisticacion, sophisticacion, from Medieval Latin sophisticātiōnis. By surface analysis, sophisticate + -ion.
sophistication.example: The police force were unable to deal with the sophistication of the criminal network.

harebell.o: From Middle English harebelle, equivalent to hare + bell.
harebell.example: Her most striking feature, then as now, was her eyes: both large and expressive, but while one was the brown of a fresh hazelnut, the other was pale bluey-violet, the colour of harebells.
harebell.exampleSense: A perennial flowering plant, Campanula rotundifolia, native to the Northern Hemisphere, with blue, bell-like flowers.

harestail.o: The head of the grass resembles a hare's tail.

hare.o:
noun: From Middle English hare, from Old English hara (“hare”), from Proto-West Germanic *hasō ~ *haʀ-, from Proto-Germanic *hesô, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱh₂s-én-; possibly related to or influenced by Proto-Germanic *haswaz (“grey”). Cognates See also West Frisian hazze, Dutch haas, German Hase, Norwegian and Swedish hare, Icelandic heri), Old English hasu, Middle High German heswe (“pale, dull”); also Welsh cannu (“to whiten”), ceinach (“hare”), Latin cānus (“white”), cascus (“old”), Old Prussian sasnis (“hare”), Pashto سوی (soe, “hare”) and Sanskrit शश (śaśa, “hare”).

verb: From Middle English harren, harien (“to drag by force, ill-treat”), of uncertain origin. Compare harry, harass.

adj: From Middle English hore, from Old English hār (“hoar, hoary, grey, old”), from Proto-Germanic *hairaz (“grey”). Cognate with German hehr (“noble, sublime”).
hare.example: Hare is another delicious meat – it’s more ‘steaky’, darker and richer than rabbit.

validation.o: From Middle French validation. By surface analysis, validate + -ion.
validation.example: In reality, brains go overboard with this sort of fear validation. They love any chance to prove a fear is valid while ignoring all the reasons it's not.

invalidate.o: First attested in 1649; borrowed from Middle French invalider, from invalide + -er. By surface analysis, in- + validate or invalid + -ate.
invalidate.example: Telling an angry person to "calm down" can invalidate their feelings.

validate.o:
verb: First attested in 1648; borrowed from Medieval Latin validātus (“to validate”) (perhaps through Middle French valider), the perfect passive participle of validō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from validus + -ō (verb-forming suffix). By surface analysis, valid + -ate.

adj: First attested in 1586; borrowed from Medieval Latin validātus, see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and Etymolgy 1 for more.
validate.example: The data file cannot be imported because it doesn't validate.
validate.exampleSense: To have its validity successfully proven.

lichenology.example: Now lichenology has a photo-illustrated guide that should not be overlooked--the long-awaited Lichens of North America.

lichee.o: Alternative spelling of lychee. * /ˈlaɪ̯.t͡ʃi/, /laɪ̯ˈt͡ʃiː/ from Cantonese 荔枝 (lai⁶ zi¹) * /ˈlit͡ʃi/ from Hokkien 荔枝 (lē-chi) Doublet of litchi and lichi.

lichen.o: Borrowed from Latin līchēn, from Ancient Greek λειχήν (leikhḗn), from λείχω (leíkhō, “to lick”). Originally used of liverwort; the modern sense first recorded 1715.
lichen.example: The nibble marks of the stone adze were still visible, though crusted over with scale lichens in most places.
lichen.exampleSense: Any of many symbiotic organisms, being associations of algae and fungi, often found as white or yellow-to-blue–green patches on rocks, old walls, etc.

depressing.o: present participle and gerund of depress. From Middle English depressen, from Old French depresser, from Latin dēpressus, perfect participle of dēprimō (“to press down, to weigh down”), from dē- (“off, away, down, out”) + premō (“to press”).
depressing.example: The television news was depressing, so rather than start crying I turned it off.

depressant.example: Alcohol acts first as a stimulant and then as a depressant.
depressant.exampleSense: A pharmacological substance which decreases neuronal or physiological activity.

depressed.o: See the etymology of the corresponding lemma form.
depressed.example: The cubic function x³ + cx + d = 0, where one of the terms has a coefficient of zero, is a depressed cubic.
depressed.exampleSense: Reduced to a lower degree or form.

depress.o: From Middle English depressen, from Old French depresser, from Latin dēpressus, perfect participle of dēprimō (“to press down, to weigh down”), from dē- (“off, away, down, out”) + premō (“to press”).
depress.example: Depress the upper lever to start the machine.

balmy.example: The new mass hysteria is known as the Pyramid Club and began—like so many other strange and wonderful notions—somewhere under the balmy skies of California.

accumulator.o: From Latin accumulātor, agent noun of accumulō (“pile up”), accumulate + -or.
accumulator.example: He is a great accumulator of bad jokes.
accumulator.exampleSense: One who, or that which, accumulates.

upcycle.o:
verb: Blend of up- + recycle or possibly upgrade + recycle.

noun: From up + cycle.
upcycle.example: Recycling in many cases means "downcycling" – in particular cases, however, it can also mean "upcycling".
upcycle.exampleSense: To convert (waste materials, etc.) into new materials or products of higher quality and greater functionality.

twaddle.o: An alteration of twattle (1556), of unknown origin.
twaddle.example: You're talking a load of twaddle. Get your facts straight, man!
twaddle.exampleSense: Empty or silly idle talk or writing; nonsense, rubbish.

swaddle.o: From Middle English swathlen (“to bind; swaddle”), from Middle English swathel, swethel, from Old English swaþul, swæþel, sweþel, sweoþol (“swaddling cloth”), equivalent to swathe (“to wrap with fabric”) + -le (agent/instrumental suffix), the word then underwent th-stopping (its voiced th became a d). Cognate with Middle Dutch swadel (“swaddling; bandage”), Old High German swedili (“poultice”), Old English sweþian, besweþian (“to wrap; swaddle”).
swaddle.example: The baby is awake, trying to escape the swaddle I have imprisoned her in.
swaddle.exampleSense: Anything used to swaddle with, such as a cloth or band.

fictional.example: The janitor's account of the crime turned out to be entirely fictional.

fiction.o: From Middle English ficcioun, from Old French ficcion (“dissimulation, ruse, invention”), from Latin fictiō (“a making, fashioning, a feigning, a rhetorical or legal fiction”), from fingō (“to form, mold, shape, devise, feign”). Displaced native Old English lēasspell (literally “false story”); see feign, feint, figment.
fiction.example: The company’s accounts contained a number of blatant fictions.
fiction.exampleSense: A verbal or written account that is not based on actual events (often intended to mislead).

deficit.o: From French déficit, from Latin dēficit. Related to defect.
deficit.example: The crop output this year has been comparatively small, owing to the deficit in rainfall.
deficit.exampleSense: Deficiency in amount or quality; a falling short; lack.

cylindrical.o: From Latin cylindricus + -al. By surface analysis, cylinder + -ical.

feedstock.example: The filtered extract of the mash is the feedstock for the fermenter.
feedstock.exampleSense: Any bulk raw material constituting the principal input for an industrial process.

accordingly.o: From Middle English acordingli, equivalent to according + -ly.
accordingly.example: He was absent when I called, and I accordingly left my card.

look ahead.example: You should forget the past and look ahead.
look ahead.exampleSense: To consider the future, to anticipate future events.

translucent.o: From Latin trānslūcentem, accusative of trānslūcēns, present participle of trānslūcēre.
translucent.example: The window-panes, encrusted with perennial deposits of Atmosphere, were less transparent than translucent.
translucent.exampleSense: Allowing light to pass through, but diffusing it.

twilight.o: PIE word *dwóh₁ From Middle English twilight, twyelyghte, equivalent to twi- (“double, half-”) + light, literally ‘second light, half-light’. Cognate to Scots twa licht, twylicht, twielicht (“twilight”), Low German twilecht, twelecht (“twilight”), Dutch tweelicht (“twilight, dusk”), German Zwielicht (“twilight, dusk”). Compare Old English twēone lēoht (“twilight”).
twilight.example: I could just make out her face in the twilight.
twilight.exampleSense: The soft light in the sky seen before the rising and (especially) after the setting of the sun, occasioned by the illumination of the earth’s atmosphere by the direct rays of the sun and their reflection on the earth.

at will.example: I'm writing my book at will - there's no deadline or minimum word count.
at will.exampleSense: At one's preference; as one sees fit.

clueless.example: The shifting shapes mimicked the dilemma of the nearly clueless mystery of the Higgins Grove murders. As soon as the picture formed into something recognizable, it morphed into something else.

scandalous.o: From Late Middle English scandalouse (“disgraceful, shameful”), borrowed from Old French scandaleux (“scandalous”) (modern French scandaleux), from Medieval Latin scandalōsus, from Ecclesiastical Latin scandalum (“scandal”) + Latin -ōsus (suffix meaning ‘full of; prone to’ forming adjectives). Scandalum is derived from Ancient Greek σκᾰ́νδᾰλον (skắndălon, “offence, scandal; snare, trap”); further etymology uncertain, possibly from Pre-Greek or Proto-Indo-European *skend- (“to jump”) (referring to a device for climbing or jumping on, such as might be used by someone setting a trap). By surface analysis, scandal + -ous (suffix forming adjectives from nouns, denoting presence of a quality in any degree (typically an abundance), or a relation to the nouns).
scandalous.example: The thing made a big stir in the town, too, and a good many come out flatfooted and said it was scandalous to separate the mother and the children that way.

scandalize.o:
verb: From Latin scandalizō, from Ancient Greek σκανδαλίζω (skandalízō). By surface analysis, scandal + -ize.

verb: From scantle.
scandalize.example: Thou scandalizest me and irritatest my nature as much as it possibly can be irritated.

stand-alone.example: They offer an inexpensive add-on for a computer, or a stand-alone system with all the functions built in.
stand-alone.exampleSense: Operating, functioning, or existing without additions or assistance; independent; able to be separate or separated; not attached to anything.

collaborate.o: Back-formation from collaborator, from French collaborateur, or else modeled on French collaborer or directly from Late Latin collabōrātus, past participle of collabōrāre. Displaced native Old English efnwyrċan.
collaborate.example: Let's collaborate on this project, and get it finished faster.
collaborate.exampleSense: To work together with others to achieve a common goal.

cumbersome.o: From Middle English cumbyrsum, cummyrsum; equivalent to cumber (“hindrance”) + -some. Compare encumber and incumbent.
cumbersome.example: A slave’s work was as cumbersome as toiling on the fields, or in the mines.
cumbersome.exampleSense: Hard, difficult, demanding to handle or get around with.

cumber.o:
verb: From Middle English combren, aphetic form of acombren or encombren, borrowed from Old French encombrer, ultimately either from Latin cumulus or Proto-Celtic *kombereti (“to bring together”), from *kom- + *bereti (“to bear”). Cognate with German kümmern (“to take care of”).

noun: From Middle English komber, kumbre, cumbre, combre (“distress; destruction”). Used in 14th century Middle English in the very scarcely attested “destruction” sense but not in common use until the 16th century; at first chiefly Scots, where it is also spelled cummer. Further etymology is uncertain, the term is either: * an aphetic form of encomber, encumbir, encumbre (“trouble; misfortune; harm, ruin”), itself from Old French encombre (“a hindrance, difficulty”), see Etymology 1 and French encombrer for further etymology; or, * cognate with Middle High German kumber (German Kummer), Middle Low German kummer, and Dutch kommer with which it strikingly shares the meaning “trouble, distress”, ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *kumbr (“burden, trouble, sorrow”); or, * a deverbal from cumber.
cumber.example: Why had he not killed himself long ago? Why cumbered he the earth?
cumber.exampleSense: To slow down; to hinder; to burden; to encumber.

entomb.o: From Old French entomber (“deposit in a tomb”). Equivalent to en- + tomb.
entomb.example: [...] after the original Victorian station was demolished and then entombed in concrete in the 1960s, Birmingham New Street became a byword for the worst excesses of the much-loathed Brutalist architecture so widely used to reconstruct inner-city post-war Britain.

disencumber.example: Francesca was soon disencumbered of her riding-hood and cloak; and the three young people, left together, became rapidly acquainted.
disencumber.exampleSense: To remove an encumbrance or burden from (someone or something); unburden.

encumbrance.o: From Middle English encombraunce, from Old French encombrance, from encombrer.

encumber.o: From Middle English encombren, from Old French encombrer, from en- + combrer (“to hinder”) (See cumber). By surface analysis, en- + cumber.
encumber.example: He [Timothy Forsyte] had never committed the imprudence of marrying or encumbering himself in any way with children.
encumber.exampleSense: To restrict or block something with a hindrance or impediment.

unencumbered.example: The commuters from the suburbs come unencumbered with luggage, children and prams, and can almost be relied upon to find their way blindfold to their trains.

stripe.o: From Middle English stripe, strype, from Middle Dutch or Middle Low German strîpe, from Proto-West Germanic *strīpā, *strīpō, from Proto-Germanic *strīpô. Cognate with Saterland Frisian Striepe (“stripe, strip”), West Frisian stripe (“stripe”), Dutch streep (“stripe”), German Low German Striepe, Striep, Streep (“stripe”), German Streifen (“stripe, strip, band”), Danish stribe (“stripe”).
stripe.example: But when practice yielded no improvement, curses and the crack of a whip followed. Stripped, lying face down on the ground, Platt absorbed the master's rage, lash after lash striping his buttocks, shoulders, and back.
stripe.exampleSense: To lash with a whip or strap.

instantiate.o: From Latin instāntia + -ate (verb-forming suffix). By surface analysis, instance + -ate.
instantiate.example: To see and test the result of one's CSS for any particular HTML element, one must instantiate that element in a document.
instantiate.exampleSense: To represent (a concept, theme, or principle) by an instance.

inventor.o: Borrowed from Latin inventor. By surface analysis, invent + -or.

widget.o:
noun: Coined by American playwright George S. Kaufman in 1924 in his play Beggar on Horseback (1924). The preface to the 1924 play credits an earlier German work from 1911 where there is an actor Elisabeth Wigge.

noun: Blend of window + gadget.
widget.example: Suppose we have a widget factory that produces 100 units per year...
widget.exampleSense: A placeholder name for an unnamed, unspecified, or hypothetical manufactured good or product, typically as an example for purposes of explaining concepts.

negate.o: From Latin negātus, perfect passive participle of negō (“to deny, refuse, decline”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).
negate.example: Progress on the study has been negated by the lack of funds.
negate.exampleSense: To nullify or cause to be ineffective.

negation.o: From Middle English negacioun, from Old French negacion, from Latin negātiō (“a denial; negative word”). Morphologically negate + -ion.
negation.example: You get the negation of a proposition if you insert "not" (or some equivalent expression) into it in such a way as to form a contradictory of it.
negation.exampleSense: A proposition which is the contradictory of another proposition and which can be obtained from that other proposition by the appropriately placed addition/insertion of the word "not". (Or, in symbolic logic, by prepending that proposition with the symbol for the logical operator "not".)

distributive.o: From Middle French distributif, from Latin distribūtīvus.
distributive.example: If function f is distributive with respect to function g, then f(a,g(b,c))=g(f(a,b),f(a,c)).
distributive.exampleSense: A property of functions that have a rule describing how the function can be performed to the individual components of another operation.

commutate.o: Back-formation from commutation (in the late 19th century), as is commutator (noun) too.
commutate.example: Continuously rated machines shall be required to commutate successfully momentary loads of 150% of the Amperes corresponding to the continuous rating keeping the rheostat set for rated load excitation.
commutate.exampleSense: To reverse the direction of (a current).

commutative.o: From French commuter (“to substitute or switch”) + -ative (“tending to”). See commute.
commutative.example: Addition and multiplication are commutative operations but subtraction and division are not.
commutative.exampleSense: Such that the order in which the operands are taken does not affect their image under the operation.

associative.example: At present conditioning is viewed as a special case of associative learning which provides an animal (and human being alike) with die ability to discover, memorize, retrieve, and use relationships between signals and reinforcers and also to control rewards and aversive events.
associative.exampleSense: Pertaining to, resulting from, or characterised by association; capable of associating; tending to associate or unite.

barb.o:
noun: PIE word *bʰardʰéh₂ From Middle English barbe, from Middle French barbe, from Old French barbe (“beard, beard-like element”). Doublet of beard.

noun: Clipping of Barbary.

noun: Clipping of barbiturate.

noun: Corruption of bard.
barb.exampleSense: The point that stands backward in an arrow, fishhook, etc., to prevent it from being easily extracted. Hence: Anything which stands out with a sharp point obliquely or crosswise to something else.

interchange.o: From Old French entrechange, by surface analysis, inter- + change.
interchange.example: David and I were not "intimate" friends. There was always a certain old-worldly formality about our interchanges. There was something professorial and distant about David, something that commanded respect, partially, I think, because he was so respectful himself.

hex.o:
verb: First attested about 1830, from Pennsylvania German hexe (“to practice witchcraft”), from German hexen (compare Hexe (“witch”)). The noun appeared later, in the 1850s. Cognate to Norwegian Bokmål heks (“witch”) and Dutch heks (“witch”), Dutch beheksen (“to bewitch”), Old English hægtesse (“witch, hag”). Doublet of hag.

noun: Short for hexadecimal.

noun: Short for hexagon.

noun: Short for hexafluoride.

cringe.o: The verb is derived from Middle English crengen (“to bend in a haughty manner; to condescend”) [and other forms], from Old English *crenġan, *crenċġan, *crenċan (“to cause to fall or turn”) from Proto-Germanic *krangijaną (“to cause to fall; to cause to turn”), causative of Proto-Germanic *kringaną, *krinkaną (“to fall; to turn; to yield”) (> Old English crin(c)gan (“to yield; to cringe; to fall; to die, perish”)), from Proto-Indo-European *grenǵʰ- (“to turn”)). The causative suffix is from *-janą (suffix forming causatives with the sense ‘to cause to do (the action of the verb)’ from strong verbs). The English word is cognate with Danish krænge (“to turn inside out, evert”), Dutch krengen (“to careen, veer”) and Dutch kring (“circle”), Scots crenge, creenge, creinge, crienge (“to cringe; to shrug”), Swedish kränga (“to careen; to heel, lurch; to toss”), and West Frisian kringe (“to pinch; to poke; to push; to insist, urge”); and is a doublet of crinkle. The noun and adjective are derived from the verb via zero derivation.
cringe.example: He cringed as the bird collided with the window.
cringe.exampleSense: To cower, flinch, recoil, shrink, or tense, as in disgust, embarrassment, or fear.

lottery.o: Borrowed from Italian lotteria, from the same root as Old English hlot (cognate with English lot). Compare French loterie (from Middle Dutch loterie). By surface analysis, lot + -ery.
lottery.example: Dave plays the lottery almost every week, but always picks different numbers.
lottery.exampleSense: A scheme for the distribution of prizes by lot or chance, especially a gaming scheme in which one or more tickets bearing particular numbers draw prizes, the other tickets are blanks.

lot.o: From Middle English lot, from Old English hlot (“portion, choice, decision”), from Proto-West Germanic *hlut, from Proto-Germanic *hlutą. Cognate with North Frisian lod, Saterland Frisian Lot, West Frisian lot, Dutch lot, French lot, German Low German Lott, Middle High German luz. Doublet of lotto. Related also to German Los.
lot.example: We seem to be made to suffer. It's our lot in life.
lot.exampleSense: The part, or fate, that falls to one, as it were, by chance, or without one's planning.

rebuttal.example: For those who imagine the capital flows with milk and honey, or avocado and sourdough, Edmonton is your rebuttal. Once full of light industry, today it has some of the most deprived areas in England.
rebuttal.exampleSense: The act of contradicting something by making a contrary argument, or presenting contrary evidence.

denominator.o: Learned borrowing from Late Latin dēnōminātor (“that which names”).

degeneracy.example: Inveterate abuse of drinking in nonhereditarily disposed persons creates a degeneracy like the hereditary.
degeneracy.exampleSense: The state of being degenerate (in all senses).

boron.o: From the stem of borax (boro-) + -on (based on carbon). Coined by British chemist Humphry Davy as a modification of his earlier word boracium.
boron.example: The B₆-type octahedral borons are each bonded to five other boron atoms; four are part of the same octahedron, and one is external to this octahedron.
boron.exampleSense: The chemical element (symbol B) with an atomic number of 5, which is a metalloid found in its pure form as a dark amorphous powder.

velocity.o: From Middle French vélocité, from Latin vēlōcitās (“speed”), from vēlōx (“fast”), thus a doublet of veloce.
velocity.example: A car racing in a circle may retain the same speed while continually changing its velocity.
velocity.exampleSense: A vector quantity that denotes the rate of change of position with respect to time, combining speed with a directional component.

annihilate.o: Borrowed from Latin annihilātus, perfect passive participle of annihilō (“to reduce to nothing”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from ad (“to”) + nihil (“nothing”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix). See also an-.
annihilate.example: An atom bomb can annihilate a whole city.
annihilate.exampleSense: To reduce to nothing, to destroy, to eradicate.

depleted.o: simple past and past participle of deplete. Borrowed from Latin dēplētus (“empty”), from depleō. First attested in 1716; originally a medical term.
depleted.example: The depleted aerosol can spray no more since there was no propellant left.
depleted.exampleSense: Used up, expended; of which nothing is left.

tetra-.o: Borrowed from Ancient Greek τετρα- (tetra-), combining form of Ancient Greek τέτταρες (téttares), from τέσσαρες (téssares, “four”). Doublet of quadri-.

tetrahedron.o: From Ancient Greek τετράεδρον (tetráedron, “triangle-based pyramid”), from τετράεδρος (tetráedros), from τετράς (tetrás, “four”) + ἕδρα (hédra, “seat”). By surface analysis, tetra- + -hedron.

intervening.o: present participle and gerund of intervene. Back-formation from intervention, and/or from Latin interveniō (“come between”, verb).
intervening.example: This is not to criticise Ghosh's use of such lexis, but just to point out that Ghosh's use of such lexis must be regarded as examples of re-use and not as evidence of continued use over the intervening period.
intervening.exampleSense: Falling between two periods or events.

sphalerite.o: From Ancient Greek σφαλερός (sphalerós, “unstable, unsteady, precarious”) + -ite; named in 1847.
sphalerite.example: The Monte Cristo and Philadelphia sphalerites have similar mean Pb concentrations (80 ppm) that are lower than the Lucky Dog sphalerites (119 ppm).
sphalerite.exampleSense: A yellow, brown or black, sometimes red, green white or colorless mineral with cubic crystals, of a chemical formula (Zn,Fe)S, often containing also minor metals, such as cadmium, gallium, germanium and indium.

tetrahedral.example: Of the convex polyhedra with regular faces, the only ones that have tetrahedral, octahedral, or icosahedral symmetry are the Platonic and Archimedean solids.
tetrahedral.exampleSense: Of, relating to, or having the shape of a tetrahedron.

isotope.o:
noun: From iso- (“equal”) + -tope (“place”), because the different isotopes of an element always occupy the same place in the periodic table. The term was coined by Scottish doctor Margaret Todd in 1909 and first used publicly on February 27, 1913 by English chemist Frederick Soddy.

verb: Possible back-formation from isotopy.

grate.o:
noun: From Middle English grate, from a Medieval Latin crāta, from a Latin word for a hurdle; or Italian grata, from Latin cratis.

verb: From Middle English graten, from Old French grater (“to scrape”) ( > French gratter), from Frankish *krattōn, from Proto-Germanic *krattōną. Cognate with Old High German krazzon ( > German kratzen (“to scrawl”) > Danish kradse), Icelandic krassa (“to scrawl”) and Danish kratte.

adj: From Latin grātus (“agreeable”).
grate.example: I need to grate the cheese before the potato is cooked.
grate.exampleSense: To shred (things, usually foodstuffs), by rubbing across a grater.

grating.example: If, with these symptoms, are heard gratings of the teeth, irregular appetite, and sudden ebullitions of temper we may reasonably conclude that parasites are irritating the intestines and should be gotten rid of.
grating.exampleSense: The sound made by something that grates against something else.

constructive.o: From Latin cōnstrūctīvus. By surface analysis, construct + -ive.

neutron.o: From neutral + -on; by surface analysis, neutr(o)- + -on. Coined by Scottish-Australian physicist William Sutherland in 1899 in a paper in the Philosophical Magazine. Subsequent usage was sporadic and theoretical, sometimes referring to neutrinos rather than neutrons, and the modern sense was reintroduced alongside proton by Ernest Rutherford in 1920.

intercept.o: Borrowed from Latin interceptum, past participle of intercipiō.
intercept.example: Because the horizontal-axis intercept occurs when y=0 and the vertical-axis intercept occurs when x=0, we can find the intercepts algebraically.
intercept.exampleSense: The coordinate of the point at which a curve intersects an axis.

aniso-.o: Representing a combining form of Ancient Greek ἄνισος (ánisos, “unequal”), equivalent to an- + iso-.

anisotropic.example: The crystal has an anisotropic structure, as it is stronger along its length than laterally.
anisotropic.exampleSense: Having properties that differ according to the direction of measurement; exhibiting anisotropy.

tetragonal.example: The eight normals of the tetragonal scalenohedron may carry the eight faces of a semiform in other ways than asymmetrically as regards the systematic planes.
tetragonal.exampleSense: Having two equal axes and one unequal, and all angles 90°.

hexagon.o: From Latin hexagōnum, from Ancient Greek ἑξάγωνον (hexágōnon). By surface analysis, hexa- + -gon. Piecewise doublet of sexagon.

hexagonal.o: From hexagon + -al. Piecewise doublet of sexagonal.
hexagonal.example: Nuts in engineering are generally hexagonal.
hexagonal.exampleSense: Having six edges, or having a cross-section in the form of a hexagon.

centered.o: simple past and past participle of center. From Middle English center, centre, from Middle French centre, from Latin centrum, from Ancient Greek κέντρον (kéntron), from κεντεῖν (kenteîn, “to prick, goad”). Doublet of centrum. * (group theory): In the notation Z(G), the letter Z derives from the German Zentrum (“center”).

centred.o: simple past and past participle of centre. From Middle English center, centre, from Middle French centre, from Latin centrum, from Ancient Greek κέντρον (kéntron), from κεντεῖν (kenteîn, “to prick, goad”). Doublet of centrum.

polymer.o: From poly- + -mer, from Ancient Greek πολύς (polús, “many”) + μέρος (méros, “part”). Coined by Jöns Jacob Berzelius in 1833, though his definition was quite different from the modern one.
polymer.example: Similar studies of rats have employed four different intracranial resorbable, slow sustained release systems—surgical foam, a thermal gel depot, a microcapsule or biodegradable polymer beads.
polymer.exampleSense: A material consisting of such polymer molecules.

bisector.example: South Street is the bisector of Broken Dreams Boulevard.
bisector.exampleSense: A line or curve that bisects or divides a line segment, angle, or other figure into two equal parts.

pendulum.o: Borrowed from the neuter of Latin pendulus (“hanging”).
pendulum.example: The pendulum can be seen to be swinging in favour of rail, as with each issue of RAIL comes news of further intermodal service expansion.
pendulum.exampleSense: A body suspended from a fixed support so that it swings freely back and forth under the influence of gravity, commonly used to regulate various devices such as clocks. The tendency of a situation to oscillate (between two extremes).

perpendicular.o: Derived from Middle French perpendiculaire, from Old French perpendiculer, from Latin perpendiculum (“plumb line”).
perpendicular.example: In most houses, the walls are perpendicular to the floor.
perpendicular.exampleSense: At or forming a right angle (to something).

translation.o: From Middle English translacioun (“transfer, translation”), from Anglo-Norman translacioun, from Latin trānslātiō, from trānslāt-, the supine stem of trānsferō (“to transfer, transport, transform, translate”). Equivalent to translate + -ion. Displaced native Old English wending.
translation.example: This old text needs translation into modern English before it is published.
translation.exampleSense: The act of translating, in its various senses: The conversion of text from one language to another.

repetition.o:
noun: Borrowed from Latin repetitionem (accusative singular of repetitio; cf. French répétition). Doublet of repetitio. By surface analysis, repeat + -ition.

verb: From re- + petition.
repetition.example: The group went through several rounds at different courts, petitioning and repetitioning, losing again and again.

amorphous.o: From Ancient Greek ἄμορφος (ámorphos, “without form, shapeless, deformed”) (itself from ἀ- (a-, “without”) + μορφή (morphḗ, “form”) + -ous. By surface analysis, a- + -morphous.
amorphous.example: The enormous pile of spaghetti landed on the floor in an amorphous heap.
amorphous.exampleSense: Lacking a definite form or clear shape.

nexus.o: From Latin nexus (“connection, nexus; act of binding, tying or fastening together; something which binds, binding, bond, fastening, joint; legal obligation”), from nectō (“to attach, bind, connect, fasten, tie; to interweave; to relate; to unite; to bind by obligation, make liable, oblige; to compose, contrive, devise, produce”, supine stem nex-) + -tus (suffix forming verbal nouns).
nexus.example: Sunday's election pits Move Forward and the billionaire Shinawatra family's Pheu Thai against ruling parties backed by a nexus of old money, conservatives and generals with influence over key institutions involved in two decades of upheaval in Southeast Asia's second-biggest economy.
nexus.exampleSense: A connected group; a network, a web.

heuristic.o: Irregular formation from Ancient Greek εὑρίσκω (heurískō, “I find, discover”) (compare the proper Greek term εὑρετικός (heuretikós)).
heuristic.example: If a heuristic algorithm works for most of the input data or its maximum percentage error is tolerable, we may prefer the heuristic algorithm to an optimum algorithm that requires a long time.
heuristic.exampleSense: That provides a useful, but not optimal, solution to a problem. Such algorithms are typically employed either because the only known algorithms that provide optimal solutions use too much time or resources, or else because there is no known algorithm that provides an optimal solution.

saddle.o:
noun: From Middle English sadel, from Old English sadol, from Proto-West Germanic *sadul, from Proto-Germanic *sadulaz (“saddle”). Further etymology uncertain, perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *sod-dʰlo-, from *sed- (“to sit”) + *-dʰlom (a variant of *-trom (suffix forming nouns denoting instruments or tools)), though the Oxford English Dictionary says this “presents formal difficulties”. Cognates * Danish sadel * Dutch zadel * German Sattel * Icelandic söðull * Low German Sadel * Russian седло́ (sedló) * Saterland Frisian Soadel * Scots sadil * Swedish sadel * West Frisian seal

verb: From Middle English sadelen (“to put a saddle on (an animal), to saddle”) [and other forms], from Old English sadolian, sadelian, sadilian (“to saddle”), from Proto-Germanic *sadulōną (“to saddle”), from *sadulaz (“a saddle”, noun) (see further at etymology 1) + *-ōną (suffix forming denominative verbs from nouns). Cognates * Middle Dutch sādelen (modern Dutch zadelen) * Middle Low German sādelen * Old Danish sathlæ (modern Danish sadle) * Old High German satalōn, satulōn (Middle High German satelen, sateln, German satteln) * Old Norse sǫðla * Old Swedish saþla (modern Swedish sadla)
saddle.example: I saw many brave men cut down, many fall mortally wounded from their saddles.
saddle.exampleSense: A seat for a rider, typically made of leather and raised in the front and rear, placed on the back of a horse or other animal, and secured by a strap around the animal's body.
