econometrics.o: An adaptation of the French économétrie. Coined by Norwegian economist Ragnar Frisch in 1926. Compare the earlier German Oekonometrie (now generally spelt Ökonometrie), first used (in a different sense) by Polish economist Paweł Ciompa in 1910.

predictably.example: Predictably he returned to the scene of his crime, where the police were waiting to arrest him.
predictably.exampleSense: In a manner that can be expected or anticipated.

go through.example: Every morning, she went through her mail over a cup of coffee.
go through.exampleSense: To examine or scrutinize (a number or series of things).

observer.example: The only crew-member to survive the crash was the Canadian observer.
observer.exampleSense: A crew member on an aircraft who makes observations of enemy positions or aircraft

chapelry.o: From Old French chapelerie, corresponding to chapel + -ry.
chapelry.example: Similarly in the many large parishes, the curates in the outlying chapelries became financially dependent on their congregations.
chapelry.exampleSense: The district attached to a chapel; a division of a large parish which has its own district chapel.

overfly.example: My family planned to take pictures from the ground as I overflew them in the hot air balloon.

overly.o:
adv: From over + -ly (adverbial suffix).

adj: From over + -ly (adjectival suffix).
overly.example: This means, at times, long and perhaps overly discursive discussions of other taxa.

prepone.o:
verb: Blend of pre- + postpone, 1913.

verb: From Latin praepōnō.
prepone.example: If then by this inviolable tie we are one, your endowments entitle me joinct owner; a riches, I prepone to Monarchies.

concise.o: From Latin concīsus (“cut short”), from concīdere (“cut to pieces”), from caedēre (“to cut, to strike down”).
concise.example: This, however, must refer solely to the length; unfortunately they were far too broad in proportion (the fault I have always observed in them). This directly gives a slightly hoofish look, as in the concise Chinese feet.

polymorphism.o: * (object-oriented programming) Coined by British computer scientist Christopher Strachey in 1967. By surface analysis, poly- + -morphism.
polymorphism.example: Some polymorphisms can be quite stable – so stable that they span the change from an ancestral to a descendant species.
polymorphism.exampleSense: The regular existence of two or more different genotypes within a given species or population; also, variability of amino acid sequences within a gene's protein.

laureate.o: First attested during the end of the 15th century, in Middle English; borrowed from Latin laureātus, from laurea (“laurel crown, wreath”, a high reward given to poets and later to the triumphant) + -ātus (forming adjectives indicating possession) (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and -ate (noun-forming suffix)), from laureus (“of laurel”), from laurus (“laurel”). The verb was formed by metanalysis, see -ate (verb-forming suffix). Cognate with French lauréat.
laureate.example: To strew the laureate hearse where Lycid lies.

catenary.o:
adj: From Latin catenarius, from Latin catēna (“chain”).

noun: From Late Latin catenaria, in turn from Latin catēna (“chain”). Attested since 1788.
catenary.example: The result was catenary being torn down several hundred feet at a time.
catenary.exampleSense: A cable, the segments of which between supports take a catenary geometric shape, supporting in turn an overhead conductor that provides trains, trams or trolley buses with electricity, or the combination of the conductor, the cable, and supports.

spadger.o: Originally British dialect (1850s), from spadge (fronted variant of northern dialect spag) + -er. The northern dialect term spag is a derhoticised form of Scots spurg (“sparrow”), from spur (from Old Norse spǫrr (“sparrow”), suffixless cognate of Old English spearwa) + diminutive suffix -ock, with loss of vowel and voicing of -k to -g after r.
spadger.example: The broadcasting blokes are twittering away like spadgers over there.

courtly.o: From Middle English courtly, equivalent to court + -ly.
courtly.example: He swept off his hat and made a deep courtly bow.
courtly.exampleSense: Befitting of a royal court; reflecting the manners or behaviour of people at court.

countess.o: From Anglo-Norman cuntesse, Old French contesse, from Latin comitissa; equivalent to count + -ess. Doublet of contessa.
countess.example: Elizabeth Millicent Leveson-Gower is 24th Countess of Sutherland; her son will be the 25th Earl.
countess.exampleSense: A woman holding the rank of count or earl in her own right; a female holder of an earldom.

courtesy.o: From Middle English curteisie, curtesie, from Anglo-Norman curtesie, from Old French curteisie, cortoisie. Equivalent to courteous + -y (abstract noun suffix). By surface analysis, court + -esy.
courtesy.example: I offered them a ride simply as a courtesy.
courtesy.exampleSense: A polite gesture or remark, especially as opposed to an obligation or standard practice.

larboard.o: From Middle English ladde-bord, latebord, most likely referring to the side of the ship on which cargo was loaded. Changed to larboard in the 1500s by association with starboard. (Texts from the 1500s have spellings like lerbord, leereboord, larboord, corresponding to how they spell sterbord, steereboord, starboord.)

torc.o: Alternative spelling of torque. Borrowed from Latin torqueō (“to twist”).

torque.o:
noun: Borrowed from Latin torqueō (“to twist”).

noun: From French torque, from Old French, from Latin torquis; or adapted directly from Latin torquēs (“chaplet, collar, necklace of twisted metal, ring, wreath”) (cf. earlier English torques).
torque.example: The relative strengths of the various torques will depend on both the spacecraft environment and the form and structure of the spacecraft itself.
torque.exampleSense: A rotational or twisting effect of a force; a moment of force, defined for measurement purposes as an equivalent straight line force multiplied by the distance from the axis of rotation (SI unit newton metre or Nm; imperial unit pound-foot or lb·ft, not to be confused with the foot pound-force, commonly "foot-pound", a unit of work or energy)

mechanist.example: The economic spirit of a people cannot be manipulated in as simple-minded a fashion as the Keynesian mechanists imagine.
mechanist.exampleSense: A person who takes a mechanical view; someone who subscribes to mechanism.

mechanics.o: From Latin mēchanicus, from Ancient Greek μηχανικός (mēkhanikós), from μηχανή (mēkhanḗ, “machine, tool”).
mechanics.example: It was anticipated that children who encountered difficulty with the mechanics of word processing could turn to the coach for help rather than interrupt Margaret's work with a reading group.

mechatronics.example: Advanced technology to create energy-saving, resorce-saving and highly intelligent systems by integrating mechanics, electronics and software is called mechatronics.
mechatronics.exampleSense: The synergistic combination of mechanical engineering, electronic engineering and software engineering for the study of automata from an engineering perspective and the control of advanced hybrid systems.

diesel-electric.example: Brush supplied shunters to industrial clients, but the first significant main line order came from the Ceylon Government Railway in 1950 for 25 diesel-electrics.

meteoric.example: Her meteoric rise to power was followed by a slow, lackluster career at the top.
meteoric.exampleSense: Like a meteor in speed, brilliance, or ephemeralness.

mechanic.o: From Middle English mekanyk (“mechanical”), from Old French mecanique, from Latin mechanicus (“of or belonging to machines or mechanics, inventive”), from Ancient Greek μηχανικός (mēkhanikós, “pertaining to machines or contrivance, mechanic, ingenious, inventive”), from μηχανή (mēkhanḗ, “a machine, contrivance”); see machine.
mechanic.example: It was so obvious. I mean, all of Nicky's half-assed mechanics, they were real signal happy.
mechanic.exampleSense: A cheat who manipulates the cards or dice.

ministerial.o: Borrowed from Middle French ministeriel, equivalent to minister + -ial. Doublet of minstrel and ministerialis.
ministerial.example: In over a quarter of a century of writing this column, there has been no end of scandals, mishaps, errors and general cock-ups resulting from ministerial incompetence.
ministerial.exampleSense: Related to a governmental minister or ministry.

protract.o: From the past participle stem of Latin prōtrahō. By surface analysis, pro- + tract.
protract.example: This is a synopsis of our marches, which, protracted on Burckhardt’s map, gives an error of ten miles.
protract.exampleSense: To draw to a scale; to lay down the lines and angles of, with scale and protractor; to plot.

encyclopedia.o: Borrowed from New Latin encyclopēdīa, encyclopaedīa (“general education”), a univerbated form of Koine Greek ἐγκύκλιος παιδείᾱ (enkúklios paideíā, “education in the circle of arts and sciences”), from Ancient Greek ἐγκύκλιος (enkúklios, “circular”) + παιδείᾱ (paideíā, “childrearing; education”) (q.v.). Nearly all modern English usage of the word was influenced by the scope and format of the French Encyclopédie by Diderot et al. (see quotation).
encyclopedia.example: I only use the library for the encyclopedia, as we’ve got most other books here.
encyclopedia.exampleSense: A comprehensive reference work (often spanning several printed volumes) with articles (usually arranged in alphabetical order, or sometimes arranged by category) on a range of subjects, sometimes general, sometimes limited to a particular field.

infelicity.o: From in- + felicity, from Latin infelicitas.
infelicity.example: Returning to our own epistemic situation, we do not know the sense in which quantum mechanics and relativity will be taken to be approximately true after their descriptive infelicities are addressed.
infelicity.exampleSense: Something that is infelicitous or inappropriate

superficiality.example: Seeks companion with similar invisible handicap or circumstance which forced early awareness of mortality and is consequently very serious about life and has little time for superficiality.
superficiality.exampleSense: The property of being superficial, the tendency to judge by surface appearance.

eigen-.o: Borrowed from German eigen (“own”). Many of the compounds represent partial translations from German, e.g. eigenvalue from German Eigenwert. Doublet of own.

eigenvector.o: From eigen- + vector, a partial calque of German Eigenvektor. The prefix eigen- (also used in eigenvalue) was first used in 1904, by David Hilbert, and was possibly inspired by a related usage by Hermann von Helmholtz.

latent.o: From Middle English latent, latente, from Old French latent, from Latin latēns, present participle of lateō (“lie hidden”).
latent.example: There is known latent demand for rail freight and the rail freight industry is working with Scottish businesses to develop new rail freight services, as environmental concerns are beginning to change the logistics choices of Scottish producers.
latent.exampleSense: Existing or present but concealed or inactive.

infrared.example: Collisions of these 'transparent' molecules with the molecules that do have absorption bands in the infrared can have a considerable influence on the intensities of the observed absorption bands.
infrared.exampleSense: The electromagnetic radiation of a wavelength longer than visible light, but shorter than microwave radiation, having a wavelength between 700 nm and 1 mm.

mercury.o: The noun is derived from Middle English mercurie (“metallic chemical element, quicksilver; a plant, probably goosefoot (genus Chenopodium); (possibly) dog’s mercury (Mercurialis perennis); etc.”), borrowed from Late Latin mercurius (“metallic chemical element, quicksilver”), Latin Mercurius (“Mercury, the Roman god of commerce, communication, etc.; the planet Mercury; etc.”), possibly from merc-, a stem of merx (“goods, wares; merchandise”); further etymology uncertain, possibly: * from Etruscan; or * from Proto-Indo-European *merǵ- (“to divide”), or *merkʷ- (“to grasp; to take”). The suffix -urius is also thought to be from Etruscan. Noun sense 1 (“metallic chemical element”) is from the association in medieval alchemy of the seven known metals—gold, silver, quicksilver, copper, iron, tin, and lead—with the Sun, the Moon, and the planets Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn. An analogy was probably also drawn between the element being liquid at room temperature, and the Roman god Mercury’s attribute of swiftness. Noun sense 2 (“senses relating to plants”) is derived from mercurial (“(obsolete) any of the plants now known as mercury”, noun), from Middle English mercurial (“a plant, probably goosefoot (genus Chenopodium); (possibly) dog’s mercury (Mercurialis perennis)”, noun) from Anglo-Norman mercurial, Old French mercurial, or directly from their etymon Latin mercuriālis (“a plant, probably annual mercury (Mercurialis annua)”), short for herba mercuriālis (“(probably) annual mercury”, literally “herb or plant of the god Mercury”). Mercuriālis (“pertaining to the Roman god Mercury”, adjective) is derived from Mercurius (“the Roman god Mercury”) (see above) + -ālis (suffix forming adjectives of relationship from nouns). Noun sense 2.2.2.1 (“Blitum bonus-henricus”) is from the fact that this plant was often confused with annual mercury (noun sense 2.1). The verb is derived from the noun.
mercury.example: The mercury there has averaged 37.6°C, 2.3°C above the February norm.
mercury.exampleSense: Ambient pressure or temperature (from the use of mercury in barometers and thermometers).

spectra.o: plural of spectrum. From Latin spectrum (“appearance, image, apparition”), from speciō (“look at, view”). Doublet of specter. See also scope.

spectral.o:
adj: From spectr(e) + -al.

adj: From spectr(um) + -al.
spectral.example: The spectral chain-rattling and moans gave me the chills.
spectral.exampleSense: Of, or pertaining to, spectres; ghostly.

irradiation.o: From Middle French irradiacion, from Latin irradiatio. Morphologically irradiate + -ion.

irradiate.o:
adj: From Middle English irradiate (“illuminated, shining”), borrowed from Medieval Latin irradiātus, perfect passive participle of irradiō, from ir- (“against; into; on, upon”) + radiō (“to cause to radiate, irradiate; to emit beams, radiate”), from radius (“ray of light; rod, staff; spoke of a wheel”) + -ō (first conjugation verb-forming suffix) (further etymology uncertain; possibly ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *reh₁t- (“beam; pole; post”)). The adjective is attested earlier than the verb. The English word is analysable as in- (“against; into; on, upon”) + radiate.

verb: From Middle English irradiate (“illuminated, shining”) (more at etymology 1), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).
irradiate.example: An inherent protection in labeling of the shipping containers will be the prevention of irradiating the commodity again, insuring that the produce has been treated within the safety limits established by the FDA [Food and Drug Administration].
irradiate.exampleSense: To apply radiation other than visible light to (someone or something). To treat (food) with ionizing radiation to destroy pathogens.

flux.o: From Old French flux, from Latin fluxus (“flow”).
flux.example: That high a neutron flux would be lethal in seconds.
flux.exampleSense: The rate of transfer of energy (or another physical quantity), especially an electric or magnetic field, through a given surface.

concurring.o: present participle and gerund of concur. Borrowed from Latin concurro (“to run together, agree”).

concurrently.example: Concurrently with the St. Pancras-Bedford service, diesel trains have now taken over that between Kentish Town and Barking, on an even-interval basis at half-hourly intervals.
concurrently.exampleSense: In a concurrent manner; at the same time.

concurrent.o: From Middle English concurrent, from Old French concurrent, from Latin concurrēns, present active participle of concurrō (“happen at the same time”), from con- (“with”) + currō (“run”).
concurrent.example: Such are the changes which science recognizes in the wire itself, as concurrent with the visual changes taking place in the eye.
concurrent.exampleSense: Happening at the same time; simultaneous.

takeoff.example: The flight was smooth, but the takeoff was a little rough.
takeoff.exampleSense: The rising or ascent of an aircraft or rocket into flight.

partitioned.o: simple past and past participle of partition. Recorded c.1430, "division into shares, distinction," from Middle English particioun, from Old French particion (modern partition), from Latin partitio, partitionem (“division, portion”), from partitus, the past participle of partire (“to split (up), part(ition)”).

synopsis.o: From Late Latin synopsis, itself from Ancient Greek σύνοψις (súnopsis), from σύν (sún, “with or whole”) + ὄψις (ópsis, “view”) meaning whole view.

competency.o: From Late Latin competentia. Doublet of competence.
competency.example: Superfluity comes sooner by white hairs, but competency lives longer.

classify.o: From French classifier. By surface analysis, class + -ify.
classify.example: Should we classify "make up" as an idiom or as a phrasal verb?
classify.exampleSense: to identify by or divide into classes; to categorize

declassified.o: simple past and past participle of declassify. From de- + classify.

declassify.example: There are also two First Class compartments, but these have been declassified for suburban services and will be available to all customers.
declassify.exampleSense: to remove the classification from; to lift the restrictions on

to and fro.example: A light tossing to and fro and still rapidly advancing showed that one of the newcomers carried a lantern.
to and fro.exampleSense: Back and forth; with a reciprocating motion.

diffident.o: From Latin diffīdentem, present participle of diffīdere (“to mistrust”). Doublet of defiant.
diffident.example: Having therefore—but hold, as we are diffident of our own abilities, let us here invite a superior power to our assistance.

well-spoken.example: They've obviously never met before, but are getting on like a house on fire. Both are well-spoken and versed in the Queen's English.
well-spoken.exampleSense: Eloquent and able with regards to speech.

impedance.o: From impede + -ance. In sense 2 and sense 3 it was coined by English mathematician and physicist Oliver Heaviside in 1886.

procedural.example: The judge dismissed the case on procedural grounds: it wasn't the facts or the law, but just that they hadn't filed the correct forms.

case-sensitive.o: Alternative form of case. From Middle English cas, from Old French cas (“an event”), from Latin cāsus (“a falling, a fall; accident, event, occurrence; occasion, opportunity; noun case”), perfect passive participle of cadō (“to fall, to drop”).

lexicalize.example: In fact, the child will lexicalize one, two, or three elements of the semantic representation according to his lexicalization span.
lexicalize.exampleSense: To accept a term into one's own vocabulary as a distinct lexical unit.

lexical.o: From Latin lexis, from Ancient Greek λέξις (léxis, “word”) + -al.

concurrence.example: This book owes its existence to a concurrence of accidents.

cripple.o: From Middle English cripel, crepel, crüpel, from Old English crypel (“crippled; a cripple”), from Proto-Germanic *krupilaz (“tending to crawl; a cripple”), from Proto-Indo-European *grewb- (“to bend, crouch, crawl”), from Proto-Indo-European *ger- (“to bend, twist”), equivalent to creep + -le. Cognate with Dutch kreupel, Low German Kröpel, German Krüppel, Old Norse kryppill.
cripple.example: But the penny was beginning to drop: even a successful railway could be crippled by its capital costs.
cripple.exampleSense: To cause severe and disabling damage; to make unable to function normally.

sexual harassment.example: All new hires at this job are trained on how to prevent and how to respond to sexual harassment.
sexual harassment.exampleSense: Harassment in the form of unwelcome sexual advances and/or remarks.

harassment.o: Borrowed from Middle French harassement. By surface analysis, harass + -ment.

harass.o: The verb is derived from Middle French, Old French harasser (“to exhaust, tire out, wear out; to harry, torment, vex”) (modern French harasser (“to exhaust, tire out, wear out”)), possibly from Old French harer (“to set a dog on”), from Frankish *hara (“here, hither”) (a command for a dog to attack), from Proto-Germanic *hē₂r (“here, in this place”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ḱe (“here; this”) + *ís (“the (person or thing just named)”) + *-r. The noun is derived from the verb.
harass.example: I am gay and have AIDS and would very much like to write to someone. It is vey lonely here and they seem to think I'm going to die soon, though I wonder if they aren't just harassing me.
harass.exampleSense: To annoy (someone) frequently or systematically; to pester. To persistently bother (someone, or a group of people) physically or psychologically when such behaviour is illegal and/or unwanted, especially over an extended period.

mingy.o: Uncertain. Perhaps a blend of mean + stingy.

milky.o: From Middle English mylky, melky, equivalent to milk + -y. Cognate with Saterland Frisian moalkig (“milky”), West Frisian molkich (“milky”), Dutch melkig (“milky”), German Low German melkig (“milky”), German milchig (“milky”), Danish mælkig (“milky”), Swedish mjölkig (“milky”), Icelandic mjólkugur (“milky”). Doublet of milchig.
milky.example: Mrs. Anthony, their daily housekeeper, brought in the milky coffee and placed it on the breakfast table.
milky.exampleSense: Containing (an especially large amount of) milk.

lonesome.example: I sat and watched the cars pass all by my lonesome.

undercurrent.example: Her lips hardly moving, every feature steady, she undercurrented my narrative with ejaculations in French, Russian, Italian.

underflow.o: From under- + flow, modelled on overflow.

actually.o:
adv: From Middle English actually, actuelly, equivalent to actual + -ly.

intj: A calque of Tagalog talaga.
actually.example: His promises did not correspond with what he actually did.
actually.exampleSense: In act or in fact; really; in truth; positively.

actual.o: From Middle English actual, actuel (“active”), from Anglo-Norman actuel, actual, and its source Late Latin actuālis (“active, practical”), from Latin actus (“act, action, performance”), from agere (“to do; to act”) + -alis (“-al”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éǵeti, from the root *h₂eǵ-. By surface analysis, act + -u- + -al.
actual.example: They also exposed the blatant discrepancy between the west's professed values and actual foreign policies.
actual.exampleSense: Existing in reality, not just potentially; really acted or acting; occurring in fact.

binary.o: Inherited from Middle English binarie. By surface analysis, bin- + -ary.
binary.example: As our initial exposure to the base 10 number system consisted of learning how to count, it also makes sense that we might begin by learning how to count in binary.
binary.exampleSense: The bijective base-2 numeral system, which uses only the digits 0 and 1.

graphic.o: From Latin graphicus (“belonging to painting or drawing”), from Ancient Greek γραφικός (graphikós, “belonging to painting or drawing, picturesque, of or for writing; of style, lively”), from γραφή (graphḗ, “drawing, painting, writing, a writing, description, etc.”), from γράφω (gráphō, “scratch, carve”) (cognate with English carve).
graphic.example: I've just played this new computer game: the graphics are amazing.
graphic.exampleSense: A computer-generated image as viewed on a screen forming part of a game or a film etc.

graphics.o: plural of graphic. From Latin graphicus (“belonging to painting or drawing”), from Ancient Greek γραφικός (graphikós, “belonging to painting or drawing, picturesque, of or for writing; of style, lively”), from γραφή (graphḗ, “drawing, painting, writing, a writing, description, etc.”), from γράφω (gráphō, “scratch, carve”) (cognate with English carve).
graphics.example: This game is really fun, but the graphics aren't very good.
graphics.exampleSense: The art or visual representations displayed by a computer.

texting.o: Blend of text + messaging, derived from text messaging
texting.example: More typical (but still not numerous) are the textings supplied for Alleluias, or just as frequently for melismas occurring at the end of the second or third verse of Offertories.
texting.exampleSense: The words set to a piece of music.

text message.example: Similarly, Fingilish usually refers to transliterated Farsi in chatrooms, text messages, and the like.
text message.exampleSense: A brief electronic message sent between mobile phones.

textspeak.example: For 40 years the society has championed good English – and hasn't been above the occasional criticism of the Queen's own standards of English – but it has finally conceded it cannot survive in the era of textspeak and Twitter.
textspeak.exampleSense: The abbreviated, simplified form of language used in text messages, which often elides vowels and omits punctuation and capitalisation.

textual.o: From Middle English textewell, textueel, textuel, textuele, tixtuel (“learned in texts, bookish”), possibly from Latin textuālis; also compare Middle French textuele; or perhaps a coinage by Chaucer from Latin textus and Middle English -el. English spelling conformed to Latin from late 15c. By surface analysis, text + -ual.
textual.example: I see that the editor revised the document's metadata, headers, and images, but I don't see any textual changes.
textual.exampleSense: Of or pertaining to text. Of or pertaining to text as opposed to other document elements.

text.o: From Middle English text, from Old French texte, from Medieval Latin textus, from Latin textus (“style or texture of a work”), perfect passive participle of texō (“to weave”). Cognate to English texture.
text.example: I'll text the address to you as soon as I find it.
text.exampleSense: To send a text message to; i.e. to transmit text using the Short Message Service (SMS), or a similar service, between communications devices, particularly mobile phones.

alphanumeric.example: Therefore, we need a special code to represent all alphanumeric data (letters, symbols, and numbers).
alphanumeric.exampleSense: Consisting of these characters plus punctuation and other special characters.

alpha.o: From the Ancient Greek ἄλφα (álpha), the first letter of the Greek alphabet, from the Phoenician 𐤀 (ʾ, “aleph”). Doublet of alif and aleph.
alpha.exampleSense: Designates the first in an order of precedence.

phonetics.example: This dictionary shows the phonetics of the words.
phonetics.exampleSense: The study of the physical sounds of human speech, concerned with the physical properties of speech sounds (phones), and the processes of their physiological production, auditory reception, and neurophysiological perception, and their representation by written symbols.

phonetic.o: Borrowed from Latin phōnēticus, from Ancient Greek φωνητῐκός (phōnētĭkós). By surface analysis, phone + -etic.
phonetic.example: All unfamiliar names have been transcribed in phonetic spelling.
phonetic.exampleSense: Relating to the spoken rather than written form of a word or name, as opposed to orthographic.

alphabetical.o: From Latin alphabēticus + -al. By surface analysis, alphabet + -ical.
alphabetical.example: All names were placed into an alphabetical list.
alphabetical.exampleSense: According to the sequence of the letters of the alphabet.

alphabetic.o: Partly from French alphabétique and partly from its etymon Latin alphabēticus. By surface analysis, alphabet + -ic.
alphabetic.example: Upper case alphabetics can be composed of two characters: (1) a shift character; and (2) the desired alphabetic character.
alphabetic.exampleSense: An alphabetic character; a letter of the alphabet.

hexadecimal.o: 1952, from hexa- + decimal; see the Wikipedia article for more information. Piecewise doublet of sexadecimal.

hexa-.o: From Latin hexa-, from Ancient Greek ἑξα- (hexa-), from ἕξ (héx, “six”). By surface analysis, hex- + -a-. Piecewise doublet of sexa-.

distortion.o: Borrowed from Latin distortio, distortionis, from distortus.
distortion.example: The story he told was a bit of a distortion.

contortion.o: Derived from Middle French contortion, from Latin contortiō.

contort.o: Equivalent to con- + -tort; from Middle English, borrowed from Latin contortus, past participle of contorqueō, from com- + torqueō (“twist, turn”).

condom.o: Unknown. Many speculations exist. Possibly derived from Italian guantone, from guanto (“a glove”).
condom.example: However, substantial proportions of participants preferred the nonlatex condom or reported that they would recommend its use to others.
condom.exampleSense: A flexible sleeve made of latex or other impermeable material such as polyurethane or sheepskin, worn over an erect penis during sexual intercourse as a contraceptive or as a way to prevent the spread of STIs.

surtitle.o: From French sur (“over, above”), from Latin super, + title, from Latin titulum.

caption.o: Borrowed from Latin captiō (“deception, fraud”), from the past participle of capiō (“to take, to seize”) (English capture). Compare Middle English capcioun (“seizure, capture”).
caption.example: Some of the photographs are new and interesting, but many captions are amateurish, uninformative or simply careless.
caption.exampleSense: A title or brief explanation attached to an illustration, cartoon, user interface element, etc.

disport.o: The verb is derived from Middle English disporten, desporten (“to take part in entertainment, sport, etc., to pass time, amuse oneself, be merry; to amuse, entertain; to cheer, console; to behave (in a particular way), deport; to be active, to busy; to relieve (someone of a task); to prevent (someone from attending)”), from Anglo-Norman desporter, Old French desporter, deporter, depporter (“to amuse, entertain; to pass time, amuse oneself; to forbear; to stop”), from Latin deportāre, present active infinitive of dēportō (“to bring, convey; to bring or take home; to carry along or down; to banish, transport”), from dē- (prefix meaning ‘from, off’) + portō (“to bear, carry; to bring, convey”) (from Proto-Indo-European *per- (“to carry forth; fare”)). The English word is a doublet of deport and sport. The noun is derived from Middle English disport, desport (“activity providing amusement, pleasure or relaxation; entertainment, recreation; game, pastime, sport; pleasure derived from an activity; source of comfort; consolation, solace; conduct, deportment; customary behaviour, manner; act, activity; departure”), from Anglo-Norman disport, Old French desport, deport (“game, pastime, sport; pleasure, recreation; disport”), from desporter: see further above.
disport.example: What generous, ardent, imaginative soul has not a secret pleasure-place in which it disports?
disport.exampleSense: To amuse oneself divertingly or playfully; in particular, to cavort or gambol.

quip.o: From a shortening of earlier quippy, perhaps from Latin quippe (“indeed”), ultimately quid (“what”).
quip.example: He did not really mind being quipped; the city gentlemen made him used to that sort of thing.
quip.exampleSense: To taunt; to treat with quips.

anxiety.o: Borrowed from Latin ānxietās, from ānxius (“anxious, solicitous, distressed, troubled”), from angō (“to distress, trouble”), akin to Ancient Greek ἄγχω (ánkhō, “to choke”). Equivalent to anxious + -ety. See anger; angst.
anxiety.example: The inquest on keeper Davidson was duly held, and at the commencement seemed likely to cause Tony Palliser less anxiety than he had expected.
anxiety.exampleSense: An unpleasant state of mental uneasiness, nervousness, apprehension and obsession or concern about some uncertain event.

flora.example: Thirdly, I continue to attempt to interdigitate the taxa in our flora with taxa of the remainder of the world.
flora.exampleSense: Plants considered as a group, especially those of a particular country, region, time, etc.

hebetic.o: From Ancient Greek ἡβητικός (hēbētikós), equivalent to ἡβητ(ής) (hēbēt(ḗs)) (“adult”; ἡβη- (hēbē-), variant stem of ἡβᾶν (hēbân, “to reach puberty”), verbal derivative of ἥβη (hḗbē, “youth”) + -τής (-tḗs, agent suffix)) + ικός (ikós, “-ic”).

heretical.o: From Middle English, borrowed from Middle French eretical and from Medieval Latin haereticālis, from haereticus, equivalent to heretic + -al. See heretic.

heretic.o: From Middle English heretyk, heretike, from Old French eretique, from Medieval Latin or Ecclesiastical Latin haereticus, from Ancient Greek αἱρετικός (hairetikós, “able to choose, factious”), itself from Ancient Greek αἱρέω (hairéō, “to choose”).

tenuous.o: Irregularly formed from Latin tenuis (“thin, slight”) + -ous. Compare tenuious.
tenuous.example: The aether was thought to be of tenuous strands.

legitimacy.example: The legitimacy based on a revolutionary essence was replaced by legitimacy with an ultranational, ultra-Yugoslav character.
legitimacy.exampleSense: The quality or state of being legitimate or valid; validity.

curtail.o: Alteration of curtal, from Old French courtault (“which has been shortened”), itself from court (“short”) (from Latin curtus) + -ault
curtail.example: When the audience grew restless, the speaker curtailed her speech.
curtail.exampleSense: To shorten or abridge the duration of; to bring an end to; to truncate.

circumscription.example: The circumscription in the APG system of the family Malvaceae includes the former families Bombacaceae, Sterculiaceae and Tiliaceae.
circumscription.exampleSense: The definition of what does and does not belong to a given taxon, from a particular taxonomic viewpoint or taxonomic system.

restriction.o: From Middle English restriccioun, from Anglo-Norman restriction, Middle French restriction, and their source, Late Latin restrictiō, from Latin restringō. Morphologically restrict + -ion.
restriction.example: Echinorhagata is likewise supported by typical echinoderid autapomorphies, inclusive the number of trichoscalids that is reduced from 14 to 6; restriction of lateral accessory spines to females only; and an apparent restriction of the middorsal spines to appear only on segments 4 to 8.
restriction.exampleSense: The mechanism by which a cell degrades foreign DNA material.

limit.o:
noun: From Middle English limit, from Old French limit, from oblique stem of Latin līmes, līmit- (“a cross-path or balk between fields, hence a boundary, boundary line or wall, any path or road, border, limit”). Displaced native Old English ġemǣre. Doublet of limes.

verb: From Middle English limiten, from Old French limiter, from Latin līmitō (“to bound, limit, fix, determine”), from līmes; see noun.
limit.example: The sequence of reciprocals has zero as its limit.
limit.exampleSense: A value to which a sequence converges. Equivalently, the common value of the upper limit and the lower limit of a sequence: if the upper and lower limits are different, then the sequence has no limit (i.e., does not converge).

restrict.o: Borrowed from Latin restrictus, perfect passive participle of restringō (“draw back tightly; restrain, restrict”), from re- (“back, again”) + stringō (“press, tighten, compress”). Doublet of ristretto as an adjective.
restrict.example: After suffering diahrroea, the patient was restricted to a diet of rice, cold meat, and yoghurt.
restrict.exampleSense: To restrain within boundaries; to limit; to confine

mustang.o: Borrowed from Mexican Spanish mestengo, from Old Spanish mesteño (“feral animal”) or mestengo (“feral animal”).
mustang.example: Having ridden a distance of two or three miles, Garey slackened his pace, and put the mustang to a slow walk.
mustang.exampleSense: A small, hardy, naturalized (feral) horse of the North American west.

cyberattack.example: He also points out that if the US does come under cyberattack, we may be powerless to stop the attack.
cyberattack.exampleSense: An attack or intrusion by means of a computer network such as the Internet, often for the purpose of spying.

footbridge.o: From Middle English fot-brigge, equivalent to foot + bridge.
footbridge.example: The girder bridge at the head of the pass is used as a footbridge, and is roughly decked.
footbridge.exampleSense: A bridge over a road, railway, river, etc for pedestrians.

affine.example: Clearly every linear functional is affine, and every affine function is both convex and concave.
affine.exampleSense: Of or pertaining to a function expressible as f(⃑x)=A⃑x+⃑b (where A is a linear transformation and ⃑b is a constant), which, regarded as a transformation, maps parallel lines to parallel lines and finite points to finite points.

estate.o: From Middle English estat, from Anglo-Norman estat and Old French estat (French: état), from Latin status. Doublet of state and status.
estate.example: The three estates of feudal lords, clergy and royal officers met in separate chambers, and exercised an advisory role.
estate.exampleSense: A major social class or order of persons regarded collectively as part of the body politic of the country and formerly possessing distinct political rights (Estates of the realm).

phoney.o: Alternative form of phony. Of unknown origin. Perhaps an alteration of fawny (“gilt brass ring used by swindlers”) (1781), from Irish fáinne (“ring”).

rationalize.o: From French rationaliser. By surface analysis, rational + -ize.

glitch.o: Probably borrowed from Yiddish גליטש (glitsh), from German glitschig (“slippy”), from glitschen (“to slide, glide, slip”) + -ig (“-y”). Related to gleiten (“glide”). Cognate with French glisser (“to slip, slide, skid”). Popularized in the 1960s, by the US space program. Attested in 1962 by American astronaut John Glenn, in reference to spikes in electrical current.
glitch.example: My computer keeps glitching; every couple of hours it just reboots without warning.
glitch.exampleSense: To experience an unexpected, typically intermittent malfunction.

crutch.o: From Middle English crucche, from Old English cryċċ (“crutch, staff”), from Proto-West Germanic *krukkju, from Proto-Germanic *krukjō (“crutch, staff”), from Proto-Indo-European *grewg- (“wrinkle, bend”), from Proto-Indo-European *ger- (“to turn, bend”). Cognate with Scots curche, crutch (“crutch, stilts”), Dutch kruk (“crutch”), Low German krukke, Krück (“crutch”), German Krücke (“crutch”), Swedish krycka (“crutch”). Latin crucia, crucca, croccia, crocia (“crutch”), and its descendants are ultimately from the Germanic.
crutch.example: He walked on crutches for a month until the cast was removed from his leg.
crutch.exampleSense: A device to assist in motion as a cane, especially one that provides support under the arm to reduce weight on a leg.

tantamount.o: First attested in English in 1628. Either inherited from an unattested Middle English borrowing from Anglo-Norman tant amount, from amunter, from tant (“as much”) amonter (“to amount to”) or borrowed in the early 17th century from Italian tanto montare (“to amount to as much”).
tantamount.example: In this view, disagreement and treason are tantamount.
tantamount.exampleSense: Equivalent in meaning or effect; amounting to the same thing in practical terms, even if being technically distinct.

cavity.o: From Middle French cavité or Late Latin cavitās, from cav(i) (“hollow, excavated, concave”) + -tās (“-ity”, nominal suffix). First attested in the Mid-16th c.
cavity.example: Jim got two cavities filled at the dentist's office yesterday.
cavity.exampleSense: A small or large hole in a tooth caused by caries; often also a soft area adjacent to the hole also affected by caries.

hetero-.o: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ἕτερος (héteros, “other, another, different”).

remitter.o: From remit + -er (agent noun suffix), or in the legal sense + -er (action noun suffix).

herewith.o: From Middle English herwith or her-with, from late Old English herwiþ. By surface analysis, here + with.

allot.o: From Middle English allotten, from Old French aloter (Modern French allotir). à + lot. By surface analysis, al- + lot.
allot.example: Each candidate was allotted five minutes to make a presentation in front of the judges.
allot.exampleSense: To assign or designate as a task or for a purpose.

allotted.o: simple past and past participle of allot. From Middle English allotten, from Old French aloter (Modern French allotir). à + lot. By surface analysis, al- + lot.
allotted.example: The clock is ticking away the minutes in our allotted meeting time.
allotted.exampleSense: simple past and past participle of allot

lavender.o: From Middle English lavendre, from Anglo-Norman lavendre (French lavande), from Medieval Latin lavendula, possibly from Latin lividus (“bluish”), but influenced by lavō (“to wash”) due to the use of lavender in washing clothes.
lavender.example: Short shafts of dying sunlight mingled with the deepening grey, lavendering the horizon, and all nature seemed to hush as though waiting to welcome the night.
lavender.exampleSense: To decorate or perfume with lavender.

ram.o:
noun: From Middle English ram, rom, ramme, from Old English ramm (“ram”), from Proto-Germanic *rammaz (“ram”), possibly from *rammaz (“strong”). Cognate with Saterland Frisian Rom (“ram”), Dutch ram (“a male sheep”), German Ramm, Ramme (“ram”). Possibly akin also to Danish ram (“sharp; acrid; rank”), Swedish ram (“strong; perfect”), Faroese ramur (“strong; competent”), Icelandic rammur (“strong; sturdy”).

verb: From Middle English rammen, from the noun (see above). Compare Old High German rammen.

adj: Likely from Old Norse ramr, rammr (“strong, rank, bitter”), from Proto-Germanic *rammaz (“strong, overbearing; acrid, rank”), perhaps ultimately related to Etymology 1 above. Compare Scots ram (“a rank odour”). Compare also Middle English rammish (“rank, offensive in smell”).
ram.example: To build a sturdy fence, you have to ram the posts deep into the ground.
ram.exampleSense: To strike (something) hard, especially with an implement.

battering.o: present participle and gerund of batter. From Middle English batteren, batren, bateren, a frequentative of Middle English batten, baten (“to beat”), equivalent to bat + -er (frequentative suffix).
battering.example: That will prove a trickier test, the management having pinpointed Oleh Blokhin's side as "one of the favourites in the group", though they will confront an England team buoyed by this battering.

batterer.example: "This is serious," replied the potential fish batterer.

batter.o:
verb: From Middle English batteren, batren, bateren, a frequentative of Middle English batten, baten (“to beat”), equivalent to bat + -er (frequentative suffix).

noun: From Middle English bature, from Old French bateure (“the action of beating”), from batre (“to beat”). Doublet of batture.

verb: Unknown.

noun: From bat + -er (agent noun suffix).
batter.example: To the dismay of his mother, the boy put his finger into the pancake batter.
batter.exampleSense: A beaten mixture of flour and liquid (usually egg and milk), used for baking (e.g. pancakes, cake, or Yorkshire pudding) or to coat food (e.g. fish) prior to frying.

ensemble.example: Landscape gardening or landscape architecture is the art that seeks the production of the most beautiful landscape effects, ensembling the various objects of interest into a grand whole and harmonious unit.
ensemble.exampleSense: To put together in a coordinated whole.

enigmatic.o: From Latin aenigmaticus and French énigmatique, from Ancient Greek αἰνιγματικός (ainigmatikós); equivalent to enigma + -tic.
enigmatic.example: Serene, smiling, enigmatic, she faced him with no fear whatever showing in her dark eyes. The clear light of the bright autumn morning had no terrors for youth and health like hers.

signed.o: simple past and past participle of sign. From Middle English signe, sygne, syng, seine, sine, syne, from Old English seġn (“sign; mark; token”) and Old French signe, seing (“sign; mark; signature”); both from Latin signum (“a mark; sign; token”); root uncertain. Doublet of signum and signal. Partially displaced native token.
signed.example: The signed check could be cashed.

abasement.o: From Middle English abaissement, from Middle French abaissement (“astonishment”). Equivalent to abase + -ment. Compare French abaissement.

self-abasement.example: Self-abasement is a state of excessive, unwarranted humility self-inflicted humiliation and degradation.

blame.o:
noun: From Middle English blame, borrowed from Old French blame, blasme, produced from the verb blasmer, which in turn is derived from Late Latin blastēmāre, variant of blasphēmāre, from Ancient Greek βλασφημέω (blasphēméō). Doublet of blaspheme. Displaced native Old English tǣling (“blame”) and tǣlan (“to blame”).

verb: From Middle English blamen, borrowed from Old French blasmer, from Late Latin blasphēmāre (“to reproach, to revile”), from Ancient Greek βλασφημέω (blasphēméō). Compare blaspheme, a doublet. Overtook common use from the native wite (“to blame, accuse, reproach, suspect”) (from Middle English wīten, from Old English wītan).
blame.example: After what happened at the wedding, I wouldn't blame you if you never spoke to them again.
blame.exampleSense: To assert or consider that someone is the cause of something negative; to place blame; to attribute responsibility (for something negative or for doing something negative).

piss off.example: It pisses people off that I am thin and I don't make any effort.

pissed off.o: simple past and past participle of piss. From Middle English pisse (noun) and pissen (verb), from Old French pissier, possibly from Vulgar Latin *pīssiāre, probably of imitative origin. Compare Old Norse pissa (“to urinate, piss”). Displaced Old English miċġe (“urine”) and mīgan (“to urinate”).

piss.o: From Middle English pisse (noun) and pissen (verb), from Old French pissier, possibly from Vulgar Latin *pīssiāre, probably of imitative origin. Compare Old Norse pissa (“to urinate, piss”). Displaced Old English miċġe (“urine”) and mīgan (“to urinate”).
piss.example: Monster, I do smell all horse-piss; at which my nose is in great indignation.

annoyed.o: simple past and past participle of annoy. From Middle English anoyen, from Old French anoier (“to bother, disturb”), from Late Latin inodiāre (“to make loathsome”), derived from Latin odium (“loathing, hatred”). Displaced native Old English dreċċan, gremman.

superficial.o: Borrowing from Late Latin superficiālis (“of or belonging to the surface”), from superficiēs (“top, surface”) + -ālis (“-al”, adjectival suffix).
superficial.example: Secondly, I continue to base my concepts on intensive study of a limited suite of collections, rather than superficial study of every packet that comes to hand.
superficial.exampleSense: Not thorough, deep, or complete; concerned only with the obvious or apparent.

weirdo.o: From weird + -o (“person with characteristic”). First attested in the early 1950s, in American English. The similar word weirdie (“odd, unconventional person”) is attested from earlier, in 1887; in Scottish English.
weirdo.example: What's going on in this weirdo town?

denude.o: From Middle French dénuder, from Latin dēnūdāre, from dē- + nūdus (“bare”).
denude.example: Widespread deforestation has led to lands being denuded.
denude.exampleSense: To divest of all covering; to make bare or naked; to strip.

nude.o: Entered English 1493 as a legal term, meaning "unsupported, not formally attested," from Middle English nud, from Latin nūdus (“naked, bare”).
nude.example: Michelangelo's David is a well-known standing male nude; Michelangelo also created several other nudes.
nude.exampleSense: A painting, sculpture, photograph or other artwork or mass-media-reproduced image depicting one or more human figure(s) in a state of near or total undress.

favour.example: I need a favour. Could you lend me £5 until tomorrow, please?

extinctive.example: Even with mild degrees of anxiety the ineffectiveness of the extinctive mechanism is striking.
extinctive.exampleSense: Tending or serving to extinguish, or make extinct.

burn out.example: After six months of twelve-hour workdays, most people just burn out and quit.
burn out.exampleSense: To tire due to overwork; to overwork to their limit.

extinguish.o: Borrowed from Latin extinguo (“to put out (what is burning), quench, extinguish, deprive of life, destroy, abolish”), from ex (“out”) + stinguere (“to put out, quench, extinguish”). Doublet of extinct.
extinguish.example: Many patients can extinguish their phobias after a few months of treatment.
extinguish.exampleSense: To put an end to (something) completely; to annihilate, to destroy. To bring about the extinction of (a conditioned reflex).

die out.example: Shepard: I thought you always needed another species to serve as one of the parents.

go out.example: They were going to stay in and read, but instead went out shopping.
go out.exampleSense: To leave one's abode to go to public places, especially for recreation or entertainment.

countrywoman.example: (to Prince Philip) You don't think I would have preferred to grow up out of the spotlight? Away from court, away from the scrutiny and the visibility? A simpler life, happier life, as a wife, a mother, an ordinary English countrywoman?
countrywoman.exampleSense: A woman who lives in the country (countryside) or has retained country ways.

brethren.o: From Early Modern English brethren, plural of brother, from Middle English brethren, from Middle English brethere, brether + -en (plural ending). Ultimately from Old English brōþor, brōþru (“brothers, brethren”), influenced by Old English brēþer, dative singular of brōþor (“brother”). Equivalent to brother + -en (plural ending). Compare German Brüder (“brothers, brethren”). More at brother. The vowel change (from o to e) is called umlaut.
brethren.example: The principle still sounds good, but our astronomical knowledge is limited, and we haven't yet discovered any such brethren solar systems.
brethren.exampleSense: Of or akin to; related; like

disunity.example: Others support either the North or the Free State; and so where there is disunity there is dissension.
disunity.exampleSense: The lack of unity or cohesion.

cohesion.o: Attested from the late 17th century, borrowed from French cohésion, from Latin cohaesiō, cohaesiōnem.
cohesion.example: Unit cohesion is important in the military.
cohesion.exampleSense: State of cohering, or of working together.

solidarity.o: By surface analysis, from English solidary + -ity, or from French solidarité (“solidarity”), from solidaire (“characterized by solidarity”), from Latin solidum (“whole sum”), neuter of solidus (“solid”).
solidarity.example: A long time union member himself, Phil showed solidarity with the picketing grocery store workers by shopping at a competing, unionized store.
solidarity.exampleSense: A bond of unity or agreement between individuals, united around a common goal or against a common enemy, such as the unifying principle that defines the labor movement; mutual support within a group.

unity.o: From Middle English unite, from Anglo-Norman, Old French unité, from Latin ūnitās, from ūnus (“one”) + noun of state suffix -itās, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *óynos (“one, single”), hence distantly related to one and an. By surface analysis, unite + -y. Displaced native Old English ānnes (literally “oneness”).
unity.example: Alan Pardew's current squad has been put together with a relatively low budget but the resolve and unity within the team is priceless.
unity.exampleSense: Oneness; the state or fact of being one undivided entity.

unite.o: From Middle English uniten, from Latin ūnītus, perfect passive participle of ūniō.
unite.example: I hope this song can unite people from all different cultures.

union.o: From Middle English unyoun, from Old French union, from Late Latin ūniō, ūniōnem (“oneness, unity”), from Latin ūnus (“one”). Doublet of unio.
union.example: Actors have to be union to get work here.
union.exampleSense: Belonging to, represented by, or otherwise pertaining to a labour union.

toggle joint.example: A toggle joint, which used a lever system to multiply power, replaced the screw mechanism for forcing down the impression-forming platen.
toggle joint.exampleSense: A mechanical linkage of the type of an elbow or knee joint, consisting of two bars so connected that they may be brought quite or nearly into a straight line, and made to produce great endwise pressure when brought into this position.

pin.o: From Middle English pinne, from Old English pinn (“pin, peg, bolt”), from Proto-Germanic *pinnaz, *pinnō, *pint- (“protruding point, peak, peg, pin, nail”), from Proto-Indo-European *bend- (“protruding object, pointed peg, nail, edge”). Related to pen (“enclosure”). Cognate with Dutch pin (“peg, pin”), Low German pin, pinne (“pin, point, nail, peg”), German Pinn, Pinne (“pin, tack, peg”), Bavarian Pfonzer, Pfunzer (“sharpened point”), Danish pind (“pin, pointed stick”), Norwegian pinn (“stick”), Swedish pinne (“peg, rod, stick”), Icelandic pinni (“pin”). More at pintle. No relation to classical Latin pinna (“fin, flipper, wing-like appendage, wing, feather”), which was extended to mean "ridge, peak, point" (compare pinnacle), and often confused with Latin penna (“wing, feather”). More at feather and pen (Etymology 3).
pin.example: Pull the pin out of the grenade before throwing it at the enemy.
pin.exampleSense: A cylinder often of wood or metal used to fasten or as a bearing between two parts.

archfiend.o: From arch- + fiend. Compare German Erzfeind, Dutch aartsvijand.
archfiend.example: Seven chief demons, seven archfiends, aid Ahriman in his struggle against the forces of light.
archfiend.exampleSense: A chief fiend (devil, demon or monster).

fiend.o: From Middle English fend, feend (“enemy; demon”), from Old English fēond (“enemy”), Proto-West Germanic *fijand, from Proto-Germanic *fijandz. Cognates Cognate with Scots fient (“fiend”), Saterland Frisian Fäind (“enemy, fiend, foe”), Cimbrian faint (“enemy, fiend”), Dutch vijand (“enemy”), German Feind (“enemy, fiend, foe”), Vilamovian faeind, fajnd (“enemy”), Yiddish פֿײַנד (faynd), פֿײַנט (faynt, “enemy”), Danish fjende (“adversary, enemy, foe”), Icelandic fjandi (“enemy; fiend, demon, devil”), Norwegian Bokmål, Norwegian Nynorsk and Swedish fiende (“enemy”), Old Norse fjándi (“enemy; devil”), Gothic 𐍆𐌹𐌰𐌽𐌳𐍃 (fiands), 𐍆𐌹𐌾𐌰𐌽𐌳𐍃 (fijands, “enemy, foe”). The Old Norse and Gothic terms are present participles of the corresponding verbs fjá/𐍆𐌹𐌾𐌰𐌽 (fijan, “to hate”), from Proto-Indo-European *peh₁- (“to hate”) (compare Sanskrit पीयति (pī́yati, “(he) reviles”)).
fiend.example: I am back in San Francisco at the Clift Hotel, fiending for my fix.
fiend.exampleSense: To yearn; to be desperate (for something, especially drugs).

deluge.o: From Middle English deluge, from Old French deluge, alteration of earlier deluvie, from Latin dīluvium, from dīluō (“wash away”). Doublet of diluvium.
deluge.example: Some areas were deluged with a month's worth of rain in 24 hours.

deletion.o: From Latin dēlētiōnem (“destruction, effacement”), from the past-participle stem of dēlēre (“to blot out, destroy, efface”). Equivalent to delete + -ion.

decisional.example: The procedures should also make plain that a decisional official, whether or not challenged, may voluntarily abstain from participating in a particular proceeding.
decisional.exampleSense: Having the power or authority to make decisions.

delusional.example: You're delusional if you think that plan will work.
delusional.exampleSense: Suffering from delusions; having false or faulty beliefs.

ethos.o: From Ancient Greek ἦθος (êthos, “character; custom, habit”). Cognate to Sanskrit स्वधा (svadhā́, “habit, custom”).
ethos.example: To slip past censors, Chinese bloggers have become masters of comic subterfuge, cloaking their messages in protective layers of irony and satire. This is not a new concept, but it has erupted so powerfully that it now defines the ethos of the Internet in China.
ethos.exampleSense: The character or fundamental values of a person, people, culture, or movement.

stereotyping.o: present participle and gerund of stereotype. Borrowed from French stéréotype (adjective), equivalent to stereo- + type. Printing sense is from 1817; the “conventional, formulaic, and oversimplified conception, opinion, or image” sense is recorded from 1922 in Walter Lippmann’s book Public Opinion.

stereotypically.example: It makes up an estimated 73 percent of the U.S. food supply, and contains stereotypically “unhealthy” products like sodas, candies and hot dogs as well as seemingly “healthy” ones like whole grain breads, breakfast cereals, flavored yogurts and plant milks.
stereotypically.exampleSense: In a stereotypical manner or way.

stereotypical.example: Tics are brief, stereotypical behaviors that are initiated by an unconscious urge that can be temporarily suppressed.

reaction.o: Inherited from Middle English reaccion, from Old French reaction, from Latin reāctiō, from the verb reagō, from re- (“again”) + agō (“to act”); more at re-, action; equivalent to react + -ion.
reaction.example: When I last tried to eat strawberries I had a terrible allergic reaction.
reaction.exampleSense: An action or statement in response to a stimulus or other event.

reactor.example: It limits the rights of nonweapon countries to develop an export business in civilian reactor technology.
reactor.exampleSense: A device which uses atomic energy to produce heat.

react.o: From re- + act. Piecewise doublet of redact.
react.example: Every body reacts on the body that impels it from its natural state.
react.exampleSense: To return an impulse or impression; to resist the action of another body by an opposite force

racist.o: 1932 (noun), 1938 (adjective). Formed from racism (1928), paralleling French raciste (1892). Replaced older racialist (1910). Equivalent to race + -ist.
racist.example: Narrators demonstrated resistance coping techniques through direct confrontation with aggressors, such as racists, sexists, homophobes, elitists, and misogynoirists.
racist.exampleSense: A person who believes in or supports racism; a person who believes that a particular race is superior to others, or who discriminates against other races.

antiracism.example: Switzerland’s antiracism legislation has previously been applied to Holocaust denial.
antiracism.exampleSense: Acting to combat or prevent racism.

ostracism.o: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ὀστρακισμός (ostrakismós, “banishment by means of voting with pot shards”), from ὀστρακίζω (ostrakízō, “ostracize”) + -ισμός (-ismós, “-ism”), from ὄστρακον (óstrakon, “clay pot”).
ostracism.example: Witnesse the Ostracisme amongst the Athenians, and the Petalisme among the Siracusans.
ostracism.exampleSense: In ancient Athens (and some other cities), the temporary banishment by popular vote of a citizen considered dangerous to the state.

racism.o: Borrowed from French racisme, equivalent to race + -ism.
racism.example: It is altogether inaccurate to suggest that Europe is being indoctrinated with Fascism or Racism.
racism.exampleSense: The belief that there are distinct human races with inherent differences which determine their abilities, and generally that some are superior and others inferior.

amigo.o: Borrowed from Spanish amigo (“friend”), from Latin amīcus (“friend”), derived from amāre (“to love”). Compare French ami, Italian amico, Portuguese amigo and Romanian amic. Doublet of amicus.
amigo.example: I don’t remember electing you dictator, amigo.

ashore.o: From a- + shore; see also onshore.
ashore.example: Swum ashore, man, like a duck. I can swim like a duck, I'll be sworn.

speed up.example: You shouldn't speed up your car when you go around corners.
speed up.exampleSense: To accelerate (something): to increase its speed, to make it go faster.

closure.o: From Middle English closure, from Old French closure, from Late Latin clausura, from Latin claudere (“to close”); see clausure and cloture (etymological doublets) and close.
closure.example: At any time they could have stopped discussion by closuring amendments and by closuring the clause under discussion.
closure.exampleSense: To end the parliamentary debate on (an issue) by closure.

budget.o: Recorded since 1432 as Middle English bogett, bouget, bowgette (“leather pouch”), borrowed from Old French bougette, the diminutive of bouge (“leather bag, wallet”) (also the root of bulge), itself from Late Latin bulga (“leather bag, bellow”), which derives from Gaulish *bolgā (compare Old Irish bolg (“bag”), Breton bolc’h (“flax pod”)), a common root with the Germanic family (compare Dutch balg (“bellows”)), from the Proto-Indo-European *bʰelǵʰ-. More at belly.
budget.example: We're on a budget, so we can't afford to eat at that restaurant.
budget.exampleSense: The amount of money or resources earmarked for a particular institution, activity or timeframe. A relatively small amount of available money.

realize.o: PIE word *reh₁ís Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *(H)reh₁-der. Proto-Indo-European *(H)reh₁ís Proto-Italic *reis Classical Latin rēs Proto-Indo-European *h₂el-der.? Proto-Italic *-ālis Latin -ālis Late Latin reālisder. Old French reelbor. Middle English real English real Proto-Indo-European *-id- Proto-Indo-European *-yéti Proto-Indo-European *-idyéti Proto-Hellenic *-íďďō Ancient Greek -ῐ́ζω (-ĭ́zō)bor. Late Latin -izōder. Middle French -iserbor. Middle English -isen English -ize English realize From real (adjective) + -ize (suffix denoting the making of what is indicated by the word it is attached to), possibly modelled after French réaliser, Middle French réaliser (“to make real; to convert (something) into assets or cash”), from real (“actual, real”) + -iser (suffix denoting the making of what is indicated by the word it is attached to). Real is derived from Old French reel, from Latin reālis (“actual, real”), from rēs (“deed; event; matter; thing”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *reh₁ís (“goods; wealth”)) + -ālis (suffix forming adjectives of relationship).
realize.example: The objectives of the project were never fully realized.
realize.exampleSense: To convert (something imaginary or planned, as a goal or idea) into reality; to bring into real existence, to make real.

acquire.o: From Middle English acqueren, from Old French aquerre, from Latin acquirō; ad- + quaerō (“to seek for”). See quest.
acquire.example: No virtue is acquired in an instant, but by degrees, step by step.
acquire.exampleSense: To gain, usually by one's own exertions; to get as one's own.

vendor.o: Borrowed from Anglo-Norman vendor (Old French vendeor), from Latin venditor (“seller”), from vendere (“to sell, cry up for sale, praise”), contraction of venundare, venumdare, also, as originally, two words venum dare (“to sell”), from venum (“sale, price”) + dare (“to give”).
vendor.example: Strawberry Perl contains vendored copies of some CPAN modules, designed to allow them to run on Windows.
vendor.exampleSense: As the software vendor, to bundle one's own, possibly modified version of dependencies with a standard program.

iteration.o: From Latin iterātiō, from iterō. Morphologically iterate + -ion.
iteration.example: The code calculates the appropriate value at each iteration.
iteration.exampleSense: A single repetition of the code within such a repetitive process.

verification.o: From Middle French verification (modern French vérification) or its etymon Medieval Latin vērificātiō. By surface analysis, verificate + -ion.
verification.example: The detective needs verification of your whereabouts last night.

i.e..o: From Latin i. e., an abbreviation of id est (“that is”).
i.e..example: While the final episode was made, the show itself was immediately cancelled after the penultimate episode i.e. the final episode never aired.
i.e..exampleSense: That is, namely, in other words, that is to say.

zed.o: From Middle English zed, zedde, zede, from Old French zede, from Late Latin zeta, from Ancient Greek ζῆτα (zêta), from Hebrew ז (zayin) with influence from βῆτα (bêta), ἦτα (êta) and θῆτα (thêta). The letter had a rare usage in Old English, such as in bezt, where it represented "ts" (compare the German, Italian, and Finnish pronunciation of Z). For the sleep sense, see zzz. The zombie sense comes from the initial letter. Doublet of zeta. Cognate to Spanish zeta, German Zett, French zède, Italian zeta, and perhaps Portuguese zê.
zed.example: Zzz...With all those ʻzedsʼ I'll be sending you to sleep.
zed.exampleSense: The name of the Latin-script letter Z/z.

respectably.example: A respectably attired solicitor came to read the will.
respectably.exampleSense: In a respectable manner; so as to gain respect.

respectable.example: His accomplishments, morals, loyalty, and stature make him a respectable person.

respecting.o: present participle and gerund of respect. From Middle English respect, from Old French respect, also respit (“respect, regard, consideration”), from Latin respectus (“a looking at, regard, respect”), perfect passive participle of respiciō (“look at, look back upon, respect”), from re- (“back”) + speciō (“to see”). Doublet of respite.
respecting.example: I wrote to him respecting the proposed lawsuit.

resentful.example: Is it serving Hashem to be machmir and resentful, rather than adhere to the letter of the law and be relaxed and happy?
resentful.exampleSense: Harboring resentment, full of resentment, at a given moment.

enfold.o: Alteration of earlier infold, from Middle English infolden, equivalent to en- + fold.

exfoliate.o: From Late Latin exfoliō (“to strip of leaves”), from ex- (“out of”) + folium (“leaf”); compare effoliate and French exfolier.

vibration.o: From French vibration, from Latin vibrātiō (“a shaking or brandishing”), from vibrō (“shake, vibrate”); see vibrate. Morphologically vibrate + -ion.
vibration.example: The procession circled the district, symbolically purging the area of its “evil,” which paraders described as the “bad vibrations” from tourists and youths in Hippie clothes not living up to Hippie standards.
vibration.exampleSense: An instinctively sensed emotional aura or atmosphere.

decoherence.o: First attested 1902 (OED) in the electrical engineering sense "the resetting of a coherer." From decohere (also 1902) + -ence, representing the verbal noun (compare decohesion, decoherency). The quantum mechanics concept was introduced in 1970 by German physicist H. Dieter Zeh, writing in the journal Foundations of Physics.
decoherence.example: A detailed investigation of decoherence during gating due to a bosonic environment was performed in the original work of Loss and DiVincenzo. Since then, there have been many studies of leakage and decoherence in the context of the quantum-dot quantum computing proposal.
decoherence.exampleSense: Loss of quantum coherence (phase relation between the quantum states of particles) in a physical system as it interacts with its environment.

upswing.example: Newspapers reported an upswing in the company's sales last month.
upswing.exampleSense: An upward trend or an increase in activity.

synapse.o: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek σύναψις (súnapsis, “conjunction”), from συνάπτω (sunáptō, “to clasp”). Introduced by neurophysiologist Charles Scott Sherrington.

megawatt.example: SAN FRANCISCO, July 23 — Pacific Gas & Electric, Northern California’s major utility, is announcing a commitment on Wednesday to purchase 550 megawatts of solar power to be generated by troughlike arrays of mirrors spread over nine square miles in the Mojave Desert.
megawatt.exampleSense: One million (1 000 000) watts, abbreviated as MW.

neuroleptic.o: Borrowed from French neuroleptique, coined by Jean Delay and Pierre Deniker in 1955. Constructed from Ancient Greek νεῦρον (neûron, “neuron”) and λῆψις (lêpsis), noun form of λαμβάνω (lambánō, “take hold of”).
neuroleptic.example: The mechanisms underlying the appearance of the parkinson-like symptoms during neuroleptic treatments are not ascertained.

bulky.o: From Middle English bulki, boulky, equivalent to bulk + -y.
bulky.example: Needless to say, one's seat must be booked in advance and a platoon of urbane officials, one to each door of the train, awaits passengers to usher them to their seats and relieve them of their bulkier baggage.
bulky.exampleSense: Being large in size, mass, or volume; big, fat or muscular

crossbar.o: From Middle English crose bar, equivalent to cross- + bar.
crossbar.example: The effervescent Suarez then went close again as he worked space for a shot after a mazy run but could not keep his close-range shot below the crossbar.
crossbar.exampleSense: The top of the goal structure.

tabular.o: From Late Latin tabulāris. By surface analysis, tabula + -ar, or, by surface analysis, table + -ar. Compare fabular.

cooperate.o: Originated 1595–1605 from Late Latin cooperātus, perfect passive participle of cooperor (“to work with”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix) for more. Equivalent to co- + operate. Displaced native Old English efnwyrċan.
cooperate.example: In polling by the Pew Research Center in November 2008, fully half the respondents thought the two parties would cooperate more in the coming year, versus only 36 percent who thought the climate would grow more adversarial.
cooperate.exampleSense: To work or act together, especially for a common purpose or benefit.

times.o: Multiplication sense from the idea that something is repeated or added together a given number of times.
times.example: Modern times are so very different from the past.
times.exampleSense: The circumstances of a certain time.

time.o: From Middle English tyme, time, from Old English tīma (“time, period, space of time, season, lifetime, fixed time, favorable time, opportunity”), from Proto-West Germanic *tīmō, from Proto-Germanic *tīmô (“time”), from Proto-Indo-European *deh₂imō, from Proto-Indo-European *deh₂y- (“to divide”). Related to tide. Not related to Latin tempus. Cognates * Scots tym, tyme (“time”) * Alemannic German Zimen, Zīmmän (“time, time of the year, opportune time, opportunity”) * Danish time (“hour, lesson”) * Elfdalian taime (“hour”) * Faroese tími (“hour, lesson, time”) * Icelandic tími (“time, season”) * Norwegian time (“lesson, hour”) * Swedish timma, timme (“hour”).
time.example: Let's synchronize our watches so we're not on different time.
time.exampleSense: The measurement under some system of region of day or moment.

match.o:
noun: From Middle English macche, mecche, from Old English mæċċa, ġemæċċa (“companion, mate, wife, one suited to another”), from Proto-West Germanic *makkjō, *gamakkjō (“partner, equal”), from Proto-Germanic *makô, from Proto-Indo-European *mag- (“to knead, work”). Compare Danish mage (“mate”), Icelandic maki (“spouse”).

verb: From Middle English macchen (“to marry; be paired with”), from the noun (see above).

noun: From Middle English macche, mecche (“wick (of a candle)”), from Old French mesche, meische, from Vulgar Latin micca (compare Catalan metxa, Spanish mecha, Italian miccia), which in turn is probably from Latin myxa (“nozzle, curved part of a lamp”), from Ancient Greek μύξα (múxa, “lamp wick”).
match.example: He struck a match and lit his cigarette.
match.exampleSense: A device made of wood or paper, at the tip coated with chemicals that ignite with the friction of being dragged (struck) against a rough dry surface.

donor.o: From Middle English donoure, donour; from Anglo-Norman donour, from Old French doneur (See French donneur).
donor.example: The charity raised $2,000 from various donors.

disequilibrium.example: The world of the angelic hierarchy was an evolutionary stream of light in a steady-state, but the creation of Adam from matter disturbs that primordial steady-state; it generates the creative disequilibrium necessary for change, transformation, and evolution.
disequilibrium.exampleSense: The loss of equilibrium or stability, especially due to an imbalance of forces.

equilibrium.o: From Latin aequilībrium, from equal + lībra (“balance”).

valency.o: From Late Latin valentia and Latin valentia (“bodily strength; health; vigour”) + English -y (suffix forming abstract nouns denoting a condition, quality, or state). Valentia is derived from valēns (“healthy, strong, vigorous”) + -ia (suffix forming feminine abstract nouns); while valēns is the present active participle of valeō (“to be healthy, sound, or well; to be strong; to have influence or power, etc.”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂welh₁- (“to rule; powerful, strong”). Sense 1 (“combining capacity of an atom”) and sense 3 (“number of arguments a verb can have”) are possibly from valence + -y.
valency.example: Some etymons appear to have greater valency than others when it comes to the formation of portmanteau words.
valency.exampleSense: Alternative form of valence (“the combining capacity of an atom, functional group, or radical determined by the number of atoms of hydrogen with which it will unite, or the number of electrons that it will gain, lose, or share when it combines with other atoms, etc.”) The capacity of something to combine with other things, as for example the capability of a vaccine as measured by the number of pathogen serotypes that it can counteract.

valence.o:
noun: Etymology 1, noun sense 1.1 (“combining capacity of an atom”) and etymology 1, noun sense 3 (“one-dimensional value assigned by a person to an object, situation, or state”) are borrowed from German Valenz + English -ence (suffix meaning ‘having the condition or state of’). Valenz is a clipping of Quantivalenz (“(archaic) valence in chemistry”), from English quantivalence, from Latin quantus (“how much”) + English -i- (interfix inserted between morphemes of Latin origin for ease of pronunciation) + Latin valentia (“bodily strength; health; vigour”) (whence Late Middle English valence (“medicinal preparation made from plants”); ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂welh₁- (“to rule; powerful, strong”)). Quantivalence was coined by F. O. Ward who communicated it to the German chemist August Wilhelm von Hofmann (1818–1892), leading him to coin the German word Quantivalenz. Doublet of value. Etymology 1, noun sense 2 (“number of arguments a verb can have”) was formed by analogy to the use of the word in chemistry: see above.

noun: A variant of valance.
valence.example: In this assignment you will analyze each of the following sentences and determine the valence of the highlighted verb.
valence.exampleSense: The number of arguments that a verb can have, including its subject, ranging from zero to three or, less commonly, four.

partition.o: Recorded c.1430, "division into shares, distinction," from Middle English particioun, from Old French particion (modern partition), from Latin partitio, partitionem (“division, portion”), from partitus, the past participle of partire (“to split (up), part(ition)”).
partition.example: And good from bad find no partition.
partition.exampleSense: An action which divides a thing into parts, or separates one thing from another.

stay.o:
verb: From Middle English steyen, staien, from Old French estayer, estaier (“to fix, prop up, support, stay”), from estaye, estaie (“a prop, stay”), from Middle Dutch staeye (“a prop, stay”), a contracted form of staede, stade (“a prop, stay, help, aid”) (compare Middle Dutch staeyen, staeden (“to make firm, stay, support, hold still, stabilise”)), from Proto-West Germanic *stadi (“a site, place, location, standing”), from Proto-Germanic *stadiz (“a standing, place”), from Proto-Indo-European *stéh₂tis (“standing”). Influenced by Old English stæġ ("a stay, rope"; see below). Cognate with Old English stede (“a place, spot, locality, fixed position, station, site, standing, status, position of a moving body, stopping, standing still, stability, fixity, firmness, steadfastness”), Swedish stödja (“to prop, support, brace, hold up, bolster”), Icelandic stöðug (“continuous, stable”). More at stead, steady. Sense of "remain, continue" may be due to later influence from Old French ester, esteir (“to stand, be, continue, remain”), from Latin stāre (“stand”), from the same Proto-Indo-European root above; however, derivation from this root is untenable based on linguistic and historical grounds. An alternative etymology derives Old French estaye, estaie, from Frankish *stakā, *stakō (“stake, post”), from Proto-Germanic *stakô (“stake, bar, stick, pole”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)teg- (“rod, pole, stick”), making it cognate with Old English staca (“pin, stake”), Old English stician (“to stick, be placed, lie, remain fixed”). Cognate with Albanian shtagë (“a long stick, a pole”). More at stake, stick.

noun: From Middle English stay, from Old French estaye, estaie (“a prop, a stay”), from Middle Dutch staeye (“a prop, stay”), a contracted form of staede, stade ("a prop, stay, help, aid"; compare Middle Dutch staeyen, staeden (“to make firm, stay, support, hold still, stabilise”)), from Old Dutch *stad (“a site, place, location, standing”), from Proto-Germanic *stadiz (“a standing, place”), from Proto-Indo-European *steh₂- (“to stand”). See above.

noun: From Middle English stay, from Old English stæġ (“stay, a rope supporting a mast”), from Proto-West Germanic *stag, from Proto-Germanic *stagą (“stay, rope”), from Proto-Indo-European *stek-, *stāk- (“stand, pole”), from Proto-Indo-European *steh₂- (“to stand”). Cognate with Dutch stag (“stay”), German Stag (“stay”), Swedish stag (“stay”), Icelandic stag (“stay”).

adj: From Middle English *steȝe, from Old English *stǣġe, an apocopated variant of stǣġel (“steep, abrupt”), from Proto-West Germanic *staigil (“steep”), see sty.
stay.example: The engineer insisted on using stays for the scaffolding.
stay.exampleSense: A guy, rope, or wire supporting or stabilizing a platform, such as a bridge, a pole, such as a tentpole, the mast of a derrick, or other structural element.

mainstay.o: From Middle English main stai, equivalent to main + stay (“rope”).
mainstay.example: Like show dogs, dog actors became a mainstay in European and American contexts from the early nineteenth century with the convergence of public sentiment for dogs and popular interest in training them.
mainstay.exampleSense: Someone or something that can be depended on to make a regular contribution.

textbook.example: Well done everyone, the tree fell exactly where we planned. That was textbook.
textbook.exampleSense: Done exactly correctly, in an exemplary way that might be described in a textbook.

supplementary.example: Thus, leucine is already being seen as a pharmaconutrient of great relevance for the supplementary feeding of malnourished and frail elderly and for specific subpopulations.
supplementary.exampleSense: Additional; added to supply what is wanted.

panoptic.example: Divested of egotistic obsession, an ordinary human being could achieve the panoptic vision of a sage.

tortious.o: Inherited from Middle English torcious, from Anglo-Norman torcious. By surface analysis, tort + -ious.

tort.o:
