noun: From Middle English tort (“(uncountable) wrong; (countable) an injury, a wrong”), from Old French tort (“misdeed, wrong”) (modern French tort (“an error, wrong; a fault”)), from Medieval Latin tortum (“injustice, wrong”), a noun use of a neuter singular participle form of Latin tortus (“crooked; twisted”), the perfect passive participle of torqueō (“to bend or twist awry, distort”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *terkʷ- (“to spin; to turn”). Cognates * Galician torto (“(adjective) bent; crooked; twisted; (noun, archaic) harm, offence; injustice, wrong, tort”) * Italian torto (“(adjective) bent; crooked; twisted; (noun, archaic) injustice, wrong”) * Norwegian Bokmål tort (dated, now only in fixed expressions) * Norwegian Nynorsk tort (dated, now only in fixed expressions) * Occitan tort * Old French tort (modern French tort) * Portuguese torto (“(adjective) bent; crooked; twisted; (noun, archaic) harm, offence; injustice, wrong”) * Spanish tuerto (“injury, offence”)

adj: From Middle English tort, torte (“contorted, crooked; twisted”), from Old French tort, torte (“crooked; twisted”), or from its etymon Latin tortus (“crooked; twisted”): see further at etymology

adj: A variant of tart.

adj: A variant of taut.

noun: Clipping of tortoise.

noun: Clipping of tortoiseshell.

repent.o:
verb: From Middle English repenten, from Old French repentir, from Vulgar Latin *repaenitīre, from Late Latin paenitīre, from Classical Latin paenitēre. Compare Modern French repentir.

adj: From Latin rēpēns, present participle of rēpō (“to creep”).
repent.example: I tell you, Nay: but, except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish.
repent.exampleSense: To be sorry for sin as morally evil, and to seek forgiveness; to cease to practice sin and to love.

fury.o:
noun: From Middle English furie, from Old French furie, from Latin furia (“rage”).

noun: Borrowed from Latin fur (“thief”).
fury.example: The building of the railway in this notable beauty spot roused the great Victorian writer John Ruskin to fury.

debater.exampleSense: One who debates or participates in a debate; one who argues.

hypersonic.o: From hyper- + sonic. Doublet of supersonic.
hypersonic.example: He said there was worry among intelligence and military officials that China or Russia could be experimenting with hypersonic technology.
hypersonic.exampleSense: Equal to, or greater than, or capable of achieving, five times the speed of sound.

hypergolic.o: From Ancient Greek ὑπέρ (hupér) + ἔργον (érgon, “work”) + -ol + -ic, after the model of German Hypergol and hypergolisch. Equivalent to hypergol + -ic.
hypergolic.example: The chemical reaction range of hypergolic mixtures varies from slow and barely visible to an instantaneous and highly visible explosive force.

hyperbolic.o:
adj: From Latin hyperbolic(us), from Ancient Greek ὑπερβολικός (huperbolikós). First attested in the 15th century. By surface analysis, hyperbol(e) + -ic.

adj: First attested in 1676. By surface analysis, hyperbol(a) + -ic.
hyperbolic.example: In this configuration the on-axis image is produced at the real hyperbolic focus (fₛ₂) but off-axis performance suffers.
hyperbolic.exampleSense: Of or pertaining to a hyperbola.

hypertrophy.o: From French hypertrophie, from Ancient Greek ὑπέρ (hupér, “over, excessive”) + τροφή (trophḗ, “nourishment”), equivalent to hyper- + -trophy.
hypertrophy.example: Ectopic chondrocyte hypertrophy has been demonstrated in OA, suggesting that the pathogenetical process involves a recapitulation of endochondral ossification [ 11 – 13 ].
hypertrophy.exampleSense: An increase in the size of an organ or tissue due to the enlargement of its individual cells.

atrophy.o: Borrowed from French atrophie, from Latin atrophia, from Ancient Greek ἀτροφία (atrophía, “a wasting away”), from ἄτροφος (átrophos, “ill-fed, un-nourished”), from ἀ- (a-, “not”) + τροφή (trophḗ, “nourishment”), from τρέφω (tréphō, “to fatten”). Equivalent to a- + -trophy.
atrophy.example: Boy. I love summer vacation. I can feel my brain beginning to atrophy already.

resettlement.example: The domestic resettlement infrastructure is also under strain after years of low admissions under the Trump administration that resulted in agencies shuttering offices and losing staff.
resettlement.exampleSense: The transportation of a group of people to a new settlement.

repentant.o: From Middle English repentant, from Old French repentant, present participle of repentir. By surface analysis, repent + -ant.
repentant.example: I cannot believe that God wants us to kill no matter if this man is a sinner. God’s greatest commandment is one of love, not hate and revenge. I believe that this man is repentant for his wrongdoings. He has asked for forgiveness.
repentant.exampleSense: Feeling or showing sorrow for wrongdoing.

refinement.example: There was no bathroom in the cabin. Such refinements don't exist in the woods, apparently.

presentment.o: From Anglo-Norman presentment, presentement, Middle French presentement, corresponding to present + -ment.
presentment.example: the presentment of a nuisance, a libel, etc.
presentment.exampleSense: The notice taken by a grand jury of any offence from their own knowledge or observation, without any bill of indictment laid before them.

resentment.o: From resent + -ment, after Middle French and French ressentiment (in Old French as recentement), from an archaic usage of the verb ressentir via Old French sentir, from Latin sentiō, sentīre (“to feel”). Compare Italian risentimento, Portuguese ressentimento, and Spanish resentimiento. Doublet of resentiment and ressentiment, the former attested slightly earlier.
resentment.example: He retains so vivid resentments of the more solid morality.
resentment.exampleSense: The state of holding something in the mind as a subject of contemplation, or of being inclined to reflect upon it; feeling; impression.

p: interfix used before Latinate suffixes appended to nouns ending with -itude or -tude
multitudinous.o: Learned borrowing from Latin multitūdin- (the oblique stem of multitūdō (“great number (of people), multitude”)) + English -ous (suffix forming adjectives from nouns, denoting the presence of a quality in any degree (typically an abundance)). Multitūdō is derived from multus (“many; much”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *mel- (“to be late; to worry”)) + -tūdō (suffix forming abstract nouns denoting a condition or state). By surface analysis, multitude + -in- (interfix used before Latinate suffixes appended to nouns ending with -itude or -tude) + -ous.
multitudinous.example: In multitudinous London the memory of A. V. Laider and his trouble had soon passed from my mind.

sign in.example: In order to get into the office after hours, you'll have to sign in at the security desk.
sign in.exampleSense: To sign one's name on a list when entering a place, to indicate one's arrival.

sky-high.example: They had to bid against a private buyer, which pushed the price sky high.

incentivise.example: The boss will incentivise the workforce by offering bonuses.
incentivise.exampleSense: Non-Oxford British English standard spelling of incentivize.

incentivize.example: The US government seeks to incentivize home ownership through a favorable tax system.
incentivize.exampleSense: To provide incentives for; to encourage.

incurvate.o: The verb is first attested in 1578, the adjective in 1647; borrowed from Latin incurvātus, perfect passive participle of incurvō, see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and -ate (verb-forming suffix).
incurvate.example: He noted that the flower's petals were incurvate.

infuriate.o: First attested in 1667; borrowed from Medieval Latin infuriātus (“enraged”), perfect passive participle of infuriō (“to enrage”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from Latin furia (“rage, fury, frenzy”); perhaps via Italian infuriato.

lumbago.o: The noun is borrowed from Late Latin lumbāgō (“backache of the lumbar region”), from Late Latin lumbus (“lumbar”), Latin lumbus (“loin”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *lendʰ- (“loins”)) + -āgō (suffix forming nouns describing objects, animals, and plants). The verb is derived from the noun.
lumbago.example: Sir Oswald Feiling winced as he turned to go home. He had felt a warning twinge of lumbago.
lumbago.exampleSense: Backache of the lumbar region or lower back, which can be caused by muscle strain or a slipped disc.

hernia.o: Borrowed from Latin hernia (“protruded viscus”). See also yarn and cord.

lumbar.o: From Latin lumbāris, from lumbus (“loin”) + -āris. See loin.
lumbar.example: The lumbar spine supports the upper body and transmits the weight of the upper body to the pelvis and lower limbs.
lumbar.exampleSense: Related to the lower back or loin, specifically the five vertebrae between the rib cage and the pelvis.

hypertensive.example: The recorded causes of kidney disease were as follows: diabetic nephropathy (in 21% of the patients), nephroangiosclerosis and glomerulonephritis (18%), interstitial nephropathy (7%), hypertensive nephropathy (5%), polykystosis (5%) and other recorded diagnoses (hereditary disease, solitary kidney, dysglobulinemia, and systemic disease) (22%).
hypertensive.exampleSense: Of, pertaining to, or causing hypertension.

hypertension.example: Once stroke was classified by a risk factor-free method, the stronger relationship between hypertension and lacunar versus nonlacunar infarction patients disappeared.
hypertension.exampleSense: The disease or disorder of abnormally high blood pressure.

monolithic.o: From French monolithique. By surface analysis, monolith + -ic.
monolithic.example: A monolithic chunk of titanium with facets for cutting, wrenching, and prying.
monolithic.exampleSense: Consisting of a single piece of homogeneous material as opposed to a composite material or an assembly of multiple parts.

elaboration.o: From Middle French élaboration. Morphologically elaborate + -ion.

mathematician.o: From Middle English mathematicion, from Middle French mathematicien, from mathematique f sg (“mathematics”) (from Latin mathēmatica, feminine of mathēmaticus, from Ancient Greek μαθηματικός (mathēmatikós, “fond of learning”), from μάθημα (máthēma, “knowledge, learning”) + -ικός (-ikós)) + Middle French -ien (from Latin -iānus). Displaced native Old English rīmcræftiga. By surface analysis, mathematic + -ian.

abacus.o: From Late Middle English abacus, abagus, agabus (“abacus; art of counting with an abacus”), from Latin abacus, abax (“sideboard or table with a slab at the top; slab at the top of a column; counting board, sand table; board for playing games”) (compare Late Latin abacus (“art of arithmetic”)), from Ancient Greek ἄβαξ (ábax, “slab, counting board; board covered with sand for drawing; plate; dice-board”). Doublet of abaque and abac. The plural form abaci is reinforced from Latin abacī.
abacus.example: I’ve heard merchants still use an abacus for adding things up in China.
abacus.exampleSense: A device used for performing arithmetical calculations; (rare) a table on which loose counters are placed, or (more commonly) an instrument with beads sliding on rods, or counters in grooves, with one row of beads or counters representing units, the next tens, etc.

capacitor.o: From capacity + -or. Capacitor replaced the term condenser (coined by Alessandro Volta in 1782) to disambiguate it from steam condenser. The coiner is unknown but the change was recommended in 1926 by British Standard Glossary of Terms in Electrical Engineering.

admiralty.o: From French amirauté, for an older amiralté (“office of admiral”), from Late Latin admīrālitās. See admiral. Analyzable as admiral + -ty.

retardation.example: [...] the effect is automatically to select a braking force which is higher at above 40 m.p.h., in the initial stages of retardation, but is reduced as the speed falls below 40 m.p.h.
retardation.exampleSense: Deceleration; reduction in the magnitude of velocity.

p: suffix with meaning "person or thing that is the object or subject of that performed verb", -ed
retardate.o: From retard + -ate (suffix with meaning "person or thing that is the object or subject of that performed verb", -ed). Compare retarded an French retardé.

retarder.example: The substance acted as a retarder to the chemical reaction because it radically changed the pH.

retarded.example: This kind of plant is usually of a retarded growth.
retarded.exampleSense: Delayed; delayed in development, hindered; impeded.

impactful.example: Everyone knows that vividly presented information is impactful and persuasive.

qubit.o: Blend of quantum + bit, a play on cubit (“historical unit of length”). Coined by American physicist Benjamin Schumacher in 1995.
qubit.example: Quantum computing, on the other hand, is based on quantum bits, or qubits.
qubit.exampleSense: A quantum bit; the basic unit of quantum information described by a superposition of two states; a quantum bit in a quantum computer capable of being in a state of superposition.

indeterminable.o: From Middle French indeterminable, from Late Latin indeterminabilis.

indeterminate.example: It bears an affinity to the problem of indeterminate architecture—the indeterminate residential area.
indeterminate.exampleSense: Designed to allow the incorporation of future changes whose nature is not yet known.

indeterminism.o: Borrowed from French indéterminisme, equivalent to in- + determinism.
indeterminism.example: This parallelism brings in conflicts and directional indeterminisms which cannot be solved by the CU.
indeterminism.exampleSense: A situation in which there are multiple valid options for next step in a process.

fermion.o: From Fermi + -on. Named after Italian-American physicist Enrico Fermi. Coined by English physicist Paul Dirac in 1945 in a lecture titled "Developments in Atomic Theory".
fermion.example: The fermions treated by the Standard Model are the (composite) baryons and the (elementary) leptons and quarks.
fermion.exampleSense: Any elementary or composite particle that has half-integer spin and thus obeys Fermi–Dirac statistics and the Pauli exclusion principle (equivalently, a particle for which the wavefunction of any system of identical such particles changes sign whenever two are swapped); a baryon, a lepton or a quark;

boson.o:
noun: From Bose + -on. Named after Indian physicist Satyendra Nath Bose (1894–1974); coined by English physicist Paul Dirac in 1945 in a lecture titled Developments in Atomic Theory.

noun: Clipping of boatswain.

sigmoid.o: Borrowing from Ancient Greek σῑγμοειδής (sīgmoeidḗs, “of the shape of sigma”), from σῖγμᾰ (sîgmă, “sigma”) + -ο- (-o-) + -ειδής (-eidḗs, “-oid, -like”); Equivalent to sigma + -oid. Compare with French sigmoïde.

epoch-making.example: The prime minister, Tony Blair, described the terrorist attacks on America as having "epoch-making proportions" as parliament was recalled for an emergency session today.
epoch-making.exampleSense: Constituting an epoch; opening a new era; introducing new conceptions or a new method in the treatment of a subject; highly novel and influential.

epochal.example: It had been an epochal decade for cancer epidemiology, but equally, an epochal decade for tobacco.
epochal.exampleSense: Highly important or significant; monumental, epoch-making.

epoch.o: From Medieval Latin epocha, from Ancient Greek ἐποχή (epokhḗ, “a check, cessation, stop, pause, epoch of a star, i.e., the point at which it seems to halt after reaching the highest, and generally the place of a star; hence, a historical epoch”), from ἐπέχω (epékhō, “to hold in, check”), from ἐπι- (epi-, “upon”) + ἔχω (ékhō, “to have, hold”). Doublet of epoche.
epoch.example: Now during the time of the glacial epoch the greatest distance of the sun in winter was 98¼ millions of miles, whereas it is now, in winter, only 91½ millions of miles, the mean distance being taken as 93 million miles.
epoch.exampleSense: A geochronologic unit of hundreds of thousands to millions of years; a subdivision of a period, and subdivided into ages (or sometimes subepochs).

stochastic.o: From Ancient Greek στοχαστικός (stokhastikós), from στοχάζομαι (stokházomai, “aim at a target, guess”), from στόχος (stókhos, “an aim, a guess”).
stochastic.example: In the evening, while she bathed, waiting for him to enter the bathroom as she powdered her body, he crouched over the blueprints spread between the sofas in the lounge, calculating a stochastic analysis of the Pentagon car park.

convex.o: Borrowed from Middle French convexe, from Latin convexus (“arched”).
convex.example: This will convex the fan and hold the cards more rigidly in place.
convex.exampleSense: To cause to form a convex curve or surface; to make convex.

jujube.o: From Middle English jujube, from Medieval Latin jujuba or Old French jujube, perhaps via Old Occitan from Classical Latin zīzyphum, zīzyphus, from Ancient Greek ζίζυφον (zízuphon)․ First attested in the 14th century.

flippy.example: And at that point I start to feel faint and my stomach starts doing that weird flippy thing.

stretch out.example: Please don't stretch out your sweater by pulling it on and off carelessly.
stretch out.exampleSense: To extend (something) fully, in space, time or use.

stretcher.example: A twelve-by-fourteen canvas would not pin in his box, so he had to make a stretcher for it, and very neatly he made it, out of strips of butter-box.
stretcher.exampleSense: A frame on which a canvas is stretched for painting.

stretchy.example: Not just comfort, but luxurious comfort — the stretchy, yawny, sleepy kind — is his portion.
stretchy.exampleSense: Inclined to stretch, as from weariness.

standby.example: The restaurant, Hop Louie, was a Chinatown standby for decades before closing in 2016.
standby.exampleSense: Something that is standard, well-tested, or frequently used.

stand by.example: I can't simply stand by and watch you ruin your life.
stand by.exampleSense: To do nothing. To be inactive in a situation.

flawless.example: The pianist’s performance this evening was flawless.
flawless.exampleSense: Without flaws, defects, or shortcomings; perfect.

epilogue.o: Borrowed from Middle French epilogue, from Latin epilogus, from Ancient Greek ἐπίλογος (epílogos, “a conclusion, peroration of a speech, epilogue of a play”), from ἐπιλέγω (epilégō, “to say in addition”). Eclipsed Middle English lenvoie (“epilogue”) borrowed ultimately from Old French. Equivalent to epi- + -logue.

filth.o: From Middle English filth, from Old English fȳlþu, from Proto-West Germanic *fūliþu, equivalent to foul + -th (abstract nominal suffix).
filth.example: Before we start cooking we need to clean up the filth in this kitchen.
filth.exampleSense: Dirt; foul matter; that which soils or defiles.

filthy.o: From Middle English filthy, filthi, equivalent to filth + -y.
filthy.example: The coaches were filthy outside and did not appear to have been painted or washed for years. Inside there were uncomfortable seats covered with a cane-like material.

absorber.example: Old Lady Dacier’s bluntness in speaking of her grandson would have shocked Lady Wathin as much as it astonished, had she been less of an ardent absorber of aristocratic manners.

camera.o: Learned borrowing from Latin camera (“chamber or bedchamber”), from Ancient Greek καμάρα (kamára, “anything with an arched cover, a covered carriage or boat, a vaulted chamber, a vault”), of Old Iranian origin, from Proto-Iranian *kamarā- (“something curved”), from *kamárati, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *kmárati, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kh₂em- (“to bend, curve”). Doublet of chamber. (device): An ellipsis of camera obscura, from New Latin camera obscura (“dark chamber”), because the first cameras used a pinhole and a dark room.
camera.example: I'm talking about the way the camera flies up above the skater when you leap into the air. No one had done it before.
camera.exampleSense: The viewpoint in a three-dimensional game or simulation.

dial.o: The original meaning was 'sundial' and/or 'clock dial'; from Middle English diall, from Middle French dyal, from Latin diālis (“daily, concerning the day”), because of its use in telling the time of day, from Latin diēs (“day”). Compare Spanish dial and día (“day”).
dial.example: His hands were too fat to operate the dial on the telephone.
dial.exampleSense: A disk with finger holes on a telephone; used to select the number to be called.

solidify.o: From French solidifier. By surface analysis, solid + -ify.
solidify.example: Emerging from Kennaway Tunnel, the train sweeps to the right, affording views of the recent work to solidify the railway here.

purity.o: From pure + -ity, from Old French purete, from Latin puritas.

carve out.example: Fortunes were carved out of the property of the crown.
carve out.exampleSense: To create (a reputation, chance, role, rank, career, victory) by hard work, or as if by cutting.

oxidation.o: From French oxydation, equivalent to oxide + -ation. See oxidate.
oxidation.example: As a demonstration, we first establish the correctness of the Jacobian matrices for kinetic models of hydrogen, methane, ethylene, and isopentanol oxidation, then demonstrate the performance achievable on CPUs and GPUs using pyJac via matrix evaluation timing comparisons..
oxidation.exampleSense: The combination of a substance with oxygen.

resultant.o: From Latin resultāns, present participle of resultō.

impurity.o: From impure + -ity. From Middle French impurité, from Latin impuritas.
impurity.example: Even animals in the Jewish system cause impurity only when they are dead.
impurity.exampleSense: The condition of being impure; because of contamination, pollution, adulteration or insufficient purification.

plasma.o: From Late Latin plasma (“mold”), from Ancient Greek πλάσμα (plásma, “something formed”).
plasma.example: However, it displayed some unique copper magic routines and plasma effects.
plasma.exampleSense: A visual effect in which cycles of changing colours are warped in various ways to give the illusion of liquid organic movement.

ingot.o: From Middle English ingot (“mould for casting metal”), of uncertain origin. In all likelihood the same word as Middle French lingot, but the direction of borrowing is hard to establish, particularly as the word appears simultaneously (ca. 1390) in both languages. * Assuming English origin, from Old English ingoten, past participle of inġēotan (“to pour in”), derived from Proto-Germanic *geutaną (“to pour”, whence archaic English yote). Compare Old English ingyte (“a pouring-in, infusion”), which is formed with a related noun (Proto-Germanic *gutiz, whence German Guss, Swedish göt). Also related with English gote, goit. * Assuming French origin, from a diminutive of Old Occitan lenga (“tongue”), so called because of the elongated form. (The presence or absence of initial l- has to do, in any case, with rebracketing of the French definite article.)

photo-.o: From Ancient Greek φωτο- (phōto-), the combining form of φῶς (phôs, “light”).

electrode.o: Coined by British scientist Michael Faraday in 1833, first used in his Diary (laboratory notebook) from the Ancient Greek words ἤλεκτρον (ḗlektron, “amber”) (from which the word electricity is derived) and ὁδός (hodós, “way”). By surface analysis, electro- + -ode

police station.example: In trying to stop him from exploiting more children, I was ensuring my parents and my siblings would be ostracised. She begged me not to go to the police station.
police station.exampleSense: A building serving as the headquarters of a branch of the police force, and sometimes as a temporary place of confinement for offenders.

short circuit.example: In the motor control room aft, a crewman crashed against the main electrical switchboard, short-circuiting it with his body, and all power aboard was lost.
short circuit.exampleSense: To cause a short circuit in.

plan.o: Borrowed from French plan (“flat surface, ground plot, map”), from Latin plānus. Some sources also argue for influence or alteration of French plant, from plantar, from Latin plantāre (“set, fix in place”). Compare plane, plain.
plan.example: Seen in plan, the building had numerous passageways not apparent to visitors.
plan.exampleSense: A two-dimensional drawing of a building as seen from above with obscuring or irrelevant details such as roof removed, or of a floor of a building, revealing the internal layout; as distinct from the elevation.

torturer.example: My destruction might indeed arrive a few months sooner; but if my torturer should suspect that I postponed it, influenced by his menaces, he would surely find other, and perhaps more dreadful means of revenge.

torture.o: From Middle English torture, from Old French torture, from Late Latin tortūra (“a twisting, writhing, of bodily pain, a griping colic;” in Medieval Latin “pain inflicted by judicial or ecclesiastical authority as a means of persuasion, torture”), from Latin tortus (whence also tort), past participle of torquēre (“to twist”).
torture.example: Using large dogs to attack bound, hand-cuffed prisoners is clearly torture.
torture.exampleSense: The infliction of severe pain or anguish, especially as an interrogation technique or punishment; (usually in the plural) a technique, method, or device which is designed to inflict such anguish.

dice.o: From Middle English dys, plural of dy. See the etymology of die (etymology 2) for further information. The voiceless /s/ was most likely retained because the word felt like a collective term rather than a plural form (compare pence), and the spelling dice is a result of the pronunciation.
dice.example: Tyrion found Timmett dicing with his Burned Men in the barracks.

syntax.o: Partly from Late Latin syntaxis and partly from its etymon, Ancient Greek σύνταξις (súntaxis), from σύν (sún, “together”) + τάξις (táxis, “arrangement”), from τάσσω (tássō, “to arrange”). Doublet of syntaxis.

make up one's mind.example: I can't make up my mind whether to have ice cream or cake.
make up one's mind.exampleSense: To decide; to reach a conclusion.

complainant.o: From Old French complaignant, present participle of complaindre.

millimeter.o: From French millimètre, as if milli- + meter.

monger.o:
noun: The noun is derived from Middle English mongere, mangere (“dealer, merchant, trader”), from Old English mangere (“dealer, merchant, trader”), from Proto-West Germanic *mangārī (“dealer, merchant, monger”), from Latin mangō (“dealer, trader”) + Proto-West Germanic *-ārī (suffix forming agent nouns, especially denoting occupations). The further etymology of mangō is uncertain; the following possibilities have been suggested: * From Ancient Greek μαγγανεύω (manganeúō, “to use charms or philtres; to cheat, play tricks; to dress food artificially to make it appear better”), from μάγγᾰνον (mángănon, “means of bewitching, charm, philtre”) (possibly from Proto-Indo-European *meng- (“to dress, embellish, trim”); or from Arabic ن ج ل (n j l, root relating to pouring out or thrusting)) + -εύω (-eúō, suffix forming denominative verbs of activity or condition). * From Latin *manicō, *manigō (“deal, trade; to handle, manage (?)”), from manus (“hand”); further etymology uncertain, possibly ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)meh₂- (“to beckon, signal”), or *mon-u-. The verb is either derived from the noun, or is a back-formation from mongering (adjective or noun).

noun: Origin uncertain, possibly from monger (“dealer or trader in a specific commodity”) (etymology 1); or related to Middle English mangbot (“type of fishing boat used on the Thames”).
monger.example: Once these fears have been mongered, their spread is irresistible.

gossipy.example: ‘Tell me who you saw and what they said,’ she says, in one of her gossipy moods.

gossip.o: From Middle English godsybbe, godsib (“a close friend or relation, a confidant; a godparent”), from Old English godsibb (“godparent, sponsor”), equivalent to god + sib. Doublet of godsib. For sense evolution to "gossip, discussing others' personal affairs," compare French commérage.
gossip.example: Be careful what you say to him: he’s a bit of a gossip.
gossip.exampleSense: Someone who likes to talk about other people's private or personal business.

parity.o:
noun: From Middle French parité, from Late Latin paritās, from Latin pār (“equal”). Equivalent to pari- + -ty.

noun: From Latin paritas, from pariō (“give birth”).
parity.example: Parity is always preserved in such operations.
parity.exampleSense: Senses related to classification into two sets. A set with the property of having all of its elements belonging to one of two disjoint subsets, especially a set of integers split in subsets of even and odd elements.

amplifier.example: The football team is not an extension of Iran’s leaders, but is in fact the opposite, seen as an amplifier for freedom, group expression, modernity.
amplifier.exampleSense: Anything that amplifies, or makes something larger or more intense.

homey.example: Susan added some homey touches to her office.

homie.o: Earliest known reference is in the tune The House of Blue Lights (1946) by Ella Mae Morse and Freddie Slack, when Morse improvises a spoken-word intro. Equivalent to home + -ie.
homie.exampleSense: A close friend or fellow member of a youth gang.

sexism.example: The sexism of making and promoting violent films for men and romantic comedies for women.
sexism.exampleSense: Attitudes or actions that are based on or promote the expectation that people adhere to stereotypical social roles (gender roles) based on sex.

sadism.o: From French sadisme and German Sadismus. Named after the Marquis de Sade, famed for his libertine writings depicting the pleasure of inflicting pain to others. The word for "sadism" (sadisme) was coined or acknowledged in the 1834 posthumous reprint of French lexicographer Boiste's Dictionnaire universel de la langue française; it is reused along with "sadist" (sadique) in 1862 by French critic Sainte-Beuve in his commentary of Flaubert's novel Salammbô; it is reused (possibly independently) in 1886 by Austrian psychiatrist Krafft-Ebing in Psychopathia Sexualis which popularized it; it is directly reused in 1905 by Freud in Three Essays on the Theory of Sexuality which definitively established the word.

phrenology.example: Phrenology involves feeling the bumps in the skull to determine an individual's psychological attributes.
phrenology.exampleSense: The pseudo-science which studies the relationships between a person's character and the morphology (structure) of the skull.

docker.o:
noun: From dock (verb) + -er.

noun: From dock (noun) + -er.

dicker.o: From Middle English diker (“measure of ten”), from Late Latin dacra (“a dicker”), from Latin decuria (“a ten of something”), from decem (“ten”).
dicker.example: In the brilliant sparkle of the morning when everything that was not superlatively blue was superlatively green, I dickered with a man who was taking a party up the inlet that he should drop me off at the village I was headed for.
dicker.exampleSense: To bargain, haggle or negotiate over a sale.

dick.o:
noun: Ultimately from Dick, pet form of the name Richard. The name Dick came to mean everyman, whence the word acquired its other meanings.

noun: A shortening and alteration of detective.

noun: A shortening and alteration of declaration.

num: Borrowed from Cumbric *deg, from Proto-Brythonic *deg. Cognate with Welsh deg.
dick.example: You better try and get some dick and take your mind off this bullshit.

overshoe.example: “I will take some brandy,” said Edna, shivering as she removed her gloves and overshoes.
overshoe.exampleSense: A shoe worn over an ordinary shoe, as: To protect from water or mud.

thematic.o: From Ancient Greek θεματικός (thematikós), from θέμα (théma, “theme”). Equivalent to theme + -atic.
thematic.example: A considerable number of derived nominals, especially thematic nouns, also exhibited o-grade roots.
thematic.exampleSense: Of a word stem, ending in a vowel that appears in or otherwise influences the noun or verb's inflection.

galoshes.o: plural of galosh. From Middle English galoche, from Old French galoche (“shoe with a wooden sole”), but further history is uncertain. further theories * From Vulgar Latin *galopium or Late Latin calopedia (“a wooden shoe; a shoe with a wooden sole”), from Ancient Greek κᾱλοπόδιον (kālopódion), diminutive of κᾱλόπους (kālópous, “shoemaker's block”), compound of κᾶλον (kâlon, “wood”) and πούς (poús, “foot”). (More at holt and foot.) * From Late Latin gallicula, diminutive of Latin gallica (solea) (“Gallic (sandal)”). * From Old French galette (“flat round cake”), from galet (“pebble”).

sneaker.o: From sneak + -er. The shoes sense is a reference to the quietness of the shoes.
sneaker.example: Beshrew the man who on such a day as this, the general festival, should affect to stand aloof. I am none of those sneakers. I am free of the corporation, and care not who knows it.

modulate.o: From Latin modulor (“to measure, regulate, modulate”) + -ate (verb-forming suffix), from modulus (“measure”). Compare module, modulus. By surface analysis, modul(e) + -ate.
modulate.example: "Can you tell?" she asked, in a trembling but well modulated and sensual voice.
modulate.exampleSense: To regulate, adjust or adapt To change the pitch, intensity or tone of one's voice or of a musical instrument

modulation.o: From Late Middle English modulacion, modulacioun (“act of making music or singing; harmony; melody, song”), from Middle French modulation (modern French modulation), and directly from its etymon Latin modulātiō (“regular or rhythmical measure, modulation; inflection of tone; (architecture) calculation of measurements from a standard unit; (Late Latin) act of making music or singing; melody, song”), from modulātus (“modulated”) + -iō (suffix forming abstract nouns from verbs). Modulātus is a perfect participle of modulor (“to beat time; to make music or sing; to measure; etc.”), from modulus (“rhythmical measure, interval; rhythm; small interval or measure, etc.”) + -or (suffix forming certain inflections of verbs); and modulus is from modus (“measure; method; etc.”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *med- (“to measure; etc.”)) + -ulus (diminutive suffix). By surface analysis, modulat(e) + -ion (suffix denoting an action or process, or its result).
modulation.example: The Rings of the VVind-pipe, are fitted for the Modulation of the Voice.
modulation.exampleSense: Modification or regulation of something to achieve an appropriate measure or proportion; (countable) an instance of this. Variation of the intensity, pitch, and tone of the sound of a musical instrument or voice; inflection; (countable) an instance of this.

amplitude.o: Borrowed from Middle French amplitude, from Latin amplitūdō, from amplus (“large”). By surface analysis, ample + -itude.
amplitude.example: As the two topped the ridge there burst on them the strong scarlet light of a red-curtained English inn. It stood sideways in the road, as if standing aside in the amplitude of hospitality.
amplitude.exampleSense: The measure of the size of something, especially its width or breadth; largeness, magnitude.

baud.o: Borrowed from French baud. Named for French inventor Jean-Maurice-Émile Baudot (1845-1903).
baud.example: To reach the Backroom Bulletin Board, call (718) 849-6699 with a computer, using either the 300 or 1200 baud setting on the modem.
baud.exampleSense: A unit of data transmission symbol rate; the number of signalling events per second.

stool.o:
noun: From Middle English stool, from Old English stōl (“chair, seat”), from Proto-West Germanic *stōl, from Proto-Germanic *stōlaz (“chair”), from Proto-Indo-European *stoh₂los (“frame, rack, stand”), from *steh₂- (“to stand”). Cognates Cognate with North Frisian stuul, stölj, Stööl (“chear”), Saterland Frisian Stoul (“chear”), West Frisian stoel (“chair, seat”), Dutch stoel (“chair”), German Stuhl (“chair”), Low German Stohl (“chair”), Luxembourgish Stull (“chair”), Vilamovian śtül (“chair”), Yiddish שתוהל (shsuhl), שטול (shtul, “chair”), Danish, Norwegian Bokmål, Norwegian Nynorsk, and Swedish stol (“chair”), Faroese stólur (“chair”), Icelandic stóll (“chair”), Crimean Gothic stul (“seat”), Gothic 𐍃𐍄𐍉𐌻𐍃 (stōls, “chair; throne”), Russian стул (stul, “chair”), Estonian tool (“chair”), Finnish tuoli (“chair”); also Breton and Cornish sevel (“to erect, rise; to build; to lift; to compose; to earn”), Irish sáil, sál (“heel”), Scottish Gaelic sàil (“heel”), Welsh sefyll (“to stand; to stop; to sit”), Latin sistō (“to set; to stop; to stand; to stabilise”), Umbrian 𐌔𐌄𐌔𐌕𐌖 (sestu, “to place”), Greek στέκω (stéko), στέκομαι (stékomai, “to stand up”), Albanian shtoj (“to add; to augment; to accumulate”), Lithuanian stálas (“table”), Old Prussian stallan (“table”), Belarusian, Bulgarian, Macedonian, and Russian стол (stol, “table”), Czech stůl (“table”), Polish stół (“table”), Serbo-Croatian сто̑, сто̑л, stȏ, stȏl (“table”), Slovak stôl (“table”), Slovene stol (“chair”), Armenian երթալ (ertʻal), էթալ (ētʻal, “to go”), Central Kurdish ستوون (stûn, “column”), Pashto ستن (stən, “needle; awl; pin; syringe; post; hand; dragonfly”), Persian ایستادن (ēstādan / istâdan), وایسادن (vâysâdan), وایستادن (vâystâdan, “to stand up; to step; to stay”), ستون (sotun / sutūn, “column”), Northern Kurdish rawestîn (“to stand up”), stûn (“column”), Ossetian стын (styn, “to stand up”), Hittite 𒋾𒄑𒍣 (tiezzi, “to step; to place oneself”), Tocharian A ṣtäm- (“to stand”), Tocharian B stäm- (“to stand”), Sanskrit तिष्ठति (tiṣṭhati, “to stand; to stay”). More at stand. The medical use derives from sense 2 (seat used for defecation).

noun: From Latin stolo. See stolon.
stool.example: Two days prior to the consultation, an abdominal radiograph was done because the patient hadn't stooled in a week. No signs of obstruction and no abnormal accumulations of stool were found.

cancellation.example: Then, in January, a creeping tsunami of train cancellations, triggered by major staff absences as a result of the aggressive transmissibility of Omicron, heaped further misery on rail users.
cancellation.exampleSense: The act, process, or result of cancelling; as, the cancellation of certain words in a contract, or of the contract itself.

sine.o: Borrowed from Latin sinus (“curve, bend; bosom”), a translation of Arabic جَيْب (jayb, “bosom”), a misidentification of the notation جيب (j-y-b), written without vowel diacritics, standing for Arabic جِيبَ (jība, “sine”), in turn from Sanskrit ज्या (jyā, “sine, chord, bowstring”) through the similar Sanskrit जीव (jīva, “sine, chord, life, existence”). Doublet of sinus.

cerate.o: From Middle English cerate, cerote, from Latin cērātum, from cēra (“wax”), see -ate (noun-forming suffix)

systematically.example: Taxonomy seeks to systematically name all living organisms; each species has one name and everyone can figure out what that name is.
systematically.exampleSense: In an organized manner; utilising a system.

clarified.o: simple past and past participle of clarify. From Middle English clarifien, from Old French clarifiier, from Latin clārificō, clārificāre; clārus (“clear”) + faciō, facere (“make”). Semantically clear + -ify.
clarified.example: Clarified butter is made by removing water and impurities from butter.

uncreative.example: Her artwork was judged to be competent but uncreative.
uncreative.exampleSense: Not creative. Deficient in or devoid of creativity and originality.

commence.o: From Middle English commencen, comencen (also as contracted comsen, cumsen), from Anglo-Norman comencer, from Vulgar Latin *cominitiāre, formed from Latin com- + initiō (whence English initiate).
commence.example: The speeches commenced three days of workshops, seminars, and cultural activities.

proportional.example: For example, according to the gas laws, pressure is directly proportional to temperature: the quotient derived from pressure (numerator) and temperature (denominator) will be constant; however, pressure is inversely proportional to volume, meaning that the product between volume and pressure will be constant.
proportional.exampleSense: At a constant ratio (to). Two magnitudes (numbers) are said to be proportional if the second varies in a direct relation arithmetically to the first. Symbol: ∝.

parabola.o: Borrowed from New Latin parabola, from Ancient Greek παραβολή (parabolḗ), from παραβάλλω (parabállō, “to set side by side”), from παρά (pará, “beside”) + βάλλω (bállō, “to throw”). Doublet of parable, parole, and palaver.

starry-eyed.example: He was so starry-eyed when he started, but reality ground him down, and he became both more realistic and more practical.
starry-eyed.exampleSense: Having naively optimistic hopes or outlooks.

starry.o: From Middle English sterry, equivalent to star + -y.
starry.example: Despite a starry cast, the film performed poorly at the box office.

polynomial.o: From poly- + -nomial, from νομός (nomós, “portion, part”), by analogy with binomial.
polynomial.example: Unfortunately, an analogous attack on the octic polynomial becomes exceedingly complicated.
polynomial.exampleSense: An expression consisting of a sum of a finite number of terms, each term being the product of a constant coefficient and one or more variables raised to a non-negative integer power, such as a_nxⁿ+a_n-1xⁿ⁻¹+...+a_0x⁰.

quadratic.o: From French quadratique (1765), from Latin quadrātus + -ique (English -ic), form of quadrō (“to make square”), from quādrus (“square”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kʷetwóres (“four”), whence also Latin quartus (“fourth”).
quadratic.example: A linear or even a quadratic relation between the overall gain in efficiency η and the modularity Q would have been easily explained through S1 Fig, which shows a quadratic (inverse) relation between interedges fraction and modularity.
quadratic.exampleSense: Of a polynomial, equation or function, second-degree: involving the second power (square) of a variable but no higher powers, as ax²+bx+c.

cohort.o: From Latin cohors (stem cohort-); borrowed into Old English as coorta, but reintroduced into Middle English as cōhort and chōors via Old French cohorte. Doublet of court.
cohort.example: Three cohorts of men were assigned to the region.
cohort.exampleSense: Any division of a Roman legion, normally of about 500 or 600 men (equalling about six centuries).

sadist.o: From the name of the Marquis de Sade; see sadism.

sadistic.example: Together, with the help of the drunkard Haymitch (Woody Harrelson), the only District 12 citizen ever to win the Games, they challenge tributes that range from sadistic volunteers to crafty kids like the pint-sized Rue (Amandla Stenberg) to the truly helpless and soon-to-be-dead.
sadistic.exampleSense: Delighting in or feeling pleasure from the pain or humiliation of others.

systole.o: Borrowed from New Latin, from Ancient Greek συστολή (sustolḗ), from συστέλλω (sustéllō, “to contract”), from σύν (sún, “together”) + στέλλω (stéllō, “to send”).
systole.example: A double systole catapulted him into full consciousness again, and he promised his uncorrected self that he would limit his daily ration of cigarettes to a couple of heartbeats.
systole.exampleSense: The rhythmic contraction of the heart, by which blood is driven through the arteries.

unfold.o:
verb: From Middle English unfolden, from Old English unfealdan (“to unfold”), equivalent to un- + fold.

verb: From un- + fold (“to confine into a fold or pen”).
unfold.example: Pity me not, but lend thy serious hearing To what I shall unfold.
unfold.exampleSense: To lay open to view or contemplation; to bring out in all the details, or by successive development; to reveal.

mull.o:
verb: Inherited from Middle English molle, mulle (“dust, rubbish”), possibly from Old English myl (“dust, mould”), from Proto-West Germanic *muli, a deverbal formation from *mulljan and thus cognate with Dutch mul (“dust, mould”), German Müll (“rubbish”), Swedish moln (“cloud”) and related to English mill (“to grind”). Alternatively, from Middle French mol or its etymon Latin mollis (“soft”). Some verbal senses are supplied by Middle English mollen (“to soften, dissolve”), from Old French moillier, from Latin *molliāre (“to steep”), itself from mollis; compare moil.

noun: Shortened from mulmul.

noun: From Scottish Gaelic maol.

noun: Borrowed from Danish muld, from Old Norse mold.
mull.example: The merchandise in this case consists of Madras mulls — thin cotton cloth.

parable.o:
noun: From Middle English parable, from Old French parable, parabole, from Late Latin parabola, from Ancient Greek παραβολή (parabolḗ, “comparison”). Doublet of parabola, parole, and palaver.

adj: From Latin parābilis, from parāre (“to prepare, procure”).
parable.example: Catholic homilies normally draw on at least one Biblical lecture, often parables.
parable.exampleSense: A short narrative illustrating a lesson (usually religious/moral) by comparison or analogy.

aeroballistics.o: From aero- + ballistics, itself from ballista + -ics or by surface analysis, ballistic + -s.

sophomore.o: From earlier sophumer, from the obsolete sophom, sophum (“sophism or dialectical exercise”), from Ancient Greek σόφισμα (sóphisma). Likely influenced by Ancient Greek σοφός (sophós, “wise”) + μωρός (mōrós, “fool”). Compare oxymoron (literally “sharp-dull”), a similar contradiction.
sophomore.example: She was very mature for a sophomore and had several friends who were juniors or even seniors.
sophomore.exampleSense: A second-year undergraduate student in a college or university, or a second-year student in a four-year secondary school or high school.

bracket.o: From earlier bragget, *bracket, from Middle English *braget, *braket (attested in braket nail), from Old French braguette (“the opening in the fore part of a pair of breeches, one's fly”), a diminutive of Old French brague (“knickers, britches”), from Old Occitan braga, from Latin brāca (“pants”), from Transalpine Gaulish *brāca, from Proto-Germanic *brāks, an early form of Proto-Germanic *brōks (“leggings, breeches, trousers”).
bracket.example: To determine if your frame has this bottom bracket type, look for a notched and possibly knurled lockring on the left side (the side without the chainrings).
bracket.exampleSense: Any intermediate object that connects a smaller part to a larger part, the smaller part typically projecting sideways from the larger part.

make-up.example: Joe and Joanne had a big fight, and then apologized and had incredible make-up sex.
make-up.exampleSense: Of or relating to a reconciliation.

citation.o: From Middle English citacioun, from Old French citation, from Latin citātiō. By surface analysis, cite + -ation.
citation.example: It's a simple citation of facts.

permission.o: From Middle English permision, permission, permissioun, permyssion, from Middle French permission, from Latin permissiō. Equivalent to permit + -ion. Mostly replaced native English leave, from Old English lēaf (“permission”).
permission.example: Sire, do I have your permission to execute this traitor?
permission.exampleSense: authorisation; consent (especially formal consent from someone in authority)

prior.o:
adj: The adjective is a learned borrowing from Latin prior (“earlier, former, previous, prior; in front; (figurative) better, superior”), from Proto-Italic *priōs (“earlier, previous”, literally “more before”), ultimately from *pri (“before”) (from Proto-Indo-European *pró (“leading to, toward”) and its etymon *per- (“before, in front; first”)) + *-jōs (suffix forming comparative adjectives). Doublet of before, fore, and former. The adverb and noun are derived from the adjective.

noun: From Middle English priour, prior (“head or deputy head of a monastery or other religious house; predecessor; superior”), from Old English prior, from Anglo-Norman priour, prior, priur, and Old French prior, priur (modern French prieur), and directly from their etymon Latin prior (“ancestor; predecessor”) (whence Late Latin prior (“superior of a religious house or order; abbot; deputy abbot; head of a guild”)), a noun use of prior (“former, previous, prior”, adjective): see etymology
prior.example: Lady Marney, duly warned of the impending catastrophe, was experiencing all the advantages of prior information.
prior.exampleSense: Coming before in order or time; earlier, former, previous.

acknowledgement.o: Alternative spelling of acknowledgment. From acknowledge + -ment.

hydro.o: From the prefix hydro-, from Ancient Greek ὕδωρ (húdōr, “water”). By surface analysis, hydr- (“water”) + -o-. The Canadian "electricity" sense is owing to hydroelectricity being the prevalent source of electricity in much of Canada and many electric companies having the word Hydro in their names.
hydro.example: Those members also get unlimited tanning, half-priced drinks and hydro and chair massages.

hydrant.o: An irregular formation: hydr- + -ant, originally US English. By surface analysis, hydrate + -ant.
hydrant.example: A horde of dirty children play about the dripping hydrant, the only thing in the alley that thinks enough of its chance to make the most of it: it is the best it can do.
hydrant.exampleSense: An outlet from a liquid/fluid main often consisting of an upright pipe with a valve attached from which fluid (e.g. water or fuel) can be tapped.

evacuation.o: From Middle English evacuacioun, from Old French evacuation, from Late Latin ēvacuātiō. Equivalent to evacuate + -ion.
evacuation.example: A large evening meal, deep sleep in a better bed than hers, a full evacuation, a hot bath (her own house had only a cold shower), a breakfast of bacon and eggs and sausages from Crabbe's boy — these had smoothed and restored her.
evacuation.exampleSense: Voidance of any matter by the natural passages of the body or by an artificial opening; defecation; urination; also, a diminution of the fluids of an animal body by cathartics, venesection, or other means.

evacuee.o: From French évacué, évacuée, from évacuer, equivalent to evacu(ate) + -ee.
evacuee.example: In the three weeks since, the city has repeatedly relocated evacuees on short notice. To reopen schools, it bused many to armories, turning drill floors into open dormitories for the first time since a 1980s lawsuit halted the practice.
evacuee.exampleSense: A person who has been evacuated, especially a civilian evacuated from a dangerous place in time of war

requisite.o: From Latin requīsītus, perfect passive participle of requīrō (“to require, seek, ask for”), from which English require.
requisite.example: Please submit the requisite papers before the end of the financial year.

nookie.o:
noun: Possibly from Dutch neuken (“to fuck”). Compare cognate and synonymous German Low German nöken, nucken.

noun: Possibly from or related to German Nuckel (“pacifier; teat”), nuckeln (“to suck”), both attested from the 17th century, in which case the German brand name NUK, though officially an acronym, could be named after the generic word.
nookie.example: I came home early and caught them on the couch having a bit of nookie.
nookie.exampleSense: Sex or other sexual activity, especially if illicit.

proprietor.example: Here the proprietor has had the good sense of holding on to the good old fashion of giving his customers their moneyworth of good wines and liquors.

propriety.o: From late Middle English proprietee, propretee, propriete (“ownership”), borrowed from Anglo-Norman propreté, Middle French proprieté, from Latin proprietās. By surface analysis, prop(e)r + -iety. Doublet of property.
propriety.example: Now, if we may, with propriety, refer to the people one question, why may we not, with equal propriety, refer another?
propriety.exampleSense: Suitability, fitness; the quality of being appropriate.

deepen.example: The water deepens as you go toward the middle of the channel.

maximize.exampleSense: To make as large as possible.

synergistic.example: Farber and Lasker struck up a synergistic partnership that would stretch over decades.
synergistic.exampleSense: Of or pertaining to synergy or synergism; synergic; co-operative, working together, interacting, mutually stimulating.

tenure.o: From Middle English tenure, from Anglo-Norman, from Old French tenure, from Vulgar Latin *tenitura, from *tenitus, from Latin tentus (from teneō) + -ura.
tenure.example: Carsley ended his six-game tenure as England's interim manager in the same way he started it, with a comfortable victory over the nation he represented with distinction as a player.
tenure.exampleSense: A status of possessing a thing or an office; an incumbency.

efficiency.o: From Latin efficientia, equivalent to efficient + -cy.
efficiency.example: The efficiency of the planning department is deplorable.
efficiency.exampleSense: The extent to which a resource is used for the intended purpose. The extent to which time is well used for the intended task.

product.o: From Middle English product, from Latin prōductus, perfect participle of prōdūcō, first attested in English in the mathematics sense.
product.example: They improve their product every year; they export most of their agricultural production.
product.exampleSense: Anything that is produced; a result. The amount of an artifact that has been created by someone or some process.

subtract.o: Borrowed from Latin subtractus, perfect passive participle of subtrahō (“to draw from beneath; withdraw, remove”); from sub (“under”) + trahō (“to draw, pull, drag”).
subtract.example: If you subtract the $100 for gas from the total cost, it was a fairly inexpensive trip.
subtract.exampleSense: To remove or reduce; especially to reduce a quantity or number

cosine.o: From co- + sine, short for complementi sinus in Latin, meaning “sine of the complement”. Doublet of cosinus.

symbolic.o: From French symbolique or directly from Latin symbolicus, from Ancient Greek συμβολικός (sumbolikós, “of or belonging to a symbol”), equivalent to symbol + -ic.

seamlessly.example: Imagine this: you walk into work and the camera above the doors scans your face, opening them seamlessly without you lifting a finger.

proprietary.o: From French propriétaire, from Latin proprietārius. By surface analysis, propriety + -ary. Compare with the Latin proprietas (“property”) and proprius (“ownership”).
proprietary.example: The continuous profitability of the company is based on its many proprietary products.
proprietary.exampleSense: Created or manufactured exclusively by the owner or licensee of intellectual property rights, as with a patent or trade secret.

figurine.o: Borrowed from French figurine, equivalent to figure + -ine.

affray.o: From Middle English affraien (“to terrify, frighten”), borrowed from Anglo-Norman afrayer (“to terrify, disquiet, disturb”) and Old French effreer, esfreer (“to disturb, remove the peace from”) (compare modern French effrayer), from Vulgar Latin *exfridāre. The second part of this is in turn from Frankish *friþu (“security, peace”), from Proto-Germanic *friþuz (“peace”), from *frijōną (“to free; to love”), from Proto-Indo-European *prāy-, *prēy- (“to like, love”). Cognate with Old High German fridu (“peace”), Old English friþ (“peace, frith”), Old English frēod (“peace, friendship”), German Friede (“peace”). More at free, friend.
affray.example: The affray in the busy marketplace caused great terror and disorder.
affray.exampleSense: The fighting of two or more persons, in a public place, to the terror of others.

defray.o: From Middle French desfrayer, French défrayer, from dé- + Old French fraier (“to spend”).
defray.example: In order to help defray the substantial costs involved, they then raised revenue through taking advertisements.
defray.exampleSense: To pay or discharge (a debt, expense etc.); to meet (the cost of something).

odeum.o: Partly from Middle French odéum and partly from Latin ōdēum. By surface analysis, ode + -eum.

ode.o:
noun: From Middle French ode, from Late Latin ōda, from Ancient Greek ᾠδή (ōidḗ, “song”). Doublet of Aoede.

noun: Shortening.

motto.o: Borrowed from Italian motto (“a word, a saying”), from Latin muttum (“a mutter, a grunt”), late 16th c. Doublet of mot.
motto.example: You have to be in it to win it — that's my motto.

illegitimacy.o: From illegitimate + -cy; may also be analyzed as il- + legitimacy.

illegitimate.o: First attested in 1536, from Latin illēgitimus, most likely an adapted borrowing of Middle French illegitime, equivalent to il- + legitimate, see -ate (etymology 1, 2 and 3).
illegitimate.example: I am a bastard begot, bastard instructed, bastard in mind, bastard in valour, in every thing illegitimate.
illegitimate.exampleSense: Not sanctioned by marriage. Born to unmarried parents.

bonk.o: Of imitative origin. Compare English bang, bounce, bump.
bonk.example: Sophie (Katrin Cartlidge) What is a proper relationship?

rebate.o: From Old French rabatre < batre. See also abate.
rebate.example: For your existing windows, the glazing rebates will also have to be deepened to provide the extra gap.
rebate.exampleSense: A rectangular groove made to hold two pieces (of wood etc) together; a rabbet.

jollification.example: I shall go down with you on Wednesday in time for the jollification on Thursday. I always enjoy that day; they are such nice, friendly people, those good Hollingford ladies.

jollity.o: From Middle English jolyfte, from Old French joliveté (“gaiety, cheerfulness; amorous passion; life of pleasure”), from jolif. Equivalent to jolly + -ty.
jollity.example: The youngsters, not immediately within sight, seemed rather bright and desirable appurtenances than otherwise; the incidents of daily life were not without humorousness and jollity in their aspect there.
jollity.exampleSense: The state of being jolly; jolliness, cheerfulness.

ray.o:
noun: Via Middle English, borrowed from Old French rai, from Latin radius (“staff, stake, spoke”). Doublet of radius.

noun: From Middle English raye, rayȝe, from Old French raie, from Latin raia, of uncertain origin. Compare Middle English reyhhe, reihe, reȝge (“ray, skate”), from Old English reohhe (“ray”).

verb: Shortened from array.

noun: From its sound, by analogy with the letters chay, jay, gay, kay, which it resembles graphically.

noun: Alternative forms.
ray.example: I saw a ray of light through the clouds.
ray.exampleSense: A beam of light or radiation.

kip.o:
noun: 1325–75, Middle English kipp, from Middle Dutch kip, from Middle Low German kip (“pack, bundle of hides”).

noun: 1760–70, probably related to Danish kippe (“dive, hovel, cheap inn”) and Middle Low German kiffe (“hovel”). From the same distant Germanic root as cove.

verb: From Middle English kippen, from Old Norse kippa (“to pull; snatch”) or Middle Dutch kippen (“to grasp, seize, catch”). Cognate with Norwegian kippe (“to snatch”), Swedish kippa (“to snatch; jerk”); Dutch kippen (“to seize; catch”). Perhaps conflated with some senses of Middle English kepen (“to keep, observe, guard, take possession of, snatch”) (see keep).

noun: 1910–15, Americanism, abbreviated from kilo + pound.

noun: 1950–55, from Lao ກີບ (kīp).

noun: Unknown. Perhaps related to Yorkshire and Lincolnshire dialect kep, to toss up into the air. Or else, perhaps related to German Kippe (“stub”).

noun: From kip (“sleep, lie down”).
kip.example: He took off his thick black coat and threw it to Harry.
kip.exampleSense: To sleep; often with the connotation of a temporary or charitable situation, or one borne out of necessity.

scale.o:
noun: From Middle English scale, from Latin scāla, usually in plural scālae (“a flight of steps, stairs, staircase, ladder”), for *skand-slā, from scandō (“to climb”); see scan, ascend, descend, etc. Doublet of scala.

noun: From Middle English scale, from Old French escale, from Frankish and/or Old High German skala, from Proto-Germanic *skalō. Cognate with Old English sċealu (“shell, husk”), whence the modern doublet shale. Further cognate with Dutch schaal, German Schale, French écale.

noun: Inherited from Northern Middle English scale (non-Northern scole), from Old Norse skál (“bowl”) from Proto-Germanic *skēlō. Compare Danish skål (“bowl, cup”), Dutch schaal, German Schale, Old High German scāla, Old English scealu (“cup”).
scale.example: The magnitude of an earthquake is measured on the open-ended Richter scale.
scale.exampleSense: An ordered, usually numerical sequence used for measurement; means of assigning a magnitude.

tollbooth.o: Alternative spelling of toll. From Middle English toll, tol, tolle, from Old English toll m or n and toln f (“toll, duty, custom”), from Proto-West Germanic *toll, *tolnu, from Proto-Germanic *tullaz, *tullō (“that which is counted or told, reckoning”), from Proto-Indo-European *del- (“calculation, fraud”). Cognate with Saterland Frisian Tol (“toll”), Dutch tol (“toll”), German Zoll (“toll, duty, customs”), Danish told (“toll, duty, tariff”), Swedish tull (“toll, customs”), Icelandic tollur (“toll, customs”). More at tell, tale. Alternate etymology derives Old English toll from Medieval Latin tolōneum, tolōnium, alteration (due to the Germanic forms above) of Latin telōneum, from Ancient Greek τελώνιον (telṓnion, “toll-house”), from τέλος (télos, “tax”).

abrogate.o: First attested in 1526, from Middle English abrogat (“abolished”), from Latin abrogātus, perfect passive participle of abrogō (“repeal”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), formed from ab (“away”) + rogō (“ask, inquire, propose”). See rogation.
abrogate.example: Whose laws, like those of the Medes and Persian, they cannot alter or abrogate.
abrogate.exampleSense: To annul by an authoritative act; to abolish by the authority of the maker or their successor; to repeal; — applied to the repeal of laws, decrees, ordinances, the abolition of customs, etc.

egesta.o: From Latin ēgesta (“discharged [matter etc.]”), plural of Latin ēgestum (“[that which is] discharged”), an adjectivization of the perfect passive participle of Latin to discharge; to carry out.

ecstatics.o: plural of ecstatic. Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἐκστατικός (ekstatikós). By surface analysis, ecstasy + -tic.

ecstatic.o: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἐκστατικός (ekstatikós). By surface analysis, ecstasy + -tic.
ecstatic.example: The moment of ejaculation in mammiferous animals is accompanied by universal excitement of the whole body, a kind of slight convulsion, which terminates in a comatose or exstatic state.

ecstasy.o: From Old French estaise (“ecstasy, rapture”), from Latin ecstasis, from Ancient Greek ἔκστασις (ékstasis), from ἐξίστημι (exístēmi, “to displace”), from ἐκ (ek, “out”) and ἵστημι (hístēmi, “to stand”).
ecstasy.example: They were thrown into ecstasies of suspicion by finding that we possessed a French translation of Hitler's Mein Kampf.
ecstasy.exampleSense: A state of emotion so intense that a person is carried beyond rational thought and self-control.

quiche.o: Borrowed from French quiche, from Lorraine Rhine Franconian Küeche (“cake”), from Middle High German kuoche (German Kuchen, English kuchen), from Old High German kuocho, kuohho, from Proto-Germanic *kōkô (English cookie), from Proto-Indo-European *gog- (“ball-shaped object”), whence also English cake (via Proto-Germanic *kakǭ (“cake”)). Compare Persian کوکو (kuku, “quiche”). More at cake. The sexually alluring sense originates from the 2013 Australian TV sitcom Ja'mie: Private School Girl, where it is defined as "a step above hot".
quiche.example: I'm not even bragging, but me and my friends are pretty much quiche.
quiche.exampleSense: Extremely appealing to look at; sexually alluring.

quickie.example: We had a quickie; I didn’t come & was only telling of the future where there was better bed fucks & us living contentedly as we walked slowly across town again to her home.

lenient.o: From Middle French lénient, from Latin lēniēns (whence -i- + -ent), present participle of lēnīre (“to soften, soothe”), from lēnis (“soft”).
lenient.example: The standard is fairly lenient, so use your discretion.
lenient.exampleSense: Lax; not strict; tolerant of dissent or deviation.

boi.example: You, tattooed, butch boi with experience and a leash.
boi.exampleSense: A male bottom (i.e. submissive partner), defined not by junior age, but by his obedient role and submission to the dominant "top".

demote.o: From de- (“down”) + promote (“advance in rank/status (ending abstracted)”).
demote.example: James was demoted from branch manager to assistant manager due to his poor discipline.
demote.exampleSense: To lower the rank or status of.

starlight.example: Bright starlight enabled us to see much of the country.
starlight.exampleSense: Light emitted from stars other than the Sun.

stoplight.example: The rear lamps are combined with the service stoplights and are contained in stoplight part and blackout marker light assemblies at the rear of the vehicle.
stoplight.exampleSense: A light on the rear of a vehicle that is activated when braking; a brake light.

spotlight.example: We spotlight the star, but the supporting cast has all the great lines in this scene.

symmetrize.o: Either from French symétriser or symmetry + -ize.

symmetric.o: From symmetry + -ic, from Latin symmetria, from Ancient Greek συμμετρία (summetría).
symmetric.example: "Is a sibling of" is a symmetric relation.
symmetric.exampleSense: Of a relation R on a set S, such that xRy if and only if yRx for all members x and y of S (that is, if the relation holds between any element and a second, it also holds between the second and the first).

cubicle.o: From Late Middle English cubicle, from Latin cubiculum (“bedroom”). Doublet of cubiculum.
cubicle.example: I sit in a cubicle and I update bank software for the 2000 switch.
cubicle.exampleSense: A small separate part or one of the compartments of a room, especially in a work environment.

probation.o: Inherited from Middle English probacioun, from Middle French probation, from Old French probacion, from Latin probatio (“a trying, inspection, examination”), from probare, past participle probatus (“to test, examine”); see probate, probe, prove.
probation.example: You'll be on probation for first six months. After that, if you work out, they'll hire you permanently.
probation.exampleSense: A period of time when a person occupies a position only conditionally and may be removed if certain conditions are not met.

stationery.example: We can pick up more paper and pens at the stationery store.

stationary.o: From Latin stationarius, from statio, ultimately from stō (“to stand”). Doublet of stationer.
stationary.example: The train remained stationary for a few moments, before lurching forward along the track.

serpent.o: From Middle English serpent, from Old French serpent (“snake, serpent”), from Latin serpēns (“snake”), present active participle of serpere (“to creep, crawl”), from Proto-Italic *serpō, from Proto-Indo-European *serp-. In this sense, displaced native Old English nǣdre (“snake, serpent”), whence Modern English adder. Compare Sanskrit सर्प (sarpa, “snake”), which is a descendant of the same Proto-Indo-European word as serpent.
serpent.example: He falls into it, who has digg'd a Pit.
serpent.exampleSense: A snake, especially a large or dangerous one.

slip up.example: I hope I don't slip up during my presentation.
slip up.exampleSense: To err, falter; to make a mistake, especially a seemingly small error.

slippy.o: From slip + -y. Compare Old English slipiġ (“slippy, slimy, viscid”).
slippy.example: It was darker now and there were stones and bits of wood on the strand and slippy seaweed.

bracer.o: From Middle English bracer, from Old French braceure; equivalent to brace + -er.
bracer.example: To prevent the bow string from hanging on the left arm, it is covered with a piece of smooth leather, fastened on the outside of the arm, this is called a bracer.
bracer.exampleSense: A covering to protect the arm of the bowman from the vibration of the string.

transmigrate.o: Borrowed from Latin trānsmigrō. By surface analysis, trans- + migrate.

transmitter.example: Epinephrine and dopamine are two other catecholamine transmitters.
transmitter.exampleSense: One who or that which transmits something (in all senses).

transmit.o: From Middle English transmitten, borrowed from Latin trānsmittō (“transmit”, verb, literally “across-send”).
transmit.example: A Mayday call was transmitted by the stricken vessel.
transmit.exampleSense: To send out a signal (as opposed to receive).

lithium.o: From New Latin lithium, from Ancient Greek λίθος (líthos, “stone”) + -ium.
lithium.example: Already, beautiful places are being wrecked by an electric vehicle resource rush. Lithium mining, for example, is now poisoning rivers and depleting groundwater from Tibet to Bolivia.
lithium.exampleSense: The simplest alkali metal, the lightest solid element, and the third lightest chemical element (symbol Li) with an atomic number of 3. It is a soft, silvery metal.

profusion.o: From Middle French profusion, from Late Latin profusio.
profusion.example: His hair, in great profusion, streamed down over his shoulders.
profusion.exampleSense: abundance; the state of being profuse; a cornucopia

propulsive.o: Formed from Latin prōpulsus with the suffix -ive.

propulsion.o: Borrowed from Medieval Latin propulsio, propulsionis, from the past participle of Latin propello (“to drive forward, drive forth, drive away, drive out”).
propulsion.example: This propulsion provides an initial velocity for the vehicle in a short time span.

backroom.example: The vote for a new prime minister will involve plenty of backroom bargaining, while Thailand struggles to revive its faltering economy.

backdrop.example: Against a backdrop of falling interest rates, the new savings account is looking less appealing.

uncountable.example: Cantor’s “diagonal proof” shows that the set of real numbers is uncountable.
uncountable.exampleSense: Incapable of being put into one-to-one correspondence with the natural numbers or any subset thereof.

uncontrollability.example: These are the images that demonstrate the force — the mesmerizing uncontrollability that is at the heart of weather's primal draw, and that holds the power to make weather fanatics out of even those of us whose first instinct is to run.

uncontrollable.example: She got the uncontrollable urge for some chocolate.
uncontrollable.exampleSense: Not able to be controlled, contained or governed.

uncontrolled.example: Into the gnarled uncontrolled hand swaying over the bunk the dog laid his paw.

legislature.o: 1676, from stem of legislator + -ure, cognate with French législature.

legislative.example: The legislative framework provides much opportunity for correction and amendment of poorly thought out bills.
legislative.exampleSense: Making, or having the power to make, a law or laws; lawmaking.

soundtrack.example: The world, in turn, watched, clicked, cried, danced, sang along, swooned, caravanned to stadiums and movie theaters, let her work soundtrack their lives.
soundtrack.exampleSense: To provide, or to act as the sound or music component of a film

paycheck.o: From pay (“wages or salary”) + check (“a means of payment”).
paycheck.example: He was delighted after getting his first paycheck, but subsequently blew it all on the horses.
paycheck.exampleSense: Money received on payday as payment for work performed.

punchy.o:
adj: From punch + -y.

adj: From punch (“short fat person”) + -y.
punchy.example: I was so sleep-deprived I was starting to get punchy.
punchy.exampleSense: Behaving or appearing punch-drunk, reacting poorly.

spat.o:
verb: From Old English spittan, spætan.

noun: Uncertain; perhaps related to spit.

noun: Shortening of spatterdash, from spatter + dash. 1779.

noun: 1804. American English, probably imitative.

noun: Attested from 1823.

noun: From Latin spatium (“space”).
spat.example: There was no sink in the room so we spat out the window.
spat.exampleSense: simple past and past participle of spit

perceptive.example: He is so perceptive when it comes to other people's feelings.
perceptive.exampleSense: Having or showing keenness or sharpness of perception, insight, understanding, or intuition.

predecease.example: Frederick, Prince of Wales, predeceased his father and never became king.

surcease.o: From Anglo-Norman surseser, from Old French sursis, past participle of surseoir, from Latin supersedēre. Spelling later influenced by association with unrelated cease, which likely also influenced the meaning. Related to supersede.
surcease.example: And first of all, it is more then time, there were an ende and surcease made of this immodest and deformed manner of writting latelie entertained, whereby matter of religion is handled in the stile of the stage.
surcease.exampleSense: Cessation; stop, stopping; end. Respite, intermission.

deceased.o: From decease + -ed, from Middle English deceas via Old French [Term?], from Latin dēcessus (“departure”), equivalent to dēced-, variation of dēcēdō, dēcēdere (“to go away”).
deceased.example: The executor's commission for winding up the deceased estate was 3.5%.

decease.o: From Old French deces (Modern French décès), from Latin dēcessus (“departure”).
decease.example: After which usurped victorie, he presently deceased: and partly through the excessive joy he thereby conceived.

unceasingly.example: All concerned, more particularly those in charge of the depots, worked unceasingly for long hours.

shallows.o: plural of shallow. From Middle English schalowe (“not deep, shallow”); apparently related to Middle English schalde, schold, scheld, schealde (“shallow”), from Old English sċeald (“shallow”), from Proto-Germanic *skal-, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kelh₁- (“to parch, dry out”). Related to Low German Scholl (“shallow water”). See also shoal.
shallows.example: You'll have to navigate carefully through these shallows.
shallows.exampleSense: An area in a large body of water with many shallow areas.

turnaround.example: They tried to reduce their turnaround on incoming paperwork.
turnaround.exampleSense: The carrying out of a task; the time required to carry it out.

reverse gear.example: Reverse gear, air-operated, is incorporated in the transmission.
reverse gear.exampleSense: A gear in a vehicle transmission which, when selected, makes the vehicle to move in the direction the driver has the back.

twister.o: From Middle English twyster, equivalent to twist + -er.
twister.example: He, twirling his twister, makes a twist of the twine.
twister.exampleSense: An instrument used in twisting or making twists.

twisty.example: The document is divided up into a number of sections controlled by twisties.
twisty.exampleSense: A collapsible element having a marker such as a small triangle that rotates between horizontal and vertical positions to indicate whether the content is currently hidden or expanded.

go ahead.example: Go ahead and eat without me. I expect to be very late.
go ahead.exampleSense: Used to grant permission for or to give endorsement of a suggestion or proposal.

go-ahead.o: Deverbal from go ahead. As a name for footwear, from the fact that one can't easily step backwards wearing them.
go-ahead.example: You can start as soon as you get the go-ahead from the president.
go-ahead.exampleSense: Approval, agreement, or instruction to begin or proceed.

accord.o:
noun: From Middle English accord, from Old French acort, from acorder (see verb below).

verb: From Middle English accorden, acorden, borrowed from Old French acorder (compare modern French accord and accorder), from Vulgar Latin *accordāre, from Latin concordāre via prefix substitution (with Latin ad-), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ḱḗr ~ *ḱr̥d-, and thus distantly related to English heart (via Proto-Germanic *hertô).
accord.example: These all continued with one accord in prayer and supplication, with the women, and Mary the mother of Iesus, and with his brethen.
accord.exampleSense: Agreement or concurrence of opinion, will, or action.

gratify.o: From French gratifier, from Latin grātificō (“to do a favor to, oblige, please, gratify”), from grātus (“kind, pleasing”) + faciō (“to make”).

antagonist.o: From Latin antagonista, from Ancient Greek ἀνταγωνιστής (antagōnistḗs, “opponent”) (ἀντί (antí, “against”) + ἀγωνιστής (agōnistḗs, “a combatant, pleader, actor”)), from ἀνταγωνίζομαι (antagōnízomai, “to antagonize”).
antagonist.example: A flexor, which bends a part, is the antagonist of an extensor, which extends it.
antagonist.exampleSense: A muscle that acts in opposition to another.

antagonism.o: From Ancient Greek ἀνταγωνιστής (antagōnistḗs, “opponent”), from ἀνταγωνίζομαι (antagōnízomai, “antagonize”), from ἀγών (agṓn, “contest”) (English agon).
antagonism.example: Their longstanding antagonism is manifested in frequent scuffles and shouting matches.
antagonism.exampleSense: A strong natural dislike or hatred; antipathy.

rehearse.o: From Middle English rehersen, from Anglo-Norman reherser (“to repeat word-for-word”).
rehearse.example: It was plain that he'd been rehearsed a lot, but he wasn't letter-perfect by any manner of means.
rehearse.exampleSense: To cause to rehearse; to instruct by rehearsal.

retroactive.o: First attested in 1610. From French rétroactif, equivalent to retro- + active.
retroactive.example: Rather, he hoped there was some legal trickeration he could deploy to get a retroactive water right filed and end-run the opposition.
retroactive.exampleSense: Extending in scope, effect, application or influence to a prior time or to prior conditions

retrofit.o: The verb is derived from retro- (prefix meaning ‘back; backward’) + fit (“to equip, supply”). The noun, which is first attested later than the verb, is either derived: * from the verb (see above); or * from retro- + fit (“act of fitting; conformity of elements one to another”).
retrofit.example: Trams dating from 2012 have been retro-fitted with lithium batteries, with the conversions starting in 2018.
retrofit.exampleSense: To supply (a device, structure, etc.) with new components or parts that were not previously available or installed; to modernize.

retroact.example: In their eyes the past was good or bad for itself, and the present good or bad for itself, and an evil past could no more shadow a virtuous present than a virtuous present could retroact to brighten or redeem an ugly past.
retroact.exampleSense: To act retrospectively or in opposition

retro.o: Borrowed from French rétro, ultimately from Latin retro.
retro.example: Richard Leacock's 1981 film portrait, Louise Brooks, was shown during a retro of Ms. Brooks's films at the Walker Art Center.

squat.o:
adj: From Middle English squatten, from Old French esquatir, escatir (“compress, press down, lay flat, crush”), from es- (“ex-”) + quatir (“press down, flatten”), from Vulgar Latin *coactire (“press together, force”), from Latin coāctus, perfect passive participle of cōgō (“force together, compress”). The sense “nothing” is synchronically analyzable as a clipping of diddly-squat, although diachronically the direction of derivation is uncertain.

noun: From Latin squatina.
squat.example: Sit in a squat, with your feet a comfortable distance apart.
squat.exampleSense: A position assumed by bending deeply at the knees while resting on one's feet.

board.o:
noun: Board (duplicate bridge) From Middle English boord, boorde, bord, bourd, burd, from Old English bord, from Proto-West Germanic *bord, from Proto-Germanic *burdą (“board, plank; edge; table”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰers- (“tip, top”) + *-dʰeti or *bʰerH- (“to pierce; to strike”) + *-dʰeti. The senses "food" and "council" are by metonymy from the sense "table".
