falsity.o: Corresponding to false + -ity. From Middle French fausseté, Old French falseté, from Late Latin falsitas, from Latin falsus.
falsity.example: The belief that the world is flat is a falsity.
falsity.exampleSense: Something that is false; an untrue assertion.

falsify.o: From French falsifier, from Late Latin falsificāre (“make false, corrupt, counterfeit, falsify”), from Latin falsificus, from falsus (“false”), corresponding to false + -ify.
falsify.example: The Irish bards use to forge and falsify everything as they list, to please or displease any man.
falsify.exampleSense: To alter so as to make false; especially when done with intent to deceive.

impersonate.example: The conman managed to impersonate several executives.
impersonate.exampleSense: To pretend to be (a different person); to assume the identity of, especially when there is an intent to deceive.

impersonal.o: From French impersonnel, from Latin impersōnālis, from im- (“not”) + persōnālis (“personal”), equivalent to im- + personal.
impersonal.example: She sounded impersonal as she gave her report of the Nazi death camps.

slide show.o: Alternative spelling of slideshow. From slide + show.

sideshow.example: An emergency brake to limit in-work benefits for EU migrants is a “sideshow” that will fail to reduce the number of arrivals to the UK, Alan Johnson has said.
sideshow.exampleSense: An incidental spectacle that diverts attention from a larger concern.

glare.o: From Middle English glaren, from Old English *glærian, from Proto-West Germanic *glarōn. Cognate with dialectal Middle Dutch glariën (“to glisten; sparkle”), Low German glaren (“to shine brightly; glow; burn”), Middle High German glaren (“to shine brightly”). Related to glower, glass.
glare.example: He walked in late, with the teacher glaring at him the whole time.

perch.o:
noun: From Middle English perche, from Old French perche, from Latin perca, from Ancient Greek πέρκη (pérkē, “perch”), cognate with περκνός (perknós, “dark-spotted”). Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *perḱ-, whence also Old English forn (“trout”), German Forelle (“trout”).

noun: From Middle English perche, from Old French perche, from Latin pertica (“staff, long pole, measuring rod”).
perch.example: [W]inning Wimbledon at just 19 years, earning her rightful place on the perch as world number one.
perch.exampleSense: A position that is secure and advantageous, especially one which is prominent or elevated.

cum.o:
prep: Learned borrowing from Latin cum (“with”).

noun: Variant of come, attested (in the basic sense "come, move from further to nearer, arrive") since Old English. The sexual sense of come is attested since the 1650s. In this sense and spelling, attested from 1970s.
cum.example: Despite claims to the contrary, a woman can cum from anal sex alone.
cum.exampleSense: To have an orgasm, to feel the sensation of an orgasm.

bluebell.example: The cutting sides were gay with heather in bloom, and masses of dainty Scots bluebells, while patches of clear sky overhead were bringing life and colour to the sea.
bluebell.exampleSense: Various flowering plants with blue, usually pendulous, flowers. In other genera Scottish bluebell (harebell) (Campanula rotundifolia)

pressure.example: Apply pressure to the wound to stop the bleeding.
pressure.exampleSense: A pressing; a force applied to a surface.

genome.o: From earlier genom, from German Genom, coined by German botanist Hans Winkler in 1920 as a blend of Gen (“gene”) + Chromosom (“chromosome”). By surface analysis, gen(e) + -ome, or a blend of gen(e) + (chromos)ome. Spelling altered to reflect the surface analysis.

unfair.o: From Middle English unfair (“unattractive, unseemly”), from Old English unfæġer (“ugly”), equivalent to un- + fair.
unfair.example: It was unfair for the boss to give larger bonuses to his friends.

paternity.o: From Middle French paternité, from Old French, from Latin paternitās (“paternity”), from paternus (“of or pertaining to a father, paternal”) + -itās, from pater (“father”).
paternity.example: The author asserted her right to paternity on the book's copyright page.

lychee.o: * /ˈlaɪ̯.t͡ʃi/, /laɪ̯ˈt͡ʃiː/ from Cantonese 荔枝 (lai⁶ zi¹) * /ˈlit͡ʃi/ from Hokkien 荔枝 (lē-chi) Doublet of litchi and lichi.

dictum.o: From Latin dictum (“proverb, maxim”), from dictus (“having been said”), perfect passive participle of dico (“to say”). Compare Spanish dicho (“saying”). Doublet of dict.
dictum.example: 1. The utmost in steam producing capacity permitted by weight and dimensions; in other words, capacity to boil water—H. A. Ivatt's old dictum.
dictum.exampleSense: An authoritative statement; a dogmatic saying; a maxim, an apothegm.

accede.o: First attested in the early 15th century. From Middle English acceden, from Latin accēdō (“approach, accede”), formed from ad (“to, toward, at”) + cēdō (“move, yield”) (English cede). Compare French accéder. Unrelated to ascend, aside from the common ad prefix.
accede.example: Maintenon had been governess to the children in the late 1670s before acceding to the king's favours.
accede.exampleSense: To come to an office, state or dignity; to attain, assume (a position).

cathode.o: From Ancient Greek κατα- (kata-, “down”) and ὁδός (hodós, “journey, way”), equivalent to Ancient Greek κάθοδος (káthodos, “way down, descent”). Coined by English polymath William Whewell in 1834 for Michael Faraday, who introduced it later that year. By surface analysis, cath- (alternative form of cata-) + -ode.

anode.o: From Ancient Greek ἀνα- (ana-, “up”) and ὁδός (hodós, “path”), forming the New Greek compound ἄνοδος (ánodos). Coined by English polymath William Whewell in 1834 for Michael Faraday, who introduced it later that year. By surface analysis, an- (“up, forward, away”) + -ode (“way”).

four-square.o: Alternative spelling of foursquare. From Middle English foure square; equivalent to four + square.

icy.o: From ice + -y; cf. Old English īsiġ.
icy.example: I wasn't all the way icy. It wasn't like I could just give a girl a baby and forget about them.
icy.exampleSense: Characterized by coldness of manner; frigid; cold.

aftermath.example: In contrast to most projections of the aftermath of nuclear war, in this there is no rioting or looting.
aftermath.exampleSense: That which happens after, that which follows, usually of strongly negative connotation in most contexts, implying a preceding catastrophe.

immortal.o: From Latin immortālis, from prefix im- (“not”) (from in-) + mortālis (“mortal”) (from mors (“death”), combining form mort- + adjectival suffix -alis), equivalent to im- + mortal. Displaced native undeadly, from Old English undēadlīċ. The term referring to the Persian soldiers was a Calque of Ancient Greek ἀθάνατος (athánatos). One suggestion claimed that "Immortals" were named by the ancient Greeks because wounded soldiers were quickly replaced, while another claimed that it was because Greek informants confused Old Persian *anauša- (“immortal, without death”) with Old Persian *anūšiya- (“companion, royal bodyguard”).
immortal.example: The brutal insouciance of her fellow immortals — whether her sharp-tongued mother, Perse; or chilly Hermes; or righteous Athena enraged — proves increasingly alien to this thoughtful and compassionate woman who learns to love unselfishly.
immortal.exampleSense: One who is not susceptible to death.

immoral.example: Let marriage be held in honor among all, and let the marriage bed be undefiled, for God will judge the sexually immoral and adulterous.
immoral.exampleSense: Breaching principles of natural law, rectitude, or justice, and so inconsistent with the demands of virtue, purity, or "good morals"; not right, not moral. (Compare unethical, illegal.)

sea cucumber.o: From sea + cucumber, named in reference to its appearance. The term first appeared in common use in the 19th century, and is a calque of French concombre de mer according to the Oxford English Dictionary.

majesty.o: From Middle English majeste, mageste, from Old French majesté, from Latin maiestātem, (literally, "the quality of being greater”). Ultimately derived from Proto-Indo-European *meǵh₂s (“great”) See mega-.

offense.o: From Middle English offence, from Old French offense, from Latin offensa (“a striking against; displeasure; injury”).
offense.example: The popular late Middle Ages fictional character Robin Hood, dressed in green to symbolize the forest, dodged fines for forest offenses and stole from the rich to give to the poor. But his appeal was painfully real and embodied the struggle over wood.
offense.exampleSense: The act of offending. A crime or sin.

forward.o:
adj: From Middle English foreward, from Old English foreweard (“forward, inclined to the front, fore, early, former”), from Proto-Germanic *fura- (“fore-”), *warþaz (“turned”), equivalent to fore + -ward. Cognate with Dutch voorwaarts (“forward”), German vorwärts (“forward”).

noun: From Middle English foreward, from Old English foreweard (“condition, bargain, agreement, contract, treaty, assurance”), equivalent to fore- + ward (“ward, keeping”). Cognate with Scots forward (“covenant, compact”), Dutch voorwaarde (“condition, terms, proviso, stipulation”). More at fore-, ward.
forward.example: The forward battalion took a hammering.
forward.exampleSense: Situated toward or at the front of something. Situated toward or near the enemy lines.

jail.o: Inherited from Middle English gayole, borrowed from Anglo-Norman jaiole, from Late Latin caveola, from Latin cavea (“cage”) + -ola (diminutive ending). Doublet of caveola and related to cage. More at cajole. Fully displaced native Middle English quartern (“prison, jail, cell”), from Old English cweartern (“jail, prison”). Partially displaced native Middle English lok, from Old English loc (“enclosure, pen; jail, prison”), whence lock; and Middle English carcern, from Old English carcern, from Latin carcer (“prison, jail”). Compare these Old English words, all meaning “jail”: heaþor, heolstorloca (means also “jail cell”), clūstorloc, dung (also “dungeon”), hlinræced, nirwþ, nīedcleofa, hearmloca, and nearu.
jail.example: It has jailed environmental activists and is planning to limit the power of judicial oversight by handing a state-approved body a monopoly over bringing environmental lawsuits.

guilty.o: From Middle English gilty, gulty, from Old English gyltiġ (“offending, guilty”); equivalent to guilt + -y.
guilty.example: Do you have a guilty conscience?

abuser.example: Child sexual abusers are highly manipulative in their befriending of parents and children and are able to deceive all types of family.
abuser.exampleSense: One who abuses someone or something.

serially.example: All tickets are serially numbered by machine as they are printed, and while two tickets of the same number should not occur, it could possibly happen through a fault in the printing machine.
serially.exampleSense: In series, one after the other, as opposed to in parallel.

asexually.example: One of the pioneers was a French plant scientist named Georges Morel who figured out how to produce asexually thousands of identical orchids from one plant through cloning instead of breeding from seed.
asexually.exampleSense: In an asexual manner; without having sex.

udder.o: From Middle English udder, uddyr (also as uther, iddyr), from Old English ūder (“udder; breast”), from Proto-Germanic *ūdarą, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁ówHdʰr̥ (“udder”). Cognate with Saterland Frisian Jadder (“udder”), Dutch uier (“udder”), German Euter (“udder”), Swedish juver (“udder”), Icelandic júgur (“udder”), Vedic Sanskrit ऊधर् (ū́dhar), Ancient Greek οὖθαρ (oûthar), Latin ūber.

dating.o: present participle and gerund of date. From Middle English date, from Old French date, datil, datille, from Latin dactylus (likely via Old Provençal datil), from Ancient Greek δάκτυλος (dáktulos, “finger”) (from the resemblance of the date to a human finger), probably a folk-etymological alteration of a word from a Semitic source such as Arabic دَقَل (daqal, “variety of date palm”) or Hebrew דֶּקֶל (deqel, “date palm”). Doublet of dactyl and dactylus.
dating.example: Janet was surprised at how much casual dating had changed since she was last single.
dating.exampleSense: A form of romantic courtship typically between two individuals with the aim of assessing the other's suitability as a partner in an intimate relationship or as a spouse.

apartment.o: From French appartement, from Italian appartamento, from Spanish apartamiento (“separation, seclusion”). See apart and -ment.
apartment.example: I am Jonathan. I am in apartment B4. — I am in apartment C2.
apartment.exampleSense: A complete domicile occupying only part of a building, especially one for rent; a flat.

arrest.o: From Middle English arest (noun) and aresten (verb), from Old French areste (noun) and arester (“to stay, stop”, verb), from Vulgar Latin *arrestō, from Latin ad- (“to”) + restō (“to stop, remain behind, stay back”), from re- (“back”) + stō (“to stand”), from Proto-Indo-European *steh₂- (“to stand”), equivalent to ad- + rest. Compare French arrêter (“to stop”).
arrest.example: State police made a total of 15 drug-related arrests across the city.
arrest.exampleSense: The process of arresting a criminal, suspect etc.

footage.o: From foot (unit of length) + -age. Video footage is so called because movie film and television tape was measured in feet. The same term is still applied by analogy to digital videos which are stored on hard drives or microchips. Compare typologically French métrage.
footage.example: The footage we shot at the riot yesterday got ruined.
footage.exampleSense: An amount of film or tape that has been used to record something.

body-con.o: Alternative form of bodycon. From Japanese ボディコン (bodikon) (clipping of English body conscious), name of a fashion subculture among young Japanese women in the mid-to-late 1980s and early 1990s.

life.o: From Middle English lyf, from Old English līf, from Proto-West Germanic *līb, from Proto-Germanic *lībą (“life, body”), from *lībaną (“to remain, stay, be left”), from Proto-Indo-European *leyp- (“to stick, glue”). Cognate with Scots life, leif (“life”), Saterland Frisian Lieuw (“body”), West Frisian liif (“body”), Cimbrian laip (“body”), Dutch lijf (“body”) and leven (“life”), German Leib (“body; womb”) and Leben (“life”), Low German Lief (“body; life”), Luxembourgish Leif, Läif (“body”), Vilamovian łaowa (“life”), Yiddish לײַב (layb, “body”), Danish, Norwegian Bokmål, Norwegian Nynorsk, and Swedish liv (“life; waist”), Faroese lív (“life”), Icelandic líf (“life”). Related to belive. The sense "biography" is likely a semantic loan from Medieval Latin vīta (“biography; hagiography”).
life.example: “My Continental prominence is improving,” I commented dryly.
life.exampleSense: A period of time during which something has existence. The period during which one (a person, an animal, a plant; a civilization, species; a star; etc) is alive.

drug.o:
noun: From Middle English drogge (“medicine”), from Middle French drogue, drocque (“tincture, pharmaceutical product”) (c. 1462), from Middle Dutch or Middle Low German droge, as in droge vate (“dry vats, dry barrels”), mistaking droge for the contents, which were usually dried herbs, plants or wares. Droge comes from Middle Dutch drōghe (“dry”), from Old Dutch drōgi (“dry”), from Proto-Germanic *draugiz (“dry, hard”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dʰerǵʰ- (“to strengthen; become hard or solid”), from *dʰer- (“to hold, hold fast, support”). Cognate with English dry, Dutch droog (“dry”), German trocken (“dry”).

verb: Germanic ablaut formation. If old, a doublet of drew, from Middle English drug, drog, drugh, drogh, from Old English drōg, from Proto-Germanic *drōg; compare Dutch droeg, German trug, Swedish drog. If secondary, probably formed by analogy with dug.
drug.example: Aspirin is a drug that reduces pain, acts against inflammation and lowers body temperature.
drug.exampleSense: A substance used to treat an illness, relieve a symptom, or modify a chemical process in the body for a specific purpose.

hydrated.o: simple past and past participle of hydrate. From French hydrate, from Ancient Greek ὕδωρ (húdōr, “water”) + -ate.
hydrated.example: We took the powdered milk and hydrated it until it was drinkable.
hydrated.exampleSense: simple past and past participle of hydrate

hydrate.o: From French hydrate, from Ancient Greek ὕδωρ (húdōr, “water”) + -ate.
hydrate.example: A lotion can hydrate the skin.
hydrate.exampleSense: To take up, consume or become linked to water.

evection.o: From Latin evectiōnem, from evectiō (“act of carrying”), from evect-, past participle stem of evehō (“to carry together”), combination of ex- and vehō.

other world.o: Alternative form of otherworld. From Middle English othyr world, oþerr werelld, oþer world, from Old English ōþer weoruld, equivalent to other + world.

otherworldly.o: From other world (“a world beyond death; a world other than the everyday world”) + -ly (suffix meaning having the likeness of, resembling forming adjectives).
otherworldly.example: Dana has the otherworldly temperament of a mystic.
otherworldly.exampleSense: Of, concerned with, or preoccupied with a different world than that of the tangible here and now, such as a heavenly, spiritual, or imaginary world.

appease.o: From Middle English apesen, from Old French apeser (“to pacify, bring to peace”).
appease.example: It's been slowly hacked back, amid fears of escalating costs, by politicians who have also increased those costs by adding expensive structures such as tunnels to appease opponents.
appease.exampleSense: To make quiet; to calm; to reduce to a state of peace; to dispel (anger or hatred).

appraise.o:
verb: From Middle English apreisen, from Old French aprisier (“apraise, set a price on”) (compare modern French apprécier), from Late Latin appretiare, from ad- + Latin pretium (“price, value”) (English precious), from which also appreciate, a doublet.

verb: Form of apprise in use since 1706 but considered incorrect by some.
appraise.example: At the end of the contract, you will be appraised by your line manager.
appraise.exampleSense: To judge the performance of someone, especially a worker.

withdrawn.o: past participle of withdraw. PIE word *wí From Middle English withdrawen, withdrauen (“to depart, leave, move away; (reflexive) to go away; (reflexive) to leave someone’s service; (often reflexive) to draw back or retreat (from a battlefield or dangerous place), withdraw; to abandon, desert; to go, go forth; to move; of the sea, water, etc.: to (cause to) ebb, recede, subside; to disappear; to slacken, wane; (often reflexive) to cease, stop; to desist, refrain; (reflexive) to go back on, recant; to avoid, eschew; to bring under control, contain, suppress; to curb, curtail; to delay, put off; to demur, refuse; to carry or take away, deprive of, remove; to contract, draw away or in, retract; to deny, refuse; to revoke; to withhold; to divert; to separate; to adopt, borrow, imitate”) [and other forms], from with- (prefix meaning ‘away; back’) + drawen, drauen (“to drag, pull, tow, tug, draw [and other senses]”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dʰregʰ- (“to drag, pull; to run”)); see further at with- and draw. The English word is analysable as with- + draw.

stipulate.o:
verb: From Latin stipulātus, perfect active participle of stipulor (“to demand a formal promise, stipulate”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

adj: From stipule + -ate (adjective-forming suffix).
stipulate.example: In general, steel springs were stipulated for primary suspension, although rubber was accepted for auxiliary springing; hydraulic dampers were specified and the use of laminated springs ruled out.
stipulate.exampleSense: To require (something) as a condition of a contract or agreement.

forget.o: From Middle English forgeten, forgiten, foryeten, forȝiten, from Old English forġietan (“to forget”) [influenced by Old Norse geta ("to get, to guess")], from Proto-West Germanic *fragetan (“to give up, forget”). Equivalent to for- + get. Cognate with : * Scots forget, forȝet (“to forget”), * West Frisian fergette, ferjitte, forjitte (“to forget”), * Dutch vergeten (“to forget”), * German vergessen (“to forget”).
forget.example: I forgot my car keys in the living room.

forest.o: Inherited from Middle English forest, from Old French forest, from Early Medieval Latin forestis. The Latin could be: * from foris (“outside”), as in forestis (silva) "(wood) outside," * or from Frankish or Proto-West Germanic *furhisti (“forest, fir-grove, wooded land”), equivalent to fir + hurst. In which case, related to Old English fyrhþe (“forested land”), Old High German forst, forsti (“forest”), Old Norse fýri (“pine forest”). Doublet of frith. Cognate with Dutch vorst (“copse, grove, woodland”), German Forst (“forest”). In this sense, mostly displaced the native Middle English wode, from Old English wudu (modern English wood) and Middle English wald, wold, wæld, from Old English wald, weald (modern English wald, weald, wold).
forest.example: From the view-point of national economy professor Fehér communicates to us most interesting facts, which he has established in an important question now of actuality : in the subject of foresting the Great Hungarian Plains.
forest.exampleSense: To cover an area with trees.

forfend.o: From Middle English forfenden (“to ward off, protect, prohibit”), equivalent to for- + fend.

forfeiture.o: From Middle English forfeture, from Old French forfaiture.
forfeiture.example: We conclude that the government has forfeited any claim of forfeiture, so we proceed to consider the merits.
forfeiture.exampleSense: Any loss occasioned by one's own actions.

forfeit.o: From Middle English forfait from ca. 1300, from Old French forfait (“crime”), originally the past participle of forfaire (“to transgress”), and Medieval Latin foris factum. During the 15th century, the sense shifted from the crime to the penalty for the crime.
forfeit.example: He who murders pays the forfeit of his own life.
forfeit.exampleSense: A thing forfeited; that which is taken from somebody in requital of a misdeed committed; that which is lost, or the right to which is alienated, by a crime, breach of contract, etc.

indicate.o: Borrowed from Latin indicātus, perfect passive participle of indicō (“to point out, indicate”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from in- (“in, to”) + dicō (“to declare, (originally) to point”). See also diction and index.
indicate.example: The guard blew his whistle to indicate imminent departure.
indicate.exampleSense: To point out; to discover; to direct to a knowledge of; to show; to make known.

domicile.o: Inherited from Middle English domicelle, domicylie, from Middle French domicile and directly from Latin domicilium.
domicile.example: The answer depends on which state he was domiciled in at his death.
domicile.exampleSense: To have a domicile in a particular place.

cypress.o: From Middle English cipres, from Old French cipres (French cyprès), from Late Latin cypressus; compare Hebrew גֹּפֶר (gōp̄er), the name of the tree whose wood was used to make the ark (Genesis. vi:14), also κύπρος (relating to aromatic pitch).
cypress.example: Have a tree or two the witches particularly like, such as the alder, larch, cypress and hemlock; then, to counteract any possible evil effects, there must be a holly, yew, hazel, elder, mountain ash or juniper.
cypress.exampleSense: An evergreen coniferous tree with flattened shoots bearing small scale-like leaves, whose dark foliage is sometimes associated with mourning, in family Cupressaceae, especially the genera Cupressus and Chamaecyparis.

big time.example: A Wheel of Fortune contestant was about to win a shot at the million dollar grand prize when he bumbled his answer and lost out big time.
big time.exampleSense: By a large margin; with great significance.

monetize.o: From French monétiser From Latin monēta (whence monnaie) + -iser.
monetize.example: We considered monetizing our computer help forums by inserting ad banners.
monetize.exampleSense: To make an activity profit-generating, particularly in computer and Internet-related activities.

dependant.example: Mrs. Smith has this morning exercised the privilege of riches upon a poor dependant cousin, by sending me on business to London.

fix.o: From Middle English fixen, borrowed from Old French *fixer (attested only as ficher, fichier; > English fitch), from fix (“fastened; fixed”), from Latin fīxus (“immovable; steady; stable; fixed”), from fīgō (“to drive in; stick; fasten”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeygʷ- (“to jab; stick; set”). Related to dig.
fix.example: And Cash told me of cases where two hips take a fix together and then one pulls out his badge.
fix.exampleSense: A single dose of a narcotic drug, especially when injected.

affix.o: Borrowed from Latin affixus, perfect passive participle of affigere (from ad- + figere). By surface analysis, af- + fix.
affix.example: Look thou no further, but affix thine eye/On that bright, shiny, round, still moving mass,/The house of blessed gods, which men call sky,/All sow'd with glist'ring stars more thick than grass...
affix.exampleSense: To fix or fasten figuratively; with on or upon.

taught.o: From Middle English taught(e), tau(h)t(e), from Old English tāhte, tǣhte, from Proto-Germanic *taihtē.

issuance.example: A cover of Bobby Day's "Rockin' Robin" held down the number-96 slot for a week in 1964, but later issuances did not do as well.

form.o: From Middle English forme (“shape, figure, manner, bench, frame, seat, condition, agreement, etc.”), borrowed from Old French forme, from Latin fōrma (“shape, figure, image, outline, plan, mold, frame, case, etc., manner, sort, kind, etc.”). In sense "division grouping school students" (now dated), derived from public school nomenclature later adopted by state schools. It is sometimes said to be from the sense of "bench", where students of certain ages would sit together, though this is disputed, or alternatively from the sense of "established method of expression or practice".
form.example: As for the notion that it’s not how Sunak would have won, that doesn’t mean a whole lot coming from a guy whose recent form includes losing to Liz Truss.
form.exampleSense: To do with structure or procedure. Past history (in a given area); a habit of doing something.

placid.o: Borrowed from French placide, from Latin placidus (“peaceful, calm, placid”), from placeō (“please, satisfy”).
placid.example: April advanced to May: a bright serene May it was; days of blue sky, placid sunshine, and soft western or southern gales filled up its duration.

registry.o: A variant of registery, from Middle English regestery (“?a record book; ?a bookmark”), partly from Medieval Latin regesterium, registerium and probably also partly formed with -ery. Equivalent to register + -y.
registry.example: Regulations may specify the minimum size of lot; the allowable closures for surveys; the types of corner marks to be used; the minimum width of streets, and the procedure for dedicating them; the rules for registry of plats; and other matters.

degree.o: From Middle English degre, borrowed from Old French degré (French: degré), itself from Latin gradus, with the prefix de-.
degree.example: To what degree do the two accounts of the accident concur?
degree.exampleSense: The amount that an entity possesses a certain property; relative intensity, extent.

appliable.o: From Middle English appliable, applyable; equivalent to apply + -able.
appliable.example: He that forgets not how Antiquity named this the Conjugall or wedding number, and made it the Embleme of the most remarkable conjunction, will conceive it duely appliable unto this handsome Oeconomy, and vegetable combination [...].
appliable.exampleSense: Able to be put into use or applied; applicable.

inapplicable.example: The argument is inapplicable to the case.
inapplicable.exampleSense: Not applicable; that does not apply or cannot be applied; unsuitable or irrelevant.

applicable.o: From Old French applicable, from Medieval Latin applicabilis.
applicable.example: This rule is not applicable to the longer-standing members of the club.

particular.o: From Middle English particuler, from Anglo-Norman particuler, Middle French particuler, particulier, from Late Latin particularis (“partial; separate, individual”), from Latin particula (“(small) part”). Equivalent to particle + -ar. Compare particle.
particular.example: I don't appreciate your particular brand of cynicism.
particular.exampleSense: Specialised; characteristic of a specific person or thing.

wallcovering.example: There is no reason not to paper one wall with your favorite wallcovering — the wall with the fireplace, say, or the one where you plan to park the sofa — and paint adjacent walls a complementary color.
wallcovering.exampleSense: A covering for a wall, such as wallpaper

covering.o:
verb: Present participle or participial adjective from cover (verb) + -ing; or, from Middle English coverynge, participle form of coveren, keveren (“to cover”).

noun: From Middle English coverynge, -inge, keverynge, -inge [verbal noun of coveren, keveren (“to cover”)]; or, verbal noun from cover (verb) + -ing.

submission.o:
noun: From Middle English submissioun, from Old French soubmission, from Latin submissio, from submitto.

noun: From sub- + mission.
submission.example: Any submissions received after Friday will have marks deducted for lateness.
submission.exampleSense: The act of submitting or giving e.g. a completed piece of work.

unduly.example: The speaker unduly criticized his opponent and later apologized for this.
unduly.exampleSense: Undeservedly; in a way that is not warranted.

duly.o: From Middle English duely, dewly, dulyche, dueliche, duweliche (“rightly, properly”), equivalent to due + -ly.
duly.example: The inquest on keeper Davidson was duly held, and at the commencement seemed likely to cause Tony Palliser less anxiety than he had expected.

latex.o: Borrowed from New Latin latex (“clear fluid which is part of a humour or bodily fluid”), a later use of Latin latex (“water; liquid, fluid”). Potentially a borrowing from Ancient Greek λᾰ́τᾰξ (lắtăx, “drop of wine”), reformed by analogy to other nouns in -ex. The semantic shift, however, from drop of wine to water is difficult to explain and may indicate that both words originated from a separate language. Perhaps from the same root as Proto-Celtic *latis (Old Irish laith (“liquid, beer”), Welsh llad (“beer”)) or Proto-Germanic *ladjō- (Old High German letto (“clay, loam”), Old Norse leðja (“mud, dregs”)) or from a Pre-Greek language.

locate.o: Borrowed from Latin locātus, perfect passive participle of locō (“to place”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from locus (“place”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix). Cognate with French louer; see also local and lieu.
locate.example: The captives and emigrants whom he brought with him were located in the trans-Tiberine quarter.
locate.exampleSense: To place; to set in a particular spot or position.

port.o:
noun: From Old English port, borrowed from Latin portus (“port, harbour”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *pértus (“crossing”) (and thus a distant doublet of ford). The directional sense, attested since at least the 1500s, derives from ancient vessels with the steering oar on the right (see etymology of starboard), which therefore had to moor with their left sides facing the dock or wharf. Doublet of fjard, fjord, firth, ford, and Portus.

noun: Inherited from the Old English port, from the Latin porta (“passage, gate”), reinforced by the Old French porte. Doublet of porta.

verb: From Old French porter, from Latin portāre (“carry”). Akin to transport, portable.

noun: Named from Portuguese Porto, a city in Portugal where the wines were originally shipped from.

noun: Clipping of portmanteau.

noun: Clipping of portfolio.
port.example: Gamers can't wait until a port of the title is released on the new system.
port.exampleSense: A program that has been adapted, modified, or recoded so that it works on a different platform from the one for which it was created; the act of this adapting.

contraposition.example: The expression “Allon” indicates the unique character of this relationship: that of being together in contraposition. I belong to the Allon, and yet detach myself from it.

cosmopolitanism.o: From cosmopolitan + -ism. The sense referring obliquely to Jewishness comes from the long era in which all Jews lived in the Jewish diaspora because Jews had been banished from the ancient Jewish homeland and no new homeland yet existed. In Soviet use it was rooted in fear of transnationalism generally but took on coded or dogwhistle antisemitic qualities that were not explicitly separable from the generality.
cosmopolitanism.example: To present the world anthropologies project (WA), this article explores the existence of three kinds of anthropological cosmopolitanisms and cosmopolitics: imperial, liberal, and radical.
cosmopolitanism.exampleSense: The idea that all of humanity belongs to a single moral community.

decipher.o: As decypher, but not retaining the y from the Old French etyma of cipher (cyfre, cyffre); the i spelling tends to be preferred etymologically, being consistent with its cognates, the French déchiffrer and the Italian decifrare, and with their common ancestor, the Medieval Latin cifra, cifera, ciphra. By surface analysis, de- + cipher.
decipher.example: Truly, we need human infirmity to teach us human nature, and that to Louis had been as a sealed book; he had only seen the coloured and gilded outside: too late he had to decipher the rough and gloomy page within.
decipher.exampleSense: To make sense of a complex situation.

cypher.o: Alternative spelling of cipher. 14th century. From Middle English cifre, from Old French cyfre, cyffre (French chiffre), ultimately from Arabic صِفْر (ṣifr, “zero, empty”), from صَفَرَ (ṣafara, “to be empty”). Doublet of chiffre and zero. Sense 8 (a fault in an organ valve) may be a different word.

password.o: From pass + word. The sentry-passing sense predates the cryptographic sense and was its inspiration.
password.example: A strong password has a mixture of lowercase and uppercase letters, numbers, and punctuation marks.
password.exampleSense: A string of characters used to log in to a computer or network, to access a level in a video game, and so on; archetypally a word but nowadays often an alphanumeric string or a phrase.

cipher.o: 14th century. From Middle English cifre, from Old French cyfre, cyffre (French chiffre), ultimately from Arabic صِفْر (ṣifr, “zero, empty”), from صَفَرَ (ṣafara, “to be empty”). Doublet of chiffre and zero. Sense 8 (a fault in an organ valve) may be a different word.
cipher.example: The message was written in a simple cipher. Anyone could figure it out.
cipher.exampleSense: A method of transforming a text in order to conceal its meaning.

tamper.o:
noun: From tamp + -er.

verb: From Middle French temprer (“to temper, mix, meddle”). Doublet of temper.
tamper.example: Prosecutors argued that he would tamper with witnesses if bail was granted.
tamper.exampleSense: To try to influence someone, usually in an illegal or devious way; to try to deal (with someone).

unhampered.example: The bare arms and thighs and unhampered breasts of young American womanhood are brushing contentedly against him.

attest.o: PIE word *tréyes Borrowed from Middle French attester, from Latin attestor (“to witness to, bear witness”), from at-, combining form of ad (“to”) + testor (“to bear witness”), from testis (“a witness”).
attest.example: Dishonour not your Mothers: now attest that those whom you call'd Fathers, did beget you.
attest.exampleSense: To affirm to be correct, true, or genuine.

supereminent.o: From Middle French supereminent, and its source, Late Latin supereminens, adjectival use of Latin superēminēre (corresponding to super- + eminent).
supereminent.example: The conservatives had come into power just after his marriage, and he had held honourable though not supereminent office.
supereminent.exampleSense: Superior to or notable above all others; outstanding; supremely remarkable.

telemetry.example: We have also installed river level monitors and scour telemetry on more than 25 bridges across our network, and over the next two years we will continue to increase the number of locations fitted with these technologies.
telemetry.exampleSense: The science, and associated technology, of the automatic recording and transmission of data from a remote source to a receiving station for analysis.

tele-.o: From Ancient Greek τῆλε (têle, “at a distance, far off, far away, far from”).

thereafter.o: From Middle English therafter, theraftir, þerefter, þerafter, þeræfter, from Old English þǣræfter (“after that; thereafter”), equivalent to there + after. Cognate with Saterland Frisian deerätter (“thereafter”), West Frisian dêrefter (“behind that; thereafter”), Dutch daarachter (“behind that; thereafter”), German Low German daarachter (“behind that”), Danish derefter (“thereafter”), Swedish därefter (“thereafter”).
thereafter.example: He left; thereafter we never met again.
thereafter.exampleSense: After that, from then on; thenceforth.

promotional.example: Collect five promotional vouchers to claim your prize.
promotional.exampleSense: Of or relating to an advertising promotion; serving to promote a service, institution, business, etc.

generic.o: From Middle French générique, from Latin genus (“genus, kind”) + -ic.
generic.example: Capri pants can be a generic term for any cropped slim pants.
generic.exampleSense: Very broad; pertaining or appropriate to large classes or groups as opposed to specific instances.

course.o: From Middle English cours, from Old French cours, from Latin cursus (“course of a race”), from currō (“run”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ḱers- (“to run”). Doublet of cursus and cour.
course.example: I need to take a French course.
course.exampleSense: A sequence of events. A learning programme a series of lectures or lessons in a particular subject

predicate.o:
noun: From Middle English predicat(e), from Old French predicat (French prédicat), from Medieval Latin praedicātum (“thing said of a subject, predicate”), substantivized from the nominative neuter singular of praedicātus, the perfect passive participle praedicō (“to proclaim”), see -ate (noun-forming suffix); see also Etymology 2 below. The adjective was derived from the noun by metanalysis, see -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

verb: From Latin praedicātus, perfect passive participle of praedicō (“to publish, declare, proclaim”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), further from prae- (“before”) + dicō (“to proclaim, dedicate”), related to dīcō (“to say, tell”). Doublet of preach.
predicate.example: A propositional variable may be treated as a nullary predicate.
predicate.exampleSense: A term of a statement, where the statement may be true or false depending on whether the thing referred to by the values of the statement's variables has the property signified by that (predicative) term.

drop-in.example: We need the ultimate drop-in biofuel to make use of our expensive oil-based infrastructure.
drop-in.exampleSense: Fit to substitute for some element in a complex system without changes to the existing infrastructure.

configuration.o: From Middle French configuration, from Latin cōnfigūrātiō. Morphologically configure + -ation.

predetermined.o:
adj: From pre- + determined.

verb: See the etymology of the corresponding lemma form.

unaffected.o:
adj: From un- + affected.

verb: See the etymology of the corresponding lemma form.
unaffected.example: Since I work from home, I was unaffected by the office move.

scale up.example: Transects can be taken in localised settings and compared to local visual environments, as in this pilot study. But the technique can be scaled up to larger situations by taking multiple transects from multiple locales and combining the data.
scale up.exampleSense: To change a process in order to allow for greater quantities.

pastel.o:
noun: Borrowed from French pastel, from Italian pastello (“pastel”), from Medieval Latin pastellum (“dough, paste”), from Latin pasta (“dough, paste”), ultimately from Ancient Greek πάστη (pástē, “dough, paste”). Doublet of pastegh, pastiglia, pastila, pastilla, and pastille.

noun: Borrowed from Spanish pastel, ultimately the same word as Etymology
pastel.example: Wool was dyed in the pastel vat.

vigil.o: From Middle English vigile (“a devotional watching”), from Old French vigile, from Latin vigilia (“wakefulness, watch”), from vigil (“awake”), from Proto-Indo-European *weǵ- (“to be strong, lively, awake”). Doublet of Wigilia. See also wake and vigor, from the same root.
vigil.example: A vigil was held for Ms. Cheptegei on Wednesday night, Ms. Indimuli said, with many women praying that she would survive.
vigil.exampleSense: An instance of keeping awake during normal sleeping hours, especially to keep watch or pray.

vigilance.o: Borrowed from Middle French vigilance, from Latin vigilantia.
vigilance.example: But you must remember, my fellow-citizens, that eternal vigilance by the people is the price of liberty, and that you must pay the price if you wish to secure the blessing.

vigilant.o: From French vigilant or its source, Latin vigilans, present participle of vigilare (“stay awake”), from vigil (“awake”). Doublet of vigilante, from Spanish. Displaced Old English wacor.
vigilant.example: Be vigilant for signs of disease in your garden.
vigilant.exampleSense: Watchful, especially for danger or disorder; alert; wary

prioritize.o: From priority + -ize. First attested in 1967 as U.S. government jargon, becoming more widespread through the 1970s and ’80s, but still denounced as officialese by purists into the 1990s.
prioritize.example: Skinimalism prioritizes skin health and lets your natural beauty shine through.
prioritize.exampleSense: To value, do, or choose something first, or before other things.

irrespectively.example: This suggests that consistency plays a role irrespectively of frequency.
irrespectively.exampleSense: Without regard to conditions; not taking circumstances into consideration.

telecommunication.o: From French télécommunication. Equivalent to tele- + communication.

telecommunications.o: plural of telecommunication. From French télécommunication. Equivalent to tele- + communication.

surplus.o: From Middle English surplus, from Middle French surplus. Compare French surplus.
surplus.example: The latest shipment of goods is surplus to our needs.
surplus.exampleSense: Being or constituting a surplus; more than sufficient.

mellow.o: The adjective is derived from Late Middle English melowe, melwe (“ripe, mellow; juicy; sweet”) [and other forms]; further etymology uncertain, possibly: * from an attributive use of melow, melowe, melewe, mele (“meal from ground grain or legumes; flour; kernel of barley or lentils”) [and other forms], from Old English melo, melu (“meal (edible part of a grain or pulse); flour”), from Proto-Germanic *melwą (“ground corn; meal; flour”), from Proto-Indo-European *melh₂- (“to crush; to grind”); or * a variant of Middle English merow, merowe, meruw (“soft, tender; of a person: frail; of love: unstable, variable”) [and other forms], from Old English meru, mearu (“soft, tender; delicate, frail; callow”) [and other forms], from Proto-Germanic *marwaz (“soft, mellow; brittle, delicate”), from Proto-Indo-European *mer(w)- (“to rub; to pack”). The noun and verb are both derived from the adjective. The etymology of noun sense 3 (“close friend; lover”) is unknown, but may also be derived from the adjective. Cognates * Dutch murw (“tender”) * German mürbe (“soft, tender”) * German Low German möör (“tender”) * Old Norse mör (“tender; aching”) (Icelandic meyr (“tender”)) * Saterland Frisian muur (“tender”) * West Frisian murf (“tender”)
mellow.example: The fervour of early feeling is tempered and mellowed by the ripeness of age.
mellow.exampleSense: To cause (a person) to become calmer, gentler, and more understanding, particularly from age or experience.

jitter.o:
noun: Possibly alteration of chitter (“to tremble, shiver”), from Middle English chittern (“to twitter, chatter”). Ultimately onomatopoeic; compare didder and teeter as well as German zittern.

noun: From jit + -er.
jitter.example: Now you have mirror-clear TV without picture flopover, jitter, tear!
jitter.exampleSense: An abrupt and unwanted variation of one or more signal characteristics.

opportunism.o: From French opportunisme, equivalent to opportune + -ism.

opportunist.o: From French opportuniste, equivalent to opportune + -ist.
opportunist.example: James Milner's angled free-kick was headed on to the post by the tireless Bent and Lampard the opportunist was perfectly placed to stoop and head in from virtually on the goal-line.
opportunist.exampleSense: Someone who takes advantage of any opportunity to advance their own situation, placing expediency above principle.

opportunity.o: From opportune + -ity, from Middle French opportunité, from Latin opportūnitās.
opportunity.example: Having a holiday is a great opportunity to relax.

opportunistic.example: The danger now isn't so much from the AIDS virus itself as from opportunistic infections.
opportunistic.exampleSense: Taking advantage of situations that arise.

experience.o: From Middle English experience, from Old French, from Latin experientia (“a trial, proof, experiment, experimental knowledge, experience”), from experiens, present participle of experiri (“to try, put to the test, undertake, undergo”), from ex (“out”) + peritus (“experienced, expert”), past participle of *periri (“to go through”); see expert and peril. Displaced native Old English āfandung (“experience”) and āfandian (“to experience”).
experience.example: Whence has it all the materials of reason and knowledge? To this I answer in one word, from experience.
experience.exampleSense: A collection of events and/or activities from which an individual or group may gather knowledge, opinions, and skills.

parley.o: From Middle English parlai (“speech, parley”), from Old French parler (“to talk; to speak”), from Late Latin parabolō, from Latin parabola (“comparison”), from Ancient Greek παραβολή (parabolḗ), from παρά (pará, “beside”) with βολή (bolḗ, “throwing”). Doublet of palaver.
parley.example: We yield on parley, but are stormed in vain.
parley.exampleSense: A conference, especially one between enemies.

sunlight.o: From Middle English sonnelight, sunneliht, from Old English sunnan lēoht (“sunlight”), equivalent to sun + light. Cognate with Dutch zonlicht (“sunlight”), German Low German Sünnenlücht (“sunlight”), German Sonnenlicht (“sunlight”).
sunlight.example: Sunlight on the skin gives you vitamin D.
sunlight.exampleSense: All the electromagnetic radiation given off by the Sun, especially that in the visible spectrum that bathes the Earth.

arbitral.o: From French arbitral, from Latin arbitrālis, from arbiter.

screenshot.o: From screen + shot (“(photography) single unbroken sequence of photographic exposures”).
screenshot.example: To help to improve the software, make sure to screenshot any bugs you find.
screenshot.exampleSense: To take a screenshot of something.

modulus.o: Learned borrowing from French module as Latin modulus. Doublet of module and mold.

snip.o: From Dutch snippen (“to snip; shred”) or Low German snippen (“to snip; shred”), of imitative origin. Compare snap.
snip.example: It was true about the fanmaking; the table and floor were littered with snips of paper.
snip.exampleSense: A piece cut out by snipping.

regain.o: From Middle French regaigner (French regagner). By surface analysis, re- + gain.
regain.example: Sarkozy's total will be seen as a personal failure. It is the first time an outgoing president has failed to win a first-round vote in the past 50 years and makes it harder for Sarkozy to regain momentum.
regain.exampleSense: To get back; to recover possession of.

live it up.example: Love in an elevator. Livin' it up when I'm going down!
live it up.exampleSense: To enjoy oneself, to have fun.

labyrinth.o: From Middle English laberynt, laberynthe, from Latin labyrinthus, from Ancient Greek λᾰβύρῐνθος (lăbúrĭnthos, “a maze”).
labyrinth.example: Above all, he flatters the men by emphasising their numerical victory: a British regiment may have turned into a troop, but it left behind it 'labyrinthed legions' of dead Russians.
labyrinth.exampleSense: to render lost and confused, as if in a labyrinth

dwelling.o:
noun: From Middle English dwellynge, dwellyng (“delay, continuance, abode”), equivalent to dwell + -ing. More at dwell.

verb: See the etymology of the corresponding lemma form.
dwelling.example: The old house served as a dwelling for Albert.
dwelling.exampleSense: A house or place in which a person lives; a habitation, a home.

supportive.example: I had a very supportive coach who helped me.

wholehearted.o: From whole + hearted. First appears before 1628 in the publications of John Preston, a clergyman in the Church of England.

shimmer.o:
verb: From Middle English schimeren, from Old English sċymrian, sċimrian, sċimerian, from Proto-Germanic *skimarōną. Cognate with Dutch schemeren, German schimmern.

noun: From shim + -er.
shimmer.example: He’d aimed film lamps at the rectangular pools, which sent reflections up the gallery wall in veined and fractured shimmers.
shimmer.exampleSense: A faint or veiled and tremulous gleam or shining.

withered.o: simple past and past participle of wither. From Middle English widren, wydderen (“to dry up, shrivel”), related to or perhaps an alteration of Middle English wederen (“to expose to weather”), from Old English wederian (“to expose to weather, exhibit a change of weather”). Cognates From Proto-Germanic: Dutch verwederen, Dutch verweren (“to erode by weather”), German verwittern, wittern (“to be ruined by weather; to erode”), Swedish vittra (“wither”). More at weather.
withered.example: Lying on the floor was a dead man, in evening dress, with a knife in his heart. He was withered, wrinkled, and loathsome of visage. It was not till they had examined the rings that they recognized who it was.
withered.exampleSense: Shrivelled, shrunken or faded, especially due to lack of water.

proxy.o:
adj: Inherited from Middle English procucie, contraction of procuracie, from Anglo-Norman procuracie, from Medieval Latin procuratia, from Latin prōcūrātiō, from Latin prōcūrō (“to manage, administer”) (English procure). Compare proctor.

noun: proximity + -y.
proxy.example: I have no man's proxy: I speak only for myself.
proxy.exampleSense: The authority to act for another, especially when written.

suffix.o: Borrowed from Latin suffīxus (“suffix”), from sub- (“under”) + fīxus (perfect passive participle of fīgere (“to fasten, fix”)), equivalent to sub- + -fix.
suffix.exampleSense: A morpheme added at the end of a word to modify the word's meaning.

detached.o: simple past and past participle of detach. From Old French destachier, from the same root as attach; compare French détacher and Portuguese and Spanish destacar.

fan.o:
noun: Inherited from Middle English fan, inherited from Old English fann (“a winnowing, fan”), derived from Latin vannus (“fan for winnowing grain”), derived from Proto-Indo-European *h₂weh₁- (“to blow”). Cognates * Latin ventus (“wind”) * Dutch wan (“winnowing basket”) * German Wanne (“winnowing basket”) * Swedish vanna (“a fan for winnowing”) * Old English windwian (“to fan, winnow”). More at winnow.

noun: Clipping of fanatic, originally in US baseball slang. Possibly influenced by fancy (“group of sport or hobby enthusiasts”), i.e. fancy boy (“fan”).

noun: From Cantonese 分. Doublet of fen and hoon.
fan.example: I am a big fan of libraries.
fan.exampleSense: A person who is fond of something or someone, especially an admirer of a performer or aficionado of a sport.

arrivisme.example: This was hardly arrivisme on my part: I was “down” with my fellow American radicals, not conspiring with a bunch of aristos and expats.
arrivisme.exampleSense: The state or behaviour of an arriviste.

arriviste.example: The second class in the bureaucracy, among whom are to be found most of the men occupying political posts just below the top, consists of arrivistes, who are enthusiastic Bolsheviks because of the material success of Bolshevism.
arriviste.exampleSense: An upstart or newcomer; nouveau riche; parvenu; an ambitious, brash or arrogant person who has yet to integrate with his or her new social group.

lilac.o: From obsolete French lilac (now lilas), from Arabic لِيلَك (līlak).

successor.o: From Anglo-Norman successour, from Latin successor.
successor.example: George W. Bush was successor to Bill Clinton as President of the US.
successor.exampleSense: A person or thing that immediately follows another in holding an office or title.

exempt.o: From Middle French exempt, from Latin exemptus, past participle of eximō.
exempt.example: His income is so small that it is exempt from tax.
exempt.exampleSense: Free from a duty or obligation.

exemption.o: From Old French exemption, from Latin exemptiō, from eximō, equivalent to exempt + -ion.

colossus.o: From Latin colossus, from Ancient Greek κολοσσός (kolossós, “large statue, especially the colossus of Rhodes”), from an unknown Pre-Greek etymon (and erroneously associated with κολοφών).
colossus.example: What I love about the colossi is that they actually feel colossal : they move ponderously around, sending out tremours with each step; their ancient husks richly detailed with dirt and plant life.
colossus.exampleSense: Any creature or thing of gigantic size.

colonial.example: None of them are, so to speak, idle men. Many of them are emigrants, not of the soil born and bred colonials.
colonial.exampleSense: A person from a country that is or was controlled by another.

colossal.o: From French colossal, formed from Latin colossus, from Ancient Greek κολοσσός (kolossós, “giant statue”).
colossal.example: A single puppy can make a colossal mess.
colossal.exampleSense: Extremely large or on a great scale.

fetus.o: A learned borrowing from Latin fētus (“offspring”). Doublet of fawn.
fetus.example: Several feti were removed from every rats' uterus, stripped of their membranes and allowed to lie in the peritoneal cavity connected to the placenta by the umbilical cord and with the placenta still attached to the uterine wall.
fetus.exampleSense: An unborn or unhatched vertebrate showing signs of the mature animal.

faeces.o: Alternative spelling of feces. From Latin faecēs, nominative plural of faex (“residue, dregs”), further origin unknown; possibly borrowed from a substrate language.
faeces.example: The fact that dogs have a well developed sense of smell suggests that they might be able to use the odour of faeces as a means of communicating.
faeces.exampleSense: UK, Canada, Ireland, South Africa, Australia, and New Zealand standard spelling of feces.

sign up.example: After much deliberation we decided to sign up for satellite TV.
sign up.exampleSense: To agree to purchase some good or service.

concord.o:
noun: From French concorde, Latin concordia, from concors (“of the same mind, agreeing”); con- + cor, cordis (“heart”). See heart, and compare accord.

noun: After Concord, Massachusetts, where the variety was developed.

verb: From French concorder, from Latin concordō.
concord.example: The foot of a fine was a copy of an agreement ( the final concord ) reached in a court of law, usually the Court of Common Pleas, following a dispute over land ownership.
concord.exampleSense: An agreement between the parties to a fine of land in reference to the manner in which it should pass, being an acknowledgment that the land in question belonged to the complainant. See fine.

antiquity.o: From Middle English antiquyte, antiquite, antiquytee, a borrowing from Old French antiquité, antiquitet, from Latin antiquitas, from antiquus. Equivalent to antique + -ity. See antique, antic. Compare with French antiquité.
antiquity.example: Cicero was an eloquent orator of antiquity.
antiquity.exampleSense: Ancient times; faraway history; former ages.

ambiguity.o: From Middle English ambiguite, from Old French ambiguite (French ambiguïté), from Latin ambiguitas, equivalent to ambiguous + -ity.
ambiguity.example: His speech was made with such great ambiguity that neither supporter nor opponent could be certain of his true position.

longevity.o: Early 17th century, learned borrowing from Latin longaevitās, from longaevus (“ancient, aged”) + -itās. The first part is related to English long and this association led to the alternative pronunciation with /ŋ/.
longevity.example: Grandpa had incredible longevity: he lived to be 105 years old!
longevity.exampleSense: The quality of being long-lasting, especially of life.

amen.o: Inherited from Middle English amen, from Old English āmen, from Ecclesiastical Latin āmēn, from Ancient Greek ἀμήν (amḗn), from Biblical Hebrew אָמֵן (ʾāmēn, “certainly, verily”) (cognate with Arabic آمِينَ (ʔāmīna), Classical Syriac ܐܡܝܢ (ʾāmên)). In Old English, it was used only at the end of the Gospels; elsewhere, it was translated as sōþlīċe! (“truly, indeed!”), swā hit is (“so it is”), and sīe! (“[so] be it!”).
amen.example: [H]is `Amens' were ejected at the pulpit with the severity of a reprimand.

albumen.o: Learned borrowing from Late Latin albūmen (“egg white, albumen; type of eye disease”) (whence Late Middle English albuminium (“clear fluid in the eyeball between the cornea and lens, aqueous humour”)), from Latin albus (“white”, adjective) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *albʰós (“white”, adjective)) + -men (suffix forming nouns), modelled after ferrūmen (“cement; glue”). The plural form albumina is a learned borrowing from Late Latin albūmina.
albumen.example: The various elements found in food are the following: Starch, sugar, fats, albumen, mineral substances, indigestible substances.
albumen.exampleSense: The white part of an egg; being mostly the protein albumin and water.

acumen.example: Finally, the acumina of all the narrowly lanceolate leaves of both species tend to be straight rather than curved.
acumen.exampleSense: A sharp, tapering point extending from a plant.

alliance.o: From Middle English alliaunce, from Old French aliance (French alliance). Equivalent to ally + -ance. Compare with Doric Greek ἁλία (halía, “assembly”). See also al-.

inquisition.o: From Old French inquisicion, from Latin inquisitio, from inquirere. The sense implying persecution is influenced by the name of the Spanish Inquisition, which is a cardinal exemplar of government inquisitions that give inquisitions a bad name.
inquisition.example: The justices in eyre had it formerly in charge to make inquisition concerning them by a jury of the county.
inquisition.exampleSense: The finding of a jury, especially such a finding under a writ of inquiry.

inquisitive.o: Late 14th century, from Old French inquisitif, from Late Latin inquisitivus, from Latin inquisitus, past participle of inquirere. See also inquire.
inquisitive.example: No, no, Bertha; we must not give them reason to say that their neighbours are inquisitive.

tattoo.o:
noun: From earlier tattaow, tattow, a borrowing from a Polynesian language, e.g. Samoan tatau (“tattoo; to tap, to strike”).

noun: From earlier tap-to, borrowed from Dutch taptoe, from tap (“tap; faucet on a cask”) + toe (“to; shut”). More at tap, to.

noun: From Hindi टट्टू (ṭaṭṭū).
tattoo.example: His shirt sleeves were turned up, so upon his brawny arms his tattooes were visible.
tattoo.exampleSense: An image made in the skin with ink and a needle.

afternoons.o: plural of afternoon. From Middle English afternone, after-non, equivalent to after- + noon.

dittography.o: From Ancient Greek διττός (dittós, “double”) + -graphy. Not related to English ditto.

ditto.o: First attested in 1625. From regional Italian ditto, variant of detto, past participle of dire (“to say”), from Latin dīcō (“to say, to speak”). Not related to English dittography. The specific meaning of making copies of paper comes from ditto machine, a genericization from the brand name of a spirit duplicator.
ditto.example: The Communists believed that Prakasam, the Prime Minister, never tried to check the bureaucracy but dittoed every action of the corrupt officials and police.
ditto.exampleSense: To repeat the aforesaid, the earlier action etc.

escort.o: Borrowed from French escorte, itself borrowed from Italian scorta.
escort.example: Three local yobs have also joined, but they have not reckoned on a redoubtable Conductor and two local revenue protection officers who soon escort them off the train!
escort.exampleSense: To accompany (a person) in order to compel them to go somewhere (e.g. to leave a building).

dissolute.o: From Middle English dissolute, from Latin dissolutus.
dissolute.example: [H]e illustrated the hypocrisy of his party; and was often known to exercise his talent of drinking a company of dissolutes under the table.
dissolute.exampleSense: An immoral person devoted to sensual pleasures.

provincial.o: From Middle English provincial, from Old French provincial, from Latin prōvinciālis (“of a province”), equivalent to province + -ial.
provincial.example: The Franciscan provincial Diego de Landa set up a local Inquisition which unleashed a campaign of interrogation and torture on the Indio population.
provincial.exampleSense: A monastic superior, who, under the general of his order, has the direction of all the religious houses of the same fraternity in a given district, called a province of the order.

wearing thin.o: present participle and gerund of wear. Inherited from Middle English weren, werien, from Old English werian (“to clothe, cover over; put on, wear, use; stock (land)”), from Proto-West Germanic *waʀjan, from Proto-Germanic *wazjaną (“to clothe”), from Proto-Indo-European *wes- (“to dress, put on (clothes)”). Cognate to Sanskrit वस्ते (váste), Ancient Greek ἕννυμι (hénnumi, “put on”), Latin vestis (“garment”) (English vest), Albanian vesh (“dress up, wear”), Tocharian B wäs-, Old Armenian զգենում (zgenum), Welsh gwisgo, Hittite 𒉿𒀸- (waš-). Originally a weak verb (i.e. with a past tense in -ed), it became irregular during the Middle English period by analogy with verbs like beren (whence bear) and teren (whence tear).

cheeky.o: From cheek + -y. Compare typologically barefaced, bald-faced; Italian sfacciato (< Latin ex- + faciēs); French effronté, Italian sfrontato (< Latin ex- + frons), Polish czelny (< czoło).
cheeky.example: The Young Turks, as might have been expected, wrote in their customary flippant, cheeky style.
cheeky.exampleSense: Impudent; impertinent; impertinently bold, often in a way that is regarded as endearing or amusing.

neutral.o: From Middle French neutral (compare modern French neutre), from Latin neutrālis. By surface analysis, neuter + -al.
neutral.example: The heart can not possibly remain neutral, but constantly takes part one way or the other.
neutral.exampleSense: Favoring neither the supporting nor opposing viewpoint of a topic of debate; unbiased.

correspondent.o: From Latin, via Middle French or directly, from Medieval Latin correspondēns, present participle of correspondeō.
correspondent.example: Action correspondent or repugnant unto the law.

correspond.o: From Middle French correspondre, from Latin com- (“with”) + respondeo (“to match, to answer to”), equivalent to co- + respond.
correspond.example: I've been corresponding with my German pen pal for three years.
correspond.exampleSense: to exchange messages, especially by postal letter, over a period of time.

pal.o: PIE word *bʰréh₂tēr Borrowed from Angloromani pal (“brother, friend”), from Romani phral (“brother”), from Sanskrit भ्रातृ (bhrātṛ, “brother”). Doublet of bhai, brother, bru, frater, friar, and vai.
pal.example: Don't you threaten me, pal – I'll report you to the police.
pal.exampleSense: An informal term of address, often used ironically in a hostile way.

responser.example: In the evening two responsers are appointed on the part of the bride, and as many for the bridegroom: they are expected to answer such questions as the Qází may think proper to ask.
responser.exampleSense: One who responds, or gives responses.

sponsorship.example: The university awarded five sponsorships to the five most qualified applicants.
sponsorship.exampleSense: The aid or support provided by a sponsor; backing or patronage.

sponsion.o: From Latin spōnsiō, from spondēre (“to promise solemnly”).

complain.o: From Middle English complaynen, from Old French complaindre, from Medieval Latin complangere (“to bewail, complain”), from Latin com- (“together”) + plangere (“to strike, beat, as the breast in extreme grief, bewail”); see plain, plaint.
complain.example: If you get cheated by the Better Business Bureau, who do you complain to?
complain.exampleSense: To make a formal accusation or bring a formal charge.

republican.o: From republic + -an, partly after French républicain.
republican.example: The Roman emperors were republican magistrates named by the senate.
republican.exampleSense: Of or belonging to a republic.

senate.o: From Middle English senat, from Old French senat, from Latin senātus (“council of elders; a senate”), from senex (“old”).

ingratitude.o: From in- + gratitude, from Old French ingratitude, from Late Latin ingrātitūdō. By surface analysis, in- + Latin grat(us) + -itude.
ingratitude.example: Blondie: Tut, tut. Such ingratitude after all the times I saved your life.
ingratitude.exampleSense: A lack or absence of gratitude; thanklessness.

photosynthesis.example: Oxygen levels on Earth skyrocketed 2.4 billion years ago, when cyanobacteria evolved photosynthesis: the ability to convert water and carbon dioxide into carbohydrates and waste oxygen using solar energy.
photosynthesis.exampleSense: Any process by which plants and other photoautotrophs convert light energy into chemical energy. principally, oxygenic photosynthesis, any process by which plants and algae convert water and carbon dioxide into carbohydrates and waste oxygen using solar energy.

instrumentation.example: They changed the woodwind instrumentation to piccollos and saxophones, and as a result it sounded much more clumsy.
instrumentation.exampleSense: The arrangement of a musical composition for performance by a number of different instruments; instrumental composition; composition for an orchestra or military band.

persuasion.o: From French persuasion and its source, Latin persuāsiō, from persuādēre, from suādēre (“to advise, recommend”).
persuasion.example: Some of the shopowners were resistant to the extortion, so the mafia did some persuasion.
persuasion.exampleSense: An argument or other statement intended to influence one's opinions or beliefs; a way of persuading someone. All activity attempting to influence or control others' behavior or profession of beliefs, from convincing to threatening, assault, or battery.

persuasively.example: The eloquent speaker persuasively stated her argument.
persuasively.exampleSense: In a manner intended to convince or persuade.

storyteller.example: "Charlotte is the best storyteller I ever heard," said Fern, poking her dish towel into a cereal bowl.
storyteller.exampleSense: A person who relates stories through one medium or another to an audience.

snorkelling.o: present participle and gerund of snorkel. Borrowed from German Schnorchel (“(submarine) snorkel”), related to schnarchen (“to snore”). Thus named because of the submarine snorkel's functional similarity to a nose and because of its noise when in use. The anglicized spelling was first recorded in 1945. See, for example, Mark S. Watson, "New Epoch in Sea War", The Baltimore Sun, December 31, 1945, p. 8: "The Germans' earlier quest of the last important objective, it will be remembered, had produced the Snorkel, a long exhaust tube whose vent reached above water and permitted a submerged vessel to discharge its Diesel fumes in open air."

storytelling.example: Dynamic typography reinvigorates the storytelling genre by anthropomorphizing fonts, defibrillating calligraphy, creating rhythmic, ambient moodscapes without sacrificing speed or lushness.
storytelling.exampleSense: The act and skills of presenting stories and tales.

descriptive.o: From Latin dēscriptīvus (“containing a full description”).
descriptive.example: He draws eclectically on studies of baboons, descriptive anthropological accounts of hunter-gatherer societies and, in a few cases, the fossil record.
descriptive.exampleSense: Describing and seeking to classify, as opposed to normative or prescriptive.

tier.o:
noun: From tie + -er.

noun: From Middle French tier, from Old French tire (“rank, sequence, order, kind”), probably from tirer (“to draw, draw out”). Alternatively, from a Germanic source related to Middle English tir (“honour, glory, power, rule”), Old English tīr (“glory, honour, fame”), Old Norse tírr (“glory, honour, renown”).
tier.example: At various points during the (too frequent, mostly boring, school play-tier) dialogue.
tier.exampleSense: A rank or grade; a stratum.

crater.o: First coined 1613, from Latin crātēr (“basin”), from Ancient Greek κρᾱτήρ (krātḗr, “mixing-bowl, wassail-bowl”).
crater.example: He cratered into that snow bank about five seconds after his first lesson.

tipster.example: Does anybody know what Jon Riglar is doing now? (SU Tipster for about 6 years - Zapchat!).
tipster.exampleSense: One who provides tips or hints on how to succeed at a game.

denounce.o: From Old French denuncier, from Latin dēnūntiō (“to announce, to denounce, to threaten”), from de + nūntiō (“to announce, to report, to denounce”), from nūntius (“messenger, message”). Doublet of denunciate.
denounce.example: It is the latest step towards an airline-style advance booking-only system, which rail users have denounced as signalling the end of affordable, immediate travel.
denounce.exampleSense: To criticize or speak out against (someone or something); to point out as deserving of reprehension, etc.; to openly accuse or condemn in a threatening manner; to invoke censure upon; to stigmatize; to blame.

report.o: From Middle English reporten, from Anglo-Norman reporter, from Latin reportāre (“to carry back, return, remit, refer”), from re- + portāre.
report.example: A report by the telecommunications ministry on the phone network revealed a severe capacity problem.
report.exampleSense: A piece of information describing, or an account of certain events given or presented to someone, with the most common adpositions being by (referring to creator of the report) and on (referring to the subject).

retailer.example: Publishers typically sell hardcover books to retailers at half the list price, while retailers set consumer prices.
retailer.exampleSense: A retail sales company or salesman.

vertex.o: Late Middle English, borrowed from Latin vertex (“whirl, eddy; top, crown, peak, summit”). Doublet of vortex.

subsidiary.o: From Middle French subsidiaire, from Latin subsidiarius (“belonging to a reserve”).
subsidiary.example: They constituted a useful subsidiary testimony of another state of existence.

group.o: From French groupe (“cluster, group”), from Italian gruppo, groppo (“a knot, heap, group, bag (of money)”). In the "group theory" sense, calqued from French groupe, a term coined by the young French mathematician Évariste Galois in 1830. Cognate with German Kropf (“crop, craw, bunch”); Old English cropp, croppa (“cluster, bunch, sprout, flower, berry, ear of corn, crop”) (whence English crop); Dutch krop (“craw”), Icelandic kroppr (“hump, bunch”). Doublet of crop and croup.
group.example: Throughout this section, we shall assume the existence of finitely presented groups with unsolvable word problem.
group.exampleSense: A set with an associative binary operation, under which there exists an identity element, and such that each element has an inverse.

high-profile.example: Bats host many high-profile viruses that can infect humans, including severe acute respiratory syndrome and Ebola.

free up.example: You can free up space on your hard disk by deleting temporary files.

front-line.o: Alternative spelling of front. From Middle English front, frunt, frount, from Old French front, frunt, from Latin frōns, frontem (“forehead”). Doublet of frons.

man-hour.example: Since 1950 our agricultural output per man-hour has actually doubled!

tech.o: Clipping of technology, technician, and technique.
tech.example: In high school, he attended the tech program, studying construction trades.

proofread.example: To Veronique Kaemerer and her eng. 101 students, Michael Horanburg and Brady Meador for their proofreads.

metrics.o: plural of metric. From French métrique (1864), from New Latin metricus (“pertaining to the system based on the meter”), from metrum (“a meter”); see meter. By surface analysis, metre + -ic.

classified.o:
verb: From classify + -ed.

noun: From classified advertisement, by shortening.
classified.example: We do not discuss specific interrogation techniques because they are classified information.
classified.exampleSense: Formally assigned by a government to one of several levels of sensitivity, usually (in English) top secret, secret, confidential, and, in some countries, restricted; thereby making disclosure to unauthorized persons illegal.

kidnapping.o: present participle and gerund of kidnap. From kid + nap (“to nab; to grab”). Originally Thieves' cant, referring to the practice of stealing children and shipping them to colonies or plantations as laborers. First attested c. 1680.

assault.o: From Middle English assaut, from Old French noun assaut, derived from the past participle of the verb assalir, from Late Latin assalīre, from Latin ad (“at, towards”) + salīre (“jump”). See also assail. Spelling Latinized around 1530 to add an l.
assault.example: The army made an assault on the enemy.
assault.exampleSense: A violent onset or attack with physical means, for example blows, weapons, etc.

robbery.o: From Middle English robberie, robry, roberie, from Old French roberie, from the verb rober (“to steal; to pillage”) + -ie. Ultimately from unattested Frankish *raubōn. By surface analysis, rob + -ery. Compare Dutch roverij (“robbery”), Norwegian Bokmål røveri (“robbery”), German Räuberei (“robbery, banditry”). Displaced native Old English rēaflāc.

tire.o:
verb: From Middle English tiren, tirien, teorien, from Old English tȳrian, tēorian (“to fail, cease, become weary, be tired, exhausted; tire, weary, exhaust”), of uncertain origin. Possibly from Proto-West Germanic *teuʀōn (“to cease”), which is possibly from Proto-Indo-European *dews- (“to fail, be behind, lag”). Compare Ancient Greek δεύομαι (deúomai, “to lack”), Sanskrit दोष (dóṣa, “crime, fault, vice, deficiency”).

noun: Probably from Middle English tir(e) (“equipment, furnshings, ornament”). See the details at tyre.

verb: From Middle English tire, from Old French tirer (“to draw or pull”), akin to English tear (“to rend”).

hit.o:
verb: Inherited from Middle English hitten (“to hit, strike, make contact with”), from Old English hittan (“to meet with, come upon, fall in with”), from Old Norse hitta (“to strike, meet”), from Proto-Germanic *hittijaną (“to come upon, find”), from Proto-Indo-European *kh₂eyd- (“to fall; fall upon; hit; cut; hew”). Cognates Cognate with West Frisian hitte (“to meet”), Dutch hitten (“to hit, encounter”), Danish hitte (“to find”), Faroese, Icelandic, Swedish hitta (“to meet”), Norwegian Nynorsk hitta, hitte (“to meet; to find”), Latin caedō (“to kill”), Albanian qit (“to hit, throw, pull out, release”). Probably also related to Dutch hei (“mallet”), German Heie (“wooden hammer, mallet”). (something very successful): Compare typologically striking, Russian порази́тельный (porazítelʹnyj) (<~ порази́ть (porazítʹ) <~ рази́ть (razítʹ)).

pron: From Middle English hit (“it”), from Old English hit (“it”), from Proto-Germanic *hit (“this, this one”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱe-, *ḱey- (“this, here”). Cognate with Dutch het (“it”). More at it; also note 'it.
hit.example: Where am I going to get my next hit?
hit.exampleSense: A dose of an illegal or addictive drug.

real-time.example: If not real-time, in-person backup, he at least needed to tell Davenport what was going on, and where he was headed.
real-time.exampleSense: Communicated as the events being responded to occur; communicated or proceeding without much delay.

billboard.example: Bleak factory buildings and billboard-cluttered avenues look as beautiful, through the camera’s eye, as churches and pastoral landscapes.
billboard.exampleSense: A very large outdoor sign, generally used for advertising.

headline.example: Once again I take typewriter in hand to express my opinion on two very different issues. Good luck in deciding what to headline this letter.
headline.exampleSense: To give a headline to a page or section of a text.

neighborhood.o: From an alteration of earlier neighborred (“neighborhood”), from Middle English neȝeburredde, neheborreden, equivalent to neighbor + -red; the term being interpreted as neighbor + -hood. For change in suffix (-red to -hood), compare brotherhood. Cognates Cognate with Scots nichbourheid (“neighbourhood”). Compare also Dutch naburigheid (“neighbourhood”).
neighborhood.exampleSense: The residential area near one's home.

assistant.o: From Middle English assistent, from Middle French assistant, from assister. By surface analysis, assist + -ant.

storefront.example: Brands are now able to set up storefronts to sell within Facebook and Instagram, where they were previously relegated to advertising for outside sales channels.
storefront.exampleSense: An e-commerce website offering goods or services to the public.

navigation.o: Borrowed from Middle French navigation, from Latin nāvigātiōnem, accusative singular of nāvigātiō (“sailing, navigation”), from nāvigō (“sail”). Morphologically navigate + -ion.

conversational.example: My aim is to become conversational in German.

augmented reality.example: Augmented Reality enhances a user's perception of and interaction with the real world. The virtual objects display information that the user cannot directly detect with his own senses.
augmented reality.exampleSense: The merging of a view of the real-world environment upon a digital image in real time.

continental.example: No former king had involved himself so frequently in the labyrinth of continental alliances.
continental.exampleSense: Of or relating to a continent or continents.

asterisk.o: [and other forms], from Late Latin asteriscus (“asterisk; small star”), from Ancient Greek ἀστερῐ́σκος (asterĭ́skos, “asterisk; small star”), from ᾰ̓στήρ (ăstḗr, “celestial body (star, planet, and other lights in the sky such as meteors)”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eHs- (“to burn; to glow”)) + -ῐ́σκος (-ĭ́skos, diminutive suffix). Doublet of asteriscus and piecewise doublet of starrish. Noun sense 1.1.2 (“something which is of little importance or which is marginal”) refers to the use of an asterisk to denote a footnote or marginal note in a text; in other words, information that is not important enough to be incorporated into the main text. Noun sense 1.1.3 (“blemish in an otherwise outstanding achievement”) refers to the use of an asterisk in a sporting record to indicate that the record is qualified in some manner (for example, that the sportsperson was found to have taken performance-enhancing drugs at the time). The verb is derived from the noun.
