asterisk.example: The Hôtels marked with one asterisc are Restaurants also. Those marked with two asteriscs have Table d'Hôte.
asterisk.exampleSense: A small star; also (by extension), something resembling or shaped like a star. The star-shaped symbol *, which is used in printing and writing for various purposes, including to refer a reader to a note at the bottom of a page or in a margin, and to indicate the omission of letters or words; a star.

denote.o: From Middle French denoter, from Latin denotare, from de- (“complete”) and notare (“to mark out”).
denote.example: The prefix pre- denotes "before", as in preview.
denote.exampleSense: To refer to literally; to convey as objective meaning.

creative.o: Borrowed from Late Latin creativus, from Latin creō. Equivalent to create + -ive. Displaced native Old English orþanclīċ.
creative.example: The design team has completed the creative for next month's multi-part ad campaign.
creative.exampleSense: Artistic material used in advertising, e.g. photographs, drawings, or video.

drive-thru.o: Alternative spelling of drive-through. Deverbal from drive through.

drive-through.example: I switched banks so that I could use a drive-through branch near my home.
drive-through.exampleSense: Of an establishment, providing service to occupants of automobiles while they are in their still-running vehicle, especially when the vehicle does not park in a parking space and the goods received are not consumed until the vehicle vacates the lane.

come to life.example: We want to know exactly how the first cells came to life on earth.
come to life.exampleSense: To become alive, to be given life; to be brought into existence.

scratch the surface.example: This beginners' course only scratches the surface of the subject.
scratch the surface.exampleSense: To barely begin; to see or do only a fraction of what is possible.

size.o:
noun: Attested since the 14th century, originally meant a “law or regulation that determines the amount to be paid”, from Middle English syse, sise (“regulation, control, limit”), from Old French cise, sise, aphetism of assise (“assize”), from the verb asseoir (“to sit down”), from Latin assidēre, composed of ad- (“to, towards, at”) + sedeō (“sit; settle down”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *sed-. Displaced native Old English miċelnes (literally “bigness”).

noun: From Middle English syse, of unclear origin; related to Old Italian sisa (“a glue used by painters”), perhaps ultimately related to size / syse (“amount”), or perhaps shortened from assisa, from assiso (“to make to sit, to seat, to place”)
size.example: The size of the building seemed to have increased since I was last there.
size.exampleSense: The dimensions or magnitude of a thing; how big something is.

showcase.example: I think the demonstration really showcases the strengths of the software.
showcase.exampleSense: To display, demonstrate, show, or present.

psycho.o:
adj: Clipping of psychotic or psychopath + -o (“person with characteristic”). Compare sicko.

noun: Clipping of psychology.
psycho.example: The loony bin up on the hill is full of psychos.
psycho.exampleSense: A person who is psychotic, psychopathic, or (broadly) otherwise insane.

psychedelic.o: From Ancient Greek ψυχή (psukhḗ, “mind, soul”) + δῆλος (dêlos, “manifest, visible”) + English -ic (prefix forming adjectives with the sense ‘of or pertaining to’), coined by the English psychiatrist Humphry Osmond (1917–2004) in a 1956 letter to Aldous Huxley.
psychedelic.example: I was going to become a three-drug connection to all my friends, psychedelics, hash and pot.
psychedelic.exampleSense: Any psychoactive substance (such as LSD or psilocybin) which, when consumed, causes perceptual changes (sometimes erratic and uncontrollable), visual hallucination, and altered awareness of the body and mind.

psyche.o:
noun: Learned borrowing from Latin psychē, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ψυχή (psukhḗ, “soul”).

noun: Shortened form of psychology, from French psychologie, from Latin psychologia, from Ancient Greek ψυχή (psukhḗ, “soul”) and -λογία (-logía, “study of”)

gild.o: From Middle English gilden, gulden, from Old English gyldan (“to gild, to cover with a thin layer of gold”), from Proto-West Germanic *gulþijan, from Proto-Germanic *gulþijaną, from Proto-Germanic *gulþą (“gold”).
gild.example: High above the city, on a tall column, stood the statue of the Happy Prince. He was gilded all over with thin leaves of fine gold, for eyes he had two bright sapphires, and a large red ruby glowed on his sword-hilt.
gild.exampleSense: To cover with a thin layer of gold; to cover with gold leaf.

follow up.example: Send a letter, then follow up promptly with a telephone call.
follow up.exampleSense: To take further actions remaining after an event; to continue, revisit, or persist; especially, to maintain communication or verify.

follow-up.example: It could have been much worse for City before the break, but goalkeeper Joe Hart saved Jamie Mackie's long-range shot and Helguson's headed follow-up - although the latter was offside - before Bothroyd hit the post with another header.
follow-up.exampleSense: A shot on goal directly following another that has been saved.

bobby.o: From the given name of Sir Robert Peel, who established London’s police force.
bobby.example: The following is the Victorian code of practice as it refers to the welfare of bobby calves.
bobby.exampleSense: A calf that is slaughtered in its first month, usually because it has no mother or because it is undersized or otherwise defective.

sledding.o: present participle and gerund of sled. From Middle English sledde, from Middle Dutch sledde or Middle Low German sledde (compare Dutch slee, slede, Low German Sleden), from Proto-Germanic *slidô (compare Saterland Frisian sliede, German Schlitten, Norwegian slede). Doublet of sleigh; also related to slide.

adulation.o: From French adulation, from Latin adulātio (“flattery”).
adulation.example: He was uncomfortable with the adulation from his fans.

movable.o: From Old French movable. By surface analysis, move + -able.
movable.example: The owners had supplied the vessel with a movable derrick for the purpose of raising the gangways of the vessel when in port, in order to discharge cargo.
movable.exampleSense: Capable of being moved, lifted, carried, drawn, turned, or conveyed, or in any way made to change place or posture; not fixed or stationary.

mutant.o: From Latin mūtāns, present participle of mūtō. By surface analysis, muta- + -ant.
mutant.example: Scientists have created a mutant enzyme that breaks down plastic drinks bottles—by accident.
mutant.exampleSense: Of, relating to, undergoing (i.e. mutating), or resulting from change or mutation; that has undergone mutation.

mutable.o: From Middle English mutable, from Old French mutable, from Latin mutabilis (“liable to change”). By surface analysis, muta- + -able.
mutable.example: Hypothesis 6.14: Entropy levels within the social group may vary but must be maintained below maximum entropy on certain relevant variables (e.g., on the six globals and five mutables).
mutable.exampleSense: Something mutable; a variable or value that can change.

meandering.o: present participle and gerund of meander. From Latin Maeander, from Ancient Greek Μαίανδρος (Maíandros) – a river in Asia Minor (present day Turkey) known for its winding course (modern Turkish Menderes).

snooper.example: Bradly was embarrassed, detected in the character of a snooper. But he had to come on, short of bolting back in his tracks.

cosmopolitan.o: From cosmopolit(e) + -an. Compare metropolitan and megalopolitan.
cosmopolitan.example: Domestication and the evolution of anthrophilic traits in houseflies and some drosophilids have allowed certain species to attain cosmopolitan status.
cosmopolitan.exampleSense: Growing or living in many parts of the world; widely distributed.

terracing.o: present participle and gerund of terrace. Borrowed from French terrasse, from Old Occitan terrassa, from Vulgar Latin *terrācea, from terra (“land”). Doublet of terrasse.

terracotta.example: A dull red or terracotta brown is far better, and sets off the foliage of Palms or Ferns to greater advantage.

subterranean.o: From Latin subterrāneus + -an. Compare subterrane and subterraneous.
subterranean.example: Today is that most sacred of American holidays. A day when people from all walks of life set aside their differences and focus their undivided attention on the prognostication abilities of a subterranean rodent.
subterranean.exampleSense: Below ground, under the earth, underground.

subterrane.o: From Latin subterrāneus. Doublet of subterraneous.
subterrane.example: I watched men in moon suits bury drums of nuclear waste and I thought of the living rocks down there, the subterrane process, the half-life, the atoms that decay to half the original number.

disinter.example: Why disinter dead faith from mouldering hidden?
disinter.exampleSense: To bring out, as from a grave or hiding place; to bring from obscurity into view.

inter.o: From Middle English enteren, borrowed from Old French enterrer, enterer, from Vulgar Latin *interrāre (“to put in earth”).

terrorism.o: From French terrorisme, from terreur + -isme. By surface analysis, terror + -ism. The word first appears in English in 1795 in reference to the Jacobin radicals of France, who ruled during the Reign of Terror.

terrible.o: Inherited from Middle English terrible, from Old French terrible, from Latin terribilis (“frightful”), from terreō (“to frighten, terrify, alarm; to deter by terror, scare (away)”). Compare terror, deter. By surface analysis, terror + -ible. Displaced Old English atol and sliþe, while also largely overtaking grimm.
terrible.example: He paid a terrible price for his life of drinking.
terrible.exampleSense: Intense; extreme in degree or extent.

examine.o: From Middle English examinen, examenen, from Old French examiner, from Latin exāmināre.
examine.example: The new study examines development activities for different AI technologies worldwide.
examine.exampleSense: To observe or inspect carefully or critically.

thoughtful.o: From Middle English thoȝtful, thohtful, equivalent to thought + -ful. Compare Dutch gedachtenvol, Swedish tankfull.
thoughtful.example: Most thoughtful people eventually solve the puzzle.

intolerance.o: Borrowed from French intolérance, itself from in- (“not”) + tolérance or borrowed from Latin intolerantia (“insolence, insufferableness; (very rare) intolerance”). By surface analysis, in- + tolerance.
intolerance.example: Religious intolerance is a serious problem in Brazil.

richness.o: Inherited from Middle English richenesse; by surface analysis, rich + -ness.
richness.example: By using the same classification system for all the dictionaries surveyed, it was possible to compare the lexical richness of each against the other.
richness.exampleSense: The state of having many examples or cases; abundance; profusion.

globalization.example: He presents Hitler’s rise as an element of the collapse of a republic confronting dilemmas of globalization with imperfect instruments and flawed leaders.
globalization.exampleSense: US and Oxford British English standard spelling of globalisation.

globalized.o: simple past and past participle of globalize. From global + -ize.

judgement.o: Alternative spelling of judgment. From Middle English juggement, borrowed from Old French jugement, from Late Latin iūdicāmentum, from Latin iūdicō. Partially displaced doom. By surface analysis, judge + -ment.

celerity.o: From Old French celeritee (compare French célérité), from Latin celeritas, from celer (“fast, swift”).
celerity.example: ...and many endeavours have been made, not only to transmit signals with celerity, but also to transmit more than one communication at the same time along the same wire.
celerity.exampleSense: The speed of symbol transmission, now called baud rate.

celery.o: From French céleri, from Lombard selleri, a plural of Latin selīnum, from Ancient Greek σέλῑνον (sélīnon). Displaced English march (“celery, smallage”) and smallage (“wild celery”).

iridescent.o: Coined around 1800, from Latin iris, iridis (“rainbow”) + -escent.

peekaboo.example: The model was wearing a peekaboo swimsuit.
peekaboo.exampleSense: With holes, slits or transparent fabric to reveal what is normally hidden.

emesis.o: From Ancient Greek ἔμεσις (émesis), from ἐμέω (eméō, “vomit”). Compare ἔμετος (émetos, “vomit”, noun). By surface analysis, suffixed with -esis.
emesis.example: Syrup of ipecac almost always forces an emesis.
emesis.exampleSense: The act or process of vomiting.

mindful.o:
adj: From Middle English myndeful, myndefull, from Old English ġemyndful (“of good memory”), equivalent to mind + -ful.

noun: From mind + -ful.
mindful.example: I think being mindful may help you to appreciate life more.
mindful.exampleSense: Of or pertaining to mindfulness; sustaining meta-attention of the contents of one's own mind in the present moment.

banner.o:
noun: From Middle English baner, from Old French baniere (Modern bannière), of Germanic origin. More at band.

noun: From ban + -er.
banner.example: The year just closed has been the banner year for New-Hampshire Home Missions. The amount raised for the cause is $505,38 more than ever was raised before in any one year.

pumpkin.o: Alteration of pompion, pumpion (“pumpkin”) with the diminutive -kin, from Middle French pompon, from Latin pepō (whence English pepo), from Ancient Greek πέπων (pépōn, “large melon”), from πέπων (pépōn, “ripe”), from πέπτω (péptō, “ripen”). The first attestation is from 1647. The alternative theory that it may be from Massachusett pôhpukun (“grows forth round”) is false. The automotive sense is by fancied resemblance.
pumpkin.example: Nevertheless, the comprehensive comparative analysis of pumpkin viromes across various geographic regions by NGS remains deficient.
pumpkin.exampleSense: A domesticated plant, in species Cucurbita pepo, similar in growth pattern, foliage, flower, and fruit to the squash or melon.

apocryphal.example: Many scholars consider the stories of the monk Teilo to be apocryphal.
apocryphal.exampleSense: Of doubtful authenticity, or lacking authority; not regarded as canonical.

locale.o: From French local (adj), nominal use of the adjective.
locale.example: Being near running water and good shade, the explorers decided it was a good locale for setting up camp.

essence.o: From Middle English essence, from Middle French essence, from Latin essentia (“the being or essence of a thing”), from an artificial formation of esse (“to be”), to translate Ancient Greek οὐσία (ousía, “being”), from ὤν (ṓn), present participle of εἰμί (eimí, “to be, exist”).
essence.example: She bathed the face of the sleeper with some essence, raised her in her arms, and called upon her name.
essence.exampleSense: An extract or concentrate obtained from a plant or other matter used for flavouring, or as a restorative.

setback.o: Deverbal from set back. Compare drawback.
setback.example: After some initial setbacks, the expedition went safely on its way.
setback.exampleSense: An obstacle, delay, disadvantage, or blow (an adverse event which slows down, or prevents progress towards a desired outcome).

discouraging.o: present participle and gerund of discourage. From Middle French descourager (modern French décourager), from Old French descouragier, from des- and corage. By surface analysis, dis- + courage.
discouraging.example: August 6, 1841, Lydia Ann Barclay, letter to J. B.

in disguise.example: The celebrity went unnoticed by her fans because she was in disguise.

overcomplex.example: But in the early days of the scheme the new machines created some problems for the fitters, who found them over-complex and their faults hard to diagnose after many years' experience of small, simple steam locomotives.

overcommit.exampleSense: To make excessive commitments, either beyond one's ability or beyond what is reasonable

overcome.o: Inherited from Middle English overcomen, inherited from Old English ofercuman (“to overcome, subdue, compel, conquer, obtain, attain, reach, overtake”). By surface analysis, over- + come. Cognate with Dutch overkomen, German überkommen, Danish overkomme, Swedish överkomma.
overcome.example: We shall overcome because Carlyle is right; "no lie can live forever".

flip-flop.o: Onomatopoeic. Most probably an imitation of the sound produced when walking in them.
flip-flop.example: On the break for strong left, everything remains the same, except for the flip-flop of positions.
flip-flop.exampleSense: A change of places; an inversion or swap.

flophouse.o: From flop + house, originally hobo slang, presumably from slang flop (“lie down to sleep”).
flophouse.example: We even visited some drunken seamen in a flophouse on Mission Street that she knew; they offered us whisky.
flophouse.exampleSense: A cheap hotel or boarding house where many people sleep in large rooms.

floppy.example: "Ja, our job is not to think or make decisions. We just here to slay floppies," remarked Koos.
floppy.exampleSense: An insurgent in the Rhodesian Bush War, called as such for the way they "flop" when shot.

accomplice.o: First attested in 1550. From a complice, from Middle English complice, from Old French complice (“confederate”), from Latin complicāre (“fold together”). The article a became part of the word, through the influence of the word accomplish.

pro.o:
noun: From Late Middle English pro, from Latin prō (“on behalf of”).

noun: Clipping of professional.

noun: Clipping of prostitute.

noun: Clipping of proproctor.

noun: Clipping of prophylaxis.
pro.example: He is pro exercise but against physical exertion, quite a conundrum.

inauspicious.example: And shake the yoke of inauspicious stars.

auspicious.o: From auspice + -ious, from Latin auspicium (“augury”), from auspex (“augur”), possibly via French.
auspicious.example: It was a boast of Napoleon, that the very weather owned the influence of his auspicious star—his triumphal entry, his procession, or his fête, were always marked by sunshine.
auspicious.exampleSense: Of good omen; indicating future success.

auspice.o: From Middle French auspice, from Latin auspicium, in turn from auspex.
auspice.example: The circle of vultures was not a good auspice.

abbey.o: From A.D. 1250 in Middle English abbey, abbeye (“convent headed by an abbot”) (compare archaic English abbaye), itself borrowed from Old French abaïe, abbaïe, abeïe, abbeïe (Modern French abbaye) from Late Latin or Ecclesiastical Latin abbātia, from Classical Latin abbās (“abbot”). Doublet of abbacy and Opatija. See abbot.
abbey.example: From 1199 to 1203 William Punchard was the abbot of the abbey of Rievaulx, which was part of the Cistercian order of monks.
abbey.exampleSense: A monastery or society of people, secluded from the world and devoted to religion and celibacy, which is headed by an abbot or abbess; also, the monastic building or buildings.

elide.o: From Latin ēlīdō (“to knock, dash or strike out”), from ex- (“out, away”) + laedō (“to strike, collide, hurt”) (whence e- (“assimilated form of ex-”)).
elide.example: Graham Hough's apparently objective assertion that 'Ozymandias' is 'extremely clear and direct', for example, elides the question of 'to whom?'.

exile.o: From Middle English exil, borrowed from Old French essil, exil, from Latin exsilium, exilium (“state of exile”), derived from exsul, exul (“exiled person”).
exile.example: She lived as an exile, and did her best to make the most out of such life.
exile.exampleSense: Someone who is banished from his home or country.

antic.o:
adj: Probably from Italian antico (“ancient”), used to describe ancient wall paintings from classical times, from Latin antiquus (“venerable”). See also Italian grottesco (“grotesque”). Doublet of antique.

noun: From anticipation.
antic.example: I'm fed up with your constant antics in class. Please behave yourself!
antic.exampleSense: A ludicrous gesture or act; ridiculous behaviour; caper.

anti.o: Conversion of the prefix anti- to an adjective.
anti.example: On one occasion, franchise supporters accused antis of dumping lemons, wet sponges, rolls of ticker tape, bags of water, and garbage pails on innocent suffrage supporters parading outside the anti-suffrage offices.
anti.exampleSense: A person opposed to a concept or principle.

bumper.example: The company sells screw-on rubber bumpers and feet.
bumper.exampleSense: Any mechanical device used to absorb an impact, soften a collision, or protect against impact.

bummer.o:
noun: Borrowed from German Bummler (“a drifter, a stroller, a rambler, a loiterer, a laggard”).

noun: From bum (“make unhappy”) + -er (agent noun suffix), originally US drug slang.

noun: From bum (“engage in anal sex”) + -er (agent noun suffix).

adj: From bum + -er (comparative suffix).
bummer.example: You know, the kind of guy who would, if he wasn't gay, probably be shouting ‘Oi, gay boy!’ or ‘You bummer!’ or even ‘Oi, paki!’ or what have you. They're not enlightened.

district.o: From French district, from Medieval Latin districtus (“a district within which the lord may distrain, also jurisdiction”), from Latin districtus, past participle of distringere (“to draw asunder, compel, distrain”), from dis- (“apart”) + stringere (“to draw tight, strain”). Doublet of Detroit.

disjoint.o: From Middle English disjoynen, from Old French desjoindre (“disjoin”), from Latin disiungō, from dis- + iungō (“join”).

disquieting.example: It is never possible to settle down to the ordinary routine of life at sea until the screw begins to revolve. There is an hour or two, after the passengers have embarked, which is disquieting and fussy.
disquieting.exampleSense: Causing mental trouble or anguish; upsetting; making uneasy.

disquietude.example: For with Rosilia, to the regret of the past and self-accusation, was added the contemplation of a dark futurity, seldom affording a gleam of hope to cheer and solace her disquietude.
disquietude.exampleSense: A state of disquiet, uneasiness, or anxiety.

disquiet.example: He felt disquieted by the lack of interest the child had shown.
disquiet.exampleSense: To make (someone or something) worried or anxious.

ludicrousness.example: The full ludicrousness of the thing dawned upon me so forcibly that I forgot all about my excitement and scare, and laughed aloud.
ludicrousness.exampleSense: The state or quality of being ludicrous.

ludicrous.o: Learned borrowing from Latin lūdicrus. First attested in 1619.
ludicrous.example: He made a ludicrous attempt to run for office.
ludicrous.exampleSense: Idiotic or unthinkable, often to the point of being funny; amusing by being plainly incongruous or absurd.

sentience.o: From sentient, from Latin sentiēns, present participle of sentiō (“feel, sense”). Compare with sentence, its equivalent formation from Classic Latin sententia (for *sentientia).
sentience.example: The science of animal sentience is far from a firm one; there's no way of knowing exactly what any animal is feeling.
sentience.exampleSense: The state or quality of being sentient; possession of consciousness or sensory awareness.

sentient.o: From Latin sentiēns (“feeling, perceiving”), present active participle of sentiō.
sentient.example: Not even a microbe? I don't want to blow up something that could evolve into a sentient species in a couple of billion years.

nadir.o: From Medieval Latin nadir, from Arabic نَظِير السَّمْت (naẓīr as-samt), composed of نَظِير (naẓīr, “counterpart, corresponding to”) and السَّمْت (as-samt, “the zenith”).
nadir.example: The myth describes the dangerous moment of the nadir, the dead of winter, the moment when it is not known whether the world will be re-created and another cycle will bring on another spring.
nadir.exampleSense: The lowest point; time of greatest depression.

futurity.example: Charles's was just an exciting consciousness; and he paced the streets, sometimes roused into disdain of the busy and thoughtless crowd around, but oftener lost in gloomy dreams of that futurity whose depths he was so soon to explore.

weightlessly.example: The astronaut hung weightlessly in the capsule.

avalanche.o: From French avalanche, from Franco-Provençal (Savoy) avalançhe, blend of aval (“downhill”) and standard lavençhe, from Vulgar Latin *labanka (compare Occitan lavanca, Italian valanga), of uncertain origin, perhaps an alteration of Late Latin lābīna (“landslide”) (compare Franco-Provençal (Dauphiné) lavino, Romansh lavina), from Latin lābēs, from lābor (“to slip, slide”).
avalanche.example: Yes, but she talked it away. She uses a whole language to herself. Her discourse is an avalanche of words, beneath which the hearers are overwhelmed.
avalanche.exampleSense: A sudden, great, or irresistible descent or influx; anything like an avalanche in suddenness and overwhelming quantity.

defective.o: From Middle English defectif, defective, from Old French defectif, from Late Latin dēfectīvus.
defective.example: It is likely that the long evolutionary trajectory of Mycoplasma went from a reductive autotroph to oxidative heterotroph to a cell-wall–defective degenerate parasite. This evolutionary trajectory assumes the simplicity to complexity route of biogenesis, a point of view that is not universally accepted.

definitely.example: Joe definitely doesn't know how to drive a tractor.

definitively.example: Far from making the kind of statement of hard fact that editors had readily made regarding claims about Trump’s racism, the article fails to definitively state that the laptop is not, in fact, Russian disinformation.
definitively.exampleSense: In a way that is not only decisive, but also conclusive and final.

definition.o: From Middle English diffinicioun, from Middle French definition, from Latin dēfīnītiō, from dēfīniō. Equivalent to define + -ition.
definition.example: Your definition of "elephant" needs to be more precise than "a big animal with large ears".
definition.exampleSense: A statement of the meaning of a word or word group or a sign or symbol (dictionary definitions).

accredit.o: * First attested in the 1610s. * From French accréditer, from à (“to”) + to credit, from crédit (“credit”). * See credit.
accredit.example: February 17, 1793, William Cowper, letter to Samuel Rose, Esq.
accredit.exampleSense: To put or bring into credit; to invest with credit or authority; to sanction.

irrupt.o: From Latin irruptus, past participle of irrumpō.

irrevocable.o: From Middle French irrévocable, from Latin irrevocabilis; equivalent to ir- + revoke + -able.

convoke.o: Borrowed from Middle French convoquer, from Latin convocare, from con- (“with”) + vocō (“to call”). Doublet of convocate.

rugged.o:
adj: From Middle English rugged, roggyd, ruggyd, derived from Old Norse rǫgg (“tuft, shagginess”), equivalent to rug (“rough, woollen material”) + -ed. Compare Old Swedish ruggoter (“wrinkled”), Swedish rugga (“to roughen”), Swedish ruggig (“shaggy”), Icelandic rögg (“shagginess”), Old Norse raggaðr (“tufted”), dialectal Danish raggad (“shaggy”).

adj: From rug + -ed.
rugged.example: Many women and men delude themselves into thinking that only the hardest and most rugged man is attractive and to many it may be the case.

laconism.o: From Latin Laconia, from Ancient Greek Λακεδαίμων (Lakedaímōn, “the region surrounding the city of Sparta”).
laconism.example: “Well, where have you been?” he said to her with offhand laconism.

laconic.o: From Latin Lacōnicus (“Spartan”), from Ancient Greek Λακωνικός (Lakōnikós, “Laconian”). Laconia was the region inhabited and ruled by the Spartans, who were known for their brevity in speech.
laconic.example: His sense was strong and his style laconic.
laconic.exampleSense: Using as few words as possible; pithy and concise.

banditry.example: The merchant refused to travel in the region due to the ongoing banditry.
banditry.exampleSense: Acts characteristic of a bandit; armed robbery.

bandit.o: Borrowed from Italian bandito (“outlawed”), a derivative of Italian bandire (“to ban”), from Late Latin bandīre, an alteration (due to Gothic 𐌱𐌰𐌽𐌳𐍅𐌾𐌰𐌽 (bandwjan, “to signal”)) of Late Latin bannīre (“to ban”), from Frankish *bannan (“to ban”). Doublet of bandito.
bandit.example: As the sanctuary was bandited at least once, it may be that the silver wine cups I have are from the treasure.
bandit.exampleSense: To rob, or steal from, in the manner of a bandit.

gunship.example: I'm sending down five more dropships, combat EMVs, and a thopter gunship.
gunship.exampleSense: An armed helicopter tasked to attack the enemy.

copter.o: Clipping of helicopter; see also -copter § Etymology.

conduce.o: PIE word *ḱóm From Late Middle English conducen (“to guide, lead; (surgery) to draw together (edges of a wound, or parts of a torn sinew); to set (a broken bone)”), borrowed from Latin condūcere, the present active infinitive of condūcō (“to bring, draw, or lead together, assemble, collect; to contribute to something by being useful, be of use, be conducive to”), from con- (prefix denoting a bringing together of several things) + dūcō (“to conduct, guide, lead, lead away”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dewk- (“to draw, pull; to lead (pull behind oneself)”)). Doublet of conduct and conn.
conduce.example: Anecdotes aside, many historians are skeptical that trade, as a general rule, conduces to peace.
conduce.exampleSense: To contribute or lead to a specific result.

condole.o: PIE word *ḱóm Learned borrowing from Ecclesiastical Latin condolēre, the present active infinitive of condoleō (“to feel severe pain, suffer greatly; to suffer with or feel another’s pain, condole”), from Latin con- (prefix denoting a being or bringing together of several things) + doleō (“to suffer physical pain, hurt; to be sorry, grieve for, deplore, lament”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *delh₁- (“to divide, split”)).
condole.example: ― So sad to look at his face, Miss Douce condoled.
condole.exampleSense: Followed by with: to express condolence to, or sympathetic sorrow with, someone; to lament in sympathy with someone.

condone.o: Learned borrowing from Latin condōnāre (“to forgive”).
condone.example: Rule-utilitarianism is unlikely to condone torturing a child, but it does imply that the torturing of a child is less evil if the torturer shares his pleasure with other sadists-perhaps by inviting an audience, or broadcasting it on the Internet.
condone.exampleSense: To allow, accept or permit (something that is considered morally wrong, offensive, or generally disliked).

monopoly.o: From Latin monopōlium, from Ancient Greek μονοπώλιον (monopṓlion, “a right of exclusive sale”), from μόνος (mónos, “sole”) + πωλέω (pōléō, “to barter, sell”). By surface analysis, mono- + -poly.
monopoly.example: A land monopoly renders its holder(s) nearly almighty in an agricultural society.
monopoly.exampleSense: An exclusive control over the trade or production of a commodity or service through exclusive possession.

virtuosity.o: From virtuoso + -ity (“quality of”); the terminal -o drops out. Compare Middle English vertuosite (“virtuous quality or character”).

virtu.o: Alternative form of vertu. Borrowed from Italian virtù, †vertù (“moral worth, virtue (13th century); determination, perseverance, military valour (14th century); study of the liberal or fine arts; appreciation of, taste for, or expertise in the fine arts; objets d'art collectively (16th century)”); or from French vertu (“virtue”), ultimately from Latin virtūt-, virtus (“virtue”). Doublet of virtue; compare also virtuoso.

dear.o:
adj: From Middle English dere, from Old English dēore, dīere, dīore, dȳre (“of great value or excellence, expensive, beloved”), from Proto-West Germanic *diurī, from Proto-Germanic *diurijaz (“dear, precious; expensive”), probably from Proto-Indo-European *dʰegʷʰ- (“to burn; hot, warm”). Cognates Cognate with Yola dear (“dear”), Saterland Frisian djuur (“precious, dear, costly, expensive”), Alemannic German tüür (“expensive”), Dutch dier, duur (“expensive”), German teuer (“expensive”), Vilamovian taojer, tojer (“dear”), West Flemish diere (“expensive”), Yiddish טײַער (tayer, “expensive”), Danish, Norwegian Bokmål, Norwegian Nynorsk, and Swedish dyr (“expensive”), Faroese dýrur (“expensive”), Icelandic dýr (“expensive”), Finnish tyyris (“expensive”), Livonian tõurõz (“dear”), Northern Sami divrras (“expensive”).

adj: From Middle English dere (“fierce, severe, hard, deadly”), from Old English dēor, dȳr (“brave, bold; severe, dire, vehement”), from Proto-Germanic *deuzaz. Cognate with the above.
dear.example: My dear man, you ought to think twice about who you're trying to blackmail.
dear.exampleSense: An ironic way to start (often after my) addressing an inferior or someone one dislikes.

brothel.o:
noun: Short for brothel-house (“house of prostitution”), from brothel (“a wretch; scoundrel; lecher; harlot; prostitute”) + house, influenced by bordel. For more on brothel (“a wretch”), see below.

noun: From Middle English brothel, brodel, brodelle, brethel (“a wretch, a depraved man or woman”) (compare also Middle English bretheling (“a wretch”)), apparently from an unrecorded Old English *brēoþel (“degenerative, corruptive”), related to Old English ābrēoþan (“to unsettle, degrade, ruin, frustrate, degenerate, deteriorate, fall away”); Old English ābroþen (“degenerate, base, trifling”); both ultimately from Proto-Germanic *breuþaną (“to fall apart; crumble”). The expected modern English form would be *broddle (see fiddle); the failure of the change from /ðl/ to /dl/ may be because of the intervening schwa in the word's uninflected forms, influence from the verb, or most likely, a dialectal development (compare stathel besides staddle).

dichotomous.o: From Late Latin dichotomos, from Ancient Greek διχότομος (dikhótomos, “cut in half”). By surface analysis, dichotomy + -ous.
dichotomous.example: Genus Riccia L. Plants are thalloid, forming rosettes or loose, dichotomous patches.
dichotomous.exampleSense: Dividing or branching into two mutually exclusive pieces.

dichotomize.example: The apostolical benediction dichotomizes all good things into grace and peace.
dichotomize.exampleSense: To separate into two parts, to classify into two classes, or to categorize into two categories.

dichotomy.example: But in the fallacy of false dichotomy, not only do the two alternatives fail to be jointly exhaustive, but they are not even likely. As a result, the disjunctive premise is false, or at least probably false.
dichotomy.exampleSense: The division of a class into two disjoint subclasses that are together comprehensive, as the division of human into female and male.

tacky.o:
adj: From tack + -y.

adj: Sense “in poor taste” from 1888, from earlier sense meaning shabby or seedy. Also see tackey (“neglected horse”), Southern US colloquialism from 1800s, later extended to people.
tacky.example: This paint isn't dry yet; it's still a bit tacky.

watcher.o: From Middle English wacchere, wachere, wacher, equivalent to watch + -er.

tenaciously.example: He continued tenaciously, doggedly continuing over all obstacles.

dusky.example: I like it when it is dusky, just before the street lights come on.

foundry.o: From French fonderie. By surface analysis, found (“to melt (metals)”) + -ry (“place; process”).
foundry.example: Chang gained trust by allaying fears that TSMC would steal designs, as pure-play foundries have no use of them; TSMC stealing from chip designers would be like a printing press stealing plots from novelists.
foundry.exampleSense: A plant that produces chips out of semiconductors in the microelectronics industry.

radix.o: PIE word *wréh₂ds Learned borrowing from Latin rādīx (“a root”). Doublet of radish.

mantissa.o: Borrowed from Latin mantissa, mantīsa, of unknown origin (said by Festus to be a loanword from Etruscan, but it may actually be from Celtic, possibly through Etruscan mediation). Coincidentally, proparoxytone Greek μάντισσα (mántissa) means "female foreteller", as in χαρτομάντισσα (chartomántissa, “cartomancer”) or χειρομάντισσα (cheiromántissa, “chiromancer”).

operand.o: From Late Latin operandum. By surface analysis, operate + -and. Doublet of operandum.
operand.example: When the microprocessor decodes the JSR opcode, it stores the operand into the TEMP register and pushes the current contents of the PC ($00 0128) onto the stack.
operand.exampleSense: A quantity to which an operator is applied (in 3-x, the operands of the subtraction operator are 3 and x).

adoption.o: Borrowed from French adoption, from Latin adoptio, allied to adoptare (“to adopt”). Equivalent to adopt + -ion.
adoption.example: A Chinese baby girl was given away for adoption.
adoption.exampleSense: The state of being adopted; the acceptance of a child of other parents as if he or she were one's own child.

deindividuation.o: From de- + individuation, first described in 1952 by Leon Festinger and colleagues.
deindividuation.example: Digital media allow almost unlimited opportunity for wilful deindividuation. They almost require it. The implications of those liberties, of the ubiquity of anonymity and the language of the crowd, are only beginning to be felt.
deindividuation.exampleSense: The situation where antinormative behaviour is released in groups in which individuals are not seen or paid attention to as individuals; immersion in a group to the point at which the individual ceases to be seen as such.

individualized.o: simple past and past participle of individualize. From individual + -ize.

individualised.o: simple past and past participle of individualise. From individual + -ise.

personalized.o: simple past and past participle of personalize. From personal + -ize.

personalize.example: Gloria Hull, best known as a Black Feminist literary critic, expands and personalizes her examination of creative thought in her first collection of poetry, Healing Heart.
personalize.exampleSense: To imbue something with one's personality.

customize.o: From custom + -ize. First attested in 1934 in American English.

imprecise.example: Rushdie oxymoronically notes that Hobson-Jobson ‘can be wonderfully imprecise at times’ (1985: 82).
imprecise.exampleSense: Not precise or exact; containing some error or uncertainty.

diagnostics.example: The diagnostics were extensive, with scores of laboratory tests.
diagnostics.exampleSense: The process of arriving at a diagnosis (through diagnostic efforts: tests, analysis, thought). Diagnostic methods considered collectively.

diagnose.o: Back-formation from diagnosis. Compare also sclerose (verb).
diagnose.example: Mechanics use this extremely portable tool to diagnose engine faults, clear fault codes, and export data.
diagnose.exampleSense: To determine the cause of a problem.

athletics.o:
noun: From athletic: see -ics. Probably formed on the model of gymnastics.

noun: See the etymology of the corresponding lemma form.
athletics.example: The University of Phoenix, a for-profit educational institution, has turned the traditional relationship between athletics and higher education on its head, reducing it to its commercially exploitive essence.
athletics.exampleSense: Physical activities such as sports and games requiring stamina, fitness and skill.

analytics.o: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀναλυτικά (analutiká, “science of analysis”).

disintegrate.example: There is a Latvian gentleman named Theodore Nemor living at White Friars Mansions, Hampstead, who claims to have invented a machine of a most extraordinary character which is capable of disintegrating any object placed within its sphere of influence.
disintegrate.exampleSense: To undo the integrity of; to break into parts. To cause to break up into infinitesimal parts through the use of a disintegrator.

redintegration.o: From the Latin redintegrātiō (“renewal, restoration, repetition”).
redintegration.example: Is McClelland’s concept of ‘motive’ yet another example of explanation masquerading as analysis? This is obviously so in his definition which includes the reference to redintegration of affect.
redintegration.exampleSense: The reinstatement of a memory upon the presentation of a stimulus element that was a part of the stimulus complex that had aroused the event.

disintegration.example: The sample exhibited an activity of three disintegrations per second.
disintegration.exampleSense: The process of radioactive decay. The radioactive decay of a single atom.

integration.o: From French intégration, from Latin integratio. Morphologically integrate + -ion.
integration.example: One has, in fact, the old choice of regarding the higher integrations as queer offthrows of an infinitely improbable lower-order accident, or as the explanatory foundation of all that leads up to them.
integration.exampleSense: The act or process of making whole or entire.

sector.example: What are your opinions about this practice? Does it have a parallel outside the lusophone sector? Do you know of other stories other than YUGA? Does this mean micronationalism is changing? Is it good, bad, or irrelevant?
sector.exampleSense: A zone; a designated area. A community or subculture within the wider intermicronational community.

bait.o:
noun: From Middle English bayte, bait, beite, from Old Norse beita (“food, bait”), from Proto-Germanic *baitō (“that which is bitten, bait”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeyd- (“to cleave, split, separate”). Cognate with German Beize (“mordant, corrosive fluid; marinade”), Old English bāt (“that which can be bitten, food, bait”). Related to bite.

verb: From Middle English bayten, baiten, beiten, from Old Norse beita (“to bait, cause to bite, feed, hunt”), from Proto-Germanic *baitijaną (“to cause to bite, bridle”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeyd- (“to cleave, split, separate”). Cognate with Icelandic beita (“to bait”), Swedish beta (“to bait, pasture, graze”), German beizen (“to cause to bite, bait”), Old English bǣtan (“to bait, hunt, bridle, bit”).

verb: French battre de l'aile or des ailes, to flap or flutter.

adj: Etymology unknown.
bait.example: And than they com into a lowe medow that was full of swete floures, and there thes noble knyghtes bayted her horses.
bait.exampleSense: To feed and water (a horse or other animal), especially during a journey.

groundbreaking.o: From ground + breaking, in reference to the practice of breaking ground at the beginning of a new building or construction.
groundbreaking.example: The latest model includes several groundbreaking features and improvements.
groundbreaking.exampleSense: Innovative; new, different; doing something that has never been done before.

equitable.o: From French équitable, from Old French, from equité (“equity”).
equitable.example: Security can be obtained but by defined rights, and these can be ensured only by equitable laws.

wellness.o: From Middle English welnes, welenes. By surface analysis, well + -ness.
wellness.example: Diet and exercise are cornerstones of wellness.
wellness.exampleSense: The quality or state of being in good health (sometimes emphasizing both health and safety).

encompass.o: From Middle English encompassen. By surface analysis, en- + compass.
encompass.example: This book on English grammar encompasses all irregular verbs.
encompass.exampleSense: To include completely; to describe fully or comprehensively.

reformation.o:
noun: From Middle English reformacioun, reformation, from Middle French reformation and Latin refōrmātiō, refōrmātiōnis (“reform, change”), from refōrmō (“transform, reshape”), from re- + fōrmō (“shape, form”). By surface analysis, reform + -ation.

noun: Originally a variant of Etymology

reformed.o: simple past and past participle of reform. From Middle English reformen, from Old French reformer, from Latin reformo, reformare. As a noun since 1660s, from French réforme.
reformed.example: The town was one of the strongholds of the Reformed faith.
reformed.exampleSense: Corrected; amended; restored to purity or excellence; said, specifically, of the whole body of Protestant churches originating in the Reformation, or, in a more restricted sense, of those who separated from Martin Luther on the doctrine of consubstantiation, etc., and carried the Reformation, as they claimed, to a higher point.

reform.o: From Middle English reformen, from Old French reformer, from Latin reformo, reformare. As a noun since 1660s, from French réforme.
reform.example: Major reform is needed to improve the efficiency in the factory.
reform.exampleSense: The change of something that is defective, broken, inefficient or otherwise negative, in order to correct or improve it

ingrowth.example: Ingrowth is a common problem with toenails.

growth.o: From grow + -th (abstract nominal suffix). Compare Old Frisian grēd ("meadow, pasture"; > North Frisian greyde (“growth, pasture”)), Middle High German gruote, gruot (“greens, fresh growth, shoot”), Old Norse gróðr ("growth, crop"; > Faroese grøði, Danish grøde (“fruits”), Swedish gröda (“crop, harvest”)). More at grow.
growth.example: Struggle, disappointment, and criticism all contribute to a person's growth.
growth.exampleSense: An increase in psychological strength or resilience; an increased ability to overcome adversity.

transformative.o: From Medieval Latin transformātīvus (“transformative”), from Latin trānsfōrmātus (“transformed”) + -īvus (suffix attached to the perfect passive participial stems of verbs, forming deverbal adjectives meaning ‘doing or related to doing [the verb]’). Trānsfōrmātus is the perfect passive participle of trānsfōrmō (“to transform”), from trāns- (prefix meaning ‘across; beyond; through’) + fōrmō (“to fashion, form, format, shape”) (from fōrma (“appearance, figure, form, shape”); further etymology unknown, perhaps related to Ancient Greek μορφή (morphḗ, “a form, shape”)). The English word is analysable as transform + -ative.

transform.o: From Middle English transformen, from Old French transformer, from Latin transformo, transformare, from trans (“across”, preposition) + forma (“form”).
transform.example: Be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind.
transform.exampleSense: To change the nature, condition or function of; to change in nature, disposition, heart, character, etc.; to convert.

health-care.o: Alternative spelling of health. Inherited from Middle English helthe, from Old English hǣlþ, from Proto-West Germanic *hailiþu, from Proto-Germanic *hailiþō, from *hailaz + *-iþō. Cognate with Old High German heilida. Analyzable as whole, hale, or heal + -th (abstract nominal suffix). More at heal. Doublet of wholth.
health-care.example: You trust that your health-care providers are people of integrity, and if they made a serious mistake that harmed you, they would be honest about it.

sustained.o: simple past and past participle of sustain. From Middle English susteinen, sustenen, from Old French sustenir (French soutenir), from Latin sustineō, sustinēre (“to uphold”), from sub- (“from below, up”) + teneō (“hold”, verb).
sustained.example: Similar studies of rats have employed four different intracranial resorbable, slow sustained release systems—surgical foam, a thermal gel depot, a microcapsule or biodegradable polymer beads.
sustained.exampleSense: Held continuously at a certain level.

insubstantial.o: Probably from Middle French insubstantiel, from Latin insubstantiālis, from in- + substantiālis. By surface analysis, in- + substantial.
insubstantial.example: The bridge was insubstantial and would not safely carry a car.
insubstantial.exampleSense: Lacking substance; not real or strong.

thickness.o: From Middle English thikkenesse, thiknesse, from Old English þicnes (“thickness, viscosity, density, hardness; obscurity, cloud, darkness; thicket; depth, a thick body, anything thick or heavy”), from Proto-West Germanic *þikkwīnassī (“thickness”), equivalent to thick + -ness. Cognate with West Frisian tsjokkens (“thickness”), Old High German dickinessī, dikkinissi, diknissi (“thickness, density”). Eclipsed non-native Middle English crassitude (“thickness”) from Latin crassitūdō (“thickness”).
thickness.example: The thickness of the Earth's crust varies from two to 70 kilometres.
thickness.exampleSense: A measure of how thick (in dimension) something is.

skinny.o: From Middle English skinny (“resembling skin”), equivalent to skin + -y. The meaning associated with lack of fat or muscle possibly derives from the phrase skin and bones; the meaning associated with nudity refers to the exposed skin.
skinny.example: She called to get the skinny on the latest goings-on in the club.
skinny.exampleSense: The details or facts; especially, those obtained by gossip or rumor.

resection.example: Most articles published after this date, however, mention the resectioning of fat around the eyes as an essential constituent of corrective lid surgery.
resection.exampleSense: To excise part or all of a tissue or organ.

resect.o: Borrowed from Latin resectus, past participle of resecare (“to cut off”), formed in turn from re- + secare (“to cut”).
resect.example: The tumor was resected after chemotherapy.
resect.exampleSense: To remove (some part of an organ or structure) by surgical means.

uncharted.o: From un- + charted. Piecewise doublet of uncarded.
uncharted.example: Far out in the uncharted backwaters of the unfashionable end of the Western Spiral arm of the Galaxy lies a small unregarded yellow sun.

decrypt.o: From de- + -crypt, from Ancient Greek κρυπτός (kruptós, literally “hidden, concealed, private, secret”).
decrypt.example: The decrypts were being obtained from the traffic of 78 German stations by the end of 1941, and of 147 stations by the end of 1942.

cryptographic.example: The storage of cryptographic secrets is one of the paramount requirements in building trustworthy systems.

digit.o: From Middle English digit, from Latin digitus (“a finger; a number”). Doublet of digitus and dedo.
digit.example: Jai grabbed Andrew’s shoulders with the same three digits he had used to grab the ancient doubter’s skull and spun him around.
digit.exampleSense: A narrow extremity of the human hand or foot: a finger, thumb, or toe.

uniform.o: Borrowed from Middle French uniforme, from Latin uniformis.
uniform.example: The Hooverette [housedress] can be worn as a dress or as an apron.
uniform.exampleSense: A distinctive outfit that serves to identify members of a group, company, prison inmates, etc.

proven.o: From Scottish English, as past participle of preve, a Middle English variant of prove – compare woven (from weave) and cloven (from cleave), both of which feature -eve → -oven. Preve died out in England, but survived in Scotland, where proven developed, initially in a legal context, as in “The jury ruled that the charges were not proven.” See usage notes for historical usage patterns. Earlier, from Late Latin probō (“test, try, examine, approve, show to be good or fit, prove”, verb), from Latin probus (“good, worthy, excellent”), from Proto-Indo-European *pro-bʰuH-s (“being in front, prominent”), from *pro-, *per- (“toward”) + *bʰuH- (“to be”). Morphologically prove + -n.
proven.example: Mass lexical comparison is not a proven method for demonstrating relationships between languages.
proven.exampleSense: Having been proved; having proved its value or truth.

tidewater.example: Their mission in life was to tote bituminous coal out of the mountain fastness of West Virginia and move it west to the gateways of Deepwater, Columbus and Toledo and east to tidewater at Hampton Roads.
tidewater.exampleSense: Water affected by the flow of the tide, especially tidal streams.

unimpeachable.example: “Patriotism” makes for a slogan that is so unimpeachable it’s arguably even manipulative; as a matter of strategy, it’s harder for opponents to vote against the USA PATRIOT Act than, say, the Enhanced Security Act.
unimpeachable.exampleSense: Not able to be impeached or reproached.

impeachment.o: From Middle English empechement (“hindrance, impediment, obstacle, obstruction; legal accusation or charge; act of calling into question or discrediting; challenge to a claim or right”), and thence either: * from Middle English empechen, empeschen, empesche, enpechen, impechen (“to cause to get stuck; of a ship: to run aground; to block, obstruct; to hinder, impede; to prevent; to interfere with, harm; to criticize, disparage; to bring charges against; to formally accuse of treason or another high crime”) (from Anglo-Norman empecher, Old French empechier, empeechier) + -ment (suffix forming action nouns, concrete nouns, and nouns indicating a result or a condition or state); or * from Old French empechement, empeechement, empeschement (“obstacle”) (modern French empêchement (“impediment, obstacle”)), from empeechier (“to fetter; to hinder”), empescher (“to inhibit, prevent”) + -ment (suffix forming nouns from verbs). The English word is analysable as impeach + -ment. Old French empechier, empeechier and empescher (compare modern French empêcher) are derived from Late Latin impedicāre (“to catch; to entangle”), present active infinitive of Latin impedicō (“to entangle; to fetter”), from im- (variant of in-) + pedica (“fetter, shackle; snare, trap”) (from pēs (“foot”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ped- (“to step, walk; to fall, stumble”)) + -ō. In senses 1.2 (“accusation that a person has committed a crime”) and 1.3 (“act of impeaching or charging a public official with misconduct”), the word has been used in place of Latin impetere, the present active infinitive of impetō (“to assail, attack, rush upon”).
impeachment.example: There is even a gender gap in support for impeachment, with more American women than men in favor of the House inquiry – and Trump’s removal from office.
impeachment.exampleSense: The act of calling into question or challenging the accuracy or propriety of something. The act of impeaching or charging a public official with misconduct, especially if serious, often with the aim of having the official dismissed from office.

impeach.o: From Middle English empechen, borrowed from Anglo-Norman empecher, from Old French empeechier (“to hinder”), from Latin impedicāre (“to fetter”). Cognate with French empêcher (“to prevent”).
impeach.example: President Clinton was impeached by the House in November 1998, but since the Senate acquitted him, he was not removed from office.
impeach.exampleSense: To bring a legal proceeding against a public official.

dome.o: Borrowed from Middle French dome, domme (modern French dôme), from Italian duomo, from Latin domus (ecclesiae) (literally “house (of the church)”), a calque of Ancient Greek οἶκος τῆς ἐκκλησίας (oîkos tês ekklēsías). Doublet of domus and duomo.
dome.example: Was he in trouble, half a ton of rubble landed on the top of his dome.

malnutrition.example: It is predictable that some of these infections occur in individuals immunocompromised by malnutrition or underlying disease (notably cancer or AIDS) or by immunosuppressive therapy.

nourish.o: From Middle English norischen, from Old French nouriss-, stem of one of the conjugated forms of norrir, from Latin nutriō (“to suckle, feed, foster, nourish, cherish, preserve, support”).
nourish.example: He planteth an ash, and the rain doth nourish it.
nourish.exampleSense: To feed and cause to grow; to supply with food or other matter which increases weight and promotes health.

ingestion.o: Borrowed from Latin ingestionem, accusative of ingestio (“a pouring in”), action noun of the perfect passive participle of ingerere (“pour in”), from in- (“in, into”) + gero (“to carry, to bear”).
ingestion.example: Ingestion is the first step of your big data pipeline. You will have to onboard the data in your instance of Spark, whether it is in local mode or cluster mode.
ingestion.exampleSense: Intake of data into a computer system.

interlace.o: From Middle English entrelacen, from Anglo-Norman entrelacer, from Old French inter- + lacer (“weave”).
interlace.example: The opportunity was also taken to remove one of the few examples of gauntleted tracks in this country, interlacing the down fast and slow lines over the bridge.

interleave.example: The Godfather Returns (Random House; 430 pages), by the non-Sicilian Mark Winegardner, is not precisely a sequel; it’s interleaved into the gaps between the three movies.
interleave.exampleSense: To intersperse (something) at regular intervals between the parts of a thing or between items in a group.

seam.o:
noun: From Middle English seem, seme, from Old English sēam (“seam”), from Proto-West Germanic *saum, from Proto-Germanic *saumaz (“that which is sewn”). Cognate with Dutch zoom (“hem, edge”), German Saum (“hem, edge”), Danish and Norwegian Bokmål søm (“seam”), Norwegian Nynorsk saum (“seam”), Swedish söm (“seam”).

verb: From the noun seam.

noun: From Old English sēam (“a burden”), from Latin sagma (“saddle”).

noun: From Middle English seym (“grease”), from Old French saim (“fat”). Compare French saindoux (“lard”).
seam.example: Seam'd o'er with wounds which his own sabre gave.
seam.exampleSense: To mark with a seam or line; to scar.

seamless.o: From Middle English seemles, semeles, semles, Old English *sēamlēas, equivalent to seam + -less. Cognate with Norwegian Bokmål sømløs (“seamless”), Swedish sömlös (“seamless”).

permutation.o: From Middle English permutacioun, permutacyoun, from Old French permutacïon, promutatïon and Medieval Latin permūtātiōnem, accusative of permūtātiō. Morphologically permute + -ation.
permutation.example: There are six permutations of three elements, e.g. {abc, acb, bac, bca, cab, cba}.
permutation.exampleSense: An ordering of a finite set of distinct elements.

overview.example: Gouldner, on the other hand, overviewed all of sociology as it exists in the Western world today, using Talcott Parsons as a "representative" example of its dominant mode of thought.
overview.exampleSense: To engage in an overview; to provide a brief summary.

discrete.o: From Old French discret, from Latin discrētus, past participle of discernō (“divide”), from dis- + cernō (“sift”). Doublet of discreet.
discrete.example: It's not that there aren't measurable, quantifiable differences between all these categories we impose upon things, it's just that for the most part they fit not into discrete units, but into a continuum.

dimensional.example: What is the meaning of an n-dimensional space when n is greater than three, and what purposes can it serve?
dimensional.exampleSense: Having dimension or dimensions; three-dimensional. Appended to cardinal numbers or algebraic symbols to form adjectives meaning "having the stated number of dimensions".

multiplication.o: Borrowed from Middle French, from Old French multiplicacion, from Latin multiplicatio, multiplicationem; ~equivalent to multiplicate + -ion.

midwinter.o: From Middle English midwinter, mydwinter, mydwynter, from Old English midwinter, from Proto-West Germanic *midiwintru, from Proto-Germanic *midjawintruz (“midwinter”), equivalent to mid- + winter. Cognate with West Frisian midwinter (“midwinter”), Dutch midwinter (“midwinter”), German Mittwinter (“midwinter”), Danish midvinter (“midwinter”), Swedish midvinter (“midwinter”).
midwinter.example: Except for the mid-winter period, when the 11.30 a.m. from Paddington and its opposite number will be withdrawn - Torquay now has seven daily expresses to and from Paddington as compared with five down and six up previously.

hyperspace.example: We can only get to the Nimrodian Galaxy if we go through hyperspace.
hyperspace.exampleSense: A notional space orthogonal to the usual dimensions of space-time often used for faster-than-light travel.

birch.o: PIE word *bʰerHǵós From Middle English birche, birk, from Old English birċe, bierċe, from Proto-West Germanic *birkijā, from Proto-Germanic *birkijǭ, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰerHǵos. Cognates Compare West Frisian bjirk, German Birke, variant of *berkō (compare Dutch berk, Danish birk, Swedish björk, Norwegian bjørk), Sanskrit भूर्ज (bhūrjá), Lithuanian béržas, Czech bříza, Ossetian бӕрз (bærz), Russian берёза (berjóza)), Latin fraxinus (“ash tree, ash javelin”), Albanian bredh.
birch.example: The Mexica were always washing, in water obtained through the aqueduct, or in the lake, and would often go to the popular baths in the numerous stone steam houses (where birching, with grasses, or massage was also available).
birch.exampleSense: To punish as though one were using a stick, bundle of twigs, or rod made of birch wood.

attestation.o: From Middle French attestation, from Latin attestātiō; by surface analysis, attest + -ation.
attestation.example: The eastern-most attestation of Sl skola in the meaning of synagogue appears to be in Smolensk Russian.
attestation.exampleSense: An appearance in print or otherwise recorded on a permanent medium.

unmatched.o: simple past and past participle of unmatch. From un- + match.

hands down.o:
adv: The origin of this colloquialism seems to have its roots in mid-19th century horseracing. When a horse jockey is nearing the finish line far ahead of the competition, "with victory certain", he could drop his hands, relaxing his hold on the reins, and "still win the race". By the late 19th century the phrase was being used in non-racing contexts to mean 'with no trouble at all.'

verb: See hand down.
hands down.example: That is a rather difficult task, hands down.

trade-off.example: In writing, there's often a trade-off between being concise and being complete.
trade-off.exampleSense: Any situation in which the quality or quantity of one thing must be decreased for another to be increased.

unbridled.example: She jumped into the project with unbridled enthusiasm.

unbridle.example: If we unbridle our greed and lust we will be nothing but animals.

tile.o:
noun: From Middle English tile, tyl, tigel, tiȝel, teȝele, from Old English tiġele, tieġle, tiġle (“tile, brick”), from Proto-West Germanic *tigulā (“tile, brick”), from Proto-Germanic *tigulǭ (“tile, brick”), from Latin tēgula, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)teg- (“to cover”). Doublet of tegula. Cognates Cognate with Saterland Frisian Tichel (“tile”), Dutch tichel (“brick”), tegel (“tile”), German Ziegel (“brick, roof tile”), Luxembourgish Zill (“brick, tile”), Danish tegl (“brick”), Faroese tigul (“tile”), Icelandic tigl (“brick, tile”), Norwegian Nynorsk tegl (“brick, roof tile”), Swedish tegel (“brick, tile”), Asturian teya (“tile”), Catalan teula (“tile”), French tuile (“tile”), Galician telha, tella (“roof tile”), Italian tegola (“roof tile”), Mirandese teilha (“roof tile”), Portuguese telha (“roof tile”), Spanish teja (“roof tile”), Belarusian цэ́гла (céhla, “brick”), Czech cihla (“brick”), Polish cegła (“brick”), Serbo-Croatian cígla (“brick”), Ukrainian це́гла (céhla, “brick”), Finnish tiili (“brick, tile”).

verb: See tiler (“doorkeeper at a Masonic lodge”).

rhetorician.o: From Middle English rethoricien, from Old French retoricien; equivalent to rhetoric + -ian.
rhetorician.example: In his classicising Troilus and Criseyde, set with pagan aplomb in ancient Troy, he approvingly quotes the rhetorician Geoffrey of Vinsauf’s New Poetics.
rhetorician.exampleSense: An expert or student of rhetoric.

rhetorical question.example: Are you nuts? Don't answer that – it's a rhetorical question.
rhetorical question.exampleSense: A question to which the asker does not expect an answer.

rhetorically.o: From Middle English retorycally; equivalent to rhetorical + -ly.

rhetorical.o: From Middle English rethorycal, rethoricalle, rethorycall, from rethorik, rhetoric (noun) or Latin rēthoricus, rhētoricus, from Ancient Greek ῥητορικός (rhētorikós, “concerning public speaking”). By surface analysis, rhetoric + -al.
rhetorical.example: A rhetorical question is one used merely to make a point, with no response expected.
rhetorical.exampleSense: Part of or similar to rhetoric, the use of language as a means to persuade.

device.o: From Middle English devis, devise, devyce, devys, devyse, from Old French devis and devise, from Latin dīvīsus, past participle of dīvidō (“to divide”). Doublet of devise (noun).
device.example: He disappointeth the devices of the crafty, so that their hands cannot perform their enterprise.
device.exampleSense: A project or scheme, often designed to deceive; a stratagem; an artifice.

seniority.o: From Middle English senyoryte, from Medieval Latin senioritas, from Latin senior (“elder”).
seniority.example: It's an old-fashioned company, with parking spaces and other perks doled out on the basis of seniority.
seniority.exampleSense: A measure of the amount of time a person has been a member of an organization, as compared to other members, and with an eye towards awarding privileges to those who have been members longer.

sincerely.o: From sincere + -ly, from Latin sincērus (“pure, clean, sound”).
sincerely.example: Please consider the proposal carefully and let me know what you decide.
sincerely.exampleSense: A conventional formula for ending a letter, used when the salutation addresses the person for whom the letter is intended by his or her name.

insincerity.example: His insincerity was obvious to all; he was neither honest nor believable.
insincerity.exampleSense: Property of being insincere, lacking sincerity or truthfulness.

sincerity.o: From Middle English sinceritie, from Old French sincerité and Medieval Latin sincēritās; both from Latin sincēritās, from sincērus + -tās. Equivalent to sincere + -ity.
sincerity.example: I protest, in the sincerity of love.
sincerity.exampleSense: The quality or state of being sincere.

burn the midnight oil.o: Originally referring to the act of burning lamp oil in oil lamps for light at night. The collocation midnight oil in its literal sense is attested from mid 17th c.
burn the midnight oil.example: She was burning the midnight oil to finish her part of the project.
burn the midnight oil.exampleSense: To work studiously, especially late into the night.

snowed under.o: simple past and past participle of snow. The noun is derived from Middle English snaw, snou, snow (“snow; accumulation of snow; snowfall; snowstorm; whiteness”), from Old English snāw (“snow”), from Proto-West Germanic *snaiw (“snow”), from Proto-Germanic *snaiwaz (“snow”), from Proto-Indo-European *snóygʷʰos (“snow”), from *sneygʷʰ- (“to snow”). The verb is derived from Middle English snouen (“to snow; (figurative) to shower”), from snou, snow (noun) (see above) + -en (suffix forming the infinitive of verbs). Displaced Old English snīwan, whence English snew (obsolete). Verb etymology 1, verb sense 2.3.2 (“to convince or hoodwink (someone)”) probably refers to a person being blinded or confused by a snowstorm. The adjective comes from the phrase a snowball's chance in hell, also see snowball clause at Wikipedia. Cognates * Scots snaw (“snow”) * Yola sneew, sneow, snow, snowe (“snow”) * North Frisian Sne, sni, snii, snii'e, snä, snäi (“snow”) * Saterland Frisian Snee (“snow”) * West Frisian snie (“snow”) * Alemannic German schnee, schnei, schnia, schné, schnìj (“snow”) * Bavarian schnea, sghneab (“snow”) * Cimbrian snea, snèa (“snow”) * Dutch snee, sneeuw (“snow”) * German Schnee (“snow”) * Limburgish Schnië, snieë (“snow”) * Luxembourgish Schnéi (“snow”) * Mòcheno schnea (“snow”) * Vilamovian śnej, šnej, śnyi (“snow”) * Yiddish שניי (shney, “snow”) * Danish sne (“snow”) * Elfdalian sniųo (“snow”) * Faroese snjógvur (“snow”) * Icelandic snjár, snjór, snær (“snow”) * Norwegian Bokmål sne, snø (“snow”) * Norwegian Nynorsk snjo, snø (“snow”) * Swedish snö (“snow”) * Gothic 𐍃𐌽𐌰𐌹𐍅𐍃 (snaiws, “snow”) * Irish sneachta (“snow”) * Manx sniaghtey (“snow”) * Scottish Gaelic sneachd, sneachda (“snow”) * Welsh nyf (“snow”) * Latin nix (“snow”) * Ancient Greek νίψ (níps, “snow”) * Latvian snìegs (“snow”) * Lithuanian sniẽgas (“snow”) * Belarusian, Russian, and Macedonian снег (sneg, “snow”) * Bulgarian сняг (snjag, “snow”) * Czech sníh (“snow”) * Polish śnieg, śmiég (“snow”) * Serbo-Croatian сне̑г, сније̑г, snȇg, snig, snijȇg (“snow”) * Slovak sneh (“snow”) * Slovene sneg (“snow”) * Ukrainian сніг (snih, “snow”) * Shughni жиниҷ (žiniǰ, “snow”) * Avestan 𐬯𐬥𐬀𐬉𐬲𐬀𐬌𐬙𐬌 (snaēžaⁱti, “to snow”) * Sanskrit स्नेह (snéha, “grease, oil”)
snowed under.example: We are completely snowed under at work because it is the end of the tax year.
snowed under.exampleSense: Having a lot of things to do, usually work-related; tied up.

mend.o:
verb: From Middle English menden (“to cure; to do good to, benefit; to do or make better, improve; to get better, recover; to keep in a good state; to put right, amend; to reform, repent”), the aphetic form of amenden (“to alter, change (especially for the better); to atone; to chastise, punish; to correct, remedy, amend; to cure; to excel, surpass; to forgive; to get or make better, improve; to make ready; to mend, repair, restore; to get well, recover; to relieve”), or from its etymon Anglo-Norman amender and Old French amender (“to cure; to fix, repair; to set right, correct”) (modern French amender), from Latin ēmendāre, the present active infinitive of ēmendō (“to atone; to chastise, punish; to correct, remedy, amend; to cure”), from ē- (variant of ex- (prefix meaning ‘away; out’)) + mendum (“defect; error, fault”) (from Proto-Indo-European *mend- (“defect; fault”)) + -ō (suffix forming first-conjugation verbs).

noun: Partly: * (chiefly etymology 2 sense 2 (“recompense; restoration or reparation”)) from Middle English mend, mende (“cure, remedy; damages, recompense; atonement; penance; relief”), the aphetic form of amende, amendes (“retribution, amends; a fine; atonement; penance”) (though attested slightly earlier); or directly from its etymon Anglo-Norman amende, Middle French amende, and Old French amende (“a fine”) (modern French amende), from amender (verb) (see etymology 1); and * from mend (verb).
mend.example: My trousers have a big rip in them and need mending.
mend.exampleSense: To physically repair (something that is broken, defaced, decayed, torn, or otherwise damaged).

delicious.o: From Middle English delicious, from Anglo-Norman delicious, from Old French delicious, delicieux, from Late Latin dēliciōsus (“delicate, delicious”), from dēliciae (“delights”), plural of dēlicia (“pleasure”), from delicere (“to allure, to entice”), from de- (“away”) + laciō (“to lure, deceive”), from Proto-Italic *lakjō (“to draw, pull”), of unknown ultimate origin. Displaced native Old English ārlīċ (“delicious”).
delicious.example: But the houses are so delicious and the way they're townscaped on to hilly bits is absolutely wonderful.
delicious.exampleSense: Pleasing to a person's taste; pleasing to the eyes or mind.

unperson.o: From un- + person. Coined by George Orwell in 1949 as part of the Newspeak in his novel Nineteen Eighty-Four, where it refers to a person who has been executed or has fallen out of favor; whose entire history has been erased.
unperson.example: With his identity stolen, he became an unperson, unable to prove his existence to the government.
unperson.exampleSense: A person who has been stripped of rights, identity, or humanity.

unceasing.example: To handle the unceasing traffic increase, immense sums of money are being expended in dealing with bottlenecks.

unpleasantness.example: Given the behaviour of the members, who do normally come to Lord’s, this seemed a bizarre attempt to offload the unpleasantness on hoi polloi taking advantage of some rare £25 tickets.
unpleasantness.exampleSense: The property of being unpleasant or disagreeable.

unpleasant.o: From Middle English unplesaunt, equivalent to un- + pleasant.

scruple.o: From Old French scrupule, from Latin scrūpulus (“(literally) a small sharp or pointed stone; uneasiness of mind, anxiety, doubt, trouble; scruple”) and scrūpulum (“one twenty-fourth of an ounce”), diminutives of scrūpus (“a rough or sharp stone; anxiety, uneasiness”); perhaps akin to Ancient Greek σκύρος (skúros, “the chippings of stone”), from ξυρόν (xurón, “razor”), from ξύω (xúō, “to scrape”), from Proto-Indo-European *ksew-. Doublet of escropulo and escrupulo.
scruple.example: The most ancient hour was divided into 1,080 scruples. The Jews suppose Issachar to have brought it from heaven.
scruple.exampleSense: A Hebrew unit of time equal to ¹⁄₁₀₈₀ hour.

scrummy.example: There's an all day menu, with lots of fish dishes such as fish soup, tuna, and monkfish. Pudding might include a scrummy rosemary panacotta.

scrumptious.o: Probably from scrimp (“to put on short allowance, limit, straiten; to be frugal”) + -ious (suffix forming adjectives denoting the presence of a quality in any degree (usually an abundance)), possibly modelled after scrimption (“small portion, little bit, scrap”). If that hypothesis is true, then scrumpy may be related, via roots referring to little amounts. Douglas Harper instead derives the word from sumptuous. As the early cites in British English have a clearly different sense from the early cites in American English, only to merge together later, it may be that there were originally two unrelated words.
scrumptious.example: Barbara Cartland scratched out this trusty 19th-century romancer concerning the scrumptious Serena Staverly (Diana Rigg), who has the dreadful misfortune to be lost in a game of cards to the flint-hearted Lord Justin.
scrumptious.exampleSense: Of a person or thing: excellent, wonderful; also, very aesthetically pleasing or attractive; good enough to eat.

strip off.example: The feathers strip off much more easily and cleanly while the bird is yet warm.

rip-off.example: He promised to mail me a refund, but it was just a rip-off.

wheel.o: From Middle English whel, from Old English hwēol, from Proto-West Germanic *hwehwl, from Proto-Germanic *hwehwlą, *hweulō, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷekʷlóm, *kʷékʷlos, *kʷékʷléh₂, reduplication of *kʷel- (“to turn”) and a suffix (literally "(the thing that) turns and turns"). See also West Frisian tsjil, Dutch wiel, Danish, Norwegian Bokmål, Norwegian Nynorsk, and Swedish hjul; also Tocharian B kokale (“cart, wagon”), Ancient Greek κύκλος (kúklos, “cycle, wheel”), Avestan 𐬗𐬀𐬑𐬭𐬀 (caxra), Sanskrit चक्र (cakrá); and Latin colō (“to till, cultivate”), Tocharian A and Tocharian B käl- (“to bear; bring”), Ancient Greek πέλω (pélō, “to come into existence, become”), Old Church Slavonic коло (kolo, “wheel”), Albanian sjell (“to bring, carry, turn around”), Avestan 𐬗𐬀𐬭𐬀𐬌𐬙𐬌 (caraⁱti, “it circulates”), Sanskrit चरति (cárati, “it moves, wanders”). Doublet of chakra, chakram, charkha, chukker, cycle, cyclus, and kike.
wheel.example: Then I went down to the potter's house, and, behold, he wrought a work on the wheels.
wheel.exampleSense: A circular device capable of rotating on its axis, facilitating movement or transportation or performing labour in machines. A potter's wheel.

sparse.example: The Leicester to Grimsby service will become hourly throughout (with some extensions to Cleethorpes as at present), while a new hourly Peterborough to Doncaster service via Spalding, Sleaford and Lincoln will join up two routes with a sparse service at present.

nickname.o: From Middle English neke name, alteration (due to a rebracketing of an ekename as a nekename) of earlier ekename (“nickname”), from eke (“additional”) + name. Compare Old Norse aukanafn, auknafn, auknefni, Faroese eyknevni, Danish øgenavn, Norwegian Nynorsk aukenamn, Swedish öknamn, and German Low German Ökelname. For other similar cases of incorrect division, see also apron, daffodil, newt, orange, umpire.
nickname.example: "The Big Apple" is a common nickname for New York City.
nickname.exampleSense: A familiar, invented name for a person or thing used instead of the actual name of the person or thing, often based on some noteworthy characteristic.

stall.o:
noun: From Middle English stall, stalle, from Old English steall (“standing place, position”), from Proto-Germanic *stallaz, from Proto-Indo-European *stel- (“to place, put, post, stand”). Cognate with French étal, Italian stallo, German Stall, Swedish stall.

noun: From Middle English stallen (“to abide, dwell, place in a location, stop, come to a standstill”), partly from Old French estaler, ultimately from the same origin as Etymology 1 (see above); and partly from Middle English stalle (“fixed position, stall”).
stall.example: The pilot stalled the plane by pulling the nose up too high at a slow airspeed.
stall.exampleSense: To cause to exceed the critical angle of attack, resulting in loss of lift.

training.o: present participle and gerund of train. From Middle English trayne (“train”), from Old French train (“a delay, a drawing out”), from traïner (“to pull out, to draw”), from Vulgar Latin *traginō, from *tragō, from Latin trahō (“to pull, to draw”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *tregʰ- (“to pull, draw, drag”). The verb was derived from the noun in Middle English. For the meaning to teach compare typologically Russian ната́скивать (natáskivatʹ) (akin to тащи́ть (taščítʹ)).
training.example: Becoming more aware of the progress that scientists have made on behavioral fronts can reduce the risk that other natural scientists will resort to mystical agential accounts when they exceed the limits of their own disciplinary training.
training.exampleSense: The activity of imparting and acquiring skills.

influence.o: From Middle English influence, from Old French influence (“emanation from the stars affecting one's fate”), from Medieval Latin īnfluentia, from Latin īnfluēns (“flowing in”), present active participle of īnfluō (“flow into”), from in- (“in-”) + fluō (“flow”). Doublet of influenza.
influence.example: I'm not able to exercise influence over him.
influence.exampleSense: An action exerted by a person or thing with such power on another to cause change.

crayfish.o: Alteration (by folk etymological influence of fish) of Middle English crevis (whence modern dialectal crevis), from Old French crevice ("crayfish"; > Modern French: écrevisse), from Frankish *krebitja (“crayfish”), diminutive of Frankish *krebit (“crab”), from Proto-Germanic *krabitaz (“crab, cancer”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *gerbʰ-, *grebʰ- (“to scratch, crawl”), or from a substrate word folk-etymologically influenced by this root. Akin to Old High German krebiz (Modern German Krebs (“crustacean, crab, crayfish”)), Middle Low German krēvet (“crab, crayfish”), Dutch kreeft (“crayfish, lobster”), Old English crabba (“crab”). More at crab. Doublet of crevette, crevis, and Krebs.

cray.o:
noun: Clipping of crayfish.

adj: Clipping of crazy, with -y to clarify pronunciation. Compare vacay (“vacation”).
cray.example: That small of a fine for that kind of blatant disregard is cray.

insanely.example: Gloating silently, she laved handfuls of hot sand over her, her mind alternating sanely and insanely.
insanely.exampleSense: In an insane manner; not sanely.

insane.o: From Latin īnsānus (“unsound in mind; mad, insane”), from in- + sānus (“sound, sane”), equivalent to in- + sane.
insane.example: That guy is insane at FPS games.

intima.o: Borrowed from Latin intima, feminine form of intimus (“innermost”).

contrite.o: From Middle English contrit, from Old French contrit, from Latin contrītus (literally “ground to pieces”), perfect passive participle of conterō (“grind, bruise”), from con- + terō (“rub, wear away”).

suspensive.o: Learned borrowing from Latin suspēnsīvus. First attested in 1557. By surface analysis, suspense + -ive.
suspensive.example: Effect of an appeal – In principle, an appeal has a suspensive effect (Art. 51(1) VRP). The term suspensive effect denotes the fact that the legal consequence prescribed by the ruling does not become effective until the conclusion of the appeal procedure.
