pensive.o: From Middle English pensif, pensyfe, pencyve, from Old French pensif (“thoughtful”), from penser (“to think”) (from Latin pēnsō) + -if (English -ive).
pensive.example: Through the deep grass the faces of the three children glowed like pensive moons.

approachable.exampleSense: Easily approached; easy to talk to.

incredibly.example: Incredibly, when he died they found he had left a million dollars to the Poetry Foundation.
incredibly.exampleSense: Used to note the surprising or hard-to-believe nature of what is being said and suggest that it is nevertheless true.

incredulity.o: Attested since 1430. From Middle English incredulite, from Old French incredulité, from Late Latin incredulitas, from Latin incredulus (“unbelieving”) + -itas (“-ity”), equivalent to incredulous + -ity.
incredulity.example: Wide went her eyes in wonder and incredulity, as she beheld this seeming apparition risen from the dead.
incredulity.exampleSense: Unwillingness or inability to believe; doubt about the truth or verisimilitude of something; disbelief.

reassure.o: From Old French rasseürer (French rassurer), from re- + asseürer; as if re- + assure.
reassure.example: The boy's mother reassured him that there was no monster hiding under the bed.
reassure.exampleSense: To assure anew; to restore confidence to; to free from fear or self-doubt.

assuredness.example: A lack of assuredness in defence, with Spurs missing holding midfielder Scott Parker, also did not help the home side and Norwich took advantage to score the winner.
assuredness.exampleSense: The state or quality of being assured.

assure.o: From Old French asseurer (Modern French assurer), from Latin ad- + securus (“secure”). Cognate with Spanish asegurar. Doublet of assecure.
assure.example: I assure you that the program will work smoothly when we demonstrate it to the client.
assure.exampleSense: To give (someone) confidence in the trustworthiness of (something).

spokesperson.o: From spoke (“past participle of speak”) + -s- + person.
spokesperson.example: Biden and his spokespeople have proudly touted his signature COVID relief bill as a major stimulus for policing in a national context already characterized by globally unparalleled police spending.
spokesperson.exampleSense: A person who acts as the voice of another person or a group of people.

spokeswoman.o: From spoke (“past participle of speak”) + -s- + woman.

spoken.example: Algebra is not a spoken language like French or Spanish, it is a math language.

spokesman.o: From spoke (“past participle of speak”) + -s- + man.
spokesman.example: President Moon Jae-in proposed the plan this week during a meeting with government officials, his spokesman said.
spokesman.exampleSense: One who speaks as the voice of another person or a group of people.

pull off.example: After about a mile, we pulled off the main road onto a dirt track.
pull off.exampleSense: To turn off a road (onto the side of the road, or onto another road).

ingressive.example: This spring is the ingressive source of the water that flows through the cave.
ingressive.exampleSense: Being a source or channel through which water enters or once entered an area.

unimpressive.example: In a culture dominated by the young, fun and hard-bodied, the middle-aged big man struggles for visibility; he is dismissed as unimpressive, a cultural dead weight.
unimpressive.exampleSense: Lacking the ability to impress, inability to produce an impression.

simulant.example: Due to its low cost and close visual likeness to diamond, cubic zirconia has remained the most gemologically and economically important diamond simulant since 1976.
simulant.exampleSense: Something that simulates something else such as a gemstone.

simular.o: From Latin simulārius, from simulō (“to simulate”).
simular.example: Christ calleth the Pharisees hypocrites, that is to say, simulars, and painted sepulchres.
simular.exampleSense: One who pretends to be what he is not; one who, or that which, simulates or counterfeits something; a pretender.

stemma.o: Borrowed from Latin stemma, from Ancient Greek στέμμα (stémma).

banishment.example: He has been in banishment from his home country for well over four years.
banishment.exampleSense: The state of being banished, exile.

banish.o: From Middle English banishen, from Old French baniss-, extended stem of banir (“to proclaim, ban, banish”), of Germanic origin and Old English bannan, from Proto-Germanic *bannaną (“curse, forbid”). Compare French bannir. Doublet of ban.
banish.example: He was banished from the kingdom for his crimes.
banish.exampleSense: To send someone away and forbid that person from returning.

ousting.o: present participle and gerund of oust. From Anglo-Norman ouster, oustier, from Old French oster (modern French ôter), from post-classical Latin obstare (“to remove”), classical obstāre (“to obstruct, stand in the way of”). Not related to out.

ouster.o:
noun: From Old French ouster, oustre, a nominalization of Anglo-Norman oustre (“to oust”).

noun: From oust + -er.
ouster.example: The announcement blindsided employees, many of whom learned of the sudden ouster from an internal announcement and the company’s public facing blog.
ouster.exampleSense: The forceful removal of a politician or regime from power; a coup; an ousting.

oust.o: From Anglo-Norman ouster, oustier, from Old French oster (modern French ôter), from post-classical Latin obstare (“to remove”), classical obstāre (“to obstruct, stand in the way of”). Not related to out.
oust.example: The protesters became so noisy that they were finally ousted from the meeting.

wither.o:
verb: From Middle English widren, wydderen (“to dry up, shrivel”), related to or perhaps an alteration of Middle English wederen (“to expose to weather”), from Old English wederian (“to expose to weather, exhibit a change of weather”). Cognates From Proto-Germanic: Dutch verwederen, Dutch verweren (“to erode by weather”), German verwittern, wittern (“to be ruined by weather; to erode”), Swedish vittra (“wither”). More at weather.

noun: See the etymology of the corresponding lemma form.

adv: From Middle English wither, from Old English wiþer (“again, against”, adverb in compounds), from Proto-West Germanic *wiþr (“against, toward”). Cognates From Proto-Germanic: Low German wedder (“against”), Dutch weer (“again, back”), German wider (“against, contrary to”), German wieder (“again”), Gothic 𐍅𐌹𐌸𐍂𐌰 (wiþra), Old Norse viðr. More at with.

verb: From Middle English witheren, from Old English wiþerian (“to resist, oppose, struggle against”). Cognates From Proto-Germanic: Middle Dutch wideren, Old High German widarōn.
wither.example: States thrive or wither as moons wax and wane.
wither.exampleSense: To lose vigour or power; to languish; to pass away.

converged.o: simple past and past participle of converge. From Latin convergere, from con- (“together”) + vergere (“to bend”).

tracking.o: present participle and gerund of track. From Middle English trak, tracke, from Old French trac (“track of horses, trail, trace”), of uncertain origin. Likely from a Germanic source, either Old Norse traðk ("a track; path; trodden spot"; > Icelandic traðk (“a track; path; tread”), Faroese traðk (“track; tracks”), Norwegian tråkke (“to trample”)) or from Middle Dutch trec, *trac, treck ("line, row, series"; > Dutch trek (“a draft; feature; trait; groove; expedition”)), German Low German Treck (“a draught; movement; passage; flow”). See tread, trek.

tracker.example: At the time, tracking chiptunes (i.e. using trackers) was the fundamental method of chipmusic-making.
tracker.exampleSense: A type of computer software for composing music by aligning notes or samples on parallel timelines.

as far as.example: As far as the choice makes any difference, I prefer the second option.
as far as.exampleSense: To the degree or extent that.

when it comes to.example: I’d prefer to keep things straightforward and stick in the lovely, tasty yolks, too. After all, there’s no such thing as too rich when it comes to brownies.

bank statement.example: Turian Merchant: This isn't a proof of purchase.
bank statement.exampleSense: A communication from a bank to a person holding an account in that bank, usually issued monthly, detailing the value of the holdings in that account and the effects of all transactions occurring with respect to that account.

overstatement.example: The story he gave was something of an overstatement of the facts.
overstatement.exampleSense: An exaggeration; a statement in excess of what is reasonable.

statement.o:
noun: From state + -ment.

verb: Back-formation from statementing or back-formation from statemented.
statement.example: However, it is the responsibility of the programmer to ensure that the control ultimately reaches the last statement of the range.
statement.exampleSense: An instruction in a computer program, especially one that returns no value, as opposed to a function call.

put out.example: One of the accident victims had to be put out by the passers-by.
put out.exampleSense: To cause something to go out, particularly To extinguish (fire).

national.o: From Middle French national, corresponding to nation + -al.
national.example: Import tariffs were raised for the national interest.
national.exampleSense: Pertaining to a nation or country, especially as a whole; affecting, shared by, or existing throughout all of a nation.

citizen.o: From Middle English citeseyn (“inhabitant of a city or town”), citezein, citisein, from Anglo-Norman citesain (“city-dweller, town-dweller”), citesein, citezein, alteration of citeien from cite (“city”) + -ien (“-ain”) (probable variant of cithein perhaps influenced by dainzain (“denizen”), deinzein), from Old French cite (“city”) + -ien (whence French citoyen), from earlier citet, from Latin civitatem, citatem, from civis. See also city. Displaced native Old English burhsittend and Old English ceasterware.
citizen.example: Assistant: You'll meet with the managing director and Dr Sinita Brahmachari, the engineer who designed the chair.
citizen.exampleSense: A legally recognized member of a state, with associated rights and obligations; a person considered in terms of this role.

repatriate.o: Borrowed from Latin repatriare, from re- + patria (“homeland”). Cognate to repair (“to return”).
repatriate.example: Greece repatriated an Athenian frieze from France, arranging for it to be sent back to Athens.
repatriate.exampleSense: To return or restore (artworks, museum exhibits, etc.) to their country of origin.

repatriation.o: Either a learned borrowing from Medieval Latin repatriātiō (“act of restoring someone to their homeland”) or from Italian repatriazione and remodelled after words in -ation. By surface analysis, repatriate + -ion.

undercut.o: From Middle English undercutten, equivalent to under- + cut.
undercut.example: The fact that, to cover low tariffs on bulk commodities, the railways have to charge very high rates on high-value goods, such as manufactures, has provided road operators with a golden opportunity to undercut the railway.
undercut.exampleSense: To sell (something) at a lower price, or to work for lower wages, than a competitor.

chequer.o: See checker. (fruit): Apparently in allusion to the chequered or spotted appearance of the fruit. According to the Oxford English Dictionary, “the surmises that chequer may be a corruption of choker, and that ‘choker’ may once have been the name, are gratuitous.”
chequer.example: Our minds are, as it were, chequered with truth and falsehood.

denominate.o: PIE word *h₁nómn̥ Inherited from Middle English denominat(e) (“named, called”), borrowed from Latin dēnōminātus, perfect passive participle of dēnōminō, see -ate (etymology 1, 2 and 3). By surface analysis, de- + nominate.
denominate.example: Oil is denominated in dollars, so changes in the strength of the dollar affect oil prices everywhere.
denominate.exampleSense: To express in a monetary unit.

nomination.o: From Middle English nominacion, nomination, from Middle French nominacion and its etymon Latin nōminātiō, from the verb nōminō (“to name; to nominate”). By surface analysis, nominate + -ion.

capitol.o: From Middle English Capitolie, via Anglo-Norman capitolie, Old French capitoile, from Latin Capitōlium (“Capitoline Hill, its temples; any similar citadel”), from the oblique stem of caput (“head”) + -ō (noun-forming suffix) or -ōlus (“-ole”, diminutive suffix) + -ium (toponym-forming suffix). Compare Latin capitō and capitulum. As a French magistrate, via French capitoul, from Capitole, the town hall of Toulouse. Doublet of Capitolium and capitoul.
capitol.example: The state capitol is located smack-dab in the middle of the state's capital.
capitol.exampleSense: Any building or complex of buildings in which a legislature meets.

wear away.example: As the sensitiveness which greeted my new position wore away, I began to rather like the freedom of my new character.

wear.o:
verb: Inherited from Middle English weren, werien, from Old English werian (“to clothe, cover over; put on, wear, use; stock (land)”), from Proto-West Germanic *waʀjan, from Proto-Germanic *wazjaną (“to clothe”), from Proto-Indo-European *wes- (“to dress, put on (clothes)”). Cognate to Sanskrit वस्ते (váste), Ancient Greek ἕννυμι (hénnumi, “put on”), Latin vestis (“garment”) (English vest), Albanian vesh (“dress up, wear”), Tocharian B wäs-, Old Armenian զգենում (zgenum), Welsh gwisgo, Hittite 𒉿𒀸- (waš-). Originally a weak verb (i.e. with a past tense in -ed), it became irregular during the Middle English period by analogy with verbs like beren (whence bear) and teren (whence tear).

verb: From Middle English weren, werien, from Old English werian (“to guard, keep, defend; ward off, hinder, prevent, forbid; restrain; occupy, inhabit; dam up; discharge obligations on (land)”), from Proto-West Germanic *warjan, from Proto-Germanic *warjaną (“to defend, protect, ward off”), from Proto-Indo-European *wer- (“to close, cover, protect, save, defend”). Cognate with Scots wer, weir (“to defend, protect”), Dutch weren (“to aver, ward off”), German wehren (“to fight”), Swedish värja (“to defend, ward off”), Icelandic verja (“to defend”).
wear.example: He wears eyeglasses.  She wears her hair in braids.
wear.exampleSense: To have on: To have or carry on one's person habitually, consistently; or, to maintain in a particular fashion or manner.

drip.o:
verb: From Middle English drippen, druppen, from Old English drypan, from Proto-Germanic *drupjaną (“to fall in drops, drip”), from Proto-Germanic *drupô (“drop”). Akin to West Frisian drippe (“to drip”), Dutch druipen, druppelen (“to drip”), German Low German drüppen (“to drip”), German tropfen, tröpfeln (“to drip”), Norwegian Bokmål dryppe, Norwegian Nynorsk drypa (“to drip”).

noun: From Middle English drippe, from the verb (see above). Compare West Frisian drip (“drip”), Dutch drup (“drip”), Danish dryp (“drip”). (style, swagger): Compare the verb sense "to have a superabundance of valuable things".

noun: Acronym.
drip.example: Listening to the tap next door drip all night drove me mad!
drip.exampleSense: To fall one drop at a time.

furl.o: Perhaps from Old French ferlier, modern French ferler.
furl.example: When he heard a voice thus calling to him, he was standing at the door of his box, with a flag in his hand, furled round its short pole.
furl.exampleSense: To lower, roll up and secure (something, such as a sail or flag)

unfurl.example: They unfurled the flag at the start of the festival.
unfurl.exampleSense: To unroll or release something that had been rolled up, typically a sail or a flag.

plenty.o: From Anglo-Norman plent(é) + -y, from Middle English plentie, plentee, plente, from Anglo-Norman plenté, from Old French plenté, from Latin plēnitātem, accusative of plēnitās (“fullness”), from plenus (“complete, full”), from Proto-Indo-European *pl̥h₁nós (“full”), from which English full also comes, via Proto-Germanic. Related to the Latin derivatives replenish, plenary, complete, deplete, replete.
plenty.example: We are lucky to live in a land of peace and plenty.

nice.o:
adj: From Middle English nyce, nice, nys, from Old French nice, niche, nisce (“simple, foolish, ignorant”), from Latin nescius (“ignorant, not knowing”); compare nesciō (“to know not, be ignorant of”), from ne (“not”) + sciō (“to know”).

verb: Name of a Unix program used to invoke a script or program with a specified priority, with the implication that running at a lower priority is "nice" (kind, etc.) because it leaves more resources for others.
nice.example: What's difficult is when you think someone is saying something nice about you, but you're not quite sure.

transparency.o: Borrowed from Medieval Latin trānspārentia, equivalent to transparent + -cy.
transparency.example: John Lehmann's narrator Jack Marlowe is such a transparency, and his fiction is totally formless.

ungracious.o: From Middle English ungracious; equivalent to un- + gracious.
ungracious.example: One might have hoped for more about the Widened Lines and about the G.C. approach to Marylebone—but it is ungracious to point to omissions when so much is contained within 260 pages.

graciously.o: From Middle English graciously, graciousliche; equivalent to gracious + -ly.

gracious.o: From Middle English gracious, from Old French gracieus, from Latin gratiosus, from gratia (“esteem, favor”). See grace. Displaced native Old English hold (“gracious”). Doublet of gracioso and grazioso.
gracious.example: The gracious movements of the figure skaters impressed the judges.
gracious.exampleSense: full of grace; graceful; charming; elegant (in appearance, conduct, movement)

liner.o:
noun: From line (verb) + -er.

noun: From line (noun) + -er (relational suffix) or -er (measurement suffix) (sense 5).
liner.example: With her luxurious furnishings and spacious accommodation the Invicta, which is 350-ft. long and has a gross tonnage of 4,178, resembles a small liner.
liner.exampleSense: A large passenger-carrying ship, especially one on a regular route; an ocean liner.

air force.example: When you're in the air force you have to be prepared to launch missiles at people from the air.
air force.exampleSense: A branch of the military mainly devoted to air warfare, as opposed to (land) army and (sea) navy.

force.o:
noun: From Middle English force, fors, forse, from Old French force, from Late Latin fortia, a noun derived from the neuter plural of Latin fortis (“strong”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰerǵʰ- (“to rise, high, hill”).

verb: From Middle English forcen, from Old French forcier, from Late Latin *fortiāre, from Latin fortia.

noun: From Middle English force, forz, fors, from Old Norse fors (“waterfall”), from Proto-Germanic *fursaz (“waterfall”). Cognate with Icelandic foss (“waterfall”), Norwegian foss (“waterfall”), Swedish fors (“waterfall”). Doublet of foss.

verb: From Middle English forcen, forsen, a use of force, with confusion of farce (“to stuff”).
force.example: He was, in the full force of the words, a good man.
force.exampleSense: Strength or energy of body or mind; active power; vigour; might; capacity of exercising an influence or producing an effect.

clarify.o: From Middle English clarifien, from Old French clarifiier, from Latin clārificō, clārificāre; clārus (“clear”) + faciō, facere (“make”). Semantically clear + -ify.
clarify.example: Leave the wine for 24 hours and it will clarify.
clarify.exampleSense: To make or become clear or bright by freeing from impurities or turbidity.

once and for all.example: They replaced the entire door, in hopes of correcting the sticking and squeaking once and for all.

astronomically.example: The calculated answer was astronomically large.
astronomically.exampleSense: In the extreme, very (typically very large).

astronomical.o: Attested since at least 1550, from Middle French astronomique or directly from Latin astronomicus, from Ancient Greek ἀστρονομικός (astronomikós).
astronomical.example: Finally, all men saw that astronomical knowledge lied not, and they awaited the comet.

rip off.example: I can't believe how the car dealerships try to rip off their customers.
rip off.exampleSense: To cheat or swindle, especially by charging an excessively high or unfair price.

overstate.example: He was suggested not to overstate at the interview.
overstate.exampleSense: To exaggerate; to state or claim too much.

executive order.example: Today I will sign a series of historic executive orders. With these actions, we will begin the complete restoration of America, and the revolution of common sense.
executive order.exampleSense: An ordinance issued by the authority of the head of the executive branch of government.

consequently.o: From Middle English consequentely, consequentliche, consequently; equivalent to consequent + -ly.
consequently.example: He didn't wake up early. Consequently, he was late to work.
consequently.exampleSense: As a result or consequence of something; subsequently.

inconsequential.example: You will never know the exact atomic time when you started reading this phrase; of course, that's inconsequential.
inconsequential.exampleSense: Having no consequence; not consequential; of little importance.

consequential.example: The more profound and consequential the issue, the more stubborn our denial.

remaining.example: May I have the only remaining cake?
remaining.exampleSense: Which remains, especially after something else has been removed.

consist of.example: The fieldwork consists of counting the species along the shoreline.
consist of.exampleSense: To be composed or made up of something.

strengthen.o: From rare Middle English strengthenen (14th c.), from earlier strengthen (12th c.), where -en is the infinitive ending. Probably the original form was reinterpreted as strength + -en around the time when the infinitive ending was being apocopated in late Middle English.
strengthen.example: A little hardship, and a little struggling with the rougher elements of life, will perchance but strengthen and increase his courage, and prepare him for the conflicts and struggles of after years.
strengthen.exampleSense: To make strong or stronger; to add strength to; to increase the strength of; to fortify.

overtime.example: Workers are usually paid extra for working overtime.
overtime.exampleSense: Working time outside of one's regular hours.

equipment.o: From equip + -ment, or from French équipement.
equipment.example: The sports shop sells different kits of famous clubs, and equipment from all kind of sports.
equipment.exampleSense: Any items used in equipping something or someone, for example things needed for an expedition or voyage.

rare earth.o: From rare + earth. First use appears c. 1841 in the publications of Henry Minchin Noad. See cite below.
rare earth.example: The metallic base of yttria, a very rare earth, discovered in a mineral called godolinite.
rare earth.exampleSense: Any of the naturally occurring oxides of the lanthanide metals; they are widely distributed in relatively small concentrations and are used in glassmaking, ceramic glazes etc.

unfreeze.example: The indictment said that after Mr. Bankman-Fried received confirmation that the accounts were unfrozen, the rest of the bribe money was paid.
unfreeze.exampleSense: To release previously suspended financial assets.

harmful.o: From Middle English harmful, from Old English *hearmful (suggested by hearmfullīċ (“harmful; hurtful”)), equivalent to harm + -ful. Cognate with German harmvoll, Danish harmfuld, Swedish harmfull.
harmful.example: Wear a hat to protect your skin from harmful sunlight.
harmful.exampleSense: Causing or likely to cause harm or damage; injurious.

hateful.o: From Middle English hateful. By surface analysis, hate + -ful.

hopefulness.example: "In the Memory of the Forest" is remarkable for the acuity of its moral vision and the vivacity of its language; what makes it extraordinary is its persuasive hopefulness.

hopefully.o: From hopeful + -ly. The use as a sentence adverb first gained currency in the United States and has been explained as a possible calque of German hoffentlich.
hopefully.example: She was buried with her mom and hopefully they are together now.
hopefully.exampleSense: It is hoped that; I hope; we hope.

hopeful.example: It looks hopeful that my father will be able to walk again.

seriously.o: From Middle English seriously, sereously, ceryously, seryowslech (“earnestly”), equivalent to serious + -ly.
seriously.example: Jeremy, meanwhile, was the fun-lover, like me, who didn't always take it too seriously.
seriously.exampleSense: In a serious or literal manner.

serious.o: From Middle English seryows, from Old French serieux, from Medieval Latin sēriōsus, an extension of Latin sērius (“grave, earnest, serious”), possibly ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *swer- (“heavy”). (If this root is correct, cognate with German schwer (“heavy, difficult, severe”), Old English swǣr (“heavy, grave, grievous”). More at swear, sweer. However, see sērius for an alternative derivation of the Latin.)
serious.example: This is a serious problem. We'll need our best experts.

unfairly.example: The carnival games were unfairly difficult, and hardly anybody won a prize.
unfairly.exampleSense: In a manner that is unfair.

far.o:
adj: Inherited from Middle English ferre, fer, Old English feor, feorr, from Proto-Germanic *ferrai

noun: From Latin far. Doublet of farro.
far.example: He built a time machine and travelled far into the future.
far.exampleSense: To, from or over a great distance in space, time or other extent.

dependent.o: From Middle English dependaunt, dependent, from Middle French dependant (present participle of dependre (“to depend”)) and Latin dēpendēns (present participle of dēpendeō (“to depend”)). By surface analysis, depend + -ent.
dependent.example: With two children and an ailing mother, she had three dependents in all.
dependent.exampleSense: A person who relies on another for support or sustenance, particularly financial support.

conductor.o: Borrowed from Middle French conductour, from Old French conduitor, from Latin conductor.
conductor.example: Falling conductors may come in contact with grounded objects or puddles of water.
conductor.exampleSense: Something that can transmit electricity, heat, light, or sound.

supply chain.example: Two months after gas and food shortages caused shudders of anxiety across the country, Britain continues to face challenges in its supply chain.
supply chain.exampleSense: A system of organizations, people, technology, activities, information and resources involved in moving a product or service from the supplier to the customer.

onshore.example: Like most storms, Hurricane Katrina weakened as it came onshore, and by Monday evening the National Hurricane Center had downgraded it to a tropical storm.
onshore.exampleSense: From the sea towards the land.

appointment.o: From Middle English appoyntement, apoyntement, from Old French appointement, equivalent to appoint + -ment.
appointment.example: His appointment as treasurer was deemed suitable.
appointment.exampleSense: The act of appointing a person to hold an office or to have a position of trust

appoint.o: From Middle English apointen, borrowed from Old French apointier (“to prepare, arrange, lean, place”) (French appointer (“to give a salary, refer a cause”)), from Late Latin appunctō (“to bring back to the point, restore, to fix the point in a controversy, or the points in an agreement”); Latin ad + punctum (“a point”). See point.
appoint.example: The hotel is beautifully designed and beautifully appointed in a classic, modern style that manages to be both serene and luxurious at the same time.
appoint.exampleSense: To furnish or equip (a place) completely; to provide with all the equipment or furnishings necessary; to fit out.

disappoint.o: From Middle French desapointer (compare French désappointer). The word originally meant to "dispossess of appointed office", and eventually broadened to mean "to frustrate the expectations or desires of" and "defeat the realization or fulfillment of".
disappoint.example: Here are officers enough at Meryton to disappoint all the young ladies in the country.
disappoint.exampleSense: To sadden or displease (someone) by underperforming, or by not delivering something promised or hoped for.

mention.o: Inherited from Middle English mencioun, mention, from Old French mention, from Latin mentiōnem, accusative of mentiō (“a mention, calling to mind”).
mention.example: I will make mention of thy righteousness.
mention.exampleSense: A speaking or noticing of anything, usually in a brief or cursory manner.

high-stakes.example: But it was in the early 2000s that the high-stakes TV pop contest really arrived, along with promises that it would propel a few lucky auditionees to obscene levels of success and fame.

security.o: From secure + -ity, from Middle English securite, from Middle French securité (modern sécurité), from Latin sēcūritās, from Latin sēcūrus (“safe, secure”), from sē- (“without”) + cūra (“care”); see cure. Similar to Latin sine cūrā (“without care, carefree”), which led to English sinecure. Doublet of surety.
security.example: Chad always carries a gun for his own security.
security.exampleSense: The condition of not being threatened, especially physically, psychologically, emotionally, or financially.

maladministration.o: PIE word *h₂éd From mal- (prefix meaning ‘bad; badly’) + administration.
maladministration.example: To combat maladministration and improve government efficiency, the ombudsman was established to function as an independent watchdog.
maladministration.exampleSense: Faulty, improper, or inefficient administration or management, especially by a government body; (countable) an instance of this.

administration.o: From Middle English administracioun, from Old French administration, from Latin administratio, from administrare; see administer; compare French administration. Equivalent to administrate + -ion.
administration.example: Successive US administrations have had similar Middle East policies.
administration.exampleSense: The executive part of government; the persons collectively who are entrusted with the execution of laws and the superintendence of public affairs; the chief magistrate and his cabinet or council; or the council, or ministry, alone, as in Great Britain.

overweigh.o: From Middle English overweȝen; equivalent to over- + weigh. First known attestation in the Ancrene Wisse ("luue ouerweið hit").

overweight.example: We also over-weight such vaine future conjectures, which infant-spirits give us.
overweight.exampleSense: To place excessive weight or emphasis on; to overestimate the importance of.

oversight.o: From over- + sight. Verb sense 2 is a semantic loan from German Aufsicht.
oversight.example: A small oversight at this stage can lead to big problems later.
oversight.exampleSense: An omission; something that is left out, missed, or forgotten.

cenotaph.o: From French cénotaphe, from Ancient Greek κενός (kenós, “empty”) + τάφος (táphos, “tomb”). By surface analysis ceno- + -taph.
cenotaph.example: But age is heart-wearied and tempest-torn: it is the crumbling cenotaph of fear and hope!
cenotaph.exampleSense: A monument, generally in the form of an empty tomb, erected to honour the dead whose bodies lie elsewhere, especially members of the armed forces who died in battle.

cynic.o: From Middle English cynike, cynicke, from Middle French cynique, from Latin cynicus, from Ancient Greek κυνικός (kunikós), originally derived from the portico in Athens called Κυνόσαργες (Kunósarges), the earliest home of the Cynic school, later reinterpreted as being derived from κύων (kúōn, “dog”), in a contemptuous allusion to the uncouth and aggressive manners adopted by the members of the school.
cynic.example: The cynic surfaced, reminding him that she'd been accused of trying to spring the baby trap on Brad Comfort.
cynic.exampleSense: A person whose outlook is scornfully negative.

civil.o: From Middle English cyvyl, civil, borrowed from Old French civil, from Latin cīvīlis (“relating to a citizen”), from cīvis (“citizen”). Cognate with Old English hīwen (“household”), hīrǣden (“family”). More at hind; hird. (polite): Compare typologically urbane (<< Latin urbs), courteous (akin to court).
civil.example: She went into civil service because she wanted to help the people.
civil.exampleSense: Having to do with people and government office as opposed to the military or religion.

dye.o:
noun: From Middle English deye, from Old English dēah, dēag (“color, hue, dye”), from Proto-West Germanic *daugu (“color, shade”), from *daugan (“to conceal, be dark”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰewh₂- (“to smoke, raise dust, camouflage”). Cognates Cognate with Old High German tougan (“dark, secretive”), tougal (“dark, hidden, covert”), Old English dēagol, dīegle (“dark, hidden, secret”), Old English dohs, dox (“dusky, dark”). See dusk.

verb: Fom Middle English deien, from Old English dēagian, from the noun.
dye.example: You look different. Have you had your hair dyed?
dye.exampleSense: To colour with dye, or as if with dye.

bunkum.o: From buncombe, from “speaking to (or for) Buncombe County, North Carolina”, a county in North Carolina named for Edward Buncombe. In 1820, Felix Walker, who represented the county in the U.S. House of Representatives, rose to address the question of admitting Missouri as a free or slave state, his first attempt to speak on the subject after nearly a month of solid debate, right before the vote was to be called. To the exasperation of colleagues, he began a long and wearisome speech, explaining that he was speaking not to Congress but "to Buncombe." He was ultimately shouted down by his colleagues, though his speech was published in a Washington paper and his persistence made "buncombe" (later respelled "bunkum") a synonym for meaningless political claptrap and later for any kind of nonsense, at first only in the jargon of Washington and then in common usage.
bunkum.example: The part of that word to focus on is bunk, short for bunkum, which is what these types attack with vigor and all the obsessiveness of the bunkum spreaders themselves.
bunkum.exampleSense: Senseless talk; nonsense; a piece of nonsense.

debark.o:
verb: From French débarquer, from de- (Old French des-) + barque (“bark, small ship”).

verb: From de- + bark (“covering of tree”).

verb: From de- + bark (“(of a dog) make the noise”).
debark.example: On these photographs, the wide strips can be seen debarked from a horse chestnut tree (left) and from a poplar (right). This seems to be typical for trees with high moisture content.
debark.exampleSense: To remove the bark from a tree, especially one that has been felled.

debunk.o: From de- (“away”) + bunk (“nonsense”) (from bunkum, from Buncombe County) 1923.
debunk.example: The explosion story was thoroughly debunked on National Public Radio in November 1999.
debunk.exampleSense: To discredit, or expose to ridicule the falsehood or the exaggerated claims of something.

metis.o:
noun: Borrowed from French métis, from Late Latin mixticius, from Latin mixtus (“mixed”). Akin to mestizo, which came from Spanish. More at Metis.

noun: From Ancient Greek μῆτις (mêtis).

sweet potato.example: The sweet potato is the article referred to as potato by Shakespeare and other English writers, previous to the middle of the seventeenth century.
sweet potato.exampleSense: The tuber of this plant cooked as a vegetable.

morsel.o: From Middle English morsel, from Old French morsel, from Medieval Latin morsellum (“a bit, a little piece”), diminutive of Latin morsum (“a bit”), neuter of morsus, perfect passive participle of mordeo (“to bite”). Compare French morceau, whence the English doublet morceau.
morsel.example: Didn't even a morsel of decency remain in his brother?

disappointment.example: Even a trip to beautiful California can be a disappointment.
disappointment.exampleSense: Something or someone that disappoints: that which causes disappointment.

dissimulation.o: Inherited from Middle English dissimulacioun, from Old French dissimulation, from Latin dissimulātiō; equivalent to dissimule + -ation.
dissimulation.example: Perhaps it was best to tell Ethel at once: if ever she went into society at all, she would inevitably hear of it, and her own concealment would have the appearance of a dissimulation,—the furthest from her thoughts.
dissimulation.exampleSense: The act of concealing the truth; hypocrisy or deception.

partnership.o: From partner + -ship. Cognate with Danish partnerskab, Dutch partnerschap, German Partnerschaft, Norwegian Bokmål partnerskap, Norwegian Nynorsk partnerskap, Swedish partnerskap, and West Frisian partnerskip.

pick out.o: From pick + out. Compare Saterland Frisian uutpikke (“to pick out”), Dutch uitpikken (“to pick out”).
pick out.example: Very often husbands would patronise my boutique and pick out something for the little lady and, in passing, pick out something for themselves.

entitlement.example: The auxiliary members of the royal family often have the greatest capacity to inflame public scepticism about monarchy, and Prince Harry once seemed determined to personify the entitlement and pointlessness that could have jeopardised the continuity of the crown.
entitlement.exampleSense: The right to have something, whether actual or perceived.

aggressiveness.example: It was a randy aggressiveness he had enjoyed because he had not used or needed it before.
aggressiveness.exampleSense: The state or quality of being aggressive.

fulfilling.o: present participle and gerund of fulfill. From Middle English fulfillen, from Old English fullfyllan (“to fill full”). By surface analysis, full- + fill.
fulfilling.example: Absolute promises have therefore a sufficiency in themselves to bring about their own fulfillings; the conditional have not so.

fulfill.o: From Middle English fulfillen, from Old English fullfyllan (“to fill full”). By surface analysis, full- + fill.
fulfill.example: My lady is positively fulfilled of grace.
fulfill.exampleSense: To fill full; fill to the utmost capacity; fill up.

long-lasting.example: This long-lasting gum keeps its flavor for almost an hour.
long-lasting.exampleSense: Persisting or enduring for a long time.

bombshell.example: Singer and Jeffreys had focused their attention on cancer risk, but the bombshell of the report was the danger to children.
bombshell.exampleSense: Something that is very surprising, shocking, amazing or sensational.

blonde bombshell.o: Derived from bombshell (“a very attractive woman”).

blonde.o: From Middle French blonde f. See blond.
blonde.example: Most women who blonde their hair today have been doing it for several years.

and so forth.o: Dates back at least to Old English and swā forþ.
and so forth.example: Don't forget to pack weather items appropriate for the climate: sunscreen, rain gear, and so forth.
and so forth.exampleSense: Indicates that a list continues in a similar manner.

first class.example: - How was your holiday? - It was first class.

make peace.example: Both countries can rebuild now that they have made peace with each other.
make peace.exampleSense: To end hostilities; to reach a peace agreement; to initiate or resume a cordial relationship after a period of animosity.

multiple.o: From French multiple, itself from Late Latin multiplus.
multiple.example: Multiple registrations are an increasing problem for many social networking sites.
multiple.exampleSense: Having more than one element, part, component, or function, having more than one instance, occurring more than once, usually contrary to expectations (can be followed by a singular).

experimental.exampleSense: Pertaining to or founded on experiment.

experiential.example: Atheists argue that there is no experiential confirmation for the existence of a god.
experiential.exampleSense: Of, related to, encountered in, or derived from experience.

relational.o: From relation + -al. The database sense is from the definition of relation as a set of ordered tuples.
relational.example: Of these three great groups of feelings the first are extremely unrelational; the second are somewhat more relational; and the third are relational in a comparatively high degree.

emotional.example: The 'movement' was simultaneously emotional and motoric, and essentially autonomous (thus distinguishing it from passive jerkings and other pathology).
emotional.exampleSense: Determined by strong emotion rather than purely logical reasoning.

sense.o: From Middle English sense, from Old French sens, sen, san (“sense, perception, direction”); partly from Latin sēnsus (“sensation, feeling, meaning”), from sentiō (“feel, perceive”); partly of Germanic origin (whence also Occitan sen, Italian senno), from Vulgar Latin *sennus (“sense, reason, way”), from Frankish *sinn ("reason, judgement, mental faculty, way, direction"; whence also Dutch zin, German Sinn, Swedish sinne, Norwegian sinn). Both Latin and Germanic from Proto-Indo-European *sent- (“to feel”).
sense.example: So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense.
sense.exampleSense: The meaning, reason, or value of something. A single conventional use of a word; one of the entries or definitions for a word in a dictionary.

reel.o: From Middle English reel, reele, from Old English rēol, hrēol, from Proto-West Germanic *hrehul, from Proto-Germanic *hrehulaz, *hrahilaz, from Proto-Indo-European *krek- (“to weave, beat”). Cognate with Icelandic ræl, hræll.
reel.example: The traditional reel Within a Mile of Dublin, for instance, distorts until it reaches something quasi-industrial.
reel.exampleSense: The music of this dance; often called a Scottish (or Scotch) reel.

look out.example: While you're in the city center, look out for the dodgy street vendors.
look out.exampleSense: To be vigilant and aware often as an imperative to alert a person to danger.

sane.o: Learned borrowing from Latin sānus (“healthy; sane”). Doublet of sound.
sane.example: Shepard: What's wrong with your assistant?
sane.exampleSense: Mentally sound; possessing a rational mind; having the mental faculties in such condition as to be able to anticipate and judge the effect of one's actions in an ordinary manner.

unwavering.o: From un- (prefix meaning ‘not’) + wavering (“being in doubt, indecisive”).
unwavering.example: [T]he religious orders who were most unwavering in their allegiance to the papacy, were pressing their opposition to the divorce into rebellion.
unwavering.exampleSense: Not wavering. Always on course and steady.

self-destruct.example: The submarine was primed to self-destruct.

self-questioning.example: Obama’s thoughtfulness is obvious to anyone who has observed his political career, but in this book he lays himself open to self-questioning.
self-questioning.exampleSense: The contemplation of one's actions, beliefs, etc.

self-restraint.example: His lack of self-restraint led to several ugly scenes of debauchery and violent outburst.
self-restraint.exampleSense: Self-control, control over one's emotions, passions and actions.

self-interest.example: I cannot abandon my husband for the sake of self-interest and personal gain.
self-interest.exampleSense: One's personal interest or advantage, especially when pursued without regard for others.

reality.o: From French réalité (“quality of being real”), from Middle French realité (“property, possession”), from Medieval Latin reālitās, from Late Latin reālis (“real”), equivalent to real + -ity. Recorded since 1550 as a legal term in the sense of “fixed property” (compare real estate, realty); the sense “real existence” is attested from 1647. First attested in c. 1540.
reality.example: The reality of the crash scene on TV dawned upon him only when he saw the victim was no actor but his friend.
reality.exampleSense: The state of being actual or real; realness.

sell.o:
verb: From Middle English sellen, from Old English sellan (“give; give up for money”), from Proto-West Germanic *salljan, from Proto-Germanic *saljaną, from Proto-Indo-European *selh₁-. Cognates Cognate with Scots sell (“to sell”), Danish sælge (“to sell”), Norwegian Bokmål selge (“to sell”), Norwegian Nynorsk selja, selje (“to sell”), Swedish sälja (“to sell”), Faroese and Icelandic selja (“to sell”), Gothic 𐍃𐌰𐌻𐌾𐌰𐌽 (saljan, “to pay tribute, make an offer”).

noun: From French selle, from Latin sella.

noun: From Old Saxon seill or Old Norse seil. Cognate with Dutch zeel (“rope”), German Seil (“rope”).
sell.example: If thou wilt be perfect, go and sell that thou hast, and give to the poor.
sell.exampleSense: To transfer goods or provide services in exchange for money.

goddess.o: From Middle English goddesse, equivalent to god + -ess, formed about 1350. The figurative meaning is first found in Edmund Spenser's Shepheardes calender (1579). Displaced Old English gyden.
goddess.example: The girls who had tormented me in high school had fallen, hard, from their pedestals. The cheerleader goddesses were Wal-Mart moms, wearing enough eyeliner and dark shadow to supply a Goth nightclub for a month.
goddess.exampleSense: A woman honored or adored as physically attractive or of superior charm and intelligence.

settle.o:
verb: From a merger of two verbs: * Middle English setlen, from Old English setlan (“to settle, seat, put to rest”), from Old English setl (“seat”) (compare Dutch zetelen (“to be established, settle”)) and * Middle English sahtlen, seihtlen (“to reconcile, calm, subside”), from Old English sahtlian, ġesehtlian (“to reconcile”), from Old English saht, seht (“settlement, agreement, reconciliation, peace”) (see saught, -le). German siedeln (“to settle”) is related to the former of the two verbs, but is not an immediate cognate of either of them.

noun: From Middle English settle, setle, setel, setil, seotel, from Old English setl (“that upon which one sits, a seat, a settle, a place to sit”), from Proto-Germanic *setlaz (“a seat; arm-chair”), representing Proto-Indo-European *sed-lo-, from *sed- (“sit”). Cognate with Dutch zetel, German Sessel, Latin sella.
settle.example: Chyle [...] runs through all the intermediate colors until it settles in an intense red.
settle.exampleSense: To establish or become established in a steady position: To become stationary or fixed; to come to rest.

deal.o:
noun: From Middle English del, dele, from Old English dǣl (“part, share, portion”), from Proto-West Germanic *daili, from Proto-Germanic *dailiz (“part, deal”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰ(h₁)-oy-lo- (“part, watershed”). Cognate with Scots dele (“part, portion”), West Frisian diel (“part, share”), Dutch deel (“part, share, portion”), German Teil (“part, portion, section”), Danish, Slovene, and Swedish del (“part”), Icelandic deila (“division, contention”), Gothic 𐌳𐌰𐌹𐌻𐍃 (dails, “portion”). Related to Old English dāl (“portion”). More at dole.

verb: From Middle English delen, from Old English dǣlan (“to divide, part”), from Proto-West Germanic *dailijan, from Proto-Germanic *dailijaną (“to divide, part, deal”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰail- (“part, watershed”). Cognates Cognate with West Frisian diele (“to divide, separate”), Dutch delen, German teilen, Swedish dela; and with Lithuanian dalinti (“divide”), Russian дели́ть (delítʹ).

noun: From Middle English dele (“plank”), from Middle Low German dele, from Old Saxon thili, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *þiljǭ (“plank, board”); cognate with Old English þille. Doublet of thill.
deal.example: We need to finalise the deal with Henderson by midnight.
deal.exampleSense: A particular instance of trading (buying or selling; exchanging; bartering); a transaction.

informed.o:
verb: From inform + -ed.

adj: From in- + formed; the first sense probably uses in- (“in”), while the second sense uses in- (“prefix of negation”).
informed.example: An informed young man delivered a lecture on the history of modern art.
informed.exampleSense: Instructed; having knowledge of a fact or area of education.

testosterone.example: Mammalian testes contain almost no testosterone because it is sent out into the body as quickly as it is made.
testosterone.exampleSense: A steroid hormone that stimulates development of male secondary sexual characteristics, produced mainly in the testes, but also in the ovaries and adrenal cortex.

cheater.o:
noun: From cheat + -er. The sense referring to welding hood lenses was inspired by cheaters (plural) as a pair of reading glasses.

noun: From Middle English chetour, a variant of eschetour, from Old French eschetour, escheteur, equivalent to escheat + -er.
cheater.example: The Old Viper's an old cheater, an old hornswoggler.
cheater.exampleSense: Someone who cheats; something that cheats.

cheat on.example: I was disqualified for cheating on my final exam.
cheat on.exampleSense: Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see cheat, on.

cheat.o:
verb: Verb from Middle English achetan, variant of escheten, from Old French escheat, past participle of escheoir, escheoiter, from Late Latin *excadēre (“fall away, fall out”), from (Latin) ex- + cadere (“fall”). Displaced native Old English beswīcan. Noun from verb and/or Middle English chete, aphetic form of achete, escheat, eschete (“the reversion of property to the state”), from Anglo-Norman eschete and Old French eschet, escheit, escheoit (“that which falls to one”), past participle of escheoir (“to fall”) (modern French échoir), from Late Latin *excadēre (“fall away, fall out”), from (Latin) ex- + cadere (“fall”). Doublet of escheat.

noun: Inherited from Middle English chet (“low-quality bread”), of unknown origin; compare manchet.
cheat.example: When I consider life, 'tis all a cheat.
cheat.exampleSense: An act of deception or fraud; that which is the means of fraud or deception.

predictability.example: England's fans responded by loudly rallying to Maguire's cause but there was a grim predictability about what happened in the 67th minute, the defender lazily sticking out a leg to divert Robertson's cross past helpless keeper Aaron Ramsdale.

opposite sex.example: The divorce rate for opposite sex marriages is increasing.
opposite sex.exampleSense: Heterosexual, or otherwise relating to a relationship between a woman and a man.

non-.o:
prefix: (“not”), from Old French non- and Medieval Latin nōn (“not”), from Old Latin noinu, noinom, from ne oinom (“not one”).

prefix: From Latin nōnus (“ninth”).

dissatisfied.example: The good news for dissatisfied users of Birmingham New Street is that none of these criticisms have gone unnoticed.
dissatisfied.exampleSense: Not satisfied (e.g. with the quality of something).

majority.o: From Middle French maiorité, from Medieval Latin maiōritātem, accusative of Latin maiōritās, from Latin maior (“greater”). Morphologically major + -ity.
majority.example: Those opposing the building plans were in the majority, so the building project was canceled.
majority.exampleSense: More than half (50%) of some group.

vastness.example: He had a feeling that he was lost in the vastness of a huge forest.

vast.o: From Middle French vaste, from Latin vastus (“void, immense”). Related to waste and German Wüste.
vast.example: Last spring, the periodical cicadas emerged across eastern North America. Their vast numbers and short above-ground life spans inspired awe and irritation in humans—and made for good meals for birds and small mammals.
vast.exampleSense: Very great in size, amount, degree, intensity, or especially extent.

impressed.o: simple past and past participle of impress. From Middle English impressen, from Latin impressus, perfect passive participle of imprimere (“to press into or upon, stick, stamp, or dig into”), from in (“in, upon”) + premere (“to press”).

impress.o: From Middle English impressen, from Latin impressus, perfect passive participle of imprimere (“to press into or upon, stick, stamp, or dig into”), from in (“in, upon”) + premere (“to press”).
impress.example: That first view of the Eiger impressed itself on my mind.
impress.exampleSense: To produce a vivid impression of (something).

normal distribution.example: It begins with the normal distribution, which is the limiting form of the sample sum over an arbitrary population.
normal distribution.exampleSense: Any of a family of continuous probability distributions such that the probability density function is the Gaussian function

hangout.o: From hang + out, as a deverbal from hang out.
hangout.example: Every Friday, Geoff and his group of friends all met at their favorite hangout to talk and have a good time.
hangout.exampleSense: A place for hanging out; an informal meeting-place.

hang out.example: When a dog pants, its tongue often hangs out of its mouth.
hang out.exampleSense: Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see hang, out.

cross-.o: From Middle English cros-, crosse- (“relating to a cross, forming a cross, in the shape of a cross or x”), from the noun (see cross) and also from across.
cross-.example: . See visuals for difference between crossband and crossbuck.

insightful.example: Appendix 4 lays out the current analysis of the liner train concept, concluding the report with perhaps its most insightful innovation.

privy.o: From Middle English pryvy, prive, from Old French privé (“private”), from Latin prīvātus (“deprived”), perfect passive participle of prīvō (“to bereave, deprive; to free, release”). Doublet of private.
privy.example: Nonetheless, in the dark and privy stillness of our minds there are few of us who are not still haunted by worrisome doubts.

abase.o: From Late Middle English abaishen, abashen, abaisse, abassen, abesse, abessen (“to be upset; to embarrass; to surprise; to confound; to bend down, stoop; to abase, degrade, disgrace”), from Middle French abaisser, from Old French abaissier, abessier (“to prostrate oneself; to lower, reduce”) (also compare Old French esbahir (“to amaze”), Vulgar Latin abbassiāre (“to lower”)), from a- (prefix indicating movement towards something) (from Latin ad (“toward, to”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éd (“at, to”)) + baissier (“to lower”) (from Medieval Latin bassus (“short of stature, low; base”), possibly from Ancient Greek βᾰ́σῐς (bắsĭs, “foot; base, foundation”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʷem- (“to step”)). The spelling of the English word has been influenced by base, thus ostensibly analyzable as a- (“towards”) + base. There exist verb cognates in galloromance languages such as Catalan abaixar (“lower; abase”) and Occitan abaissar, and similar word construction in other romance languages as Spanish abajo (“down, downstairs; below”).

abashed.o: simple past and past participle of abash. Attested from 1303, as Middle English abaisen, abaishen, abashen (“lose one's composure, be upset”), from the later 14th-century also transitive "to make ashamed, to perplex or embarrass"; from Anglo-Norman abaïss, from Middle French abair, abaisser (“lose one's composure, be startled, be stunned”), from Old French esbaïr, (French ébahir), from es- (“utterly”) + baïr (“to astonish”), from Medieval Latin *exbadō, from ex- (“out of”) + bado (“to gape, yawn”), an onomatopoeic word imitating a yawn, see also French badaud (“rubbernecker”).
abashed.example: So spake the Lord Goldry Bluszco, standing in great pride and splendour beneath the starry canopy, and scowling terribly on the Ambassador from Witchland, so that the Ambassador was abashed and his knees smote together.

abash.o: Attested from 1303, as Middle English abaisen, abaishen, abashen (“lose one's composure, be upset”), from the later 14th-century also transitive "to make ashamed, to perplex or embarrass"; from Anglo-Norman abaïss, from Middle French abair, abaisser (“lose one's composure, be startled, be stunned”), from Old French esbaïr, (French ébahir), from es- (“utterly”) + baïr (“to astonish”), from Medieval Latin *exbadō, from ex- (“out of”) + bado (“to gape, yawn”), an onomatopoeic word imitating a yawn, see also French badaud (“rubbernecker”).
abash.example: The stare seemed to abash Poirot.
abash.exampleSense: To make ashamed; to embarrass; to destroy the self-possession of, as by exciting suddenly a consciousness of guilt, mistake, or inferiority; to disconcert; to discomfit.

unabashed.example: For the third time Allan looked at his lawyer. And for the third time his lawyer looked back at him quite unabashed.

stare.o:
verb: From Middle English staren, from Old English starian (“to stare”), from Proto-West Germanic *starēn, from Proto-Germanic *starjaną, *starāną (“to be fixed, be rigid”), from Proto-Indo-European *ster-. Cognate with Dutch staren (“to stare”), German starren (“to stare”), German starr (“stiff”). More at start.

noun: From Middle English star, ster, from Old English stær (“starling”), from Proto-Germanic *starô (“starling”), from Proto-Indo-European *stor- (“starling”). Cognate with German Star (“starling”), Danish stær (“starling”), Swedish stare (“starling”), Norwegian Nynorsk stare (“starling”), Icelandic stari (“starling”). Compare also Old English stearn (“a type of bird, starling”).
stare.example: Take off all the staring straws, twigs and jags in the hive.
stare.exampleSense: To stand out; to project; to bristle.

lick.o:
verb: From Middle English likken, from Old English liccian, from Proto-West Germanic *likkōn, from Proto-Germanic *likkōną (“to lick”), from Proto-Indo-European *leyǵʰ- (“to lick”). Sense evolution towards violence unclear; not paralleled in any other Germanic language. Cognates Cognate with Dutch lekken, likken (“to lick”), German lecken (“to lick”), Vilamovian łaekia, łakia, łȧḱkja (“to lick”), Yiddish לעקן (lekn, “to lick”), French lécher (“to lick”), Friulian lecâ (“to lick”), Italian leccare (“to lick”), Lombard leccà (“to lick”), Norman litchi (“to lick”), Occitan lecar (“to lick”); also Faroese and Icelandic sleikja (“to lick”), Breton leat (“to lick”), Irish and Scottish Gaelic ligh (“to lick”), Welsh llyfu (“to lick”), Latin lingō (“to lick”), Ancient Greek λείχω (leíkhō, “to lick up”), Latvian làizît (“to lick”), Lithuanian laižyti (“to lick”), Bulgarian ли́жа (líža, “to lick”), Czech lízat (“to lick”), Macedonian лиже (liže, “to lick”), Polish lizać (“to lick”), Russian лиза́ть (lizátʹ, “to lick”), Serbo-Croatian ли́зати, lízati (“to lick”), Slovene lizati (“to lick”), Ukrainian лиза́ти (lyzáty, “to lick”), Armenian լիզել (lizel, “to lick”), Central Kurdish لستن (listin, “to lick”), Northern Kurdish alastin, alêstin, alistin, alîstin (“to lick”), Persian لیسیدن (lēsīdan / lisidan, “to lick”), Sanskrit लिह् (lih), रिह् (rih, “to lick; to eat”).

noun: Back-formation from hit a lick, which see. Ultimately from liquor.
lick.example: She licked the last of the honey off the spoon before washing it.
lick.exampleSense: To lap; to take in with the tongue.

immure.o: From Middle English enmuren and Middle French emmurer, both from Old French enmurer, from Latin immūrō, from in- + mūrus (“wall”). Modern spelling is modelled after the Latin.
immure.example: Mattes creates a perversely sympathetic character: one who is so immured and immersed in his own self-pity/-hatred that his only connection to life is to dominate and control those with whom he connects.
immure.exampleSense: To cloister, confine, imprison or hole up: to lock someone up or seclude oneself behind walls.

demurely.o: From Middle English demurely; equivalent to demure + -ly.
demurely.example: `I am a hairdresser, but I was advertising as a model,' said Miss A demurely.

demure.o: Inherited from Middle English demure, demwre, an abbreviation of Anglo-Norman de mure port (“with a mature demeanor”) (compare Old French meur from Latin mātūrus): *si il seyt coy e de mure port (Amur curteiz) (“he sits quietly and with a mature appearance”) * Documents illustrating the history of Scotland, CLV, 1306, Orders for the custody of Scottish prisoners, CLV: …et que eles soient de bon et meur port (“…with a good and mature demeanor”) * mss. Arundel, 220: ke cely qe vus amerez soyt de gentil manere, coy, de meure porture (“with a mature demeanor”) * (Monastic rule): de aunciene dame de meure porture ke pusse les plus ieuenes rieueler e endoctriner (“an old lady with a mature demeanor able to rule and educate the young girls”).
demure.example: Miss Lizzy, I have no doubt, would be as demure and coquettish, as if ten winters more had gone over her head.
demure.exampleSense: Affectedly modest, decorous, or serious; making a show of gravity.

apparent.o: From Middle English apparaunt, aparaunt, from Old French aparent, aparant, in turn from Latin appārēns, appārentis, present participle of appāreō.
apparent.example: When I came to Renfield's room I found him lying on the floor on his left side in a glittering pool of blood. When I went to move him, it became at once apparent that he had received some terrible injuries.
apparent.exampleSense: Clear or manifest to the understanding; plain; evident; obvious; known; palpable; indubitable.

wild.o: From Middle English weilde, wield, wielde, wijlde, wild, wilde, wyld, wylde, wyled, wyyld, from Old English wilde, from Proto-West Germanic *wilþī, from Proto-Germanic *wilþijaz (“wild”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂welh₁- (“hair; wool”). Cognates Cognate with North Frisian wil (“wild”), Saterland Frisian wíeld, wüüld (“wild”), West Frisian wyld (“wild”), Bavarian wüd (“wild”), Central Franconian weld (“wild”), Cimbrian bill (“crazy, mad; wild; stupid”), Dutch, German, and Low German wild (“wild”), Luxembourgish wëll (“wild; savage”), Vilamovian wyłd (“wild”), Yiddish ווילד (vild, “wild; savage”), Danish and Swedish vild (“wild”), Faroese villur (“wild”), Icelandic villtur (“wild; lost; barbaric, savage; uncultivated; untamed”), Norwegian Bokmål and Norwegian Nynorsk vill (“wild”), vill (“lost”), Gothic 𐍅𐌹𐌻𐌸𐌴𐌹𐍃 (wilþeis, “wild”); also Cornish gwlan (“wool”), Irish and Scottish Gaelic olann (“wool”), Manx ollan (“wool”), Welsh gwlân (“wool”), Latin vellus (“fleece, wool”), villus (“hair, shaggy hair”), Ancient Greek λάχνη (lákhnē, “woolly hair; thin hair; soft nap or pile on cloth; quills hedgehog; leafage”), Lithuanian valai (“hair of the horse tail”), Belarusian во́лас (vólas, “single hair”), Czech and Slovak vlas (“single hair”), Macedonian влас (vlas, “fluff; thread (of hair)”), Polish włos (“single hair”), Russian and Ukrainian во́лос (vólos, “single hair”), Serbo-Croatian вла̑с, vlȃs (“single hair”), Slovene las (“hair on top of head; nap, pile”), Armenian գեղմ (geġm, “fleece, wool”), Central Kurdish پرچ (pirç, “fax, headhair”), Northern Kurdish hirî (“wool”), Persian گرس (gors, “curl, ringlet; braid”), Hittite 𒋠𒀸 (SÍG-aš, “wool”), Tocharian A urṇ (“the circles of white hair between the brows of the Buddha or other deity”), Tocharian B *ūrṇ (“the circles of white hair between the brows of the Buddha or other deity”), Sanskrit वल्श (valśa, “branch, shoot, twig”).
wild.example: After mending the lion's leg, we returned him to the wild.
wild.exampleSense: The undomesticated state of a wild animal.

message.o: From Middle English message, from Old French message, from Early Medieval Latin missāticum, derived from Latin mittere (“send”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *meyth₂- (“to exchange”). Partially displaced Old English ærende (whence errand).
message.example: Please message the final report by fax.
message.exampleSense: To send (something) as a message; usually refers to electronic messaging.

lie.o:
verb: From Middle English lien, liggen, from Old English liċġan, from Proto-West Germanic *liggjan, from Proto-Germanic *ligjaną, from Proto-Indo-European *legʰ-. Cognates Cognate with Yola lee, lidge (“to lie”), leigh, leiough (“to idle”), North Frisian lade, lai, laie, lei, lii, läde, läie (“to lie; to lay”), Saterland Frisian lääse (“to lie; to lay”), West Frisian lizze (“to lie”), Alemannic German ligge (“to lie”), Central Franconian lijje (“to lie”), Dutch and Dutch Low Saxon liggen (“to lie”), German liegen (“to lie”), German Low German ligge, liggen (“to lie”), Luxembourgish leien (“to lie”), Yiddish ליגן (lign, “to lie”), Danish and Norwegian Bokmål ligge (“to lie”), Faroese and Icelandic liggja (“to lie”), Norwegian Nynorsk ligge, liggja, liggje (“to lie”), Swedish ligga (“to lie”), Gothic 𐌻𐌹𐌲𐌰𐌽 (ligan, “to lie, to rest”); and with Irish laigh, luigh (“to lie”), Manx lhie (“lie; lay”), Scottish Gaelic laigh (“lie; lay”), Faliscan 𐌋𐌄𐌂𐌄𐌕 (lecet, “he lies down”), Latin lectus (“bed”), South Picene 𐌅𐌄𐌉𐌀𐌕 (veiat, “to lie”), Ancient Greek λέχομαι (lékhomai, “to lie down”), Albanian lag (“band, encampment, troop”), Belarusian ляжа́ць (ljažácʹ, “to lie”), Bulgarian лежа́ (ležá, “to lie”), Czech ležet (“to lie”), Macedonian лежи (leži, “to lie”), Polish leżeć (“to lie”), Russian лежа́ть (ležátʹ, “to lie”), Serbo-Croatian лѐжати, lèžati (“to lie”), Slovene ležáti (“to lie”), Ukrainian лежа́ти (ležáty, “to lie”), Tocharian B lyäk- (“to lie”). As a noun for position, the noun has the same etymology above as the verb.

verb: From Middle English lien (“to lie, tell a falsehood”), from Old English lēogan (“to lie”), from Proto-West Germanic *leugan, from Proto-Germanic *leuganą (“to lie”), from Proto-Indo-European *lewgʰ- (“to announce, tell publicly”). Cognates Cognate with Scots lee (“to lie”), North Frisian jooge, leeg, löög (“to lie”), Saterland Frisian ljooge (“to lie”), West Frisian lige (“to lie”), Bavarian liagn (“to lie”), Dutch liegen (“to lie”), German lügen (“to lie”), Luxembourgish léien (“to lie”), Danish lyve (“to lie”), Faroese lúgva (“to lie”), Icelandic ljúga (“to lie”), Norwegian Bokmål juge, lyge, lyve (“to lie”), Norwegian Nynorsk ljuga, ljuge, lyga, lyge (“to lie”), Scanian ljuğa (“to lie”), Swedish ljuga (“to lie”), Gothic 𐌻𐌹𐌿𐌲𐌰𐌽 (liugan, “to lie”); also Breton le (“vow”), Cornish li (“oath”), Welsh llw (“oath, pledge, vow; curse, swear word”), Latvian lùgt (“to ask; to request; to seek; to plead; to solicit; to invoke; to desire”), Belarusian ілга́ць (ilhácʹ), лга́ць (lhácʹ, “to lie”), Bulgarian лъжа (lǎža, “to lie”), Czech lhát (“to lie”), Kashubian łżec (“to lie”), Macedonian ла́же (láže, “to lie”), Polish łgać (“to lie”), Russian лгать (lgatʹ, “to lie”), Serbo-Croatian ла̀гати, làgati (“to lie”), Slovak luhať (“to lie”), Slovene lagáti (“to lie”).

noun: From Middle English lie, from Old English lyġe (“lie”), from Proto-Germanic *lugiz (“lie”), from Proto-Indo-European *lewgʰ- (“to announce, tell publicly”). Cognates Cognate with Saterland Frisian Löägene (“a lie”), Dutch leugen, logen, loogen (“a lie”), German Lug, Lüge, Lügen (“a lie”), German Low German Lögen (“a lie”), Luxembourgish Ligen (“a lie”), Yiddish ליגן (lign, “a lie”), Danish and Norwegian Bokmål løgn (“a lie”), Icelandic lygi, lygn (“a lie”), Norwegian Nynorsk lygn, løgn (“a lie”), Swedish lögn (“a lie”); also Bulgarian лъжа́ (lǎžá, “а lie”), Czech lež (“a lie”), Russian ложь (ložʹ, “а lie”), Polish łeż (“a lie”), Serbo-Croatian ла̑ж, laž (“a lie”), Slovak lož (“a lie”), Slovene lȃž (“a lie”).
lie.example: Ying-yang county lies 70 li southwest of the modern Teng-feng county, Honan.

sexuality.o: Learned borrowing from New Latin sexuālitās. By surface analysis, sexual + -ity.
sexuality.example: Listening to teenage girls on the telephone discuss for an hour who held whose hand at a party underscores the universal adolescent fascination with burgeoning sexuality.
sexuality.exampleSense: Sexual activity; concern with, or interest in, sexual activity.

sexually.example: He was sexually active by the age of fifteen.

sexual.o: Borrowed from Latin sexuālis. By surface analysis, sex + -ual.
sexual.exampleSense: Characterised by sexual feelings or behaviour; possessing sexuality.

underactive.example: Thus a person with an underactive thyroid can gain weight even on a low-calorie diet.

unattractive.example: In Britain, nearly 2,500 steam locomotives were built, 999 to new designs. Although the latter were modern, they were still labour-intensive to man and maintain, during a period of full employment when working for poor pay in the dirty railway environment was unattractive.
unattractive.exampleSense: Lacking the power to attract interest.

hottie.o: From hot + -ie. Sense “stolen vehicle” perhaps from hot-wired.
hottie.example: You guys are pathetic. I'm gonna find myself a little hottie.
hottie.exampleSense: A physically or sexually attractive person.

hots.example: I mean, this girl obviously has the hots for you man. Why do you think she's calling you?
hots.exampleSense: A condition of physical attraction toward (for) someone.

hot.o: From Middle English hot, hoot, from Old English hāt (“hot”), from Proto-West Germanic *hait, from Proto-Germanic *haitaz (“hot”), from Proto-Indo-European *keHy- (“to heat; to become hot”). Cognates Cognate with Yola hoat, hoate, hote (“hot”), West Frisian hjit, hyt (“hot”), Bavarian hoaß (“hot”), Central Franconian heeß (“hot”), Dutch heet (“hot”), German heiss, heiß, heyß (“hot”), Vilamovian haas, haes, hȧś, hǡs (“hot”), Yiddish הייס (heys, “hot”), Danish hed (“hot”), Faroese and Icelandic heitur (“hot”), Norwegian Bokmål and Swedish het (“hot”); also Lithuanian kaitra (“heat”). Related to heat. Superseded non-native Middle English chaud, from Old French chaut (“hot”); and early Modern English calent, from Latin calēns (“hot”).
hot.example: He forgot that the frying pan was hot and burned his hand.
hot.exampleSense: Relating to heat and conditions which produce it. Having or giving off a high temperature.

feel like.example: I didn't feel like working yesterday, so I called in sick.
feel like.exampleSense: To have a desire for something, or to do something.

provocative.o: Borrowed from Middle French provocatif, and its source, Late Latin provocativus, from Latin provocare.
provocative.example: She used by way of Provocative, to read the wanton Verses of her Paramour in the day time [...].
provocative.exampleSense: Something that provokes an appetite, especially a sexual appetite; an aphrodisiac.

provocation.o: From Middle English provocacioun, from Old French provocacion, from Late Latin prōvocātiō, prōvocātiōnem, from Latin prōvocō. By surface analysis, provoke + -ation. Doublet of provokatsiya.
provocation.example: When it's time to check for provocation, ask the patient about what makes their chief complaint better or worse.
provocation.exampleSense: The second step in OPQRST regarding the investigation of what makes the symptoms MOI or NOI improve or deteriorate.

brand.o: From Middle English brand, from Old English brand (“fire; flame; burning; torch; sword”), from Proto-West Germanic *brand, from Proto-Germanic *brandaz (“flame; flaming; fire-brand; torch; sword”), derived from Proto-Germanic *brinnaną (“to burn”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *bʰrewh₁- (“to boil; brew”). Cognate with Scots brand, West Frisian brân (“fire”), Dutch brand, German Brand, Danish brand, Swedish brand (“blaze, fire”), Icelandic brandur, French brand (< Germanic). More distantly cognate with Proto-Slavic *gorěti (“to burn”).
brand.example: The indelible word "homosexual," like a brand that grew deeper and redder every day, became increasingly hard to conceal and to ignore.
brand.exampleSense: A mark or scar made by burning with a hot iron, especially to mark cattle or to classify the contents of a cask.

red alert.example: Another red alert last night. Lasted only five minutes, Possibly just a friendly plane with its IFF turned off.
red alert.exampleSense: A warning that indicates an emergency situation.

alertness.example: THE human body was meant to have a midafternoon nap, according to a new consensus among sleep researchers who are studying the biological rhythms of sleep and alertness.
alertness.exampleSense: The quality of being alert or on the alert.

alertly.example: I walked fast to avoid being overtaken. Every crossing was a danger, every passenger a thing to watch alertly.
alertly.exampleSense: In an alert manner; with alertness.

potentiality.example: A new year is filled with potentiality.
potentiality.exampleSense: The quality of being or having potential.

denigration.example: To nostalgic eyes they became absolutely and almost mercifully unrecognisable. Nor did they escape a full measure of denigration.

denigrate.o: Derived from Latin dēnigrātus, the perfect passive participle of dēnigrō (“to blacken”) [see -ate (verb-forming suffix)], from dē- (“of; from”) + nigrō (“to blacken”) [from niger (“black”)]. Cognate with Middle English denigart(e) (“darkened, discolored”).
denigrate.example: You have no right to denigrate people and things that you have no personal experience with.
denigrate.exampleSense: To treat as worthless; belittle, degrade or disparage.

vet.o:
noun: Clipping of veterinarian.

noun: Clipping of veteran.

verb: Possibly by analogy from Etymology 1, in the sense of "verifying the soundness [of an animal]"
vet.example: Colin Cameron, a vet who examined the dead animal, said there was "no doubt the kitten would have suffered unnecessarily" before dying.

awesomeness.example: The bogan likes playing Epic Leads because the bogan is on an inexorable quest for maxtreme awesomeness.

trashy.example: It was nonsense this being in love; there wasn't such a thing as love outside of trashy novelettes.
trashy.exampleSense: Like trash; having low quality, especially of books and films.

creator.o: From Middle English creatour, from Old French creator, creatur, creatour, from Latin creātor, agent noun from perfect passive participle creātus (“created”), from verb creō (“to create”) + agent suffix -or. Mostly displaced native Old English wyrhta (modern English wright).
creator.example: Kenneth E. Iverson was the creator of APL.
creator.exampleSense: Something or someone which creates or makes something.

et cetera.o: From Middle English et cetera, from Latin et cētera (“and the other things; and the rest of the things”).

kind of.o: From a reanalysis of kind of in a phrase such as a kind of merry dance from “a kind + of + merry dance” (a type among merry dances) to “a + kind-of merry + dance” (a somewhat merry dance).
kind of.example: I'm getting kind of tired. Could we finish tomorrow?

in general.o: Inherited from Middle English in general.

naivete.o: Alternative spelling of na. From Middle English na, from Old English nā, from Old English ne (“not”) + ā (“ever”). More at no.

naivety.o: From naive + -ity, English analogue of naïveté (naïf + -eté) borrowed from French.

no comment.example: Wrex: And Shepard--I like what you've done with the Normandy. Got tired of always hanging around the cargo bay before.
no comment.exampleSense: A refusal to make the obvious impolite retort.

commentary.o: From Middle French commentaire, from Latin commentārius, commentārium (“notebook”), compare French commentaire. See comment.
commentary.example: We listened to the football commentary while watching the match.
commentary.exampleSense: An oral relation of an event, especially broadcast by television or radio, as it occurs.

for sure.example: I would buy one of those for sure.

over.o:
adj: From Middle English over, from Old English ofer, ofor, ouer, from Proto-West Germanic *obar, from Proto-Germanic *uber (“over”), from Proto-Indo-European *upér (“above; over”). Cognates Cognate with Scots ower (“over”), Yola oer, ower, owr (“over”), Saterland Frisian uur (“over”), West Frisian oer (“over, across”), Cimbrian übar (“over”), Dutch over (“over”), German ober, über, ueber (“over, above”), Limburgish euver, övver (“over”), Low German över, üöver (“over”), Luxembourgish iwwer (“over”), Mòcheno iber (“over”), Yiddish איבער (iber, “over”), Danish and Norwegian Bokmål over (“over”), Elfdalian yvyr (“over”), Faroese yvir (“over”), Icelandic yfir (“over”), Norwegian Nynorsk over, yver, yvi (“over”), Swedish över (“over”), Gothic 𐌿𐍆𐌰𐍂 (ufar, “over”); also Breton and Cornish war (“on, over”), Irish ar (“on”), Manx er (“on”), Scottish Gaelic air (“on, upon”), Latin super (“above, over”), Ancient Greek ῠ̔πείρ (hŭpeír), ὑπέρ (hupér), ῠ̔́περ (hŭ́per, “above, over”), Albanian epër (“above, high, overhead, up, upward”), Armenian վեր (ver, “up”), Avestan 𐬎𐬞𐬀𐬌𐬭𐬌 (upaⁱri, “above, over”), Persian بر (bar, “on; onto; upon”), Sanskrit उपरि (upari, “above, over”). Doublet of uber, super, and hyper.

noun: From Middle English over (“riverbank, seashore, brink”), from Old English ōfer (“riverbank, seashore, brink, edge, margin, border”), from Proto-Germanic *ōferaz. Cognate with Dutch oever (“riverbank, shore”), German Ufer (“shore, shoreline, riverbank”), Low German Över (“shore, riverbank”).
over.example: I'll have to work over the weekend.

overwork.o:
verb: From Middle English overwerken, possibly from Old English oferwyrċan (“to overwork, overlay”), equivalent to over- + work. Cognate with Dutch overwerken (“to overwork”).

noun: From Middle English overwerc, from Old English oferweorc, oferġeweorc (“an overwork, superstructure, tomb”), equivalent to over- + work.
overwork.example: For some years locomotives and coaches have been overworked and undermaintained to a degree without precedent in British railway history, and the leeway in maintenance now to be made up is very great.
overwork.exampleSense: To make (someone or something) work too hard.

invulnerable.o: From Middle French invulnérable, from Latin invulnerābilis, from vulnerābilis, from vulnerō (“to wound”), from vulnus (“wound”), equivalent to in- + vulnerable.
invulnerable.example: His gaze went to Hirken, who stood gloating behind invulnerable transparisteel.
invulnerable.exampleSense: Incapable of being injured; not vulnerable.

seducer.example: But Ted Farrell couldn't stop; that armful of active girl was too much for the wise precautions of a seducer. He kept panting, "Don't be a nark, Cora," while struggling to hold her down.
seducer.exampleSense: Someone who seduces, especially a man who seduces a woman.

seductress.example: Even though she didn't think of herself as a seductress, her effect on men showed she was one.

seductive.o: From Latin sēduct-, past-participle stem of sēdūcere, + -ive.
seductive.example: Evil is said to be seductive, which is one reason why people do what they know they shouldn't.

seduction.o: Borrowed from Middle French séduction, from Latin sēductiō, from sēdūcō. Equivalent to seduce + -tion.
seduction.example: It is with no small degree of irony that I confess that immersing myself in an interdisciplinary project has warmed me to the seductions of disciplinary perspectives.
seduction.exampleSense: A seductive aspect of something; appeal.

intimacy.example: He recognized the tone as the one used by friendly sisters to discuss the infirmities of their husbands. It was Shama’s plea to a sister to exchange intimacies, to show support.

chat up.example: Have you been chatting up my girlfriend?
chat up.exampleSense: To talk to (someone) in a friendly, open, or casual manner, sometimes also in a charming or affected manner, usually to curry favor, and sometimes flirtatiously with the intention of establishing a romantic or sexual encounter or relationship with that person.

pick up.example: I've tried his home number a couple times, but it isn't picking up.
pick up.exampleSense: To receive calls; to function correctly.

leading.o:
verb: From Middle English ledinge, ledynge, ledand, ledande, ledende, from Old English lǣdende, from Proto-West Germanic *laidijandī, from Proto-Germanic *laidijandz, present participle of Proto-Germanic *laidijaną (“to lead”), equivalent to lead + -ing. Compare West Frisian liedend, Dutch leidend, German leitend, Swedish ledande, Icelandic leiðandi.
