noun: From Middle English leding, ledyng, ledinge, ledunge, equivalent to lead + -ing. Cognate with Dutch leiding (“conduit, leading, guidance, leadership”), German Leitung (“line, conduit, cable”).

noun: From Middle English leedynge, equivalent to lead (chemical element) + -ing; so named because in metal typesetting (letterpress and hot metal typesetting), pieces of lead (slugs, strips, blocks, etc) were often the mechanical means of producing the gap.
leading.example: The stock market can be a leading economic indicator.

blandness.example: But generally, these summits have been real snoozers, producing statements of such vague blandness that they make G-20 resolutions read like Harry Potter page-turners.
blandness.exampleSense: The state, quality, or characteristic of being bland. Lack of interest or appeal.

bloodless.o: From Middle English blodles, from Old English blōdlēas (“bloodless”). Cognate with Dutch bloedeloos (“bloodless”), German blutlos (“bloodless”), Danish blodløs (“bloodless”), Swedish blodlös (“bloodless”), Icelandic blóðlaus (“bloodless”). By surface analysis, blood + -less.
bloodless.example: Now and then a gaudy peacock would run from his shelter in the lauhala trees, but no wild boars came out, so we returned from our raid bloodless and spoilless.
bloodless.exampleSense: Taking place without loss of blood.

shameless.o: From Middle English schameles, shameles, from Old English sċamlēas, sċeamlēas (“without shame; shameless”), from Proto-Germanic *skamalausaz (“shameless”), equivalent to shame + -less. Cognate with West Frisian skamteleas (“shameless”), Dutch schaamteloos (“shameless”), German schamlos (“shameless”), Danish skamløs (“shameless”), Swedish skamlös (“shameless”), Icelandic skammlaus (“shameless; unashamed”).

shameful.o: From Middle English schameful, schamfull, from Old English *sċeamfull, sċeomfull, equivalent to shame + -ful. Cognate with Danish skamfuld (“shameful, shamefast, ashamed”).

openness.o: From Middle English *opennesse, from Old English openness (“openness, publicity”), equivalent to open + -ness. Cognate with Old High German offannussi (“disclosure, revelation, openness”).
openness.example: "Instead of openness, there was the cunning tactics of cover-up and a complete failure by General De Chastelain to deal with the vital numerics of decommissioning," said Ian Paisley, 79, the Protestant preacher who heads the Democratic Unionists, Northern Ireland's largest party.

penne.o: Borrowed from Italian penne, plural of penna.

reflector.example: Most reflectors on leadership are comfortable thinking of "ethical" and "unethical" as modifiers of leadership.
reflector.exampleSense: One who reflects on something; one who thinks or considers at length.

inflection.o: From older inflexion, borrowed from Middle French inflexion, itself borrowed from Latin inflexiōnem (“alteration”, literally “bending”). The English spelling with ⟨ct⟩ is due to influence from inflect or related words like correction.
inflection.example: Recite every inflection for each of these words.
inflection.exampleSense: Any form produced by such an instance of a change, such as the principal parts for any given stem: any of the declined or conjugated forms that constitute its declension or conjugation.

deflection.o: From Latin dēflexiō, from dēflectere (“to deflect”; participle stem dēflex-) + -iō (suffix forming abstract nouns). The non-etymological spelling deflection is taken from the present stem dēflect-, associated with collection, dissection, etc. By surface analysis, deflect + -ion.
deflection.example: Russell's goalbound shot took a deflection off a defender and went out for a corner.
deflection.exampleSense: The act of deflecting or something deflected.

genuflect.o: PIE word *ǵónu From around 1620–1630 from Medieval Latin genūflectō (“to bend the knee”) equivalent to the Latin genū (“knee”) + flectō (“to bend”).
genuflect.example: At high Mass the deacon and subdeacon stand on either side, genuflect too, and answer.
genuflect.exampleSense: To briefly enter a position that touches one knee to the ground in a manner that is typically associated with formal homage or religious worship.

inflect.o: From Latin īnflectō, from in- (“in”) + flectō (“to bend”).
inflect.example: The actress has a great skill of being able to inflect her voice to any situation.
inflect.exampleSense: To change the tone or pitch of the voice when speaking or singing.

deflect.o: From Latin deflecto, from de- (“away”) + flecto (“to bend”).
deflect.example: The Prime Minister deflected some increasingly pointed questions by claiming he had an appointment.

flection.o: An alteration of flexion, from Latin.

undulatory.example: His body was contracted and bent towards them, and described an undulatory movement like that of a worm writhing.
undulatory.exampleSense: That undulates, or that causes undulations

undulate.o:
verb: First attested in 1664; borrowed from New Latin undulātus, the perfect passive participle of undulō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from an unattested *undula (“small wave”), diminutive of Latin unda (“wave”).

adj: Borrowed from Late Latin undulātus (“undulated”), see -ate (adjective-forming suffix).
undulate.example: Breath vocalized, i.e., vibrated and undulated.
undulate.exampleSense: To cause to move in a wavelike motion.

fingertip.o: From finger + tip. Compare tiptoe and toetip.
fingertip.example: They were all professional to their fingertips, knew each other very well, and knew their disciplines backwards.
fingertip.exampleSense: The tip of the human finger.

containerize.example: 1. First and foremost, containerize or dockerize the Spring Boot app using a Dockerfile.
containerize.exampleSense: To run an application in a software container.

container.o: From Middle English conteyner, equivalent to contain + -er.
container.example: The specifiers of the Freightliner network had the foresight to base the rail journey on carrying ISO containers which are 8ft wide and originally 8ft tall (although now increased to a height of 9ft 6ins), with a variety of lengths.
container.exampleSense: A very large, typically metal, box used for transporting goods.

swipe.o: From earlier swip (with a short vowel), from Middle English swippen, swype (“to move violently”), from Old English sweopian, swipian, swippan (“to scourge, strike, beat, lash”), from Proto-West Germanic *swippjan, *swipōn, *swipēn, from Proto-Germanic *swipōną, *swipjaną, *swipāną (“to move”), from Proto-Indo-European *sweyb- (“to bend, sway, swing, sweep, swerve, turn”). Cognate with German schwippen (“sway back and forth”), Danish svippe (“to smack; crack a whip”), Icelandic svipa (“riding crop, whip”). Related to sweep, swoop.
swipe.example: Some New Yorkers are moving beyond the swipe to venture into flirtatious panel discussions and speed dating sessions.
swipe.exampleSense: An act of interacting with a touch screen by drawing the finger rapidly across it.

flamen.o: Borrowed from Latin flāmen (“ancient Roman priest devoted exclusively to one deity”).

ancillary.o: From Latin ancillāris (“ancillary; relating to female slaves”), from ancilla (“slave-woman”).
ancillary.example: The cafeteria is primarily used by students and staff (academic, administrative, and ancillary).

profiling.o: present participle and gerund of profile. From French profil, from Italian profilo (“a border”), later also proffilo (“a side-face, profile”), from Latin pro (“before”) + filo (“a line, stroke, thread”), from filum (“a thread”); see file. Doublet of purfle.

nook.o: From Middle English noke, nok (“nook, corner, angle”), of uncertain origin. Perhaps from Old English hnoc, hnocc (“hook, angle”), from Proto-Germanic *hnukkaz, *hnukkô (“a bend”), from Proto-Indo-European *knewg- (“to turn, press”), from Proto-Indo-European *ken- (“to pinch, press, bend”). If so, then also related to Scots nok (“small hook”), Norwegian dialectal nok, nokke (“hook, angle, bent object”), Danish nok (“hook”), Swedish nock (“ridge”), Faroese nokki (“crook”), Icelandic hnokki (“hook”), Dutch nok (“ridge”) or Dutch hoek (“corner”), Low German Nocke (“tip”), Old Norse hnúka (“to bend, crouch”), Old English ġehnycned (“drawn, pinched, wrinkled”). Also cognate with Scots neuk, nuk (“corner, angle of a square, angular object”).
nook.example: The back of the used book shop was one of her favorite nooks; she could read for hours and no one would bother her or pester her to buy.
nook.exampleSense: A hidden or secluded spot; a secluded retreat.

eviction.o: Borrowed from Middle French éviction, from Late Latin ēvictiō, from Latin ēvincō.

skid.o:
noun: From Middle English *skid, from Old Norse skíð (“a billet of wood, a beam or plank on which something rests”), from Proto-Germanic *skīdą (“log, clapboard”), from Proto-Indo-European *skey-t-, *skey- (“to split, divide, separate”). Cognate with English shide, from Middle English schyd, schyde, schide (“plank, beam”), German Scheit (“piece of wood, log”). Doublet of ski.

noun: Shortening of stepkid.

noun: Shortened from script kiddie, probably via skiddie.
skid.example: They skidded around the corner and accelerated up the street.
skid.exampleSense: To slide in an uncontrolled manner as in a car with the brakes applied too hard, the wheels sliding with limited spinning.

sample.o: Inherited from Middle English saumple, sample, from Old French essample (“example”), from Latin exemplum. Doublet of example and exemplum.
sample.example: He looked down into Glen Doone first, and sniffed as if he were smelling it, like a sample of goods from a wholesale house; and then he looked at the hills over yonder, and then he stared at me.
sample.exampleSense: A part or snippet of something taken or presented for inspection, or shown as evidence of the quality of the whole; a specimen.

sampling.o: present participle and gerund of sample. Inherited from Middle English saumple, sample, from Old French essample (“example”), from Latin exemplum. Doublet of example and exemplum.

coniferous.o: From Latin. By surface analysis, cone + -i- + -ferous (“bearing”), or conifer + -ous (“pertaining to”), as reflected in the meanings.
coniferous.example: During the first part of the oligocratic stage, leaching of brown soils produces acid podzols that favour coniferous woodlands and heaths.
coniferous.exampleSense: Of, or pertaining to, a conifer.

timbering.example: The timbering and centring used for the construction of the main arch were exceptionally massive, and were acclaimed as masterpieces of joinery in contemporary reports on the progress of the work.
timbering.exampleSense: Any structure, partial structure, or other item made from timber.

powerhouse.example: The company has been a powerhouse in its industry for many years.
powerhouse.exampleSense: Any source of power, energy or strength; a source of influence or inspiration

snowball.o: From Middle English snoweball, snoweballe, snaweballe, snayballe, equivalent to snow + ball. Cognate with Scots snawbaw, German Schneeball, Luxembourgish Schnéiball, Dutch sneeuwbal, Afrikaans sneeubal, Limburgish snieëbal, West Frisian sniebal, Saterland Frisian Sneebaal, Sneebal, Swedish snöboll, Elfdalian sniųoboll, Danish snebold, Norwegian Bokmål snøball, Norwegian Nynorsk snøball and Icelandic snjóbolti.
snowball.example: It didn't take long to eat a packetful of snowballs - they are simply delicious.
snowball.exampleSense: A small cake, typically cream-filled and covered in chocolate icing and desiccated coconut.

snowfall.example: There has been snowfall every day this week.
snowfall.exampleSense: An instance of falling of snow.

mandarin.o:
noun: From Portuguese mandarim, mandarij, from Malay menteri, manteri, and its source, Sanskrit मन्त्रिन् (mantrin, “minister, councillor”), from मन्त्र (mantra, “counsel, maxim, mantra”) + -इन् (-in, an agent suffix).

noun: From French mandarine, feminine of mandarin, probably formed as Etymology 1, above, from the yellow colour of the mandarins' costume.
mandarin.example: LIKE THE MANDARINS of old, the rulers of China live behind high walls. When they emerge, which they rarely do, they travel in cars with rear windows curtained like sedan chairs.
mandarin.exampleSense: A high government bureaucrat of the Chinese Empire.

template.o: Alteration of templet, probably from French templet, diminutive of temple (“a weaver's stretcher”), variant of tempe, from Latin tempora (“temple”). Alteration of second syllable due to analogy with plate. Cognate with Faroese tamba (“to stretch out, relax”), Icelandic þamb (“a stretched, bloated, or extended belly”).
template.example: Metal phosphates that are templated by transition-metal complexes are rare.
template.exampleSense: To provide a template or pattern for.

predominance.o: From predominant + -ance. By surface analysis, pre- + dominance.
predominance.example: Inside classrooms and lecture theatres, all signage is in English, as is the signage in the staff office blocks. There were only three exceptions to this complete predominance of English.
predominance.exampleSense: The condition or state of being predominant; ascendancy, domination, preeminence, preponderance.

act.o:
noun: From Middle English acte, from Old French acte, from Latin ācta (“register of events”), plural of āctum (“decree, law”), from agere (“to do, to act”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éǵeti. Compare German Akte (“file”). Partially displaced deed, from Old English dǣd (“act, deed”).

adv: Clipping of actually.
act.example: The pivotal moment in the play was in the first scene of the second act.
act.exampleSense: A division of a theatrical performance.

puffin.o: From Middle English poffin, poffoun, puffon, equivalent to puff + -ing, or perhaps ultimately from Middle Cornish (compare Breton poc'han (“puffin”)).

metropolis.o: Borrowed from Late Latin mētropolis, from Ancient Greek μητρόπολις (mētrópolis, “mother city”), from μήτηρ (mḗtēr, “mother”) + πόλις (pólis, “city (state)”). By surface analysis, metro- + -polis. Doublet of metropole.
metropolis.example: An immense metropolis, like London, is calculated to make men selfish and uninteresting.
metropolis.exampleSense: A large, busy city, especially as the main city in an area or country or as distinguished from surrounding rural areas.

metro.o:
noun: From French métro, clipping of métropolitain (from Ancient Greek μήτηρ (mḗtēr, “mother”) + πόλις (pólis, “city”)), as in the Chemin de fer métropolitain, an early name for the Paris Métro. This name was a direct translation of "Metropolitan Railway", which was the original name of the earliest part of the London Underground, constructed in 1863.

noun: Clipping of metropolitan.
metro.example: I hurry to the underground. ... I am waiting for the next metro; I'll take it.
metro.exampleSense: A rapid transit rail transport system, or a train in such systems, generally underground and serving a metropolitan area.

hesitant.o: Borrowed from Latin haesitans, present participle of haesitare (“to stick fast, to hesitate”).
hesitant.example: I am hesitant to recommend him as a manager because he has a short temper.
hesitant.exampleSense: Tending to hesitate, wait, or proceed with caution or reservation.

aging.example: The aging artist could no longer steadily hold the brush.

metallic.o: From Latin metallicus, from metallum (“metal”), from Ancient Greek μέταλλον (métallon). Equivalent to metal + -ic.
metallic.example: These chemical distinctions then, to which we have referred, are quite independent of physical condition. For instance, amongst the most metallic of the metals is a gas.

ecumenical.o: From ecumenic + -al. By surface analysis, ecumene + -ical.
ecumenical.example: Within Europe, the church's ecumenical partnerships have demonstrated that ecclesial unity may have political resonances.
ecumenical.exampleSense: Pertaining to the universal Church, representing the entire Christian world; interdenominational; sometimes by extension, interreligious.

recalcitrant.o: Borrowed from French récalcitrant, in derived from Latin recalcitrāns, recalcitrantis, present participle of recalcitrō, recalcitrāre (“be disobedient, kick back [as a horse]”), from calx (“heel”), 1820s.
recalcitrant.example: His nimble fancy was recalcitrant to mental discipline.
recalcitrant.exampleSense: Marked by a stubborn unwillingness to obey authority.

hop.o:
noun: From Middle English hoppen, from Old English hoppian (“to hop, spring, leap, dance”), from Proto-West Germanic *huppōn, from Proto-Germanic *huppōną (“to hop”), from Proto-Indo-European *kewb- (“to bend, bow”). Cognate with Dutch hoppen (“to hop”), German hopfen, hoppen (“to hop”), Danish hoppe (“to hop, leap, jump”), Swedish hoppa (“to hop, leap, jump”), Icelandic hoppa (“to hop, skip”).

noun: From Middle English hoppe, from Middle Dutch hoppe, from Old Dutch *hoppo, from Proto-Germanic *huppô, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *(s)keup (“tuft, hair of the head”), referring to the plant's appearance. Cognate with German Hopfen and French houblon.
hop.example: The frog crossed the brook in three or four hops.

get around.example: The tide was too high, and we couldn't get around the rocks.
get around.exampleSense: To move to the other side of (something, such as an obstruction) by deviating from a direct course or following a curved path.

waddle.o: From Middle English wadelen, frequentative form of waden, equivalent to wade + -le. Compare Saterland Frisian wuttelje (“to waddle”), Old High German wadalōn (“to roam; wander”), Middle High German wadelen, wedelen (“to wander; rove”), German wedeln (“to waggle”). First known use in English in a version of the Song of Roland around the year 1400.
waddle.example: The pond was another favourite place to visit. Moorhens strutted from the neighbouring bushes, and a bevy of Muscovy ducks, a study in black, white and red, waddled from the farmyard hard by to enjoy a refreshing splash.
waddle.exampleSense: To walk with short steps, tilting the body from side to side.

some.o: From Middle English som, sum, from Old English sum (“some, a certain one”), from Proto-West Germanic *sum, from Proto-Germanic *sumaz (“some, a certain one”), from Proto-Indo-European *sem- (“one, whole”). Cognate Scots sum, some (“some”), North Frisian som, sam, säm (“some”), West Frisian sommige, somlike (“some”), dialectal Dutch som, saom (“some”), standard Dutch sommige (“some”), Low German somige (“some”), German dialectal summige (“some”), Danish somme (“some”), Swedish somlig (“some”), Norwegian sum, som (“some”), Icelandic sumur (“some”), Gothic 𐍃𐌿𐌼𐍃 (sums, “one, someone”). More at same.
some.exampleSense: A nonzero, unspecified quantity or number of (an unbounded set of countable things).

preconception.example: He told RAIL: "We had no preconceptions, but you would assume a newer train to have better air quality than an older one. We found that was not necessarily the case.
preconception.exampleSense: An opinion formed before obtaining adequate evidence, especially as the result of bias or prejudice.

sunbeam.o: From Middle English sonnebeem, sonne beem, from Old English sunnbēam, sunnebēam (“sunbeam”), equivalent to sun + beam.
sunbeam.example: I cut-in various other material to this; for instance, a shot of a rushing brook in springtime, with dancing sunbeams reflected in the water; of birds splashing in the village pond; and, finally, of a laughing child.
sunbeam.exampleSense: A visible, narrow, and intense (relative to ambient light) ray of sunlight.

anti-virus.o: Alternative spelling of antivirus. From anti- + virus.

claustrophobia.o: From Latin claustrum (“a shut-in place”), from Latin claudō (“to shut, close; to imprison, confine”) + -phobia. First attested in the British Medical Journal.
claustrophobia.example: The first scenes, which take place in a minitheater that keeps shrinking, will be painful for anyone with even a tinge of claustrophobia.
claustrophobia.exampleSense: The fear of closed, tight places.

sick.o:
adj: From Middle English sik, sike, seek, seke, seok, from Old English sēoc (“sick, ill”), from Proto-West Germanic *seuk, from Proto-Germanic *seukaz, from Proto-Indo-European *sewg- (“to be troubled or grieved”). See also West Frisian siik, Dutch ziek, German siech, Norwegian Bokmål syk, Norwegian Nynorsk and Swedish sjuk, Danish syg; also Middle Irish socht (“silence, depression”), Old Armenian հիւծանիմ (hiwcanim, “to be weakening”). The "very good, excellent" sense is an ameliorative semantic shift from the original sense of "in poor health". Compare similar semantic development in terrific and wicked.

verb: Variant of sic, itself an alteration of seek.
sick.example: Old man to pickney, so wave unno hand if you with me /To see the sufferation sick me.

feeling.o: From Middle English felynge, equivalent to feel + -ing.
feeling.example: The wool on my arm produced a strange feeling.

sensibility.o: From Late Middle English sensibilite (“physical ability to sense or perceive; sensitivity to pain; type of perception by a sense organ; perception, understanding; image imprinted on the mind during perception; (philosophy) capacity of the soul to receive information from the senses, perceptibility; (in the plural) the senses”), from Middle French sensibilité and Old French sensibilité (“characteristic or state of being capable of sensation”) (modern French sensibilité), and from their etymon Late Latin sēnsibilitās (“intelligence; perception, sensation; sensitiveness; meaning or sense of words”), from Latin sēnsibilis (“detectable; perceptible, sensible”) (from sentiō (“to perceive with the senses, feel, sense; to be aware or sensible of; etc.”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *sent- (“to perceive; to think”)) + -bilis (suffix forming adjectives denoting a capacity or worth of being acted upon)) + -tās (suffix forming abstract nouns denoting states of being). By surface analysis, sensible + -ity (suffix forming nouns). Sense 6 (“in the philosophy of Immanuel Kant: emotion or feeling as opposed to the will”) is a use of the word as a calque of German Sinnlichkeit (“receptivity and devotion to what is experienced by the senses; desire for or openness to eroticism, sensuality”).
sensibility.example: By poetic ethic I am speaking about the intention to act on, and incorporate into a narrative configuration, values and beliefs that promote a poetic ontology and a poetic sensibility.
sensibility.exampleSense: Emotional or artistic awareness; keen sensitivity to matters of feeling or creative expression.

aggressive.o: From aggress + -ive. Compare with French agressif.
aggressive.example: This paper describes how aggressive loop unrolling is done in a retargetable optimizing compiler.
aggressive.exampleSense: Exploiting every opportunity to be applied.

aspersion.example: No criminality can be infered or punishment inflicted, but for writing, printing, uttering, or publishing false, scandalous and malicious aspersions against the government.
aspersion.exampleSense: An attack on somebody's reputation or good name, often in the phrase to cast aspersions upon….

asperse.o: From Latin aspersus, past participle of aspergere.

vermicelli.o: From Italian vermicelli, plural of vermicello (“little worm”), from verme (“worm”), from Latin vermis + -cello (“diminutive suffix”).

vesicle.o: From Middle French vesicule, from Latin vēsīcula. By surface analysis, vesic- + -le. Doublet of vesicule.
vesicle.example: It frequently contains holes, or vesicles, especially nearer the surface of a flow where gas has escaped.
vesicle.exampleSense: A small cavity formed in volcanic rock by entrapment of a gas bubble during solidification.

broth.o: From Middle English broth, from Old English broþ (“broth”), from Proto-West Germanic *broþ (“broth”), from Proto-Germanic *bruþą (“broth”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰrewh₁- (“to seethe, roil, brew”). Akin to Old English breowan (“to brew”), equivalent to brew + -th (abstract nominal suffix).

pilaf.o: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish پلاو (modern Turkish pilav), from Classical Persian پلاو (pilāw), from Hindi पुलाव (pulāv)/Urdu پُلاؤ (pulāo), from Sauraseni Prakrit *𑀧𑀼𑀮𑀸𑀕 (*pulāga), from Sanskrit पुलाक (pulāka), which is probably of Dravidian origin. Akin to Tamil புழுக்கு (puḻukku, “cooked rice”). Doublet of pulao.
pilaf.example: Charlie Vaughn, the tribal chairman, dismissed his critics at the opening as people who are "eating tofu and pilaf and sitting in Phoenix with their plasma-screen TVs".
pilaf.exampleSense: A dish made by browning grain, typically rice, in oil and then cooking it with a seasoned broth, to which meat and/or vegetables may be added.

emergency brake.example: At 0725, the driver operated the emergency brakes to no immediate effect. [...] As the train passed through Platform 11 at around 30mph, the train manager realised there was a problem and applied the emergency brake, bringing the train to a stand [...].
emergency brake.exampleSense: A brake which can be used by passengers in a vehicle to stop in event of an emergency.

emergent.o: From Latin ēmergēns, present participle of ēmergō. The medical sense is a back-formation from emergency.
emergent.example: Bleeding manifestations in chronic DIC are more subacute than in acute DIC, but may become emergent as DIC progresses.

concern.o: Borrowed from Middle French concerner, from Medieval Latin concernō, concernere (“I distinguish, have respect to”), from Latin concernō (“to mix, sift, or mingle together, as in a sieve”), combined form of con- + cernō (“distinguish”).
concern.example: Mark’s health was of great concern to Connie.
concern.exampleSense: That which affects one’s welfare or happiness. A matter of interest to someone.

privacy.example: I need my privacy, so please stay out of my room.
privacy.exampleSense: The state of being secluded from the presence, sight, or knowledge of others.

excessively.example: The application form was excessively complicated.

exceptive.example: In 1813, Unitarians were set free from legal penalties by the repeal, so far as they were concerned, of the exceptive clauses of the Toleration Act, this relief coming twenty years after Charles James Fox had tried to secure it for them.

overall.o: From Middle English overall, overal, from Old English ofer eall, ofer ealle (“over all”), equivalent to over + all. Compare Saterland Frisian oural, uural (“everywhere”), West Frisian oeral (“everywhere”), Dutch overal (“everywhere”), German Low German overall, överall (“everywhere; all over”), German überall (“all over; everywhere”), Danish overalt (“everywhere”), Swedish överallt (“everywhere; overall”).
overall.example: Overall, there is not enough evidence to form a clear conclusion.

expectancy.example: O, what a noble mind is here o’erthrown!

expect.o: From Latin expectāre, infinitive form of exspectō (“look out for, await, expect”), from ex (“out”) + spectō (“look at”), frequentative of speciō (“see”).
expect.example: I expect to be able to walk again after getting over my broken leg.
expect.exampleSense: To predict or believe that something will happen

healthcare.example: There are many groups trying to claim healthcare marketing as part of their activity.

instance.o: Borrowed from Middle French instance, from Latin īnstantia (“a being near, presence, also perseverance, earnestness, importunity, urgency”), from īnstāns (“urgent”); see instant.
instance.example: Some compilers will allow statics to be inlined, but then incorrectly create multiple instances of the inlined variable at run-time.
instance.exampleSense: A specific occurrence of something that is created or instantiated, such as a database, or an object of a class in object-oriented programming.

instant.o:
noun: From Middle English instant (“infinitely short period of time”), from Old French instant (“assiduous, at hand”, adjective), from Latin īnstāns, īnstantis (“present, pressing, urgent”, literally “standing near”), present active participle of īnstō (“to stand upon, be nearby”), from in- (“after”) + stō (“to stand”). Compare Old English instede (“immediately, on the spot, at once”). More at in, stand.

adj: From French instant and Middle English instant, both from Old French, from Latin instans (“standing by, being near, present, also urgent, importunate”), present participle of instō (“to stand upon, press upon, urge, pursue, insist”), from in (“on, upon”) + stō (“to stand”); see state.

verb: Ultimately from Latin īnstāre; its precise evolution is uncertain. OED hints at (unattested) Middle French *instanter.
instant.example: I refer to your letter of the 16th instant in regard to traffic disruption.

discerning.o: present participle and gerund of discern. From Middle English discernen, from Old French discerner, from Latin discernere (“to separate, divide, distinguish, discern”), from dis- (“apart”) + cernere (“to distinguish”); see certain.
discerning.example: The discerning customer will appreciate our new range of quality clothing.
discerning.exampleSense: Of keen insight or good judgement; perceptive.

discern.o: From Middle English discernen, from Old French discerner, from Latin discernere (“to separate, divide, distinguish, discern”), from dis- (“apart”) + cernere (“to distinguish”); see certain.
discern.example: Meanwhile the brig had altered her tack, and was moving slowly to the east. Three hours later and the keenest eye could not have discerned her top-sails above the horizon.
discern.exampleSense: To detect with the senses, especially with the eyes.

fallow.o:
noun: [Alt: A photograph of a ploughed field.] From Middle English falwe, from Old English fealh, fealg (“fallow land”), from Proto-West Germanic *falgu (compare Saterland Frisian Falge, West Frisian falig, felling, Dutch valg, German Felge), from Proto-Indo-European *polḱéh₂ (“arable land”) (compare Gaulish olca, Russian полоса́ (polosá)).

verb: From Middle English falowen, falwen, from Old English fealgian (“to fallow; break up land”), from Proto-West Germanic *falgōn (“to fallow”). Cognate with Dutch valgen (“to plow lightly; fallow”), German Low German falgen (“to till; dig a hole”).

adj: [Alt: A photograph of a light brown deer.] From Middle English falwe, from Old English fealu, from Proto-West Germanic *falu, from Proto-Germanic *falwaz (compare West Frisian feal, Dutch vaal, German falb, fahl, French fauve), from Proto-Indo-European *polwos (compare Lithuanian pal̃vas (“sallow, wan”), Russian поло́вый (polóvyj, “wan, light yellow”), Serbo-Croatian plâv (“blond, blue”), Ancient Greek πολιός (poliós, “grey”)), from Proto-Indo-European *pelH- (“pale, gray”).
fallow.example: By a complete summer fallow, land is rendered tender and mellow. The fallow gives it a better tilth than can be given by a fallow crop.
fallow.exampleSense: The ploughing or tilling of land, without sowing it for a season.

curry.o:
noun: 1747 (as currey, first published recipe for the dish in English), from Tamil கறி (kaṟi), influenced by existing Middle English cury (“cooking”), from Middle French cuyre (“to cook”) (whence also cuisine), from Vulgar Latin cocere, from Latin coquere. Earlier cury found in 1390 cookbook Forme of Cury (Forms of Cooking) by court chefs of Richard II of England.

verb: From Middle English currayen, from Old French correer (“to prepare”), presumably from Vulgar Latin *conredare, from Latin com- (a form of con- (“with; together”)) + a verb derived from Proto-Germanic *raidaz. More at ready.

verb: Named after American mathematician Haskell Curry.

verb: Possibly derived from currier, a common 16th- to 18th-century form of courier, as if to ride post, to post. Possibly influenced by scurry.
curry.example: Your short horse is soon curried.
curry.exampleSense: To groom (a horse); to dress or rub down a horse with a curry comb.

gully.o:
noun: Origin uncertain. Possibly from a variant of Middle English golet (“esophagus, gullet”), from Old French goulet, from Latin gula (“throat”). Shift in meaning in Middle English to "water channel, ravine" may have been influenced by Middle English gylle, gille, galle (“deep narrow valley, ravine”); see gill. Compare Dutch geul. Alternatively, from a diminutive of dialectal gull (“fissue, chasm”) + -y (diminutive suffix). See gull, gullick.

noun: From Scots gully, of unknown origin.
gully.example: Older boys play gali cricket, while young girls watch them shyly from a distance.

gullible.o: Origin uncertain. Either from gull (“to dupe, trick, fool”) + -ible; or alternatively from Middle English gole, goll, gol (“an unfledged bird, silly fellow”), perhaps from Old Norse gulr (“yellow, pale”), from the hue of its down.
gullible.example: Spurious accounts that snare the gullible are readily available. Skeptical treatments are much harder to find.
gullible.exampleSense: A gullible person; someone easily fooled or tricked.

vein.o: From Middle English veyne, borrowed from Anglo-Norman veine, from Latin vēna (“a blood-vessel; vein; artery”) of uncertain origin. See vēna for more. Doublet of vena. Displaced native edre, from ǣdre (whence edder).
vein.example: The nurse hovered her vein finder to locate the veins in the patient's body.
vein.exampleSense: A blood vessel that transports blood from the capillaries back to the heart.

artery.o: Late Middle English arterie, borrowing from Old French artaire and Latin artēria (“a windpipe; an artery”), from Ancient Greek ᾰ̓ρτηρῐ́ᾱ (ărtērĭ́ā, “windpipe; artery”).
artery.example: But the importance of the railways as main arteries of the national economy remains undimmed, just as their fascination for the railway enthusiast is surely undiminished.
artery.exampleSense: A major transit corridor in a system of roads, rivers, or railway lines.

glamour.o: Borrowed from Scots glamour (“magic”), alteration of Middle English gramere (“grammar”), from Old French gramaire. Doublet of glamoury, gramarye, grammar, and grimoire. A connection has also been suggested with Old Norse glámr (“the moon", also "the name of a ghost”, poetic byname, literally “the pale one”) and glámsýni (“glamour, illusion”, literally “glam-sight”). From Grettir's Saga aka Grettis Saga, one of the Sagas of Icelanders, after the hero has been cursed by Glam, aka Glamr: "...he was become so fearsome a man in the dark, that he durst go nowhither alone after nightfall, for then he seemed to see all kinds of horrors. And that has fallen since into a proverb, that "Glam lends eyes", or gives Glamsight to those who see things nowise as they are."
glamour.example: The idea of being a movie star has lost its glamour for me.
glamour.exampleSense: Any excitement, appeal, or attractiveness associated with a person, place, or thing; that which makes something appealing.

ensue.o: From Old French ensu-, stem of some conjugated forms of ensuivre (“follow close upon, come afterward”) (French ensuivre), from Latin īnsequere, from īnsequi (“to pursue, follow, follow after; come next”), from in- (“upon”) (see in-) + sequi (“follow”) (see sequel).
ensue.example: Give three freshmen six bottles of wine, and hilarity will ensue.
ensue.exampleSense: To occur afterwards, as a result or effect.

rump.o: From Middle English rumpe, from Old Norse rumpr (“rump”), from Middle Low German rump (“the bulk or trunk of a body, trunk of a tree”), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *rumpō (“trunk of a tree, log”). The ultimate origin could be related to Proto-Germanic *hrimpaną (“to wrinkle”) (Dutch rimpel and German rümpfen (“to wrinkle”)); outside of Germanic, compare Ancient Greek ῥάμφος (rhámphos, “crooked beak”). Cognate with Icelandic rumpur (“rump”), Swedish rumpa (“rump”), Dutch romp (“trunk, body, hull”), German Rumpf (“hull, trunk, torso, trunk”). In the sense of remnant, first attested in the Rump Parliament of 1648; its original meaning here was a reference to the rotten, unclean hindquarters of an animal, gradually morphing to refer to the "remnant" aspect of the Parliament rather than its perceived unsavory nature.
rump.example: SEIGISMUNDO If she hadn't gone rumping around the world. Rubbing up on this and that man for her sport.
rump.exampleSense: To ramble; to move (or talk) aimlessly.

despotic.o: From Ancient Greek δεσποτικός (despotikós) via French despotique, equivalent to despot + -ic.
despotic.example: The despotic king dissolved the parliament, and took personal control of the country.
despotic.exampleSense: Acting or ruling as a despot, tyrannical.

despotism.o: From French despotisme; equivalent to despot + -ism.
despotism.example: The iron hand of despotism has quenched the last spark of liberty; hunted down like a wild beast, I am watching an opportunity to fly my degraded and enslaved country.
despotism.exampleSense: Government by a despot or despots: rule by a singular authority, either a single person or a tight-knit group, which rules with absolute power, especially in a cruel and oppressive way.

tribute.o: PIE word *tréyes From Middle English tribut (14th c.), from Middle French tribut, from Latin tributum (“tribute”, literally “a thing contributed or paid”), past participle of tribuere (“to assign, allot”), usually derived from tribus (“tribe”, which see).
tribute.example: The Ancient Romans made their conquered countries pay tribute.
tribute.exampleSense: A payment made by one nation to another in submission.

outlook.o:
noun: From out- + look.

noun: From out + look. Perhaps influenced by Chinese 外表 (literally “outside + surface”) and English look (“appearance”). Same etymology as Cantonese outlook.
outlook.example: He has a positive outlook on life.
outlook.exampleSense: An attitude or point of view.

step up.o: Ellipsis of step up to the plate (“take one's turn at bat, take responsibility”).
step up.example: They will need to step up production if they are going to compete.
step up.exampleSense: To increase, augment, or advance, especially by one or more steps.

gloom.o: From Middle English *gloom, *glom, from Old English glōm (“gloaming, twilight, darkness”), from Proto-West Germanic *glōm, from Proto-Germanic *glōmaz (“gleam, shimmer, sheen”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰley- (“to gleam, shimmer, glow”). The English word is cognate with Norwegian glom (“transparent membrane”), Scots gloam (“twilight; faint light; dull gleam”).
gloom.example: A sullen gloom and furious disorder prevailed by fits.
gloom.exampleSense: Cloudiness or heaviness of mind; melancholy; aspect of sorrow; low spirits; dullness.

doom and gloom.example: His sister was all doom and gloom after she lost the part.
doom and gloom.exampleSense: Something considered indicative of feelings of pessimism and despair.

dealership.example: I visited the car dealership today.
dealership.exampleSense: A place that sells items, especially cars.

dealer.o: From Middle English delare, from Old English dǣlere, from Proto-West Germanic [Term?]. By surface analysis, deal + -er. Cognate with Saterland Frisian Deeler, West Frisian dieler, Dutch deler, German Teiler, Swedish delare.
dealer.example: That used car dealer gave me a great deal on my 1962 rusted-out Volkswagen bug!
dealer.exampleSense: One who deals in goods, especially automobiles; a middleman.

inventory.o: From Middle English inventorie, from Medieval Latin inventōrium, alteration of Late Latin inventārium, from Latin inveniō (“to find out”).
inventory.example: The inventory included several items that one wouldn't normally think to find at a cheese shop.
inventory.exampleSense: A detailed list of all of the items on hand.

double-digit.example: Taiwan proposed on Thursday $19 billion in defence spending for next year, a double-digit increase on 2022 that includes funds for new fighter jets, weeks after China staged large-scale military exercises around the island it views as its territory.
double-digit.exampleSense: Being a number between 10 and 99 inclusive, a number that requires two digits to write in base 10.

kick out.example: I was driving and the motor just kicked out.
kick out.exampleSense: To stop, stall, or disconnect suddenly.

kick off.example: A week after we kicked off her calf that cow was still bawling.
kick off.exampleSense: To force the weaning of a bovine cow's calf by restricting the calf's access to its mother's udders, whether by literally kicking it away or another method.

kick up.example: See, that rod there is supposed to kick up to engage the gear.

kick in.example: I took my medication an hour ago, and it hasn't kicked in yet.
kick in.exampleSense: To begin, contribute or join in on To start, connect, or take effect, especially in a sudden way; to begin functioning.

stock up.example: Q: What about fuel oil? A: We plan to stock up before November.
stock up.exampleSense: To acquire or increase stock or inventory.

stock.o:
noun: From Middle English stok, from Old English stocc, from Proto-West Germanic *stokk, from Proto-Germanic *stukkaz (“tree-trunk”). Modern senses are mostly referring either to the trunk from which the tree grows (figuratively, its origin and/or support/foundation), or to a piece of wood, stick, or rod. The senses of "supply" and "raw material" arose from a probable conflation with steck (“an item of goods, merchandise”) or the use of split tally sticks consisting of foil or counterfoil and stock to capture paid taxes, debts or exchanges. Doublet of chock.

noun: From Italian stoccata.
stock.example: After that last screw-up of mine, my stock is pretty low around here.
stock.exampleSense: The capital raised by a company through the issue of shares; the total of shares held by an individual shareholder. The measure of how highly a person or institution is valued.

cutback.example: Fifteen more proposals to reverse historical cutbacks in passenger services and the size of the rail network have secured development funding.
cutback.exampleSense: A reduction of some sort in an existing program or service.

quarter.o:
noun: From Middle English quarter, from Anglo-Norman quarter, from Latin quartarius, from quartus. Compare Spanish cuarto (“room, quarters; quarter”). Doublet of quartier.

verb: Borrowed from French cartayer.
quarter.example: I ate a quarter of the pizza.
quarter.exampleSense: A fourth part of something. Each of four equal parts into which something can be divided; a fourth part.

bureau.o: Unadapted borrowing from French bureau, earlier "coarse cloth (as desk cover), baize", from Old French burel (“woolen cloth”), diminutive of *bure (compare Middle French bure (“coarse woolen cloth”), French bourre (“hair, fluff”)), from Late Latin burra (“wool, fluff, shaggy cloth, coarse fabric”); akin to Ancient Greek βερβέριον (berbérion, “shabby garment”). Doublet of burel and borrel, taken from Old French.
bureau.example: Ashley Johnson is an energy, trade and economics expert at the National Bureau of Asian Research, based in the United States.
bureau.exampleSense: An administrative unit of government; office.

gross.o: From Middle English gros (“large, thick, full-bodied; coarse, unrefined, simple”), from Old French gros, from Latin grossus (“big, fat, thick”, in Late Latin also “coarse, rough”), of uncertain further origin but perhaps related to Proto-Celtic *brassos (“great, violent”).
gross.example: The film grossed $464 million worldwide, ensconcing her in the Hollywood A-list.
gross.exampleSense: To earn money, not including expenses.

e-commerce.example: The last thing you need to do before launching the e-commerce site is enable credit card processing.
e-commerce.exampleSense: Commercial activity conducted via the Internet.

adviser.example: The call, which is the first known conversation between the presidents since Trump assumed office last month, came as as Trump makes clear to his advisers he wants to bring the Ukraine conflict to a swift end.

advisory.example: The advisory committee could only offer advice, but since that was almost always accepted they had real power.

pocketbook.o: 1610s, from pocket + book, popularized in its sense as a paperback by the success of Pocket Books in the United States after its 1939 launch.
pocketbook.example: The publishers brought out small format pocketbooks of the whole of their nature series.
pocketbook.exampleSense: A small book, particularly (US) a paperback or (UK) notebook able to fit into a pocket (of any genre, from reference work to fine art).

adjustment.o: From French ajustement, or else adjust + -ment.
adjustment.example: The credit card company made an adjustment to my account to waive the late fee.
adjustment.exampleSense: The settling or balancing of a financial account

microcosm.o: From French microcosme, from Latin microcosmus, from Ancient Greek μικρός (mikrós, “small”) + κόσμος (kósmos, “universe, order”); micro- + -cosm.
microcosm.example: The method is relatively labour intensive (24-30 microcosms are run) and more difficult to interpret when compared with other microcosm methods (Shannon et al. 1986; Cairns & Cherry 1993).
microcosm.exampleSense: A small natural ecosystem; an artificial ecosystem set up as an experimental model.

cost.o:
verb: From Middle English costen, from Old French coster, couster (“to cost”), from Medieval Latin cōstō, from Latin cōnstō (“stand together”).

noun: From Middle English cost, coust, from costen (“to cost”), from the same source as above.

noun: From Middle English cost, from Old English cost (“option, choice, possibility, manner, way, condition”), from Old Norse kostr (“choice, opportunity, chance, condition, state, quality”), from Proto-Germanic *kustuz (“choice, trial”) (or Proto-Germanic *kustiz (“choice, trial”)), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵéwstus (“to enjoy, taste”). Cognate with Icelandic kostur, German dialectal Kust (“taste, flavour”), Dutch kust (“choice, choosing”), North Frisian kest (“choice, estimation, virtue”), West Frisian kêst (“article of law, statute”), Old English cyst (“free-will, choice, election, the best of anything, the choicest, picked host, moral excellence, virtue, goodness, generosity, munificence”), Latin gustus (“taste”). Related to choose. Doublet of gusto.

noun: From Middle English coste, from Old French coste, from Latin costa. Doublet of coast and cuesta.
cost.example: The total cost of the new complex was an estimated $1.5 million.
cost.exampleSense: Amount of money, time, etc. that is required or used.

end up.example: The band usually ends up their concerts with their biggest hit song.

barbie.o:
noun: Clipping of barbecue + -ie (diminutive suffix).

noun: Clipping of barbiturate + -ie (diminutive suffix).

roaming.o: present participle and gerund of roam. From Middle English romen, from Old English rāmian, from Proto-Germanic *raimōną (“to wander”), from *raim- (“to move, raise”), from *h₃reyH- (“to move, lift, flow”). Akin to Old English ārǣman (“to arise, stand up, lift up”), Old High German rāmēn (“to aim”) ( > archaic German rahmen (“to strive”)), Middle Dutch rammen (“to night-wander, to copulate”), rammelen (“to wander about, ramble”). More at ramble.
roaming.example: That last problem did intrude on Hazzard’s roamings, and when she refers to the living city it is with periodic references to thefts of cars and wallets, with a warning not to carry anything “snatchable” by the thieves on motorcycles who whiz through the streets.

fuzz.o:
noun: Uncertain. Some dictionaries suggest a Germanic source; compare Low German fussig (“loose; spongy”), Dutch voos (“unsound; rotten”). Others, such as Webster's New College Dictionary, suggest a back-formation from fuzzy. The Oxford English Dictionary suggests, “Perhaps imitative of the action of blowing away light particles.”

noun: Unknown. Godfrey Irwin (1930) suggests a possible connection to fuss, "over-particular", excessive bother.
fuzz.example: His cheeks were like peaches, with much the same sort of fuzz over them.
fuzz.exampleSense: A frizzy mass of hair or fibre.

choppy.example: Commander Birch was a trifle uneasy when he found there was more than a popple on the sea; it was, in fact, distinctly choppy.

puff.o:
noun: From Middle English puff, puf, from Old English pyf (“a blast of wind, puff”), from Proto-West Germanic *puf(f)- (“to blow, puff”), of imitative origin. Cognate with Dutch puf (“puff, wind, fart”), Middle Low German puf, pof (“puff”).

verb: From Middle English puffen, from Old English pyffan (“to breathe out, blow with the mouth”). Compare Dutch puffen, German Low German puffen, German puffen, Danish puffe, Swedish puffa.
puff.example: The clearing north will puff the clouds away.
puff.exampleSense: To drive with a puff, or with puffs.

puffy.example: A puffy fat man in a tracksuit came jogging around the corner.

crystalline.o: From Middle English cristallyn, cristallyne, from Old French cristallin and its etymon Latin crystallinus, from Ancient Greek κρυστάλλινος (krustállinos), from κρύσταλλος (krústallos, “crystal”) + -ῐνος (-ĭnos, adjectival suffix). By surface analysis, crystal + -ine.
crystalline.example: not in his favoured midfield role, either but as a false No 9: the sort of role Guardiola only hands to his chosen, crystalline few: Mario Götze at Bayern Munich (less successfully), Lionel Messi at Barcelona (a little more so).

enflame.o: A variant of inflame; by surface analysis, en- (prefix meaning ‘in, into’) + flame.

dreamlike.example: Her kiss sent me into a dreamlike state of bliss.
dreamlike.exampleSense: Like something from a dream; having a sense of vagueness, insubstantiality, or incongruousness.

rug.o: Uncertain; probably of North Germanic origin; perhaps inherited via Middle English *rugge (suggested by Middle English ruggy (“hairy, shaggy, bristly”) and rugged (“hairy, shaggy, rugged”)), from Old Norse rǫgg (“shagginess, tuft”), from Proto-Germanic *rawwō (“long wool”), probably related to *rūhaz (“rough”), related to English rag and rough. Cognate with dialectal Norwegian rugga (“coarse coverlet”), Swedish rugg (“rough entangled hair”), related to English rag and rough. Compare also Old English rȳhe (“rug, rough covering, blanket”).
rug.example: They then cut down a quantity of gum-tree leaves for a bed, and threw their rugs upon them ready for bed-time.
rug.exampleSense: A (usually thick) piece of fabric used for warmth (especially on a bed); a blanket.

periwig.o: Alteration of Middle French perruque. Doublet of peruke.

wig.o: Clipping of periwig, itself an alteration of French perruque. The meaning of "to reprimand" perhaps came from this being something a bigwig would do or perhaps from the expressions to flip one's wig, wigs on the green, or dash my wig!
wig.example: That guy must be high. Look how he's wigging.
wig.exampleSense: To act in an extremely emotional way; to be overly excited, irritable, nervous, or fearful; behave erratically.

tequila.o: Borrowed from Mexican Spanish tequila, from Tequila, a town in Jalisco.
tequila.example: For a moment the bottle of tequila at the bottom of the garden gleamed on his soul, then the Consul stumbled into his bedroom.
tequila.exampleSense: An alcoholic liquor distilled from the fermented juice of the Central American century plant Agave tequilana.

pounce.o:
noun: From French ponce, from Latin pūmex. Doublet of pumice.

noun: From Middle English pounce, probably akin to punch. Possibly from Old French ponchonner (compare French poinçonner).
pounce.example: Again the cat jolted the bed with a pounce.

radiant.o: From Middle English radyant, from Latin radiāns, radiantis, present participle of radiāre (“to emit rays or beams”).
radiant.example: Nurse Cramer had a cute nose and a radiant, blooming complexion dotted with fetching sprays of adorable freckles that Yossarian detested.

radiate.o:
verb: Learned borrowing from Latin radiātus, perfect passive participle of radiō (“to radiate, furnish with spokes, give out rays, radiate, shine”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from radius (“a spoke, ray”).

adj: Learned borrowing from Latin radiātus (see Etymology 1 and -ate (adjective-forming suffix) for more).

noun: From a substantivation of the above adjective through the associated taxon's name (Radiata), see -ate (noun-forming suffix).
radiate.example: Oban is not a terminus; its routes radiate by sea, rail and road.
radiate.exampleSense: To extend, send or spread out from a center like radii.

radiance.example: Girt with omnipotence, with radiance crowned.
radiance.exampleSense: The quality or state of being radiant; shining, bright or splendid.

hematite.o: From Middle French hematite, from Latin (lapis) haematites, from Ancient Greek αἱματίτης (haimatítēs) λίθος (líthos, “blood-red stone”), from αἷμα (haîma, “blood”). By surface analysis, hemat- + -ite.

turquoise.o: From Middle French turquoise, from Old French (pierre) turquoise (“Turkish (stone)”), from turc + -ois. The stone, mined near Nishapur in the Khorasan region of Persia, was originally brought to Europe through Turkey. Doublet of Turkish.

scow.example: This steamboat was exactly like a decked scow.
scow.exampleSense: A large flat-bottomed boat, having broad, square ends.

scowler.example: Attending Bradly for company when he went abroad with his painting traps failed to account for itself under the heading of a diversion. Old Mudgy surpassed himself as a scowler and mumbler when engaged in the practice of his art.

wafer.o: From Middle English wafre, from Anglo-Norman wafre, waufre (Old French gaufre), from a Germanic source. Compare Middle Low German wāfel, Middle Dutch wafel (“honeycomb”), West Flemish wafer. See also waffle.
wafer.example: The house supplied him with a wafer for his present purpose, with which, having sealed his letter, he returned hastily towards the brook side, in order to search for the things which he had there lost.
wafer.exampleSense: A soft disk originally made of flour, and later of gelatin or a similar substance, used to seal letters, attach papers etc.

mar.o:
verb: Inherited from Middle English merren, from Old English mierran (“to mar, disturb, confuse; scatter, squander, waste; upset, hinder, obstruct; err”), from Proto-Germanic *marzijaną (“to disturb, hinder”), from Proto-Indo-European *mers- (“to annoy, disturb, neglect, forget, ignore”). Cognate with Scots mer, mar (“to obstruct, impede, spoil, ruin”), Dutch marren (“to push along, delay, hinder”), dialectal German merren (“to entangle”), Icelandic merja (“to bruise, crush”), Gothic 𐌼𐌰𐍂𐌶𐌾𐌰𐌽 (marzjan, “to annoy, bother, disturb, offend”), Lithuanian miršti (“to forget, lose, become oblivious, die”), Armenian մոռանալ (moṙanal, “to forget, fail”), Sanskrit मृष् (mṛṣ, “forget, neglect”).

noun: Variant of mere.

noun: See mayor.
mar.example: For concealing deep mars, some manufacturers offer putty sticks in colors that match their panels.

cane.o: From Middle English cane, canne, from Old French cane (“sugar cane”), from Latin canna (“reed”), from Ancient Greek κάννα (kánna), from Akkadian 𒄀 (qanû, “reed”). Doublet of canna and kaneh. Related to channel and canal.
cane.example: The teacher gave his student the cane for throwing paper.
cane.exampleSense: The stem of such a plant adapted for use as a tool Corporal punishment by beating with a cane.

mistletoe.o: From Middle English mistelto, mistilto (“European mistletoe”), from Old English misteltān (“mistletoe”), from mistel (“mistletoe; basil; birdlime”) + tān (“sprig, shoot, twig”), possibly as a calque of Old Norse mistilteinn; equivalent to mistle + tan (“twig”). This was mistaken for the plural of tā (“toe”). Cognate with Danish mistelten (“mistletoe”), Norwegian misteltein (“mistletoe”), Icelandic mistilteinn (“mistletoe”). Compare also the simplex form West Frisian mistel (“mistletoe”), Dutch mistel (“mistletoe”), German Mistel (“mistletoe”), Swedish mistel (“mistletoe”).
mistletoe.example: In Martigny I first observed the custom, common throughout many parts of Switzerland, of hanging mistletoes over the house doors; a superstition for which I have not been able to get any reason rendered.
mistletoe.exampleSense: Any of numerous hemiparasitic evergreen plants of the order Santalales with white berries that grow in the crowns of apple trees, oaks, and other trees, such as the European mistletoe (Viscum album) and American mistletoe or eastern mistletoe (Phoradendron leucarpum).

underneath.o: From Middle English undernethe, undernethen, from Old English underneoþan (“underneath”), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *underniþer. Equivalent to under- + neath.
underneath.example: connected with it underneath, you see a very fine hair-spring.

wallet.o: From Middle English walet (“a bag, knapsack”), of uncertain origin. Possibly from an assumed Old Northern French *walet (“a roll; bag; a knapsack”), from Proto-Germanic *wal- (“to roll”). More at walk, well, wallow.
wallet.example: The thief stole all the money and credit cards out of the old man's wallet.
wallet.exampleSense: A small case, often flat and often made of leather, for keeping money (especially paper money), credit cards, etc.

consumer.example: This new system favours the consumer over the producer.
consumer.exampleSense: Someone who trades money for goods or services as an individual.

relief.o:
noun: From Old French relief (“assistance”), from Old French relever (“to relieve”), from Latin relevare (“to raise up, make light”). See also relieve.

noun: From Italian rilievo, from rilevare (“to raise”), from Latin relevō (“to raise”).
relief.example: Relief arrived quickly after the disaster.
relief.exampleSense: Aid or assistance offered in time of need.

escalate.example: A small fight escalated into a big fight.
escalate.exampleSense: To increase (something) in extent or intensity; to intensify or step up.

stalemate.example: The North Korean nuclear issue, stalemated for the past three years, is now back in play again—not before time.
stalemate.exampleSense: To bring about a stalemate, in which no advance in an argument is achieved.

stale.o:
adj: From Middle English stale, from Old French estal (“fixed position, place”), but probably originally from Proto-Germanic *stāną (“to stand”): compare West Flemish stel in the same sense for ‘beer’ and ‘urine’.

noun: From Middle English stale, from Old English stalu, from Proto-Germanic *stal-; compare English stell from this root. The development was paralleled by the ablaut which became English steal, from Middle English stele, from Old English stela, from Proto-Germanic *stel-. Both are from the same Proto-Indo-European root *stel-, *stol- (“to place, establish”), whence also Ancient Greek στελεός (steleós, “handle”). See also English stele.

noun: From Middle English stale, from Old French estal (“place, something placed”) (compare French étal), from Frankish stal, from Proto-Germanic *stallaz, earlier *staþlaz. Related to stall and stand.

noun: Noun from Middle English stale, from Anglo-Norman estal (“urine”), from Middle Dutch stal (“urine”). Cognate with Middle Low German stal (“horse urine; bowel movement”). Verb from Middle English stalen, from Old French estaler (“urinate”), related to Middle High German stallen (“to piss”).

noun: From Middle English stale (“bird used as a decoy”), probably from uncommon Anglo-Norman estale (“pigeon used to lure hawks”), ultimately from Proto-Germanic, probably *standaną (“to stand”). Compare Old English stælhran (“decoy reindeer”) and Northumbrian stællo (“catching fish”).
stale.example: Gif ony stal in the yet of the gilde...he sall gif iiijd. to the mendis.
stale.exampleSense: To urinate, especially used of horses and cattle.

official.o: From Middle English official, from Old French official, from Latin officiālis, from Latin officium (“duty, service”), by surface analysis, office + -ial.
official.example: Officials in the Firefly administration assure the Sylvanians they don't want war either.
official.exampleSense: An office holder, a person holding an official position in government, sports, or other organization.

marathon.o: From French marathon, coined in 1894 by linguist Michel Bréal for the first modern time Olympic Games after Ancient Greek Μαραθών (Marathṓn), a town northeast of Athens. Phidippides the Greek ran the distance from Marathon to Athens to deliver a message regarding the Battle of Marathon. The modern sport of marathon running is based on a run approximately the same distance. The toponym itself comes from μάραθον (márathon, “fennel”) and refers to the prevalence of the plant in the area.
marathon.example: He had a cleaning marathon the night before his girlfriend came over.

lower.example: I could never lower myself enough to buy second-hand clothes.
lower.exampleSense: To humble oneself; to do something one considers to be beneath one's dignity.

whopping.example: Doss and I run the house, cooking dinner—whopping great pots of stew and rice, sewing and darning clothes, ironing, bathing the kids, blacking the grate, scrubbing the doorstep, running errands.

whop.o: From Middle English whappen, a variant of wappen (“to strike; fling; shoot; stun”), probably of imitative origin. Compare Old Norse vappa (“to waddle”).
whop.example: He angrily whopped the book onto the table.
whop.exampleSense: To throw or move (something) quickly, usually with an impact.

pros and cons.o: From Latin prō (“for, on behalf of”) and contrā (“against”).

backward and forward.o: Alternative form of backwards. From backward + -s. See also -s (“used in the formation of certain adverbs: backwards, downwards, inwards, etc.”).

rollback.o: The noun is a deverbal from roll back. The verb is a back-formation from the noun despite being redundant to roll back.
rollback.example: Politically, Brzezinski was a centrist, or conservative, Democrat. He criticised both the Eisenhower administration’s “rollback” policy towards communism in Europe, and the Nixon-Kissinger detente.
rollback.exampleSense: The strategy of forcing a change in the major policies of a state, usually by replacing its ruling regime, or by totally annihilating an enemy's armed forces and occupying the country, as was done in World War II to Italy, Germany, and Japan.

cool down.example: We had to cool down the equipment with water before using it.
cool down.exampleSense: To cause (something) to become cooler; to reduce the temperature of.

talk.o:
verb: From Middle English talken, talkien, from Old English *tealcian (“to talk, chat”), from Proto-West Germanic *talkōn, from Proto-Germanic *talkōną (“to talk, chatter”), frequentative form of Proto-Germanic *talōną (“to count, recount, tell”), from Proto-Indo-European *dol-, *del- (“to aim, calculate, adjust, count”), equivalent to tell + -k. Cognates Cognate with Low German taalken (“to chatter, gossip, talk”). Related also to Bavarian zoin (“to pay”), Cimbrian zaln (“to pay”), Dutch talen (“to care, long; to speak; to say”), German zahlen (“to pay”), Mòcheno zoln (“to pay”), Danish and Norwegian Bokmål tale (“to talk, speak”), Faroese, Icelandic, and Swedish tala (“to speak, talk”), Norwegian Nynorsk tala (“to speak, talk”); also Latin dolus (“deceit, deception, fraud, guile, treachery, trickery; malice; artifice, device, stratagem”), Ancient Greek δόλος (dólos, “deceit, trick; wiles; bait”), Armenian տող (toġ, “line (in a text)”). More at tale. Despite the surface similarity, unrelated to Proto-Indo-European *telkʷ- (“to talk”) (due to Grimm's law), which is the source of loquacious.

noun: From Middle English talk, talke (“conversation; discourse”), from the verb (see above).
talk.example: We need to have a talk about your homework.
talk.exampleSense: A conversation or discussion; usually serious, but informal.

breakthrough.o: From break + through. Compare German Durchbruch and Dutch doorbraak (“breakthrough”, literally “through-break”).
breakthrough.example: Albert Einstein is credited with making some of the greatest breakthroughs in modern physics.
breakthrough.exampleSense: Any major progress; such as a great innovation or discovery that overcomes a significant obstacle.

accumulation.o: From Middle English acumulacyon, from Middle French accumulation and its etymon, Latin accumulātiō, accumulātiōnis. By surface analysis, accumulate + -ion. First attested in the late 15th century. Doublet of accumulatio.

agnostic.o: Coined by Thomas Henry Huxley in 1870. Either from Ancient Greek ἄγνωστος (ágnōstos, “ignorant, not knowing”), or from a- + Gnostic, deriving (either way) from Ancient Greek ἀ- (a-, “not”) + γιγνώσκω (gignṓskō, “I know”).
agnostic.example: She left the church when she had become agnostic.
agnostic.exampleSense: Doubtful or uncertain about the existence or demonstrability of God or other deity.

inversion.example: Question formation involves the phenomenon commonly known as subject-auxiliary inversion, a change in word order in which the auxiliary moves in front of the subject.
inversion.exampleSense: Deviation from standard word order by putting the predicate before the subject. It takes place in questions with auxiliary verbs and in normal, affirmative clauses beginning with a negative particle, for the purpose of emphasis.

subserve.o: Borrowed from Latin subservire; by surface analysis, sub- + serve.
subserve.example: Their principles will cease to be dear to them, whenever they shall cease to subserve the purposes of good order.
subserve.exampleSense: To serve to promote (an end); to be useful to.

impassive.o: From im- (prefix meaning ‘not’) + passive (“which is, or is capable of being, acted on; (obsolete) which suffers, or may suffer, pain, death, etc.”, adjective).
impassive.example: It was a victory that clearly meant so much to Van Gaal as the normally impassive manager raced from his seat in the technical area to celebrate Lingard's winner.

orient.o:
name: The noun is derived from Middle English orient, oriente, oryent, oryente, oryentte (“the east direction; eastern horizon or sky; eastern regions of the world, Asia, Orient; eastern edge of the world”), borrowed from Anglo-Norman orient, oriente, and Old French orient (“east direction; Asia, Orient”) (modern French orient), or directly from its etymon Latin oriēns (“the east; daybreak, dawn; sunrise; (participle) rising; appearing; originating”), present active participle of orior (“to get up, rise; to appear, become visible; to be born, come to exist, originate”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃er- (“to move, stir; to rise, spring”). The adjective is derived from Middle English orient (“eastern; from Asia or the Orient; brilliant, shining (characteristic of jewels from the Orient)”), from Middle English orient (noun); see above.

verb: The verb is derived from French orienter (“to orientate; to guide; to set to north”) from French orient (noun) (see above) + -er (suffix forming infinitives of first-conjugation verbs).
orient.example: Give him time to orient himself within the new hierarchy.
orient.exampleSense: To familiarize (oneself or someone) with a circumstance or situation.

future-proof.example: It’s not easy to buy a future-proof laptop because the industry is moving in the opposite direction.
future-proof.exampleSense: Capable of surviving changes made in the future; not liable to become outdated.

domain.o: From Middle English demayne, demain (“rule”), from Old French demeine, demaine, demeigne, domaine (“power”), (French domaine), from Latin dominium (“property, right of ownership”), from dominus (“master, proprietor, owner”). Doublet of demesne and dominium, and closely related to dominion and domino. See also dame, and compare demain, danger, dungeon.
domain.example: Dealing with complaints isn't really my domain: get in touch with customer services.
domain.exampleSense: A field or sphere of activity, influence or expertise.

domineering.o: present participle and gerund of domineer. From Dutch domineren, from Middle French dominer.
domineering.example: In strange contrast to the hardly tolerable constraint and nameless invisible domineerings of the captain's table, was the entire care-free license and ease, the almost frantic democracy of those inferior fellows the harpooneers.
domineering.exampleSense: The act of one who domineers.

domineer.o: From Dutch domineren, from Middle French dominer.

deposition.o: From Middle English deposicion, from Old French deposicion (French déposition), from Latin depositio.
deposition.example: So, Andover featured in the Glorious Revolution, which involved the deposition of Catholic fraterniser James II and his replacement by stout Protestants William and Mary.
deposition.exampleSense: The removal of someone from office.

cucumber.o: From Middle English cucumer, cucumber, from Old French cocombre, ultimately from Latin cucumis, cucumerem (possibly through an Old Occitan intermediate). Probably of Pre-Italic substrate origin. First attested in the late 14c. Displaced native English earthapple (see which for more), which has since acquired other senses.
cucumber.example: That Wolf is one cool cucumber.
cucumber.exampleSense: A person who is calm and self-possessed.

leverage.o: From lever + -age. The verb likely comes from martial arts/judo usage, where one would "use an opponent's leverage (i.e. their weight, height, centre of balance, etc.)" against them in order to defeat them.
leverage.example: Leverage is great until something goes wrong with your investments and you still have to pay your debts.
leverage.exampleSense: The use of borrowed funds with a contractually determined return to increase the ability to invest and earn an expected higher return, but usually at high risk.

rendering.o: present participle and gerund of render. From Middle English renderen, rendren, from Old French rendre (“render, give back”), from Late Latin rendere, from Latin reddere (“make, give back”).
rendering.example: Sophia broke down here. Even at this moment she was subconsciously comparing her rendering of the part of the forlorn bride with Miss Marie Lohr's.

whiteout.example: The slightest reference to national security is accepted as excuse enough for a news whiteout.
whiteout.exampleSense: The suppression of a story by the media, analogously to deleting information with correction fluid.

braise.o: From French braise (“live coals”) and braiser (“to braise”, from the noun), from Old French brese (“embers”), from Old Low Franconian/Old Dutch; akin to Norwegian/Swedish braseld (“sparkling fire”), Norwegian/Swedish dialectal brasa (“to roast”), Danish dialectal brase (“to flambé, enflame”). Perhaps from Gothic *𐌱𐍂𐌰𐍃𐌰 (*brasa, “glowing coal”), from Proto-Germanic *brasō (“gleed, crackling coal”), Proto-Indo-European *bʰres- (“to crack, break, burst”). Cognate with Icelandic brasa (“to harden by fire”). See burst.
braise.example: Pot roast is typically a braise, as is osso buco.
braise.exampleSense: A dish (usually meat) prepared by braising.

carry-out.example: A simpler scheme is to connect the carry-ins and carry-outs of the units in a ripple chain. This approach is most common in chip design because the wiring for the carry-lookahead tree is hard to design and area-consuming.
carry-out.exampleSense: A command that exports a carry (bit or digit that is carried in an addition operation) from the current column of an addition operation.

envoy.o: From French envoyé (“envoy, messenger”), from envoyer (“send”).

annuity.o: From French annuité, from Medieval Latin annuitās, from Latin annuus (“annual”). Cf. annuality.

annual.o: First attested around 1382, borrowed from Late Latin annuālem, annuālis, related to Latin annālis, adjective form of annus (“year”). Used to categorize plants since 1710.
annual.example: I read the magazine, but I usually don't purchase the annuals.
annual.exampleSense: An annual publication; a book, periodical, journal, report, comic book, yearbook, etc., which is published serially once a year, which may or may not be in addition to regular weekly or monthly publication.

annum.o: From Latin per annum (“yearly”), from annus (“year”).

peninsula.o: Borrowed from Latin paenīnsula, from paene (“almost”), and īnsula (“island”).
peninsula.example: Man cancelling Lisa's inauguration as president: I sentence you to a lifetime of horror on Monster Island. Don't worry, it's just a name.
peninsula.exampleSense: A piece of land projecting into water from a larger land mass.

outsourcing.o: present participle and gerund of outsource. From out- + source.

punch out.example: The ump punched out the batter with relish to close out the game.
punch out.exampleSense: To rule (by an umpire) that a pitch is a called third strike, often done emphatically.

clock out.example: If we clock out now we can be at the bar by happy hour.
clock out.exampleSense: To end work; to officially record a time when one terminates a period of work.

clock in.example: We clocked in at 7:30, but didn't actually do any work until at least 8.
clock in.exampleSense: To begin working time, especially by punching in (entering a workplace by punching a time card with the time clock).

clock off.example: Most of the staff have already clocked off for the night, you should do the same.
clock off.exampleSense: to leave work, especially by recording the leaving time on a machine

punch in.example: I'm going to punch in a bit early today to get more work done.
punch in.exampleSense: To enter a workplace by punching a timecard.

clock on.example: His birthday was another reminder of his life clocking on.

meander.o: From Latin Maeander, from Ancient Greek Μαίανδρος (Maíandros) – a river in Asia Minor (present day Turkey) known for its winding course (modern Turkish Menderes).
meander.example: And as to the lands that were within the national meander boundaries, that description was based upon a state survey?
meander.exampleSense: A path on which the directions, distances, and elevations are noted, as a part of a land survey.

dean.o:
noun: From Middle English den, deen (“dean”), from Anglo-Norman deen and continental Old French deien (modern French doyen), from Latin decānus. Doublet of doyen.

noun: Related to den.

dignitary.example: Chinese dignitaries traveled with us from place to place, and when ready to depart from Urumchi, or Tihwa, we were introduced to the high officials who were going along in the plane.
dignitary.exampleSense: An important or influential person, or one of high rank or position.

dignify.o: From Old French dignifier, from Late Latin dignificare, from dignus (“worthy”) + ficare (in comp.), facere (“to make”). See deign and fact.
dignify.example: I will not dignify that comment with a response.
dignify.exampleSense: To treat as worthy or acceptable; to indulge or condone by acknowledging.

indignity.o: Borrowed from Latin indignitās, indignitātem. Equivalent to indign + -ity.

amidst.o: From amids + -t (excrescent), from amid + -s (genitive). By surface analysis, amid + -st (excrescent). Root amid from Middle English amidde, amiddes, on midden, from Old English on middan (“in the middle”), from midd (“central”) (English mid).
amidst.example: Be a philosopher ; but amidst all your philosophy, be still a man.
amidst.exampleSense: In the midst or middle of; surrounded or encompassed by; among.

arsenal.o: From Italian arsenale, from Arabic دَار الصِّنَاعَة (dār aṣ-ṣināʕa, “manufacturing shop”), from دَار (dār) + صِنَاعَة (ṣināʕa).
arsenal.example: He arrived with a large arsenal of cleansers and tools, and got right to work.
arsenal.exampleSense: Any supply of aid collected to prepare a person or army for hardship

jagged.o: simple past and past participle of jag. The noun is from late Middle English jagge, from Old English giagga, giacga. The ultimate origin could be sound-symbolic of sudden movement, compare with jam, rag and Middle English dag, of which jag may be a palatalised variant. The verb is from jaggen, from Old English giacgian.

jag.o:
noun: The noun is from late Middle English jagge, from Old English giagga, giacga. The ultimate origin could be sound-symbolic of sudden movement, compare with jam, rag and Middle English dag, of which jag may be a palatalised variant. The verb is from jaggen, from Old English giacgian.

noun: Circa 1597; originally "load of broom or furze", variant of British English dialectal chag (“tree branch; branch of broom or furze”), from Old English ċeacga (“broom, furze”), from Proto-Germanic *kagô (compare dialectal German Kag (“stump, cabbage, stalk”), Swedish dialect kage (“stumps”), Norwegian dialect kage (“low bush”), of unknown origin.
jag.example: Even if you hadn’t been drowned, you would have been smashed to pieces by the terrible weight of water against the countless jags of rock.

federal.o: From French fédéral, from Latin stem foeder- of foedus (“covenant, league, treaty, alliance”).

favored.o: simple past and past participle of favor. From Middle English favour, favor, faver, from Anglo-Norman favour, from mainland Old French favor, from Latin favor (“good will; kindness; partiality”), from faveō (“to be kind to”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeh₂weh₁yeti (“to be favourable to”), from the root Proto-Indo-European *bʰeh₂- (“to shine, glow light”). Respelled in American English to more closely match its Latin etymon. Compare also Danish favør (“favor”), Irish fabhar (“favor”), from the same Romance source.

base.o:
noun: From Middle English base, bas, baas, from Old French base, from Latin basis, from Ancient Greek βάσις (básis). Doublet of basis and bass.

adj: From Middle English base, bas, from Old French bas, from Late Latin bassus (“low”). Cognate with Spanish bajo, Italian basso and base.

noun: Probably a specific use of Etymology 1, above; perhaps also a development of the plural of bar.

noun: Variant forms.
base.example: Use the globe he inhabits as a base wherewith to measure the magnitude and distance of the sun and planets.
base.exampleSense: A line in a survey which, being accurately determined in length and position, serves as the origin from which to compute the distances and positions of any points or objects connected with it by a system of triangles.

resurrection.o: From Middle English resurreccioun, resurrection, from Anglo-Norman resurrectiun, Old French resurrection (French: résurrection), and their etymon Late Latin resurrēctiōnem (accusative of resurrēctiō) from Latin resurgō (“to rise again”), from re- (“again”), + surgō (“to rise”). By surface analysis, resurrect + -ion. Displaced native Old English ǣrist.
resurrection.example: But the rest of the dead lived not again until the thousand years were finished. This is the first resurrection.

resurrect.o: From Latin resurrēct-, past participial stem of resurgō, after resurrection.
resurrect.example: Why resurrect the idea almost 25 years later?
resurrect.exampleSense: To bring back to view or attention; to reinstate.

inflate.o: From Latin īnflātus, perfect passive participle of īnflō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix). Doublet of inblow.
inflate.example: The balloon will inflate if you blow into it.
inflate.exampleSense: To enlarge by filling with air (or a gas).

inflation.o: From Middle English, borrowed from Old French inflation (“swelling”), from Latin īnflātiō (“expansion", "blowing up”), from īnflātus, the perfect passive participle of īnflō (“blow into, expand”), from in (“into”) + flō (“blow”). By surface analysis, inflate + -ion.
inflation.example: Due to inflation, the monthly gym fee is rising by 10% from January.
inflation.exampleSense: An increase in the general level of prices or in the cost of living.

preview.o: From pre- + view; compare Old French preveü, past participle of preveoir (“to foresee”).

ghost.o: The noun is derived from Middle English gost, from Old English gāst, gǣst (“breath, spirit, soul, ghost”) (compare modern English Holy Ghost), from Proto-West Germanic *gaist, from Proto-Germanic *gaistaz, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰéysdos, from *ǵʰéysd- (“anger, agitation”). The h in the spelling appears in the Prologue to William Caxton’s Royal Book, printed in 1484, in a reference to the “Holy Ghoost”.
