It was likely influenced by Middle Dutch gheest, a common variant of geest. Both Caxton and his assistant Wynkyn de Worde had connections to the Low Countries. Doublet of geist. The adjective and verb are derived from the noun. The verb gained prominence in the 2010s. cognates * Danish gast (“ghost”), gejst (“enthusiasm”) * Dutch geest (“ghost, spirit”) * German Geist (“ghost, spirit”) * Luxembourgish Geescht (“ghost, spirit, spectre, phantom”) * Saterland Frisian Gäist, Jeest (“ghost, spirit”) * Scots gaist, ghaist (“ghost”) * Swedish gast (“ghost”) * Vilamovian gȧjst (“ghost, spirit”) * West Frisian geast (“ghost, spirit”) * Yiddish גײַסט (gayst, “ghost, spirit”) * Yola gaast (“ghost”)
ghost.example: Everyone believed that the ghost of an old lady haunted the crypt.
ghost.exampleSense: The disembodied soul; the soul or spirit of a deceased person; a spirit appearing after death.

casualty.o: From casual, from Middle French casuel, from Medieval Latin casualitas and Late Latin cāsuālis (“happening by chance”), from Latin cāsus (“event”) (English case), from cadere (“to fall”). Originally meaning “a chance event” (compare casual, as in “casual encounter”), it developed a negative meaning as “an unfortunate event”, especially the loss of a person.
casualty.example: Among recent casualties is the S.B.B.'s branch from Nyon to Divonne-les-Bains, just across the French frontier, closed to all traffic at the commencement of the winter service.
casualty.exampleSense: Someone or something adversely affected by a decision, event or situation.

tweet.o: Onomatopoeic of the sound made by a bird. Compare twitter. The social media senses evolved from earlier Twitter update, twit (noun), twitter (verb).
tweet.example: [Ignatz, dropping Officer Pupp's police whistle into the lake:] The fishes will have lots of fun tweeting tweets on it.
tweet.exampleSense: The sound of a bird; any short high-pitched sound or whistle.

stance.o: From Middle English staunce (“place to stand; battle station; position; standing in society; circumstance, situation; stanchion”), from Old French estance (“predicament; situation; sojourn, stay”) (compare modern French stance (“stanza; position one stands in when golfing”)), from Italian stanza (“room, standing place; stanza”), from Vulgar Latin *stantia, from Latin stō (“to stand; to remain, stay”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *steh₂- (“to stand (up)”). The word is cognate with Spanish estante (“shelf”) and a doublet of stanza. The verb is derived from the noun. Compare typologically Czech postoj (“stance (the way of holding a body); stance (point of view)”) (cognate via PIE). Also see position, posture.
stance.example: The fencer’s stance showed he was ready to begin.
stance.exampleSense: The manner, pose, or posture in which one stands.

partisan.o:
noun: From French partisan, from Italian partigiano (“defender of a party”), from parte (“part”). Doublet of partigiano. Attested in English from the late 15th century in the noun sense of "party adherent", and in related adjective senses from the 16th century. The "guerrilla fighter" sense influenced by Serbo-Croatian partizan, Russian партиза́н (partizán), from the same source. The sense of "guerrilla fighter" is from c. 1690. The adjective in the military sense dates from the early 18th century.

noun: From French partizaine, from Middle French partizaine, partisanne etc., from Italian partigiana, related to Etymology 1 above (apparently because it was seen as a typical weapon of such forces).
partisan.example: Salisbury and his attendants were also now drawing near, with bills and partisans brandished, and bows already bended.
partisan.exampleSense: A long-handled spear with a triangular, double-edged blade having lateral projections, in some forms also used in boar hunting.

polarize.o: From French polariser, equivalent to polar + -ize.
polarize.example: To polarize, and indeed, to artificially distinguish between the secular and the religious is to dismiss the inarguable Judeo-Christian foundation of contemporary secular institutions.
polarize.exampleSense: To cause to have a polarization.

multifaceted.example: Joanne was a multifaceted individual; she knew how to bargain both with Wall Street brokers and push-cart vendors.
multifaceted.exampleSense: Having many aspects; nuanced or diverse.

lumber.o: Exact origin unknown. The earliest recorded reference for the noun was to heavy, useless objects such as old, discarded furniture. Perhaps from the verb lumber in reference to meaning "awkward to move"; Online Etymological Dictionary thinks this may derive from the same root as lame. Possibly influenced by Lumbar, an obsolete variant of Lombard, the Italian immigrant class known for being pawnbrokers and money-lenders in early England. Compare English lumpish.
lumber.example: 2002, Russell Allen, "Incantations of the Apprentice", on Symphony X, The Odyssey.
lumber.exampleSense: To move clumsily and heavily; to move slowly.

fracking.o:
noun: From frack (“fracture”) + -ing.

adj: From frack + -ing.
fracking.example: As we said before, will someone please agree on a fracking dual videocard standard?

petroleum.o: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin petroleum. Doublet of petrol.
petroleum.example: Coal and petroleum do not occur hap-hazard in nature, but the aggregate occurrence of each product in any region forms a definite, limited horizon, which, in its continuance, is independent of the bedding plane.
petroleum.exampleSense: A flammable liquid ranging in color from clear to very dark brown and black, consisting mainly of hydrocarbons, occurring naturally in deposits under the Earth's surface.

rebound.o:
noun: From Old French rebondir.

verb: see rebind
rebound.example: I knew for sure if Griffin blocked shots and rebounded the basketball my Ravens would become champions.
rebound.exampleSense: To catch the ball after it has hit the rim or backboard without scoring a basket for the other team.

lag.o: Of unknown origin. Possibly of North Germanic origin.
lag.example: Spun glass mattresses are used for lagging the boiler, which has three Ross pop safety valves on the front ring.
lag.exampleSense: To cover (for example, pipes) with felt strips or similar material.

in conjunction with.example: The new shed, in conjunction with the existing multiple-unit shed, goes far to provide a complete diesel motive power depot at Stratford, [...].

conjunction.o: From Old French conjonction, from Latin coniūnctiō (“joining”), from coniungere (“to join”).
conjunction.example: A comma is placed between short members of compound sentences, connected by and, but, for, nor, or, because, whereas, that expressing purpose (so that, in order that), and other conjunctions.
conjunction.exampleSense: A word used to join other words, phrases, or clauses together into sentences. (The specific conjunction used shows how the two joined parts are related semantically.)

disruption.o: From Latin disruptionem, from disrumpere. By surface analysis, disrupt + -ion.
disruption.example: There was great disruption in the classroom when the teacher left.

freight.o:
noun: From Late Middle English freight, freght, freyght [and other forms], a variant of fraught, fraght (“transport of goods or people, usually by water; transportation fee; transportation facilities; cargo or passengers of a ship; (figuratively) burden; ballast of a ship; goods; a charge”), from Middle Dutch vracht, vrecht, and Middle Low German vrecht (“cargo, freight; transportation fee”), from Old Saxon frāht, frēht, from Proto-West Germanic *fra- (from Proto-Germanic *fra- (prefix meaning ‘completely, fully’)) + *aihti (from Proto-Germanic *aihtiz (“possessions, property”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eyḱ- (“to come into possession of, obtain; to own, possess”)). The English word can be analysed as for- + aught, and is a doublet of fraught. Cognates * French fret (“cargo, freight; transportation fees; rental of a ship”) * Old English ǣht (“livestock; possession, property; power”) * Old High German frēht (“earnings”) * Portuguese frete (“cargo, freight; transportation fees”) * Spanish flete (“cargo, freight; charter (hire of a vehicle for transporting cargo)”) * Swedish frakt c (“cargo, freight; transportation fees”)

verb: The verb is derived from Late Middle English freighten, freghten, a variant of fraughten, fraghten (“to load (a ship with cargo or passengers); to hire (a ship) for transporting goods; to provide fully (with goods, money, etc.); to stow away”), and then either: * from fraught, fraght (noun) (see etymology 1) + -en (suffix forming the infinitive form of verbs); or * from Middle Dutch vrachten, vrechten (“to load (a ship with cargo or passengers); to hire (a ship) for transporting goods, to fraught”), from vracht, vrecht (noun) (see etymology 1) + -en (suffix forming the infinitive form of verbs). The adjective is: * derived from Middle English freght, freight, freyght, the past participle of fraughten (verb) (see above); and/or * a contraction of freighted, the past participle of the verb.
freight.example: The freight shifted and the trailer turned over on the highway.
freight.exampleSense: Goods or items in transport; cargo, luggage.

modal.o:
adj: From Middle French modal, from Medieval Latin modālis (“pertaining to a mode”), from Latin modus (“mode”). Compare to French, Spanish, and Portuguese modal and Italian modale. By surface analysis, mod(e) + -al.

noun: A genericized trademark of Lenzing AG.
modal.example: Modal screen elements are subtrees which, when activated, disable all elements external to them. Examples of modals are yes-no message boxes and the application itself.
modal.exampleSense: A modal window, one that cannot be closed until a decision is made.

intermodal.example: It created inter-city and intermodal services, which were genuinely world leading. And it undeniably pushed British Railways into the modern era.
intermodal.exampleSense: Relating to more than one mode of transport.

generative.o: Inherited from Middle English generatyve. By surface analysis, generate + -ive. Compare French génératif.
generative.example: This ceremony seals the covenant in the flesh of the male generative organ.

vacation.o: Inherited from Middle English vacation, vacacion, vacacioun, from Anglo-Norman vacacioun, from Old French vacacion, vacation, from Latin vacātiō. Equivalent to vacate + -ion.
vacation.example: Spring vacation offers a good opportunity to travel.
vacation.exampleSense: An extended period of time away from work or school.

indigene.o: From Middle French indigène, from Latin indigena.
indigene.example: The price for all this chutzpah was that Malraux then had to take up the cause of the colonial indigenes as if it really mattered to him.

indigent.o: From Middle English indigent, from Old French indigent, from Latin indigēns, present participle of indigeō (“to need”), from indu (“in, within”) + egeō (“to be in need, want”).
indigent.example: The influx of indigents overwhelmed the city's meagre social services and affordable accommodation.
indigent.exampleSense: A person in need, or in poverty.

flattop.o: From flat + top. Sense of “aircraft carrier” attributed to the message, “Scratch one flattop,” radioed during the Battle of the Coral Sea by LCDR Robert E. Dixon to the USS Lexington, whose commanding officer credited the pilot with coining the standard USN slang.

flatten.example: As there was a lot of damage, we chose the heavy roller to flatten the pitch.
flatten.exampleSense: To make something flat or flatter.

flat.o:
adj: (“level piece of ground, flat edge of a weapon”), from the adjective. The algebraic sense was coined by Serre in a 1956 paper, originally as French plat.

noun: From an alteration (due to Scots flatt (“a level part of a structure”)) of Scots flet, flett (“inner part of a house”), from Middle English flet (“dwelling”), from Old English flet, flett (“ground floor, dwelling”), from Proto-West Germanic *flati, from Proto-Germanic *flatją (“floor”), from Proto-Germanic *flataz (“flat”), from Proto-Indo-European *pleth₂- (“flat”). Akin to Old Frisian flet, flette (“dwelling, house”). More at flet, flat₁.

verb: From Middle English flatten, from Old French flatir (“to knock or strike down, dash”), from Frankish *flattjan (“to move the palm of the hand”), from Proto-Germanic *flatjaną (“to make flat, flatten”).
flat.example: The key of E♭ has three flats.
flat.exampleSense: A note played one chromatic semitone lower than a natural, denoted by the symbol ♭ placed after the letter representing the note (e.g., B♭) or in front of the note symbol (e.g. ♭♪).

flattery.o: From Middle English flaterye, flaterie, from Old French flaterie, from the verb flater (“to flatter”). By surface analysis, flatter + -y (forming abstract nouns).
flattery.example: Don't you know that some of his contributions here are pure flattery?
flattery.exampleSense: Excessive praise or approval, which is often insincere and sometimes contrived to win favour.

pull over.example: Can you pull over just after the post office? My house is next door.
pull over.exampleSense: To come to a stop, and turn off the road (i.e. onto the roadside or hard shoulder).

selfie.o: From self + -ie. Attested since 2002, originally Australian English.
selfie.example: I shall take this photograph myself. This must be what they call a selfie.
selfie.exampleSense: A photographic self-portrait, especially one taken manually (not using a timer, tripod etc.) with a small camera or mobile phone.

fairyland.example: The children built a fairyland cottage out of gingerbread, decorated with gumdrops and peppermint sticks.
fairyland.exampleSense: Having qualities ascribed to fairies and their realm; fanciful, delicate, surreal, or diminutive.

capitalistic.o: From capitalist + -ic, probably after German kapitalistisch. Derived from Proto-Indo-European *káput (“head”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kap-.
capitalistic.example: This gloomy view of the capitalistic production system envisioned ceaseless warfare among the major powers.
capitalistic.exampleSense: Of or pertaining to capitalism or to capitalists.

clutch.o:
verb: From Middle English clucchen, clicchen, cluchen, clechen, cleken, from Old English clyċċan (“to clutch, clench”), from Proto-West Germanic *klukkjan, from Proto-Germanic *klukjaną, from Proto-Germanic *klu- (“to ball up, conglomerate, amass”), from Proto-Indo-European *glew- (“to ball up; lump, mass”). Cognate with Swedish klyka (“clamp, fork, branch”). The noun is from Middle English cleche, cloche, cloke ("claw, talon, hand"; compare Scots cleuk, cluke, cluik (“claw, talon”)), of uncertain origin, with the form probably assimilated to the verb. Alternative etymology derives Old English clyċċan from Proto-Germanic *klēk- (“claw, hand”), from Proto-Indo-European *glēk-, *ǵlēḱ- (“claw, hand; to clutch, snatch”). If so, then cognate with Irish glac (“hand”).

noun: Variant form of cletch, from Middle English cleken (“to hatch”), perhaps from Old Norse klekja (“to hatch”).
clutch.example: He is the player who has come through so often in the clutch during his days at Camarillo.

fusion.o: First appears c. 1555, in a translation by Richard Eden. From Middle French fusion, from Latin fūsiōnem (the accusative of fūsiō), from fusus, past participle of fundō (“to pour; to melt”) (see also found). Doublet of foison.
fusion.example: Below the temperature of fusion of the solid phase, the growth rate of the solid/ liquid interface at low undercooling is affected mainly by undercooling.
fusion.exampleSense: The act of merging separate things, or the result thereof. The act of melting or liquefying something by heating it.

refuse.o:
adj: Borrowed into late Middle English from Middle French refusé, past participle of refuser (“to refuse”). Displaced native Middle English wernen (“to refuse”) likely due to the similar sounding Middle English warnen

verb: From Middle English refusen, from Old French refuser, from Vulgar Latin *refūsāre, a blend of Classical Latin refūtāre (whence also refute) and recūsāre (whence also recuse).

verb: From re- + fuse.
refuse.example: I asked the star if I could have her autograph, but she refused.
refuse.exampleSense: To decline a request or demand, forbear; to withhold permission.

infusion.o: From Middle English infusioun, from Old French infusion, from Latin infusio, infusionem (“a pouring into, a wetting, a dyeing, a flow”), from infundo.
infusion.example: An extract of rooibos and chamomile makes a refreshing infusion.
infusion.exampleSense: A product consisting of a liquid which has had other ingredients steeped in it to extract useful qualities.

photon.o: From photo- + -on. Coined by American physicist Leonard Troland in 1916 as a unit of light hitting the retina, and later popularized in a more modern sense by Gilbert N. Lewis, with the term gaining acceptance in the physics community by the late 1920s.
photon.example: The single-imaging optic of the mammalian eye offers some distinct visual advantages. Such lenses can take in photons from a wide range of angles, increasing light sensitivity. They also have high spatial resolution, resolving incoming images in minute detail.
photon.exampleSense: The quantum of light and other electromagnetic energy, regarded as a discrete particle having zero rest mass, no electric charge, and an indefinitely long lifetime. It is a gauge boson.

photogenic.example: The company hired the spokesperson for his photogenic face.

caprice.o: Borrowed from French caprice, from Italian capriccio, from caporiccio (“fright, sudden start”). Doublet of capriccio.
caprice.example: The only difference between a caprice and a life-long passion is that a caprice lasts a little longer.

capsize.o: Attested since 1788. Origin unknown. Possibly related to Spanish chapuzar (“to sink by the head”).
capsize.example: But what if carrying sail capsize the boat?

impudent.o: From Middle English impudent, originally meaning immodest, shameless, from Latin impudēns (“shameless”), ultimately from in- + pudere (“to feel shame”).
impudent.example: The impudent children would not stop talking in class.
impudent.exampleSense: Not showing due respect; bold-faced, impertinent.

pudendum.o: From Latin pudenda (“that whereof one ought to feel shame”), substantive use of the neuter plural gerundive of pudet (“it shames”); in Latin the usage in the plural form (to mean external genitalia), was far more common than the singular form, as is also the case in English.

troupe.o: Attested 1825; Unadapted borrowing from French troupe, which see for more. Doublet of troop, and possibly also of thorp and dorp.

niggle.o: First attested in 1599. Origin uncertain, but likely borrowed from dialectal Norwegian nigla (“to be stingy, to busy oneself with trifles”), ultimately from Old Norse hnøggr (“stingy; miserly”), related to Old English hnēaw (“stingy; niggardly”). More at niggard.
niggle.example: I can see him now with his one eye closed as he came niggling along, and didn't he just give me a grandfather's blessing!

embezzle.o: From Middle English embesilen, from Anglo-Norman embesiler, embesillier, embeseillier (“to steal, cause to disappear”), from em- + Old French besillier (“to torment, destroy, gouge”), of unknown origin.
embezzle.example: You let Dunsey have it, sir? And how long have you been so thick with Dunsey that you must collogue with him to embezzle my money?
embezzle.exampleSense: To steal or misappropriate money that one has been trusted with, especially to steal money from the organisation for which one works.

poultry.o: From Middle English pultrie, from Old French pouleterie, from poulet, diminutive of poule (“hen”), from Latin pullus (“chick”). By surface analysis, poult + -ry. For the development of Middle English /u/ to modern /oʊ/, /əʊ/ before /lt/, /ld/, /ln/, compare boult, boulder, colter/coulter, poultice, shoulder, won't.

intentional.o: Borrowed from Medieval Latin intentiōnālis. By surface analysis, intention + -al.
intentional.example: It should, however, be borne in mind that even in the cohortative proper, the -ah does not add to the simple imperfect the ‘intentional’ signification expressed by that mood: the signification is already there, and the new termination merely renders it more prominent.
intentional.exampleSense: Reflecting intention; marking an expenditure of will in the shape of a matter.

tropic.o: From Late Latin tropicus (“of or pertaining to the solstice, as a noun, one of the tropics”), from Ancient Greek τροπικός (tropikós, “of or pertaining to a turn or change; or the solstice; or a trope or figure; tropic; tropical; etc.”), from τροπή (tropḗ, “turn; solstice; trope”).
tropic.example: The binding of oxygen to hemoglobin is allosterically regulated by various tropic factors, such as BPG and acidity.
tropic.exampleSense: Having the quality of indirectly inducing a biological or chemical change in a system or substrate.

fain.o:
adj: From Middle English fain (“enjoyable, pleasing; fond of; glad, pleased; good, suitable; happy, joyful”), from Old English fægen (“happy, joyful, fain”), from Proto-West Germanic *fagan (“glad”), from Proto-Germanic *faganaz (“glad”), from Proto-Indo-European *peḱ- (“joyful; pretty”). Cognates * Old Norse fagna (“to rejoice”), feginn (“glad, joyful”) * Gothic 𐍆𐌰𐌲𐌹𐌽𐍉𐌽 (faginōn, “to rejoice”) * Old High German fehan, gifehan (“to rejoice”) * Old Saxon fagan, fagin

adv: From Middle English fain (“eagerly, willingly; gladly, joyfully”), from fain (adjective): see etymology

verb: From Middle English fainen (“to be glad or joyful, rejoice; to make happy, gladden; to welcome; of an animal: to show happiness, as by wagging the tail; to act fawningly or flatteringly”), from Old English fæġnian (“to be glad, rejoice; to celebrate; to be delighted with, applaud; to wish for”), from Proto-West Germanic *faginōn (“to be glad, rejoice; to make glad, gladden”), from Proto-Germanic *faginōną (“to be glad, rejoice”), from *faganaz (“glad”): see further at etymology
fain.example: Man and Birds are fayne of climbing high.
fain.exampleSense: Chiefly followed by to, or (obsolete) for or of: eager or willing, or inclined.

crystal clear.o: From Middle English cristal cleer. Emphatic form of clear in visual and metaphorical “understandable” senses. Compare clear as a bell (“very clear (of sound)”).
crystal clear.example: Reread through the manual until the instructions are crystal clear in your head.
crystal clear.exampleSense: Completely clear (in various senses). Without ambiguity or doubt; completely understood.

coil.o:
noun: From Middle English coilen, from Old French coillir, cuillir (“to gather, pluck, pick, cull”) (modern French cueillir), from Latin colligō (“to gather together”), past participle collectus, from com- (“together”) + legō (“to gather”); compare legend. Doublet of cull.

noun: Unknown.
coil.example: The wild grapevines that twisted their coils or tendrils from tree to tree.
coil.exampleSense: Something wound in the form of a helix or spiral.

skein.o:
noun: The noun is derived from Middle English skaine, skayne (“quantity of string, thread, etc., wound on a reel; the string, thread, etc., so wound”), from Old French escaigne (modern French écagne, écaigne (Picardy)); further etymology uncertain, probably from Proto-Celtic, from Proto-Indo-European *skend- (“to split off”). The verb is derived from noun. cognates * Irish scáinne (“skein, clew”)

noun: From Dutch scheen (“strip of metal or wood; (anatomy) shin”), from Middle Dutch schene, from Old Dutch *skina, from Proto-West Germanic *skinu (“bar; track; (anatomy) shin; spine”), from Proto-Germanic *skinō (“piece; plate; rim; (anatomy) shinbone”), probably from Proto-Indo-European *skey- (“to dissect; to split”). Doublet of shin.
skein.example: “How horribly unjust of you!” cried Lord Henry, tilting his hat back and looking up at the little clouds that, like ravelled skeins of glossy white silk, were drifting across the hollowed turquoise of the summer sky.
skein.exampleSense: A quantity of yarn, thread, etc. put up together in an oblong shape, after it is taken from the reel. A skein of cotton yarn is formed by eighty turns of the thread around a fifty-four inch reel.

yawnsome.example: This yawnsome tract is possibly the most over-rated play of all time.
yawnsome.exampleSense: Characterised or marked by yawning; boring; dull.

yarn.o: From Middle English yern, yarn, from the Old English ġearn (“yarn, spun wool”), from Proto-West Germanic *garn, from Proto-Germanic *garną (“yarn”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰorn-, *ǵʰerH- (“tharm, guts, intestines”). Cognates Akin to West Frisian jern, Dutch garen (“yarn”), German Garn (“yarn”), Danish garn, Swedish garn (“yarn, thread”), Icelandic garn (“yarn”), Latin hernia (“rupture”), Ancient Greek χορδή (khordḗ, “string”), Sanskrit हिर (hira, “band”). Compare also the obsolete doublet garn.
yarn.example: Statistically, this person is also likely to be male and well off, but more essentially this person wants to be educated, to be obsessed, wants more than just a good yarn.
yarn.exampleSense: A story, a tale, especially one that is incredible.

oversubscribe.example: The operator says its apprenticeship scheme is always oversubscribed, with more and more roles offered every year.
oversubscribe.exampleSense: To subscribe to an extent that is greater than the availability.

fortnight.o: From Middle English fourtenyght, fourtene nyght, from Old English fēowertīene niht (literally “fourteen nights"; the Anglo-Saxons counted by nights), equivalent to fourteen + night. Compare sennight.
fortnight.example: On being kicked the girl fell desperately in love with Henri, and for a fortnight they lived together and spent a thousand francs of Henri's money.

firefight.example: His goal: a patch of high ground called Sperwan Ghar, where he and his men firefought a thousand Taliban to take the hill and call in the air strikes critical to turning the tide.

foresight.o: From Middle English forsight, forsyght, forsichte (since 14th c.), a calque of Latin providentia. By surface analysis, fore- + sight. Compare Scots foresicht, Saterland Frisian Foarsicht, archaic Dutch voorzicht (now voorzichtigheid), German Vorsicht (all “caution, foresight”).
foresight.example: Having the foresight to prepare an evacuation plan may have saved their lives.
foresight.exampleSense: The ability to foresee or prepare wisely for the future.

reckon.o: From Middle English rekenen, from Old English recenian (“to pay; arrange, dispose, reckon”) and ġerecenian (“to explain, recount, relate”); both from Proto-West Germanic *rekanōn (“to count, explain”), from Proto-West Germanic *rekan (“swift, ready, prompt”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃reǵ- (“to make straight or right”). Cognate with Scots rekkin (“to enumerate, mention, narrate, rehearse, count, calculate, compute”), Saterland Frisian reekenje (“to calculate, figure, reckon”), West Frisian rekkenje (“to account, tally, calculate, figure”), Dutch rekenen (“to count, calculate, reckon, charge”), German Low German reken (“to reckon”), German rechnen (“to count, reckon, calculate”), Danish regne (“to calculate”), Swedish räkna (“to count, calculate, reckon”), Norwegian Nynorsk rekna (“to calculate”), Icelandic reikna (“to calculate”), Latin rectus (“straight, right”). See also reck, reach.
reckon.example: I reckoned above two hundred and fifty on the outside of the church.
reckon.exampleSense: To count; to enumerate; to number; also, to compute; to calculate.

reck.o: From Middle English recken, rekken, reken, from Old Norse rœkja (compare Old English rēċċan, rēċan (“to care, reck, take care of, be interested in, care for, desire”); whence English retch), from Proto-Germanic *rōkijaną (“to care, take care”), from Proto-Indo-European *rēǵ-, *rēg- (“to care, help”). Cognate with obsolete Dutch roeken, Low German roken, ruken (“to reck, care”), German geruhen (“to deign, condescend”), Icelandic rækja (“to care, regard, discharge”), Danish røgte (“to care, tend”), Swedish rykta (“to groom”). See reckon.
reck.example: Little thou reck'st of this sad store!
reck.exampleSense: To take account of (someone or something); to care for; to consider, to heed, to regard.

recklessness.o: From Middle English reklesnes, reklesnesse, rekelesnesse (also assibilated as rechelesnes, reccheleesnesse), from Old English rēcelēasnes (“recklessness, carelessness, negligence”), equivalent to reckless + -ness.
recklessness.example: His recklessness repeatedly put him in danger.
recklessness.exampleSense: The state or quality of being reckless or heedless, of taking unnecessary risks.

reckless.o: From Middle English rekles, reckeles, rekkeles, (also recheles), from Old English rēcelēas (“reckless, careless, negligent”), equivalent to reck + -less. Cognate with West Frisian roekeleas (“reckless”), Dutch roekeloos (“reckless”), German Low German ruuklos (“careless”), German ruchlos (“careless, notorious”).
reckless.example: Escalation is the film’s nuclear energy source. It’s there, of course, in the downright lunatic stunts performed by [Tom] Cruise, again defying good sense and his own advancing years to top his previous feats of reckless self-endangerment.
reckless.exampleSense: Indifferent or oblivious to danger or the consequences thereof.

predictable.example: Despite the predictable squalling on some of the Twilight fanblogs, the two leads are impeccably cast.

rollout.example: The pilot kept a vigilant eye out for runway obstructions throughout the rollout.
rollout.exampleSense: The phase of a landing after touchdown but before the aircraft slows to taxi speed.

call upon.o: Alternative form of call. From Middle English callen, from Old English ċeallian (“to call, shout”) and Old Norse kalla (“to call; shout; refer to as; name”); both from Proto-Germanic *kalzōną (“to call, shout”), from Proto-Indo-European *golH-so- (“voice, cry”), from *gel(H)- (“to vocalize, call, shout”). Cognates * Scots call, caw, ca (“to call, cry, shout”) * Dutch kallen (“to chat, talk”) * German Low German kallen (“to speak, talk”) * German kallen (“to call”) * Swedish kalla (“to call, refer to, beckon”) * Norwegian kalle (“to call, name”) * Danish kalde (“to call, name”) * Icelandic kalla (“to call, shout, name”) * Welsh galw (“to call, demand”) * Polish głos (“voice”) * Lithuanian gal̃sas (“echo”) * Russian голос (golos, “voice”) * Albanian gjuhë (“language, tongue”).

eye-popping.o: The image is of a viewer's eyes opening wide to the point of popping out.
eye-popping.example: And most eye-popping of all, Rep. Matt Gaetz – a political bomb-thrower who has faced federal and congressional investigations into alleged unsavory personal conduct – is now President-elect Trump’s nominee for U.S. attorney general.

what if.o: Dates back at least to Old English hwæt ġif, of the same meaning. A similar expression occurs in Latin in the Vulgate, Acts 23:9, "Factus est autem clamor magnus. Et surgentes quidam pharisaeorum, pugnabant, decentes: Nihil mali inveniumus in homine isto: quid si Spiritus locutus est ei, aut angelus?" ("And there arose a great cry. And some of the Pharisees rising up, strove, saying: We find no evil in this man. What if a spirit hath spoken to him, or an angel?" Douay-Rheims translation)
what if.example: What if we could learn to get along? What would happen then?
what if.exampleSense: Used to introduce a speculation about a future event.

what-if.example: Each man was running over the what ifs in his mind.
what-if.exampleSense: A speculation as to what might have happened if something else had happened earlier.

invite.o:
verb: From Middle French inviter, from Latin invītō. Displaced native English lathe

noun: From the verb invite.
invite.example: We invited our friends round for dinner.
invite.exampleSense: To ask for the presence or participation of someone or something.

invitation.o: From Middle English invitacioun, ynvytacioun, from Latin invītātio, reinforced by Middle French invitation. By surface analysis, invite + -ation. Displaced native Middle English lathinge from Old English laþung (see dialectal English lathing).
invitation.example: We need to print off fifty invitations for the party.
invitation.exampleSense: A document or verbal message conveying an invitation.

napery.o: From Middle English naperie, from Anglo-Norman naperie, Middle French naperie, from Old French nape + -erie.
napery.example: She led the way through a wide hall into a charming room, where a table was already spread in its dainty napery and silver.

bell.o:
noun: Inherited from Middle English belle, from Old English belle, from Proto-West Germanic *bellā, from Proto-Germanic *bellǭ, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰel-. Cognate with West Frisian belle, bel (“bell”), Dutch bel (“bell”), Low German Belle, Bel (“bell”), Danish bjælde (“bell”), Faroese bjølla (“bell”), Icelandic bjalla (“bell”), Norwegian bjelle (“bell”), Swedish bjällra (“bell”).

verb: From Middle English bellen, from Old English bellan (“to bellow; make a hollow noise; roar; bark; grunt”), from Proto-Germanic *bellaną (“to sound; roar; bark”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰel- (“to sound; roar; bark”). Cognate with Scots bell (“to shout; speak loudly”), Dutch bellen (“to ring”), German Low German bellen (“to ring”), German bellen (“to bark”), Swedish böla (“to low; bellow; roar”).
bell.example: In a cowslip's bell I lie.
bell.exampleSense: Anything shaped like a bell, such as the cup or corolla of a flower.

thrifty.o: From Middle English thrifty, threfty, thryfty, þrifti, equivalent to thrift + -y.
thrifty.example: But, Gentlemen, the gallant Admiral has told you he has two loves; and he seems to have made a prudent choice, and been a very thrifty wooer.
thrifty.exampleSense: Thriving, prosperous, successful; (of an animal or plant) growing rapidly or vigorously.

frugal.o: From Middle French, from Latin frugalis (“virtuous, thrifty”). Displaced native Old English spærhende (literally “spare-handed”).

frugality.o: Borrowed from Middle French frugalité. By surface analysis, frugal + -ity.
frugality.example: With the frugality that hard graft begets, his mate limited both his and her own tobacco, so he must not smoke all afternoon.
frugality.exampleSense: The quality of being frugal; prudent economy; thrift.

thrift.o: From Middle English thrift, thryfte, þrift, from Old Norse þrift (“thriving condition, prosperity”). Equivalent to thrive + -t.
thrift.example: His thrift can be seen in how little the trashman takes from his house.
thrift.exampleSense: The characteristic of using a minimum of something (especially money).

superstitious.o: From Old French superstitieux, from Latin superstitiōsus, from superstitio + -ōsus.

cultus.o: From Latin cultus (“cultivation, culture”). See cult.
cultus.example: Among the rituals which members of their family had inaugurated in other states of Greece, was a peculiar cultus of Hermes (Mercury) at Stymphalus in Arcadia.
cultus.exampleSense: Established or accepted religious rites or customs of worship; state of religious development.

superstition.o: From Middle French superstition, from Latin superstitio (“superstition”), from superstāre (“to stand above, to stand upon, to survive”) + -tiō (“-tion: forming nouns”), from super- (“above, over, upon”) + stāre (“to stand”).

exclusivity.example: The exclusivity period of a product on the market can also be extended through nonpatent exclusivities.

solid.o:
adj: From Middle English solide, borrowed from Old French solide, from Latin solidus (“solid”), from Proto-Indo-European *solh₂-i-dʰ-o-s (“entire”), suffixed form of root *solh₂- (“integrate, whole”). Doublet of sol, sold, soldo, solidus, sou, and xu.

noun: From Middle English solid, from the adjective, Middle French solide, or Latin solidum. Doublet of solidum.
solid.example: Radiohead's on tour! Have you heard their latest album yet? It's quite solid.
solid.exampleSense: Excellent, of high quality, or reliable.

drag.o:
noun: From Middle English draggen (“to drag”), early Middle English dragen (“to draw, carry”), confluence of Old English dragan (“to drag, draw, draw oneself, go, protract”) and Old Norse draga (“to draw, attract”); both from Proto-Germanic *draganą (“to draw, drag”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰregʰ- (“to draw, drag”). Verb sense influenced due to association with the noun drag (“that which is hauled or dragged”), related to Low German dragge (“a drag-anchor, grapnel”). Cognate with Danish drægge (“to dredge”), Danish drage (“to draw, attract”), Swedish dragga (“to drag, drag anchor, sweep”), Swedish draga (“to draw, go”), Icelandic draga (“to drag, pull”). Doublet of draw.

noun: Possibly from English drag (“to pull along a surface”) because of the sensation of long skirts trailing on the floor, or from Yiddish טראָגן (trogn, “to wear”)
drag.example: When designing cars, manufacturers have to take drag into consideration.
drag.exampleSense: Resistance of a fluid to something moving through it.

adore.o: From Middle English *adoren, aouren, from Old French adorer, aorer, from Latin adōrō (“to pray to”), from ad (“to”) + ōrō (“to speak”).
adore.example: The great mass of the population abhorred Popery and adored Monmouth.
adore.exampleSense: To love with one's entire heart and soul; regard with deep respect and affection.

admire.o: From Middle English admyren, borrowed from Middle French admirer, from Latin admīror, from ad + mīror (“wonder at”).
admire.example: He had always admired the work ethos and family values of his friend.
admire.exampleSense: To estimate or value highly; to hold in high esteem.

cape.o:
noun: From Middle English cape, gappe, cap, from Old French cap (“cape, headland”), from Latin caput (“head”). Doublet of capo, caput, chef, and chief, and distantly with head and Howth. For sense development, compare English ness (“a promontory point, cape”) from a root related to nose, Bulgarian нос (nos) (the same PIE root). Also compare coast (<< Latin costa).

noun: From French cape, from Old Occitan capa, from Late Latin cappa (“cape”). The second sense ("superhero") is metonymic from the fact that many superheroes wear capes. Likewise, the verb sense "defend, praise" alludes to the stereotypical depiction of superheroes wearing capes when they come to people's defense. (Compare caped crusader.) Doublet of capa and cappa.
cape.example: The white fur that caped his neck and shoulders stood on end.
cape.exampleSense: To cover (as) with or like a cape.

emoji.o: Borrowed from Japanese 絵文字(えもじ) (emoji), from 絵(え) (e, “picture”) + 文字(もじ) (moji, “character”). False cognate of English emotion and emoticon.
emoji.example: Apple wants to introduce new emojis to better represent people with disabilities. A guide dog, a wheelchair user and prosthetic limbs are just some of the symbols it's suggested.
emoji.exampleSense: A digital graphic icon with a unique code point used to represent a concept, object, person, animal or place, originally used in Japanese text messaging but since adopted internationally in other contexts such as social media. Or, by extension, any non-standard emoji-like image inserted inline in text, i.e. an image emoticon.

frosty.o: From Middle English frosty, forsty, from Old English forstiġ, fyrstiġ (“frosty”), from Proto-West Germanic *frostag, *frustīg, By surface analysis, frost + -y. Cognates Cognate with West Frisian froastich (“frosty”), Dutch vorstig (“frosty”), German Low German fröstig (“frosty”), German frostig (“frosty”), Swedish frostig (“frosty”). Compare also Saterland Frisian froasterch (“frosty”), German Low German frösterg (“frosty”).
frosty.example: The frosty beverage gave him a brain freeze.
frosty.exampleSense: Having frost on it or in it.

regression.o: Learned borrowing from Latin regressio. Equivalent to regress + -ion. The statistics sense comes from regression to the mean.
regression.example: Few of these groups or communities that are classed as "savage" show no traces of regression from a more advanced cultural stage.
regression.exampleSense: An action of regressing, a return to a previous state.

megapixel.example: This camera has a resolution of three megapixels.
megapixel.exampleSense: One million pixels, used as a unit of resolution of digital cameras.

sky-blue.o: Alternative form of sky. The noun is derived from Middle English sky (“sky; cloud; mist”), also spelled ski, skie, [and other forms], from Old Norse ský (“cloud”), from Proto-Germanic *skiwją (“cloud; sky”), from *skiwô (“cloud; cloud cover, haze; sky”) (whence Old English sċēo (“cloud”) and Middle English skew (“air; sky; (rare) cloud”)), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kewH- (“to cover; to conceal, hide”). Partly displaced Old English heofon, which survives in the reflex heaven, still sometimes used in the sense of sky, but usually in high or poetic register. The verb is derived from the noun. Cognates The English word is cognate with Old English scēo (“cloud”), Old Saxon scio, skio, skeo (“light cloud cover”), Danish, Swedish and Norwegian Bokmål sky (“cloud”), Old Irish ceo (“mist, fog”), Irish ceo (“mist, fog”). It is also related to Old English scūa (“shadow, darkness”), Latin obscūrus (“dark, shadowy”), Sanskrit स्कुनाति (skunāti, “he covers”). See also hide, hose, house, hut, shoe.
sky-blue.example: Except for an eye-catching sky-blue container boldly and attractively featuring the B.T.C.'s "door-to-door" arrow symbol [...], there were no outlandish colour schemes or lettering styles.

aggregation.example: The difference between an association and an aggregation is entirely conceptual and is focused strictly on semantics.
aggregation.exampleSense: Kind of object composition which does not imply ownership.

quadrant.o:
noun: Inherited from Middle English quadrant, from Old French cadran, quadrant and its etymon Latin quadrāns, -antis (“fourth part of something, quarter”). Doublet of quadrans.

noun: Inherited from Middle English quadrant, quadrante, from Latin quadrātum; form influenced by Etymology
quadrant.example: There is an outcourt or quadrant, whereof one side is a gallery to walk in, being in length six hundred feet.

cove.o:
noun: From Middle English cove, from Old English cofa (“chamber; den”), from Proto-West Germanic *kobō, from Proto-Germanic *kubô. Cognate with Dutch koof (“cove”), German Low German Koov (“small room”), German Koben (“nook, shed”), Icelandic kofi (“hut, shack”). This word has probably survived as long as it has due to its coincidental phonetic resemblance to the unrelated word English cave. Also unrelated to Spanish cueva, which itself is a cognate of cave.

noun: Attested in Britain a. 1570, from Romani kodo (“this one, him”, pronounced KOTHO /koðo/, ultimately undergoing th-fronting to KOV /kov/ in English), or perhaps directly from Romani kova (“that person”).

verb: Borrowed from French couver, from Old French cover (“to hatch (eggs)”), from Latin cubāre (“to lie down, recline; to incubate; to be broody”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ḱewb- (“to lie down”). Cognates * Italian covare
cove.example: There are several excellent snorkelling spots in the shallow coves around Chimei, and one-day tours (NT$1100 to NT$1300, including transport and food) can be arranged beforehand by your hotel or home-stay.
cove.exampleSense: A small coastal inlet, especially one having high cliffs protecting vessels from prevailing winds; bight.

zen.o: From Zen. In more general use, popularized by Eugen Herrigel's 1948 Zen in the Art of Archery and Robert M. Pirsig's 1974 Zen and the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance.
zen.example: Greggs: You hung over? Just sayin', you look like shit.
zen.exampleSense: Alternative letter-case form of Zen: of or related to Zen Buddhism, particularly its focus on indirect teaching of wisdom through riddles and stories.

naive.o: Borrowed from French naïve, feminine form of naïf, from Latin nātīvus (“native, natural”). Doublet of native.
naive.example: The salarians believed the genophage would be used as a deterrent, a position the turians viewed as naive. Once the project was complete, the turians mass produced and deployed it. The krogan homeworld, their colonies, and all occupied worlds were infected.
naive.exampleSense: Lacking worldly experience, wisdom, or judgement; unsophisticated.

courier.o: From a convergence of Middle English corour, currour, from Old French coreor, agent noun of corir (“to run”), and Middle English courier, a borrowing of Middle French courrier, from Italian corriere.
courier.example: You can always find musicians. There are more trackers than coders, pixelers, organizers, couriers, and designers combined.
courier.exampleSense: A user who earns access to a topsite by uploading warez.

shipment.example: Shipment of hazardous waste on this route is strictly prohibited.

analytical.o: Compare with French analytique. See analysis.

ecliptic.o:
noun: Borrowed from Latin eclīptica. So named because an eclipse can occur only when the Moon lies on this plane.

adj: From Middle English ecliptik, from Latin eclīpticus.

lineate.o:
verb: First attested in 1558; borrowed from Medieval Latin līneātus, perfect passive participle of līneō (“to draw a line; (classically) to reduce to a straight line, make straight”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from līnea (“a line”).

adj: First attested in 1643; borrowed from Latin delineātus, participial adjective, see Etymology 1 and -ate (adjective-forming suffix) for more.

liberality.o: From Middle English liberalite, from Old French liberalité, from Latin līberālitās (“a noble, kind, or friendly disposition; generosity”), equivalent to liberal + -ity.
liberality.example: She preferred that Lord Rotheles's liberality should take a purely personal direction. Whatever decorations might be lavished upon her dressing-room, the dowager would have to leave them behind her; not so those which filled the prodigality of red morocco cases on her toilette.
liberality.exampleSense: The property of being liberal; generosity; charity.

lineation.example: Lineation is very much a matter of syntax, organizing the poem's grammar across its lines in ways significant and central to the poem's meaning.
lineation.exampleSense: The way in which line breaks are inserted in a poem

subscriber.example: Our magazine has over ten thousand subscribers.
subscriber.exampleSense: A person who subscribes to a publication or a service.

inbound.example: Smith inbounds the ball to Johnson.
inbound.exampleSense: To pass a ball inbounds; to throw the ball in.

encourage.o: From Middle English encouragen, encoragen, from Anglo-Norman encoragier, from Old French encoragier. Displaced native Old English hiertan, tyhtan, and trymman. By surface analysis, en- + courage.
encourage.example: Delia's coach encouraged her to focus on the positives.
encourage.exampleSense: To mentally support; to motivate, give courage, hope or spirit.

encouraging.o: present participle and gerund of encourage. From Middle English encouragen, encoragen, from Anglo-Norman encoragier, from Old French encoragier. Displaced native Old English hiertan, tyhtan, and trymman. By surface analysis, en- + courage.
encouraging.example: Although there is no cure for the disease yet, the research results are encouraging.
encouraging.exampleSense: Giving courage, confidence or hope; auspicious.

pay off.example: I had to pay off the judge to get my license back.
pay off.exampleSense: To bribe, especially to deter oversight.

teem.o:
verb: From Middle English temen (“to bear, to support”), from Anglian Old English tēman (“to give birth”) (West Saxon Old English tīeman), from Proto-West Germanic *taumijan (“to bridle”), from Proto-Germanic *taumijaną, from *taumaz ("bridle", continued in Modern English as team).

verb: From Middle English temen (“to drain”), from Old Norse tœma, from Proto-Germanic *tōmijaną (“to empty, make empty”). Related to English toom (“empty, vacant”). More at toom.

verb: From Middle English temen (“to be suitable, befit”), from Old English *teman, from Proto-Germanic *temaną (“to fit”). Cognate with Low German temen, tamen (“to befit”), Dutch betamen (“to befit”), German ziemen. See also tame (adjective) and compare beteem.
teem.example: “Are you sure they’re good lodgings?” she asked.

serpentine.o: From Middle English serpentine, from Old French serpentin, from Latin serpentīnus, from serpēns (“serpent”), equivalent to serpent + -ine.
serpentine.example: There are serpentine species of lizards which do not have legs.
serpentine.exampleSense: Having the form or shape of a snake.

barrow.o:
noun: From Middle English berwe, bergh, from Old English beorg (“mountain, hill, mound, barrow, burial place”), from Proto-West Germanic *berg, from Proto-Germanic *bergaz (“hill, mountain”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰérǵʰos (“hill”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰerǵʰ- (“to rise up, ascend; to be elevated, up high”). Doublet of berg and bergh. Cognates Cognate with Scots burrow (“mound, tumulus, barrow”), North Frisian Bārig, beerch, beeri, beerj, berag, berig, berri, bärj (“mountain”), Saterland Frisian Bierich, Bíerig, Bäirch (“mountain”), West Frisian berch (“mountain”), Cimbrian pèrge (“mountain”), Dutch berg (“mountain”), German Berg (“mountain”), German Low German Barg (“mountain”), Limburgish berg, Bärrech (“hill, mountain”), Luxembourgish Bierg (“mountain”), Mòcheno pèrg (“mountain”), Yiddish באַרג (barg, “mountain”), Danish bjerg (“mountain”), Elfdalian bjärr (“hill, mountain”), Faroese berg, bjarg (“cliff”), bjørg (“cliffs”), Icelandic, Norwegian Bokmål, Norwegian Nynorsk, and Swedish berg (“mountain”); also Northern Luri برگ (berg, “mountain”), Polish brzeg (“bank, shore”), Russian бе́рег (béreg, “bank, shore”).

noun: From Middle English barowe, barwe, barewe, from Old English bearwe (“basket, handbarrow”), from Proto-West Germanic *barwā, *barwijā, from Proto-Germanic *barwǭ, *barwijǭ (“stretcher, bier”) (compare Low German Berwe, Old Norse barar (plural), Middle High German radebere (“wheelbarrow”)), from *beraną (“to bear”). More at bear.

noun: From Middle English barow, bareȝ, bareh, from Old English bearg, bearh (“boar”), from Proto-West Germanic *barug, *barah, from Proto-Germanic *barugaz, *barahaz. Cognate with Old Frisian barch, Old Saxon barug, Old High German barug (German Borg), Old Norse bǫrgr.

noun: From Middle English *berwe, *borwe, *bergh (attested in hamberwe and berwham (“horse-collar”)), from Middle English berwen (“to protect”), from Old English beorgan (“to protect”).

barrow boy.o: From barrow + boy. First use appears c. 1939. See cite below. The slang usage dates from the 1980s.
barrow boy.example: The "barrow boy" commodities trader may well have no aspirations to old-style middle class tastes.
barrow boy.exampleSense: A financial industry worker from a working class or lower middle class family background.

sardine.o:
noun: Borrowed from French sardine (cognate with Spanish sardina, Italian sardina), Latin sardīna; from Ancient Greek σαρδίνη (sardínē).

noun: Pliny states that its name was ultimately derived from Sardis, in Lydia, where the sard was first discovered; but probably ultimately derived from Persian sered ("yellowish-red").
sardine.example: No one on Monhegan says they saw them, but a man sardining says he saw it headed there, or at least some boat with people atop it.

swamp.o: Early attestations (starting in 1624) are from North America, but the term was probably in local use in Britain earlier. The etymology is not entirely certain; it is probably a fusion of Middle English swam (“swamp, muddy pool, bog, marsh”, also “fungus, mushroom”) — from Old English swamm (“mushroom, fungus, sponge”), from Proto-West Germanic *swamm, from Proto-Germanic *swambaz, *swammaz — and Middle English sompe (“marsh, morass”), from either Middle Dutch somp, sump (“marsh, swamp”) or Middle Low German sump (“marsh, swamp”) (from Old Saxon *sump (“swamp, marsh”)), both from Proto-West Germanic *sump, from Proto-Germanic *sumpaz. *Swambaz, *swammaz and *sumpaz are likely related to each other, but it is unclear whether they are of Indo-European origin or are substrate words or wanderworts. The word has alternatively been suggested to be a borrowing from Dutch zwamp (“swamp, marsh, fen”). Other cognates include Middle Low German swamp (“sponge, mushroom”), Dutch zomp (“swamp, lake, marshy place”), German Low German Sump (“swamp, bog, marsh”), German Sumpf (“swamp”), Swedish sump (“swamp”). Related also to Dutch zwam (“fungus, punk, tinder”), German Schwamm (“mushroom, fungus, sponge”), Swedish svamp (“mushroom, fungus, sponge”), Icelandic svampur, sveppur (“fungus”), Gothic 𐍃𐍅𐌿𐌼𐍃𐌻 (swumsl, “a ditch”). Related to sump, swim.
swamp.example: Some small Marshes and Swamps there are, but more profitable than hurtfull.
swamp.exampleSense: A piece of wet, spongy land; low ground saturated with water; soft, wet ground which may have a growth of certain kinds of trees, but is unfit for agricultural or pastoral purposes (a type of wetland). (Compare marsh, bog, fen.)

commentariat.o: Probably a blend of commentary + proletariat, perhaps after proprietariat and salariat. Perhaps compare also secretariat.
commentariat.example: From Boston, a man who finally joined the commentariat by making his debut on CNBC’s Hardball, Esquire Magazine writer-at-large, Charlie Pierce!
commentariat.exampleSense: All the pundits and commentators of the news media collectively.

commentate.o: Back-formation from commentator. Equivalent to comment + -ate (verb-forming suffix).
commentate.example: For the radio audience he will commentate on the match.
commentate.exampleSense: To provide a commentary; to act as a commentator; to maintain a stream of comments about some event.

premeditate.o: Learned borrowing from Latin praemeditātus, past participle of praemeditor (“to premeditate”). By surface analysis, pre- + meditate.

goggle.o: From 14th century Middle English gogelen (“to roll (eyes), to look sideways”). Earlier source is unknown. The noun is attested from the 17th century. Compare Irish gog (“a nod, a slight motion”).
goggle.example: Come and have a goggle at Fauzia’s new car!
goggle.exampleSense: A wide-eyed stare or affected rolling of the eye.

take aback.o: From take + aback, see the two entries for their respective etymology.
take aback.example: In a way, he was taken aback by the absence of discouragement.
take aback.exampleSense: To surprise or shock; to discomfit.

balk.o:
noun: From Middle English balke, from Old English balca, either from or influenced by Old Norse bálkr (“partition, ridge of land”), from Proto-Germanic *balkô. Cognate with Dutch balk (“balk”), German Balken (“balk”), Italian balcone (“balcony”).

noun: From Middle English balok, ballok (“knob”), from Old English bealluc (“testicle”, literally “little ball”). Doublet of ballock and bollocks.
balk.example: The best advice you can receive regarding balking is to always maintain poise and composure on the mound.
balk.exampleSense: To make a deceptive motion to deceive another player.

aridity.o: Borrowed from Latin āriditās (“dryness”); equivalent to arid + -ity.

overdrawn.o: past participle of overdraw. From over- + draw.

overdraft.example: The bank have given me an overdraft of $2000.
overdraft.exampleSense: The maximum amount that may be overdrawn.

overset.o: PIE word *upér The verb is derived from Middle English oversetten (“to place or set over, cover; to assail; to defeat, overcome, overpower, overthrow; to defer; to discredit, refute; to disregard, overlook, set aside; to hinder; to oppress; to repulse”), from Old English ofersettan (“to put in a position of authority; to overcome or be overcome; to set over”), from Proto-West Germanic *ubarsattjan (“to place above, set over; to establish, install”), from *ubarsittjan (“to abstain from, neglect; to occupy, possess; to sit over or upon”), from *ubar- (prefix meaning ‘above, over’) + *sittjan (“to sit”) (from Proto-Germanic *sitjaną (“to sit”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *sed- (“to sit”)). By surface analysis, over- (prefix meaning ‘above, higher; excessive, excessively’) + set (verb). Doublet of oversit. Verb sense 1.2.3 (“to translate (a text)”) is probably a calque of German übersetzen. The adjective is derived from overset, the past participle form of the verb. The noun is also derived from the verb. cognates * Dutch overzetten (“to ferry, transport, translate”) * Old High German ubarsezzen (Middle High German übersetzen, modern German übersetzen (“to cross over, translate”)) * Saterland Frisian uursätte (“to cross over, translate”) * Swedish översätta (“to translate”) * West Frisian oersette (“to translate”)
overset.example: [A] certain Calypso-Island detains him at the very outset; and as it were falsifies and oversets his whole reckoning.
overset.exampleSense: To throw (something, such as an organization, a plan, etc.) into confusion or out of order; to subvert, to unsettle, to upset.

sinew.o: From Middle English synwe, synewe (“tendon; ligament or other connective tissue; muscle; nerve; leaf vein”), from Old English sinu (“tendon, sinew; nerve”), from Proto-West Germanic *sinu, from Proto-Germanic *sinwō, *senawō (“sinew”), from Proto-Indo-European *snéh₁wr̥ (“sinew, tendon”), from *(s)neh₁- (“to twist (threads), spin, weave”). The word is cognate with sinnow (“sinew”), Scots senon, sinnon, Saterland Frisian Siene (“sinew”), West Frisian senuw, sine (“sinew; nerve”), Dutch zenuw (“nerve, sinew”), German Sehne (“tendon, sinew; cord”), Icelandic sin (“tendon”), Danish sene (“tendon, sinew”), Swedish sena (“sinew”), Avestan 𐬯𐬥𐬁𐬎𐬎𐬀𐬭 (snāuuar, “tendon, sinew”), Ancient Greek νεῦρον (neûron, “tendon; nerve; cord”), Latin nervus (“tendon, sinew; nerve”), Sanskrit स्नावन् (snāván, “sinew, tendon; muscle”), Tocharian B ṣñor (“sinew”). Doublet of nerve and neuron.
sinew.example: Good company and good discourse are the very sinews of virtue.
sinew.exampleSense: That which gives strength or in which strength consists; a supporting factor or member; mainstay.

gadget.o: Unknown. First used in print by Robert Brown in 1886 (see quote in definition section). Might come from French gâchette or gagée, or from the French family name Gaget, an industrialist who produced promotional gadgets in collaboration with the project to build the statue of Liberty.
gadget.example: A Spectre gadget was found in the Linux kernel's implementation of system interrupts.
gadget.exampleSense: A sequence of machine code instructions crafted as part of an exploit that attempts to divert execution to a memory location chosen by the attacker.

pretension.o:
noun: From Middle English pretencioun, pretensioun, from Medieval Latin prētēnsiō.

verb: From pre- + tension.
pretension.example: As a foreign stamp gazette it is nowhere. An article on Stamp Collecting, by J. E. Gray, “reprinted from one of his books,” and a catalogue of stamps constitute its sole attraction. We are surprised to find such sounding pretentions so poorly supported.
pretension.exampleSense: A claim or aspiration to a particular status or quality.

sidelines.o: plural of sideline. From side + line.

execute.o: From Old French executer (French exécuter), from Latin exsecutus, past participle of exsequor (“to follow (up/through)”, particularly in the sense “to go through with a deed or punishment”), from ex- (“out”) + sequor (“to follow”).
execute.example: According to international treaties, it is illegal to execute prisoners of war.
execute.exampleSense: To kill, especially as punishment for a capital crime.

exec.example: An upcoming problem to be thrashed out at a meeting of diskery reps and execs of the American Federation of Radio Artists (AFRA), is the degree of AFRA's jurisdictional claim over singers on records.
exec.exampleSense: An executive; a person employed at the executive level.

brief.o: From Middle English breef, breve, bref, from Old French brief, bref, from Latin brevis (“short”), from Proto-Indo-European *mréǵʰus (“short, brief”). Doublet of breve and merry.
brief.example: Her skirt was extremely brief but doubtless cool.
brief.exampleSense: Occupying a small distance, area or spatial extent; short.

briefing.example: The president received a briefing on the situation before going to the press conference.
briefing.exampleSense: A concise summary of a current situation.

cap.o:
noun: Inherited from Middle English cappe, from Old English cæppe, from Proto-West Germanic *kappā (“covering, hood, mantle”), from Late Latin cappa, itself from Latin caput. Doublet of cape, chape, and cope.

noun: Various clippings.

noun: From Scots cap, an alteration of earlier cop, from Middle English cop, from Old English copp (“a cup, vessel”), from Proto-West Germanic *kopp, from Proto-Germanic *kuppaz.
cap.example: He took the cap off the bottle and splashed himself with some cologne.

qualify.o: Borrowed from Middle French qualifier (“to qualify”). Equivalent to quality + -fy.
qualify.example: He had qualified himself for municipal office by taking the oaths to the sovereigns in possession.
qualify.exampleSense: To make someone, or to become competent or eligible for some position or task.

wavy.o:
adj: From wave + -y.

noun: See wavey.
wavy.example: The blue and white wavies breed in the barren grounds and feed chiefly on berries.

headquarters.example: As though on an incendiary rampage, the fires systematically devoured the contents of Edison's headquarters and facilities.
headquarters.exampleSense: The center of an organization's operations or administration.

mild.o: From Middle English milde, from Old English milde (“mild”), from Proto-Germanic *mildijaz (“mild”), from Proto-Indo-European *melh₂- (“to beat, pound, grind”). Cognate with Scots mild, myld (“mild”), Saterland Frisian milde (“mild”), West Frisian myld (“mild”), Dutch mild (“mild”), Low German milde (“mild”), German mild (“mild”), Danish, Swedish and Norwegian Bokmål mild (“mild”), Icelandic mildur (“mild”), Latin mollis (“soft, gentle”), Lithuanian malonus (“pleasing, pleasant, kind”), Old Norse mildr.
mild.exampleSense: Of only moderate severity; not strict.

fere.o:
noun: From Middle English fere, from (Northumbrian) Old English fǣra, aphetic form of ġefēra (whence also Middle English y-fere).

adj: From Middle English fer, from Anglo-Norman fer, from Old French fier. Compare Latin ferus (“wild”).
fere.example: And Cambel tooke Cambrina to his fere.
fere.exampleSense: A person's spouse, or an animal's mate.

maid.o: From Middle English mayde, maide, abbreviation of Middle English maiden from Old English mæġden (Old English mǣden). Ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *magaþ, from Proto-Germanic *magaþs (“girl, virgin”).
maid.example: You are betrothed both to a maid and man.
maid.exampleSense: A virgin, now female but originally one of either gender.

future.o: From Middle English future, futur, from Old French futur, from Latin futūrus, irregular future active participle of sum (“to be”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰuH- (“to become, be”). Cognate with Old English bēo (“to become, will be; to be”). More at be. Doublet of futur. Displaced native Old English tōweard, which took on a different meaning as toward, and Middle English afterhede (“future”, literally “afterhood”) in the given sense.
future.example: Again, it's unlikely they will return to traffic, but futures have been secured for four that will be heading to heritage railways [...].
future.exampleSense: The likely prospects for or fate of someone or something in time to come.

financial year.example: As yet, we don't know what the comparable figures will be like for the current financial year which ends in March 2022, but we can have a good stab at approximating them.

financial.example: For financial reasons, we're not going to be able to continue to fund this program.

pace.o:
noun: From Middle English pase, from Anglo-Norman pas, Old French pas, and their source, Latin passus. Doublet of pas and fathom; compare also pass. Cognate with pass, Spanish pasear, paso.

prep: From Latin pāce (“in peace”), ablative form of pāx (“peace”).

noun: Alteration of archaic Pasch.
pace.example: Netherlands, one of the pre-tournament favourites, combined their undoubted guile, creativity, pace and attacking quality with midfield grit and organisation.
pace.exampleSense: A way of stepping. A manner of walking, running or dancing; the rate or style of how someone moves with their feet.

gallop.o: From Middle English galopen (“to gallop”), from Old French galoper (compare modern French galoper), from Frankish *wala hlaupan (“to run well”), from *wala (“well”) + *hlaupan (“to run”), from Proto-Germanic *hlaupaną (“to run, leap, spring”), from Proto-Indo-European *klaup-, *klaub- (“to spring, stumble”). Possibly also derived from a deverbal of Frankish *walhlaup (“battle run”) from *wal (“battlefield”) from a Proto-Germanic word meaning "dead, victim, slain" from Proto-Indo-European *wel- (“death in battle, killed in battle”) + *hlaup (“course, track”) from *hlaupan (“to run”). More at well, leap, valkyrie. See also the doublet wallop, coming from the same source through an Old Northern French variant.
gallop.example: Gallop lively down the western hill.
gallop.exampleSense: To ride at a galloping pace.

trot.o:
noun: From Middle English trotten, from Old French trotter, troter (“to go, trot”), from Medieval Latin *trottō, *trotō (“to go”), from Frankish *trottōn (“to go, run”), from Proto-Germanic *trudōną, *trudaną, *tradjaną (“to go, step, tread”), from Proto-Indo-European *dreh₂- (“to run, escape”). Cognate with Old High German trottōn (“to run”), Modern German trotten (“to trot, plod”), Gothic 𐍄𐍂𐌿𐌳𐌰𐌽 (trudan, “to tread”), Old Norse troða (“to walk, tread”), Old English tredan (“to step, tread”). Doublet of trade and tread.

noun: Short for foxtrot, whose rhythms influenced the genre.
trot.example: Dogs have a variety of gaits. Most dogs have the walk, trot, pace, and gallop.
trot.exampleSense: A gait of a four-legged animal between walk and canter, a diagonal gait (in which diagonally opposite pairs of legs move together).

verdure.o: Inherited from Middle English verdure, from Middle French verdure, from Old French verdure, from Late Latin *viridūra, from viridis (“green”) + -ūra (abstract noun-forming suffix).
verdure.example: Through the brazen hours that followed high noon, we crept onwards through a tunnel of glittering verdure.
verdure.exampleSense: The greenness of lush or growing vegetation (greenery); also: the vegetation itself.

hillbilly.o: From hill + billy (“fellow”). Compare Scots chapman billie (“travelling salesman”).
hillbilly.example: Hillbillying troubadors, the bohemians of a new world, not cafe society but more like the poor white origins of an Elvis Presley.
hillbilly.exampleSense: To emphasize one's rural or humble upbringing; to use unsophisticated charm.

stowage.example: We'll have to pay the stowage if we want our crate back.
stowage.exampleSense: A charge for stowing and storage.

latchet.o:
noun: From Middle English lachet, from Old French lachet, variant of lacet, diminutive of laz (“lace”).

noun: From latch + -et.
latchet.example: a stronger than I commeth after me, whos shue latchett I am not worthy to stoupe doune and unlose.
latchet.exampleSense: A thong or cord, especially one used to fasten a shoe.

latch.o:
verb: From Middle English lacchen (“to seize, catch, grasp”, verb), from Old English læċċan (“to grasp, take hold of, catch, seize”), from Proto-Germanic *lakjaną, *lakwijaną, *lakkijaną (“to seize”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)leh₂g-, *(s)leh₂gʷ- (“to take, seize”). Cognate with Middle Dutch lakken (“to grasp, catch”).

noun: From Middle English latche, lacche (“a latch; a trap”), from lacchen (“to seize, catch, grasp”), from Old English læċċan (“to grasp, take hold of, catch, seize”). See above for more.

verb: Compare French lécher (“to lick”).
latch.example: The cleverly constructed latch which Clayton had made for the door had sprung as Kerchak passed out; nor could the apes find means of ingress through the heavily barred windows.
latch.exampleSense: A fastening for a door that has a bar that fits into a notch or slot, and is lifted by a lever or string from either side.

humbling.o: present participle and gerund of humble. From Middle English humble, from Old French humble, umble, humle, from Latin humilis (“low, slight, hence mean, humble”) (compare Greek χαμηλός (khamēlós, “on the ground, low, trifling”)), from humus (“the earth, ground”), humi (“on the ground”). See homage, and compare chameleon, humiliate. Displaced native Old English ēaþmōd.

pigmeat.example: A fire burned on the rock and fat dripped from the roasting pigmeat into the invisible flames.
pigmeat.exampleSense: The meat or flesh of a pig, used especially for food; pork.

transcendent.o: From transcend + -ent, or borrowed from Latin trānscendēns.
transcendent.example: Both stood silent, gazing on each other; Walter was actually lost in admiration of Lady Marchmont's transcendent beauty.

transcend.o: From Middle English transcenden, from Old French transcender, from Latin transcendō (“to climb over, step over, surpass, transcend”), from trans (“over”) + scandō (“to climb”); see scan; compare ascend, descend.
transcend.example: Shepard: What do you want from us? Slaves? Resources?
transcend.exampleSense: To pass beyond the limits of something.

pundit.o: Borrowed from Hindi पंडित (paṇḍit) / Urdu پنڈت (panḍit), from Sanskrit पण्डित (paṇḍita, “scholar, learned man, teacher, philosopher”). Doublet of pandit.
pundit.example: This week we introduce Jenny Walker, who will be The Observer's expert pundit for the duration of the World Cup.
pundit.exampleSense: An expert in a particular field, especially as called upon to provide comment or opinion in the media; a commentator, a critic.

orchard.o: From Middle English orchard, orcherd, from Old English orċeard, ortġeard, a compound of *ort (probably from Proto-Germanic *urtiz, a dissimilated variant of Proto-Germanic *wurt- (“wort (plant)”), later incorrectly associated with unrelated Latin hortus (“garden”)) + ġeard (see hortyard and yard, which ironically is etymologically linked with hortus). Cognate with Swedish örtagård (“herb garden”), Gothic 𐌰𐌿𐍂𐍄𐌹𐌲𐌰𐍂𐌳𐍃 (aurtigards, “orchard”), Old High German orzōn (“to cultivate a field”). Equivalent to wort + yard. More at root.

blunt.o:
adj: From Middle English blunt, blont, from Old English *blunt, probably of North Germanic origin, possibly related to Old Norse blunda (“to doze”) (> Icelandic blunda, Swedish blunda, Danish blunde).

verb: From Middle English blunten, blonten, from the adjective (see above).
blunt.example: The murderous knife was dull and blunt.
blunt.exampleSense: Having a thick edge or point; not sharp.

perplexed.o: simple past and past participle of perplex. From Old French, from Latin perplexus (“entangled, confused”), from per (“through”) + plexus, perfect passive participle of plectō (“plait, weave, braid”).
perplexed.example: The scientists were perplexed by the new discovery.

assimilate.o:
verb: First attested in the early 15ᵗʰ century, in Middle English; Middle English assimilaten (“to become similar; to make like”), from assimilat(e) (“assimilated”, also used as the past participal of assimilaten) + -en (verb-forming suffix), borrowed from Late Latin assimilātus, variant of Latin assimulātus (“made similar, imitated”), perfect passive participle of assimulō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from ad + simulō (“to imitate, copy”), from similis (“like, similar”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *sem- (“together, one”). Doublet of assemble.

adj: First attested in the early 15ᵗʰ century, in Middle English; from Middle English assimilat(e) (“made like”, used as the participle of assimilaten), see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and Etymology 1 for more; the noun was derived from the participle through substantivization, see -ate (noun-forming suffix). Participial usage up until Early Modern English.
assimilate.example: The aliens in the science-fiction film wanted to assimilate human beings into their own race.
assimilate.exampleSense: To absorb (a person or people) into a community or culture.

scrutinize.example: Those pronounced him youngest who scrutinized his face the closest.
scrutinize.exampleSense: To examine something with great care or detail, as to look for hidden or obscure flaws.

commencement.o: From French commencement; analyzable as commence + -ment.
commencement.example: The time of Henry VII nearly coincides with the commencement of what is termed modern history.
commencement.exampleSense: The first existence of anything; act or fact of commencing; the beginning.

pulse.o:
noun: From Late Middle English pulse, Middle English pous, pouse (“regular beat of arteries, pulse; heartbeat; place on the body where a pulse is detectable; beat (of a musical instrument); energy, vitality”) [and other forms], from Anglo-Norman puls, pous, pus, and Middle French pouls, poulz, pous [and other forms], Old French pous, pulz (“regular beat of arteries; place on the body where a pulse is detectable”) (modern French pouls), and from their etymon Latin pulsus (“beat, impulse, pulse, stroke; regular beat of arteries or the heart”), from pellō (“to drive, impel, propel, push; to banish, eject, expel; to set in motion; to strike”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *pel- (“to beat, strike; to drive; to push, thrust”)) + -sus (a variant of -tus (suffix forming action nouns from verbs)).

verb: From Late Middle English pulse, Middle English pulsen (“to pulse, throb”), from Latin pulsāre, the present active infinitive of pulsō (“to push; to beat, batter, hammer, strike; to knock on; (figuratively) to drive or urge on, impel; to move; to agitate, disquiet, disturb”), the frequentative of pellō (“to drive, impel, propel, push; to banish, eject, expel; to set in motion; to strike”); see further at etymology

noun: From Middle English puls (“(collectively) seeds of a leguminous plant used as food; leguminous plants collectively; a species of leguminous plant”), Early Middle English pols (in compounds), possibly from Anglo-Norman pus, puz, Middle French pouls, pols, pous, and Old French pous, pou (“gruel, mash, porridge”) (perhaps in the sense of a gruel made from pulses), or directly from their etymon Latin puls (“meal (coarse-ground edible part of various grains); porridge”), probably from Ancient Greek πόλτος (póltos, “porridge made from flour”), from Proto-Indo-European *pel- (“dust; flour”) (perhaps by extension from *pel- (“to beat, strike; to drive; to push, thrust”), in the sense of something beaten).
pulse.example: Her pulse was thready and weak.
pulse.exampleSense: The nature or rate of this beat as an indication of a person's health.

pulverization.o: From French pulvérisation. By surface analysis, pulverize + -ation.

pulverise.o: From Middle English pulverizen, from Latin pulverizō, pulverizāre, from pulvis (“powder”). Compare French pulvériser. By surface analysis, pulver (“powder”) + -ise.

convent.o:
noun: From Middle English convent, variant of covent, from Old French covent, from Latin conventus, perfect participle of the verb convenio (whence ultimately convene), see con- + venio. Doublet of coven.

verb: From Latin convenio (past participle conventus), whence also convene; so of the same ultimate origin as Etymology
convent.example: ...an usual ceremony at their [the witches'] convents or meetings...

gland.o:
noun: Late 17th century borrowing from French glande, alteration of Old French glandre, from Latin glandulae (“throat glands, tonsils”), plural of glandula (“a little acorn”), from glāns (“an acorn”) + -ula (diminutive nominal suffix).

noun: Early 19th century, probably from Scots glam (“vice, clamp”), probably from a variant of clam (“clam; clamp, vise”). Related to clamp.

watt.o: Named after Scottish engineer James Watt. For the surname, see Watt.

asap.example: I feel the impatience in her voice, the desire to sell all her stuff asap and return home.

voltage.o: From volt + -age, ultimately derived from the name of Alessandro Volta, inventor of the modern battery.
voltage.example: The voltage between the wires is too low to produce a spark.
voltage.exampleSense: The difference in electrostatic potential between two points in space, especially between live and neutral conductors or the earth.

volt.o:
noun: Named after Italian physicist Alessandro Volta. For the surname, see Italian Volta.

noun: From French volte.
volt.example: If the volt, ampere and ohm were taken as the absolute units, the practical units would be the ampere, begohm and begavolt, names just as convenient as ampere, coulomb and farad.
volt.exampleSense: In the International System of Units, the derived unit of electrical potential and electromotive force (voltage); the potential difference across a conductor when a current of one ampere uses one watt of power. Symbol: V

vitality.o: From vital + -ity, from Middle French vitalité, from Latin vitalitas (“vital force, life”), from vitalis (“vital”); see vital.

advisable.example: Perhaps it will be advisable for me to state my reasons for marrying.

splint.o: From Middle English splint, splent, splente, from Middle Low German splinte, splente or Middle Dutch splint, splinte. Cognate with Old High German splinza (“bar, bolt, latch”). All ultimately from Proto-Germanic *splintǭ, *splintō (“piece of wood, splinter”), from Proto-Germanic *splint-, *splind- (“to split”), from a nasalized form of *splītaną (“to split”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)pley- (“to split, splice”).
splint.example: [...] I saw in the white men's ward that little chap tossing on his back, with his arm in splints, and quite light-headed.
splint.exampleSense: A device to immobilize a body part.

tome.o: From Middle French tome, from Latin tomus (“section of larger work”), from Ancient Greek τόμος (tómos, “section, roll of papyrus, volume”), from τέμνω (témnō, “to cut, separate”).
tome.example: The professor pulled a dusty old tome from the bookshelf.

department.o: From Middle English departement (“ceasing, end”), from Middle French département. Later senses borrowed from Modern French département. Doublet of département.
department.example: The departments were the bricks from which the edifice of the nation was to be constructed.
department.exampleSense: A territorial division; a district; especially, in France, one of the districts into which the country is divided for governmental purposes, similar to a county in the UK and in the USA. France is composed of 101 départements organized in 18 régions, each department is divided into arrondissements, in turn divided into cantons.

frigid.o: Borrowed from Latin frīgidus (“cold”), from frīgeō (“to be cold”), from frīgus (“cold, coldness”), from Proto-Indo-European *sríHgos.
frigid.example: A frigid, fine rain was falling.

sushi.o: Borrowed from Japanese 寿司(すし) (sushi, “sushi (sour rice)”), ultimately from archaic conjugation 酸(す)し (sushi, “sour, vinegared”) of modern adjective 酸(す)い (sui, “sour, vinegared”).
sushi.example: For the vegetarians, she served cucumber sushi.
sushi.exampleSense: A Japanese dish made of small portions of sticky white rice flavored with vinegar, usually wrapped in seaweed and filled or topped with fish, vegetables or meat.

alluring.example: Lookout heights and Smoky Mountains have allurings all their own.
alluring.exampleSense: The act or habit of enticing or attracting in order to seek a benefit or advantage.

allurement.example: He read the letter aloud. Sophia listened with the studied air of one for whom, even in these days, a title possessed some surreptitious allurement.
