white.o: Inherited from Middle English whit, hwit, from Old English hwīt, from Proto-West Germanic *hwīt, from Proto-Germanic *hwītaz, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱweydós, a byform of *ḱweytós (“bright; shine”). Cognates * West Frisian wyt * Dutch wit * German weiß * German weiss * Norwegian Bokmål hvit * Norwegian Nynorsk kvit * Swedish vit * Danish hvid * Lithuanian šviẽsti (“to gleam”), šviesa (“light”) * Old Church Slavonic свѣтъ (světŭ, “light”), свѣтьлъ (světĭlŭ, “clear, bright”) * Persian سفید (sefid, “white”), Persian سپید (sepid, “white”) * Avestan 𐬯𐬞𐬀𐬉𐬙𐬀 (spaēta, “white”) * Sanskrit श्वेत (śvetá, “white, bright”)
white.example: I've got to hit the streets; I've got to move this white.
white.exampleSense: Any object or substance that is of the color white. Cocaine.

melancholy.o: From Middle English malencolie, from Old French melancolie, from Ancient Greek μελαγχολία (melankholía, “atrabiliousness”) (from μέλας (mélas), μελαν- (melan-, “black, dark, murky”) + χολή (kholḗ, “bile”)), referring to the humour which ancient Hippocratic and later Galenic medicine associated with sadness and despondency. Compare the Latin ātra bīlis (“black bile”). The adjectival use is a Middle English innovation, perhaps influenced by the suffixes -y, -ly. Doublet of melancholia.
melancholy.example: My mind was troubled with deep melancholy.
melancholy.exampleSense: Great sadness or depression, especially of a thoughtful or introspective nature.

rework.example: You'll have to rework the crank assembly to incorporate the changes.

imperfection.o: From Old French imperfeccion, see im- + perfection.
imperfection.example: You can accept your imperfection or try to improve.
imperfection.exampleSense: Those qualities or features that are imperfect; the characteristic, state, or quality of being imperfect.

decode.example: The cryptographer decoded the secret message and sent the result to the officer.
decode.exampleSense: To convert from an encrypted form to plain text.

monotonous.example: [L]istening for a moment, she heard the monotonous and heavy tread of the soldier echoing through the passage.
monotonous.exampleSense: Tedious, repetitious, or lacking in variety.

monotony.o: From French monotonie, from Late Latin monotonia, from Ancient Greek μονοτονία (monotonía, “sameness of tone, monotony”).
monotony.example: Yet second-hand romance and second-hand emotion are surely better than the dull, soul-killing monotony which life brings to most of the human race.
monotony.exampleSense: Tedium as a result of repetition or a lack of variety.

monotone.o: From the post-Classical Latin monotonus (“unvarying in tone”) or its etymon the Ancient Greek μονότονος (monótonos, “steady”, “unwavering”); compare cognate adjectives, namely the French monotone, the German monoton, the Italian monotono, and the Spanish monótono, as well as the slightly earlier English noun monotony and adjective monotonical.
monotone.example: When Tima felt like her parents were treating her like a servant, she would speak in monotone and act as though she were a robot.
monotone.exampleSense: A single unvaried tone of speech or a sound.

tease out.example: Well, early in the days of vitamin and mineral discovery, chickens were the research models for studies that eventually teased out information that we take for granted today.
tease out.exampleSense: To work out, procure, or extract, usually by processes involving subterfuge, diligence, manipulation, or coaxing.

salute.o: Borrowed from Latin salūtō (“to greet; to wish health to”), from salūs (“greeting, good health”), related to salvus (“safe”).
salute.example: The soldiers greeted the dignitaries with a crisp salute.
salute.exampleSense: An utterance or gesture expressing greeting or honor towards someone, (now especially) a formal, non-verbal gesture made with the arms or hands in any of various specific positions.

sage.o:
adj: From Middle English sage, from Old French sage (11th century), from Vulgar Latin *sapium, from Latin sapere (“to taste, to discern, to be wise”). The noun meaning "man of profound wisdom" is recorded from circa 1300. Originally applied to the Seven Sages of Greece.

noun: From Middle English sauge, from Middle French sauge, from Old French salje, from Latin salvia, from salvus (“healthy”), see safe. Doublet of salvia.

intj: Borrowed from Japanese sage (sage), from 下げる (sageru, “to lower”). From 2channel.
sage.example: CHAPTER VII. In which Jack makes some very sage reflections, and comes to a very unwise decision.

basic.example: Rice is a basic for many Asian villagers.
basic.exampleSense: A necessary commodity, a staple requirement.

impatient.o: From Old French impacient (modern French impatient), from Latin impatiēns. By surface analysis, im- + patient.
impatient.example: The impatient man will not give himself time to be informed of the matter that lies before him.
impatient.exampleSense: Restless, short of temper, and intolerant of delays.

sequence.o: From Middle English sequence, from Old French sequence (“a sequence of cards, answering verses”), from Late Latin sequentia (“a following”), from Latin sequēns (“following”), from sequī (“to follow”); see sequent.
sequence.example: Complete the listed tasks in sequence.
sequence.exampleSense: The state of being sequent or following; order of succession.

dog days.o: Calque of Latin diēs caniculārēs (“puppy days”), a calque of Ancient Greek κυνάδες ἡμέραι (kunádes hēmérai, “dog days”), from κυνάς (kunás, “of or related to dogs”), from Κῠ́ων (Kŭ́ōn, “the Dog”) in reference to the star Sirius, which appears in Homeric Greek as "Orion's dog". The return of Sirius to the night sky (its heliacal rising), occurring in antiquity around July 25 (Athens) or 29 (Rome), was considered by the Greeks and Romans to herald what were considered the hottest, least healthy, and least lucky days of summer.
dog days.example: The dog days of August have often spelled trouble for the world economy.
dog days.exampleSense: The unpleasantly hot days of late summer.

homecoming.o: From Middle English hom-comyng, home komyng, home-cumyng, home-commynge, equivalent to home + coming. Probably an alteration of earlier Middle English hom-come, homkome, hame-come, ham-cume, from Old English hāmcyme (“homecoming; return”).
homecoming.example: Many alumni come back for homecoming, and many freshmen are advised to flee.
homecoming.exampleSense: In colleges and high schools, a tradition centred around a football game, a parade and the "coronation" of a Homecoming Queen.

bomb.o: From French bombe, from Italian bomba, from Latin bombus (“a booming sound”), from Ancient Greek βόμβος (bómbos, “booming, humming, buzzing”), imitative of the sound itself. Doublet of bombe. Compare boom.
bomb.example: "The hard Brexiteers have built a bomb under the UK automotive industry and the EU have lit it," they said.
bomb.exampleSense: An explosive device used or intended as a weapon, especially, one dropped from an aircraft. Events or conditions that have a speedy destructive effect.

windscreen.example: Oh no! A vandal has just smashed our windscreen! Susan, can you go and call the insurance company?
windscreen.exampleSense: A transparent screen made of glass, located at the front of a vehicle in order to protect its occupants from the wind and weather.

summarise.example: Before summarising his report, Beeching looks at other factors "influencing the future role of the railways".

summarize.example: Jim was asked to summarize the document by Wednesday.

bot.o:
noun: Unknown. Possibly a modification of Scottish Gaelic boiteag (“maggot”), but the word already existed in Middle English, so the reverse direction of borrowing is likely. Possibly from Middle Low German [Term?].

verb: From bottom.

noun: Clipping of robot.
bot.example: One deer, later found to be heavily parasitized by bots, suffered severe vomiting attacks during the early spring.
bot.exampleSense: The larva of a botfly, which infests the skin of various mammals, producing warbles, or the nasal passage of sheep, or the stomach of horses.

entropy.o: First attested in 1867, as the translation of German Entropie, coined in 1865 by Rudolph Clausius in analogy to Energie (“energy”), replacing the root of Ancient Greek ἔργον (érgon, “work”) by Ancient Greek τροπή (tropḗ, “transformation”)).

fax.o:
noun: From Middle English fax, from Old English feax (“hair, head of hair”), from Proto-West Germanic *fahs, from Proto-Germanic *fahsą (“hair, mane”), from Proto-Indo-European *poḱsom (“hair”, literally “that which is combed, shorn, or plucked”), from Proto-Indo-European *peḱ- (“to comb, shear, pluck”). Cognate with Dutch vas (“headhair”), German Fachs (“head-hair”), Norwegian faks (“mane”), Icelandic fax (“mane”), Sanskrit पक्ष्मन् (pákṣman, “eyelash, hair, filament”).

noun: Clipping of facsimile, first attested 1979.

noun: Formed with -x from facts; the pronunciation of facts and fax is identical in certain varieties of English.
fax.example: He already has the copy of the other fingerprints that Leo faxxed to him for comparison.
fax.exampleSense: To send a document via a fax machine.

division.o: PIE word *dwóh₁ From Middle English divisioun, from Old French division, from Latin dīvīsiō, dīvīsiōnem, noun of process form from perfect passive participle dīvīsus (“divided”), from dīvidō (“divide”). Doublet of divisio.
division.example: I've got ten divisions to do for my homework.
division.exampleSense: A calculation that involves this process.

conscience.o: From Middle English conscience, from Old French conscience, from Latin conscientia (“knowledge within oneself”) (a calque of Ancient Greek σῠνείδησῐς (sŭneídēsĭs)), from consciens, present participle of conscire (“to know, to be conscious (of wrong)”), from com- (“together”) + scire (“to know”).
conscience.example: Your conscience is your highest authority.
conscience.exampleSense: The ethical or moral sense of right and wrong, chiefly as it affects a person’s own behaviour and forms their attitude to their past actions.

auxiliary.o: From Latin auxiliārius (“assistant, ally”), equiv. to auxiliāris (“helping, aiding”), from auxilium (“help, aid”), from augēre (“to increase”).
auxiliary.example: A drive to exploit the Highlands as a winter sports area, with all the necessary auxiliaries, such as chair lifts in the Cairngorms, shows increasing promise, [...].
auxiliary.exampleSense: A person or group that acts in an auxiliary manner.

graduate.o:
noun: From Middle English graduat(e) (“(noun) a graduate of a university; (adjective) graduate, having graduated”, also used as the past participle of graduaten (“to graduate”)), borrowed from Medieval Latin graduātus (“graduated, graduate”), perfect passive participle of graduō (“to graduate”) (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from gradus (“step”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix). The noun is originally derived within Latin from the adjective via substantivization, see -ate (noun-forming suffix). Sense 10 of the verb, relating to Japanese entertainment, is a semantic loan from Japanese 卒業 (sotsugyō).

verb: From Middle English graduaten (“to graduate”), from (adjective) graduat(e) (also used as the past participle of graduaten) + -en (verb-forming suffix), from Medieval Latin graduātus, see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and Etymology 1 for more.
graduate.example: If the government wants graduates to stay in the country they should offer more incentives.
graduate.exampleSense: A person who is recognized by a university as having completed the requirements of a degree studied at the institution.

bail.o:
noun: From Middle English baille, from the Old French verb bailler (“to deliver or hand over”) and noun bail (“lease”), from Latin bāiulāre (“carry or bear”), from baiulus (“porter; steward”) (English: bailiff).

verb: From a shortening of bail out, ultimately same as above.

noun: From Middle English beyle, from Old English bīeġels, from bīeġan + -els.

verb: Borrowed from French baillier.
bail.example: The Eighth Amendment to the US Constitution forbids excessive bail, and state bail laws are usually designed to prevent discrimination in setting bail.
bail.exampleSense: Security, usually a sum of money, exchanged for the release of an arrested person as a guarantee of that person's appearance for trial.

nightingale.o:
noun: Inherited from Middle English nyghtyngale, nightingale, niȝtingale, alteration (with intrusive n) of nyghtgale, nightegale, from Old English nihtegala, nihtegale (“nightingale; night-raven”, literally “night-singer”), from Proto-West Germanic *nahtigalā (“nightingale”), equivalent to a compound of night + gale. Cognate with Saterland Frisian Noachtegoal (“nightingale”), Dutch nachtegaal (“nightingale”), German Low German Nachtigall (“nightingale”), German Nachtigall (“nightingale”), Danish nattergal (“thrush nightingale”), Swedish näktergal (“nightingale”), Icelandic næturgali (“nightingale”).

noun: Named after Florence Nightingale.
nightingale.example: The oaks around were the home of a tribe of nightingales.
nightingale.exampleSense: A Eurasian and African songbird, Luscinia megarhynchos, family Muscicapidae, famed for its beautiful singing at night; a common nightingale.

greet.o:
verb: From Middle English greten, from Old English grētan, from Proto-West Germanic *grōtijan, from Proto-Germanic *grōtijaną. Cognate with Dutch groeten, German grüßen, grüssen.

adj: From Middle English greet, grete (“great”).

verb: From a blend of two Old English verbs, grētan, grǣtan (itself from Proto-West Germanic *grātan); and of Old English grēotan (itself from *greutan), both meaning "to weep, lament". Possibly reinforced in Northern England and Scotland by Old Norse gráta, whence also Danish græde, Norwegian gråte, Swedish gråta, all meaning "to cry, to weep".
greet.example: A brilliant dawn greeted her eyes as she looked out of the window.

ravenous.o: From Middle English ravenous, ravynous, from Old French ravineus. By surface analysis, ravin + -ous. As seen at raven and ravin, the word comes from a root referring to predation, not from the root referring to ravens (corvid birds); but folk etymology notes that the latter hypothesis seems plausible because ravens can often seem ravenous (especially as nestlings).
ravenous.example: Ravenous, I order one more wine and a selection of cheese and biscuits.

raven.o:
noun: From Middle English raven, reven (“raven (Corvus corax); carrion crow (Corvus corone); rook (Corvus frugilegus) (?); the constellation Corvus; gall nuts of the Aleppo oak (Quercus infectoria) used to make black ink”), from Old English hræfn (“raven”), from Proto-West Germanic *hrabn (“raven”), from Proto-Germanic *hrabnaz (“raven”), probably from Proto-Indo-European *ḱrep- (“to crackle; to rattle”) or *ḱer- (“to croak, crow”), probably ultimately onomatopoeic, referring to the bird’s call.

noun: A variant of ravin, from Middle English ravin, ravine, raven (noun).
raven.example: The raven is both a scavenger, who ravens a dead animal almost like a vulture, and a bird of prey, who commonly ravens to catch a rodent.

wand.o: From Middle English wand, wond, from Old Norse vǫndr (“switch, twig”), from Proto-Germanic *wanduz (“rod”), from Proto-Indo-European *wendʰ- (“to turn, twist, wind, braid”). Cognate with Icelandic vendi (“wand”), Danish vånd (“wand, switch”), German Wand (“wall, septum”), Gothic 𐍅𐌰𐌽𐌳𐌿𐍃 (wandus, “rod”).
wand.example: Love is that blessed wand which wins the waters from the hardness of the heart.
wand.exampleSense: A hand-held narrow rod, usually used for pointing or instructing, or as a traditional emblem of authority. A stick or rod used by a magician (a magic wand), conjurer or diviner (divining rod).

not yet.example: The rubric in Exhibit 3.2 provides criteria for exemplary, acceptable, and not yet acceptable work.
not yet.exampleSense: Not for the moment, though expected later.

sort of.o: From sort (noun) + of. The adverbial use is derived from the use of the term as an adjective in phrases such as “a sort of [something]”.
sort of.example: It sort of makes sense the way he explains it, but I still don't really understand.
sort of.exampleSense: Approximately; in a way; partially; not quite; somewhat.

sort.o:
noun: From Middle English sort, soort, sorte (cognate Dutch soort, German Sorte, Danish sort, Swedish sort), borrowed from Old French sorte (“class, kind”), from Latin sortem, accusative form of sors (“lot, fate, share, rank, category”).

verb: From Middle English sorten, from Old French sortir (“to allot, sort”), from Latin sortīre (“draw lots, divide, choose”), from sors.
sort.example: Sort the letters in those bags into a separate pile for each language.
sort.exampleSense: To separate items into different categories according to certain criteria that determine their sorts.

watchtower.example: A "watchtower" Website, keeping track of paedophile groups around the world, is expected to be up and running next year. The campaign will also liaise with law enforcement agencies around the world and share information on suspected Internet paedophiles.
watchtower.exampleSense: An observation tower in which a lookout keeps watch over prisoners, or looks out for fires, etc.

current.o: From Middle English curraunt, borrowed from Old French curant (French courant), present participle of courre (“to run”), from Latin currere (“to run”) (present participle currens). Doublet of courant.
current.example: The mantle is important to our discussion in that its viscous nature can conduct convection currents that have effects on the crust upon which we live.
current.exampleSense: The generally unidirectional movement of a gas or fluid.

glider.o: From Middle English glider, glydare, equivalent to glide + -er.
glider.example: In Conway's Life interesting effects can be obtained by colliding gliders.
glider.exampleSense: In the Game of Life, a particular configuration of five cells that recurs periodically at fixed offsets and appears to "walk" across the grid.

village.o: From Middle English village, from Old French village, from Latin vīllāticus, ultimately from Latin villa (English villa). Broadly overtook Old English wic, þorp, and ham. The Philippine sense is due to its frequent use in the names of gated communities.
village.example: There are six blocks in our village, each having ten lots.

cowardly.o: From Middle English *cowardly (adjective) and cowardly (adverb), equivalent to coward + -ly. Displaced native Old English earg.
cowardly.example: The cowardly rascals that ran from the battle.
cowardly.exampleSense: Showing cowardice; lacking in courage; weakly fearful.

optical.example: Optical telescopes don't work when it is cloudy.
optical.exampleSense: Of, or relating to visible light.

syntactic.o: From New Latin syntacticus, from Ancient Greek συντακτικός (suntaktikós).
syntactic.example: The sentence “I saw he” contains a syntactic mistake.
syntactic.exampleSense: Of, related to or connected with syntax.

transformer.example: While initial reports Thursday traced the glow to a transformer explosion or a fire, Mr. McGee said there was no fire, and there were no transformers involved.
transformer.exampleSense: A static device that transfers electric energy from one circuit to another by magnetic coupling; primarily used to transfer energy between different voltage levels, which allows the most appropriate voltages for power generation, transmission and distribution to be chosen separately.

trans-.o: Borrowed from Latin trans- (“across, beyond, on the far side”).

tense.o:
noun: From Middle English tens, from Old French tens (modern French temps), from Latin tempus. Doublet of tempo and tempus.

adj: Borrowed from Latin tēnsus, one form of the past participle of tendō (“stretch”).
tense.example: The driver and the man shouted angrily at each other and I tensed, ready for violence. But soon everyone in the tap-tap joined in, capping remarks, joking, telling chicken and goat stories.

peculiarity.example: I had often heard of Miss Marchmont, and of her peculiarities (she had the character of being very eccentric), but till now had never seen her.
peculiarity.exampleSense: That which is peculiar; a special and distinctive characteristic or habit; particularity.

peculiarly.example: Having red hair and freckles is a characteristic that is peculiarly Northern European.
peculiarly.exampleSense: Strongly associated with; in a manner that is peculiar or restricted to some person or place. Mostly or solely associated with.

skyline.example: Our arrival at Worcester is heralded by the appearance of the city's cathedral tower, a solid square structure that's dominated the skyline since the 12th century.
skyline.exampleSense: The horizontal silhouette of a city or building against the sky.

quote.o: From Middle English quoten, coten (“to mark (a book) with chapter numbers or marginal references”), from Old French coter, from Medieval Latin quotāre (“to distinguish by numbers, number chapters”), itself from Latin quotus (“which, what number (in sequence)”), from quot (“how many”) and related to quis (“who”). The sense developed via “to give as a reference, to cite as an authority” to “to copy out exact words” (since 1680); the business sense “to state the price of a commodity” (1866) revives the etymological meaning. The noun, in the sense of “quotation,” is attested from 1885; see also usage note, below.
quote.example: The writer quoted the president's speech.
quote.exampleSense: To repeat (the exact words of a person).

shortlist.o: Alternative form of short. From Middle English schort, short, from Old English sċeort, sċort (“short”), from Proto-West Germanic *skurt, from Proto-Germanic *skurtaz (“short”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker-. Doublet of shirt, skirt, and curt. Cognates Cognate with Scots short, schort (“short”), French court, Dutch kort, German kurz, Old High German scurz (“short”) (whence Middle High German schurz), Old Norse skorta (“to lack”) (whence Danish skorte), Albanian shkurt (“short, brief”), Latin curtus (“shortened, incomplete”) and Proto-Slavic *kortъkъ. See more at shirt.
shortlist.example: First and Trenitalia were initially shortlisted for the East Midlands franchise but withdrew from bidding to focus on the West Coast Partnership, while Trenitalia was shortlisted as a sole entity for the South Eastern franchise but again withdrew from the competition.
shortlist.exampleSense: To place something on a short list.

whelm.o: From Middle English whelmen (“to turn over, capsize; to invert, turn upside down”), perhaps from Old English *hwealmnian, a variant of *hwealfnian, from hwealf (“arched, concave, vaulted; an arched or vaulted ceiling”), from Proto-West Germanic *hwalb, from Proto-Germanic *hwalbą (“arch, vault”), from Proto-Indo-European *kʷelp- (“to curve”). Cognates The English word is cognate with Dutch welven (“to arch”), Old Saxon bihwelvian (“to cover, hide”), German wölben (“to bend, curve, arch”), Icelandic hvelfa (“to overturn”), German Walm (“a vaulted roof”), Icelandic hvolf (“vaulted ceiling”), Ancient Greek κόλπος (kólpos, “bosom, hollow, gulf”). The noun is derived from the verb.
whelm.example: A whelm was a wooden drainpipe, a hollowed-out tree trunk, "whelmed down" or turned with the concavity downwards to form an arched watercourse.
whelm.exampleSense: A wooden drainpipe, a hollowed out tree trunk, turned with the cavity downwards to form an arched watercourse.

overwhelmed.o: simple past and past participle of overwhelm. Inherited from Middle English overwhelmen, equivalent to over- + whelm.

overwhelming.example: The vote was taken at once, and it was agreed by an overwhelming majority that rats were comrades.

overwhelm.o: Inherited from Middle English overwhelmen, equivalent to over- + whelm.
overwhelm.example: Joy overwhelmed her when she realized that she had won a million dollars.

uncertainty.o: From Middle English uncerteynte; equivalent to un- + certainty or uncertain + -ty.
uncertainty.example: It's a full circle. Over the past 43 years, RAIL has reported on how the railways have gone from uncertainty under government control to sectorisation, privatisation, and back to uncertainty under government control.
uncertainty.exampleSense: Doubt; the condition of being uncertain or without conviction.

uncertain.o: From Middle English uncerteyn. By surface analysis, un- + certain.
uncertain.example: Thinking about the uncertain refines our perception of the certain, and generally this takes place in a framework in which the uncertain is the future and the certain is the present.

contextualise.o: Alternative spelling of contextualize. From contextual + -ize.
contextualise.example: "Secrets of the London Underground is completely unscripted. It is just me and Tim going to a location, and I have to contextualise where we are.

embedding.example: “A major reason we chose to study word embeddings is that they have been spectacularly successful in the last few years in helping computers make sense of language,” said Arvind Narayanan, a computer scientist at Princeton University and the paper’s senior author.
embedding.exampleSense: A representation of a unit of text (such as a word or token) as a vector, which encodes the context in which it is used.

disenthral.o: Alternative spelling of disenthrall. From dis- + enthrall.

cherry tomato.o: From its resemblance to a cherry.

cascade.o: From French cascade, from Italian cascata, from cascare (“to fall”), from Vulgar Latin *cāsicāre, derived from Latin cadere, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ḱh₂d-.
cascade.example: In the first week of May, Sharp began his summit push.
cascade.exampleSense: A waterfall or series of small waterfalls.

indentured.example: As a result, many Black people remained unfairly enslaved and indentured in the so-called free territory. This was not legal slavery (also known as de jure slavery), but slavery in practice (de facto slavery).

transcribe.o: Learned borrowing from Latin trānscrībere (“to write again in another place, transcribe, copy”).
transcribe.example: The doctor made several recordings today which she will transcribe into medical reports tomorrow.
transcribe.exampleSense: To make such a conversion from live or recorded speech to text.

trampoline.o: From Spanish trampolín and/or Italian trampolino; in English, a genericized trademark based on the Spanish word trademarked in 1936, but attested since 1798.
trampoline.example: Though the name of the Four Cleos may not be familiar, their pranks are. They perform on that apparatus resembling a spring mattress, which has been dubbed the “trampoline,” owing to some confusion with the Anglicised form of tremplin (springboard).
trampoline.exampleSense: A gymnastic and recreational device consisting of a piece of taut, strong fabric or rubber stretched over a (usually steel) frame using many coiled springs as anchors.

transistor.o: Blend of transfer + resistor. Said to have been coined by American engineer John Robinson Pierce in 1947, who used transresistance as the basis for forming transistor.

transient.o: From Late Latin transiēnt- (for classical transeunt-), stem of transiēns, present participle of trānsīre (“to go over, to pass”).
transient.example: The overhead in loading transients is a big time-waster.
transient.exampleSense: A module that generally remains in memory only for a short time.

abomination.o: From Middle English abominacioun, from Middle French abomination (“horror, disgust”), from Late Latin abōminātiō, abōminātiōnem (“abomination”) Doublet of abominatio.
abomination.example: Appalled by a child she found hideous, Philyra begged the gods to free her from having to rear such an abomination.
abomination.exampleSense: That which is abominable, shamefully vile; an object that excites disgust and hatred (often with religious undertones).

abominable.o: From Middle English abhomynable, from Old French abominable, from Late Latin abōminābilis (“deserving abhorrence”), from abōminor (“abhor, deprecate as an ill omen”), from ab (“from, away from”) + ōminor (“forebode, predict, presage”), from ōmen (“sign, token, omen”). Formerly erroneously folk-etymologized as deriving from Latin ab- + homo, literally "away from humankind," and therefore spelled abhominable, abhominal (Hence, Shakespeare puns on this when Hamlet speaks of incompetent actors that "imitate humanity abominably.")
abominable.example: The parish stank of idolatry, abominable rites were practiced in secret, and in all the bounds there was no one had a more evil name for the black traffic than one Alison Sempill, who bode at the Skerburnfoot.
abominable.exampleSense: Worthy of, or causing, abhorrence, as a thing of evil omen; odious in the utmost degree; very hateful; detestable; loathsome; execrable.

abominate.o: First attested in 1644. Perhaps a back-formation from abomination. Alternatively, perhaps from Late Latin abōminātus, past participle of abōminarī (“to deprecate as an ill omen”), from ab + ominari (“to forebode, presage”), from omen.

boot.o:
noun: From Middle English boote, bote (“shoe”), from Old French bote (“a high, thick shoe”). Of obscure origin, but probably related to Old French bot (“club-foot”), bot (“fat, short, blunt”), from Old Frankish *butt, from Proto-Germanic *buttaz, *butaz (“cut off, short, numb, blunt”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰewt-, *bʰewd- (“to strike, push, shock”); if so, a doublet of butt. Compare Old Norse butt (“stump”), Low German butt (“blunt, plump”), Old English bytt (“small piece of land”), buttuc (“end”). More at buttock and debut.

noun: From Middle English boote, bote, bot, from Old English bōt (“help, relief, advantage”), from Proto-West Germanic *bōtu, from Proto-Germanic *bōtō (“atonement, improvement”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰed- (“good”). Akin to Old Norse bót (“bettering, remedy”) (Danish bod), Gothic 𐌱𐍉𐍄𐌰 (bōta), German Buße. Doublet of bote (a borrowing from Middle English).

noun: Clipping of bootstrap.

noun: From bootleg (“to make or sell illegally”), by shortening.
boot.example: The body is constructed of welded steel panels, with the bonnet, doors and boot lid in aluminium on steel frames.
boot.exampleSense: The luggage storage compartment of a sedan or saloon car.

spite.o: From Middle English spit, a shortening of despit (whence despite), from Old French despit, from Latin dēspectum (“looking down on”), from Latin dēspiciō (“to look down, despise”). Compare also North Frisian spīt, spīd (“regret”), Saterland Frisian Spiet (“regret, remorse”), West Frisian spyt (“regret”), Dutch spijt (“regret, remorse”), German Low German Spiet (“anger, regret, remorse”), German Spiet (“annoyance, vexation”), Swedish spit (“insult, outrage, annoyance”), Norwegian spit (“insult, outrage, annoyance”).
spite.example: She soon married again, to spite her ex-husband.
spite.exampleSense: To treat maliciously; to try to hurt or thwart.

knight.o:
noun: From Middle English knight, knyght, kniht, from Old English cniht (“boy; servant, knight”), from Proto-West Germanic *kneht.

verb: From Middle English knighten, kniȝten, from the noun. Cognate with Middle High German knehten.
knight.example: The king knighted the young squire.

knighthead.o: From knight + head; sometimes decorated with a carving of a man's head.

mogul.o:
noun: Figurative use of Moghul, which originally meant Mongol, or person of Mongolian descent. In this context, it refers to the Mughal Empire (Mughal being Persian or Arabic for "Mongol") of the Indian subcontinent that existed between 1526 and 1857: the early Mughal emperors claimed a heritage dating back to the Mongol ruler Genghis Khan. The modern meaning of the word is supposedly derived from the storied riches of the Mughal emperors, which, for example, produced the Taj Mahal.

noun: From dialectal German Mugel or from dialectal Norwegian mugje (“heap, mound”).
mogul.example: On the same slope, choose a steeper traverse track on a short mogul field that passes over a series of small moguls, and repeat the avalement movements.
mogul.exampleSense: A hump or bump on a skiing piste.

oceanic.o: Borrowed from Latin ōceanicus; equivalent to ocean + -ic. Doublet of oceany.
oceanic.example: Nevertheless, the capacity of fleshy fruits to be dispersed by oceanic currents (resulting from their floatability and viability after prolonged exposure to saltwater) cannot be evaluated without empirical experimentation [3 ,7 ,10 ,16 ].
oceanic.exampleSense: Living in, produced by, or frequenting the ocean.

soda.o: From Italian soda. Sense 4 is an ellipsis of soda water.
soda.example: A waiter brought his aperitif, which was a small scotch and soda, and as he sipped it gratefully he sighed.
soda.exampleSense: Carbonated water (water impregnated with pressurised carbon dioxide, originally made with sodium bicarbonate).

refuel.example: In his statement, Miliband said the two flights had refuelled at Diego Garcia. Each one had a single detainee on board who did not leave the aircraft.

proximity.o: From proxim(ate) + -ity, from Middle French proximité, from Latin proximitās, proximitāt-, from proximus.
proximity.example: The proximity of the heat source allowed it to be detected by the sensor.
proximity.exampleSense: Closeness; the state of being near as in space, time, or relationship.

proximal.o: From Latin proximus, superlative form of prope (“near, nigh”).

representation.o:
noun: From Late Middle English representacioun, from Old French representacion, from Latin repraesentātiō. By surface analysis, represent + -ation.

noun: From re- + presentation.
representation.example: The Venus of Willendorf was an early representation of the female body.

encode.example: The blotchy black mark she impresses on my hand will still be there tomorrow morning, a confused barcode, unsure of what exactly it encodes.
encode.exampleSense: To convert source information into another form.

gazelle.o: Unadapted borrowing from Middle French gazelle, from Old French gazel, from Arabic غَزَال (ḡazāl).

salience.o: From Latin saliēns, salientis (whence -ence), from saliō.

hound.o:
noun: From Middle English hound, from Old English hund, from Proto-West Germanic *hund, from Proto-Germanic *hundaz. Doublet of canine. Cognate with Dutch hond (“dog”), German Hund (“dog”), Danish, Norwegian Bokmål, Norwegian Nynorsk, and Swedish hund (“dog”), Faroese and Icelandic hundur (“dog”). In 14th-century England, hound was the general word for all domestic canines, and dog referred to a subtype resembling the modern mastiff and bulldog (much as the distinction between Hund and Dogge in contemporary German). By the 16th century, dog had become the general word, and hound had begun to refer only to breeds used for hunting.

verb: From Middle English hounden, from the noun (see above).

noun: From Middle English hownde, hount, houn, probably from Old Norse húnn, from Proto-Germanic *hūnaz.
hound.example: We both thought we saw what had the appearance to be a fox, and hounded the dogs at it, but they would not pursue it.
hound.exampleSense: To urge on against; to set (dogs) upon in hunting.

pixel.o: pix (“pictures”), + el(ement); often taken to be a blend of “picture” and “element”. The ⟨x⟩ stems from the abbreviation pics being sometimes also written as pix, which has been in use since the 1880s. First attested in 1965.
pixel.example: In the tomographic images of the 30-day-old cheeses, the gantry had to be removed with image processing techniques: first, the binarised image (grey level larger than 10⁴) was eroded with a disk of three pixels.
pixel.exampleSense: One of the tiny dots that make up the representation of an image in a computer's memory.

yep.o: Representing yeah pronounced with the mouth snapped closed at the end. Compare yup, nope, welp, and ope. Compare also German jap (“yep”).
yep.example: I'll take that as a yep, then.

yup.o:
noun: Representing yeah pronounced with the mouth snapped closed at the end (excrescent IPA⁽ᵏᵉʸ⁾: /p/). Compare yep, nope, welp, and ope.

noun: Shortening.
yup.example: She'd ask him a question that couldn't be answered by a "yup" or a "nope.

misdiagnosis.example: They have suffered from misdiagnoses, lapses in treatment, a lack of access to specialized food and physical therapy, displacement and the unrelenting stress of war.

issuer.example: A request for a nonreviewable ruling must be submitted by an issuer or holder.
issuer.exampleSense: One who issues, emits, or publishes.

loan.o:
noun: From Middle English lone, lane, from Old Norse lán, from Proto-Germanic *laihną, from Proto-Indo-European *leykʷ- (“to leave (over)”). Cognate with Icelandic lán, Swedish lån, Danish lån, German Lehen (“fief”), Dutch leen (“fief”), West Frisian lien, North Frisian leen (“fief; loan; office”), Scots lane, lain, len, Old English lǣn. More at lend.

noun: From Scottish Gaelic lòn (“marshy meadow”) (compare lèana (“wet meadow, marsh, meadow”)).
loan.example: All loans from the library, whether books or audio material, must be returned within two weeks.
loan.exampleSense: A sum of money or other property that a natural or legal person borrows from another with the condition that it be returned or repaid over time or at a later date (sometimes with interest).

salient.o: The heraldic sense “leaping” and the sense “projecting outward” are borrowed from Latin salientem, the accusative form of saliēns (“springing, leaping”) (whence -ent), present participle of saliō (“leap, spring”, verb). The senses “prominent” and “pertinent” are relatively recent, and derive from the phrase salient point, which is a calque of the Latin punctum saliēns, a translation of Aristotle's term for the embryonal heart visible in (opened) eggs, which he thought seemed to move already. Compare also the German calque der springende Punkt.
salient.example: On April 26 the First Division had gone into the line in the Montdidier salient on the Picardy battlefront.
salient.exampleSense: An outwardly projecting part of a fortification, trench system, or line of defense.

catching.o: present participle and gerund of catch. From Middle English cacchen, from Anglo-Norman cachier, variant of Old French chacier, from Late Latin captiāre, from Latin captāre, frequentative of capere. Akin to Modern French chasser (from Old French chacier) and Spanish cazar, and thus a doublet of chase. Compare ketch. Via PIE cognate with have. Displaced Middle English fangen ("to catch"; > Modern English fang (verb)), from Old English fōn (“to seize, take”); Middle English lacchen ("to catch" and heavily displaced Modern English latch), from Old English læċċan. The verb became irregular, possibly under the influence of the semantically similar latch (from Old English læċċan), whose past tense was lahte, lauhte, laught (Old English læhte), until becoming regularised in Modern English.
catching.example: Bomb guy looked her up and down, not because he was an attractive man and she was possibly a catching woman.

catch-up.example: Rapid expansion of Britain's transport network during the 'railway mania' of the 19th century meant that the testing of engineering principles often played catch-up to the ambitions of progress.
catch-up.exampleSense: An act of catching up or attempting to catch up.

saint.o:
noun: From Middle English saint, seint, sainct, seinct, sanct, senct, partly from Old English sanct (“saint”) and confluence with Old French saint, seinte (Modern French saint); both from Latin sānctus (“holy, consecrated”, in Late Latin as a noun, “a saint”), past participle of sancīre (“to render sacred, make holy”), akin to sacer (“holy, sacred”). Doublet of Sanctus. Displaced native Middle English halwe (“saint”) from Old English hālga (“saint, holy one”) (> Modern English hallow (“saint”)).

verb: From Middle English saynten, seinten, sonten, partly from Anglo-Norman saintir and partly from the noun Middle English seint, seynt (see above).
saint.example: Thanks for looking after the house while I'm away. You're a saint!
saint.exampleSense: A person with similarly overwhelming positive qualities; one who does good.

lawsuit.example: My ex-fiancé filed a lawsuit against me for a false restraining order and defamation.
lawsuit.exampleSense: In civil law, a case where two or more people disagree and one or more of the parties take the case to a court for resolution.

sue.o: From Middle English seuen, sewen, siwen, borrowed from Anglo-Norman suer, siwer et al. and Old French sivre (“to follow after”) (modern French suivre), from Vulgar Latin *sequere (“to follow”), from Latin sequi. Cognate with Italian seguire and Spanish seguir. Doublet of segue. Related to suit.
sue.example: I plan to sue you for everything you have.
sue.exampleSense: To file a legal action against someone, generally a non-criminal (civil) action.

fermentation.o: From Middle English fermentacioun, from Latin fermentātiō, fermentātiōnem. By surface analysis, ferment + -ation.
fermentation.example: The universal fusion of races, languages, and customs, which had gone on for four centuries under Roman rule, had produced a corresponding fusion of creeds, an universal fermentation of human thought and faith.
fermentation.exampleSense: A state of agitation or excitement; a ferment.

anaerobic.o: From French anaérobie, from Ancient Greek ἀν- (an-, “not”) + ἀήρ (aḗr, “air”) + βίος (bíos, “life”) + -ic. By surface analysis, an- + aerobic.

imperialism.example: Though most of the cases here cover European encounters with non-Europeans, it is not the intention of the book to give the impression that genocide is a function of European colonialism and imperialism alone.
imperialism.exampleSense: The policy of forcefully extending a nation's authority by territorial gain or by the establishment of economic and political dominance over other nations.

firefly.o: Endocentric compound of fire + fly, because the insects glow; whence also lightning bug. Compare glow fly, glowworm, and lanternfly. Compare typologically Ancient Greek λαμπυρίς (lampurís, “glowworm”) (<+ πῦρ (pûr)).

concatenate.o: From the perfect passive participle stem of Latin concatēnāre (“to link or chain together”), from con- (“with”) + catēnō (“chain, bind”), from catēna (“a chain”).

sora.o: Early 19th-century sources observe that this term was in use in Virginia; presumably it is from an Indigenous American language of that area.

constitutional.o: PIE word *ḱóm From constitution + -al (suffix meaning ‘of or pertaining to’ forming adjectives). Constitution is derived from Middle English constitucioun, constitucion (“edict, law, ordinance, regulation, rule, statute; body of laws or rules, or customs; body of fundamental principles; principle or rule (of science); creation”) from Old French constitucion (modern French constitution), a learned borrowing from Latin cōnstitūtiō, cōnstitūtiōnem (“character, constitution, disposition, nature; definition; point in dispute; order, regulation; arrangement, system”), from cōnstituō (“to establish, set up; to confirm; to decide, resolve”) (from con- (prefix indicating a being or bringing together of several objects) + statuō (“to set up, station; to establish; to determine, fix”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *steh₂- (“to stand (up)”))) + -tiō (suffix forming nouns relating to actions or the results of actions), -tiōnem (accusative singular of -tiō).
constitutional.example: The Supreme Court ruled against the applicant and found the statute constitutional.
constitutional.exampleSense: In compliance with or valid under a legal or political constitution.

navel.o: From Middle English navel, navele, from Old English nafola, from Proto-West Germanic *nabulō, from Proto-Germanic *nabalô (“navel”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃nóbʰōl (“navel”), diminutive of *h₃nebʰ- (“hub; navel”). Cognates Cognate with West Frisian nâle (“navel”), Dutch navel (“navel”), German Nabel (“navel”), Vilamovian nowuł (“navel”), Yiddish נאָפּל (nopl, “navel”), Danish, Norwegian Bokmål, and Norwegian Nynorsk navle (“navel”), Icelandic nafli (“navel”), Swedish navel (“navel”); also Irish imleacán (“navel”), Scottish Gaelic ilmeag, imleag (“navel; nave”), Kashmiri ناب (nāb, “navel”), Latin umbilīcus (“navel”), Greek αφαλός (afalós), ομφαλός (omfalós, “navel”), Old Prussian nabis (“navel”), Armenian անիվ (aniv, “wheel”), Central Kurdish ناوک (nawik, “navel”), Persian ناف (nâf, “navel”), Sanskrit नाभि (nābhi, “navel; centre”), Doublet of omphalos. More at nave.
navel.example: This contributed to a rapid rise in planted acreage in northern California, especially in navels, which are more suited to growing conditions there.

nave.o:
noun: Ultimately from Latin nāvem, singular accusative of nāvis, possibly via a Romance source. Doublet of nef and nau.

noun: From Middle English nave, from Old English nafu, from Proto-West Germanic *nabu, from Proto-Germanic *nabō (compare Dutch naaf, German Nabe, Swedish nav), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃nebʰ- (“navel, hub”) (compare Latin umbō (“shield boss”), Latvian naba, Sanskrit नभ्य (nabhya)).

arcade.o: Unadapted borrowing from French arcade, from Italian arcata (“the arch of a bridge”), from Latin arcus (“an arc”). Not etymlogically related to Arcadia.
arcade.example: The walk down to the Underground station is equally easy, as you pass through the restored undercroft along an arcade of two-way spanning 'quadripartite' arches.

pandanus.o: From New Latin pandanus, from Malay pandan.
pandanus.example: A girl of fifteen, perhaps, was plaiting pandanus-leaf to make a hat, and an old woman was sitting on her haunches smoking a pipe.
pandanus.exampleSense: Any of various palm-like plants in the genus Pandanus.

juggle.o: From Middle English jogelen, partly a back-formation of Middle English jogeler (“juggler”), and partly a borrowing from Old French jogler, jongler (“to have fun with someone”), a conflation of Latin joculāri (“to jest; joke”) and Old French jangler (“to regale; entertain; have fun; trifle with; tease; mess around; gossip; boast; meddle”), from Frankish *jangalōn (“to chit-chat with; gossip”), akin to Middle Dutch jankelen (“to murmur; whisper; mumble; grumble”), frequentative of Middle Dutch janken (“to moan; groan; complain”). Related also to Middle Low German janken (“to sigh; moan; lament”), Dutch jengelen (“to whine; whimper”) Dutch janken (“to whine; wimper”).
juggle.exampleSense: To manipulate objects, such as balls, clubs, beanbags, rings, etc. in an artful or artistic manner. Juggling may also include assorted other circus skills such as the diabolo, devil sticks, hat, and cigar box manipulation as well.

juggler.o: From Middle English jogeler, jogelour, iogular, partly continuing Old English ġeogolere (“juggler; magician; wizard”) and partly from Anglo-Norman jogelour, jugelur, Old French jongleur (“juggler”), equivalent to juggle + -er. Doublet of jongleur.
juggler.example: Baraka was part trickster and part provocateur, a brilliant juggler of genres, ideas, and identities, whose career spanned nearly six decades.
juggler.exampleSense: Agent noun of juggle; one who either literally juggles objects, or figuratively juggles tasks.

modality.example: In general, pharmacotherapy is less effective as a single modality approach than psychotherapy when treating chronic depression with an Axis II disorder.
modality.exampleSense: A method of diagnosis or therapy.

dandelion.o: From Middle English dentdelyon, from Old French dent de lion (“lion's tooth”), also in Latin dēns leōnis, referring to the jagged shape of the plant's leaves. The term is now rare in French (together with liondent, calque from Germanic), but compare Spanish diente de león, Portuguese dente-de-leão, Italian dente di leone, German Löwenzahn, Norwegian Bokmål løvetann, Welsh dant y llew, all descendants, calques, or loan translations of the Latin term. First attested in the late 14th c. Displaced various words, including native Old English ǣġwyrt, native Middle English houndes-tooth, and English tell-time and swine's snout; and mostly displaced English cankerwort, monk's head, and pissabed.
dandelion.example: There are asexual variants among all sorts of creatures, including jellyfish, dandelions, lichens and lizards.
dandelion.exampleSense: Any of the several species of plant in the genus Taraxacum, characterised by yellow flower heads and notched, broad-ended leaves, especially the common dandelion (Taraxacum officinale).

fawn.o:
noun: From Middle English fawne, fowne, foun, from Old French faon, foon, feon, from Vulgar Latin *fētōnem, from Latin fētus (“offspring, young”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁(y)- (“to suckle, nurse”). Displaced native Old English hindċealf (literally “deer calf”). Doublet of fetus.

verb: From Middle English fawnen, from Old English fagnian, alternative form of fæġnian (“to celebrate”), whence Middle English fainen, English fain. Cognate with Old Norse fagna. See also fain.
fawn.example: You showed your teeth like apes, and fawned like hounds.
fawn.exampleSense: To seek favour by flattery and obsequious behaviour.

inferiority complex.o: Calque of German Minderwertigkeitskomplex (literally “complex of lesser value”), coined in 1920 by Alfred Adler.

haughtiness.o: From Middle English hauteynesse, hautenesse, from Middle English hautein (“proud, haughty”), from Old French hautain + Middle English -nesse. Reanalysed in Modern English as haughty + -ness.

haughty.o: From earlier hauty, haultic, with spelling change in imitation of English naughty and English high, from Middle English hautein, hautain (with -ein, -ain becoming -y through the form hautenesse standing for *hauteinnesse; see haughtiness), from Middle English haute (“self-important”), from Old French haut, hault (“high, lofty”), from Frankish *hauh, *hōh (“high, lofty, proud”) and Latin altus (“high, deep”).

bluster.o: From Middle English blusteren (“to wander about aimlessly”); however, apparently picking up the modern sense from Middle Low German blüstren (“to blow violently”; compare later Low German blustern, blistern). Related to blow, blast. Compare also Saterland Frisian bloasje (“to blow”), bruusje (“to bluster”).
bluster.example: When confronted by opposition his reaction was to bluster, which often cowed the meek.

fragility.o: Borrowed from Middle French fragilité, from Latin fragilitās. Doublet of frailty. Morphologically fragile + -ity.

unpretentious.example: Cheltenham Spa station had opened in June 1840 as Cheltenham, being renamed Cheltenham Spa (Lansdown) in February 1925 and taking on its modern name of Cheltenham Spa in January 1948 - an oddity in itself as its town is plain, unpretentious Cheltenham.

pretentiousness.example: Possibly her sheer pretentiousness, or that she knew everything about everything, or maybe because she treated her reporters like underoxygenated platypies.

pretentious.o: From French prétentieux, from prétention, from Latin praetēnsus (“false or hypocritical profession”), past participle of praetendō. Note that pretentious is spelled with a ‘t’, unlike related pretense, pretension. This is due to the French spelling: *-sious does not occur as an English suffix, though -sion and -tion both do.
pretentious.example: Their song titles are pretentious in the context of their basic lyrics.
pretentious.exampleSense: Marked by an unwarranted claim to importance or distinction.

windfall.o: From Middle English windfal, wyndfall, equivalent to wind + fall. Cognate with Middle High German wintval, wintfal, German Windfall.
windfall.example: They couldn't reach the branches, so they ate the windfalls.
windfall.exampleSense: A fruit that has fallen from a tree naturally, as from wind.

flamboyant.o: Borrowed from French flamboyant (“flaming, wavy”), participle of flamboyer (“to flame”), from Old French flamboier, from flambe (“flame”). The architectural style derives its name from the flame-like shapes in the tracery.
flamboyant.example: S. Pierre is a flamboyant church, the details passing into Renaissance.
flamboyant.exampleSense: Referring to the final stage of French Gothic architecture from the 14th to the 16th centuries.

paradigmatic.o: From French paradigmatique, from Ancient Greek πᾰρᾰδειγμᾰτῐκός (părădeigmătĭkós).

paradigm.o: From Middle English paradygme, from Late Latin paradīgma, from Ancient Greek παράδειγμα (parádeigma, “pattern”), from παραδείκνυμι (paradeíknumi, “I show [beside] or compare”) + -μα (-ma, suffix forming nouns concerning the results of actions). Doublet of paradigma.
paradigm.example: The paradigm of "to sing" is "sing, sang, sung". The verb "to ring" follows the same paradigm.
paradigm.exampleSense: A set of all forms which contain a common element, especially the set of all inflectional forms of a word or a particular grammatical category.

tune.o: From Middle English tune, an unexplained variant of tone, from Old French ton, from Latin tonus, from Ancient Greek τόνος (tónos, “a tone”). Doublet of tone, ton, and tonus.
tune.example: Tune to Channel 6 for all your favourite daytime shows.
tune.exampleSense: To adjust the frequency on a radio or TV set, so as to receive the desired channel.

fine-tune.example: Jim fine-tuned the radio until the sound was perfect.
fine-tune.exampleSense: To make small adjustments to (something) until it is optimal.

proctor.o: Inherited from Middle English procatour, procutour, contraction of procuratour; compare proxy. Doublet of procurator and procurer.

invigilator.o: From invigilate + -or, from Latin invigilatus, past participle of invigilo.

adversary.o: From Middle English adversarie, from Anglo-Norman aversaire (in Wace's Life of Saint Margaret) and Old French aversier, aversaire (French adversaire), from Latin adversārius, from adversus (“turned toward”). By surface analysis, adverse + -ary.
adversary.example: He prepared to fight his adversary.

adversarial.example: Canada uses an adversarial system of criminal justice, whereas France uses an inquisitorial model.
adversarial.exampleSense: In which issues are tried through the presentation of evidence and argument by adverse parties, with no or limited inquiry by the court's own initiative.

brocade.o: From Occitan brocada and Spanish and Portuguese brocado, influenced by French brocart, from Italian broccato, from brocco, ultimately from Gaulish.
brocade.example: … his desire to stand in brocade and sing Rhadames in Aida was like my eagerness to go far, far beyond fellow intellectuals of my generation who had lost the imaginative soul.
brocade.exampleSense: A thick heavy fabric into which raised patterns have been woven, originally in gold and silver; more recently any cloth incorporating raised, woven patterns.

temperament.o: Inherited from Middle English temperament, borrowed from Middle French tempérament, from Latin temperāmentum.
temperament.example: President Taft did not have the temperament either to dominate or to work with his Congress.
temperament.exampleSense: A person's usual manner of thinking, behaving or reacting.

hatred.o: From Middle English haterede, hatrede (“hatred”), from hate (“hate”) + -rede (“suffix denoting state or condition”), equivalent to hate + -red; compare sibred, Scots luferent. Related to Icelandic hatur (“hatred”).
hatred.example: Fears and hatreds pay no attention to facts.

malice.o: From Middle English malice, borrowed from Old French malice, from Latin malitia (“badness, bad quality, ill-will, spite”), from malus (“bad”).
malice.example: Robert Truswell may have been a belligerent and malicing man, a jury heard this morning during the trial of George Kieran Daunt.
malice.exampleSense: To intend to cause harm; to bear malice.

minivan.o: From mini- + van. First widely used in the 1980s, when this class of vehicles became widely popular as an alternative to station wagons (estate cars). Attested earlier in technical usage, usually as mini-van.

pickup.example: Hey, thanks for the drink, but if this is a pickup, I'm not interested.
pickup.exampleSense: An instance of approaching someone and engaging in romantic flirtation and courting with the intent to pursue romance, a date, or a sexual encounter.

disassemble.example: To perform the repair it was necessary to disassemble most of the mechanism.
disassemble.exampleSense: To take to pieces; to reverse the process of assembly.

hold.o:
verb: Derived from Middle English holden, derived from Old English healdan, derived from Proto-West Germanic *haldan, derived from Proto-Germanic *haldaną (“to tend, herd”), maybe derived from Proto-Indo-European *kel- (“to drive”). Doublet of halt. Cognates *West Frisian hâlde *Low German holden, holen *Dutch houden *German halten *Danish *Norwegian Bokmål holde *Norwegian Nynorsk halda. Compare Latin celer (“quick”), Tocharian B käl- (“to goad, drive”), Ancient Greek κέλλω (kéllō, “to drive”), Sanskrit कलयति (kalayati, “to impel”).

noun: Alteration (due to hold) of hole. Cognate with Dutch hol (“hole, cave, den, cavity, cargo hold”), Dutch holte (“cavity, hollow, den”).

adj: From Middle English hold, holde, from Old English hold (“gracious, friendly, kind”), from Proto-West Germanic *holþ, from Proto-Germanic *hulþaz (“favourable, gracious, loyal”), from Proto-Indo-European *kel- (“to tend, incline, bend, tip”). Cognate with German hold (“gracious, friendly, sympathetic, grateful”), Danish and Swedish huld (“fair, kindly, gracious”), Icelandic hollur (“faithful, dedicated, loyal”), German Huld (“grace, favour”).
hold.example: War has a hold on our cultural imaginations as an inevitable force, it is peace that has no benefactor.

psychiatrist.example: Pass the chalk. Dr. Levine was there with a friend and fellow psychiatrist (detect a pattern?), Alexa Albert, Coco’s mother, who squinted up into the sun as her daughter effortlessly sailed skyward. Dr. Albert is an acrophobe.
psychiatrist.exampleSense: A medical doctor specializing in psychiatry.

psychiatric.example: Some women with postpartum depression and thyroid imbalance may require antidepressants and psychiatric therapy.

psychiatry.o: Borrowed from French psychiatrie. First attested in 1846.

psychic.o: From Ancient Greek ψυχικός (psukhikós, “relative to the soul, spirit, mind”). Earlier referred to as "psychical"; or from Ancient Greek ψυχή (psukhḗ, “soul, mind, psyche”). First appeared (as substantive) 1871 and first records 1895.
psychic.example: You must be psychic—I was just about to say that.
psychic.exampleSense: Relating to or having the abilities of a psychic.

psychical.o: From Ancient Greek ψυχικός (psukhikós) + -al. By surface analysis, psyche + -ical.
psychical.example: Who could say where the fleshly impulse ceased, or the psychical impulse began?
psychical.exampleSense: Performed by or pertaining to the psyche (the mind, spirit, or both): mental, psychic.

matcha.o: Borrowed from Japanese 抹茶 (matcha), from 抹 (matsu, “to wipe, to rub”) + 茶 (cha, “tea”).

coefficient.o: From French coefficient. Coined by French mathematician François Viète. Or influenced by (New) Latin coefficient-, which is the stem of coefficiens, which is a substantivation of the present active participle of coefficio, which comes from co- and efficio.
coefficient.example: Nevertheless, there was some substance to the notion that acclaim and merit were coefficient.

regressive.o: Borrowed from Latin regressīvus, equivalent to regress + -ive.
regressive.example: He likes experimenting with flamboyant clothes! That’s it! It’s weird and regressive to think that means he is making a statement about his sexual orientation or gender identity. Let the man wear his “clowncore” jumpsuits in peace.
regressive.exampleSense: That tends to return, revert or regress.

chunk.o: Variant of chuck; or alternatively a diminutive of chump (“chunk; block”) + *-k (diminutive suffix) (compare hunk from hump, etc.). Also compare Dutch schonk.
chunk.example: He's chunked right before the next battle so he has to regen HP.
chunk.exampleSense: Deal a substantial amount of damage to an opponent.

quantification.o: Coined by Scottish philosopher Sir William Hamilton: "quantification of the predicate".

hug.o: From earlier hugge (“to embrace, clasp with the arms”) (1560), probably representing a conflation of huck (“to crouch, huddle down”) and Old Norse hugga (“to comfort, console”), from hugr (“mind, heart, thought”), from Proto-Germanic *hugiz (“mind, thought, sense”), cognate with Icelandic hugga (“to comfort”), Old English hyġe (“thought”) (whence high (Etymology 2)).
hug.example: They hugged for what seemed like an eternity.
hug.exampleSense: To embrace by holding closely, especially in the arms.

huggy.example: Gordy, who looks sort of like a bear cub, only not cute, is a very huggy person.
huggy.exampleSense: Tending to hug; affectionate in a physical way.

pouch.o: From Middle English pouche, poche, borrowed from Old Northern French pouche, from Old French poche, puche (whence French poche; compare also the Anglo-Norman variant poke), of Germanic origin: from Frankish *poka (“pouch”) (compare Middle Dutch poke, Old English pohha, dialectal German Pfoch). Doublet of poke; compare pocket.
pouch.example: He pouched his mouth, and reared himself up and swelled; but answered me not.

bolster.o: From Middle English bolster, bolstre, from Old English bolster (“pillow”), from Proto-West Germanic *bolstr, from Proto-Germanic *bulstraz (“pillow, cushion”). Cognate with Scots bowster (“bolster”), West Frisian bulster (“mattress”), Dutch bolster (“husk, shell”), German Polster (“bolster, pillow, pad”), Swedish bolster (“soft mattress, bolster”), Icelandic bólstur (“pillow”).
bolster.example: My health too has been better since you took away that Montero cap. I have left off cayenned eggs and such bolsters to discomfort.
bolster.exampleSense: That which supports or promotes; a catalyst.

shore up.o: From shore (“to provide with support”) + up. Shore is derived from Late Middle English shoren (“to prop, to support”) [and other forms], from shore (“a prop, a support”) [and other forms], + -en (suffix forming the infinitive form of verbs); while shore (noun) is from Middle Dutch schore, schare (“a prop, a stay”) (modern Dutch schoor), and Middle Low German schōre, schāre (“a prop, a stay; barrier; stockade”) (compare Old Norse skorða (“a prop, a stay”) (Norwegian skor, skorda)); further etymology unknown.
shore up.example: He needed something bold and dramatic to shore up his failing candidacy.
shore up.exampleSense: To reinforce or strengthen (something at risk of failure).

arbitrarily.example: The number or classes or potential offerers of satellite services should not be [limited] arbitrarily.

semi.o: The prefix semi- (from Latin) used as a noun.
semi.example: All night we couldn′t hear each other speak because of the sound of semis changing gear to get over the hill.
semi.exampleSense: A semi-trailer; a tractor-trailer; an eighteen-wheeler; an artic.

snoop.o: From Dutch snoepen (“to pry, eat in secret, sneak”). Related to Dutch and Low German snappen (“to bite, seize”), Dutch snavel (“beak, bill, pecker, neb”), German Schnabel (“beak, bill, mouth”). More at snap.
snoop.example: If I had not snooped on her, I wouldn't have found out that she lied about her degree.
snoop.exampleSense: To secretly spy on or investigate, especially into the private personal life of others.

mendacity.o: From Late Latin mendacitas, from Latin mendāx (“deceitful, deceptive, lying”) + -itās (suffix forming nouns indicating a state of being). Mendāx is derived from mentior (“to deceive, lie”) (from mēns, mentis (“mind; intellect; judgment, reasoning”), from Proto-Indo-European *méntis (“thought”)) + -āx (suffix forming adjectives expressing a tendency or inclination), or from Proto-Indo-European *mend- (“to fault”). By surface analysis, Latin mendāc- + -ity.
mendacity.example: So now the hard Brexiters say, with astonishingly cynical mendacity, that Britain would be better off going it alone.
mendacity.exampleSense: The fact or condition of being untruthful; dishonesty.

disc.o: From French disque, from Latin discus, from Ancient Greek δίσκος (dískos, “disk, quoit, platter”). Doublet of dais, desk, discus, dish, disk, and diskos.
disc.example: A coin is a disc of metal.
disc.exampleSense: A thin, flat, circular plate or similar object.

robustness.example: Robustness was considered to be an essential feature because of the comparatively high starting effort and the generally rough work for which the locomotives are to be used.

plain text.example: Using the sophisticated code was useless since the spy merely stole the plain text from the waste basket.
plain text.exampleSense: Text or any data that is to be encrypted (as opposed to ciphertext).

p: to carry, bear, or convey; to bring
transport.o: Inherited from Middle English transporten, a borrowing from Old French transporter (“carry or convey across”), from Latin trānsportāre (“to carry over, take across, carry, convey, remove, transport”), from trāns- (“across, over, to the farther side of”) + portō (“to bear, carry, convey, take”). By surface analysis, trans- (“beyond, across, through”) + port (“to carry, bear, or convey; to bring”).
transport.example: The transport of goods is not included in the price given on the website.

aggregate.o:
noun: From Middle English aggregat(e) (“a sum, unit, complex, aggregate”), borrowed from New Latin aggregātum (“an aggregate”), substantivized from the nominative neuter singular of aggregātus, the perfect passive participle of aggregō (“to flock together”), from ad- (“at, to, toward”)) + gregō (“to flock or group”), from grex (“flock”, greg- in compounds) + -ō (verb-forming suffix). See also egregious and gregarious. See also ag-.

adj: From Middle English aggregat(e) (“aggregated”, used as the past participle of aggregaten), see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and Etymology 1 for more.

verb: From Middle English aggregaten (“to aggregate”), from its earlier borrowed past participle aggregat(e) + -en (verb-forming suffix), from Latin aggregātus, see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and Etymology 1 for more.
aggregate.example: He explained that engineers had been able to examine the bridge visually, and had started surveying likely sites for access roads and where to place the heavyweight crawler crane. NR was also ordering the aggregates needed for the access roads.
aggregate.exampleSense: Solid particles of low aspect ratio added to a composite material, as distinguished from the matrix and any fibers or reinforcements; especially the gravel and sand added to concrete.

flit.o:
noun: From Middle English flitten, flytten, from Old Norse flytja (“to move”), from Proto-Germanic *flutjaną, from Proto-Indo-European *plewd- (“to flow; run”). Cognate Icelandic flytja, Swedish flytta, Danish flytte, Norwegian flytte, Faroese flyta. Compare also Saterland Frisian flitskje (“to rush; run quickly”).

noun: Short for fl(ow control un)it or fl(ow control dig)it.
flit.example: After this manner did the late Warden of Barchester Hospital accomplish his flitting, and change his residence.
flit.exampleSense: To move house (sometimes a sudden move to avoid debts).

flush.o:
noun: From Middle English flusshen, fluschen, of uncertain origin. Compare dialectal flusk (“to fly at, startle a bird out of the bush”) and flusker (“to flutter, fly irregularly”). Perhaps related to Middle English flasshen, flasschen, flaschen, see flash; or a Middle English blend of flowen (“to flow”) + guschen (“to gush”). Compare Saterland Frisian flutskje, German Low German flutschen, German flutschen.

adj: Same as Etymology 3, according to The American Heritage Dictionary of the English Language.

noun: Probably from Etymology 1, according to The American Heritage Dictionary of the English Language.

noun: Various similar terms are found in dialectal English and Scots as flash and flosh (older Scots flosche), and the variation goes back to Middle English flushe, flosche, flashe, flaske. The DSL suggests a relation between flush, English flash (“pool”), and Middle English flosche, but influence from other water-related senses of flush and flash is also conceivable.

noun: Probably from Middle French flus (“flow”), cognate with flux.
flush.example: There must be somebody home: I just heard the toilet flushing.
flush.exampleSense: To be cleansed by being flooded with generous quantities of water.

firmware.o: From firm + -ware, coined in an article in 1967 as an intermediary term between hardware and software.

entity.o: From the Medieval Latin entitās, from ēns (“being”) (stem: ent-) + -tās (compare essentia), see there for more information.
entity.example: The organisational and administrative tasks involved in welding the railways into a single entity have also received much publicity.
entity.exampleSense: That which has a distinct existence as an individual unit, often used for organizations which have no physical form.

multiplex.o: Learned borrowing from Latin multiplex, from multi- + -plex.

coherent.o: From Middle French coherent, from Latin cohaērēns, from co- + haereō. By surface analysis, cohere + -ent.
coherent.example: Perhaps Khrushchev did have a coherent plan in mind at the time he placed the nuclear missiles in Cuba.

acronym.o: Borrowed from German Akronym (from Ancient Greek ἄκρον (ákron, “end; peak”) + ὄνυμα (ónuma, “name”)), modelled after Homonym and Synonym, first attested in German in the early 1900s and in English in 1940. By surface analysis, acro- (prefix meaning ‘beginning; high’) + -onym (suffix meaning ‘name’)
acronym.example: Pee-gee-enn. It's an acronym, that's what it is. That's what they call words made up of initials.
acronym.exampleSense: An abbreviation formed by the initial letters of other words. Generally such abbreviations, including those pronounced as individual letters (initialisms such as "TNT").

wise.o:
adj: From Middle English wys, wyse, from Old English wīs (“wise”), from Proto-Germanic *wīsaz (“knowledgeable, wise”), from Proto-Indo-European *wéydos (“seeing; knowledge”), from *weyd- (“to see”). Cognates Cognate with West Frisian wiis (“wise”), Dutch wijs (“wise”), German weis, weise (“wise”), Low German wies (“wise; clever”), Danish, Norwegian Bokmål, Norwegian Nynorsk, and Swedish vis (“wise”), Icelandic vís (“wise; certain”), Gothic *𐍅𐌴𐌹𐍃 (*weis, “wise”); also Irish fios (“knowledge; information”), Manx fys (“knowledge; information”), Scottish Gaelic fhios, fios (“knowledge; information”), Welsh gwys, gwŷs (“citation, summons”), Latin videō (“to look, perceive, see; to note, observe; to comprehend, understand”), Greek είδος (eídos, “form, kind, type”), Albanian vizë (“line, stripe, track; dash”), Latvian veids (“form, kind, mode, type”), Lithuanian veidas (“face; appearance, aspect, look”), Belarusian ве́даць (vjédacʹ, “to know”), Bulgarian вям (vjam, “to know”), Czech vědět (“to know”), Polish wiedzieć (“to know”), Russian ве́дать (védatʹ, “to know”), Serbo-Croatian vedeti, viedieti (“to know”), Slovak vedieť (“to know”), Slovene vedeti (“to know”), Ukrainian ві́дати (vídaty, “to know”), Armenian գիտեմ (gitem, “I know”), գիտենալ (gitenal), գիտնալ (gitnal, “to know”), Avestan 𐬬𐬀𐬉𐬛 (vaēd, “find”), 𐬬𐬌𐬛 (vid, “to know”), Persian نوید (navid / nawīd, nuwēd, “invitation; annunciation; good news”), Tocharian A ime (“awareness, consciousness, memory, thought”), Tocharian B īme (“awareness, consciousness, memory, thought”), ūwe (“educated, learned, knowledgeable”), Sanskrit वेदस् (vedas, “knowledge, science; property, wealth”). Compare wit.

noun: From Middle English wise, from Old English wīse, from Proto-Germanic *wīsō. Cognate with Dutch wijze, German Weise, Norwegian vis, Swedish visa, vis, Italian guisa, Spanish guisa. Compare -wise. Doublet of guise.

verb: From Middle English wisen (“to advise, direct”), from Old English wisian (“to show the way, guide, direct”), from Proto-West Germanic *wīsōn, from Proto-Germanic *wīsōną (“to show the way, dispense knowledge”), from Proto-Indo-European *weyd- (“to know”). Compare Dutch wijzen (“to indicate, point out”), German weisen (“to show, indicate”), Danish and Norwegian Bokmål vise (“to show”), Norwegian Nynorsk visa (“to show”).
wise.example: Be careful: the boss is wise to your plan to call out sick.

shim.o:
noun: Unknown; from Kent. Originally a piece of iron attached to a plow; sense of “thin piece of wood” from 1723, sense of “thin piece of material used for alignment or support” from 1860.

noun: Blend of she + him.
shim.example: The second adjustment [to a door that keeps swinging open] will require the screws to be loosened, and a shim or packing piece pushed behind the hinge to bring it into line.
shim.exampleSense: A thin piece of material, sometimes tapered, used for alignment or support.

morose.o: From French morose, from Latin mōrōsus (“particular, scrupulous, fastidious, self-willed, wayward, capricious, fretful, peevish”), from mōs (“way, custom, habit, self-will”). See moral.
morose.example: If there is any boy or man who loves to be melancholy and morose, and who cannot enter with kindly sympathy into the regions of fun, let me seriously advise him to shut my book and put it away. It is not meant for him.
morose.exampleSense: Sullen, gloomy; showing a brooding ill humour.

clockwork.example: Many contrivances for making model horses move up and down as on roundabouts were patented in 1887, and toy horses pulling toy carts were made to imitate galloping by means of clockwork.
clockwork.exampleSense: A mechanism powered by a coiled spring and regulated by some form of escapement; the power is transmitted through toothed gearwheels and used to drive a mechanical clock, toy, or other device.

carrousel.o: Alternative spelling of carousel. From French carrousel, from Italian carosello, from Sicilian caruseḍḍu and/or Neapolitan carusiello. Uncertain. Some suggested a derivation from carro (“cart”), from Latin carrus, but this does not fit the criteria of an appropriate morphological reconstruction. Not believed to be related to carousal.

recurrence.o: From recurrent + -ence, cognate with Latin recurrentia, from recurrēns (“returning back, recurring”), form of recurrō (“to return, to recur”) (English recur).
recurrence.example: I shall insensibly go on from a rare to a frequent recurrence to the dangerous preparations.
recurrence.exampleSense: The instance of recurring; frequent occurrence.

recurrent.o: From Latin recurrens, present participle of recurrere. Morphologically recur + -ent.
recurrent.example: The patient complained of recurrent chest pain.

implicate.o:
verb: First attested in the 15th century, in Middle English; inherited from Middle English implicaten (poorly attested), from implicat(e) (“wrapped, entwined; involved, connected (with)”, possibly also used as the past participle of implicaten) + -en (verb-forming suffix), borrowed from Latin implicātus, perfect passive participle of implicō (“to entangle, involve”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from plicō (“to fold”). Doublet of imply and employ.

noun: First attested in the first part of the 15ᵗʰ century, in Middle English; inherited from Middle English implicat(e) (“wrapped, entwined; incolved, connected (with)”), see -ate (adjective-forming suffix), -ate (noun-forming suffix) and Etymology 1 for more.
implicate.example: The evidence implicates involvement of top management in the scheme.
implicate.exampleSense: To show to be connected or involved in an unfavorable or criminal way.

tera-.o: From Ancient Greek τέρας (téras, “monster”). Also from Ancient Greek τέτταρες (téttares, “four”), by analogy with tetra- for being the fourth power of 10³. Doublet of terato-.

infinity.o: From Middle English infinite, from Old French infinité, from Latin īnfīnitās (“unlimitedness”), from negative prefix in- (“not”), + fīnis (“end”), + noun of state suffix -tās.

memorial.o: From Late Latin memoriale, neuter of memorialis. By surface analysis, memory + -ial.
memorial.example: This succession of Aspirate, Soft, and Hard, may be expressed by the memorial word ASH.

bafflement.example: The cartoon characters on the front cover, the irritatingly meaningless track names . . . make it seem like a concept album about global warming for kids. Since the lyrics remain a bafflement, it might well be.
bafflement.exampleSense: Something that causes a state of confusion or puzzlement.

magnificent.o: From Middle English magnificent, from Middle French magnificent, from Latin magnificentior, comparative of magnificus (“great in deeds or sentiment, noble, splendid, etc.”), from magnus (“great”) + -ficēns, a form of -ficiēns, the regular form, in compounds, of faciēns, a participle of facere (“to do”).
magnificent.example: “Do I fidget you ?” he asked apologetically, whilst his long bony fingers buried themselves, string, knots, and all, into the capacious pockets of his magnificent tweed ulster.
magnificent.exampleSense: Grand, elegant or splendid in appearance.

magnific.o: From Middle French magnifique, and its source, Latin magnificus. Doublet of magnifico.

leak.o: From Middle English leken (“to let water in or out”), from Old English *lecan (“to leak”), Middle Dutch leken (“to leak, drip”) or Old Norse leka (“to leak, drip”); all from Proto-Germanic *lekaną (“to leak, drain”), from Proto-Indo-European *leg- (“to leak”). Cognate with Dutch lekken (“to leak”), German lechen, lecken (“to leak”), Danish lække (“to leak”), Swedish läcka (“to leak”), Norwegian Bokmål lekke (“to leak”), Faroese, Icelandic, and Norwegian Nynorsk leka (“to leak”). Related also to Old English leċċan (“to water, wet”), Albanian lag, lak (“to damp, make wet”). See also leach, lake. (divulgation, disclosure of information): Compare typologically Bulgarian изтичане (iztičane), Polish przeciek, Russian уте́чка (utéčka) (akin to течь impf or f (tečʹ)).
leak.example: The leaks by Chelsea Manning showed the secrets of the US military.
leak.exampleSense: A divulgation, or disclosure, of information previously held secret.

interrelate.example: The inability of the gay movement as a whole to interrelate AIDS work with the many other items on its political agenda left vast segments of the lesbian and gay community sitting on the sidelines wondering how and why to plug in.
interrelate.exampleSense: To form relationships between multiple things.

interpolate.o: From Latin interpolātus, perfect passive participle of interpolō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix). Compare French interpoler.
interpolate.example: When interpolating an explanatory gloss, please enclose it in square brackets to make clear that it is interpolated.
interpolate.exampleSense: To introduce (something) between other things; especially to insert (possibly spurious) words into a text.

shuffle.o: Originally the same word as scuffle, and properly a frequentative of shove.
shuffle.example: He shuffled out of the room.
shuffle.exampleSense: To move in a slovenly, dragging manner; to drag or scrape the feet in walking or dancing.

dilate.o:
verb: First attested in 1393, in Middle English; inherited from Middle English dilaten, from Old French dilater, from Latin dīlātō (“to spread out”), from dī- + lātus (“wide”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix). Doublet of dilatate.

verb: First attested in 1399, in Middle English; inherited from Middle English dilaten (“to delay, tarry”), borrowed from Latin dīlātus, perfect passive participle of Latin dīfferō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)). If so, Doublet of defer and differ; see also infer, relate and refer, collate and confer, delate and defer, as well as prefer and prelate among others. Alternatively, from Latin dīlātō, see Etymology

adj: First attested in 1471, in Middle English; borrowed from Latin dīlātus, see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and Etymology 2 for more.
dilate.example: His heart dilates and glories in his strength.
dilate.exampleSense: To become wider or larger; to expand.
