First attested circa second half of 14th century, from the similarity between the sizzling sound of food cooking in a frying pan and that of musical pipes, from Canterbury Tales http://www.gutenberg.org/etext/2383 by Geoffrey Chaucer: :: "He singeth brokking¹ as a nightingale. / He sent her piment, mead, and spiced ale, / And wafers² piping hot out of the glede³: / And, for she was of town, he proffer'd meed." :: ¹ quavering, ² cakes, ³ coals

piping.o: present participle and gerund of pipe. From Middle English pīpe, pype (“hollow cylinder or tube used as a conduit or container; duct or vessel of the body; musical instrument; financial records maintained by the English Exchequer, pipe roll”), from Old English pīpe (“pipe (musical instrument); the channel of a small stream”), from Proto-West Germanic *pīpā. Reinforced by Vulgar Latin *pīpa, from Latin pipire, pipiare, pipare, from pīpiō (“to chirp, peep”), of imitative origin. Displaced native Old English fealh and Old English þrūh. Doublet of fife. Cognate with Dutch pijp, German Pfeife, Danish pibe, Norwegian Bokmål and Norwegian Nynorsk pipe, Swedish pipa, Faroese and Icelandic pípa. The “storage container” and “liquid measure” senses are derived from Middle English pīpe (“large storage receptacle, particularly for wine; cask, vat; measure of volume”), from pīpe (above) and Old French pipe (“liquid measure”). In specific contexts, calques similar units of measure such as Portuguese pipa. The verb is from Middle English pīpen, pypyn (“to play a pipe; to make a shrill sound; to speak with a high-pitched tone”), from Old English pīpian (“to pipe”).
piping.example: His piping voice could be heard above the hubbub.

pipe.o: From Middle English pīpe, pype (“hollow cylinder or tube used as a conduit or container; duct or vessel of the body; musical instrument; financial records maintained by the English Exchequer, pipe roll”), from Old English pīpe (“pipe (musical instrument); the channel of a small stream”), from Proto-West Germanic *pīpā. Reinforced by Vulgar Latin *pīpa, from Latin pipire, pipiare, pipare, from pīpiō (“to chirp, peep”), of imitative origin. Displaced native Old English fealh and Old English þrūh. Doublet of fife. Cognate with Dutch pijp, German Pfeife, Danish pibe, Norwegian Bokmål and Norwegian Nynorsk pipe, Swedish pipa, Faroese and Icelandic pípa. The “storage container” and “liquid measure” senses are derived from Middle English pīpe (“large storage receptacle, particularly for wine; cask, vat; measure of volume”), from pīpe (above) and Old French pipe (“liquid measure”). In specific contexts, calques similar units of measure such as Portuguese pipa. The verb is from Middle English pīpen, pypyn (“to play a pipe; to make a shrill sound; to speak with a high-pitched tone”), from Old English pīpian (“to pipe”).
pipe.example: In former days every tavern of repute kept such a room for its own select circle—a club, or society, of habitués, who met every evening for a pipe and a cheerful glass.
pipe.exampleSense: Meanings relating to a smoking implement. A hollow stem with a bowl at one end used for smoking, especially a tobacco pipe but also including various other forms such as a water pipe.

well.o:
adv: From Middle English wel, wal, wol, wele, from Old English wel (“well, abundantly, very, very easily, very much, fully, quite, nearly”), from Proto-Germanic *wela, *wala (“well”, literally “as wished, as desired”), from Proto-Indo-European *welh₁- (“wish, desire”). Cognates Cognate with Yola vella, waal, wel, well, wull (“well”), Cimbrian boll, bóol (“well”), Dutch wel (“well”), German wohl, wol, woll (“well”), Danish, Icelandic, Norwegian Bokmål, and Norwegian Nynorsk vel (“well”), Faroese væl (“well”), Swedish väl, waͤl (“well”), Gothic 𐍅𐌰𐌹𐌻𐌰 (waila, “well”). Related to will.

noun: From Middle English welle, from Old English wielle (“well”), from Proto-West Germanic *wallijā, from Proto-Germanic *wallijǭ (“well, swirl, wave”), from Proto-Indo-European *welH- (“to turn; wind; roll”). Cognate with West Frisian wel (“well”), Dutch wel (“well”), German Low German Well (“well”), German Welle (“wave”), Danish væld (“well; spring”), Swedish väl (“well”), Icelandic vella (“boiling; bubbling; eruption”).

verb: From Middle English wellen, from a merger of Old English weallan (intransitive) and wiellan (transitive), both meaning “to boil.” Further from Proto-Germanic *wallaną and *wallijaną. Doublet of wall. Cognate with German wallen (“boil, seethe”), Danish vælde (“gush”), Norwegian Nynorsk vella and outside Germanic, with Albanian valë (“hot, boiling”).
well.example: The woman said unto him, Sir, thou hast nothing to draw with, and the well is deep.
well.exampleSense: A hole sunk into the ground as a source of water, oil, natural gas or other fluids.

acquisition.o: From Middle English, borrowed from Old French acquisicion, from Latin acquisītiō, from acquīrō, acquīrere; equivalent to acquire + -ition.
acquisition.example: The acquisition of sports equipment can be fun in itself.
acquisition.exampleSense: The act or process of acquiring.

merger.o:
noun: From merge + -er.

noun: From Anglo-Norman merger (verb used as noun).

paella.o: Borrowed from Catalan paella (“pot; pan”), from Old French paelle, from Latin patella (“plate, small pan”). Doublet of patella and possibly pail.

pubescent.o: From Middle French pubescent, from Latin pubescens (“to become hairy, downy, or an adult”).

diagonal.o: From Middle French diagonal, from Latin diagōnālis, from Ancient Greek διαγώνιος (diagṓnios, “from angle to angle”), from διά (diá, “across”) + γωνία (gōnía, “angle”).
diagonal.example: The visitors' undoing was caused by a diagonal ball from the right which was nodded into the six-yard area by Ian Evatt and finished off by Campbell.
diagonal.exampleSense: Having a slanted or oblique direction.

tensor.o: Borrowed from New Latin tensor (“that which stretches”), equivalent to tense + -or. Anatomical sense from 1704. Introduced in the 1840s by William Rowan Hamilton as an algebraic quantity unrelated to the modern notion of tensor. The contemporary mathematical meaning was introduced (as German Tensor) by Woldemar Voigt (1898) and adopted in English from 1915 (in the context of general relativity), obscuring the earlier Hamiltonian sense. The mathematical object is so named because an early application of tensors was the study of materials stretching under tension. (See, for example, Cauchy stress tensor on Wikipedia.Wikipedia )
tensor.example: The tensor #92;alpha#95;#123;ij#125; should really be called a “tensor of second rank,” because it has two indexes. A vector—with one index—is a tensor of the first rank, and a scalar—with no index—is a tensor of zero rank.
tensor.exampleSense: A mathematical object that describes linear relations on scalars, vectors, matrices and other algebraic objects, and is represented as a multidimensional array.

sidebar.example: May we have a moment to discuss your proposition? Sidebar!
sidebar.exampleSense: A short conversation between a smaller portion of a group held outside the hearing of the rest of the group.

potato.o: Borrowed from Spanish patata, itself borrowed from Taíno batata (“sweet potato”).
potato.example: Do not let your child have potato for another year; he will probably take milk well enough after he is weaned.
potato.exampleSense: Solanum tuberosum or its edible starchy tuber.

reconstruction.example: The reconstruction of the medieval bridge began last year.
reconstruction.exampleSense: The act of restoring something to an earlier state.

reconstruct.example: [...] after the original Victorian station was demolished and then entombed in concrete in the 1960s, Birmingham New Street became a byword for the worst excesses of the much-loathed Brutalist architecture so widely used to reconstruct inner-city post-war Britain.

carbonate.o:
noun: From French carbonate, equivalent of carbon + -ate (“suffix used for salts of acids ending in -ic”).

verb: From carbon + -ate (verb-forming suffix).

glomerate.o: Borrowed from Latin glomerātus, perfect passive participle of glomero (“to glomerate”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

glom.o:
verb: From Scottish English glom, glaum (“to grab or snatch at”), a variant of clam, claum (“to clutch, seize, grasp, reach for”), from Middle English *clammen, from Old English clæmman (“to pinch, press, inclose”), from Proto-West Germanic *klammjan. Related to clamp.

verb: Variant of glaum, gloom (“to frown, scowl, stare at”).
glom.example: Bisexuals, she said, glommed onto lesbians because they feared their fathers, or had been devastated by ex-boyfriends.
glom.exampleSense: To grab hold of, seize; catch, grab or latch onto.

agglomerate.o: From Latin agglomerātus, past participle of agglomerō (“to wind into a ball”), from ad- (“to”) + glomerō (“to wind into a ball”), from glomus (“a ball”), akin to globus (“a ball”).

monk.o:
noun: From Middle English monk, from Old English munuc, from Proto-West Germanic *munik, from Late Latin monicus, variant of monachus, from Ancient Greek μοναχός (monakhós, “single, solitary”), from μόνος (mónos, “alone”).

noun: By shortening.
monk.example: Good people, if you're ever short of a job, don't take up monking for a living.

commander.o: From Middle English comaundour, commaunder, comaunder, borrowed from Old French comandeor, cumandeur, from comander. By surface analysis, command + -er. See command.
commander.example: Shepard: I don't take orders from you anymore, remember?
commander.exampleSense: A naval officer whose rank is above that of a lieutenant commander and below that of captain.

battalion.o: From Middle French battaillon (modern French bataillon).

sinuous.example: We followed every bend of the sinuous river.
sinuous.exampleSense: Having curves in alternate directions; meandering.

anaesthetic.o: Alternative spelling of anesthetic. From an- + esthetic, or Latinized form of Ancient Greek ἀναίσθητος (anaísthētos, “insensible”) + -ic, from ἀν- (an-, “un-”) + αἰσθητικός (aisthētikós, “perceptible”).

nunnery.o: From Middle English nonnery, nonnerie, equivalent to nun + -ery. (brothel): Compare typologically Czech nevěstinec (< nevěstka < nevěsta).
nunnery.example: Get thee to a nunnery, why wouldst thou be a breeder of sinners?
nunnery.exampleSense: The residence of a female religious community, a monastery for nuns.

indispensable.o: Borrowed from Middle French indispensable, from Medieval Latin indispensābilis, corresponding to in- + dispensable.
indispensable.example: An indispensable component of a heart-healthy diet.
indispensable.exampleSense: Absolutely necessary or requisite; that one cannot do without.

dispensable.example: The difference in absorption rate is not surprising since whey has a high percentage of indispensable amino acids, which are absorbed more rapidly than dispensable amino acids.
dispensable.exampleSense: Not essential to be taken in as part of an organism's diet, as it can be synthesized de novo.

mint.o:
noun: From Middle English mynt, münet (“money, coin”), from Old English mynet (“coin”), from late Proto-West Germanic *munit, from Latin monēta (“place for making coins, coined money”), from the temple of Juno Moneta (named for Monēta mother of the Muses), where coins were made. Doublet of money and manat. The verb is from the noun; Old English mynetian (“to mint”) is a parallel formation.

noun: From Middle English mynte, from Old English minte (“mint plant”), from Proto-West Germanic *mintā (“mint”), from Latin menta, probably from a lost Mediterranean language either through Ancient Greek μίνθη (mínthē), μίνθα (míntha) or directly. Akin to Old Norse minta (“mint”). Doublet of mentha.

verb: From Middle English minten, from Old English myntan (“to mean, intend, purpose, determine, resolve”), from Proto-West Germanic *muntijan (“to think, consider”), from Proto-Indo-European *men-, *mnā- (“to think”). Cognate with Saterland Frisian mintsje, muntsje (“to aim, target”), Dutch munten (“to aim at, target”), German Low German münten (“to aim at”), German münzen (“to aim at”), Dutch monter (“cheerful, gladsome, spry”), Gothic 𐌼𐌿𐌽𐍃 (muns, “thought, opinion”), Old English munan (“to be mindful of, consider, intend”). More at mind.
mint.example: Beeple’s collaged JPG was made, or “minted,” in February as a “nonfungible token,” or NFT.

mix up.example: She mixed up peat moss, humus, and compost to make potting soil.
mix up.exampleSense: To mix or blend thoroughly and completely.

conspiracy.o: From Middle English conspiracie, from Anglo-Norman conspiracie, from Latin cōnspīrātiō, from conspire + -acy.
conspiracy.example: Conspiracies, like all other exercises of human ingenuity, are of very different kinds. The gloomy plots arranged in old Italian halls...
conspiracy.exampleSense: An agreement or arrangement between multiple parties to do something harmful, immoral or subversive; an instance of collusion.

conspicuous.o: From Latin conspicuus (“visible, striking”), from cōnspicere (“to notice”), from con- (“with, together”) + specere (“to look at”).
conspicuous.example: He was conspicuous by his absence.

carousel.o: From French carrousel, from Italian carosello, from Sicilian caruseḍḍu and/or Neapolitan carusiello. Uncertain. Some suggested a derivation from carro (“cart”), from Latin carrus, but this does not fit the criteria of an appropriate morphological reconstruction. Not believed to be related to carousal.
carousel.example: After collecting his suitcase at the baggage carousel, he left the airport.
carousel.exampleSense: A continuously revolving device for item delivery.

potty.example: The noise that the neighbour's kids were making was driving Fred potty.

decadent.o: From French décadent, a back-formation from décadence (see -ent), from Medieval Latin dēcadentia, from Late Latin dēcadēns, present participle of dēcadō, dēcidō (“sink, fall; perish”), from Latin dē- + cadō (“fall”).
decadent.example: As societies grow decadent, the language grows decadent, too. Words are used to disguise, not to illuminate, action: you liberate a city by destroying it. Words are to confuse, so that at election time people will solemnly vote against their own interests.
decadent.exampleSense: Characterized by moral or cultural decline.

decadence.o: From French décadence, from Medieval Latin decadentia (“decay”), from *decadens (“decaying”), present participle of *decadere (“to decay”); see decay.

salad.o: PIE word *sḗh₂l From Middle English salade, from Old French salade, borrowed from Northern Italian salada, salata (compare insalata), from Vulgar Latin *salāta, from *salāre, from Latin saliō, from sal (“salt”). Vegetables were seasoned with brine or salty oil-and-vinegar dressings during Roman times.
salad.example: Lafeu. ’Twas a good lady, ’twas a good lady: we may pick a thousand salads ere we light on such another herb.
salad.exampleSense: A food made primarily of a mixture of raw or cold ingredients, typically vegetables, usually served with a dressing such as vinegar or mayonnaise.

taxicab.o: Shortened from taximeter cab, equivalent to taxi + cab.

taxis.o:
noun: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek τάξις (táxis, “arrangement, order”).

noun: See taxi.

taxi.o: Shortened from taximeter cab, taximeter (“automatic meter that records distance and fare”) from French taximètre, from German Taxameter (whence also English taxameter), coined from Medieval Latin taxa (“tax, charge”). More at tax, task. The aviation sense originally derived from a slang term for training aircraft used for practicing ground operations, which were said to drive around the airfield like a taxicab, and subsequently applied to all aircraft ground movements.
taxi.example: Seat belts must be kept fastened during taxi, takeoff, turbulence, and landing.
taxi.exampleSense: The movement of an aircraft across an airport's surface under its own power; a phase of aircraft operation involving this movement.

cab.o:
noun: Clipping of cabriolet.

noun: From Hebrew קב (káv).

noun: Clipping of cabinet.

noun: Clipping of cabernet sauvignon
cab.example: Dad looked up to catch sight of the man in the crane’s cab. He knew that DEVILISH smirk anywhere. It was Fingers.
cab.exampleSense: A similar compartment in other vehicles.

taximeter.o: Borrowed from French taximètre, from German Taxameter, coined from Medieval Latin taxa (“tax, charge”), from Proto-Indo-European *teh₂g- (“to touch, handle”).

prepossessing.o: From prepossess + -ing. Attested in 1610s with the meaning of "getting possession of (ground or land) beforehand". The meaning "to possess (a person) beforehand with a feeling, notion, etc." developed in 1630s, acquiring by the 40s of the same century the meaning of "to cause (someone) to have a favorable opinion of something, preoccupy the mind or heart of".
prepossessing.example: He was a frank, prepossessing fellow, but I saw that he could add nothing to his original account.
prepossessing.exampleSense: Tending to invite favor; attracting confidence, favor, esteem, or love; attractive

daisy.o: From Middle English dayesye, from Old English dæġes ēage (“daisy”, literally “day's eye”) due to the flowers closing their blossoms during night. The rhyming slang comes from daisy roots for boots.
daisy.example: Then Dan drew the sheath-knife and tested the edge of it on the gunwale.

thumbs-up.example: He stood outside the dressing room and thumbs-upped or thumbs-downed each choice.
thumbs-up.exampleSense: To approve with a thumbs-up sign.

slap.o: From Middle English slappen, of uncertain origin, possibly imitative. Compare Low German Slappe (“slap”), whence also German Schlappe (“defeat”). Compare also Italian sleppa (“slap”).
slap.example: He gave me a friendly slap on the back as a sign of camaraderie.
slap.exampleSense: A blow, especially one given with the open hand, or with something broad and flat.

flick.o: From Middle English flykke (“light blow or stroke”). Later uses apparently interpreted as a back-formation from flicker. The use of flick to mean a film or movie derives from the fact that early films had a low frame rate, thus causing the film to "flick" rapidly when projected onto a screen.
flick.example: Using her hands like windshield wipers, she tried to flick snow away from her mouth. When she clawed at her chest and neck, the crumbs maddeningly slid back onto her face. She grew claustrophobic.
flick.exampleSense: To move or hit (something) with a short, quick motion.

whiskey.o:
noun: Variant of usque, abbreviation of usquebaugh, from Irish uisce beatha, calque of Medieval Latin aqua vītae (“water of life”). Compare akvavit, aquavit, aqua vitae, eau de vie, and water of life from the same source and vodka from a Russian diminutive for water in reference to the dilution of pure grain spirits.

noun: From whisk + ey.

barber.o: PIE word *bʰardʰéh₂ From Middle English barbour, from Anglo-Norman barbour, from Old French barbeor, from barbe (“beard”), from Latin barba.
barber.example: There's also a barber's shop and that staple of railway stations up and down the UK - a WH Smith.
barber.exampleSense: A person whose profession is cutting the hair and beards of usually male customers.

act up.example: Acting up is always recommended when you find yourself under a new boss.
act up.exampleSense: To perform the duties of an appointment senior to that actually held; to deputise for a superior.

elf.o: From Middle English elf, from Old English ielf, ælf, from Proto-West Germanic *albi, from Proto-Germanic *albiz. Ultimately probably derived from Proto-Indo-European *h₂elbʰós (“white”). Doublet of alf, awf, and oaf. The modern fantasy literature sense was popularised by the works of J.R.R. Tolkien.
elf.example: Eve, Danish legend of her concealing her unwashed children, from whom come elfs, trolls, &c.
elf.exampleSense: A luminous spirit presiding over nature and fertility and dwelling in the world of Álfheim (Elfland). Compare angel, nymph, fairy.

humiliation.o: From Middle French humiliation, from Late Latin humiliātiō, from humiliāre (“to humiliate”); see humiliate. Equivalent to humiliate + -ion.
humiliation.example: They listened to the sound of Fanny’s retreating footsteps. ‘Well, well!’ said Marcus. ‘Oh, take no notice Jess. You know what our Frances Maud is like! It’s nothing to cry about!’ To her humiliation Jessamy found there were tears trickling down her cheeks.
humiliation.exampleSense: The state of being humiliated, humbled or reduced to lowliness or submission.

humiliating.o: present participle and gerund of humiliate. Borrowed from Late Latin humiliātus, perfect passive participle of humiliō (“to abase, humble”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from Latin humilis (“lowly, humble”), from humus (“ground; earth, soil”); see humble.
humiliating.example: The most rapid and most seductive transition in all human nature is that which attends the palliation of a ravenous appetite. There is something humiliating about it.
humiliating.exampleSense: Liable to humiliate, degrade, shame or embarrass someone.

humiliated.o: simple past and past participle of humiliate. Borrowed from Late Latin humiliātus, perfect passive participle of humiliō (“to abase, humble”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from Latin humilis (“lowly, humble”), from humus (“ground; earth, soil”); see humble.

humiliate.o: Borrowed from Late Latin humiliātus, perfect passive participle of humiliō (“to abase, humble”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from Latin humilis (“lowly, humble”), from humus (“ground; earth, soil”); see humble.

humility.o: From Middle English humilite, from Old French (h)umilité, from Latin humilitas (“lowness, meanness, baseness, in Late Latin humility”), from humilis (“low, lowly, humble, earth”). Equivalent to humble + -ity, with /mb/ reduced to /m/ (compare plumbing). Displaced native Old English ēaþmōdnes. Doublet of omertà.
humility.example: She had established a character for humility, discretion, noiselessness and religion which Mrs. Piper greatly regretted losing.
humility.exampleSense: The characteristic of being humble; humbleness in character and behavior.

fast-food.example: Estimate the number of calories in a fast-food that has 14g of fat.

stay-at-home.example: Both the hardy long-distance travelers and the butterfly stay-at-homes face continual danger from predators.
stay-at-home.exampleSense: A person or animal that prefers to stay at home rather than socialize or travel.

husband.o: Inherited from Middle English husbonde, from Old English hūsbonda, from hūs + bonda. Calque of Old Norse húsbóndi. By surface analysis, house + bond.
husband.example: You should start dating so you can find a suitable husband.
husband.exampleSense: A man in a marriage or marital relationship, especially in relation to his spouse.

move up.example: “She’s upset she has to walk me down the aisle,” Serena told Maggie.
move up.exampleSense: To reschedule (something) to an earlier date or time.

situation.o: From Middle English situacioun, situacion, from Middle French situation, from Medieval Latin situatio (“position, situation”), from situare (“to locate, place”), from Latin situs (“a site”). By surface analysis, situate + -ion.
situation.example: The United States is in an awkward situation with debt default looming.
situation.exampleSense: The combination of circumstances at a given moment; a state of affairs.

funeral.o: Borrowed from Middle French funerailles pl (“funeral rites”), from Medieval Latin fūnerālia (“funeral rites”), originally neuter plural of Late Latin fūnerālis (“having to do with a funeral”), from Latin fūnus (“funeral, death, corpse”), origin unknown, perhaps ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dʰew- (“to die”). Singular and plural used interchangeably in English until circa 1700. The adjective funereal is first attested 1725, by influence of Middle French funerail, from Latin funereus, from funus. First attested in 1437. Displaced native Old English līcþeġnung (literally “dead body service”).
funeral.example: Many mourners turned up at the local artist's funeral to pay homage.
funeral.exampleSense: A ceremony to honor and remember a deceased person, often distinguished from a memorial service by the presence of the body of the deceased.

senseless.o: From sense + -less. Compare Saterland Frisian sinloos (“senseless, foolish”).
senseless.example: What a senseless waste of money.
senseless.exampleSense: Lacking meaning or purpose; without common sense.

stricken.o: From Middle English striken, ystriken, from Old English stricen, ġestricen, from Proto-West Germanic *strikan, from Proto-Germanic *strikanaz, past participle of Proto-Germanic *strīkaną (“to strike”). Cognate with Saterland Frisian strieken, Dutch gestreken, German Low German streken, German gestrichen.
stricken.example: The town was stricken by a devastating earthquake that left many buildings in ruins.

kitchen.o: From Middle English kichene, kichen, from Old English cyċen, cyċene, from Proto-West Germanic *kukinā, a borrowing from Late Latin cocīna, from earlier coquīna (“kitchen; cuisine”), from coquō (“to cook”), from Proto-Indo-European *pekʷ- (“to cook, become ripe”). In other languages, the cognate term often refers both to the room and the type of cooking. In English, the distinction is generally made via the etymological twins kitchen (“room”) (Latin via Germanic) and cuisine (“type of cooking”) (Latin via French).
kitchen.exampleSense: A room or area for preparing food.

emotionless.example: Overhanging her precarious body was a jaundiced face whose skin resembled a sheet of parchment paper punctured by two emotionless eyes.

motionless.example: Nothing was to be seen save flat meadows, cows for the most part feeding unconcernedly, and silvery pollard willows motionless in the warm sunlight.
motionless.exampleSense: At rest, stationary, immobile, not moving.

ambulance.o: Borrowed from French ambulance, which replaced hôpital ambulant (“moving hospital”) via the suffix -ance, from Latin ambulō (“to walk; to go about”).
ambulance.example: Ambulancing patients with acute obstruction over cobble and rails should not be tolerated; better render the necessary service where the patient is found.

blender.example: A blender is added to a wig in the same way that a quick front is added. It can be added at the same time as the fronting lace is added or after the wig is completed.
blender.exampleSense: A piece of fabric sewn into the front of a theatrical wig to make it blend in with the performer's natural hair.

unannounced.example: The Major Stations category is keenly contested, with 24 other large city centre termini and major rail hub stations all vying for recognition. As ever, the NRA's expert panel of judges visited each as unannounced mystery shoppers.

drop.o:
noun: From Late Middle English droppe, Middle English drope (“small quantity of liquid; small or least amount of something; pendant jewel; dripping of a liquid; a shower; nasal flow, catarrh; speck, spot; blemish; disease causing spots on the skin”) [and other forms], from Old English dropa (“a drop”), from Proto-West Germanic *dropō (“drop (of liquid)”), from Proto-Germanic *drupô (“drop (of liquid)”),, from *dreupaną (“to drip, droop”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰrebʰ- (“to drip, drop”). Cognates Cognate with Saterland Frisian Droupe, Druppe (“drop”), Dutch drop, drup (“droplet”), German Tropfen (“drop”), German Low German Drüpp (“drop”), Luxembourgish Drëps (“drop”), Vilamovian tropa, troppa (“drop”), Yiddish טראָפּן (tropn, “drop”), Danish dråbe (“drop”), Faroese and Icelandic dropi (“drop”), Norwegian Bokmål dråpe (“drop”), Norwegian Nynorsk drope (“drop”), Swedish droppe (“drop”).

verb: From Middle English droppen, dropen (“to fall in drops, drip or trickle down; to scatter, sprinkle; to be covered with a liquid; to give off moisture; of an object: to drop, fall; of a living being: to fall to the ground”) [and other forms], from Old English droppian, dropian (“to drop”), from Proto-West Germanic *dropōn, from Proto-Germanic *drupōną (“to fall in drops, drip”), ultimately from *dreupaną (“to hang, droop; drop, drip”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰrebʰ- (“to drip, drop”). Cognates Cognate with West Frisian drippe (“to drip”), Dutch druipen (“to drip”), German triefen (“to drip”), Yiddish טריפֿן (trifn, “to drip”), Icelandic drjúpa (“to drip”), Norwegian Nynorsk drjupa, drypa, drype (“to drip”), Swedish drypa (“to drip”).
drop.example: Put three drops of oil into the mixture.
drop.exampleSense: A small quantity of liquid, just large enough to hold its own round shape through surface tension, especially one that falls from a source of liquid.

curiosity.o: From Middle English curiosite, variant of curiouste, from Anglo-Norman curiouseté, from Latin cūriōsitātem, accusative of cūriōsitās. By surface analysis, curious + -ity. Displaced native Old English firwitt.
curiosity.example: He put the strangely shaped rock in his curiosity cabinet.
curiosity.exampleSense: A unique or extraordinary object which arouses interest.

neigh.o: Inherited from Middle English neyen, from Old English hnǣġan, from Proto-West Germanic *hnaijan, from Proto-Germanic *hnajjaną (“to neigh”). Cognate with dialectal Dutch neien, Middle Low German neigen, Swedish gnägga, Icelandic hneggja.

revolver.o: From revolve + -er, coined by American inventor Samuel Colt in 1835.
revolver.example: The debt is split between $6.5bn of term loans, as well as $6bn of senior and junior bonds and a $500mn revolver.
revolver.exampleSense: Synonym of revolving line of credit, a form of credit permitting the holder to repeatedly borrow money.

polish.o: From Middle English polishen, from Old French poliss-, stem of some of the conjugated forms of polir, from Latin polīre (“to polish, make smooth”), from Proto-Indo-European *pelh₂- (“to drive, strike, thrust”), from the notion of fulling cloth.
polish.example: He polished up the chrome until it gleamed.
polish.exampleSense: To shine; to make a surface very smooth or shiny by rubbing, cleaning, or grinding.

come across.example: He came across with the rest of the money when we mentioned our lawyer.
come across.exampleSense: To produce what was desired; to come up with the goods.

thud.o: From Middle English thudden (“to strike with a weapon”), from Old English þyddan (“to strike, press, thrust”), from Proto-Germanic *þuddijaną, *þiudijaną (“to strike, thrust”), from Proto-Germanic *þūhaną, *þeuhaną (“to press”), from Proto-Indo-European *tūk- (“to beat”). Cognate with Old English þoddettan (“to strike, push, batter”), Old English þȳdan (“to strike, stab, thrust, press”), Old English þēowan (“to press”), Albanian thundër (“a hoof, talon, a shaft", figuratively, "oppression, torment”).
thud.example: At the same instant two arrows thudded into the carcass of the deer over which he knelt, passing but a few inches from his head.
thud.exampleSense: To make the sound of a dull impact.

thunk.o:
verb: By analogy with past participles ending in "-unk", such as drunk and sunk.

intj: Onomatopoeic.

noun: Said by the inventors to be from the irregular jocular past tense of think (see Etymology 1), being coined when they realised that the type of an argument in ALGOL 60 could be predetermined at compile time (with a little compile-time “thought”).
thunk.example: I was thunked on the head by his stick.
thunk.exampleSense: To strike against something, without breakage, making a "thunk" sound.

acropetal.o: From Ancient Greek ἄκρον (ákron, “the top”) + Latin petō, petere (“fall, rush out”) + -al.

acropolis.o: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ἀκρόπολις (akrópolis), from ἄκρος (ákros, “topmost”, “tip”, “summit”) + πόλις (pólis, “city”); By surface analysis, acro- + -polis.

acro-.o: From international scientific vocabulary, per above.

delimit.o: From French délimiter, from Late Latin dēlīmitō (“to mark out the limits”), from dē- + līmitō (“to limit, to bound”); see limit.
delimit.example: Data items in the computer file were delimited by commas.

calibre.o: Alternative form of caliber. From French calibre (“bore of a gun, size, capacity (literally, and figuratively), also weight”), from Italian calibro.

caliber.o: From French calibre (“bore of a gun, size, capacity (literally, and figuratively), also weight”), from Italian calibro.
caliber.example: A snort of about the calibre of an explosion in an ammunition dump escaped my late father's sister.

avatar.o: First use appears c. 1784, in The Hindu Wife; or, The Enchanted Fruit, by William Jones. Borrowed from Hindustani अवतार (avtār) / اوتار (avtār), from Sanskrit अवतार (avatāra, “descent of a deity from a heaven”), a compound of अव (ava, “off, away, down”) and the vṛddhi-stem of the root तॄ (tṝ, “to cross”) (whence तरति (tarati)). In the computing sense, some use appeared in video games in the 1980s, such as the online roleplaying game Habitat (1985) by Lucasfilm Games (today LucasArts), by Chip Morningstar and Randy Farmer, later versions of the Ultima series (following religious use in Ultima IV: Quest of the Avatar (1985)), and the pen and paper role-playing game Shadowrun (1989). Also popularized by the novel Snow Crash (1992) by Neal Stephenson.
avatar.example: ...that a new avatar of Mrs. Siddons has appeared at Covent Garden, in the shape of her niece Fanny Kemble...
avatar.exampleSense: The embodiment of an idea or concept; an instantiation, especially a personification or incarnation.

deference.example: By tidying his room, he showed deference to his mother.
deference.exampleSense: The willingness to carry out the wishes of others.

confluence.o: From late Middle English confluence, from Late Latin cōnfluentia (“a flowing together, conflux”), from cōnfluēns (present participle of cōnfluō (“to flow or run together”)) + -ia (nominal suffix).
confluence.example: We encountered an abandoned boat at the confluence of the Mississippi and Ohio Rivers.
confluence.exampleSense: The act of combining that occurs where two rivers meet. The place where two rivers, streams, or other continuously flowing bodies of water meet and become one, especially where a tributary joins a river.

confluent.o: From Latin cōnfluēns, present participle of cōnfluō.

p: not, do the opposite of, undo
desensitize.o: From de- (“not, do the opposite of, undo”) + sensitize. First attested in the 1900s.
desensitize.example: Working in an Operating Room desensitized me to the sight of blood.
desensitize.exampleSense: To cause to become less sensitive or insensitive.

languid.o:
adj: Borrowed from Middle French languide (“fatigued, weak; apathetic, indifferent”) (modern French languide), or from its etymon Latin languidus (“faint, weak; dull; slow, sluggish; ill, sick, unwell; (figuratively) inactive, inert, listless”), from langueō (“to be faint or weak; (figuratively) to be idle, inactive, or listless”) (from Proto-Indo-European *(s)leg-, *(s)leh₁g- (“to weaken”)) + -idus (suffix meaning ‘tending to’ forming adjectives). See also the related languish. Cognates * Italian languido (“languid; languishing”) * Portuguese lânguido (“languid; listless”) * Spanish lánguido (“languid, weak”)

noun: A variant of languet.
languid.example: His thick, heavy, languid, lustreless black hair fell down behind his ears on to his shoulders, in that musicianlike way that is so offensive to the normal Englishman.
languid.exampleSense: Of a thing: lacking energy, liveliness, or strength; inactive, slow-moving, weak.

tipsy.o: From tips + -y. Compare artsy, folksy, and sudsy.
tipsy.example: I was too tipsy to protest.
tipsy.exampleSense: Slightly drunk, fuddled, staggering, foolish as a result of drinking alcoholic beverages.

payroll.example: We can spread a rumor this cop was dirty. Look, Tom, we have newspaper people on the payroll, don't we?

vested.o: simple past and past participle of vest. Derived from French veste (“a vest, jacket”), from Latin vestis (“a garment, gown, robe, vestment, clothing, vesture”), from Proto-Indo-European *wéstis, from *wes- (“to be dressed”) (English wear). Cognate with Sanskrit वस्त्र (vastra) and Spanish vestir.
vested.example: All legislative Powers herein granted shall be vested in a Congress of the United States, which shall consist of a Senate and House of Representatives.
vested.exampleSense: Settled, fixed or absolute, with no contingencies.

dogsbody.o: From dog + -s- + body. 1818, British navy slang (dog's body), originally derogatory reference to unappetizing pease pudding (compare dog's breakfast), as if it were made of mashed dog meat. In 20th century applied to low-ranked sailors, thence menial servants in wider usage.
dogsbody.example: Who chose this face for me? This dogsbody to rid of vermin.
dogsbody.exampleSense: A person who does menial work, a servant.

wangle.o: Blend of wag + dangle, first attested 1810–1820. Alternatively, from an alteration of waggle or wankle.
wangle.example: “My dear old lad,” he said, briskly, “this must be remedied! Oh, positively! This must be remedied at once! I suppose my things wouldn’t fit you? No. Well, I tell you what. We’ll wangle something from my father-in-law.
wangle.exampleSense: To obtain through deceitful or manipulative methods.

whimper.o: From dialectal whimp (“to whine”) + -er (frequentative suffix). Compare German wimmern (“to whimper, whine”).
whimper.example: The lonely puppy began to whimper as soon as we left the room.
whimper.exampleSense: To cry or sob softly and intermittently.

gratitude.o: From French gratitude, from Medieval Latin grātitūdō (“thankfulness”), from Latin grātus (“thankful”). Displaced Old English þancung.

bay.o:
noun: From French baie, from Late Latin baia, probably ultimately from Iberian or Basque badia. Partly displaced native Old English byht, whence bight.

noun: From Middle English baye, baie, from Old English beġ (“berry”), as in beġbēam (“berry-tree”), conflated with Old French baie, from Latin bāca (“berry”).

noun: From Middle English, from Old French baee, beee, from the verb beer (“gape open”), from Early Medieval Latin batāre. Compare Modern French baie. More at bevel, badinage.

noun: From the root *bai, combined with aphetized form of abay; verbal form of baier, abaier.

adj: From Middle English bay, bai, from Old French bai, from Latin badius (“reddish brown, chestnut”).
bay.example: This hotel has a great view across the bay.
bay.exampleSense: A body of water (especially the sea) contained by a concave shoreline.

limousine.o: Borrowed from French limousine, from region Limousin, originally an adjective referring to the city Limoges, from Latin Lemovices (adjective Lemovicīnus), name of a Gaulish tribe in central France, most likely a reference to their elm bows and spears, of same ultimate origin as elm.

solicit.o: From Middle English soliciten, solliciten, from Old French soliciter, solliciter, borrowed from Latin sollicitō (“stir, disturb; look after”), from sollicitus (“agitated, anxious, punctilious”, literally “thoroughly moved”), from sollus (“whole, entire”) + perfect passive participle of cieō (“shake, excite, cite, to put in motion”).
solicit.example: If you want to lose your virginity, you should try to solicit some fine looking women.
solicit.exampleSense: To persuade or incite one to commit some act, especially illegal or sexual behavior.

dump.o:
noun: From Middle English dumpen, dompen, probably from Old Norse dumpa (“to thump”) (whence Danish dumpe (“to fall suddenly”)), of uncertain origin, possibly imitative of falling, similar to thump.

noun: See dumpling.

noun: Cognate with Scots dump (“hole in the ground”), Norwegian dump (“a depression or hole in the ground”), German Low German dumpen (“to submerge”), Dutch dompen (“to dip, sink, submerge”).
dump.example: The capons were leaden representations of cocks and hens pitched at by leaden dumps.
dump.exampleSense: A lead counter used in the game of chuck-farthing.

secession.example: That year, secession was enacted on account of unreasonable policies.

commonplace.o: A calque of Latin locus commūnis, referring to a generally applicable literary passage, itself a calque of Ancient Greek κοινὸς τόπος (koinòs tópos).
commonplace.example: The smallest commonplace of domestic life, so amiable to the healthy mind, lacerates like a blade.
commonplace.exampleSense: Something that is ordinary; something commonly done or occurring.

chatter.o:
noun: From Middle English chateren, from earlier cheteren, chiteren (“to twitter, chatter, jabber”), of imitative origin. Compare Saterland Frisian tjoaterje (“to chatter”), West Frisian tsjotterje (“to chatter”), Dutch schateren, schetteren (“chatter”), Dutch koeteren (“jabber”), Middle Low German kidderen (“to chatter”), German Low German queteln (“to chatter”), dialectal German kaudern (“to gobble (like a turkey)”), Danish kvidre (“to twitter, chirp”).

noun: From chat + -er.
chatter.example: He was so cold that his teeth were chattering.
chatter.exampleSense: To make a noise by rapid collisions.

laptop.o: From lap (“upper legs of a seated person”) + top, modeled after desktop.
laptop.example: Over time, the difference in size between laptops and notebooks became a matter of no more than an inch or two in length and width, and a fraction of an inch in thickness.

scratchy.example: The FM station two hundred miles away was receivable, but the audio was too scratchy to positively identify.
scratchy.exampleSense: Noisy, lossy; marred by white noise or static as a result of poor or low signal, interference or unfavourable atmospheric conditions.

oblige.o: From Middle English obligen, from Old French obligier, obliger, from Latin obligō, obligāre, from ob- + ligō. Doublet of obligate, taken straight from Latin.
oblige.example: He obliged me by not parking his car in the drive.
oblige.exampleSense: To do (someone) a service or favour (hence, originally, creating an obligation).

significance.o: Inherited from Middle English significaunce, from Middle French significance, from Old French significance, from Latin significantia. Doublet of signifiance.
significance.example: As a juror your opinion is of great significance for the outcome of the trial.
significance.exampleSense: The extent to which something matters; importance

cautious.example: He took a few cautious steps toward the cave.
cautious.exampleSense: Using or exercising caution; careful; tentative

fortune.o: From Middle English fortune, from Old French fortune, from Latin fortuna (“fate, luck”). The plural form fortunae meant “possessions”, which also gave fortune the meaning of “riches”.
fortune.example: My vast fortune was a result of inheritance and stock market nous.
fortune.exampleSense: One's wealth; the amount of money one has, especially if it is vast.

run-off.example: Twelve laps later, Leclerc locked up at the first chicane and clattered over the run-off area. Again, Hamilton got a run on him, and this time Leclerc defended robustly through the flat-out Curva Grande, moving very late to block Hamilton to the Ferrari's left.
run-off.exampleSense: A run-off area; a paved area around the track at a spot that drivers are likely to go off, as opposed to a gravel trap, grass or a barrier.

subsidence.o: Latin subsidens, subsidentis, present participle of subsidere. Equivalent to subside + -ence.
subsidence.example: The subdual or subsidence of the more violent passions.
subsidence.exampleSense: The process of becoming less active or severe.

remind.o: From mid 17th century, equivalent to re- + mind (“to remember”). Probably suggested by obsolete rememorate with the same sense. Displaced Old English myndgian.
remind.example: His eyes were green and every cat I see to this day reminds me of the exact contour of his face.
remind.exampleSense: To cause one to experience a memory (of someone or something); to bring to the notice or consideration (of a person).

remainder.o: From Middle English remaindre, remeigner, from Anglo-Norman remaindre, with infinitive used as noun.
remainder.example: My son ate part of his cake and I ate the remainder.
remainder.exampleSense: A part or parts remaining after some has/have been removed or already occurred.

methane.example: Cattle emit a large amount of methane.
methane.exampleSense: The simplest aliphatic hydrocarbon, CH₄, being a constituent of natural gas, and one of the most abundant greenhouse gases.

clearance.example: The plane got clearance from air traffic control, and we were off.
clearance.exampleSense: A permission for a vehicle to proceed, or for a person to travel.

waterlogged.example: The sudden inundation from the remnants of Ida transformed familiar scenes of life in New York into otherworldly and waterlogged chaos on Wednesday night.

in demand.example: Importantly, apprenticeships provide an alternate route into employment, giving people from all backgrounds the chance to build in-demand skills and a career for life.

commodity.o: Inherited from Middle English commoditee, borrowed from Anglo-Norman commoditee, from Latin commoditās.
commodity.example: Although they were once in the forefront of consumer electronics, the calculators have become a mere commodity.
commodity.exampleSense: Undifferentiated goods characterized by a low profit margin, as distinguished from branded products.

pulp.o: From Middle English pulpe, from Latin pulpa.
pulp.example: The hard-hitting, action packed, thud and blunder adventure fantasy was a commodity during that somber decade: Americans paid money to forget their troubles, and the pulps were willing to sell.
pulp.exampleSense: A magazine or book containing lurid subject matter and characteristically printed on rough, unfinished paper.

substantially.example: For the first time since the Great Depression, median family income has fallen substantially over an entire decade. Income grew slowly through most of the last decade, except at the top of the distribution, before falling sharply when the financial crisis began.
substantially.exampleSense: In a strong or substantial manner; considerably.

buffer.o:
noun: From buff + -er.

noun: Agent noun from obsolete verb buff (“make a dull sound when struck”) (mid-16c.), from Old French buffe (“blow”). The “boatswain's mate” sense is said to be popularly explained by the mate being a “buffer”, that is intermediary, between officers and men, but various other explanations have also been proposed.

noun: In reference to buff leather.
buffer.example: I keep a savings buffer of three months' worth of living expenses.
buffer.exampleSense: Anything used to isolate or minimize the effect of one thing on another. A reserve of funds set aside for use only when adverse circumstances prevail.

die.o:
verb: From Middle English deyen, probably from Old Norse deyja, from Proto-Germanic *dawjaną (“to die”). Displaced native Old English sweltan, whence Modern English swelt, and Old English steorfan, whence modern starve.

noun: From Middle English dee, from Old French de (Modern French dé), from Latin datum, from datus (“given”), the past participle of dō (“to give”), from Proto-Indo-European *deh₃- (“to lay out, to spread out”). Doublet of datum. Replaced Old English tasul, tesul (“die”), from Latin tessella (“die, cube”).

noun: Variant spelling.

adv: Borrowed from Latin die (“[in a] day”), locative of Latin dies (“day”).
die.example: I rolled the die and moved 2 spaces on the board.
die.exampleSense: An isohedral polyhedron, usually a cube, with numbers or symbols on each side and thrown in games of chance.

rugby.o:
noun: From the name of Rugby School in Rugby, in Warwickshire, England, United Kingdom, where the modern game was developed in the 19th century. The place name Rugby is attested in the Domesday Book as Old English Rocheberie (probably equivalent to rook (“Corvus frugilegus, a bird of the crow family”) + -by (suffix indicating a village or town)), possibly from *Hrōcebyriġ, dative singular of *Hrōceburh, from hrōc (“rook”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ker- (“to crow”)) + burh, burg (“castle, fort, stronghold; city; town”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰerǵʰ- (“hill, mountain; high, lofty; to rise”)).

noun: Genericized trademark from Rugby, a brand of rubber cement by Bostik.
rugby.example: The two rugbies split following a debate about amateurism.
rugby.exampleSense: A form of football in which players can hold or kick an ovoid ball; rugby football. The ball cannot be handled forwards and points are scored by touching the ball to the ground in the area past the opponent's territory or by kicking the ball between goalposts and over a crossbar.

gamble.o: From earlier gamel, from Middle English *gamlen, *gamelen, variant of Middle English gamenen, from Old English gæmnian, gamnian, gamenian (“to joke; play”), related to Old English gamen (“joy; mirth; pleasure; entertainment; pastime; sport; game”), equivalent to game + -le. Compare Old Danish gammel, Middle High German gamel (“pleasure; fun”). More at game.
gamble.example: Mark won half a million dollars gambling on horses.
gamble.exampleSense: To play risky games, especially casino games, for monetary gain.

erotica.o: From neuter plural of Latin eroticus (“amatory”), from Ancient Greek ἐρωτικός (erōtikós). By surface analysis, erotic + -ica.
erotica.example: In fact, eighteenth-century British erotica has been the subject of unremitting attention for the last two decades.
erotica.exampleSense: Erotic literature, art, decoration, or other such work.

motivate.o: From motive + -ate (verb-forming suffix). Compare French motiver.
motivate.example: The weekly staff meeting was meant to motivate employees.
motivate.exampleSense: To provide someone with an incentive to do something; to encourage; to actuate.

militate.o: First attested in 1598; borrowed from Latin mīlitātus, perfect passive participle from mīlitō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix). Semantically from its cognate, French militer.
militate.example: There are a number of theoretical concerns which might seem to militate against the successful creation of a dictionary of Indian English.
militate.exampleSense: To give force or effect toward; to influence.

allergy.o: Borrowed from German Allergie. Coined by Austrian pediatrician Clemens von Pirquet in 1906 from Ancient Greek ἄλλος (állos, “other”) + ἔργον (érgon, “work, activity”), on the model of Energie.
allergy.example: He has an allergy to reality TV.
allergy.exampleSense: An antipathy, as toward a person or activity.

inevitability.example: Surveillance capitalism is a human creation. It lives in history, not in technological inevitability.

amazon.o: From Amazon, from Ancient Greek Ἀμαζών (Amazṓn).
amazon.example: Although the evidence for real Amazons is thin, women athletes are often dubbed amazons.

fraud.o: Inherited from Middle English fraude (recorded since 1345), from Old French fraude, a borrowing from Latin fraus (“deceit, injury, offence”).
fraud.example: But electric vehicles and the batteries that made them run became ensnared in corporate scandals, fraud, and monopolistic corruption that shook the confidence of the nation and inspired automotive upstarts.
fraud.exampleSense: Any act of deception carried out for the purpose of unfair, undeserved or unlawful gain.

necklace.example: Frustrated residents tied the hands of two suspected criminals, put tyres around their necks and then set them alight. In a manifestation of growing disillusionment with the criminal justice system, residents of Bramfischerville, west of Johannesburg, on Tuesday abducted and necklaced two suspected burglars.
necklace.exampleSense: To informally execute by necklacing; by setting on fire a petrol-filled rubber tyre which has been put around the bound victim's neck.

fast food.example: The best evidence is that Sandals, the fast-food king of island weddings, now markets the term weddingmoons.
fast food.exampleSense: Anything standardized, quickly available, and inexpensive, often, of low value.

single-use.example: Filtrona Plastics, Victoria, has supplied Malaysia with $20 000 worth of single-use plastic ware for hospitals and laboratories.
single-use.exampleSense: Designed or intended to be used one time and then discarded or disposed of.

one-time.example: Has the one-time wonder fuel become the new asbestos – not to say mustard gas?
one-time.exampleSense: Of or pertaining to a specific period of time in the past, not extending to the present.

mandatory.o: From Late Latin mandatorius (“of or belonging to a mandator”), from mandātor (“one who commands”), equivalent to mandate + -ory; see mandate.
mandatory.example: Attendance at a school is usually mandatory for children.
mandatory.exampleSense: obligatory; required or commanded by authority.

ready-made.o: From Middle English redye made, equivalent to ready + made.
ready-made.example: During the 1830s and 1840s, ready-made standardized shoes and clothing increasingly challenged the custom-made products of small handicraft workshops.
ready-made.exampleSense: Made in advance to a standard specification.

immersed.o: simple past and past participle of immerse. Borrowed from Latin immersus, from immergō, from in + mergō.
immersed.example: Sori in the axils of lamina branches, partly immersed; involucre bell- or trumpet-shaped, or obconical, usually 2-lipped; receptacle generally exserted.
immersed.exampleSense: Lowered or sunken relative to a reference surface.

immersive.example: An immersive system usually allows the user to move around physically so it is important that the real world allows sufficient space for this to happen safely.

immersion.o: From late Middle English, borrowed from Late Latin immersiō, immersiōnem (“dipping”).
immersion.example: Jesus did not become known as a baptizer (cf. however John 3:26 and 4:1), but we can recognize the same ritual structure in his healing practice as in John's immersion.
immersion.exampleSense: The act of immersing or the condition of being immersed. The total submerging of a person in water as an act of baptism.

immerse.o: Borrowed from Latin immersus, from immergō, from in + mergō.
immerse.example: Thus, in mathematical terms a Klein bottle cannot be "embedded" but only "immersed" in three dimensions as an embedding has no self-intersections but an immersion may have them.

contain.o: From Middle English, borrowed from Old French contenir, from Latin continēre (“to hold or keep together, comprise, contain”), combined form of con- (“together”) + teneō (“to hold”).
contain.example: If that subgraph contains the vertex in question then it must be spanning.
contain.exampleSense: To have as an element or subset.

superpower.example: The year 1945 marked the end of Europe's global hegemony and confirmed the US and the Soviet Union as global superpowers.
superpower.exampleSense: A sovereign state with dominant status on the globe and a very advanced military, especially the United States or formerly the Soviet Union.

stagnation.o: From stagnate + -ation (suffix denoting an action or process, or its result), Stagnate is derived from stagnāt-, the participial stem of Latin stagnāre, the present active infinitive of stāgnō (“of waters: to cover the land as a lake, to become a pool, to stagnate”), from stāgnum (“body of standing water (lake, swamp, etc.)”) (possibly from Proto-Indo-European *steh₂g- (“to drip; to seep”)) + -ō (suffix forming regular first-conjugation verbs).
stagnation.example: Factors known to encourage the growth of harmful bacteria inside cooling systems include the stagnation of the water.
stagnation.exampleSense: The state of being stagnant, without circulation.

outpace.example: The youngster outpaced his grandfather and ran on ahead.
outpace.exampleSense: To go faster than; to exceed the pace of.

basin.o: From Middle English basyn, from Old French bacin, from Vulgar Latin *baccinum (“wide bowl”).
basin.example: The fountains were plashing musically into marble and alabaster basins.
basin.exampleSense: A depression, natural or artificial, containing water.

exhale.o: From Middle French exhaler, from Latin exhalare, from ex (“out”) + halare (“to breathe”).
exhale.example: Above was a tiled roof – though from that imperfect tiling exhaled stench and pestilence.
exhale.exampleSense: To pass off in the form of vapour; to emerge.

sagacious.o: Coined between 1600 and 1610. Borrowed from Latin sagāx, + -acious.

pea.o:
noun: Back-formation from pease, an original singular reinterpreted as a plural. Further from Middle English pese (“a pea”), from Old English pise, from Latin pisa, pisum, from Ancient Greek πίσον (píson).

noun: From having the appearance of a pea (see English etymology 1), the edible seed of Pisum sativum, the pea plant.

noun: From Middle English pe, po, poue, pa, paue, from Old English pēa, pāwa (“peacock”) (compare Old English pāwe (“peahen”)) and Old Norse pái (“peacock”), both from Proto-Germanic *pāwô (“peacock”), from Latin pāvō (“peacock”). Cognate with Saterland Frisian Pau, West Frisian pau, Dutch pauw, German Pfau. Doublet of Pavo.
pea.example: Below, long rows of peas put forth their white-winged flowers, tempting the small butterflies to flutter round their inanimate likenesses;...
pea.exampleSense: A plant, Pisum sativum, member of the legume (Fabaceae) family.

distinguishing.o: present participle and gerund of distinguish. From Middle English distingwen, from Old French distinguer, from Latin distinguere (“to separate, divide, distinguish, set off, adorn, literally mark off”), from di-, dis- (“apart”) + stinguere, related to English stink. Compare extinguish.
distinguishing.example: It has no obvious distinguishing characteristics, and therefore people are constantly ascribing to it the characteristics of other similar species.

distinguish.o: From Middle English distingwen, from Old French distinguer, from Latin distinguere (“to separate, divide, distinguish, set off, adorn, literally mark off”), from di-, dis- (“apart”) + stinguere, related to English stink. Compare extinguish.
distinguish.example: The soldier distinguished himself in combat and received a medal.
distinguish.exampleSense: To make noticeably different or better from others through accomplishments.

slick.o: From Middle English slicke, slike, slyke, from Old English slīc (“sleek, smooth; crafty, cunning, slick”), from Proto-Germanic *slīkaz (“sleek, smooth”), from Proto-Indo-European *sleyg-, *sleyǵ- (“to glide, smooth, spread”). Akin to Dutch sluik, dialectal Dutch sleek (“even, smooth”), Old Norse slíkr (“sleek, smooth”), Old English slician (“to make sleek, smooth, or glossy”).
slick.example: You'll go much faster if you put on slicks.
slick.exampleSense: A tire with a smooth surface instead of a tread pattern, often used in auto racing.

p: suffix used in all noble gases
neon.o: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek νέον (néon), neuter of νέος (néos, “new”), from earlier *νέϝος (*néwos), from Proto-Hellenic *newos, from Proto-Indo-European *néwos. By surface analysis, neo- + -on (suffix used in all noble gases).

pipeline.example: An oil pipeline has been opened from the Caspian Sea.
pipeline.exampleSense: A conduit made of pipes used to convey water, gas or petroleum, etc.

ingest.example: The plane's engine ingested a large bird and flamed out.
ingest.exampleSense: To cause (an undesired object or fluid) to enter the engine, generally via the intake.

recurring.o: present participle and gerund of recur. Learned borrowing from Latin recurrō (“to hurry or run back; to return, revert”), from re- (prefix meaning ‘back, backwards’) + currō (“to hasten, hurry; to move, travel; to run”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ḱers- (“to run”)). cognates * Anglo-Norman recurre, recorre (“to have recourse to”) * Catalan recórrer * Italian ricorrer * Old French recourir (Middle French recourir; modern French recourir (“to have recourse to; to run again; to run back”)) * Old Occitan recorre * Portuguese recorrer * Spanish recorrer
recurring.example: Winter, here, is a dimension of all reality, not one-fourth of the spiritual year's endless recurrings.
recurring.exampleSense: A recurrence; a coming round again.

recur.o: Learned borrowing from Latin recurrō (“to hurry or run back; to return, revert”), from re- (prefix meaning ‘back, backwards’) + currō (“to hasten, hurry; to move, travel; to run”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ḱers- (“to run”)). cognates * Anglo-Norman recurre, recorre (“to have recourse to”) * Catalan recórrer * Italian ricorrer * Old French recourir (Middle French recourir; modern French recourir (“to have recourse to; to run again; to run back”)) * Old Occitan recorre * Portuguese recorrer * Spanish recorrer
recur.example: Over the last few days her mind had time and again recurred to these elusive beings and those few elusive comments.
recur.exampleSense: To speak, write or think about something again; to return or go back (to a subject).

labor-intensive.example: Picking beans is a very labor-intensive activity, there's no machine made that can do it.
labor-intensive.exampleSense: Requiring a great deal of work, especially physical and manual effort versus capital.

capital-intensive.example: Petroleum is the most productive and capital-intensive industry while apparel is the least productive and least capital intensive.
capital-intensive.exampleSense: Needing a relatively large expenditure on capital, especially when compared to that spent on labour.

supercar.example: As much of Seattle tries to sleep, the Hellcat supercar goes on the prowl, the howls of its engine and the explosive backfires from its tailpipes echoing off the high-rise towers downtown.

deafen.o: From deaf + -en (verbal suffix). Compare Middle English deven, deaven (“to make deaf”), Old English ādēafian (“to deafen”) and Old English ādȳfan, Dutch verdoven (“to stupefy, deafen”), German betäuben (“to stun, stupefy, deafen”).

absolution.o: From Middle English absolucion, absolucioun, from Old French absolution, from Latin absolūtiōnem, accusative singular of absolūtiō (“acquittal”), from absolvō (“absolve”). See also absolve.
absolution.example: Governments granting absolution to the nation.
absolution.exampleSense: An absolving, or setting free from guilt, sin, or penalty; forgiveness of an offense.

solution.o: From Middle English solucioun, from Old French solucion (French solution), from Latin solūtiōnem, accusative singular of solūtiō, from the verb solvō. Compare solve, -tion.
solution.example: All too often, computer technology is treated as a solution in search of a problem. In fact, it is not uncommon for people working with computers to become critical of the problem because it doesn't seem to fit the solution they have generated.
solution.exampleSense: An act, plan or other means, used or proposed, to solve a problem.

irresolution.o: Probably from Middle French irresolution (modern French irrésolution), from ir- + resolution (“resolution”); compare Italian irresoluzione. By surface analysis, ir- + resolution.
irresolution.example: Again he paced the chamber; but an involuntary movement of awe and inquietude constantly led his eye towards the alcove. He drew near it with irresolution.
irresolution.exampleSense: Lack of resolution; lack of decision or purpose; vacillation.

resolution.o: Recorded since 1412, as Middle English resolucioun (“dissolution”), either from Anglo-Norman resolucion or directly from Latin resolūtiō (“a loosening, solution”), from resolvō (“to loosen”), itself from the intensive prefix re- + solvō (“to loosen”). By surface analysis, recognizably related to resolve and -tion.
resolution.example: Printing at higher resolution will cause a reduction in performance.
resolution.exampleSense: The degree of fineness with which an image can be recorded or produced, often expressed as the number of pixels per unit of length (typically an inch).

dunk.o: From Pennsylvania German dunke, from Middle High German dunken, from Old High German dunkōn (“to dip, submerge, dunk”), from Proto-West Germanic *þunkōn (“to make wet”), possibly from Proto-Germanic *þunkōną, from Proto-Indo-European *teng- (“to moisten, wet”). Cognate with German tunken (“to dunk”), Latin tingō (“to wet, moisten”), Ancient Greek τέγγω (téngō, “to wet, moisten”). Related to taint, tincture, tint.
dunk.example: I like to dunk my donut in my apple cider.
dunk.exampleSense: To submerge briefly in a liquid.

oppose.o: From Middle English opposen, from Old French opposer, from Latin ob (“before, against”) + Medieval Latin pono (“to put”), taking the place of Latin opponere (“to oppose”).
oppose.example: There is still time to oppose this plan.
oppose.exampleSense: To attempt to stop the progression of; to resist or antagonize by physical means, or by arguments, etc.; to contend against.

pandemic.o:
adj: From Ancient Greek πάνδημος (pándēmos, “of or belonging to all the people, public”) + English -ic (suffix forming adjectives from nouns with the sense ‘of or pertaining to’). πάνδημος is derived from παν- (pan-, prefix meaning ‘all, every’) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂- (“to protect, shepherd”)) + δῆμος (dêmos, “the common people; free citizens, sovereign people”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *deh₂- (“to divide, share”)). Compare Late Latin pandēmus (“affecting all the people, general, public”).

adj: See Pandemic.
pandemic.example: The chaotic breakdown of public health as World War I dragged on is widely recognized as exacerbating the disease burden of the pandemic outbreak of influenza in 1918.
pandemic.exampleSense: Of a disease: epidemic over a wide geographical area and affecting a large proportion of the population; also, of or pertaining to a disease of this nature.

anticipated.o: simple past and past participle of anticipate. Borrowed from Latin anticipātus, perfect passive participle of anticipō (“to anticipate”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from ante- (“before”), + capiō (“to take”, cip- when prefixed) + -ō (verb-forming suffix). See capable.

battle.o:
noun: From Middle English batel, batell, batelle, batayle, bataylle, borrowed from Old French bataille, from Late Latin battālia, variant of battuālia (“fighting and fencing exercises”) from Latin battuō (“to strike, hit, beat, fight”), of uncertain origin. Possibly from a Gaulish or Proto-Germanic root from Proto-Indo-European *bʰedʰ- (“to stab, dig”), related to Old English beado (“battle”); or possibly from a Proto-Indo-European *bʰew- (“to hit, strike, beat”). Doublet of battalia and battel. Displaced native Old English ġefeoht, beado, camp, and wīg (“battle”), among others.

adj: From Early Modern English batell, probably from Middle English *batel (“flourishing”), from Old English *batol (“improving, tending to be good”), from batian (“to get better, improve”) + -ol ( + -le).
battle.example: She has been battling against cancer for years.
battle.exampleSense: To join in battle; to contend in fight

polyester.example: Her short stout body was packed into pale pink polyester pants and a matching buttonfront vest.

court.o: From Middle English court, from Old French cort, curt, from Late Latin cōrs, contracted from Latin cohors. Doublet of cohort. Professional tennis players playing on a tennis court (noun sense 5) in New Delhi, India
court.example: The court started proceedings at 11 o'clock.
court.exampleSense: The administration of law. The persons officially assembled under authority of law, at the appropriate time and place, for the administration of justice; an official assembly, legally met together for the transaction of judicial business; a judge or judges sitting for the hearing or trial of cases.

strung.o: simple past and past participle of string. From Middle English string, streng, strynge, from Old English strenġ, from Proto-West Germanic *strangi, from Proto-Germanic *strangiz (“string”), from Proto-Indo-European *strengʰ- (“rope, cord, strand; to tighten”). Cognate with Scots string (“string”), Dutch streng (“cord, strand”), Low German strenge (“strand, cord, rope”), German Strang (“strand, cord, rope”), Danish streng (“string”), Swedish sträng (“string, cord, wire”), Icelandic strengur (“string”), Latvian stringt (“to be tight, wither”), Latin stringō (“to tighten”), Ancient Greek στραγγαλόομαι (strangalóomai, “to strangle”), from στραγγάλη (strangálē, “halter”), Ancient Greek στραγγός (strangós, “tied together, entangled, twisted”).

string.o:
noun: From Middle English string, streng, strynge, from Old English strenġ, from Proto-West Germanic *strangi, from Proto-Germanic *strangiz (“string”), from Proto-Indo-European *strengʰ- (“rope, cord, strand; to tighten”). Cognate with Scots string (“string”), Dutch streng (“cord, strand”), Low German strenge (“strand, cord, rope”), German Strang (“strand, cord, rope”), Danish streng (“string”), Swedish sträng (“string, cord, wire”), Icelandic strengur (“string”), Latvian stringt (“to be tight, wither”), Latin stringō (“to tighten”), Ancient Greek στραγγαλόομαι (strangalóomai, “to strangle”), from στραγγάλη (strangálē, “halter”), Ancient Greek στραγγός (strangós, “tied together, entangled, twisted”).

verb: From Middle English stryngen, strengen, from the noun (see above).
string.example: In 1933, disgusted and discouraged after a string of commercial failures, Clara quit the film business forever. She was twenty-six.
string.exampleSense: A series of items or events.

regularity.o: Borrowed from Middle French regularite, from Old French regularite, from Late Latin rēgulāritās, rēgulāritātem, from rēgulāris; see regular. By surface analysis, regular + -ity.
regularity.example: I have been watching that show with regularity.
regularity.exampleSense: The condition or quality of being regular

topspin.example: The tennis star was famed for her topspin.
topspin.exampleSense: A rotational motion, especially that given to a ball, in which the upper surface spins in the direction of motion.

specification.o: From Middle French specification, from Medieval Latin specificationem (accusative of specificatio).

rather.o: From Middle English rather, from Old English hraþor, comparative of hraþe (“soon, early, fast”). More at rathe. Cognate with Dutch radder (“faster”), comparative of Dutch rad (“fast; quick”), German Low German radd, ratt (“rashly; quickly; hastily”), German gerade (“even; straight; direct”). By surface analysis, rathe + -er.
rather.example: It wasn't supposed to be popular; rather, it was supposed to get the job done.
rather.exampleSense: Used to introduce a contradiction; on the contrary.

maximization.example: Monopolies engaging in profit maximization will produce at the quantity where its marginal revenue equals marginal cost.
maximization.exampleSense: The act of raising something to its greatest value or extent.

stringer.example: A startled man looked out the office window and then rushed for the door, but the boys were too quick for him. They were lying behind a wooden stringer in the lot before he even got near the door.
stringer.exampleSense: A horizontal timber that supports upright posts, or supports the hull of a vessel.

touring.o: present participle and gerund of tour. From Old French tour, tourn, from the verb torner, tourner.
touring.example: Finally, there was the 40-hp machine from the previous year, on the 120-inch wheelbase and listed in four body styles, tourings and roadsters.

tournament.o: From Old French tornoiement (Modern French tournoiement) from the verb tornoier.
tournament.example: England secured their place at Euro 2012 with a scrambled draw in Montenegro - but Wayne Rooney was sent off and will miss the start of the tournament.
tournament.exampleSense: A series of games; either the same game played many times, or a succession of games related by a single theme; played competitively to determine a single winning team or individual.

outsider.example: Johnny was an outsider at this year's karate tournament, but he still managed to win second place out of sheer determination.
outsider.exampleSense: A competitor or contestant who has little chance of winning; a long shot.

generous.o: From Middle French genereux, and its source, Latin generōsus (“of noble birth”), from genus (“race, stock”).
generous.example: She's been extremely generous with her winnings.
generous.exampleSense: Willing to give and share unsparingly; showing a readiness to give more (especially money) than is expected or needed.

scab.o: From Middle English scabb, scabbe (also as shabbe, schabbe > English shab), from Old English sċeabb and Old Norse skabb, both from Proto-Germanic *skabbaz (“scab, scabies”), from Proto-Indo-European *skabʰ- (“to cut, split, carve, shape”). Doublet of shab. Cognate with German Schabe (“scabies”), Danish skab (“scab, scabies”), Swedish skabb (“scab, scabies”), Latin scabies (“scab, itch, mange”). Related also to Old English scafan (“to scrape, shave”), Latin scabere (“to scratch”), English shabby.
scab.example: Scab was the terror of the sheep farmer, and the peril of his calling.
scab.exampleSense: The mange, especially when it appears on sheep.

candid.example: My candid opinion was that it was all rubbish!

recondite.example: They afford a lesson to the modern metaphysical and recondite writers not to overvalue their works.
recondite.exampleSense: Difficult, obscure. Deliberately employing abstruse or esoteric allusions or references; intentionally obscure.

tamer.o:
noun: From tame (verb) + -er (suffix forming agent nouns).

adj: From tame (adjective) + -er (suffix forming comparative adjectives).
tamer.example: Only Enid could dare him at such a time, and even she felt occasionally that sinking of the heart which the bravest of tamers may experience as he unbars the gate of the cage.

deafness.o: From Middle English deefnesse; equivalent to deaf + -ness.

deaf.o: From Middle English def, deef, from Old English dēaf, from Proto-West Germanic *daub, from Proto-Germanic *daubaz, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰewbʰ- (“to whisk, smoke, darken, obscure”). Cognate with Ancient Greek τυφλός (tuphlós, “blind”). See also dumb. Doublet of daff, dof, and dowf. Cognate with Dutch doof, German taub, Danish and Norwegian Bokmål døv, Norwegian Nynorsk dauv, Swedish döv, Faroese deyvur, Icelandic daufur.
deaf.example: Those people are deaf to reason.
deaf.exampleSense: Unwilling to listen or be persuaded; determinedly inattentive; regardless.

blind.o: From Middle English blynd, from Old English blind, from Proto-West Germanic *blind, from Proto-Germanic *blindaz. Cognate with Danish, Dutch, German, Norwegian Bokmål, Norwegian Nynorsk, and Swedish blind, Faroese and Icelandic blindur.
blind.example: Field biologists use blinds, and so do hunters.
blind.exampleSense: A place where people can hide in order to observe wildlife.

fidelity.o: 15th century, from Middle English [Term?], from Middle French fidélité, from Latin fidēlitās, from fidēlis (“faithful”), from fidēs (“faith, loyalty”) (English faith), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰidʰ-, zero-grade of *bʰeydʰ- (“to command, to persuade, to trust”) (English bide). Doublet of fealty.
fidelity.example: By placing them closer to the source, we can reduce the number of messages in the system and this in turn is likely to improve the fidelity of the system.
fidelity.exampleSense: The degree to which a system accurately reproduces an input.

live stream.o: Alternative form of livestream. From live + stream.
live stream.example: The concert was transmitted via satellite and live stream.
live stream.exampleSense: A real-time broadcast of audio or video over the Internet.

robe.o: From Middle English robe, roobe, from Old French robe, robbe, reube (“booty, spoils of war, robe, garment”), from Frankish *rouba, *rauba (“booty, spoils, stolen clothes”, literally “things taken”), from Proto-Germanic *raubō, *raubaz, *raubą (“booty, that which is stripped or carried away”), from Proto-Indo-European *Hrewp- (“to tear, peel”). cognates and related terms Akin to Old High German roup (“booty”) (Modern German Raub (“robbery, spoils”)), Old High German roubōn (“to rob, steal”) (Modern German rauben (“to rob”)), Old English rēaf (“spoils, booty, dress, armour, robe, garment”), Old English rēafian (“to steal, deprive”). Cognate with Spanish ropa (“clothing, clothes”). More at rob, reaf, reave.

bate.o:
verb: Inherited from Middle English baten (“to abate”), an apheretic form of abaten, from Old French abatre (“to knock down”).

noun: * Noun: From the verb, or directly from the noun debate. * Verb: From Middle English bate (“contention”), from Old French batre (French battre), from Latin battere.

noun: Borrowed from Swedish beta (“maceration, tanning”).

verb: Formed by analogy with eat → ate or other Class 5 strong verbs (compare gave, obsolete spake, etc.), with which it shares an analogous past participle (eaten → beaten).

noun: Variant of beat (“rhythm”).
bate.example: Also about Autumne bate the earth from about the roots of Olives, and lay them bare, but in stead thereof put good mucke thereto.
bate.exampleSense: To cut off, remove, take away.

illustrious.o: From Latin illūstris (“bright, shining; distinguished, prominent, illustrious”) + -ous (suffix forming adjectives from nouns, to denote possession or presence of a quality in any degree). Illūstris is derived from illūstrō (“to brighten, illuminate; to make famous or illustrious”), from in- (“in, inside”) + lūstrō (“to purify by making a sacrifice; to brighten, illuminate”) (from lūstrō (“purificatory sacrifice”), possibly ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *lewk- (“bright; to shine”) or *lewh₃- (“to wash”)).
illustrious.example: Really, for a man who had been out of practice for so many years, it was a splendid laugh, a most illustrious laugh. The father of a long, long line of brilliant laughs!

slang.o:
noun: First use appears c. 1756, meaning "special vocabulary of tramps or thieves", origin unknown. Not believed to be connected with language or lingo. Possibly derived from a North Germanic source, then possibly related to Nordic language: Danish slænge, Icelandic and Norwegian Nynorsk slengja, Norwegian slenge, Swedish slänga (“to (carelessly) sling, throw, hurl; throw away, to dispose of; to flail”), with derivational nouns such as slæng, sleng, släng etc. Compare the compound: Danish slængenavn, Norwegian slengenavn, Norwegian Nynorsk slengenamn, Swedish slängnamn (“nickname, byname, informal name”, literally “sling-name”), and the phrases: Norwegian Nynorsk slengja kjeften, Swedish slänga käften (“to abuse verbally”, literally “to sling one's jowl”), Swedish slänga ur sig (“to say something hastily, carelessly, thoughtlessly”, literally “to throw out of oneself”), also Swedish (regional) slänga (“careless, nonchalant girl”, literally “sling + feminine suffix -a”).

noun: Compare sling.

verb: The same as sling which is also used in this sense. The vowel exhibits the lowering of /ɪ/ before /ŋ/ distinguishing for African American Vernacular English, as in thang for thing, but the word has spread with this pronunciation outside the accents that exhibit this feature.
slang.example: [F]or a detailed analysis see Liberman (2008 157ff) who sees it as one of a number of terms found in pan-European slangs meaning concealment and/or cheating.
slang.exampleSense: A particular variety of slang; the slang used by a particular group.

sift.o: From Middle English syften, from Old English siftan, from Proto-West Germanic *siftijan.
sift.example: Sifting through the work of great orators like Philostratus and Quintilian they identify numerous examples of classical irony, metaphor, comparison, etc. which are missing in Paul.
sift.exampleSense: To examine (something) carefully. [with through] To carefully go through a set of objects, or a collection of information, in order to find something.
