rheology.o: Coined by American scientist Eugene C. Bingham in 1920, following a suggestion by a colleague, Markus Reiner; inspired by aphorism πάντα ῥεῖ (pánta rheî, “everything flows”) by Simplicius of Cilicia. Formed from Ancient Greek ῥέω (rhéō, “flow”) + -logy (“study of”, suffix ultimately from Ancient Greek). See also rheo-.
rheology.example: Curious as to whether other had explored the connection between Oreos and rheology, Owens found mention of a 2016 Princeton University study in which physicists first reported that indeed, when twisting Oreos by hand, the cream almost always came off on one wafer.
rheology.exampleSense: The branch of physics that studies the deformation and flow of matter.

wicked.o:
adj: From Middle English wicked, wikked, an alteration of Middle English wicke, wikke (“morally perverse, evil, wicked”). Of uncertain origin. Possibly from an adjectival use of Old English wiċċa (“wizard, sorcerer”), from Proto-West Germanic *wikkō (“necromancer, sorcerer”), though the phonology makes this theory difficult to explain. Alternatively, perhaps related to English wicker, Old Norse víkja (“to bend to, yield, turn, move”), Swedish vika (“to bend, fold, give way to”), English weak. The "excellent, awesome" sense is an ameliorative semantic shift from the original sense of "evil, mischievous". Compare similar semantic development in terrific and sick.

verb: See wick.
wicked.example: Genuine cowards follow wicked people and cannot reliably sustain any virtue.

wince.o: From Middle English wyncen, from Anglo-Norman winchir (compare Old French guenchir), from Frankish *wankjan, related to *winkijan (“to flex, bend”). See also German winken.
wince.example: I will not stir, nor wince, nor speak a word.
wince.exampleSense: To flinch as if in pain or distress.

winker.o:
noun: From wink (“blinking of only one eye”) + -er (suffix forming agent nouns).

noun: Clipping of tiddlywinker.
winker.example: Take the winkers off that donkey's face, and let him get a bit to eat; there's grass enough, God knows, and it's good grass.
winker.exampleSense: A thing which is used to wink with, or which winks. Chiefly in the plural: synonym of blinker (“a shield attached to the bridle of a horse or other domesticated animal to prevent it from seeing things behind it and to its side”)

deserve.o: From Middle English deserven, from Old French deservir, from Latin dēserviō, from dē- + serviō.
deserve.example: After playing so well, the team really deserved their win.
deserve.exampleSense: To be entitled to, as a result of past actions; to be worthy to have.

scramble.o: Origin uncertain. Perhaps from earlier dialectal scramble, scrammel (“to collect or rake together with the hands”), from scramb (“to pull or scrape together with the hands”) + -le (frequentative suffix) (compare Dutch schrammen (“to graze, brush, scratch”)); or alternatively from a nasalised form of scrabble (“to scrape or scratch quickly”).
scramble.example: As half-time approached Fabregas had another chance to give Barcelona the lead. He collected an incisive Messi pass and this time beat Cech, who required Cole to scramble back and clear the ball off the line.
scramble.exampleSense: To move hurriedly to a location, especially by using all limbs against a surface.

anaphylaxis.o: Borrowed from French anaphylaxie, coined by French physiologist and parapsychologist Charles Richet and French zoologist Paul Portier from the Ancient Greek ᾰ̓νᾰ- (ănă-, “(intensifier) thoroughly”) from ᾰ̓νᾰ́ (ănắ, “to, again, upon”) and φύλαξις (phúlaxis, “protection, watching, guarding”).

shank.o: Inherited from Middle English sceonke, schank, schanke, shanke, schonke, sconke, sschanke, from Old English sċanca, sċeanca, sċeonca (“leg”), from Proto-West Germanic *skankō, from Proto-Germanic *skankô (“shank; thigh”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)keng- (“to hobble, limp; to tilt”). Cognates Cognate with West Frisian skonk (“leg”), Dutch schenkel (“shank”), German and Luxembourgish Schenkel (“thigh”), Danish skank (“shank; leg”), Norwegian Nynorsk skank, skonk (“thigh; foot”), Swedish skank, skånk (“leg”); also Cornish kamm (“pace, step”), Irish céim (“pace, step”), Manx keim (“degree, pace, stage, step”), Scottish Gaelic ceum (“pace, step”), Welsh cam (“pace, step”), Greek σκάω (skáo), σκάζω (skázo, “to burst, explode”), Bulgarian and Macedonian шега́ (šegá, “jest, joke; prank”).
shank.example: Edward I of England was nicknamed Edward Longshanks.
shank.exampleSense: The part of the leg between the knee and the ankle.

cramp.o: From Middle English crampe, from Old French crampe (“cramp”), from Frankish *krampa (“cramp”), from Proto-West Germanic *krampu, from Proto-Germanic *krampō (“cramp, clasp”). Distant relative of English crop.
cramp.example: You're going to need to cramp the wheels on this hill.
cramp.exampleSense: To restrain to a specific physical position, as if with a cramp.

inaugurate.o:
verb: Either: * borrowed from French inaugurer (“to inaugurate”), from Latin inaugurō (“to take omens from the flight of birds, to divine, practise augury; to approve, consecrate, or inaugurate on the basis of omens; to install”) with common assimilation of French -er with English -ate (verb-forming suffix) * or a Learned borrowing from Latin inaugurātus, perfect passive participle of inaugurō, see etymology at -ate; Further from in- (“against; into; on, upon; to, towards”) + augurō (“to act as an augur, interpret omens, augur; to foretell, predict; to conjecture, guess”), from augur (“soothsayer, augur”) + -ō (first conjugation verb-forming suffix) (further etymology uncertain; see the entry).

adj: Borrowed from Latin inaugurātus (“having been taken as an omen, divined; having been approved, consecrated, or inaugurated on the basis of omens; installed, having been installed”) (the perfect passive participle of inaugurō (verb): see etymology 1). See -ate (adjective-forming suffix).
inaugurate.example: On February 22nd, at an event featuring film stars, astronauts and technology gurus, Acciona, a Spanish conglomerate, is due to inaugurate a new power plant a few miles from Las Vegas.
inaugurate.exampleSense: To dedicate (something, as a building or a monument) for public access or use with a formal ceremony.

inaugural.o: From French inaugural, from inaugurer, from Latin augurare (“to take omens”).
inaugural.example: The inaugural of the President will take place in March.

inauguration.example: The inauguration of the new bar was a success, with plenty of discounts.
inauguration.exampleSense: The formal beginning, initiation, or entry into service of any movement, enterprise, building, event, etc.

satellite.o: From Middle French satellite, from Latin satelles (“attendant”). Ultimately perhaps of Etruscan origin.
satellite.example: Many telecommunication satellites orbit at 36000km above the equator.
satellite.exampleSense: A man-made apparatus designed to be placed in orbit around a celestial body, generally to relay information, data etc. to Earth.

eager.o:
adj: Inherited from Middle English egre, eger, from Old French aigre, egre (modern French aigre), from Latin ācrus, variant of ācer (“sharp, keen”); see acid, acerb, etc. Compare vinegar, alegar.

noun: See eagre.
eager.example: I was eager to show my teacher how much I'd learned over the holidays.
eager.exampleSense: Desirous; keen to do or obtain something.

indenture.o: From Anglo-Norman endenture, from Old French endenteure, from endenter (“to dent”). The name of the contract derives from the irregular dent-shaped cut (indentation) used to prove the authenticity of the two parts, similar to a chirograph.
indenture.example: And so the schoolmistress reconciled the recommendation to her conscience, and the indentures were cancelled, and the apprentice was free.
indenture.exampleSense: A contract which binds a person to work for another, under specified conditions, for a specified time (often as an apprentice).

lard.o:
noun: From Middle English lard, from Old French lard (“bacon”), from Latin lārdum, lāridum (“bacon fat”).

verb: From Middle English larden, from Old French larder and Medieval Latin lārdō.
lard.example: [The oak] with his nuts larded many swine.

switchback.o: The noun is derived from switch (“to turn (a train) from one railway track to another using a switch”, verb) + back (“so as to reverse direction and return”, adverb). The verb is derived from the noun.
switchback.example: Marriage was the switchback, the giant racer, the lobster teas, the guarantee that one would never be alone.
switchback.exampleSense: A railway track on a steep slope in a zigzag formation, in which a train travels in a reverse direction at each switch.

frazzle.o: Originally an East Anglian word. Either from a variant of the now obsolete fazle (“to unravel”), altered due to influence from fray, or from a blend of fazle and fray. fazle comes from earlier fasel, which was inherited from Middle English facelyn (“[of the end of a rope, or of cloth] to unravel”). Middle English facelyn was a verbal derivative of the noun fasylle (“frayed edge”), which was in turn a derivative (with the diminutive suffix -el) of Old English fæs (“fringe, border”), from Proto-West Germanic *fas, from Proto-Germanic *fasōn. Related to German Faser (“fibre”).
frazzle.example: After dealing with the children all day, I just can't help feeling frazzled.

ginseng.o: Borrowed from Hokkien 人參 /人参 (jîn-sim, “ginseng”). Doublet of ninzin.
ginseng.example: When the Afghan princes find it necessary to employ Chob-Chini, (the Jin-seng, or China root so celebrated as a purifier, tonic, and aphrodisiac) they choose the spring season.
ginseng.exampleSense: The root of such a plant, or an extract of these roots.

billowy.example: He was shabby and careless, with inkstains on the sleeves of his jacket, and his cravat was large and billowy, under a chin shaped like the toe of an old boot.
billowy.exampleSense: Swelling or swollen into large waves; full of billows or surges; resembling billows.

noontime.o: From noon + time, perhaps an innovation of earlier English noontide (“noontime”), from Middle English noon tijd, from Old English nōntīd (“noontime”). Eclipsed non-native Middle English merian, merion (“noontime”) from Old French meriiene, merīane (“noontime”).

eventide.o: From Middle English eventyde, from Old English ǣfentīd, derived from ǣfen (“evening”) + tīd (“time”). By surface analysis, even + -tide.
eventide.example: The mist rises from the lake at eventide.

scarecrow.o: The noun is derived from scare (“to frighten, startle, terrify”) + crow (“bird of the genus Corvus”). The word displaced other terms such as bogle (now dialectal, dated), sewel or shewel, and shoy-hoy (perhaps imitative of the cry of crows). The verb is derived from the noun.
scarecrow.example: An arctic wind whooshes down Columbus Avenue like the IRT express, catching her bags, scarecrowing her arms, and threatening to take her broad-brimmed hat downtown.
scarecrow.exampleSense: To cause (a person, their body, etc.) to look awkward and stiff, like a scarecrow (noun sense 1). To splay (one's arms) away from the body, like the arms of a scarecrow.

crow.o:
noun: From Middle English crowe, from Old English crāwe, from Proto-West Germanic *krāā, from Proto-Germanic *krēǭ (compare West Frisian krie, Dutch kraai, German Krähe), from *krēaną (“to crow”). See below.

verb: The verb is from Middle English crowen, from Old English crāwan (past tense crēow, past participle crāwen), from Proto-West Germanic *krāan, from Proto-Germanic *krēaną, from imitative Proto-Indo-European *gerH- (“to cry hoarsely”). The noun is from Middle English crowe, from the verb. Compare Dutch kraaien, German krähen, Lithuanian gróti, Russian гра́ять (grájatʹ)). Related to croak.
crow.example: Gaslark in his splendour on the golden stairs saying adieu to those three captains and their matchless armament foredoomed to dogs and crows on Salapanta Hills.
crow.exampleSense: A bird, usually black, of the genus Corvus, having a strong conical beak, with projecting bristles; it has a harsh, croaking call.

wick.o:
noun: The noun is derived from Middle English wek, weke, wicke (“fibrous cord drawing fuel to flame of a candle, etc.; material used to make this object”), from Old English wēoce (“wick”), from Proto-West Germanic *weukā (“flax bundle; wick”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *weg- (“to weave”). It has been suggested that noun etymology 1, noun sense 2 (“penis”) is derived from Hampton Wick, used as rhyming slang for prick. If so, that sense should be placed under etymology 2. The verb is derived from the noun. cognates * Dutch wiek (“wick; wing; blade, propeller”) * German Wieche (“wick; wisp”) * Swedish veke (“wick”) * West Frisian wjok, wjuk (“wing”)

noun: From Middle English wik, wike, wich, wicke (“dwelling, home; building or land, probably enclosed, in which work is done; area, region, territory; city, town; hamlet, village”), from Old English wīc (“dwelling place, abode, lodging; temporary dwelling place, camp; place where a thing remains; town, village”), and then probably: * from Latin vīcus (“row of houses; street; quarter, neighbourhood; hamlet, village; municipal section or ward; farm”), from Proto-Italic *weikos (“village”); and/or * from Proto-West Germanic *wīhs (“burgh, village; colony, settlement; dwelling”), from Proto-Germanic *wīhsą (“settlement; village”); both ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *weyḱ- (“to enter in; to settle; settlement”). Doublet of vicus and -wich. cognates * Ancient Greek οἶκος (oîkos, “house”) (whence English eco-) * Dutch wijk (“quarter, district”) * Old Frisian wik * Old High German wîch, wih (“village”) (modern German Weichbild (“municipal area”)) * Old Saxon wic (“village”)

adj: A variant of quick.

noun: From Late Middle English wike, wyke (“corner of part of the body”), from Old Norse *vík (“angle, bend, corner”) (attested in munnvík (“corner of the mouth”)), from víkja (“to move, bend, curve; to retreat”) (related to Old Norse vikna (“to cave in, yield”)), probably from Proto-Germanic *wīkwaną (“to cease; to yield”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃weyg-, *weyg- (“to bend, turn; to wind”).

noun: Probably borrowed from Scots wick (“(noun) shot in which a bowl or stone is aimed at another so that one or other is deflected at an angle towards the tee, cannon; (verb) to strike (a bowl or curling stone) in such a manner; to (attempt to) reach the tee in this manner”), The Scots noun is probably derived from Middle English wike, wyke (“corner of part of the body”); the verb from Old Norse víkja (“to move, bend, curve; to retreat”): see further at etymology 4.

noun: Possibly from Middle English *wik (compare Old English wīc (“small bay, bight; creek, inlet”)), or from Old Norse vík (“bay; small creek, inlet”) (in place names; compare *vík (“angle, bend, corner”), attested in munnvík (“corner of the mouth”)), from Proto-Germanic *wīkō (“bay; fjord, inlet”), from Proto-Indo-European *weyg- (“to bend, turn; to wind”), *weyk- (“to bend, curve”).

noun: Probably a clipping of wicker.
wick.example: Trim the wick fairly short, so that the flame does not smoke.
wick.exampleSense: A bundle, twist, braid, or woven strip of cord, fabric, fibre, or other porous material in a candle, oil lamp, kerosene heater, or the like, that draws up liquid fuel, such as melted tallow, wax, or the oil, delivering it to the base of the flame for conversion to gases and burning; any other length of material burned for illumination in small successive portions.

dissection.o: Borrowed from Latin dissectiōnem, perhaps via Middle French dissection. By surface analysis, dissect + -ion.

delusion.example: Hess, always a muddled man though not so doltish as Rosenberg, flew on his own to Britain under the delusion that he could arrange a peace settlement.
delusion.exampleSense: That which is falsely or delusively believed or propagated; false belief; error in belief.

contravene.o: From Middle French contravenir (French contrevenir), from Latin contraveniō.
contravene.example: It was a construction in wood, with manifold “features” suggestive of the villa, the bungalow, the chateau, the palace; it united all tastes and contravened all conventions.
contravene.exampleSense: To act contrary to an order; to fail to conform to a regulation or obligation.

poke.o:
verb: From Middle English poken, perhaps from Middle Dutch poken or Middle Low German poken, both from Proto-West Germanic *pukōn or similar, which is itself of uncertain origin, but may be from an imitative Proto-Germanic root *puk-. Doublet of poach. Compare Nordic cognates Swedish påka (“to poke, muck with a stick”), påk (“club, limb; dagger”), pykel (“small poker”), dialectal Norwegian pauka (“to walk stomping, etc”), pauk (“weak, slow person”). Central European noun-cognates refer to “dagger, bad knife, poker (for a fireplace)”, with analog verbs. To a Proto-Germanic *pauk-, *puk-, meanig, “to stick, muck with a stick”.

noun: From Middle English poke, from Anglo-Norman poke (whence pocket), from Frankish *poka. More at pocket. Doublet of pouch.

noun: Clipping of pocan (“pokeweed”) or directly borrowed from Powhatan pocan. See pocan for more.

noun: Borrowed from Hawaiian poke (literally “to cut crosswise into pieces”).
poke.example: Old Fred is the slowest old poke, isn't he? Suppose I try, Paul.

observation.o: From Middle English observacion, borrowed from Middle French observacion. Also a borrowing from French observation and a learned borrowing from Latin observātiō(n-). Morphologically observe + -ation.
observation.example: The physics of elementary particles in the 20th century was distinguished by the observation of particles whose existence had been predicted by theorists sometimes decades earlier.
observation.exampleSense: The act of observing, and the fact of being observed (see observance)

observe.o: From Middle French observer, from Old French observer, from Latin observō (“to watch”), from ob- (“before”) + servō (“to keep”), from Proto-Indo-European *ser- (“to guard”). Cognate with Gothic 𐍃𐌰𐍂𐍅𐌰 (sarwa, “weapons, armour”), Old English searu (“device”).
observe.example: Please observe all posted speed limits.
observe.exampleSense: To follow or obey the custom, practice, or rules (especially of a religion).

scram.o:
verb: Probably either: * a clipping of scramble by apocope; or * from dialectal German schramm, the imperative singular form of schrammen (“to scratch, scrape”), from Late Middle High German schramm, schramme (“a graze, scratch”); further etymology unknown.

verb: Uncertain; the verb is possibly derived from etymology

verb: The verb is a variant of dialectal English scramb (“to pull or rake together with the hands; to gather a handful of something from the ground; to scratch with the claws or nails; to pull down violently; to tear off; to maul about; a handful of something from the ground”), possibly related to Dutch schrammen (“to graze, scratch”) and German schrammen (“to scratch, scrape”); see etymology

verb: Origin unknown.
scram.example: [T]wo vampires had picked up the guy who needed a new face, and they scrammed.
scram.exampleSense: To leave in a hurry; to go away.

nonobservance.o: From Middle English non-observaunce, nonn observance, equivalent to non- (“no”, adjective) + observance.

observance.o: From Old French observance, from Latin observantia. Equivalent of observe + -ance.
observance.example: Thomas Merton was a monk in the Order of Cistertians of the Strict Observance.
observance.exampleSense: A rule governing a religious order, especially in the Roman Catholic church.

purpose.o:
noun: From Middle English purpos, from Old French purposer (“to propose”) (with conjugation altered based on poser), from Latin prō- (“forth”) + pōnere (“place, put”), hence Latin prōpōnō, prōpōnere. By surface analysis, pur- + pose (“halt, pause, put, place”).

verb: From Middle English purposen, from Old French purposer (“to propose”).
purpose.example: The exceptionally small gate-leg table served the purpose of a tea table admirably.

patience.o: Inherited from Middle English pacience, from Old French pacience (modern French patience), from Latin patientia (“suffering; endurance, patience”), from patiens, present active participle of patior (“suffer, experience, wait”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *peh₁- (“to hurt”). Displaced Old English ġeþyld.
patience.example: Musical perfection requires practice and a lot of patience.

perseverance.o: From Middle English perseveraunce, from Old French perseverance, from Latin persevērantia.
perseverance.example: It had taken nine years from the evening that Truman first showed up with a pie plate at her mother's door, but his dogged perseverance eventually won him the hand of his boyhood Sunday school crush.
perseverance.exampleSense: Continuing in a course of action without regard to discouragement, opposition or previous failure.

felid.o: By surface analysis, an appellativization from Felid(ae) minus -ae (a pattern that recurs with many -idae names); by surface analysis, feline + -id.

fetid.o: Borrowed from Latin fētidus (“having offensive odour”), originally fēteō (“to stink”).
fetid.example: I caught the fetid odor of dirty socks.

lost-and-found.o: Alternative form of lost. From Middle English loste, losede (preterite) and Middle English lost, ilost, ilosed (past participle), from Old English losode (preterite) and Old English losod, ġelosod, equivalent to lose + -t.

poker.o:
noun: From poke + -er.

noun: American English, perhaps from first element of German Pochspiel, from German pochen, perhaps from French poque. First appeared in the 19th century.

noun: Compare Danish pokker (“the deuce, devil”), and English puck.
poker.example: The lids have very pleasant designs pokered on with a hot needle.
poker.exampleSense: To poke with a utensil such as a poker or needle.

porno.o: Clipping of pornographic or pornography. Attested from mid-20th century.
porno.example: In any case, porno is littered—porno is heaped—with the deaths of feelings.

porn.o: Clipping of pornography. First attested in the mid-20th century.
porn.example: I just delete the porn before someone else uses the computer.

theory.o: Borrowed from Middle French théorie, a learned borrowing from Late Latin theōria, borrowed from Ancient Greek θεωρία (theōría), from θεωρός (theōrós, “spectator”) + -ῐ́ᾱ (-ĭ́ā).
theory.example: In its most proper acceptation, theory means the completed result of philosophical induction from experience.
theory.exampleSense: A coherent statement or set of ideas that explains observed facts or phenomena and correctly predicts new facts or phenomena not previously observed, or which sets out the laws and principles of something known or observed; a hypothesis confirmed by observation, experiment etc.

theoretic.o: English theory + -etic, from Latin theōrēticus, from Ancient Greek θεωρητικός (theōrētikós).
theoretic.example: We shall, therefore, only very humbly submit whether the whole statement be not rather too theoretic and somewhat too darkly adumbrated in ambiguous phraseology for plain, uncollegian understandings.
theoretic.exampleSense: Concerned with theories or hypotheses rather than with practical matters.

meditate.o: First attested in 1560; borrowed from Latin meditātus, perfect active participle of meditor (“to think or reflect upon, consider, design, purpose, intend”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), morphologically as if frequentative of medeor (“to heal, to cure, to remedy”); in sense and in form near to Ancient Greek μελετάω (meletáō, “to care for, attend to, study, practise, etc.”). Participial usage up until Early Modern English.
meditate.example: He lay and meditated the sluggishness of his bowels. This created pictures of chrome and porcelain and attendant circumstances.

lavatory.o:
noun: From Middle English lavatorie, from Late Latin lavātōrium, from Latin lavāre (“to wash”) + -ium (forming places related to an activity). As a place to pan gold, via Spanish lavadero. Doublet of lavatorium and laver. See also lave.

adj: From Latin lavātōrius.
lavatory.example: Americans don't know 'WC' and Brits mock 'bathroom' but everyone usually understands 'toilet' or 'lavatory'.
lavatory.exampleSense: A room containing a toilet: a bathroom (US) or WC (UK).

sport utility vehicle.o: Extant since the 1970s in the technical usage of the auto industry, where at the time it sometimes included a virgule as sport/utility vehicle; in common use among the general public since the early 1990s, when this class of vehicles first became widely popular as an alternative to station wagons and minivans.

leaning.o:
noun: From Middle English lening, leninge, from Old English hlinung (“leaning; resting; place of rest”), equivalent to lean + -ing.

verb: See the etymology of the corresponding lemma form.

workaholic.example: All workaholics should move to Hong Kong, where working hours average over 50 per week.
workaholic.exampleSense: A person who feels compelled to work excessively, including while at home.

commonweal.o: From Middle English comun wele, commen wele, comune wele, equivalent to common (“public”) + weal (“well-being”). By the 1520s used by some authors as the equivalent of res publica (republic), alongside commonwealth from about the same time.
commonweal.example: He yearns for the days when people, for reasons of the commonweal, did what they were told.
commonweal.exampleSense: The common good; public wellbeing or prosperity

impetus.o: Borrowed from Latin impetus (“a rushing upon, an attack, assault, onset”), from impetō (“to rush upon, attack”), from in- (“upon”) + petō (“to seek, fall upon”).
impetus.example: The outbreak of World War II in 1939 gave a new impetus to receiver development.
impetus.exampleSense: Anything that impels; a stimulating factor.

doll.o:
noun: From Doll, pet form of the given name Dorothy. Etymology 1, noun sense 7 was coined and popularized by American writer Jacqueline Susann in 1966 through her book Valley of the Dolls (1966) and the film adaptation Valley of the Dolls (1967).

noun: Probably variant of archaic dool (“boundary marker”).

noun: Clipping of dollar.

verb: Possibly same as dull (whence Middle English doll).
doll.example: "They didn't sell cigarettes where you were, doll?" Palmer asked.
doll.exampleSense: A term of endearment: darling, sweetheart.

threat.o:
noun: From Middle English threte, thret, thrat, thræt, threat, from Old English þrēat (“crowd, swarm, troop, army, press; pressure, trouble, calamity, oppression, force, violence, threat”), from Proto-Germanic *þrautaz, closely tied to Proto-Germanic *þrautą (“displeasure, complaint, grievance, labour, toil”), from Proto-Indo-European *trewd- (“to squeeze, push, press”). Cognate with Scots thret, threte, threit (“threat”), Middle High German drōz (“annoyance, disgust, horror, terror, fright”), Middle Low German drōt (“threat, menace, danger”), Faroese treyt (“struggle, labour, distress”), Icelandic þraut (“struggle, labour, distress”), Belarusian, Bulgarian, Macedonian, Russian, and Ukrainian труд (trud, “work, labour”), Czech trud (“effot, hard work”), Polish trud (“hard work”), Serbo-Croatian trȗd (“effort, hard work”).

verb: From Middle English threten, from Old English þrēatian (“to press, oppress, repress, correct, threaten”), derived from Proto-Indo-European *trewd- (“to squeeze, push, press”). Cognate with Scots threit (“to threaten”), Dutch verdrieten (“to sadden, displease”), Middle Low German drēten (“to threaten”), German verdrießen (“to bother, vex”), Faroese tróta (“to run out”), Icelandic þrjóta (“to run out, end”), Norwegian tryte (“to run out, end”), Swedish tryda (“to run out”), Gothic 𐌿𐍃𐌸𐍂𐌹𐌿𐍄𐌰𐌽 (usþriutan, “to harass, torment”), Latin trūdō (“to push”), Albanian ndrydh (“to sprain, supress, withdraw”), Belarusian трудзіць (trudzicʹ, “to burden, tire”), Bulgarian тру̀дя (trùdja, “to work”), Czech trudit (“to toil, worry”), Polish trudzić (“to toil, worry”), Russian труди́ть (trudítʹ, “to burden, tire”), Serbo-Croatian trúditi (“to try, make and effot”), Ukrainian труди́ти (trudýty, “to toil, tire”).
threat.example: There is no terror, Cassius, in your threats.
threat.exampleSense: An expression of intent to injure or punish another.

defence.o:
noun: From Middle English defens, defense, from Old French defens, defense, from Late Latin dēfēnsa (“protection”). Displaced Old English bewering.

verb: From Middle English defencen, defensen, from Old French defenser or its etymon, Latin dēfēnsō.
defence.example: Better manned and more strongly defenced.
defence.exampleSense: To furnish with defences; to fortify.

employment.o: From employ (itself from Middle French employer, from Middle French empleier, from Latin implicō (“enfold, involve, be connected with”), itself from in- + plicō (“fold”)) + -ment.
employment.example: At the period just preceding the advent of Bartleby, I had two persons as copyists in my employment, and a promising lad as an office-boy.

decision-making.o: Alternative form of decision. Derived from Middle French, from Latin dēcīsiō, dēcīsiōnis, from dēcīdō (“to decide”).
decision-making.example: But what if Google's biggest problem isn't a lack of flexibility or the speed of its decision-making, but a fundamental cultural inability to create new lines of business that can keep the company growing? What if it's just a gargantuan one-trick pony?

feces.o: From Latin faecēs, nominative plural of faex (“residue, dregs”), further origin unknown; possibly borrowed from a substrate language.
feces.example: We are also extracting DNA, both from blood collected during immobilizations and from hyena feces.
feces.exampleSense: Digested waste material (typically solid or semi-solid) discharged from a human or other mammal's stomach to the intestines; excrement.

fecal.o: From Middle French fecal, from Latin faex, equivalent to feces + -al.
fecal.example: Differential biochemical or physiological characteristics which correlate with aerogenesis at elevated incubation temperatures will be adapted towards a fecal coliform procedure and towards converting a total coliform procedure under development to give a fecal coliform count as well.

defecate.o: Borrowed from Latin dēfaecātus, the perfect passive participle of dēfaecō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix). See also faeces; cognate with French déféquer.
defecate.example: Till the soul be defecate from the dregs of sense.
defecate.exampleSense: Freed from pollutants, dregs, lees, etc.; refined; purified.

defecation.o: 17th century, borrowed from Late Latin dēfaecātiō.
defecation.example: The juice after it leaves the mill has a more or less green color, due to the presence of large quantities of chlorophyl and other vegetable substances, which must be removed. This process is known as defecation.
defecation.exampleSense: Any of several processes for the removal of impurities, or for clarifying various materials.

rainy.o: From Middle English reyny, from Old English reġniġ, from Proto-West Germanic *regnag, from Proto-Germanic *regnagaz (“rainy”), equivalent to rain + -y. Cognate with Saterland Frisian rienig (“rainy”), West Frisian reinich (“rainy”), Dutch regenig (“rainy”), German regnig (“rainy”), Swedish regnig (“rainy”).
rainy.example: Due to the rainy weather, we decided not to play in the park.

regrowth.example: The eventual regrowth of the forest to its primeval state will take centuries, if not millennia.

keystone.o: From key + stone. Definition 4 (retail) possibly originated in the jewelry industry in the magazine called "Jewelers' Circular-Keystone".
keystone.example: The tunnel, which is 1,000 yd. long, had been closed to passenger traffic since November 17, 1949, after some of the keystones had worked loose.
keystone.exampleSense: The top stone of an arch.

fig.o:
noun: From Middle English fige, fygge (also fyke, from Old English fīc, see fike), borrowed from Anglo-Norman figue, borrowed from Old French figue, from Old Occitan figa, from Vulgar Latin *fīca (“fig”), from Latin fīcus (“fig tree”), from a pre-Indo European language, perhaps Phoenician 𐤐𐤂 (pg, literally “ripe fig”) (compare Biblical Hebrew פַּגָּה (paggâ, “early fallen fig”), Classical Syriac ܦܓܐ (paggāʾ), dialectal Arabic فَجّ (fajj), فِجّ (fijj)). (Another Semitic root (compare Akkadian 𒈠 (tīʾu, literally “fig”)) was borrowed into Ancient Greek as σῦκον (sûkon) (whence English sycophant; Boeotian τῦκον (tûkon)) and Armenian as թուզ (tʻuz).) The soap-making sense derives from the resemblance of the granulations in and texture of the soap to those of a fig. Doublet of fico.

verb: Variation of fike.

verb: See figging.
fig.example: And the eyes of them both were opened, and they knew that they were naked; and they sewed fig leaves together, and made themselves aprons.
fig.exampleSense: A fruit-bearing tree or shrub of the genus Ficus that is native mainly to the tropics.

topsoil.example: Little grew on the farm, after the floods from the hurricane washed away the topsoil.
topsoil.exampleSense: The upper layer of soil, typically most fertile and in which it is the easiest to start new plants.

rearing.example: We studied blowfly rearings in various environmental conditions.

restoration.o: From Middle English restoracion, altered from restauracion (from Latin restaurātiō) by partly deriving from restoren + -acion. By surface analysis, restore + -ation.
restoration.example: The restoration of this medieval church involved undoing all the Victorian modifications.
restoration.exampleSense: The process of bringing an object back to its original state; the process of restoring something.

drone.o:
noun: From Middle English drane, dron, drone, from Old English drān, drǣn, from Proto-West Germanic *drānu, from Proto-Germanic *drenô, *drēnuz (“drone”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰreh₁n- (“bee, drone, hornet”). Cognates Cognate with Saterland Frisian Droane (“drone”), Dutch dar (“drone”), German Drohne (“drone”), Limburgish dreen, Droon (“drone”), Danish, Norwegian Bokmål, and Norwegian Nynorsk drone (“drone”), Swedish drönare (“drone”); also Belarusian тру́цень (trúcjenʹ, “drone”), Bulgarian търтей (tǎrtej, “drone”), Czech trubec (“drone”), Macedonian трут (trut, “drone”), Polish trąd, trut, truteń (“drone”), Russian and Ukrainian тру́тень (trútenʹ, “drone”), Serbo-Croatian тру̑т, trȗt (“drone”), Slovak trúd (“drone”), Slovene trot (“drone”). The etymology of the sense of "remote-controlled aircraft" is disputed; theories include early military UAVs dumbly flying on preset paths.

verb: From Middle English drounen (“to roar, bellow”), from Proto-West Germanic *drunnjan, from Proto-Germanic *drunjaną (“to drone, roar, make a sound”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰer- (“to roar, hum, drone”). Cognate with Scots drune (“to drone, moan, complain”), Dutch dreunen (“to drone, boom, thud”), Low German drönen (“to drone, buzz, hum”), German dröhnen (“to roar, boom, rumble”), Danish drøne (“to roar, boom, peel out”), Swedish dröna (“to low, bellow, roar”), Icelandic drynja (“to roar”).
drone.example: Several images of the compound were obtained via a drone overflight.
drone.exampleSense: A remotely operated vehicle. An aircraft operated by remote control, especially an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV).

recreational.example: This is perhaps what we call recreational reading and we may be doing something useful in supplying it, if not anything strictly educational or even librarious.

formerly.example: Xenia Robertson, formerly known as Xenia Isaamov, is from Ukraine.
formerly.exampleSense: at some time in the past

long-term.example: Asari Cultural VI: Due to our lifespan-sometimes reaching 1,000 years of age-we are patient in our decisions, and prefer long-term solutions over short-term gains.
long-term.exampleSense: Extending over a relatively long time period.

invasive.o: PIE word *h₁én The adjective is derived from Middle English invasif (“of a weapon: offensive”), from Middle French invasif, Old French invasif (“invasive”) (modern French invasif), from Medieval Latin invāsīvus, from Latin invāsus (“entered; invaded”) + -īvus (suffix forming adjectives). Invāsus is the perfect passive participle of invādō (“to enter; to invade”), from in- (prefix meaning ‘in, inside’) + vādō (“to go; to rush; to walk”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *weh₂dʰ- (“to go, proceed; to pass, traverse”)). The noun is derived from the adjective.
invasive.example: Two patients developed cancer in the upper urinary tract, and 3 eventually developed invasive cancer.
invasive.exampleSense: Of a carcinoma or other abnormal growth: that invades healthy tissue, especially rapidly.

link.o:
noun: From Middle English linke, lenke, from a merger of Old English hlenċe, hlenċa (“ring; chainlink”) and Old Norse *hlenkr, hlekkr (“ring; chain”); both from Proto-Germanic *hlankiz (“ring; bond; fettle; fetter”), from Proto-Germanic *hlankaz (“bendsome, flexible”), from Proto-Indo-European *kleng-, *klenk- (“to bend; twist; wind”). Used in English since the 14th century. Related to lank. Cognates Cognate with Low German Lenk (“link”), Danish lænke (“chain; link”), Elfdalian lekk (“link”), Icelandic hlekkur (“link”), Norwegian Bokmål lenke (“chain; link”), Norwegian Nynorsk lenke, lenkje (“chain; link”), Swedish länk (“chain; link”).

noun: Plausibly a modification of Medieval Latin linchinus (“candle”), an alteration of Latin lynchinus, itself from Ancient Greek λύχνος (lúkhnos, “lamp”).

verb: Unknown.
link.example: The third link of the silver chain needs to be resoldered.
link.exampleSense: One element of a chain or other connected series.

proliferate.example: The flowers proliferated rapidly all spring.
proliferate.exampleSense: To increase in number or spread rapidly; to multiply.

call forth.example: They were called forth as witnesses.
call forth.exampleSense: To summon, to call to speak.

attend.o: PIE word *h₂éd From Middle English attenden, atenden (“to devote oneself (to a task, etc.); to pay attention to (something), to look after; to consider (something); to expect or look forward to (something); to intend to do (something); to help or serve (someone), attend upon; to take care of (something)”), from Old French atendre (“to await, wait for; to expect; to intend”), from Latin attendere, adtendere (“to pay attention to, attend; to direct or turn toward”), from ad- (“prefix meaning ‘to, towards’”) + tendō (“to direct one’s course; to extend, stretch; to exert, strive”). Doublet of attempt and tend.
attend.example: [T]he two captains, Peleg and Bildad, could attend to everything necessary to fit the vessel for the voyage.
attend.exampleSense: Senses relating to caring for or waiting on someone, or accompanying or being present. Followed by to: to take action with respect to someone or something; to deal with.

diagnosis.o: From Latin diagnōsis, from Ancient Greek διάγνωσις (diágnōsis), from διαγιγνώσκω (diagignṓskō, “to discern”), from διά (diá, “through”) + γιγνώσκω (gignṓskō, “to know”).
diagnosis.example: Her diagnosis of the current economic situation is that central banks are overcorrecting.
diagnosis.exampleSense: The process of, or an instance of, identification of the nature and cause of something (of any nature).

avenue.o: Borrowed from French avenue, from Old French avenue, feminine past participle of avenir (“approach”), from Latin adveniō, advenīre (“come to”, from ad (“to”) + veniō, venīre (“come”)).
avenue.example: Boulevards typically (but not exclusively) go east to west; avenues usually run north to south.
avenue.exampleSense: A broad street, especially one bordered by trees or, in cities laid out in a grid pattern, one that is on a particular side of the city or that runs in a particular direction.

urgency.example: Arsenal lacked urgency and inspiration until shortly before half-time, Wheater's block denying Van Persie from close range before Walcott drilled wide.
urgency.exampleSense: The quality or condition of being urgent.

exhibit.o: From Latin exhibitus, perfect passive participle of exhibeō (“to hold forth, present, show, display”), from ex (“out of, from”) + habeō (“to have, hold”); see habit.
exhibit.example: I now exhibit this bloody hammer.
exhibit.exampleSense: To submit (a physical object) to a court as evidence.

exclusively.o: From Middle English exclusyvely; equivalent to exclusive + -ly.
exclusively.example: These new shoes are made exclusively out of recycled cardboard.
exclusively.exampleSense: to the exclusion of anything or anyone else; solely or entirely

positive.o: From Old French positif, from Latin positivus, from the past participle stem of ponere (“to place”). Compare posit.
positive.example: The box was not empty – I felt some positive substance within it.
positive.exampleSense: Characterized by the existence or presence of distinguishing qualities or features, rather than by their absence.

aggravate.o: The adjective is first attested in 1471 in Middle English, the verb in 1530; from Latin aggravātus, perfect passive participle of aggravō (“to add to the weight of, make worse, oppress, annoy”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from ad- (“to”) + gravō (“to make heavy”), from gravis (“heavy”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix). See grave and compare aggrieve and aggrege. Participial usage of the adjective up until Early Modern English. By surface analysis, ag- + grave (“heavy”) + -ate (“verb suffix”).
aggravate.example: If both were to aggravate her parents, as my brother and sister do mine.
aggravate.exampleSense: To exasperate; to provoke or irritate.

cure.o:
noun: From Middle English cure, borrowed from Old French cure (“care, cure, healing, cure of souls”), from Latin cura (“care, medical attendance, cure”). Displaced native Old English hǣlu, but this survived as heal.

verb: From Middle English curen, from Old French curer, from Latin cūrāre. Partially displaced Old English ġehǣlan, whence Modern English heal.

noun: From curiosity.
cure.example: The smoke and heat cures the meat.
cure.exampleSense: To prepare or alter, especially by chemical or physical processing for keeping or use.

oddity.example: An Avonside 0-4-4T with outside cylinders, bought by the S.M.A. in 1882 and scrapped in 1892 as a dismal failure, was one of the motive power oddities (some of them mortgaged).
oddity.exampleSense: An odd or strange thing or opinion.

uncritical.example: More importantly, the rehearsing of that information has been almost completely uncritical, indicating a lack of recourse to any further information about the term.
uncritical.exampleSense: Lacking critique or critical examination; undiscriminating.

phenomena.o: The plural form of phenomenon, formed according to the Ancient Greek -ον (-on) → -α (-a) pluralisation pattern.
phenomena.example: A new musical prodigy has turned up in Cincinnati more wonderful than all the infant phenomenas in that line that have appeared for many a day.

achieve.o: From Middle English achieven, acheven, from Anglo-Norman achever, Old French achever, achiever et al., apparently from Late Latin *accapāre, from ad (“to”) + caput (“head”) + -ō (verbal suffix), or alternatively a construction based on Old French chief (“head”). Compare Catalan, Occitan, Portuguese and Spanish acabar, French achever.
achieve.example: Some are born great, some achieve greatness.
achieve.exampleSense: To obtain, or gain (a desired result, objective etc.), as the result of exertion; to succeed in gaining; to win.

miracle.o: From Middle English miracle, from Old French miracle, from Latin mīrāculum (“object of wonder”), from mīror (“to wonder at”), from mīrus (“wonderful”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)meyh₂- (“to smile, to be astonished”). Doublet of milagro and miraculum. Partially displaced native wonder, from Old English wundor (“miracle, wonder”).
miracle.example: An example of a miracle associated with Muhammad is the splitting of the moon.
miracle.exampleSense: An event that appears inexplicable by the laws of nature and so is held to be supernatural in origin.

miraculous.o: From Middle French miraculeux. Displaced native Old English wundorlīċ.

posture.o: Borrowed from Middle French posture, from Italian postura, from Latin positūra (“position, situation”). Doublet of positura.
posture.example: If you're finished posturing in front of the mirror, can I use the bathroom now?
posture.exampleSense: to put one's body into a posture or series of postures, especially hoping that one will be noticed and admired

fluent.o: From Latin fluens (“flowing”), present active participle of fluō (“to flow”).
fluent.example: The clerk had, I'm afraid, a shrew of a wife—shrill, vehement, and fluent.
fluent.exampleSense: Able to use a language accurately, rapidly, and confidently.

verbally.example: Dumbstruck with joy, she was unable to express herself verbally, but the gratitude in her face was evident to all.
verbally.exampleSense: In a verbal manner; with words; by speaking.

aphasia.o: From French aphasie, from Ancient Greek ἀφασία (aphasía), from ἄφατος (áphatos, “speechless”), from ἀ- (a-, “not”) + φάσις (phásis, “speech”). Equivalent to a- + -phasia.
aphasia.example: The Doctor came over in three minutes, and heard the story. ‘It's aphasia,’ he said.
aphasia.exampleSense: A partial or total loss of language skills due to brain damage. Usually, damage to the left perisylvian region, including Broca's area and Wernicke's area, causes aphasia.

expressive.example: These adults performed significantly more poorly than a group of 28 control adults on all measures of articulation and expressive and receptive language.
expressive.exampleSense: Conveying the speaker's emotions and/or attitudes, in addition to the denotative or literal meaning.

melodic.o: Borrowed from French mélodique. By surface analysis, melody + -ic.
melodic.example: Debussy's melody is fractional, fragmentary. But at the core all his music is melodic and melody is its main motive force.
melodic.exampleSense: Of, relating to, or having melody.

underappreciated.o: simple past and past participle of underappreciate. From under- + appreciate.
underappreciated.example: As a regular rail user who has only ever been a leisure passenger, I agree that it's now an under-appreciated market.
underappreciated.exampleSense: Not valued or appreciated as highly as one should be.

recount.o:
noun: From Old Northern French and Anglo-Norman recunter, variant of Old French reconter.

noun: From re- + count.
recount.example: The old man recounted the tale of how he caught the big fish.
recount.exampleSense: To tell; narrate; to relate in detail

dissociation.o: Borrowed from French dissociation, from Latin dissociātiō(n).
dissociation.example: Project MONARCH could be best described as a form of structured dissociation and occultic integration, carried out in order to compartmentalize the mind into multiple personalities within a systematic framework.
dissociation.exampleSense: A defence mechanism where certain thoughts or mental processes are compartmentalised in order to avoid emotional stress to the conscious mind.

amusia.o: From Late Latin amusia, from Ancient Greek ἀμουσία (amousía, “without harmony”), from ἄμουσος (ámousos, “without song”). The Muses were the nine daughters of Zeus and the goddesses of arts and sciences.

torment.o: From Middle English torment, from Old French torment, from Latin tormentum (“something operated by twisting”), from torquere (“to twist”).
torment.example: They brought unto him all sick people that were taken with divers diseases and torments.
torment.exampleSense: Any extreme pain, anguish or misery, either physical or mental.

trauma.example: Jailing her on Wednesday, magistrate Liz Clyne told Robins: "You have shown little remorse either for the death of the kitten or the trauma to your former friend Sarah Knutton." She was also banned from keeping animals for 10 years.
trauma.exampleSense: An emotional wound leading to psychological injury.

cerebrate.o:
verb: First attested in 1874; from Latin cerebrum (“brain”) + -ate (verb-forming suffix); likely a back-formation from cerebration.

noun: From (obsolete) cerebric acid + -ate (“salt or ester”).

cerebrum.o: Inherited from Middle English cerebrum, from Latin cerebrum (“a brain; a skull”); see there for more.

cerebral.o:
adj: Borrowing from French cérébral, from Latin cerebrum (“a brain”); equivalent to cerebrum + -al.

adj: Semantic loan from Sanskrit मूर्धन्य (mūrdhanya, “pertaining to the head”).
cerebral.example: Certainly, “Capital” is a cerebral read and the dangers of the world Marx lived in are not all the same as ours.
cerebral.exampleSense: Intellectual rather than emotional or physical.

torrid.o: From Latin torridus, from torreō (“parch, scorch”).
torrid.example: Tomás O'Leary had a torrid time behind the forwards, fumbling on the floor, hesitant with his kicks.

terrain.o: Unadapted borrowing from French terrain, from Latin terrenum (“land, ground”), neuter of terrenus (“consisting of earth”), from terra (“earth”).
terrain.example: This approach requires the aircraft to stay at an altitude of at least 3000 feet MSL until crossing the VOR in order to maintain terrain clearance.
terrain.exampleSense: The surface of the earth; the ground.

torrent.o:
noun: Borrowed from French torrent, from Italian torrente, from Latin torrentem, accusative of torrēns (“burning, seething, roaring”), from Latin torrēre (“to parch, scorch”).

noun: From BitTorrent and the file extension it uses for metadata (.torrent); ultimately from etymology 1, carrying the notion of the flow of information.
torrent.example: A torrent of green and white water broke over the hull of the sail-boat.
torrent.exampleSense: A violent flow, as of water, lava, etc.; a stream suddenly raised and running rapidly, as down a precipice.

arise.o: From Middle English arisen, from Old English ārīsan (“to arise, get up; rise; spring from, originate; spring up, ascend”), from Proto-Germanic *uzrīsaną (“to rise up, arise”), equivalent to a- + rise. Cognate with Scots arise, aryse (“to arise, rise up, come into existence”), Middle Low German errīsen (“to stand up, arise”), Old High German irrīsan (“to rise up, fall”), Gothic 𐌿𐍂𐍂𐌴𐌹𐍃𐌰𐌽 (urreisan, “to arise”). Eclipsed Middle English sourden, sorden, borrowed from Old French sordre, sourdre (“to arise, originate, fly up”).
arise.example: A cloud arose and covered the sun.
arise.exampleSense: To spring up; to come into action, being, or notice; to become operative, sensible, or visible; to begin to act a part; to present itself.

arose.o: simple past of arise. From Middle English arisen, from Old English ārīsan (“to arise, get up; rise; spring from, originate; spring up, ascend”), from Proto-Germanic *uzrīsaną (“to rise up, arise”), equivalent to a- + rise. Cognate with Scots arise, aryse (“to arise, rise up, come into existence”), Middle Low German errīsen (“to stand up, arise”), Old High German irrīsan (“to rise up, fall”), Gothic 𐌿𐍂𐍂𐌴𐌹𐍃𐌰𐌽 (urreisan, “to arise”). Eclipsed Middle English sourden, sorden, borrowed from Old French sordre, sourdre (“to arise, originate, fly up”).
arose.example: The amniote egg is most likely to have arose along the portion of the phylogeny denoted by the solid shading, and is less likely to have arose along the portion denoted by the cross-hatched shading.

craft.o: (“strength, skill”), from Old English cræft (“strength, skill”), from Proto-West Germanic *kraftu, from Proto-Germanic *kraftuz (“strength, power”); further origin obscure. Cognate with Dutch kracht (“strength, power, force”), German Kraft (“strength, power, force, energy, employee”), Danish, Norwegian Bokmål, Norwegian Nynorsk, and Swedish kraft (“strength, power, force”), Faroese and Icelandic kraftur (“strength”).
craft.example: Quite near could also be seen several ancient wooden warships, and always a variety of craft slipping up and down the tideway.
craft.exampleSense: A vehicle designed for navigation in or on water or air or through outer space . Boats, especially of smaller size than ships. Historically primarily applied to vessels engaged in loading or unloading of other vessels, as lighters, hoys, and barges.

consume.o: From Middle English consumen, from Old French consumer, from Latin cōnsūmere, cōnsūmō, from con- (“with, together”) + sūmō (“take; consume”), from sub- + emō (“to buy, take”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁em- (“to take, distribute”), possibly related to the root *nem- (“to take or give one's due”).
consume.example: The building was consumed by fire.

lightning.example: Although we did not see the lightning, we did hear the thunder.
lightning.exampleSense: A flash of light produced by short-duration, high-voltage discharge of electricity within a cloud, between clouds, or between a cloud and the earth.

liberal.o: The adjective is from Old French liberal, from Latin līberālis (“befitting a freeman”), from līber (“free”); it is attested since the 14th century. The noun is first attested in the 1800s.
liberal.example: The result was usually that such helpers got a liberal sprinkling of mud over their clothing.

spark.o:
noun: From Middle English sparke, sperke, from Old English spearca, from Proto-West Germanic *sparkō (compare Saterland Frisian Spoorke, West Frisian spark, Dutch spark, German Low German Sparke, German Sparke), perhaps from Proto-Germanic *sparkaz (“lively, energetic”), from Proto-Indo-European *sperg- (“to strew, sprinkle”) (compare Breton erc’h (“snow”), Latin spargō (“to scatter, spread”), sparsus (“scattered”), Lithuanian sprógti (“to germinate”), Ancient Greek σπαργάω (spargáō, “to swell”), Avestan 𐬟𐬭𐬀𐬯𐬞𐬀𐬭𐬈𐬔𐬀 (frasparega, “branch, twig”), Sanskrit पर्जन्य (parjanya, “rain, rain god”)).

noun: Probably Scandinavian, akin to Old Norse sparkr (“sprightly”).
spark.example: Byron sparked the cigarette. He sucked it dramatically and thrust it into Marko's hand.

sprinkle.o: From Middle English sprenkelen, sprynklen, from Middle Dutch sprenkelen, equivalent to sprink + -le (frequentative suffix). Cognate with Dutch sprenkelen (“to sprinkle”), German Low German sprenkeln (“to sprinkle; dapple”), German sprenkeln (“to sprinkle”).
sprinkle.example: The confectioner sprinkled icing sugar over the cakes.
sprinkle.exampleSense: To cause (a substance) to fall in fine drops (for a liquid substance) or small pieces (for a solid substance).

contemporary.o: From Medieval Latin contemporārius, from Latin con- (“with, together”) + temporārius, an adjective derived from tempus (“time”).
contemporary.example: The early mammals inherited the earth by surviving their saurian contemporaries.
contemporary.exampleSense: Someone or something belonging to the same time period (as someone or something else)

heed.o: From Middle English heden, from Old English hēdan (“to heed, take care, observe, attend, guard, take charge, take possession, receive”), from Proto-West Germanic *hōdijan (“to heed, guard”), from Proto-Indo-European *kadʰ- (“to heed, protect”). Cognate with West Frisian hoedje (“to heed”), Dutch hoeden (“to heed”), German hüten (“to heed”).
heed.example: Then for a few minutes I did not pay much heed to what was said, being terribly straitened for room, and cramped with pain from lying so long in one place.

take heed.example: The king spoke and the lords took heed.

newfangled.o: From new + fangled, from obsolete fangle (“to fashion”).
newfangled.example: [US president Donald Trump] might have in mind a newfangled protectionism that lasts generations.
newfangled.exampleSense: New and often needlessly novel or gratuitously different; recently devised or fashionable, especially when not an improvement.

old-fashioned.o: From old + fashioned. The cocktail (which goes back to at least the early 1800s) got its name in the late 1800s as more complicated cocktails became common and those who preferred simpler drinks began asking for old-fashioned cocktails.
old-fashioned.example: You can’t stay the night, because my parents are a bit old-fashioned.
old-fashioned.exampleSense: Of a person, preferring the customs of earlier times and the old-style ways.

tear.o:
verb: From Middle English teren, from Old English teran (“to tear, lacerate”), from Proto-Germanic *teraną (“to tear, tear apart, rip”), from Proto-Indo-European *der- (“to tear, tear apart”). Cognate with Scots tere, teir, tair (“to rend, lacerate, wound, rip, tear out”), Dutch teren (“to eliminate, efface, live, survive by consumption”), German zehren (“to consume, misuse”), German zerren (“to tug, rip, tear”), Danish tære (“to consume”), Swedish tära (“to fret, consume, deplete, use up”), Icelandic tæra (“to clear, corrode”). Outside Germanic, cognate to Ancient Greek δέρω (dérō, “to skin”), Albanian ther (“to slay, skin, pierce”). Doublet of tire.

noun: From Middle English tear, teer, teere, ter, tere, tyar, tyear, tyer, tær (“tear”), from Old English teagor, tēar, tæher, from Proto-West Germanic *tahr, from Proto-Germanic *tahrą (“tear”), from Proto-Indo-European *dáḱru- (“tear”). Cognates Cognate with German Zähre (“tear”), Danish, Norwegian Bokmål, and Norwegian Nynorsk tåre (“tear”), Faroese and Icelandic tár (“tear”), Swedish tår (“tear”), Gothic 𐍄𐌰𐌲𐍂 (tagr, “teardrop”); also Cornish dager (“tear; drop”), Irish deoir (“tear”), Manx jeir (“tear”), Scottish Gaelic deur (“tear; drop”), Welsh deigryn (“tear”), Latin dacrima, dacruma, lachryma, lacrima, lacruma, lacryma (“tear”), Greek δάκρυ (dákry, “tear”), Armenian արտոսր (artosr, “tear”).
tear.example: Ryan wiped the tear from the paper he was crying on.
tear.exampleSense: A drop of clear, salty liquid produced from the eyes by crying or irritation.

torn.o: past participle of tear. From Middle English teren, from Old English teran (“to tear, lacerate”), from Proto-Germanic *teraną (“to tear, tear apart, rip”), from Proto-Indo-European *der- (“to tear, tear apart”). Cognate with Scots tere, teir, tair (“to rend, lacerate, wound, rip, tear out”), Dutch teren (“to eliminate, efface, live, survive by consumption”), German zehren (“to consume, misuse”), German zerren (“to tug, rip, tear”), Danish tære (“to consume”), Swedish tära (“to fret, consume, deplete, use up”), Icelandic tæra (“to clear, corrode”). Outside Germanic, cognate to Ancient Greek δέρω (dérō, “to skin”), Albanian ther (“to slay, skin, pierce”). Doublet of tire.
torn.example: I'm torn between pizza and hamburgers.
torn.exampleSense: Unable to decide between multiple options.

underpinning.o: present participle and gerund of underpin. From under- + pin.
underpinning.example: This house's underpinning is not up to standard.
underpinning.exampleSense: A support or foundation, especially as a structure of masonry that supports a wall.

preface.o: Late 14th century, from Middle English preface, prefas, from Old French preface (from which derives the modern French préface), from Medieval Latin prefātia, for classical Latin praefātiō (“a saying beforehand”), from praefor (“to speak beforehand”), from prae- (“beforehand”) + for (“to speak”).
preface.example: The book included a brief preface explaining the author's motivations for writing.
preface.exampleSense: A beginning or introductory portion that comes before the main text of a document or book, typically serving to contextualize or explain the writing of the book and sometimes to acknowledge others' contributions; especially, such a discussion written by the work's own author.

self-promotion.example: The resources channelled to those institutions which showed themselves most adept at formfilling, self-promotion and presentation were inadequate to sustain the quality they claimed.
self-promotion.exampleSense: The purposeful act of presenting oneself to others in a favorable way, often viewed by others negatively as forceful, exaggerated, or self-indulgent.

pontiff.o: Borrowed from Middle French pontife m, from Latin pontifex m. Doublet of pontifex.
pontiff.example: In several respects John turned out to be an unexpected figure as supreme pontiff.
pontiff.exampleSense: A bishop of the early Church; now specifically, the Pope.

pontifical.example: If the editio princeps was an attempt to create an authoritative version of the pontifical, such was not yet attainable.
pontifical.exampleSense: A book containing the offices, or formulas, used by a pontiff.

erudite.o: From Latin ērudītus, participle of ērudiō (“educate, train”), from e- (“out of”) + rudis (“rude, unskilled”). Doublet of erudit.
erudite.example: Perhaps his erudite mind does not quite yet grasp how to transform his beloved scholarly explorations into effective papal politics.
erudite.exampleSense: Learned, scholarly, with emphasis on knowledge gained from books.

born.o:
verb: From Middle English born, boren, borne, iborne, from Old English boren, ġeboren, from Proto-West Germanic *boran, *gaboran, from Proto-Germanic *buranaz, past participle of Proto-Germanic *beraną (“to bear, carry”), equivalent to bear + -en. Cognate with Saterland Frisian gebooren (“born”), West Frisian berne (“born”), Dutch geboren (“born”), German geboren (“born”), Swedish boren (“born”).

noun: Dialectal variant of burn.
born.example: Although not born in the country, she qualifies for nationality through her grandparents.
born.exampleSense: past participle of bear; given birth to.

pathetic.o: From Middle French pathétique, from Latin patheticus, from Ancient Greek παθητικός (pathētikós, “subject to feeling, capable of feeling, impassioned”), from παθητός (pathētós, “one who has suffered, subject to suffering”), from πάσχω (páskhō, “to suffer”). By surface analysis, path- + -etic.
pathetic.example: Well you'd better think of something because middle-aged tramps aren't cute, they're pathetic.
pathetic.exampleSense: Arousing scorn or contempt, often due to miserable inadequacy.

enchanted.o: simple past and past participle of enchant. From Middle English enchaunten, from Old French enchanter, from Latin incantāre. Doublet of incant.

profess.o: From Old French professer, and its source, the participle stem of Latin profitērī, from pro- + fatērī (“to confess, acknowledge”).
profess.example: This swayed the balance decisively in Mary's favour, and she was professed on 8 September 1578.
profess.exampleSense: To administer the vows of a religious order to (someone); to admit to a religious order.

confess.o: From Middle English confessen, from Anglo-Norman confesser, from Old French confesser, from Latin confessus (Old French confés), past participle of cōnfiteor (“to confess, admit”) from con- + fateor (“to admit”). Displaced Middle English andetten (“to confess, admit”) (from Old English andettan). Doublet of confiteor. Sense 6 is a calque of 告白 (kokuhaku).
confess.example: Our beautiful votary took an opportunity of confessing herself to this celebrated father.
confess.exampleSense: To unburden (oneself) of sins to God or a priest, in order to receive absolution.

prolific.o: First use appears c. 1635. From French prolifique and its etymon Latin prōlificus, from prōlēs (“offspring”) + -ficus (“making”).
prolific.example: However appealing Antibes may be to migrant authors, indigenous ones are relatively scarce. A notable exception is Jacques Audiberti, Antibes-born novelist and prolific playwright who wrote in the turn-of-the-century surrealist style, with titles that translate as Slaughter, or In Favour of Infanticide.
prolific.exampleSense: Similarly producing results or performing deeds in abundance.

specialty.o: From Middle English specialte, Old French specialte, especialte, from Latin specialitas.
specialty.example: They cook well overall, but their true specialty is pasta.
specialty.exampleSense: That in which one specializes; a chosen expertise or talent.

specialised.o: simple past and past participle of specialise. From special + -ise.
specialised.example: Specialised long-reach excavators with a clamshell grab then reach though the openings to lift the spoil to the surface, which is then deposited in articulated dump trucks (ADTs).
specialised.exampleSense: Non-Oxford British English standard spelling of specialized.

specialise.example: [Oily Cart] specialises in creating spectacular productions for young people with complex disabilities.
specialise.exampleSense: Non-Oxford British English standard spelling of specialize.

review.o: From Middle English revewe, reveue, from Old French reveüe, revue (Modern French: revue), feminine form of reveü, past participle of reveoir (French: revoir), from Latin revideō, from re- +videō (“see, observe”) (English: video). Equivalent to re- + view. Compare retrospect. Doublet of revue.
review.example: The newspaper review was full of praise for the play.
review.exampleSense: An account intended as a critical evaluation of a text or a piece of work.

malady.o: From Middle English maladie, from Old French maladie (“sickness, illness, disease”), from malade (“ill, sick”), from Latin male habitus (“ill-kept, not in good condition”), 1st century AD. See also malice and habit.
malady.example: The maladies of the body may prove medicines of the mind.
malady.exampleSense: Any ailment or disease of the body; especially, a lingering or deep-seated disorder.

melody.o: From Middle English melodie, melodye, from Old French melodie, from Latin melodia, from Ancient Greek μελῳδίᾱ (melōidíā, “singing, chanting”), from μέλος (mélos, “musical phrase”) + ἀοιδή (aoidḗ, “song”), contracted form ᾠδή (ōidḗ).
melody.example: There is a melody upon the Earth as though ten thousand streams all sang together for their homes that they had forsaken in the hills.
melody.exampleSense: A sequence of notes that makes up a musical phrase

centenary.o: From Latin centēnārius (“containing 100; local official overseeing a hundred”) either directly or via French centenaire, from centēnī (“100 each”) + -ārius (“-ary”), from centum (“hundred”). Doublet of centner, kantar, and quintal.
centenary.example: In the midst of a world war many centenaries pass unnoticed, but one which fell on August 2, namely, the opening of Fenchurch Street station, is deserving of record.
centenary.exampleSense: Synonym of centennial: a hundredth anniversary.

strike out.example: Dave asked the new girl to the dance but he struck out.
strike out.exampleSense: To fail; to be refused a request or to have a proposal not be accepted, in particular a request for a (hopefully romantic) date.

structure.o: From Middle French structure, from Latin structūra (“a fitting together, adjustment, building, erection, a building, edifice, structure”), from struere, past participle structus (“pile up, arrange, assemble, build”). Compare construct, instruct, destroy, etc.
structure.example: The birds had built an amazing structure out of sticks and various discarded items.
structure.exampleSense: A cohesive whole built up of distinct parts.

eternity.o: From Middle English eternyte, from Old French eternité, from Latin aeternitās. Displaced native Old English ēcnes.
eternity.example: This theory regards creation as an act of God in eternity past.

overshoot.o: From Middle English overshoten, oversheten (“to shoot beyond, shoot past, pour down from above”), perhaps continuing Old English ofersċēotan (“to shoot down”), equivalent to over- + shoot.
overshoot.example: Let's see if we can predict and correct for the overshoot.
overshoot.exampleSense: The amount by which something goes too far.

tropology.o: From Late Latin tropologia, from Late Greek τροπολογία (tropología), equivalent to trope + -ology.
tropology.example: He must distinguish the historical information from the allegory, divide the allegory from the tropology, and separate the tropology from the anagogy.
tropology.exampleSense: The interpretation of scripture or other work in order to educe moral or figurative meaning; a treatise of such interpretation.

tropo-.o: From Ancient Greek τρόπος (trópos, “turn, way, manner, style”).

troposphere.o: Borrowed from French troposphère. Equivalent to tropo- + -sphere.

stratosphere.o: From French stratosphère, a word coined by its discoverer, meteorologist Léon Teisserenc de Bort. From strato- + -sphere.
stratosphere.example: Variation in height of the stratosphere (isothermal layer).
stratosphere.exampleSense: The region of the uppermost atmosphere where temperature increases along with the altitude due to the absorption of solar ultraviolet radiation by ozone. The stratosphere extends from the tropopause (10–15 kilometers) to approximately 50 kilometers, where it is succeeded by the mesosphere.

billow.o: From Middle English *bilwe, borrowed from Old Norse bylgja, from Proto-Germanic *bulgijō. Cognates include Danish bølge (“wave”); Norwegian Bokmål bølge (“wave”), Norwegian Nynorsk bylgje (“wave”); Swedish bölja (“wave”); German Low German Bulge, Bulg, Bülg (“billow, wave”); German Bulge (“billow, wave”). Compare bellow, bawl.
billow.example: 1893 August, Rudyard Kipling, "Seal Lullaby", in "The White Seal", National Review.
billow.exampleSense: A large wave, swell, surge, or undulating mass of something, such as water, smoke, fabric or sound

billowing.o: present participle and gerund of billow. From Middle English *bilwe, borrowed from Old Norse bylgja, from Proto-Germanic *bulgijō. Cognates include Danish bølge (“wave”); Norwegian Bokmål bølge (“wave”), Norwegian Nynorsk bylgje (“wave”); Swedish bölja (“wave”); German Low German Bulge, Bulg, Bülg (“billow, wave”); German Bulge (“billow, wave”). Compare bellow, bawl.
billowing.example: The Bible is full of passages designed to meet and relieve those billowings and heavings of the soul, but without a devotional spirit such passages can never be appreciated or comprehended.
billowing.exampleSense: The act of something that billows; a billow.

nervously.example: He paced nervously as he waited for the important phone call.
nervously.exampleSense: In a nervous manner; feeling or displaying nervousness.

subtlety.o: From Middle English sotilte, from Old French sutilté, inherited from Latin subtīlitās, from subtīlis (“subtle”). Equivalent to subtle + -ty. Doublet of subtility.
subtlety.example: [H]e had a lifetime of skill in interpreting his father's gestures: those bent knees meant that something of great subtlety was about to be revealed.
subtlety.exampleSense: The quality of being subtle. The quality of being scarcely noticeable or difficult to discern. (of things)

broadcast.o: From broad + cast. First attested in the mid 18th century, in the agricultural use of spreading seeds.
broadcast.example: However, truth and lies can usually be confirmed or denied by speaking with eyewitnesses of events in order to verify what took place. The amount of time separating the event in question from when it was broadcasted also makes a difference.
broadcast.exampleSense: To transmit a message over a wide area; specifically, to send an email in a single transmission to a (typically large) number of people.

betide.o: From Middle English bityden [and other forms]; from bi- (prefix forming verbs, usually with a completive, figurative, or intensive sense) + tyden (“to come about, happen, occur; to befall, become of, happen to (someone); to be the fate of (someone); to await (someone); to fare, get along”); tyden is derived from Old English tīdan (“to befall, betide, happen”), related to tīd (“time; season; hour”) (both ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *deh₂- (“to divide, share”) or its extended form *deh₂-y-, whence *dh₂ítis (“time”)) + -an (suffix forming the infinitive of most verbs). The English word is analysable as be- + tide (“(obsolete) to happen, occur”).
betide.example: If he were dead what would betide of me.
betide.exampleSense: Chiefly in the third person: to happen; to take place; to bechance, to befall.

betoken.o: From Middle English bitoknen, bitacnen, from Old English betācnian (“to betoken, signify, designate”), from Proto-West Germanic *bitaiknijan. Equivalent to be- + token. Cognate with Dutch betekenen (“to mean, signify”), German bezeichnen (“to call, designate”), Swedish beteckna (“to represent, designate, indicate”) and Danish betegne (“to represent, designate, indicate”).
betoken.example: “ Ah ! hospitable land, thou (nevertheless) betokenest war,” i. e., although hospitable, thou nevertheless betokenest war. — Bello.
betoken.exampleSense: To foreshow by present signs; indicate something future by that which is seen or known.

horizon.o: Inherited from Middle English orisonte, orisoun, from Middle French horizon, horizonte, from Old French orisonte, orison, via Latin horizōn, from Ancient Greek ὁρίζων (horízōn), from ὅρος (hóros, “boundary”).
horizon.example: A tall building was visible on the horizon.
horizon.exampleSense: The visible horizontal line (in all directions) where the sky appears to meet the earth in the distance.

tortoise.o: From Middle English tortuse, tortuce, tortuge, from Medieval Latin tortuca, of uncertain origin. May be from Late Latin tartarūcha, from tartarūchus, from Ancient Greek ταρταροῦχος (tartaroûkhos, literally “holder of Tartarus [the land of the damned dead in Greek myths]”), because it used to be thought that tortoises and turtles came from the underworld and they were commonly paired with such infernal beasts; see Τάρταρος (Tártaros). Or, from Latin tortus (“twisted”). The French-looking Modern English spelling tortoise may be influenced by porpoise. Displaced native Old English byrdling.

turtle.o:
noun: Modification of Middle English tortou, tortu, from Old French tortüe (under the influence of Middle English turtel, turtur (“turtledove”), see Etymology 2 below), from Old Occitan tortuga (compare Spanish tortuga), the same source of tortoise (see there for more). Displaced native Old English byrdling (See birdling).

noun: From Middle English turtle, tortle, turtel, turtul, from Old English turtle, turtla (“turtledove”), ultimately from Latin turtur (“turtledove”), of imitative origin.
turtle.example: Of these, 80 turtled (65%), 26 hunted and turtled (20%), and 18 hunted (15%).
turtle.exampleSense: To hunt turtles, especially in the water.

trade wind.o: Compound of trade (“course, path (of running)”, from 14th c.) + wind, because of their consistent linear direction. Associations with transatlantic trade are a later folk etymology.
trade wind.example: They rode the trade winds going west.
trade wind.exampleSense: A steady wind that blows from east to west above and below the equator.

nag.o:
noun: From Middle English nagg, nage, nagge (“horse, small riding horse, pony”), cognate with Dutch negge, neg (“horse”), German Nickel (“small horse”). Perhaps related to English neigh.

verb: Probably from a North Germanic source; compare Swedish nagga (“to gnaw, grumble”), Danish nage (“to nag, bother”), Icelandic nagga (“to complain”). Compare typologically fret, Bulgarian глождя (gloždja), Russian глода́ть (glodátʹ), грызть (gryztʹ), по́едом есть (pójedom jestʹ), е́дкий (jédkij).
nag.example: The notion that he forgot something nagged him the rest of the day.
nag.exampleSense: To bother with persistent thoughts or memories.

nagging.o: present participle and gerund of nag. From Middle English nagg, nage, nagge (“horse, small riding horse, pony”), cognate with Dutch negge, neg (“horse”), German Nickel (“small horse”). Perhaps related to English neigh.

reconnoitre.o: From French reconnoître (obsolete spelling of reconnaître), from Latin recognoscere (“to recognise”). There is also an obsolete 19th-century British English spelling reconnaitre, influenced by the modern French form.
reconnoitre.example: Our scout will reconnoitre the path ahead of our troops.
reconnoitre.exampleSense: To perform a reconnaissance (of an area; an enemy position); to scout with the aim of gaining information.

reconnoiter.o: From French reconnoître (obsolete spelling of reconnaître), from Latin recognoscere (“to recognize”). Contrarily, there is also an obsolete 19th-century British English spelling reconnaitre (now reconnoitre).
reconnoiter.example: Our scout will reconnoiter the path ahead of our troops.
reconnoiter.exampleSense: To perform a reconnaissance (of an area; an enemy position); to scout with the aim of acquiring information.

downwind.example: ... the aftermath of the dust-storm came up and caught us both, and drove us downwind like pieces of paper.
downwind.exampleSense: in the same direction as the wind is blowing

upwind.o:
adj: From up- + wind.

verb: From Middle English upwinden, equivalent to up- + wind (verb).

headwind.o: From Middle English *hedwind, from Old English hēafodwind, equivalent to head + wind. Cognate with Old Norse höfuðvindr.
headwind.example: "Domestic economic activity has been gaining traction in spite of formidable headwinds from external developments," the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) said in its monthly bulletin.
headwind.exampleSense: A strong force that impedes or reverses progress.

prevailing.example: In Sydney at 9 am, by far the most prevailing wind is a westerly, particularly during the colder two-thirds of the year.

throw.o:
verb: From Middle English throwen, thrawen, from Old English þrāwan (“to turn, twist”), from Proto-West Germanic *þrāan, from Proto-Germanic *þrēaną (“to twist, turn”), from Proto-Indo-European *terh₁- (“to rub, rub by twisting, twist, turn”). Cognate with Scots thraw (“to twist, turn, throw”), West Frisian triuwe (“to push”), Dutch draaien (“to turn”), Low German draien, dreien (“to turn (in a lathe)”), German drehen (“to turn”). Displaced warp as the word for hurling and was displaced by warp as the word for twisting. The use in computing comes from the fact, that in programming languages a statement reporting an error interrupts normal processing and sends an error object up the function calling stack until a handling statement intercepts it. Thus an “object” is “thrown” and “flies” until it is “catched”.

noun: From Middle English, from Old English þrāh, þrāg (“space of time, period, while”). Of uncertain origin. Perhaps related to Gothic 𐌸𐍂𐌰𐌲𐌾𐌰𐌽 (þragjan, “to run”).

noun: See throe.
throw.example: Football tickets are expensive at fifty bucks a throw.
throw.exampleSense: A single instance, occurrence, venture, or chance.

yacht.o: Circa 1557; variant of yaught, earlier yeaghe (“light, fast-sailing ship”), from Dutch jacht (“yacht; hunt”), in older spelling jaght(e), short for jaghtschip (“light sailing vessel, fast pirate ship”, literally “pursuit ship”), compound of jacht and schip (“ship”). In the 16th century the Dutch built light, fast ships to chase the ships of pirates and smugglers from the coast. The ship was introduced to England in 1660 when the Dutch East India Company presented one to King Charles II, who used it as a pleasure boat, after which it was copied by British shipbuilders as a pleasure craft for wealthy gentlemen.
yacht.example: You are a true yachtsman! Are you a member of the local yacht club?
yacht.exampleSense: A slick and light ship for making pleasure trips or racing on water, having sails but often motor-powered. At times used as a residence offshore on a dock.

acidify.o: From acid + -ify, from Latin acidus (“sour, acid”); compare French acidifier.

avidity.o: From Middle English avidite, from Old French avidite (modern French avidité), from Latin aviditās (“avidity, covetousness”), equivalent to avid + -ity.

avid.o: From French avide, from Latin avidus (“eager, desirous; greedy”), from aveō (“wish, desire, long for, crave”).
avid.example: A blanket disdain for indigenous foods doesn't explain the delay, because Spain was avid to adopt a different New World root.
avid.exampleSense: enthusiastic; keen; eager; showing great interest in something or desire to do something
