oxide.exampleSense: A binary chemical compound of oxygen with another chemical element.

atmosphere.o: Borrowed from French atmosphère, from New Latin atmosphaera, from Ancient Greek ἀτμός (atmós, “steam”) + σφαῖρα (sphaîra, “sphere”); corresponding to atmo- + -sphere.
atmosphere.example: To most people, the huge ice sheets of Antarctica and Greenland are merely water that once was snow. To glaciologists and climatologists, they are storehouses of the Earth's former atmospheres.
atmosphere.exampleSense: The gases surrounding the Earth or any astronomical body.

pore.o:
noun: From Middle English pore, from Old French pore, from Latin porus, from Ancient Greek πόρος (póros, “passage”). Displaced native English sweat hole from Middle English swet hole, which might have been a reformation of Old English swātþȳrel (literally “sweat hole”), which competed with līcþēote (literally “body pipe”).

verb: From Middle English poren, pouren, puren (“to gaze intently, look closely”), from Old English *pūrian, from Proto-West Germanic *pūrōn, suggested by Old English spyrian (“to investigate, examine”). Akin to Saterland Frisian puurje (“to question, investigate; pry, prod”), West Frisian poarje (“to poke, prod”), Middle Dutch poren (“to pore, look”), Dutch porren (“to poke, prod, stir, encourage, endeavour, attempt”), Low German purren (“to poke, stir”), Danish purre (“to poke, stir, rouse”), dialectal Swedish pora, pura, påra (“to work slowly and gradually, work deliberately”), Old English spor (“track, trace, vestige”). Compare also Middle English puren, piren (“to look, peer”). See peer.
pore.exampleSense: By extension any small opening or interstice, especially one of many, or one allowing the passage of a fluid.

mantle.o: From Middle English mantel, from Old English mæntel, mentel (“sleeveless cloak”), from Proto-West Germanic *mantel; later reinforced by Anglo-Norman mantel, both from Latin mantellum (“covering, cloak”) (French manteau), diminutive of mantum (Spanish manto), probably from Gaulish *mantos, *mantalos (“trodden road”), from Proto-Celtic *mantos, *mantlos, from Proto-Indo-European *menH- (“tread, press together; crumble”). Compare Icelandic möttull. Doublet of manteau.
mantle.example: The crust (a mere 1% of the Earth's volume) is made of lighter melt products from the mantle.
mantle.exampleSense: The layer between Earth's core and crust.

magma.example: By the pathside, there are occasional large boulders that shown black crystals the size of a fingernail; these are pyroxene minerals that had time to crystallise out deep within the chamber of liquid rock – or magma – beneath the volcano.
magma.exampleSense: The molten matter within the earth, the source of the material of lava flows, dikes of eruptive rocks, etc.

combat.o: 16th century, borrowed from Middle French combat, deverbal from Old French combatre, from Vulgar Latin *combattere, from Latin com- (“with”) + battuere (“to beat, strike”).
combat.example: It has proven very difficult to combat drug addiction.

solace.o: From Old French solas, from Latin sōlācium (“consolation”), root from Proto-Indo-European *selh₂- (“mercy, comfort”).
solace.example: You cannot put a monetary value on emotional solace.
solace.exampleSense: Comfort or consolation in a time of loneliness or distress.

shot.o:
adj: The past participle of shoot.

noun: Inherited from Middle English schot, from Old English sceot, from Proto-Germanic *skutą; compare the doublet scot.
shot.example: He'd make a bad soldier, since he's a lousy shot.
shot.exampleSense: Someone who shoots (a gun, longbow, etc.); a person reckoned as to their aim.

microbe.o: Borrowed from French microbe, from Ancient Greek μικρός (mikrós, “small”) and βίος (bíos, “life”). By surface analysis, micro- + -obe.

differentiate.o: From New Latin differentiātus, perfect passive participle of differentiō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (noun-forming suffix)), from Latin differentia (“difference”); see difference.
differentiate.example: In Chapter IV we learned that every animal consists of a body, or soma, formed of cells that are differentiated from the germ cells usually at an early stage of development.
differentiate.exampleSense: To (cause to) go through a process of development called differentiation; to make or become different in form or function.

stem cell.example: Stem cells are characterized by their ability to self-renew and to produce numerous differentiated cell types, and are directly responsible for generating and maintaining tissues and organs.
stem cell.exampleSense: A primal undifferentiated cell from which a variety of other cells can develop through the process of cellular differentiation.

fatten.example: The news spread, about the bastard caterer who was toying with their religious sentiments, trampling on their beliefs, polluting their beings, all for the sake of fattening his miserable wallet.
fatten.exampleSense: To make thick or thicker (often something containing paper, especially money).

mouse.o: Inherited from Middle English mous, from Old English mūs, from Proto-West Germanic *mūs, from Proto-Germanic *mūs, from Proto-Indo-European *múHs. Cognates Germanic cognates include Old Frisian mūs, Old Saxon mūs (German Low German Muus), Dutch muis, Old High German mūs (German Maus), Old Norse mús (Danish, Norwegian Bokmål, Norwegian Nynorsk, and Swedish mus, Faroese and Icelandic mús). Indo-European cognates include Ancient Greek μῦς (mûs), Latin mūs, Spanish mur, Armenian մուկ (muk), Old Church Slavonic мꙑшь (myšĭ) (Russian мышь (myšʹ)), Albanian mi, Persian موش (muš), Northern Kurdish mişk, Sanskrit मूष् (mūṣ). The computing sense was coined by American engineer Bill English in 1965 and first used publicly in a publication titled "Computer-Aided Display Control", in reference to the similarity with the animal.
mouse.example: I had just moused to the File menu and the pull-down menu repeated the menu bar's hue a dozen shades lighter.
mouse.exampleSense: To navigate by means of a computer mouse.

mice.o: From Middle English mys, mice, muis, mise, mis, from Old English mȳs (“mice”), from an umlauted form of Proto-Germanic *mūsiz (“mice”), nominative and vocative plural of Proto-Germanic *mūs (“mouse”). Compare Scots mice, mise, myse, myce (“mice”), West Frisian mûzen (“mice”), Dutch muizen (“mice”), German Mäuse (“mice”), Swedish möss (“mice”), Faroese mýs (“mice”), Icelandic mýs (“mice”). More at mouse.
mice.example: That cat's mysin, he doesn't see the dog coming.
mice.exampleSense: To be distracted or inattentive (possibly alluding to a cat being distracted by a mouse).

bona fide.o: Unadapted borrowing from Latin bonā fidē (“in good faith”).
bona fide.example: Although he failed, the prime minister made a bona fide attempt to repair the nation's damaged economy.
bona fide.exampleSense: In good faith; sincere; without deception or ulterior motive.

svelte.o: Borrowed from French svelte, from Italian svelto (“stretched out”), past participle of svellere (“to pluck out, root out”), from Vulgar Latin *exvellere, from ex + vellere (“to pluck, stretch”).
svelte.example: My first priority was to help Trumps lose her pudgy look and gain a healthier, svelter size.

abdominals.o: plural of abdominal. First attested in 1746. From New Latin abdōminālis, from Latin abdōmen. Equivalent to abdomin- + -al. Compare French abdominal.

abdominal.o: First attested in 1746. From New Latin abdōminālis, from Latin abdōmen. Equivalent to abdomin- + -al. Compare French abdominal.

abdomen.o: First attested in 1541 as labdomen. Borrowed from Middle French abdomen as well as from its etymon Latin abdōmen, possibly from abdō (“conceal”), from ab (“away”) + -dō (“put, place”).
abdomen.example: He was all bent over complaining of pains in the abdomen.
abdomen.exampleSense: The cavity of the belly, which is lined by the peritoneum, and contains the viscera; often restricted in humans to the part between the diaphragm and the commencement of the pelvis, the remainder being called the pelvic cavity.

attributable.example: His lack of conversation is attributable to his shyness.

insulin.o: From Latin īnsula (“island”) (named for the islets of Langerhans, where insulin is produced) + -in.
insulin.example: Nationally the average insulin price nearly tripled from 2002 through 2013, and prices have risen 10% or more a year since then, forcing many diabetics to ration their insulin.
insulin.exampleSense: A polypeptide hormone that regulates carbohydrate metabolism (in various animals including humans).

complication.o: Borrowed from Middle French complication, from Latin complicatio, complicationem. Morphologically complicate + -ion.
complication.example: the snaky complication in the Caduceus or rod of Hermes.

complice.example: Our Saviour was accused that he would Destroy the Temple. The first Martyr Steven was stoned as a Complice.

endocrine gland.example: An endocrine gland is one that secretes its products directly into the bloodstream.
endocrine gland.exampleSense: Any of various glands that secrete hormones directly into the blood or lymph and not through a duct.

endocrinology.example: The first journal devoted to endocrinology wasnʼt founded until 1917.
endocrinology.exampleSense: The study of the endocrine glands of the human body, the hormones produced by them, and their related disorders.

endorse.o: Alteration influenced by Medieval Latin indorsare of Middle English endosse, from Old French endosser (“to put on the back”), from Latin dossum, alternative form of dorsum (“back”), from which also dorsal (“of the back”). That is, the ‘r’ was dropped in Latin dossum, which developed into Old French and then Middle English endosse, and then the ‘r’ was re-introduced into English via the Medieval Latin indorsare, which had retained the ‘r’. Note that the alternative spelling indorse also uses the initial ‘i’ from Latin (in-, rather than en-), but this form is now rare.
endorse.example: The court endorsed his driving record with three penalty points for the drink-driving.
endorse.exampleSense: To add penalty points to one's driving licence as a result of a road traffic offence.

imprint.o:
noun: From Old French empreinte, from the past participle of empreindre, from Latin imprimere.

verb: From Middle English emprinten, enprinten, from Old French empreinter, from the past participle of empreindre, from Latin imprimere.
imprint.example: From their Belmont Avenue address they issued such memorable titles as I Peddle Jazz, Camera Bait, Our Flesh Was Cheap, Lesbian Twins, and His Sex, His Problem under at least four different imprints—Saber, Fabian, Vega, and National Library Books.
imprint.exampleSense: The name and details of a publisher or printer, as printed in a book etc.; a publishing house.

impregnate.o: The adjective is first attested in 1540, the verb in 1605; borrowed from Medieval Latin impraegnātus, perfect passive participle of Latin impraegnō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix). Doublet of impregn; participial usage of the adjective up until Early Modern English.
impregnate.example: It takes a little time for the personal fatty acids to impregnate new shoes or boots, but from the scent point of view leather is a sponge, and the personal scent is left.
impregnate.exampleSense: To fill pores or spaces with a substance.

vainly.o: Inherited from Middle English vaynly, veynly, vaynely, veynely, equivalent to vain + -ly.
vainly.example: She searched vainly for her reflection in the shattered mirror.
vainly.exampleSense: In a vain pursuit; to no avail.

vastly.example: After Trump spoke with Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau in April 2017, the two sides offered vastly different accounts of what was discussed.

whittle.o:
noun: From Middle English whittel (“large knife”), an alteration of thwitel, itself from thwiten (“to whittle”), from Old English þwītan (“to strike down, whittle”), from Proto-Germanic *þwītaną, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *twey- (“to shake, hurl, toss”). Compare Old Norse þveita (“to hurl”), Ancient Greek σείω (seíō, “I shake”). Related to thwite and thwaite.

noun: From Middle English whytel, from Old English hwītel (“cloak, blanket”), from Proto-West Germanic *hwītil, from Proto-Germanic *hwītilaz, equivalent to white + -le; akin to Icelandic hvítill (“white bedcover, sheet, linen”).
whittle.example: The Sheffield whittle was the common knife of the country, which every one carried for general purposes, who was not entitled by rank to wear a sword.
whittle.exampleSense: A knife; especially, a clasp knife, pocket knife, or sheath knife.

counseling.o: present participle and gerund of counsel. From Middle English counseil, conseil, from Old French conseil, from Latin cōnsilium, of unknown origin but possibly from either com- + calō (via a phonetic variant of concilium) or cōnsulō.

counsel.o:
noun: From Middle English counseil, conseil, from Old French conseil, from Latin cōnsilium, of unknown origin but possibly from either com- + calō (via a phonetic variant of concilium) or cōnsulō.

verb: From Middle English counseilen, from Old French conseiller, from Latin cōnsilior, from cōnsilium.
counsel.example: He counseled his daughter to resist the lure of hatred and bitterness.

elimination.o: Borrowed from Latin ēliminātiō, from eliminate + -ion.
elimination.example: Everton require at least 3 goals in the second leg to avoid elimination from the FA Cup.
elimination.exampleSense: The act of excluding a losing contestant from a match, tournament, or other competition.

carb.example: She lifted her thumb off the carb and breathed in the thick smoke.
carb.exampleSense: The hole on a pipe which is covered and opened to control the inflow of air.

cue.o:
noun: From Middle English cu (used for half a farthing, from q as an abbreviation for Latin quadrāns (“quarter of an as”)), from Latin cū, kū. Compare French ku.

noun: From earlier qu, abbreviation of Latin quandō (“when”), marked on actor's play copy where they were to begin.

noun: Variant of queue, from French queue (“tail”).
cue.example: When my cue comes, call me, and I will answer.
cue.exampleSense: The last words of a play actor's speech, serving as an intimation for the next actor to speak; any word or words which serve to remind an actor to speak or to do something; a catchword.

gut.o: From Middle English gut, gutte, gotte, from Old English gutt (usually in plural guttas (“guts, entrails”)), from Proto-Germanic *gut-, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰewd- (“to pour”). Related to English gote (“drain”), Old English ġēotan (“to pour”). More at gote, yote. The verb is from Middle English gutten, gotten (“to gut”).
gut.exampleSense: To remove or destroy the most important parts of.

equivalence.o: From French équivalence, from Medieval Latin aequivalentia.

budge.o:
verb: Borrowed from Middle French bouger, from Old French bougier, from Vulgar Latin *bullicāre (“to bubble; seethe; move; stir”), from Latin bullīre (“to boil; seethe; roil”). More at boil.

noun: From Middle English bouge, bougie, bugee, from Anglo-Norman bogé, from Anglo-Latin *bogea, bulgia, related to Latin bulga (“a leathern bag or knapsack”). Doublet of bulge.

noun: Perhaps related to booze.
budge.example: The Minister for Finance refused to budge on the new economic rules.
budge.exampleSense: To yield in one’s opinions or beliefs.

needle.o: From Middle English nedle, from Old English nǣdl, from Proto-West Germanic *nāþlu, from Proto-Germanic *nēþlō, from pre-Germanic *neh₁-tleh₂, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)neh₁- (“to spin, twist”). Cognates Cognate with Saterland Frisian Näddele (“sewing needle”), Dutch naald (“needle”), German Nadel (“needle, pin, crochet hook”), nähen (“sew”), Luxembourgish Nol (“needle”), Vilamovian nöłd (“needle”), Yiddish נאָדל (nodl, “needle, pin”), Danish, Norwegian Bokmål, Norwegian Nynorsk, Swedish nål (“needle”), Elfdalian ną̊l (“needle”), Faroese, Icelandic nál (“needle”), Gothic 𐌽𐌴𐌸𐌻𐌰 (nēþla, “sewing needle”), Finnish neula (“needle”). Further related with Welsh nyddu, Latin nēre, Sanskrit स्नायति (snāyati, “wraps up, winds”). Related to snood.
needle.example: The seamstress threaded the needle to sew on a button.
needle.exampleSense: A long, thin, sharp implement usually for piercing as in sewing, embroidery, acupuncture, tattooing, body piercing, medical injections, sutures, etc; or a blunt but otherwise similar implement used for forming loops or knots in crafts such as darning, knitting, tatting, etc.

espousal.o: From Middle English espousal, espousaille, from Old French espousailles, from Latin sponsalia (“a betrothal”), neuter plural of sponsalis, from spōnsus (“one betrothed, a spouse”); see spouse. By surface analysis, espouse + -al.

expose.o: From Middle English exposen, from Old French exposer (“to lay open, set forth”), from Latin expōnō (“set forth”), with contamination from poser (“to lay, place”). Doublet of expone and expound (via Old French espondre (“to set forth, explain”)), from the same Latin term.
expose.example: You understand that by using the Services, you may be exposed to Content that might be offensive, harmful, inaccurate or otherwise inappropriate, or in some cases, postings that have been mislabeled or are otherwise deceptive.
expose.exampleSense: To reveal, uncover, make visible, bring to light, introduce (to).

espouse.o: From Middle English espousen, borrowed from Old French espouser, from Latin spōnsāre (frequentative of spondeō), from Proto-Indo-European *spend-.
espouse.example: Among those leavers who believe Brexit has not gone well, many blame politicians for handling it badly – a narrative espoused by the former Ukip leader Nigel Farage, who recently claimed that “Brexit has failed”.
espouse.exampleSense: To accept, support, or take on as one’s own (an idea or a cause).

prerogative.o: From Anglo-Norman prerogative (noun), from Latin praerogātīva (“previous verdict; claim, privilege”), noun use of the feminine singular of praerogātīvus (“having first vote; privileged”).
prerogative.example: Despite being a constitutional monarchy, the British sovereign still retain many royal prerogatives.
prerogative.exampleSense: A right, or power that is exclusive to a monarch etc, especially such a power to make a decision or judgement.

wallpaper.example: He is letting her select the wallpapers for the whole house.
wallpaper.exampleSense: A style or design of such material.

predispose.o: Either a back-formation from predisposition or borrowed from Middle French predisposer.

hang.o:
verb: From Middle English hangen, hongen, from a fusion of Old English hōn (“to hang, be hanging”, transitive verb) and hangian (“to hang, cause to hang”, intransitive verb), respectively from the transitive verb Proto-West Germanic *hą̄han and the intransitive verb *hangēn; also probably influenced by Old Norse hengja (“to suspend”) and hanga (“to be suspended”); all from Proto-Germanic *hanhaną and *hangāną, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱenk- (“to waver, be in suspense”). See also Dutch hangen, Low German hangen and hängen, German hängen, Norwegian Bokmål henge, Norwegian Nynorsk henga; also Gothic 𐌷𐌰𐌷𐌰𐌽 (hāhan), Hittite 𒂵𒀀𒀭𒂵 (/⁠kānk-⁠/, “to hang”), Sanskrit शङ्कते (śáṅkate, “is in doubt, hesitates”), Latin cūnctārī (“to delay”).

noun: From hang sangwich, Irish colloquial pronunciation of ham sandwich.

noun: Alteration of dang, itself a minced oath of damn.
hang.example: Hang those lights from the ceiling.
hang.exampleSense: To cause (something) to be suspended, as from a hook, hanger, hinges, or the like.

subscribe.o: From Middle English subscriben, subskryben, from Latin subscrībere (“write beneath”). By surface analysis, sub- + scribe. Compare its native English equivalent underwrite.
subscribe.example: The capital which had been subscribed to this bank, at two different subscriptions, amounted to one hundred and sixty thousand pounds, of which eighty per cent only was paid up.
subscribe.exampleSense: To agree to buy shares in a company.

virus.o: From Middle English virus, from Latin vīrus (“poison, slime, venom”), via rhotacism from Proto-Italic *weizos, from Proto-Indo-European *wisós (“fluidity, slime, poison”). First use in the computer context by David Gerrold in his 1972 book When HARLIE Was One.
virus.example: Under electron microscopy, a few viruses were seen floating near the cells.
virus.exampleSense: A submicroscopic, non-cellular structure that consists of a core of DNA or RNA surrounded by a protein coat, that requires a living host cell to replicate, and that sometimes causes disease in the host organism (such agents are often classed as nonliving infectious particles and less often as microorganisms). An individual particle thereof: synonym of virion.

metabolic.o: Borrowed from Ancient Greek μεταβολικός (metabolikós), from μεταβολή (metabolḗ, “change”) + -ικός (-ikós), thus by surface analysis, metabola + -ic. Compare metabolism.

fry.o:
verb: Inherited from Middle English fryen, borrowed from Old French frire, from Latin frīgō. Cognate with Ancient Greek φρύγω (phrúgō, “to roast, bake”), Sanskrit भृज्जति (bhṛjjati, “to roast, grill, fry”). Replaced native Middle English hirsten, from Old English hierstan (“to fry”). Related to bhurji, bhujia (“fried Indian snacks”).

noun: From Middle English frie (“spawn of fish, young or small fish, offspring, progeny, children”), probably from Old Norse frjó (“seed, semen”), from Proto-Germanic *fraiwą (“seed, semen, offspring”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)per-, *(s)prey- (“to strew, sow”). Cognate with Icelandic frjó (“pollen, seed”), Icelandic fræ (“seed”), Swedish frö (“seed, embryo, grain, germ”), Danish and Norwegian frø (“seed”), Gothic 𐍆𐍂𐌰𐌹𐍅 (fraiw, “seed”). Likely merging with Old French froiz, froie (“spawn, spawning”), from froier, freier (“to spawn”), from Latin fricō (“to rub”). Compare friable.

noun: Dialectal, of obscure origin. Perhaps related to or a corruption of frith (“a wood, forest", also "brushwood, wattle”), from Middle English fryth, frith (“forest, woodland, a fence of brush or wattle, hedge”).
fry.example: You tellin' me a shrimp fried this rice?
fry.exampleSense: A method of cooking food. To cook (something) in hot fat.

predetermine.o: From Latin praedēterminō; equivalent to pre- + determine.

overabundance.o: From Middle English overaboundaunce, equivalent to over- + abundance.

baffling.o: present participle and gerund of baffle. The origin of the verb is uncertain; it is possibly: * from French bafouer, baffoüer (“to abuse, revile; to confuse, baffle; to deceive; to flout; to scorn”), imitative of someone making a disdainful sound by expelling air quickly through pouted lips (compare Occitan baf (interjection expressing disdain)); or * from French befer, beffer, beffler (“(obsolete) to deceive; to mock, ridicule”) (compare Old French befe, beffe, buffe (“deception; mockery”); beferie (“deceit; quibbling”)), possibly from bafouer: see above. The noun is derived from the verb. Cognates * Italian beffare (“(verb) to deride, mock”), beffa (“(noun) banter; mockery”) * Occitan bafar (“(verb) to deride, mock”), bafa (“(noun) banter; mockery”) * Old Spanish bafa (modern Spanish befa (“(noun) banter; mockery”)) * Spanish befar (“(verb) to deride, mock”)
baffling.example: [T]he primitive concept of the generative act was one of awe and worship, accorded to a force which was incomprehensible and baffling.

baffle.o:
verb: The origin of the verb is uncertain; it is possibly: * from French bafouer, baffoüer (“to abuse, revile; to confuse, baffle; to deceive; to flout; to scorn”), imitative of someone making a disdainful sound by expelling air quickly through pouted lips (compare Occitan baf (interjection expressing disdain)); or * from French befer, beffer, beffler (“(obsolete) to deceive; to mock, ridicule”) (compare Old French befe, beffe, buffe (“deception; mockery”); beferie (“deceit; quibbling”)), possibly from bafouer: see above. The noun is derived from the verb. Cognates * Italian beffare (“(verb) to deride, mock”), beffa (“(noun) banter; mockery”) * Occitan bafar (“(verb) to deride, mock”), bafa (“(noun) banter; mockery”) * Old Spanish bafa (modern Spanish befa (“(noun) banter; mockery”)) * Spanish befar (“(verb) to deride, mock”)

verb: The origin of the verb is uncertain; it is possibly from Scots bauchle (“to annoy; to cause harm or trouble to; to disgrace; to jilt; to treat with contempt”), from bauchle (“useless or worn-out person or thing; clumsy work, bungle; clumsy or untidy person; contemptible person; laughing stock”); further etymology uncertain, possibly related to bauch (“feeble, sorry; backward, foolish”, adjective), possibly related to Old Norse bagr (“awkward, clumsy”), bāgr (“hard up, poor; uneasy”) The noun is derived from the verb.
baffle.example: Tanker trucks use baffles to keep the liquids inside from sloshing around.
baffle.exampleSense: A device used to dampen, muffle, restrain, or otherwise control the movement of a fluid, or waves travelling through a fluid such as light or sound; specifically, a surface positioned inside an open area to inhibit direct motion from one place to another without preventing motion altogether.

serene.o:
adj: From Middle English, borrowed from Latin serēnus (“clear, cloudless, untroubled”).

noun: Borrowed from Middle French serein, from Old French serein (“evening”), from Vulgar Latin *serānum, from substantive use of sērum, neuter of sērus (“late”) + -ānus suffix.
serene.example: A serene sky and verdant fields filled me with ecstasy.
serene.exampleSense: Fair and unclouded (as of the sky); clear; unobscured.

tranquil.o: Borrowed from Middle French tranquille, from Latin tranquillus, from trāns- + the root of quiēs (“rest, quiet, peace”), ultimately from *kʷyeh₁- (“to rest”).
tranquil.example: Some time passed before I felt tranquil even here: I had a vague dread that wild cattle might be near, or that some sportsman or poacher might discover me.
tranquil.exampleSense: Free from emotional or mental disturbance.

hostage.o: From Middle English hostage, ostage, from Old French hostage, ostage. This, in turn, is either from Old French hoste (“host”) + -age (in which case the sense development is from taking someone into "lodging" to taking them into "captivity", to applying the term to a captive), or is from Vulgar Latin obsidāticum (“condition of being held captive”), from Latin obses (“hostage, captive”), with the initial h- added under the influence of hoste or another word. Displaced native Old English ġīsl.
hostage.example: One of the hostages pretends to be pregnant and is released at Benghazi Airport, where the aircraft refuels.
hostage.exampleSense: A person seized in order to compel another party to act (or refrain from acting) in a certain way, because of the threat of harm to the hostage.

booth.o: Inherited from Middle English bothe, from Old East Norse *bóð, from Proto-Germanic *bōþō, *būþiz, *buþǭ, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰuH-. Compare Middle Low German bôde, Middle Dutch boede, German Bude.

boorishness.example: No refinement in him would now have surprised her; but neither would any outbreak of boorishness.
boorishness.exampleSense: The state or characteristic of being a boor or of being boorish; boorish behaviour.

boor.o: Borrowed from Dutch boer (“peasant”). Doublet of bauer, Boer, and bower (“peasant, farmer”). For the meaning development from Proto-Indo-European *bʰuH-, compare with other derived from this term Russian обыва́тель (obyvátelʹ, “the average man/citizen, the man in the street, philistine, resident, inhabitant”), Polish bydło (“cattle, rabble”) (whence Russian бы́дло (býdlo, “rabble, uncultured or stupid people, sheeple”)). Compare typologically with pagan (see more).
boor.example: Not swear it, now I am a gentleman? Let boors and franklins say it, I’ll swear it.

pretext.o: From Latin praetextum (“an ornament, etc., wrought in front, a pretense”), neuter of praetextus, past participle of praetexere (“to weave before, fringe or border, allege”).
pretext.example: The reporter called the company on the pretext of trying to resolve a consumer complaint.
pretext.exampleSense: A false, contrived, or assumed purpose or reason; a pretense.

patronize.o: From patron + -ize (verb ending); or from Old French patroniser, from Medieval Latin patronizāre (“to lead a galley as patron”). Piecewise doublet of patternize.
patronize.example: Of course, [Jack] Nicholson patronises him [co-star Morgan Freeman], much as a hare might a tortoise, except that hares can't arch an eyebrow and smirk.
patronize.exampleSense: To assume a tone of unjustified superiority toward; to talk down to, to treat condescendingly.

couplet.o: From French couplet, from couple + -et. Doublet of cabaletta.
couplet.example: The dichotomous keys are constructed so that each couplet presents a set of alternative choices.
couplet.exampleSense: A set of two things, particularly A pair of two mutually exclusive choices in a dichotomous key.

terrific.o: From French terrifique, and its source, Latin terrificus (“terrifying”), from terrēre (“to frighten, terrify”) + -ficus, related to facere (“to make”). By surface analysis, terrify + -ic. The sense of excellent or amazing is an ameliorative semantic shift from the original sense of terrifying. Compare similar semantic development in sick and wicked.
terrific.example: The car came round the bend at a terrific speed.
terrific.exampleSense: Very strong or intense; excessive, tremendous.

asylum.o: From Latin asylum, from Ancient Greek ἄσυλον (ásulon).

consort.o: Borrowed from Middle French, ultimately from Latin cōnsors. As “companion or partner”, via Middle English consorte.
consort.example: Being itself inferior and consorting with an inferior faculty it begets inferior offspring.

bureaucratic.o: Borrowed from French bureaucratique, from bureaucrate (“bureaucrat”) or bureaucratie (“bureaucracy”) + -ique (“-ic”), equivalent to bureaucrat + -ic or bureau + -cratic.
bureaucratic.example: European Union is legalistic, bureaucratic and runs by precedent.
bureaucratic.exampleSense: Of or pertaining to bureaucracy or the actions of bureaucrats.

bureaucrat.o: From French bureaucrate, equivalent to bureau + -crat.
bureaucrat.example: Coristine, who had signed onto the telemeeting using a non-government email address, gave the bureaucrats swift marching orders, telling them he needed access to the federal department’s contract and payment systems before reportedly making them justify their jobs at the $1 billion-budget administration.
bureaucrat.exampleSense: An official who is part of a bureaucracy.

bureaucracy.o: From bureau + -cracy, from French bureaucratie, coined by Jean Claude Marie Vincent de Gournay from bureau (“office”) + -cratie (“rule of”).
bureaucracy.example: However, when Britain left the European Union, ferries started to ply a direct sea link from Ireland, to save hauliers from custom's bureaucracy of driving via Britain.
bureaucracy.exampleSense: Government by bureaus or their administrators or officers.

invincibility.o: From Middle French invincibilité, from Latin invincibilitas.

invincible.o: From Middle French invincible, from Latin invincibilis (“unconquerable”), from in- (“not”) + vincibilis (“conquerable”), from vincere (“to conquer”).

metabolise.o: Alternative spelling of metabolize. From Ancient Greek μετᾰβολή (metăbolḗ, “change, mutation”) + -ize.

metabolism.o: From Ancient Greek μεταβολή (metabolḗ, “change”) + -ism, from μεταβάλλω (metabállō, “to change, to alter”) + -η (-ē, action noun suffix).

billiards.o: From French billard, originally referring to the wooden cue stick, diminutive of Old French bille (“log, tree trunk”), from Vulgar Latin *bilia, probably of Gaulish origin (compare Old Irish bile (“large tree, tree trunk”)), from Proto-Celtic *belyos (“tree”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰolh₃yos (“leaf”), from *bʰleh₃- (“blossom, flower”).

billiard.o:
noun: From French billard with the insertion of the second i and orthographic representation of the French palatalized /j/ sound, originally referring to the wooden cue stick, diminutive of Old French bille (“log, tree trunk”), from Vulgar Latin *bilia, probably of Gaulish origin (compare Old Irish bile (“large tree, tree trunk”)), from Proto-Celtic *belyos (“tree”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰolh₃yos (“leaf”), from *bʰleh₃- (“blossom, flower”).

num: From French billiard, equivalent to bi- (“two”) + -illiard.

bole.o:
noun: From Middle English bole, from Old Norse bolr, akin to Danish bul and German Bohle (“plank”). See also bulwark (“defensive wall”).

noun: From Ancient Greek βῶλος (bôlos, “clod or lump of earth”): compare French bol. Doublet of bolus.
bole.example: Good Iznik has strong colours well-contained within their outlines and a very clean, clear white. The red colour, made with Armenian bole (an earthy clay) should be thick and proud of the surface.
bole.exampleSense: Any of several varieties of friable earthy clay, usually coloured red by iron oxide, and composed essentially of hydrous silicates of alumina, or more rarely of magnesia.

badass.o: From bad + ass (“buttocks; one's self or person”).
badass.example: Yeah. So stop with the pity party. You really are pretty badass right about now.
badass.exampleSense: Having an extreme appearance, attitude, or behavior that is considered admirable.

crust.o: From Middle English cruste, from Anglo-Norman and Old French cruste, from Latin crusta (“hard outer covering”), from Proto-Indo-European *krustós (“hardened”), from *krews- (“to form a crust, begin to freeze”), related to Old Norse hroðr (“scurf”), Old English hruse (“earth”), Old High German hrosa (“crust, ice”), Latvian kruvesis (“frozen mud”), Ancient Greek κρύος (krúos, “frost, icy cold”), κρύσταλλος (krústallos, “crystal, ice”), Avestan 𐬑𐬭𐬎𐬰𐬛𐬭𐬀- (xruzdra-, “hard”), Sanskrit क्रूड् (krūḍ, “thicken, make hard”). Doublet of crusta.
crust.example: The crust (a mere 1% of the Earth's volume) is made of lighter melt products from the mantle.
crust.exampleSense: The outermost layer of the lithosphere of the Earth.

perpetuate.o:
verb: (16th century) From earlier perpetuat, learned borrowing from Latin perpetuātus (“perpetuated”), perfect passive participle of perpetuō (“to cause to continue uninterruptedly, to proceed with continually, to make perpetual, perpetuate”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from perpetuus (“everlasting, perpetual”) + -ō (first conjugation verb-forming suffix), from per- (“thoroughly, very”) + petō (“to ask, request; to look for; to make for (somewhere)”) + -uus (forms adjectives from verbal stems), literally “that is asked with great zeal, over and over again”, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *peth₂- (“to spread out; to fly”). Cognates * Catalan perpetuar * Italian perpetuare * Old French perpetué (adjective) (Middle French perpetué (adjective)); Middle French perpétuer (verb) (modern French perpétuer (verb)) * Old Occitan perpetuar * Portuguese perpetuar * Spanish perpetuar

adj: From earlier preparat (see Etymology 1 and -ate (adjective-forming suffix) for more).
perpetuate.example: [T]he Constitution's doctrine of enumerated powers and federalism also plays a role in perpetuating individual rights.
perpetuate.exampleSense: To make (something) perpetual; to make (something) continue for an indefinite time; also, to preserve (something) from extinction or oblivion.

perpetually.o: From Middle English perpetuelly; equivalent to perpetual + -ly.
perpetually.example: Now her work dropped on her knee, and her book fell from her hand; she was perpetually seeking excuses for change of place; and the change brought added discomfort.
perpetually.exampleSense: Seeming to never end; endlessly; constantly.

perpetual.o: From Middle English perpetuel, from Old French perpetuel, from Latin perpetuālis (“universal”), from perpetuus, from petō.
perpetual.example: There are perpetual requests for changes as new payloads and new demands and modifications are suggested by the users.

adversity.o: From Old French adversité, from Latin adversitātem, the accusative singular of adversitās, from adversus, the perfect passive participle of advertō (“to turn toward”).
adversity.example: These are the people who will overcome the adversity, chaos, and destruction of combat and defeat the enemy in war.
adversity.exampleSense: The state of adverse conditions; state of misfortune or calamity.

utter.o:
adj: PIE word *úd The adjective is derived from Middle English outre, utter, uttre (“situated on the outside of, exterior”), from Old English ūtera (“exterior, outer”, literally “more out”), the comparative form of ūt (“out”). Piecewise doublet of outer. The noun is derived from the adjective.

verb: PIE word *úd From Middle English outren, utteren (“to display for sale; to market; to sell; to say, speak; to put into words, express, tell; to make known, reveal”), partly: * from outre, utter (adjective, adverb) (see etymology 1 and etymology 3) + -en (suffix forming the infinitives of verbs); and * from Middle Dutch uteren (“to announce, make known”) (modern Dutch uiteren); or from Middle Low German üteren, ütern (“to demonstrate, show; to speak; to sell; etc.”) (modern Low German ütern), from Old Dutch or Old Saxon ūtan, probably from Proto-West Germanic *ūtanā (“from outside or without; outside of”). Compare Middle High German ūzeren, whence German äußern (“to express, say, utter”))

adv: PIE word *úd From Middle English outre, utter (“away, out; further away or out; out in the open; outside, without; to a greater extent”), partly: * from outre, utter (adjective) (see etymology 1); and * from Old English ūtor, the comparative form of ūt (“out; outdoors, outside”, adverb).
utter.example: For thy mouth uttereth thine iniquity, and thou choosest the tongue of the crafty.
utter.exampleSense: Senses relating to expressing sounds, etc., or disclosing something To verbally express or report (a desire or emotion, an idea or thought, etc.).

holy.o: From Middle English ali, aly, hale, halege, hali, halȝe, hayly, holi, holia, holie, holiȝ, holy, hooly, oli, oly, wholy, woly, from Old English hāleġ, hāliġ (“holy, sacred; healthy, sound”), from Proto-West Germanic *hailag, from Proto-Germanic *hailagaz (“holy, sacred”), from Proto-Germanic *hailaz (“healthy; whole”), from Proto-Indo-European *kéh₂ilos (“intact, whole; complete; hale, healthy, sound”), equivalent to whole + -y and a doublet of later wholly. Cognates Cognate with Scots halie, haly (“holy”), Yola holly, holy (“holy”), Saterland Frisian helig (“holy”), Alemannic German, Dutch, and German heilig (“holy, sacred”), Cimbrian hòolig (“holy”), Luxembourgish helleg (“holy”), Vilamovian haeliḱ, haliky, hȧlikjy, hǡliḱ (“holy”), Yiddish הייליק (heylik, “holy”), Danish and Norwegian Bokmål hellig (“holy”), Faroese heilagur (“holy”), Icelandic heilagur, helgur (“holy”), Norwegian Nynorsk heilag, heilag’u (“holy”), Swedish helig (“holy”), Gothic 𐌷𐌰𐌹𐌻𐌰𐌲𐍃 (hailags, “holy”); also Latin cael, caelus, caelum, coelus, coelum (“heaven; sky; climate, weather”), Belarusian цэ́лы (cély, “entire, whole”), Bulgarian цял (cjal, “entire, full, intact, whole; real, regular, veritable”), Czech and Slovak celý (“whole”), Macedonian цел (cel, “entire, whole”), Polish cały (“entire, whole”), Russian це́лый (célyj, “entire, whole”), Serbo-Croatian це̏о, ци̏јел, ци̏о, cȅo, cȉjel, cȉo (“entire, whole”), Slovene cel (“whole”), Ukrainian ці́лий (cílyj, “entire, whole”). More at whole.
holy.example: I'm planning to visit the holy city of Jerusalem this Christmas.
holy.exampleSense: Dedicated to a religious purpose or a god.

unhallow.example: Nay, the very Ostentation of the Thorn, is a Weakness, and I might have said a Vice too; for the Vanity Unhallows the very Virtue, especially where it is Accompany'd with Detraction.

hallowed.o: From Middle English halwed (“hallowed, sacred, sanctified”), from Old English ġehālgod (“hallowed, sacred, sanctified”), past participle of hālgian (“to hallow, make holy”). Equivalent to hallow + -ed. More at hallow.

hallow.o:
noun: Inherited from Middle English halwe (“a saint, holy thing, shrine”), from Old English hālga (“a holy one, saint”), from Proto-Germanic *hailagô (“holy one”), from *hailagaz (“holy”), from Proto-Germanic *hailaz (“whole, safe, hale”), from Proto-Indo-European *kéh₂ilos (“safe, unharmed”). Cognate with Scots halow, hallow (“saint”), German Heiliger (“saint (male)”) / Heilige (“saint (female)”). More at holy, whole.

verb: Inherited from Middle English halwen (“to hallow, sanctify”), from Old English hālgian (“to hallow, sanctify, make holy”), from Proto-Germanic *hailagōną (“to make holy”), from *hailagaz (“holy”), from Proto-Germanic *hailaz (“whole, safe, hale”), from Proto-Indo-European *kéh₂ilos (“safe, unharmed”). Cognate with Dutch heiligen (“to hallow”), German heiligen (“to hallow”). More at holy.

verb: Inherited from Middle English halowen, from halow (interjection), from Old English ēalā (“O!, alas!, oh!, lo!”, interjection), probably conflated with Old French halloer.
hallow.example: All Hallows Eve (or Halloween), the night before All Hallows Day (now more commonly known as "All Saints' Day").
hallow.exampleSense: A saint; a holy person; an apostle.

etiquette.o: 1740, from French étiquette (“property, a little piece of paper, or a mark or title, affixed to a bag or bundle, expressing its contents, a label, ticket”), from Middle French estiquette (“ticket, memorandum”), from the Old French verb estechier, estichier, estequier (“to attach, stick”), (compare Picard estiquier (“to stick, pierce”)), from Frankish *stekan, *stikkjan (“to stick, pierce, sting”), from Proto-Germanic *stikaną, *stikōną, *staikijaną (“to be sharp, pierce, prick”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)teyg- (“to be sharp, to stab”). Akin to Old High German stehhan (“to stick, attach, nail”) (German stechen (“to stick”)), Old English stician (“to pierce, stab, be fastened”). The French Court of Louis XIV at Versailles used étiquettes (literally “little cards”) to remind courtiers to keep off of the grass and similar rules. More at stick (verb) and stitch. Doublet of ticket.
etiquette.example: Cycling's complex etiquette contains an unwritten rule that riders in contention for a race win should not be penalised for sheer misfortune.
etiquette.exampleSense: The customary behavior of members of a profession, business, law, or sports team towards each other.

rite.o:
noun: Via Middle English and Old French, from Latin ritus.

adj: Variation of right.
rite.example: But he had to perform the rites of hospitality, had to behave politely to his ally.

anime.o:
noun: Borrowed from Japanese アニメ (anime), an abbreviation of アニメーション (animēshon), itself borrowed from English animation, from Latin animātiō, from animāre.

noun: Borrowed from French animé (“animated”) (from the insects that are entrapped in it); or native name.
anime.example: I can draw an anime version of you, if you want.
anime.exampleSense: An artistic style originating in, and associated with, Japanese animation, and that has also been adopted by a comparatively low number of animated works from other countries.

feminist.o: First attested in 1852. Ultimately from Latin fēminīnus, from fēmina (“woman”). See also feminine, feminism.
feminist.example: Feminist struggle takes place anytime anywhere any female or male resists sexism, sexist exploitation, and oppression.
feminist.exampleSense: relating to or in accordance with feminism.

feminize.example: Parabiosis experiments on primitive vertebrates showed inversion of sex in either direction, males were feminized and females masculinized.

feminism.o: From French féminisme circa 1837, ultimately from Latin fēminīnus, from fēmina (“woman”). In the original sense of “women's movement or advocacy”, the French word was probably directly derived from fēmina, as if from Neo-Latin feminismus. First recorded in English in 1851, originally meaning “the state of being feminine”. Sense of “advocacy of women's rights” is from 1895.
feminism.example: Women are still forbidden to smoke there... Ardent though we are in feminism, we applaud this stand...
feminism.exampleSense: A social theory or political movement which argues that legal and social restrictions on women must be removed in order to bring about equality of the sexes in all aspects of public and private life.

feminine.o: From Middle English feminine, femynyne, femynyn, from Old French feminin, feminine, from Latin fēminīnus, from fēmina (“woman”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁-m̥h₁n-eh₂ (“(the one) nursing, breastfeeding”). Related to fetus, feminism, filial, fellatio.
feminine.example: Her letters are remarkably deficient in feminine ease and grace.
feminine.exampleSense: Having the qualities stereotypically associated with women: nurturing, not aggressive.

damn.o: From Middle English dampnen, from Old French damner, from Latin damnāre (“to condemn, inflict loss upon”), from damnum (“loss”).
damn.example: The new hires aren't worth a damn.
damn.exampleSense: A small, negligible quantity, being of little value; a whit or jot.

ideologue.o: Borrowed from French idéologue (circa 1800), from earlier idéologie (“ideology”) (1796). Classical compound on Ancient Greek roots, equivalent to ideo- + -logue.
ideologue.example: The concept of ideology has its origins in the 19th century and was first used as a technical word by Destutt de Tracy. He was also considered the first ideologue, since he applied this word as a substitute for metaphysics.
ideologue.exampleSense: A person who advocates an ideology, especially as an official or preeminent advocate.

ideology.o: Borrowed from French idéologie, from idéo- + -logie (equivalent to English ideo- + -logy). Cognate with, but not derived from, idea. Coined 1796 by Antoine Destutt de Tracy. Modern sense of “doctrine” attributed to use of related idéologue (“ideologue”) by Napoleon Bonaparte as a term of abuse towards political opponents in early 1800s.
ideology.example: A dictatorship bans things, that do not conform to its ideology, to secure its reign.
ideology.exampleSense: Doctrine, philosophy, body of beliefs or principles belonging to an individual or group.

contingency.example: There was also the imperative necessity of creating a reserve fund for unforeseen contingencies, and the question ever present was how was money to be found.
contingency.exampleSense: A possibility; something which may or may not happen. A chance occurrence, especially in finance, unexpected expenses.

contingence.o: Borrowed from Latin contingentia (whence con- + and -ence), from contingēns, present passive participle of contingō (“to make contact with, to be touching”).

epic.o:
noun: From Middle French épique, from Latin epicus, from Ancient Greek ἐπικός (epikós), from ἔπος (épos, “word, story”).

adj: From epi-, from Ancient Greek ἐπί (epí, “on top of”).
epic.example: The Icelandic epic took all night to recite.
epic.exampleSense: An extended narrative poem in elevated or dignified language, celebrating the feats of a deity, demigod (heroic epic), other legend or traditional hero.

feudist.example: After two years away, Rosie O’Donnell — actress, Broadway booster, consummate feudist — is returning to the stage.
feudist.exampleSense: One who takes part in feuds.

feudal.o: From Old French feodal, from Medieval Latin feodalis, from feodum, feudum, fevum (“fief, fee”), from Frankish *fehu (“cattle, owndom, property, fee”), from Proto-Germanic *fehu (“cattle”). By surface analysis, feud (“estate”) + -al. More at fee.

feud.o:
noun: Inherited from Northern Middle English fede, feide, from Old French faide, feide, fede, from Proto-West Germanic *faihiþu (“hatred, enmity”) (corresponding to foe + -th), from Proto-Indo-European *peyḱ- (“hostile”). Cognate to Old English fǣhþ, fǣhþu, fǣhþo (“hostility, enmity, violence, revenge, vendetta”), German Fehde, and Dutch vete (“feud”) (directly inherited from Proto-West Germanic) alongside Danish fejde (“feud, enmity, hostility, war”) and Swedish fejd (“feud, controversy, quarrel, strife”) (borrowed from Middle Low German).

noun: From Medieval Latin feudum. Doublet of fee, fief, and feoff.
feud.example: The two men began to feud after one of them got a job promotion and the other thought he was more qualified.

incomprehension.example: Stephen blushed; and his father looked from one to the other in a state of utter incomprehension.
incomprehension.exampleSense: Lack of comprehension or understanding; inability to understand.

look.o: From Middle English loken, lokien, from Old English lōcian, from Proto-West Germanic *lōkōn. Further origin unknown, no certain cognates outside Germanic. Cognate with Scots luke, luik, leuk (“to look, see”), West Frisian lôkje, loaitsje (“to look”), Dutch loeken (“to look”), German Low German löken. Likely also related to German lugen (“to peek”), Alemannic German luege (“to look”), Yiddish לוגן (lugn).
look.example: Look how they massacred my boy.
look.exampleSense: To try to see, to pay attention to with one’s eyes. As a transitive verb, often in the imperative; chiefly takes relative clause as direct object.

glee.o:
noun: From Middle English gle, from Old English glēo, glīġ, glēow, glīw (“glee, pleasure, mirth, play, sport; music; mockery”), from Proto-West Germanic *glīw, from Proto-Germanic *glīwą (“joy, mirth”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰlew- (“to joke, make fun, enjoy”). Cognate with Scots gle, glie, glew (“game, play, sport, mirth, joy, rejoicing, entertainment, melody, music”), Icelandic glý (“joy, glee, gladness”), Ancient Greek χλεύη (khleúē, “joke, jest, scorn”). A poetic word in Middle English, the word was obsolete by 1500, but revived late 18c.

verb: From Middle English gleen, glewen, from Old English glēowian (“to sing, play an instrument, jest”), from Proto-West Germanic *glīwōn, from Proto-Germanic *glīwōną. Cognate with Icelandic glýja (“to be gleeful”).
glee.example: I watched with glee while your kings and queens fought for ten decades for the gods they made.
glee.exampleSense: Joy; happiness; great delight, especially from one's own good fortune or from another's misfortune.

tweak.o: From Middle English twikken, from Old English twiccian (“to pluck”), from Proto-West Germanic *twekkōn (“to fasten; clamp; pinch”). Related to twitch. The drug-related sense may be a blend of twitch and freak.
tweak.example: If we tweak the colors towards blue, it will look more natural.

quantitative.o: From Late Latin quantitātīvus. By surface analysis, quantity + -ative.

quantifiable.example: If the human factor in production is reduced through automation, the process becomes more quantifiable.

cannibalise.example: The female black widow spider is known to cannibalise the male.
cannibalise.exampleSense: To eat (parts of) another of one's own species.

intra-.example: intramercurial is between the planet Mercury and the sun, intrapetiolar is situated between the petiole and the stem, intraaxillary Situated below the point where a leaf joins the stem.
intra-.exampleSense: In between two entities: Spatially located in between the root entity and a reference point.

frenzy.o: From Middle English frensy, frenesie, from Old French frenesie, from Latin phrenesis, from Ancient Greek *φρένησις (*phrénēsis), a later equivalent of φρενῖτις (phrenîtis, “inflammation of the brain”): see frantic and frenetic. Doublet of phrenesis.
frenzy.example: The poet's eye in a fine frenzy rolling.
frenzy.exampleSense: A violent agitation of the mind approaching madness; rage.

crave.o: From Middle English craven, from Old English crafian (“to crave, ask, implore, demand, summon”), from Proto-West Germanic *krafōn, from Proto-Germanic *krafjaną (“to demand”). Cognate with Danish kræve (“to demand, require”), Swedish kräva (“to crave, demand”), Icelandic krefja (“to demand”), Norwegian kreve (“to demand”).
crave.example: I humbly crave your indulgence to read this letter until the end.
crave.exampleSense: To ask for earnestly; to beg; to claim.

snatch.o: From Middle English snacchen, snecchen (“to snap; seize”), from Old English *snæċċan, *sneċċan, from Proto-West Germanic *snakkjan, from Proto-Germanic *snakjaną (“to whiff, sniff, catch wind of; to taste-test, nibble”), related to Proto-Germanic *snakōną (“to breathe, blow, sigh”) and *snakkōną (“to blather, jabber, chatter”). Cognate with Middle Dutch snacken (“to snap [of a dog]”), Norwegian Nynorsk snaka (“to snatch [of animals]”). Related also to Dutch snakken (“to sob, pant, long for”), Low German snacken (“to chatter”), German schnacken (“to chat”), Danish snakke (“to chat”) and Norwegian snakke (“to chat”). Related to snack.
snatch.example: She snatched the letter out of the secretary's hand.

disregard.example: The government's disregard for the needs of disabled people is outrageous.
disregard.exampleSense: The act or state of deliberately not paying attention or caring about something.

period.o: From Middle English periode, from Middle French periode, from Medieval Latin periodus, from Ancient Greek περίοδος (períodos, “circuit, orbit, a recurring interval of time, path around”), from περι- (peri-, “around”) + ὁδός (hodós, “way”). Displaced native Middle English tide (“interval, period, season”), from Old English tīd (“time, period, season”), as well as Middle English elde (“age, period”), from Old English ieldu (“age, period of time”).
period.example: Gretzky scored in the last minute of the second period.
period.exampleSense: Each of the intervals, typically three, of which a game is divided.

terrify.o: From Middle French terrifier, from Latin terrificare.

volume.o: From Middle English volume, from Old French volume, from Latin volūmen (“book, roll”), from volvō (“roll, turn about”).
volume.example: The room is 9×12×8, so its volume is 864 cubic feet.
volume.exampleSense: A three-dimensional measure of space that comprises a length, a width and a height. It is measured in units of cubic centimeters in metric, cubic inches or cubic feet in English measurement.

intangible.o: Borrowed from Middle French intangible, from Medieval Latin intangibilis, from Late Latin tangibilis, from Latin tango.
intangible.example: Diaghilev's love for Nijinsky was as deep and as sincere and reliant as a bond could be, it being based on all those intangibles of love that cannot be enumerated.

intellectual property.example: One area of current change concerns intellectual properties and intellectual property rights.
intellectual property.exampleSense: Any individual work that is protected under intellectual property law.

intellectual.o: From Old French intellectuel, from Latin intellectualis.
intellectual.example: A good deal of nonsense is written about sport and entertainment. Many of us can, with pleasant ease, suspend a severely intellectual task for a few hours to witness a first-class football match.
intellectual.exampleSense: Suitable for exercising one's intellect; perceived by the intellect

intelligent.o:
adj: From Middle French intelligent, from Latin intellegēns (“discerning”), present active participle of intellegō (“understand, comprehend”), itself from inter (“between”) + legō (“choose, pick out, read”).

noun: Partly from Russian интеллиге́нт (intelligént) and partly from the adjective.
intelligent.example: The engineer had a very intelligent design proposal for the new car.

intellect.o: Borrowed from Late Latin intellēctus (“understanding, intellect”), from Latin intellegō (“understand; reason”), from inter (“between, among”) + legō (“read”), with connotation of bind.
intellect.example: They were chosen because of their outstanding intellect.
intellect.exampleSense: The capacity of that faculty (in a particular person).

run out.o: Alternative form of runout. Deverbal from run out.
run out.example: The option will run out next week and I can't get it extended.
run out.exampleSense: To expire; to come to an end; to be completely used up or consumed.

reshape.example: Intentional skull reshaping is found in burials across Asia, Europe and Mesoamerica.
reshape.exampleSense: To make into a different shape.

come up.example: I came up the ladder carefully, holding the bucket in my right hand.
come up.exampleSense: Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see come, up.

outsource.example: Read said maintenance would be outsourced, with "positive discussions" held with two companies.
outsource.exampleSense: To transfer the management and/or day-to-day execution of a business function to a third-party service provider.

intimidation.o: From intimidate + -ion. Compare French intimidation; perhaps modeled on it.

intimidating.o: present participle and gerund of intimidate. From Medieval Latin intimidātus, perfect passive participle of Latin intimidō (“to intimidate, terrify”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from in- (“in”) + timidus (“afraid, timid”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix); see timid.

intimidated.o: simple past and past participle of intimidate. From Medieval Latin intimidātus, perfect passive participle of Latin intimidō (“to intimidate, terrify”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from in- (“in”) + timidus (“afraid, timid”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix); see timid.

timidity.o: From timid + -ity, from Middle French timidité, from Latin timiditātem.

timid.o: From Middle French timide, from Latin timidus (“full of fear, fearful, timid”), from timeō (“to fear”).
timid.example: John's a very timid person. I doubt he'll be brave enough to face his brother.

intimidate.o: From Medieval Latin intimidātus, perfect passive participle of Latin intimidō (“to intimidate, terrify”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from in- (“in”) + timidus (“afraid, timid”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix); see timid.
intimidate.example: He's trying to intimidate you. If you ignore him, hopefully he'll stop.
intimidate.exampleSense: To make timid or afraid; to cause to feel fear or nervousness; to deter, especially by threats of violence.

neurosis.example: On inquiry it was found that this neurosis corresponded in time with the oncome of the catamenia.
neurosis.exampleSense: A mental disorder, less severe than psychosis, marked by anxiety or fear which differ from normal measures by their intensity, which disorder results from a failure to compromise or properly adjust during the developmental stages of life, between normal human instinctual impulses and the demands of human society.

neurology.o: From New Latin neurologia. By surface analysis, neuro- + -logy.

neuronal.example: Nicotine, a stimulant found in tobacco, long used by Native Americans, taught scientists about the existence of our own nicotinic receptors, which influence neuronal excitement.
neuronal.exampleSense: Of, or relating to a neuron.

neurone.o: Alternative spelling of neuron. From New Latin, from Ancient Greek νεῦρον (neûron, “nerve”), doublet of nerve and sinew. By surface analysis, neuro- + -on.

neuron.o: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek νεῦρον (neûron, “nerve”), doublet of nerve and sinew. By surface analysis, neuro- + -on.

neuro-.o: From Ancient Greek νευρο- (neuro-), combining form of νεῦρον (neûron, “sinew, tendon, cord”). By surface analysis, neur- + -o-.
neuro-.example: There's been a proliferation of “neuro-” fields. Some, like neuroendocrinology and neuroimmunology, are stodgy old institutions by now.
neuro-.exampleSense: Nerves, nervous tissue, or the nervous system.

up-and-coming.example: The theater likes to feature up-and-coming singers and comedians.
up-and-coming.exampleSense: Emerging; aspiring; beginning to attract attention or critical acclaim.

dietitian.o: Irregular spelling of diet + -ician, probably influenced by dietetic.
dietitian.example: The dietitian works with the client to develop meal planning that meets the client's needs based on healthy food choices.
dietitian.exampleSense: A person who studies or practices dietetics.

celebrate.o: From Middle English celebraten, from celebrat(e) (“celebrated”, also used as the past participle of celebraten) + -en, borrowed from Latin celebrātus, perfect passive participle of celebrō (“frequent, go to in great numbers, celebrate, honor, praise”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from celeber (“frequented, populous”). Displaced native Old English fæġnian.
celebrate.example: I was promoted today at work—let’s celebrate!
celebrate.exampleSense: To engage in joyful activity in appreciation of an event.

celebrated.o: simple past and past participle of celebrate. From Middle English celebraten, from celebrat(e) (“celebrated”, also used as the past participle of celebraten) + -en, borrowed from Latin celebrātus, perfect passive participle of celebrō (“frequent, go to in great numbers, celebrate, honor, praise”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from celeber (“frequented, populous”). Displaced native Old English fæġnian.
celebrated.example: She became a celebrated actress, but never won any major awards.

shabby.o: The adjective is derived from shab (“(obsolete except UK, dialectal) scaly skin disease; skin disease of sheep; crust forming over wound, scab”) + -y (suffix meaning ‘having the quality of’ forming adjectives). The verb is derived from the adjective. Cognates * Dutch schabbig (“poor, needy, shabby”) * Middle High German schebic (modern German schäbig (“shabby”)) * Middle Low German schabbich (“miserable”) (modern Low German schabbig, schäbbig) * Scots shabby (“in poor health, ill”) * Swedish sjabbig (“shabby, mangy, scruffy”), skabbig (“scabby”)
shabby.example: It was voted a shabby excuse.
shabby.exampleSense: Of a person, their behaviour, etc.: despicable, mean; also, not generous; stingy, tight-fisted.

habitual.o: The adjective is derived from Late Middle English habitual (“of one's inherent disposition”), from Medieval Latin habituālis (“customary; habitual”), from Latin habitus (“character; disposition; habit; physical or emotional condition; attire, dress”) + -ālis (suffix forming adjectives of relationship); analysable as habit + -ual. Habitus is derived from habeō (“to have; to hold; to own; to possess”) (possibly ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʰeh₁bʰ- (“to grab, take”)) + -tus (suffix forming action nouns from verbs). The noun is derived from the adjective.
habitual.example: Professor Franklein took his habitual seat at the conference table.

occurrence.o: From Middle French occurrence, from Medieval Latin occurrentia. Morphologically occur + -ence.

suspect.o: From Old French suspect, from Latin suspectus, perfect passive participle of suspiciō (“mistrust, suspect”), from sub (“under”), + speciō (“watch, look at”).
suspect.example: I suspect him of being the thief.

aberration.o: A learned borrowing from Latin aberrātiō(n) (“relief, diversion”), first attested in 1594, from aberrō (“wander away, go astray”), from ab (“away”) + errō (“wander”). Compare French aberration. By surface analysis, aberrat(e) + -ion.
aberration.example: Only by submitting to the aberration could the human traders travel safely through the territory of Zularn.
aberration.exampleSense: Any creature with supernatural powers not found in the organized classes of beings in a given setting.

aberrant.o: From Latin aberrāns, present active participle of aberrō (“go astray; err”), from ab (“from”) + errō (“to wander”). See aberr.
aberrant.example: The more aberrant any form is, the greater must have been the number of connecting forms which, on my theory, have been exterminated.
aberrant.exampleSense: Deviating from the ordinary or natural type; exceptional; abnormal.

exclaim.o: From Middle French exclamer, from Latin exclāmō, exclāmāre (“call out”), from ex- + clāmō (“to call”).
exclaim.example: Must she be forc’d, t’exclaime th’iniurious wrong?
exclaim.exampleSense: To say suddenly and with strong emotion.

prowess.o: From Middle English prowesse, prouwesse, proues, prouesce, prouesse (“bravery in battle; act of bravery; excellence; nobility of character; intelligence”), from Old French proeche, proesce, proeësche (“goodness; excellence; bravery”), from Old French preu, prou, prouz, proz, pruz (“good; excellent; brave”). Compare English proud.
prowess.example: If it is deemed of so much importance, why has no attention been paid to the effects of general friendship, such as certain military prowesses, in which you see a portion of a regiment sacrifice itself in support of another portion?
prowess.exampleSense: An act of prowess. An act of distinguished bravery or courage; a heroic deed.

salvable.o: From Latin salvare (“to save”), from salvus (“safe”). Compare savable.

salvage.o:
noun: From Old French salver (see also save, from a variant form), from Late Latin salvare (“to make safe, secure, save”), from Latin salvus (“safe”) with the English suffix -age.

noun: See the etymology of the corresponding lemma form.

noun: Borrowed from Spanish salvaje, from Catalan salvatge, from Late Latin *salvāticus, alteration of Latin silvāticus (“wild”, literally “of the woods”). Confused false friends; English salvage and Tagalog salbahe (“mischievous, naughty”).
salvage.example: [...] the debris was hurled down the hillside on to the line and swept the engine off the track and into the sea; the engine in question, ex-Cambrian 0-6-0 No. 874, was not considered to be worth salvage, and was abandoned.
salvage.exampleSense: The similar rescue of property liable to loss; the property so rescued.

salvation.o: From Middle English savacioun, from Old French savaciun, salvaciun, from Latin salvātiō. Displaced native Old English hǣlu.
salvation.example: Collective salvation is not possible without personal salvation, but the latter is achievable.
salvation.exampleSense: The process of being saved, the state of having been saved (from hell).

bushmeat.o: From bush + meat, as a calque of French viande de brousse.

decimate.o: The verb is first attested in 1591, the noun in 1641; borrowed from Latin decimātus, perfect passive participle of decimō (“to kill one tenth; to tithe”) (see, from -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (noun-forming suffix)), from decimus (“tenth”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix). As a noun, via Latin decimatus (“tithing area; tithing rights”).
decimate.example: Shall we decimate them? That sounds good, nice word. Remove one-tenth of the population!
decimate.exampleSense: To kill one-tenth of (a group), (historical, specifically) as a military punishment in the Roman army selected by lot, usually carried out by the surviving soldiers.

tragicomic.example: The pirates threatened to kill Captain Phillips if attacked, and the result was tragicomic: the world’s most powerful navy vs. a lifeboat.
tragicomic.exampleSense: Of, pertaining to, or resembling tragicomedy; having both tragic and comic aspects.

tragical.o: Ultimately from Ancient Greek τραγικός (tragikós) + Latin -ālis. By surface analysis, tragic + -al.
tragical.example: Fortunately the illness passed away without serious consequences; yet it seemed the first break in our festivities, and was followed by an event of a most tragical nature.

culinary.o: Borrowed from French culinaire, itself a borrowing from Latin culīnārius, from culīna (“kitchen”).
culinary.exampleSense: Relating to the practice of cookery or the activity of cooking.

compressor.o: From compress + -or, or from New Latin compressor.

compress.o:
verb: From Middle English compressen, from Old French compresser, from Late Latin compressare (“to press hard/together”), from Latin compressus, the past participle of comprimō (“to compress”), itself from com- (“together”) + premō (“press”).

noun: From Middle French compresse, from compresse (“to compress”), from Late Latin compressare (“to press hard/together”), from Latin compressus, the past participle of comprimō (“to compress”), itself from com- (“together”) + premō (“press”).
compress.example: The same strength of expression, though more compressed, runs through his historical harangues.
compress.exampleSense: To make smaller; to press or squeeze together, or to make something occupy a smaller space or volume.

outpost.example: The outpost did not have enough ammunition to resist a determined assault.
outpost.exampleSense: A military post stationed at a distance from the main body of troops.

logistics.o: From French logistique, coined or popularized 1830 by Antoine-Henri Jomini from logis (“lodging place”), in phrases maréchal des logis (“marshall of lodging”) (see maréchal des logis), major-général des logis (“major-general of lodging”). Possibly influenced by existing mathematical term logistique, of Ancient Greek origin; see logistic.

logistic.o:
adj: From French logistique, from Ancient Greek λογιστικός (logistikós, “practiced in arithmetic; rational”), from λογίζομαι (logízomai, “I reason, I calculate”), from λόγος (lógos, “reason, computation”), whence English logos, logic, logarithm, etc.; modern mathematical use influenced by related logarithmic. Sense of “logistic function” by Pierre François Verhulst (1845) in French, then borrowed into English. Verhulst does not explain his choice of naming, but he contrasts it with the logarithmic curve (also from λόγος (lógos)), and it is presumably by analogy with arithmetic and geometric (other divisions of mathematics), as his discussion of arithmetic growth and geometric growth precede his discussion of logistic growth. The term logistic and logistical also found occasional mathematical use in English prior to 1800, from the same Greek origin.

adj: From French logistique, from loger (“to lodge”) or logis (“lodging place”).

logistical.example: Feeding all those people will be a logistical nightmare.

primal.o: Probably partly from Medieval Latin prīmālis, from Latin prīmus (“first”) + -ālis, and partly from prime + -al.
primal.example: Primaling on the infant level seems so genuinely babyish that the unsophisticated observer may mistake it for psychotic behavior.
primal.exampleSense: To take part in primal therapy.

unaccustomed.example: Later that day, whether from the accumulated effect of seeing hunger, from the unaccustomed food or from the sun, I get sick.
unaccustomed.exampleSense: To which one is not accustomed, unfamiliar

depopulation.o: Inherited from Middle English depopulacion (also spelled depopulacyoun, depopolacion), borrowed from Latin dēpopulātiō. By surface analysis, depopulate + -ion.

overpopulation.example: I hope for another end, though not, indeed, from any of the three remedies for over-population commonly suggested by economists. These three are, in brief—Colonization; Bringing in of waste lands; or Discouragement of Marriage.
overpopulation.exampleSense: An excessive number of occupants (people, animals, plants, etc.) in a particular area; specifically, when the number of occupants exceeds the ability of that area to provide for them.

regional.o: From Middle French régional, from Latin regiōnālis.
regional.example: In the CPE^([Customer Premises Equipment]) market, all seven regionals are selling several sizes of private branch exchanges (PBX) and key systems for smaller customers.
regional.exampleSense: An entity or event with scope limited to a single region.

singularize.example: There’s a word that we use in consumer behavior — it singularizes the couple and communicates that this couple is like no other.

singularity.o: From Middle English singularite, from Old French singularité, from Late Latin singulāritās (“singleness”), from Latin singulāris (“single”). By surface analysis, singular + -ity.
singularity.example: I took notice of this little figure for the singularity of the instrument.
singularity.exampleSense: The state of being singular, distinct, peculiar, uncommon or unusual.

singular.o: From Middle English singuler, from Old French, from Latin singulāris (“alone of its kind”), from Latin singulus (“single”).
singular.example: A singular experiment cannot be regarded as scientific proof of the existence of a phenomenon.
singular.exampleSense: Being only one of a larger population; single, individual.

baboon.o: Inherited from Middle English babewin, baboin, from Old French babouin, from baboue (“grimace; muzzle”) (whence French babouin), from an imitative origin. According to Oxford English Dictionary, it was an imitative base *bab-, which is in turn from the (reduplicated) syllable ba, characteristic of early infantile vocalization (and expressive of the movement of the lips in speech). French babouin was also borrowed into other European languages. Confer Vulgar Latin babouinus ("a grimace"), Vulgar Latin babuinare ("to paint marginal figures in manuscripts"), Italian babbuino, babuino (“baboon”), Dutch baviaan (“baboon”), German Pavian (“baboon”) For the sense of infant imitation, see English babble (“to blather”), English babe (“darling”), English baby (“infant”).
baboon.example: He draws eclectically on studies of baboons, descriptive anthropological accounts of hunter-gatherer societies and, in a few cases, the fossil record.
baboon.exampleSense: An Old World monkey of the genus Papio, having dog-like muzzles and large canine teeth, cheek pouches, a short tail, and naked callosities on the buttocks.

lust.o:
noun: From Middle English lust, from Old English lust (“lust, pleasure, longing”), from Proto-West Germanic *lustu, from Proto-Germanic *lustuz. Akin to Old Saxon, Dutch lust, Old Frisian, Old High German, German Lust, Swedish lust, Danish lyst, Icelandic lyst, Old Norse losti, Gothic 𐌻𐌿𐍃𐍄𐌿𐍃 (lustus), and perhaps to Sanskrit लष् (laṣ), लषति (laṣati, “to desire”) and Albanian lushë (“bitch, savage dog, promiscuous woman”), or to English loose. Compare list (“to please”), listless.

verb: From Middle English lusten, from the noun.
lust.example: Seeing Leslie fills me with a passionate lust.
lust.exampleSense: A feeling of strong desire, especially such a feeling driven by sexual arousal.

wanderlust.o: Borrowed from German Wanderlust (“an urge to travel; a love of the ‘great outdoors’”), from wandern (“to wander; to hike”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *wendʰ- (“to turn; to wind”)) + Lust (“a desire, a wish to do or have something; fun, pleasure”) (possibly ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *lewH- (“to separate; to set free; to untie”)); analysable as wander + lust.
wanderlust.example: If you find yourself suffering from an attack of Wanderlust, this is the book for you!
wanderlust.exampleSense: A strong impulse or longing to travel.

zombie.o: First attested in the 18th century. Partially through Louisiana Creole zombi (“zombie; ghost”), Haitian Creole zonbi (“zombie”), and French zombi (“zombie”). Ultimately from a Bantu language. Compare Kongo nzambi (“god”), zumbi (“fetish”), and Kimbundu nzumbi (“ghost”) (see Portuguese zumbi, Sranan Tongo dyumbi), and Caribbean folklore's jumbie (“a spirit or demon”).
zombie.example: The maitre d’ introduced us and I had a zombie with him. Those zombies are wicked.
zombie.exampleSense: A cocktail of rum and fruit juices.

rancor.o: First attested in the 13th century as Middle English rancour, from Old French rancor, from Latin rancor (“rancidity, grudge, rancor”), from ranceō (“to be rotten or putrid”), from which also English rancid.
rancor.example: I could almost see the rancor in his eyes when he challenged me to a fight.
rancor.exampleSense: A feeling of long-lasting ire for another, sometimes to the point of hatred, over a perceived wrongdoing; bitterness.

elegy.o: From Middle French elegie, from Latin elegīa, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ἐλεγείᾱ (elegeíā), ellipsis of ἐλεγείᾱ ᾠδή (elegeíā ōidḗ, “an elegiac song”).

elegiac.o: From Middle French élégiaque, from Latin elegīacus, from Ancient Greek ἐλεγειακός (elegeiakós).

summer house.o: Alternative spelling of summerhouse. From Middle English somer-hous, from Old English sumerhūs, sumorhūs, equivalent to summer + house. Compare Dutch zomerhuis, German Sommerhaus, Danish sommerhus, Swedish sommarhus.
summer house.example: One [old passenger coach], still used as a summer house, has been stripped of its wheels and repainted fairly recently in bright green, while the other, still in begrimed olive-green, has descended to the level of a chicken house.

verse.o:
noun: From Middle English vers, from a mixture of Old English fers and Old French vers; both from Latin versus (“a line in writing, and in poetry a verse; (originally) row, furrow”), from vertō (“to turn around”).

verb: Back-formation from versus, misconstrued as a third-person singular verb verses.
verse.example: It is not rhyming and versing that maketh a poet.

doodle.o:
noun: Originally dialectal, from Low German dudeldopp (“simpleton”). Influenced by dawdle. Compare also German dudeln (“to play (the bagpipe)”). The word doodle first appeared in the early 17th century to mean a fool or simpleton. German variants of the etymon include Dudeltopf, Dudentopf, Dudenkopf, Dude and Dödel. American English dude may be a derivation of doodle. The meaning "fool, simpleton" is intended in the song title "Yankee Doodle", originally sung by British colonial troops prior to the American Revolutionary War. This is also the origin of the early eighteenth century verb to doodle, meaning "to swindle or to make a fool of". The modern meaning emerged in the 1930s either from this meaning or from the verb "to dawdle", which since the seventeenth century has had the meaning of wasting time or being lazy.

noun: Extracted from Labradoodle, itself a blend of labrador and poodle
doodle.example: The bored student doodled a submarine in his notebook.

material.o: From Middle English material, from Late Latin māteriālis, from Latin māteria (“wood, material, substance”), from māter (“mother”). Displaced native Middle English andweorc, andwork (“material, matter”) (from Old English andweorc (“matter, substance, material”)). Doublet of materiel.
material.example: As we age, the major arteries of our bodies frequently become thickened with plaque, a fatty material with an oatmeal-like consistency that builds up along the inner lining of blood vessels.
material.exampleSense: The substance that something is made or composed of.

exposition.o: From Middle English exposicioun, from Old French esposicion, from Latin expositiō, from expōnere (“to put forth”). The sense meaning "exhibition" is a later semantic loan from French exposition.
exposition.example: My reviewer said she couldn't picture the setting for my story, so I'm improving the exposition.
exposition.exampleSense: The act or process of declaring or describing something through either speech or writing, in nonfiction or in fiction; the portions and aspects of a piece of writing that exist mainly to describe or explain a set of things (such as, in fiction, the setting, characters and other non-plot elements).

daunting.example: Abd-ool-Azeez gave the stranger a daunting look, but coolly proceeded.

daunt.o: From Middle English daunten, from Old French danter, donter (“to tame”), from Latin domitō (“tame”, verb), frequentative of Latin domō (“tame, conquer”, verb), from Proto-Italic *domaō, from Proto-Indo-European *demh₂- (“to domesticate, tame”). Doublet of dompt.

pastime.o: From earlier passtime, pass-time, from Middle English passe tyme, passetyme, calque of Middle French passetemps.
pastime.example: Nor would there be an opportunity for the media's favorite pastime of exposing conflict among his advisors.
pastime.exampleSense: Something which amuses, and serves to make time pass agreeably.

superintendent.o: From Ecclesiastical Latin superintendens, a calque of Ancient Greek ἐπίσκοπος (epískopos); thence being distantly related to English bishop.

superintend.example: Herb Abbott, the foreman, who superintended the whole operation and filled in wherever he was needed.
superintend.exampleSense: To oversee the work of others; to supervise.

civic.o: Borrowed from Latin cīvicus (“pertaining to a city or citizens”).
