civic.example: Thousands of people came to the Civic Center to show off their civic pride.
civic.exampleSense: Of, relating to, or belonging to a city, a citizen, or citizenship; municipal or civil.

post.o:
noun: (“pillar, door-post”) and Old French post (“post, upright beam”), both from Latin postis (“door, post, doorpost”).

noun: Borrowed from Middle French poste, from Italian posta (“stopping-place for coaches”), feminine of posto (“placed, situated”).

noun: Probably from French poste.

prep: Borrowed from Latin post.

noun: Clipping of post-production.

noun: Clipping of post mortem.
post.example: As hard as this may seem for some people to understand, my adamant stand in favor of President Clinton leaving his post was not personal.
post.exampleSense: An appointed position in an organization, job.

lead.o:
noun: From Middle English led, leed, from Old English lēad (“lead”), from Proto-West Germanic *laud (“lead”), possibly borrowed from Proto-Celtic *ɸloudom, from Proto-Indo-European *plewd- (“to flow”). Cognate with Scots leid, lede (“lead”), North Frisian lud, luad (“lead”), West Frisian lead (“lead”), Dutch lood (“lead”), Low German Lod (“solder, plummet”), German Lot (“solder, plummet, sounding line”), Swedish lod (“solder, plummet”), Icelandic lóð (“a plumb, weight”), Irish luaidhe (“lead”) Latin plumbum (“lead”), Finnish luoti (“bullet”). Doublet of loth. More at flow. * (graphite in a pencil): Graphite was once believed to be a form of lead; see black lead and plumbago.

verb: From Middle English leden, from Old English lǣdan (“to lead”), from Proto-West Germanic *laidijan, from Proto-Germanic *laidijaną (“to cause one to go, lead”), causative of Proto-Germanic *līþaną (“to go”), from Proto-Indo-European *leyt- (“to leave, die”). Cognate with West Frisian liede (“to lead”), Dutch leiden (“to lead”), German leiten (“to lead”), Danish and Norwegian Bokmål lede (“to lead”), Norwegian Nynorsk leia (“to lead”), Swedish leda (“to lead”), Faroese and Icelandic leiða (“to lead”). Related to Old English līþan (“to go, travel”).

verb: Perhaps from a confusion or conflation with read, which has a single spelling for both past and present tenses, but has differing pronunciations in the same way as lead, i.e. the present's vowel is /i/, and the past's is /ɛ/. See also red and redd, the obsolete spellings of read.
lead.example: The guide was able to lead the tourists through the jungle safely.
lead.exampleSense: To guide or conduct. To guide or conduct in a certain course, or to a certain place or end, by making the way known; to show the way, especially by going with or going in advance of, to lead a pupil; to guide somebody somewhere or to bring somebody somewhere by means of instructions.

excel.o: From Middle English excellen, from Old French exceller, from Latin excellere, excelsum; ex (“out”) + *cellō, an unattested verb root found in culmen (“height, top”); Compare French exceller. See also culminate, column.
excel.example: But it is as a destroyer of grasshoppers that the dickcissel excels.
excel.exampleSense: To be much better than others.

maternal.o: PIE word *méh₂tēr The adjective is derived from Late Middle English maternal, maternall, from Middle French maternel (“maternal”) (modern French maternel (“maternal; native”)), or from its etymon Late Latin māternālis (“maternal”), from Latin māternus (“maternal; related to the mother or her side of the family”) + -ālis (suffix forming adjectives of relationship from nouns). Māternus is derived from māter (“mother”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *méh₂tēr (“mother”)) + -rnus (suffix forming adjectives). The English word is cognate with Italian maternale, materno, Portuguese maternal, materno, Spanish maternal, materno. The noun is derived from the adjective.
maternal.example: Undernutrition occurs when dietary intake cannot meet nutritional requirements. The synthesis of maternal and fetal tissue or breast milk, and the associated costs of maternal maintenance increase nutrient requirements during pregnancy and lactation.
maternal.exampleSense: Derived from the mother as opposed to the foetus during pregnancy.

oblivion.o: Inherited from Middle English oblivion, from Anglo-Norman oblivion, from Latin oblīviō (“forgetfulness”), from oblīvīscor (“to forget”).
oblivion.example: They tried to bomb them into oblivion.
oblivion.exampleSense: The state of being completely forgotten, of being reduced to a state of non-existence, extinction, or nothingness, including through war and destruction. (Figuratively) for an area like hell, a wasteland.

oblivious.o: From Middle English oblivious, from Latin oblīviōsus (“forgetful, oblivious”), formed from oblīvium (“forgetfulness, oblivion”) + -ōsus (“full of, overly, prone to”), from oblīvīscor (“to forget”).
oblivious.example: Your grandmother is completely oblivious to her surroundings.
oblivious.exampleSense: Lacking awareness; unmindful; unaware, unconscious of.

childproof.example: They attempted to make the house childproof by covering all sharp corners with soft foam.

demo-.o: From Ancient Greek δημο- (dēmo-), from δῆμος (dêmos, “people”).

demotic.o: First attested in 1822, from Ancient Greek δημοτικός (dēmotikós, “common”), from δημότης (dēmótēs, “commoner”), from δῆμος (dêmos, “the common people”).

hieroglyph.o: First attested around 1598, a back-formation from hieroglyphic (1580s), from Middle French hiéroglyphique, from Late Latin hieroglyphicus, from Ancient Greek ἱερογλυφικός (hierogluphikós) (Plutarch τά ἱερογλυφικά [γράμματα] "hieroglyphic [writing]), ἱερόγλυφος (hierógluphos, “carver of hieroglyphs”) (Ptolemy), a compound of ἱερός (hierós, “sacred, holy”) and γλυφή (gluphḗ, “carved work”), a calque of Egyptian mdw-nṯr (“the god’s word”), nTr-md. By surface analysis, hiero- + glyph.
hieroglyph.example: Hieroglyphs were discovered on the wall inside the temple.
hieroglyph.exampleSense: An element (individual sign or glyph) of a hieroglyphic writing system.

hiero-.o: From Ancient Greek ἱερο- (hiero-), from ἱερός (hierós, “sacred, holy”).

alphabet.o: From Middle English alphabete, borrowed from Classical Latin alphabētum, from Ancient Greek ἀλφάβητος (alphábētos), from ἄλφα (álpha) and βῆτα (bêta), the names of the first two letters of the Greek alphabet, Α (A) and Β (B), lowercase forms α and β. The Greek names derived from aleph, the name of the Phoenician letter 𐤀 (ʾ, “ox”) and beth, the name of the letter 𐤁 (b, “house”), so called because they were pictograms of those objects, having developed from the Egyptian hieroglyphs F1 (𓃾) and pr (𓉐). Doublet of alfabeto.
alphabet.example: In the first year of school, pupils are taught to recite the alphabet.
alphabet.exampleSense: The set of letters used when writing in a language.

instrument.o: From Middle English instrument, from Old French instrument, from Latin īnstrūmentum (“an implement, tool”), From īnstruō (“build, construct; arrange”) + -mentum.
instrument.example: The bold are but the instruments o' the wise.
instrument.exampleSense: A person used as a mere tool for achieving a goal.

retinal.o:
adj: From retina + -al (“of or pertaining to”).

noun: From retina + -al (“aldehyde”).

retina.o: From Middle English rethina, borrowing from Medieval Latin rētīna (“retina”, feminine noun), ellipsis of tunica rētīna (“net-like tunic”), used to describe the blood vessel system at the back of the eye. The phrase is attested in the 12th century in Guillelmus the abbot and Gerard of Cremona—the latter may have created this phrase as a translation for Arabic طَبَقَة شَبَكِيَّة (ṭabaqa šabakiyya) "net-like layer", which translates Ancient Greek ἀμφιβληστροειδής χῐτών (amphiblēstroeidḗs khĭtṓn, “retina”), which is attested in the ancient medical writer Galen.

theorize.o: From theory + -ize. First use appears c. 1599 in the text A pil to purge melancholie.
theorize.example: Autistic rhetoric scholar Melanie Yergeau theorizes neuroqueer as a kind of “asocially perverse” motioning.
theorize.exampleSense: To formulate a theory, especially about some specific subject.

shape.o: From Middle English schap, schape, from Old English ġesceap (“shape, form, created being, creature, creation, dispensation, fate, condition, sex, gender, genitalia”), from Proto-West Germanic *ga- + *skap, from Proto-Germanic *ga- + *skapą (“shape, nature, condition”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kep- (“to split, cut”). The verb is from Middle English shapen, schapen, from Old English scieppan (“to shape, form, make, create, assign, arrange, destine, order, adjudge”), from Proto-West Germanic *skappjan, from Proto-Germanic *skapjaną (“to create”), from the noun. The noun is cognate with Middle Dutch schap (“form”), Middle High German geschaf (“creature”), Icelandic skap (“state, condition, temper, mood”). The verb is cognate with Dutch scheppen, German schaffen, Swedish skapa (“create, make”), Norwegian Bokmål skape (“create”). Doublet of -ship.
shape.example: What shape shall we use for the cookies? Stars, circles, or diamonds?
shape.exampleSense: A graphical representation of an object's form or its external boundary, outline, or external surface.

hypothesise.example: They hypothesise the behaviour might have evolved as a means to avoid predators at the bottom of bodies of water.
hypothesise.exampleSense: Non-Oxford British English standard spelling of hypothesize.

elect.o: Borrowed from Latin ēlēctus, past participle of ēligō (“to pick out, choose, elect”), from ē- (“out”) + legō (“to pick out, pick, gather, collect, etc.”); see legend. Cognate to eclectic, which is via Ancient Greek rather than Latin, hence prefix ἐκ (ek), rather than e- (from ex).
elect.exampleSense: Who has been elected in a specified post, but has not yet entered office.

entry.o: Inherited from Middle English entre, from Old French entree (feminine past participle of the verb entrer, Modern French entrée). From Latin intrō. Doublet of entrada and entrée.
entry.example: What does the entry for 2 August 2005 say?
entry.exampleSense: A record made in a log, diary or anything similarly organized; (computing) a datum in a database.

paleontologist.example: In the late nineteenth century, paleontologists began to catalog the many curious correspondences exhibited by fossils gathered on different continents.

paleontology.o: Attested since 1836 (as palæontology). From French paléontologie (attested since 1822). By surface analysis, paleo- (“ancient”) + onto- (“being”) + -logy (“study”).

unclaimed.example: Any unclaimed items of luggage may be destroyed.

taphonomy.example: Some cases may have an innocent explanation based in taphonomy, the processes by which bodies are preserved over long spans of time.
taphonomy.exampleSense: The study of the fate of the remains of organisms after they die, especially the study of fossilization.

epitaph.o: From Old French epitafe, from Late Latin epitaphium (“eulogy”), from Ancient Greek ἐπιτάφιος (epitáphios, “relating to a funeral”), from ἐπί (epí, “over”) + τάφος (táphos, “tomb”). By surface analysis epi- + -taph.
epitaph.example: Let me rather be epitaphed the inventor of the English Hexameter.

contender.example: In April 2014, towards the end of Özil’s first season at Arsenal – which had been marked by highs and lows – Wenger predicted the German would be a contender for the player of the year awards in 2014‑15.
contender.exampleSense: Someone who has a viable chance of winning a competition.

ambitious.o: From Middle English ambitious, from Middle French ambitieus, from Latin ambitiosus, from ambitio; see ambition. Compare with French ambitieux. By surface analysis, ambit + -ious.

diabetes mellitus.o: Learned borrowing from New Latin diabetes mellitus (“diabetes of the sweet type”) (from the fact that in centuries past, physicians sometimes tasted a patient's urine to help diagnose the illness).
diabetes mellitus.example: Patients initially may seek medical attention for diabetes mellitus, which becomes clinically manifest a few years after the onset of pancreatalgia.
diabetes mellitus.exampleSense: A medical disorder commonly called diabetes, characterized by varying or persistent hyperglycemia (high blood sugar levels), especially after eating. It is classified in two types, which are different etiologically but similar in clinical effects: type 1 and type 2.

dilettante.o: From Italian dilettante, present participle of dilettare (“to delight”), from Latin dēlectāre (“to delight”).

genie.o: From French génie (“genius, genie”), a phono-semantic matching of Arabic جِنِّيّ (jinniyy).

authoritative.example: This book is the world's most authoritative guide to insect breeding habits.
authoritative.exampleSense: Highly accurate or definitive; treated or worthy of treatment as a scholarly authority

sleek.o: A late variant of slick; cognate to German schleichen (Old High German slihhan) and Dutch slijk (“mud, slime”). Compare slink.
sleek.example: 'Are these the Carrara marbles?' the lady queried. 'Yes, madam,' responded the sleek salesman.
sleek.exampleSense: Dated form of slick (“convincing but untrustworthy”).

coupon.o: From French coupon, from couper (“to cut”).
coupon.example: Jenna coupons and she goes through three magazines a day to find the coupons.
coupon.exampleSense: To use coupons to a such extent that makes the user actively looking for coupons in magazines, online and whatever they can be found.

goose.o: PIE word *ǵʰh₂éns From Middle English goos, gos, from Old English gōs, from Proto-West Germanic *gans, from Proto-Germanic *gans, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰh₂éns. Cognates Compare West Frisian goes, North Frisian göis (also Fering-Öömrang dialect North Frisian gus; Sölring dialect North Frisian Guus; Heligoland dialect North Frisian gus), Low German Goos, Gans, Dutch gans, German Gans, Danish, Swedish and Norwegian gås, Icelandic gæs, Irish gé, Latin ānser, Latvian zùoss, Russian гусь (gusʹ), Albanian gatë, Ancient Greek χήν (khḗn), Avestan 𐬰𐬁 (zā), Sanskrit हंस (haṃsá). * The tailor's iron is so called from the likeness of the handle to the neck of a goose.
goose.example: Here are the three strange men have exposed themselves to me, the two obscene phone callers, the time I was goosed by an employer.
goose.exampleSense: To sharply poke or pinch the buttocks, or prod between the buttocks, of (a person).

pop.o:
noun: From Middle English pop, poppe (“a blow; strike; buffet”) (> Middle English poppen (“to strike; thrust”, verb)), of onomatopoeic origin – used to describe the sound, or short, sharp actions. The physics sense is part of a facetious sequence "snap, crackle, pop", after the mascots of Rice Krispies cereal.

noun: From papa or poppa.

adj: Clipping of popular.

noun: Clipping of population.

noun: From colloquial Russian поп (pop) and Попъ (Pop), from Old Church Slavonic попъ (popŭ), from Byzantine Greek πάπας (pápas) (see pope). Doublet of pope.
pop.example: Listen to the pop of a champagne cork.
pop.exampleSense: A loud, sharp sound, as of a cork coming out of a bottle, especially when the contents are pressurized by fizziness.

concealed.o: simple past and past participle of conceal. From Middle English concelen, from Old French conceler (“hide, disguise”), from Latin concēlō, concēlāre (“carefully disguise”).
concealed.example: Certainly after a very concealed mannner; so concealed that no man has been able to find it.

tenacious.o: From Latin tenāx (“holding fast, clinging”), from tenēre (“to hold”), + -ious.

tenacity.o: From Middle French ténacité, from Latin tenācitās (whence -acity).
tenacity.example: — Our opponents may be younger, faster and less out of shape than we are, but we have something they’ll never have!
tenacity.exampleSense: The quality or state of being tenacious, or persistence of purpose; tenaciousness.

vulgarly.example: Rosemary peeled off Sloane Square, Hartnell, decorations-will-be-worn, fog primroses, crumpets by the fire, and let fly vulgarly at Vythilingam.
vulgarly.exampleSense: In a vulgar manner; obscenely or unrefinedly.

vulgar.o: From Middle English vulgare, from Latin vulgāris, from volgus, vulgus (“mob; common folk”), from Proto-Indo-European *welH-. Compare Welsh gwala (“plenty, sufficiency”), Ancient Greek ἁλία (halía, “assembly”), εἰλέω (eiléō, “to compress”), Old Church Slavonic великъ (velikŭ, “great”).
vulgar.example: The mechanical process of multiplying books had brought the New Testament in the vulgar tongue within the reach of every class.
vulgar.exampleSense: Having to do with ordinary, common people.

untainted.example: Time was when Love and I were well acquainted.
untainted.exampleSense: Not tainted; free of contamination; pure.

ugliness.example: There was some ugliness at the council meeting.

cynical.o: Originated 1542, from Classical Latin cynicus (“Cynic/cynic”, adjective) + -al. By surface analysis, cynic + -al. In reference to dogs, with allusion to the ultimate etymology (Ancient Greek κυνικός (kunikós, “doglike”)).
cynical.example: I hope it is no very cynical asperity not to confess obligations where no benefit has been received.
cynical.exampleSense: Of or relating to the belief that human actions are motivated only or primarily by base desires or selfishness.

astonishingly.example: Famous hotels, for instance, are astonishingly commonplace.
astonishingly.exampleSense: In an astonishing manner; so as to surprise or astonish.

chop chop.o: Alternative form of chop-chop. From Chinese Pidgin English, from Cantonese 速速 (cuk1 cuk1, “quick”). Recorded in English since the 1830s (see citations for adverb). Recorded as a Chinese term in 1795.

chop.o:
noun: From Middle English choppen, chappen (“to chop”), of uncertain origin, possibly onomatopoeic, or a variant of chap (“to become cracked”). Cognate with Scots chap (“to chop”). Compare also Saterland Frisian kappe, kapje (“to hack; chop; lop off”), Dutch kappen (“to chop, cut, hew”), German Low German kappen (“to cut off; clip”), German kappen (“to cut; clip”), German dialectal chapfen, kchapfen (“to chop into small pieces”), Albanian copë (“piece, chunk”), Old English *ċippian (in forċippian (“to cut off”)). Perhaps related to chip.

verb: Uncertain, perhaps a variant of chap (“cheap”). Compare Middle English copen (“to buy”), Dutch kopen (“to buy”).

noun: From Middle English choppe (“jaw, jawbone”), related to Middle English cheppe (“one side of the jaw, chap”). Perhaps ultimately related to Etymology 1 above.

noun: Borrowed from Hindi छाप (chāp, “stamp”). Closely related to the similarly descended Malay word cap, which likely reinforced the English usage within the Malay world.

noun: Shortening.

verb: Shortening of chopper.
chop.example: Out of a Greediness to get both, he Chops at the Shadow, and Loses the Substance.
chop.exampleSense: To do something suddenly with an unexpected motion; to catch or attempt to seize.

fugitive.o: From Middle English fugitive, fugityve, fugityf, fugitife, fugytif, fugitif, from Latin fugitīvus, from fugitō, from fugiō.
fugitive.example: Her son Thomas was fugitived in the persecution.
fugitive.exampleSense: To render someone a fugitive; to drive into escape or exile.

nutshell.o: From Middle English notschelle, from Old English hnutsċiell, from Proto-West Germanic *hnutskallju, equivalent to nut + shell. Cognate with Saterland Frisian Nuteskele, Nuteskil (“nutshell”), Dutch notenschaal (“nutshell”), German Nussschale (“nutshell”).

diverge.o: From Medieval Latin dīvergō (“bend away from, go in a different direction”), from Latin dī- + vergō (“bend”).
diverge.example: Both stories start out the same way, but they diverge halfway through.
diverge.exampleSense: To become different; to run apart; to separate; to tend into different directions.

await.o: From Middle English awaiten, from Old Northern French awaitier (“to lie in wait for, watch, observe”), originally especially with a hostile sense; itself from a- (“to”) + waitier (“to watch”). More at English wait.
await.example: Glorious rewards await the good in heaven; eternal suffering awaits mortal sinners in hell.
await.exampleSense: To be in store for; to be ready or in waiting for.

itinerant.o: From Late Latin itinerantem, present active participle of itineror (“travel”), from itiner-. By surface analysis, Latin itiner- + -ant.
itinerant.example: The Greek term translated as “apostle” derives from the concept of being sent, thus underlining the missionary and more itinerant nature of the ministry.
itinerant.exampleSense: Habitually travelling from place to place.

itinerancy.example: I went through a period of itinerancy in my youth.
itinerancy.exampleSense: The state or quality of being itinerant.

illiteracy.example: Illiteracy is widespread in certain areas of the country.
illiteracy.exampleSense: The inability to read and write.

contrast.o: From French contraster, from Latin contrāstāre (“to resist", "to withstand”), from contrā (“against”) + stō, stāre (“to stand”).
contrast.example: Ohh, you can't fool me. This thing's top of the line! It's got two contrast knobs!
contrast.exampleSense: A difference in lightness, brightness or hue between two colours that makes them more or less distinguishable. A control on a television, etc, that adjusts the amount of contrast in the images being displayed.

earnest.o:
noun: From Middle English ernest, eornest, from Old English eornest, eornost, eornust (“earnestness, zeal, seriousness, battle”), from Proto-Germanic *ernustuz (“earnest, strength, solidity, struggle, fight”), a derivative of Proto-Germanic *arniz (“efficient, capable, diligent, sure”), from Proto-Indo-European *er- (“to cause to move, arouse, increase”). Cognate with West Frisian earnst (“earnest, seriousness”), Dutch ernst (“seriousness, gravity, earnest”), German Ernst (“seriousness, earnestness, zeal, vigour”), Icelandic ern (“brisk, vigorous”), Gothic 𐌰𐍂𐌽𐌹𐌱𐌰 (arniba, “secure, certain, sure”). The adjective is from Middle English eornest, from Old English eornoste (“earnest, zealous, serious”), from the noun. Cognate with North Frisian ernste (“earnest”), Middle Low German ernest, ernst (“serious, earnest”), German ernst (“serious, earnest”).

noun: Uncertain; apparently related to erres. Compare also arles.

verb: From earn + -est.
earnest.example: Now he that hath wrought us for the selfsame thing is God, who also hath given unto us the earnest of the Spirit.
earnest.exampleSense: A sum of money paid in advance as a deposit; hence, a pledge, a guarantee, an indication of something to come.

squander.o: Earliest uses (late 16th c.) "to spend recklessly or prodigiously", also "to scatter over a wide area". Of unknown origin. Perhaps a blend of scatter + wander. Compare Danish skvætte (rare)/skvatte (“to splash”) (nominalised: skvæt), Icelandic skvetta (“to squirt”), Swedish skvätta (“to splash”), Norwegian Bokmål skvette.

avert.o: From Middle English averten, adverten, from Old French avertir (“turn, direct, avert; turn the attention, make aware”), from Latin āvertere, from ab + vertō (“to turn”).
avert.example: I averted my eyes while my friend typed in her password.

predicament.o: From Middle English predicament, from Old French predicament, from Late Latin praedicāmentum (“that which is predicated, a predicament, category”).
predicament.example: Culture, for me, is the effort to provide a coherent set of answers to the existential predicaments that confront all human beings in the passage of their life.
predicament.exampleSense: An unfortunate or trying position or condition.

fold.o:
verb: The verb is from Middle English folden, from Old English fealdan, from Proto-West Germanic *falþan, from Proto-Germanic *falþaną (“to fold”), from Proto-Indo-European *pel- (“to fold”). Cognate with Dutch vouwen, German falten. The noun is from Middle English folde, falde, itself derived from the verb.

noun: The noun is from Middle English fold, fald, from Old English fald, falæd, falod (“fold, stall, stable, cattle-pen”), from Proto-West Germanic *falud, from Proto-Germanic *faludaz (“enclosure”). Akin to Scots fald, fauld (“an enclosure for livestock”), Dutch vaalt (“dung heap”), Middle Low German valt, vālt (“an inclosed space, a yard”), Danish fold (“pen for herbivorous livestock”), Swedish fålla (“corral, pen, pound”). The verb is from Late Middle English fooldyn, itself derived from the noun.

noun: From Middle English folde, from Old English folde (“earth, land, country, district, region, territory, ground, soil, clay”), from Proto-Germanic *fuldǭ, *fuldō (“earth, ground; field; the world”). Cognate with Old Norse fold (“earth, land, field”), Norwegian and Icelandic fold (“land, earth, meadow”).
fold.example: It was Erik Meijer who coined the name hylomorphism to describe a computation that consists of a fold after an unfold. The unfold produces a data structure and the fold consumes it.
fold.exampleSense: Any of a family of higher-order functions that process a data structure recursively to build up a value.

privatise.example: A senior rail source said: "Frankly, no one believes being on the government books is temporary. The only bits of the railway still genuinely privatised are the freight trains and the rolling stock owners.
privatise.exampleSense: Non-Oxford British English standard spelling of privatize.

repeal.o: From Anglo-Norman repeler, from Old French rapeler (“to call back, call in, call after, revoke”), from Latin repellō (“drive or thrust back”), from re- and pellō (“push or strike”). Doublet of repel.
repeal.example: Wednesday June 02, 2021, Has the Northern Ireland Protocol undermined the United Kingdom?
repeal.exampleSense: An act or instance of repealing.

prudent.o: Inherited from Middle English prudent, from Old French prudent, from Latin prūdēns, contracted from prōvidēns (“foresight”) (English providence), the present participle of prōvideō (“to forsee; to provide for”). Unrelated to prude. Doublet of provident. Displaced native Old English glēaw.
prudent.example: His prudent career moves reliably brought him to the top.

judicious.o: From French judicieux, ultimately derived from Latin iudico. Related to judge, judicial.
judicious.example: This project has stripped away modern PVCu and aluminium shop fronts to reveal original or 1930s Art Deco work, with judicious repairs and replacements as necessary, plus stonework repairs and the restoration of traditional London Transport signage.
judicious.exampleSense: Having, characterized by, or done with good judgment or sound thinking.

bother.o: Borrowed from Scots bauther, bather (“to bother”). Origin unknown. Perhaps related to Scots pother (“to make a stir or commotion, bustle”), also of unknown origin. Compare English pother (“to poke, prod”), variant of potter (“to poke”). More at potter. Perhaps related to Irish bodhaire (“noise”), Irish bodhraim (“to deafen, annoy”).
bother.example: Would it bother you if I smoked?
bother.exampleSense: To annoy, to disturb, to irritate; to be troublesome to, to make trouble for.

deflation.example: The great deflation of the northern economy occurred with the rupturing of the Mackenzie Valley pipe dream.

deflate.o: From de- + (in)flate. Coined in 1891, in reference to balloons. Equivalent to Latin dē- (“away, from”) + Latin flō (“blow”) + -ate (verb-forming suffix).
deflate.example: Never had a problem, guess I've never had to deflate multiple files!
deflate.exampleSense: To compress (data) according to a particular algorithm.

ramify.o: Borrowed from Middle French ramifier, from Medieval Latin ramificō (“to branch, ramify”), from Latin rāmus (“a branch”) + -ficō (causative suffix).
ramify.example: The cortical, hemispheral or superficial veins ramify on the surface of the brain and return the blood from the cortical substance into the venous sinuses.
ramify.exampleSense: To divide into branches or subdivisions.

ramification.o: From Middle French ramification, or its source, Medieval Latin rāmificātiō. By surface analysis, ramify + -ication.
ramification.example: What, then, is my Scheme? It is a very simple one, although in its ramifications and extensions it embraces the whole world.
ramification.exampleSense: An offshoot of a decision, fact etc.; a consequence or implication, especially one which complicates a situation.

liquidate.o: Learned borrowing from Late Latin liquidātus (“liquid; clear”, adjective) + English -ate (suffix forming verbs, and forming adjectives with the sense ‘characterized by [the specified things]’). Liquidātus is the perfect passive participle of liquidō (“to turn into a liquid, melt; to make clear”), from Latin liquidus (“fluid, liquid; clear, transparent”) + -ō (suffix forming regular first-conjugation verbs); while liquidus is from liqueō (“to be fluid or liquid; to be clear or transparent”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *wleykʷ- (“to make wet; moist”)) + -idus (suffix meaning ‘tending to’ forming adjectives). By surface analysis, liquid (adjective) + -ate. Verb sense 1.2.3 (“to kill; to abolish or eliminate”) is a semantic loan from Russian ликвиди́ровать (likvidírovatʹ); while verb sense 1.2.4 and verb sense 2 (business-related senses) were influenced by French liquider and Italian liquidare, all ultimately from Latin liquidus (see above).
liquidate.example: Her only relative was a niece in Boston, who arranged for a local lawyer to liquidate Mrs. Garner’s property.
liquidate.exampleSense: To convert (assets) into cash; to encash, to realize, to redeem.

asset.o: Back-formation from assets, from Anglo-Norman asetz, from Old French assez (“enough”). Compare Middle English asseth.
asset.example: My assets consist of stocks in companies that pay a dividend, and a few apartments that pay me rental income.
asset.exampleSense: A thing or quality that has value, especially one that generates cash flows.

postponement.example: The lawyer asked for a postponement in the trial so he could spend more time preparing before it began.
postponement.exampleSense: A delay, as a formal delay in a proceeding.

postpone.o: From Latin postpōnō (“to put after; to postpone”) from post (“after”) + pōnō (“to put; to place”), compare forestall.
postpone.example: Significant rail projects have been mothballed before in the face of changed circumstances – in particular, the LNER Woodhead project which was postponed due to wartime conditions and not revived until 1948, as money became available after nationalisation.
postpone.exampleSense: To delay or put off an event, appointment, etc.

post-.o: From Latin post (“after, behind”). Cognate with Spanish pues (“well, so, then”)

dwindling.o: present participle and gerund of dwindle. Frequentative form of dwine, from Middle English dwynen, from Old English dwīnan (“to waste away”), from Proto-West Germanic *dwīnan, from Proto-Germanic *dwīnaną. It is equivalent to dwine + -le, akin to Old Norse dvena, dvína, Dutch verdwijnen (“to disappear, dwindle”).
dwindling.example: There is dwindling support for New Labour.

dwindle.o: Frequentative form of dwine, from Middle English dwynen, from Old English dwīnan (“to waste away”), from Proto-West Germanic *dwīnan, from Proto-Germanic *dwīnaną. It is equivalent to dwine + -le, akin to Old Norse dvena, dvína, Dutch verdwijnen (“to disappear, dwindle”).
dwindle.example: The larger the empire, the more dwindles the mind of the citizen.
dwindle.exampleSense: To fall away in quality; degenerate, sink.

covet.o: From Middle English coveten, coveiten, coveyten, from Old French covoitier (modern French convoiter), from covoitié (“desire”), presumably modified from Latin cupiditas.
covet.example: No! He covets. That is his nature. And how do we begin to covet, Clarice? Do we seek out things to covet? Make an effort to answer now.
covet.exampleSense: To wish for with eagerness; to desire possession of, often enviously.

bind.o: From Middle English binden, from Old English bindan, from Proto-West Germanic *bindan, from Proto-Germanic *bindaną, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰéndʰ-e-ti, from *bʰendʰ- (“to tie”). See also West Frisian bine, Dutch binden, Low German binnen, binden, German binden, Danish, Norwegian Bokmål, and Norwegian Nynorsk binde, Faroese, Icelandic, and Swedish binda; also Welsh ben (“cart”), Latin offendīx (“knot, band”), Lithuanian beñdras (“partner”), Albanian bind (“to convince, to awe, to spell”), Ancient Greek πεῖσμα (peîsma, “cable, rope”), Persian بستن (bastan, “to bind”), Sanskrit बन्धति (bándhati). Doublet of bandana.
bind.example: We bind the variable n to the value 2, and xs to "abcd".
bind.exampleSense: To associate an identifier with a value; to associate a variable name, method name, etc. with the content of a storage location.

adhere.o: From Middle English *adheren (suggested by Middle English adherande (“adhering, adherent”, present participle)), from Latin adhaerēre, adhaesum: ad (“to”) + haerēre (“to stick”). Compare French adhérer.
adhere.exampleSense: To stick fast or cleave, as a glutinous substance does; to become joined or united.

cousin.o: The noun is derived from Middle English cosin, cosine, cosyn (“blood relative, kinsman or kinswoman; any relative; nephew or niece; first cousin; grandson or granddaughter; descendant; godchild or godparent, or a relative of a godchild or godparent; (figurative) closely related or similar thing”) [and other forms], and then: * from Anglo-Norman cosen, cosin [and other forms], Middle French cosin, and Old French cosin (“collateral male relative more distant than one’s brother; form of address used by a monarch to male monarchs or nobles”) [and other forms] (modern French cousin); and * from Anglo-Norman cosine, Middle French cosine, and Old French cosine (“collateral female relative more distant than one’s sister; form of address used by a monarch to female monarchs or nobles”) [and other forms] (modern French cousine), from Latin cōnsobrīnus (“maternal cousin; first cousin; relation”) (possibly through Vulgar Latin *cōsuīnus, from *cōsobīnus), from con- (prefix denoting a bringing together of several objects) + sobrīnus (“maternal cousin; sister’s son; any nephew”) (from a noun use of Proto-Italic *swezrīnos (“of or belonging to a sister”, adjective) (with the first syllable influenced by Latin soror (“sister”)), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *swésōr (“sister”), possibly from *swé (“self”) + *h₁ésh₂r̥ (“blood”) (that is, a woman of one’s own blood) or *-sōr (feminine suffix)). The verb is derived from the noun.
cousin.example: Although we were cousins, we grew up like sisters.
cousin.exampleSense: Chiefly with a qualifying word: Any relation (especially a distant one) who is not a direct ancestor or descendant but part of a person's extended family; a kinsman or kinswoman. When used without a qualifying word: the child of a person's parent's brother (that is, an uncle) or sister (an aunt); a cousin-german, a first cousin.

deride.o: Learned borrowing from Latin dērīdēre, the present active infinitive of dērīdeō (“to laugh at, make fun of, mock, deride”), from dē- (prefix denoting putting down or subjecting to indignity) + rīdeō (“to laugh; to laugh at, mock, ridicule”) (further etymology uncertain, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *wert- (“to rotate; to turn”) (referring to turning the mouth to smile) or *wreyd- (“to carve; to scratch”)). cognates * Old French dérider (rare), derire

ersatz.o: Borrowed from German Ersatz (“replacement, substitute”), a back-formation from ersetzen (“to replace, to substitute”).
ersatz.example: The crowd wandered out to a huge party on the ersatz city blocks of the Paramount lot.
ersatz.exampleSense: Made in imitation; artificial, especially of a poor quality.

apace.o: From Middle English apās (“step by step, slowly; quickly, rapidly; at once, promptly”), from Old French à pas (“at a quick pace”).
apace.example: Construction of the new offices is proceeding apace.

bend.o: From Middle English benden, from Old English bendan (“to bind or bend (a bow), fetter, restrain”), from Proto-West Germanic *bandijan, from Proto-Germanic *bandijaną (“to bend”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰendʰ- (“to bind, tie”). Cognate with Middle High German benden (“to fetter”), Danish bænde (“to bend”), Norwegian bende (“to bend”), Faroese benda (“to bend, inflect”), Icelandic benda (“to bend”). Related to bind, band, bond.
bend.example: If you bend the pipe too far, it will break.
bend.exampleSense: To cause (something) to change its shape into a curve, by physical force, chemical action, or any other means.

du jour.o: Borrowed from French du jour (literally “of the day”).
du jour.example: Beth came to the party with her boyfriend du jour.
du jour.exampleSense: Currently stylish; en vogue; trendy; favoured now but likely temporary; latest.

catastrophe.o: From Ancient Greek καταστροφή (katastrophḗ), from καταστρέφω (katastréphō, “to overturn”), from κατά (katá, “down, against”) + στρέφω (stréphō, “to turn”).
catastrophe.example: Between these high lights accumulated disaster, social catastrophe.
catastrophe.exampleSense: Any large and disastrous event of great significance.

flammable.o: Back-formation from inflammable, which is used to avoid confusion with non-flammable, as the prefix in- is often used to mean "un-; non-", although it was originally meant in a sense closely related to en-.
flammable.example: With her play Diamond Lil, she discovered a way to sneak her flammable subject matter past the censors.
flammable.exampleSense: Very likely to cause fighting or controversy; extremely contentious.

gimmick.o: Unknown. Possibly a rough anagram of magic or from gimme.
gimmick.example: The box had a gimmick to make the coin appear to vanish.
gimmick.exampleSense: A trick or device used to attain some end.

novelty.o: From Middle English novelte, from Old French novelté (Modern French nouveauté), from the adjective novel, ultimately from Latin novellus. By surface analysis, novel + -ty.
novelty.example: Men In Black 3 lacks the novelty of the first film, and its take on the late ’60s feels an awful lot like a psychedelic dress-up party, all broad caricatures and groovy vibes.
novelty.exampleSense: The state of being new or novel; newness.

defy.o: From Old French desfier, from Vulgar Latin *disfidare (“renounce one's faith”), from Latin dis- (“away”) + fidus (“faithful”). Meaning shifted in the 14th century from "be disloyal" to "challenge". Contrast confide, fidelity, faith.
defy.example: If you defy your teacher you may end up in detention.

bunker.o:
noun: The origin of the noun is uncertain; the earliest sense is sense 7.1 (“box or chest, the lid of which serves as a seat”), from Scots bunker (“bench; pew; window-seat; sand pit (especially in golf); coal receptacle; sleeping berth, bunk”), from Early Scots bunker, bunkur, bonker (“a chest or box, often serving as a seat”), probably from Old Norse bunki (“a heap”) (probably whence bunk (“sleeping berth in a ship, train, etc.”)), from Proto-Germanic *bunkô (“a heap, pile; a bump, lump, a crowd”), perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *bʰenǵʰ- (“thick”) or *bʰeg- (“to billow, swell; to arch, bend, curve (?)”). Compare Middle Low German bunge (“drum, container”), Middle High German bunge (“drum”). Sense 1 (“hardened shelter designed to protect the inhabitants from falling bombs or other attacks”) was derived from German Bunker during World War II, which was itself from bunker (“large bin or container for storing coal”) (sense 5). The verb is derived from the noun.

noun: From bunk (“to fail to attend school or work without permission, to play truant”) + -er (suffix forming agent nouns indicating a person or thing that does an action).

noun: Clipping of mossbunker, a variant of mossbanker, from Dutch marsbanker (“common scad or Atlantic horse mackerel (Trachurus trachurus)”), from Marsdiep (“deep tide-race between Den Helder and Texel in the Netherlands”) + bank (“shallow part of the sea near a coast”) + -er (suffix forming nouns denoting male inhabitants of a place).
bunker.example: More than 10,000 people were bunkering in 20 emergency shelters across the disaster zone, not all of them cyclone-rated.
bunker.exampleSense: Often followed by down: to take shelter in a bunker or other place.

fractional.example: The two women exchanged a glance, then a fractional nod of agreement.

minuscule.o: From French minuscule, from Latin minuscula, feminine of minusculus (“rather less, rather small”), from minus (“less, smaller”) + -culus (diminutive suffix).
minuscule.example: By the eighth century, Irish scribes had refined everyday cursive writing in minuscule to allow its use for the production of quality vellum books.
minuscule.exampleSense: Either of the two medieval handwriting styles minuscule cursive and Caroline minuscule.

plentiful.o: From Middle English plentiful, plentyfull, plentefull, equivalent to plenty + -ful.
plentiful.example: She accumulated a plentiful collection of books.
plentiful.exampleSense: Existing in large number or ample amount.

cosmos.o:
noun: From Middle English cossmos (“the universe; the world”), borrowed from Ancient Greek κόσμος (kósmos, “order; universe; the earth, the world; decoration, ornament”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ḱens- (“to announce, proclaim; to put in order”). The plural form cosmoi is a learned borrowing from Ancient Greek κόσμοι (kósmoi).

noun: Borrowed from translingual Cosmos (genus name), from New Latin cosmos, from Ancient Greek κόσμος (kósmos, “decoration, ornament; order; universe; the earth, the world”) (referring to its elegant leaves); see further at etymology

noun: See the etymology of the corresponding lemma form.
cosmos.example: People were attracted to him as bees are attracted to cosmos or dahlia stalks.
cosmos.exampleSense: Any of various mostly Mexican herbs of the genus Cosmos having radiate heads of variously coloured flowers and pinnate leaves.

squeak.example: If he be obstinate, put a civil question to him upon the rack, and he squeaks, I warrant him.

inhale.o: From Latin inhalare (“to breathe on (breathe in)”), from in (“in, into, on”) + halare (“to breathe”).
inhale.example: Now have client take slower, normal breaths through the nose and notice how the abdomen moves slightly outward with each inhale and then deflates with each exhale.

inert.o: From French inerte, from Latin iners (“inactive, inert”).

odorless.example: They were taken unawares and overcome when the room filled with a lethal, odorless gas.

odourless.example: They were taken unawares and overcome when the room filled with a lethal, odourless gas.

odour.example: So after learning a great deal about iron founding and much more about pike fishing, one regretfully took leave of a shop full of kindly characters and proceeded to a worse lot of odours in the brass foundry.

helium.o: From New Latin helium, from Ancient Greek ἥλιος (hḗlios, “sun”) (because its presence was first theorised in the Sun's atmosphere) with the suffix + -ium. Probably coined by Norman Lockyer. This suffix is unusual, because it is usually used only for metallic elements. It is likely that Lockyer, being an astronomer, was unaware of the usual chemical conventions.
helium.example: It was an enormous balloon filled with helium, that elemental gas forged from hydrogen in the nuclear furnace of the stars.
helium.exampleSense: The second lightest chemical element (symbol He) with an atomic number of 2 and atomic weight of 4.002602, a colorless, odorless and inert noble gas.

depletion.o: Borrowed from Latin depletio, depletionem, from depleō.

ringing.o: present participle and gerund of ring. From Middle English ryng, from Old English hring (“ring, circle”), from Proto-West Germanic *hring, from Proto-Germanic *hringaz (“ring”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)krengʰ-, extended nasalized form of *(s)ker- (“to turn, bend”). Doublet of rank and rink, as well as indirectly range. Cognates * West Frisian ring * Low German Ring * Dutch ring * German Ring * Swedish ring * Finnish rengas More distantly cognate with Proto-Slavic *krǫgъ (whence Bulgarian кръг (krǎg), Polish krąg, Russian круг (krug)).
ringing.example: They declare ringing confirmation for their theories even in the face of feeble data.

presage.o: From Middle English presage, from Latin praesāgium.
presage.example: That brief moment after the election four years ago, when many Americans thought Mr. Obama’s election would presage a new, less fractious political era, now seems very much a thing of the past.

onset.o: From on- + set. Compare Old English onsettan (“to impose; oppress, bear down”). For semantic parallels for the meaning to assault, compare cognate Russian насе́сть pf (naséstʹ), наседа́ть impf (nasedátʹ).
onset.example: There is surely no greater wisdom than well to time the beginnings and onsets of things.

barometric.example: A low barometric pressure is characteristic of hurricanes.
barometric.exampleSense: Of or pertaining to atmospheric pressure.

barometer.o: From baro- + -meter. Coined in 1665 by Robert Boyle as a name for the instrument invented by Torricelli some 20 years earlier; soon thereafter borrowed from English into various languages.
barometer.example: The weakest members of society become social barometers or canaries in a coal mine.
barometer.exampleSense: Anything used as a gauge or indicator.

baro-.o: From Ancient Greek βάρος (báros, “weight”), from βαρύς (barús, “heavy”).

calibrate.example: Trent Alexander-Arnold was prominent in the early running, stepping up from right-back into midfield, calibrating his passing range. He had already teed up Harry Kane for a free header – the captain headed high – when he sent Anthony Gordon clean through.
calibrate.exampleSense: To check or adjust by comparison with a standard.

compass.o:
noun: From Middle English compas (“a circle, circuit, limit, form, a mathematical instrument”), from Old French compas, from Medieval Latin compassus (“a circle, a circuit”), from Latin com- (“together”) + passus (“a pace, step, later a pass, way, route”); see pass, pace.

verb: From Middle English compassen (“to go around, make a circuit, draw a circle, contrive, intend”), from Old French compasser; from the noun; see compass as a noun.
compass.example: You would sound me from my lowest note to the top of my compass.
compass.exampleSense: The range of notes of a musical instrument or voice.

numb.o: From the past participle of nim (“to take”). Compare German benommen (“dazed, numb”) and Old Norse numinn. The final ⟨b⟩ is a later addition; it was never pronounced, and did not appear in the original word.
numb.example: The dentist gave me novocaine to numb my tooth before drilling, thank goodness.
numb.exampleSense: To cause to become numb (physically or emotionally).

boggle.o: Variation or derivation of bogle, possibly cognate with bug.
boggle.example: The horror of the deed and its consequences boggle the imagination.
boggle.exampleSense: (literally or figuratively) to stop or hesitate as if suddenly seeing a bogle.

mind-boggling.example: Faced with a mind-boggling selection of special-purpose shampoos, he gave up and simply purchased something inexpensive with a pleasant fragrance.
mind-boggling.exampleSense: That causes the mind to boggle; that is beyond one's ability to understand or figure out.

mind-numbing.o: From mind + numbing. Compare Old English ġemynd-benimming (“lethargy”, noun, literally “numbing of the mind, mind-numbing”).
mind-numbing.example: The story described the main character's wristwatch in mind-numbing detail.
mind-numbing.exampleSense: Excessively boring, tedious, or dull; repetitive; of an activity, etc., lacking any interest or variety that might serve as intellectual stimulation.

mind-bending.example: The book contains fifteen mind-bending mazes.

marvel.o: First attested from 1300, from Middle English merveile, from Old French merveille (“a wonder”), from Vulgar Latin *miribilia, from Latin mīrābilia (“wonderful things”), from neuter plural of mīrābilis (“strange, wonderful”), from mīror (“to wonder at”), from mīrus (“wonderful”). Doublet of mirabilia.
marvel.example: Marueile not, my brethren, if the world hate you.
marvel.exampleSense: To become filled with wonderment or admiration; to be amazed at something.

en route.o: From French en route, from en (“in”) + route (“route”).
en route.example: The shipment is en route to the buyer.

necessitate.o: From earlier necessitat, from Medieval Latin necessitātus, perfect past participle of necessitō (“to make necessary”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix, of participial origin)), from Classical Latin necessitās (“necessity, need”) + -ō. Necessitās is derived from necesse (“unavoidable”) (from ne- (“not”) + cessus (“conceded, given up, yielded”). By surface analysis, necessitō + -ate.
necessitate.example: The early departure of her plane necessitated her waking up at 4 a.m.
necessitate.exampleSense: To make necessary; to behove; to require (something) to be brought about.

necessaries.example: Mechanically he returned home, gathered together a few small necessaries and special treasures he was fond of, and put them in a satchel; acting with slow deliberation, moving about the room like a sleep-walker; listening ever with parted lips.

equatorial.example: That plant is best suited to equatorial climates.
equatorial.exampleSense: Of, near, or relating to the equator.

temperate.o: The adjective is first attested in 1380, in Middle English, the verb in 1540; borrowed from Latin temperātus, perfect passive participle of temperō (“to moderate, forbear, combine properly”), see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and -ate (verb-forming suffix). See temper. Displaced native Old English ġemetegod.
temperate.example: The temperate sleeps, and spirits light as air.

ingenious.o: Borrowed from Middle French ingénieux, from Old French engenious, from Latin ingeniōsus (“endowed with good natural capacity, gifted with genius”), from ingenium (“innate or natural quality, natural capacity, genius”), from in- (“in”) + gignere (“to produce”), Old Latin genere. See also engine.
ingenious.example: He sent me an ingenious reply to an email.

appearance.o: Borrowed from Middle French apparence, from Latin apparentia, from appareo. Morphologically appear + -ance. Doublet of apparence and apparency. Displaced native Old English hīew (“the way something looks or seems”) and ætīewednes (“act of appearing or coming into view”).
appearance.exampleSense: The act of appearing or coming into sight; the act of becoming visible to the eye.

derivation.o: From Middle English derivacioun, borrowed from Middle French dérivation, from Latin dērīvātiō, dērīvātiōnem. Morphologically derive + -ation.

murky.o: From Middle English mirky. Related to Old Norse myrkr, Russian мрак (mrak) and its Slavic cognates. By surface analysis, murk + -y.
murky.example: Mr. Farrier, 39, said he often questioned the moral implications of his trips. “It’s very ethically murky territory,” Mr. Farrier said.

murk.o:
adj: From Middle English merke, mirke, from Old English mirce, myrce (“dark, gloomy, evil”) and Old Norse myrkr (“dark, murky”), both from Proto-Germanic *merkuz (“dark”), from Proto-Indo-European *mergʷ- (“to flicker; to darken; to be dark”). Cognate Danish mørk (“dark”), Norwegian mørk (“dark”), Swedish mörk (“dark”), Icelandic myrkur (“dark”), as also Albanian murg (“dark”), Proto-Slavic *morkъ (“darkness”), Lithuanian márgas (“multicolored”), murzinas (“dirty, spoiled”), Ancient Greek ἀμορβός (amorbós, “dark”).

noun: From Middle English mirke, merke, from Old English mirce, myrce (“darkness, gloom”) and Old Norse myrkr (“darkness, gloom”), both from Proto-Germanic *merkwą, *mirkwiz (“darkness”), Proto-Indo-European *mergʷ- (“to flicker; to darken; to be dark”).

verb: From Middle English mirken, probably from Old Norse myrkja, myrkva (“to make dark, darken”), from Proto-Germanic *mirkwijaną, *mirkwajaną (“to make dark”), from Proto-Indo-European *mergʷ- (“to flicker; to darken; to be dark”).

verb: Possibly an alteration of merc, from clipping of mercenary. First attested in the 1990s.
murk.example: O great star disappear’d—O the black murk that hides the star!
murk.exampleSense: Darkness, or a dark or gloomy environment.

prolong.o: Either a back-formation from prolongation, or from Old French prolonguer or porloignier, from Latin prōlongō, from prō + longō. Doublet of purloin.
prolong.example: The government shouldn't prolong deciding on this issue any further.
prolong.exampleSense: To put off to a distant time; to postpone.

emollient.o: From French émollient, from Latin emolliēns, present active participle of ēmolliō (“make soft”), from ex- + molliō, from mollis (“soft”). By surface analysis, e- + Latin moll- + -i- + -ent.
emollient.example: Attentive conversation is an emollient I lack sorely aboard Prophetess & the doctor is a veritable polymath.
emollient.exampleSense: Anything soothing the mind, or that makes something more acceptable.

earthy.o: From Middle English erthy, equivalent to earth + -y. Compare German erdig (“earthy”), Swedish jordig (“earthy”).
earthy.example: The earthy smell of fresh turned loam told me the farmer had started plowing this morning, the definitive sign of spring for me.

musky.o:
adj: From musk + -y.

noun: Shortening of muskellunge.

musk.o: From Middle English muske, borrowed from Old French musc, from Late Latin muscus, from Ancient Greek μόσχος (móskhos), from Middle Persian [script needed] (mwšk' /⁠muʃk⁠/) whence Persian مشک (mošk). Ultimately from Sanskrit मुष्क (muṣka, “testicle”), the shape of the gland of animals secreting the substance being compared to human testicles, a diminutive of मूष् (mūṣ, “mouse”), the shape of human testicles being compared to mice, from Proto-Indo-European *muh₂s (“mouse”). Cognate with mouse.
musk.example: I was so excited I could smell my own musk.
musk.exampleSense: The scent of human genitalia when aroused or unwashed.

dung.o:
noun: From Middle English dung, dunge, donge, from Old English dung (“dung; excrement; manure”), from Proto-West Germanic *dungu, from Proto-Germanic *dungō (“dung”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰengʰ- (“to cover”). Superseded non-native Middle English fen (“dung, excrement, filth”), from Old French fien, fiente (“dung, manure”).

verb: See ding

verb: unknown

intj: Onomatopoeic.
dung.example: She had been dunging the roses and was fairly covered in muck.

innards.example: He took the cover off his computer and looked at the innards.
innards.exampleSense: The inner workings of something; the insides or guts.

lump.o: From Middle English lumpe, from a Germanic base akin to Proto-Germanic *limpaną (“to glide, go, hang loosely”). Compare Dutch lomp (“rag”), German Low German Lump (“rag”), German Lumpen (“rag”) and Lump (“ragamuffin”).
lump.example: People tend to lump turtles and tortoises together, when in fact they are different creatures.
lump.exampleSense: To treat as a single unit; to group together in a casual or chaotic manner (as if forming an ill-defined lump of the items).

resinous.o: Borrowed from Middle French résineux; cf. Latin resinosus. By surface analysis, resin + -ous.

hyper.o: Shortenings, all ultimately from the prefix hyper-.
hyper.example: Why do I want to snort coke so I can be extremely hyper and talk nonstop?

vomit.o: From Middle English vomiten, from Latin vomitāre (“vomit repeatedly”), frequentative form of vomō (“be sick, vomit”), from Proto-Indo-European *wemh₁- (“to spew, vomit”). Cognate with Old Norse váma (“nausea, malaise”), Old English wemman (“to defile”). More at wem.
vomit.example: For all tables are full of vomite and filthinesse, so that there is no place cleane.
vomit.exampleSense: The regurgitated former contents of a stomach; vomitus.

squid.o:
noun: Unknown. Perhaps a sailors' alteration of squirt.

noun: Possibly a blend of stupid + quick; "stupid, quick, under-dressed and imminently dead", a claimed origin, is probably a backronym.

noun: Calque of Korean 오징어 (ojing'eo).
squid.example: Can you lend me five squid? I feel like a bacon sarnie.

acrid.o: From Latin ācris, from ācer (“sharp”); probably assimilated in form to acid. Compare eager.
acrid.example: The bombardier beetle sprays acrid secretions to defend itself.

fount.o:
noun: Clipping of fountain, on the pattern of the pair mount, mountain.

noun: A variant of font, influenced by fount (etymology 1) being a synonym of font (“natural source of water, spring”).

verb: Variant of found.
fount.example: He is a real fount of knowledge!
fount.exampleSense: That from which something flows or proceeds; a source.

bitumen.o: From Middle English bithumen, bitumen, from Latin bitūmen. Doublet of bitume.
bitumen.example: The development of water reticulation occurred in parallel with street work — forming, kerbing, channelling and bitumening.
bitumen.exampleSense: To cover or fill with bitumen.

chronicler.example: But he was also a natural chronicler: one senses that, even as his schemes collapsed, this aesthetic Arab Quixote knew the stories would make great material for his witty, sharp, melancholic writings.
chronicler.exampleSense: A person who writes a chronicle or chronicles.

whaler.o: From whale + -er. In sense 1, displaced Old English hwælhunta (literally “whale hunter”).
whaler.example: For a whaler's wife to have been “ 'round the Cape” half a dozen times, or even more, was nothing extraordinary.
whaler.exampleSense: One who hunts whales; a person employed in the whaling industry.

resin.o: From Middle English resyn, resyne, from Old French résine, from Latin resīna. Doublet of rosin.

carcass.o: Dated from the late 13th Century C.E.; from Anglo-Norman carcois, possibly related to Old French charcois. Cognate with French carcasse. But cf. also Avestan 𐬐𐬀𐬵𐬭𐬐𐬁𐬯𐬀 (kahrkās, “vulture”), and Middle Persian [Book Pahlavi needed] (klkʾs /⁠kargās⁠/, “vulture”), whence Persian کرکس (karkas, “vulture”).
carcass.example: Instead, the majority of studies involve freezing the carcasses until time permits the analysis.
carcass.exampleSense: The body of a dead animal.

carcase.o: Alternative form of carcass. Dated from the late 13th Century C.E.; from Anglo-Norman carcois, possibly related to Old French charcois. Cognate with French carcasse. But cf. also Avestan 𐬐𐬀𐬵𐬭𐬐𐬁𐬯𐬀 (kahrkās, “vulture”), and Middle Persian [Book Pahlavi needed] (klkʾs /⁠kargās⁠/, “vulture”), whence Persian کرکس (karkas, “vulture”).
carcase.example: Silence has sometimes a remarkable power of showing itself as the disembodied soul of feeling wandering without its carcase, and it is then more impressive than speech.

recover.o:
verb: From Middle English recoveren, rekeveren, from Anglo-Norman recoverer and Old French recovrer, from Latin recuperāre, alternative form of reciperāre. Doublet of recuperate. The noun is from Middle English recover, from the verb.

verb: From re- + cover.
recover.example: For days telescopes surveyed the skies to recover the small asteroid.
recover.exampleSense: To get back, to regain (a physical thing; in astronomy and navigation, sight of a thing or a signal).

gob.o:
noun: From Middle English gobbe (also Middle English gobet), from Old French gobet, gobe (“lump, mouthful”), from Transalpine Gaulish *gobbo- (“neb, muzzle”).

noun: Probably from Irish gob, Scottish Gaelic gob (“beak, mouth”).

noun: Back-formation from gobbing, or a specified use of Etymology 1, above.

noun: Shortened from gobby or gobshite.
gob.example: He spat a big ball of gob on to the pavement.

costly.o: From Middle English costly, costely, costeley, equivalent to cost + -ly.
costly.example: Individual mistakes proved costly for Wigan who, particularly after the half-time introduction of Hugo Rodallega, dominated for long periods.

guesswork.o: From guess + work. Compare Dutch giswerk (“guesswork”).

remedy.o: From Middle English remedie, from Old French *remedie, remede, from Latin remedium (“a remedy, cure”), from re- (“again”) + mederi (“to heal”). Doublet of remeid.

spit.o:
noun: The noun is from Middle English spit, spite, spete, spette, spyte, spytte (“rod on which meat is cooked; rod used as a torture instrument; short spear; point of a spear; spine in the fin of a fish; pointed object; dagger symbol; land projecting into the sea”), from Old English spitu (“rod on which meat is cooked; spit”), from Proto-Germanic *spitō (“rod; skewer; spike”), *spituz (“rod on which meat is cooked; stick”), from Proto-Indo-European *speyd-, *spey- (“sharp; sharp stick”). The English word is cognate with Dutch spit, Low German Spitt (“pike, spear; spike; skewer; spit”), Danish spid, Swedish spett (“skewer; spit; type of crowbar”). The verb is derived from the noun, or from Middle English spiten (“to put on a spit; to impale”), from spit, spite: see above. The English verb is cognate with Middle Dutch speten, spitten (modern Dutch speten), Middle Low German speten (Low German spitten, modern German spießen (“to skewer, to spear”), spissen (now dialectal)) and Danish spidde.

verb: The verb is from Middle English spē̆ten, spete (“to spit (blood, phlegm, saliva, venom, etc.); of a fire: to emit sparks”), from Old English spǣtan (“to spit; to squirt”); or from Middle English spit, spitte, spitten (“to spit (blood, phlegm, saliva, venom, etc.); of a fire: to emit sparks”), from Old English spittan, spyttan (“to spit”), both from Proto-Germanic, from Proto-Indo-European *sp(y)ēw, *spyū, ultimately imitative; compare Middle English spitelen (“to spit out, expectorate”) and English spew. The English word is cognate with Danish spytte (“to spit”), North Frisian spütte, Norwegian spytte (“to spit”), Swedish spotta (“to spit”), Old Norse spýta (Faroese spýta (“to spit”), Icelandic spýta (“to spit”)). The noun is derived from the verb; compare Danish spyt (“spit”), Middle English spit, spytte (“saliva, spittle, sputum”), spet (“saliva, spittle”), spē̆tel (“saliva, spittle”), North Frisian spiit.

noun: The noun is from Middle Dutch speet, spit, Middle Low German spêdt, spit (Low German spit); the word is cognate with Dutch spit, North Frisian spatt, spet, West Frisian spit. The verb is from Middle English spitten (“to dig”), from Old English spittan (“to dig with a spade”), possibly from spitu (“rod on which meat is cooked; spit”); see further at etymology
spit.example: The wag zigzagged across the field, bumping over ruts in the soil and tangled grass as a stream of bullets followed them from the high-mounted railguns, spitting sparks from the metal sides of the wag.
spit.exampleSense: To emit or expel in a manner similar to evacuating saliva from the mouth.

spittle.o:
noun: Alteration of dialectal spattle (by association with spit (noun)), from Old English spātl, which is related to spǣtan (whence spit (verb)).

noun: Representing a frequentative form of spit (“a spade's depth”), equivalent to spit + -le.
spittle.example: "Who are you?!" he blurted into the woman's palm, and she shook it off in obvious disgust, wiping spittle onto his D-class uniform.
spittle.exampleSense: Spit, usually frothy and of a milky coloration.

irritant.o: From French irritant, equivalent to irritate + -ant.
irritant.example: The states elected Harry, Duke of Anjou, for their king, with this clause irritant; that, if he did violate any part of his oath, the people should owe him no allegiance.
irritant.exampleSense: Rendering null and void; conditionally invalidating.

muse.o:
noun: From Middle French muse, from Latin Mūsa, from Ancient Greek Μοῦσα (Moûsa).

verb: From Middle English musen, from Old French muser.

noun: From French musse. See muset.
muse.example: Yoko Ono was John Lennon's wife, lover, and muse.

emulsifier.example: The lecithin in egg yolks is often used as an emulsifier.
emulsifier.exampleSense: A substance that helps an emulsion form, or helps keep an emulsion from separating.

emulsion.o: Borrowed from French émulsion, from New Latin ēmulsiō, ēmulsiōnis, based on Latin ēmulgeō (“to milk out, extract”).
emulsion.example: Mayonnaise is an emulsion where egg is used to keep oil and water mixed.
emulsion.exampleSense: A stable suspension of small droplets of one liquid in another with which it is immiscible.

excess.o: From Middle English exces (“excess, ecstasy”), from Old French exces, from Latin excessus (“a going out, loss of self-possession”), from excedere, excessum (“to go out, go beyond”). See exceed.
excess.example: The excess of heavy water was given away to the neighbouring country.
excess.exampleSense: The state of surpassing or going beyond a limit; the state of being beyond sufficiency, necessity, or duty; more than what is usual or proper.

hell.o:
name: From Middle English hel, hell, helle, hælle, from Old English hel, hell, from Proto-West Germanic *hallju, from Proto-Germanic *haljō (“hell, netherworld”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱel- (“to cover”). First attested in c. 725. Cognates Cognate with Yola helle (“hell”), Saterland Frisian Hälle (“hell”), West Frisian hel (“hell”), Alemannic German Hell (“hell”), Cimbrian hélla (“hell”), Dutch hel (“hell”), German Hölle (“hell”), Limburgish hel, Héll, Höll (“hell”), Luxembourgish Häll (“hell”), Vilamovian heł, hełł (“hell”), Danish helvede (“hell”), ihjel (“to death”), Faroese helviti (“hell”), Icelandic hel (“death, hell”), helvíti (“hell”), Norwegian Nynorsk hel (“death, underworld”), helvete (“hell”), Swedish helvete (“hell”), ihjäl (“to death”), Gothic 𐌷𐌰𐌻𐌾𐌰 (halja, “hell”), Estonian koll (“bugbear”), Finnish koljo (“giant; evil spirit; devil”); also Cornish keles (“to conceal, hide”), Irish ceil (“to conceal, hide; to cover up”), Welsh celu (“to conceal, hide”), Faliscan 𐌂𐌄𐌋𐌀 (cela, “tomb”), Latin cella (“hut, storeroom; barn, granary”), Greek κολεός (koleós, “vagina; sheath; scabbard; coleus”), Lithuanian šalmas (“helmet”), Belarusian шало́м (šalóm, “helmet”), Bulgarian and Macedonian шлем (šlem, “helmet”), Old Polish szłom (“helmet”), Russian шело́м (šelóm), шлем (šlem, “helmet”), Serbo-Croatian шле̏м, шље̏м, šlȅm, šljȅm (“helmet”), Ukrainian шолом (šolom, “helmet”), Sanskrit शर्मन् (śarman, “safety, shelter; house; bliss, happiness, joy”). Also related to the Hel of Germanic mythology. See also hele.

verb: From German hellen (“to brighten, burnish”). Related to Dutch hel (“clear, bright”) and German hell (“clear, bright”).

verb: From Middle English hellen, from Old Norse hella (“to pour”), from Proto-Germanic *halþijaną (“to incline, tip; to pour out, empty”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱel- (“to lean, incline”). Cognate with Icelandic hella (“to pour”), Norwegian helle (“to pour”), Swedish hälla (“to pour”). See also English hield.
hell.example: Thou shalt beat him with the rod, and shalt deliver his soul from hell.
hell.exampleSense: A place of torment where some or all sinners are believed to go after death and evil spirits are believed to be.

gerontic.o: First attested in the late 19th century. From Ancient Greek γέρων (gérōn, “old man”).
gerontic.example: The gerontic population of the U.S., those of 65 and over, numbered 3.1 million in 1900.
gerontic.exampleSense: Of or pertaining to old age or the elderly.

geronto-.o: Derived from Ancient Greek γέροντος (gérontos, “old man”).

incompatible.example: My phone is incompatible with the latest version of this app.
incompatible.exampleSense: Of two things: that cannot coexist; not congruous because of differences; unable to function together due to dissimilarities.

consist.o:
verb: From Middle French consister, from Latin consistō (“stand together, stop, become hard or solid, agree with, continue, exist”), from com- (“together”) + sistō (“to cause to stand, stand”).

noun: From consist (verb).
consist.example: The train's consist included a baggage car, four passenger cars, and a diner.
consist.exampleSense: A lineup or sequence of railroad carriages or cars, with or without a locomotive, that form a unit.

empowerment.example: Hence, the anonymity that digital technological tools can provide ultimately leads to empowerment of student opinion and input.
empowerment.exampleSense: The achievement of political, social or economic power by an individual or group.

enmesh.example: They take their time sizing each other up since they both know their motives might not be entirely honest. Tentatively they find warmth and companionship in each other. However, before long, they get enmeshed in Hale’s diabolical schemes.

pupil.o:
noun: From Middle English pupille, from Anglo-Norman pupille (“orphan”), from Latin pūpillus (“orphan, minor”), variant of pūpulus (“little boy”), from pūpus (“child, boy”).

noun: From Middle English pupille, from Old French pupille, from Latin pūpilla (“pupil; little girl, doll”), named because of the small reflected image seen when looking into someone's eye.
pupil.example: Plato was Socrates' pupil, and in turn Aristotle was Plato's pupil.
pupil.exampleSense: One who studies under supervision of a renowned expert in their field.

homophone.o: From French homophone; equivalent to homo- (“same”) + -phone (“sound”).

homo-.o:
prefix: From Ancient Greek ὁμός (homós, “same”). By surface analysis, hom- + -o-.

prefix: Back-formation from homosexual, ultimately from Ancient Greek ὁμός (homós, “same”).

prefix: Back-formation from homologue, ultimately from Ancient Greek ὁμός (homós, “same”).

homo.o:
noun: Clipping of homosexual.

noun: Clipping of homogenized.

noun: From Latin homō̆ (“a human being, man, person”), sometimes as a shortening of Homo sapiens. Doublet of gome, hombre, ombre, and omi.
homo.example: I heard that he's a homo, but he hasn't come out of the closet yet.

compelling.example: There are compelling reasons why a manager should have previous experience.
compelling.exampleSense: Strongly or irresistibly evoking interest or attention.

compel.o: From Middle English compellen, borrowed from Middle French compellir, from Latin compellere, itself from com- (“together”) + pellere (“to drive”). Displaced native Old English nīedan.
compel.example: The Queen has nothing but the power to execute the laws, to adjust grievances and to compel order.
compel.exampleSense: To exact, extort, (make) produce by force.

linguist.example: President Donald Trump has "turned words into weapons" -- and journalists are providing additional ammunition.
linguist.exampleSense: One who studies linguistics. One who studies modern-day linguistics, that is, linguistic science.

object.o: From Old French object, from Medieval Latin obiectum (“object”, literally “thrown against”), from obiectus, perfect passive participle of obiciō (“to throw against”), from ob- (“against”) + iaciō (“to throw”), as a calque of Ancient Greek ἀντικείμενον (antikeímenon). Doublet of objectum and objet.
object.example: Similarly, there is a category whose objects are groups and whose arrows are the homomorphisms from one group to another.
object.exampleSense: An instance of one of the two kinds of entities that form a category, the other kind being the arrows (also called morphisms).

acceptance.o: * First attested in 1528–1530. Probably partly from Middle French acceptance (from Old French accepter (“accept”)) and partly from accept + -ance.
acceptance.example: But what acts shall amount to such an acceptance is often a question of great nicety and difficulty.
acceptance.exampleSense: An agreeing to the action, proposals, or terms of another by some act which results in the conclusion of a legally binding contract; the reception or taking of a thing bought as that for which it was bought, or as that agreed to be delivered, or the taking of possession of a thing as owner.

engaging.o: present participle and gerund of engage. From Middle English engagen, from Old French engagier (“to pledge, engage”), from Old French en- (“in, under”) + gage (“pledge”), from Frankish *wadi (“pledge”), from Proto-Germanic *wadją (“pledge, guarantee”), from Proto-Indo-European *wedʰ- (“to pledge, redeem a pledge; guarantee, bail”), equivalent to en- + gage. Cognate with Old English weddian (“to engage, covenant, undertake”), German wetten (“to bet, wager”), Icelandic veðja (“to wager”). More at wed.
engaging.example: I found the first of the Harry Potter books a very engaging read.
engaging.exampleSense: Tending to engage attention or interest; engrossing, interesting; enthralling.

recite.o:
verb: From Middle English reciten, from Old French reciter, from Latin recitō.

verb: From re- + cite.
recite.example: Janice is able to recite pi to 100 decimals.
recite.exampleSense: To repeat aloud (some passage, poem or other text previously memorized, or in front of one's eyes), often before an audience.

rote.o:
noun: From Middle English rote (“custom, habit, wont, condition, state”), further origin unknown. Found in the Middle English phrase bi rote (“by heart, according to form, expertly”), c. 1300. Some have proposed a relationship either with Old French rote/rute (“route”), or Latin rota (“wheel”) (see rotary), but the OED calls both suggestions groundless. Another explanation might be the metaphorical comparison between anything repetitive and playing the rote.

noun: From Old Norse rót n (“tossing, pitching (of sea)”), perhaps related to rauta (“to roar”); see hrjóta. Compare Middle English routen (“to roar, bellow, storm, rage, howl”).

noun: From Middle English rote, from Old French rote, probably of German origin; compare Middle High German rotte, and English crowd (“a kind of violin”).
rote.example: He could perform by rote any of his roles in Shakespeare.
rote.exampleSense: Mechanical routine; a fixed, habitual, repetitive, or mechanical course of procedure.

polar.o: Learned borrowing from Late Latin polāris. By surface analysis, pole + -ar.
polar.example: After all, to go into outer space is not so much worse, if at all, than a polar expedition.
polar.exampleSense: Of or having a pole or polarity, as: Of, relating to, measured from, or referred to a geographic pole (the North Pole or South Pole); within the Arctic or Antarctic circles.

polarise.o: From French polariser, equivalent to polar + -ise.

heated.o: simple past and past participle of heat. From Middle English hete, from Old English hǣtu, from Proto-West Germanic *haitī, from Proto-Germanic *haitį̄ (“heat”), from Proto-Indo-European *keHy- (“heat; hot”). Cognate with Scots hete (“heat”), Saterland Frisian Hatte (“heat”), Old High German heizī (“heat”). Related also to Dutch hitte (“heat”), German Hitze (“heat”), Swedish hetta (“heat”), Faroese and Icelandic hiti (“heat”). Related to hot.

fishery.example: This fishery, which at its peak produced more than 80,000 tons a year, is now in decline.
fishery.exampleSense: A place related to fishing A place where fish or other seafood are caught: a fishing ground (for example, a territorial one).

air.o: From Middle English aire, from Old French air, from Latin āēr, from Ancient Greek ἀήρ (aḗr). Displaced native Old English lyft. More at lift, loft.
air.example: Open the window and let some air into the room.
air.exampleSense: The substance constituting Earth's atmosphere: a gaseous mixture of nitrogen, oxygen, and various trace gases. The substance of the atmosphere seen as an agency of freshness.

marina.o: From Latin marinus (“of the sea, marine”), by way of Italian marina and Spanish marina.
marina.example: It's a peaceful marina with not too many boats and yachts.

appreciation.o: From French appréciation. By surface analysis, appreciate + -ion.
appreciation.example: We give to you this trophy as a token of our appreciation of all your years of service.
appreciation.exampleSense: A fair valuation or estimate of merit, worth, weight, etc.; recognition of excellence; gratitude and esteem.

alum.o:
noun: From Middle English alum, alym, alyme, from Anglo-Norman alum, alun, from Latin alūmen.

noun: Clipping of alumnus and alumna (> alumn- > alum), by the removal of the originally Latin gender-specific nominative singular case endings -us (masculine) and -a (feminine).
alum.example: A natural astringent and antiseptic, potassium alum was coveted for its medicinal and cosmetic properties.
alum.exampleSense: An astringent salt, usually occurring in the form of pale crystals, much used in the dyeing and tanning trade and in certain medicines, and now understood to be a double sulphate of potassium and aluminium (K₂SO₄·Al₂(SO₄)₃·24H₂O).

gravel.o: From Middle English gravel, grauel, from Old French gravele, diminutive of grave (“gravel, seashore”), from Medieval Latin grava, ultimately from Proto-Celtic *grāwā (“gravel, pebbles”) (compare Breton groa, Cornish grow, Welsh gro), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰroh₁weh₂, from *gʰreh₁w- (“to grind”). Compare also Old English græfa (“coal”).
gravel.example: We kept quietly on our way until we reached a place in the road that had been freshly graveled, and where the surface was covered with stones just suited to our use.
gravel.exampleSense: To apply a layer of gravel to the surface of a road, etc.

shallow.o: From Middle English schalowe (“not deep, shallow”); apparently related to Middle English schalde, schold, scheld, schealde (“shallow”), from Old English sċeald (“shallow”), from Proto-Germanic *skal-, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kelh₁- (“to parch, dry out”). Related to Low German Scholl (“shallow water”). See also shoal.
shallow.example: Sauté the onions in a shallow pan.
shallow.exampleSense: Having little depth; significantly less deep than wide.

aerial.o: From Latin āeri(us) + -al, from Ancient Greek ἀέριος (aérios), from ἀήρ (aḗr, “air”) + -ιος (-ios). By surface analysis, aer- (“air”) + -ial.
aerial.example: The seabirds put on an astonishing aerial display.
aerial.exampleSense: Living or taking place in the air.

responsive.o: From Middle French responsif, from Late Latin responsivus.
responsive.example: Now, let's briefly explore two different approaches for creating sites for a multiple audience: multiserving and responsive design.
responsive.exampleSense: automatically resizing and repositioning elements to fit the available space

weir.o: From Middle English were, from Old English wer, from werian (“to dam up”), from Proto-West Germanic *warjan, from Proto-Germanic *warjaną, from Proto-Indo-European *wer- (“to cover”); Cognate with Old Norse ver (“station for fishing”), Sanskrit वृणोति (vṛṇóti). Related to warranty.
weir.example: The weir catch of mackerel at Monomoy and along Cape Cod has been a failure.
weir.exampleSense: A fence placed across a river to catch fish.

elaborate.o: 1575, from Late Latin ēlabōrātus (“worked out”), past participle of ēlabōrō (“to work out”), from ē- (“out, forth, fully”) + labor (“work, toil, exertion”). More at e-, labour.
elaborate.example: The notion of blood purity was first elaborated in Europe, where it was used to separate Old Christians from Spain’s New Christians—women and men of Jewish and Muslim origin whose ancestors had converted to Christianity.
elaborate.exampleSense: Тo develop in detail or complexity.

procure.o: From Middle English procuren, from Old French procurer, from Late Latin prōcūrāre (“to manage, administer”), from prō (“on behalf of”) + cūrō (“to care for”).
procure.example: By all means possible they procure to have gold and silver among them in reproach.
procure.exampleSense: To contrive; to bring about; to effect; to cause.

precedented.o: c. 1650 precedent + -ed, possibly a back-formation from unprecedented.
precedented.example: We have a right to take any method that is legal and is precedented.

multitude.o: From Middle English multitude, multitud, multytude (“(great) amount or number of people or things; multitudinous”), borrowed from Old French multitude (“crowd of people; diversity, wide range”), or directly from its etymon Latin multitūdō (“great amount or number of people or things”), from multus (“many; much”) + -tūdō (suffix forming abstract nouns indicating a state or condition). The English word is analysable as multi- + -itude.
