multitude.example: A torrential rain poured down from the floodgates of the angry heavens upon the bared heads of the assembled multitude which numbered at the lowest computation five hundred thousand persons.
multitude.exampleSense: A great amount or number, often of people; abundance, myriad, profusion.

quay.o: The current spelling replaced the spelling key in the 1690s to emulate the spelling but (at least originally) not the pronunciation of the equivalent modern French quai. From Middle English kay, key, kaye, keye, from Old French kay, cail, from Gaulish *kagyum, cagiíun (“enclosure”), from Proto-Celtic *kagyom (“pen, enclosure”) (compare Welsh cae (“field”)), from Proto-Indo-European *kagʰyóm (“enclosure”). Doublet of hedge and hey (“choreographic figure”).

suffice.o: From Middle English suffisen, from Middle French souffire, from Latin sufficiō (“supply, be adequate”), from sub (“under”) + faciō (“do, make”). Cognate with French suffire.
suffice.example: For this plum cake, two eggs should suffice.
suffice.exampleSense: To be enough or sufficient; to meet the need (of anything); to be adequate; to be good enough.

patchy.example: Added to these woes was the Treasury's demands for across-the-board train operator cost-cutting of broadly 10%. Passenger rail's slow, patchy and fragile recovery had the stuffing knocked out of it once more.
patchy.exampleSense: Not constant or continuous; intermittent or uneven.

patch.o:
noun: From Middle English patche, of uncertain origin. Perhaps an alteration of earlier Middle English placche (“patch, spot, piece of cloth”), from Old English *plæċċ, *pleċċ (“a spot, mark, patch”), from Proto-West Germanic *plakkju, from Proto-Germanic *plakjō (“spot, stain”). For the loss of l compare pat from Middle English platten. Germanic cognates would then include Middle English plecke, dialectal English pleck (“plot of ground, patch”), West Frisian plak (“place, spot”), Low German Plakk, Plakke (“spot, piece, patch”), Dutch plek (“spot, place, stain, patch”), Dutch plak (“piece, slab”), Swedish plagg (“garment”), Faroese plagg (“cloth, rag”). Or, possibly a variant of Old French pieche, dialectal variant of piece (“piece”). Compare also Old Occitan petaç (“patch”).

noun: Perhaps borrowed from Italian pazzo or paggio; the form influenced by folk etymological association with patch (Etymology 1).
patch.example: His sleeves had patches on the elbows where different fabric had been sewn on to replace material that had worn away.
patch.exampleSense: A piece of cloth, or other suitable material, sewed or otherwise fixed upon a garment to repair or strengthen it, especially upon an old garment to cover a hole.

postmodern.example: What I am objecting to is that aspect of postmodern thought that rejects the idea of any objective reality.
postmodern.exampleSense: Of, relating to, or having the characteristics of postmodernism, especially as represented in art, architecture, literature, science, or philosophy that reacts against an earlier modernism.

unparalleled.example: The candidate experienced unparalleled support in the last election.
unparalleled.exampleSense: Having no parallel; without equal; lacking anything similar or worthy of comparison.

para-.o:
prefix: From Ancient Greek παρα- (para-, “beside, next to”).

prefix: From French para-, from Italian para-, from para, imperative of parare (“to defend, shield, shroud”), from Latin parō (“to prepare”).

prefix: From parachute.

prefix: From Paralympic.

localised.o: simple past and past participle of localise. From local + -ise.
localised.example: On more than one other occasion, torrential rain has caused signal failures as well as localised flooding.

immensely.exampleSense: Greatly; hugely; extremely; vastly; to a great extent.

crook.o:
noun: From Middle English croke, crok, from Old English *crōc (“hook, bend, crook”), from Proto-West Germanic *krōk, from Proto-Germanic *krōkaz (“bend, hook”), from Proto-Indo-European *greg- (“tracery, basket, bend”). Cognate with Dutch kreuk (“a bend, fold, wrinkle”), Middle Low German kroke, krake (“fold, wrinkle”), Danish krog (“crook, hook”), Swedish krok (“crook, hook”), Icelandic krókur (“hook”). Compare typologically Czech křivák (< křivý < Proto-Slavic *krivъ, whence also *krivьda).

verb: From Middle English crooken, croken, crokien, from Old English *crōcian, from Proto-West Germanic *krōkōn (“to bend, wrinkle”), from the noun (see above). Cognate with Dutch kreuken (“to crease, rumple”), German Low German kröken (“to bend, offend, suppress”).

adj: From crooked (“dishonestly come by”).
crook.example: He crooked his finger toward me.
crook.exampleSense: To bend, or form into a hook.

encroach.o: From Middle English encrochen, from Old French encrochier (“to seize”), from Old French en- + croc (“hook”), of Germanic origin. More at crook.
encroach.example: He never allows work to encroach upon his family life.
encroach.exampleSense: to intrude unrightfully on someone else’s rights or territory

rise.o:
verb: From Middle English risen, from Old English rīsan, from Proto-West Germanic *rīsan, from Proto-Germanic *rīsaną (“to rise”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁rey- (“to arise, rise”). According to Kroonen (2013), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃er- (“to rise, spring”). See also raise. Cognates Cognate with Dutch rijzen (“to rise”), German reisen (“to fall”), Limburgish rieze (“to rise”), Faroese and Icelandic rísa (“to rise”), Norwegian Nynorsk risa, rise (“to rise”), Gothic *𐍂𐌴𐌹𐍃𐌰𐌽 (*reisan, “to rise”) (whence 𐌿𐍂𐍂𐌴𐌹𐍃𐌰𐌽 (urreisan, “to arise”)). Non-Germanic cognates include Cornish ardh (“height”), Irish arad, ard, árd (“high, tall”), Manx ard (“high, tall”), Scottish Gaelic àrd (“high”), Welsh ardd (“hill, upland”), Latin orior (“to rise”), Ancient Greek ἔρις (éris, “quarell, strife; contention, rivalry”) (whence Greek έριδα (érida, “feud”)), Albanian rashë (“to have fallen; to have flopped”), Bulgarian ръст (rǎst, “size; stature; growth”), Czech růst (“growth”), Macedonian раст (rast, “growth, height”), Polish rost, wzrost (“growth”), Russian рост (rost, “growth”), Serbo-Croatian ра̑ст, rȃst (“growth”), Slovene rȃst (“growth”), Old Armenian յառնեմ (yaṙnem, “to arise, rise”) (whence Armenian հառնել (haṙnel, “to rise up”)), Persian رمبیدن (rombidan, “to collapse”), Tocharian A ar- (“to evoke”), Tocharian B er- (“to evoke”), Hittite 𒀀𒊏𒀀𒄑𒍣 (arāwanzi, “to rise”), Sanskrit ऋ (ṛ, “to rise”).

noun: From Middle English ris, rys, from Old English hrīs, from Proto-Germanic *hrīsą (“twig; shoot”). More at rice.
rise.example: The path rises as you approach the foot of the hill.
rise.exampleSense: To move, or appear to move, physically upwards relative to the ground. To slope upward.

pristine.o:
adj: From Middle French pristin, borrowed from Latin prīstinus.

adj: From Ancient Greek πρίστις (prístis, “saw, sawfish”).
pristine.example: The beach back is in pristine condition after a council-led cleanup.
pristine.exampleSense: Unspoiled; still with its original purity; uncorrupted or unsullied.

broad.o:
adj: From Middle English brood, brode, from Old English brād (“broad, flat, open, extended, spacious, wide, ample, copious”), from Proto-West Germanic *braid, from Proto-Germanic *braidaz (“broad, wide”), of uncertain origin. Cognates Cognate with Yola brode (“broad”), North Frisian bread, breeđ, briad, briid, briidj (“wide”), Saterland Frisian and West Frisian breed (“broad, wide”), Bavarian brad, broad (“broad, wide”), Central Franconian and Luxembourgish breet (“broad, wide”), Dutch breed (“broad, wide”), German breit (“broad, wide”), Vilamovian braat (“broad, wide”), Yiddish ברייט (breyt, “broad, wide”), Danish and Swedish bred (“broad, wide”), Faroese and Icelandic breiður (“broad, wide”), Norwegian Bokmål bred, brei (“broad, wide”), Norwegian Nynorsk brei, breid (“broad, wide”), Gothic 𐌱𐍂𐌰𐌹𐌸𐍃 (braiþs, “broad, wide”).

noun: Early 20th century, apparent phono-semantic matching of German Braut (“bride”, also “girlfriend”, and more generally “broad, chick”).
broad.example: Lee: I wrote that line for you. Maeve: A bit broad, if you ask me.

spill.o: From Middle English spillen, from Old English spillan, spildan (“to kill, destroy, waste”), from Proto-West Germanic *spilþijan, from Proto-Germanic *spilþijaną (“to spoil, kill, murder”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)pel- (“to sunder, split, rend, tear”). Cognate with Dutch spillen (“to use needlessly, waste”), French gaspiller ("to waste, squander" < Germanic), Bavarian spillen (“to split, cleave, splinter”), Danish spilde (“to spill, waste”), Swedish spilla (“to spill, waste”), Icelandic spilla (“to contaminate, spoil”). See also spool.
spill.example: I spilled some sticky juice on the kitchen floor.
spill.exampleSense: To drop something so that it spreads out or makes a mess; to accidentally pour.

contemplate.o: First attested in the 1590s; borrowed from Latin contemplātus, the perfect active participle of contemplor (“to observe, survey, gaze (at), contemplate”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix). See also template.
contemplate.example: If a treaty contains any stipulations which contemplate a state of future war.

suspicion.o: From Middle English suspecioun, borrowed from Latin suspīciō, suspīciōnem, from suspicere, from sub- (“up to”) with specere (“to look at”). Perhaps partly through the influence of Old French sospeçon (or rather the Anglo-Norman form suspecioun). Equivalent to suspect + -ion.
suspicion.example: "I've been suspicioning here was where they got their information right along," the sheriff commented, and slipped the handcuffs on the landlord.

abscond.o: Either borrowed from Middle French abscondre or directly from Latin abscondō (“hide”); formed from abs, ab (“away”) + condō (“put together, store”), from con- (“together”) + *dʰeh₁- (“to put, place, set”). * Cognate with sconce (“a type of light fixture”).
abscond.example: You abscond the fuck outta there and find a place to hide.
abscond.exampleSense: To flee, often secretly; to steal away.

ill-informed.example: Despite their age, and a spot of ill-informed mainstream media criticism, there is plenty of life left in the HSTs.

notoriously.o: From Middle English notoryously, equivalent to notorious + -ly.
notoriously.example: Orton himself notoriously defaced library books before starting to write books himself.
notoriously.exampleSense: In a notorious or notable manner; as is commonly known.

notorious.o: From Late Middle English notoryous, from Medieval Latin nōtōrius (“evident, known; famous, well-known; infamous”), from Latin nōtus (“known, recognized; familiar, widely known; famous, well-known; infamous”) + -tōrius (suffix forming adjectives). Nōtus is the perfect passive participle of nōscō (“to become acquainted with or learn about (something); (rare) to be familiar with, recognize”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ǵneh₃- (“to know; to recognize”). cognates * Catalan notori (“well-known”) * Middle French notoire (Anglo-Norman notoire, notoir, notore, notorie, modern French notoire (“notorious; well-known”)) * Italian notorio (“notorious; well-known”) * Portuguese notorjo (obsolete), notório (“illustrious; open, public; notorious”) * Spanish notorio (“apparent, clear, obvious; well-known”)
notorious.example: Simon Forman was notorious in his day, and was a man of many reverses.
notorious.exampleSense: Senses with an unfavourable connotation. Of a person or entity: generally or widely known for something negative; infamous.

notoriety.o: Derived from Middle French notoriété, from Medieval Latin nōtōrietās, from nōtōrius, from nōtus (“known”), perfect passive participle of nōscō (“get to know”). By surface analysis, notorious + -ety.
notoriety.example: [H]e who portrays examples of disinterestedness and intrepidity, confers on virtue the notoriety and homage that are due to it, and rouses in the spectators, the spirit of salutary emulation.
notoriety.exampleSense: An infamous or notorious condition or reputation.

untamed.o: From Middle English untamed, untemed, equivalent to un- + tamed and/or untame + -ed. Compare Dutch ongetemd (“untamed”), German ungezähmt (“untamed”), Danish utæmmet (“untamed”), Swedish otämd (“untamed”), Icelandic ótamin (“untamed”).
untamed.example: The mustang is an untamed horse that roams where it wants, with little interest in humans.
untamed.exampleSense: Wild, uncontrolled, especially of animals not domesticated or trained to human contact.

negotiation.o: Borrowed from Middle French négociation, or from Latin negotiatio (“the carrying on of business, a wholesale business”), from negotiari (“to carry on business”). By surface analysis, negotiate + -ion.
negotiation.example: The specifics of the contract are still under negotiation.
negotiation.exampleSense: The process of achieving agreement through discussion.

contemn.o: From Middle English contempnen, from Old French contemner, from Latin contemnō (“to scorn”). See also contempt.
contemn.example: I was perturbed by the suspicion that the anguish of love contemned was alloyed in her broken heart with the pangs, sordid to my young mind, of wounded vanity.
contemn.exampleSense: To disdain; to value at little or nothing; to treat or regard with contempt.

contemptuous.example: I don't know that guy, but he just gave me a contemptuous look.
contemptuous.exampleSense: Showing contempt; expressing disdain; showing a lack of respect.

contempt.o: From Latin contemptus (“scorn”), from contemnō (“to scorn, despise”), from com- + temnō (“to despise”). Displaced native Old English forsewennes.
contempt.example: Justice Merchan has yet to issue a ruling on whether to find Mr. Trump in contempt.
contempt.exampleSense: Open disrespect or willful disobedience of the authority of a court of law or legislative body.

mercy.o: From Middle English mercy, merci, from Anglo-Norman merci (compare continental Old French merci, mercit), from Latin mercēs (“wages, fee, price”), from merx (“wares, merchandise”). Displaced native Old English mildheortnes (literally "mildheartedness"). Cognate with French merci, whence the doublet merci.
mercy.example: Have mercy on the poor and assist them if you can.
mercy.exampleSense: Forgiveness or compassion, especially toward those less fortunate.

release.o:
noun: From Middle English relesen, relessen, from Old French relaisser (variant of relascher).

verb: From re- + lease.
release.example: The video store advertised that it had all the latest releases.
release.exampleSense: Anything recently released or made available (as for sale).

ruler.o: From Middle English reuler; equivalent to rule + -er.
ruler.example: The carcharhinids are unquestionably the rulers of the seas, because of their abundance, their strength and speed, and their unchallenged position as the number one predators in the marine ecosystem.
ruler.exampleSense: A person who rules or governs; someone or something that exercises dominion or controlling power over others.

rule.o:
noun: From Middle English reule, rewle, rule, borrowed from Old French riule, reule, from Latin regula (“straight stick, bar, ruler, pattern”), from regō (“to keep straight, direct, govern, rule”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃réǵeti (“to straighten; right”), from the root *h₃reǵ-; see regent. Doublet of rail, regal, regula, and rigol.

verb: From Middle English reulen, rulen, borrowed from Old French riuler, from Latin regulāre (“to regulate, rule”), from regula (“a rule”); see regular and regulate.

noun: Related to revel.
rule.example: That's a ruled case with the school-men.
rule.exampleSense: To establish or settle by, or as by, a rule; to fix by universal or general consent, or by common practice.

craftsman.example: Dilettanteism presupposes art as botchwork does handicraft; and the Dilettante holds the same relation to the artist that the botcher does to the craftsman.
craftsman.exampleSense: One who is highly skilled at one's trade; an artisan or artificer.

harmony.o: From Middle English armonye, from Old French harmonie, armonie, from Latin harmonia, from Ancient Greek ἁρμονία (harmonía, “joint, union, agreement, concord of sounds”), either from or cognate with ἁρμόζω (harmózō, “to fit together”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂er- (“to join, fit, fix together”). First attested in 1602. Doublet of harmonia.

harmonious.o: From Middle French harmonieux; by surface analysis, harmony + -ous.

strife.o: From Middle English strif, stryf, striffe, from Old French estrif, noun derived from estriver, from Frankish *strīban; compare Dutch strijven. More at strive.

enlighten.o: Formerly also inlighten, from Middle English enlightenen, inlightnen, a hybrid formed from inlighten (“to enlighten, illuminate”), from Old English inlīhtan, onlīhtan, enlīhtan (“to enlighten, illuminate, give light to, give sight to”) and lightnen (“to enlighten, illuminate”) (equivalent to light + -en). Cognate with Dutch inlichten (“to enlighten, inform”), Old High German inliuhten (“to enlighten, illuminate”), Gothic 𐌹𐌽𐌻𐌹𐌿𐌷𐍄𐌾𐌰𐌽 (inliuhtjan, “to enlighten, illuminate”). More at inlight, -en.
enlighten.example: Care to enlighten me, if you think I'm so benighted?
enlighten.exampleSense: To make something clear to (someone); to give knowledge or understanding to.

complete.o: From Middle English compleet (“full, complete”), borrowed from Old French complet or Latin completus, past participle of compleō (“to fill up, to complete”) (whence also complement, compliment), from com- + pleō (“to fill, to fulfill”) (whence also deplete, replete, plenty), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *pleh₁- (“to fill”) (English full).
complete.example: My life will be complete once I buy this new television.
complete.exampleSense: With all parts included; with nothing missing; full.

boarding.example: Load profiles are a standard analysis tool showing passenger activity (boardings, alightings) and passenger load at each stop along a route in a single direction.
boarding.exampleSense: The act of people getting aboard a ship aircraft, train, bus, etc.; embarkation.

apart.o: From Middle English apart, aparte, a-part, a part, from Anglo-Norman a part, from Latin ad partem (“to the side”).
apart.example: Joking apart, what do you think?

set out.example: This contract sets out all the terms of the agreement as we discussed.
set out.exampleSense: To explain something, or give exact details, usually in writing.

conviction.o: From late Middle English conviction, from Anglo-Norman conviction, from Latin convictiō, from convictus, the past participle of convincō (“to convict”). Equivalent to convict + -ion.
conviction.example: From G. R. Ratts , Game Warden , fines collected on conviction of violation of State game law .
conviction.exampleSense: The state of being found or proved guilty.

at a loss.example: His policies may be ineffective, but he is never at a loss for words.
at a loss.exampleSense: Not sure; uncertain; lacking further ideas, direction, or ability.

criminal.o: From Middle English cryminal, borrowed from Anglo-Norman criminal, from Late Latin criminalis, from Latin crimen (“crime”).
criminal.example: His long criminal record suggests that he is a dangerous man.
criminal.exampleSense: Of or relating to crime or penal law.

convict.o: From Middle English convicten, from Anglo-Norman convicter, from Latin convictus, the past participle of convincō (“to convict”). Doublet of convince. Displaced native Old English forwyrċan (“to convict, condemn”).
convict.example: His remarks convicted him of a lack of sensitivity.
convict.exampleSense: To find guilty, as a result of legal proceedings, or (informal) in a moral sense.

living.o:
verb: From Middle English livynge, libbyng, livinde, livand, livende, libbinde, libbende, from Old English lifiġende, lifiende, libbende, from Proto-West Germanic *libbjandī, from Proto-Germanic *libjandz (“living”), present participle of Proto-Germanic *libjaną (“to live”), equivalent to live + -ing. Cognate with West Frisian libbend (“living”), Dutch levend (“living”), German lebend (“living”), Swedish levande (“living”), Icelandic lifandi (“living”).

noun: From Middle English livynge, libbynge, equivalent to live + -ing. Cognate with Middle Dutch levinge, (whence Dutch leving (“way of life, living”)), Middle Low German lēvinge (“living”).
living.example: This is the living image of Fidel Castro.

destitute.o:
adj: From Middle English destitute, destitut, from Latin dēstitūtus.

verb: From Middle English destituten, from the adjective (see above).
destitute.example: In thee is my trust; leave not my soul destitute.

deindustrialization.example: The U.K. is now an object lesson for other countries dealing with a dark triad of deindustrialization, degrowth, and denigration of foreigners.
deindustrialization.exampleSense: A decrease in industrial activity or capacity.

industrialization.o: From French industrialisation. Analyzable as industrial + -ization or industrialize + -ation.
industrialization.example: It was during this period of industrialization that the individualistic world view of classical liberalism became the dominant ideology of capitalism.
industrialization.exampleSense: A process of social and economic change whereby a human society is transformed from a preindustrial to an industrial state.

feed.o:
verb: From Middle English feden, from Old English fēdan (“to feed”), from Proto-West Germanic *fōdijan, from Proto-Germanic *fōdijaną (“to feed”), from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂- (“to guard, graze, feed”). Cognate with West Frisian fiede (“to nourish, feed”), Dutch voeden (“to feed”), Danish føde (“to bring forth, feed”), Swedish föda (“to bring forth, feed”), Icelandic fæða (“to feed”), and more distantly with Latin pāscō (“feed, nourish”, verb) through Indo-European. More at food, fodder.

noun: From Middle English fede, fed, from the verb (see above). Alternatively, perhaps from Old Norse fœða (“nourishment, food”), from Proto-Germanic *fōdijaną (“to feed”), whence also Old English fēdan (“to feed”).

verb: See the etymology of the corresponding lemma form.
feed.example: DR SIMEON: I said I'd feed you. I didn't say who to.
feed.exampleSense: To give (someone or something) to (someone or something else) as food.

omnivore.o: From the Latin omnivorus. By surface analysis, omni- + -vore.
omnivore.example: Bears are omnivores: they can eat plants, but they also eat fish.
omnivore.exampleSense: An animal which is able to consume both plants (like a herbivore) and meat (like a carnivore).

arthritis.o: From Latin arthrītis, from Ancient Greek ἀρθρῖτις (arthrîtis, “joint-disease, gout”), from ἄρθρον (árthron, “a joint”). By surface analysis, arthr- + -itis.
arthritis.example: She identified the dry grasp and the finger joints (both the Simpsons were dry-handed, and in the early stages of arthritis, so Dr Simpson had diagnosed).
arthritis.exampleSense: Inflammation of a joint or joints causing pain and/or disability, swelling and stiffness, and due to various causes such as infection, trauma, degenerative changes or metabolic disorders.

arthrodia.o: From Ancient Greek ἀρθρωδία (arthrōdía), from ἀρθρώδης (arthrṓdēs, “well articulated”). By surface analysis, arthr- + -ode + -ia.

jellyfish.o: From jelly + fish. From being an aquatic creature (i.e. fish) that is gelatinous (“jelly”). Despite the name, jellyfish are not biologically classified as fish. The term appeared in the mid-19th century and displaced various older terms such as sea jelly (now much less common), blubber/sea blubber, nettle/sea nettle (both now referring to specific jellyfish species), and, in scientific literature, medusa.
jellyfish.example: There are asexual variants among all sorts of creatures, including jellyfish, dandelions, lichens and lizards.
jellyfish.exampleSense: An almost transparent aquatic animal; any one of the acalephs, especially one of the larger species, having a jellylike appearance.

jelly.o:
noun: Inherited from Middle English gele. Doublet of gelee.

adj: Clipping of jealous + -y (informal adjective ending).
jelly.example: Sam floored him perpetually, and beat his face to a jelly, without getting a scratch.
jelly.exampleSense: Any substance or object having the consistency of the dessert or preserve.

persevere.o: From Middle English perseveren, from Old French perseverer, from Latin persevērāre (“to continue steadfastly, persist, persevere”), from perseverus (“very strict or earnest”), from per (“through, by the means of”) + severus (“strict, earnest”). Doublet of perseverate.

flagship.example: After Russia’s flagship in the Black Sea, the Moskva, sank last week, the authorities said that the entire crew of more than 500 had been rescued.
flagship.exampleSense: The ship occupied by the fleet's commander (usually an admiral); it denotes this by flying his flag.

celestial.o: (“relating to the heavens or sky; (Christianity) relating to heaven, divine, heavenly”), borrowed from Old French celestial (modern French céleste), from Medieval Latin caelestiālis (“celestial”), or directly from its etymon Latin caelestis (“of or in the heavens, heavenly; (figurative) of the gods, divine; etc.”), from caelum (“heaven; sky”) (ultimate etymology uncertain, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *kéh₂ilom (“whole”)) + -estris (suffix meaning ‘dwelling or located in’ forming adjectives from nouns). The adverb and noun are derived from the adjective. Adjective sense 2.2 (“of or relating to China”) and noun sense 3 (“native of China”) refer to Celestial Empire (a calque of Mandarin 天朝 (Tiāncháo, “(literary) the Chinese Empire, China”), from 天 (tiān, “heaven; sky”) + 朝 (cháo, “dynasty; emperor’s reign; imperial court; etc.”)), a dated name for China when it was subject to imperial rule.
celestial.example: For the celestials communicate by the psychic dispatch. Scriptures prove that.

dredge.o:
noun: From Scots dreg-boat, dreg-bot (from Old English *dreċġ); or alternatively from Middle Dutch dregghe (“drag-net”), probably ultimately from the same root as drag.

noun: From Middle English dragge, from Old French dragee, dragie, from Latin tragēmata, from Ancient Greek τραγήματα (tragḗmata, “spices”), plural of τράγημα (trágēma, “dried fruit”).
dredge.example: Dredge the meat with the flour mixture you prepared earlier.
dredge.exampleSense: To sprinkle (food) with spices or seasonings, using a dredge.

soul.o:
noun: From Middle English soule, sowle, saule, sawle, from Old English sāwol (“soul, life, spirit, being”), from Proto-West Germanic *saiwalu, from Proto-Germanic *saiwalō (“soul”), of an uncertain ultimate origin (see there for further information). Cognates Cognate with Scots saul, sowel (“soul”), Saterland Frisian Seele (“soul”), West Frisian siel (“soul”), Alemannic German Seel (“soul”), Central Franconian Siel (“soul”), Dutch ziel (“soul”), German Seele (“soul”), German Low German Seel (“soul”), Luxembourgish Séil (“soul, spirit”), Vilamovian zejł, zəjł, zyił (“soul”), Gothic 𐍃𐌰𐌹𐍅𐌰𐌻𐌰 (saiwala, “soul”). Scandinavian homonyms seem to have been borrowed from Old Saxon sēola. Modern Danish sjæl (“soul”), Icelandic sál (“soul”), Norwegian Bokmål sjel (“soul”), Norwegian Nynorsk sjel, sål (“soul”), Swedish själ (“soul”), Finnish sielu (“soul”) may have come from Old English sāwol.

verb: Borrowed from French souler (“to satiate”).
soul.example: Fifty souls were lost when the ship sank.

bounce.o: From Middle English bounsen, bunsen (“to beat, thump”), cognate with Scots bunce, bonce (“to bounce”). Of uncertain origin. Perhaps imitative, related to bump, or related to Middle English bonchen (“to pound, beat”) and Dutch bonken (“to bump”). Compare Saterland Frisian bumzje (“to pound, bang, bounce”), West Frisian bûnzje (“to throb, bounce, pulsate”), Dutch bonzen (“to thump, knock, throb, bounce”), German Low German bunsen, bumsen (“to beat, bounce”), German bumsen (“to thud, bang, pound”).
bounce.example: Nobody took umbrage and bounced me out of the Union for being a pro.
bounce.exampleSense: To eject violently, as from a room; to discharge unceremoniously, as from employment.

penetrate.o: From Latin penētrātus, perfect passive participle of penētrō (“to put, set, or place within, enter, pierce, penetrate”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from penes (“within, with”) by analogy to intrō (“to go in, enter”). Compare French pénétrer.
penetrate.example: His weapons have been destroyed; his body has been or can be penetrated. In other words, he is rapable.
penetrate.exampleSense: To insert the penis into an orifice, such as a vagina, mouth, or anus.

penetrant.example: Young Bob's oddly penetrant voice was raised, to his father's uneasiness, in opposition to Grayson, and thus providentially deflected the ordeal from Charles.

pneumatic.o: From Latin pneumaticus, from Ancient Greek πνευματικός (pneumatikós, “relating to wind or air”), from πνεῦμα (pneûma, “wind, air, breath, spirit”), from πνέω (pnéō, “to blow, breath”).
pneumatic.example: "Every one says I'm awfully pneumatic," said Lenina reflectively, patting her own legs.

pneumo-.o:
prefix: From Ancient Greek πνεύμων (pneúmōn, “lung”).

prefix: From Ancient Greek πνεῦμα (pneûma, “air”).

pneuma.o: From Ancient Greek πνεῦμα (pneûma, “wind, breath, spirit”), from πνέω (pnéō, “I blow, breathe”). Doublet of neume.
pneuma.example: With swaying arms they wail in pneuma over the recreant Bloom.

dismantle.o: From Middle French desmanteler, itself from des- (“dis-”), mantel (“coat”) + -er (verbal suffix). By surface analysis, dis- + mantle. Compare typologically uncloak, reveal, unmask.
dismantle.example: In order to grant the rich these pleasures, the social contract is reconfigured. The welfare state is dismantled. Essential public services are cut so that the rich may pay less tax.
dismantle.exampleSense: To take apart; to disassemble; to take to pieces.

sub-surface.o: Alternative spelling of subsurface. From sub- + surface.
sub-surface.example: The next two stages of new signalling equipment went live on London Underground's sub-surface lines at the beginning of September.

seep.o: Variant of sipe, from Middle English *sipen, from Old English sipian, from Proto-Germanic *sipōną, derivative of *sīpaną, from Proto-Indo-European *seyb-, *sib- (“to pour out, drip, trickle”). See also Middle Dutch sīpen (“to drip”), German Low German siepern (“to seep”), archaic German seifen (“to trickle blood”); also Latin sēbum (“suet, tallow”), Ancient Greek εἴβω (eíbō, “to drop, drip”)). See soap.
seep.example: The water steadily seeped in through the thirl.
seep.exampleSense: To ooze or pass slowly through pores or other small openings, and in overly small quantities; said of liquids, etc.

rim.o:
noun: From Middle English rim, rym, rime, from Old English rima (“rim, edge, border, bank, coast”), from Proto-Germanic *rimô, *rembô (“edge, border”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *rem-, *remə- (“to rest, support, be based”). Cognate with Saterland Frisian Rim (“plank, wooden cross, trellis”), Old Saxon rimi (“edge; border; trim”), Icelandic rimi (“a strip of land”).

verb: From a variation of ream.

noun: From Middle English rim, rym, ryme, reme, from Old English rēoma (“membrane, ligament”), from Proto-West Germanic *reumō.

noun: Unknown.
rim.example: That's... our galaxy. We're beyond the rim.
rim.exampleSense: An edge around something, especially when circular.

strike.o: From Middle English stryken, from Old English strīcan, from Proto-West Germanic *strīkan, from Proto-Germanic *strīkaną, from Proto-Indo-European *streyg- (“to stroke, rub, press”). Cognate with Dutch strijken, German streichen, Danish stryge, Icelandic strýkja, strýkva.
strike.example: It was then I knew I had made my third mistake. Yes, three strikes right across the plate, and as I hollered "Honey, please wait" she was gone.
strike.exampleSense: A status resulting from a batter swinging and missing a pitch, or not swinging at a pitch when the ball goes in the strike zone, or hitting a foul ball that is not caught.

purification.o: From Old French purificacion, from Latin pūrificātiō.

lotion.o: From Middle English locion, borrowed from Latin lōtiō, lōtiōnem (“a washing”), from lavō (“to wash”); see lave. Doublet of lavation.
lotion.example: I would finish my daily ranging session by lotioning his legs, and lotioning and rubbing his feet.
lotion.exampleSense: To cover or treat with a lotion.

acute.o: From Late Middle English acute (“of a disease or fever: starting suddenly and lasting for a short time; of a humour: irritating, sharp”), from Latin acūta, from acūtus (“sharp, sharpened”), perfect passive participle of acuō (“to make pointed, sharpen, whet”), from acus (“needle, pin”). The word is cognate to ague (“acute, intermittent fever”). As regards the noun, which is derived from the verb, compare Middle English acūte (“severe but short-lived fever; of blood: corrosiveness, sharpness; musical note of high pitch”).
acute.example: The teacher pointed out the acute angle.

mount.o:
noun: From Middle English mount, munt, from Old English munt, from Latin mōns (“a hill, mountain”), from a root seen also in ēmineō (“to project, to protrude”) (English eminent). Doublet of mons. Not related to mound.

noun: From Middle English mounten, from Anglo-Norman munter, from Vulgar Latin *montāre (“climb”), from Latin montem (“mountain”). Compare modern French monter.
mount.example: “My Continental prominence is improving,” I commented dryly.
mount.exampleSense: To attach (an object) to a support, backing, framework etc.

multinational.example: AS a young student at the multinational Aramco school in Dhahran, Saudi Arabia, Fadi Jaber, a son of Palestinian refugees, always preferred his American classmates’ cupcakes, brownies and chocolate chip cookies to his mother’s pastries: knafah, qatayef and baklawah.
multinational.exampleSense: Of, or involving more than two nations (externally between countries or internally in a country).

illiterate.o: First attested in 1425–1475, in Middle English; from Middle English illiterat(e) (“uneducated, ignorant of Latin”), borrowed from Latin illīterātus, illitterātus (“unlearned, ignorant”), itself from in- (“un-”) + līterātus, litterātus (“furnished with letters”) (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from lītera, littera (“letter, character”). The noun was derived from the adjective by substantivization, see -ate (noun-forming suffix).
illiterate.example: We might also provide education plus reading and writing services to adult illiterates.
illiterate.exampleSense: An illiterate person, one either not able to read and write or not knowing how.

paw.o:
noun: From Middle English pawe, from Old French poue, poe, from Vulgar Latin *pauta. Further origin unknown, perhaps from Frankish *pōta, from Frankish *pōtōn (“to put, stick, plant”), from Proto-Germanic *putōną, whence also Old English potian (“to push”), pȳtan (“to put out, poke out”). See more at put. Doublet of pote, put, and putt. Cognate with Dutch poot, poten (“to plant”), Low German Pote, German Pfote, Icelandic pota (“to stick”).

noun: The word probably has an origin in baby talk. See pa.
paw.example: He paweth in the valley, and rejoiceth in his strength: he goeth on to meet the armed men.
paw.exampleSense: To draw the forefoot along the ground; to beat or scrape with the forefoot.

beak.o:
noun: From Middle English bec, borrowed from Anglo-Norman bec, Old French bec, from Latin beccus, from Gaulish *bekkos, from Proto-Celtic *bekkos (“beak, snout”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *bak-, *baḱ- (“pointed stick, peg”). Cognate with Breton beg (“beak”). Compare Saterland Frisian Bäk (“mouth; muzzle; beak”); Dutch bek (“beak; bill; neb”).

noun: Unknown; originally cant; first recorded in 17thC; probably related to obsolete cant beck "constable".
beak.example: Typical Yankee detractor, nize your beak.

spy.o: From Middle English spien, aphetic variant of earlier espien (“to espy”), from Old French espier (“to spy”), from Frankish *spehōn (“to spy”), from Proto-Germanic *spehōną (“to see, look”), from Proto-Indo-European *speḱ- (“to look”). Akin to German spähen (“to spy”), Dutch spieden (“to spy”). The noun displaced native Old English sċēawere (literally “watcher”), which was also the word for "mirror." In this sense, the verb displaced Old English sċēawian, which was also the word for "to watch" and became the Modern English word show. Distant cognate vie PIE with Latin speculātor, Ancient Greek κατάσκοπος (katáskopos). Compare typologically Russian согляда́тай (sogljadátaj) (akin to гляде́ть (gljadétʹ)).
spy.example: One in reading, skipped over all sentences where he spied a note of admiration.
spy.exampleSense: To spot; to catch sight of; to espy.

refugee.o: From French réfugié, past participle of réfugier (“to take refuge, to seek refuge”), from Old French refuge (“hiding place”) from Latin refugium (“a place of refuge, place to flee back to”), originally describing French Huguenots fleeing religious persecution after the revocation of the Edict of Nantes in 1685. Noun sense 1 was "one seeking asylum" until 1914, when it evolved to mean more generally "one fleeing home" (first applied in this sense to civilians in Flanders heading west to escape fighting in World War I). By surface analysis, refuge + -ee. Displaced native Old English flīema.
refugee.example: Why did the SDP dream eventually fade? Partly because it succeeded far better inside parliament than out. It might attract some inner-city Catholic traditionalist Labour refugees from Labour's left, but many of those were already gentrifying.
refugee.exampleSense: A person who flees one place or institution for another.

refuge.o: From Middle English refuge, from Old French refuge, from Latin refugium, from re- + fugiō (“flee”). Doublet of refugium.
refuge.example: Among these macaques, although activity cycles are quite variable from location to location, refuging is a common characteristic.
refuge.exampleSense: To return to a place of shelter.

thorn.o: From Middle English thorn, þorn, from Old English þorn, from Proto-West Germanic *þorn, from Proto-Germanic *þurnaz, from Proto-Indo-European *tr̥nós, from *(s)ter- (“stiff”). Cognates Near cognates include West Frisian toarn, Low German Doorn, Dutch doorn, German Dorn, Danish and Norwegian torn, Swedish torn, törne, Gothic 𐌸𐌰𐌿𐍂𐌽𐌿𐍃 (þaurnus). Further cognates include Old Church Slavonic трънъ (trŭnŭ, “thorn”), Russian тёрн (tjorn), Polish cierń, Kamkata-viri taňi, tai (“thorn”), Sanskrit तृण (tṛ́ṇa, “grass”).
thorn.example: See also Etymology of ye (definite article).
thorn.exampleSense: A letter of Latin script (capital: Þ, small: þ), borrowed from the futhark; today used only in Icelandic to represent the voiceless dental fricative, but originally used in several early Germanic scripts, including Old English where it represented the dental fricatives that are today written th (Old English did not have phonemic voicing distinctions for fricatives).

throng.o: From Middle English throng, thrang, from Old English þrang, ġeþrang (“crowd, press, tumult”), from Proto-Germanic *þrangwą, *þrangwō (“throng”), from *þrangwaz (“pressing, narrow”), from *þrinhwaną (“to press, to push; to force”), from Proto-Indo-European *trenkʷ- (“to beat; pound; hew; press”). Cognate with Dutch drang, German Drang. Compare also German Gedränge (“throng”) and Persian ترنجیدن (Trenjidan, “to beat, to push”). Compare typologically crowd (see there for more).
throng.example: Much people followed him, and thronged him.
throng.exampleSense: To crowd or press, as persons; to oppress or annoy with a crowd of living beings.

amphibian.o: Learned borrowing from Latin amphibius [from Ancient Greek ἀμφίβιος (amphíbios), from ἀμφίς (amphís, “of both kinds”) + βίος (bíos, “life”)] + -an.

precipitation.o: From Middle French précipitation, from Latin praecipitātiō, praecipitātiōnem. By surface analysis, precipitate + -ion.
precipitation.example: South Korea’s Ministry of Environment said in a news release that no major precipitation was observed after the cloud seeding operation.
precipitation.exampleSense: Any or all of the forms of water particles, whether liquid or solid, that fall from the upper atmosphere (e.g., rain, hail, snow or sleet). It is a major class of hydrometeor, but it is distinguished from cloud, fog, dew, rime, frost, etc., in that it must fall. It is distinguished from cloud and virga in that it must reach the ground.

precipitate.o:
verb: From Latin praecipitātus, perfect passive participle of praecipitō (“throw down, hurl down, throw headlong”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) for more), from praeceps (“head foremost, headlong”) (praecipit- in its oblique stem), from prae (“before”) + -ceps (“headed”).

adj: From Latin praecipitātus (see Etymology 1 and -ate (adjective-forming suffix) for more).

noun: From New Latin praecipitātum. Equivalent to Latin praecipitō + -ate (noun-forming suffix).
precipitate.example: It will precipitate tomorrow, but we don't know whether as rain or snow.
precipitate.exampleSense: To have water in the air fall to the ground, for example as rain, snow, sleet, or hail; be deposited as condensed droplets.

precipitant.o: The adjective is borrowed from Middle French précipitant, Old French precipitant (“acting hastily, hasty, rash; acting, happening, or moving rapidly; pressing”) (modern French précipitant), and from their etymon Late Latin praecipitans (“hasty, rash”), an adjective use of Latin praecipitāns, the present participle of praecipitō (“to cast down; to throw headlong”), from praeceps (“head first, headlong; (figurative) hasty, rash”) (from prae (“before; in front”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *preh₂- (“before; in front”)) + -ceps (suffix meaning ‘having a head with specified characteristics’) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kap- (“a head”))). The adverb and noun are derived from the adjective.

crawler.o:
noun: From crawl (“to move slowly, by dragging the body along the ground”) + -er.

noun: From crawl (“to act in a servile manner”) + -er. From the Australian convict period (1788–1850); a prisoner who was purposely and extensively abused by an overseer (also a convict) and thereby driven to escape but who, finding it impossible to survive in the Australian bush, surrenders to this overseer, who would then have his penal term reduced. The particular crawler was picked for his weak personality and might escape and return a number of times increasing his own penal term each time. According to James Tucker, some convict overseers had their sentences extensively reduced using this odious practice.
crawler.example: These serve as an algorithmic way to judge the “mobileness” of a site, and similar algorithms are likely to be used by the search crawlers.
crawler.exampleSense: A software bot that autonomously follows connected paths such as links between web pages.

vital.o: From Middle English vital, from Old French vital, from Latin vītālis (“of life, life-giving”), from vīta (“life”), from vīvō (“to live”). Doublet of jiva and quick.
vital.example: I ought to go upright and vital, and speak the rude truth in all ways.

insular.o: Learned borrowing from Latin īnsulāris (“of or belonging to an island”), from īnsula (“an island”), of uncertain origin.
insular.example: There now is your insular city of the Manhattoes, belted round by wharves as Indian isles by coral reefs.
insular.exampleSense: Of or being, pertaining to, situated on, or resembling an island or islands.

insula.o: From Latin īnsula (“island”). Doublet of isle.
insula.example: All mammals have insulas that read their body condition, Dr. Craig said.
insula.exampleSense: A structure of the human brain located within the lateral sulcus.

tract.o:
noun: From Middle English tract, tracte, traht (“a treatise, exposition, commentary”), from Old English traht, tract (“a treatise, exposition, commentary, text, passage”); and also from Middle English tract, tracte (“an expanse of space or time”); both from Latin tractus (“a haul, drawing, a drawing out”), the perfect passive participle of trahō. Doublet of trait.

verb: From Latin tractus, the participle stem of trahere (“to pull, drag”).

verb: From Latin tractāre, from tractō, from trahō + -tō.
tract.example: The church clergy at that writ the best collection of tracts against popery that ever appeared.
tract.exampleSense: A brief treatise or discourse on a subject.

thorny.o: From Middle English thorny, þorny, þorni, from Old English þorniġ, from Proto-West Germanic *þornag. By surface analysis, thorn + -y.
thorny.example: Six weeks into the renegotiation of the North American Free Trade Agreement, the thorniest issues surrounding the pact remain unresolved.

underscore.example: By convention, Rubyists usually underscore their method names.
underscore.exampleSense: To underline; to mark a line beneath text.

existential.o: The adjective is a learned borrowing from Late Latin existentiālis, exsistentiālis (“coming into or relating to existence”) + English -al (suffix meaning ‘of or pertaining to’ forming adjectives; and forming nouns of verbal action). Existentiālis, exsistentiālis are derived from Late Latin existentia, exsistentia (“existence”) + Latin -ālis (suffix forming adjectives of relationship); and existentia, exsistentia from Latin existēns, exsistēns (“being, existing; appearing, emerging; becoming”) (the present active participle of existō, exsistō (“to be, exist; to appear, emerge; to become”), from ex- (prefix meaning ‘away; out’) + sistō (“to cause to stand; to place, set; to halt, stop”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *steh₂- (“to stand (up)”))) + -ia (suffix forming feminine abstract nouns). The noun is derived from the adjective.
existential.example: Here, therefore, we seek to assemble and assess the evidence to provide an overview of how serious trade is as an existential threat to avian taxa in Sundaic Indonesia.
existential.exampleSense: Concerning the very existence of something, especially with regard to extinction.

existent.o: From Latin existens, from existere. By surface analysis, exist + -ent.

frater.o: PIE word *bʰréh₂tēr Learned borrowing from Latin frāter (“brother”). Doublet of bhai, brother, bru, friar, pal, and vai.

fraternal.o: PIE word *bʰréh₂tēr Borrowed from Middle French fraternel, from Medieval Latin frāternālis (“fraternal”), from Latin frāternus (“of or pertaining to a brother, fraternal”), from frāter (“brother”).
fraternal.example: The rate of natural fraternal embryo fusion is not well documented.
fraternal.exampleSense: Of twins or embryos, produced from two different eggs and sperm, and genetically distinct.

apparel.o: From Old French apareillier. Doublet of parrel.
apparel.example: They which are gorgeously appareled, and live delicately, are in kings’ courts.
apparel.exampleSense: To dress or clothe; to attire.

explicit.o:
adj: Borrowed from French explicite, from Latin explicitus (“disentangled, easy”), variant of explicātus.

phrase: Abbreviated from Latin explicitus est liber (“the book is set in order, ended”).
explicit.example: I gave explicit instructions for him to stay here, but he followed me, anyway.

yoghurt.o: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish یوغورت (yoğurt). Ultimately from Proto-Turkic *yogrut.
yoghurt.example: Many icecream shops now sell soft-serve yoghurts, icecreams and ice-desserts that are high in carbos and low in fat.

recession.o: Borrowed from Latin recessiō, from recēdō (“recede, retreat”), from re- (“back”) + cēdō (“to go”). By surface analysis, recess + -ion.
recession.example: Bilateral medial rectus muscle recession when angle is stable. Controversy exists regarding optimal timing of surgery. If greater than 40 prism diopter esotropia, some recommend bimedial recession with resection of one lateral rectus muscle.
recession.exampleSense: A procedure in which an extraocular muscle is detached from the globe of the eye and reattached posteriorly.

currency.o: Borrowed from Medieval Latin currentia. By surface analysis, current + -cy.
currency.example: Fear of punishment has no currency with me as long as I remain convinced of the larger value of what I have done.
currency.exampleSense: The state of being current; general acceptance, recognition or use.

lunar.o: From Middle English lunar (“shaped like the crescent moon”), from Latin lūnāris (“of or pertaining to the moon, lunar”) (possibly through Middle French lunaire (modern French lunaire (“lunar”)), from lūna (“the Moon; crescent shape”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *lewk- (“bright; to shine”)) + -is (suffix forming adjectives).
lunar.example: The scaphoid and lunar (wrist bones) are separate, whereas in Carnivores they are united perhaps to give greater strength to the wrist.
lunar.exampleSense: The middle bone of the proximal series of the carpus in the wrist, which is shaped like a half-moon.

inhibition.o: From Middle English inhibicioun, inhibicione from Old French inibicion, from Latin inhibitio. Morphologically inhibit + -ion.

incapable.o: Borrowed from Middle French incapable, equivalent to in- + capable.
incapable.example: A pint glass is incapable of holding more than a pint of liquid.

dia-.o: From Ancient Greek prefix δια- (dia-), from διά (diá, “through, across, by, over”).

short.o: From Middle English schort, short, from Old English sċeort, sċort (“short”), from Proto-West Germanic *skurt, from Proto-Germanic *skurtaz (“short”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker-. Doublet of shirt, skirt, and curt. Cognates Cognate with Scots short, schort (“short”), French court, Dutch kort, German kurz, Old High German scurz (“short”) (whence Middle High German schurz), Old Norse skorta (“to lack”) (whence Danish skorte), Albanian shkurt (“short, brief”), Latin curtus (“shortened, incomplete”) and Proto-Slavic *kortъkъ. See more at shirt.
short.example: Our meeting was a short six minutes today. Every day for the past month it’s been at least twenty minutes long.

pregnant.o:
adj: From Middle English preignant, from Old French preignant, pregnant, also prenant (compare archaic Modern French prégnant), and their source, Latin praegnāns (“pregnant”), probably from prae- (“pre-”) + *gnāscī, an archaic form of nāscī (“to be born”). Displaced Old English bearnēacen (literally "child-enlarged").

adj: Apparently from Middle French pregnant, preignant (“pressing, compelling”), present participle of prembre (“to press”), from Latin premere (“to press”).
pregnant.example: I went to the doctor and, guess what, I’m pregnant!
pregnant.exampleSense: Carrying developing offspring within the body.

vitamin.o: First use appears c. 1920, originally vitamine (1912), from Latin vīta (“life”) (see vital) + amine (see amino acids). Vitamine coined by Polish biochemist Casimir Funk after the initial discovery of aberic acid (thiamine), when it was thought that all such nutrients would be amines. The term had become ubiquitous by the time it was discovered that vitamin C, among others, had no amine component. In 1920, British biochemist Jack Drummond proposed that the final -e be dropped to deemphasize the amine reference. The ending -in was acceptable because it was used for natural substances of undefined composition. Drummond also introduced the lettering system of nomenclature (Vitamin A, B, C, etc.) at this same time.

can.o:
verb: From Middle English can, first and third person singular of connen, cunnen (“to be able, know how”), from Old English can(n), first and third person singular of cunnan (“to know how”), from Proto-West Germanic *kunnan, from Proto-Germanic *kunnaną, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵneh₃- (whence also know). Doublet of con. See also: canny, cunning.

noun: From Middle English canne, from Old English canne (“glass, container, cup, jar”), from Proto-Germanic *kannǭ (“can, tankard, mug, cup”).
can.example: Soup in a can lasts for years.
can.exampleSense: A container or vessel, especially for liquids, usually made of metal. A sealed metal container, cylindrical or cuboid in form, typically used to store preserved foods.

ease.o: From Middle English ese, eise, aise, from Anglo-Norman ese (“ease”), from Old French eise, aise (“elbow room; opportunity”), of uncertain and obscure origin. Apparently related to Provençal ais, Italian agio and asio, Sicilian aciu and Portuguese azo. Sometimes ascribed to Vulgar Latin *āsia or *āsium, possibly from Latin ānsa (“handle, haft”) or Frankish *ansiju (“handle, loophole, eyelet; cup-handle; arms akimbo, elbow room”), but more often derived from Vulgar Latin *adjace(m), from Latin adjacēns (“adjacent, neighbouring”), present participle of adjaceō (“lie next to, border on”), though the forms and senses are difficult to trace clearly. Alternatively, possibly from a non-Latin source such as Germanic or Celtic on the basis of the conflicting forms which appear in various Romance languages. Compare Old English īeþe (“easy”), Gothic 𐌰𐌶𐌴𐍄𐌹 (azēti, “ease; pleasure”), *𐌰𐌶𐌴𐍄𐍃 (*azēts, “easy”), Breton eaz, ez (“easy”), Irish adhais (“easy; leisure”). See also eath. The verb is from Middle English esen, ultimately of the same origin.
ease.example: His inheritance catapulted him into a life of ease.
ease.exampleSense: Comfort, a state or quality lacking unpleasantness Freedom from financial effort or worry; affluence.

jungle.o: Borrowed from Hindustani (Hindi जंगल (jaṅgal) / Urdu جَن٘گَل (jaṅgal)), from Sauraseni Prakrit 𑀚𑀁𑀕𑀮 (jaṃgala), from Sanskrit जङ्गल (jaṅgala, “arid or sterile region, desert”), from a substrate language. First appears c. 1776 in a translation by Nathaniel Halhed.
jungle.exampleSense: A place where people behave ruthlessly, unconstrained by law or morality.

nurture.o: From Middle English norture, noriture, from Old French norriture, norreture, from Late Latin nutritura (“nourishment”), from Latin nutrire (“to nourish”).
nurture.example: The problem is aggravated by the fact that much of the gay sub-culture is not conducive to the nurture of the radical ego integrity of which Erikson speaks.
nurture.exampleSense: The act or process of encouraging the growth or development of something.

surgeoncy.example: Before she is able to have her own practice, she has to complete her house surgeoncy.
surgeoncy.exampleSense: The office or employment of a surgeon, either in the naval or military service, or in a hospital as a resident or house officer.

surgeon.o: From Middle English surgien, borrowed from Anglo-Norman surgien, sirogen (Old French surgien et al.), from Vulgar Latin *chīrurgiānus, from Latin chīrūrgia (“surgery”), from chīrurgus (“surgeon”), borrowed from Ancient Greek χειρουργός (kheirourgós), from χείρ (kheír, “hand”) + ἔργον (érgon, “work”). Doublet of chirurgeon.
surgeon.example: The surgeon refused to operate because the patient was her son.
surgeon.exampleSense: One who performs surgery; a doctor who performs operations on people or animals.

juvenile.o: Borrowed from Latin iuvenīlis (“youthful; juvenile”), from iuvenis (“young; a youth”) + -īlis (suffix forming adjectives indicating a relationship or a pertaining to). Iuvenis is ultimately derived from Proto-Indo-European *h₂yuh₁en- (“young”), from *h₂óyu (“long life; lifetime”) (from *h₂ey- (“age; life”)) + *h₁én (“in”).
juvenile.example: [T]he juvenile justice system became firmly established as the legitimate institution for responding to juvenile delinquency and misconduct during 1900 and 1960.

delinquency.o: Borrowed from Late Latin dēlinquentia, derived from Latin dēlinquēns, present participle of dēlinquō (“to transgress, err”). By surface analysis, delinquent + -cy

delinquent.o: Borrowed from Middle French délinquant, ultimately from Latin delinquens, present participle of delinquo.
delinquent.example: The company made a new effort to collect delinquent payments.
delinquent.exampleSense: Of a payment or other financial obligation: late or otherwise unfulfilled.

dynamite.o: Coined by Alfred Nobel in 1867. Ultimately from Ancient Greek δύναμις (dúnamis, “power”) + -ite, most likely under the influence of dynamo or dynamic.
dynamite.example: Gradually the construction gangs cut and dynamited their way through some of the most difficult country in the world.
dynamite.exampleSense: To blow up with dynamite or other high explosive.

fertiliser.o: Alternative spelling of fertilizer. From fertilize + -er.

drainage.example: In the forward part of the cyclone, drainage katabasis is checked; but its highest intensity is observed in the rear part of the cyclone.

pine.o:
noun: From Middle English pyne, from Old English *pīne, from Proto-West Germanic *pīnā, from Latin pīnus, see there for more. Doublet of pinus. Possibly related to fat.

noun: From Middle English pyne, pine, probably from Old English *pīne (“pain”), from Proto-West Germanic *pīnā (“pain, torment, torture”), possibly from Latin poena (“punishment”), from Ancient Greek ποινή (poinḗ, “penalty, fine, bloodmoney”). Cognate to pain. Entered Germanic with Christianity; cognate to Middle Dutch pinen, Old High German pīnōn, Old Norse pína.

verb: From Middle English pynen, from Old English pīnian (“to torment”), from Proto-West Germanic *pīnōn, from Proto-West Germanic *pīnā (“pain, torment, torture”), from the noun (see above). Cognate with German peinigen (“to torment, torture”), Icelandic pína (“to torment”).
pine.example: The northern slopes were covered mainly in pine.
pine.exampleSense: Any coniferous tree of the genus Pinus.

foil.o:
noun: From Middle English foyle, from Middle French fueille, from Old French fueille (“plant leaf”), from Late Latin folia, the plural of folium, mistaken as a singular feminine. The literary sense is from the practice of backing a gem with metal foil to make it shine more brilliantly. Doublet of folio and folium, distantly also with phyllo and phyllon.

verb: From Middle English foilen (“spoil a scent trail by crossing it”), from Old French fouler (“tread on, trample”), ultimately from Latin fullō (“to trample, full”).

noun: From French foulis.

verb: From mnemonic acronym FOIL (“First Outside Inside Last”).

verb: See file.
foil.example: Blunt as the fencer's foils, which hit, but hurt not.
foil.exampleSense: A very thin sword with a blunted (or foiled) tip

giant.o: From Middle English geaunt, geant, from Old French geant, gaiant (Modern French géant) from Vulgar Latin *gagās, gagant-, from Latin gigās, gigant-, from Ancient Greek γίγας (gígas, “giant”). Cognate to giga- (“1,000,000,000”). Largely Displaced native Old English ent, eoten, and þyrs. Compare Modern English ent (“giant tree-man”), ettin ("a giant"), and thurse ("a giant").
giant.example: "It's barbarous, Norsus." "It's Rome," said the giant flatly.
giant.exampleSense: A very tall and large person.

gigantic.o: From Ancient Greek γιγαντικός (gigantikós), ultimately from γίγας (gígas, “giant”). According to the Poly-Olbion project coined by Michael Drayton in 1612.
gigantic.example: This band is going to be gigantic.

overhead.o:
adj: From Middle English owerheved, over-hed, over hede (adverb), from Old English oferhēafod (adverb), equivalent to over- + head. Compare German Low German overhoopt, överhoopt, German überhaupt. Piecewise doublet of overchief.

noun: (Sense 1) Abbreviation of overhead projector. : (Sense 2) Back-formation from overhead projector.
overhead.example: Place your luggage in the overhead lockers.
overhead.exampleSense: Located above, especially over the head.

perturb.o: From Late Middle English perturben (“to disturb (someone) mentally, disquiet; to cause disorder to (something), confuse; to hinder (something)”), from Old French perturber, and from its etymon Latin perturbāre, the present active infinitive of perturbō (“to confuse; to alarm, disturb, trouble, perturb”), from per- (intensifying prefix) + turbō (“to agitate, disturb, unsettle, perturb; to upset”) (from turba (“disorder, disturbance, turmoil”) (possibly from Ancient Greek τῠ́ρβη (tŭ́rbē, “confusion, disorder, tumult”), either from Pre-Greek, or Proto-Indo-European *(s)twerH- (“to agitate, stir up; to urge on, propel”)) + -ō (suffix forming infinitives of regular first-conjugation verbs)).

manipulative.example: Some children need manipulatives to learn math basics, Dr. Clements said, but only as a starting point.
manipulative.exampleSense: A manipulable object designed to demonstrate a mathematical concept.

blindness.o: From Middle English blyndnes, blyndnesse, from Old English blindnes (“blindness”), equivalent to blind + -ness.
blindness.example: A tormenting hunger shuddered through her and she wished she could put aside the power. Oh, to be as others were — blind in that safest of all blindnesses, living only the hypnoidal half-life into which birth-shock precipitated most humans.
blindness.exampleSense: Want of intellectual or moral discernment; mental darkness; ignorance, heedlessness.

albeit.o: From the Middle English expression al be it (that), itself shortened from althagh it be that (“although it be that”), and thus composed from al (“completely, entirely”) + be (3rd person singular present subjunctive of been (“to be”)) + it.
albeit.example: There’s an easy, albeit expensive, way to fix the national crisis in forensic crime labs.

refusal.o: From Middle English refusell; equivalent to refuse + -al.
refusal.example: Your refusal to carry out your duties resulted in your sacking.

browse.o: From Middle English browsen, from Old French brouster, broster (“to nibble off buds, sprouts, and bark; browse”), from brost (“a sprout, shoot, bud”), from a Germanic source, perhaps Frankish *brust (“shoot, bud”), from Proto-Germanic *brustiz (“bud, shoot”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰrews- (“to swell, sprout”). Cognate with Bavarian Bross, Brosst (“a bud”), Old Saxon brustian (“to sprout”). Doublet of brut, breast, and brush.
browse.example: I stopped in several bookstores to browse.
browse.exampleSense: To scan, to casually look through in order to find items of interest, especially without knowledge of what to look for beforehand.

hold back.example: He's a year older than his classmates, because he was held back in second grade.
hold back.exampleSense: To delay the progress of, especially in school.

subsidise.example: The government wants to subsidise healthcare products for the elderly.
subsidise.exampleSense: Non-Oxford British English standard spelling of subsidize.

subside.example: The tumults of war will subside.
subside.exampleSense: To fall into a state of calm; to be calm again; to settle down; to become tranquil; to abate.

subsidy.o: From Middle English subsidy, subsidie, from Anglo-Norman subsidee, subsidie, from Old French subside, from Latin subsidium (support, assistance), from subsido from sub- (“below”) + sīdō (“sit”).
subsidy.example: Manufacturing firms are supported by government subsidies in some countries.
subsidy.exampleSense: Financial support or assistance, such as a grant.

assemblage.o: Borrowed from French assemblage. By surface analysis, assemble + -age.

arbitrary.o: From Middle English arbitrarie, Latin arbitrārius (“arbitrary, uncertain”), from arbiter (“witness, on-looker, listener, judge, overseer”).
arbitrary.example: Benjamin Franklin's designation of "positive" and "negative" to different charges was arbitrary.
arbitrary.exampleSense: Based on individual discretion or judgment; not based on any objective distinction, perhaps even made at random.

meltdown.o: From melt (verb) + down (adverb), a deverbal from melt down (verb).
meltdown.example: Not only that, but wishcycling is playing a big role in the current global recycling meltdown.
meltdown.exampleSense: A situation being likened to a nuclear meltdown; a crisis.

insomnia.o: Borrowed from Latin īnsomnia, from Latin in- (“without”) + somnus (“sleep”, noun) + -ia, equivalent to in- + somn- + -ia.
insomnia.exampleSense: A sleeping disorder that is known for its symptoms of unrest and the inability to sleep.

wakefulness.example: Similarly, the brain-penetrating Hrh2 antagonist zolantidine had no effect on light-induced phase shift as shown for hamsters, or the lengths or distributions of NREM, REM and wakefulness states as shown on rats.

tension.o: Borrowed from Middle French tension, from Latin tēnsiō.
tension.example: My tensions with Eric over his alleged past actions have been fully resolved.
tension.exampleSense: The condition of being held in a state between two or more forces, which are acting in opposition to each other.

intensification.example: [...] moreover, the layout fortunately allows for the likely intensification of the suburban service.
intensification.exampleSense: The act or process of intensifying, or of making more intense.

mow.o:
verb: From Middle English mowen (participle mowen), from Old English māwan (past tense mēow, past participle māwen), from Proto-West Germanic *māan, from Proto-Germanic *mēaną, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂meh₁- (“to mow, reap”). Cognate with Saterland Frisian mjo (“to mow”), Dutch maaien (“to mow”), German mähen (“to mow”), Luxembourgish méien (“to mow”), Danish meje (“to mow”), Swedish meja (“to mow”); see also Hittite [script needed] (ḫamešḫa, “spring/early summer”, literally “mowing time”), Latin metō (“to harvest, mow”), Ancient Greek ἀμάω (amáō, “to mow”).

noun: From Middle English mowe, from Old French moe (“grimace”), from Frankish *mauwa (“pout, protruding lip”), from Proto-Germanic *mawwō (“muff, sleeve”). Akin to Middle Dutch mouwe (“protruding lip”). Doublet of moue ("pout").

noun: From Middle English mowe, form Old English mūga, mūha, from Proto-West Germanic *mūgō, *mūhō, from Proto-Germanic *mūgô, *mūhō; perhaps connected to Ancient Greek μύκων (múkōn, “heap”). Cognate with Norwegian muge (“heap, crowd, flock”).
mow.example: I consider it would engender a stiff, tame, cautious mode of play, with only now and then a mow, or a chopping hit.
mow.exampleSense: A shot played with a sweeping or scythe-like motion.

tenant.o:
noun: From Middle English tenaunt, from Anglo-Norman tenaunt and Old French tenant, present participle of tenir (“to hold”), from Latin tenēre (“hold, keep”).

noun: Possibly just a modification of tenet, but note obsolete tenent (“tenet”).
tenant.example: Long even before the last tenant had occupied it, the room had been regarded with fear and aversion, and the end of that last tenant had in no way lightened the gloom that hung about the place.
tenant.exampleSense: One who holds a lease (a tenancy).

tenancy.example: Most gay people know oppresion as fear of losing a job, losing a tenancy or family ties.
tenancy.exampleSense: Synonym of lease (an interest in land, its related contract or the document containing that contract); more commonly used when a lease is short-term or has a periodic rent that is not merely nominal.

overplay.example: The first few shots went wonderfully, but Robin overplayed the last and lost.
overplay.exampleSense: To accidentally hit (one's golf ball) beyond "the green".

affluence.o: From Old French affluence, from Latin affluentia. Only relation to antonym indigence is common Latinate suffix; affluence only acquired sense of wealth in 16th century English and French, while indigentia meant “poverty” or “lack” in Latin.
affluence.example: They had achieved affluence, but aspired to true wealth.

affluent.o: Borrowed from Middle French affluent, borrowed in turn from Latin affluentem, accusative singular of affluēns, present active participle of affluō (“flow to or towards; overflow with”), from ad (“to, towards”) + fluō (“flow”) (cognate via latter to fluid, flow). Sense of “wealthy” (plentiful flow of goods) c. 1600, which also led to nominalization affluence. By surface analysis, af- + fluent.
affluent.example: The Upper East Side is an affluent neighborhood in New York City.
affluent.exampleSense: Abounding in goods or riches; having a moderate level of material wealth.

sobering.o: present participle and gerund of sober. Inherited from Middle English sober, from Old French sobre, from Latin sōbrius, from se- (“without”) + ebrius (“intoxicated”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁egʷʰ- (“drink”). In the sense "not drunk," displaced native undrunken, from Old English undruncen.
sobering.example: It was a sobering thought that I had almost killed myself. That was something I wouldn't soon do on purpose again.
sobering.exampleSense: Causing more sober thought or concern.

sober.o: Inherited from Middle English sober, from Old French sobre, from Latin sōbrius, from se- (“without”) + ebrius (“intoxicated”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁egʷʰ- (“drink”). In the sense "not drunk," displaced native undrunken, from Old English undruncen.
sober.example: The night air may have sobered him a bit by the time they got back to Beattock.

cistern.o: From Middle English cisterne, from Old French cisterne (Modern French citerne) from Latin cisterna, from cista (“box”), from Ancient Greek κίστη (kístē, “box”). Doublet of cisterna.
cistern.example: It is possible to connect your tank to your toilet cistern and/or garden, so that even if the water is not drinkable it still can be used productively to make major water savings.
cistern.exampleSense: In a flush toilet, the container in which the water used for flushing is held; a toilet tank.

equation.o: From Old French, from Latin aequātiō (“an equalizing”). Morphologically equate + -ion
equation.example: The cultural equation of love with suffering is similar to the equation of love with an experience of both transcendence and consummation in which love is affirmed in an ostentatious display of self loss.
equation.exampleSense: The act or process of equating two or more things, or the state of those things being equal (that is, identical).

take advantage of.example: He took advantage of the swimming pool every day of his visit.
take advantage of.exampleSense: To use or make use of.

petty.o: The adjective is derived from Middle English peti, pety (“little, small; minor”) [and other forms], from Anglo-Norman petit, Middle French petit, and Old French peti, petit, pitet (“young; little, small; inferior; insignificant”) (modern French petit), ultimately of imitative origin. It is no longer thought that the word is derived from Celtic. Doublet of petit and petite. The noun is derived from the adjective.
petty.example: My cousin is so petty—I forgot his birthday and he's been making snarky comments all week.
petty.exampleSense: Inclined to cause frustration or annoyance to others out of spite over minor grievances; extremely vindictive.

dilapidate.o:
verb: From Latin dilapidō (“to scatter, consume, throw away”) + -ate (verb-forming suffix), from dis- (“asunder”) + lapidō (“to stone”), from lapis (“stone”). Compare French dilapider.

adj: Learned borrowing from Latin dīlapidātus, perfect passive participle of dilapidō (“squander, consume, throw away”), see Etymology 1 and -ate (adjective-forming suffix) for more.
dilapidate.example: The patrimony of the bishopric of Oxon was much dilapidated.

mentality.example: 1978, Edward Proffitt, "Romanticism, Bicamerality, and the Evolution of the Brain", The Wordsworth Circle, Vol. 9, No.1, reprinted in Kuijsten, 2016, page 129.
mentality.exampleSense: The characteristics of a mind described as a system of distinctive structures and processes based in biology, language, or culture, etc.; a mental system.

readily.o: From Middle English redily, rediliche. By surface analysis, read(i) + -ly.
readily.example: The suspect readily answered all questions the police officers asked him.
readily.exampleSense: Without unwillingness or hesitation; showing readiness.

arrival.o: From Middle English arivaile, arivaille, arrival, arryvaile, arryvaylle, aryvayle, aryvaylle, from Middle French arrivaille, from arriver; equivalent to arrive + -al.
arrival.example: The early arrival of the bride created a stir.
arrival.exampleSense: The act of arriving (reaching a certain place).

address.o: From Middle English adressen (“to radise erect, adorn”), from Old French adrecier (“to straighten, address”) (modern French adresser), from Proto-Romance *addīrēctiāre, from ad- (“to; towards”) + *dīrēctiāre (“to guide; to direct”), from Latin dīrēctus (“straight; right”), from dīrigō (“to lay straight; to direct”), itself from regō (“to govern, to rule”). Cognate with Spanish aderezar (“to garnish; dress (food); to add spices”).
address.example: The President's address is 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue NW in Washington, D.C.
address.exampleSense: Direction. A description of the location of a property, usually with at least a street name and number, name of a town, and now also a postal code; such a description as superscribed for direction on an envelope or letter.

animosity.o: From French animosité, from Latin animositas (“courage, spirit, vehemence”), from animosus, from animus (“courage, spirit, mind”); see animose, animate.

softball.example: This will give you someone with whom you can trade softball complaints, which any veteran game-goer will tell you is the key to a good time.
softball.exampleSense: A game similar to baseball but played with a larger and softer ball which can be thrown overhand or underhand.

brick.o: From Late Middle English brik, bryke, bricke, from Middle Low German and Middle Dutch bricke ("cracked or broken brick; tile-stone"; modern Dutch brik), ultimately related to Proto-West Germanic *brekan (“to break”), whence also Old French briche and French brique (“brick”). Compare also German Low German Brickje (“small board, tray”). Related to break. The social media slang sense derives from memes about building up one's feed “brick by brick”, analogizing bricks with reels that inform the algorithm.
brick.example: This wall is made of bricks.
brick.exampleSense: A hardened rectangular block of mud, clay etc., used for building.

tidy.o: From Middle English tidy, tydy, tidi (“timely, seasonal, opportune”), from tide (“time”) + -y. Cognate with Saterland Frisian tiedig (“timely, early”), Dutch tijdig (“timely”), German Low German tiedig (“timely”), German zeitig (“seasonal, timely”), Danish tidig (“timely”), Swedish tidig (“timely”).
tidy.example: She always kept her desk immaculately tidy; nothing was ever out of place.

makeover.example: This room is a mess; it needs a makeover.
makeover.exampleSense: A major change in the use of something, or in the appearance of something or someone; a radical transformation.

vandalism.o: Borrowed from French vandalisme, first used by Henri Grégoire to decry the pillage and destruction of art in the course of the French Revolution, in reference to the East Germanic tribe of the Vandals, which looted Rome in 455. By surface analysis, vandal + -ism.
vandalism.example: As we turned down the street I was appalled by the vandalism: spray paint and smashed windows that were everywhere.
vandalism.exampleSense: Willful damage to or destruction of any property, such as graffiti or defacement.

ghetto.o: Borrowed from the name of the Venetian Ghetto, whose etymology and original source language is uncertain. Compare Italian ghetto.
ghetto.example: Invent is undoubtedly the wrong word, but the push from government was crucial in getting the Internet out of its academic ghetto.
ghetto.exampleSense: An isolated, self-contained, segregated subsection, area or field of interest; often of minority or specialist interest.

gauge.o: From Middle English gauge, gaugen, from Anglo-Norman, Old Northern French gauger (compare Modern French jauger from Old French jaugier), from gauge (“gauging rod”), from Frankish *galgā (“measuring rod, pole”), from Proto-Germanic *galgô (“pole, stake, cross”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰalgʰ-, *ǵʰalg- (“perch, long switch”). Cognate with Old High German galgo, Old Frisian galga, Old English ġealga (“cross-beam, gallows”), Old Norse galgi (“cross-beam, gallows”), Old Norse gelgja (“pole, perch”). Doublet of gallows.
gauge.example: I'm talking about cocking a gauge in between your eyes.
gauge.exampleSense: A shotgun (synecdoche for 12 gauge shotgun, the most common chambering for combat and hunting shotguns).

pour.o: From Middle English pouren (“to pour”), of uncertain origin. Perhaps from Old Northern French purer (“to sift (grain), pour out (water)”), from Latin pūrō (“to purify”), from pūrus (“pure”). Compare Middle Dutch afpuren (“to pour off, drain”). To pour displaced several Middle English verbs: * schenchen, schenken (“to pour”), from Old English sċenċan (“to pour out”) and Old Norse skenkja, from Proto-Germanic *skankijaną. Compare dialectal English shink, skink. * yeten, from Old English ġēotan (“to pour”), from Proto-Germanic *geutaną. * birlen (“to pour, serve drink to”), from Old English byrelian (“to pour, serve drink to”). * hellen (“to pour, pour out”), from Old Norse hella (“to pour out, incline”). * temen (“to pour out, empty”), from Old Norse tœma (“to pour out, empty”). Compare archaic English teem.
pour.example: to pour out sand or dust.
pour.exampleSense: To cause (liquid, or liquid-like substance) to flow in a stream, either out of a container or into it.

insulate.o: From Latin īnsula (“isle, island”) + -ate (verb-forming suffix) or from Late Latin īnsulātus (“made an island”), see etymology at -ate. First attested in the 16th century; the general verb īnsulō (“insulate”) is attested only in New Latin and postdates the English term, but influence from an otherwise unattested Medieval Latin counterpart cannot be ruled out. Piecewise doublet of isolate.
insulate.example: Ceramic can be used to insulate power lines.
insulate.exampleSense: To separate a body or material from others, e.g. by non-conductors to prevent the transfer of electricity, heat, etc.

pageantry.example: The world seemed decked for some holiday or prouder pageantry, with silken streamers flying, ...
pageantry.exampleSense: A pageant; a colourful show or display, as in a pageant.

vagina.example: The epithelial lining of the vagina consists of many layers of flattened cells. Changes in the condition of these cells during the menstrual cycle can be detected by swabbing the lining and looking at the cells under a microscope.
vagina.exampleSense: A sex organ leading from the vulval vestibule/urogenital sinus to the cervix of the uterus for copulation and birth in female therian mammals.

take off.example: If you take off for Thanksgiving you must work Christmas and vice versa.
take off.exampleSense: To absent oneself from (work or other responsibility), especially with permission.

crash course.example: He got a crash course in babysitting when his sister dropped off his nephew for the afternoon.
crash course.exampleSense: A quick, intense course of learning, especially one which is informal or hurried.

straightforward.example: For the most part they are of straightforward design and the largest group is the ex-Prussian "T16" Class 0-10-0 of Type "94", [...].

cyber.o: Originally from cybernetics, before becoming a stand-alone word.
cyber.example: ...a cross between metal, punk, goth, cyber, and rock.

truck.o:
noun: Perhaps a shortening of truckle, related to Latin trochus (“iron hoop, wheel”) from Ancient Greek τροχός (trokhós).

verb: From Middle English truken, troken, trukien, from Old English trucian (“to fail, run short, deceive, disappoint”), from Proto-West Germanic *trokōn (“to fail, miss, lack”), from Proto-Indo-European *derew-, *derwu- (“to tear, wrap, reap”), from Proto-Indo-European *der- (“to flay, split”). Cognate with Middle Low German troggelen (“to cheat, deceive, swindle”), Dutch troggelen (“to extort”), German dialectal truggeln (“to flatter, fawn”).

verb: From dialectal truck, truk, trokk, probably of North Germanic origin, compare Norwegian dialectal trokka, trakka (“to stamp, trample, go to and fro”), Danish trykke (“to press, press down, crush, squeeze”), Swedish trycka. More at thrutch.

verb: From Middle English trukien, from unrecorded Anglo-Norman and Old French words, from Latin trocāre, from Frankish *trokan. Related to Etymology 2.
