noun: From Middle English ware, from Old Norse vár (“spring”), from Proto-Germanic *wazrą. Cognate with Icelandic vor (“spring”), Swedish vår (“spring”), Danish vår (“spring”), Scots ware, wair (“spring”).
ware.example: Artisans sell their ware in the historic district at the lower level of the Soldier's Barracks.
ware.exampleSense: Goods or a type of goods offered for sale or use.

lobster.o: From Middle English loppestere, lopster, from Old English loppestre, lopustre, lopystre, of uncertain origin. Some believe it to be a corruption of Latin lō̆custa (“grasshopper, locust”) + the Old English feminine agent suffix -estre. In Latin, the phrase lō̆custa marīna (literally "sea-grasshopper") signified a type of crustacean (shrimp or lobster). Alternatively, from Old English lobbe, loppe (“spider”) + the Old English feminine agent suffix -estre, equivalent to lop + -ster.
lobster.example: 1991, Markus Grosskopf, "Shit and Lobster", Helloween, Pink Bubbles Go Ape.
lobster.exampleSense: A crustacean of the Nephropidae family, dark green or blue-black in colour turning bright red when cooked, with a hard shell and claws, which is used as a seafood.

vineyard.o: Equivalent to vine + yard; from Middle English vyneȝerd (circa 1300), following earlier Old English wīnġeard (“wine yard, vine yard”), with vine (from Old French vigne (“vine, vineyard”), from Latin vīnea) replacing native Old English wīn (“wine, vine”). The earlier wīnġeard may have had the sense of “vine” already, with /w/ → /v/ facilitated by common v-/w- interchange. Compare Dutch wijngaard (literally “wine garden”) and German Weingarten alongside contracted Wingert. (Dutch gaard, German Garten are cognate to English yard.)
vineyard.example: The vineyard of Château Margaux stands as the producer of one of the world's greatest and most sought-after red wines.
vineyard.exampleSense: A grape plantation, especially one used in the production of wine.

vine.o: From Middle English vyne, from Anglo-Norman vigne, from Vulgar Latin vīnia, from Latin vīnea (“vines in a vineyard”), from vīneus (“related to wine”), from vīnum (“wine”), from Proto-Italic *wīnom, from Proto-Indo-European *wóyh₁nom (“vine, wine”), from *weh₁y- (“to twist, wrap”). Doublet of wine.
vine.example: They picked the grapes off the vine.
vine.exampleSense: The climbing plant that produces grapes.

jetty.o:
noun: The noun is derived from Late Middle English gete, jette, jetti (“projecting upper storey of a building, overhang; breakwater, pier, jetty”), from Anglo-Norman geté, getee, getté, and Middle French geté, getee, jeté (“projecting upper storey of a building; breakwater, pier”) (modern French jetée), a noun use of the past participle of geter, jeter, from Old French geter, jeter (“to throw”) from Late Latin iectāre, the present active infinitive of iectō (“to throw”), probably from Latin iactō (“to cast, hurl, throw”), from iaciō (“to cast, hurl, throw”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(H)yeh₁- (“to throw”)) + -tō (frequentative suffix). Compare jet (“(obsolete) protruding part”), jutty. The verb is derived from the noun.

adj: From jet (“(obsolete) protruding part, projection”, noun) or jet (“to jut, project, protrude”, verb) + -y (suffix forming adjectives with the sense ‘having the quality of’).

adj: From jet (“hard, black form of coal; colour of jet coal”, noun) + -y (suffix forming adjectives with the sense ‘having the quality of’).

verb: From jet (“(obsolete) to strut; to walk with a lofty or haughty gait”, verb) + -y (suffix added for metrical reasons, or forming informal terms).

wharf.o: From Middle English wharf, from Old English hwearf (“heap, embankment, wharf”); related to Old English hweorfan (“to turn”), Old Saxon hwerf (whence German Werft and Warft), Dutch werf, Old High German hwarb (“a turn”), hwerban (“to turn”), Old Norse hvarf (“circle”), and Ancient Greek καρπός (karpós, “wrist”).
wharf.example: Commerce pushes its wharves into the sea.
wharf.exampleSense: An artificial landing place for ships on a riverbank or shore.

pastoral.o: From Middle French, Old French pastoral, from Latin pāstōrālis, from pāstor (“shepherd”), + adjective suffix -ālis.
pastoral.example: He wanders west as far as Memphis, a solitary migrant upon that flat and pastoral landscape.
pastoral.exampleSense: Relating to rural life and scenes, in particular of poetry.

pastor.o: From Middle English pastour, from Old French pastor (Modern French pasteur), from Latin pāstor.
pastor.example: As they pastored churches in Georgia and Texas, they supported talented black politicians who were unable to win statewide office.
pastor.exampleSense: To serve a congregation as pastor

butter.o:
noun: PIE word *gʷṓws Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *gʷṓws Proto-Hellenic *gʷous Ancient Greek βοῦς (boûs) Proto-Indo-European *tewh₂- Proto-Indo-European *-rós Proto-Indo-European *tuh₂rós Proto-Hellenic *tūrós Ancient Greek τυρός (turós) Ancient Greek βούτῡρον (boútūron)bor. Latin būtȳrumbor. Proto-West Germanic *buterā Old English butere Middle English buter English butter From Middle English buter, butter, from Old English butere, from Proto-West Germanic *buterā, from Latin būtȳrum, from Ancient Greek βούτῡρον (boútūron, “cow cheese”), compound of βοῦς (boûs, “ox, cow”) and τῡρός (tūrós, “cheese”). Cognate with Dutch boter and German Butter.

noun: From butt + -er.
butter.example: Butters such as cocoa, illippe, kokum, mango, murumuru, sal (shorea) and shea occur naturally and are obtained directly from the plant.
butter.exampleSense: Any of various substances made from other (especially plant-based) oils or fats, used in moisturizers, cosmetics, etc.

maize.o: Borrowed from Spanish maíz, from Taíno *mahis, *mahisi, from Proto-Arawak *marikɨ. Cognate with Lokono marisi, Wayuu maiki.

fertile.o: From Middle English, from Middle French fertile, from Old French fertile, from Latin fertilis (“fruitful, fertile”), from ferō (“to bear, carry”).
fertile.example: Most women at the age of fifty are not fertile.

legendary.o: From legend + -ary; from Medieval Latin legendārius. Earlier it was a noun meaning "a collection of legends" (1510s) (Medieval Latin legendārium, Old French legendier), from Latin legenda. In English, both the noun and the adjective first appeared in the 16th century.
legendary.example: And it was a fitting victory for Liverpool as Anfield celebrated the 100th anniversary of the birth of their legendary Scottish manager Bill Shankly.
legendary.exampleSense: Having unimaginable greatness; excellent to such an extent to evoke stories.

exercise.o: From Middle English exercise, from Old French exercise, from Latin exercitium.
exercise.example: The teacher told us that the next exercise is to write an essay.
exercise.exampleSense: Any activity designed to develop or hone a skill or ability.

roger.o:
intj: From Roger, used circa 1940 in UK and US military communication to represent "R" when spelling out a word. "R" is the first letter in received, used to acknowledge understanding a message. "Roger" for "received" was in spoken usage in air traffic radio parlance by 1950.

verb: Possibly from Old High German Hrotger via Shelta roger.
roger.example: The Explorer radio operator rogered receipt of the War Room's signal.

endeavour.example: And such were Prais'd who but endeavour'd well.

trite.o:
adj: From Latin trītus (“worn out”), perfect passive participle of terō (“to wear away, wear out”).

noun: Unadapted borrowing from Latin tritē, from Ancient Greek τρίτη (trítē, literally “third [string]”).
trite.example: McPedro the cactus: How to woo a woman! On yehr fahrst date, don’t bring her cut flowers! That’s inhumane! And trite!
trite.exampleSense: Often in reference to a word or phrase: used so many times that it is commonplace, or no longer interesting or effective; worn out, hackneyed.

galvanic.o: From French galvanique, named after Italian physiologist Luigi Aloisio Galvani (1737–1798) + -ique.
galvanic.example: [S]he was quivering like a galvanic battery with the suppressed force of some powerful emotion.
galvanic.exampleSense: Of or pertaining to galvanism; electric.

galvanise.o: From French galvaniser, from galvanisme, named after Italian physiologist Luigi Aloisio Galvani (1737–1798). By surface analysis, galvano- + -ise.

contradictory.o: Borrowed from Late Latin contradictorius, from Latin contradico. Equivalent to contradict + -ory.
contradictory.example: Our attitudes toward sharks are contradictory. We fear them and yet we seek them out.

rigour.o: From Middle English rigour, from Anglo-Norman, from Old French rigor, from Latin rigor (“stiffness, rigidity, rigor, cold, harshness”), from rigere (“to be rigid”). Compare French rigueur.

maverick.o: Named after Texan lawyer and politician Samuel Maverick (1803–1870), who refused to brand his cattle. For probable origin and meaning, see Maverick. The poker noun sense (“a queen and a jack as a starting hand in Texas hold ’em”) may be from the theme song of the US Western television series Maverick (1957–1962), which says of the eponymous protagonist that “[g]amblin’ is his game” and that he is “livin’ on jacks and queens”.
maverick.example: Long Bill was a graduate of the camp and trail. Luck and thrift, a cool head, and a telescopic eye for mavericks had raised him from cowboy to be a cowman.

set off.example: What a tragedy, that someone would set off a bomb in a crowded place.
set off.exampleSense: To cause to explode, let off.

anarchy.o: From New Latin anarchia, from Ancient Greek ἀναρχία (anarkhía). By surface analysis, an- + -archy.
anarchy.example: It was total anarchy in the clothes shop on Black Friday as soon as they opened the doors.

come to terms with.example: Until he comes to terms with the likelihood of failure, he will not succeed.
come to terms with.exampleSense: To accept or resign oneself to something emotionally painful.

dictate.o:
noun: First attested in 1581; borrowed from Latin dictātum (“a thing said, something dictated”), substantivized from the nominative neuter singular of dictātus, the perfect passive participle of dictō (“pronounce or declare repeatedly; dictate”), frequentative of dīcō (“say, speak”). Doublet of diktat.

verb: First attested in 1577; borrowed from Latin dictātus, perfect passive participle of dictō (“to pronounce or declare repeatedly; to dictate”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), frequentative of dīcō (“say, speak”).
dictate.example: The French teacher dictated a passage from Victor Hugo.
dictate.exampleSense: To speak in order for someone to write down the words.

dictator.o: From Latin dictātor (“a chief magistrate”), from dictō (“dictate, prescribe”), from dīcō (“say, speak”). By surface analysis, dictate + -or, literally “one who dictates”. Compare Old English tictator (“absolute ruler of the Roman Republic”).
dictator.example: "The reason why Xi Jinping got very upset in terms of when I shot that balloon down with two box cars full of spy equipment in it was he didn't know it was there," Biden said.
dictator.exampleSense: A totalitarian leader of a country, nation, or government.

dictatorship.example: There were no elections during Franco's dictatorship.
dictatorship.exampleSense: A government which exercises autocratic rule.

proletarian.o: From Latin proletarius (“a man whose only wealth is his offspring, or whose sole service to the state is as father”), from proles (“offspring, posterity”).

proletariat.o: Borrowed from French prolétariat, from prolétaire + -at, from Latin proletārius, from prōlēt- (“offspring”) + -ārius, from stem of prōlēs, from pro- + *olēs (“growth”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂el- (“to grow, nourish”). By surface analysis, Latin prōlēt- + -ary + -at.
proletariat.example: Of all the classes that stand face to face with the bourgeoisie to-day, the proletariat alone is a really revolutionary class. The other classes decay and finally disappear in the face of modern industry; the proletariat is its special and essential product.
proletariat.exampleSense: Wage earners collectively; people who own no capital and depend on their labour for survival; the working class, especially when seen as engaged in a class struggle with the bourgeoisie (“the capital-owning class”).

assembly.o: From Middle English assemblee, from Anglo-Norman asemblee (Old French asemblee, French assemblée). By surface analysis, assemble + -y.
assembly.example: In order to change the bearing, you must first remove the gearbox assembly.
assembly.exampleSense: A set of pieces that work together in unison as a mechanism or device.

empower.example: Regulations have been made under the Civil Aviation Acts of 1949, 1980 and 1982 which empower Inspectors of Accidents to do these things.
empower.exampleSense: To give permission, power, or the legal right to do something.

tangential.example: The archoplasm divides and forms a very large spindle which first lies tangential to the surface of the nucleus.
tangential.exampleSense: Merely touching, positioned as a tangent.

tricky.example: A tricky salesman can sell anything.

grapple.o:
verb: From Middle English *grapplen (“to seize, lay hold of”), from Old English *græpplian (“to seize”) (compare Old English ġegræppian (“to seize”)), from Proto-Germanic *graipilōną, *grabbalōną (“to seize”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰrebʰ- (“to take, seize, rake”), equivalent to grab + -le. Cognate with Dutch grabbelen (“to grope, scramble, scrabble”), German grabbeln (“to rummage, grope about”) and grapsen, grapschen (“to seize, grasp, grabble”). Influenced in some senses by grapple (“tool with claws or hooks”, noun) (see below). See further at grasp.

noun: From Middle English *grapple, *graple, from Old French grappil (“a ship's grapple”) (compare Old French grappin (“hook”)), from Old French grape, grappe, crape (“hook”), of Germanic origin, from Frankish *krappō (“hook”), from Proto-Indo-European *grep- (“hook”), *gremb- (“crooked, uneven”), from Proto-Indo-European *ger- (“to turn, bend, twist”). See further at grape. Influenced in some senses by grapple (“seize”, verb) (see above).

noun: Blend of grape + apple.
grapple.example: The men scrambled down the three ropes that had been grappled up the shaft.
grapple.exampleSense: To fasten, as with a grapple; (by extension) to fix; to join indissolubly.

mob.o:
noun: From Middle English mob, short for mobile, from Latin mōbile (vulgus) (“fickle (crowd)”).

noun: Alteration of mab.

noun: Clipping of mobile. The video-gaming sense is sometimes reported as an abbreviation of man or beast or of mobile object, but these are backronyms.
mob.example: Had every Athenian citizen been a Socrates, every Athenian assembly would still have been a mob.
mob.exampleSense: A large or disorderly group of people; especially one bent on riotous or destructive action.

dedicated.o: simple past and past participle of dedicate. From Middle English dedicaten (“to dedicate”), from dedicat(e) (“dedicated”, also used as the past participle of dedicaten) + -en (verb-forming suffix), from Latin dēdicātus, the perfect passive participle of dēdicō (“to dedicate, proclaim”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

pedal.o: Borrowed from French pédale, Latin pedāl(is). By surface analysis, ped- + -al.
pedal.example: There are three pedals on manual cars, two on automatics.
pedal.exampleSense: A lever operated by one's foot that is used to control or power a machine or mechanism, such as a bicycle or piano.

disseminate.o: Borrowed from Latin dissēminātus, the perfect passive participle of dissēminō (“to broadcast, disseminate”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), further from dis- (“asunder, in all directions”) + sēminō (“to plant, sow”), from sēmen (“seed”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix). See also Middle English disseminat(e) (“disseminated”).
disseminate.example: The values of the human rights movement have disseminated throughout the world.

charcoal.o: From Middle English charcole, from charren (“to change, turn”) + cole (“coal”), from Old English cierran (“to change, turn”) + col (“coal”). By surface analysis, char (Etymology 3 [verb]) + coal.
charcoal.example: But through the oligopoly, charcoal fuel proliferated throughout London's trades and industries. By the 1200s, brewers and bakers, tilemakers, glassblowers, pottery producers, and a range of other craftsmen all became hour-to-hour consumers of charcoal.
charcoal.exampleSense: impure carbon obtained by destructive distillation of wood or other organic matter, that is, heating it in the absence of oxygen.

trailer.o: From trail + -er. The film sense derives from the fact that previews were formerly shown after the main feature, rather than before as is usual today, that is trailing after the main feature.
trailer.example: At the end of the day, we put the snowmobiles back on the trailer.
trailer.exampleSense: An unpowered wheeled vehicle (not a caravan or camper) that is towed behind another, and used to carry equipment, etc., that cannot be carried in the leading vehicle.

culvert.o: Origin obscure, with a number of possible etymologies suggested: * a dialectal word, * a word related to the name of the now-forgotten inventor, * a derivation from French couvert (“covered”), although couvert is not used in this sense and the French translation of culvert is ponceau or buse de drainage, * a derivation from an unrecorded Dutch word, possibly *coul-vaart, a combination of Dutch coul-, from French couler (“to flow”), and Dutch vaart (“a trip by boat, a canal”).
culvert.example: A raft of twigs stayed upon a stone, suddenly detached itself, and floated towards the culvert.
culvert.exampleSense: A channel crossing under a road or railway for the draining of water.

vigorous.o: From Anglo-Norman vigrus, from Old French vigoros (French vigoureux), from Medieval Latin vigorosus, from Latin vigor. Doublet of vigoroso.
vigorous.example: Life in the country will be fuller, richer, and more comfortful, because it is freer, healthier, and more vigorous.

incent.o: Back-formation from incentive. Clipping of incentivize
incent.example: We try to incent people to do it earlier, which levels the load.
incent.exampleSense: To provide an incentive to (a person or organization).

fiscal.o:
adj: From Middle French fiscal, from Latin fiscus (“treasury”) – see fiscus and fisc.

noun: From Spanish fiscal, ultimately from Latin fiscus (“treasury”).

noun: After Afrikaans fiskaal (“public official, hangman”).
fiscal.example: The allotment is $22 million less than the Pentagon spent on military bands in fiscal 1990.

favourable.o: From Middle English favourable, from Old French favorable, from Latin favōrābilis, from favor. By surface analysis, favour + -able.
favourable.example: The rain stopped at a favourable time for our tennis match.
favourable.exampleSense: Convenient or at a suitable time; opportune.

weathered.o: simple past and past participle of weather. From Middle English weder, wedir, from Old English weder, from Proto-West Germanic *wedr, from Proto-Germanic *wedrą, from Proto-Indo-European *wedʰrom (=*we-dʰrom), from *h₂weh₁- (“to blow”). Cognates Cognate with Scots wather (“weather”), Saterland Frisian Weeder (“weather”), Cimbrian bèttar (“weather”), Dutch weder, weer (“weather”), German Wetter (“weather”), Low German Weder (“weather”), Luxembourgish Wieder (“weather”), Yiddish וועטער (veter, “weather”), Danish vejr (“weather”), Faroese, Icelandic veður (“weather”), Norwegian Bokmål vær (“weather”), Norwegian Nynorsk veder, vêr (“weather”), Swedish väder (“weather”); also more distantly related to Russian вёдро (vjódro, “fair weather”) and perhaps Albanian vrëndë (“light rain”). Other cognates include Sanskrit निर्वाण (nirvāṇa, “blown or put out, extinguished”).
weathered.example: In this scene Lupita, the neophyte, is counselled by more weathered professionals about the rules and regulations of whoring.

impoverish.o: From Middle English empoverishen, impoverishen, empoverischen, enpoverisshen, Anglo-Norman empoveriss-, from Old French empoverir, from em- + povre, from Latin pauper (“poor”) (English poor).
impoverish.example: That exuberant crop quickly impoverishes any fertile soil.
impoverish.exampleSense: To weaken in quality; to deprive of some strength or richness.

radically.example: The reasons for this growing disconnect are myriad and complex but the situation is exacerbated by the reality that those English players who do smash through our game's "glass ceiling" command radically inflated transfer fees.
radically.exampleSense: In a radical manner; fundamentally; very.

stagnant.o: From French stagnant, from Latin stagnans, present participle of stagno (“to form a pool of standing water”).

prohibitive.o: From Middle English prohibitif, prohibityve, from Medieval Latin prohibitīvus, from prohibit-, past-participle stem of Latin prohibēre. By surface analysis, prohibit + -ive.
prohibitive.example: Some countries are more prohibitive than others when it comes to hot topics like euthanasia and cloning.
prohibitive.exampleSense: Tending to prohibit, preclude, or disallow.

lotus.o: Unadapted borrowing from Latin lōtus, from Ancient Greek λωτός (lōtós). Doublet of lote. First attested in the 1540s. Ultimately from Hebrew לוֹט (lōṭ, “myrrh”, literally “covering, envelope”).
lotus.example: Since the '60s ended abruptly on January 1, 1970, everyone, protestors, police and all, fell to the ground in a full lotus.

plume.o:
noun: From Late Middle English plum, plume (“feather; plumage”), from Anglo-Norman plum, plume, from Old French plume, plome (“feather, plumage”), from Latin plūma (“feather, plumage”) (compare Late Latin plūma (“pen, quill”)), from Proto-Italic *plouksmā, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *plewk- (“to fly”). Doublet of pluma.

verb: Sense 1 (“to adorn, cover, or furnish with feathers or plumes”) is derived from Anglo-Norman plumer (“to cover with or provide with feathers”), or its etymon Latin plūmāre, the present active infinitive of plūmō (“to grow feathers, to fledge; to cover with feathers, to feather; to embroider with a feathery pattern”) (and compare Late Latin plūmō (“to attach feathers to arrows; of a hawk: to pluck the feathers from prey; (figurative) to celebrate, praise”)), from plūma (“feather; plumage; down”) (see etymology 1) + -ō (suffix forming regular first-conjugation verbs). Senses 2–4 (“to arrange and preen the feathers of; to congratulate (oneself) proudly; to strip of feathers”) are from Late Middle English plumen (“to remove the feathers from a bird; of a hawk: to pluck the feathers or the head from prey”) [and other forms], from Anglo-Norman and Middle French plumer (“to remove the feathers from a bird; to pull out (hairs, especially from a moustache); to rob”), from plūma (see etymology 1). Sense 5 (“to fan out or spread in a cloud”) is derived from plume (noun).
plume.example: Leave no black plume as a token of that lie thy soul hath spoken!
plume.exampleSense: A feather of a bird, especially a large or showy one used as a decoration.

wizard.o: From Middle English wysard, wysarde, equivalent to wise + -ard. A uniquely medieval Anglo-Saxon word with no known morphologically exact cognates inside the Germanic family; did not gain distinct sense of "occultist, magic user" (as opposed to a philosopher or sage) until circa 1500s, aligning roughly with the starting English Renaissance. However, via Proto-Indo-European *weyd- cognate with Proto-Celtic *druwits (whence English druid), Proto-Slavic *vědьma (Polish wiedźma, Russian ве́дьма (védʹma)), Russian веду́н (vedún). The sense of "old (male) virgin" is from a Japanese Internet meme in which virgins who are typically friendless, shy outcasts and loners who don't fit in anywhere legendarily gain magical powers upon reaching 30 years of age; popularized ultimately by 4chan and adjacent online incel spaces. Compare typologically specialist (<< Latin speciō).
wizard.example: The wizard conjured up a large fireball.
wizard.exampleSense: Someone, usually male, who uses (or has skill with) magic, mystic items, and magical and mystical practices.

foe.o:
adj: From Middle English fo (“foe; hostile”), from earlier yfoh, yvo, ifa (“foe”), from Old English ġefāh (“enemy”), from fāh (“hostile”), from Proto-West Germanic *faih, from Proto-Germanic *faihaz (compare Old Frisian fāch (“punishable”), Middle High German gevēch (“feuder”)), from Proto-Indo-European *peyk/ḱ- (“to hate, be hostile”) (compare Middle Irish óech (“enemy, fiend”), Lithuanian pi̇̀ktas (“evil”)).

noun: Acronym of [ten to the power of] fifty-one ergs, due to equalling 10⁵¹ ergs; coined by Gerald Brown of Stony Brook University in his work with Hans Bethe.

pater.o: Borrowed from Latin pater (“father”). Doublet of ayr, faeder, father, padre, and père.

pudency.o: From Latin pudentia, from Latin pudet (“it shames”).

impertinent.o: Inherited from Middle English impertinent, from Middle French impertinent, from Old French impertinent, from Latin impertinēns; by surface analysis, im- + pertinent.
impertinent.example: How impertinent that grief was which served no end!
impertinent.exampleSense: Not pertaining or related to (something or someone); Irrelevant or useless.

pertinent.o: Inherited from Middle English pertinent, borrowed from Old French pertinent and Latin pertinēns, pertinentem.
pertinent.example: Fourthly, I have made an effort to call the attention of the reader to the pertinent literature.
pertinent.exampleSense: Important with regard to (a subject or matter); pertaining; relevant.

mop.o:
noun: From Middle English mappe (also as mappel), perhaps borrowed from Walloon mappe (“napkin”), from Latin mappa (“napkin, cloth”). Believed to be from a Semitic source, variously claimed as Phoenician or Punic (the latter by Quintilian). Compare Modern Hebrew מַפָּה (mapá, “a map; a cloth”) (shortened from מַנְפָּה (manpah, “fluttering banner, streaming cloth”)). Doublet of map, nape, and nappe.

noun: From Middle English moppe (“fool, simpleton; derisive gesture; child, baby, doll”), of obscure origin, but compare Proto-West Germanic *mauwu (“pout, protruding lip”). Compare Low German mop, mops (“simpleton; pugnosed dog”), Dutch mop, mops (“pugnosed dog”), and the verb mope.
mop.example: He gave the floor a quick mop to soak up the spilt juice.
mop.exampleSense: A wash with a mop; the act of mopping.

mosquito.o: Borrowed from Spanish mosquito (“gnat”), diminutive of mosca (“fly”), from Latin musca (“fly”), from Proto-Indo-European *mūs- (“fly, stinging fly, gnat”). Cognate with West Flemish meuzie (“mosquito”), dialectal Swedish mausa (“fly”), Lithuanian musė (“a fly”) and Sicilian muschitta (“midge”). See also midge. First attested in the 1580s.
mosquito.example: We lit a driftwood fire to help keep the mosquitoes away. It was partially successful.
mosquito.exampleSense: A small flying insect of the family Culicidae, the females of which bite humans and animals and suck blood, leaving an itching bump on the skin, and sometimes carrying diseases like malaria, dengue and yellow fever.

mile.o: From Middle English myle, mile, from Old English mīl, from Proto-West Germanic *mīliju, a borrowing of Latin mīlia, mīllia, plural of mīle, mīlle (“mile”) (literally ‘thousand’ but used as a short form of mīlle passūs (“a thousand paces”)).
mile.exampleSense: The international mile: a unit of length precisely equal to 1.609344 kilometers established by treaty among Anglophone nations in 1959, divided into 5,280 feet or 1,760 yards.

mileometer.o: Alternative form of milometer. From mile + -o- + -meter.

milage.o: Alternative spelling of mileage. From mile + -age.

meek.o: From Middle English meek, meke, meoc, probably a borrowing from Old Norse mjúkr (“soft; meek”), from Proto-Germanic *meukaz, *mūkaz (“soft; supple”), from Proto-Indo-European *mewg-, *mewk- (“slick, slippery; to slip”); compare Old English smēag (“subtle, stealthy, etc.”) and smūgan. Cognate with Swedish and Norwegian Nynorsk mjuk (“soft”), Norwegian Bokmål myk (“soft”), and Danish myg (“supple”), Dutch muik (“soft, overripe”), dialectal German mauch (“dry and decayed, rotten”), Mauche (“malanders”). Compare as well Welsh mwyth (“soft, weak”), Latin ēmungō (“to blow one's nose”), Tocharian A muk- (“to let go, give up”), Lithuanian mùkti (“to slip away from”), Ancient Greek μύσσομαι (mússomai, “to blow the nose”), Sanskrit मु॒ञ्चति॑ (muñcáti, “to release, let loose”).
meek.example: What if they were wolves instead of lambs? They'd eat her all the sooner if she was meek to them. Fight or be eaten.

quit.o:
adj: From Middle English quiten, quyten, from Anglo-Norman quitter, Old French quitter, from quitte (“acquitted, quit”), ultimately from Latin quietus, which itself derives from Proto-Indo-European *kʷyéh₁-ti-s, from *kʷyeh₁- (“to rest”). Doublet of coy, quite, quiet, and quietus. Compare Dutch kwijten (“to quit”), German Low German quitten (“to quit”), German quitten, quittieren, Danish kvitte, Swedish qvitta, kvitta (“to quit, leave, set off”), Icelandic kvitta.

noun: Probably of imitative origin.
quit.example: After having to work overtime without being paid, I quit my job.
quit.exampleSense: To resign from (a job, office, position, etc.).

admission.o: Borrowed from Latin admissio, admissionis; compare French admission. See admit.
admission.example: I request admission for two adults.
admission.exampleSense: Permission to enter, or the entrance itself; admittance; entrance; access

alias.o: From Latin alias (“at another time; at another place, elsewhere, under other circumstances, otherwise”). See else and alien.
alias.example: Hitherto the commanding influence of Sir Robert Evelyn's character had sunk his own into insignificance—now he had no "rival near the throne," alias the bench of county magistrates.
alias.exampleSense: Otherwise; at another time; in other circumstances; otherwise called; also known as; formerly known as.

likewise.o: From Middle English lykewise, lykewyse, lyke wyse, lijk wise, a shortened form of Middle English in lik wise (“in like wise”); equivalent to like + -wise. Compare with otherwise.
likewise.example: Public transportation is virtually inaccessible in this country; likewise, its hospitals are also not very user-friendly.

blush.o:
noun: From Middle English blusshen, bluschen, blusschen, blisshen, from Old English blysċan (“to be red; shine”), perhaps from Proto-Germanic *blaskijaną, from *blasǭ (“burning candle; torch”) or alternatively from Proto-Germanic *bluskijaną, from *blusjǭ (“torch”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰel-. Cognate with Middle Low German blöschen (“to blush”). Compare also Old English blysian (“to burn; blaze”), Dutch blozen (“to blush”), Danish blusse (“to blush”), Old Norse blys (“torch”), Danish blus (“blaze”).

noun: Unknown; attested in the late 15th century.
blush.example: He wasn't used to this much attention, so he blushed as he saw dozens of pairs of eyes watching him.
blush.exampleSense: To become red or pink in the face (and sometimes experience an associated feeling of warmth), especially due to shyness, love, shame, excitement, or embarrassment.

obscene.o: From Middle French obscene (modern French obscène (“indecent, obscene”)), and from its etymon Latin obscēnus, obscaenus (“inauspicious; ominous; disgusting, filthy; offensive, repulsive; indecent, lewd, obscene”). The further etymology is uncertain, but may be from ob- (prefix meaning ‘towards’) + caenum (“dirt, filth; mire, mud”) (possibly ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ḱweyn- (“to make dirty, soil; filth; mud”)) or scaevus (“left, on the left side; clumsy; (figurative) unlucky”) (from Proto-Indo-European *skeh₂iwo-). If from caenum, the unexpected extra -s- may be from a variant form of the original PIE root; a similar -s- exists in ex-.
obscene.example: All masturbation is obscene, for [Roger] Scruton, also because it "involves a concentration on the body and its curious pleasures" [...].

endow.o: From Late Middle English endowen, endouen, enduen, indouen, indw (“to provide with assets, a livelihood, or privileges; to bestow, grant; (figuratively) to favour; to endow”), from Anglo-Norman endouer, from Old French en- (prefix meaning ‘in, into’) + douer (“to endow”) (from Latin dōtāre (present active infinitive of dōtō (“to endow”)); modern French douer). Dōtō is derived from dōs (“dowry; endowment, gift”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *deh₃- (“to give”)) + -ō (suffix forming regular first-conjugation verbs).
endow.example: I am weak; but surely the spirits who assist my vengeance will endow me with sufficient strength.
endow.exampleSense: To enrich or furnish with some faculty or quality.

accuracy.example: The jury doubted the accuracy of the witness' comments.
accuracy.exampleSense: Exact conformity to truth, or to a rule or model; degree of conformity of a measure to a true or standard value.

uprise.o: From Middle English uprisen, from Old English ūprīsan (“to rise up”), equivalent to up- + rise. Cognate with Icelandic upprisa (“resurrection”), Middle Low German oprīsinge (“uprising”). Compare also Icelandic uppreisn (“an uprising, revolt”).
uprise.example: They had decided to uprise rather than face punishment, and they wanted all the help they could get.
uprise.exampleSense: To rebel or revolt; to take part in an uprising.

foot.o: From Middle English fot, fote, foot, from Old English fōt, from Proto-West Germanic *fōt, from Proto-Germanic *fōts, from Proto-Indo-European *pṓds. Doublet of pes, pie (“Spanish unit of length”), and pous. Cognates *Scots fit (“foot”) *Yola voote (“foot”) *North Frisian fut, fötj (“foot”) *Saterland Frisian Fout (“foot”) *West Frisian foet (“foot”) *Cimbrian buus, vuaz, vuus (“foot”) *Dutch voet (“foot”) *Dutch Low Saxon voot (“foot”) *German Fuß, Fuss (“foot”) *German Low German Faut, Foot (“foot”) *Gottscheerish vúəs (“foot”) *Luxembourgish Fouss (“foot”) *Mòcheno vuas (“foot”) *Vilamovian füs (“foot”) *Yiddish פֿוס (fus, “foot”) *Danish fod (“foot”) *Faroese and Icelandic fótur (“foot”) *Jamtish fót (“foot”) *Norwegian Bokmål, Norwegian Nynorsk, and Swedish fot (“foot”) *Gothic 𐍆𐍉𐍄𐌿𐍃 (fōtus, “foot”).
foot.example: The flag pole at the local high school is about 20 feet high.
foot.exampleSense: A unit of measure equal to twelve inches or one third of a yard, equal to exactly 30.48 centimetres.

validity.o: From valid + -ity, borrowed from Middle French validité, from Late Latin validitas.

impute.o: Borrowed from Middle French imputer, from Latin imputō (“to bring into the reckoning, charge, impute”).
impute.example: We ascribe or impute motives to others and avow them or confess to them in ourselves.
impute.exampleSense: To attribute or ascribe (responsibility or fault) to a cause or source.

impudence.o: From Middle French impudence, from Latin impudentia.

impertinence.o: Borrowed from Middle French impertinence, from impertinent (“impertinent”); by surface analysis, im- + pertinent.
impertinence.example: The musical has always had a lightness of touch, an impertinence that resembles gay humor.

encounter.o: From Middle English encountren, from Anglo-Norman encountrer, Old French encontrer (“to confront”), from encontre (“against, counter to”), from Late Latin incontrā (“in front of”) itself from Latin in (“in”) + contrā (“against”).
encounter.example: As they have planned the encounters, they mostly have control over the time limits.
encounter.exampleSense: A meeting, especially one that is unplanned or unexpected.

regress.o: (verb) From Latin regressus, past participle of regredior (“to go back”), from re- (“back”) + gradior (“to go”). Doublet of regressus.
regress.example: Its bearing on the progress or regress of man is not an inconsiderable question.
regress.exampleSense: The act of passing back; passage back; return; retrogression.

in short.example: It was, in short, saved before - and looks to be once more.
in short.exampleSense: As a summary; as a shortened version of what has been told or what would have been told.

disapprove.example: She disapproves of rap music because of its sometimes aggressive lyrics.
disapprove.exampleSense: To condemn; to consider wrong or inappropriate; used with of.

approve.o:
verb: From Middle English aproven, appreoven, appreven, apreven, borrowed from Old French aprover, approver, approuvir, appreuver (“to approve”), from Latin approbō, from ad + probō (“to esteem as good, approve, prove”). Doublet of approbate. By surface analysis, ad- + prove.

verb: From Middle English approuen, approven, from Old French aprouer; a- + a form apparently derived from the pro, prod, in Latin prōsum (“be useful or profitable”). Compare with improve.
approve.example: We approve the measure of the administration, for it is an excellent decision.
approve.exampleSense: To regard as good; to commend; to be pleased with; to think well of.

individualistic.example: A few examples will demonstrate the cultural basis of individualistic, greedy, and anticooperative behavior.
individualistic.exampleSense: Interested in oneself rather than others; egocentric.

individualist.example: Miró was too much of an individualist to simply subscribe to an aesthetic party platform of Mediterranean art, which wanted to move forward, but only at a safe trot.
individualist.exampleSense: Someone who does as they wish, unconstrained by external influences.

notice.o: Borrowed from Middle French notice, from the Latin nōtitia. Doublet of notitia.
notice.example: I gave her her mandatory two weeks' notice and sacked her.
notice.exampleSense: Advance notification of termination of employment, given by an employer to an employee or vice versa.

strip.o:
noun: From alteration of stripe or from Middle Low German strippe, of uncertain ultimate origin, perhaps derived from a lost strong verb Proto-Germanic *strīpaną, with no clear cognates outside of Germanic except for Irish sríab (“line, stripe”).

verb: From Middle English strepen, strippen, from Old English strīepan (“plunder”), from Proto-Germanic *strēpōną, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ter(h₁)- (“to be stiff; be rigid; exert”). Probably related to German Strafe (“deprivation, fine, punishment”).
strip.example: Squeeze a strip of glue along the edge and then press down firmly.
strip.exampleSense: A long, thin piece of any material; any such material collectively.

comic.o: From Latin comicus, from Ancient Greek κωμικός (kōmikós, “relating to comedy”), from κῶμος (kômos, “carousal”).
comic.example: She started out as a joke-writer on the radio, and first performed as a comic at the ages of 30.

rouse.o:
noun: From Middle English rousen, from Anglo-Norman reuser, ruser, originally used in English of hawks shaking the feathers of the body, from Latin recūsō, by loss of the medial 'c.' Doublet of recuse. Figurative meaning “to stir up, provoke to activity” is from 1580s; that of “awaken” is first recorded 1590s.

noun: First attested in the late 16th Century. From carouse, from rebracketing of the phrase “drink carouse” as “drink a rouse”.
rouse.example: Tom, you and the boy rouse the cable up—get about ten fathoms on deck, and bend it.
rouse.exampleSense: To pull by main strength; to haul.

arouse.example: I can't wear wool underwear: it tends to arouse me at inappropriate times.
arouse.exampleSense: To sexually stimulate. To cause an erection of the penis or other physical signs of sexual arousal, such as fluid secretion.

reverence.o: From Middle English reverence (noun) and reverencen (verb), from Old French reverence and Latin reverentia, from Latin revereor (“to stand in awe, respect, revere”), from re- + vereor, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *wer- (“to cover, heed, notice”).
reverence.example: When discords, and quarrels, and factions, are carried openly and audaciously, it is a sign the reverence of government is lost.

revere.o: Borrowed from French révérer, ultimately from Latin revereor, from re- + vereor (“to fear”).

compatriot.o: Borrowed from French compatriote, itself borrowed from Latin compatriota. By surface analysis, com- + patriot. Displaced native Old English ġelanda.
compatriot.example: However Russian Pavlyuchenko stunned his compatriots with an unstoppable 25-yard drive into the top corner.

patriotic.o: From French patriotique, from Late Latin patriōticus, from Ancient Greek πατριωτικός (patriōtikós), from πατριώτης (patriṓtēs), equivalent to patriot + -ic.
patriotic.example: Most patriotics in copper or brass are common. They are rare in off-metals.
patriotic.exampleSense: A postage stamp, Civil War token, etc. bearing a patriotic design.

patriotism.example: The most extraordinary positive development in Czechoslovakia since its creation in 1918, the tumultuous outpouring of patriotism and protest was dared by students and intellectuals and soon embraced steel-workers and elderly pensioners.
patriotism.exampleSense: Love of one's country; devotion to the welfare of one's compatriots; passion which inspires one to serve one's country.

patri-.o: From Latin pater (“father”), or from Greek πατρια (patria, “tribe, family”).

hot key.o: Alternative form of hotkey. From hot + key.

shortcut.example: There are shortcuts to some of my favourite applications on my desktop.
shortcut.exampleSense: A file that points to the location of another file and serves as a quick way to access it.

voice mail.o: Alternative form of voicemail. From voice + mail, genericized trademark.

supervisor.o: Attested since the 15th century C.E.; from Middle English supervisor, supervisour, supervysor, supervysour, from Latin supervīsor, from supervideō, in turn from super + videō. By surface analysis, supervise + -or.
supervisor.example: I had learned a lot about supervising by observing other supervisors—the good things and the not-so-good things they did.
supervisor.exampleSense: A person with the official task of overseeing the work of a person or group, or of other operations and activities.

triangulate.o:
verb: From Latin triangulum + -ate or Medieval Latin *triangulāt-, the past participial stem of *triangulō. Compare French trianguler.

adj: From Latin triangulātus. By surface analysis, tri- + angulate.
triangulate.example: "I'll give you a check now," I said abruptly, and saw Selina's green eyes triangulate angrily on my face.
triangulate.exampleSense: To locate by means of triangulation.

conversation.o: From Middle English conversacioun, from Old French conversacion and its etymon, Latin conversātiōnem, accusative singular of conversātiō (“conversation”), from conversor (“abide, keep company with”). Doublet of conversazione. Morphologically converse + -ation.
conversation.example: I had an interesting conversation with Nicolas yesterday about how much he's getting paid.
conversation.exampleSense: Expression and exchange of individual ideas through talking with other people; also, a set instance or occasion of such talking.

incoming.o:
adj: From in (adverb) + coming (adjective).

noun: From Middle English incomming, in comyng, in-comyng, incomyng, in-comynge, incomynge, inne comyng, yn comyng, equivalent to in (adverb) + coming (noun).
incoming.example: Incoming tides cause a tidal bore in many rivers.
incoming.exampleSense: Coming (or about to come) in; arriving.

field.o: From Middle English feeld, feld (“field”), from Old English feld (“field”), from Proto-West Germanic *felþu (“field”), from Proto-Germanic *felþuz (“field”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *pleh₂- (“field, plain”) or *pleth₂- (“flat”) (with schwebeablaut). Cognates Cognate with Scots feld, feild (“field”), North Frisian fial, fälj (“field”), Saterland Frisian Fäild (“field”), West Frisian fjild (“field”), Dutch veld (“field”), German and Luxembourgish Feld (“field”), Vilamovian fald (“field”), Danish, Norwegian Bokmål, and Norwegian Nynorsk felt (“field”), Swedish fält (“field”), Finnish pelto (“field”), Asturian and Leonese platu (“plate”), Aragonese and Spanish plato (“plate”), Catalan plat (“plate”), French plat (“dish”), Galician, Mirandese, and Portuguese prato (“plate”), Italian piatto (“plate”), Latin *plattus (“flattened”), Greek πλατύς (platýs, “wide, broad”). Doublet of plate. Related also to Middle English flat (“flat”), Old English folde (“earth, land, territory”), Old English folm (“palm of the hand”). More at flat, fold. Not related to English felt.
field.example: He needs some time in the field before his judgment can be trusted.
field.exampleSense: Any of various figurative meanings, often dead metaphors. Any of certain structures serving cognition. A realm of practical, direct or natural operation, contrasted with an office, classroom, or laboratory.

launch.o:
verb: From Middle English launchen (“to throw as a lance”), Old French lanchier, another form (Old Northern French/Norman variant, compare Jèrriais lanchi) of lancier, French lancer, from lance.

noun: From Portuguese lancha (“barge, launch”), apparently from Malay lancar (“quick, agile”). Spelling influenced by the verb above.
launch.example: My class was wearing butter-yellow pique dresses, and Momma launched out on mine. She smocked the yoke into tiny crisscrossing puckers, then shirred the rest of the bodice.
launch.exampleSense: To move with force and swiftness like a sliding from the stocks into the water; to plunge; to begin.

prototype.o: From French prototype or Late Latin prototypon, from Ancient Greek πρωτότυπος (prōtótupos, “original; prototype”), from πρωτο- (prōto-, “first”) (from πρῶτος (prôtos, “first; earliest”)) + τῠ́πος (tŭ́pos, “blow, pressing; sort, type”) (from τύπτω (túptō, “to beat, strike”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)tewp- (“to push; to stick”)). The word is analysable as proto- + -type.
prototype.example: A robin is a prototype of a bird; a penguin is not.
prototype.exampleSense: An instance of a category or a concept that combines its most representative attributes.

videotape.o: From video + tape, a trademark of media company Ampex.

paraphernalia.o: Borrowed from Medieval Latin paraphernālia (“goods which a wife brings over and above her dowry”), use as noun (short for paraphernālia bona (“paraphernal goods”)) of neuter plural of paraphernālis, from Late Latin parapherna + Latin -ālis (suffix forming adjectives), from Ancient Greek παράφερνα (parápherna), a compound of παρά (pará, “beside”) + φερνή (phernḗ, “dowry”). In the propertied classes, a dowry was placed under the control of the husband, while the paraphernalia which she brought with her remained the wife’s property.
paraphernalia.example: He has an impressive collection of bicycling paraphernalia, but he doesn't ride very often anymore.
paraphernalia.exampleSense: Miscellaneous items, especially the set of equipment required for a particular activity.

executive.o: From Middle French executif, from Latin executivus, from Latin exsequi, from ex- ‘out’ + sequi ‘follow’.
executive.example: She works in an office with an executive bathroom.

in-house.o: Alternative spelling of in. PIE word *h₁en Preposition and verb from Middle English in, from Old English in, from Proto-Germanic *in. Adverb, noun and adjective from Middle English in, from Old English inn and inne, from Proto-Germanic *innai. Sense 1/2 "in"/"into" are from the original PIE prefix, with locative/accusative case respectively. Sense 3/4 "qualification"/"means" are from the PIE metaphor of all infinitives coming from locatives.
in-house.example: MUTV, United’s in-house channel, was so confused by all the changes it announced before kick-off that Matic would be playing as a centre-half.

interject.o: From Latin interiectus, perfect passive participle of intericiō (“place between”).

panorama.o: From pan- (“all”) + Ancient Greek ὅρᾱμᾰ (hórāmă, “view”). Coined by Robert Barker (painter) in 1792.

lithology.example: The ‘monomict’ meteorites are samples of a single lithology while the polymict meteorites are those containing two or more lithologies.
lithology.exampleSense: The general composition of a rock or rock sequence.

lithosphere.example: Then we indicate some of the more pertinent characteristics of oceanic and continental lithospheres.
lithosphere.exampleSense: The rigid, mechanically strong, outer layer of the Earth; divided into twelve major plates.

geological.o: From Renaissance Latin geōlogia + -ical; first attested slightly earlier than geology. By surface analysis, geo- + -logical.

canvass.o:
verb: The verb is derived from canvas (“type of coarse cloth woven from hemp”). The connection between “to toss (someone) in a (canvas) sheet; (by extension) to batter, beat, or thrash (someone or something); etc.” and “to seek the support of voters or a constituency in a forthcoming election or poll” is not entirely clear. The noun is derived from the verb. It has been suggested that noun sense 4.2 (“rejection (at an election, of a suit, etc.)”) may refer to the canvas bag used by journeymen mechanics which they used to pack up their tools after they had completed their jobs, in which case it is not derived from the verb but directly from canvas (noun).

noun: A variant of canvas (noun).
canvass.example: The police are canvassing the neighbourhood for information about the missing child.
canvass.exampleSense: To seek or solicit donations, information, opinions, support, etc. from (people or a place)

kismet.o: From Ottoman Turkish قسمت (kısmet, “fate, destiny”) (Turkish kısmet), from Arabic قِسْمَة (qisma, “division, lot, destiny”).
kismet.example: Sexualised Catholicism, at the dawn of MTV, was Madonna’s first stroke of kismet.
kismet.exampleSense: Fate; a predetermined or unavoidable destiny.

vaunt.o:
verb: From Middle English vaunten, from Anglo-Norman vaunter, variant of Old French vanter, from Latin vānus (“vain, boastful”).

noun: From French avant (“before, fore”). See avant, vanguard.
vaunt.example: Charity vaunteth not itself, is not puffed up.
vaunt.exampleSense: To boast of; to make a vain display of; to display with ostentation.

flout.o: Perhaps from Middle English flouten (“to play the flute”); compare with Dutch fluiten.
flout.example: The manoeuvres of Microsoft and HP appear to comply with the letter of the regulations, even if they flout their spirit.
flout.exampleSense: To express contempt for (laws, rules, etc.) by word or action.

flaunt.o:
verb: Of North Germanic origin. Perhaps related to Norwegian flanta (“to show off, wander about”), Icelandic flana (“to rush about, act rashly or heedlessly”) and then also to French flâner (“to wander around, loiter”). Alternatively, it could be related to Swedish flankt (“loosely, flutteringly”) (compare English flaunt-a-flaunt), from flanka (“waver, hang and wave about, ramble”), a nasalised variant of flakka (“to waver”), related to Middle English flacken (“to move to and fro, flutter, palpitate”). See flack.

verb: By confusion with flout.
flaunt.example: She’s always flaunting her designer clothes.

eloquent.o: From Old French eloquent, from Latin eloquens (“speaking, having the faculty of speech, eloquent”), present participle of eloquor (“to speak out”), from e (“out”) + loquor (“to speak”).

monody.o: From Latin monodia, from Ancient Greek μονῳδία (monōidía).
monody.example: All directions in life were blocked to him. He could not think, he could not sleep, his heart thudded to a deadening monody of fear. Fear that is itself the penalty of all things feared.
monody.exampleSense: A composition having a single melodic line.

quiescent.o: Learned borrowing from Latin quiēscēns, quiēscentem.
quiescent.example: The bats were quiescent at that time of day, so we slowly entered the cave.

expedite.o: From Latin expedītus (“unimpeded, unfettered”), perfect passive participle of expediō (“bring forward, set right”).
expedite.example: He expedited the search by alphabetizing the papers.

carbon.o: Borrowed from French carbone, coined by Antoine Lavoisier, from Latin carbō, carbōnem (“charcoal, coal”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *kerh₃- (“to burn”). By surface analysis, carbo- + -on.
carbon.example: Carbon is the most common element in our bodies—indeed, in all living things on earth.
carbon.exampleSense: The chemical element (symbol C) with an atomic number of 6. It can be found in pure form for example as graphite, a black, shiny and very soft material, or diamond, a colourless, transparent, crystalline solid and the hardest known material.

anal.o: Borrowed from Latin ānālis. By surface analysis, anus + -al. Psychological sense shortened from anal-retentive.
anal.example: Please don't touch his furniture, as he can get very anal about things like that.
anal.exampleSense: Of a person, compulsive and stubborn, obsessed with neatness and accuracy, supposedly from not having progressed beyond the anal stage.

acre.o: From Middle English acre, aker, from Old English æcer (“field where crops are grown”), from Proto-West Germanic *akr, from Proto-Germanic *akraz (“field”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éǵros (“field”). Doublet of agriculture. Cognate with Scots acre, aker, acker (“acre, field, arable land”), North Frisian ecir (“field, a measure of land”), West Frisian eker (“field”), Dutch akker (“field”), German Acker (“field, acre”), Norwegian åker (“field”) and Swedish åker (“field”), Icelandic akur (“field”), Latin ager (“land, field, acre, countryside”), Ancient Greek ἀγρός (agrós, “field”), Sanskrit अज्र (ájra, “field, plain”).
acre.example: Buried within the Mediterranean littoral are some seventy to ninety million tons of slag from ancient smelting, about a third of it concentrated in Iberia. This ceaseless industrial fueling caused the deforestation of an estimated fifty to seventy million acres of woodlands.
acre.exampleSense: An English unit of land area (symbol: a. or ac.) originally denoting a day's ploughing for a yoke of oxen, now standardized as 4,840 square yards or 4,046.86 square metres.

mediocre.o: From the late Middle English medioker, from the French médiocre, from the Middle French médiocre, from the Classical Latin mediocris (“in a middle state”, “of middle size”, “middling”, “moderate”, “ordinary”, from medius (“middle”) + ocris (“rugged mountain”)); compare mediocrely and mediocrity.
mediocre.example: I'm pretty good at tennis but only mediocre at racquetball.
mediocre.exampleSense: Not excellent or outstanding, usually disappointingly so.

outcompete.example: While individual Neanderthals were perhaps as inquisitive, imaginative and creative as individual Sapiens, superior networking enabled Sapiens to swiftly outcompete Neanderthals.
outcompete.exampleSense: To be more successful than a competitor; especially to thrive in the presence of an organism that is competing for resources.

punishment.o: From Middle English punishement, from Old French punissement, from punir (“to punish”). Equivalent to punish + -ment. Displaced native Old English wīte.
punishment.example: The naughty children were given a punishment by their teachers.
punishment.exampleSense: The act (action) or process of punishing, imposing and/or applying a sanction, typically by an authority or a person in authority (for example: a parent or teacher), especially when disappointed or dissatisfied with the behavior or actions of a child, student, or someone else being looked after.

vinegar.o: From Middle English vynegre, from Old French vinaigre from Old French vyn egre, based on Latin vīnum (“wine”) + Latin ācer (“sour”). Displaced Old English æċed (survived in Middle English eced).

dematerialize.example: Some magicians claim they can dematerialize their bodies and re-materialize them in a different location.
dematerialize.exampleSense: To cause something to disappear by making it immaterial.

stimulus.example: From the beginning of the show to the end, vanity is the sole stimulus and reward of action—vanity, that never looks beyond the present.
stimulus.exampleSense: An external phenomenon that has an influence on a system, by triggering or modifying an internal phenomenon; for example, a spur or incentive that drives a person to take action or change behaviour.

shack.o:
noun: Unknown. Some scholars derive this word from Mexican Spanish jacal, from Nahuatl xacalli (“adobe hut”). Alternatively, the word may instead come from ramshackle/ramshackly (e.g., old ramshackly house) or perhaps it may be a back-formation from shackly. Compare Tavringer Romani hak (“place, house”), Traveller Norwegian hak (“place”).

noun: Obsolete variant of shake. Compare Scots shag (“refuse of barley or oats”).

adj: From shagged or shagged out.
shack.example: All the poor old shacks about the town found a friend in Deacon Marble.
shack.exampleSense: A shiftless fellow; a low, itinerant beggar; a vagabond; a tramp.

hedonism.o: From Ancient Greek ἡδονή (hēdonḗ, “pleasure”) + English -ism. First attested in 1856.

bask.o: Inherited from Middle English basken, from Old Norse baðask (“to take a bath”, literally “to bathe oneself”), mediopassive form from underlying baða (“to bathe”) + sik (“oneself”), from Proto-Germanic *baþōną and *sek. Doublet of English bathe.
bask.example: There will be no problems with visibility, or the highly changeable Highland weather, as Scotland basks in what is reported to be the country's hottest September day for more than a century.
bask.exampleSense: To bathe in warmth; to be exposed to pleasant heat.

considerate.example: It was very considerate of you to give up your place for your friend.
considerate.exampleSense: Consciously thoughtful and observant (often of other people and their rights, needs, feelings and comfort).

inconsiderable.o: From Middle French inconsidérable. By surface analysis, in- + considerable.
inconsiderable.example: There will be inconsiderable rises in British Railways day return fares in the London Area; those priced at 2s. and over are unchanged, as are the ordinary single fares.
inconsiderable.exampleSense: Too unimportant to be worthy of attention.

curb.o: From Middle French courbe (“curve, curved object”), from Latin curvus (“bent, crooked, curved”). Doublet of curve.
curb.example: Where pinching want must curb her warm desires.

oppress.o: From Middle English oppressen, from Old French oppresser, from Medieval Latin oppressare (“to press against, oppress”), frequentative of Latin opprimere, past participle oppressus (“to press against, press together, oppress”), from ob (“against”) + premere, past participle pressus (“to press”); see press.
oppress.example: The rural poor were oppressed by the land-owners.
oppress.exampleSense: To keep down by unjust force.

oppression.o: From Middle English oppression, from Old French oppression, from Latin oppressiō (“a pressing down, violence, oppression”), from opprimō; see oppress.
oppression.example: Our oppression was lifted by the reappearance of the sun.

lure.o:
noun: From Anglo-Norman lure, from Old French loirre (Modern French leurre), from Frankish *lōþr, from Proto-Germanic *lōþr-, perhaps ultimately related to *laþō (“invitation, calling”), or from Proto-Indo-European *leh₂- (“to hide”). Compare English allure, also from Old French. Probably related to German Luder (“bait”).

noun: Borrowed from Icelandic lúðr.
lure.example: Professor is what you become after teaching for twenty to thirty years. Research Professor is what you then want to become, so you can finally stop worrying about students and do the research that lured you into academia in the first place!
lure.exampleSense: To attract by temptation, appeal, or guile.

allure.o:
noun: From Middle English aluren, from Old French aleurer, alurer, from a (“to, towards”) (Latin ad) + leurre (“lure”). By surface analysis, al- + lure.

noun: From Middle English alure, alour, from Old French alure, aleure (“walk, gait”), from aler (“to go”) + -ure.
allure.example: Injustice doth allure them; as the honour of their vertuous actions enticeth the good.

brain drain.o: Coined by spokesmen for the Royal Society of London in the early 1950s to describe the outflow of scientists and technologists to the United States and Canada.

witch.o:
noun: The noun is from Middle English wicche, from Old English wiċċe (“(female) witch; sorceress”) and wiċċa (“(male) witch; sorcerer; warlock”), deverbative from wiċċian (“to practice sorcery”), from Proto-Germanic *wikkōną (compare West Frisian wikje, wikke (“to foretell; to warn”), German Low German wicken (“to soothsay”), Dutch wikken, wichelen (“to dowse; to divine”)), from Proto-Indo-European *wik-néh₂-, derivation of *weyk- (“to consecrate; to separate”); akin to Latin victima (“sacrificial victim”), Lithuanian viẽkas (“life-force”), Sanskrit वि॒नक्ति॑ (vinákti, “to set apart; to separate out”). Possibly related to wicked; see that entry for more. The verb derives from the noun.

verb: From Middle English wicchen, from Old English wiċċian, from Proto-Germanic *wikkōną, from Proto-Indo-European *wik-néh₂-, derivation of *weyk-. In the senses arising in Middle English and later probably aphetic from bewitch.

noun: Compare wick.

noun: Chosen for its euphemistic rhyme.
witch.example: He cannot abide the old woman of Brentford; he swears she's a witch.
witch.exampleSense: A person (now usually particularly a woman) who uses magical or similar supernatural powers to influence or predict events.

jam.o:
noun: First attested in the early 18th c. as a verb meaning “to press, be pressed, be wedged in”. Compare dialectal jammock (“to press, squeeze, crush into a soft mass, chew food"; also "a soft, pulpy substance”). Perhaps from Middle English chammen, champen ("to bite upon something, gnash the teeth"; whence modern champ, chomp), of uncertain origin; probably originally onomatopoeic. The "performance" sense is first attested with regards to jazz in 1929, and its origin, though uncertain, is likely metaphorical, "something sweet made by the combination of many things", with influence from jamboree.

noun: Borrowed from Persian جامه (“garment”) and/or Hindustani (Hindi जामा (jāmā) / Urdu جامہ (jāma)), meaning "garment, robe". Related to pajamas and pyjamas.
jam.example: A single accident can jam the roads for hours.
jam.exampleSense: To cause congestion or blockage. Often used with "up".

sewage.o: From sewer (“system of pipes used to remove human waste and to provide drainage”) + -age or from sew (“to drain or draw off water”) + -age.

sew.o:
verb: From Middle English sewen, sowen, from Old English siwian, seowian, seowan (“to sew, mend, patch, knit together, link, unite”), from Proto-Germanic *siwjaną (“to sew”), from Proto-Indo-European *syewH- (“to sew”). Cognate with Scots sew, North Frisian saie, sei, Saterland Frisian säie, Danish, Norwegian Bokmål, Norwegian Nynorsk, and Swedish sy, and, more distantly, Polish szyć, Russian шить (šitʹ), Latin suō, Sanskrit सीव्यति (sī́vyati). Related to seam.

verb: Back-formation from sewer (“a drain”).

noun: From Middle English sew (“broth”), from Old English sēaw (“sap, juice”), from Proto-West Germanic *sauw.
sew.example: She [Kate Spade] took the label, which originally had been on the inside of the bag, and sewed it to the outside.
sew.exampleSense: To use a needle to pass thread repeatedly through (pieces of fabric) in order to join them together.

garrison.o: From Middle English garisoun, garysoun, from Old French garison, guarison, from guarir + -ison, ultimately of Germanic origin; thus a doublet of warison. Compare guard, ward; the modern meaning is influenced by (now obsolete) garnison.

butt.o:
noun: From Middle English but, butte (“goal, mark, butt of land”), from Old English byt, bytt (“small piece of land”) and *butt (attested in diminutive Old English buttuc (“end, small piece of land”) > English buttock), from Proto-West Germanic *butt, from Proto-Germanic *buttaz (“end, piece”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰudʰnós (“bottom”), later thematic variant of Proto-Indo-European *bʰudʰmḗn ~ *bʰudʰn-, perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *dʰewbʰ- (“deep”). Cognate with Norwegian butt (“stump, block”), Icelandic bútur (“piece, fragment”), Low German butt (“blunt, clumsy”). Influenced by Old French but, butte (“but, mark”), ultimately from the same Germanic source. Compare also Albanian bythë (“buttocks”), Ancient Greek πυθμήν (puthmḗn, “bottom of vessel”), Latin fundus (“bottom”) and Sanskrit बुध्न (budhná, “bottom”), from the same Proto-Indo-European root. Related to bottom, boot. PIE word *bʰudʰmḗn

verb: From Middle English butten, from Anglo-Norman buter, boter (“to push, butt, strike”), from Frankish *bautan (“to hit, beat”), from Proto-Germanic *bautaną (“to beat, push”). Cognate with Old English bēatan (“to beat”). More at beat.

noun: From late Middle English bote, but, butte (“wine cask”), of disputed origin. Probably (1) from Anglo-Norman but, from Old French bot (“barrel, wine-skin”), Late Latin buttis (“cask”); (2) alternatively, a later form of Middle English bitte, bit, butte (“leather bottle”), from Old English bytt, byt, from Proto-West Germanic *buttjā, from Vulgar Latin *buttia and thus a doublet of boccia.

noun: From Middle English but, butte, botte (“flounder; plaice; turbot”), possibly derived from sense 1 (“blunt end”), meaning "blunt-headed fish." Compare Dutch bot and the second element of English halibut. Cognate with West Frisian bot, German Low German Butt, German Butt, Butte, Swedish butta.

noun: Variant of putt.

noun: Originally apparently a less-desired cut, named either due to its often being packed in butts (“casks”) for storage and shipping, or from the use of butt to refer to "the larger or thicker end of something, in distinction from the sharp or narrow end" or "the waste end".
butt.example: I put out my hand and felt the meat-chopper hanging to the wall. In a flash I was after him. [...] With one last touch of humanity I turned the blade back and struck him with the butt.
butt.exampleSense: An end of something, often distinguished in some way from the other end. The blunt back part of an axehead or large blade. Also called the poll.

borne.o: From Middle English boren, iborne, from Old English boren, ġeboren, past participle of Old English beran (“to carry, bear”).
borne.example: In the last rays of the setting sun, you could pick out far away down the reach his beard borne high up on the white structure, foaming up stream to anchor for the night.

waste.o:
noun: From Middle English wast, waste (“a waste”, noun), from Anglo-Norman, Old Northern French wast, waste (“a waste”), from Frankish *wōstī (“a waste”), from Proto-Germanic *wōstaz, *wōstuz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁weh₂- (“empty, wasted”). Displaced native Middle English wernen (“to refuse”) likely due to the similar sounding Middle English warnen

adj: From Middle English wast, waste (“waste”, adjective), from Anglo-Norman, Old Northern French wast (“waste”), from Frankish *wōstī (“waste, empty”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁weh₂- (“empty, wasted”). Cognate with Old High German wuosti, wuasti (“waste, empty”), German wüst, Old Saxon wōsti (“desolate”), Old English wēste (“waste, barren, desolate, empty”).

verb: From Middle English wasten (“to waste, lay waste”), from Anglo-Norman, Old Northern French waster (“to waste, devastate”) (compare also the variant gaster and French gâter from a related Old French word); the Anglo-Norman form waster was either from Frankish *wōstijan (“to waste”), from Proto-Indo-European *wāsto- (“empty, wasted”), or alternatively from Latin vastāre and influenced by the Frankish; the English word was assisted by similarity to native Middle English westen ("to waste"; > English weest). Cognate with Old High German wuostan, wuastan, wuostjan (“to waste”) (Modern German wüsten), Old English wēstan (“to lay waste, ravage”). Displaced native Old English essian and strȳndan. Largely overtook Old English forspillan and wēstan.
waste.example: Wasted by such a course of life, the infirmities of age daily grew on him.
waste.exampleSense: To wear away by degrees; to impair gradually; to deteriorate; to diminish by constant loss; to use up; to consume; to spend; to wear out.

log.o:
noun: From Middle English logge, logg (first recorded in Anglo-Latin as loggum), of uncertain origin, but probably from Old Norse lóg, lág (“felled tree, log”), derived from Old Norse liggja (“to lie”). If so, then cognate with Norwegian låg (“fallen tree”), Dutch loog (“wood, timber, lumber”). Alternatively, directly from Norwegian låg (“fallen tree”), which could have been borrowed through the Norwegian timber trade. However the Old Norse/Middle Norwegian vowel is long while Middle English vowel is short.

noun: Clipping of logbook, itself from log (etymology 1) + book, from a wooden float (chip log) used to measure speed.

verb: Ellipsis of log out, itself from Etymology 2.

noun: From Hebrew לֹג.

noun: A clipping of logarithm.
log.example: They walked across the stream on a fallen log.
log.exampleSense: The trunk of a dead tree, cleared of branches.

elm.o: From Middle English elme, elm, from Old English elm, from Proto-West Germanic *elm, from Proto-Germanic *elmaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁élem (“mountain elm”). See also dialectal Low German Elm, dialectal German Ilm, archaic German Ilme, Norwegian and Swedish alm; also Irish leamh, Latin ulmus, Albanian ulzë (“maple”).
elm.example: The village is a dignified place of thatch, half-timbering, box hedges and neat farms, set among elms (though not as many as formerly, since Dutch elm disease took its toll) on the level plain of the Pewsey Vale.
elm.exampleSense: A tree of the genus Ulmus of the family Ulmaceae, large deciduous trees with alternate stipulate leaves and small apetalous flowers.

sewer.o:
noun: From Middle English sewer, seuer, from Anglo-Norman sewere (“water-course”), from Old French sewiere (“overflow channel for a fishpond”), from Vulgar Latin *exaquāria (“drain for carrying water off”), from Latin ex (“out of, from”) + aquāria (“of or pertaining to waters”) or from a root *exaquāre.

noun: From Middle English seware, seuere, from Anglo-Norman asseour, from Old French asseoir (“find a seat for”), from Latin assidēre, present active participle of assideō (“attend to”), from ad (“to, towards, at”) + sedeō (“sit”).

noun: sew + -er
sewer.example: One of the hidden glories of Victorian engineering is proper drains. Isolating a city’s effluent and shipping it away in underground sewers has probably saved more lives than any medical procedure except vaccination.
sewer.exampleSense: A pipe or channel, or system of pipes or channels, used to remove human waste and to provide drainage.

sanitary.o: 19th century, borrowed from French sanitaire, formed from Latin sanitas (“health”). Analysable as sanity + -ary.
sanitary.example: When I made evening rounds, I saw women with their hair rolled, using the sanitaries for rollers.

contradict.o: Derived from Latin contrādictus (“contradicted”), the past participle of contrādīcō (“speak against”) (originally two words).
contradict.example: The prime minister contradicted herself during her speech.
contradict.exampleSense: To say things that conflict with each other.

ceaseless.example: Buried within the Mediterranean littoral are some seventy to ninety million tons of slag from ancient smelting, about a third of it concentrated in Iberia. This ceaseless industrial fueling caused the deforestation of an estimated fifty to seventy million acres of woodlands.

dress.o: PIE word *dwís The verb is from Middle English dressen, dresse (“to arrange, put in order”), from Anglo-Norman, Old French dresser, drecier (modern French dresser), from Late Latin *dīrēctiāre (“to guide, direct”), from Classical Latin dīrēctus, whence English direct. Further akin to Latin regō. The noun is derived from the verb. Compare typologically adorn (<< Latin ōrnō < ōrdō, whence also ōrdinō, English order, ornament); Russian наряжа́ть (narjažátʹ), наря́д (narjád) (akin to ряд (rjad), поря́док (porjádok)).
dress.example: The fashion designer was proud to have dressed the queen for the charity event.
dress.exampleSense: To design, make, provide, or select clothes (for someone).

whisk.o:
noun: From Middle English whisk, borrowed from Old Norse visk, from Proto-Germanic *wiskaz, *wiskō (“bundle of hay, wisp”), from Proto-Indo-European *weys-. Cognates Cognate with Danish visk, Dutch wis, German Wisch, Latin virga (“rod, switch”), viscus (“entrails”), Lithuanian vizgéti (“to tremble”), Czech věchet (“wisp of straw”), Sanskrit वेष्क (veṣka, “noose”). Compare also Old English wiscian (“to plait”), granwisc (“awn”). The unetymological wh- is probably expressive of the sound; compare the same development in whip and onomatopoeias such as whack and whoosh.

noun: So called from the rapid action of sweeping the cards off the table after a trick has been won.
whisk.example: The chef prepared to whisk the egg whites for the angel's food cake.
whisk.exampleSense: In cooking, to whip e.g. eggs or cream.

peat.o:
noun: Inherited from Northern Middle English pete (recorded in Latin text as peta), of uncertain origin; perhaps from a Celtic language such as an unattested Pictish or Brythonic source, in turn possibly from Proto-Brythonic *peθ (“portion, segment, piece”); if so, it would be a doublet of piece.

noun: Probably from Middle Dutch pete (“godmother or godfather”) (modern Dutch peet (“godparent, old woman, grandmother; godchild”)), related to dialectal German Pfette, Pfetter (“godfather; godchild”)), German Pate (“godfather, sponsor”), Patin (“godmother”). Or alternatively, related to pet (“a favourite”).

florist.o: From French fleuriste, from Latin floris (“genitive singular of flōs, flower”), + -ist.

bonsai.o: From Japanese 盆栽 (bonsai), from Middle Chinese 盆 (MC bwon, “bowl”) + 栽 (MC tsoj|dzojH, “to plant”).
bonsai.example: Could I be a father who was, so to speak, bonsaiing his children, trimming urban roots, and then twisting the emerging branches?
bonsai.exampleSense: To make into a bonsai by restricting the roots and pruning.

curvy.example: A city is entangled in straight lines, while nature is curvy. Fast is straight, but slow is curvy and patient.

hesitate.o: Borrowed from Latin haesitātus, perfect passive participle of haesitō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), intensive of haereō (“to hesitate, stick fast; to hang or hold fast”). Displaced native Old English wandian. Compare French hésiter.
hesitate.example: He hesitated whether to accept the offer or not; men often hesitate in forming a judgment.
hesitate.exampleSense: To stop or pause respecting decision or action; to be in suspense or uncertainty as to a determination.

medicine.o: From Middle English medicin, from Middle French medicine, from Old French medecine, from Latin medicīna (“the healing art, medicine, a physician's shop, a remedy, medicine”), feminine of medicīnus (“of or belonging to physic or surgery, or to a physician or surgeon”), from medicus (“a physician, surgeon”). The extended sense of "Indigenous magic" is a calque of Ojibwe mashkiki (“medicine”) or mide (or cognates in related languages) when used in compounds such as Grand Medicine Society, medicine lodge, medicine dance, medicine bag, medicine wheel, medicine man, Medicine Line, and bad medicine or place names such as Medicine Hat, Medicine Creek, etc.
medicine.example: She's studying medicine at university because she wants to be a doctor in the future.
medicine.exampleSense: The study of the cause, diagnosis, prognosis and treatment of disease or illness.

p: the art of preparing drugs, a drug, especially laxatives
pharmacist.o: From pharmacy (“the art of preparing drugs, a drug, especially laxatives”) + -ist.
pharmacist.example: By Admir, pharmacist by profession and hobby dronist by passion.
pharmacist.exampleSense: A health professional who controls, formulates, preserves, and dispenses medications and provides medical advice and counseling on how medicines should be used in order to achieve maximum benefit, and minimal side effects in order to avoid drug interactions.

competitively.example: For example, kalicludin 1-3 from A. sulcata binds competitively to Kv1.2 channels to paralyse the prey rapidly.

prescript.o: Latin praescriptum: compare Old French prescript.
prescript.example: Nor did he ever with so much regret submit unto any prescript, as when his physicians, after his great fever that he had in Oxford , required him to eat suppers.

prescription.o: Borrowed from Middle French, from Old French prescripcion, from Latin praescriptio (“preface; pretext; something written ahead of time”), from prae- (“pre-, before”) + scribere (“to write”) + -tio (“-tion, forming nouns”). Equivalent to prescribe + -tion.
prescription.example: Many powerful pain killers are prescription drugs in the U.S.
prescription.exampleSense: only available with a physician or nurse practitioner's written prescription (of a drug, etc.)

medication.o: From Middle English medicacioun, from Middle French médication and its etymon Latin medicātiō, from medicārī (“to heal, cure”), from medicus (“a physician, surgeon”), from medērī (“to heal”). Equivalent to medicate + -ion.
medication.example: Are you going to be be like this all day? It’s like I’ve not took^([sic – meaning taken]) my medication.
medication.exampleSense: A medicine, or all the medicines regularly taken by a patient.

description.o: From Middle English descripcioun, from Old French description and its etymon, Latin dēscrīptiō, noun of action of dēscrībō (“to describe”). Equivalent to describe + -tion.
description.example: The zoo had no lions, tigers, or cats of any description.
description.exampleSense: A set of characteristics by which someone or something can be recognized.

unexceptional.example: Uncle Shemp was alarmingly unexceptional. He had no detectable lifestyle, and his only accomplishment was the fact that he was a lifelong member of the general public.

exceptionable.example: The subject however is rendered still more exceptionable by the aukward and ridiculous manner in which it is here treated.
exceptionable.exampleSense: Liable to cause disapproval, objection or debate.

exceptionally.example: The shed, a steel-framed structure with a single-span roof devoid of intermediate support, is exceptionally well-lit by continuous glazing on the roof and along much of the sides, while there is fluorescent roof lighting for night work.
exceptionally.exampleSense: To an unusual, remarkable or exceptional degree.

exceptional.example: The quality of the beer was exceptional.
exceptional.exampleSense: Better than the average; superior due to exception or rarity.

exception.o: From Middle English exception, excepcioun, from Anglo-Norman excepcioun, from Old French excepcion, from Latin exceptiō. Equivalent to except + -ion.
exception.example: That rule is usually true, but there are a few exceptions.
exception.exampleSense: That which is excluded from others; a person, thing, or case, specified as distinct, or not included.

speciality.o: From special + -ity, from Middle French spécialité, from Old French specialte, especialte, from Latin specialitas.
speciality.example: They cook well overall, but their true speciality is pasta.

overnight.o: Inherited from Middle English overnyght, from Old English ofer niht (“through the night, overnight”), equivalent to over + night. Verbal use (late 19th c.) may have been influenced by German übernachten (16th c.), though it could also have developed independently. Compare also Dutch overnachten (“to overnight”), Middle Low German ȫvernachten (“to overnight”), West Frisian oernachtsje (“to overnight”), Saterland Frisian uurnoachtje (“to overnight”).
overnight.example: Let it run overnight and we'll check on it in the morning.
overnight.exampleSense: During or throughout the night, especially during the evening or night just past.

number.o:
