enhance.exampleSense: To augment or make something greater.

outperform.example: Rail has continued to outperform bus operations, where a decline in ridership continues.
outperform.exampleSense: To perform better than something or someone.

fundament.o: From Middle English, from Old French fundement, fondement, from Latin fundāmentum (“foundation”), from fundō (“to lay the bottom, to found”). Doublet of fondamento.
fundament.example: It [the Sphincter Ani] serves to purse up the Fundament, and so hinders the involuntary Evacuation of the Fæces.
fundament.exampleSense: The bottom; the buttocks or anus.

algorithm.o: From Middle English algorisme, augrym, from Anglo-Norman algorisme, augrim, from Medieval Latin algorismus, from Arabic الخَوَارِزْمِيّ (al-ḵawārizmiyy), the nisba of Persian mathematician Muḥammad ibn Mūsā al-Khwārizmī and a toponymic name meaning "the Chorasmian". The spelling change (-s- > -th-) was influenced by unrelated Ancient Greek ἀριθμός (arithmós) (whence English arithmo-).
algorithm.example: It’s a computer – an algorithm – and if you’ve been in Iran lately, they take you out of the system.
algorithm.exampleSense: A collection of ordered steps that solve a mathematical problem. A precise step-by-step plan for a computational procedure that possibly begins with an input value and yields an output value in a finite number of steps.

disembody.example: Jerusha turned, a flush on her cheeks that wasn't makeup, a swath of steam from the vaporizer swirling around her chest, disembodying her head.
disembody.exampleSense: To separate (a part of the body) from the body.

disembodied.o: simple past and past participle of disembody. From dis- + embody.
disembodied.example: Silence has sometimes a remarkable power of showing itself as the disembodied soul of feeling wandering without its carcase, and it is then more impressive than speech.
disembodied.exampleSense: Having no material body, immaterial; incorporeal or insubstantial.

disruptive.o: From disrupt + -ive. In the business sense popularized by Clayton Christensen and Joseph Bower, see 1995 citation.
disruptive.example: Children who exhibit disruptive behaviour may be expelled from school.

embodiment.example: You are the very embodiment of beauty.
embodiment.exampleSense: A physical entity typifying an abstract concept.

embody.example: The soul, while it is embodied, can no more be divided from sin.
embody.exampleSense: To represent in a physical or concrete form; to incarnate or personify.

capable.o: Borrowed from Middle French capable, from Late Latin capābilis.
capable.example: He does not need help; he is capable of eating on his own.
capable.exampleSense: Able and efficient; having the ability needed for a specific task; having the disposition to do something; permitting or being susceptible to something.

occupy.o: From Middle English occupien, occupyen, borrowed from Old French occuper, from Latin occupāre (“to take possession of, seize, occupy, take up, employ”), from ob (“to, on”) + capiō (“to take”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kap- (“to seize, grab”). Doublet of occupate, now obsolete.
occupy.example: The better apartments were already occupied.
occupy.exampleSense: To take or use space. To live or reside in.

occupant.o: Borrowed from Middle French occupant (present participle of occuper) or Latin occupāns, occupantis (present participle of occupō). By surface analysis, occupy + -ant.

occupational.example: Boredom is an occupational hazard if you are a checkout operator.
occupational.exampleSense: Of, belonging, or relating to an occupation (in any sense).

occupation.o: From Middle English occupacioun, borrowed from Middle French occupacion, occupation, from Latin occupātiō, occupātiōnis, from occupō (“occupy, seize”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kap- (“to seize, grab”). By surface analysis, occupy + -ation.
occupation.example: The early years of Norman occupation saw a frenzy of castle building.
occupation.exampleSense: The control of a nation or region by a hostile military or paramilitary force.

workforce.example: The rail sector's ageing workforce (28% of workers are over 50 years old) means that about 15,000 people could retire from the industry by 2025.
workforce.exampleSense: All the workers employed by a specific organization or state, or on a specific project.

intuitive.o: Borrowed from Middle French intuitif, from Medieval Latin intuitivus, from Latin intueri.
intuitive.example: I'm real intuitive, everyone is, we're just conditioned not to trust it.
intuitive.exampleSense: Having a marked degree of intuition.

intuition.o: From Middle French intuition, from Medieval Latin intuitiō (“a looking at, immediate cognition”), from Latin intueor (“to look at, consider”), from in- (“in, on”) + tueor (“to look, watch, guard, see, observe”). Equivalent to intuit + -ion.

intuit.o: A back-formation from intuition and intuitive; compare Latin intuitus (“observed; considered”), perfect participle of intueor (“to look at, upon or towards; to observe, regard; to consider, contemplate”), from in- (“in, inside”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁én (“in”)) + tueor (“to look or gaze at”). Related to tuition, tutor.
intuit.example: Bhandat frowned. The words had made no impression on him. And Mr Biswas knew for sure then, what he had intuited and dismissed: Bhandat was deaf.
intuit.exampleSense: To know intuitively or by immediate perception.

telecom.o:
noun: Clipping of telecommunications.

noun: Abbreviation of telephone company.
telecom.example: However, HS2 believes it could sell mobile and broadband providers access to spare capacity in the fibre-optic cabling and telecoms masts being built to support the railway's signalling and telecoms.

poetry.o: From Middle English poetrye, poetrie, a borrowing from Old French pöeterie, pöetrie, from Medieval Latin poētria, from poēta (“poet”), from Ancient Greek ποιητής (poiētḗs, “poet; author; maker”). Displaced native Old English lēoþcræft.
poetry.example: More people write poetry than read it.
poetry.exampleSense: Literature composed in verse or language exhibiting conscious attention to patterns and rhythm.

flame.o:
noun: From Middle English flawme, blend of Old French flame and flambe, flamble, the first from Latin flamma, the second from Latin flammula, diminutive of flamma, both from pre-Latin *fladma; Proto-Italic *flagmā, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰel- (“to shimmer, gleam, shine”). Displaced native Old English līeġ.

verb: From Middle English flawmen, from Old French flamber, flammer.
flame.example: The main blaze of it is past, but a small thing would make it flame again.
flame.exampleSense: To produce flames; to burn with a flame or blaze.

jet black.o: Alternative spelling of jet-black. From jet + black.

jet.o:
noun: Borrowed from French jet (“spurt”, literally “a throw”), from Old French get, giet, from Vulgar Latin *iectus, *jectus, from Latin iactus (“a throwing, a throw”), from iacere (“to throw”). See abject, ejaculate, gist, jess, jut. Cognate with Spanish echar.

noun: From Middle English get, geet, gete, from a northern form of Old French jayet, jaiet, gaiet, from Latin gagātēs, from Ancient Greek Γαγάτης (Gagátēs), from Γάγας (Gágas, “a town and river in Lycia”). Doublet of gagate.

noun: Borrowed from French jet.
jet.example: Farmers may either dip or jet sheep with chemicals.
jet.exampleSense: To spray with liquid from a container.

pitch-black.o: From pitch (“tar”) + black. Compare West Frisian pikswart (literally “pitch-black”), Dutch pikzwart (literally “pitch-black”), German pechschwarz (literally “pitch-black”), Swedish becksvart (literally “pitch-black”), Icelandic biksvartur (literally “pitch-black”).

pitch-dark.example: The assassin crept into the royal bedchamber only after it was pitch-dark.
pitch-dark.exampleSense: Absolutely dark or black; as dark as pitch.

tsunami.o: Borrowed from Japanese 津波 (tsunami), from 津 (tsu, “harbour”) + 波 (nami, “wave”).
tsunami.example: A wave simulator in the tank can re-enact tsunamis and northeasters, and imitate wave conditions from midocean.
tsunami.exampleSense: A very large and destructive wave, generally caused by a tremendous disturbance in the ocean, such as an undersea earthquake or volcanic eruption; often a series of waves (a wave train).

infringe.o: Borrowed from Latin īnfringō, īnfringere (“to break off, break, bruise, weaken, destroy”), from in (“in”) + frangere (“to break”).

contravention.example: Their contravention of the treaty increased international tensions.
contravention.exampleSense: The act of contravening (a rule, regulation, law, or order) or of not fulfilling (an obligation, promise, or agreement).

violate.o:
verb: From Middle English violaten (“to defile, render impure”), from violat(e) (“defiled, desecrated”, also used as the past participle of violaten) + -en, borrowed from Latin violātus, perfect passive participle of violō (“to treat with violence (whether bodily or mental)”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix). Ultimately from vīs (“strength, power, force, violence”).

adj: From Middle English violat, from Classical Latin violātus.
violate.example: If you don't have a job, you can't pay the money, then you get violated and have to go back to prison.
violate.exampleSense: To cite (a person) for a parole violation.

seasoning.o:
noun: From season + -ing.

verb: From Middle English seasonyng, present participle of Middle English sesounen (“to season”), equivalent to season + -ing.
seasoning.example: To distinctify the seasoning, add grated fresh ginger, finely minced green chili (serrano or jalapeno), or chopped fresh herbs: cilantro, mint, thyme.
seasoning.exampleSense: Something used to add taste or flavour to food, such as salt and pepper or other condiment, herb or spice.

ubiquitous.o: From ubiquity + -ous, from Medieval Latin ubīquitās, from Latin ubīque (“everywhere”), from ubī̆ (“where”) + -que (“each, ever”). Compare ubiety.
ubiquitous.example: In Christianity, Hinduism and Judaism, God is ubiquitous.

adopt.o: From Middle French adopter, from Latin adoptō; ad + optō (“to choose, desire”), equivalent to ad- + opt.
adopt.example: A friend of mine recently adopted a Chinese baby girl found on the streets of Beijing.
adopt.exampleSense: To take (a child, heir, friend, citizen, etc.) by choice into a relationship. To take voluntarily (a child of other parents) to be in the place of, or as, one's own child.

fame.o: From Middle English fame, from Old French fame (“celebrity, renown”), itself borrowed from Latin fāma (“talk, rumor, report, reputation”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰéh₂-meh₂, from *bʰeh₂- (“to speak, say, tell”). Cognate with Ancient Greek φήμη (phḗmē, “talk”). Related also to Latin for (“speak, say”, verb), Old English bōian (“to boast”), Old English bēn (“prayer, request”), Old English bannan (“to summon, command, proclaim”). More at ban. Displaced native Old English hlīsa.
fame.example: I find thou art no less than fame hath bruited.
fame.exampleSense: The state of being famous or well-known and spoken of, especially for something positive.

offend.o: From Middle French offendre, from Latin offendō (“strike, blunder, commit an offense”), from ob- (“against”) + *fendō (“strike”).
offend.exampleSense: To hurt the feelings of; to displease; to make angry; to insult.

defend.o: From Middle English defenden, from Old French defendre, deffendre (Modern French défendre), from Latin dēfendō (“to ward off”), from Proto-Italic *fendō, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʷʰen-. Displaced native Old English bewerian.

biographee.example: Where the biographee is the founder of a school, the biography will be mentioned in conjunction with the treatment of the school.
biographee.exampleSense: One about whom a biography is written; the subject of a biography.

biography.o: Borrowed from New Latin biographia, from Ancient Greek βιογραφίᾱ (biographíā), from βίος (bíos, life) + -γραφία (-graphía, writing).
biography.example: There are many biographies of Benjamin Franklin.
biography.exampleSense: A person's life story, especially one published.

leave behind.example: The wound I got in my car accident left behind a massive scar.

entail.o:
verb: From Middle English entaillen, from Old French entaillier, entailler (“to notch”, literally “to cut in”); from prefix en- + tailler (“to cut”), from Late Latin taliare, from Latin talea. Compare late Latin feudum talliatum (“a fee entailed, i.e., curtailed or limited”).

noun: From Middle English entaille (“carving”), from Old French entaille (“incision”), from the verb entailler. See above.
entail.example: God's immateriality entails the divine attribute of incorporeality, that God is neither a body nor embodied.

investigation.o: From Middle English investigacioun, from Old French investigacion, from Latin investigatio. Morphologically investigate + -ion.
investigation.example: Despite thorough investigation, the perpetrator of the attacks remains unknown.
investigation.exampleSense: The act of investigating; the process of inquiring into or following up; research, especially patient or thorough inquiry or examination

investigate.o: Recorded since circa 1510, a back-formation from investigation on the basis of -ate (verb-forming suffix), from Latin investīgātiō (“a searching into”), from investīgātus, the perfect passive participle of investīgō, equivalent to in- + vestigate. Displaced native Old English undersēċan (literally “to search under or between”).
investigate.example: "Why don't you investigate?" he demanded. And investigate I did.
investigate.exampleSense: To conduct an inquiry or examination.

sideline.example: The coach stood on the sidelines and bellowed commands at the team.
sideline.exampleSense: The area outside the playing field beyond each sideline.

aloft.o: From Old Norse á lopti (“in the sky”); equivalent to a- + loft.
aloft.example: I think you said something concerning the manner in which yonder ship has anchored, and of the condition they keep things alow and aloft?
aloft.exampleSense: In the top, at the masthead, or on the higher yards or rigging.

descendant.o: From Middle English dessendaunte, borrowed from Middle French, from Latin dēscendēns, present participle of descendere, from dē + scandere (“to climb, ascend”).
descendant.example: The direct descendant of this form is the Slavic aorist: Sb.-Cr. nȍsī, dȍnosī.
descendant.exampleSense: A word or form in one language that is descended from a counterpart in an ancestor language.

respect.o: From Middle English respect, from Old French respect, also respit (“respect, regard, consideration”), from Latin respectus (“a looking at, regard, respect”), perfect passive participle of respiciō (“look at, look back upon, respect”), from re- (“back”) + speciō (“to see”). Doublet of respite.
respect.example: He is an intellectual giant, and I have great respect for him.
respect.exampleSense: an attitude of consideration or high regard

tectonic.o: 1650s, in sense of building, from Late Latin tectonicus, from Ancient Greek τεκτονικός (tektonikós, “pertaining to building”), from Ancient Greek τέκτων (téktōn, “carpenter, joiner, maker”), from Proto-Indo-European *teḱ- (“to make”) (from which also texture). In sense of geology, attested 1894. By surface analysis, Ancient Greek τέκτων (téktōn) + -ic (“pertaining to”).
tectonic.example: A boiling hot rock planet with extreme tectonic activity, Parnassus is home to many volcanic mountains. Surface scans reveal several geothermal and solar power stations, tapping the planet's abundant energy.
tectonic.exampleSense: Of, relating to, or caused by large-scale movements of the Earth's (or a similar planet's) lithosphere.

plausible.o: From Latin plausibilis (“deserving applause, praiseworthy, acceptable, pleasing”), from the participle stem of plaudere (“to applaud”).

laterally.example: The trial running tests which were made with the vehicles showed that they ride very steadily laterally, with almost complete absence of oscillation at all speeds.
laterally.exampleSense: Relating to the direction to the side.

lifetime.o: From Middle English lyftyme, equivalent to life + time. Cognate with Icelandic líftími (“lifetime”). Compare also Saterland Frisian Lieuwendstied, Dutch leeftijd and levenstijd, German Low German Levenstied, German Lebenszeit, Danish livstid, Swedish livstid.
lifetime.example: I've been waiting a lifetime for a train.

controvert.o: Borrowed from Medieval Latin contrōvertere, from Latin contrō- (“against”) + vertere (“to turn”).
controvert.example: [T]hat women from their education and the present state of civilized life, are in the same condition, cannot, I think, be controverted.
controvert.exampleSense: To argue against (something or someone); to contradict, to deny.

edition.o: From French édition, from Latin ēditiō, from ēdere (“to publish”).
edition.example: The first edition was soon sold.
edition.exampleSense: The whole number of copies of a work printed and published at one time.

rest.o:
noun: From Middle English rest, reste, from Old English ræst, from Proto-West Germanic *rastu, from Proto-Germanic *rastō, of uncertain origin; possibly derived from Proto-Indo-European *h₁reh₁- (“to rest”) or *Hre(h₁)s- (“to flow, rush”). Cognate with West Frisian rêst (“rest”), Dutch rust (“rest”), German Rast (“rest”), Swedish rast (“rest”), Norwegian rest (“rest”), Icelandic röst (“rest”), Old Irish árus (“dwelling”), German Ruhe (“calm”), Albanian resht (“to stop, pause”), Welsh araf (“quiet, calm, gentle”), Lithuanian rovà (“calm”), Ancient Greek ἐρωή (erōḗ, “rest, respite”), Avestan 𐬀𐬌𐬭𐬌𐬨𐬈 (aⁱrime, “calm, peaceful”), Sanskrit रमते (rámate, “he stays still, calms down”), Gothic 𐍂𐌹𐌼𐌹𐍃 (rimis, “tranquility”). Related to roo.

verb: From Middle English resten, from Old English restan, from Proto-West Germanic *rastijan (“to rest”), from Proto-Indo-European *ros-, *res-, *erH- (“rest”). Cognate with Dutch rusten (“to rest”), Middle Low German resten (“to rest”), German rasten (“to rest”), Danish raste (“to rest”), Swedish rasta (“to rest”).

noun: From Middle English reste, from Old French reste, from Old French rester (“to remain”), from Latin restō (“to stay back, stay behind”), from re- + stō (“to stand”). Replaced native Middle English lave (“rest, remainder”) (from Old English lāf (“remnant, remainder”)).

verb: From Middle English resten, from Old French rester, from Latin restō.

verb: Aphetic form of arrest.
rest.example: I need to get a good rest tonight; I was up late last night.
rest.exampleSense: Relief from work or activity by sleeping; sleep.

reputation.o: 14c. "credit, good reputation", from Middle English reputacion, reputacioun, reputation, reputatioun, from Anglo-Norman reputacion, reputacioun, Middle French reputation (French réputation), and their etymon Latin reputātiōnem (“consideration, thinking over”), noun of action from past participle stem of reputō (“reflect upon, reckon, count over”), from the prefix re- (“again”) + putō (“reckon, consider”). By surface analysis, repute + -ation. Displaced native Old English hlīsa (“reputation, fame”)
reputation.example: Sometimes a man makes a reputation, deserved or otherwise, by a single action.
reputation.exampleSense: What somebody or something is known for.

drift.o: From Middle English drift, dryft (“act of driving, drove, shower of rain or snow, impulse”), from Old English *drift (“drift”), from Proto-Germanic *driftiz (“drift”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰreybʰ- (“to drive, push”). Equivalent to drive + -t; cognate with North Frisian drift (“drift”), Saterland Frisian Drift (“current, flow, stream, drift”), Dutch drift (“drift, passion, urge”), German Drift (“drift”) and Trift (“drove, pasture”), Danish drift (“impulse, instinct”), Swedish drift (“impulse, instinct”), Icelandic drift (“drift, snow-drift”).
drift.example: a drift of snow, of ice, of sand, of plants, etc.
drift.exampleSense: Movement; that which moves or is moved. A mass of matter which has been driven or forced onward together in a body, or thrown together in a heap, etc., especially by wind or water.

strive.o: From Middle English striven (“to strive”), from Old French estriver (“to compete, quarrel”), from Frankish *strīban (“to exert, make an effort”) from Proto-Germanic *strībaną, or from Frankish *stribēn (“to strive”) from Proto-Germanic *stribāną. As this verb is conjugated as if it were a strong verb (like drive, ride, and write), it is possible this word may instead be inherited from an unattested Old English *strīfan or *strifian, which would itself also be inherited from Proto-Germanic *strībaną.
strive.exampleSense: To try to achieve a result; to make strenuous effort; to try earnestly and persistently.

deliberative.o: From Middle French délibératif, from Latin deliberativus.
deliberative.example: [T]he court of jurisdiction is to be distinguished from the deliberative body, the advisers of the crown.

deliberate.o: Inherited from Middle English deliberat(e), borrowed from Latin dēlīberātus, perfect passive participle of dēlīberō (“to consider, weigh well”) (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from dē- + *līberō / lībrō (“to weigh”)), from *libera / libra (“a balance”); see librate. Doublet of deliber.
deliberate.example: It is now time for the jury to deliberate the guilt of the defendant.
deliberate.exampleSense: To consider carefully; to weigh well in the mind.

morale.example: After the layoffs, morale was at an all time low; the staff were so dispirited nothing was getting done.
morale.exampleSense: The capacity of people to maintain belief in an institution or a goal, or even in oneself and others.

p: to pierce, to be fastened, to adhere
sticker.o: From stick (“to pierce, to be fastened, to adhere”) + -er (“agent”).
sticker.example: Also out of Africa: a huge hammered copper floor mirror stickered at $449.
sticker.exampleSense: To mark as the sticker price

delude.o: From Middle English deluden, borrowed from Latin dēlūdō (“mock, deceive”), from de + lūdō (“to make sport of, to mock”). See ludicrous.
delude.example: To delude the nation by an airy phantom.
delude.exampleSense: To deceive into believing something which is false; to lead into error; to dupe.

deluded.o: simple past and past participle of delude. From Middle English deluden, borrowed from Latin dēlūdō (“mock, deceive”), from de + lūdō (“to make sport of, to mock”). See ludicrous.
deluded.example: He was deluded to think that she cared in the slightest.

serve.o: From Middle English serven, from Old French servir, from Latin serviō (“be a slave; serve”), from Latin servus (“slave; servant”), which perhaps derives from Etruscan (compare Etruscan proper names 𐌔𐌄𐌓𐌅𐌉 (servi), 𐌔𐌄𐌓𐌅𐌄 (serve)), or from Proto-Indo-European *ser- (“watch over, protect”).
serve.example: The bust also served to remind the public that the Mafia is not harmless.
serve.exampleSense: To be effective. To have a given use or purpose; to function for something or to do something.

paradoxically.example: Cottagecore is related to grandmacore, faeriecore, farmcore and goblincore; other nostalgia-ridden aesthetic communities that, paradoxically, thrive on many of the most popular internet platforms of the day.
paradoxically.exampleSense: In a paradoxical manner; so as to create a paradox.

paradoxical.example: It is the ambiguity of language only which can make this proposition appear either doubtful or paradoxical. When properly explained and understood, it is almost self-evident.

administer.o: From Middle English administren, from Old French aminister, from Latin administrare (“to manage, execute”), from ad (“to”) + ministrare (“to attend, serve”), from minister (“servant”); see minister.
administer.example: Located in the northwestern side of the Black Sea, Snake Island, or called ostriv Zmiyinyy in Ukrainian and Insula Serpilor in Romanian, is currently administered by Ukraine but claimed by Romania.
administer.exampleSense: To manage or supervise the conduct, performance or execution of; to govern or regulate the parameters for the conduct, performance or execution of; to work in an administrative capacity.

viable.o: Borrowed from French viable (further from Latin vīta), with semantic influence of Latin viābilis (“passable”).
viable.example: Barker believed that evidence was emerging that a "solid proportion" of operations were "grossly uneconomic", and that no amount of improvement in equipment would make them viable. He suggested that "while the superstructure of the report is correct, the foundations require radical re-examination".

proponent.o: From Latin prōpōnēns, present participle of prōpōnō (“to put forward; propose”).
proponent.example: Proponents of the race — notably Mayor Michael R. Bloomberg and Mary Wittenberg, director of the marathon — said the event would provide a needed morale boost, as well as an economic one.
proponent.exampleSense: One who supports something; an advocate.

elixir.o: From Medieval Latin elixir (“philosopher's stone”), from Arabic اَلْإِكْسِير (al-ʔiksīr, “philosopher's stone”), from Ancient Greek ξηρίον (xēríon, “powder for drying wounds”), from ξηρός (xērós, “dry”).
elixir.example: The subcommittee's report to the Council on Pharmacy and Chemistry shows that the action of somnos is practically identical with that of a 5 per cent elixir of hydrated chloral.
elixir.exampleSense: A sweet flavored liquid (usually containing a small amount of alcohol) used in compounding medicines to be taken by mouth in order to mask an unpleasant taste.

genuine.o: From Latin genuīnus (“innate, native, natural”), from genus, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵenh₁-.

intended.o: simple past and past participle of intend. From Middle English intenden, entenden (“direct (one’s) attention towards”), borrowed from Old French entendre, from Latin intendō, intendere. See also intensive. Doublet of entendre. Largely displaced native Old English myntan (“to mean, intend; to think, suppose”), whence dialectal mint.
intended.example: His mother had died lately, watched over, as I was told, by his Intended.

undo.o: From Middle English undōn, from Old English ondōn, from Proto-West Germanic *andadōn (“to undo”), equivalent to un- + do. Cognate with West Frisian ûndwaan, ûntdwaan (“to undo; rid”), Dutch ontdoen (“to undo”).
undo.example: Woe is me, for I am undone!
undo.exampleSense: To impoverish or ruin, as in reputation; to cause the downfall of.

effectiveness.example: The effectiveness of the drug was well established.
effectiveness.exampleSense: The property of being effective, of achieving results.

effective.o: From French effectif, from Latin effectīvus (“productive; effective”), from efficiō (“to make; to bring about”), equivalent to effect + -ive.
effective.example: Whosoever is an effective, real cause of doing his neighbour wrong, is criminal.
effective.exampleSense: Producing a decided or decisive effect.

subtle.o:
adj: The adjective is derived from Middle English sotil, soubtil, subtil (“of a person, the mind, etc.: clever, ingenious, penetrating; cunning, sly; insidious; delicate, fine; not dense, light, thin; finely powdered; narrow, slender; etc.”), borrowed from Anglo-Norman sotel, subtil, sutil, Middle French soutil, subtil, sutil, and Old French sotil, soutil, subtil, sutil (“of an object: skilfully designed or made; delicate, fine; slender, thin; of an intangible thing: difficult to understand; of a person: discerning, shrewd; devious, sly; etc.”) (modern French subtil), from Latin subtīlis (“of texture: delicate, fine; slender, thin; accurate, keen; having fine judgment; etc.”), from sub (“below, under”) + tēla (“warp (threads running lengthwise in a loom); web”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *tetḱ- (“to create, produce; to cut, hew”), from *teḱ- (“to beget, sire”)). The word displaced Old English smēag (literally “creeping”). The modern and Middle English (and French) spellings with -b- are influenced by Latin subtīlis; the letter was probably never pronounced. The noun is derived from Middle English sotil, soubtil, subtil (“wise person; sophisticated people collectively”), from the adjective.

verb: Partly from both of the following: * From Middle English sotilen, subtile, subtilien (“to reflect on (something); to become mentally keen; to connive, scheme; to contrive, invent; to become pure or thin; to (cause something to) become light or thin; (medicine) to lighten or reduce (a diet)”), from Anglo-Norman sotiller, soutiller, sutiller, Middle French soutiller, soutillier, and Old French soutillier (“to make thin; to sharpen; to split hairs when arguing; to scheme, plot”), from Old French sotil, soutil, subtil, sutil (noun) (see etymology 1) + -ier (suffix forming infinitives of first-conjugation verbs), partly influenced by Late Latin subtīliāre, the present active infinitive of subtīliō (“to act craftily; to diminish”), from Latin subtīlis (adjective) (see etymology 1) + -ō (suffix forming regular first-conjugation verbs). * From subtle (adjective).
subtle.example: The difference is subtle, but you can hear it if you listen carefully.

self-esteem.example: People with high self-esteem think they're more popular, charming, and socially skilled than other people, but objective studies find no difference.
self-esteem.exampleSense: Confidence in one's own worth; self-respect.

esteem.o: First at end of 16th century; borrowed from Middle French estimer, borrowed from Latin aestimō. See estimate and aim, an older word, partly a doublet.
esteem.example: The Earth, which I esteem unable to reflect the rays of the Sun.
esteem.exampleSense: To judge; to estimate; to appraise

conflate.o: Attested since 1541: from Latin cōnflātus, past passive participle of cōnflō (“fuse, kindle, blow together”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).
conflate.example: Why the redactor created this conflate version, despite its inconsistencies, is a matter of conjecture.
conflate.exampleSense: Combining elements from multiple versions of the same text.

nor.o:
conj: From Middle English nauther, from nother. Cognate with neither. By surface analysis, not + or.

noun: From Etymology 1 (sense 2 above), reinterpreted as not + or or negation + or.
nor.example: Nor did I stop to think, but ran.
nor.exampleSense: And... not (introducing a negative statement, without necessarily following one).

hand out.example: He jumped onto the deck and handed her out of the gondola.

applause.o: From Latin applausus, from applaudō (“to strike against, to applaud”) (whence applaud).
applause.example: Livy never gets her share of those applauses, but it is because the people do not know. Yet she is entitled to the lion's share.
applause.exampleSense: The act of applauding; approbation and praise publicly expressed by the clapping of hands, stamping or tapping of the feet, acclamation, huzzas, or other means; marked commendation.

applaud.o: From Middle English applauden, from Latin applaudere (“to clap the hands together, applaud”), from ad (“to”) + plaudere (“to strike, clap”).
applaud.example: After the performance, the audience applauded for five minutes.
applaud.exampleSense: To express approval (of something) by clapping the hands.

consonance.o: From Middle English consonance, from Middle French consonance, from Latin cōnsonantia. Doublet of consonancy. By surface analysis, con- + son- + -ance.
consonance.example: Like a musical string, the optic nerve responds to the waves with which it is in consonance, while it refuses to be excited by others of almost infinitely greater energy, whose period of recurrence are not in unison with its own.

resonance.o: From Old French resonance (French résonance), from Latin resonantia (“echo”), from resonō (“to resound”).
resonance.example: One of the most important developments beyond the original concept of magnetic resonance is so-called double resonance in which, as the name suggests, one excites one resonant transition of a system while simultaneously monitoring a different transition.
resonance.exampleSense: The increase in the amplitude of an oscillation of a system under the influence of a periodic force whose frequency is close to that of the system's natural frequency.

assonance.o: From French assonance, from Latin assonāre; by surface analysis, a- + son- + -ance.

dissonance.o: Borrowed from Middle French dissonance, from Latin dissonantia; by surface analysis, dis- + son- + -ance.
dissonance.example: In this polyphony of images in the unconscious which is beyond and outside historical time, there are complex harmonies but no dissonances: the images do not clash, but that, of course, is an aesthetic judgment and not a scientific one.

characteristic.o: From Ancient Greek χαρακτηριστικός (kharaktēristikós), from χαρακτηρίζω (kharaktērízō, “to designate by a characteristic mark”), from χαρακτήρ (kharaktḗr, “a mark, character”). By surface analysis, character + -istic.
characteristic.example: Similarly, the characteristic for .003 is −3, and the characteristic for .0003 is −4.
characteristic.exampleSense: The integer part of a logarithm.

climate.o: From Middle English climat, from Old French climat, from Latin clima, from Ancient Greek κλίμα (klíma, “latitude”, literally “inclination”).
climate.example: And the effects from climate change are already extreme.
climate.exampleSense: The long-term manifestations of weather and other atmospheric conditions in a given area or country, now usually represented by the statistical summary of its weather conditions during a period long enough to ensure that representative values are obtained (generally 30 years).

implementation.example: His implementation works, but it needs some fine-tuning.
implementation.exampleSense: A result of implementing something; a finished product, system or device.

implement.o: Borrowed from Late Latin implēmentum (“a filling up”), from Latin impleō (“to fill up”).
implement.example: They carried an assortment of gardening implements in the truck.
implement.exampleSense: A tool or instrument for working with.

impediment.o: From Middle English impediment, borrowed from Latin impedimentum.
impediment.example: We were all on foot, officers and men alike. Our horses, baggage, and impediments had been left at Brashear to follow the column of General Emory.
impediment.exampleSense: Baggage, especially that of an army; impedimenta.

impassion.o: From Italian impassionare. By surface analysis, im- + passion.
impassion.example: Baseball remains a formidable item, yet scarcely capable of balancing the scale against the sports—football, cricket, racing, pelota, bull-fighting—which, in Europe, impassion the common people, and draw most of their champions from the common people.

imitation.o: From Middle English imitacioun, from Middle French imitacion, from Old French imitacion, from Latin imitatio.

failure.o: From Anglo-Norman failer, from Old French faillir (“to fail”). Equivalent to fail + -ure.
failure.example: For Liverpool, their season will now be regarded as a relative disappointment after failure to add the FA Cup to the Carling Cup and not mounting a challenge to reach the Champions League places.
failure.exampleSense: State or condition of not meeting a desirable or intended objective, opposite of success.

refer.o: From Middle English referren, from Old French referer, from Latin referre. The noun (used in journalism) is from the verb. Doublet of relate. See also infer, collate and confer, delate and defer, as well as prelate and prefer among others.
refer.example: He referred the matter to the principal.
refer.exampleSense: To submit to (another person or group) for consideration; to send or direct elsewhere.

infer.o: From Latin inferō, from Latin in- (“in, at, on; into”) + Latin ferō (“bear, carry; suffer”) (cognate to Old English beran, whence English bear), from Proto-Italic *ferō, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰéreti (“to bear, carry”), from the root *bʰer-. Literally “carry forward”, equivalent to “bear in”, as in concluding from a premise. Doublet of inbear.
infer.example: It is dangerous to infer too much from martial bluster in British politics: at the first hint of trouble, channelling Churchill is a default tactic for beleaguered leaders of all sorts.
infer.exampleSense: To introduce (something) as a reasoned conclusion; to conclude by reasoning or deduction, as from premises or evidence.

former.o:
adj: Inherited from Middle English former, comparative of forme (“first”), from Old English forma (“first”), descended from Proto-Germanic *frumô. Parallel to prior (via Latin), as comparative form from same Proto-Indo-European root. Related to first and fore (thence before), from Proto-Germanic.

noun: Inherited from Middle English formere. By surface analysis, form + -er.
former.example: The former is a good idea but the latter is not.
former.exampleSense: First of aforementioned two items. Used with the, often without a noun.

worth.o:
adj: From Middle English worth, from Old English weorþ, from Proto-West Germanic *werþ, from Proto-Germanic *werþaz (“worthy, valuable”); from Proto-Indo-European *wert-. Cognate with Scots wirth (“worth”), Cimbrian bèart (“worth, value”), Dutch waard, weerd (“worth”), German wert (“worth”) (the source of Polish wart (“worth”), Ukrainian вартість (vartistʹ, “worth, value”), etc), Luxembourgish wäert (“worth”), Yiddish ווערט (vert), ווערד (verd, “worth, value”), Danish værd (“worth”), Faroese and Icelandic verður (“worth”), Norwegian Bokmål verdt (“worth”), Norwegian Nynorsk verd (“worth”), Swedish värd (“worth”), Gothic 𐍅𐌰𐌹𐍂𐌸 (wairþ, “worth, value”), Welsh gwerth (“worth, value”).

verb: From Middle English worthen, wurthen, werthen (“to be; exist; come into being; come into existence”), from Old English weorþan (“to come into being; be made; become; arise; be”), from Proto-West Germanic *werþan, from Proto-Germanic *werþaną (“to come about; happen; come into being; become”), from Proto-Indo-European *wert- (“to turn; turn out”). Cognate with Dutch worden, dated Low German warrn, German werden, Old Norse verða (Norwegian verta, Swedish varda), Latin vertere.
worth.example: My house now is worth double what I paid for it.
worth.exampleSense: Having a value of; proper to be exchanged for.

instillation.o: From Middle French instillation, from Latin instillatio.

instill.example: It is important to instill discipline in a child at an early age.
instill.exampleSense: To cause a quality to become part of someone's nature.

argue.o: From Middle English arguen, from Old French arguer, from Latin arguere (“to declare, show, prove, make clear, reprove, accuse”), q.v. for more. Displaced native Old English flītan and reċċan.
argue.example: He argued that America should stop Lend-Lease convoying because it needed to fortify its own Army with the supplies.
argue.exampleSense: To present (a viewpoint or an argument therefor).

destine.o: From Middle English destinen, from Old French destiner. Doublet of destinate.

note.o:
noun: From Middle English note, from Old English not, nōt (“note, mark, sign”) and Old French note (“letter, note”), both from Latin nota (“mark, sign, remark, note”).

noun: From Middle English note (“use, usefulness, profit”), from Old English notu (“use, enjoyment, advantage, profit, utility”), from Proto-West Germanic *notu, from Proto-Germanic *nutō (“enjoyment, utilisation”), from Proto-Indo-European *newd- (“to acquire, make use of”). Cognate with West Frisian not (“yield, produce, crop”), Dutch genot (“enjoyment, pleasure”), Dutch nut (“usefulness, utility, behoof”), German Nutzen (“benefit, usefulness, utility”), Icelandic not (“use”, noun). Related also to Old English notian (“to enjoy, make use of, employ”), Old English nēotan (“to use, enjoy”), Old High German niozan (“to use, enjoy”) (Modern German genießen (“to enjoy”)), Modern German benutzen (“to use”). Related to nait.
note.example: Garson: Drop me a note sometime. I'd love to hear how we're doing.
note.exampleSense: A written or printed communication or commitment. A short informal letter; a billet.

indication.o: From Old French indication, from Latin indicātiō (“a showing, indicating the value of something; valuation”), from indicō (“point out, indicate, show; value”); see indicate; compare French indication, Spanish indicación, Italian indicazione. By surface analysis, indicate + -ion.
indication.example: Influenza and suspected influenza are FDA-approved indications for oseltamivir.
indication.exampleSense: Any symptom or occurrence in a disease that serves to direct to suitable remedies; the problem that warrants and prompts the use of a diagnostic test, imaging mode, or treatment (e.g., medication, surgical procedure).

coax.o:
verb: Originally (1586) in the slang phrase to make a coax of, from earlier noun coax, cox, cokes "fool, simpleton", itself of obscure origin, perhaps related to cock (“male bird, pert boy”). The modern spelling is from 1706.

noun: Shortened from coaxial
coax.example: They coaxed the rope through the pipe.
coax.exampleSense: To carefully manipulate (someone or something) into a particular desired state, situation or position.

major.o: From Middle English major, from Latin maior, comparative of magnus (“great, large; noble, important”), from Proto-Indo-European *méǵh₂yōs (“greater”), comparative of *meǵh₂- (“great”). Compare West Frisian majoar (“major”), Dutch majoor (“major”), French majeur. Doublet of mayor. Noun sense 1 is a shortening of sergeant major, perhaps after Spanish mayor in the same sense.
major.example: He used to be a major in the army.
major.exampleSense: A rank of officer in the army and the US air force, between captain and lieutenant colonel.

poster.o:
noun: From post + -er.

noun: From post + -er, from post (“travel, dispatch”).
poster.example: I saw a poster for the film on the side of a bus.
poster.exampleSense: An advertisement to be posted on a pole, wall etc. to advertise something.

version.o: Borrowed from Middle French version, from Medieval Latin versiō, from Latin vertō (“to turn”). Used in English since 16th century.
version.example: He gave another version of the affair.
version.exampleSense: An account or description from a particular point of view, especially as contrasted with another account.

mindset.example: Earth Day is a way of propagating and celebrating the environmentalist mindset.
mindset.exampleSense: A way of thinking; an attitude or opinion, especially a habitual one.

mind.o: From Middle English minde, munde, imynde, imunde, ȝemynde, ȝemunde, from Old English mynd, ġemynd (“mind, memory”), from Proto-West Germanic *mundi, *gamundi, from Proto-Germanic *mundiz, *gamundiz (“memory, remembrance”), from Proto-Indo-European *méntis (“thought”) (compare also mantis, via Greek), from the root *men- (“to think”). Cognate with Old High German gimunt ("mind, memory, remembrance"; Middle High German munst (“love, benevolence, joy”)), Old Norse mynd (“image, model”), Gothic 𐌲𐌰𐌼𐌿𐌽𐌳𐍃 (gamunds, “remembrance, memory, mind”). Related also to Danish minde (“memory”), Norwegian Bokmål, Norwegian Nynorsk, and Swedish minne (“memory”), Faroese and Icelandic minni (“memory, recall, recollection”), Latin mēns (“mind, reason”), Sanskrit मनस् (mánas), Ancient Greek μένος (ménos), Albanian mënd (“mind, reason”). Related to mantra. Compare also Old English myntan (“to mean, intend, purpose, determine, resolve”). More at mint.
mind.example: Mind you don't knock that glass over.
mind.exampleSense: To pay attention or heed to so as to obey; hence to obey; to make sure, to take care (that).

instead.o: From in + stead, from Middle English ine (“in”) + stede (“stead”). Related to German statt.
instead.example: I was going to go shopping, but I went dancing instead.
instead.exampleSense: In the place of something (usually mentioned earlier); as a substitute or alternative.

destiny.o: From Middle English destine et al., from Old French destinee, from Latin dēstinō (English destine). Displaced Old English wyrd.
destiny.example: There were two kinds of beardom opposed here, two futures, two destinies.
destiny.exampleSense: The fixed order of things; invincible necessity; an irresistible power or agency conceived of as determining the future, whether in general or of an individual.

progressive.o: From the Middle French progressif, from the Latin prōgressīvus, from prōgredior (perfect participial stem: prōgress-) + -īvus. Displaced native Old English forþgenġe. By surface analysis, progress + -ive.
progressive.example: The progressives want to legalise gay marriage.
progressive.exampleSense: One with liberal or progressive political beliefs.

quantify.o: From Medieval Latin quantifico (introduced by Sir William Hamilton in logic).
quantify.example: The statement (#92;forallx#92;in#92;mathbb#123;R#125;)#92;,2x#61;x#43;x quantifies over the real numbers.
quantify.exampleSense: To relate a statement (called a predicate) to a given set using a quantifier—either for all (denoted ∀) or there exists (denoted ∃).

seek.o: From Middle English seke, seken, from Old English sēċan, sēċean, sœ̄ċan, from Proto-West Germanic *sōkijan, from Proto-Germanic *sōkijaną (“to seek”), from Proto-Indo-European *séh₂gyeti (“to seek out”), from *seh₂g- (“to follow, trace”). Cognates Cognate with Yola zeek (“to seek”), North Frisian schük, sjuk, säke (“to search, seek”), Saterland Frisian säike (“to search, seek”), West Frisian sykje (“to seek”), Alemannic German sueche, süeche (“to search, seek”), Bavarian suacha, suachn (“to search”), Central Franconian söke (“to search”), Cimbrian züuchan (“to seek”), Dutch zoeken (“to seek”), Low German söken (“to seek”), German suchen (“to seek”), Luxembourgish sichen (“to seek; to fetch”), Vilamovian zihia, zihja (“to seek”), Yiddish זוכן (zukhn, “to search, seek”), Danish søge (“to seek; to apply”), Faroese søkja (“to seek”), Icelandic sækja (“to seek”), Norwegian Bokmål søke (“to seek; to apply”), Norwegian Nynorsk søka, søke, søkja, søkje (“to seek; to apply”), Swedish söka (“to search”), Gothic 𐍃𐍉𐌺𐌾𐌰𐌽 (sōkjan, “to seek”); also Cornish hedhes (“to reach; to achieve; to manage”), Welsh haeddu (“to deserve, merit”), Latin sāgiō (“to perceive quickly or keenly with the senses”), Ancient Greek ἡγέομαι (hēgéomai, “to go before, precede; to lead; to believe, hold”), Albanian gjegj (“to answer; to obey”), Hittite 𒊭𒀀𒆠𒄑𒍣 (ša-a-ki-ez-zi, “to seek out”). The Middle English and later Modern English hard /k/ derives from Old English sēcð, the third person singular.
seek.example: When the alarm went off I sought the exit in a panic.
seek.exampleSense: To try to reach or come to; to go to; to resort to.

sought.o: simple past and past participle of seek. From Middle English seke, seken, from Old English sēċan, sēċean, sœ̄ċan, from Proto-West Germanic *sōkijan, from Proto-Germanic *sōkijaną (“to seek”), from Proto-Indo-European *séh₂gyeti (“to seek out”), from *seh₂g- (“to follow, trace”). Cognates Cognate with Yola zeek (“to seek”), North Frisian schük, sjuk, säke (“to search, seek”), Saterland Frisian säike (“to search, seek”), West Frisian sykje (“to seek”), Alemannic German sueche, süeche (“to search, seek”), Bavarian suacha, suachn (“to search”), Central Franconian söke (“to search”), Cimbrian züuchan (“to seek”), Dutch zoeken (“to seek”), Low German söken (“to seek”), German suchen (“to seek”), Luxembourgish sichen (“to seek; to fetch”), Vilamovian zihia, zihja (“to seek”), Yiddish זוכן (zukhn, “to search, seek”), Danish søge (“to seek; to apply”), Faroese søkja (“to seek”), Icelandic sækja (“to seek”), Norwegian Bokmål søke (“to seek; to apply”), Norwegian Nynorsk søka, søke, søkja, søkje (“to seek; to apply”), Swedish söka (“to search”), Gothic 𐍃𐍉𐌺𐌾𐌰𐌽 (sōkjan, “to seek”); also Cornish hedhes (“to reach; to achieve; to manage”), Welsh haeddu (“to deserve, merit”), Latin sāgiō (“to perceive quickly or keenly with the senses”), Ancient Greek ἡγέομαι (hēgéomai, “to go before, precede; to lead; to believe, hold”), Albanian gjegj (“to answer; to obey”), Hittite 𒊭𒀀𒆠𒄑𒍣 (ša-a-ki-ez-zi, “to seek out”). The Middle English and later Modern English hard /k/ derives from Old English sēcð, the third person singular.

capability.o: Formed in Modern English as capable + -ity.
capability.example: Enforcing a security policy means controlling the rights users can acquire to data. In a capability machine, a user’s rights are defined by the capabilities he (or a process acting on his behalf) can obtain and the access rights conferred by those capabilities.
capability.exampleSense: A digital token allowing a user or process to interact in a specified way with an object that is subject to access control.

author.o: From Middle English auctour, from Anglo-Norman autour, from Old French autor, from Latin auctor, from augeō (“to increase, originate”). The h, also found in Middle French autheur, is unetymological as there is no h in the original Latin spelling. The OED attributes the h to contamination by authentic. Doublet of auteur.
author.example: The copyright of any original writing belongs initially and properly to its author.
author.exampleSense: The originator or creator of a work, especially of a literary composition; or, one of the creators of a collaborative work.

supplant.o: From Middle English supplanten, supplaunten, from Old French supplanter, from Latin supplantō (“trip up”), from sub (“from below, under”) + planta (“sole”).
supplant.example: Will online dictionaries ever supplant paper dictionaries?
supplant.exampleSense: To take the place of; to replace, to supersede.

innate.o: The adjective is first attested in the 1420s, the verb in 1602; from Middle English innat(e) (“innate, inborn”), borrowed from Latin innātus (“inborn, innate”) (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), perfect active participle of innāscor (“to be born in, grow up in”), from in- (“in, at on”) + nāscor (“to be born”); see natal, native. The verb is derived from the adjective, see -ate (verb-forming suffix).
innate.example: Ironically, given France's innate reluctance to permit competition at home, the first breach in Renfe's monopoly came from SNCF offshoot Ouigo España in 2021.
innate.exampleSense: Inborn; existing or having existed since birth.

cedar.o: From Middle English cedre, probably from Old French cedre, from Latin cedrus, from Ancient Greek κέδρος (kédros). Some suggest that the Middle English word was partially from Old English ċeder, but the gap in attestation between the two words makes this proposal unlikely. Possible doublet of citrus.
cedar.example: There had been dry seasons, accumulations of dust, wind-blown seeds, and cedars rose wonderfully out of solid rock.
cedar.exampleSense: A coniferous tree of the family Cupressaceae, especially of the genera Juniperus, Cupressus, Calocedrus, or Thuja.

ride.o: From Middle English riden, from Old English rīdan, from Proto-West Germanic *rīdan, from Proto-Germanic *rīdaną (“to ride”), from Proto-Indo-European *Hreydʰ- (“to ride”), from *h₃reyH- (“to move”), from *h₃er- (“to move, stir”). Cognates From Proto-Germanic: North Frisian ride, ridj, rir (“to ride”), West Frisian ride (“to ride”), Dutch rijden, ryden (“to ride; to drive”), German reiten, reuten (“to ride”), German Low German rieden (“to ride; to drive”), Limburgish rieje (“to ride; to drive”), Luxembourgish reiden (“to ride”), Vilamovian raeita, rajta (“to ride”), Danish ride (“to ride”), Faroese and Icelandic ríða (“to ride”), Norwegian Bokmål ri, ride (“to ride”), Norwegian Nynorsk ri, rida, ride (“to ride”), Swedish rida (“to ride”). From Indo-European: Cornish ardh (“height”), Irish arad, ard, árd (“high, tall”), Manx ard (“high, tall”), Scottish Gaelic àrd (“high”), Welsh ardd (“hill, upland”), Latin irrītō (“to excite, incite, stimulate; to exasperate”), Ancient Greek ὀρῑ́νω (orī́nō, “to move, stir”), Albanian rashë (“to have fallen; to have flopped”), Russian ре́ять (réjatʹ, “to fly, hover, soar”), Armenian հառնել (haṙnel, “to get up; to rise up”), Northern Kurdish rîtin (“to shit”), Persian ریدن (ridan, “to shit; to fuck up, to screw up”), Tocharian A ar- (“to evoke; to produce, yield”), Tocharian B er- (“to evoke; to produce, yield”), Hittite 𒅈𒉡𒊻𒍣 (ar-nu-uz-zi, “to address, send”), Sanskrit रीति (rīti, “course, motion; current, stream; line, row”).
ride.example: In an elaborately built, indoor San Francisco, passengers ride cable cars through quiet, hilly streets.
ride.exampleSense: To be transported in a vehicle; to travel as a passenger.

cowboy.o: PIE word *gʷṓws From cow + boy. More on Wikipedia.
cowboy.example: Derwood Bailey cowboyed for 50 cents a day, a noon meal, and a gallon of oats for his horse.
cowboy.exampleSense: To work as a cowboy, herding cattle.

irrespective.example: According to this doctrine, it must be resolved wholly into the absolute, irrespective will of God.
irrespective.exampleSense: Without regard for conditions, circumstances, or consequences; unbiased; independent; impartial.

assortment.example: This box has an assortment of chocolates. There's a picture on the cover so you know which is which.
assortment.exampleSense: A collection of varying but related items.

supplement.o: From Latin supplementum (“that which is added to supply a shortage”), from supplere (“to provide something”).
supplement.example: AI models will not completely replace the humans, she said, but will serve as a “supplement” intended to aid in the brand’s representation of various sizes, skin tones and ages.
supplement.exampleSense: Something added; especially, such an addition added to make up for a deficiency.

warden.o:
noun: From Middle English wardein, from Anglo-Norman wardein, from warder (“to guard”), variant of Old French guarder (“to guard”) (whence modern French garder, also English guard), from Proto-Germanic *ward-; related to Old High German wartēn (“to watch”). Compare guardian, French gardien, from Old French guardian, guardein. Compare also ward and reward. Doublet of guardian.

noun: From Middle English wardon, origin uncertain; perhaps from Anglo-Norman or Anglo-Latin wardo, -ōnis.
warden.example: In September, come Grapes; Apples; Poppies of all colours; Peaches; Melo-Cotones; Nectarines; Cornelians; Wardens; Quinces.

maze.o: From Middle English mase, from Middle English masen (“to perplex, bewilder”); or perhaps from Old English *mæs (“delusion, bewilderment”); akin to Old English āmasian (“to perplex, confound”), Icelandic masa (“to chatter”). More at amaze.
maze.example: She rowed back alone, the simple soul that was in her forwandered and mazed with excess of joy.

lorry.o: Uncertain; perhaps from dialectal English lurry (“to lug or pull about, drag”) (compare dialectal lurry-cart), or from the forename Laurie. First attested in early to middle 19th century.
lorry.example: Ties should never be hauled on a motor car, but they may safely be hauled on a lorrie car properly coupled to a motor car.
lorry.exampleSense: A large, low, horse-drawn, four-wheeled cart without sides; also, a similar wagon modified for use on railways.

desperation.o: From Middle English desperacion, desperacioun, desperation, disparacion, disperacion, disperacioun, dispiracioune, dysperacioun, from Middle French desperation and its etymon Latin dēspērātiō, dēspērātiōnis. By surface analysis, desperate + -ion.
desperation.example: The mass of men lead lives of quiet desperation. What is called resignation is confirmed desperation.
desperation.exampleSense: A state of despair, or utter hopelessness; abandonment of hope.

aspiration.o:
noun: From aspire + -ation.

noun: From aspirate + -ion or borrowed from Latin aspīrātiō.
aspiration.example: Riley has an aspiration to become a doctor.
aspiration.exampleSense: The act of aspiring or ardently desiring; an ardent wish or desire, chiefly after what is elevated or spiritual (with common adjunct adpositions being to and of).

aspire.o: From Middle English aspiren, from Old French aspirer, from Latin aspīrō (“breathe on; approach; desire”).
aspire.example: This match, to which you have the presumption to aspire, can never take place.
aspire.exampleSense: To have a strong desire or ambition to achieve something.

pavement.o: From Middle English pament, from Anglo-Norman pavement and reinforced by Middle French pavement; both from Latin pavīmentum (“paved surface or floor”), from pavīre (“to beat, to ram, to tread down”). Morphologically pave + -ment.
pavement.example: The antirunway munitions are specifically designed to cause maximum destruction to airfield pavements.
pavement.exampleSense: A paving (paved part) of a road or other thoroughfare; the roadway or road surface.

flyover.example: As our train to Paris dashed through the labyrynthine flyovers at Porchefontaine, barely a mile from Versailles, the 75 m.p.h. limit was already almost attained.
flyover.exampleSense: A road or railway that passes over another, allowing routes to cross without interruption.

prostate.o:
noun: Borrowed from Middle French prostate, a learned borrowing from Medieval Latin prostata.

adj: From pro- + state.
prostate.example: Finally, Paul made me get my prostate checked. As I say, he's already left a legacy. But if you haven't chaps, please get yourself checked over - it's worth it.

clever.o: From East Anglian dialectal English cliver (“expert at seizing”), from Middle English cliver (“tenacious”). * perhaps from Old English *clifer, clibbor (“clinging”); * or perhaps from Dutch, Low German, or East/Saterland Frisian (compare kluftich (“clever, prudent”), probably derived from Proto-West Germanic *kleuban (“to cleave, split”)); * or dialectal Norwegian klover (“ready, skillful”), itself borrowed from Middle Low German klever, related to kleven (“to stick”), from Old Saxon klibōn, from Proto-West Germanic *klibēn, related to the Old English word above; * possibly influenced by Old English clifer (“claw, hand”) (compare clawian (“to claw”)). Related to cleave. Perhaps influenced by Welsh celfydd (“talented, dexterous, expert”). Compare typologically Czech chytrý, Russian хи́трый (xítryj) (akin to хвата́ть (xvatátʹ)), also note схва́тывать на лету́ (sxvátyvatʹ na letú).
clever.example: I felt they expected me to say clever things, and I never could think of any till after the party was over.

adverse.o: First attested around 1374, from Old French avers (French adverse), from Latin adversus (“turned against”), past participle of advertere, from ad- (“to”) + vertere (“to turn”). See also versus.
adverse.example: Northbound expresses have the hardest work to perform, with adverse grades predominating from Willesden to Tring.
adverse.exampleSense: Unfavorable; antagonistic in purpose or effect; hostile; actively opposing one's interests or wishes; contrary to one's welfare; acting against; working in an opposing direction.

gardening leave.example: Until September Mr Orcel was head of the investment bank at Switzerland’s UBS. He had been due to succeed José Antonio Álvarez in April, after “gardening leave”.

gardenia.o: From New Latin, named after Scottish naturalist Dr. Alexander Garden.
gardenia.example: Heed remembered the baby-powder smell from the bowl of gardenias, their edges browning like toast.

excuse.o: From Middle English excusen (verb) and excuse (noun), borrowed from Old French escuser (verb) and excuse (noun), from Latin excūsō, excūsāre (“to excuse, allege in excuse, literally, free from a charge”), from ex (“out”) + causa (“a charge”); see cause, accuse and recuse. Displaced native Old English lād (“an excuse”) and lādian (“to excuse”).
excuse.example: I excused myself from the proceedings to think over what I'd heard.
excuse.exampleSense: To allow to leave, or release from any obligation.

outdoors.o:
adv: From out + doors (plural of door), probably as a shortening of out of doors. Alternatively, from outdoor (adjective) + -s (adverbial genitive suffix).

verb: See the etymology of the corresponding lemma form.
outdoors.example: He won't leave his house: he's afraid of the outdoors.
outdoors.exampleSense: The environment outside of enclosed structures.

agreement.o: From Middle English agrement, agreement, from Old French agrement, agreement. Doublet of agrément. Morphologically agree + -ment.
agreement.example: The UK and US negotiators were nearing agreement.
agreement.exampleSense: An understanding between entities to follow a specific course of conduct.

underpin.example: You should underpin the mine roof to prevent further collapse.
underpin.exampleSense: To support from below with props or masonry.

gardening.example: Gardening, then, is a sort of refined farming upon a limited scale.
gardening.exampleSense: The process or action of cultivating the soil, particularly in a garden; the care of a garden; horticulture.

subconscious.example: The sense of smell can be a subconscious influence on our actions.
subconscious.exampleSense: Occuring in the part of our mind that we are not normally aware of.

soak up.example: The tissue soaked up all of the spilled milk.
soak up.exampleSense: To absorb or draw in a substance, especially all of that substance.

sponge.o: From Middle English sponge, from Old English spunge, taken from Latin spongia, from Ancient Greek σπογγιά (spongiá), from σπόγγος (spóngos). Displaced native Old English swamm (“fungus, sponge”).
sponge.example: She removed Stranleigh’s coat with a dexterity that aroused his imagination. The elder woman returned with dressings and a sponge, which she placed on a chair.
sponge.exampleSense: A piece of porous material used for washing (originally made from the invertebrates, now often made of plastic).

moody.o: From Middle English mody, modi, from Old English mōdiġ (“brave”), from Proto-Germanic *mōdagaz (“courageous”). By surface analysis, mood + -y.
moody.example: Both Garry and Wally were dressed in dodgy suits and looked ready to hit the streets of Peckham to sell moody goods.
moody.exampleSense: Of dubious origin; counterfeit or stolen.

bass.o:
adj: A respelling of base under the influence of Italian basso (“low”).

noun: From Middle English bace, bas, alteration of bars, from Old English bærs (“a fish, perch”), from Proto-West Germanic *bars, from Proto-Germanic *barsaz (“perch”, literally “prickly”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰórsos (“prickle, thorn, scale”). Cognate with Dutch baars (“perch, bass”), German Barsch (“perch”). More at barse.

noun: A corruption of bast.
bass.example: The giant spoke in a deep, bass, rumbling voice that shook me to my boots.
bass.exampleSense: Of sound, a voice or an instrument, low in pitch or frequency.

recruitment.example: 'The recruitment of 72 new drivers means that we will have the resource to deliver additional services' said the spokesman.
recruitment.exampleSense: The process or art of finding candidates for a post in an organization, or recruits for the armed forces.

program.o: Borrowed from French programme, from Late Latin programma (“a proclamation, edict”), from Ancient Greek πρόγραμμα (prógramma, “a written public notice, an edict”), from προγράφω (prográphō, “to set forth as a public notice”), from πρό (pró, “before”) + γράφω (gráphō, “to write”). Doublet of programma.
program.example: He programmed the DVR to record his favorite show.
program.exampleSense: To enter a program or other instructions into (a computer or other electronic device) to instruct it to do a particular task.

breath.o: From Middle English breeth, breth, from Old English brǣþ (“odor, scent, stink, exhalation, vapor”), from Proto-West Germanic *brāþi (“vapour, waft, exhalation, breath”) (compare German Brodem (“haze, vapor; breath”), of a different but related formation).
breath.example: I could hear the breath of the runner behind me.
breath.exampleSense: The act or process of breathing.

programme.example: The programme about Greek architecture starts at 9:00 on Channel 4.
programme.exampleSense: British, New Zealand, and India standard spelling of program.

intervention.o: From Middle French intervention, from Latin interventiō. Morphologically intervene + -tion.
intervention.example: Fernando Torres was recalled in place of the suspended Didier Drogba and he was only denied a goal in the opening seconds by Laurent Koscielny's intervention - a moment that set the tone for game filled with attacking quality and littered with errors.
intervention.exampleSense: The action of intervening; interfering in some course of events.

discreet.o: From Middle English discrete, from Old French discret, from Latin discrētus, from past participle of discernere. Doublet of discrete.
discreet.example: John just doesn't understand that laughing at Mary all day is not very discreet.
discreet.exampleSense: Respectful of privacy or secrecy; exercising caution in order to avoid causing embarrassment; quiet; diplomatic.

discretion.o: From Middle English discrecioun, from Old French discretion, from Late Latin discrētiō, from Latin discerno. Equivalent to discreet + -ion.
discretion.example: The police came and searched us at their discretion because we were shouting at each other's faces.
discretion.exampleSense: The freedom to make one's own judgements. The authority to exercise one's own judgement in making decisions that have effect.

crypto-.o: Derived from Ancient Greek κρῠπτός (krŭptós, “hidden, secret”).

delegate.o:
noun: From Middle English delegat, from Old French delegat, from Latin dēlēgātus substantivized from the nominative masculine singular of dēlēgātus, the perfect passive participle of dēlēgō (“to send, assign, delegate”), see -ate (noun-forming suffix). See also legate.

verb: From the above noun by metanalysis or directly borrowed from Latin dēlēgātus, see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and Etymology 1 for more.

adj: From Middle English delegat(e) (“delegated”, used as a past participle and adjective), used as the past participle of delegate up until Early Modern English, see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and Etymology 1 for more.
delegate.example: The war on Covid-19 was delegated to the health secretary, Matt Hancock, a paralysed NHS and scientists publicly feuding over dud data.
delegate.exampleSense: To commit (a task or responsibility) to someone, especially a subordinate.

dispel.o: From Middle English dispelen, from Latin dispellere (“to disperse; to dispel”).
dispel.example: “My dispel didn't work,” she said finally. “He wasn't a blood witch, Sunny,” I said.
dispel.exampleSense: An act or instance of dispelling.

literary.example: He has long outlived his century, the term commonly fixed as the test of literary merit.

litchi.o: Ultimately from Hokkien 荔枝 (lē-chi). Doublet of lichi and lychee.

beer.o:
noun: From Middle English ber, bere, from Old English bēor (“beer”) (Oxford OED notes: "rare, except in poetry"), from Proto-West Germanic *beuʀ, from Proto-Germanic *beuzą (“beer”) (putatively from Proto-Indo-European *bʰewsóm), meaning “brewer's yeast”. However, also see the "beer" entry on EtymOnline (q.v.), which links a connection to monastic Vulgar Latin *biber (“a drink, beverage”), from Latin bibere (“to drink”). Samuel Johnson in his famous 18th-century A Dictionary of the English Language guessed it was from (unattested) Welsh *bîr; he distinguished it in his time from ale — the ancient usual word — by beer being older-aged and/or smaller. Cognate with Saterland Frisian Bjoor (“beer”), West Frisian bier (“beer”), Dutch bier (“beer”), German Low German Beer (“beer”), German Bier (“beer”), dialectal Swedish bjor, bör (“beer”), Norwegian Nynorsk bjor (“beer”), Faroese bjór (“beer”), Icelandic bjór (“beer”).

noun: From Middle English beere, equivalent to be + -er.
beer.example: Beer is brewed all over the world.
beer.exampleSense: An alcoholic drink fermented from starch material, commonly barley malt; often with hops or some other substance (like gruit) to impart a bitter flavor.

concentrated.o: simple past and past participle of concentrate. (early 17th century) From a Romance language, see French concentrer, Italian concentràre, Spanish concentrar; alternatively from Medieval Latin/New Latin concentrō + -ate (verb-forming suffix). Compare also earlier concentre and German konzentrieren. By surface analysis, con- + center (centr- in compounds) + -ate (verb-forming suffix).
concentrated.example: The concentrated fire from the enemy destroyed our fortifications.
concentrated.exampleSense: Intense; directed towards a specific location.

palm.o:
noun: From Middle English palme, from Old English palm, palma (“palm-tree, palm-branch”), from Latin palma (“palm-tree, palm-branch, palm of the hand”), from Proto-Indo-European *pl̥h₂meh₂, *pl̥h₂emeh₂ (“palm of the hand”), from Proto-Indo-European *pleh₂- (“flat”). Cognate with Dutch palm, German Palme, Danish palme, Icelandic pálmur (“palm”).

noun: From Middle English palme, paume, from Old French palme, paulme, paume (“palm of the hand, ball, tennis”), from Latin palma (“palm of the hand, hand-breadth”), from Proto-Indo-European *pl̥h₂(e)meh₂ (“palm of the hand”), from Proto-Indo-European *pleh₂- (“flat”). Doublet of palmo, palma, and pam. Cognate with Ancient Greek παλάμη (palámē, “palm of the hand”), Old English folm (“palm of the hand”), Old Irish lám (“hand”).
palm.example: The open palm of desire wants everything.
palm.exampleSense: The inner and somewhat concave part of the human hand that extends from the wrist to the bases of the fingers.

suppose.o: From Middle English supposen, borrowed from Old French supposer, equivalent to prefix sub- (“under”) + poser (“to place”); corresponding in meaning to Latin supponere (“to put under, to substitute, falsify, counterfeit”), suppositum. See pose.
suppose.example: Suppose that A implies B and B implies C. Then A implies C.

afterglow.example: Why did dusk and fir-scent and the afterglow of autumnal sunsets make people say absurd things?
afterglow.exampleSense: The glow seen in the sky after sunset.

glow.o:
verb: The verb is derived from Middle English glouen, glowen (“to give off heat and light without flame; of a thing: to be heated until red hot; to be brightly coloured; to shine brightly; (figurative) to be filled with emotion; of the face, etc.: to turn red, flush; etc.”), and then either: * from Old English glōwan (“to glow”) (a strong verb), from Proto-West Germanic *glōan (“to glow”); or * because the Middle English and modern English words are weak verbs, possibly from Old Norse *glówa, thought to be a variant of glóa (“to glow”), also a weak verb; both from Proto-Germanic *glōaną (“to glow”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰleh₁- (“to shine, glow; to be shining, glowing”). Possibly a doublet of glass. The noun is derived from the verb. cognates * Dutch gloeien * Finnish loistaa * German glühen * Norwegian glo * Old Norse glóa (Danish glo, Icelandic glóa, Swedish glo) * Saterland Frisian gloie, glöie, gluuje * West Frisian gloeie

verb: From Late Middle English glouen (“to gaze, stare”); further etymology uncertain, possibly either: * from glouen, glowen (“to give off heat and light without flame; of a thing: to be heated until red hot; to be brightly coloured; to shine brightly; (figurative) to be filled with emotion; of the face, etc.: to turn red, flush; etc.”); or * from Old Norse glóa (“to shine”) (whence Norwegian Nynorsk glo (“to stare”) and Swedish glo (“to stare”)). See further at etymology
glow.example: He had a bright red glow on his face.
glow.exampleSense: The brilliance or warmth of color in an environment or on a person (especially one's face).

jog.o: Of uncertain origin. Originally with the meaning of "to shake up and down." Possibly from Middle English joggen, a variant of jaggen (“to pierce, prod, stir up, arouse”); see jag (“sharp projection”). Or, perhaps an early alteration of English shog (“to jolt, shake; depart, go”), from Middle English shoggen, schoggen (“to shake up and down, jog”), from Middle Dutch schocken (“to jolt, bounce”) or Middle Low German schoggen, schocken (“to shog”), ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *skukkōn (“to move, shake, tremble”), possibly related to *skakan (“to shake, stir”). More at shock.
jog.example: I saw her jogging in the forest yesterday.
jog.exampleSense: To move at a pace between walking and running, to run at a leisurely pace.

daze.o: From Middle English, back-formation from dazed. Compare Old Norse dasask (“to become weary”), with reflexive suffix -sk, Swedish dasa (“lie idly”), and Icelandic dasask (“to make weary with cold”). Also compare Proto-Germanic *dusāną, to slumber. Alternatively from Middle Dutch dasen (“act silly”).

dazzle.example: Dazzled by the headlights of the lorry, the deer stopped in the middle of the street.
dazzle.exampleSense: To confuse or overpower the sight of (someone or something, such as a sensor) by means of excessive brightness.

naos.o: From Ancient Greek ναός (naós, “inner part of the temple”).
naos.example: The simplest form of the rectangular temple was that in which the two side walls were carried out from the naos to form the porch at one or both extremities of the building.
naos.exampleSense: The inner part of an ancient Greek temple, containing a statue of the temple's deity and surrounded by a colonnaded portico; (by extension) the Roman cella, which it later gave rise to.

eligible.o: From Middle French eligible, from Latin eligibilis, from ēligō (“to select, to choose”).
eligible.example: Federal agencies report that only about 1 percent of eligible students take advantage of switching schools and fewer than 20 percent of eligibles receive extra tutoring.

seduce.o: Borrowed from Latin sēdūcō (“to lead apart or astray”), from sē- (“aside, away, astray”) + dūcō (“to lead”); see duct. Compare adduce, conduce, deduce, etc. and Middle English seduct.
seduce.example: Your father was seduced by the dark side of The Force.
seduce.exampleSense: To beguile or lure (someone) away from duty, accepted principles, or proper conduct; to lead astray.

deduce.o: From Late Middle English deducen (“to demonstrate, prove, show; to argue, infer; to bring, lead; to turn (something) to a use; to deduct”), borrowed from Latin dēdūcere, the present active infinitive of dēdūcō (“to lead or bring out or away; to accompany, conduct, escort; (figuratively) to derive, discover, deduce”); from dē- (prefix meaning ‘from, away from’) + dūcere (the present active infinitive of dūcō (“to conduct, guide, lead; to draw, pull; to consider, regard, think”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dewk- (“to lead; to draw, pull”)).
deduce.example: If you leave this Isle, and got to the court of England, see what regard there will be paid to the old pedigree that deduces your descent from kings and conquerors.
deduce.exampleSense: To examine, explain, or record (something) in an orderly manner.

reduce.o: From Middle English reducen, from Old French reduire, from Latin redūcō (“reduce”); from re- (“back”) + dūcō (“lead”). See duke, and compare with redoubt.
reduce.example: to reduce weight, speed, heat, expenses, price, personnel etc.
reduce.exampleSense: To bring down the size, quantity, quality, value or intensity of something; to diminish, to lower.

duce.o: Borrowed from Italian duce. Doublet of doge, duc, duke, and dux.

chronical.example: A convulsive Asthma is a periodical and chronical Disease; but a suffocating Catarrh is more properly reckoned an acute Disease.

chronic.o: From chronical, from Old French cronike, from Latin chronicus, from Ancient Greek χρονικός (khronikós, “of time”), from χρόνος (khrónos, “time”). By surface analysis, chron- + -ic.
chronic.example: Chronic patients must learn to live with their condition.
chronic.exampleSense: Of a person, suffering from an affliction that is prolonged or slow to heal.

commingle.example: This vibrant stir-fry from Christian Reynoso is Chifa cooking — the cuisine that commingles Chinese and Peruvian elements — and it’s utterly delicious.

blend.o: From Middle English blenden, either from Old English blandan, blondan, ġeblandan, ġeblendan or from Old Norse blanda (“to blend, mix”) (which was originally a strong verb with the present-tense stem blend; compare blendingr (“a blending, a mixture; a half-breed”)), whence also Danish blande, or from a blend of the Old English and Old Norse terms; both ultimately from Proto-Germanic *blandaną (“to blend; mix; combine”). Compare Middle Dutch blanden (“to mix”), Gothic 𐌱𐌻𐌰𐌽𐌳𐌰𐌽 (blandan), Old Church Slavonic блєсти (blesti, “to go astray”).
blend.example: To make hummus you need to blend chickpeas, olive oil, lemon juice and garlic.
blend.exampleSense: To mingle; to mix; to unite intimately; to pass or shade insensibly into each other.

walkabout.o: Deverbal from walk about, originally in Australian Pidgin English; the Australian aboriginal word wokabat is derived from this term.

informal.example: Students and faculty members lunch at the cafeteria and naturally communicate freely with one another in a relaxed and informal setting.

automobile.o: From French automobile, from Ancient Greek αὐτός (autós, “self”) + French mobile (“moving”), from Latin mōbilis (“movable”), equivalent to auto- (“self”) + mobile.
automobile.example: The misguided youngsters are yachting, attending the races, playing the "stage Johnny," automobiling, playing poker for high stakes, overliving at home, on expensive shopping tours, attending box parties to the theatre, visiting high-priced restaurants, etc., etc.

vehicle.o: Borrowed from French véhicule, from Latin vehiculum (“a carriage, conveyance”), from vehō, vehere (“to carry”).
vehicle.example: But electric vehicles and the batteries that made them run became ensnared in corporate scandals, fraud, and monopolistic corruption that shook the confidence of the nation and inspired automotive upstarts.
vehicle.exampleSense: A conveyance; a spacious device for carrying or transporting substances, objects, people or animals.

exhaust.o: From Latin exhaustus, past participle of exhaurīre (“to draw out, drink up, empty, exhaust”), from ex (“out”) + haurīre (“to draw (especially water), drain”).
exhaust.example: My grandfather seemingly never exhausts his supply of bad jokes.
exhaust.exampleSense: To use up; to deplete, drain or expend wholly, or until the supply comes to an end

reluctance.o: From reluct + -ance. From Latin relū̆ctor (“to struggle against, oppose, resist”) + -ance, from re- (“back”) + luctor (“to struggle”).
reluctance.example: That is to say, the total number of ampere-hours, including the drop of gilbertage, due to magnetic flux traversing the reluctance of the circuit, must be equal to zero.
reluctance.exampleSense: That property of a magnetic circuit analogous to resistance in an electric circuit.

liter.o: Alternative form of litre. From French litre, from Medieval Latin litra, from Ancient Greek λίτρα (lítra, “a Sicilian coin, a measure of weight”). Related to Latin lībra. Doublet of arratel, libbra, Libra, libra, lira, litra, livre, and rottol.

radius.o: Borrowed from Latin radius (“ray”). Doublet of ray.
radius.example: Fatima claims to have visited all the bars within a five-mile radius of her Manhattan apartment.
radius.exampleSense: A line segment between any point of a circle or sphere and its center.

monster.o: From Middle English monstre, from Old French monstre, mostre, moustre, from Latin mōnstrum. Displaced native Old English fīfel and Old English þyrs.
monster.example: O, 'twas a din to fright a monster's ear,/ to make an earthquake.
monster.exampleSense: A terrifying and dangerous creature, especially one of an imaginary or mythical kind.

mad.o:
