noun: From Middle English barnin, bearne, beerne, beornen, berne, bernen, birne, burne, burnen, bærnen, which arose via the metathesis of branne, brennen, brennyn, brynne, from Old English beornan, biernan, birnan, byrnan, from Proto-West Germanic *brinnan, from Proto-Germanic *brinnaną (“to burn”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰrenw-, present stem from *bʰrewh₁- (“to boil; to brew”). The East Midland forms were heavily influenced by Old Norse brenna, brinna (“to burn”). Doublet of brew. The late metathesis of East Midland brin- to birn- (and subsequently burn-) parallels the phonological development of bird and dirt from brid and drit. As this metathesized form became the Chancery Standard, it completely displaced the semantic functions and weak conjugation paradigm of the native Old English bærnan (weak), alongside the surviving remnants of byrnan (strong). Cognates Cognate with Cimbrian prönnan (“to burn”), Dutch barnen, branden (“to burn”), German brinnen (“to burn”), Luxembourgish brennen (“to burn”), Vilamovian brīn (“to burn”), Yiddish ברענען (brenen, “to burn”), Danish brænde (“to burn”), Faroese and Icelandic brenna (“to burn”), Norwegian Bokmål brenne (“to burn”), Norwegian Nynorsk brenna, brenne (“to burn”), Swedish brinna (“to burn”), Gothic 𐌱𐍂𐌹𐌽𐌽𐌰𐌽 (brinnan, “to burn”); also Cornish bros (“blazing, boiling”), Irish bruth (“heat; eruption; surf”), Welsh brwd (“eager, keen; passionate, zealous”), Latin defrutum (“grape must reduced by boiling”), Ancient Greek πορφύρω (porphúrō, “to boil, heave”), Albanian burth (“Cyclamen hederifolium; mouth burning”), Armenian աղբյուր (aġbyur, “fountain, spring”), Sanskrit भुर्वन् (bhurvan, “runnel, spring”). More at brew.

noun: From Northern Middle English burn, from Old English burne, burna (“spring, fountain”), Proto-West Germanic *brunnō, from Proto-Germanic *brunnô, *brunō. Cognate with Scots burn (“stream”), Cimbrian, Mòcheno prunn (“well, spring”), Dutch bron (“well”), German Bronnen, Brun, Brunnen (“well”), Luxembourgish Buer, Bur (“well”), Yiddish ברונעם (brunem, “well”), Danish brønd (“well”), Faroese brunnur, bruður (“well”), Icelandic brunnur (“well”), Norwegian Bokmål, Scanian brønn (“well”), Norwegian Nynorsk brunn, brønn (“well”), Swedish brunn (“well”), Gothic 𐌱𐍂𐌿𐌽𐌽𐌰 (brunna, “source, wellspring”), Crimean Gothic brunna (“spring, fountain, source”). Also Albanian burim (“spring, fountain”), Ancient Greek φρέαρ (phréar, “well, reservoir”), Old Armenian աղբիւր (ałbiwr, “fount”). Doublet of bourn. More at brew.
burn.example: She burned the child with an iron, and was jailed for ten years.
burn.exampleSense: To injure (a person or animal) with heat or chemicals that produce similar damage.

ken.o:
verb: From Middle English kennen (“to give birth, conceive, generate, beget; to develop (as a fetus), hatch out (of eggs); to sustain, nourish, nurture”), from Old English cennan (“to give birth, conceive, generate, beget”), from Proto-West Germanic *kannjan, from Proto-Germanic *kanjaną.

verb: Northern English dialects and Scots language from Middle English kennen, from Old English cennan (“make known, declare, acknowledge”) originally “to make known”, causative of cunnan (“to become acquainted with, to know”), from Proto-West Germanic *kannijan, from Proto-Germanic *kannijaną, causative of *kunnaną (“be able”), from which comes the verb can. Cognate with West Frisian kenne (“to know; recognise”), Dutch kennen (“to know”), German kennen (“to know, be acquainted with someone/something”), Norwegian Bokmål kjenne, Norwegian Nynorsk kjenna, Old Norse kenna (“to know, perceive”), Swedish känna (“to know, feel”), Danish kende (“to know”). See also: can, con.

noun: From a nautical abbreviation of Middle English kenning, present participle of the verb kennen (“to make known, point out, reveal; to direct, instruct, teach; to know, perceive”).

noun: Of unknown origin. Perhaps from kennel.

noun: From Hebrew קֵן (qēn, “nest”).

noun: Borrowed from Japanese 間.

noun: Borrowed from Japanese 剣.
ken.example: Ah thought he wis being harsh, flippant and show-oafy, until ah got sae far in. Now ah ken precisely what the cunt meant.

priority.o: From Old French priorite, from Latin priōritās. Surface analysis: prior + -ity.
priority.example: She needs to get her priorities straight and stop playing games.
priority.exampleSense: A goal of a person or an organisation.

first aid.example: He slipped and fell under the wagon's wheels, losing his left leg. His presence of mind was quite amazing. The report notes that Webb's knowledge of first aid probably saved his life, and he was able to instruct others who came to help him.
first aid.exampleSense: Basic medical care given to an injury victim, usually where the injury is slight or where better care is not available.

vacancy.o: From Late Latin vacantia. Doublet of vacance.
vacancy.example: Whenever there is a vacancy in the office of the Vice President, the President shall nominate a Vice President who shall take office upon confirmation by a majority vote of both Houses of Congress.

uphill.example: For a large part of this game, England once again looked like a team suffering from the rigours of a long season and faced an uphill task when Hofmann put Germany in front.

delighted.o: simple past and past participle of delight. Attested from the 13th century, from Middle English delite, from Old French deleiter, deliter, from Latin dēlectāre (“to delight, please”), frequentative of dēlicere (“to allure, entice”), from dē- (“away”) + laciō (“to lure, to deceive”), from Proto-Italic *lakjō (“to draw, pull”), of unknown ultimate origin. Doublet of delect. Related with delectation, delicate, delicious and dilettante. The modern unetymological spelling (instead of expected delite) is influenced by light and other words ending in -ight, such as might, bright, etc. The -gh- may also be an attempt to represent the Latin -c-; compare obsolete indight for indict.

novel.o:
adj: From Middle English novel, from Old French novel (“new, fresh, recent, recently made or done, strange, rare”) (modern nouvel, nouveau), from Latin novellus (“new, fresh, young, modern”), diminutive of novus (“new”). Doublet of nouveau.

noun: Borrowed from Italian novella, from Latin novella, feminine of novellus. Doublet of novella.

noun: From Middle English novel, from Old French novelle, from Latin novella, feminine of novellus.

noun: Borrowed from Latin novella, feminine of novellus.
novel.example: Libum is a cake made of Honey (sugar is a nouvelle, since the discovery of America), meale and oyle.

availability.o: From available + -ity; attested since the early 1800s.
availability.example: What is your availability this week?

commit.o: Inherited from Middle English committen, itself borrowed from Latin committō (“to bring together, join, compare, commit (a wrong), incur, give in charge, etc.”), from com- (“together”) + mittō (“to send”). See mission.
commit.example: Every Git commit represents a single, atomic changeset with respect to the previous state.
commit.exampleSense: The act of committing (e.g. a database transaction), making it a permanent change; such a change.

squash.o:
noun: From Middle English squachen, squatchen, from Old French esquacher, escachier, from Vulgar Latin *excoāctiāre, from Latin ex + coāctāre. Probably influenced by Middle English quashen, quassen, from Old French esquasser, escasser (“to crush, shatter, destroy, break”), from Vulgar Latin *exquassare, from Latin ex- + quassare (“to shatter”) (see quash).

noun: Shortening of Narragansett askutasquash (“[a vegetable] eaten green (or raw)”), from askut (“green, raw”) + asquash (“eaten”).

noun: Clipping of musquash.
squash.example: Ivor had acquired more than a mile of fishing rights with the house; he was not at all a good fisherman, but one must do something; one generally, however, banged a ball with a squash-racket against a wall.
squash.exampleSense: A sport played in a walled court with a soft rubber ball and bats like tennis racquets.

verdant.o: From Middle French verdoyant, from Old French verb verdier, verdoier, from vert (“green”), from Vulgar Latin *virdis, from Latin viridis.
verdant.example: It was a verdant and delightful valley, watered by a rivulet ...
verdant.exampleSense: Abundant in verdure; lush with vegetation.

metric.o: From French métrique (1864), from New Latin metricus (“pertaining to the system based on the meter”), from metrum (“a meter”); see meter. By surface analysis, metre + -ic.
metric.example: How to measure marketing? Use these key metrics for measuring marketing effectiveness.
metric.exampleSense: A measure for something; a means of deriving a quantitative measurement or approximation for otherwise qualitative phenomena (especially used in engineering).

collar.o: From Middle English coler, borrowed from Old French coler (Modern French collier), from Late Latin collāre, from Latin collāris, from collum (“neck”). Cognate with Gothic 𐌷𐌰𐌻𐍃 (hals, “neck”), Old English heals (“neck”). Compare Spanish cuello (“neck”). More at halse. Doublet of collet.
collar.example: Make sure your dog has a collar holding an identification tag.
collar.exampleSense: Clothes that encircle the neck. A band or chain around an animal's neck, used to restrain and/or identify it.

attention.o: From Middle English attencioun, borrowed from Latin attentio, attentionis, from attendere, past participle attentus (“to attend, give heed to”); see attend. Equivalent to attend + -tion.
attention.example: The attention mechanism is an important part of these models and plays a very crucial role. Before Transformer models, the attention mechanism was proposed as a helper for improving conventional DL models such as RNNs.
attention.exampleSense: A kind of prioritisation technique in neural networks that assigns soft weights between tokens from two (or more) input sequences in order to compute the required output.

flew.o:
verb: From Middle English flew, flow, from Old English flēag, flug-, from Proto-Germanic *flaug, *flug-, past tense forms of Proto-Germanic *fleuganą (“to fly”). Compare Saterland Frisian flooch (“flew”), West Frisian fleach (“flew”), Dutch vloog (“flew”), German flog (“flew”), Danish fløj (“flew”), Swedish flög (“flew”), Icelandic flaug (“flew”).

noun: Unknown.
flew.example: The raging hound's flews were twisted upwards in an angry snarl.
flew.exampleSense: The thick, dangling upper lip of certain breeds of dog, or the canine equivalent of the upper lip.

round up.example: During the Holocaust, the Nazis rounded up Jews into ghettos and concentration camps.
round up.exampleSense: To collect or gather (something) together. To arrest or detain a group of people based on collective (rather than individualized) cause or suspicion, often as a form of targeted persecution.

ranger.example: He saw men long dead whom he had rangered with, saw Pedro Flores and Pea Eye and a redheaded whore he had taken up with for a month in his riverboating days.

range.o: From Middle English rengen, from Old French rengier (“to range, to rank, to order,”), from the noun renc, reng, ranc, rang (“a rank, row”), from Frankish *hring, from Proto-Germanic *hringaz (“ring, circle, curve”). Doublet of ring.
range.example: Maccabeus ranged his army by hands.
range.exampleSense: To set in a row, or in rows; to place in a regular line or lines, or in ranks; to dispose in the proper order.

routinely.example: We routinely test the fire extinguishers but no one ever expects them to fail.
routinely.exampleSense: Done by rote or habit, as part of a routine, without attention or concern.

routine.o: Unadapted borrowing from French routine. By surface analysis, route + -ine. Further from Latin rupta via. Compare typologically travel << Latin tripālium, whence also travail, note the inverse semantic vector from a subjective state (toil) to an objective action (journey). Also compare Czech běžný (< běžet), Russian обихо́д (obixód), обихо́дный (obixódnyj) (akin to ходи́ть (xodítʹ)).
routine.example: Pepper's forgiven me in the quiet, hurt way women sometimes forgive. She doesn't cry. She doesn't smile either. She's being routine.

afield.o: From Middle English afeld, a-felde, o felde, on felde, from Old English on felde (“afield”, literally “in (the) field”), equivalent to a- (“on”) + field.
afield.example: Whether things could have been different is an open question, and one that would take us far afield from the focus of this book.
afield.exampleSense: Away (from the home or starting point, physical or conceptual); usually preceded by far (or farther, further).

waterfront.example: The wide prospect up stream was grey and lowering, the long still-distant waterfront of Dundee, and the Fife shore were alike colourless, and there was ample evidence of rough weather not far ahead.
waterfront.exampleSense: The land alongside a body of water.

invoke.o: From Middle English *invoken, envoken, borrowed from Old French envoquer, from Latin invocāre (“to call upon”), itself from in- + vocare (“to call”). Doublet of invocate.
invoke.example: In certain Christian circles, invoking the Bible constitutes irrefutable proof.
invoke.exampleSense: To appeal for validation to a (notably cited) authority.

picturesque.o: From picture + -esque, a calque of French pittoresque, from picture (“a picture, painting”).
picturesque.example: We looked down onto a beautiful, picturesque sunset over the ocean.
picturesque.exampleSense: Resembling or worthy of a picture or painting; having the qualities of a picture or painting; pleasingly beautiful.

springtime.example: Georgian and Regency houses cluster picturesquely around the sloping village green, which in springtime is carpeted with daffodils.
springtime.exampleSense: The season of spring, between winter and summer.

spring.o:
verb: From Middle English springen, from Old English springan (“to spring, leap, bounce, sprout forth, emerge, spread out”), from Proto-West Germanic *springan, from Proto-Germanic *springaną (“to burst forth”), from Proto-Indo-European *spre(n)ǵʰ- (“to move, race, spring”), from *sperǵʰ- (“to hurry”). Cognates * Saterland Frisian springe * West Frisian springe * Dutch springen * German Low German springen * German springen * Danish springe * Swedish springa * Norwegian springe * Faroese springa * Icelandic springa (“to burst, explode”). Other possible cognates include Lithuanian spreñgti (“to push (in)”), Old Church Slavonic прѧсти (pręsti, “to spin, to stretch”), Latin spargere (“to sprinkle, to scatter”), Ancient Greek σπέρχω (spérkhō, “to hasten”), Sanskrit स्पृहयति (spṛháyati, “to be eager”). Some newer senses derived from the noun.

noun: From Middle English spryng (“a wellspring, tide, branch, sunrise, kind of dance or blow, ulcer, snare, flock”); partly from Old English spring (“wellspring, ulcer”), from Proto-West Germanic *spring, from Proto-Germanic *springaz (“a wellspring, fount”); and partly from Old English spryng (“a jump”), from Proto-West Germanic *sprungi, from Proto-Germanic *sprungiz (“a jump”). Further senses derived from the verb and from clippings of day-spring, springtime, spring tide, etc. Its sense as the season, first attested in a work predating 1325, gradually replaced Middle English lenten, lente, from Old English lencten (“spring, Lent”) as that word became more specifically liturgical. Compare fall.
spring.example: We jumped so hard the bed springs broke.
spring.exampleSense: Something which springs, springs forth, springs up, or springs back, particularly A mechanical device made of flexible or coiled material that exerts force and attempts to spring back when bent, compressed, or stretched.

negotiate.o: c. 1598; borrowed from Latin negōtiātus, perfect active participle of negōtior (“to do business, trade”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from negotium (“business”) + -or, from nec (“not”) + otium (“leisure, ease, inactivity”).
negotiate.example: Novak Djokovic earlier had negotiated his own tricky passage through the fifth day.
negotiate.exampleSense: To succeed in coping with, getting over or navigate a hazard or obstacle.

outright.o: From Middle English outright. By surface analysis, out + right.
outright.example: I have just responded outright to that question.

twofold.o: PIE word *dwóh₁ From Middle English twofold, from Old English twēofeald. Equivalent to two + -fold; cognate to Icelandic tvöfalt and Dutch tweevoudig.
twofold.example: 1874, Ernest Myers (transl.), The Extant Odes of Pindar, translated into English, Pythian Ode III, page 65.
twofold.exampleSense: Having two parts, especially two different parts.

grid.o: Back-formation or clipping of griddle or gridiron.
grid.example: McLaren's Lewis Hamilton fought up from the back of the grid to eighth, with team-mate Jenson Button taking ninth.
grid.exampleSense: The pattern of starting positions of the drivers for a race.

diesel.o: From German Diesel, named after inventor Rudolf Diesel, who developed a heavy-duty engine in Germany (1892–1897) and perfected it throughout his life.
diesel.example: The only reason the VW bug has a solenoid is to prevent it from dieseling.
diesel.exampleSense: For a spark-ignition internal combustion engine to continue running after the electrical current to the spark plugs has been turned off. This occurs when there's enough heat in the combustion chamber to ignite the air and fuel mixture without a spark, the same way that heat and pressure cause ignition in a diesel engine.

scarcity.o: Inherited from Middle English scarsite, from Old Northern French escarsete; by surface analysis, scarce + -ity.
scarcity.example: The crucial and intersecting challenges of scarcities, both emerging and intensifying, will consume China’s custodians over the next decade.
scarcity.exampleSense: An inadequate amount of something; a shortage.

particle.o: From Middle French particule, and its source, Latin particula (“small part, particle”), diminutive of pars (“part, piece”). Semantically displaced native Old English grot whence modern English groat.
particle.example: What, he asked himself, does quantum theory have to say about the familiar properties of particles such as position?
particle.exampleSense: Any of various physical objects making up the constituent parts of an atom; an elementary particle or subatomic particle.

trap.o:
noun: From Middle English trappe, from Old English træppe, treppe (“trap, snare”) (also in betræppan (“to trap”)) from Proto-West Germanic *trappjā (“trap, snare”), from Proto-West Germanic *trappjan (“to step”), from Proto-Germanic *trapjaną (“to tread, stamp”), from Proto-Indo-European *drebʰ- (“to step, trip, trample”). Cognate with Dutch trap (“step, stair”), German Low German Trapp (“step, stair”). Akin also to West Frisian traap (“stepping, treading, stairway”), German Treppe (“step, stair”), Old English træppan (“to step, tread”). Connection to "step" is "that upon which one steps". French trappe and Spanish trampa are ultimately borrowings from Germanic.

noun: Borrowed from Swedish trapp (“step, stair, stairway”), from Middle Low German trappe (“stair, step”).

verb: Akin to Middle English trappe (“trappings, gear”), and perhaps from Old Northern French trape, a byform of Old French drap, a word of the same origin as English drab (“a kind of cloth”).

noun: Clipping of trapezius.
trap.example: They shot out of the school gates like greyhounds out of the trap.
trap.exampleSense: Any device used to hold and suddenly release an object.

still.o:
adj: From Middle English stille (“motionless, stationary”), from Old English stille (“still, quiet”), from Proto-West Germanic *stillī, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)telH- (“to be silent; to be still”). Cognate with Scots stil (“still”), Saterland Frisian stil (“motionless, calm, quiet”), West Frisian stil (“quiet, still”), Dutch stil (“quiet, silent, still”), Low German still (“quiet, silent, still”), German still (“still, quiet, tranquil, silent”), Swedish stilla (“quiet, silent, peaceful”), Icelandic stilltur (“set, quiet, calm, still”). Related to stall. (noun: Falkland Islander): Military slang, short for still a Benny, since the military had been instructed not to refer to the islanders by the derogatory term Benny (which see).

noun: Via Middle English stillen, clip of distillen; Old French distiller; Latin distillare, from dis- + stillare, from Latin stilla.

verb: Inherited from Old English stillan.

verb: Aphetic form of distil, or from Latin stillare.
still.example: The guilt being great, the fear doth still exceed.
still.exampleSense: To an even greater degree. Used to modify comparative adjectives or adverbs.

distill.example: Carbonic acid is a limpid colourless body, extremely fluid, and floating upon the other contents of the tube. It distills readily and rapidly at the difference of temperature between 32° and 0°.

sheet.o:
noun: From Middle English schete; partly from Old English sċīete (“a sheet, a piece of linen cloth”); partly from Old English sċēata (“a corner, angle; the lower corner of a sail, sheet”); and Old English sċēat (“a corner, angle”); all from Proto-Germanic *skautijǭ, *skautaz (“corner, wedge, lap”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kewd- (“to throw, shoot, pursue, rush”). Cognate with North Frisian skut (“the fold of a garment, lap, coattail”), West Frisian skoat (“sheet; sail; lap”), Dutch schoot (“the fold of a garment, lap, sheet”), German Low German Schote (“a line from the foot of a sail”), German Schoß (“the fold of a garment, lap”), Danish skød (“lap, skirt”), Icelandic skaut (“the corner of a cloth, a line from the foot of a sail, the skirt or sleeve of a garment, a hood”), Norwegian skaut (“headdress”), Swedish sköt (“sheet”).

noun: A minced oath of shit.
sheet.example: A sheet of paper measuring eight and one-half inches wide by eleven inches high is a popular item in commerce.
sheet.exampleSense: A piece of paper, usually rectangular, that has been prepared for writing, artwork, drafting, wrapping, manufacture of packaging (boxes, envelopes, etc.), and for other uses. The word does not include scraps and irregular small pieces destined to be recycled, used for stuffing or cushioning or paper mache, etc. In modern books, each sheet of paper is typically folded in half, to produce two leaves and four pages. In the absence of folding, "leaf" and "sheet" are equivalent.

glazing.o: Inherited from Middle English glasynge; equivalent to glaze + -ing.
glazing.example: Before new glazier's putty can be applied, the various bits of old glazing must be scraped off.
glazing.exampleSense: The material used in such act or process; glaze.

glaze.o: From Middle English glasen, from glas (“glass”) (Modern English glass), from Old English glæs, from Proto-Germanic *glasą. Related to glazen. In the sense of "overcompliment", originated in November 2021 and popularized throughout 2022, and allegedly suggests the spattering of semen on the complimented person, following "the visual of a donut being glazed"; could be derived by analogy of sugarcoating first before a sexual connotation is taken separately. The noun is from the verb.
glaze.example: An overfired biscuit has insufficient porosity for glazing.
glaze.exampleSense: To apply a thin, transparent layer of coating.

film.o: From Middle English filme, from Old English filmen (“film, membrane, thin skin, foreskin”), from Proto-West Germanic *filmīn-, from Proto-Germanic *filmīn- (“thin skin, membrane”) (compare Proto-Germanic *felma- (“skin, hide”)), from Proto-Indo-European *pél-mo- (“membrane”), from *pel- (“to cover, skin”). Cognate with Old Frisian filmene (“thin skin, human skin”), Middle Dutch velm, vilm (“fleece, film, membrane”), Old High German felm (“peel, skin, wrap”), Old English *felma (in ǣġerfelma (“egg membrane”)). Related also to Dutch vel (“sheet, skin”), German Fell (“skin, hide, fur”), Swedish fjäll (“fur blanket, cloth, scale”), Norwegian fille (“rag, cloth”), Lithuanian plėvē (“membrane, scab”), Russian плева́ (plevá, “membrane”), Ancient Greek πέλμα (pélma, “sole of the foot”). More at fell. Sense of a thin coat of something is 1577, extended by 1845 to the coating of chemical gel on photographic plates. By 1895 this also meant the coating plus the paper or celluloid.
film.example: Her legs folded under her, and her eyes filmed over.
film.exampleSense: To cover or become covered with a thin skin or pellicle.

by.o: From Middle English by, bi, from Old English bī (“by; near; around”), from Proto-West Germanic *bī, from Proto-Germanic *bi (“near; by; around; about”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁epi. Cognate with West Frisian by (“by; near”), Afrikaans by (“at; by; near”), Saterland Frisian bie (“near; by”), Dutch bij (“near; by”), German Low German bi (“by; near; at”), German bei (“by; near; at”).
by.example: We will send it by the first week of July.
by.exampleSense: Not later than (the given time); not later than the end of (the given time interval).

generate.o:
verb: From Latin generō (“beget, procreate, produce”) + -ate (verb-forming suffix), from genus (“a kind, race, family”, gener- in compounds) + -ō; see genus. Compare Italian generare, French générer (and its older (and now obsolete) English cognate from Middle French, gender (“engender, breed, copulate”)).

adj: Learned borrowing from Latin generātus, perfect passive participle of generō (“beget, procreate, produce”). See Etymology 1 and -ate (adjective-forming suffix) for more.
generate.example: The Ecclesiastical Commission was generated by Sir Robert Peel and bore the marks of Peel’s personality; bureaucratic, capable and cold.
generate.exampleSense: To bring into being; give rise to.

litre.o:
noun: From French litre, from Medieval Latin litra, from Ancient Greek λίτρα (lítra, “a Sicilian coin, a measure of weight”). Related to Latin lībra. Doublet of arratel, libbra, Libra, libra, lira, litra, livre, and rottol.

noun: Borrowed from Spanish litre.
litre.example: You should be able to fill four cups with one litre of water.
litre.exampleSense: The metric unit of fluid measure, equal to one cubic decimetre. Symbol: L, l, or ℓ.

gulf.o: From Middle English gulf, goulf, golf, from Old French golf, from Italian golfo, from Late Latin colfos, from Ancient Greek κόλπος (kólpos, “bosom, gulf”), of obscure origin, but possibly from Proto-Indo-European *kʷelp- (“to curve, arch”).
gulf.example: Of course, there was no arguing against this, but one thing was clear, we could not attempt that leap in the dark; the only thing to do was to wait for the ray of light which pierced through the gulf at sunset.
gulf.exampleSense: A hollow place in the earth; an abyss; a deep chasm or basin.

confront.o: From Middle French confronter, borrowed from Medieval Latin cōnfrontāre, from con- + frontem (“front, forehead”).
confront.example: It is important that police officers learn to deescalate situations in which someone confronts them aggressively.
confront.exampleSense: To stand or meet facing, especially in competition, hostility or defiance; to come face to face with

sustain.o: From Middle English susteinen, sustenen, from Old French sustenir (French soutenir), from Latin sustineō, sustinēre (“to uphold”), from sub- (“from below, up”) + teneō (“hold”, verb).
sustain.example: A foundation sustains the superstructure; an animal sustains a load; a rope sustains a weight.
sustain.exampleSense: To keep from falling; to bear; to uphold; to support.

bore.o:
verb: From Middle English boren, from Old English borian (“to pierce”), from Proto-West Germanic *borōn, from Proto-Germanic *burōną. Compare Danish bore, Norwegian Bokmål bore, Dutch boren, German bohren, Old Norse bora. Cognate with Latin forō (“to bore, to pierce”), Latin feriō (“strike, cut”) and Albanian birë (“hole”). Sense of wearying may come from a figurative use such as "to bore the ears"; compare German drillen.

noun: From Middle English *bore, bare, a borrowing from Old Norse bára (“billow, wave”), from Proto-Germanic *bērō (“that which bears or carries”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰer- (“to bear”). Cognate with Icelandic bára (“billow, wave”), Faroese bára (“billow, wave”). Doublet of bier.
bore.example: My neighbour is such a bore when he talks about his coin collection.
bore.exampleSense: One who inspires boredom or lack of interest; an uninteresting person.

borehole.example: Extensive borehole information and tendered contract prices make these cost estimates much more plausible than earlier estimates.
borehole.exampleSense: A hole bored into the ground to collect samples for analysis or to extract oil or water.

portable.o: From Middle English portable, from Middle French portable and Latin portābilis. By surface analysis, port (“to carry”) + -able.
portable.example: How do Java and C# create cross-platform, portable programs, and why can't C++ do the same?
portable.exampleSense: Of software: able to be run on multiple hardware or operating systems.

decade.o: From Middle English decade, from Old French decade, from Late Latin decādem (“(set of) ten”), from Ancient Greek δεκάς (dekás), from δέκα (déka, “ten”). In reference to a span of ten years, originally a clipping of the phrase decade of years. By surface analysis, dec- + -ade. Doublet of decad and dekad.
decade.example: Athletes' use of herbal supplements has skyrocketed in the past two decades.
decade.exampleSense: A group, set, or series of ten A period of ten years , particularly such a period beginning with a year ending in 0 and ending with a year ending in 9.

proof.o: From Middle English proof, from Old French prove, from Late Latin proba (“a proof”), from Latin probō (“to prove”); see prove; compare also the doublet probe.
proof.example: And these men scour the printed proof for error, blunder, and misspelling.
proof.exampleSense: A proof sheet; a trial impression, as from type, taken for correction or examination.

roof.o:
noun: From Middle English rof, from Old English hrōf (“roof, ceiling; top, summit; heaven, sky”), from Proto-Germanic *hrōfą (“roof”). Cognate with Scots ruif (“roof, ceiling”), Dutch roef (“cabin on a boat”), Icelandic hróf (“shed”), Irish cró (“pen, barn, cabin”), Proto-Slavic *stropъ (“roof, ceiling”). Compare Faroese rógv (“something high up”).

verb: From Middle English rofen, roven (“to roof”), from the noun (see above).
roof.example: A trench about ten feet deep was dug in the ground and roofed over with sticks and earth so as to form a dark tunnel.
roof.exampleSense: To cover or furnish with a roof.

heel.o:
noun: From Middle English hele, from Old English hēla, from Proto-West Germanic *hą̄hilō, from Proto-Germanic *hanhilaz, diminutive of Proto-Germanic *hanhaz (“heel, hock”), equivalent to hock + -le. More at hock. Compare North Frisian haiel, West Frisian hyl, Dutch hiel, German Low German Hiel, Danish and Norwegian hæl, Swedish häl.

verb: Probably inferred from hielded, the past tense of hield, from Middle English helden, heelden, from Old English hyldan, hieldan (“to incline”), cognate with Old Norse hella (“to pour out”) (whence Danish hælde (“lean, pour”)).

verb: See hele (“conceal, keep secret, cover”).
heel.example: Boiled mutton was in one, and the heel of a damper in another.
heel.exampleSense: A crust end-piece of a loaf of bread.

hail.o:
noun: From Middle English hayl, haul, from Old English hæġl, hæġel, hagol (“hail”), from Proto-West Germanic *hagl, from Proto-Germanic *haglaz, of uncertain origin. Either from Proto-Indo-European *kagʰlos (“pebble”); or alternatively from *ḱoḱló-, a reduplication of *ḱel- (“cold”). Cognate with Saterland Frisian Hail (“hail”), West Frisian heil (“hail”), Low German Hagel (“hail”), German Hagel (“hail”), Dutch and Swedish hagel (“hail”), Danish, Norwegian Bokmål, Norwegian Nynorsk, and Icelandic hagl (“hail”). Compare also Old Norse héla (“frost”). Doublet of haglaz, if the second etymology (“cold”) is correct. Root-cognates outside of Germanic include Ancient Greek κάχληξ (kákhlēx, “pebble”), or alternatively Sanskrit शिशिर (śíśira, “cool, cold”), possibly also Lithuanian šešėlis (“shade, shadow”), depending on the etymology.

verb: From Middle English haylen, haulien, hawelien, from Old English hagolian, hagalian (“to hail”), from Proto-West Germanic *haglōn, from Proto-Germanic *haglōną (“to hail”), from the noun (see above). Cognate with Saterland Frisian hailje (“to hail”), West Frisian heilje (“to hail”), Dutch hagelen (“to hail”), German Low German hageln (“to hail”), German hageln (“to hail”), Danish hagle (“to hail”), Swedish hagla (“to hail”), Norwegian Nynorsk hagle, hagla (“to hail”), Faroese hegla (“to hail”), Icelandic hagla (“to hail”).

adj: From Middle English heyl (“healthy, sound”), from Old Norse heill, from Proto-Germanic *hailaz (“whole, entire, healthy”). The verb is from Middle English heilen, itself from the adjective. Doublet of whole, hale, and heil.
hail.example: Their lack of good intelligence also meant that they vastly overestimated the size of their foes for far too long, hails of armor-piercing shells doing comparatively little damage compared to the high explosive that they should have been using.
hail.exampleSense: A rapid, intense barrage by a large number of projectiles or other objects.

wage.o:
noun: From Middle English wage, from Anglo-Norman wage, from Old Northern French wage, a northern variant of Old French gauge, guage (whence modern French gage), Medieval Latin wadium, from Frankish *waddī (cognate with Old English wedd), from Proto-Germanic *wadją (“pledge”), from Proto-Indo-European *wedʰ- (“to pledge, redeem a pledge”). Akin to Old Norse veðja (“to pledge”), Gothic 𐍅𐌰𐌳𐌹 (wadi), Dutch wedde. Compare also the doublet gage. More at wed.

verb: From Middle English wagen (“to pledge”), from Anglo-Norman, Old Northern French wagier, a northern variant of Old French guagier (whence modern French gager), itself either from guage or from a derivative of Frankish *waddī, possibly through a Vulgar Latin intermediate *wadiō from *wadium (see the noun above). See Medieval Latin wadiō and wadium for more.
wage.example: The two are waging war, and the one triumphs by the destruction of the other.
wage.exampleSense: To conduct or carry out (a war or other contest).

spam.o: The original sense (canned ham) is a proprietary name registered by Geo. A. Hormel & Co. in U.S., 1937. It is presumed to be a conflation of either "spiced ham" or "shoulder of pork and ham" but was soon extended to other kinds of canned meat. Hormel spells the trademarked name in all upper case. The use for unsolicited and unwanted email derives from a Monty Python's Flying Circus sketch. In the 1970 sketch, a group of Vikings in a restaurant repeatedly chant the word "spam". The earliest recorded real-life use for this sense occurs around 1993 which finds reference in a newsgroup post dated March 31, 1993, but the term may have been in use on "Multi-User Dungeons" (MUDs) in the 1980s.
spam.example: I get far too much spam.

stash.o:
noun: Unknown. Perhaps a blend of stick + cache or stow + cache.

noun: Apheretic clipping of mustache.
stash.example: He stashed his liquor in the cabinet under the bar.
stash.exampleSense: To hide or store away for later use.

radio-.o: Derived from Latin radius (“ray”). By surface analysis, clipping of radiation + -o-.

baked.o: simple past and past participle of bake. From Middle English baken, from Old English bacan (“to bake”), from Proto-West Germanic *bakan, from Proto-Germanic *bakaną (“to bake”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeh₃g- (“to roast, bake”). Cognate with West Frisian bakke (“to bake”), Dutch bakken (“to bake”), Low German backen (“to bake”), German backen (“to bake”), Norwegian Bokmål bake (“to bake”), Danish bage (“to bake”), Norwegian Nynorsk and Swedish baka (“to bake”), Ancient Greek φώγω (phṓgō, “roast”, verb).
baked.example: SATURNINUS: Go fetch them hither to us presently.
baked.exampleSense: That has been cooked by baking.

profit.o: From Middle English profit, from Old French profit (Modern French profit), from Latin prōfectus (“advance, progress, growth, increase, profit”), from proficiō (“to go forward, advance, make progress, be profitable or useful”). Doublet of profect.
profit.example: Let no man anticipate uncertain profits.
profit.exampleSense: Total income or cash flow minus expenditures. The money or other benefit a non-governmental organization or individual receives in exchange for products and services sold at an advertised price.

purify.o: From Middle English purifien, purifyen, from Old French purifier, purifiier, from Latin pūrificō, pūrificāre, from pūrus (“pure; clean”).
purify.example: The modern arts deviate from the standards set forth by the divine—art should be used to purify one’s heart and improve one’s morality.
purify.exampleSense: To cleanse, or rid of impurities.

indifference.o: From Middle French indifférence, from Late Latin indifferentia. By surface analysis, in- + difference.
indifference.example: His daughter's indifference towards the sexist group made him wonder if she was even human.

apathy.o: From French apathie, from Latin apathīa, from Ancient Greek ἀπάθεια (apátheia, “impassibility”, “insensibility”, “freedom from emotion”), from ἀπαθής (apathḗs, “not suffering or having suffered”, “without experience of”), from ἀ- (a-, “not”) + πάθος (páthos, “anything that befalls one”, “incident”, “emotion”, “passion”). Doublet of apatheia, which was borrowed directly from Ancient Greek.
apathy.example: I opened it with apathy; the theory which he attempts to demonstrate and the wonderful facts which he relates soon changed this feeling into enthusiasm.
apathy.exampleSense: Lack of emotion or motivation; lack of interest or enthusiasm towards something; disinterest (in something).

inability.o: From earlier inhability (“disqualification for office”), equivalent to in- + ability. Compare Middle French inhabilité, Medieval Latin inhabilitās.

adaptiveness.example: With female adaptiveness she fell in with his humour, and looked at the world through his eyes.
adaptiveness.exampleSense: The state or quality of being adaptive; capacity to adapt.

gear.o: From Middle English gere, a borrowing from Old Norse gervi, from Proto-Germanic *garwijaną (“to prepare”). See also adjective yare, yar from the same root via Old English.
gear.example: This shop is not really geared towards people of our age.
gear.exampleSense: To design or devise (something) so as to be suitable (for a particular type of person or a particular purpose).

boredom.exampleSense: An instance or period of being bored; A bored state.

outcome.example: A quality automobile is the outcome of the work of skilled engineers and thousands of workers.
outcome.exampleSense: That which is produced or occurs as a result of an event or process.

productive.o: Borrowed from Late Latin productivus, equivalent to product + -ive.

mutation.o: Late 14th century as Middle English mutacioun, from Latin mūtātiō, both directly and via Old French mutacion.
mutation.example: Names for a group: A flute or mutation of thrushes.

mutate.o: First attested in 1796; back-formation from mutation on the basis of -ate (verb-forming suffix), ultimately from Latin mūtō (“to exchange; to change, to vary”). Doublet of moult.
mutate.example: The virus has mutated into a more resilient version.

domesticate.o:
verb: First attested in 1620; either borrowed from Middle French domestiquer (Modern French domestiquer) or directly from Medieval Latin domesticātus, perfect passive participle of domesticō (“to domesticate”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix). By surface analysis, domestic + -ate.

noun: First attested in 1860; borrowed from Medieval Latin domesticātus (“domesticated”), see Etymology 1 and -ate (noun-forming suffix).
domesticate.example: The Russians claim to have successfully domesticated foxes.
domesticate.exampleSense: To adapt to live with humans.

edible.o: From Late Latin edibilis, from Latin edō (“eat”). Doublet of eatable.
edible.example: Although stale, the bread was edible.
edible.exampleSense: Capable of being eaten without disgust or disrelish.

staple.o:
noun: From Middle English staple, from Anglo-Norman estaple, Old French estaple (“market, (trading) post”), from Late Latin stapula, from Frankish *stapul, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *stapulaz (“post”), from Proto-Indo-European *stebʰ- (“post, stem”). Compare staff. Doublet of étape and etymology 2.

noun: From Middle English stapel (“staple, pillar, post”), from Old English stapol (“post, pillar”), from Proto-West Germanic *stapul, from Proto-Germanic *stapulaz, from Proto-Indo-European *stebʰ- (“post, stem”). See also Old English steppan (“to step”) and Old French estaple (“post”). Consider also stapes (“stirrup”), from Latin. Doublet of étape and etymology
staple.example: Tow is flax with short staple.
staple.exampleSense: Short fiber, as of cotton, sheep’s wool, or the like, which can be spun into yarn or thread.

resign.o:
verb: From Anglo-Norman resigner, Middle French resigner, and its source, Latin resignāre (“to unseal, annul, assign, resign”), from re- + signāre (“to seal, stamp”). Piecewise doublet of re-sign.

verb: From re- + sign.
resign.example: He had no choice but to resign the game and let his opponent become the champion.
resign.exampleSense: To submit passively; to give up as hopeless or inevitable.

tape.o: From Middle English tape, tappe, from Old English tæppa, tæppe (“ribbon, tape”); further origin unclear. Probably akin to Old Frisian tapia (“to pull, rip, tear”), Middle Low German tappen, tāpen (“to grab, pull, rip, tear, snatch”), Middle High German zāfen, zāven (“to pull, tear”).
tape.example: Jones broke the tape in 47.77 seconds, a new world record.
tape.exampleSense: Finishing tape, stretched across a track to mark the end of a race.

tape measure.example: Reappearing, tape-measure in hand, he went into the bedroom and took slow and accurate measurements, whistling delightedly to find that his pre-mortem theoretical calculations and post-mortem practical measurements hardly varied.
tape measure.exampleSense: A graduated flexible ribbon used for measuring lengths.

dormitory.o: From Middle English dormitory, dormytory, dormytorye, borrowed from Latin dormītōrium (“a sleeping-room”), from dormiō (“to sleep”). Doublet of dormitorium and dorter.

contest.o: PIE word *tréyes From French contester, from Old French, from Latin contestor (“to call to witness”).
contest.example: The troops contested every inch of ground.
contest.exampleSense: To strive earnestly to hold or maintain; to struggle to defend.

bacon.o: From Middle English bacoun (“meat from the back and sides of a pig”), from Anglo-Norman bacon, bacun (“ham, flitch, strip of lard”), from Old Low Frankish *bakō (“ham, flitch”), from Proto-Germanic *bakô, *bakkô (“back”), an extension of *baką, whence English back, which see for more. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeg- (“back, buttocks; to vault, arch”). Cognate with Old Saxon baco (“back”), Dutch bake (“ham, side of bacon”), Old High German bahho (“ham, side of bacon”), whence German Bache f (“wild sow”), Alemannic German Bache m (“bacon”). (police): Extension of pig (“police”).
bacon.example: They fried the fish with bacon and were astonished, for no fish had ever seemed so delicious before.
bacon.exampleSense: Cured meat from the sides, belly, or back of a pig.

barbecue.o: From mid-17th century. Borrowed from Spanish barbacoa, from Taíno barbakoa (“framework of sticks”), the raised wooden structure the natives used to either sleep on or cure meat. Originally “meal of roasted meat or fish”. Doublet of balbacua and barbacoa.
barbecue.example: She ordered a plate of barbecue with a side of slaw.
barbecue.exampleSense: Meat, especially pork or beef, which has been cooked in such an apparatus (i.e. smoked over indirect heat from high-smoke fuels) and then chopped up or shredded.

smoky.o: From Middle English smoky, smokie, equivalent to smoke + -y.
smoky.example: I smelled it the moment I entered—that sweet smoky reek.
smoky.exampleSense: Having a flavour or odour like smoke; flavoured with smoke.

halal.example: Is this kosher? I hear you ask. Is it halal? Can this really be viewed as strict adherence to the letter and spirit of the competition?
halal.exampleSense: In accordance with standards or usual practice; allowable.

gown.o: From Middle English gowne, from Anglo-Norman goune, gune (“fur-trimmed coat, pelisse”), from Old French goune, from Late Latin gunna (“leather garment, a fur”). Cognate with Manx gooyn, Irish gúna.
gown.example: In the perennial town versus gown battles, townies win some violent battles, but the collegians are winning the war.
gown.exampleSense: The university community, especially as contrasted with the local populace.

attraction.o: From Middle English attraccioun, from Old French attraction, from Latin attractio from past participle of attrahō (= ad + trahō), equivalent to attract + -ion.
attraction.example: Star Tours is a very cool Disney World attraction.
attraction.exampleSense: An event, location, or business that has a tendency to draw interest from visitors, and in many cases, local residents.

nightlife.example: Rio de Janeiro boasts the best nightlife in South America.

canter.o:
noun: Short for Canterbury pace, from the supposed easy pace of medieval pilgrims to Canterbury.

noun: From cant + -er.
canter.example: From lawn-sleeved ranters to kerbstone canters, From bishops to Army lasses.
canter.exampleSense: One who makes hypocritical pretensions to goodness; one who uses canting language.

afterwards.o: From Middle English afterwardes, from Old English æfteweard (“behind”) + -s (“(adverbial genitive)”). By surface analysis, after + -wards.
afterwards.example: Another Karadeniz cross led to Cudicini's first save of the night, with the Spurs keeper making up for a weak punch by brilliantly pushing away Christian Noboa's snap-shot.
afterwards.exampleSense: At a later or succeeding time.

afterward.o: Inherited from Middle English afterward, from Old English æfterweard; equivalent to after + -ward.

observatory.o: Borrowed from French observatoire, equivalent to observe + -atory.

astronomy.o: From Middle English astronomie, astronemy, from Old French astronomie, equivalent to astro- + -nomy. Displaced native Old English tungolcræft.

ceramics.example: “The Global Africa Project” at the Museum of Arts & Design tries to survey this pervasiveness, in terms of contemporary visual endeavors of all kinds: jewelry, fashion, architecture, basketry, ceramics, painting, utilitarian design.
ceramics.exampleSense: The art or science of making ceramic objects.

ceramic.o: From Ancient Greek κεραμικός (keramikós, “potter's”), from κέραμος (kéramos, “potter's clay”), perhaps from a pre-Hellenic word or from Proto-Indo-European *kerh₂- (“to heat, burn, fire”).
ceramic.example: Joan made the dish from ceramic.
ceramic.exampleSense: A hard, brittle, inorganic, nonmetallic material, usually made from a material, such as clay, then firing it at a high temperature.

sandwich.o: Named after its supposed inventor, the Earl of Sandwich (see Sandwich).
sandwich.example: And the only "care" I could offer was egg sandwichs and Lilly's unfaltering attention.
sandwich.exampleSense: A dish or foodstuff where at least one piece, but typically two or more pieces, of bread serves as the wrapper or container of some other food.

rep.o:
noun: Clippings of various words beginning with rep.

noun: Back-formation from reps, misinterpreted as a plural.
rep.example: When I requested tickets for Nassau, my rep just put me on hold.

cast.o: From Middle English casten, from Old Norse kasta (“to throw, cast, overturn”), from Proto-Germanic *kastōną (“to throw, cast”), of unknown origin. Cognate with Scots cast (“to cast, throw”), Danish kaste (“to throw”), Swedish kasta (“to throw, cast, fling, toss, discard”), Icelandic kasta (“to pitch, toss”). In the sense of "flinging", displaced native warp. The senses relating to broadcasting are based on that same term; compare -cast.
cast.example: The cast would need a great deal of machining to become a recognizable finished part.
cast.exampleSense: An object made in a mould.

dip.o:
noun: From Middle English dippen, from Old English dyppan, from Proto-West Germanic *duppjan, from Proto-Germanic *dupjaną; see *daupijaną (“to dip”). Related to deep.

noun: Back-formation from dippy.

noun: Shortenings.
dip.example: The sailor rushed to the flag hoist to dip the flag in return.
dip.exampleSense: To lower (a flag), particularly a national ensign, to a partially hoisted position in order to render or to return a salute. While lowered, the flag is said to be “at the dip.” A flag being carried on a staff may be dipped by leaning it forward at an approximate angle of 45 degrees.

downhill.example: Moraines are found at the downhill end of a glacier.
downhill.exampleSense: Located towards or at the bottom of a slope or hill.

lantern.o: From Middle English lanterne (13th century), via Old French lanterne from Latin lanterna (“lantern”), itself a corruption of Ancient Greek λαμπτήρ (lamptḗr, “torch”) (see lamp, λάμπω (lámpō)) by influence of Latin lucerna (“lamp”). The spelling lanthorn was current during the 16th to 19th centuries and originates with a folk etymology associating the word with the use of horn as translucent cover. For the verb, compare French lanterner to hang at the lamppost. Displaced native Old English lēohtfæt (literally “light-container”).
lantern.example: The station also boasts a large semi-domed French pavilion roof with fish-scale tiles and iron cresting, plus a rectangular hall with arcaded upper storey and wooden lantern.
lantern.exampleSense: An open structure of light material set upon a roof, to give light and air to the interior.

ingress.o: From Latin ingressus, from the verb ingredior.
ingress.example: "We ingressed North Vietnam over Cam Pha on a westerly heading," reported Captain Madden.
ingress.exampleSense: To enter (a specified location or area)

resemblance.o: From Anglo-Norman resemblance, from Old French (compare French ressemblance). Morphologically resemble + -ance.
resemblance.example: His wife and sister had too many points of resemblance, not to entertain a strong and mutual dislike.
resemblance.exampleSense: The quality or state of resembling.

assemble.o: From Middle English assemblen, from Old French assembler (“to assemble”), from Medieval Latin assimulāre (“to bring together”), from ad- + simulō (“copy, imitate”), from similis (“like, similar”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *sem- (“together, one”). Doublet of assimilate.
assemble.example: The handman reads copy and assembles type by hand, including straight composition, tables and display.

assembler.example: The system includes an 8080 and a Z80 assembler, a Tektronix format downloader and other utilities.
assembler.exampleSense: A program that reads source code written in assembly language and produces executable machine code, possibly together with information needed by linkers, debuggers and other tools.

wagon.o: Borrowed from Middle Dutch wagen, from Old Dutch *wagan, from Proto-West Germanic *wagn, from Proto-Germanic *wagnaz (“wagon”), from Proto-Indo-European *weǵʰ- (“to transport”). Generally displaced native cognate wain, from Old English wæġn, of which it is a doublet. Related also to way, weigh. Sense 8 (“woman of loose morals; obnoxious woman”) is probably a derogatory and jocular reference to a woman being “ridden”, that is, mounted for the purpose of sexual intercourse. The verb is derived from the noun.
wagon.example: These wagons and pack-mules will include transportation for all personal baggage, mess chests, cooking utensils, desks, papers, &c.
wagon.exampleSense: A heavier four-wheeled (normally horse-drawn) vehicle designed to carry goods (or sometimes people).

volk.o:
noun: Borrowed from Afrikaans volk. Doublet of folk.

noun: From Middle English volk, southern form of folk; compare vixen.
volk.example: No doubt a mampus of volk of our own rank will be down here in their carriages as soon as 'tis known.

treat.o: From Middle English treten, from Anglo-Norman treter, Old French tretier, traiter, from Latin tractāre (“to pull", "to manage”), from the past participle stem of trahere (“to draw", "to pull”).
treat.example: It was such a treat to see her back in action on the London stage.
treat.exampleSense: An unexpected gift, event etc., which provides great pleasure.

realistic.example: A realistic novel about the Victorian poor.
realistic.exampleSense: Relating to the representation of objects, actions or conditions as they actually are or were.

solitary.o: From Middle English solitarie, borrowed from Latin sōlitārius. Doublet of solitaire.
solitary.example: He brooded and intrigued fantastically. He was becoming one of the big-time solitaries. And he wasn't meant to be a solitary. He was meant to be in active life, a social creature.
solitary.exampleSense: One who lives alone, or in solitude; an anchorite, hermit or recluse.

soli.o: plural of solo. Borrowed from Italian solo, from Latin sōlus, probably related to se (“himself”).

put off.example: I'm too busy to see Mr Smith today. I'll have to put him off.

scope.o:
noun: From Italian scopo (“purpose”), from Latin scopus (“target”), from Ancient Greek σκοπός (skopós), from σκέπτομαι (sképtomai), from Proto-Indo-European *speḱ-. Etymologically related to skeptic and spectrum.

noun: From Latin scopa.
scope.example: Before scoping the investigation and developing a work plan, it is necessary to establish reasonable goals and objectives.
scope.exampleSense: To define the scope of something.

situate.o: Borrowed from Late Latin situātus, past participle of Medieval Latin situō (“to locate, place”), from Latin situs (“a site”).
situate.example: In the following sections, I situate my work more explicitly within several contemporary contexts.
situate.exampleSense: To place or put into an intangible place or position, such as social, ethical, fictional, etc.

reinforce.example: He reinforced the handle with a metal rod and a bit of tape.
reinforce.exampleSense: To strengthen, especially by addition or augmentation.

embed.example: The torus S¹#92;timesS¹ can be embedded in #92;mathbb#123;R#125;³.
embed.exampleSense: To define a one-to-one function from one set to another so that certain properties of the domain are preserved when considering the image as a subset of the codomain.

depot.o: From French dépôt, from Old French depost, from Medieval Latin dēpositum, from Latin, participle of dēpōnō, dēpōnere. Doublet of deposit.
depot.example: Similar studies of rats have employed four different intracranial resorbable, slow sustained release systems—surgical foam, a thermal gel depot, a microcapsule or biodegradable polymer beads.
depot.exampleSense: A storage facility, in particular, a warehouse.

acoustics.example: The acoustics in the opera house gave the whole concert a spooky sound.
acoustics.exampleSense: The properties of a space that affect how sound carries.

impose.o: The verb is derived from Late Middle English imposen (“to place, set; to impose (a duty, etc.)”), borrowed from Middle French imposer, and Old French emposer, enposer (“to impose (a duty, tax, etc.)”) (modern French imposer), from im-, em- (variants of en- (prefix meaning ‘in, into’)) + poser (“to place, put”), modelled after: * Latin impōnere (“to place or set (something) on; (figurative) to impose (a duty, tax, etc.)”), from im- (variant of in- (prefix meaning ‘on, upon’)) + pōnō (“to place, put; etc.”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂pó, *h₂epó (“away; off”) + *tḱey- (“to cultivate; to live; to settle”)); and * Latin impositus (“established; put upon, imposed”), the perfect passive participle of impōnō: see above. The noun is derived from the verb.
impose.example: Sanctions were imposed on the country that had made an unprovoked attack on its neighbour.
impose.exampleSense: To apply, enforce, or establish (something, often regarded as burdensome as a restriction or tax: see sense 1.2.2) with authority.

spectacle.o: From Middle English spectacle, from Middle French spectacle, from Latin spectāculum (“a show, spectacle”), from spectō (“to see, behold”), frequentative of speciō (“to see”). See species. Doublet of spectaculum.
spectacle.example: The horse race was a thrilling spectacle.
spectacle.exampleSense: An exciting or extraordinary scene, exhibition, performance etc.

venue.o: From Middle English venu, from Old French venue, the feminine singular past participle of the verb venir (to come). Doublet of veny.
venue.example: The twelve men who are to try the cause must be of the same venue where the demand is made.
venue.exampleSense: A neighborhood or near place; the place or county in which anything is alleged to have happened; also, the place where an action is laid, or the district from which a jury comes.

fortress.o: Early 14 c., from Old French forteresce, forteresse, forterece (“strong place, fortification”), variant of fortelesse, from Medieval Latin fortalitia, from Latin fortis (“strong”) (see fort) + -itia, added to adjectives to form nouns of quality or condition. French -ess, from Latin -itia is also in words such as duress, prowess, largesse and richesse. For change of medial -l- to -r- in Old French, compare orne (“elm”) from ulmus; chartre from cartula and chapitre from capitulum. First attested in the 12th century.
fortress.example: Like the Mesolithic age of 10,000-8000 B.C., the period 6000-4000 B.C. seems to be one of the fall of fortresses and the rise of pastoral nomadism.
fortress.exampleSense: A fortified place; a large and permanent fortification, sometimes including a town; for example a fort, a castle; a stronghold; a place of defense or security.

versatile.o: From Latin versātilis (“turning easily”), from versātus, past participle of versō (“to turn, change”), frequentative of vertō (“to turn”).
versatile.example: The versatile anther is an important step up in flowering plant evolution and it may be the most widespread of all simple anther types.
versatile.exampleSense: Capable of moving freely in all directions.

amphitheatre.o: From Latin amphitheatrum, from Ancient Greek ἀμφιθέατρον (amphithéatron) from ἀμφί (amphí, “on both sides”) + θέᾱτρον (théātron, “theatre”).
amphitheatre.example: Ancient Roman amphitheatres were mostly oval or circular in plan, with seating tiers that surrounded the central performance area, like a modern open-air stadium.
amphitheatre.exampleSense: An open, outdoor theatre (which may be a theatre in the round, or have a stage with seating on only one side), especially one from the classical period of ancient Greece or Rome, or a modern venue of similar design.

amphi-.o: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ἀμφίς (amphís), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂m̥bʰi (“round about, around”), possibly from *h₂énts, from *h₂ent- (“face, forehead; front”) + *-s. Doublet of ambi-.
amphi-.example: amphicribral is when the phloem surrounds the xylem, amphigynous refers to when the oogonial stalk is surrounded, amphiphyte is when a plant grows on the surrounding edges of a wetland.

emblematic.example: All was dreary—all was emblematic of that change and barrenness which passes away from nature, but never from the heart;...
emblematic.exampleSense: Serving as, or relating to a symbol, emblem or illustration of a type.

emblem.o: From Old French embleme, from Latin emblēma (“raised ornaments on vessels, tessellated work, mosaic”), from Ancient Greek ἔμβλημα (émblēma, “an insertion”), from ἐμβάλλειν (embállein, “to put in, to lay on”). Doublet of emblema.
emblem.example: The medical trucks were emblazoned with the emblem of the Red Cross.
emblem.exampleSense: A representative symbol, such as a trademark or logo.

arena.o: Borrowed from Latin arēna (“sand; arena”), from earlier harēna, from Old Latin hasēna, possibly from Etruscan; compare Sabine fasēna.
arena.exampleSense: The sand-covered centre of an amphitheatre where contests were held in Ancient Rome.

soar.o: From Middle English soren, from Old French essorer (“to fly up, soar”), from Vulgar Latin *exaurare (“to rise into the air”), from Latin ex (“out”) + aura (“the air, a breeze”), from Ancient Greek αὔρα (aúra, “breath”). Compare aura, and exhale.
soar.example: The pump prices soared into new heights as the strike continued.
soar.exampleSense: To rise, especially rapidly or unusually high.

sceptic.o: Alternative spelling of skeptic. Borrowed from Middle French sceptique (but with a pronunciation closer to that of the Latin etymon), or possibly directly from Late Latin scepticus (originally attested only in the plural Scepticī (“the sect of Skeptics”)), from Proto-Italic *spektos (“see, observing”), from *speḱ- (“to see”), compare to σκοπέω (skopéō, “to view, examine”).
sceptic.example: As I said, my experience was: I travelled to Russia as a sceptic person and I returned as a European.

dominate.o:
verb: Borrowed from Latin dominātus, perfect active participle of dominor (“to rule, have dominion”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from dominus (“lord, master”) + -or (verb-forming suffix).

adj: Ultimately from Latin dominor (“rule, have dominion”), either from Latin dominātus, the perfect active participle of dominor (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), or via phonetic alteration of the synonym dominant, from Latin domināns, the present active participle of the same. Compare the pairs predominate / predominant and obstinate / obstinant.

noun: Borrowed from Latin dominātus (“rule, command”), from dominus + -ātus, see -ate (forms nouns denoting rank or office, a regime handled by people of such rank).
dominate.example: Individual mistakes proved costly for Wigan who, particularly after the half-time introduction of Hugo Rodallega, dominated for long periods.
dominate.exampleSense: To enjoy a commanding position in some field

grand.o:
adj: From Middle English grand, grond, graund, graunt, from Anglo-Norman graunt, from Old French grant, from Latin grandis. Doublet of grande and grandee.

noun: From granddaughter, grandfather, grandmother, grandson, etc.
grand.example: His simple vision has transformed into something far more grand.
grand.exampleSense: Large, senior (high-ranking), intense, extreme, or exceptional Great in size, and fine or imposing in appearance or impression; illustrious, dignified, magnificent.

portion.o: From Middle English porcioun, borrowed from Old French porcion, accusative of Latin portiōnem (“a share, part, portion, relation, proportion”), from portiō, akin to pars (“part”); see part. Compare proportion.
portion.example: Father, giue me the portion of goods that falleth to me.
portion.exampleSense: The part of an estate given or falling to a child or heir; an inheritance.

speculation.o: From Middle English speculacioun, speculation, from Old French speculation (compare French spéculation), from Late Latin speculātiō, speculātiōnem, from Latin speculor. Morphologically speculate + -ion.
speculation.example: To his speculations on these subjects he gave the lofty name of the "Oracles of Reason".
speculation.exampleSense: A conclusion to which the mind comes by speculating; mere theory; notion; conjecture.

mesh.o: From Middle English mesche, from Old English masc (“net”) (perhaps influenced in form by related Old English mæscre (“mesh, spot”)), from the related Proto-Germanic *maskwǭ and *maskrǭ respectively, from Proto-Indo-European *mezg- (“to knit, twist, plait”). Akin to Old High German māsca (“mesh”), Old Saxon maska (“net”), Old Norse mǫskvi, mǫskun (“mesh”).
mesh.example: The music meshed well with the visuals in that film.
mesh.exampleSense: To fit in; to come together harmoniously.

snowmobile.example: From the manufacture of snowgoing equipment such as snow cats, it diversified first into that of snowmobiles (and later skidoos, or water scooters), then into railcar and locomotive manufacture, and finally into the manufacture of small (less than 100-seat) commercial aircraft.
snowmobile.exampleSense: A vehicle with skis at the front and a caterpillar track at the rear, used for travelling over snow, sometimes as sport.

hut.o:
noun: From Middle English *hutte, hotte, from both Old English hōd and Old English hȳdan (“to hide”) and influenced by Anglo-Norman hute or hutte, from Middle French hutte, from Old French hute (“hut”), hute (“cottage”), from Old High German hutta (“hut, cottage”), from Proto-Germanic *hudjǭ, *hudjō (“hut”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kewt- (“to deck; cover; covering; skin”). Cognate with German Hütte (“hut”), Dutch hut (“hut”), West Frisian hutte (“hut”), Saterland Frisian Hutte (“hut”), Danish hytte (“hut”), Norwegian Bokmål hytte (“hut”), Swedish hydda (“hut”). Related to hide.

intj: A short, sharp sound of command. Compare hey, hup, etc.
hut.example: His troops, hutted among the heights of Morristown, were half fed, half clothed, and inferior in number to the garrison of New York.
hut.exampleSense: To provide (someone) with shelter in a hut.

head off.example: The government took steps to head off summertime shortages of gasoline.
head off.exampleSense: To avoid the undesirable consequences of; to prevent.

lap.o:
noun: From Middle English lappe, from Old English læppa (“skirt or flap of a garment”), from Proto-West Germanic *lappō, from Proto-Germanic *lappô (“cloth; rag”), of uncertain origin, possibly Proto-Indo-European *leb- (“to hang loosely”). Cognate with Dutch lap (“cloth; rag”), German Lappen (“cloth; lobe; flap”), Icelandic leppur (“rag; patch”).

verb: From Middle English lappen (“to fold, wrap”) from earlier wlappen (“to fold, wrap”), from Old English *wlappan, *wlæppan, *wlappian (“to wrap”), from Proto-Germanic *wlapp-, *wrapp- (“to wrap, fold, roll up, turn”), from Proto-Indo-European *werb- (“to bend, turn”). Cognate with Middle Dutch lappen (“to wrap up, embrace”), dialectal Danish vravle (“to wind”), Old Italian goluppare (“to wrap, fold up”) (from Germanic). Doublet of wrap. Also related to envelop, develop. The sense of "to get a lap ahead (of someone) on a track" is from 1847, on notion of "overlapping." The noun meaning "a turn around a track" (1861) is from this sense.

verb: From Middle English lappen, from Old English lapian, from Proto-West Germanic *lapōn, from Proto-Germanic *lapōną, *lapjaną (“to lick; lap”), from imitative Proto-Indo-European *leh₂b- (“to lap, lick”); akin to Old High German laffen (“to lick”), Old Norse lepja, Danish labe, Old Saxon lepil, German Löffel (“spoon”). Cognate with Latin lambere (“lick”). French lamper is a loanword from German. Compare Danish leffe, dialect German läffeln.
lap.example: The second boat got a lap of half its length on the leader.
lap.exampleSense: The state or condition of being in part extended over or by the side of something else; or the extent of the overlapping.

relay.o:
noun: From Middle French relai (“reserve pack of hounds”), from relaier (“to exchange tired animals for fresh”); literally, "to leave behind", from Old French relaier (“to leave behind”), from re- + laier (“to leave”), of uncertain origin.

verb: From re- + lay.
relay.example: The CCTV cameras relay what's going on to the headquarters.

sit back.example: Please just sit back and watch the show.
sit back.exampleSense: To recline while still in a seated position, with one's back on the frame of the seat.

negligible.o: From negligence/negligent + -ible, as if from New Latin *negligibilis, from Latin neglegō (“to neglect”) + -ibilis (“-ible”).
negligible.example: We found errors, but their effects were negligible.
negligible.exampleSense: Able to be neglected, ignored or excluded from consideration; too small or unimportant to be of concern.

sled.o: From Middle English sledde, from Middle Dutch sledde or Middle Low German sledde (compare Dutch slee, slede, Low German Sleden), from Proto-Germanic *slidô (compare Saterland Frisian sliede, German Schlitten, Norwegian slede). Doublet of sleigh; also related to slide.
sled.example: "Mush!" he yelled at the dogs pulling the sled.
sled.exampleSense: A vehicle on runners, used for conveying loads over the snow or ice, and often pulled by sled dogs.

glide.o: From Middle English gliden, from Old English glīdan, from Proto-West Germanic *glīdan, from Proto-Germanic *glīdaną, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰleydʰ-. Cognate with West Frisian glide, glydzje, Low German glieden, Dutch glijden, German gleiten, Norwegian Nynorsk gli, Danish glide, Swedish glida, Finnish liitää.
glide.example: The water over which the boats glided was black and smooth, rising into huge foamless billows, the more terrible because they were silent.
glide.exampleSense: To move softly, smoothly, or effortlessly.

increment.o: From Middle English encrement, increment, from Latin incrēmentum, from incrēscō (whence increase), from in- + crēscō (“grow”). Equivalent to increase + -ment.
increment.example: The others will return at night, [...] pushing their experiments and nudging their projects toward completion in small, painful increments.

dashboard.o: From dash (“to sprinkle; to splatter”) + board for meaning
dashboard.example: Log in to the dashboard to change your account settings.
dashboard.exampleSense: A graphical user interface in the form of or resembling a motor car dashboard.

dash.o: From Middle English daschen, dassen, from Danish daske (“to slap, strike”), related to Swedish daska (“to smack, slap, spank”), of obscure origin. Compare German tatschen (“to grope, paw”), Old English dwǣsċan (“to quell, put out, destroy, extinguish”). See also dush.
dash.example: The only other times you'll be asked for a dash is from beggars.
dash.exampleSense: A bribe or gratuity; a gift.

bash.o:
verb: From Middle English *basshen, *basken, likely from Old Norse *baska (“to strike”), akin to Swedish basa (“to baste, whip, lash, flog”), Danish baske (“to beat, strike, cudgel”), German patschen (“to slap”)

verb: From Middle English baschen, baissen. See abash.
bash.example: They had a big bash to celebrate their tenth anniversary.
bash.exampleSense: A large party; a gala event.

cursor.o: Borrowed from Latin cursor (“runner”), from currō (“run”) + -or (agentive suffix). Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European.
cursor.example: The only other problem is that there's a nagging tendency for the highlight to overrun when cursoring through file lists.
cursor.exampleSense: To navigate by means of the cursor keys.

pressured.o: simple past and past participle of pressure. From Latin pressūra.

vain.o:
adj: From Middle English veyn, from Old French vain, from Latin vānus (“empty”).

verb: A conversion of the adjectival form of vain. The only use of this verb in English appears c. 1628 in the writings of Owen Felltham.
vain.example: Let no man deceive you with vain words.
vain.exampleSense: Having no real substance, value, or importance; empty; void; worthless; unsatisfying.

vanity.o: From va(i)n + -ity, from Middle English vanite, from Old French vanité, from Latin vānitas, from vānus, whence English vain. Doublet of vanitas.
vanity.example: She was sitting in front of her vanity, brushing out her hair.
vanity.exampleSense: A dressing table used to apply makeup, preen, and coif hair, in which the table is normally quite low and similar to a desk.

accent.o:
noun: Inherited from Middle English accent, from Medieval Latin accentus and Old French accent, acent, both from Latin accentus, past participle of accinō (“sing to, sing along”), from ad- + canō (“to sing”). The word accent had been borrowed into Old English already, but was lost and reborrowed in Middle English.

verb: From Middle French accenter, from Old French accenter, from Latin accentō, from accentus.
accent.example: The name Cézanne is written with an acute accent.
accent.exampleSense: A mark or character used in writing, in order to indicate the place of the spoken accent, or to indicate the nature or quality of the vowel marked.

go off.example: One day I'll go off, but until then, I'm in charge around here.
go off.exampleSense: To fall unconscious; to go to sleep; to die.

leave.o:
verb: From Middle English leven, from Old English lǣfan (“to leave”), from Proto-West Germanic *laibijan, from Proto-Germanic *laibijaną (“to let stay, leave”), causative of *lībaną (“to stay, remain”), from Proto-Indo-European *leyp- (“to stick; fat”). Cognate with Old Frisian lēva (“to leave”), dialectal Dutch loven (“to have left over, save, keep”), Old Saxon lēvian, Old High German leiban (“to leave”), Old Norse leifa (“to leave over”) (whence Icelandic leifa (“to leave food uneaten”), Swedish leva (“to leave”)), lifna (“to be left”) (whence Danish levne). More at lave, belive. The noun is attested since the 19th century, with earliest references to billiards.

noun: From Middle English leve, from Old English lēaf (“permission, privilege”), from Proto-Germanic *laubō, *laubą (“permission, privilege, favour, worth”), from Proto-Indo-European *lewbʰ- (“to love, hold dear”). Cognate with obsolete German Laube (“permission”), Swedish lov (“permission”), Icelandic leyfi (“permission”). Related to Dutch verlof, German Urlaub, Erlaubnis, Verlaub. See also love.

verb: From Middle English leven, from Old English līefan (“to allow, grant, concede; believe, trust, confide in”), from Proto-West Germanic *laubijan, from Proto-Germanic *laubijaną (“to allow, praise”), from Proto-Indo-European *lewbʰ- (“to love, hold dear”). Cognate with German erlauben (“to allow”), German glauben (“to believe”), Icelandic leyfa (“to allow”).

verb: From Middle English leven, from lef (“leaf”). More at leaf.

verb: From French lever. Compare levy. Compare also Middle English leve, a variant of levy that may have been monosyllabic.
leave.example: I've been given three weeks' leave by my boss.
leave.exampleSense: Permission to be absent; time away from one's work.

marked.o:
adj: From mark (“sign, characteristic, visible impression”) + -ed. Less common disyllabic pronunciation (/ˈmɑː.kɪd/) is likely an analogy derived from markedness (explaining its restriction to sense 2).

verb: See the etymology of the corresponding lemma form.
marked.example: The eighth century BC saw a marked increase in the general wealth of Cyprus.

fairly.o: From Middle English fayrly, fayrely, vayrliche, equivalent to fair + -ly.
fairly.example: A jury is expected to ensure that the accused is fairly judged.
fairly.exampleSense: In a fair manner; fair; not biased or skewed or favouring a certain party

carriage.o: From Middle English cariage, from Old Northern French cariage, from carier (“to carry”).
carriage.example: The runner has a very low arm carriage.
carriage.exampleSense: The manner or posture in which one holds or positions a body part, such as one's arm or head.

triple.o: PIE word *tréyes From Middle English triple (also þripell), from Latin triplus. Doublet of treble.
triple.example: Give me a triple serving of mashed potatoes.
triple.exampleSense: Of three times the quantity; treble.

bustle.o: From Middle English bustlen, bustelen, bostlen, perhaps an alteration of *busklen (> Modern English buskle), a frequentative of Middle English busken (“to prepare; make ready”), from Old Norse búask (“to prepare oneself”); or alternatively from a frequentative form of Middle English busten, bisten (“to buffet; pummel; dash; beat”) + -le. Compare also Icelandic bustla (“to splash; bustle”). The etymology of noun sense 3 is uncertain, perhaps related to busk (“strip in a corset”) or German Buschel.
bustle.example: The commuters bustled about inside the train station.
bustle.exampleSense: To move busily and energetically with fussiness (often followed by about).

rush hour.example: It takes 30 minutes to drive there, but maybe 2 hours during the rush hour.
rush hour.exampleSense: The times of the day when traffic jams are commonplace, due mainly to people commuting to or from work.

sacrifice.o:
noun: (“act of offering a life or object to a deity; the life or object so offered”), from Anglo-Norman sacrefiz, and Old French sacrifice, sacrifise (modern French sacrifice), from Latin sacrificium (“something offered to a deity, sacrifice”), from sacrum (“sacrifice, sacrificial rite”) + faciō (“to do, to make”) + -ium (suffix forming abstract nouns). The noun sacrum is the nominalized neuter of the adjective sacer (“devoted to a deity for sacrifice; holy, sacred”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *seh₂k- (“ceremony, ritual; to make sacred”), and the verb faciō is ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁- (“to do; to place, put”). Related Latin formations include sacrificus (“of or pertaining to sacrifice, sacrificial”) and sacrificō (“to make a sacrifice”). Displaced native Old English blōt and hūsl. Cognates * Italian sagrifizio * Occitan sacrifici * Portuguese sacrificio * Spanish sacrificio

verb: From Middle English sacrificen (“to offer a sacrifice to a deity”), from sacrifice (see etymology 1) + -en (suffix forming infinitives of verbs).
sacrifice.example: [H]e bought a green shawl for Mrs. Bolton, and a yellow one for Fanny: the most brilliant "sacrifices" of a Regent-street haberdasher's window.
sacrifice.exampleSense: A monetary loss incurred by selling something at less than its value; also, the thing thus sold.

swing.o: From Middle English swyngen, from Old English swingan, from Proto-West Germanic *swingan, from Proto-Germanic *swinganą (compare Low German swingen, German schwingen, Dutch zwingen, Swedish svinga), from Proto-Indo-European *swenk-, *sweng- (compare Scottish Gaelic seang (“thin”)). Related to swink.
swing.example: A ship swings with the tide.
swing.exampleSense: To turn round by action of wind or tide when at anchor.

slash.o:
noun: Late Middle English, originally a verb of uncertain etymology. Perhaps of imitative origin, or possibly from Old French esclachier (“to break in pieces”), a variant of esclater, which is likely a Germanic borrowing, from Frankish *slaitan (“to slit, tear”). Used in the Wycliffe Bible as slascht (see 1 Kings 5:18) but otherwise unattested until 16th century. Conjunctive use from various applications of the punctuation mark ⟨/⟩. See also slash fiction.

noun: Uncertain. Compare Scots slash (“large splash”), possibly from Old French esclache. Slang use for urination attested from the 1950s.

noun: Uncertain. Compare British dialectal slashy (“wet and dirty, miry”) and Scots slash (“act of walking forcefully through water or mud”) and slatch (“wet and muddy place, mire”). Perhaps related to Swedish slask (“slush”). Compare also slash (“clearing in a forest”): in many cases it is difficult to tell whether that sense or this one is meant. (Also compare flash (“a marsh; a pool of water”).)

noun: See slatch
slash.example: We passed over the shoulder of a ridge and around the edge of a fire slash, and then we had the mountain fairly before us.
slash.exampleSense: Something resembling such a mark: A clearing in a forest, particularly one made by logging, fire, or other violent action.

bungalow.o: Borrowed from Gujarati બંગલો (baṅglo, “Bengali-style house; a detached house situated between a garden or a field”). Compare Hindi बंगला (baṅglā, “Bengali”), Bengali বাংলা (baṅla, “Bengal”). Doublet of bangalo and Bangla.
bungalow.example: My aunt can't manage the stairs any more, so she's moving to a bungalow.
bungalow.exampleSense: A single-storey house, typically with rooms all on one level, or sometimes also with upper rooms set into the roof space.

brochure.o: 1748, from French brochure (“stitched work”), from brocher (“to stitch”), from Old French brochier (“to pierce”), from broche (“awl”), from Vulgar Latin brocca, from Latin broccus (“pointy-toothed”). Doublet of broach.
brochure.example: Have a look in the Acme brochure for a new vacuum cleaner.
