veterinary.exampleSense: Of or relating to the medical or surgical treatment of non-human animals, especially domestic and farm animals.

individual.o: PIE word *dwóh₁ From Medieval Latin indīviduālis, from Latin indīviduum (“an indivisible thing”), neuter of indīviduus (“indivisible, undivided”), from in + dīviduus (“divisible”), from dīvidō (“divide”).
individual.example: As we can't print them all together, the individual pages will have to be printed one by one.
individual.exampleSense: Relating to a single person or thing as opposed to more than one.

entrance.o:
noun: From Middle French entrance (“entry”). Replaced native Middle English ingang (“entrance, admission”), from Old English ingang (“ingress, entry, entrance”).

verb: From en- + trance (“daze”).
entrance.example: Beware of entrance to a quarrel.
entrance.exampleSense: The entering upon; the beginning, or that with which the beginning is made; the commencement; initiation.

cave.o:
noun: From Middle English cave, borrowed from Old French cave, from Latin cava (“cavity”), from cavus (“hollow”). Cognate with Tocharian B kor (“throat”), Albanian cup (“odd, uneven”), Ancient Greek κύαρ (kúar, “eye of needle, earhole”), Old Armenian սոր (sor, “hole”), Sanskrit शून्य (śūnya, “empty, barren, zero”). Displaced native Old English sċræf. More at cavum, cavus and cage.

intj: Borrowed from Latin cavē, second-person singular present active imperative of caveō (“to beware”). Used at Eton College, Berkshire.
cave.example: My room was a cozy cave where I could escape from my family.
cave.exampleSense: A place of retreat, such as a man cave.

bin.o:
noun: From Middle English bynne, from Old English binn (“crib, manger”), from Late Latin benna or a Celtic language, possibly Proto-Brythonic *benn (“cart, carriage”) (whence Middle Welsh benn, Old Breton benn (“caisson”), modern Welsh ben), from Proto-Celtic *bend(n)ā (whence Gaulish benna). Compare German Benne (“wheelbarrow”) and Middle Dutch benne (“basket”), whence modern Dutch ben and as a borrowing, West Frisian bin (both "wicker basket").

noun: From Arabic بِن (bin, “son”).

contraction: Contraction of being.

verb: Pronunciation spelling of been.

noun: Clipping of binary.
bin.example: British journalists shun complete respectability, feeling a duty to be ready to savage the mighty, or rummage through their bins. Elsewhere in Europe, government contracts and subsidies ensure that press barons will only defy the mighty so far.
bin.exampleSense: A container for rubbish or waste.

staff.o: From Middle English staf, from Old English stæf (“letter of the alphabet”), from Proto-West Germanic *stab, from Proto-Germanic *stabaz. Cognate with Dutch staf, German Stab, Danish stav, Swedish stav. Sense of "group of military officers that assists a commander" and similar meanings, attested from 1702, is influenced by or is even from German Stab.
staff.example: The case was that of a murder. It had an element of mystery about it, however, which was puzzling the authorities. A turban and loincloth soaked in blood had been found; also a staff.
staff.exampleSense: A long, straight, thick wooden rod or stick, especially one used to assist in walking.

litter.o: Inherited from Middle English litere, borrowed from Anglo-Norman litere, from Old French litiere (“bedding; bed of loose straw; litter”), from Late Latin lectuāria, from Latin lectus + -āria.
litter.example: He ordeyned lyttyers for the wounded knyghtes.
litter.exampleSense: A mobile bed or couch transported upon or suspended from poles placed over human shoulders or animal backs. Synonym of stretcher, such a vehicle used for transporting the sick and injured, inclusive of designs carried in the hand.

lunchbox.example: The performance difference between desktops and lunchboxes was practically nil.
lunchbox.exampleSense: A luggable; an early laptop computer, usually a unit with a handle and a fold-out keyboard.

woodwork.o: From Middle English woodewerk (“carpentry”), equivalent to wood + work.
woodwork.example: Some woodwork and the plaster ceiling medallions have been duplicated to match the originals.
woodwork.exampleSense: Something made from wood, especially cabinets and trim (e.g., baseboards, doorframes) made from millwork.

forthcoming.o:
adj: The adjective is derived from forth (“forwards”) + coming (“approaching (adjective)”); or from Middle English forth commyng, *forthcominge, present participle of forth-comen (“to come forth; to appear, issue”), from Old English forþcuman (“to come forth, come forward”) (present participle *forþcumende), from forþ- (“forth; forward”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *per- (“before, in front; first”)) + cuman (“to come”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʷem- (“to step”)). Compare Dutch voortkomend (“coming forth, originating from (verb)”), German fortkommend (“getting away; progressing (verb)”). The noun is derived from forth (“forwards”) + coming (“arrival”).

verb: From forthcome + -ing.
forthcoming.exampleSense: Available when needed; in place, ready.

voyage.o: From Middle English viage, borrowed from Anglo-Norman viage and Old French voiage, from Latin viaticum. The modern spelling is under the influence of Modern French voyage. Doublet of viaticum.
voyage.example: A mind forever voyaging through strange seas of thought alone.
voyage.exampleSense: To go on a long journey.

spice.o:
noun: Inherited from Middle English spice, from Old French espice (modern épice), from Late Latin speciēs (“spice, good, ware”), from Latin speciēs (“kind, sort”). Doublet of species.

noun: Formed by analogy with lice and mice as the plurals of louse and mouse. First attested use Christopher Morley in “Morley's Magnum” (1935). Made popular by Robert A. Heinlein in Time Enough for Love (1973).
spice.example: What spice level do you want for your pad thai? I recommend mild.

extinction.o: From late Middle English, borrowed from Latin extinctio (“extinction, annihilation”), from extinguere, past participle extinctus (“to extinguish”); see extinguish.
extinction.example: The extinction of a species once so numerous seemed incredible.
extinction.exampleSense: The action of making or becoming extinct; annihilation.

emission.o:
noun: First attested in 1607. From Middle French émission, from Latin ēmissiō (“sending forth”), from ēmittō (“send out”), from ex (“from, out of”) + mittō (“send”).

noun: Borrowed from French émission.
emission.example: Camden motive power depot has been much criticised for its emission of smoke in a residential neighbourhood and its complete dieselisation is rapidly taking place.
emission.exampleSense: The act of emitting; the act of sending forth or putting into circulation.

railing.example: During the war, everyone's railings were taken away to make bombers.
railing.exampleSense: A fence or barrier consisting of one or more horizontal rails and vertical supports.

patio.o: From Spanish patio, either from Old Occitan patu or pati (compare Occitan and Catalan pati), from Late Latin pactus, from Latin pactum (“pact, agreement, bargain”), hence a doublet of pact, or alternatively from Latin patēre (“to lie open”).
patio.example: The flat looks out on a patio on one side and a churro café on the other.
patio.exampleSense: An inner courtyard typical of traditional houses in some regions of Spain.

herb.o: From Middle English herbe, erbe, from Old French erbe (French herbe), from Latin herba. Initial h was restored to the spelling in the 15th century on the basis of Latin, but it remained mute until the 19th century and still is for many speakers. Doublet of yerba.
herb.example: If any medicinal herbs used by witches were supposedly evil, then how come people from at least the past benefited from the healing properties of such herbs?
herb.exampleSense: A plant whose roots, leaves or seeds, etc. are used in medicine.

dominance.example: Shepard: Too many lives were lost at that base. I'm not sorry it's gone.
dominance.exampleSense: Being in a position of power, authority or ascendancy over others.

hemp.o: Inherited from Middle English hemp, from Old English henep, from Proto-West Germanic *hanapi, from Proto-Germanic *hanapiz. Doublet of cannabis and canvas.

linen.o: From Middle English lynnen, lynen, from Old English līnen (“linen", "made of flax”), from Proto-West Germanic *līnīn (“made of flax”), from Proto-Germanic *līną (“flax”), from Proto-Indo-European *līno- (“flax”), equivalent to line + -en. Cognate with Latin līnum (“flax”) and thus also Linum. More at line.
linen.example: She put the freshly cleaned linens into the linen closet.
linen.exampleSense: Domestic textiles, such as tablecloths, bedding, towels, underclothes, etc., that are made of linen or linen-like fabrics of cotton or other fibers; linens.

hardship.o: From Middle English hardshipe, equivalent to hard + -ship.
hardship.example: When you visit the museum, we invite you to make a donation of $10 if this will not be a hardship.
hardship.exampleSense: A burden, a source of difficulty that could impose a barrier.

garment.o: From Middle English garment, garement, garnement, from Old French garnement, guarnement, from Old French garnir, guarnir (“to protect, fortify, clothe, garnish, adorn”), from Frankish *warnijan (“to ward off, refuse, deny”). More at English garnish.
garment.example: The highest state in which the soul completely casts away its garment of flesh and becomes a disembodied spirit.
garment.exampleSense: The visible exterior in which a thing is invested or embodied.

modification.o: From Middle English modificatioune, from Middle French modification and its etymon Latin modificātiō (“a measuring”), from modificāre (“to limit, control, modify”); see modify. By surface analysis, modify + -ication.
modification.example: The Chinese word "kòu tóu" had a modification made to become the English "kowtow".
modification.exampleSense: a change to a word when it is borrowed by another language

packet.o: From Middle English pacquet; either from Middle French pacquet, or formed independently from pak and -et.
packet.example: (archaic) a travel bag containing clothing, nightwear and other accessories.
packet.exampleSense: A small pack or package; a little bundle or parcel

tractor.o: Formed from Latin tractus, perfect passive participle of trahere (“to pull”), + agent noun suffix -or.
tractor.example: EWS are also denying any rumours of tractors going to Spain, then again they denyed the rumours of tractors going to France until the contract was signed!

intense.o: From Late Middle English intens, intense (“ardent, fervent; extreme, great, intense”), borrowed from Old French intense (modern French intense), or directly from its etymon Latin intēnsus (“strained, stretched tight; intense; attentive; violent; (rare) eager, intent”), the perfect passive participle of intendō (“to stretch out, strain”), from in- (prefix meaning ‘in, inside, within’) + tendō (“to extend, stretch”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *tend- (“to extend, stretch”)).
intense.example: As the night came on the yellow stars grew more intense overhead, but the lambent glow in the north did not pale.
intense.exampleSense: Of a thing: possessing some characteristic to an extreme or very high or strong degree.

adolesce.o: Back-formation from adolescence. First attested in 1859.

adolescent.o: First attested ?1440, from Middle English adolescent, from Middle French adolescent or directly from Latin adolescentem, accusative form of adolescens, present participle of adolēscere (“to become adult, grow up”), from ad- (“to”) + alēscere (“to grow or become nourished”). The adjective first appeared in 1785.
adolescent.example: Again, voice change is not easy and vulnerability plays a big part, but if choral teachers and adolescent singers approach it with the right mindframe, the experience can be empowering, enlightening, and restorative for all involved.
adolescent.exampleSense: Of, relating to, or at the age of adolescence; at the stage between being a child and an adult.

methodology.o: From French méthodologie. By surface analysis, method + -ology.
methodology.example: For example, an agile methodology should promote the frequent delivery of working systems rather than a single big bang delivery.
methodology.exampleSense: A collection of methods, practices, procedures and rules used by those who work in some field.

coincidence.o: From Middle French coincidence (French coïncidence). By surface analysis, coincide + -ence.
coincidence.example: It is sheer coincidence that the cartoon resembles the local politician.
coincidence.exampleSense: Of events, the appearance of a meaningful connection when there is none.

cuisine.o: Borrowed from French cuisine (“cooking, culinary art, kitchen”), from Late Latin cocīna, from earlier coquīna (“kitchen”). Doublet of kitchen.
cuisine.example: French cuisine is considered to be one of the world's most refined and elegant styles of cooking.
cuisine.exampleSense: A characteristic style of preparing food, often associated with a place of origin.

nucleus.o: Learned borrowing from Latin nucleus (“kernel, core”). The earliest uses refer to the head of a comet and the kernel of a seed, both recorded in Lexicon Technicum in 1704. The sense in atomic physics was coined by British scientist Michael Faraday in 1844 in a theoretical meaning.
nucleus.example: This collection will form the nucleus of a new library.
nucleus.exampleSense: An initial part or version that will receive additions.

cardboard.example: MUMMER 3 pulls out an inflated cushion with a very cardboard crown on it.
cardboard.exampleSense: Made of or resembling cardboard; (figurative) flat or flavorless.

attic.o: From the practice of decorating the top storey of building facades in the Attic architectural style. From French attique, from Latin atticus, from Ancient Greek Ἀττικός (Attikós).
attic.example: We went up to the attic to look for the boxes containing our childhood keepsakes.
attic.exampleSense: The space, often unfinished and with sloped walls, directly below the roof in the uppermost part of a house or other building, generally used for storage or habitation.

resilience.o: From Latin resiliō (“to spring back”) + English -ence.
resilience.example: Network Rail previously said it is determined to build upon the "significant changes" it has made since the accident, which have "helped us to manage the risk of severe weather to the network". It has invested millions to improve the resilience of the railway.
resilience.exampleSense: The positive capacity of an organizational system or company to adapt and return to equilibrium after a crisis, failure or any kind of disruption, including: an outage, natural disasters, man-made disasters, terrorism, or similar (particularly IT systems, archives).

depression.o: From Middle English depression, depressioun, from Old French depression, from Latin dēpressiō. Equivalent to depress + -ion.
depression.example: I used to suffer from depression, but now I'm mostly content with my life.
depression.exampleSense: A state of mind producing serious, long-term lowering of enjoyment of life or inability to visualize a happy future.

inspiration.o: From Middle English inspiracioun, from Old French inspiration, from Late Latin īnspīrātiōnem (nominative: īnspīrātiō), from Latin īnspīrātus (past participle of inspīrō). By surface analysis, inspire + -ation. Displaced native Old English onbryrdnes (literally “in-pricked-ness”).
inspiration.example: The trip was an inspiration to her for writing a book.
inspiration.exampleSense: A person, object, or situation which quickens or stimulates an influence upon the intellect, emotions or creativity.

capitalism.o: Borrowed from French capitalisme (“the condition of one who is rich”); equivalent to capital + -ism. Derived from Proto-Indo-European *káput (“head”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kap-. First used in English by novelist William Thackeray in The Newcomes [1854-1855].

ardent.o: First attested circa 14th century as Middle English ardaunt, borrowed from Anglo-Norman ardent and Old French ardant, from Latin ardentem, accusative of ardēns, present participle of ardeō (“to burn”).
ardent.example: Nor gushing tears, nor ardent prayers, shall shake our firm decree.
ardent.exampleSense: Full of ardor; expressing passion, spirit, or enthusiasm.

initiation.o: Borrowed from Middle French initiation, from Latin initiātiō. Morphologically initiate + -ion.

jealous.o: First attested in 1382. From Middle English jelous, gelous, gelus, from Old French jalous, from Late Latin zelosus, from Ancient Greek ζῆλος (zêlos, “zeal, jealousy”). Doublet of zealous.
jealous.example: I began my fence or wall; which, being still jealous of my being attacked by somebody, I resolved to make very thick and strong.

meditation.o: From Old French meditacion, from Latin meditatio, from meditatus, the past participle of meditārī (“to meditate, to think over, consider”), itself from Proto-Indo-European *med- (“to measure, limit, consider, advise”).
meditation.example: Her book is less a cookbook than a meditation on the craft of cookery.
meditation.exampleSense: A contemplative discourse, often on a religious or philosophical subject.

scary.o:
adj: From scare + -y.

noun: From dialectal English scare (“scraggy”).
scary.example: She was hiding behind her pillow during the scary parts of the film.

kingfisher.o: Originally king's fisher, from Middle English kyngys fyschare; equivalent to king + fisher. So named for obscure reasons.

texture.o: Borrowed from Middle French texture, borrowed from Latin textūra (“a weaving, web, texture, structure”), from textus, past participle of texere (“to weave”). See text. Doublet of tessitura.
texture.example: The beans had a grainy, gritty texture in her mouth.
texture.exampleSense: The feel or shape of a surface or substance; the smoothness, roughness, softness, etc. of something.

machinery.example: All Mr. Yeats's grotesque machinery of sowlths and tevishes and sheogues leaves us without a shudder; his fantasies are stage-properties of the most unillusive kind.
machinery.exampleSense: The machines constituting a production apparatus, in a plant etc., collectively.

apprenticeship.example: Entry to shop grades is by apprenticeship, boys bring taken as apprentices on leaving school.
apprenticeship.exampleSense: The system by which a person learning a craft or trade is instructed by a master for a set time under set conditions.

apprentice.o: From Middle English apprentice, apprentesse, apprentyse, apprentis, from Old French aprentis, plural of aprentif, from Old French aprendre (verb), Late Latin apprendō, from Classical Latin apprehendō. Compare typologically Latin discipulus (akin to capiō); Russian ухвати́ть (uxvatítʹ), нахвата́ться (naxvatátʹsja), схва́тывать на лету́ (sxvátyvatʹ na letú), and, for another aspect, быть на подхва́те (bytʹ na podxváte) (both akin to хвата́ть (xvatátʹ)).
apprentice.example: Joe apprenticed three different photographers before setting up his own studio.

animation.o: Learned borrowing from Latin animatiō, from animō, equivalent to animate + -ion.
animation.example: Perhaps an inanimate thing supplies me, while I am speaking, with whatever I possess of animation.
animation.exampleSense: The condition of being animate or alive.

skeleton.o:
noun: From New Latin sceleton, from Ancient Greek σκελετόν (skeletón), the neuter of σκελετός (skeletós, “dried up, withered, dried body, parched, mummy”), from σκέλλω (skéllō, “dry, dry up, make dry, parch”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kelh₁- (“to parch, wither”); compare Ancient Greek σκληρός (sklērós, “hard”).

noun: The etymology of the term is disputed between two versions. * From the sled used, which originally was a bare frame, like a skeleton. * From Norwegian kjaelke (a type of ice sled) through a bad anglicization as "skele".
skeleton.example: The skeleton of the organisation is essentially the same as it was ten years ago, but many new faces have come and gone.
skeleton.exampleSense: The central core of something that gives shape to the entire structure.

affordable.example: The bill seeks to make IVF treatment more affordable by mandating coverage for fertility treatments under employer-sponsored insurance and certain public insurance plans.
affordable.exampleSense: Able to be afforded; inexpensive or reasonably priced.

pavilion.o: From Middle English pavilloun, from Anglo-Norman pavilloun, from Latin pāpiliōnem, form of pāpiliō (“butterfly, moth”) (due to resemblance of tent to a butterfly’s wings), of unknown origin. Doublet of papilio and papillon. Cognate to French pavillon (“pavilion”) and papillon (“butterfly”), and similar terms in other Romance languages.

pedestrian.o: Borrowed from Latin pedester, root pedestri- (from pedes) + -an (suffix forming adjectives).
pedestrian.example: The piezoelectric pedestrian tubeways depicted for Shanghai 2121 will provide all-weather pedestrian transportation citywide.
pedestrian.exampleSense: Of or intended for those who are walking.

knitting.o: From Middle English knyttynge; equivalent to knit + -ing.
knitting.example: She put down her knitting and went to answer the phone.
knitting.exampleSense: Material that has been, or is being knitted.

knit.o: From Middle English knytten, from Old English cnyttan (“to fasten, tie, bind, knit; add, append”), from Proto-West Germanic *knuttijan, from Proto-Germanic *knutjaną, *knuttijaną (“to make knots, knit”). Cognate with Low German knütten and Old Norse knýta (whence Danish knytte, Norwegian Nynorsk knyta). More at knot.
knit.example: The first generation knitted to order; the second still knits for its own use; the next leaves knitting to industrial manufacturers.
knit.exampleSense: To turn thread or yarn into a piece of fabric by forming loops that are pulled through each other. This can be done by hand with needles or by machine.

sweetener.example: Some examples of the sweeteners include aspartame, saccharin, sucralose and stevia. The W.H.O.’s announcement contradicts previous studies that have said these sweeteners don’t offer any health benefits but also do not cause harm.
sweetener.exampleSense: Something added to food to sweeten its taste, especially an artificial substitute for sugar.

artificial.o: From Middle English artificial (“man-made”) via Old French (modern French artificiel), from Latin artificiālis from artificium (“skill”), from artifex, from ars (“skill”), and -fex, from facere (“to make”). Displaced native Old English cræftlīċ.
artificial.example: In Alberta, for example, policy documents reinforce an artificial distinction between leadership-related activity and management.
artificial.exampleSense: Not natural or normal: imposed arbitrarily or without regard to the specifics or normal circumstances of a person, a situation, etc.

horticulture.o: 17th century, from the Latin word hortus (“garden”) + culture (on the model of agriculture). By surface analysis, horti- + cult + -ure.

sandal.o:
noun: From Middle English sandal (“sandal”), from Old French sandale, from Latin sandalium, from Ancient Greek σανδάλιον (sandálion), diminutive of σάνδαλον (sándalon, “sandal”), of unknown origin. Often mistakenly parsed as related to sand.

noun: From Middle English sandal (“sandalwood”), from Medieval Latin sandalum, from Byzantine Greek σάνδανον (sándanon), σάνταλον (sántalon), from Arabic صَنْدَل (ṣandal), from Middle Persian [script needed] (cndl /⁠čandal⁠/, “sandalwood”), from Sanskrit चन्दन (candana, “sandalwood”). Doublet of santalum.

noun: From Arabic صَنْدَل (ṣandal), the same word as the shoe sandal, just applied for boats of the shape of this shoe.

accessible.o: First attested in 1400, from French, from Late Latin accessibilis, from accessus, perfect passive participle of accēdō (“approach”), equivalent to access + -ible.
accessible.example: At first sight it would seem that the deep interior of the sun and stars is less accessible to scientific investigation than any other region of the universe.

correlation.o: From Middle French corrélation. Morphologically correlate + -ion.
correlation.example: For example, scientists can use data from larger studies about the correlation between antibody levels and vaccine efficacy in adults to make a prediction about vaccine efficacy in children.
correlation.exampleSense: One of the several measures of the linear statistical relationship between two random variables, indicating both the strength and direction of the relationship.

faculty.o: From Middle English faculte (“power, property”), from Old French faculte, from Latin facultas (“capability, ability, skill, abundance, plenty, stock, goods, property; in Medieval Latin also a body of teachers”), another form of facilitas (“easiness, facility, etc.”), from facul, another form of facilis (“easy, facile”); see facile. Doublet of facility.
faculty.example: She transferred from the Faculty of Science to the Faculty of Medicine.

ethical.o: From ethic + -al, from Late Latin ethicus (“moral, ethical”), from Ancient Greek ἠθικός (ēthikós, “of or for morals, moral, expressing character”), from ἦθος (êthos, “character, moral nature”).
ethical.example: The philosopher Kant is particularly known for his ethical writings.
ethical.exampleSense: Of or relating to the study of ethics.

faulty.example: They replaced the faulty wiring and it has worked fine ever since.
faulty.exampleSense: Having or displaying faults; not perfect; not adequate or acceptable.

controversial.o: From Latin contrōversiālis, from contrōversia + -ālis. By surface analysis, controversy + -al.
controversial.exampleSense: Arousing controversy—a debate or discussion of opposing opinions.

catering.o: present participle and gerund of cater. From Middle English catour (“acater, provisioner”), aphetic form of acatour (“acater”), from Old French acater (“to buy, to purchase”). Equivalent to cate + -er.
catering.example: Professional jealousies are always confined to the more ignorant; and education alone will enable us to rise above our catchpenny caterings to the prejudices and jealousies of the uninformed.
catering.exampleSense: The act of one who caters (to something).

fragile.o: Borrowed from Middle French fragile, from Latin fragilis, formed on frag-, the root of frangere (“to break”). Cognate with fraction, fracture and doublet of frail.
fragile.example: She caught the fragile vase before it could shatter on the floor.
fragile.exampleSense: Easily broken, not sturdy; of delicate material.

album.o: Borrowed from Latin album (“blank white writing tablet”), from albus (“white”).

virtuous.o: From Middle English vertuous, borrowed from Anglo-Norman vertuous, vertous, ultimately from Late Latin virtuōsus, from Latin virtūs. By surface analysis, virtue + -ous. Doublet of virtuoso and piecewise doublet of virtùous.
virtuous.example: Successful communities need strong, selfless leaders and a virtuous people.
virtuous.exampleSense: Full of virtue; having excellent moral character.

hawk.o:
noun: Inherited from Middle English hauk, hauke, hawke, havek, from Old English hafoc, from Proto-West Germanic *habuk, from Proto-Germanic *habukaz, controversially derived from Proto-Indo-European *kopuǵos, perhaps ultimately derived from *kap- (“seize”). Cognate with West Frisian hauk, German Low German Haavke, Dutch havik, German Habicht, Swedish hök, Danish høg, Norwegian Bokmål hauk, Norwegian Nynorsk hauk, Faroese heykur, Icelandic haukur, Finnish haukka, Estonian haugas; also Latin capys, capus (“bird of prey”), Albanian gabonjë, shkabë (“eagle”), Russian ко́бец (kóbec, “falcon”), Polish kobuz (“Eurasian Hobby”)).

noun: Uncertain; perhaps from Middle English hache (“battle-axe”), or from a variant use of the above, for this compare with Russian со́кол (sókol, “falcon, but also a hawk (plaster's tool), mortarboard”).

verb: Back-formation from hawker.

noun: Probably imitative, like hock (“cough”), hack (“cough”), although see the latter entry for more.
hawk.example: President Donald Trump has spent years playing the role of a China hawk.
hawk.exampleSense: An advocate of aggressive political positions and actions.

evaluative.example: The college's position has always been that the opinion of students and colleagues was an important part of the evaluative process leading to tenure decisions.
evaluative.exampleSense: Relating to the assignment of value to a person, thing, or event.

rationale.o:
noun: From Late Latin ratiōnāle.

noun: From Latin ratiōnāle.
rationale.example: the local bishop, H.E. Gregor Maria Hanke, is shown wearing that rarest of liturgical garments, the rationale.
rationale.exampleSense: A liturgical vestment worn by some Christian bishops of various denominations.

introductory.o: Borrowed from Late Latin intrōductōrius, from Latin intrōductus.
introductory.example: He enrolled in an introductory wine-making course.
introductory.exampleSense: Introducing; giving a preview or idea of.

courtyard.example: She sat in the courtyard, enjoying the garden.
courtyard.exampleSense: An area, open to the sky, partially or wholly surrounded by walls or buildings.

automotive.example: But electric vehicles and the batteries that made them run became ensnared in corporate scandals, fraud, and monopolistic corruption that shook the confidence of the nation and inspired automotive upstarts.
automotive.exampleSense: Of, or relating to motor vehicles.

apron.o: Rebracketing of napron (a napron → an apron), from Middle English naperoun, napron, apron, from Old French napperon, diminutive of nappe (“tablecloth”), from Latin mappa (“napkin”). For other similar cases of rebracketing, see adder, daffodil, newt, nickname, orange, trickle, umpire.

inscription.example: The coin bears an inscription in Latin.

mechanism.o: Learned borrowing from New Latin mechanismus.
mechanism.example: A very rare polymorphism in the prion protein gene recently has been identified that appears to protect against prion disease; this finding, in addition to providing greater understanding of the prionlike mechanisms of neurodegenerative disorders, might lead to potential treatments.
mechanism.exampleSense: A group of entities, such as objects, that interact together.

durable.o: From Middle English durable, from Old French durable, from Latin dūrābilis (“lasting, permanent”), from dūrō (“harden, make hard”).
durable.example: In a frictionless world with perfect rental markets, there is an unambiguous cost associated with the use of a durable for a single period.
durable.exampleSense: A durable thing, one useful over more than one period, especially a year.

cushion.o: From Middle English quysshyn, from later Old French coissin (modern coussin), from Vulgar Latin *coxīnus (“seat pad”), derived from Latin coxa (“hip, thigh”) (with the suffix possibly after Latin pulvīnus (“pillow”)), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *koḱs- (“joint, limb”).
cushion.example: Interest coverage is important because it is an indicator of how much cushion a company has in making its interest payments.
cushion.exampleSense: a sufficient quantity of an intangible object (like points or minutes) to allow for some of those points, for example, to be lost without hurting one's chances for successfully completing an objective. Money kept in reserve.

claw.o:
noun: From Middle English clawe, from Old English clawu, from Proto-Germanic *klawō. Compare West Frisian klau, Dutch klauw, German Klaue, Danish, Norwegian Bokmål, Norwegian Nynorsk, and Swedish klo.

verb: From Middle English clawen, from a combination of Old English clawan/clāwan (a remodelling of *clīeġan, from Proto-West Germanic *klauwjan, from Proto-Germanic *klawjaną) and Old English clawian (from Proto-West Germanic *klawēn).
claw.example: De Gea was United's hero again within seconds of Hernandez's equaliser, diving to his left to claw away Dirk Kuyt's shot as he got on the end of a superb cross from Stewart Downing.

frustration.o: From Latin frūstrātiō (“disappointment”), related to frūstrā (“in vain”). By surface analysis, frustrate + -ion.

rumor.o: From Middle English rumour, from Old French rumeur, from Latin rūmor (“common talk”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃rewH- (“to shout, to roar”).
rumor.example: There's a rumor going round that he's going to get married.
rumor.exampleSense: A statement or claim of questionable accuracy, from no known reliable source, usually spread by word of mouth.

calculation.o: From Middle English calculation, borrowed from Latin calculatio, calculationis. Morphologically calculate + -ion.
calculation.example: As a check on these calculations we note that the total probability for 0, 1, 2, or 3 successes must be one since there are no other possibilities.

stability.o: From Middle English stabletee, stabilite, from Old French stabilité, from Latin root of stabilitas (“firmness, steadfastness”), from stabilis (“steadfast, firm”). Displaced native Old English staþolfæstnes.

spray.o:
noun: From Middle Dutch sprāien, sprayen, spraeyen (“to spray, sprinkle, spread”), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *sprēwijaną (“to spray, sprinkle”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)per- (“to sow, scatter”). Cognate with Middle High German spræjen, spræwen (“to squirt, spray, dust, splash, straw”), Danish dialectal språe (“to open up, burst forth”), Swedish dialectal språ (“to sprout, shoot forth, burst”), Norwegian dialectal spra, spræ (“to splash, splatter, spout, burst forth”), Dutch sproeien (“to spray, sprinkle”), German sprühen (“to spray, sparkle”).

noun: From Middle English spray, from Old English *spræġ, sprei (found in place names such as that of Spreyton, England), of unknown origin. Compare English sprig (“shoot, twig”).
spray.example: The bridesmaid carried a spray of lily-of-the-valley.
spray.exampleSense: A small branch of flowers or berries.

phase.o:
noun: From New Latin phasis, from Ancient Greek φάσις (phásis, “an appearance”), from φαίνω (phaínō, “to cause to appear”); compare phantasm and see face.

name: From Latin phase (“passover”), Phasa, from Hebrew פָּסַח (pésach).
phase.example: The use of the obsolete machines was gradually phased out as the new models were phased in.
phase.exampleSense: To begin—if construed with "in"—or to discontinue—if construed with out—(doing) something over a period of time (i.e. in phases).

colony.o: From Middle English colane, colonye, from Latin colōnia (“colony”), from colōnus (“farmer; colonist”), from colō (“till, cultivate, worship”), from earlier *quelō, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷel- (“to move; to turn (around)”). Doublet of Cologne, Colonia, and Köln.
colony.example: The question of ecclesiastical jurisdiction had to be answered before the colony sailed for East Florida.
colony.exampleSense: A group of people who settle such an area and maintain ties to their native country, and (later) their descendants.

initiative.o: From French initiative, from Medieval Latin *initiativus (“serving to initiate”), from Late Latin initiare (“to begin, to initiate”), from Latin initium (“beginning”), from ineo (“enter, begin”). By surface analysis, initiate + -ive.
initiative.example: Not only are all religions welcome at the Voice Community Kitchen, but experts also say such initiatives could be key to improving ethnoreligious engagement and lead to better conflict mediation in the future.

cereal.o: Borrowed from French céréale (“having to do with cereal”), from Latin Cerealis (“of or relating to Ceres”), from Ceres (“Roman goddess of agriculture”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱer- (“grow”), from which also Latin sincerus (English sincere) and Latin crēscō (“grow”) (English crescent). The adjective is equivalent to Cere(s) + -al.
cereal.example: Wheat .. is, of all the cereal seeds, the best adapted to the making of bread.

notable.o: Inherited from Middle English notable (“worthy of note, profitable, useful”), in some senses from Anglo-Norman notable (“noteworthy”), from Latin notābilis (“noteworthy, extraordinary”), from notō (“to note, mark”); in some senses from Middle English note (“benefit, profit, use, advantage”), from Old English notu (“t-use, profit, advantage, employment”) + -able; equivalent to note + -able. Compare English noteful (“useful”).
notable.example: [...] how sayest thou, that my master is become a notable lover?
notable.exampleSense: Worthy of note; remarkable; memorable; noted or distinguished.

livestock.example: In the West there are local areas with too many livestock.
livestock.exampleSense: farm animal Farm animals; animals domesticated for cultivation.

dependable.example: He was a very dependable person.
dependable.exampleSense: Able, or easily able to be depended on.

unimaginable.example: But at the microlevel it consists of an unimaginable number of atoms connected by springy chemical bonds, all jiggling around at a rate that even our fastest supercomputer might envy.
unimaginable.exampleSense: Unable to be imagined; inconceivable or mind-boggling; beyond belief.

necessity.o: From Middle English necessite, from Old French necessite, from Latin necessitās (“unavoidableness, compulsion, exigency, necessity”), from necesse (“unavoidable, inevitable”); see necessary. Doublet of Necessitas.
necessity.example: I bought a new table out of necessity. My old one was ruined.
necessity.exampleSense: The quality or state of being necessary, unavoidable, or absolutely requisite.

explosion.o: From French explosion, from Latin explōsiōnis, genitive form of explōsio, from explōdo (“to drive out by clapping”), from ex- and plōdo (“to clap or strike”). For more information see explode.
explosion.example: A man was injured by an explosion caused by drilling into a missed shot at the Mendota mine above Silver Plume, Colo.
explosion.exampleSense: A violent release of energy (sometimes mechanical, nuclear, or chemical); an act or instance of exploding.

entrepreneur.o: Borrowed from French entrepreneur (“one who undertakes or manages”), from Middle French entrepreneur, from entreprendre (“to undertake”) + -eur.
entrepreneur.example: Every rail company worth its salt wanted to connect with London. Interestingly, it was largely that way around - provincial entrepreneurs wanting to connect with the capital, rather than London capitalists seeking to spread outwards.
entrepreneur.exampleSense: A person who organizes and operates a business venture and assumes much of the associated risk.

canal.o: Borrowed from Middle French canal, from Old French canal, from Latin canālis (“channel, canal, narrow passage”), from canna (“reed, cane”), from Ancient Greek κάννα (kánna, “reed”), from Akkadian 𒄀 (qanû, “reed”), from Sumerian 𒄀𒈾 (gi.na). Doublet of channel. See also cane and -al.
canal.example: Near Rotterdam we canalled by Delfthaven.
canal.exampleSense: To travel along a canal by boat

numerous.o: From Middle English numerous from Latin numerōsus (“numerous, abundant; harmonious”), from numerus (“number”). Doublet of numerose. Analyzeable as numero- + -ous.
numerous.example: There are numerous definitions of the word 'man'.

cart.o:
noun: From Middle English cart, kart, from Old Norse kartr (“wagon; cart”), merged with native Old English cræt (“a chariot; cart”), from Proto-Germanic *krattaz, *krattijô, *kradō, from Proto-Indo-European *gret- (“tracery; wattle; cradle; cage; basket”), from *ger- (“to turn, wind”). Cognate with West Frisian kret (“wheelbarrow for hauling dung”), Dutch krat, kret (“crate; wheelbarrow for hauling dung”), German Krätze (“basket; pannier”). Wider cognates include Sanskrit ग्रन्थ (grantha, “a binding”).

noun: Clipping of cartridge.
cart.example: The grocer delivered his goods by cart.
cart.exampleSense: A small, open, wheeled vehicle, drawn or pushed by a person or animal, often with two wheels on one axle, more often used for transporting goods than passengers.

ribbon.o: From Middle English riban, ryban, ryband, from Old French riban, ruban ( > modern French ruban), of uncertain origin. Likely from a Germanic compound whose second element is cognate with English band. Compare Middle Dutch ringhband (“necklace”, literally “ring-band”).
ribbon.example: They were single-shift, frontstroke, typebar typewriters with four-bank QWERTY keyboards, inked by a ribbon.
ribbon.exampleSense: An inked strip of material against which type is pressed to print letters in a typewriter or printer.

lace.o:
noun: From Middle English lace, laace, las, from Old French las, from Vulgar Latin *laceum, based on Latin laqueus. Doublet of lasso.

verb: From Middle English lacen, lasen, from Old French lacer, lacier, lasser, lachier, from the noun (see above).
lace.example: your laces are untied, do them up!
lace.exampleSense: A cord or ribbon passed through eyelets in a shoe or garment, pulled tight and tied to fasten the shoe or garment firmly. ᵂᵖ

watermill.example: Upstream from the house is a watermill, cased in gleaming white weather-boarding, which has been restored to working order. Near by is the water-driven turbine which [Rudyard] Kipling had installed in 1902 to light his mansion with electricity.

dense.o: From Middle French dense, from Latin dēnsus, from Proto-Indo-European *dens- (“thick, dense”) (whence also Ancient Greek δασύς (dasús)).
dense.example: There are times when systems like GPT-4 seem to mimic human reasoning, but there are also times when they seem terribly dense. “These behaviors are not always consistent,” Ece Kamar, a Microsoft researcher, said.
dense.exampleSense: Slow to comprehend; of low intelligence. (of a person)

composition.o: From Middle English composicioun, borrowed from Old French composicion, from Latin compositiō, compositiōnem.
composition.example: And as for the perfume which thou shalt make, ye shall not make to yourselves according to the composition thereof: it shall be unto thee holy for the Lord.
composition.exampleSense: The proportion of different parts to make a whole.

ecologist.o: From eco- + -logist. The less common sense “environmentalist” might be from association with deep ecology, or influenced by Romance-language equivalents such as Spanish ecologista (“environmentalist”).
ecologist.example: Despite the accomplishments and the vision of radical ecologists, however, most of the world's power is presently concentrated in economic systems and political institutions that bring about environmental deterioration.
ecologist.exampleSense: An environmentalist (one who advocates for the protection of the environment).

disinfectant.o: From disinfect + -ant, borrowed from French désinfectant.
disinfectant.example: The scalpels were soaked in disinfectant before the operation so disease wouldn't be spread.
disinfectant.exampleSense: A substance that kills germs or viruses.

nectar.o: From Latin nectar, from Ancient Greek νέκταρ (néktar, “nourishment of the gods”), from Proto-Indo-European *neḱ- (“perish, disappear”) + *-tr̥h₂ (“overcoming”), from *terh₂- (“to overcome, pass through, cross over”).
nectar.example: On the lane below, more orangetips nectared on spring beauties and violets.

shelter.o: From Middle English sheltron, sheldtrume (“roof or wall formed by locked shields”), from Old English sċildtruma, sċyldtruma (“a phalanx, company (of troops), a tortoise, a covering, shed, shelter”, literally “shield-troop”), from sċyld, sċield (“shield”) + truma (“a troop of soldiers”). Cognate with Scots schilthrum, schiltrum. More at shield, and Old English trymman (“to strengthen”), from trum (“strong, firm”) at trim. Doublet of sheltron (a kind of military formation), which is the more conservative of the two.
shelter.example: Those ruins sheltered once his sacred head.
shelter.exampleSense: To provide cover from damage or harassment; to shield; to protect.

acid.o: From French acide, from Latin acidus (“sour, acid”), from aceō (“to be sour”). Doublet of agita.
acid.example: In the end, though, there is one sure way to distinguish a real hippie from his assorted sympathizers: hippies drop acid. That is, real hippies frequently, if irregularly, ingest LSD.

chemist.o: First attested 1562, borrowed from French chimiste, from Medieval Latin chimista, from earlier alchimista (literally “alchemist”), from Arabic الْكِيمِيَاء (al-kīmiyāʔ), with article اَلْ (al-) + Ancient Greek χυμεία (khumeía, “art of alloying metals”), from χύμα (khúma, “fluid”), from χυμός (khumós, “juice”), from χέω (khéō, “to pour”). The pronunciation with initial /k/ is based on the Graeco-Latin etymology rather than on the French word, where the pronunciation with /ʃ/ is based on native French orthography. As a synonym for pharmacy, a metonymous use of the proprietor to stand for their shop.
chemist.example: It was Oxford now—the matriculation photograph, posed in the stony front quad at Corpus, the pelican on top of the sundial appearing to sit on the head of the lanky, begowned chemist at the centre of the back row.
chemist.exampleSense: A person who specializes in the science of chemistry, especially at a professional level.

commercial.o: From French commercial (“of, or pertaining to commerce”), from Late Latin commercialis, from Latin commercium. By surface analysis, commerce + -ial.
commercial.example: She was in a commercial for breakfast cereal.
commercial.exampleSense: An advertisement in a common media format, usually radio or television.

unsanitary.example: A. The exterior of the premises and all structures thereon shall be kept free of all nuisances, unsanitary conditions and fire or safety hazards in the public areas and any of the foregoing shall be removed and abated promptly by the owner or manager.

luxurious.o: From Middle English luxurious, from Old French luxurios (modern French luxurieux), from Latin lū̆xuriōsus (“rank, luxuriant, profuse, excessive, immoderate”), from lū̆xuria (“rankness, luxury”), from lū̆xus (“extravagance, luxury”). By surface analysis, luxury + -ous.
luxurious.example: Invalids, and luxurious persons, require more artificial arrangements for travelling on the camel.
luxurious.exampleSense: Enjoying the pleasures of luxury, accustomed to luxury.

pumice.o: From Anglo-Norman and Old French pomis (“pumice stone”), from Latin pūmex (“pumice stone”). Doublet of pounce.

excavation.o: From Latin excavātiō (“a hollowing out”), from excavō (“to hollow out”), from ex + cavō (“to hollow out”), from cavus (“hollow”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱewh₁- (“vault, hole”). Equivalent to excavate + -ion.
excavation.example: To date, [Taco's 1982 cover of Irving Berlin's 1935] "Cheek To Cheek" and similar auditory excavations have fared poorly.

cleanliness.example: Both engines and carriages were maintained in admirable cleanliness, and a very high standard of neatness characterised the permanent way and lineside buildings.
cleanliness.exampleSense: The property of being cleanly, or habitually clean; good hygiene.

saliva.o: A learned borrowing from Latin salīva (“spittle”), replacing or merging with Middle English salive, salve (“saliva”), from the same Latin source. Further origin uncertain. Perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *salw-, *sal- (“dirt, dirty”), cognate with Old English salu (“dark, dusky”). More at sallow. Displaced Middle English slaver, slavere ("saliva"; whence Modern English slaver); and Middle English spyttle, spetel, spatel, spotel ("saliva"; whence Modern English spittle, spettle, spattle).

emperor.o: From Middle English emperour, from Anglo-Norman emperour, from Latin imperātorem, derived from imperō (“to command”). Doublet of imperator. Displaced earlier Old English casere, from Latin Caesar.
emperor.example: In imperial China, it was often a responsibility of the emperor to evaluate his predecessor after the latter's death.
emperor.exampleSense: The male monarch or ruler of an empire.

magnet.o: From Middle English magnete, via Old French magnete, Latin magnēs, magnētem (“lodestone”), from Ancient Greek μαγνῆτις [λίθος] (magnêtis [líthos], “Magnesian [stone]”), either after the Lydian city Magnesia ad Sipylum (modern-day Manisa, Turkey), or after the Greek region of Μαγνησία (Magnēsía) (whence came the colonists who founded the city in Lydia). Related to manganese, magnesia and magnesium.
magnet.example: He always had a girl on his arm – he's a bit of a babe magnet.
magnet.exampleSense: A person or thing that attracts what is denoted by the preceding noun.

trumpet.o: From Middle English trumpet, trumpette, trompette (“trumpet”), from Old French trompette (“trumpet”), diminutive of trompe (“horn, trump, trumpet”), from Frankish *trumpa, *trumba (“trumpet”), ultimately imitative. Cognate with Old High German trumpa, trumba (“horn, trumpet”), Middle Dutch tromme (“drum”), Middle Low German trumme (“drum”), Old Norse trumba (“pipe; trumpet”). More at drum. Displaced native English beme, from Middle English beme, from Old English bīeme.
trumpet.example: Cedric made a living trumpeting for the change of passersby in the subway.

industrial.o: From French industriel. By surface analysis, industry + -al.
industrial.example: This is an industrial product—it's much too strong for home use.
industrial.exampleSense: Suitable for use in such industry; industrial-grade.

critic.o: Borrowed from Middle French critique, from Latin criticus, from Ancient Greek κριτικός (kritikós, “of or for judging, able to discern”), from κρίνω (krínō, “to judge”).
critic.example: When an author has many beauties consistent with virtue, piety, and truth, let not little critics exalt themselves, and shower down their ill nature.
critic.exampleSense: One who criticizes; a person who finds fault.

symbol.o: From French symbole, from Latin symbolus, symbolum (“a sign, mark, token, symbol, in Late Latin also a creed”), from Ancient Greek σύμβολον (súmbolon, “a sign by which one infers something; a mark, token, badge, ticket, tally, check, a signal, watchword, outward sign”), from συμβάλλω (sumbállō, “to throw together, dash together, compare, correspond, tally, come to a conclusion”), from σύν (sún, “with, together”) + βάλλω (bállō, “to throw, put”).
symbol.example: "$" is the symbol for dollars in the US and some other countries.
symbol.exampleSense: A character or glyph representing an idea, concept or object.

hospitality.o: From Middle English hospitalite, from Old French hospitalité (modern French hospitalité), from Latin hospitālitās (“hospitality”), from hospitālis (“hospitable”), from hospes (“guest", "host”). Displaced native Old English cumlīþnes (literally “guest gentleness”).
hospitality.example: Please thank our hosts for their hospitality during the week that we stayed.
hospitality.exampleSense: The act or service of welcoming, receiving, hosting, or entertaining guests; an appropriate attitude of openness, respect, and generosity toward guests.

mixture.o: From Middle English, borrowed from Old French misture, from Latin mixtūra (“a mixing”), from mixtus, perfect passive participle of misceō (“mix”); compare mix.
mixture.example: The mixture of sulphuric acid and water produces heat.

dominant.example: Finally, if we suppose provisionally that the mutant genes are dominant just as often as they are recessive, selection will be far more severe in eliminating the disadvantageous dominants than in eliminating the disadvantageous recessives.
dominant.exampleSense: Of an allele, that a heterozygote for the allele has the same phenotype as the homozygote.

commerce.o: Borrowed from Middle French commerce, from Latin commercium. Doublet of comess.
commerce.example: Fifteen years of thought, observation, and commerce with the world had made him [Bunyan] wiser.
commerce.exampleSense: Social intercourse; the dealings of one person or class in society with another; familiarity.

evolution.o: Borrowed from Latin ēvolūtiō, ēvolūtiōnis (“the act of unrolling, unfolding or opening (of a book)”), from ēvolūtus, perfect passive participle of ēvolvō (“unroll, unfold”), from ex + volvō (“roll”). Compare typologically Czech vývoj, Serbo-Croatian развој, Russian разви́ть (razvítʹ), развива́ть (razvivátʹ), разви́ться (razvítʹsja), развива́ться (razvivátʹsja), Russian разви́тие (razvítije), related to Proto-Slavic *viti (whence Czech vít, Russian вить (vitʹ)).
evolution.example: The ongoing evolution of Lolita subculture fashion includes, among other things, the ballet style.
evolution.exampleSense: Process of development. Development; the act or result of developing what was implicit in an idea, argument etc.

depth.o: From Middle English depthe, from Old English *dīepþ (“depth”), from Proto-Germanic *diupiþō (“depth”), equivalent to deep + -th (abstract nominal suffix). Cognates Cognate with Scots deepth, Saterland Frisian Djüpte, West Frisian djipte (“depth; abyss, chasm”), Dutch diepte, German Low German Deepd, Luxembourgish Déift, Danish, Norwegian Bokmål dybde (“depth”), Faroese dýpd (“depth”), Icelandic dýpt, Norwegian Nynorsk djupt, dypt, and Gothic 𐌳𐌹𐌿𐍀𐌹𐌸𐌰 (diupiþa, “depth”); further to Old English diepe, German Tiefe, Icelandic dýpi, Norwegian Nynorsk djup, djupn, Swedish djup.
depth.example: The burning ship finally sunk into the depths.
depth.exampleSense: the deepest part (usually of a body of water)

journalism.o: From French journalisme (beginning of 19th century). By surface analysis, journal + -ism.

tutorial.o: The adjective is from tutor (noun) + -ial, ultimately from Latin tūtor (“watcher, protector, defender”). The noun is transferred from the adjective.
tutorial.example: The probability is that any verse of this nature, in which the lines are worn smooth, is one which has been causing tutorial ears to tingle for a generation at least; and very probably it is known in a variety of forms.
tutorial.exampleSense: Of or pertaining to a tutor; belonging to, or exercised by, a tutor.

restrained.o: simple past and past participle of restrain. From Middle English restreinen, from Old French restreindre, from Latin rēstringere (“fasten, tighten”).
restrained.example: He greeted her for the first time in three years with a restrained embrace.
restrained.exampleSense: Held back, limited, kept in check or under control.

moisture.o: From Middle English moisture, from Old French moistour (“moisture, dampness, wetness”). Compare French moiteur.

poet.o: From Middle English poete, from Old French poete, from Latin poēta (“poet, author”), from Ancient Greek ποιητής (poiētḗs, “creator, maker, author, poet”), from ποιέω (poiéō, “to make, compose”). Displaced native Old English sċop. Doublet of piyyut.

instinctive.example: When approached by a stranger, Jared clenched his fists in an instinctive manner.
instinctive.exampleSense: Driven by impulse, spontaneous and without thinking.

flavor.o: From Middle English flavour meaning “smell, odour”, usually pleasing, borrowed from Old French flaour (“smell, odour”) (cfr. Sicilian ciàguru, its etymology and semantic), from Vulgar Latin *flātor (“odour, that which blows”), from Latin flātor (“blower”), from flō, flāre (“to blow, puff”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰleh₁- (“to blow”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰel- (“to make a loud noise”). Doublet of blow and bleat.
flavor.example: Debian is one flavor of the Linux operating system.

timber.o: From Middle English tymber, from Old English timber, from Proto-West Germanic *timr, from Proto-Germanic *timrą (“building; timber”), from Proto-Indo-European *dem- (“to build; to arrange”) (see Proto-Indo-European *dṓm (“home, house”)). Cognates Cognate with Dutch timmer (“building, construction; chamber, room”), German Zimmer (“room, timber”), Luxembourgish Zëmmer (“room”), Yiddish צימער (tsimer, “room”), Danish and Norwegian Bokmål tømmer (“timber”), Faroese and Icelandic timbur (“timber, wood”), Norwegian Nynorsk timber, tymbur, tømmer (“timber”), Swedish timmer (“timber”), Gothic 𐍄𐌹𐌼𐌱𐍂𐌾𐌰𐌽 (timbrjan), 𐍄𐌹𐌼𐍂𐌾𐌰𐌽 (timrjan, “to build, construct; to edify, strengthen”); also Breton danvez (“material, matter; fabric; fortune, wealth”), Cornish devnydh (“inhredient, material, stuff; use”), Irish and Scottish Gaelic damhna (“matter”), Welsh defnydd (“material, stuff; gear, implement, instrument; application; cause, occasion, reason”), Latin domus (“home, house”), Ancient Greek δόμος (dómos, “house; household”), Albanian dhomë (“chamber, room”), Latgalian noms (“house”), Latvian nams (“house”), Lithuanian namas (“house”), Belarusian, Bulgarian, Macedonian, and Russian дом (dom, “home, house”), Czech dům (“house”), Polish, Slovak, and Slovene dom (“home, house”), Serbo-Croatian до̑м, dȏm (“home, house”), Ukrainian дім (dim, “home, house; building”), Armenian տուն (tun, “home, house; family, household”), Avestan 𐬛𐬀𐬨 (dam, “house”), Sanskrit दम् (dam, “house”), दम (dama, “home”).
timber.example: For many heads that undertake [learning], were never squared nor timbred for it.

complex.o: From French complexe, from Latin complexus, past participle of complector (“to entwine, encircle, compass, infold”), from com- (“together”) and plectō (“to weave, braid”). May be analyzed as com- + -plex. See complect. Doublet of complexus.
complex.example: Ideas thus made up of several simple ones put together, I call complex; such as beauty, gratitude, a man, an army, the universe.
complex.exampleSense: Made up of multiple parts; composite; not simple.

consumption.o: From con- + Latin sūmptus + -ion, from Middle English consumpcioun, from Old French consumpcion, from Latin cōnsūmptiō, from cōnsūmō + -tiō, from con- (“with, together”) + sūmō (“take; consume”). Equivalent to consume + -tion.
consumption.example: The consumption of snails as food is more common in France than in England.
consumption.exampleSense: The act of eating, drinking or using.

additive.o: From Late Latin additivus, from the participial stem of Latin addere (“to add”).
additive.example: It is natural to look at a finite cyclic group as an additive group.
additive.exampleSense: Whose operator is identified as addition.

medal.o: From Middle English [Term?], from Middle French medaille, medale, from Italian medaglia (originally "half a denarius"), from Early Medieval Latin medālia, feminine derived via dissimilation (/dj–lj/ > /d–lj/) from mediālia, neuter plural of Late Latin mediālis (“middle”, adjective), from Classical Latin medius.
medal.example: I wanted to medal. I was pregnant and I wanted to medal.

textile.o: Borrowed from Latin textile, substantive use of textilis (“woven”), from texō (“weave”).

poisonous.o: From Middle English poisounous, poysonouse. By surface analysis, poison + -ous.
poisonous.example: While highly poisonous to dogs, this substance is completely harmless if ingested by humans.
poisonous.exampleSense: Containing sufficient poison to be dangerous to touch or ingest.

aurora.o: Borrowed from Latin aurōra (“dawn”). Doublet of Eos.

beetroot.example: Harmon's face beetrooted. He strode from the office, stared at the cell block, and swore with artistry.
beetroot.exampleSense: To turn a bright red or purple colour.

teaspoon.example: I teaspooned some sugar into my cup.

consolidation.o: From Latin cōnsolidātiō, cōnsolidātiōnem, from cōnsolidō.
consolidation.example: These included multilobular consolidation with histiological lesions of bronchiolitis with epithelial necrosis and syncytia [14 ].
consolidation.exampleSense: A solidification into a firm dense mass. It is usually applied to induration (swelling or hardening of normally soft tissue) of a normally aerated lung.

purple.o: From Middle English purple, purpel, from Old English purpul (“purple”, adjective), taken from Old English purpure (“purple colour”, noun), from Latin purpura (“purple dye, shellfish”), from Ancient Greek πορφύρα (porphúra, “purple-fish”), perhaps of Semitic origin. Doublet of purpura and purpure. The sense of "imperial power" is from the wearing of the color purple by emperors and kings.
purple.example: Thy head as Carmelus: and the heares of thy head as a kings purple tyed to cundite pipes.
purple.exampleSense: Cloth, or a garment, dyed a purple colour; especially, a purple robe, worn as an emblem of rank or authority; specifically, the purple robe or mantle worn by Ancient Roman emperors as the emblem of imperial dignity.

odd.o: From Middle English odde, od (“odd (not even); leftover after division into pairs”), from Old Norse oddi (“odd, third or additional number; triangle”), from oddr (“point of a weapon”), from Proto-Germanic *uzdaz (“point”), from Proto-Indo-European *wes- (“to stick, prick, pierce, sting”) + *dʰeh₁- (“to set, place”). Cognate to Icelandic oddi (“triangle, point of land, odd number”), Swedish udda (“odd”), udd (“a point”), Danish od (“point of weapon””) and odde (“a headland, point”), Norwegian Bokmål odde (“a point”, “odd”, “peculiar”); related to Old English ord (“a point”). Doublet of ord ("point").
odd.example: There were thirty-odd people in the room.
odd.exampleSense: About, approximately; somewhat more than (an approximated round number).

repellent.o: From Latin repellēns. Equivalent to repel + -ent.
repellent.example: [Martin] Heidegger's repellent political beliefs do not contaminate his philosophical work.

slave.o: Inherited from Middle English sclave, from Old French sclave, from Medieval Latin sclavus (“slave”), from Late Latin Sclavus (“Slav”), traditionally assumed to be because Slavs were often forced into slavery in the Middle Ages. The Latin word is from Byzantine Greek Σκλάβος (Sklábos); see that entry and Slav for more. Displaced native Old English þēow. Thrall and bondsman/bondswoman, however, remain common synonyms. Doublet of ciao and Slav. An alternative hypothesis derives sclavus from Ancient Greek σκῡλεύω (skūleúō), σκῡλάω (skūláō, “to strip or despoil a slain enemy”).
slave.example: I was slaving all day over a hot stove.

nomadic.o: From Ancient Greek νομαδικός (nomadikós), equivalent to nomad (“a member of a society or class of herdsmen”) + -ic (forming adjectives).
nomadic.example: Neither vehicle has a set home base. Young explains: "They are 'nomadic' nationally employed assets that, rather than having a regular home depot, are generally deployed and maintained following a programme of works across the full network.
nomadic.exampleSense: Of or relating to nomads. Of or related to any habitually wandering person or animal.

nomad.o: From Middle French nomade, from Latin Nomas (“wandering shepherd”), from Ancient Greek νομάς (nomás, “roaming, wandering, esp. to find pasture”), from Ancient Greek νομός (nomós, “pasture”). Compare Numidia.
nomad.example: The life of the people called the Nomads or Grazyers...
nomad.exampleSense: A member of a society or class who herd animals from pasture to pasture with no fixed home.

ethnic.o: From Middle English ethnik, from Latin ethnicus ("pagan", "heathen"), from Ancient Greek ἐθνικός (ethnikós, “of or for a nation, heathen”), from ἔθνος (éthnos, “a company", later "a people or nation, heathens”). By surface analysis, ethno- + -ic.
ethnic.example: Coinage with the ethnic ΑΝΤΙΟΧΕΩΝ ΠΡΟΣ ΕΥΦΡΑΤΗΝ survives from the mid-second century A.D.
ethnic.exampleSense: The demonym of an Ancient Greek city.

varied.o: simple past and past participle of vary. From Middle English varien, from Old French varier, from Latin variō (“to change, alter, make different”), from varius (“different, various”); see various.
varied.example: It's a geological wonderland, with great exposures of colorful and varied sedimentary rocks.

psychology.o: From French psychologie, from Renaissance Latin psychologia, from Ancient Greek ψυχή (psukhḗ, “soul”) + -λογία (-logía, “study of”), equivalent to psycho- + -logy. The Latin term is believed by some to have been coined in a lost treatise by Croatian humanist Marko Marulić (1450–1524), but this is disputed by other scholars. It is first attested in the 1570s, at which time it was apparently already current, and may be a Hellenization of the established expression dē animā (“on the soul”) in titles.
psychology.example: For generations, historians have conjectured everything from a warped psychology to a deformed body as accounting for Elizabeth's preferred spinsterhood...
psychology.exampleSense: The mental, emotional, and behavioral characteristics pertaining to a specified person, group, or activity.

psychological.example: The film was a dark psychological thriller.
psychological.exampleSense: Relating to the mind and behavior or to the mental, emotional, and behavioral characteristics pertaining to a specified person, group, or activity.

robot.o:
noun: From German Robot, from a West Slavic language, ultimately related to Etymology 2, below.

noun: Borrowed from Czech robot, from robota (“drudgery, servitude”). Coined in the 1920 science-fiction play R.U.R. by Karel Čapek after having been suggested to him by his brother Josef. Ultimately a cognate with Old English earfoþe and German Arbeit; see dialectal erf. Doublet of etymology

noun: Referencing the origin of the name of the 4chan imageboard /r9k/ (created in 2008), so-called because it implements the ROBOT9000 algorithm by Randall Munroe to prevent the reposting of content. Possibly overlapping with the sense of robot (“a person who does not seem to have any emotions”), alluding to autism, due to the prevalence of personal stories describing awkward or embarrassing situations on the board.
robot.example: Although the robot varied from region to region, it was rarely less than burdensome.
robot.exampleSense: A system of serfdom used in Central Europe, under which a tenant's rent was paid in forced labour.

passion.o: From Middle English passioun, passion, from Old French passion (and in part from Old English passion), from Latin passio (“suffering”), noun of action from perfect passive participle passus (“suffered”), from deponent verb patior (“to suffer”), from Proto-Indo-European *peh₁- (“to hurt”), see also Old English fēond (“devil, enemy”), Gothic 𐍆𐌰𐌹𐌰𐌽 (faian, “to blame”).
passion.example: We share a passion for books.
passion.exampleSense: Any great, strong, powerful emotion, especially romantic love or extreme hate.

bubble.o: Partly imitative, also influenced by burble. Compare Middle Dutch bobbe (“bubble”) > Dutch bubbel (“bubble”), Low German bubbel (“bubble”), Danish boble (“bubble”), Swedish bubbla (“bubble”). The word was first used in its economic sense in association with the collapse of the South Sea Company in 1720, based on the metaphor of an inflated soap bubble bursting.
bubble.example: Her mouth hung slightly open and water droplets bubbled her forehead, like oversized sweat.

ultraviolet.example: Some have advocated the search for a new theory of quantum gravity, a theory which does not suffer from ultraviolet infinity problems.
ultraviolet.exampleSense: Relating to very high energies or very small distances or time spans.

violet.o: Inherited from Middle English violet, vyolet, vyolette, from Old French violette, from Latin viola (“violet”) + -ette. Cognate with Lithuanian violetinė (“purple, violet”) and Spanish violeta (“purple, violet”).
violet.example: Refreshed by their cooling bath of evening dew, the violets and other nocturnal flowers emitted a pleasant fragrance over the fields, but from the bogs and the rivulets came up now and then damp, penetrating gusts, that sent an icy chill through me.
violet.exampleSense: A plant or flower of the genus Viola, especially the fragrant Viola odorata; (inexact) similar-looking plants and flowers.

shrimp.o: From Middle English schrimpe (“shrimp, puny person”), possibly from or related to Middle Low German schrempen (“to wrinkle”), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *skrimpaz (“shrivelled”), from Proto-Germanic *skrimpaną (“to shrivel”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kerbʰ-. See also Middle High German schrimpf (“a scratch, minor wound”), Norwegian skramp (“thin horse, thin man”); also Old English sċrimman (“to shrink”) and scrimp, Middle High German schrimpfen (“to shrink, dry up”), Swedish skrympa (“to shrink”); also Lithuanian skrembti (“to crust over, stiffen”), and possibly Albanian shkrumb (“embers, ashes; crumble”).
shrimp.example: Although the line is not always sharply drawn, offshore shrimping and inshore shrimping require different strategies.

rainbow.o: From Middle English reynbowe, raynbowe, from Old English reġnboga (“rainbow”), from Proto-West Germanic *regnabogō, from Proto-Germanic *regnabugô (“rainbow”), equivalent to rain + bow (“arch”). Cognate with West Frisian reinbôge (“rainbow”), Dutch regenboog (“rainbow”), German Regenbogen (“rainbow”), Danish regnbue (“rainbow”), Swedish regnbåge (“rainbow”), Icelandic regnbogi (“rainbow”).
rainbow.example: called “rainbowing.” Different routes were color coordinated. ... Using hand-me-down equipment and learning as much as she could, Brittany began climbing outdoors. She found like-minded people and joined organizations such as Brown ...
rainbow.exampleSense: In climbing gyms where the rocks to climb are colored to indicate suggested climbing routes, to climb rocks of different colors, thereby ignoring such routes.

obligation.o: From Middle English obligacioun, from Old French obligacion, from Latin obligatio, obligationem, from obligatum (past participle of obligare), from ob- (“to”) + ligare (“to bind”), from Proto-Indo-European *leyǵ- (“to bind”).
obligation.example: I feel I'm under obligation to attend my sister's wedding, even though we have a very frosty relationship.
obligation.exampleSense: A social, legal, or moral requirement, duty, contract, or promise that compels someone to follow or avoid a particular course of action.

boiler.o:
noun: From boil + -er.

noun: Clipping of boilerplate.
boiler.example: Nearly every employer in my field has similar terms (they all come out of a legal boiler mill somewhere).

reward.o:
noun: From Middle English reward, rewarde, from Old French reward (“reward”) (compare Old French regard, whence modern French regard, and also English regard through Middle French), from rewarder (“to reward”) (compare Old French reguarder), from re- + warder (“to guard, keep”) (compare Old French guarder); the Anglo-Norman forms are derived from Old Northern French variants of Old French, ultimately of Germanic (Frankish) origin. Compare regard, warden, guard. See more below. Mostly displaced Old English mēd, whence Modern English meed. Displaced Old English lēan and edlēan.

verb: From Middle English rewarden, from Anglo-Norman rewarder (“to reward”), from re- + warder (“to guard, keep”), from Old Northern French [Term?], from Frankish *wardōn (“to guard, keep”), from Proto-Germanic *wardōną (“to guard, defend”), from Proto-Indo-European *wer- (“to cover, shelter, defend, guard, shut”). Cognate with Old Saxon wardōn (“to guard, provide for, protect”), Old English weardian (“to guard”), Old High German wartēn (“to watch, keep, look after”). More at ward. Piecewise doublet of regard. Displaced Old English lēanian. In this sense, displaced Old English ġieldan, whence Modern English yield.
reward.example: Decorations are meant to reward the most meritous acts and services.

instinct.o: From Latin īnstīnctus, past participle of īnstinguō (“to incite, to instigate”), from in (“in, on”) + stinguō (“to prick”).
instinct.example: It was a most Bedlamite catalogue of horrors, which, if true, made the wholesome moors a place instinct with tragedy.

rational.o:
adj: From Old French rationel, rational, from Latin rationalis (“of or belonging to reason, rational, reasonable; having a ratio”), from ratio (“reason; calculation”).

noun: From Old French rational, from Medieval Latin rationale (“a pontifical stole, a pallium, an ornament worn over the chasuble”), neuter of Latin rationalis (“rational”), for which see the first etymology. Translation of λογεῖον (logeîon) or perhaps λόγιον (lógion, “oracle”) in the Septuagint version of Exodus 28.
rational.example: ¾ is a rational number, but √2 is an irrational number.
rational.exampleSense: Comprising, or expressible as, a ratio Of a number, capable of being expressed as the ratio of two integers.

ration.o: From French ration. Doublet of reason and ratio.
ration.example: By the third day on the raft, we had to ration our water.
ration.exampleSense: To portion out (especially during a shortage of supply); to limit access to.

diversity.o: From Middle English diversite, from Old French diversité, from Latin dīversitās, equivalent to diverse + -ity. Displaced native Old English mislīcnes.
diversity.example: One place there were none, of course, was on the Buckingham Palace balcony, as was observed by the Bridgerton actor Adjoa Andoh – who contrasted on the ITV coverage “the rich diversity of the abbey” and “a terribly white balcony”.
diversity.exampleSense: The quality of being diverse or different; difference or unlikeness.

molt.o: simple past of melt. From Middle English melten, from a merger of Old English meltan (intransitive) and mieltan (transitive), both meaning “to melt, digest,” from Proto-West Germanic *meltan and *maltijan, from Proto-Germanic *meltaną and *maltijaną, both from Proto-Indo-European *(s)meld- (“melt”). Cognate with Icelandic melta (“to digest”).

predator.o: Borrowed from Latin praedātor, from praedor (“loot, pillage”), from praeda (“booty, spoils, prey”).
predator.example: So if you're the only thing worth eating in the middle of the ocean, the predator that grabs you will probably have gotten there by a Levy walk.
predator.exampleSense: Any animal or other organism that hunts and kills other non-plant organisms (their prey), primarily for food.

literacy.example: Prof Alan McKee, who led the project, argues that young adults should be taught “porn literacy” to help them “read porn well” and look for healthy and ethical depictions of sex.
literacy.exampleSense: The ability to understand and evaluate something.

relaxation.o: Borrowed from Latin relaxatio, relaxationis; equivalent to relax + -ation.

oyster.o: From Middle English oystre, from Old English ostre, reinforced or superseded by Anglo-Norman oistre, which is from Old French oistre, uistre (compare modern French huître); both lines (Old English and Old French) from Latin ostrea, from Ancient Greek ὄστρεον (óstreon). Doublet of ostro (“a purple dye”).
oyster.example: Cut remaining skin on back. Remove the oyster (choice dark meat in spoon-shaped bone on back) with the leg.
oyster.exampleSense: The delicate oyster-shaped morsel of dark meat contained in a small cavity of the bone on each side of the lower part of the back of a fowl.

cable.o: Recorded since c.1205 as Middle English cable, from Old Northern French cable, from Late Latin capulum (“lasso, rope, halter”), from Latin capiō (“to take, seize”). Use of the term "cable" to refer to the USD/GBP exchange rate originated in the mid-19th century, when the exchange rate began to be transmitted across the Atlantic by a submarine communications cable.
cable.example: “And now the time of tide has come; the ship casts off her cables; and from the deserted wharf the uncheered ship for Tarshish, all careening, glides to sea.
cable.exampleSense: A long object used to make a physical connection. A strong rope or chain used to moor or anchor a ship.

gill.o:
noun: From Middle English gille, gylle (“gill”), of North Germanic origin, akin to Danish gælle, Swedish gäl, Norwegian gjelle, and further to Old Norse gjǫlnar (“lips”), which also may have had the meaning of "gills" (based on Old Danish fiskegæln (“gills”)). The Old Norse word has been suggested as deriving from Proto-Germanic *gelunō (“jaw”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰel-, which would make it root-cognate to Ancient Greek χελύνη (khelúnē, “lip, jaw”), χεῖλος (kheîlos, “lip”). Displaced native Old English ċīe.

noun: From Middle English gille, from Old French gille (“a wine measure”), from Medieval Latin gillo (“earthenware jar”).

noun: From Middle English gille, from Old Norse gil.

noun: Uncertain.

noun: Clipping of gillian, from the female name Gillian.
gill.example: Gill nets are designed to catch a fish by the gills.
gill.exampleSense: A gill slit or gill cover.

tuna.o:
noun: Borrowed from United States Spanish tuna, alteration of Spanish atún, from Arabic اَلتُّنّ (at-tunn, “tuna”), from Latin thunnus, itself from Ancient Greek θύννος (thúnnos). Possibly in the sense of "darter" from thynein "to dart along". Doublet of tonno.

noun: From Taíno.

noun: Acronym of turnt up nonaffiliate.

humidity.o: From Middle English humidite, borrowed from Old French humidité, from Medieval Latin hūmiditās, from Latin ūmidus (“damp, moist, wet”). By surface analysis, humid + -ity.

tolerance.o: Inherited from Middle English toleraunce, borrowed from Old French tolerance, from Latin tolerantia (“endurance”), from tolerāns, present participle of, and participial adjective from Latin tolerō (“to endure”).
tolerance.example: Both [Ze'ev] Jabotinsky and [David] Ben-Gurion also wrote songs of praise to the Ottoman Empire, its tolerance toward ethnic minorities in general — and to Jews in particular — as well as to the democratic changes it was undergoing.
tolerance.exampleSense: The ability or practice of tolerating; an acceptance of or patience with the beliefs, opinions or practices of others; a lack of bigotry.

amber.o: From Middle English ambre, aumbre, from Old French aumbre, ambre, from Arabic عَنْبَر (ʕanbar, “ambergris”), from Middle Persian 𐭠𐭭𐭡𐭫 (ʾnbl /⁠ambar⁠/, “ambergris”). Compare English lamber, ambergris. Displaced Middle English smulting (from Old English smelting (“amber”)), Old English eolhsand (“amber”), Old English glær (“amber”), and Old English sāp (“amber, resin, pomade”). * The nucleotide sequence "UAG" is named "amber" for the first person to isolate the amber mutation, California Institute of Technology graduate student Harris Bernstein, whose last name ("Bernstein") is the German word for the resin "amber".
amber.example: Ahead, a cool breeze swept the pale morning sun across a grassy meadow turned amber by morning's frost.
amber.exampleSense: Of a brownish yellow colour, like that of most amber.

morality.o: From Anglo-Norman moralité, Middle French moralité, from Late Latin mōrālitās (“manner, characteristic, character”), from Latin mōrālis (“relating to manners or morals”), from mōs (“manner, custom”). equivalent to moral + -ity.
morality.example: It may be true that you cannot legislate morality, but behavior can be regulated.
morality.exampleSense: Recognition of the distinction between good and evil or between right and wrong; respect for and obedience to the rules of right conduct; the mental disposition or characteristic of behaving in a manner intended to produce morally good results.

migration.o: From Middle French migration and its source, Latin migrātiō, from the participle stem of migrō (“to migrate”). Morphologically migrate + -ion.
migration.example: The migration of lead from a can to the food inside it can cause lead poisoning.

protein.o: From proto- + -ein. Suggested by Jöns Jacob Berzelius in a letter to Gerardus Johannes Mulder, from French protéine and German Protein, both coined based on Ancient Greek πρωτεῖος (prōteîos, “primary”), from πρῶτος (prôtos, “first”).
protein.example: Proteins carry out the bulk of cellular functions, including relaying signals, providing structural support, and accelerating biochemical reactions.
protein.exampleSense: Any of numerous large, complex naturally-produced molecules composed of one or more long chains of amino acids, in which the amino acid groups are held together by peptide bonds.

bacteria.o:
noun: Borrowed from New Latin bacteria, plural of bactērium, from Ancient Greek βακτήριον (baktḗrion, “little rod”); by surface analysis, bacteri(um) + -a.

noun: From New Latin bactēria, from Ancient Greek βακτηρίᾱ (baktēríā, “rod, stick”).
